Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa

Homage to the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Rightly Self-Awakened One.

Majjhimanikāye

The Middle Length Discourses

Mūlapaṇṇāsa-aṭṭhakathā

Commentary on the Root Fifty

(Paṭhamo bhāgo)

(First Part)

Ganthārambhakathā

Introduction to the Text

Karuṇāsītalahadayaṃ[V 1.0001][M 1.0001][P 1.0001], paññāpajjotavihatamohatamaṃ;

Sanarāmaralokagaruṃ, vande sugataṃ gativimuttaṃ.

I pay homage to the Sugata, whose heart is cooled by compassion, who has dispelled the darkness of ignorance with the light of wisdom, who is the teacher of the world with its humans and devas, and who is freed from the five destinations.

Buddhopi buddhabhāvaṃ, bhāvetvā ceva sacchikatvā ca;

Yaṃ upagato gatamalaṃ, vande tamanuttaraṃ dhammaṃ.

I pay homage to that unsurpassed Dhamma, stainless, which the Buddha himself attained after having developed and realized the state of a Buddha.

Sugatassa orasānaṃ, puttānaṃ mārasenamathanānaṃ;

Aṭṭhannampi samūhaṃ, sirasā vande ariyasaṅghaṃ.

With my head, I also pay homage to the Noble Saṅgha, the assembly of the eight types of individuals, who are the true-born sons of the Sugata and the crushers of Māra's army.

Iti [V 1.0002] me pasannamatino, ratanattayavandanāmayaṃ puññaṃ;

Yaṃ suvihatantarāyo, hutvā tassānubhāvena.

By the power of whatever merit has been made by me, of confident mind, through this homage to the Triple Gem with these three verses, may I become one for whom all obstacles are dispelled.

Majjhimapamāṇasuttaṅkitassa idha majjhimāgamavarassa;

Buddhānubuddhasaṃvaṇṇitassa paravādamathanassa.

Of the excellent Majjhima Āgama here, which is marked by suttas of medium length, praised by the disciples of the Buddha, and which crushes the views of others.

Atthappakāsanatthaṃ, aṭṭhakathā ādito vasisatehi;

Pañcahi yā saṅgītā, anusaṅgītā ca pacchāpi.

For the purpose of explaining the meaning, the commentary which was originally compiled by the five hundred masters, and was also subsequently recited afterwards.

Sīhaḷadīpaṃ pana ābhatātha vasinā mahāmahindena;

Ṭhapitā sīhaḷabhāsāya, dīpavāsīnamatthāya.

Then it was brought to the island of Sīhaḷa by the master, the Elder Mahāmahinda, and established in the Sīhaḷa language for the benefit of the island's inhabitants.

Apanetvāna tatohaṃ, sīhaḷabhāsaṃ manoramaṃ bhāsaṃ;

Tantinayānucchavikaṃ, āropento vigatadosaṃ.

Having removed the Sīhaḷa language from that, I, rendering it into the pleasing Māgadhī language, which is faultless and in accordance with the method of the canon,

Samayaṃ [M 1.0002] avilomento, therānaṃ theravaṃsadīpānaṃ;

Sunipuṇavinicchayānaṃ, mahāvihāre nivāsīnaṃ.

Not contradicting the doctrine of the Elders residing in the Mahāvihāra, who are lamps unto the lineage of the Elders and possess extremely subtle judgment,

Hitvā punappunāgatamatthaṃ, atthaṃ pakāsayissāmi;

Sujanassa ca tuṭṭhatthaṃ, ciraṭṭhitatthañca dhammassa.

Having omitted the meaning that is repeated again and again, I shall explain the meaning of the Majjhima Nikāya for the delight of good people and for the long endurance of the Dhamma.

Sīlakathā [P 1.0002] dhutadhammā, kammaṭṭhānāni ceva sabbāni;

Cariyāvidhānasahito, jhānasamāpattivitthāro.

The discourse on virtue, the ascetic practices, and all the meditation subjects; the detailed explanation of the jhānas and attainments, together with the method of conduct.

Sabbā ca abhiññāyo, paññāsaṅkalananicchayo ceva;

Khandhādhātāyatanindriyāni ariyāni ceva cattāri.

And all the higher knowledges, and the determination of wisdom and formations; the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, and faculties; and the four noble truths.

Saccāni [V 1.0003] paccayākāradesanā suparisuddhanipuṇanayā;

Avimuttatantimaggā, vipassanābhāvanā ceva.

And the teaching on the modes of conditionality, which has an exceedingly pure and subtle method and a textual lineage that does not conflict with the canon; and the development of insight.

Iti pana sabbaṃ yasmā, visuddhimagge mayā suparisuddhaṃ;

Vuttaṃ tasmā bhiyyo, na taṃ idha vicārayissāmi.

Now, since all this has been spoken of by me in the Visuddhimagga, having made it exceedingly clear, therefore I shall not investigate it all again here.

“Majjhe visuddhimaggo, esa catunnampi āgamānañhi;

Ṭhatvā pakāsayissati, tattha yathābhāsitamatthaṃ”.

This Visuddhimagga, standing in the midst of the four Āgamas, will illuminate the meaning taught therein.

Icceva kato tasmā, tampi gahetvāna saddhimetāya;

Aṭṭhakathāya vijānatha, majjhimasaṅgītiyā atthanti.

Since it was made by me in this way, therefore, taking that Visuddhimagga also together with this commentary, you should know the meaning of the Majjhima Saṅgīti.

Nidānakathā

The Introduction

1. Tattha majjhimasaṅgīti nāma paṇṇāsato mūlapaṇṇāsā majjhimapaṇṇāsā uparipaṇṇāsāti paṇṇāsattayasaṅgahā. Vaggato ekekāya paṇṇāsāya pañca pañca vagge katvā pannarasavaggasamāyogā. Suttato diyaḍḍhasuttasataṃ dve ca suttantā. Padato tevīsuttarapañcasatādhikāni asītipadasahassāni. Tenāhu porāṇā –

1. Therein, the Majjhima Saṅgīti by name, in terms of fifties, is a collection of three fifties: the Mūlapaṇṇāsa, the Majjhimapaṇṇāsa, and the Uparipaṇṇāsa. In terms of vaggas, by making five vaggas for each fifty, it is a combination of fifteen vaggas. In terms of suttas, there are one hundred and fifty-two suttas. In terms of padas, there are eighty thousand padas with an additional five hundred and twenty-three. Therefore the ancients said:

“Asītipadasahassāni, bhiyyo pañcasatāni ca;

Puna tevīsati vuttā, padamevaṃ vavatthita”nti.

Eighty thousand padas, and five hundred more; again, twenty-three are stated. Thus the padas are determined.

Akkharato [M 1.0003] satta akkharasatasahassāni cattālīsañca sahassāni tepaññāsañca akkharāni. Bhāṇavārato asīti bhāṇavārā tevīsapadādhiko ca upaḍḍhabhāṇavāro. Anusandhito pucchānusandhi-ajjhāsayānusandhi-yathānusandhivasena saṅkhepato tividho anusandhi. Vitthārato panettha tīṇi anusandhisahassāni nava ca satāni honti. Tenāhu porāṇā –

In terms of letters, there are seven hundred and forty thousand, and fifty-three letters. In terms of bhāṇavāras, there are eighty bhāṇavāras and a half bhāṇavāra with an additional twenty-three padas. In terms of connections, there are briefly three types of connection: by way of question, by way of intention, and by way of sequence. But in detail, there are three thousand nine hundred connections herein. Therefore the ancients said:

“Tīṇi [V 1.0004] sandhisahassāni, tathā navasatāni ca;

Anusandhinayā ete, majjhimassa pakāsitā”ti.

Three thousand connections, and likewise nine hundred; these methods of connection for the Majjhima have been declared.

Tattha paṇṇāsāsu mūlapaṇṇāsā ādi, vaggesu mūlapariyāyavaggo, suttesu mūlapariyāyasuttaṃ. Tassāpi “evaṃ me suta”ntiādikaṃ āyasmatā ānandena paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikāle vuttaṃ nidānamādi. Sā panesā paṭhamamahāsaṅgīti sumaṅgalavilāsiniyā dīghanikāyaṭṭhakathāya ādimhi vitthāritā. Tasmā sā tattha vitthāritanayeneva veditabbā.

Therein, among the fifties, the Mūlapaṇṇāsa is the first; among the vaggas, the Mūlapariyāyavagga is the first; among the suttas, the Mūlapariyāyasutta is the first. Of that sutta also, the introduction beginning with 'evaṃ me sutaṃ', spoken by the Venerable Ānanda at the time of the First Great Council, is the beginning. And since that First Great Council is explained in detail at the beginning of the Sumaṅgalavilāsinī, the commentary to the Dīgha Nikāya, it should therefore be known according to the method explained in detail there.

1. Mūlapariyāyavaggo

1. The Chapter of the Root Exposition

1. Mūlapariyāyasuttavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Discourse on the Root Exposition

1. Yaṃ [V 1.0005][M 1.0004][P 1.0003] panetaṃ “evaṃ me suta”ntiādikaṃ nidānaṃ. Tattha evanti nipātapadaṃ. Metiādīni nāmapadāni. Ukkaṭṭhāyaṃ viharatīti ettha vīti upasaggapadaṃ, haratīti ākhyātapadanti iminā tāva nayena padavibhāgo veditabbo.

1. Now, with regard to this introduction beginning with 'evaṃ me sutaṃ'. Therein, the word 'evaṃ' is a particle. The words beginning with 'me' are nouns. In the phrase 'ukkaṭṭhāyaṃ viharati', 'vī' is a prefix, and 'harati' is a verb. By this method, first of all, the division of words should be understood.

Atthato pana evaṃ-saddo tāva upamūpadesasampahaṃsanagarahaṇavacanasampaṭiggahākāranidassanāvadhāraṇādianekatthappabhedo. Tathāhesa – “evaṃ jātena maccena kattabbaṃ kusalaṃ bahu”nti evamādīsu (dha. pa. 53) upamāyaṃ āgato. “Evaṃ te abhikkamitabbaṃ, evaṃ te paṭikkamitabba”ntiādīsu (a. ni. 4.122) upadese. “Evametaṃ bhagavā, evametaṃ sugatā”tiādīsu (a. ni. 3.66) sampahaṃsane. “Evamevaṃ panāyaṃ vasalī yasmiṃ vā tasmiṃ vā tassa muṇḍakassa samaṇakassa vaṇṇaṃ bhāsatī”tiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 1.187) garahaṇe. “Evaṃ bhanteti kho te bhikkhū bhagavato paccassosu”ntiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.1) vacanasampaṭiggahe. “Evaṃ byākho ahaṃ, bhante, bhagavatā dhammaṃ desitaṃ ājānāmī”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.398) ākāre. “Ehi tvaṃ, māṇavaka, yena samaṇo ānando tenupasaṅkama, upasaṅkamitvā mama vacanena samaṇaṃ, ānandaṃ, appābādhaṃ appātaṅkaṃ lahuṭṭhānaṃ balaṃ phāsuvihāraṃ puccha – ‘subho māṇavo todeyyaputto, bhavantaṃ ānandaṃ, appābādhaṃ appātaṅkaṃ lahuṭṭhānaṃ balaṃ phāsuvihāraṃ pucchatī’ti, evañca vadehi sādhu kira bhavaṃ ānando yena subhassa māṇavassa todeyyaputtassa nivesanaṃ, tenupasaṅkamatu anukampaṃ upādāyā”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 1.445) nidassane. “Taṃ kiṃ maññatha, kālāmā, ime dhammā kusalā vā akusalā [V 1.0006] vāti? Akusalā, bhante. Sāvajjā vā anavajjā vāti? Sāvajjā, bhante. Viññugarahitā vā viññuppasatthā vāti? Viññugarahitā, bhante. Samattā samādinnā ahitāya dukkhāya saṃvattanti no vā, kathaṃ vo ettha hotīti? Samattā, bhante, samādinnā ahitāya dukkhāya saṃvattanti, evaṃ no ettha hotī”tiādīsu (a. ni. 3.66) avadhāraṇe. Svāyamidha ākāranidassanāvadhāraṇesu daṭṭhabbo.

In terms of meaning, however, the word 'evaṃ' has various distinct applications, such as: simile, instruction, approval, censure, acceptance of a statement, manner, indication, and ascertainment. For instance, it appears in the sense of simile in passages such as: 'evaṃ jātena maccena kattabbaṃ kusalaṃ bahu' ('Thus, by one born a mortal, much merit should be done'). It appears in the sense of instruction in passages such as: 'evaṃ te abhikkamitabbaṃ, evaṃ te paṭikkamitabbaṃ' ('Thus you should advance, thus you should retreat'). It appears in the sense of approval in passages such as: 'evametaṃ bhagavā, evametaṃ sugatā' ('Thus it is, Blessed One; thus it is, Well-Farer'). It appears in the sense of censure in passages such as: 'evamevaṃ panāyaṃ vasalī yasmiṃ vā tasmiṃ vā tassa muṇḍakassa samaṇakassa vaṇṇaṃ bhāsati' ('Just so, this wretched woman praises that shaven-headed ascetic for any trivial reason'). It appears in the sense of acceptance of a statement in passages such as: 'evaṃ bhanteti kho te bhikkhū bhagavato paccassosuṃ' ('‘Even so, venerable sir,’ those monks replied to the Blessed One'). It appears in the sense of manner in passages such as: 'evaṃ byākho ahaṃ, bhante, bhagavatā dhammaṃ desitaṃ ājānāmi' ('In this manner, venerable sir, I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One'). It appears in the sense of indication in passages such as: 'ehi tvaṃ, māṇavaka... evañca vadehi...' ('Come, young man... and speak thus...'). It appears in the sense of ascertainment in passages such as: 'taṃ kiṃ maññatha, kālāmā... evaṃ no ettha hotī' ('What do you think, Kālāmas?... Thus it is for us in this matter'). Here, in this context, it should be understood in the senses of manner, indication, and ascertainment.

Tattha [M 1.0005] ākāraṭṭhena evaṃsaddena etamatthaṃ dīpeti – nānānayanipuṇaṃ anekajjhāsayasamuṭṭhānaṃ atthabyañjanasampannaṃ vividhapāṭihāriyaṃ dhammatthadesanāpaṭivedhagambhīraṃ sabbasattānaṃ sakasakabhāsānurūpato sotapathamāgacchantaṃ [P 1.0004] tassa bhagavato vacanaṃ sabbappakārena ko samattho viññātuṃ, sabbathāmena pana sotukāmataṃ janetvāpi evaṃ me sutaṃ, mayāpi ekenākārena sutanti.

Therein, by the word 'evaṃ' in the sense of manner, this meaning is shown: Who is capable of understanding in every way the speech of the Blessed One—which is subtle through various methods, arises from numerous noble intentions, is complete with meaning and expression, displays manifold wonders, is profound in the teaching of cause and effect and in its penetration, and reaches the ear-path of all beings according to their own respective languages? However, even after generating with all one's strength the desire to hear, it is shown that 'Thus it was heard by me,' meaning, 'By me too it was heard in one particular way.'

Nidassanaṭṭhena “nāhaṃ sayambhū, na mayā idaṃ sacchikata”nti attānaṃ parimocento evaṃ me sutaṃ, mayāpi evaṃ sutanti idāni vattabbaṃ sakalaṃ suttaṃ nidasseti.

In the sense of indication, while freeing himself from exalting himself by stating, 'I am not self-enlightened, nor was this realized by me,' he indicates the entire discourse that is now to be recounted by saying, 'evaṃ me sutaṃ' ('Thus it was heard by me'), meaning, 'By me too, it was heard thus.'

Avadhāraṇaṭṭhena “etadaggaṃ, bhikkhave, mama sāvakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ bahussutānaṃ yadidaṃ ānando, gatimantānaṃ, satimantānaṃ, dhitimantānaṃ, upaṭṭhākānaṃ yadidaṃ ānando”ti (a. ni. 1.219-223) evaṃ bhagavatā, “āyasmā ānando atthakusalo dhammakusalo byañjanakusalo niruttikusalo pubbāparakusalo”ti (a. ni. 5.169) evaṃ dhammasenāpatinā ca pasatthabhāvānurūpaṃ attano dhāraṇabalaṃ dassento sattānaṃ sotukamyataṃ janeti “evaṃ me sutaṃ, tañca kho atthato vā byañjanato vā anūnamanadhikaṃ, evameva na aññathā daṭṭhabba”nti.

In the sense of ascertainment, demonstrating his own power of retention in a manner befitting how he was praised by the Blessed One—'Monks, among my monk disciples who are learned, Ānanda is foremost... among those with intelligence... among those with mindfulness... among those with resolution... among attendants, Ānanda is foremost'—and by the General of the Dhamma—'The venerable Ānanda is skilled in the meaning, skilled in the principle, skilled in the expression, skilled in the etymology, and skilled in the sequence'—he generates in beings a desire to hear, implying: 'Thus it was heard by me, and that hearing is neither deficient nor excessive in either meaning or expression; it is to be understood as exactly so and not otherwise.'

Me-saddo tīsu atthesu dissati. Tathā hissa “gāthābhigītaṃ me abhojaneyya”ntiādīsu (su. ni. 81) mayāti attho. “Sādhu me, bhante bhagavā, saṃkhittena dhammaṃ desetū”tiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 4.88) mayhanti attho. “Dhammadāyādā me, bhikkhave, bhavathā”tiādīsu [V 1.0007] (ma. ni. 1.29) mamāti attho. Idha pana “mayā suta”nti ca “mama suta”nti ca atthadvaye yujjati.

The word 'me' is found in three meanings. Thus, in passages like 'gāthābhigītaṃ me abhojaneyyaṃ', it has the meaning of 'by me' (mayā). In passages like 'sādhu me, bhante bhagavā, saṃkhittena dhammaṃ desetu', it has the meaning of 'to me' (mayhaṃ). In passages like 'dhammadāyādā me, bhikkhave, bhavatha', it has the meaning of 'my' (mama). Here, however, it is suitable in two meanings: 'by me it was heard' (mayā sutaṃ) and 'my hearing' (mama sutaṃ).

Sutanti ayaṃ suta-saddo saupasaggo ca anupasaggo ca gamana-vissuta-kilinna-upacitānuyoga-sotaviññeyya-sotadvārānusāraviññātādianekatthappabhedo. Tathā hissa “senāya pasuto”tiādīsu gacchantoti attho. “Sutadhammassa passato”tiādīsu (udā. 11) vissutadhammassāti attho, “avassutā avassutassāti”ādīsu (pāci. 657) kilinnā kilinnassāti attho. “Tumhehi puññaṃ pasutaṃ anappaka”ntiādīsu (khu. pā. 7.12) upacitanti [M 1.0006] attho. “Ye jhānapasutā dhīrā”tiādīsu (dha. pa. 181) jhānānuyuttāti attho. “Diṭṭhaṃ sutaṃ muta”ntiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.241) sotaviññeyyanti attho. “Sutadharo sutasannicayo”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.339) sotadvārānusāraviññātadharoti attho. Idha panassa sotadvārānusārena “upadhārita”nti vā “upadhāraṇa”nti vāti [P 1.0005] attho. Me-saddassa hi mayāti atthe sati “evaṃ mayā sutaṃ sotadvārānusārena upadhārita”nti yujjati. Mamāti atthe sati “evaṃ mama sutaṃ sotadvārānusārena upadhāraṇa”nti yujjati.

The word 'suta', used with or without a prefix, has many different meanings, such as: going, renowned, stained, accumulated, diligently engaged, cognizable by ear-consciousness, and known by remembering in sequence the sound that arrived at the ear-door. For instance, in passages like 'senāya pasuto,' its meaning is 'going.' In passages like 'sutadhammassa passato,' its meaning is 'of one whose Dhamma is renowned.' In passages like 'avassutā avassutassā,' its meaning is 'stained, of one who is stained.' In passages like 'tumhehi puññaṃ pasutaṃ anappakaṃ,' its meaning is 'accumulated.' In passages like 'ye jhānapasutā dhīrā,' its meaning is 'diligently engaged in jhāna.' In passages like 'diṭṭhaṃ sutaṃ mutaṃ,' its meaning is 'cognizable by ear-consciousness.' In passages like 'sutadharo sutasannicayo,' its meaning is 'one who bears what is known by remembering in sequence the sound that arrived at the ear-door.' Here, however, its meaning is either 'borne in mind' (upadhāritaṃ) or 'the bearing in mind' (upadhāraṇaṃ) by way of remembering in sequence the sound that arrived at the ear-door. For when the word 'me' has the meaning 'by me' (mayā), it is suitable as: 'Thus by me was it heard, that is, borne in mind by way of remembering in sequence the sound that arrived at the ear-door.' And when it has the meaning 'of me' (mama), it is suitable as: 'Thus of me was the hearing, that is, the bearing in mind by way of remembering in sequence the sound that arrived at the ear-door.'

Evametesu tīsu padesu evanti sotaviññāṇādiviññāṇakiccanidassanaṃ. Meti vuttaviññāṇasamaṅgipuggalanidassanaṃ. Sutanti assavanabhāvappaṭikkhepato anūnānadhikāviparītaggahaṇanidassanaṃ. Tathā evanti tassā sotadvārānusārena pavattāya viññāṇavīthiyā nānappakārena ārammaṇe pavattibhāvappakāsanaṃ. Meti attappakāsanaṃ. Sutanti dhammappakāsanaṃ. Ayañhettha saṅkhepo “nānappakārena ārammaṇe pavattāya viññāṇavīthiyā mayā na aññaṃ kataṃ, idaṃ pana kataṃ, ayaṃ dhammo suto”ti.

Thus, among these three terms, 'evaṃ' is an indication of the function of consciousness, beginning with ear-consciousness. 'Me' is an indication of the person endowed with the aforesaid consciousness. 'Sutaṃ,' by way of rejecting the state of not-hearing, is an indication of the comprehension without deficiency, without excess, and without distortion. Furthermore, 'evaṃ' is a manifestation of the state of arising, in various ways in relation to the object, of that cognitive process which occurred by way of remembering in sequence the sound that arrived at the ear-door. 'Me' is a manifestation of the self. 'Sutaṃ' is a manifestation of the Dhamma that was heard. And here, this is the summary: 'By means of the cognitive process that occurred in various ways in relation to the object, nothing else was done by me, but this was done; this Dhamma was heard.'

Tathā evanti niddisitabbappakāsanaṃ. Meti puggalappakāsanaṃ. Sutanti puggalakiccappakāsanaṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yaṃ suttaṃ niddisissāmi, taṃ mayā evaṃ sutanti.

Furthermore, 'evaṃ' is a manifestation of what is to be indicated. 'Me' is a manifestation of the person. 'Sutaṃ' is a manifestation of the person's function. This is what is meant: 'The discourse which I shall expound, that was thus heard by me.'

Tathā evanti yassa cittasantānassa nānākārappavattiyā nānatthabyañjanaggahaṇaṃ hoti, tassa [V 1.0008] nānākāraniddeso. Evanti hi ayaṃ ākārapaññatti, meti kattuniddeso, sutanti visayaniddeso. Ettāvatā nānākārappavattena cittasantānena taṃsamaṅgino kattuvisaye gahaṇasanniṭṭhānaṃ kataṃ hoti.

Furthermore, 'evaṃ' is a designation of the various modes of that mental continuum for which there is the grasping of diverse meanings and expressions due to its operating in various ways. For 'evaṃ' is a concept of manner, 'me' is a designation of the agent, and 'sutaṃ' is a designation of the object. To this extent, by the mental continuum operating in various ways, the determination in the grasping of the object of the agent, who is endowed with that mental continuum, has been made.

Atha vā evanti puggalakiccaniddeso. Sutanti viññāṇakiccaniddeso. Meti ubhayakiccayuttapuggalaniddeso. Ayaṃ panettha saṅkhepo – mayā savanakiccaviññāṇasamaṅginā puggalena viññāṇavasena laddhasavanakiccavohārena sutanti.

Alternatively, 'evaṃ' is a designation of the person's function. 'Sutaṃ' is a designation of the function of consciousness. 'Me' is a designation of the person connected with both functions. Herein, this is the summary: 'By me—the person endowed with consciousness that has the function of hearing, and who possesses the verbal designation "function of hearing" acquired through the power of consciousness—it was heard.'

Tattha evanti ca meti ca saccikaṭṭhaparamatthavasena avijjamānapaññatti. Kiñhettha taṃ paramatthato atthi, yaṃ evanti vā meti vā niddesaṃ labhetha? Sutanti [M 1.0007] vijjamānapaññatti. Yañhi tamettha sotena upaladdhaṃ, taṃ paramatthato vijjamānanti.

Therein, 'evaṃ' and 'me' are non-existent concepts from the standpoint of ultimate, real meaning. For what is there in an ultimate sense that could obtain the designation 'evaṃ' or 'me'? 'Sutaṃ' is an existent concept. For that which is apprehended here by the ear, that exists in an ultimate sense.

Tathā evanti ca meti ca taṃ taṃ upādāya vattabbato upādāpaññatti. Sutanti diṭṭhādīni upanidhāya vattabbato upanidhāpaññatti. Ettha ca evanti vacanena asammohaṃ dīpeti. Na hi sammūḷho nānappakārapaṭivedhasamattho hoti. Sutanti vacanena sutassa asammosaṃ dīpeti. Yassa hi sutaṃ sammuṭṭhaṃ hoti[P 1.0006], na so kālantarena mayā sutanti paṭijānāti. Iccassa asammohena paññāsiddhi, asammosena pana satisiddhi. Tattha paññā pubbaṅgamāya satiyā byañjanāvadhāraṇasamatthatā, satipubbaṅgamāya paññāya atthapaṭivedhasamatthatā, tadubhayasamatthatāyogena atthabyañjanasampannassa dhammakosassa anupālanasamatthato dhammabhaṇḍāgārikattasiddhi.

Furthermore, 'evaṃ' and 'me' are concepts of dependence, because they are spoken in dependence on this or that. 'Sutaṃ' is a concept of comparison, because it is spoken in comparison with what is seen and so on. And here, by the word 'evaṃ,' he indicates non-delusion. For one who is deluded is not capable of penetrating the various aspects. By the word 'sutaṃ,' he indicates the non-forgetting of what has been heard. For one for whom what was heard has been forgotten does not, after some time, acknowledge, 'It was heard by me.' Thus, for him, the accomplishment of wisdom is through non-delusion, and the accomplishment of mindfulness is through non-forgetting. Therein, with mindfulness preceded by wisdom, there is the capability of determining the expression; with wisdom preceded by mindfulness, there is the capability of penetrating the meaning. Through the connection with the capability for both, the accomplishment of being the Treasurer of the Dhamma is achieved, from being capable of preserving the Dhamma treasury, which is complete with meaning and expression.

Aparo nayo – evanti vacanena yoniso manasikāraṃ dīpeti, ayoniso manasikaroto hi nānappakārapaṭivedhābhāvato. Sutanti vacanena avikkhepaṃ dīpeti, vikkhittacittassa savanābhāvato. Tathā hi vikkhittacitto puggalo sabbasampattiyā vuccamānopi “na mayā sutaṃ, puna bhaṇathā”ti bhaṇati. Yoniso manasikārena cettha attasammāpaṇidhiṃ pubbe ca katapuññataṃ sādheti, sammā apaṇihitattassa pubbe akatapuññassa vā tadabhāvato. Avikkhepena [V 1.0009] pana saddhammassavanaṃ sappurisūpanissayañca sādheti. Na hi vikkhittacitto sotuṃ sakkoti, na ca sappurise anupassayamānassa savanaṃ atthīti.

Another method: By the word 'evaṃ,' he indicates wise attention, because for one who attends unwisely there is an absence of penetrating the various aspects. By the word 'sutaṃ,' he indicates non-distraction, because for one with a distracted mind there is an absence of hearing. For indeed, a person with a distracted mind, even when spoken to with all completeness, says, 'It was not heard by me, speak again.' And here, through wise attention, he accomplishes right resolution of self and the state of having made merit previously, because of the absence of that wise attention for one whose self is not rightly resolved or who has not made merit previously. But through non-distraction, he accomplishes the hearing of the good Dhamma and reliance on good persons. For one with a distracted mind is not able to hear, and there is no hearing for one who does not resort to good persons.

Aparo nayo – yasmā evanti yassa cittasantānassa nānākārappavattiyā nānatthabyañjanaggahaṇaṃ hoti, tassa nānākāraniddesoti vuttaṃ. So ca evaṃ bhaddako ākāro na sammā appaṇihitattano pubbe akatapuññassa vā hoti, tasmā evanti iminā bhaddakena ākārena pacchimacakkadvayasampattiṃ attano dīpeti, sutanti savanayogena purimacakkadvayasampattiṃ. Na hi appatirūpadese vasato sappurisūpanissayavirahitassa vā savanaṃ atthi. Iccassa pacchimacakkadvayasiddhiyā āsayasuddhi siddhā hoti. Purimacakkadvayasiddhiyā payogasuddhi. Tāya ca āsayasuddhiyā adhigamabyattisiddhi, payogasuddhiyā āgamabyattisiddhi. Iti payogāsayasuddhassa [M 1.0008] āgamādhigamasampannassa vacanaṃ aruṇuggaṃ viya sūriyassa udayato yonisomanasikāro viya ca kusalakammassa arahati bhagavato vacanassa pubbaṅgamaṃ bhavitunti ṭhāne nidānaṃ ṭhapento evaṃ me sutantiādimāha.

Another method: Because it has been said that 'evaṃ' is a designation of the various modes of a mental continuum, through the occurrence of which there is the grasping of diverse meanings and expressions. And such a wholesome mode does not arise for one whose mind is not well-directed or who has not previously performed merit. Therefore, by this wholesome mode 'evaṃ', he indicates his own accomplishment of the latter pair of wheels, and by 'sutaṃ', through the practice of listening, his accomplishment of the former pair of wheels. For listening does not exist for one dwelling in an unsuitable place or for one who is devoid of the support of good persons. Thus, for him, through the accomplishment of the latter pair of wheels, purity of intention is achieved. Through the accomplishment of the former pair of wheels, purity of effort is achieved. And through that purity of intention, the accomplishment of proficiency in attainment is achieved; through purity of effort, the accomplishment of proficiency in the scriptures is achieved. Thus, the statement of one who is pure in effort and intention, and accomplished in the scriptures and in attainment, is fit to be the forerunner of the Blessed One's word—just as the rising of the dawn is the forerunner of the rising sun, and just as wise attention is the forerunner of wholesome kamma. Therefore, wishing to establish the introduction in its proper place, he said, 'Evaṃ me sutaṃ', and so on.

Aparo nayo – evanti iminā nānappakārapaṭivedhadīpakena vacanena attano atthapaṭibhānapaṭisambhidāsampattisabbhāvaṃ dīpeti. Sutanti iminā sotabbabhedapaṭivedhadīpakena dhammaniruttipaṭisambhidāsampattisabbhāvaṃ[P 1.0007]. Evanti ca idaṃ yonisomanasikāradīpakaṃ vacanaṃ bhāsamāno – “ete mayā dhammā manasānupekkhitā diṭṭhiyā suppaṭividdhā”ti dīpeti. Sutanti idaṃ savanayogadīpakaṃ vacanaṃ bhāsamāno – “bahū mayā dhammā sutā dhātā vacasā paricitā”ti dīpeti. Tadubhayenapi atthabyañjanapāripūriṃ dīpento savane ādaraṃ janeti. Atthabyañjanaparipuṇṇañhi dhammaṃ ādarena assuṇanto mahatā hitā paribāhiro hotīti ādaraṃ janetvā sakkaccaṃ dhammo sotabboti.

Another method: By this word 'evaṃ' (thus), which illuminates the penetration of meaning in its various aspects, he indicates the fact of his own accomplishment in the analytical knowledge of meaning and the analytical knowledge of ready wit. By this word 'sutaṃ' (heard), which illuminates the penetration of the divisions of what is to be heard, he indicates the fact of his own accomplishment in the analytical knowledge of the Dhamma and the analytical knowledge of language. And in speaking this word 'evaṃ', which illuminates wise attention, he indicates: 'These Dhammas have been repeatedly contemplated by me with the mind and thoroughly penetrated with wisdom.' In speaking this word 'sutaṃ', which illuminates the practice of listening, he indicates: 'Many Dhammas have been learned by me, borne in mind, and repeatedly practiced with speech.' By both of these, while indicating the completeness of meaning and phrasing, he generates reverence for listening. Indeed, one who does not listen with reverence to the Dhamma that is complete in meaning and phrasing is excluded from great benefit. Therefore, having generated reverence, the Dhamma should be listened to respectfully.

“Evaṃ me suta”nti iminā pana sakalena vacanena āyasmā ānando tathāgatappaveditaṃ dhammaṃ attano adahanto asappurisabhūmiṃ atikkamati, sāvakattaṃ paṭijānanto sappurisabhūmiṃ okkamati. Tathā asaddhammā cittaṃ vuṭṭhāpeti, saddhamme cittaṃ patiṭṭhāpeti. “Kevalaṃ sutamevetaṃ mayā [V 1.0010] tasseva pana bhagavato vacana”nti dīpento attānaṃ parimoceti, satthāraṃ apadisati, jinavacanaṃ appeti, dhammanettiṃ patiṭṭhāpeti.

But by this entire phrase, 'Evaṃ me sutaṃ,' the Venerable Ānanda, by not taking the Dhamma proclaimed by the Tathāgata as his own, transcends the domain of an unworthy person; and by acknowledging his discipleship, he enters the domain of a worthy person. Likewise, he raises his mind from the false Dhamma and establishes it in the true Dhamma. By indicating, 'This has merely been heard by me; it is the word of that same Blessed One,' he liberates himself, points to the Teacher, confirms it as the word of the Victor, and establishes the guideline of the Dhamma.

Apica “evaṃ me suta”nti attanā uppāditabhāvaṃ appaṭijānanto purimavacanaṃ vivaranto “sammukhā paṭiggahitamidaṃ mayā tassa bhagavato catuvesārajjavisāradassa dasabaladharassa āsabhaṭṭhānaṭṭhāyino sīhanādanādino sabbasattuttamassa dhammissarassa dhammarājassa dhammādhipatino dhammadīpassa dhammasaraṇassa saddhammavaracakkavattino sammāsambuddhassa vacanaṃ, na ettha atthe vā dhamme vā pade vā byañjane vā kaṅkhā vā vimati vā kattabbā”ti sabbadevamanussānaṃ imasmiṃ dhamme assaddhiyaṃ vināseti, saddhāsampadaṃ uppādetīti. Tenetaṃ vuccati –

Furthermore, with 'Evaṃ me sutaṃ,' by not acknowledging that he himself had produced it and by clarifying the teaching heard previously, he dispels the lack of faith in this Dhamma among all devas and humans and gives rise to the accomplishment of faith, declaring: 'This is the word I received in the presence of that Blessed One—who is expert in the four kinds of fearlessness, who wields the ten powers, who stands in the supreme place, who utters the lion's roar, who is the highest of all beings, the lord of Dhamma, the king of Dhamma, the sovereign of Dhamma, the lamp of Dhamma, the refuge of Dhamma, the supreme wheel-turning monarch of the true Dhamma, the Perfectly Enlightened One. Herein, no doubt or uncertainty should be entertained regarding the meaning, the text, the words, or the phrasing.' Therefore, it is said:

“Vināsayati [M 1.0009] assaddhaṃ, saddhaṃ vaḍḍheti sāsane;

Evaṃ me sutamiccevaṃ, vadaṃ gotamasāvako”ti.

By saying, 'Thus have I heard,' the disciple of Gotama dispels lack of faith and increases faith in the Dispensation.

Ekanti gaṇanaparicchedaniddeso. Samayanti paricchinnaniddeso. Ekaṃ samayanti aniyamitaparidīpanaṃ. Tattha samayasaddo –

'Ekaṃ' is a designation of numerical demarcation. 'Samayaṃ' is a designation of a demarcated time. 'Ekaṃ samayaṃ' is an elucidation of the indefinite. Therein, the word 'samaya'—

Samavāye khaṇe kāle, samūhe hetudiṭṭhisu;

Paṭilābhe pahāne ca, paṭivedhe ca dissati.

Is seen in the sense of concurrence, opportunity, time,

assembly, cause, and views;

also in attainment, abandonment,

and penetration.

Tathā hissa “appeva nāma svepi upasaṅkameyyāma kālañca samayañca upādāyā”ti evamādīsu (dī. ni. 1.447) samavāyo [P 1.0008] attho. “Ekova kho, bhikkhave, khaṇo ca samayo ca brahmacariyavāsāyā”tiādīsu (a. ni. 8.29) khaṇo. “Uṇhasamayo pariḷāhasamayo”tiādīsu (pāci. 358) kālo. “Mahāsamayo pavanasmi”ntiādīsu samūho. “Samayopi kho te, bhaddāli, appaṭividdho ahosi, bhagavā kho sāvatthiyaṃ viharati, bhagavāpi maṃ jānissati, ‘bhaddāli, nāma bhikkhu satthusāsane sikkhāya na paripūrakārī’ti, ayampi kho te, bhaddāli, samayo appaṭividdho ahosī”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 2.135) hetu[V 1.0011]. “Tena kho pana samayena uggāhamāno paribbājako samaṇamuṇḍikāputto samayappavādake tindukācīre ekasālake mallikāya ārāme paṭivasatī”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 2.260) diṭṭhi.

For instance, in passages such as, 'Perhaps tomorrow we might approach, taking into account the time and the concurrence of causes,' its meaning is concurrence (samavāyo). In passages such as, 'Monks, there is only one moment and opportunity for living the holy life,' its meaning is opportunity (khaṇo). In passages such as, 'The hot season, the scorching season,' its meaning is time (kālo). In passages such as, 'A great assembly in the forest,' its meaning is assembly (samūho). In passages such as, 'Bhaddāli, this cause was not penetrated by you... This too, Bhaddāli, was a cause not penetrated by you,' its meaning is cause (hetu). In passages such as, 'At that time, the wanderer Uggāhamāno, son of Samaṇamuṇḍikā, was dwelling in Mallikā's park... at a place for propounding views,' its meaning is view (diṭṭhi).

“Diṭṭhe dhamme ca yo attho, yo cattho samparāyiko;

Atthābhisamayā dhīro, paṇḍitoti pavuccatī”ti. –

'Whatever benefit there is in this present life, and whatever benefit pertains to the future life—through the attainment of this benefit, the steadfast one is called a sage.'

Ādīsu (saṃ. ni. 1.129) paṭilābho. “Sammā mānābhisamayā antamakāsi dukkhassā”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.24) pahānaṃ. “Dukkhassa pīḷanaṭṭho saṅkhataṭṭho santāpaṭṭho vipariṇāmaṭṭho abhisamayaṭṭho”tiādīsu (paṭi. ma. 3.1) paṭivedho. Idha panassa kālo attho. Tena saṃvacchara-utu-māsaḍḍhamāsa-ratti-diva-pubbaṇha-majjhanhika-sāyanha- paṭhamamajjhimapacchimayāma-muhuttādīsu kālappabhedabhūtesu samayesu ekaṃ samayanti dīpeti.

In such passages, its meaning is attainment (paṭilābho). In passages such as, 'Through the right overcoming of conceit, he made an end of suffering,' its meaning is abandonment (pahānaṃ). In passages such as, 'Suffering has the meaning of oppression, the meaning of being conditioned, the meaning of torment, the meaning of change, and the meaning of penetration,' its meaning is penetration (paṭivedho). Here, however, its meaning is time (kālo). Therefore, it indicates 'at one time' among the divisions of time, such as year, season, month, half-month, night, day, forenoon, midday, afternoon, the first, middle, and last watches of the night, moments, and so on.

Tattha kiñcāpi etesu saṃvaccharādīsu samayesu yaṃ yaṃ suttaṃ yamhi yamhi saṃvacchare utumhi māse pakkhe rattibhāge divasabhāge vā vuttaṃ, sabbaṃ taṃ therassa [M 1.0010] suviditaṃ suvavatthāpitaṃ paññāya. Yasmā pana “evaṃ me sutaṃ asukasaṃvacchare asukautumhi asukamāse asukapakkhe asukarattibhāge asukadivasabhāge vā”ti evaṃ vutte na sakkā sukhena dhāretuṃ vā uddisituṃ vā uddisāpetuṃ vā, bahu ca vattabbaṃ hoti, tasmā ekeneva padena tamatthaṃ samodhānetvā “ekaṃ samaya”nti āha.

In this matter, although whichever sutta was spoken in whichever year, season, month, fortnight, part of the night, or part of the day among these times beginning with the year, all of that was well known and well established with wisdom by the Elder; nevertheless, because if it were said, 'Thus have I heard: this sutta in such-and-such a year, in such-and-such a season, in such-and-such a month, in such-and-such a fortnight, in such-and-such a part of the night, or in such-and-such a part of the day,' it would not be possible to easily bear it in mind, to recite it, or to have it recited, and much would have to be said, therefore, having summarized that meaning with just a single phrase, he said, 'At one time.'

Ye vā ime gabbhokkantisamayo jātisamayo saṃvegasamayo abhinikkhamanasamayo dukkarakārikasamayo māravijayasamayo abhisambodhisamayo diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārasamayo desanāsamayo parinibbānasamayoti evamādayo bhagavato devamanussesu ativiya suppakāsā anekakālappabhedā eva samayā, tesu samayesu desanāsamayasaṅkhātaṃ [P 1.0009] ekaṃ samayanti dīpeti. Yo cāyaṃ ñāṇakaruṇākiccasamayesu aruṇākiccasamayo, attahitaparahitapaṭipattisamayesu parahitapaṭipattisamayo, sannipatitānaṃ karaṇīyadvayasamayesu dhammikathāsamayo, desanāpaṭipattisamayesu [V 1.0012] desanāsamayo, tesupi samayesu aññataraṃ sandhāya “ekaṃ samaya”nti āha.

Or, there are these times of the Blessed One, which are themselves many divisions of time and exceedingly well-known among devas and humans: the time of conception, the time of birth, the time of spiritual urgency, the time of renunciation, the time of practicing austerities, the time of conquering Māra, the time of perfect enlightenment, the time of dwelling happily in the present life, the time of teaching, the time of final Nibbāna, and so forth. Among these times, he indicates 'one time' to mean that which is designated as the time of teaching. Or, with reference to a certain one among these times as well—that is, among the times for the tasks of knowledge and compassion, the time for the task of compassion; among the times for the practice for one's own welfare and for the welfare of others, the time for the practice for the welfare of others; among the times for the two duties for those who have assembled, the time for a Dhamma talk; and among the times for teaching and for practice, the time for teaching—he said, 'At one time.'

Kasmā panettha yathā abhidhamme “yasmiṃ samaye kāmāvacara”nti ca ito aññesu suttapadesu “yasmiṃ samaye, bhikkhave, bhikkhu vivicceva kāmehī”ti ca bhummavacanena niddeso kato, vinaye ca “tena samayena buddho bhagavā”ti karaṇavacanena, tathā akatvā “ekaṃ samaya”nti upayogavacananiddeso katoti. Tattha tathā idha ca aññathā atthasambhavato. Tattha hi abhidhamme ito aññesu suttapadesu ca adhikaraṇattho bhāvenabhāvalakkhaṇattho ca sambhavati. Adhikaraṇañhi kālattho ca samūhattho ca samayo, tattha vuttānaṃ phassādidhammānaṃ khaṇasamavāyahetusaṅkhātassa ca samayassa bhāvena tesaṃ bhāvo lakkhīyati, tasmā tadatthajotanatthaṃ tattha bhummavacananiddeso kato.

Why is it that here, unlike in the Abhidhamma where the indication is made with the locative case, as in 'at which time, a sensuous-sphere [consciousness arises],' and in other sutta passages apart from this one, as in 'at which time, monks, a monk, secluded from sensual pleasures...'; and unlike in the Vinaya where it is made with the instrumental case, as in 'at that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One'—why, not having done so, is the indication 'at one time' made with the accusative case? It is done in that way there and in another way here because of the suitability of the meaning. For there, in the Abhidhamma and in other sutta passages apart from this one, the meaning of location (adhikaraṇa) and the meaning of 'the characteristic of one state by another' (bhāvena-bhāva-lakkhaṇa) are suitable. For 'samaya,' which has the meaning of time and of collection, is the location for the phenomena such as contact, etc., spoken of there; and by the existence of the 'samaya' designated as momentary conjunction and cause, the existence of those phenomena is characterized. Therefore, to illuminate that meaning, the indication is made there with the locative case.

Vinaye ca hetuattho karaṇattho ca sambhavati. Yo hi so sikkhāpadapaññattisamayo sāriputtādīhipi dubbiññeyyo, tena samayena hetubhūtena karaṇabhūtena ca sikkhāpadāni paññāpayanto sikkhāpadapaññattihetuñca apekkhamāno bhagavā tattha tattha vihāsi, tasmā tadatthajotanatthaṃ tattha karaṇavacanena niddeso kato.

And in the Vinaya, the meaning of reason (hetu) and the meaning of instrument (karaṇa) are suitable. For that time of laying down a training rule was difficult to be known even by Sāriputta and others. Because the Blessed One, laying down the training rules and considering the reason for laying down the training rules, dwelled in various places by means of that time which had become the reason and the instrument, therefore, to illuminate that meaning, the indication is made there with the instrumental case.

Idha [M 1.0011] pana aññasmiñca evaṃjātike accantasaṃyogattho sambhavati. Yañhi samayaṃ bhagavā imaṃ aññaṃ vā suttantaṃ desesi, accantameva taṃ samayaṃ karuṇāvihārena vihāsi, tasmā tadatthajotanatthaṃ idha upayogavacananiddeso katoti.

Here, however, and in another [sutta] of a similar kind, the meaning of continuous connection (accanta-saṃyoga) is suitable. For throughout whichever time the Blessed One taught this or another sutta, he dwelled continuously throughout that time with the abiding in compassion. Therefore, to illuminate that meaning, the indication is made here with the accusative case.

Tenetaṃ vuccati –

For that reason, this is said:

“Taṃ taṃ atthamapekkhitvā, bhummena karaṇena ca;

Aññatra samayo vutto, upayogena so idhā”ti.

“Having considered those respective meanings, elsewhere 'samaya' is stated with the locative and with the instrumental; here, it is stated with the accusative.”

Porāṇā [P 1.0010] pana vaṇṇayanti – “tasmiṃ samaye”ti vā – “tena samayenā”ti vā – “ekaṃ samaya”nti [V 1.0013] vā abhilāpamattabhedo esa, sabbattha bhummameva atthoti. Tasmā “ekaṃ samaya”nti vuttepi “ekasmiṃ samaye”ti attho veditabbo.

The ancients, however, explain: Whether it is 'tasmiṃ samaye' (locative), or 'tena samayena' (instrumental), or 'ekaṃ samayaṃ' (accusative), this is merely a difference in expression; in all cases, the meaning is only that of the locative. Therefore, even when 'ekaṃ samayaṃ' is said, the meaning should be understood as 'ekasmiṃ samaye' (at one time).

Bhagavāti garu. Garuñhi loke “bhagavā”ti vadanti. Ayañca sabbaguṇavisiṭṭhatāya sabbasattānaṃ garu, tasmā “bhagavā”ti veditabbo. Porāṇehipi vuttaṃ –

'Bhagavā' means a revered teacher (garu). For in the world, they call a revered teacher 'bhagavā'. And this one, because of being distinguished by all qualities, is the revered teacher of all beings. Therefore, he should be understood as 'Bhagavā'. It was also said by the ancients:

“Bhagavāti vacanaṃ seṭṭhaṃ, bhagavāti vacanamuttamaṃ;

Garugāravayutto so, bhagavā tena vuccatī”ti.

“The word 'Bhagavā' is excellent, the word 'Bhagavā' is supreme; He is a revered teacher and is endowed with that which is worthy of respect. For that reason, he is called 'Bhagavā'.”

Apica –

Furthermore:

“Bhāgyavā bhaggavā yutto, bhagehi ca vibhattavā;

Bhattavā vantagamano, bhavesu bhagavā tato”ti. –

“He had good fortune (bhāgyavā); he had broken (bhagga) the defilements; he was endowed with the glories (bhagehi yutto); he was one who analyzed (vibhattavā) the Dhamma; he was one who partook of (bhattavā) the supramundane states; and he had abandoned journeying (vanta-gamano) in the states of existence (bhavesu). Therefore, he is called 'Bhagavā'.”

Imissā gāthāya vasenassa padassa vitthārato attho veditabbo. So ca visuddhimagge buddhānussatiniddese vuttoyeva.

By means of this verse, the meaning of this word should be understood in detail. And that detailed explanation has indeed been given by me in the Visuddhimagga, in the exposition on the Recollection of the Buddha.

Ettāvatā cettha evaṃ me sutanti vacanena yathāsutaṃ dhammaṃ dassento bhagavato dhammasarīraṃ paccakkhaṃ karoti. Tena – “nayidaṃ atikkantasatthukaṃ pāvacanaṃ, ayaṃ vo satthā”ti satthu adassanena ukkaṇṭhitaṃ janaṃ samassāseti.

And by this much, with the words 'Thus have I heard,' he who shows the Dhamma as it was heard makes the Dhamma-body of the Blessed One manifest. Thereby, he consoles the people who are distressed by not seeing the Teacher, as if saying: “This teaching is not one whose Teacher has passed away; this Dhamma is your Teacher.”

Ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavāti vacanena tasmiṃ samaye bhagavato avijjamānabhāvaṃ dassento rūpakāyaparinibbānaṃ sādheti. Tena “evaṃvidhassa [M 1.0012] nāma ariyadhammassa desako dasabaladharo vajirasaṅghātasamānakāyo, sopi bhagavā parinibbuto, kena aññena jīvite āsā janetabbā”ti jīvitamadamattaṃ janaṃ saṃvejeti, saddhamme cassa ussāhaṃ janeti.

With the words 'At one time, the Blessed One,' by showing the state of the Blessed One's non-existence at that time, he establishes the final Nibbāna of the physical body. By this, he stirs with spiritual urgency the people intoxicated with the conceit of life, as if saying: “The teacher of such a noble Dhamma, the bearer of the ten powers, whose body was like a mass of diamond—even that Blessed One has attained final Nibbāna. By what other person should hope in life be generated?” And he generates enthusiasm for the True Dhamma in them.

Evanti ca bhaṇanto desanāsampattiṃ niddisati. Me sutanti sāvakasampattiṃ. Ekaṃ samayanti kālasampattiṃ. Bhagavāti desakasampattiṃ.

And by saying 'Thus,' he indicates the accomplishment of the teaching. By saying 'heard by me,' the accomplishment of the hearer. By saying 'at one time,' the accomplishment of the time. By saying 'the Blessed One,' the accomplishment of the teacher.

Ukkaṭṭhāyaṃ viharatīti ettha ukkāti dīpikā, tañca nagaraṃ “maṅgaladivaso sukhaṇo sunakkhattaṃ [V 1.0014] mā atikkamī”ti rattimpi ukkāsu ṭhitāsu māpitattā ukkaṭṭhāti vuccati. Daṇḍadīpikāsu jāletvā dhārīyamānāsu māpitattāti vuttaṃ hoti, tassaṃ ukkaṭṭhāyaṃ. Samīpatthe cetaṃ bhummavacanaṃ. Viharatīti avisesena iriyāpathadibbabrahmaariyavihāresu [P 1.0011] aññataravihārasamaṅgiparidīpanametaṃ. Idha pana ṭhānagamananisinnasayanappabhedesu riyāpathesu aññatarairiyāpathasamāyogaparidīpanaṃ. Tena ṭhitopi gacchantopi nisinnopi sayānopi bhagavā viharaticceva veditabbo. So hi bhagavā ekaṃ iriyāpathabādhanaṃ aññena iriyāpathena vicchinditvā aparipatantaṃ attabhāvaṃ harati pavatteti, tasmā viharatīti vuccati.

Here, in the phrase 'dwelling in Ukkaṭṭhā,' 'ukkā' means 'torch.' That city is called Ukkaṭṭhā because it was created with torches kept alight even at night, with the thought, 'May the auspicious day, the fortunate moment, the favorable constellation not pass by.' It is meant that it was created with torches on staffs being lit and carried. In that Ukkaṭṭhā. And this is a locative expression in the sense of proximity. 'He dwells' is a term that generally indicates being endowed with any of the abodes: the abodes of posture, divine abodes, brahma abodes, or noble abodes. Here, however, it indicates being associated with one of the postures—standing, walking, sitting, or lying down. Thus, the Blessed One should be understood as 'dwelling' whether standing, walking, sitting, or lying down. For that Blessed One, by cutting off the affliction of one posture with another, maintains and continues his existence without falling; therefore, he is said to 'dwell.'

Subhagavaneti ettha subhagattā subhagaṃ, sundarasirikattā sundarakāmattā cāti vuttaṃ hoti. Tassa hi vanassa sirisampattiyā manussā annapānādīni ādāya divasaṃ tattheva chaṇasamajjaussave karontā bhogasukhaṃ anubhonti, sundarasundare cettha kāme patthenti “puttaṃ labhāma, dhītaraṃ labhāmā”ti, tesaṃ taṃ tatheva hoti, evaṃ taṃ sundarasirikattā sundarakāmattā ca subhagaṃ. Apica bahujanakantatāyapi subhagaṃ. Vanayatīti vanaṃ, attasampadāya sattānaṃ bhattiṃ kāreti, attani sinehaṃ uppādetīti attho. Vanute iti vā vanaṃ, nānāvidhakusuma-gandhasammodamattakokilādivihaṅgamābhirutehi mandamālutacalitarukkhasākhāviṭapapallavapalāsehi ca “etha maṃ paribhuñjathā”ti sabbapāṇino yācati viyāti attho. Subhagañca taṃ vanañcāti subhagavanaṃ. Tasmiṃ subhagavane. Vanañca nāma ropimaṃ, sayaṃjātanti duvidhaṃ. Tattha veḷuvanajetavanādīni [M 1.0013] ropimāni. Andhavanamahāvanaañjanavanādīni sayaṃ jātāni. Idampi sayaṃjātanti veditabbaṃ.

Here, in the phrase 'Subhagavana,' it is 'Subhaga' (Auspicious) because of its auspicious nature; it is said to be so because of its beautiful splendor and because beautiful desires are fulfilled there. Indeed, due to the perfection of that grove's splendor, people take food and drink and, spending the day there making festivals, gatherings, and celebrations, they experience the pleasure of enjoyment. And they wish for beautiful desires there, thinking, 'May we obtain a son, may we obtain a daughter,' and for them, it happens just so. Thus, it is 'Subhaga' because of its beautiful splendor and because beautiful desires are fulfilled there. Moreover, it is 'Subhaga' also because it is beloved by many people. 'Vana' (grove) is so-called because it 'vanayati' (engenders affection); the meaning is that through its own perfection, it causes devotion in beings, it produces affection for itself. Or, it is 'vana' because it 'vanute' (requests); the meaning is that with the sounds of cuckoos and other birds, intoxicated with joy by the fragrance of various flowers, and with the branches, twigs, new shoots, and leaves of the trees stirred by a gentle breeze, it is as if it requests all living beings, saying, 'Come, enjoy me.' It is both auspicious (subhaga) and it is that grove (vana), thus it is 'Subhagavana.' In that Subhagavana. And a grove, by name, is of two kinds: planted and self-grown. Among these, Veḷuvana, Jetavana, and so on are planted. Andhavana, Mahāvana, Añjanavana, and so on are self-grown. This one, too, should be known as self-grown.

Sālarājamūleti ettha sālarukkhopi sāloti vuccati. Yathāha “seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, gāmassa vā nigamassa vā avidūre mahantaṃ sālavanaṃ, tañcassa eḷaṇḍehi sañchanna”nti (ma. ni. 1.225) “antarena yamakasālāna”nti ca (dī. ni. 2.195) vanappatijeṭṭhakarukkhopi. Yathāha –

Here, in the phrase 'Sālarājamūle,' the sāla tree is also called 'sāla.' As He said: 'Just as, monks, not far from a village or a town there might be a great sāla grove, and it might be covered with castor-oil plants,' and 'between the twin sāla trees.' The chief forest tree is also called 'sāla.' As He said:

“Taveva deva vijite, tavevuyyānabhūmiyā;

Ujuvaṃsā mahāsālā, nīlobhāsā manoramā”ti. (jā. 2.19.4);

‘In your kingdom, O king, in your very own garden-land, are great sāla trees with straight trunks, of dark-green luster, and delightful to the mind.’

Yo [V 1.0015] koci rukkhopi. Yathāha “atha kho taṃ, bhikkhave, māluvabījaṃ aññatarasmiṃ sālamūle nipateyyā”ti (ma. ni. 1.469). Idha [P 1.0012] pana vanappatijeṭṭhakarukkho adhippeto. Rājasaddo panassa tameva jeṭṭhakabhāvaṃ sādheti. Yathāha “suppatiṭṭhitassa kho brāhmaṇa dhammika nigrodharājassā”ti (a. ni. 6.54). Tattha dvedhā samāso, sālānaṃ rājātipi sālarājā, sālo ca so jeṭṭhakaṭṭhena rājā ca itipi sālarājā. Mūlanti samīpaṃ. Ayañhi mūlasaddo, “mūlāni uddhareyya, antamaso usiranāḷimattānipī”tiādīsu (a. ni. 4.195) mūlamūle dissati. “Lobho akusalamūla”ntiādīsu (dī. ni. 3.305) asādhāraṇahetumhi. “Yāva majjhanhike kāle chāyā pharati, nivāte paṇṇāni patanti, ettāvatā rukkhamūla”ntiādīsu samīpe. Idha pana samīpe adhippeto, tasmā sālarājassa samīpeti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo.

Any tree whatsoever is also called 'sāla.' As He said: 'Then, monks, that māluvā seed might fall at the base of some tree.' Here, however, the chief forest tree is intended. The word 'rāja' (king) establishes this very status as the chief. As He said: '...of the well-established righteous banyan king named Dhammika, O brahmin.' Herein, the compound can be understood in two ways: 'king of the sāla trees' (sālānaṃ rājā), thus 'sālarājā'; or 'it is a sāla tree and it is a king (rāja) in the sense of being the chief,' thus also 'sālarājā.' 'Mūla' means 'near.' For this word 'mūla' is seen in the sense of a physical root in passages such as, 'he might pull out the roots, down to the very last fiber of vetiver grass.' In passages such as, 'greed is an unwholesome root,' it is seen in the sense of a fundamental cause. In passages such as, 'as far as the shade spreads at midday, where the leaves fall when there is no wind, that far is the 'base of the tree',' it is seen in the sense of proximity. Here, however, the sense of 'proximity' is intended. Therefore, the meaning in this context should be understood as 'near the sāla tree king.'

Tattha siyā – yadi tāva bhagavā ukkaṭṭhāyaṃ viharati, “subhagavane sālarājamūle”ti na vattabbaṃ, atha tattha viharati, “ukkaṭṭhāya”nti na vattabbaṃ, na hi sakkā ubhayattha ekaṃ samayaṃ viharitunti. Na kho panetaṃ evaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Herein, an objection might be raised: 'If the Blessed One is dwelling in Ukkaṭṭhā, then it should not be said, 'in Subhagavana at the base of the sāla tree king.' And if he is dwelling there, then it should not be said, 'in Ukkaṭṭhā,' for it is not possible to dwell in both places at the same time.' But this should not be understood in that way.

Nanu avocumha “samīpatthe cetaṃ bhummavacana”nti. Tasmā yathā gaṅgāyamunādīnaṃ samīpe goyūthāni carantāni “gaṅgāya caranti, yamunāya carantī”ti vuccanti, evamidhāpi yadidaṃ ukkaṭṭhāya samīpe subhagavanaṃ sālarājamūlaṃ, tattha viharanto vuccati “ukkaṭṭhāyaṃ viharati subhagavane sālarājamūle”ti. Gocaragāmanidassanatthañhissa [M 1.0014] ukkaṭṭhāvacanaṃ, pabbajitānurūpanivāsaṭṭhānanidassanatthaṃ sesavacanaṃ.

Did we not say, 'And this is a locative expression in the sense of proximity'? Therefore, just as herds of cattle roaming near rivers like the Ganges and Yamunā are said to be 'roaming in the Ganges' or 'roaming in the Yamunā,' so too here, with regard to this Subhagavana at the base of the sāla tree king which is near Ukkaṭṭhā, one dwelling there is said to be 'dwelling in Ukkaṭṭhā, in Subhagavana at the base of the sāla tree king.' For the mention of Ukkaṭṭhā serves to indicate the village for alms-round, while the remaining words serve to indicate a dwelling place suitable for one who has gone forth.

Tattha ukkaṭṭhākittanena āyasmā ānando bhagavato gahaṭṭhānuggahakaraṇaṃ dasseti, subhagavanādikittanena pabbajitānuggahakaraṇaṃ. Tathā purimena paccayaggahaṇato attakilamathānuyogavivajjanaṃ, pacchimena vatthukāmappahānato kāmasukhallikānuyogavivajjanupāyadassanaṃ. Purimena ca dhammadesanābhiyogaṃ, pacchimena vivekādhimuttiṃ. Purimena karuṇāya upagamanaṃ, pacchimena paññāya apagamanaṃ. Purimena sattānaṃ hitasukhanipphādanādhimuttataṃ, pacchimena parahitasukhakaraṇe nirupalepanaṃ. Purimena dhammikasukhāpariccāganimittaṃ [V 1.0016] phāsuvihāraṃ, pacchimena uttarimanussadhammānuyoganimittaṃ[P 1.0013]. Purimena manussānaṃ upakārabahulataṃ, pacchimena devānaṃ. Purimena loke jātassa loke saṃvaḍḍhabhāvaṃ, pacchimena lokena anupalittataṃ. Purimena “ekapuggalo, bhikkhave, loke uppajjamāno uppajjati bahujanahitāya bahujanasukhāya lokānukampāya atthāya hitāya sukhāya devamanussānaṃ. Katamo ekapuggalo, tathāgato arahaṃ sammāsambuddho”ti (a. ni. 1.170) vacanato yadatthaṃ bhagavā uppanno, tadatthaparinipphādanaṃ, pacchimena yattha uppanno, tadanurūpavihāraṃ. Bhagavā hi paṭhamaṃ lumbinivane, dutiyaṃ bodhimaṇḍeti lokiyalokuttarāya uppattiyā vaneyeva uppanno, tenassa vaneyeva vihāraṃ dassetīti evamādinā nayenettha atthayojanā veditabbā.

Here, by mentioning Ukkaṭṭhā, the Venerable Ānanda shows the Blessed One’s support for householders; by mentioning the Subhagavana and so forth, he shows support for renunciants. Thus, the former indicates the avoidance of self-mortification through the acceptance of requisites, while the latter shows the means to avoid indulgence in sensual pleasures by abandoning sensual objects. The former also demonstrates dedication to teaching the Dhamma, the latter an inclination for seclusion. The former shows approaching through compassion, the latter withdrawing by wisdom. The former reveals an inclination for bringing about the welfare and happiness of beings, the latter demonstrates being unstained in the act of bringing about the welfare and happiness of others. The former indicates a comfortable abiding for the sake of not abandoning righteous happiness, and the latter for the sake of practicing the supramundane states. The former shows great benefit to humans, the latter to devas. The former indicates being born and having grown up in the world, the latter remaining unstained by the world. The former, in accordance with the text: 'Monks, one person arising in the world arises for the welfare of the many, for the happiness of the many, out of compassion for the world, for the good, welfare, and happiness of devas and humans. Who is that one person? The Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One,' signifies the accomplishment of the purpose for which the Blessed One arose. The latter signifies a dwelling appropriate to the place where he was born. For the Blessed One was first born in the Lumbinī Grove and secondly at the Bodhi-maṇḍa; thus, by worldly and supramundane birth, he was born in a grove itself. Therefore, this shows his dwelling in a grove itself. In this and other ways, the application of the meaning here should be understood.

Tatrāti desakālaparidīpanaṃ. Tañhi yaṃ samayaṃ viharati, tatra samaye. Yasmiñca sālarājamūle viharati, tatra sālarājamūleti dīpeti. Bhāsitabbayutte vā desakāle dīpeti. Na hi bhagavā ayutte dese kāle vā dhammaṃ bhāsati. “Akālo kho tāva bāhiyā”ti (udā. 10) ādicettha sādhakaṃ. Khoti padapūraṇamatte avadhāraṇe ādikālatthe vā nipāto. Bhagavāti lokagarudīpanaṃ. Bhikkhūti kathāsavanayuttapuggalavacanaṃ. Apicettha, “bhikkhakoti bhikkhu, bhikkhācariyaṃ ajjhupagatoti bhikkhū”tiādinā (pārā. 45) nayena vacanattho veditabbo. Āmantesīti ālapi abhāsi sambodhesīti ayamettha attho. Aññatra [M 1.0015] pana ñāpanepi hoti. Yathāha “āmantayāmi vo, bhikkhave, paṭivedayāmi vo, bhikkhave”ti. Pakkosanepi. Yathāha “ehi tvaṃ bhikkhu mama vacanena sāriputtaṃ āmantehī”ti (a. ni. 9.11).

The word ‘tatra’ (there) is an indication of place and time. For it indicates the time when he was dwelling, ‘at that time,’ and the foot of the royal sāla-tree where he was dwelling, ‘at the foot of that royal sāla-tree.’ Alternatively, it indicates a suitable place and time for speaking, for the Blessed One does not speak the Dhamma in an unsuitable place or at an unsuitable time. The statement, ‘Now is not the time, Bāhiya’ (Ud 1.10), is evidence for this. The particle ‘kho’ is used merely for filling out a phrase, for emphasis, or in the sense of ‘at the beginning.’ ‘Bhagavā’ (the Blessed One) is an indication of one who is revered by the world. ‘Bhikkhū’ (monks) is a term for persons fit to listen to the discourse. Moreover, here the meaning of the word should be understood according to the method beginning with: ‘A bhikkhu is one who begs; a bhikkhu is one who has undertaken the practice of mendicancy.’ ‘Āmantesi’ (he addressed) here means he spoke to, conversed with, or roused. Elsewhere, however, it also occurs in the sense of informing, as in: ‘I address you, monks; I make known to you, monks.’ It also occurs in the sense of summoning, as in: ‘Come, monk, and in my name, summon Sāriputta.’

Bhikkhavoti āmantanākāradīpanaṃ. Tañca bhikkhanasīlatādiguṇayogasiddhattā vuttaṃ. Bhikkhanasīlatāguṇayuttopi hi bhikkhu bhikkhanadhammatāguṇayuttopi. Bhikkhane sādhukāritāguṇayuttopīti saddavidū maññanti. Tena ca nesaṃ bhikkhanasīlatādiguṇayogasiddhena vacanena hīnādhikajanasevitaṃ vuttiṃ pakāsento uddhatadīnabhāvaniggahaṃ [P 1.0014] karoti. Bhikkhavoti iminā ca karuṇāvipphārasommahadayanayananipātapubbaṅgamena vacanena te attano mukhābhimukhe karoti. Teneva ca kathetukamyatādīpakena vacanena nesaṃ sotukamyataṃ janeti. Teneva ca sambodhanaṭṭhena [V 1.0017] sādhukaṃ savanamanasikārepi ne niyojeti. Sādhukasavanamanasikārāyattā hi sāsanasampatti.

‘Bhikkhavo’ (O monks) is an indication of the manner of address. And this is said because of their accomplishment in virtues such as the habitual practice of mendicancy. For a bhikkhu is indeed endowed with the virtue of the habitual practice of mendicancy, and also with the virtue of the nature of mendicancy; moreover, experts in grammar consider him endowed with the virtue of acting well in mendicancy. And by that word, which is established through the virtue of the habitual practice of mendicancy, by revealing a way of life practiced by both lowly and eminent people, he suppresses states of arrogance and dejection. And by this address, ‘O monks,’ a statement preceded by the casting of his eyes with a gentle heart pervaded by compassion, he makes them turn to face him. And by that very statement, which indicates the desire to speak, he generates in them a desire to listen. And by that very word, which has the meaning of rousing, he also engages them in proper hearing and attention. For the accomplishment of the Dispensation is dependent on proper hearing and attention.

Aparesupi devamanussesu vijjamānesu kasmā bhikkhūyeva āmantesīti ce. Jeṭṭhaseṭṭhāsannasadāsannihitabhāvato. Sabbaparisasādhāraṇā hi bhagavato dhammadesanā. Parisāya ca jeṭṭhā bhikkhū, paṭhamuppannattā. Seṭṭhā, anagāriyabhāvaṃ ādiṃ katvā satthucariyānuvidhāyakattā sakalasāsanapaṭiggāhakattā ca. Āsannā, tattha nisinnesu satthusantikattā. Sadāsannihitā, satthusantikāvacarattāti. Apica te dhammadesanāya bhājanaṃ, yathānusiṭṭhaṃ paṭipattisabbhāvato. Visesato ca ekacce bhikkhūyeva sandhāya ayaṃ desanātipi te eva āmantesi.

If it be asked: ‘Even though other devas and humans were present, why did he address only the monks?’ It is because of their being the eldest, the most excellent, the nearest, and ever-present. For the Blessed One’s teaching of the Dhamma is common to all assemblies. And in the assembly, the monks are the eldest because they were the first to arise. They are the most excellent because, beginning with the homeless life, they conformed to the Teacher’s conduct and were the recipients of the entire Dispensation. They are the nearest because, among those seated there, they were in the Teacher’s presence. They are ever-present because they moved about in the Teacher’s presence. Moreover, they are a vessel for the teaching of the Dhamma, because of their practice in accordance with what was taught. And specifically, he addressed only them also because this teaching was intended for certain monks.

Tattha siyā – kimatthaṃ pana bhagavā dhammaṃ desento paṭhamaṃ bhikkhū āmantesi, na dhammameva desetīti. Satijananatthaṃ. Bhikkhū hi aññaṃ cintentāpi vikkhittacittāpi dhammaṃ paccavekkhantāpi kammaṭṭhānaṃ manasikarontāpi nisinnā honti, te anāmantetvā dhamme desiyamāne – “ayaṃ desanā kinnidānā kiṃpaccayā katamāya aṭṭhuppattiyā desitā”ti sallakkhetuṃ asakkontā duggahitaṃ vā gaṇheyyuṃ, na vā gaṇheyyuṃ. Tena nesaṃ satijananatthaṃ bhagavā paṭhamaṃ āmantetvā pacchā dhammaṃ deseti.

Here it might be asked: ‘For what reason, when teaching the Dhamma, did the Blessed One first address the monks, and not just teach the Dhamma?’ It was for the purpose of generating mindfulness. For monks might be seated there thinking of other things, or with distracted minds, or reflecting on the Dhamma, or attending to their meditation subject. If the Dhamma were taught without first addressing them, they, being unable to discern, ‘What is the source of this teaching? What is its condition? Due to what occasion was it taught?’, might grasp it wrongly, or not grasp it at all. Therefore, to generate mindfulness in them, the Blessed One first addressed them and afterwards taught the Dhamma.

Bhadanteti [M 1.0016] gāravavacanametaṃ, satthuno paṭivacanadānaṃ vā, apicettha bhikkhavoti vadamāno bhagavā te bhikkhū ālapati. Bhadanteti vadamānā te bhagavantaṃ paccālapanti. Tathā bhikkhavoti bhagavā ābhāsati. Bhadanteti te paccābhāsanti. Bhikkhavoti paṭivacanaṃ dāpeti, bhadanteti paṭivacanaṃ denti. Te bhikkhūti ye bhagavā āmantesi. Bhagavato paccassosunti bhagavato āmantanaṃ paṭiassosuṃ, abhimukhā hutvā suṇiṃsu sampaṭicchiṃsu paṭiggahesunti [P 1.0015] attho. Bhagavā etadavocāti bhagavā etaṃ idāni vattabbaṃ sakalaṃ suttaṃ avoca.

‘Bhadante’ (Venerable Sir) is an expression of respect, or it is the giving of a reply to the Teacher. Furthermore, in this context, the Blessed One, saying ‘Bhikkhavo,’ addresses those monks. They, saying ‘Bhadante,’ address the Blessed One in return. Similarly, the Blessed One speaks first, saying ‘Bhikkhavo.’ They speak in response, saying ‘Bhadante.’ With ‘Bhikkhavo,’ he causes a reply to be given; with ‘Bhadante,’ they give the reply. ‘Those monks’ means those whom the Blessed One addressed. ‘They responded to the Blessed One’ means they acknowledged the Blessed One's address; having turned to face him, they listened, they accepted, they received it—this is the meaning. ‘The Blessed One said this’ means the Blessed One spoke this entire sutta that was now to be spoken.

Ettāvatā ca yaṃ āyasmatā ānandena kamalakuvalayujjalavimalasādurasasalilāya pokkharaṇiyā sukhāvataraṇatthaṃ nimmalasilātalaracanavilāsasobhitaratanasopānaṃ vippakiṇṇamuttātalasadisavālikākiṇṇapaṇḍarabhūmibhāgaṃ [V 1.0018] titthaṃ viya suvibhattabhittivicitravedikāparikkhittassa nakkhattapathaṃ phusitukāmatāya viya, vijambhitasamussayassa pāsādavarassa sukhārohaṇatthaṃ dantamaya-saṇhamuduphalaka-kañcanalatāvinaddha- maṇigaṇappabhāsamudayujjalasobhaṃ sopānaṃ viya, suvaṇṇavalayānūpurādisaṅghaṭṭanasaddasammissitakathitahasitamadhurassaragehajanavicaritassa uḷāraissariyavibhavasobhitassa mahāgharassa sukhappavesanatthaṃ suvaṇṇarajatamaṇimuttāpavāḷādijutivissaravijjotita-suppatiṭṭhitavisāladvārabāhaṃ mahādvāraṃ viya ca atthabyañjanasampannassa buddhānaṃ desanāñāṇagambhīrabhāvasaṃsūcakassa imassa suttassa sukhāvagāhaṇatthaṃ kāladesadesakavatthuparisāpadesapaṭimaṇḍitaṃ nidānaṃ bhāsitaṃ, tassa atthavaṇṇanā samattā.

Thus far, the explanation of the meaning of the introduction is concluded. This introduction was spoken by the Venerable Ānanda, adorned with indications of time, place, speaker, subject, assembly, and location, for the sake of easy comprehension of this sutta, which is endowed with meaning and phrasing and is indicative of the profundity of the teaching-knowledge of the Buddhas. It is like a bathing place with a ground portion made white with sand like scattered pearl-dust, for ease of descending into a pond with shining, spotless, sweet, and delicious water of red and blue lotuses; and like a staircase made of ivory, of smooth and soft planks, entwined with golden vines, resplendent and beautiful with the radiant light from multitudes of gems, for ease of ascending a noble palace that is enclosed by well-portioned walls and variegated railings, a repository of splendor, as if desiring to touch the path of the stars; and like a great door with well-established, wide doorposts, brilliantly illuminated by the radiant light of gold, silver, gems, pearls, coral, and so on, for ease of entering a great house, resplendent with abundant sovereignty and wealth, where the household folk move about amidst the sweet sounds of conversation and laughter, mingled with the sounds from the striking of gold bracelets, anklets, and the like.

Suttanikkhepavaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Introduction to the Sutta

Idāni “sabbadhammamūlapariyāyaṃ vo”tiādinā nayena bhagavatā nikkhittassa suttassa vaṇṇanāya okāso anuppatto. Sā panesā suttavaṇṇanā yasmā suttanikkhepaṃ vicāretvā vuccamānā pākaṭā hoti, tasmā suttanikkhepaṃ tāva vicārayissāma. Cattāro hi suttanikkhepā attajjhāsayo parajjhāsayo pucchāvasiko aṭṭhuppattikoti.

Now the occasion has arrived for the exposition of the sutta laid down by the Blessed One with the method beginning, “I will teach you the root-discourse on all phenomena.” And since this sutta exposition becomes clear when it is spoken after having considered the introduction of the sutta, therefore we shall first consider the introduction of the sutta. Indeed, there are four introductions of suttas: that due to one's own inclination, that due to the inclination of others, that due to a question, and that due to an arisen cause.

Tattha [M 1.0017] yāni suttāni bhagavā parehi anajjhiṭṭho kevalaṃ attano ajjhāsayeneva kathesi. Seyyathidaṃ, ākaṅkheyyasuttaṃ, vatthasuttaṃ, mahāsatipaṭṭhānasuttaṃ, mahāsaḷāyatanavibhaṅgasuttaṃ, ariyavaṃsasuttaṃ, sammappadhānasuttantahārako, iddhipādaindriyabalabojjhaṅgamaggaṅgasuttantahārakoti evamādīni. Tesaṃ attajjhāsayo nikkhepo.

Among these, there are those suttas that the Blessed One taught, unrequested by others, purely from his own inclination. Which are these? The Ākaṅkheyya Sutta, the Vattha Sutta, the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta, the Mahāsaḷāyatanavibhaṅga Sutta, the Ariyavaṃsa Sutta, the Sammappadhāna Suttantahāraka, the Iddhipāda-Indriya-Bala-Bojjhaṅga-Maggaṅga Suttantahāraka, and others such as these. Their introduction is that due to one's own inclination.

Yāni pana “paripakkā kho rāhulassa vimuttiparipācanīyā dhammā, yaṃnūnāhaṃ rāhulaṃ uttari āsavānaṃ khaye vineyya”nti (saṃ. ni. 4.121) evaṃ paresaṃ ajjhāsayaṃ khantiṃ manaṃ abhinīhāraṃ [P 1.0016] bujjhanabhāvañca avekkhitvā parajjhāsayavasena kathitāni. Seyyathidaṃ, cūḷarāhulovādasuttaṃ, mahārāhulovādasuttaṃ, dhammacakkappavattanaṃ, dhātuvibhaṅgasuttanti evamādīni. Tesaṃ parajjhāsayo nikkhepo.

But those suttas that were taught by the power of the inclination of others, after having considered the inclination, preference, intention, aspiration, and capacity for understanding of others, as in the case of: “Indeed, the qualities in Rāhula that are ripeners for liberation are mature. What if I were to train Rāhula further in the destruction of the taints?” Which are these? The Cūḷarāhulovāda Sutta, the Mahārāhulovāda Sutta, the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, the Dhātuvibhaṅga Sutta, and others such as these. Their introduction is that due to the inclination of others.

Bhagavantaṃ [V 1.0019] pana upasaṅkamitvā catasso parisā cattāro vaṇṇā nāgā supaṇṇā gandhabbā asurā yakkhā mahārājāno tāvatiṃsādayo devā mahābrahmāti evamādayo “bojjhaṅgā bojjhaṅgā”ti, bhante, vuccanti. “Nīvaraṇā nīvaraṇā”ti, bhante, vuccanti. Ime nu kho, bhante, pañcupādānakkhandhā. “Kiṃ sūdha vittaṃ purisassa seṭṭha”ntiādinā (su. ni. 183) nayena pañhaṃ pucchanti. Evaṃ puṭṭhena bhagavatā yāni kathitāni bojjhaṅgasaṃyuttādīni. Yāni vā panaññānipi devatāsaṃyutta-mārasaṃyutta-brahmasaṃyutta-sakkapañha-cūḷavedalla-mahāvedalla-sāmaññaphala- āḷavaka-sūciloma-kharalomasuttādīni, tesaṃ pucchāvasiko nikkhepo.

But having approached the Blessed One, the four assemblies, the four classes, nāgas, supaṇṇas, gandhabbas, asuras, yakkhas, the great kings, the Tāvatiṃsa devas and others, and Mahābrahmā, and so on, ask questions in the manner of: “Venerable Sir, what are these that are called ‘factors of enlightenment’?”; “Venerable Sir, what are these that are called ‘hindrances’?”; “Venerable Sir, are these the five aggregates subject to clinging?”; and “What here is a person’s best wealth?” and so on. The suttas taught by the Blessed One when thus questioned—such as the Bojjhaṅga Saṃyutta and others, or whatever others such as the Devatā Saṃyutta, Māra Saṃyutta, Brahma Saṃyutta, Sakkapañha Sutta, Cūḷavedalla Sutta, Mahāvedalla Sutta, Sāmaññaphala Sutta, Āḷavaka Sutta, Sūciloma Sutta, Kharaloma Sutta, and so on—the introduction of these is that due to a question.

Yāni panetāni uppannaṃ kāraṇaṃ paṭicca kathitāni. Seyyathidaṃ, dhammadāyādaṃ cūḷasīhanādaṃ candūpamaṃ puttamaṃsūpamaṃ dārukkhandhūpamaṃ aggikkhandhūpamaṃ pheṇapiṇḍūpamaṃ pāricchattakūpamanti evamādīni. Tesaṃ aṭṭhuppattiko nikkhepo.

And those suttas that were taught in dependence on an arisen cause—which are these? The Dhammadāyāda Sutta, the Cūḷasīhanāda Sutta, the Candūpama Sutta, the Puttamaṃsūpama Sutta, the Dārukkhandhūpama Sutta, the Aggikkhandhūpama Sutta, the Pheṇapiṇḍūpama Sutta, the Pāricchattakūpama Sutta, and others such as these. The introduction of these suttas is that due to an arisen cause.

Evamimesu catūsu nikkhepesu imassa suttassa aṭṭhuppattiko nikkhepo. Aṭṭhuppattiyañhi idaṃ bhagavatā nikkhittaṃ. Katarāya aṭṭhuppattiyā? Pariyattiṃ nissāya uppanne māne. Pañcasatā kira brāhmaṇā tiṇṇaṃ vedānaṃ pāragū aparabhāge bhagavato dhammadesanaṃ sutvā kāmesu ādīnavaṃ nekkhamme ca ānisaṃsaṃ sampassamānā bhagavato santike pabbajitvā nacirasseva sabbaṃ buddhavacanaṃ uggaṇhitvā pariyattiṃ nissāya mānaṃ uppādesuṃ “yaṃ yaṃ bhagavā katheti, taṃ taṃ mayaṃ khippameva jānāma, bhagavā hi tīṇi liṅgāni [M 1.0018] cattāri padāni satta vibhattiyo muñcitvā [P 1.0017] na kiñci katheti, evaṃ kathite ca amhākaṃ gaṇṭhipadaṃ nāma natthī”ti. Te bhagavati agāravā hutvā tato paṭṭhāya bhagavato upaṭṭhānampi dhammassavanampi abhiṇhaṃ na gacchanti. Bhagavā tesaṃ taṃ cittacāraṃ ñatvā “abhabbā ime imaṃ mānakhilaṃ anupahacca maggaṃ vā phalaṃ vā sacchikātu”nti tesaṃ sutapariyattiṃ nissāya uppannaṃ mānaṃ aṭṭhuppattiṃ katvā desanākusalo bhagavā mānabhañjanatthaṃ sabbadhammamūlapariyāyanti desanaṃ ārabhi.

Thus, among these four introductions, the introduction of this sutta is one based on an occasion. For it was laid down by the Blessed One on an occasion. On which occasion? Arrogance arising in dependence on scriptural learning. It is said that five hundred brahmins, masters of the three Vedas, in a later time, having heard the Blessed One’s teaching, and seeing the danger in sensual pleasures and the benefit in renunciation, went forth in the presence of the Blessed One. Not long after, they learned all the Buddha’s words and, in dependence on their scriptural learning, generated arrogance, thinking: 'Whatever the Blessed One says, we quickly understand. For the Blessed One says nothing apart from the three genders, four nominal stems, and seven grammatical cases. And when he speaks thus, for us there is no knotty point at all.' Having become disrespectful toward the Blessed One, from then on they did not regularly attend upon him or listen to the Dhamma. The Blessed One, knowing their mental disposition, thought: 'These men are incapable of realizing the path or its fruit without having removed this stake of arrogance.' The Blessed One, skilled in teaching, making the arrogance that arose in dependence on their acquired learning the occasion, began the discourse on 'The Root of All Phenomena' for the shattering of their pride.

Tattha sabbadhammamūlapariyāyanti sabbesaṃ dhammānaṃ mūlapariyāyaṃ. Sabbesanti anavasesānaṃ. Anavasesavācako hi ayaṃ sabba-saddo. So yena yena sambandhaṃ gacchati, tassa tassa anavasesataṃ dīpeti. Yathā, “sabbaṃ rūpaṃ aniccaṃ sabbā vedanā aniccā sabbasakkāyapariyāpannesu [V 1.0020] dhammesū”ti. Dhamma-saddo panāyaṃ pariyatti-sacca-samādhi-paññā-pakati-sabhāvasuññatā-puññāpatti-ñeyyādīsu dissati. “Idha bhikkhu dhammaṃ pariyāpuṇāti suttaṃ geyya”ntiādīsu (a. ni. 5.73) hi dhammasaddo pariyattiyaṃ vattati. “Diṭṭhadhammo viditadhammo”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 1.299) saccesu. “Evaṃ dhammā te bhagavanto”tiādīsu samādhimhi.

Here, "the root-discourse on all phenomena" means the root exposition of all phenomena. "All" means without remainder. The word "all" signifies 'without remainder.' Wherever it is applied, it indicates the completeness of that. For example: "All form is impermanent, all feeling is impermanent, in all phenomena included in the personality-group." The word "dhamma" is seen in contexts such as scriptural learning, truth, concentration, wisdom, nature, own-being, emptiness, merit, offense, the knowable, etc. In passages like, "Here, a monk learns the Dhamma—the suttas, the geyyas..." (AN 5.73), the word "dhamma" refers to scriptural learning. In passages like, "One who has seen the Dhamma, known the Dhamma..." (DN 1.299), it refers to truths. In passages like, "Thus are those Blessed Ones endowed with Dhamma," it refers to concentration.

“Yassete caturo dhammā, vānarinda yathā tava;

Saccaṃ dhammo dhiti cāgo, diṭṭhaṃ so ativattatī”ti. –

"O monkey king, whoever possesses these four qualities, as you do—truth, wisdom, steadfastness, and generosity—transcends what is seen."

Ādīsu (jā. 1.1.57) paññāya.

In passages such as this (Jā 1.1.57), it refers to wisdom.

“Jātidhammā jarādhammā, atho maraṇadhammino”tiādīsu pakatiyaṃ. “Kusalā dhammā”tiādīsu (dha. sa. 1.tikamātikā) sabhāve. “Tasmiṃ kho pana samaye dhammā hontī”tiādīsu (dha. sa. 121) suññatāyaṃ. “Dhammo suciṇṇo sukhamāvahātī”tiādīsu (jā. 1.10.102) puññe. “Dve aniyatā dhammā”tiādīsu (pārā. 443) āpattiyaṃ. “Sabbe dhammā sabbākārena buddhassa bhagavato ñāṇamukhe āpāthaṃ āgacchantī”tiādīsu ñeyye. Idha panāyaṃ sabhāve vattati. Tatrāyaṃ vacanattho – attano lakkhaṇaṃ dhārentīti dhammā. Mūla-saddo vitthārito eva. Idha panāyaṃ asādhāraṇahetumhi daṭṭhabbo.

In passages such as, “Subject to birth, subject to aging, and also subject to death,” it refers to nature. In passages such as, “Wholesome phenomena” (Dhs 1, Tikamātikā), it refers to own-being. In passages such as, “At that time, phenomena exist” (Dhs 121), it refers to emptiness. In passages such as, “The well-practiced Dhamma brings happiness” (J 1.10.102), it refers to merit. In passages such as, “Two indeterminate phenomena” (Pārā. 443), it refers to offenses. In passages such as, “All phenomena in every way enter the range of knowledge of the Blessed Buddha,” it refers to the knowable. Here, however, it refers to own-being. The meaning of the term is this: 'They uphold their own characteristic, thus they are dhammas.' The word 'mūla' has indeed been explained in detail. Here, however, it should be regarded as referring to the unique cause.

Pariyāyasaddo [M 1.0019][P 1.0018] “madhupiṇḍikapariyāyoti naṃ dhārehī”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.205) desanāyaṃ vattati. “Atthi khvesa brāhmaṇa, pariyāyo, yena maṃ pariyāyena sammā vadamāno vadeyya akiriyavādo samaṇo gotamo”tiādīsu (pārā. 3) kāraṇe. “Kassa nu kho, ānanda, ajja pariyāyo bhikkhuniyo ovaditu”ntiādīsu (ma. ni. 3.398) vāre. Idha pana kāraṇepi desanāyampi vattati. Tasmā “sabbadhammamūlapariyāya”nti ettha sabbesaṃ dhammānaṃ asādhāraṇahetusaññitaṃ kāraṇanti vā sabbesaṃ dhammānaṃ kāraṇadesananti vā evaṃ attho daṭṭhabbo. Neyyatthattā cassa suttassa, na catubhūmakāpi sabhāvadhammā sabbadhammāti veditabbā. Sakkāyapariyāpannā pana tebhūmakā dhammāva anavasesato veditabbā, ayamettha adhippāyoti.

The term ‘pariyāya’ is used for 'exposition,' as in ‘Remember this as the ‘Honeyball Exposition’' (MN 18). It is used for 'reason' in passages such as ‘There is, brahmin, a way by which one may rightly say of me, “The ascetic Gotama is a proponent of non-action”’ (Vin. i. 234). It is used for 'turn' in passages such as ‘Ānanda, whose turn is it today to advise the bhikkhunīs?’ (MN 146). Here, however, it is used in the sense of both reason and exposition. Therefore, ‘the exposition on the root of all phenomena’ should be understood either as 'the reason which is the unique cause of all phenomena,' or as 'the exposition on the cause of all phenomena.' Because this sutta has a meaning that must be inferred, 'all phenomena' should not be understood as the phenomena of own-being pertaining to the four planes of existence. Rather, only phenomena included in the personality-group and pertaining to the three realms should be understood without remainder. This is the intended meaning here.

Voti [V 1.0021] ayaṃ vo-saddo paccattaupayogakaraṇasampadānasāmivacanapadapūraṇesu dissati. “Kacci pana vo, anuruddhā, samaggā sammodamānā”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.326) hi paccatte dissati. “Gacchatha, bhikkhave, paṇāmemi vo”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 2.157) upayoge. “Na vo mama santike vatthabba”ntiādīsu (ma. ni. 2.157) karaṇe. “Vanapatthapariyāyaṃ vo, bhikkhave, desessāmī”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.190) sampadāne. “Sabbesaṃ vo, sāriputta, subhāsita”ntiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.345) sāmivacane. “Ye hi vo ariyā parisuddhakāyakammantā”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.35) padapūraṇamatte. Idha panāyaṃ sampadāne daṭṭhabbo.

The pronoun ‘vo’ occurs in the senses of individuality, objective, instrument, dative, possession, and as a mere sentence filler. For example, in ‘Anuruddhas, I hope you are living in harmony and mutual appreciation’ (MN 31), it is seen in the sense of individuality. In ‘Go, bhikkhus, I dismiss you’ (MN 66), it is used in the objective sense. In ‘You should not stay near me’ (MN 66), it is instrumental. In ‘Bhikkhus, I will teach you the discourse on the forest life’ (MN 17), it is dative. In ‘Sāriputta, what all of you have said is well-spoken’ (MN 32), it signifies possession. In ‘For those of you whose bodily actions are perfectly pure’ (MN 7), it is merely a sentence filler. In this context, however, it should be regarded as dative.

Bhikkhaveti patissavena abhimukhībhūtānaṃ punālapanaṃ. Desessāmīti desanāpaṭijānanaṃ.
