Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti, bhikkhave, sabbadhammānaṃ mūlakāraṇaṃ tumhākaṃ desessāmi, dutiyena nayena kāraṇadesanaṃ tumhākaṃ desessāmīti. Taṃ suṇāthāti tamatthaṃ taṃ kāraṇaṃ taṃ desanaṃ mayā vuccamānaṃ suṇātha. Sādhukaṃ manasi karothāti ettha pana sādhukaṃ sādhūti ekatthametaṃ. Ayañca sādhu saddo āyācanasampaṭicchanasampahaṃsanasundaradaḷhīkammādīsu dissati. “Sādhu me bhante bhagavā, saṃkhittena dhammaṃ desetū”tiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 4.95) hi āyācane dissati. “Sādhu, bhanteti kho so [M 1.0020] bhikkhu bhagavato bhāsitaṃ [P 1.0019] abhinanditvā anumoditvā”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 3.86) sampaṭicchane. “Sādhu, sādhu sāriputtā”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 3.349) sampahaṃsane.

‘Bhikkhus’ is a re-addressing of those who have become attentive by way of assent. ‘I will explain’ is the declaration of undertaking to teach. This is what is said: Bhikkhus, ‘I will explain to you the root cause of all phenomena; in a second way, I will explain to you the exposition of causality.’ ‘Listen to it,’ means listen to that meaning, that cause, that teaching as it is spoken by me. ‘Apply your minds well’—here ‘well’ (sādhukaṃ) and ‘good’ (sādhu) have one meaning. And this word ‘sādhu’ is seen in contexts such as requesting, accepting, praising, beauty, strengthening, etc. For example, it is seen in requesting: ‘Good, Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One briefly teach the Dhamma’ (SN 35.116). In accepting: ‘Good, Venerable Sir,’ that bhikkhu, having rejoiced and delighted in the Blessed One’s words… (MN 118). In praising: ‘Good, good, Sāriputta’ (DN 33).

“Sādhu dhammarucī rājā, sādhu paññāṇavā naro;

Sādhu mittānamaddubbho, pāpassākaraṇaṃ sukha”nti.

“Good is the king who loves the Dhamma; good is the person endowed with wisdom. Good is one who is not treacherous to friends; abstaining from evil is happiness.”

Ādīsu (jā. 2.18.101) sundare. “Tena hi, brāhmaṇa, sādhukaṃ suṇāhī”tiādīsu (a. ni. 5.192) sādhukasaddoyeva daḷhīkamme, āṇattiyantipi vuccati. Idhāpi ayaṃ ettheva daḷhīkamme ca āṇattiyañca attho veditabbo. Sundaratthepi vattati. Daḷhīkaraṇatthena hi daḷhamimaṃ dhammaṃ suṇātha suggahitaṃ gaṇhantā. Āṇattiatthena mama āṇattiyā suṇātha. Sundaratthena sundaramimaṃ bhaddakaṃ dhammaṃ suṇāthāti evaṃ dīpitaṃ hoti.

In passages such as this (Jā 2.18.101), it refers to beauty. In contexts such as ‘Well then, brahmin, listen carefully’ (AN 5.192), the word ‘sādhukaṃ’ itself signifies strengthening, and it is also said to be a command. Here too, this word should be understood in the sense of both strengthening and a command. It also functions in the sense of beauty. By way of strengthening, it means: ‘Listen firmly to this Dhamma, grasping it well.’ By way of command: ‘Listen according to my command.’ By way of beauty: ‘Listen to this beautiful, auspicious Dhamma.’ Thus, it is shown.

Manasi [V 1.0022] karothāti āvajjetha, samannāharathāti attho, avikkhittacittā hutvā nisāmetha citte karothāti adhippāyo. Idānettha taṃ suṇāthāti sotindriyavikkhepavāraṇametaṃ. Sādhukaṃ manasi karothāti manasikāre daḷhīkammaniyojanena manindriyavikkhepavāraṇaṃ. Purimañcettha byañjanavipallāsaggāhavāraṇaṃ, pacchimaṃ atthavipallāsaggāhavāraṇaṃ. Purimena ca dhammassavane niyojeti, pacchimena sutānaṃ dhammānaṃ dhāraṇūpaparikkhādīsu. Purimena ca sabyañjano ayaṃ dhammo, tasmā savanīyoti dīpeti. Pacchimena sāttho, tasmā manasi kātabboti. Sādhukapadaṃ vā ubhayapadehi yojetvā yasmā ayaṃ dhammo dhammagambhīro desanāgambhīro ca, tasmā suṇātha sādhukaṃ, yasmā atthagambhīro paṭivedhagambhīro ca, tasmā sādhukaṃ manasi karothāti evaṃ yojanā veditabbā.

‘Apply your mind’ (manasi karotha) means to advert (āvajjetha), to apply the mind (samannāharatha); this is the meaning. ‘Listen with an undistracted mind, place it in your mind’ is the intention. Here, ‘listen to it’ is for the prevention of distraction of the ear-faculty. ‘Apply your mind well’ is for the prevention of distraction of the mind-faculty by enjoining firm application in attending. And here, the former prevents the distorted grasping of the wording; the latter, the distorted grasping of the meaning. By the former, He enjoins the hearing of the Dhamma; by the latter, the retaining, examining, etc., of the teachings that have been heard. By the former, it is shown that this Dhamma is complete with wording, therefore it should be heard. By the latter, that it is complete with meaning, therefore it should be attended to. Alternatively, the word ‘well’ (sādhukaṃ) can be connected with both phrases, and the construction should be understood thus: because this Dhamma is profound in its text and profound in its exposition, therefore ‘listen well’; because it is profound in meaning and profound in penetration, therefore ‘apply your mind well.’

Bhāsissāmīti desessāmi. “Taṃ suṇāthā”ti ettha paṭiññātaṃ desanaṃ na saṃkhittatova desessāmi, apica kho vitthāratopi naṃ bhāsissāmīti vuttaṃ hoti, saṅkhepavitthāravācakāni hi etāni padāni. Yathāha vaṅgīsatthero –

‘I will speak’ (bhāsissāmi) means ‘I will teach’ (desessāmi). In this context, it is meant that ‘I will not teach the declared teaching only in brief, but I will also speak it in detail,’ for these words are indicative of concise and detailed explanation. As the Elder Vaṅgīsa said:

“Saṃkhittenapi [P 1.0020] deseti, vitthārenapi bhāsati;

Sāḷikāyiva nigghoso, paṭibhānaṃ udīrayī”ti. (saṃ. ni. 1.214);

“He teaches concisely and speaks extensively; like the melodious sound of a sāḷikā bird, He utters inspired speech.”

Evaṃ [M 1.0021] vutte ussāhajātā hutvā evaṃ bhanteti kho te bhikkhū bhagavato paccassosuṃ satthu vacanaṃ sampaṭicchiṃsu, paṭiggahesunti vuttaṃ hoti. Atha nesaṃ bhagavā etadavoca etaṃ idāni vattabbaṃ idha bhikkhavotiādikaṃ sakalaṃ suttaṃ avoca. Tattha idhāti desāpadese nipāto. Svāyaṃ katthaci lokaṃ upādāya vuccati. Yathāha – “idha tathāgato loke uppajjatī”ti (dī. ni. 1.190). Katthaci sāsanaṃ. Yathāha – “idheva, bhikkhave, samaṇo, idha dutiyo samaṇo”ti (a. ni. 4.241). Katthaci okāsaṃ. Yathāha –

When this was said, those bhikkhus, having become enthusiastic, replied to the Blessed One, ‘Even so, venerable sir.’ They accepted the Teacher’s word, they received it; so it is said. Then the Blessed One spoke this to them; He spoke this entire sutta which was now to be spoken, beginning with ‘Here, bhikkhus,’ and so on. Therein, ‘here’ (idha) is a particle in the sense of place. This word is sometimes used with reference to the world, as it is said: ‘Here the Tathāgata arises in the world.’ Sometimes, with reference to the Dispensation, as it is said: ‘Here, bhikkhus, is the ascetic; here is the second ascetic.’ Sometimes, with reference to a location, as it is said:

“Idheva tiṭṭhamānassa, devabhūtassa me sato;

Punarāyu ca me laddho, evaṃ jānāhi mārisā”ti. (dī. ni. 2.369);

“While standing right here, having become a deva and being mindful, renewed life was gained by me; thus know, O Noble One.”

Katthaci [V 1.0023] padapūraṇamattameva. Yathāha “idhāhaṃ – bhikkhave, bhuttāvī assaṃ pavārito”ti (ma. ni. 1.30). Idha pana lokaṃ upādāya vuttoti veditabbo.

In some places, it is merely for filling out the phrase. As it is said: ‘Here, bhikkhus, having eaten, I might be satisfied.’ Here, however, it should be understood as spoken with reference to the world.

2. Bhikkhaveti yathāpaṭiññātaṃ desanaṃ desetuṃ puna bhikkhū ālapati. Ubhayenāpi, bhikkhave, imasmiṃ loketi vuttaṃ hoti. Assutavā puthujjanoti ettha pana āgamādhigamābhāvā ñeyyo assutavā iti. Yassa hi khandhadhātuāyatanasaccapaccayākārasatipaṭṭhānādīsu uggahaparipucchāvinicchayarahitattā maññanāpaṭisedhako neva āgamo, paṭipattiyā adhigantabbassa anadhigatattā neva adhigamo atthi. So āgamādhigamābhāvā ñeyyo assutavā iti. Svāyaṃ –

2. ‘Bhikkhus’—He again addresses the bhikkhus in order to teach the teaching as promised. By both words combined, it is meant: ‘O bhikkhus, in this world.’ As to ‘an uninstructed worldling,’ he is to be known as ‘uninstructed’ due to the absence of learning and realization. For one who—with regard to the aggregates, elements, sense bases, truths, dependent origination, foundations of mindfulness, and so forth—is devoid of study, inquiry, and ascertainment, there is neither the learning that refutes conceiving, nor is there realization, due to not having realized that which is to be realized through practice. He, due to the absence of learning and realization, is to be known as ‘uninstructed.’ This one is:

Puthūnaṃ jananādīhi, kāraṇehi puthujjano;

Puthujjanantogadhattā, puthuvāyaṃ jano iti.

He is a ‘worldling’ (puthujjana) for reasons such as generating many (puthu) defilements; because this being is included among the many common folk; or, because this person (jano) is separate (puthu) from the noble ones.

So hi puthūnaṃ nānappakārānaṃ kilesādīnaṃ jananādīhi kāraṇehi puthujjano. Yathāha – puthu kilese janentīti puthujjanā, puthu avihatasakkāyadiṭṭhikāti puthujjanā, puthu satthārānaṃ mukhamullokikāti puthujjanā, puthu sabbagatīhi avuṭṭhitāti puthujjanā, puthu nānābhisaṅkhāre abhisaṅkharontīti puthujjanā, puthu nānāoghehi vuyhantīti puthujjanā, puthu nānāsantāpehi santappantīti puthujjanā, puthu nānāpariḷāhehi paridayhantīti puthujjanā, puthu pañcasu kāmaguṇesu rattā giddhā gadhitā [M 1.0022] mucchitā ajjhosannā laggā lagitā palibuddhāti puthujjanā, puthu pañcahi nīvaraṇehi āvuṭā nivutā [P 1.0021] ovutā pihitā paṭicchannā paṭikujjitāti puthujjanāti (mahāni. 51). Puthūnaṃ vā gaṇanapathamatītānaṃ ariyadhammaparammukhānaṃ nīcadhammasamācārānaṃ janānaṃ antogadhattāpi puthujjanā. Puthu vā ayaṃ, visuṃyeva saṅkhaṃ gato, visaṃsaṭṭho sīlasutādiguṇayuttehi ariyehi janotipi puthujjano. Evametehi “assutavā puthujjano”ti dvīhipi padehi yete –

Indeed, he is a worldling because of causes such as generating many and various defilements and so forth. As it is said: They are called puthujjanas because they generate various defilements. They are called puthujjanas because they have many personality-views not slain by the path. They are called puthujjanas because they look to the faces of various teachers. They are called puthujjanas because they have not arisen from all destinations. They are called puthujjanas because they form various formations. They are called puthujjanas because they are swept away by various floods. They are called puthujjanas because they are tormented by various torments. They are called puthujjanas because they are burned all around by various fevers. They are called puthujjanas because they are impassioned, greedy, infatuated, clinging, attached, and entangled by the five strands of sensual pleasure. They are called puthujjanas because they are obstructed, hindered, shut in, blocked, covered over, and overturned by the five hindrances. Or, they are called puthujjanas because of being included among the many beings who have gone beyond the path of counting, who are turned away from the Dhamma of the noble ones, and who have base conduct. Or, this person is a puthujjana because he is separate, has gone to a separate counting, and is unmixed with the noble people endowed with virtues such as morality and learning. Thus, by these two terms, 'the uninstructed worldling,' are meant those who—

Duve puthujjanā vuttā, buddhenādiccabandhunā;

Andho puthujjano eko, kalyāṇeko puthujjanoti. –

Two puthujjanas have been spoken of by the Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun: one is a blind puthujjana, and one is a virtuous puthujjana.

Dve [V 1.0024] puthujjanā vuttā. Tesu andhaputhujjano vutto hotīti veditabbo. Ariyānaṃ adassāvītiādīsu ariyāti ārakattā kilesehi, anaye nairiyanato, aye iriyanato, sadevakena ca lokena araṇīyato buddhā ca paccekabuddhā ca buddhasāvakā ca vuccanti, buddhā eva vā idha ariyā. Yathāha “sadevake, bhikkhave, loke…pe… tathāgato ariyoti vuccatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.1098). Sappurisāti ettha pana paccekabuddhā tathāgatasāvakā ca “sappurisā”ti veditabbā. Te hi lokuttaraguṇayogena sobhanā purisāti sappurisā. Sabbeva vā ete dvedhāpi vuttā. Buddhāpi hi ariyā ca sappurisā ca, paccekabuddhā buddhasāvakāpi. Yathāha –

Two puthujjanas have been spoken of. Among them, it should be understood that the blind puthujjana is spoken of here. In phrases such as 'one who does not see the noble ones,' the term 'noble ones' refers to the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and the Buddha's disciples, because they are far from defilements, because they do not proceed in what is unbeneficial, because they proceed in what is beneficial, and because they are to be resorted to by the world with its devas. Alternatively, here only the Buddhas are called ariyas. As it is said: 'Bhikkhus, in the world with its devas... the Tathāgata is called noble.' But here, in the term sappurisā, Paccekabuddhas and the Tathāgata's disciples are to be understood as 'true persons.' For they, because of their connection with supramundane qualities, are excellent persons; therefore, they are called sappurisā. Alternatively, all of these are spoken of in two ways. For the Buddhas are both noble ones and true persons, and so are the Paccekabuddhas and the Buddha's disciples. As it is said:

“Yo ve kataññū katavedi dhīro,

Kalyāṇamitto daḷhabhatti ca hoti;

Dukhitassa sakkacca karoti kiccaṃ,

Tathāvidhaṃ sappurisaṃ vadantī”ti. (jā. 2.17.78);

“Indeed, the wise person who is grateful and acknowledges what was done, who is a good friend and has firm devotion; for one who is suffering, he respectfully performs the task—such a person they call a true person.”

Kalyāṇamitto daḷhabhatti ca hotīti ettāvatā hi buddhasāvako vutto, kataññutādīhi paccekabuddhā buddhāti. Idāni yo tesaṃ ariyānaṃ adassanasīlo, na ca dassane sādhukārī, so ariyānaṃ adassāvīti veditabbo. So ca cakkhunā adassāvī ñāṇena adassāvīti duvidho, tesu ñāṇena adassāvī idha adhippeto. Maṃsacakkhunā hi dibbacakkhunā vā ariyā [M 1.0023] diṭṭhāpi adiṭṭhāva honti. Tesaṃ cakkhūnaṃ vaṇṇamattaggahaṇato, na ariyabhāvagocarato. Soṇasiṅgālādayopi ca cakkhunā ariye passanti. Na ca te ariyānaṃ dassāvino.

Indeed, by 'is a good friend and has firm devotion,' a disciple of the Buddha is spoken of. By 'gratitude' and so on, Paccekabuddhas and Buddhas are spoken of. Now, one who is not in the habit of seeing those noble ones, and does not approve of seeing them, should be understood as 'one who does not see the noble ones.' And that person is twofold: one who does not see with the physical eye and one who does not see with wisdom. Among them, the one who does not see with wisdom is intended here. For even if noble ones are seen with the physical eye or the divine eye, it is as if they are not seen, because those eyes grasp only the visible form and do not have as their object the state of being a noble one. Even dogs, jackals, and other animals see noble ones with the eye, but they are not seers of the noble ones.

Tatridaṃ [P 1.0022] vatthu – cittalapabbatavāsino kira khīṇāsavattherassa upaṭṭhāko vuḍḍhapabbajito ekadivasaṃ therena saddhiṃ piṇḍāya caritvā therassa pattacīvaraṃ gahetvā piṭṭhito āgacchanto theraṃ pucchi “ariyā nāma, bhante, kīdisā”ti. Thero āha “idhekacco mahallako ariyānaṃ pattacīvaraṃ gahetvā vattapaṭipattiṃ katvā sahacarantopi neva ariye jānāti, evaṃ dujjānā, āvuso, ariyā”ti. Evaṃ vuttepi so neva aññāsi. Tasmā na cakkhunā dassanaṃ dassanaṃ, ñāṇena dassanameva dassanaṃ. Yathāha “kiṃ te, vakkali, iminā pūtikāyena diṭṭhena, yo kho, vakkali[V 1.0025], dhammaṃ passati, so maṃ passatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 3.87). Tasmā cakkhunā passantopi ñāṇena ariyehi diṭṭhaṃ aniccādilakkhaṇaṃ apassanto ariyādhigatañca dhammaṃ anadhigacchanto ariyakaradhammānaṃ ariyabhāvassa ca adiṭṭhattā “ariyānaṃ adassāvī”ti veditabbo.

Herein, this is the story. It is said that an attendant of the Arahant elder who lived on Cittalapabbata, one who had gone forth in old age, one day went for alms with the elder. Carrying the elder’s bowl and robes as he followed behind, he asked the elder, 'Venerable sir, what are the noble ones like?' The elder said, 'Here, a certain one who has gone forth in old age, having taken the bowl and robes of noble ones, having performed his duties and observances, even while accompanying them, does not know the noble ones. Thus, friend, are the noble ones difficult to know.' Even when this was said, he still did not understand. Therefore, seeing with the eye is not true seeing; only seeing with wisdom is true seeing. As it is said: 'What benefit is there for you, Vakkali, in seeing this foul body? Vakkali, whoever sees the Dhamma, sees me' (SN 3.87). Therefore, even though seeing with the eye, one who does not see with wisdom the characteristics of impermanence, etc., seen by the noble ones; and who does not attain the Dhamma attained by the noble ones; because of not having seen the dhammas that make one a noble one and the state of being a noble one, should be understood as 'one who does not see the noble ones'.

Ariyadhammassa akovidoti satipaṭṭhānādibhede ariyadhamme akusalo. Ariyadhamme avinītoti ettha pana –

'Unskilled in the noble Dhamma' means unskilled in the noble Dhamma—with its divisions such as the establishments of mindfulness. As for 'untrained in the noble Dhamma'—

Duvidho vinayo nāma, ekamekettha pañcadhā;

Abhāvato tassa ayaṃ, “avinīto”ti vuccati.

Discipline is twofold, and each of these is fivefold; due to the absence of that, this one is called 'undisciplined'.

Ayañhi saṃvaravinayo pahānavinayoti duvidho vinayo. Ettha ca duvidhepi vinaye ekameko vinayo pañcadhā bhijjati. Saṃvaravinayopi hi sīlasaṃvaro satisaṃvaro ñāṇasaṃvaro khantisaṃvaro vīriyasaṃvaroti pañcavidho. Pahānavinayopi tadaṅgapahānaṃ vikkhambhanapahānaṃ samucchedapahānaṃ paṭippassaddhipahānaṃ nissaraṇapahānanti pañcavidho.

Indeed, this discipline is twofold: the discipline of restraint and the discipline of abandoning. And in these two kinds of discipline, each discipline is divided into five ways. For the discipline of restraint is fivefold: restraint by virtue, restraint by mindfulness, restraint by knowledge, restraint by patience, and restraint by energy. The discipline of abandoning is also fivefold: abandoning by substitution of opposites, abandoning by suppression, abandoning by cutting off, abandoning by tranquilization, and abandoning by escape.

Tattha “iminā pātimokkhasaṃvarena upeto hoti samupeto”ti (vibha. 511) ayaṃ sīlasaṃvaro. “Rakkhati cakkhundriyaṃ cakkhundriye saṃvaraṃ āpajjatī”ti (dī. ni. 1.213; ma. ni. 1.295; saṃ. ni. 4.239; a. ni. 3.16) ayaṃ satisaṃvaro.

Therein, 'endowed with this restraint of the Pātimokkha, fully endowed' (Vibh. 511) is the restraint by virtue. 'He guards the eye faculty, undertakes restraint in the eye faculty' (DN 1.213; MN 1.295; SN 4.239; AN 3.16) is the restraint by mindfulness.

“Yāni [M 1.0024] sotāni lokasmiṃ, (ajitāti bhagavā)

Sati tesaṃ nivāraṇaṃ;

Sotānaṃ saṃvaraṃ brūmi,

Paññāyete pidhīyare”ti. (su. ni. 1041);

“Whatever streams there are in the world,” (said the Blessed One to Ajita,) “mindfulness is their prevention. I declare the restraint of the streams; by wisdom they are closed off.”

Ayaṃ [P 1.0023] ñāṇasaṃvaro. “Khamo hoti sītassa uṇhassā”ti (ma. ni. 1.23; a. ni. 4.114; 6.58) ayaṃ khantisaṃvaro. “Uppannaṃ kāmavitakkaṃ nādhivāsetī”ti (ma. ni. 1.26; a. ni. 4.114; 6.58) ayaṃ [V 1.0026] vīriyasaṃvaro. Sabbopi cāyaṃ saṃvaro yathāsakaṃ saṃvaritabbānaṃ vinetabbānañca kāyaduccaritādīnaṃ saṃvaraṇato “saṃvaro”, vinayanato “vinayo”ti vuccati. Evaṃ tāva saṃvaravinayo pañcadhā bhijjatīti veditabbo.

This is restraint by knowledge. 'He is patient with cold and heat' (MN 1.23; AN 4.114; 6.58)—this is restraint by patience. 'He does not tolerate an arisen sensual thought' (MN 1.26; AN 4.114; 6.58)—this is restraint by energy. And all this restraint, because it restrains bodily misconduct and so forth that should be restrained and eliminated, is called 'restraint' (saṃvara); and because it eliminates them, it is called 'discipline' (vinaya). Thus, it should be understood that the discipline of restraint is divided fivefold.

Tathā yaṃ nāmarūpaparicchedādīsu vipassanāñāṇesu paṭipakkhabhāvato dīpālokeneva tamassa, tena tena vipassanāñāṇena tassa tassa anatthassa pahānaṃ. Seyyathidaṃ, nāmarūpavavatthānena sakkāyadiṭṭhiyā, paccayapariggahena ahetuvisamahetudiṭṭhīnaṃ, tasseva aparabhāgena kaṅkhāvitaraṇena kathaṃkathībhāvassa, kalāpasammasanena “ahaṃ mamā”ti gāhassa, maggāmaggavavatthānena amagge maggasaññāya, udayadassanena ucchedadiṭṭhiyā, vayadassanena sassatadiṭṭhiyā, bhayadassanena sabhaye abhayasaññāya, ādīnavadassanena assādasaññāya, nibbidānupassanāya abhiratisaññāya, muccitukamyatāñāṇena amuccitukamyatāya, upekkhāñāṇena anupekkhāya, anulomena dhammaṭṭhitiyaṃ nibbāne ca paṭilomabhāvassa, gotrabhunā saṅkhāranimittaggāhassa pahānaṃ, etaṃ tadaṅgapahānaṃnāma.

Likewise, just as darkness is dispelled by the light of a lamp, so too, by each insight knowledge which is the opposite of a defilement, that particular detriment is abandoned. As follows: by the determination of name-and-form, identity-view is abandoned; by the comprehension of conditions, the views of causelessness and dissimilar causes are abandoned; by its later stage, the overcoming of doubt, the state of perplexity is abandoned; by the comprehension of groups, the grasping of 'I' and 'mine' is abandoned; by the determination of path and not-path, the perception of 'path' in what is not the path is abandoned; by the seeing of arising, the annihilationist view is abandoned; by the seeing of passing away, the eternalist view is abandoned; by the seeing of fear, the perception of fearlessness in what is fearful is abandoned; by the seeing of danger, the perception of gratification is abandoned; by the contemplation of disenchantment, the perception of delight is abandoned; by the knowledge of the desire for liberation, the desire not to be liberated is abandoned; by the knowledge of equanimity, equanimity due to ignorance is abandoned; by conformity, the state of being contrary to the stability of phenomena and to Nibbāna is abandoned; by change-of-lineage, the grasping of the sign of formations is abandoned. This is called abandonment by substitution of opposites.

Yaṃ pana upacārappanābhedena samādhinā pavattibhāvanivāraṇato ghaṭappahāreneva udakapiṭṭhe sevālassa tesaṃ tesaṃ nīvaraṇādidhammānaṃ pahānaṃ, etaṃ vikkhambhanapahānaṃ nāma.

Furthermore, the abandoning of those various things such as the hindrances by means of concentration—differentiated into access and absorption—which prevents their state of occurrence, just as moss on the surface of water is removed by a strike with a pot: this is called abandonment by suppression.

Yaṃ catunnaṃ ariyamaggānaṃ bhāvitattā taṃtaṃmaggavato attano attano santāne “diṭṭhigatānaṃ pahānāyā”tiādinā (dha. sa. 277) nayena vuttassa samudayapakkhikassa kilesagaṇassa accantaṃ appavattibhāvena pahānaṃ, idaṃ samucchedapahānaṃ nāma. Yaṃ pana phalakkhaṇe paṭippassaddhattaṃ kilesānaṃ, etaṃ paṭippassaddhipahānaṃ [M 1.0025] nāma. Yaṃ sabbasaṅkhatanissaṭattā pahīnasabbasaṅkhataṃ nibbānaṃ etaṃ nissaraṇapahānaṃ nāma. Sabbampi cetaṃ pahānaṃ yasmā cāgaṭṭhena pahānaṃ, vinayanaṭṭhena vinayo, tasmā “pahānavinayo”ti vuccati. Taṃtaṃpahānavato vā tassa tassa vinayassa sambhavatopetaṃ [P 1.0024] “pahānavinayo”ti vuccati. Evaṃ pahānavinayopi pañcadhā bhijjatīti veditabbo.

The abandoning of the mass of defilements belonging to the side of origination—spoken of in the manner beginning 'for the abandoning of wrong views' (Dhs 277)—through their complete non-arising, due to the four noble paths having been developed in the continuity of that path-possessor: this is called abandonment by cutting off. Furthermore, the abandoning which is the tranquilization of defilements at the moment of fruition: this is called abandonment by tranquilization. That Nibbāna which is the escape from all conditioned things and is the abandonment of all conditioned things: this is called abandonment by escape. And all this abandoning, because it is 'abandoning' (pahāna) in the sense of relinquishing and 'discipline' (vinaya) in the sense of removing, is called 'abandonment-discipline' (pahānavinaya). Or, because that respective discipline arises for one who has abandoned those respective things, it is also called 'abandonment-discipline'. Thus, it should be understood that the abandonment-discipline is also divided fivefold.

Evamayaṃ saṅkhepato duvidho, bhedato ca dasavidho vinayo bhinnasaṃvarattā pahātabbassa ca appahīnattā [V 1.0027] yasmā etassa assutavato puthujjanassa natthi, tasmā abhāvato tassa ayaṃ avinītoti vuccatīti. Esa nayo sappurisānaṃ adassāvī sappurisadhammassa akovido sappurisadhamme avinītoti etthapi. Ninnānākaraṇañhi etaṃ atthato. Yathāha “yeva te ariyā, teva te sappurisā. Yeva te sappurisā, teva te ariyā. Yo eva so ariyānaṃ dhammo, so eva so sappurisānaṃ dhammo. Yo eva so sappurisānaṃ dhammo, so eva so ariyānaṃ dhammo. Yeva te ariyavinayā, teva te sappurisavinayā. Yeva te sappurisavinayā, teva te ariyavinayā. Ariyeti vā sappuriseti vā, ariyadhammeti vā sappurisadhammeti vā, ariyavinayeti vā sappurisavinayeti vā esese eke ekatthe same samabhāge tajjāte taññevā”ti.

Thus, this discipline is twofold in brief and tenfold in detail. And since this discipline—due to broken restraint and the non-abandonment of what should be abandoned—does not exist for this uninstructed ordinary person, he is therefore, due to its absence, called 'undisciplined'. This same method should be understood also in the passage: 'he does not see good persons, is unskilled in the Dhamma of good persons, and is undisciplined in the Dhamma of good persons.' For in meaning, this is without differentiation. As it is said: 'Those who are noble ones, they are good persons. Those who are good persons, they are noble ones. The Dhamma of the noble ones is indeed the Dhamma of the good persons. The Dhamma of the good persons is indeed the Dhamma of the noble ones. The disciplines of the noble ones are indeed the disciplines of the good persons. The disciplines of the good persons are indeed the disciplines of the noble ones. Whether one says "noble one" or "good person," "Dhamma of the noble ones" or "Dhamma of the good persons," "discipline of the noble ones" or "discipline of the good persons"—these are all one, of a single meaning, the same, of the same portion, of that same nature, that very thing.'

“Kasmā pana bhagavā sabbadhammamūlapariyāyaṃ vo, bhikkhave, desessāmī”ti vatvā taṃ adesetvāva “idha, bhikkhave, assutavā puthujjano ariyānaṃ adassāvī”ti evaṃ puthujjanaṃ niddisīti? Puggalādhiṭṭhānāya dhammadesanāya tamatthaṃ āvikātuṃ. Bhagavato hi dhammādhiṭṭhānā dhammadesanā, dhammādhiṭṭhānā puggaladesanā, puggalādhiṭṭhānā puggaladesanā, puggalādhiṭṭhānā dhammadesanāti dhammapuggalavaseneva tāva catubbidhā desanā.

Why, then, did the Blessed One, after saying, 'Bhikkhus, I will teach you the Discourse on the Root of All Things,' not teach it, but instead designate the ordinary person, saying, 'Here, bhikkhus, an uninstructed ordinary person does not see the noble ones'? To make that meaning clear by a Dhamma teaching established on a person. For the Blessed One's teaching is fourfold by way of Dhamma and person: a Dhamma teaching established on Dhamma, a teaching on persons established on Dhamma, a teaching on persons established on a person, and a Dhamma teaching established on a person.

Tattha, “tisso imā, bhikkhave, vedanā. Katamā tisso? Sukhā vedanā dukkhā vedanā adukkhamasukhā vedanā. Imā kho, bhikkhave, tisso vedanā”ti (saṃ. ni. 4.250) evarūpī dhammādhiṭṭhānā dhammadesanā veditabbā. “Cha dhātuyo ayaṃ putiso cha phassāyatano aṭṭhārasa manopavicāro caturādhiṭṭhāno”ti (ma. ni. 3.343) evarūpī dhammādhiṭṭhānā puggaladesanā. “Tayome, bhikkhave, puggalā santo saṃvijjamānā [M 1.0026] lokasmiṃ. Katame tayo? Andho ekacakkhu dvicakkhu. Katamo ca, bhikkhave, puggalo andho”ti? (A. ni. 3.29) evarūpī puggalādhiṭṭhānā puggaladesanā. “Katamañca, bhikkhave, duggatibhayaṃ? Idha, bhikkhave, ekacco iti paṭisañcikkhati, kāyaduccaritassa kho pāpako vipāko abhisamparāyaṃ…pe… suddhamattānaṃ pariharati. Idaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, duggatibhaya”nti (a. ni. 4.121) evarūpī [P 1.0025] puggalādhiṭṭhānā dhammadesanā.

Therein, a teaching of this kind should be understood as a Dhamma teaching established on Dhamma: 'Bhikkhus, there are these three feelings. What three? Pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. These, bhikkhus, are the three feelings.' A teaching of this kind is a teaching on persons established on Dhamma: 'This person has six elements, six bases for contact, eighteen mental investigations, and four foundations.' A teaching of this kind is a teaching on persons established on a person: 'Bhikkhus, there are these three persons existing and found in the world. What three? The blind, the one-eyed, and the two-eyed. And who, bhikkhus, is the blind person?' A teaching of this kind is a Dhamma teaching established on a person: 'And what, bhikkhus, is the fear of a bad destination? Here, bhikkhus, a certain person reflects thus: "The result of bodily misconduct is evil in the life to come..." He keeps himself pure. This, bhikkhus, is called the fear of a bad destination.'

Svāyaṃ [V 1.0028] idha yasmā puthujjano apariññātavatthuko, apariññāmūlikā ca idhādhippetānaṃ sabbadhammānaṃ mūlabhūtā maññanā hoti, tasmā puthujjanaṃ dassetvā puggalādhiṭṭhānāya desanāya tamatthaṃ āvikātuṃ, “idha, bhikkhave, assutavā puthujjano ariyānaṃ adassāvī”ti evaṃ puthujjanaṃ niddisīti veditabbo.

Here, because the uninstructed person is one for whom the basis is not fully understood, and because the conceiving—which is the root of all phenomena of personality-view intended here—has its root in non-understanding, therefore, in order to make that meaning manifest by a teaching based on the individual, having pointed out the uninstructed person, it should be understood that he designated the uninstructed person thus: 'Here, bhikkhus, an uninstructed ordinary person who has not seen the noble ones.'

Suttanikkhepavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the laying down of the Sutta is finished.

Pathavīvāravaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Section on Earth

Evaṃ puthujjanaṃ niddisitvā idāni tassa pathavīādīsu vatthūsu sabbasakkāyadhammajanitaṃ maññanaṃ dassento, pathaviṃ pathavitotiādimāha. Tattha lakkhaṇapathavī sasambhārapathavī ārammaṇapathavī sammutipathavīti catubbidhā pathavī. Tāsu “katamā ca, āvuso, ajjhattikā pathavīdhātu? Yaṃ ajjhattaṃ paccattaṃ kakkhaḷaṃ kharigata”ntiādīsu (vibha. 173) vuttā lakkhaṇapathavī. “Pathaviṃ khaṇeyya vā khaṇāpeyya vā”tiādīsu (pāci. 85) vuttā sasambhārapathavī. Ye ca kesādayo vīsati koṭṭhāsā, ayolohādayo ca bāhirā. Sā hi vaṇṇādīhi sambhārehi saddhiṃ pathavīti sasambhārapathavī. “Pathavīkasiṇameko sañjānātī”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 3.360) āgatā pana ārammaṇapathavī, nimittapathavītipi vuccati. Pathavīkasiṇajjhānalābhī devaloke nibbatto āgamanavasena pathavīdevatāti nāmaṃ labhati. Ayaṃ sammutipathavīti veditabbā. Sā sabbāpi idha labbhati. Tāsu yaṃkañci pathaviṃ ayaṃ puthujjano pathavito sañjānāti, pathavīti sañjānāti, pathavībhāgena sañjānāti, lokavohāraṃ gahetvā saññāvipallāsena sañjānāti pathavīti. Evaṃ pathavībhāgaṃ amuñcantoyeva vā etaṃ “sattoti vā sattassā”ti vā ādinā nayena sañjānāti. Kasmā evaṃ sañjānātīti na [M 1.0027] vattabbaṃ. Ummattako viya hi puthujjano. So yaṃkiñci yena kenaci ākārena gaṇhāti. Ariyānaṃ adassāvitādibhedameva vā ettha kāraṇaṃ. Yaṃ vā parato “apariññātaṃ tassā”ti vadantena bhagavatāva vuttaṃ.

Having thus designated the uninstructed person, now, showing the conceiving generated by all phenomena of personality-view in regard to objects such as earth, he said, 'earth as earth,' etc. Therein, earth is of four kinds: characteristic earth, composite earth, object earth, and conventional earth. Among these, what is spoken of in passages such as, 'And what, friends, is the internal earth element? Whatever is internal, belonging to oneself, hard, solid,' etc., is characteristic earth. What is spoken of in passages such as, 'One might dig the earth or have it dug,' etc., is composite earth. And also the twenty parts of the body beginning with hair, and external things such as iron and bronze. For that earth, together with its components such as color, is called composite earth. What is mentioned in passages such as, 'One perceives the earth kasiṇa,' etc., is object earth; it is also called sign earth. One who has obtained the earth-kasiṇa jhāna, having been reborn in a devaloka, obtains the name 'earth-deity' by way of convention. This should be understood as conventional earth. All of these are applicable here. Among these, whatever earth this uninstructed person perceives, he perceives it 'from earth,' he perceives 'earth,' he perceives by way of the earth-part; having adopted worldly convention, he perceives 'earth' through a perversion of perception. Or, not abandoning the earth-part, he perceives it in the manner of 'it is a being' or 'it belongs to a being.' It should not be said, 'Why does he perceive thus?' For the uninstructed person is like one who is mad. He grasps anything in any way whatsoever. Or, the reason here is just the distinction of not having seen the noble ones, and so on. Or it is what was said by the Blessed One himself later on when saying, 'it is not fully understood by him.'

Pathaviṃ pathavito saññatvāti so taṃ pathaviṃ evaṃ viparītasaññāya sañjānitvā, “saññānidānā [V 1.0029] hi papañcasaṅkhā”ti (su. ni. 880) vacanato aparabhāge thāmapattehi taṇhāmānadiṭṭhipapañcehi idha maññanānāmena vuttehi maññati kappeti vikappeti, nānappakārato aññathā gaṇhāti. Tena vuttaṃ “pathaviṃ maññatī”ti. Evaṃ [P 1.0026] maññato cassa tā maññanā oḷārikanayena dassetuṃ “yā ayaṃ kesā lomā”tiādinā nayena vīsatibhedā ajjhattikā pathavī vuttā. Yā cāyaṃ vibhaṅge “tattha katamā bāhirā pathavīdhātu? Yaṃ bāhiraṃ kakkhaḷaṃ kharigataṃ kakkhaḷattaṃ kakkhaḷabhāvo bahiddhā anupādinnaṃ. Seyyathidaṃ, ayo lohaṃ tipu sīsaṃ sajjhaṃ muttā maṇi veḷuriyaṃ saṅkho silā pavāḷaṃ rajataṃ jātarūpaṃ lohitaṅko masāragallaṃ tiṇaṃ kaṭṭhaṃ sakkharā kaṭhalaṃ bhūmi pāsāṇo pabbato”ti (vibha. 173) evaṃ bāhirā pathavī vuttā. Yā ca ajjhattārammaṇattike nimittapathavī, taṃ gahetvā ayamatthayojanā vuccati.

Regarding 'having perceived earth as earth': having perceived that earth with such a perverted perception, and because it is said, 'proliferations have perception as their source,' in the subsequent stage, by means of the proliferations of craving, conceit, and views which have gained strength—which are called here by the name 'conceiving'—he conceives, forms concepts, and diversifies; he grasps otherwise in various ways. Therefore it is said, 'he conceives earth.' To show these conceivings of his in a gross way, the twentyfold internal earth is spoken of in the manner beginning, 'head-hairs, body-hairs...' And in the Vibhaṅga, the external earth is spoken of thus: 'Therein, what is the external earth element? Whatever is external, hard, solid, hardness, the state of being hard, external, unappropriated. That is: iron, copper, tin, lead, silver, pearl, gem, beryl, conch-shell, stone, coral, silver, gold, ruby, cat's-eye, grass, wood, gravel, potsherd, the ground, rocks, mountains.' And taking the sign-earth, which is in the triad on internal objects, this application of the meaning is stated.

Pathaviṃ maññatīti tīhi maññanāhi ahaṃ pathavīti maññati, mama pathavīti maññati, paro pathavīti maññati, parassa pathavīti maññati, atha vā ajjhattikaṃ pathaviṃ taṇhāmaññanāya maññati, mānamaññanāya maññati, diṭṭhimaññanāya maññati. Kathaṃ? Ayañhi kesādīsu chandarāgaṃ janeti kese assādeti abhinandati abhivadati ajjhosāya tiṭṭhati. Lome, nakhe, dante, tacaṃ, aññataraṃ vā pana rajjanīyavatthuṃ. Evaṃ ajjhattikaṃ pathaviṃ taṇhāmaññanāya maññati. Iti me kesā siyuṃ anāgatamaddhānaṃ. Iti lomātiādinā vā pana nayena tattha nandiṃ samannāneti. “Imināhaṃ sīlena vā…pe… brahmacariyena vā evaṃ siniddhamudusukhumanīlakeso bhavissāmī”tiādinā vā pana nayena appaṭiladdhānaṃ paṭilābhāya cittaṃ paṇidahati. Evampi ajjhattikaṃ pathaviṃ taṇhāmaññanāya maññati.

Regarding 'he conceives earth': by three kinds of conceiving, he conceives, 'I am earth'; he conceives, 'earth is mine'; he conceives, 'another is earth'; he conceives, 'earth is another's'. Or, he conceives the internal earth with the conceiving of craving, he conceives with the conceiving of conceit, he conceives with the conceiving of view. How? This person generates desire and lust for hair and so on; he relishes the hair, delights in it, speaks of it, and remains clinging to it—and so for body hair, nails, teeth, skin, or any other lustful object. Thus he conceives the internal earth with the conceiving of craving. Or in the manner of 'Thus may my hair be in the future,' or 'Thus body hair,' etc., he brings about delight in them. Or in the manner of 'By this virtue... or by this holy life, may I become one with such smooth, soft, fine, dark hair,' etc., he directs his mind to the attainment of what has not been attained. In this way too, he conceives the internal earth with the conceiving of craving.

Tathā attano kesādīnaṃ sampattiṃ vā vipattiṃ vā nissāya mānaṃ janeti, “seyyohamasmīti vā sadisohamasmīti vā hīnohamasmīti vā”ti. Evaṃ ajjhattikaṃ [M 1.0028] pathaviṃ mānamaññanāya maññati. “Taṃ jīvaṃ taṃ sarīra”nti (ma. ni. 2.187) āgatanayena pana kesaṃ “jīvo”ti abhinivisati. Esa nayo lomādīsu. Evaṃ ajjhattikaṃ pathaviṃ diṭṭhimaññanāya maññati.

Likewise, based on the accomplishment or failure of one's own hair and so forth, one generates conceit, thinking, 'I am better,' or 'I am equal,' or 'I am inferior.' In this way, one conceives the internal earth with the conceiving of conceit. Moreover, according to the method that comes in 'what is the soul, that is the body,' one adheres to the view that hair is the 'soul.' This is the method for body hair and so forth. In this way, one conceives the internal earth with the conceiving of view.

Atha vā “yā ceva kho panāvuso, ajjhattikā pathavīdhātu, yā ca bāhirā pathavīdhātu, pathavīdhāturevesā[V 1.0030], taṃ netaṃ mamā”ti (ma. ni. 1.302) imissā pavattiyā [P 1.0027] paccanīkanayena kesādibhedaṃ pathaviṃ etaṃ mama esohamasmi eso me attāti abhinivisati. Evampi ajjhattikaṃ pathaviṃ diṭṭhimaññanāya maññati. Evaṃ tāva ajjhattikaṃ pathaviṃ tīhi maññanāhi maññati.

Or, in a way that is contrary to this process—'Friends, whatever is the internal earth element and whatever is the external earth element, that is just the earth element; that is not mine'—one adheres to the earth distinguished as hair and so on, thinking: 'This is mine, this I am, this is my self.' In this way too, one conceives the internal earth with the conceiving of view. Thus, firstly, one conceives the internal earth with the three kinds of conceiving.

Yathā ca ajjhattikaṃ evaṃ bāhirampi. Kathaṃ? “Ayañhi ayalohādīsu chandarāgaṃ janeti. Ayalohādīni assādeti abhinandati abhivadati ajjhosāya tiṭṭhati. Mama ayo mama lohantiādinā nayena ayādīni mamāyati rakkhati gopayati, evaṃ bāhiraṃ pathaviṃ taṇhāmaññanāya maññati. Iti me ayalohādayo siyuṃ anāgatamaddhānanti vā panettha nandiṃ samannāneti, imināhaṃ sīlena vā vatena vā tapena vā brahmacariyena vā evaṃ sampannaayalohādiupakaraṇo bhavissāmī”ti appaṭiladdhassa paṭilābhāya cittaṃ paṇidahati. Evampi bāhiraṃ pathaviṃ taṇhāmaññanāya maññati.

Just as with the internal, so too with the external. How? This person generates desire and passion for iron, copper, and so on. One relishes, delights in, speaks of, and abides clinging to iron, copper, and so on. By the method of 'My iron, my copper,' one cherishes, guards, and protects iron and so on. Thus, one conceives of the external earth with the conceiving of craving. Or one brings about delight in it, thinking, 'May I have this iron, copper, and so on in a future time.' Or one directs the mind toward the attainment of what has not yet been attained, thinking, 'By this morality, or observance, or austerity, or holy life, I will become one endowed with such equipment as iron, copper, and so on.' In this way, too, one conceives of the external earth with the conceiving of craving.

Tathā attano ayalohādīnaṃ sampattiṃ vā vipattiṃ vā nissāya mānaṃ janeti “imināhaṃ seyyosmīti vā, sadisosmīti vā hīnosmīti vā”ti (vibha. 832) evaṃ bāhiraṃ pathaviṃ mānamaññanāya maññati. Aye jīvasaññī hutvā pana ayaṃ “jīvo”ti abhinivisati. Esa nayo lohādīsu. Evaṃ bāhiraṃ pathaviṃ diṭṭhimaññanāya maññati.

Similarly, relying on the success or failure of one's own iron, copper, and so on, one generates conceit, thinking: 'By this I am superior,' or 'I am equal,' or 'I am inferior.' Thus, one conceives of the external earth with the conceiving of conceit. Furthermore, having the perception of a living being in regard to iron, one adheres to the view, 'This is a living being.' This is the method for copper and so on. Thus, one conceives of the external earth with the conceiving of view.

Atha vā “idhekacco pathavīkasiṇaṃ attato samanupassati. Yaṃ pathavīkasiṇaṃ, so ahaṃ. Yo ahaṃ, taṃ pathavīkasiṇanti pathavīkasiṇañca attañca advayaṃ samanupassatī”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.131) paṭisambhidāyaṃ vuttanayeneva nimittapathaviṃ “attā”ti abhinivisati. Evaṃ bāhiraṃ pathaviṃ diṭṭhimaññanāya maññati. Evampi bāhiraṃ pathaviṃ tīhi maññanāhi maññati. Evaṃ tāva “pathaviṃ maññatī”ti ettha tissopi maññanā veditabbā. Ito paraṃ saṅkhepeneva kathayissāma.

Alternatively, 'Here, a certain person regards the earth kasina as self. That which is the earth kasina, that I am. That which I am, that is the earth kasina. Thus one regards the earth kasina and the self as non-dual.' In accordance with the method stated in the Paṭisambhidāmagga, one adheres to the view that the earth as a meditation sign is 'self.' In this way, one conceives of the external earth with the conceiving of view. In this way too, one conceives of the external earth with the three conceivings. Thus, firstly, in the phrase 'one conceives earth,' all three conceivings should be understood. From this point forward, we shall speak only concisely.

Pathaviyā [M 1.0029] maññatīti ettha pathaviyāti bhummavacanametaṃ. Tasmā ahaṃ pathaviyāti maññati, mayhaṃ [V 1.0031] kiñcanaṃ palibodho pathaviyāti maññati, paro pathaviyāti maññati, parassa kiñcanaṃ palibodho pathaviyāti maññatīti ayamettha attho.

In the phrase 'one conceives in earth,' the word 'pathaviyā' is a locative expression. Therefore, one conceives, 'I am in the earth'; one conceives, 'My impediment is in the earth'; one conceives, 'Another is in the earth'; one conceives, 'Another's impediment is in the earth.' This is the meaning here.

Atha vā yvāyaṃ “kathaṃ rūpasmiṃ attānaṃ samanupassati? Idhekacco vedanaṃ… saññaṃ… saṅkhāre… viññāṇaṃ attato samanupassati, tassa evaṃ hoti, ayaṃ kho me attā, so kho pana me attā imasmiṃ rūpeti evaṃ rūpasmiṃ vā attānaṃ [P 1.0028] samanupassatī”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.131) etassa atthanayo vutto, eteneva nayena vedanādidhamme attato gahetvā tato ajjhattikabāhirāsu pathavīsu yaṃkiñci pathaviṃ tassokāsabhāvena parikappetvā so kho pana me ayaṃ attā imissā pathaviyāti maññanto pathaviyā maññati, ayamassa diṭṭhimaññanā. Tasmiṃyeva panassa attani sinehaṃ tabbatthukañca mānaṃ uppādayato taṇhāmānamaññanāpi veditabbā. Yadā pana teneva nayena so kho panassa attā pathaviyāti maññati, tadā diṭṭhimaññanā eva yujjati. Itarāyopi pana icchanti.

Alternatively, there is the method of meaning for this passage: 'How does one regard self in form? Here, a certain person regards feeling... perception... formations... consciousness as self. It occurs to him: "This indeed is my self. And this self of mine has arisen in this form." Thus one regards self in form.' By this same method, having taken mental phenomena such as feeling as self, and then, from among the internal and external earth elements, having conceived of any earth element as a location for that self, one who thinks, 'This self of mine has arisen in this earth,' conceives in the earth. This is that person's conceiving of view. For that person who generates affection and conceit based on that very self, the conceivings of craving and conceit should also be understood. But when, by that same method, one conceives, 'That self of that other person has arisen in the earth,' then only the conceiving of view is suitable. The teachers, however, also accept the other conceivings.

Pathavito maññatīti ettha pana pathavitoti nissakkavacanaṃ. Tasmā saupakaraṇassa attano vā parassa vā yathāvuttappabhedato pathavito uppattiṃ vā niggamanaṃ vā pathavito vā añño attāti maññamāno pathavito maññatīti veditabbo, ayamassa diṭṭhimaññanā. Tasmiṃyeva panassa diṭṭhimaññanāya maññite vatthusmiṃ sinehaṃ mānañca uppādayato taṇhāmānamaññanāpi veditabbā. Apare āhu pathavīkasiṇaṃ parittaṃ bhāvetvā tato aññaṃ appamāṇaṃ attānaṃ gahetvā pathavito bahiddhāpi me attāti maññamāno pathavito maññatīti.

In the phrase 'one conceives from earth,' the word 'pathavito' is in the ablative case. Therefore, one who conceives of the arising from earth or the departure from earth of oneself or another together with their accessories, according to the distinctions already mentioned, or who thinks, 'The self is other than the earth,' should be understood as one who 'conceives from earth.' This is that person's conceiving of view. For that person who generates affection and conceit in that very object conceived by the conceiving of view, the conceivings of craving and conceit should also be understood. Others say: Having developed a limited earth kasina, and then taking the self to be something else and immeasurable, one who thinks, 'My self exists even outside of the earth,' 'conceives from earth.'

Pathaviṃ meti maññatīti ettha pana kevalañhi mahāpathaviṃ taṇhāvasena mamāyatīti iminā nayena pavattā ekā taṇhāmaññanā eva labbhatīti veditabbā. Sā cāyaṃ mama kesā, mama lomā, mama ayo, mama lohanti evaṃ yathāvuttappabhedāya sabbāyapi ajjhattikabāhirāya pathaviyā yojetabbāti.

In the phrase 'one conceives "earth is mine,"' it should be understood that only a single conceiving of craving is found here, which proceeds by the method of cherishing the great earth purely through the power of craving. And this should be applied to all internal and external earth with the distinctions already stated, such as: 'My hair, my body hair, my refined iron, my raw iron.'

Pathaviṃ [M 1.0030] abhinandatīti vuttappakārameva pathaviṃ taṇhādīhi abhinandati, assādeti, parāmasati [V 1.0032] cāti vuttaṃ hoti. “Pathaviṃ maññatī”ti eteneva etasmiṃ atthe siddhe kasmā etaṃ vuttanti ce. Avicāritametaṃ porāṇehi. Ayaṃ pana attano mati, desanāvilāsato vā ādīnavadassanato vā. Yassā hi dhammadhātuyā suppaṭividdhattā nānānayavicitradesanāvilāsasampanno, ayaṃ sā bhagavatā suppaṭividdhā. Tasmā pubbe maññanāvasena kilesuppattiṃ dassetvā idāni abhinandanāvasena dassento desanāvilāsato vā idamāha[P 1.0029]. Yo vā pathaviṃ maññati, pathaviyā maññati, pathavito maññati, pathaviṃ meti maññati, so yasmā na sakkoti pathavīnissitaṃ taṇhaṃ vā diṭṭhiṃ vā pahātuṃ, tasmā pathaviṃ abhinandatiyeva. Yo ca pathaviṃ abhinandati, dukkhaṃ so abhinandati, dukkhañca ādīnavoti ādīnavadassanatopi idamāha. Vuttañcetaṃ bhagavatā “yo, bhikkhave, pathavīdhātuṃ abhinandati, dukkhaṃ so abhinandati, yo dukkhaṃ abhinandati, aparimutto so dukkhasmāti vadāmī”ti.

In 'one delights in earth,' it is meant that one delights in the earth of the kinds already stated through craving and so on, savors it, and wrongly grasps it. If it is asked, 'Since this meaning is already established by the phrase "one conceives earth," why is this stated?'—this was not analyzed by the ancients. The following, however, is our own opinion: it was stated either for the sake of the discourse's elegance or for showing the danger. For, because the Blessed One has thoroughly penetrated the Dhamma-element, he is endowed with the elegance of a teaching that is varied with numerous methods. Therefore, having first shown the arising of defilements by way of conceiving, he now teaches it by way of delighting, either for the sake of the discourse's elegance. Alternatively, whoever conceives earth, conceives in earth, conceives from earth, or conceives 'earth is mine'—because that person is unable to abandon the craving or view dependent on earth, they inevitably delight in earth. And whoever delights in earth, delights in suffering; and suffering is a danger. Thus, this was also stated for the sake of showing the danger. And this was stated by the Blessed One: 'Bhikkhus, whoever delights in the earth element, delights in suffering. Whoever delights in suffering, I say, is not liberated from suffering.'

Evaṃ pathavīvatthukaṃ maññanaṃ abhinandanañca vatvā idāni yena kāraṇena so maññati, abhinandati ca, taṃ kāraṇaṃ āvikaronto āha taṃ kissa hetu, apariññātaṃ tassāti vadāmīti. Tassattho, so puthujjano taṃ pathaviṃ kissa hetu maññati, kena kāraṇena maññati, abhinandatīti ce. Apariññātaṃ tassāti vadāmīti, yasmā taṃ vatthu tassa apariññātaṃ, tasmāti vuttaṃ hoti. Yo hi pathaviṃ parijānāti, so tīhi pariññāhi parijānāti ñātapariññāya tīraṇapariññāya pahānapariññāyāti.

Having thus spoken of conceiving and delighting founded on earth, He now, wishing to make clear the reason why that person conceives and delights, said: 'For what reason is that? I say it is because it is not fully comprehended by him.' Its meaning is: If it is asked, 'For what reason does that ordinary person conceive that earth? For what reason does he conceive and delight in it?' [The answer is:] 'I say it is because it is not fully comprehended by him.' This is said because that object is not fully comprehended by him. For whoever fully comprehends earth, that person comprehends it by means of three kinds of full comprehension: full comprehension as knowing, full comprehension as scrutinizing, and full comprehension as abandoning.

Tattha katamā ñātapariññā. Pathavīdhātuṃ parijānāti, ayaṃ pathavīdhātu ajjhattikā, ayaṃ bāhirā, idamassā lakkhaṇaṃ, imāni rasapaccupaṭṭhānapadaṭṭhānānīti, ayaṃ ñātapariññā. Katamā tīraṇapariññā? Evaṃ ñātaṃ katvā pathavīdhātuṃ tīreti aniccato dukkhato rogatoti dvācattālīsāya ākārehi, ayaṃ tīraṇapariññā. Katamā pahānapariññā? Evaṃ tīrayitvā aggamaggena pathavīdhātuyā chandarāgaṃ pajahati, ayaṃ pahānapariññā.

Herein, what is full comprehension as knowing? One fully comprehends the earth element thus: 'This earth element is internal; this is external; this is its characteristic; these are its function, manifestation, and proximate cause.' This is full comprehension as knowing. What is full comprehension as scrutinizing? Having thus known it, one scrutinizes the earth element as impermanent, as suffering, as a disease, and so on, in forty-two aspects. This is full comprehension as scrutinizing. What is full comprehension as abandoning? Having thus scrutinized it, one abandons desire and lust for the earth element by means of the highest path. This is full comprehension as abandoning.

Nāmarūpavavatthānaṃ [M 1.0031] vā ñātapariññā. Kalāpasammasanādianulomapariyosānā tīraṇapariññā. Ariyamagge ñāṇaṃ pahānapariññāti. Yo pathaviṃ parijānāti, so imāhi tīhi pariññāhi parijānāti, assa ca puthujjanassa tā pariññāyo natthi, tasmā apariññātattā [V 1.0033] pathaviṃ maññati ca abhinandati cāti. Tenāha bhagavā – idha, bhikkhave, assutavā puthujjano…pe… pathaviṃ maññati, pathaviyā maññati, pathavito maññati, pathaviṃ meti maññati, pathaviṃ abhinandati. Taṃ kissa hetu? Apariññātaṃ tassāti vadāmī”ti.

Alternatively, the determination of name-and-form is full comprehension as knowing. Knowledge beginning with the comprehension of groups and ending with conformity-knowledge is full comprehension as scrutinizing. Knowledge in the noble path is full comprehension as abandoning. Whoever fully comprehends earth, that person comprehends it by means of these three kinds of full comprehension. But for this ordinary person, those kinds of full comprehension do not exist. Therefore, due to not having fully comprehended it, he conceives and delights in earth. For that reason, the Blessed One said: 'Here, bhikkhus, an uninstructed ordinary person... conceives earth, conceives in earth, conceives from earth, conceives "earth is mine," and delights in earth. For what reason is that? I say it is because it is not fully comprehended by him.'

Pathavīvāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The exposition of the section on earth is concluded.

Āpovārādivaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Section on Water and so forth

Āpaṃ [P 1.0030] āpatoti etthāpi lakkhaṇasasambhārārammaṇasammutivasena catubbidho āpo. Tesu “tattha, katamā ajjhattikā āpodhātu. Yaṃ ajjhattaṃ paccattaṃ āpo āpogataṃ, sineho sinehagataṃ bandhanattaṃ rūpassa ajjhattaṃ upādinna”ntiādīsu (vibha. 174) vutto lakkhaṇaāpo. “Āpokasiṇaṃ uggaṇhanto āpasmiṃ nimittaṃ gaṇhātī”tiādīsu vutto sasambhārāpo. Sesaṃ sabbaṃ pathaviyaṃ vuttasadisameva. Kevalaṃ yojanānaye pana “pittaṃ semha”ntiādinā nayena vuttā dvādasabhedā ajjhattikā āpodhātu, “tattha, katamā bāhirā āpodhātu? Yaṃ bāhiraṃ āpo āpogataṃ, sineho sinehagataṃ bandhanattaṃ rūpassa bahiddhā anupādinnaṃ. Seyyathidaṃ, mūlaraso khandharaso tacaraso pattaraso puppharaso phalaraso khīraṃ dadhi sappi navanītaṃ telaṃ madhu phāṇitaṃ bhummāni vā udakāni antalikkhāni vā”ti (vibha. 174) evaṃ vuttā ca bāhirā āpodhātu veditabbā, yo ca ajjhattārammaṇattike nimittaāpo.

In the passage 'Water, from water,' here too, water is fourfold by way of characteristic, constituent, object, and convention. Among these, that spoken of in passages such as, 'Herein, what is the internal water element? Whatever internally, in oneself, is water, watery, moisture, moist, cohesion, the cohesive quality of matter, appropriated...' is water as characteristic. That spoken of in passages such as, 'Taking up the water kasiṇa, one apprehends the sign in water...' is water as constituent. All the rest is just like what was said in the section on earth. Only, in the method of application, the twelve kinds of water element spoken of in the manner of 'bile, phlegm,' etc., should be known as the internal water element. And the external water element should be known as that spoken of thus: 'Herein, what is the external water element? Whatever externally is water, watery... not appropriated. That is to say: root-sap, stem-sap, bark-sap, leaf-sap, flower-sap, fruit-sap, milk, curd, ghee, fresh butter, oil, honey, molasses, and water that is in the earth or in the sky.' And the water that is a sign in the triad of internal objects should be known as water as object.

Tejaṃ tejatoti imasmiṃ tejovārepi vuttanayeneva vitthāro veditabbo. Yojanānaye panettha “yena ca santappati, yena ca jīrīyati, yena ca pariḍayhati, yena ca asitapītakhāyitasāyitaṃ sammā pariṇāmaṃ gacchatī”ti (vibha. 175) evaṃ vuttā catuppabhedā ajjhattikā tejodhātu. “Tattha katamā [M 1.0032] bāhirā tejodhātu? Yaṃ bāhiraṃ tejo tejogataṃ usmā usmāgataṃ usumaṃ usumagataṃ bahiddhā anupādinnaṃ. Seyyathidaṃ, kaṭṭhaggi palālaggi tiṇaggi gomayaggi thusaggi saṅkāraggi indaggi aggisantāpo sūriyasantāpo kaṭṭhasannicayasantāpo [V 1.0034] tiṇasannicayasantāpo dhaññasannicayasantāpo bhaṇḍasannicayasantāpo”ti (vibha. 175) evaṃ vuttā ca bāhirā tejodhātu veditabbā.

In this section on the heat element, 'Heat, from heat,' the detailed explanation should be understood in the same way as was stated. In the method of application here, however, the four kinds of internal heat element are as stated: 'that by which one is heated, that by which one ages, that by which one is consumed with fever, and that by which what is eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted gets properly digested.' And the external heat element should be known as that spoken of thus: 'Herein, what is the external heat element? Whatever externally is heat, heat-like, warmth, warmth-like, vapor, vaporous, not appropriated. That is to say: wood-fire, grass-fire, cow-dung-fire, chaff-fire, rubbish-fire, lightning-fire, the heat of fire, the heat of the sun, the heat from a pile of wood, the heat from a pile of grass, the heat from a pile of grain, the heat from a pile of goods.'

Vāyaṃ vāyatoti imassa vāyavārassāpi yojanānaye pana “uddhaṅgamā vātā adhogamā vātā kucchisayā vātā koṭṭhāsayā vātā aṅgamaṅgānusārino vātā satthakavātā khurakavātā uppalakavātā assāso passāso”ti evaṃ vuttā ajjhattikā vāyodhātu. “Tattha katamā bāhirā vāyodhātu? Yaṃ bāhiraṃ vāyo vāyogataṃ thambhitattaṃ rūpassa bahiddhā anupādinnaṃ. Seyyathidaṃ, puratthimā vātā pacchimā vātā uttarā vātā dakkhiṇā vātā sarajā vātā arajā vātā sītā vātā uṇhā vātā parittā vātā adhimattā vātā kāḷavātā verambhavātā [P 1.0031] pakkhavātā supaṇṇavātā tālavaṇṭavātā vidhūpanavātā”ti (vibha. 176) evaṃ vuttā ca bāhirā vāyodhātu veditabbā. Sesaṃ vuttanayamevāti. Ettāvatā ca yvāyaṃ –

For this section on the wind element, 'Wind, from wind,' in the method of application, the internal wind element should be known as that spoken of thus: 'upward-going winds, downward-going winds, winds in the belly, winds in the bowels, winds that course through the limbs, knife-like winds, razor-like winds, uprooting winds, in-breath, out-breath.' And the external wind element should be known as that spoken of thus: 'Herein, what is the external wind element? Whatever externally is wind, wind-like, the quality of stiffness in matter, not appropriated. That is to say: eastern winds, western winds, northern winds, southern winds, dusty winds, dustless winds, cold winds, hot winds, gentle winds, strong winds, black winds, tempestuous winds, winds from flapping wings, winds from the wings of Supaṇṇas, winds from a palm-leaf fan, winds from a winnowing fan.' The rest is in the manner already stated. And by this much...

“Vuttamhi ekadhamme, ye dhammā ekalakkhaṇā tena;

Vuttā bhavanti sabbe, iti vutto lakkhaṇo hāro”ti. –

When one phenomenon is stated, all phenomena that share a single characteristic with it are thereby stated; thus is the characteristic method declared.

Evaṃ nettiyaṃ lakkhaṇo nāma hāro vutto, tassa vasena yasmā catūsu bhūtesu gahitesu upādārūpampi gahitameva bhavati, rūpalakkhaṇaṃ anatītattā. Yañca bhūtopādārūpaṃ so rūpakkhandho. Tasmā “assutavā puthujjano pathaviṃ āpaṃ tejaṃ vāyaṃ maññatī”ti vadantena atthato rūpaṃ attato samanupassatītipi vuttaṃ hoti. “Pathaviyā āpasmiṃ tejasmiṃ vāyasmiṃ maññatī”ti vadantena rūpasmiṃ vā attānaṃ samanupassatīti vuttampi hoti. “Pathavito āpato tejato vāyato maññatī”ti vadantena rūpato añño attāti siddhattā rūpavantaṃ vā attānaṃ attani vā rūpaṃ samanupassatītipi vuttaṃ hoti. Evametā catasso rūpavatthukā sakkāyadiṭṭhimaññanā [M 1.0033] veditabbā. Tattha ekā ucchedadiṭṭhi, tisso sassatadiṭṭhiyoti dveva diṭṭhiyo hontīti ayampi atthaviseso veditabbo.

Thus, in the Netti, the method named Lakkhaṇa (Characteristic) is stated. By its power, because when the four great elements are grasped, derived matter is also indeed grasped—as the characteristic of matter is not transcended. And whatever is primary and derived matter, that is the matter-aggregate. Therefore, by the one who says, 'The uninstructed worldling conceives earth, water, fire, and air,' it is also said in effect that one regards matter as self. By the one who says, 'One conceives in earth, in water, in fire, in air,' it is also said that one regards self in matter. By the one who says, 'One conceives from earth, from water, from fire, from air,' because it is established that the self is other than matter, it is also said that one regards self as possessing matter or matter in self. In this way, these four conceivings of identity-view that have matter as their object should be known. Among them, one is the annihilation-view, and three are eternalist-views; thus, there are only two views. This distinction of meaning should also be known.

Āpovārādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The exposition of the section on the water element and so forth is concluded.

Bhūtavārādivaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Section on Beings and so forth

3. Evaṃ [V 1.0035] rūpamukhena saṅkhāravatthukaṃ maññanaṃ vatvā idāni ye saṅkhāre upādāya sattā paññapīyanti, tesu saṅkhāresu sattesupi yasmā puthujjano maññanaṃ karoti, tasmā te satte niddisanto bhūte bhūtato sañjānātītiādimāha. Tatthāyaṃ bhūtasaddo pañcakkhandhaamanussadhātuvijjamānakhīṇāsavasattarukkhādīsu dissati. “Bhūtamidanti, bhikkhave, samanupassathā”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.401) hi ayaṃ pañcakkhandhesu dissati. “Yānīdha bhūtāni samāgatānī”ti (su. ni. 224) ettha amanussesu. “Cattāro kho, bhikkhu, mahābhūtā hetū”ti (ma. ni. 3.86) ettha dhātūsu. “Bhūtasmiṃ pācittiya”ntiādīsu (pāci. 69) vijjamāne. “Yo ca kālaghaso bhūto”ti (jā. 1.10.190) ettha khīṇāsave. “Sabbeva nikkhipissanti bhūtā loke samussaya”nti (dī. ni. 2.220) ettha sattesu. “Bhūtagāmapātabyatāyā”ti [P 1.0032] (pāci. 90) ettha rukkhādīsu. Idha panāyaṃ sattesu vattati, no ca kho avisesena. Cātumahārājikānaṃ hi heṭṭhā sattā idha bhūtāti adhippetā.

3. Having thus spoken, with form as the principal means, of conceiving that has formations as its object, now, because the worldling engages in conceiving regarding those formations on account of which beings are designated, and also regarding those beings, therefore the Blessed One, wishing to point out those beings, said, beginning with, 'One perceives beings as beings.' Therein, this word 'bhūta' is seen in the sense of the five aggregates, non-human beings, elements, what is existent, the arahant, beings, trees, and so forth. For in passages such as, 'Bhikkhus, contemplate this as what has come to be (bhūta),' it is seen in the sense of the five aggregates. In, 'Whatever beings (bhūtāni) have gathered here,' it is seen in the sense of non-human beings. In, 'Bhikkhu, the four great elements are the cause,' it is seen in the sense of the elements. In passages such as, 'There is a pācittiya offense regarding what is true (bhūtasmiṃ),' it is seen in the sense of what is existent. In, 'And he who has come to be (bhūto), a devourer of time,' it is seen in the sense of the arahant. In, 'All beings (bhūtā) in the world will lay aside their bodies,' it is seen in the sense of beings. In, 'For causing injury to a plant-being (bhūtagāma),' it is seen in the sense of trees and so forth. Here, however, this word applies to beings, but not without distinction. For, beings below the Cātumahārājikas are intended here as 'bhūta'.

Tattha bhūte bhūtato sañjānātītiādi vuttanayameva. Bhūte maññatītiādīsu pana tissopi maññanā yojetabbā. Kathaṃ? Ayañhi “so passati gahapatiṃ vā gahapatiputtaṃ vā pañcahi kāmaguṇehi samappitaṃ samaṅgibhūta”nti (a. ni. 7.50) vuttanayena bhūte subhā sukhitāti gahetvā rajjati, disvāpi ne rajjati, sutvāpi, ghāyitvāpi, sāyitvāpi, phusitvāpi, ñatvāpi. Evaṃ bhūte taṇhāmaññanāya maññati. “Aho vatāhaṃ khattiyamahāsālānaṃ vā sahabyataṃ upapajjeyya”ntiādinā (dī. ni. 3.337) vā pana nayena appaṭiladdhassa paṭilābhāya cittaṃ paṇidahati, evampi bhūte taṇhāmaññanāya maññati. Attano pana bhūtānañca sampattivipattiṃ nissāya attānaṃ vā seyyaṃ dahati. Bhūtesu ca yaṃkiñci bhūtaṃ hīnaṃ attānaṃ vā hīnaṃ, yaṃkiñci bhūtaṃ seyyaṃ[M 1.0034]. Attānaṃ vā bhūtena, bhūtaṃ vā attanā sadisaṃ dahati. Yathāha “idhekacco jātiyā vā…pe… aññataraññatarena vatthunā pubbakālaṃ parehi sadisaṃ attānaṃ dahati. Aparakālaṃ attānaṃ seyyaṃ dahati. Pare hīne dahati, yo evarūpo māno [V 1.0036] …pe… ayaṃ vuccati mānātimāno”ti (vibha. 876-880). Evaṃ bhūte mānamaññanāya maññati.

Therein, the passage beginning with, 'One perceives beings as beings,' is of the same method as that already stated. However, in passages beginning with, 'One conceives of beings,' the three conceivings should be applied. How? For this worldling, by the method stated, 'He sees a householder or a householder's son, endowed and furnished with the five cords of sensual pleasure,' grasping that beings are beautiful and happy, becomes impassioned. Having seen them, one becomes impassioned; having heard, having smelled, having tasted, having touched, or having known them, one becomes impassioned. Thus, one conceives of beings with the conceiving of craving. Or, by the method beginning with, 'Oh, would that I might attain companionship with the great khattiya families!' one directs one's mind to attain that which has not yet been attained. In this way too, one conceives of beings with the conceiving of craving. Furthermore, depending on one's own and beings' success and failure, one places oneself as superior, and among beings, places some unspecified being as inferior. Or one places oneself as inferior, and some unspecified being as superior. Or one places oneself as equal to a being, or a being as equal to oneself. As it is said: 'Here, a certain person, by birth... or by some other basis, at a former time places themself as equal to others. At a later time, they place themself as superior and place others as inferior. Whatever conceit is of such a nature... this is called conceit and excessive conceit.' Thus, one conceives of beings with the conceiving of conceit.

Bhūte pana “niccā dhuvā sassatā avipariṇāmadhammā”ti vā “sabbe sattā sabbe pāṇā sabbe bhūtā sabbe jīvā avasā abalā avīriyā niyatisaṅgatibhāvapariṇatā chasvevābhijātīsu sukhadukkhaṃ paṭisaṃvedentī”ti (dī. ni. 1.168) vā maññamāno diṭṭhimaññanāya maññati. Evaṃ bhūte tīhi maññanāhi maññati.

Furthermore, a worldling conceives of beings with the conceiving of view, thinking either, 'They are permanent, constant, eternal, not subject to change,' or, 'All beings, all living things, all creatures, all souls are without power, without strength, without energy, determined by destiny, association, and nature, and experience pleasure and pain in the six classes of birth.' Thus, one conceives of beings with the three conceivings.

Kathaṃ bhūtesu maññati? Tesu tesu bhūtesu attano upapattiṃ vā sukhuppattiṃ vā ākaṅkhati. Evaṃ tāva taṇhāmaññanāya bhūtesu maññati. Bhūtesu vā upapattiṃ ākaṅkhamāno dānaṃ deti, sīlaṃ samādiyati, uposathakammaṃ karoti. Evampi bhūtesu taṇhāmaññanāya maññati. Bhūte pana samūhaggāhena gahetvā tattha ekacce bhūte seyyato dahati, ekacce sadisato vā hīnato vāti. Evaṃ bhūtesu mānamaññanāya [P 1.0033] maññati. Tathā ekacce bhūte niccā dhuvāti maññati. Ekacce aniccā adhuvāti, ahampi bhūtesu aññatarosmīti vā maññati. Evaṃ bhūtesu diṭṭhimaññanāya maññati.

How does one conceive regarding beings? Among those various beings, one longs for one's own rebirth or the arising of happiness. Thus, firstly, one conceives regarding beings with the conceiving of craving. Alternatively, desiring rebirth among beings, one gives gifts, undertakes the moral precepts, and performs the Uposatha observance. In this way too, one conceives regarding beings with the conceiving of craving. Furthermore, having grasped beings by taking them as a group, therein one places some beings as superior, and some as equal or as inferior. Thus, one conceives regarding beings with the conceiving of conceit. Similarly, one conceives some beings as permanent and constant, and some as impermanent and inconstant, or one conceives, 'I too am one among beings.' Thus, one conceives regarding beings with the conceiving of view.

Bhūtato maññatīti ettha pana saupakaraṇassa attano vā parassa vā yato kutoci bhūtato uppattiṃ maññamāno bhūtato maññatīti veditabbo, ayamassa diṭṭhimaññanā. Tasmiṃyeva panassa diṭṭhimaññanāya maññite vatthusmiṃ sinehaṃ mānañca uppādayato taṇhāmānamaññanāpi veditabbā. Bhūte meti maññatīti ettha pana ekā taṇhāmaññanāva labbhati. Sā cāyaṃ “mama puttā, mama dhītā, mama ajeḷakā, kukkuṭasūkarā, hatthigavassavaḷavā”ti evamādinā nayena mamāyato pavattatīti veditabbā. Bhūte abhinandatīti etaṃ vuttanayameva. Apariññātaṃ tassāti ettha pana ye saṅkhāre upādāya bhūtānaṃ paññatti, tesaṃ apariññātattā bhūtā apariññātā hontīti veditabbā. Yojanā pana vuttanayeneva kātabbā.

Here, regarding 'He conceives from beings,' it should be understood that one who, with their appurtenances, whether for oneself or for another, conceives an arising from some being or other, 'conceives from beings.' This is their view-conceiving. Furthermore, in that very object conceived through view-conceiving, for one who generates affection and pride, craving-conceiving and conceit-conceiving should also be understood. Regarding 'He conceives "mine" in beings,' here only one, craving-conceiving, is obtained. And it should be understood that this occurs for one who appropriates in the manner of 'my sons, my daughters, my goats and sheep, chickens and pigs, elephants, cattle, horses, and mares,' and so on. 'He delights in beings' is just as has been explained. Regarding 'It is not fully understood by them,' here it should be understood that because the formations which are the basis for the designation of 'beings' are not fully understood, beings are not fully understood. The application, however, should be made in the same way as has been explained.

Evaṃ [M 1.0035] saṅkhepato saṅkhāravasena ca sattavasena ca maññanāvatthuṃ dassetvā idāni bhūmivisesādinā bhedena vitthāratopi taṃ dassento deve devatotiādimāha. Tattha dibbanti pañcahi [V 1.0037] kāmaguṇehi attano vā iddhiyāti devā, kīḷanti jotenti cāti attho. Te tividhā sammutidevā upapattidevā visuddhidevāti. Sammutidevā nāma rājāno deviyo rājakumārā. Upapattidevā nāma cātumahārājike deve upādāya tatuttaridevā. Visuddhidevā nāma arahanto khīṇāsavā. Idha pana upapattidevā daṭṭhabbā, no ca kho avisesena. Paranimmitavasavattidevaloke māraṃ saparisaṃ ṭhapetvā sesā cha kāmāvacarā idha devāti adhippetā. Tattha sabbā atthavaṇṇanā bhūtavāre vuttanayeneva veditabbā.

Thus, having briefly shown the basis for conceiving by way of formations and by way of beings, now, showing it in detail by distinguishing various levels and so on, He begins with 'deities as deities.' Herein, they are called 'deities' (devā) because they sport (dibbanti) by means of the five strands of sensual pleasure or by their own power; the meaning is that they play and they shine. They are of three kinds: conventional deities, deities by rebirth, and deities by purification. Conventional deities are kings, queens, and princes. Deities by rebirth are those beginning with the Cātumahārājika deities up to the deities above them. Deities by purification are arahants, those whose taints are destroyed. Here, however, deities by rebirth are to be understood, but not indiscriminately. Excluding Māra together with his retinue in the Paranimmitavasavatti deva-world, the remaining six sense-sphere deities are intended here as 'deities.' In this context, all explanation of meaning should be understood in the manner stated in the Section on Beings.

Pajāpatinti ettha pana māro pajāpatīti veditabbo. Keci pana “tesaṃ tesaṃ devānaṃ adhipatīnaṃ mahārājādīnametaṃ adhivacana”nti vadanti. Taṃ devaggahaṇeneva tesaṃ gahitattā ayuttanti mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ paṭikkhittaṃ, māroyeva pana sattasaṅkhātāya pajāya adhipatibhāvena idha pajāpatīti adhippeto. So kuhiṃ vasati? Paranimmitavasavattidevaloke[P 1.0034]. Tatra hi vasavattirājā rajjaṃ kāreti. Māro ekasmiṃ padese attano parisāya issariyaṃ pavattento rajjapaccante dāmarikarājaputto viya vasatīti vadanti. Māraggahaṇeneva cettha māraparisāyapi gahaṇaṃ veditabbaṃ. Yojanānayo cettha pajāpatiṃ vaṇṇavantaṃ dīghāyukaṃ sukhabahulaṃ disvā vā sutvā vā rajjanto taṇhāmaññanāya maññati. “Aho vatāhaṃ pajāpatino sahabyataṃ upapajjeyya”ntiādinā vā pana nayena appaṭiladdhassa paṭilābhāya cittaṃ paṇidahantopi pajāpatiṃ taṇhāmaññanāya maññati. Pajāpatibhāvaṃ pana patto samāno ahamasmi pajānamissaro adhipatīti mānaṃ janento pajāpatiṃ mānamaññanāya maññati. “Pajāpati nicco dhuvo”ti vā “ucchijjissati vinassissatī”ti vā “avaso abalo avīriyo niyatisaṅgatibhāvapariṇato chasvevābhijātīsu sukhadukkhaṃ paṭisaṃvedetī”ti vā maññamāno pana pajāpatiṃ diṭṭhimaññanāya maññatīti veditabbo.

Regarding 'Pajāpati,' here Māra should be understood as Pajāpati. Some, however, say, “This is a designation for the sovereign rulers of various deities, such as the Great Kings.” That has been rejected in the Great Commentary as inappropriate because they are already included by the term ‘deva.’ Instead, here Pajāpati is intended to refer to Māra in the sense of being the lord over the multitude of beings. Where does he reside? In the Paranimmitavasavatti deva realm. There, the Vasavatti king exercises sovereignty. Māra, exercising authority over his own retinue in one region, dwells, they say, like a rebellious prince in a frontier province. Here, the term ‘Māra’ should also be understood to include Māra’s retinue. As for the method of application here, one, seeing or hearing about Pajāpati—splendid, long-lived, and abounding in pleasure—becomes enamored and conceives through craving-conceiving. Or, thinking, “Oh, if only I could be reborn in the company of Pajāpati!” or in some similar way, one who directs their mind towards the attainment of what is unattained also conceives Pajāpati through craving-conceiving. Having attained the state of Pajāpati, and generating conceit, thinking, “I am the lord, the master of beings,” one conceives Pajāpati through conceit-conceiving. Furthermore, it should be understood that one who thinks, “Pajāpati is permanent, stable,” or “he will be annihilated, he will perish,” or “he is powerless, weak, lacking vigor, subject to a fixed nature and association, and experiences pleasure and pain only in the six classes of birth,” conceives Pajāpati through view-conceiving.

Pajāpatisminti ettha pana ekā diṭṭhimaññanāva yujjati. Tassā evaṃ pavatti veditabbā. Idhekacco “pajāpatismiṃ ye ca dhammā saṃvijjanti, sabbe te niccā dhuvā [M 1.0036] sassatā avipariṇāmadhammā”ti maññati. Atha vā “pajāpatismiṃ natthi pāpaṃ, na tasmiṃ pāpakāni kammāni upalabbhantī”ti maññati.

Regarding 'In Pajāpati,' here only one, view-conceiving, is applicable. Its occurrence should be understood as follows: Here, someone thinks, “Whatever phenomena exist in Pajāpati, all are permanent, stable, eternal, and not subject to change.” Or else, they think, “In Pajāpati, there is no evil; no evil actions are found in him.”

Pajāpatitoti [V 1.0038] ettha tissopi maññanā labbhanti. Kathaṃ? Idhekacco saupakaraṇassa attano vā parassa vā pajāpatito uppattiṃ vā niggamanaṃ vā maññati, ayamassa diṭṭhimaññanā. Tasmiṃyeva panassa diṭṭhimaññanāya maññite vatthusmiṃ sinehaṃ mānañca uppādayato taṇhāmānamaññanāpi veditabbā. Pajāpatiṃ meti ettha pana ekā taṇhāmaññanāva labbhati. Sā cāyaṃ “pajāpati mama satthā mama sāmī”tiādinā nayena mamāyato pavattatīti veditabbā. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva.

Regarding 'From Pajāpati,' here all three types of conceiving are obtained. How? Here, someone conceives the arising or passing away of oneself or another, with their appurtenances, as being from Pajāpati. This is their view-conceiving. Furthermore, in that very object conceived through view-conceiving, for one who generates affection and conceit, craving-conceiving and conceit-conceiving should also be understood. Regarding 'Pajāpati is mine,' here only one, craving-conceiving, is obtained. And it should be understood that this occurs for one who appropriates in the manner of 'Pajāpati is my teacher, my master,' and so on. The rest is just as has been explained.

Brahmaṃ brahmatoti ettha brūhito tehi tehi guṇavisesehīti brahmā. Apica brahmāti mahābrahmāpi vuccati, tathāgatopi brāhmaṇopi mātāpitaropi seṭṭhampi. “Sahasso brahmā dvisahasso brahmā”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 3.165-166) hi mahābrahmā brahmāti vuccati. “Brahmāti kho, bhikkhave[P 1.0035], tathāgatassetaṃ adhivacana”nti ettha tathāgato.

Regarding 'Brahmā as Brahmā,' here 'Brahmā' means one who is great because of various special qualities. Moreover, 'Brahmā' is also said of Mahābrahmā, the Tathāgata, a brahmin, parents, and the highest. For in passages like “a thousand Brahmā, two thousand Brahmā,” Mahābrahmā is called 'Brahmā.' In the passage, “Monks, ‘Brahmā’ is a designation for the Tathāgata,” it refers to the Tathāgata.

“Tamonudo buddho samantacakkhu,

Lokantagū sabbabhavātivatto;

Anāsavo sabbadukkhappahīno,

Saccavhayo brahme upāsito me”ti. (cūḷani. 104) –

“O brahmin, the dispeller of darkness, the Buddha, the all-seeing one, gone to the world's end, who has overcome all existence; taintless, with all suffering abandoned, the one named Truth—he is worshipped by me.”

Ettha brāhmaṇo.

Here, it refers to a brahmin.

“Brahmāti mātāpitaro, pubbācariyāti vuccare”ti. (itivu. 106; jā. 2.20.181) –

“Parents are called ‘Brahmā,’ and they are called ‘first teachers.’”

Ettha mātāpitaro. “Brahmacakkaṃ pavattetī”ti (ma. ni. 1.148; a. ni. 5.11) ettha seṭṭhaṃ. Idha pana paṭhamābhinibbatto kappāyuko brahmā adhippeto. Taggahaṇeneva ca brahmapurohitabrahmapārisajjāpi gahitāti veditabbā. Atthavaṇṇanā panettha pajāpativāre vuttanayeneva veditabbā.

Here, it refers to parents. In “he sets rolling the Brahma-wheel,” it refers to the best. Here, however, the intended meaning is the first-born Brahmā, who lives for an aeon. And by his inclusion, the Brahmā’s ministers and the Brahmā’s assembly are also understood to be included. The explanation of meaning here should be understood in the same way as explained in the Section on Pajāpati.

Ābhassaravāre [V 1.0039] daṇḍadīpikāya acci viya etesaṃ sarīrato ābhā chijjitvā chijjitvā patantī viya sarati visaratīti ābhassarā. Tesaṃ gahaṇena [M 1.0037] sabbāpi dutiyajjhānabhūmi gahitā, ekatalavāsino eva cete sabbepi parittābhā appamāṇābhā ābhassarāti veditabbā.

In the section on the Ābhassarā, their radiance, like the flame of a torch, seems to detach and scatter from their bodies; thus they are called Ābhassarā (Radiant). By their inclusion, the entire second jhāna plane is encompassed. It should be understood that all these, dwelling on a single plane, are the Parittābhā, Appamāṇābhā, and Ābhassarā.

Subhakiṇhavāre subhena okiṇṇā vikiṇṇā subhena sarīrappabhāvaṇṇena ekagghanā suvaṇṇamañjūsāya ṭhapitasampajjalitakañcanapiṇḍasassirikāti subhakiṇhā. Tesaṃ gahaṇena sabbāpi tatiyajjhānabhūmi gahitā. Ekatalavāsino eva cete sabbepi parittasubhā appamāṇasubhā subhakiṇhāti veditabbā.

In the section on the Subhakiṇhā, they are filled and permeated with beauty. By the beautiful color of their bodily radiance, they are a solid mass, splendid like a blazing lump of gold placed in a golden casket; thus they are called Subhakiṇhā. By their inclusion, the entire third jhāna plane is encompassed. It should be understood that all these, dwelling on a single plane, are the Parittasubhā, Appamāṇasubhā, and Subhakiṇhā.

Vehapphalavāre, vipulā phalāti vehapphalā. Catutthajjhānabhūmi brahmāno vuccanti. Atthanayayojanā pana imesu tīsupi vāresu bhūtavāre vuttanayeneva veditabbā.

In the section on the Vehapphalā, they are called Vehapphalā because their fruits are vast. They are called Brahmās of the fourth jhāna plane. However, the method of explaining the meaning in all these three sections should be understood in the same way as explained in the section on the Bhūtā.

Abhibhūvāre abhibhavīti abhibhū. Kiṃ abhibhavi? Cattāro khandhe arūpino. Asaññabhavassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Asaññasattā devā vehapphalehi saddhiṃ ekatalāyeva ekasmiṃ okāse yena iriyāpathena nibbattā, teneva yāvatāyukaṃ tiṭṭhanti cittakammarūpasadisā hutvā. Te idha sabbepi abhibhūvacanena gahitā. Keci abhibhū nāma sahasso brahmāti evamādinā nayena tattha tattha adhipatibrahmānaṃ vaṇṇayanti. Brahmaggahaṇeneva pana tassa gahitattā [P 1.0036] ayuttametanti veditabbaṃ. Yojanānayo cettha abhibhū vaṇṇavā dīghāyukoti sutvā tattha chandarāgaṃ uppādento abhibhuṃ taṇhāmaññanāya maññati. “Aho vatāhaṃ abhibhuno sahabyataṃ upapajjeyya”ntiādinā pana nayena appaṭiladdhassa paṭilābhāya cittaṃ paṇidahantopi abhibhuṃ taṇhāmaññanāya maññati. Attānaṃ hīnato abhibhuṃ seyyato dahanto pana abhibhuṃ mānamaññanāya maññati. “Abhibhū nicco dhuvo”tiādinā nayena parāmasanto abhibhuṃ diṭṭhimaññanāya maññatīti veditabbo. Sesaṃ pajāpativāre vuttanayameva.

In the section on Abhibhū: one overcomes, thus one is 'Abhibhū'. What does one overcome? The four formless aggregates. This is a designation for the non-percipient existence. The non-percipient devas, together with the Vehapphala devas, exist on a single plane in a single location. In whatever posture they are reborn, in that very posture they remain for their entire lifespan, having become like painted figures. Here, all of them are included by the term 'Abhibhū'. Some describe the ruling Brahmās in various places by a method beginning with, 'Abhibhū is the thousand-fold Brahmā'.
