13. Nandī [M 1.0055] dukkhassa mūlantiādīsu ca nandīti purimataṇhā. Dukkhanti pañcakkhandhā. Mūlantiādi. Iti viditvāti taṃ purimabhavanandiṃ “imassa dukkhassa mūla”nti evaṃ jānitvā. Bhavāti kammabhavato. Jātīti vipākakkhandhā. Te hi yasmā jāyanti, tasmā “jātī”ti vuttā. Jātisīsena vā ayaṃ desanā. Etampi “iti viditvā”ti iminā yojetabbaṃ. Ayañhi ettha attho “kammabhavato upapattibhavo hotīti evañca jānitvā”ti. Bhūtassāti [V 1.0058] sattassa. Jarāmaraṇanti jarā ca [P 1.0053] maraṇañca. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – tena upapattibhavena bhūtassa sattassa khandhānaṃ jarāmaraṇaṃ hotīti evañca jānitvāti.

13. And in passages such as “Delight is the root of suffering,” “delight” means craving in a previous life. “Suffering” means the five aggregates. As for “root,” etc., “having understood thus” means having known thus: “that craving of a previous existence is the root of this suffering.” “From existence” means from kamma-existence. “Birth” means the resultant aggregates. For since they arise, they are called “birth.” Alternatively, this teaching proceeds with birth as its head. This too should be connected with the phrase “having understood thus.” Indeed, the meaning here is this: “and having also known thus that from kamma-existence, rebirth-existence arises.” “Of one who has come to be” means of a being. “Aging and death” means aging and death. This is what is meant: “due to that rebirth-existence, for the being that has come to be, there is aging and death of the aggregates”; having also known thus.

Ettāvatā yaṃ bodhirukkhamūle aparājitapallaṅke nisinno sammasitvā sabbaññutaṃ patto, tassa paṭiccasamuppādassa paṭivedhā maññanānaṃ abhāvakāraṇaṃ dassento catusaṅkhepaṃ tisandhiṃ tiyaddhaṃ vīsatākāraṃ tameva paṭiccasamuppādaṃ dasseti.

By this much, He who, having sat at the foot of the Bodhi tree on the unconquered seat and contemplated, attained omniscience, now teaches that very dependent origination—with its four summaries, three connections, three divisions of time, and twenty aspects—while demonstrating that the penetration of that dependent origination is the reason for the absence of conceivings.

Kathaṃ pana ettāvatā esa sabbo dassito hotīti. Ettha hi nandīti ayaṃ eko saṅkhepo. Dukkhassāti vacanato dukkhaṃ dutiyo, bhavā jātīti vacanato bhavo tatiyo, jātijarāmaraṇaṃ catuttho. Evaṃ tāva cattāro saṅkhepā veditabbā, koṭṭhāsāti attho. Taṇhādukkhānaṃ pana antaraṃ eko sandhi, dukkhassa ca bhavassa ca antaraṃ dutiyo, bhavassa ca jātiyā ca antaraṃ tatiyo. Evaṃ catunnaṃ aṅgulīnaṃ antarasadisā catusaṅkhepantarā tayo sandhī veditabbā.

But how is this entire dependent origination shown by just this much? Herein, “delight” is one summary. From the statement “of suffering,” suffering is the second; from the statement “from existence, birth,” existence is the third; and birth, aging, and death are the fourth. Thus, firstly, these four summaries, meaning sections, are to be understood. Furthermore, the interval between craving and suffering is one connection; the interval between suffering and existence is the second; and the interval between existence and birth is the third. Thus, the three connections, which are between the four summaries and are like the intervals between four fingers, are to be understood.

Tattha nandīti atīto addhā, jātijarāmaraṇaṃ anāgato, dukkhañca bhavo ca paccuppannoti evaṃ tayo addhā veditabbā. Atīte pana pañcasu ākāresu nandīvacanena taṇhā ekā āgatā, tāya anāgatāpi avijjāsaṅkhāraupādānabhavā paccayalakkhaṇena gahitāva honti. Jātijarāmaraṇavacanena pana yesaṃ khandhānaṃ tajjātijarāmaraṇaṃ, te vuttā yevāti katvā āyatiṃ viññāṇanāmarūpasaḷāyatanaphassavedanā gahitāva honti.

Therein, “delight” is the past period; “birth, aging, and death” is the future period; and “suffering” and “existence” are the present period—thus, the three periods are to be understood. However, in the past, among the five aspects, only one, craving, is mentioned by the word “delight”; and by that, ignorance, formations, clinging, and existence, though not mentioned, are nevertheless included by way of their characteristic as conditions. By the term “birth, aging, and death,” however, the aggregates to which that birth, aging, and death belong are indeed mentioned; and for this reason, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling in the future are nevertheless included.

Evamete “purimakammabhavasmiṃ moho avijjā, āyūhanā saṅkhārā, nikanti taṇhā, upagamanaṃ upādānaṃ, cetanā bhavo iti ime pañca dhammā purimakammabhavasmiṃ [M 1.0056] idha paṭisandhiyā paccayā. Idha paṭisandhi viññāṇaṃ, okkanti nāmarūpaṃ, pasādo āyatanaṃ, phuṭṭho phasso, vedayitaṃ vedanā iti ime pañca dhammā idhūpapattibhavasmiṃ purekatassa kammassa paccayā. Idha paripakkattā āyatanānaṃ moho avijjā, āyūhanā saṅkhārā, nikanti taṇhā, upagamanamupādānaṃ, cetanā bhavo iti ime pañca dhammā idha kammabhavasmiṃ āyatiṃ paṭisandhiyā paccayā. Āyatiṃ paṭisandhi viññāṇaṃ, okkanti nāmarūpaṃ, pasādo āyatanaṃ, phuṭṭho phasso[V 1.0059], vedayitaṃ vedanā iti ime pañca dhammā āyatiṃ upapattibhavasmiṃ idha [P 1.0054] katassa kammassa paccayā”ti evaṃ niddiṭṭhalakkhaṇā vīsati ākārā idha veditabbā. Evaṃ “nandī dukkhassa mūlanti iti viditvā bhavā jāti, bhūtassa jarāmaraṇa”nti ettāvatā esa sabbopi catusaṅkhepo tisandhi tiyaddho vīsatākāro paṭiccasamuppādo dassito hotīti veditabbo.

Thus, these twenty aspects with their characteristics thus indicated are to be understood here: “In a previous kamma-existence, delusion is ignorance; striving is formations; delight is craving; grasping is clinging; volition is becoming. These five factors in a previous kamma-existence are the conditions for rebirth here. Here, rebirth is consciousness; descent is name-and-form; sensitivity is the sense bases; being touched is contact; being felt is feeling. These five factors in this rebirth-existence arise on account of kamma done previously. Here, due to the maturation of the sense bases, delusion is ignorance; striving is formations; delight is craving; grasping is clinging; volition is becoming. These five factors in this kamma-existence are the conditions for future rebirth. In the future, rebirth is consciousness; descent is name-and-form; sensitivity is the sense bases; being touched is contact; being felt is feeling. These five factors in a future rebirth-existence arise on account of kamma done here.” Thus, it should be understood that by this much—“having known thus that ‘delight is the root of suffering,’ from existence, birth arises; for one who has come to be, there is aging and death”—this entire dependent origination, with its four summaries, three connections, three divisions of time, and twenty aspects, is shown.

Idāni tasmā tiha, bhikkhave…pe… abhisambuddhoti vadāmīti ettha apubbapadavaṇṇanaṃ katvā padayojanāya atthanigamanaṃ karissāma. Tasmā tihāti tasmā icceva vuttaṃ hoti. Tikārahakārā hi nipātā. Sabbasoti anavasesavacanametaṃ. Taṇhānanti nandīti evaṃ vuttānaṃ sabbataṇhānaṃ. Khayāti lokuttaramaggena accantakkhayā. Virāgādīni khayavevacanāneva. Yā hi taṇhā khīṇā, virattāpi tā bhavanti niruddhāpi cattāpi paṭinissaṭṭhāpi. Khayāti vā catumaggakiccasādhāraṇametaṃ. Tato paṭhamamaggena virāgā, dutiyena nirodhā, tatiyena cāgā, catutthena paṭinissaggāti yojetabbaṃ. Yāhi vā taṇhāhi pathaviṃ pathavito sañjāneyya, tāsaṃ khayā. Yāhi pathaviṃ maññeyya, tāsaṃ virāgā. Yāhi pathaviyā maññeyya, tāsaṃ nirodhā. Yāhi pathavito maññeyya, tāsaṃ cāgā. Yāhi pathaviṃ meti maññeyya, tāsaṃ paṭinissaggā. Yāhi vā pathaviṃ maññeyya, tāsaṃ khayā…pe… yāhi pathaviṃ abhinandeyya, tāsaṃ paṭinissaggāti evamettha yojanā kātabbā, na kiñci virujjhati.

Now, concerning the passage 'Therefore, bhikkhus…pe… I declare as fully enlightened,' having provided an explanation for words not previously explained, we shall connect the words and conclude the meaning. 'Tasmā tiha' means simply 'tasmā' (therefore) is said. For 'ti' and 'ha' are indeed particles. 'Sabbaso' (in every way) is a word indicating 'without remainder.' 'Of cravings' refers to all cravings that are thus called 'delight.' 'Through destruction' means because of the utter destruction by the supramundane path. Terms like 'dispassion' are indeed synonyms for destruction. For those cravings that are destroyed also become dispassionate, ceased, abandoned, and relinquished. Alternatively, 'destruction' is common to the function of the four paths. Thus, it should be connected as follows: by the first path, dispassion; by the second, cessation; by the third, abandonment; by the fourth, relinquishment. Alternatively: through the destruction of the cravings by which one would perceive earth as earth; through the dispassion towards the cravings by which one would conceive earth; through the cessation of the cravings by which one would conceive in earth; through the abandonment of the cravings by which one would conceive 'from earth'; through the relinquishment of the cravings by which one would conceive 'earth is mine.' Or: through the destruction of the cravings by which one would conceive earth…pe… through the relinquishment of the cravings by which one would delight in earth. In this way, the connection should be made here; nothing contradicts.

Anuttaranti uttaravirahitaṃ sabbaseṭṭhaṃ. Sammāsambodhinti sammā sāmañca bodhiṃ. Atha vā pasatthaṃ sundarañca bodhiṃ. Bodhīti rukkhopi maggopi sabbaññutañāṇampi nibbānampi. “Bodhirukkhamūle paṭhamābhisambuddho”ti (mahāva. 1; udā. 1) ca “antarā [M 1.0057] ca bodhiṃ antarā ca gaya”nti (mahāva. 11; ma. ni. 1.285) ca āgataṭṭhānehi rukkho bodhīti vuccati. “Catūsu maggesu ñāṇa”nti (cūḷani. 121) āgataṭṭhāne maggo. “Pappoti bodhiṃ varabhūrimedhaso”ti (dī. ni. 3.217) āgataṭṭhāne sabbaññutañāṇaṃ. “Patvāna bodhiṃ amataṃ asaṅkhata”nti āgataṭṭhāne nibbānaṃ. Idha pana bhagavato arahattamaggañāṇaṃ adhippetaṃ. Apare sabbaññutañāṇantipi vadanti.

'Anuttara' means that which is without a superior, the most excellent of all. 'Sammāsambodhi' means the enlightenment correctly and by oneself. Alternatively, it means the enlightenment that is praiseworthy and good. The term 'Bodhi' can refer to the tree, the path, the knowledge of omniscience, and also Nibbāna. In passages such as, 'At the foot of the Bodhi tree, he was first fully enlightened' and 'between the Bodhi tree and Gayā,' the tree is called 'Bodhi.' In the passage, 'knowledge in the four paths,' it refers to the path. In the passage, 'The one of excellent and vast wisdom attains Bodhi,' it refers to the knowledge of omniscience. In the passage, 'Having attained Bodhi, the deathless, the unconditioned,' it refers to Nibbāna. Here, however, the Blessed One's knowledge of the Arahantship path is intended. Others say it refers to the knowledge of omniscience.

Sāvakānaṃ [V 1.0060][P 1.0055] arahattamaggo anuttarā bodhi hoti na hotīti. Na hoti. Kasmā? Asabbaguṇadāyakattā. Tesañhi kassaci arahattamaggo arahattaphalameva deti, kassaci tisso vijjā, kassaci cha abhiññā, kassaci catasso paṭisambhidā, kassaci sāvakapāramīñāṇaṃ. Paccekabuddhānampi paccekabodhiñāṇameva deti. Buddhānaṃ pana sabbaguṇasampattiṃ deti abhiseko viya rañño sabbalokissariyabhāvaṃ. Tasmā aññassa kassacipi anuttarā bodhi na hotīti.

Is the Arahantship path of the disciples 'unsurpassed enlightenment' or not? It is not. Why? Because it does not bestow all qualities. Indeed, for some of those disciples, the Arahantship path gives only the fruit of Arahantship; for some, the three true knowledges; for some, the six direct knowledges; for some, the four analytical knowledges; and for some, the knowledge of a disciple's perfections. For Paccekabuddhas, too, their Arahantship path gives only the knowledge of a Paccekabuddha. But for the Buddhas, their Arahantship path gives the accomplishment of all qualities, just as the anointing of a king bestows sovereignty over the entire world. Therefore, for any other person, the Arahantship path is not 'unsurpassed enlightenment'.

Abhisambuddhoti abhiññāsi paṭivijjhi, patto adhigatoti vuttaṃ hoti. Iti vadāmīti iti vadāmi ācikkhāmi desemi paññapemi, paṭṭhapemi vivarāmi vibhajāmi uttānīkaromīti. Tatrāyaṃ yojanā – tathāgatopi, bhikkhave…pe… pathaviṃ na maññati…pe… pathaviṃ nābhinandati. Taṃ kissa hetu, nandī dukkhassa mūlaṃ, bhavā jāti, bhūtassa jarāmaraṇanti iti viditvāti. Tattha iti viditvāti itikāro kāraṇattho. Tena imassa paṭiccasamuppādassa viditattā paṭividdhattāti vuttaṃ hoti. Kiñca bhiyyo – yasmā ca evamimaṃ paṭiccasamuppādaṃ viditvā tathāgatassa yā nandīti vuttataṇhā sabbappakārā, sā pahīnā, tāsañca tathāgato sabbaso taṇhānaṃ khayā…pe… anuttaraṃ sammāsambodhiṃ abhisambuddho. Tasmā pathaviṃ na maññati…pe… pathaviṃ nābhinandatīti vadāmīti evaṃ abhisambuddhattā na maññati nābhinandatīti vadāmīti vuttaṃ hoti.

'Fully enlightened' means: he has directly known, he has penetrated, he has attained, he has realized. 'Thus I declare' means: thus I say, I point out, I teach, I proclaim, I establish, I reveal, I analyze, I make clear. Herein, this is the application: 'The Tathāgata, monks… does not conceive earth… does not delight in earth.' For what reason? 'Because of having understood thus: "Delight is the root of suffering; from existence comes birth; for one who has come to be, there is aging and death."' Therein, in the phrase 'having understood thus,' the particle 'iti' has the meaning of 'reason.' By that, it is meant: 'because of having known, because of having penetrated this dependent origination.' And what is more: because, having understood this dependent origination in this way, the craving of the Tathāgata—which is called 'delight'—is in all its forms abandoned, and because the Tathāgata, through the utter destruction of those cravings… is fully awakened to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, therefore, 'he does not conceive earth… does not delight in earth—thus I declare.' Thus it is said: 'Because he is fully enlightened in this way, he does not conceive, does not delight—thus I declare.'

Atha vā yasmā “nandī dukkhassa mūla”ntiādinā nayena paṭiccasamuppādaṃ viditvā sabbaso taṇhā khayaṃ gatā, tasmā tiha, bhikkhave, tathāgato sabbaso taṇhānaṃ khayā…pe… abhisambuddhoti vadāmi. So evaṃ abhisambuddhattā [M 1.0058] pathaviṃ na maññati…pe… nābhinandatīti. Yattha yattha hi yasmāti avatvā tasmāti vuccati, tattha tattha yasmāti ānetvā yojetabbaṃ, ayaṃ sāsanayutti. Esa nayo sabbattha.

Alternatively: because, by understanding dependent origination in the manner beginning with 'delight is the root of suffering,' craving has in every way come to destruction, therefore, monks, I declare that the Tathāgata, through the utter destruction of all cravings… is fully enlightened. He, being thus fully enlightened, does not conceive earth… does not delight in it—thus I declare. Indeed, wherever 'therefore' is stated without 'because' being said, there 'because' should be supplied and connected; this is the proper method of the teaching. This principle should be understood everywhere.

Idamavoca bhagavāti idaṃ nidānāvasānato pabhuti yāva abhisambuddhoti vadāmīti sakalasuttantaṃ bhagavā paresaṃ paññāya alabbhaṇeyyapatiṭṭhaṃ paramagambhīraṃ sabbaññutañāṇaṃ dassento ekena puthujjanavārena ekena [P 1.0056] sekkhavārena catūhi khīṇāsavavārehi dvīhi tathāgatavārehīti aṭṭhahi [V 1.0061] mahāvārehi ekamekasmiñca vāre pathavīādīhi catuvīsatiyā antaravārehi paṭimaṇḍetvā dvebhāṇavāraparimāṇāya tantiyā avoca.

'The Blessed One said this' means: The Blessed One, wishing to reveal the knowledge of omniscience—which is supremely profound and whose foundation is unobtainable by the wisdom of others—spoke this entire discourse, from the end of the introduction up to the words 'I declare that he is fully enlightened.' He spoke it as a teaching of two recitation sections in length, having adorned it with eight great sections—one for the worldling, one for the trainee, four for the taintless ones, and two for the Tathāgata—and having embellished each of those sections with twenty-four intermediate sections concerning earth and so on.

Evaṃ vicitranayadesanāvilāsayuttaṃ panetaṃ suttaṃ karavikarudamañjunā kaṇṇasukhena paṇḍitajanahadayānaṃ amatābhisekasadisena brahmassarena bhāsamānassāpi. Na te bhikkhū bhagavato bhāsitaṃ abhinandunti te pañcasatā bhikkhū idaṃ bhagavato vacanaṃ nānumodiṃsu. Kasmā? Aññāṇakena. Te kira imassa suttassa atthaṃ na jāniṃsu, tasmā nābhinandiṃsu. Tesañhi tasmiṃ samaye evaṃ vicitranayadesanāvilāsayuttampi etaṃ suttaṃ ghanaputhulena dussapaṭṭena mukhe bandhaṃ katvā purato ṭhapitamanuññabhojanaṃ viya ahosi. Nanu ca bhagavā attanā desitaṃ dhammaṃ pare ñāpetuṃ kappasatasahassādhikāni cattāri asaṅkhyeyyāni pāramiyo pūretvā sabbaññutaṃ patto. So kasmā yathā te na jānanti, tathā desesīti. Vuttamidaṃ imassa suttassa nikkhepavicāraṇāyaṃ eva “mānabhañjanatthaṃ sabbadhammamūlapariyāyanti desanaṃ ārabhī”ti, tasmā na yidha puna vattabbamatthi, evaṃ mānabhañjanatthaṃ desitañca panetaṃ suttaṃ sutvā te bhikkhū taṃyeva kira pathaviṃ diṭṭhigatikopi sañjānāti, sekkhopi arahāpi tathāgatopi sañjānāti. Kinnāmidaṃ kathaṃ nāmidanti cintentā pubbe mayaṃ bhagavatā kathitaṃ yaṃkiñci khippameva jānāma, idāni panimassa mūlapariyāyassa antaṃ vā koṭiṃ vā na jānāma na passāma, aho buddhā nāma appameyyā atulāti uddhaṭadāṭhā viya sappā nimmadā hutvā buddhupaṭṭhānañca dhammassavanañca sakkaccaṃ āgamaṃsu.

Even though this discourse, endowed with the charm of a teaching of various methods, was spoken by the Blessed One with a sublime voice—as lovely as the call of the Karavīka bird, pleasant to the ear, and like an anointing with nectar for the hearts of the wise—those monks did not delight in the Blessed One's speech. That is, those five hundred monks did not approve of the Blessed One's words. Why? Because of their ignorance. It is said that they did not understand the meaning of this discourse; therefore, they did not delight in it. Indeed, at that time, this discourse, though endowed with the charm of a teaching of various methods, was for them like delicious food placed before a person whose mouth has been bound with a thick, heavy cloth. And yet, the Blessed One, having fulfilled the perfections for four incalculable and one hundred thousand eons in order to make others know the Dhamma he taught, attained omniscience. Why then did he teach in a way that they did not understand? This was already stated in the analysis of this discourse's exposition: 'He began the teaching called the "Discourse on the Root of All Phenomena" for the purpose of shattering conceit.' Therefore, there is nothing more to be said here. And having heard this discourse taught for the purpose of shattering conceit, those monks, thinking, 'It seems that one who holds wrong views perceives this very earth, as does a trainee, an Arahant, and a Tathāgata. What is this? How is this? Before, we quickly understood whatever the Blessed One said, but now we do not know or see the end or the limit of this Discourse on the Root. Ah, Buddhas are indeed immeasurable, incomparable!', became free from conceit, like snakes with their fangs removed, and reverently approached to attend upon the Buddha and to hear the Dhamma.

Tena [M 1.0059] kho pana samayena bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ sannisinnā imaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ “aho buddhānaṃ ānubhāvo, te nāma brāhmaṇapabbajitā tathā mānamadamattā bhagavatā mūlapariyāyadesanāya nihatamānā katā”ti, ayañcarahi tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ antarākathā vippakatā. Atha [P 1.0057] bhagavā gandhakuṭiyā nikkhamitvā taṅkhaṇānurūpena pāṭihāriyena dhammasabhāyaṃ paññattavarabuddhāsane nisīditvā te bhikkhū āha – “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti. Te tamatthaṃ bhagavato ārocesuṃ. Bhagavā etadavoca – “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepi ahaṃ ime evaṃ mānapaggahitasire vicarante nihatamāne akāsi”nti. Tato imissā aṭṭhuppattiyā idaṃ atītaṃ ānesi –

At that time, the other monks, sitting together in the Dhamma hall, raised this topic of conversation: 'Oh, the power of the Buddhas! Those monks who went forth from the brahmin caste, who were so intoxicated with the intoxication of conceit, have been made by the Blessed One, through the Discourse on the Root of All Phenomena, to have their conceit struck down.' And this conversation among those monks was not yet finished. Then the Blessed One, having emerged from the Fragrant Chamber, by a miracle appropriate to that moment, sat down on the excellent, prepared Buddha-seat in the Dhamma hall and addressed those monks: 'Monks, for what topic of conversation are you now assembled together?' They informed the Blessed One of that matter. The Blessed One said this: 'Monks, not only now; in the past, too, I made these very ones, who wandered about exalted by pride, to have their conceit struck down.' Thereupon, on account of this matter arising, he brought forth this past event:

Bhūtapubbaṃ[V 1.0062], bhikkhave, aññataro disāpāmokkho brāhmaṇo bārāṇasiyaṃ paṭivasati tiṇṇaṃ vedānaṃ pāragū sanighaṇṭukeṭubhānaṃ sākkharappabhedānaṃ itihāsapañcamānaṃ padako veyyākaraṇo lokāyatamahāpurisalakkhaṇesu anavayo, so pañcamattāni māṇavakasatāni mante vāceti. Paṇḍitā māṇavakā bahuñca gaṇhanti lahuñca, suṭṭhu ca upadhārenti, gahitañca tesaṃ na vinassati. Sopi brāhmaṇo ācariyamuṭṭhiṃ akatvā ghaṭe udakaṃ āsiñcanto viya sabbampi sippaṃ uggaṇhāpetvā te māṇavake etadavoca “ettakamidaṃ sippaṃ diṭṭhadhammasamparāyahita”nti. Te māṇavakā – “yaṃ amhākaṃ ācariyo jānāti, mayampi taṃ jānāma, mayampi dāni ācariyā evā”ti mānaṃ uppādetvā tato pabhuti ācariye agāravā nikkhittavattā vihariṃsu. Ācariyo ñatvā “karissāmi nesaṃ mānaniggaha”nti cintesi. So ekadivasaṃ upaṭṭhānaṃ āgantvā vanditvā nisinne te māṇavake āha “tātā pañhaṃ pucchissāmi, kaccittha samatthā kathetu”nti. Te “pucchatha ācariya, pucchatha ācariyā”ti sahasāva āhaṃsu, yathā taṃ sutamadamattā. Ācariyo āha –

Once upon a time, monks, a certain brahmin, renowned in all directions, resided in Bārāṇasī. He had gone to the further shore of the three Vedas, together with the Nighaṇḍu and Keṭubha texts, the texts on phonology, with the Itihāsa as the fifth. He was a master of prosody and grammar, and was completely proficient in worldly philosophy and the marks of a great man. He taught the sacred texts to five hundred young men. The young men were intelligent; they learned much and learned it quickly, they retained it well, and what they had learned did not perish. That brahmin, without keeping a 'teacher's fist,' like one pouring water into a pot, had them learn every skill and then said to those young men, 'This much skill is for the welfare of the present life and the life to come.' Those young men, having produced conceit, thought, 'Whatever our teacher knows, we also know. Now we too are teachers!' and from then on, they lived disrespectfully towards their teacher, having abandoned their duties. The teacher, knowing this, thought, 'I will subdue their conceit.' One day, he addressed those young men, who had come to attend on him, paid their respects, and were seated, saying, 'Dear sons, I will ask a question. Are you able to answer it?' They immediately replied, 'Ask, teacher! Ask, teacher!'—just as those intoxicated by the conceit of learning would do. The teacher said:

“Kālo ghasati bhūtāni, sabbāneva sahattanā;

Yo ca kālaghaso bhūto, sa bhūtapacaniṃ pacī”ti. (jā. 1.10.190) –

Time devours beings, all of them, along with itself; and the being who is a devourer of time, he has cooked that which cooks beings.

Vissajjetha tātā imaṃ pañhanti.

Answer this question, dear sons.

Te [M 1.0060] cintetvā ajānamānā tuṇhī ahesuṃ. Ācariyo āha “alaṃ tātā gacchathajja, sve katheyyāthā”ti uyyojesi. Te dasapi vīsatipi sampiṇḍitā hutvā na tassa pañhassa ādiṃ, na antamaddasaṃsu. Āgantvā ācariyassa ārocesuṃ “na imassa pañhassa atthaṃ ājānāmā”ti. Ācariyo tesaṃ niggahatthāya imaṃ gāthamabhāsi –

They, having pondered, but not knowing the answer, became silent. The teacher said, 'Enough, dear sons. Go for today; you may answer tomorrow,' and dismissed them. They, having gathered in groups of ten and twenty, could see neither the beginning nor the end of that question. They came and informed the teacher, 'We do not know the meaning of this question.' The teacher, for the purpose of rebuking them, spoke this verse:

“Bahūni [P 1.0058] narasīsāni, lomasāni brahāni ca;

Gīvāsu paṭimukkāni, kocidevettha kaṇṇavā”ti. (jā. 1.10.191) –

Many are the heads of men, hairy and large, set upon their necks; yet only someone here has ears.

Gāthāyattho – bahūni narānaṃ sīsāni dissanti, sabbāni ca tāni lomasāni sabbāni ca mahantāni [V 1.0063] gīvāyameva ca ṭhapitāni, na tālaphalaṃ viya hatthena gahitāni, natthi tesaṃ imehi dhammehi nānākaraṇaṃ. Ettha pana kocideva kaṇṇavāti attānaṃ sandhāyāha. Kaṇṇavāti paññavā. Kaṇṇacchiddaṃ pana na kassaci natthi, taṃ sutvā te māṇavakā maṅkubhūtā pattakkhandhā adhomukhā aṅguliyā bhūmiṃ vilikhantā tuṇhī ahesuṃ.

The meaning of the verse is: Many heads of men are seen, and all of them are hairy, and all are large, and they are all placed on the neck, not held in the hand like a palm-fruit. In these characteristics, there is no distinguishing factor among them. But here, 'only someone has ears'—this he said referring to himself. 'One with ears' means one with wisdom. It is not, however, that anyone lacks an ear-hole. Hearing this, those young men became crestfallen, with drooping shoulders and downcast faces, and scratching the ground with a finger, they became silent.

Atha nesaṃ ahirikabhāvaṃ passitvā ācariyo “uggaṇhatha tātā pañha”nti pañhaṃ vissajjesi. Kāloti purebhattakālopi pacchābhattakālopīti evamādi. Bhūtānīti sattādhivacanametaṃ. Kālo hi bhūtānaṃ na cammamaṃsādīni khādati, apica kho nesaṃ āyuvaṇṇabalāni khepento yobbaññaṃ maddanto ārogyaṃ vināsento ghasati khādatīti vuccati. Sabbāneva sahattanāti evaṃ ghasanto ca na kiñci vajjeti, sabbāneva ghasati. Na kevalañca bhūtāniyeva, apica kho sahattanā attānampi ghasati. Purebhattakālo hi pacchābhattakālaṃ na pāpuṇāti. Esa nayo pacchābhattakālādīsu. Yo ca kālaghaso bhūtoti khīṇāsavassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. So hi āyatiṃ paṭisandhikālaṃ khepetvā khāditvā ṭhitattā “kālaghaso”ti vuccati. Sa bhūtapacaniṃ pacīti so yāyaṃ taṇhā apāyesu bhūte pacati, taṃ ñāṇagginā paci dayhi bhasmamakāsi, tena “bhūtapacaniṃ pacī”ti vuccati. “Pajani”ntipi pāṭho. Janikaṃ nibbattikanti attho.

Then, seeing their shamelessness, the teacher said, 'Learn the question, dear ones,' and he explained the question. 'Time' means the before-meal time, the after-meal time, and so on. 'Beings' is a designation for sentient beings. For time does not eat the skin, flesh, and so on, of beings; rather, by exhausting their lifespan, beauty, and strength, by crushing their youth, by destroying their health, it is said to 'devour' and 'consume.' As for 'all of them, along with itself': thus devouring, it does not leave anything out; it devours all. And not only does it devour beings, but indeed it also devours its own self. For the before-meal time does not reach the after-meal time. This is the principle for the after-meal time and so on. As for 'the being who is a devourer of time,' this is a designation for one whose cankers are destroyed. For he, having exhausted and consumed the time for rebirth-linking in the future, is called a 'devourer of time.' As for 'he has cooked that which cooks beings': that craving which 'cooks' beings in the woeful states, he has 'cooked' it with the fire of knowledge, has burned it, has made it into ashes. Therefore he is called one who 'has cooked that which cooks beings.' There is also the reading 'pajaniṃ.' The meaning is 'that which generates, that which produces.'

Atha te māṇavakā dīpasahassālokena viya rattiṃ samavisamaṃ ācariyassa vissajjanena pañhassa atthaṃ pākaṭaṃ disvā “idāni mayaṃ yāvajīvaṃ guruvāsaṃ [M 1.0061] vasissāma, mahantā ete ācariyā nāma, mayañhi bahussutamānaṃ uppādetvā catuppadikagāthāyapi atthaṃ na jānāmā”ti nihatamānā pubbasadisameva ācariyassa vattappaṭipattiṃ katvā saggaparāyaṇā ahesuṃ.

Then those young men, seeing the meaning of the question made clear by the teacher's explanation—just as the even and uneven ground at night becomes clear by the light of a thousand lamps—thought, 'Now we will live with our teacher for as long as we live. Great indeed are these teachers! For we, having produced conceit based on our great learning, did not know the meaning of even a four-lined verse.' With their conceit struck down, just as before, they fulfilled their duties and obligations to the teacher and became destined for heaven.

Ahaṃ kho, bhikkhave, tena samayena tesaṃ ācariyo ahosiṃ, ime bhikkhū māṇavakā. Evaṃ pubbepāhaṃ ime evaṃ mānapaggahitasire [P 1.0059] vicarante nihatamāne akāsinti.

Monks, at that time I was their teacher, and these monks were the young men. Thus, in the past, too, I made these very ones, who wandered with heads held high by pride, to have their conceit struck down.

Imañca jātakaṃ sutvā te bhikkhū pubbepi mayaṃ māneneva upahatāti bhiyyosomattāya nihatamānā hutvā attano upakārakakammaṭṭhānaparāyaṇā ahesuṃ.

Having heard this Jātaka, those monks, reflecting, 'Even in the past, we were ruined only by pride,' became exceedingly humbled in their pride and made the beneficial meditation subject their sole resort.

Tato [V 1.0064] bhagavā ekaṃ samayaṃ janapadacārikaṃ caranto vesāliṃ patvā gotamake cetiye viharanto imesaṃ pañcasatānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ ñāṇaparipākaṃ viditvā imaṃ gotamakasuttaṃ kathesi –

Then the Blessed One, while wandering on a tour through the country, arrived at Vesālī and stayed at the Gotamaka Shrine. Knowing the ripeness of knowledge in these five hundred monks, he taught this Gotamaka Sutta.

“Abhiññāyāhaṃ, bhikkhave, dhammaṃ desemi no anabhiññāya, sanidānāhaṃ…pe… sappāṭihāriyāhaṃ, bhikkhave, dhammaṃ desemi no appāṭihāriyaṃ. Tassa mayhaṃ, bhikkhave, abhiññāya dhammaṃ desayato…pe… no appāṭihāriyaṃ. Karaṇīyo ovādo, karaṇīyā anusāsanī. Alañca pana vo, bhikkhave, tuṭṭhiyā alaṃ attamanatāya alaṃ somanassāya. Sammāsambuddho bhagavā, svākkhāto dhammo, suppaṭipanno saṅghoti. Idamavoca bhagavā, imasmiñca pana veyyākaraṇasmiṃ bhaññamāne dasasahassilokadhātu akampitthā”ti (a. ni. 3.126).

“Monks, I teach the Dhamma having directly known it, not without direct knowledge. I teach the Dhamma with its cause… I teach the Dhamma which leads to deliverance, not that which does not lead to deliverance. Monks, when I teach the Dhamma having directly known it… not that which does not lead to deliverance, my exhortation should be followed, my instruction should be followed. And, monks, it is indeed enough for your satisfaction, enough for your gladness, enough for your joy that: ‘The Blessed One is a Perfectly Enlightened One, the Dhamma is well-proclaimed, the Saṅgha is of good conduct.’ This the Blessed One said. And while this prose exposition was being spoken, the ten-thousandfold world-system trembled.”

Idañca suttaṃ sutvā te pañcasatā bhikkhū tasmiṃyevāsane saha paṭisambhidāhi arahattaṃ pāpuṇiṃsu, evāyaṃ desanā etasmiṃ ṭhāne niṭṭhamagamāsīti.

Having heard this Sutta, those five hundred monks, right there in their seats, attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges. Thus, this teaching reached its conclusion at this place.

Tathāgatavāraaṭṭhamanayavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the eighth method of the Tathāgata section is concluded.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

Of the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya

Mūlapariyāyasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Mūlapariyāya Sutta is concluded.

2. Sabbāsavasuttavaṇṇanā

2. The Commentary on the Sabbāsava Sutta

14. Evaṃ [V 1.0065][M 1.0062] me sutaṃ…pe… sāvatthiyanti sabbāsavasuttaṃ. Tatrāyaṃ apubbapadavaṇṇanā – sāvatthīti savatthassa isino nivāsaṭṭhānabhūtā nagarī, yathā kākandī mākandī kosambīti evaṃ tāva akkharacintakā. Aṭṭhakathācariyā pana bhaṇanti “yaṃkiñci manussānaṃ upabhogaparibhogaṃ sabbamettha atthīti sāvatthī. Satthasamāyoge ca kiṃ bhaṇḍamatthīti pucchite sabbamatthī”ti vacanamupādāya sāvatthī.

14. “Thus have I heard… at Sāvatthī.” This is the Sabbāsava Sutta. Herein, this is the explanation of terms not previously explained: Sāvatthī is the city that was the dwelling place of the sage Savattha, just as Kākandī, Mākandī, and Kosambī were. Thus say the etymologists. The commentary teachers, however, say: “Because whatever is for human beings' enjoyment and use, all is present here, it is called Sāvatthī.” And also, on account of the reply, “Everything is here,” when asked at a gathering of a caravan, “What merchandise is here?”, it is called Sāvatthī.

“Sabbadā sabbūpakaraṇaṃ, sāvatthiyaṃ samohitaṃ;

Tasmā sabbamupādāya, sāvatthīti pavuccati.

“At all times every requisite is gathered in Sāvatthī; therefore, on account of everything, it is called Sāvatthī.”

Kosalānaṃ [P 1.0060] puraṃ rammaṃ, dassaneyyaṃ manoramaṃ;

Dasahi saddehi avivittaṃ, annapānasamāyutaṃ.

“The delightful city of the Kosalans, fair to see and charming, not devoid of the ten sounds, and endowed with food and drink.”

Vuddhiṃ vepullataṃ pattaṃ, iddhaṃ phītaṃ manoramaṃ;

Aḷakamandāva devānaṃ, sāvatthipuramuttama”nti.

“Having attained growth and abundance, prosperous, thriving, and delightful; like Āḷakamandā of the devas, is the excellent city of Sāvatthī.”

Tassaṃ sāvatthiyaṃ. Jetavaneti ettha attano paccatthikajanaṃ jinātīti jeto, raññā vā attano paccatthikajane jite jātoti jeto, maṅgalakamyatāya vā tassa evaṃnāmameva katanti jeto, jetassa vanaṃ jetavanaṃ. Tañhi jetena rājakumārena ropitaṃ saṃvaddhitaṃ paripālitaṃ, so ca tassa sāmī ahosi. Tasmā jetavananti vuccati, tasmiṃ jetavane. Anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāmeti ettha sudatto nāma so gahapati mātāpitūhi katanāmavasena. Sabbakāmasamiddhitāya pana vigatamalamaccheratāya karuṇādiguṇasamaṅgitāya ca niccakālaṃ anāthānaṃ piṇḍamadāsi, tena anāthapiṇḍikoti saṅkhaṃ gato. Āramanti ettha pāṇino visesena vā pabbajitāti ārāmo, tassa pupphaphalādisobhāya nātidūranaccāsannatādipañcavidhasenāsanaṅgasampattiyā ca tato tato āgamma [V 1.0066] ramanti abhiramanti anukkaṇṭhitā hutvā nivasantīti attho. Vuttappakārāya vā sampattiyā tattha tattha gatepi attano abbhantaraṃyeva ānetvā rametīti ārāmo. So hi anāthapiṇḍikena gahapatinā jetassa rājakumārassa hatthato aṭṭhārasahi hiraññakoṭīhi koṭisantharena kīṇitvā aṭṭhārasahi hiraññakoṭīhi senāsanāni kārāpetvā aṭṭhārasahi hiraññakoṭīhi vihāramahaṃ niṭṭhāpetvā [M 1.0063] evaṃ catupaññāsahiraññakoṭipariccāgena buddhappamukhassa saṅghassa niyyādito. Tasmā “anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāmo”ti vuccati. Tasmiṃ anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme.

In that Sāvatthī. Regarding 'Jetavana': he is called Jeta because he conquers his adversaries; or, he was born when the king had conquered his adversaries, and so was called Jeta; or, this name was given to him for the sake of auspiciousness. Jeta's grove is Jetavana. For it was planted, nurtured, and protected by Prince Jeta, and he was its owner. Therefore it is called Jetavana; in that Jetavana. Regarding 'Anāthapiṇḍika's monastery': that householder's name, given by his parents, was Sudatta. But because he was endowed with all desirable things, was free from the stain of stinginess, possessed virtues such as compassion, and constantly gave alms-food to the destitute, he became known as Anāthapiṇḍika. It is a monastery (ārāma) because beings, and especially the ordained, delight (āramanti) there. Or, because of the beauty of its flowers and fruits and its possession of the five qualities of a suitable dwelling—such as being not too far and not too near—beings come from here and there and dwell there, delighting and rejoicing, free from discontent. Or, because of its aforementioned perfections, it draws even those who have gone elsewhere into itself and causes them to delight; therefore, it is an ārāma. It was bought by the householder Anāthapiṇḍika from the hand of Prince Jeta for eighteen crores of gold coins, by covering the ground with them. He had dwellings built for eighteen crores of gold coins, and completed the monastery dedication festival for eighteen crores of gold coins. Thus, with an expenditure of fifty-four crores of gold coins, it was dedicated to the Saṅgha with the Buddha at its head. Therefore, it is called 'Anāthapiṇḍika's monastery'; in that monastery of Anāthapiṇḍika.

Ettha ca “jetavane”ti vacanaṃ purimasāmiparikittanaṃ. “Anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme”ti pacchimasāmiparikittanaṃ. Kimetesaṃ parikittane payojananti. Puññakāmānaṃ diṭṭhānugatiāpajjanaṃ. Tatra hi dvārakoṭṭhakapāsādamāpane bhūmivikkayaladdhā aṭṭhārasa hiraññakoṭiyo anekakoṭiagghanakā rukkhā ca jetassa pariccāgo, catupaññāsa [P 1.0061] koṭiyo anāthapiṇḍikassa. Iti tesaṃ parikittanena evaṃ puññakāmā puññāni karontīti dassento āyasmā ānando aññepi puññakāme tesaṃ diṭṭhānugatiāpajjane niyojeti.

Herein, the phrase 'in Jetavana' is a proclamation of the former owner. 'In Anāthapiṇḍika's monastery' is a proclamation of the later owner. What is the purpose in proclaiming them? It is for causing those who desire merit to follow the example they have seen. For in this matter, in the construction of the gate-mansion, the eighteen crores of gold coins received from the sale of the land and the trees worth many crores were Prince Jeta's expenditure; fifty-four crores were Anāthapiṇḍika's. Thus, by proclaiming them, the Venerable Ānanda, showing that 'in this way, those who desire merit perform meritorious deeds,' urges other merit-seekers to follow the example they have seen.

Sabbāsavasaṃvarapariyāyaṃ vo, bhikkhaveti kasmā idaṃ suttamabhāsi? Tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ upakkilesavisodhanaṃ ādiṃ katvā āsavakkhayāya paṭipattidassanatthaṃ. Tattha sabbāsavasaṃvarapariyāyanti sabbesaṃ āsavānaṃ saṃvarakāraṇaṃ saṃvarabhūtaṃ kāraṇaṃ, yena kāraṇena te saṃvaritā pidahitā hutvā anuppādanirodhasaṅkhātaṃ khayaṃ gacchanti pahīyanti nappavattanti, taṃ kāraṇanti attho. Tattha āsavantīti āsavā, cakkhutopi…pe… manatopi sandanti pavattantīti vuttaṃ hoti. Dhammato yāva gotrabhuṃ okāsato yāva bhavaggaṃ savantīti vā āsavā, ete dhamme etañca okāsaṃ anto karitvā pavattantīti attho. Antokaraṇattho hi ayaṃ ākāro. Cirapārivāsiyaṭṭhena madirādayo āsavā, āsavā viyātipi āsavā. Lokasmiñhi cirapārivāsikā madirādayo āsavāti vuccanti. Yadi ca cirapārivāsiyaṭṭhena āsavā, eteyeva bhavitumarahanti. Vuttañhetaṃ “purimā, bhikkhave, koṭi na paññāyati avijjāya, ito pubbe avijjā nāhosī”tiādi (a. ni. 10.61). Āyataṃ vā saṃsāradukkhaṃ savanti pasavantītipi āsavā. Purimāni cettha nibbacanāni yattha kilesā āsavāti [V 1.0067] āgacchanti, tattha yujjanti, pacchimaṃ kammepi. Na kevalañca kammakilesāyeva āsavā, apica kho nānappakārakā uppaddavāpi. Suttesu hi “nāhaṃ, cunda, diṭṭhadhammikānaṃyeva āsavānaṃ saṃvarāya dhammaṃ desemī”ti (dī. ni. 3.182) ettha vivādamūlabhūtā kilesā āsavāti āgatā.

Why was this discourse, 'Bhikkhus, the method for the restraint of all taints,' spoken? For the purpose of showing the practice for the destruction of the taints, beginning with the purification of the defilements of those bhikkhus. Therein, 'the method for the restraint of all taints' means the cause for the restraint of all taints, the cause that has become restraint. The meaning is: it is that cause by which they, being restrained and shut off, reach the destruction called non-arising cessation, are abandoned, and do not proceed. Therein, 'they flow in' (āsavanti), thus they are 'taints' (āsavā). It is said that they flow in and proceed from the eye... and so on... from the mind. Or, they are 'taints' because they flow (savanti) with respect to phenomena up to the change-of-lineage stage, and with respect to location up to the peak of existence. The meaning is that they proceed having included these phenomena and this location. For this prefix 'ā' has the meaning of inclusion. Because of the meaning of being long-matured, like spirits, they are called 'taints'; also, because they are like spirits (āsavā), they are called 'taints' (āsavā). For in the world, long-matured things like spirits are called 'āsavā.' And if they are 'āsavā' because of the meaning of being long-matured, then these [defilements] too may rightly be so. For this was said: 'Bhikkhus, a first point of ignorance is not discerned, [thinking,] "Before this, ignorance did not exist,"' and so on. Or, they are also 'taints' because they cause the long suffering of saṃsāra to flow and flow forth. And here, the first two etymologies apply where defilements are called 'āsavā'; the last one also applies to kamma. And not only are kamma and defilements 'āsavā', but also various kinds of calamities. For in the discourses, in the passage, 'Cunda, I do not teach the Dhamma only for the restraint of taints in the present life,' the defilements that are the root of disputes are presented as 'āsavā'.

“Yena [M 1.0064] devūpapatyassa, gandhabbo vā vihaṅgamo;

Yakkhattaṃ yena gaccheyyaṃ, manussattañca abbaje;

Te mayhaṃ āsavā khīṇā, viddhastā vinaḷīkatā”ti. (a. ni. 4.36); –

“By which there would be rebirth among the devas, or I would be a gandhabba or a bird; by which I would go to the state of a yakkha, or attain the human state; those taints of mine are destroyed, demolished, and uprooted.”

Ettha tebhūmakañca kammaṃ avasesā ca akusalā dhammā. “Diṭṭhadhammikānaṃ āsavānaṃ saṃvarāya samparāyikānaṃ āsavānaṃ paṭighātāyā”ti (pārā. 39) ettha parūpavādavippaṭisāravadhabandhādayo [P 1.0062] ceva apāyadukkhabhūtā ca nānappakārā upaddavā. Te panete āsavā yattha yathā āgatā, tattha tathā veditabbā.

Here, kamma of the three planes and the remaining unwholesome states are 'āsavā.' In the passage, 'for the restraint of taints in the present life and for the destruction of taints in future lives,' blame from others, remorse, killing, bondage, and so on, and the various kinds of calamities that have become the suffering of the woeful states, are 'āsavā.' However, these taints should be understood in that way, wherever and in whatever way they are presented.

Ete hi vinaye tāva “diṭṭhadhammikānaṃ āsavānaṃ saṃvarāya, samparāyikānaṃ āsavānaṃ paṭighātāyā”ti dvedhā āgatā. Saḷāyatane “tayome āvuso āsavā, kāmāsavo bhavāsavo avijjāsavo”ti (a. ni. 6.63) tidhā āgatā. Aññesu ca suttantesu abhidhamme ca teyeva diṭṭhāsavena saha catudhā āgatā. Nibbedhikapariyāye – “atthi, bhikkhave, āsavā nirayagāminiyā, atthi āsavā tiracchānayonigāminiyā, atthi āsavā pettivisayagāminiyā, atthi āsavā manussalokagāminiyā, atthi āsavā devalokagāminiyā”ti (a. ni. 6.63) pañcadhā āgatā. Chakkanipāte – “atthi, bhikkhave, āsavā saṃvarā pahātabbā”tiādinā nayena chadhā āgatā. Imasmiṃ pana sutte teyeva dassanāpahātabbehi saddhiṃ sattadhā āgatāti. Ayaṃ tāva āsavapade vacanattho ceva pabhedo ca.

For, in the Vinaya, they are first presented in two ways: 'for the restraint of taints in the present life, and for the destruction of taints in future lives.' In the Saḷāyatana section, they are presented in three ways: 'Friends, there are these three taints: the taint of sensual pleasure, the taint of existence, and the taint of ignorance.' In other suttas and in the Abhidhamma, these same taints together with the taint of views are presented in four ways. In the Nibbedhika Pariyāya, they are presented in five ways: 'Bhikkhus, there are taints that lead to hell, there are taints that lead to the animal realm, there are taints that lead to the sphere of ghosts, there are taints that lead to the human world, and there are taints that lead to the deva world.' In the Chakkanipāta, they are presented in six ways, by the method beginning with, 'Bhikkhus, there are taints to be abandoned by restraint.' In this sutta, however, these same taints together with those to be abandoned by seeing are presented in seven ways. This, for now, is the word-meaning and the classification in the section on the taints.

Saṃvarapade pana saṃvarayatīti saṃvaro, pidahati nivāreti pavattituṃ na detīti attho. Tathā [V 1.0068] hi “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, divā paṭisallīyantena dvāraṃ saṃvaritvā paṭisallīyitu”nti (pārā. 77), “sotānaṃ saṃvaraṃbraūmi, paññāyete pidhīyare”ti (su. ni. 1041) ca ādīsu pidhānaṭṭhena saṃvaramāha. Svāyaṃ saṃvaro pañcavidho hoti sīlasaṃvaro satiñāṇa khanti vīriyasaṃvaroti. Tattha “iminā pātimokkhasaṃvarena upeto”ti (vibha. 511) ayaṃ sīlasaṃvaro. Pātimokkhasīlañhi [M 1.0065] ettha saṃvaroti vuttaṃ. “Cakkhundriye saṃvaramāpajjatī”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 1.213) satisaṃvaro. Sati hettha saṃvaroti vuttā. “Sotānaṃ saṃvaraṃ brūmi, paññāyete pidhīyare”ti ayaṃ ñāṇasaṃvaro. Ñāṇañhettha pidhīyareti iminā pidhānaṭṭhena saṃvaroti vuttaṃ. “Khamo hoti sītassa…pe…, uppannaṃ kāmavitakkaṃ nādhivāsetī”tiādinā (ma. ni. 1.24-26) pana nayena idheva khantivīriyasaṃvarā āgatā. Tesañca “sabbāsavasaṃvarapariyāya”nti iminā uddesena saṅgahitattā saṃvarabhāvo veditabbo.

Now, in the section on restraint: because it restrains (saṃvarayati), it is called restraint (saṃvaro). The meaning is: it shuts off, it prevents, it does not allow to proceed. For in passages such as, 'I allow, bhikkhus, one who is in seclusion during the day to shut the door and remain in seclusion,' and, 'I speak of the restraint of the streams; by wisdom they are shut off,' he spoke of restraint in the sense of shutting off. This restraint is of five kinds: restraint by virtue, restraint by mindfulness, by knowledge, by patience, and by energy. Therein, 'endowed with this Pātimokkha-restraint'—this is restraint by virtue. For here, the Pātimokkha-virtue is called restraint. In passages such as, 'He undertakes restraint in the eye-faculty,' this is restraint by mindfulness. For here, mindfulness is called restraint. 'I speak of the restraint of the streams; by wisdom they are shut off'—this is restraint by knowledge. For here, knowledge is called restraint by this [phrase] 'they are shut off,' in the sense of shutting off. And by the method beginning with, 'He is patient with cold... he does not tolerate an arisen thought of sensual pleasure,' the restraints by patience and energy are presented right here. And because they are included by this heading, 'the method for the restraint of all taints,' their nature as restraint should be understood.

Apica pañcavidhopi [P 1.0063] ayaṃ saṃvaro idha āgatoyeva, tattha khantivīriyasaṃvarā tāva vuttāyeva. “So tañca anāsanaṃ tañca agocara”nti (ma. ni. 1.25) ayaṃ panettha sīlasaṃvaro. “Paṭisaṅkhā yoniso cakkhundriyasaṃvarasaṃvuto”ti (ma. ni. 1.22) ayaṃ satisaṃvaro. Sabbattha paṭisaṅkhā ñāṇasaṃvaro. Aggahitaggahaṇena pana dassanaṃ paṭisevanā bhāvanā ca ñāṇasaṃvaro. Pariyāyanti etena dhammāti pariyāyo, uppattiṃ nirodhaṃ vā gacchantīti vuttaṃ hoti. Ettāvatā “sabbāsavasaṃvarapariyāya”nti ettha yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ vuttaṃ hoti.

Furthermore, this fivefold restraint is indeed presented here. Among them, the restraints by patience and energy have already been mentioned. Herein, 'He [avoids] that unsuitable seat and that unsuitable resort'—this is restraint by virtue. 'Having reflected wisely, he dwells restrained with the restraint of the eye-faculty'—this is restraint by mindfulness. In all cases, reflection is restraint by knowledge. But by means of grasping what has not been grasped, seeing, practicing, and developing are also restraint by knowledge. Because states (dhammā) proceed (pariyāyanti) by means of this, it is a method (pariyāyo). It is said that they go either to arising or to cessation. With this, whatever should be said regarding 'the method for the restraint of all taints' has been said.

15. Idāni jānato ahantiādīsu jānatoti jānantassa. Passatoti passantassa. Dvepi padāni ekatthāni, byañjanameva nānaṃ. Evaṃ santepi jānatoti ñāṇalakkhaṇaṃ upādāya puggalaṃ niddisati, jānanalakkhaṇañhi ñāṇaṃ. Passatoti ñāṇappabhāvaṃ upādāya, passanappabhāvañhi ñāṇaṃ. Ñāṇasamaṅgī puggalo cakkhumā viya cakkhunā rūpāni ñāṇena vivaṭe dhamme passati. Apica yonisomanasikāraṃ uppādetuṃ jānato, ayonisomanasikāro yathā na uppajjati, evaṃ passatoti ayamettha sāro. Keci panācariyā bahū papañce bhaṇanti, te imasmiṃ atthe na yujjanti.

15. Now, in the phrases beginning with 'jānato ahaṃ' ('for one who knows, I...'), 'jānato' means 'for one who knows.' 'Passato' means 'for one who sees.' Both words have the same meaning; only the expression is different. Even so, with 'jānato,' He indicates the person by referring to the characteristic of knowing, for indeed knowledge has the characteristic of knowing. With 'passato,' He indicates the person by referring to the power of knowledge, for indeed knowledge has the power of seeing. A person endowed with knowledge sees with knowledge the revealed dhammas, just as one with eyesight sees forms with the eye. Furthermore, for one who knows how to generate wise attention, and for one who sees in such a way that unwise attention does not arise—this is the essential meaning here. Some teachers, however, speak of many elaborations, but those are not suitable in this context.

Āsavānaṃ [V 1.0069] khayanti āsavappahānaṃ āsavānaṃ accantakkhayasamuppādaṃ khīṇākāraṃ natthibhāvanti ayameva hi imasmiñca sutte, “āsavānaṃ khayā anāsavaṃ cetovimutti”ntiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.438) ca āsavakkhayattho. Aññattha pana maggaphalanibbānānipi āsavakkhayoti vuccanti. Tathā hi –

The destruction of the taints (āsavānaṃ khayaṃ) means the abandoning of the taints, the bringing about of the utter destruction of the taints, the state of being exhausted, the state of non-existence. This indeed is the meaning of 'āsavakkhaya' in this sutta and also in passages such as, 'Through the destruction of the taints, the taintless liberation of mind.' Elsewhere, however, the path, fruit, and Nibbāna are also called 'the destruction of the taints.' For indeed:

“Sekhassa [M 1.0066] sikkhamānassa, ujumaggānusārino;

Khayasmiṃ paṭhamaṃ ñāṇaṃ, tato aññā anantarā”ti. (itivu. 62) –

'For the learner who is training, following the straight path, first is the knowledge in destruction, and then immediately following is final knowledge.'

Ādīsu maggo āsavakkhayoti vutto,

In these and other such passages, the path is called 'the destruction of the taints.'

“Āsavānaṃ khayā samaṇo hotī”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.438) phalaṃ.

In passages beginning with, 'Through the destruction of the taints, one becomes a recluse,' the fruit is called 'the destruction of the taints.'

“Paravajjānupassissa, niccaṃ ujjhānasaññino;

Āsavā tassa vaḍḍhanti, ārā so āsavakkhayā”ti. (dha. pa. 253) –

'For one who sees the faults of others and is ever inclined to find fault, his taints increase; he is far from the destruction of the taints.'

Ādīsu nibbānaṃ “āsavakkhayo”ti vuttaṃ.

In these and other such passages, Nibbāna is called 'the destruction of the taints.'

No ajānato no apassatoti yo pana na jānāti na passati, tassa no vadāmīti attho. Etena ye ajānato apassatopi saṃvarādīhiyeva [P 1.0064] suddhiṃ vadanti, te paṭikkhittā honti. Purimena vā padadvayena upāyo vutto, iminā anupāyapaṭisedho. Saṅkhepena cettha ñāṇaṃ āsavasaṃvarapariyāyoti dassitaṃ hoti.

As for 'not for one who does not know, not for one who does not see,' the meaning is: 'For whichever person does not know and does not see, for that person I do not declare it.' By this, those who claim that purity comes from restraint and so on, even for one who does not know and does not see, are rejected. Alternatively, by the former pair of words, the means was stated; by this pair, the rejection of the non-means is stated. And here, in brief, it is shown that knowledge is the method for the restraint of the taints.

Idāni yaṃ jānato āsavānaṃ khayo hoti, taṃ dassetukāmo kiñca, bhikkhave, jānatoti pucchaṃ ārabhi, tattha jānanā bahuvidhā. Dabbajātiko eva hi koci bhikkhu chattaṃ kātuṃ jānāti, koci cīvarādīnaṃ aññataraṃ, tassa īdisāni kammāni vattasīse ṭhatvā karontassa sā jānanā maggaphalānaṃ padaṭṭhānaṃ na hotīti na vattabbā. Yo pana sāsane pabbajitvā vejjakammādīni kātuṃ jānāti, tassevaṃ jānato āsavā vaḍḍhantiyeva, tasmā yaṃ jānato [V 1.0070] passato ca āsavānaṃ khayo hoti, tadeva dassento āha yoniso ca manasikāraṃ ayoniso ca manasikāranti.

Now, wishing to show that for which there is the destruction of the taints for one who knows, He began the question: 'And what, monks, for one who knows...?' Therein, knowing is of many kinds. Indeed, some monk who is skillful knows how to make an umbrella; another knows how to do some other task among robes and so on. For one who performs such actions while established at the head of duties, it should not be said that this knowing is not a basis for the path and fruits. However, for whichever monk, having gone forth in the Dispensation, knows how to perform medical practice and the like, for such a one who knows, the taints only increase. Therefore, showing that very thing for which there is the destruction of the taints for one who knows and sees, He said: 'Wise attention and unwise attention.'

Tattha yoniso manasikāro nāma upāyamanasikāro pathamanasikāro, aniccādīsu aniccanti ādinā eva nayena saccānulomikena vā cittassa āvaṭṭanā anvāvaṭṭanā ābhogo samannāhāro manasikāro, ayaṃ vuccati yoniso manasikāroti.

Therein, what is called 'wise attention' is attention that is a means, attention that is a path. It is the turning of the mind, the repeated turning, the adverting, the bringing to mind, and the attending to things like impermanence by the method of 'it is impermanent,' and so on, or by the method that is in conformity with the truths. This is called 'wise attention.'

Ayoniso manasikāroti anupāyamanasikāro uppathamanasikāro. Anicce niccanti dukkhe sukhanti anattani attāti asubhe subhanti ayoniso manasikāro uppathamanasikāro. Saccappaṭikulena vā cittassa āvaṭṭanā anvāvaṭṭanā ābhogo [M 1.0067] samannāhāro manasikāro, ayaṃ vuccati ayoniso manasikāroti. Evaṃ yoniso manasikāraṃ uppādetuṃ jānato, ayoniso manasikāro ca yathā na uppajjati, evaṃ passato āsavānaṃ khayo hoti.

As for 'unwise attention,' it is attention that is not a means, attention that is a wrong path. It is unwise attention, a wrong path, to regard the impermanent as 'permanent,' the suffering as 'happiness,' the not-self as 'self,' and the foul as 'beautiful.' Alternatively, it is the turning of the mind, the repeated turning, the adverting, the bringing to mind, and the attending in a way that is contrary to the truths. This is called 'unwise attention.' Thus, for one who knows how to generate wise attention, and for one who sees in such a way that unwise attention does not arise, the destruction of the taints occurs.

Idāni imassevatthassa yuttiṃ dassento āha ayoniso, bhikkhave…pe… pahīyantīti. Tena kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti, yasmā ayoniso manasikaroto āsavā uppajjanti, yoniso manasikaroto pahīyanti, tasmā jānitabbaṃ yoniso manasikāraṃ uppādetuṃ jānato, ayoniso manasikāro ca yathā na uppajjati, evaṃ passato āsavānaṃ khayo hotīti, ayaṃ tāvettha saṅkhepavaṇṇanā.

Now, wishing to show the justification for this very matter, He said: 'Monks, through unwise attention... (etc.) ... are abandoned.' What is stated by that? Because taints arise for one who attends unwisely, and are abandoned for one who attends wisely, it should therefore be known that for one who knows how to generate wise attention, and for one who sees in such a way that unwise attention does not arise, the destruction of the taints occurs. This, for now, is the brief explanation here.

Ayaṃ pana vitthāro – tattha “yoniso ayoniso”ti imehi tāva dvīhi padehi ābaddhaṃ hoti upari sakalasuttaṃ. Vaṭṭavivaṭṭavasena [P 1.0065] hi upari sakalasuttaṃ vuttaṃ. Ayoniso manasikāramūlakañca vaṭṭaṃ, yoniso manasikāramūlakañca vivaṭṭaṃ. Kathaṃ? Ayoniso manasikāro hi vaḍḍhamāno dve dhamme paripūreti avijjañca bhavataṇhañca. Avijjāya ca sati “avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā…pe… dukkhakkhandhassa samudayo hoti. Taṇhāya sati taṇhāpaccayā upādānaṃ…pe… samudayo hotī”ti. Evaṃ ayaṃ ayoniso manasikārabahulo puggalo vātavegābhighātena vippanaṭṭhanāvā viya gaṅgāvaṭṭe patitagokulaṃ viya cakkayante yuttabalibaddo [V 1.0071] viya ca punappunaṃ bhavayonigativiññāṇaṭṭhitisattāvāsesu āvaṭṭaparivaṭṭaṃ karoti, evaṃ tāva ayoniso manasikāramūlakaṃ vaṭṭaṃ.

This, however, is the detailed explanation. Therein, the entire sutta above is first connected by these two words: 'yoniso' and 'ayoniso'. For the entire sutta above was spoken by way of the round of existence (vaṭṭa) and the ending of the round (vivaṭṭa). The round has unwise attention as its root, and the ending of the round has wise attention as its root. How so? Indeed, unwise attention, when it increases, brings two dhammas to fulfillment: ignorance and craving for existence. When there is ignorance, 'with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise... (etc.) ... such is the origin of this whole mass of suffering.' When there is craving, 'with craving as condition, clinging arises... (etc.) ... such is the origin of this whole mass of suffering.' In this way, a person who abounds in unwise attention repeatedly revolves and circles through existences, wombs, destinations, stations of consciousness, and abodes of beings—like a boat wrecked by the force of the wind, like a herd of cattle fallen into a whirlpool in the Ganges, or like a yoked bull on a machine-wheel. Thus, for now, the round has unwise attention as its root.

Yoniso manasikāro pana vaḍḍhamāno – “yoniso manasikārasampannassetaṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno pāṭikaṅkhaṃ, ariyaṃ aṭṭhaṅgikaṃ maggaṃ bhāvessati, ariyaṃ aṭṭhaṅgikaṃ maggaṃ bahulīkarissatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.55) vacanato sammādiṭṭhipamukhaṃ aṭṭhaṅgikaṃ maggaṃ paripūreti. Yā ca sammādiṭṭhi, sā vijjāti tassa vijjuppādā avijjānirodho, “avijjānirodhā saṅkhāranirodho…pe… evaṃ etassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa nirodho hotī”ti (mahāva. 1) evaṃ yoniso manasikāramūlakaṃ vivaṭṭaṃ veditabbaṃ. Evaṃ imehi dvīhi padehi ābaddhaṃ hoti upari sakalasuttaṃ.

But wise attention, when developed—as stated in the discourse (SN 5.55), 'For a monk endowed with wise attention, it is to be expected that he will develop the noble eightfold path, that he will cultivate the noble eightfold path'—fulfills the eightfold path, which has right view as its chief. And that right view is knowledge; with the arising of that knowledge, ignorance ceases. 'With the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease… thus comes the cessation of this entire mass of suffering' (Mahāvagga 1). In this way, the ending of the round, rooted in wise attention, is to be understood. Thus, the entire discourse above is connected by these two terms.

Evaṃ ābaddhe [M 1.0068] cettha yasmā pubbe āsavappahānaṃ dassetvā pacchā uppatti vuccamānā na yujjati. Na hi pahīnā puna uppajjanti. Uppannānaṃ pana pahānaṃ yujjati, tasmā uddesapaṭilomatopi “ayoniso, bhikkhave, manasikaroto”tiādimāha.

When it is thus connected here, it is not fitting to speak of the arising of the taints after having first shown their abandoning. For what has been abandoned does not arise again. The abandoning of what has arisen, however, is fitting. Therefore, reversing the order of the exposition, He said: 'Monks, for one who attends unwisely…'

Tattha ayoniso manasikarototi vuttappakāraṃ ayoniso manasikāraṃ uppādayato. Anuppannā ceva āsavā uppajjantīti ettha ye pubbe appaṭiladdhapubbaṃ cīvarādiṃ vā paccayaṃ upaṭṭhākasaddhivihārikaantevāsikānaṃ vā aññataraṃ manuññaṃ vatthuṃ paṭilabhitvā, taṃ subhaṃ sukhanti ayoniso manasikaroto, aññataraññataraṃ vā pana ananubhūtapubbaṃ ārammaṇaṃ yathā vā tathā vā ayoniso manasikaroto āsavā uppajjanti, te anuppannā uppajjantīti veditabbā, aññathā hi anamatagge saṃsāre anuppannā nāma āsavā na santi. Anubhūtapubbepi ca vatthumhi ārammaṇe vā yassa pakatisuddhiyā vā uddesaparipucchāpariyattinavakammayonisomanasikārānaṃ [P 1.0066] vā aññataravasena pubbe anuppajjitvā pacchā tādisena paccayena sahasā uppajjanti, imepi anuppannā uppajjantīti veditabbā. Tesuyeva pana vatthārammaṇesu punappunaṃ uppajjamānā uppannā pavaḍḍhantīti vuccanti. Ito aññathā hi paṭhamuppannānaṃ vaḍḍhi nāma natthi.

Herein, 'for one who attends unwisely' means for one who generates unwise attention of the kind described. As for 'unarisen taints arise': here, when one who has not previously obtained requisites such as robes, or a pleasing object from an attendant, a co-resident, or a pupil, attends to it unwisely as 'beautiful' and 'pleasant'; or when one attends unwisely in any way whatsoever to some previously unexperienced object, taints arise. These should be understood as 'unarisen taints arising.' Indeed, otherwise, in beginningless saṃsāra, there are no taints that are truly unarisen. And even in the case of a previously experienced object or basis, for a person for whom taints had not arisen before—perhaps due to natural purity, or due to one of the following: recitation, questioning, study, new work, or wise attention—if they later arise suddenly due to such a condition, these too should be understood as 'unarisen taints arising.' Moreover, when they arise repeatedly in those very same objects and bases, they are said to be 'arisen and increasing.' Apart from this, for those that arose for the first time, there is no such thing as growth.

Yoniso [V 1.0072] ca kho, bhikkhaveti ettha pana yassa pakatisuddhiyā vā seyyathāpi āyasmato mahākassapassa bhaddāya ca kāpilāniyā, uddesaparipucchādīhi vā kāraṇehi āsavā nuppajjanti, so ca jānāti “na kho me āsavā maggena samugghātaṃ gatā, handa nesaṃ samugghātāya paṭipajjāmī”ti. Tato maggabhāvanāya sabbe samugghāteti. Tassa te āsavā anuppannā na uppajjantīti vuccanti. Yassa pana kārakasseva sato satisammosena sahasā āsavā uppajjanti, tato saṃvegamāpajjitvā yoniso padahanto te āsave samucchindati, tassa uppannā pahīyantīti vuccanti maṇḍalārāmavāsīmahātissabhūtattherassa viya. So kira tasmiṃyeva vihāre uddesaṃ gaṇhāti, athassa gāme piṇḍāya carato visabhāgārammaṇe kileso uppajji, so taṃ vipassanāya vikkhambhetvā vihāraṃ agamāsi. Tassa supinantepi taṃ ārammaṇaṃ na upaṭṭhāsi. So “ayaṃ kileso vaḍḍhitvā apāyasaṃvattaniko hotī”ti saṃvegaṃ janetvā ācariyaṃ āpucchitvā vihārā nikkhamma mahāsaṅgharakkhitattherassa santike [M 1.0069] rāgapaṭipakkhaṃ asubhakammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā gumbantaraṃ pavisitvā paṃsukūlacīvaraṃ santharitvā nisajja anāgāmimaggena pañcakāmaguṇikarāgaṃ chinditvā uṭṭhāya ācariyaṃ vanditvā punadivase uddesamaggaṃ pāpuṇi. Ye pana vattamānuppannā, tesaṃ paṭipattiyā pahānaṃ nāma natthi.

But here, in the phrase 'And with wise attention, bhikkhus,' it refers to one for whom, due to natural purity—as in the case of the Venerable Mahākassapa and Bhaddā Kāpilānī—or due to reasons such as recitation and questioning, the taints do not arise, and who knows: 'My taints have not been eradicated by the path. Come, let me practice for their eradication.' Then, by developing the path, he eradicates them all. For him, it is said that 'unarisen taints do not arise.' But for one who, while engaged in the practice, has taints suddenly arise due to a lapse of mindfulness, and then, stirred with urgency, strives wisely and cuts off those taints—for him, it is said that 'arisen taints are abandoned,' as in the case of the elder Mahātissabhūta who dwelt in Maṇḍalārāma. It is said that he was receiving instruction in that very monastery. Then, while walking for alms in the village, a defilement arose in him regarding an unsuitable object. He suppressed it through insight and returned to the monastery. That object did not appear to him even in a dream. Reflecting, 'This defilement, if it grows, will lead to the lower realms,' he aroused a sense of urgency, took leave of his teacher, left the monastery, and approached the elder Mahāsaṅgharakkhita. Taking up the meditation on foulness as an antidote to lust, he entered a thicket, spread out his rag-robe, sat down, and with the path of non-returning, severed the lust related to the five cords of sensual pleasure. Rising, he paid respects to his teacher and, on the next day, resumed his course of recitation. As for those taints that are arising in the present moment, there is no such thing as their abandoning by means of practice.

16. Idāni “uppannā ca āsavā pahīyantī”ti idameva padaṃ gahetvā ye te āsavā pahīyanti, tesaṃ nānappakārato aññampi pahānakāraṇaṃ āvikātuṃ desanaṃ vitthārento atthi, bhikkhave, āsavā dassanā pahātabbātiādimāha yathā taṃ desanāpabhedakusalo dhammarājā. Tattha dassanā pahātabbāti dassanena pahātabbā. Esa nayo sabbattha.

16. Now, taking up this very phrase, 'and arisen taints are abandoned,' the Dhammarāja, the King of Dhamma skilled in the divisions of the teaching, wishing to expand the teaching in order to reveal in various ways another cause for the abandoning of those taints that are abandoned, said: 'Bhikkhus, there are taints to be abandoned by seeing,' and so on. Herein, 'to be abandoned by seeing' means to be abandoned by means of seeing. This is the method in all cases.

Dassanāpahātabbaāsavavaṇṇanā

The Exposition of Taints to be Abandoned by Seeing.

17. Idāni [P 1.0067] tāni padāni anupubbato byākātukāmo “katame ca, bhikkhave, āsavā dassanā pahātabbā”ti pucchaṃ katvā mūlapariyāyavaṇṇanāyaṃ vuttanayeneva “idha, bhikkhave, assutavā puthujjano”ti puggalādhiṭṭhānaṃ desanaṃ ārabhi. Tattha manasikaraṇīye dhamme nappajānātīti āvajjitabbe samannāharitabbe dhamme na pajānāti. Amanasikaraṇīyeti tabbiparīte. Esa nayo sesapadesupi. Yasmā pana ime dhammā manasikaraṇīyā, ime amanasikaraṇīyāti [V 1.0073] dhammato niyamo natthi, ākārato pana atthi. Yenā ākārena manasikariyamānā akusaluppattipadaṭṭhānā honti, tenākārena na manasikātabbā. Yena kusaluppattipadaṭṭhānā honti, tenākārena manasikātabbā. Tasmā “ya’ssa, bhikkhave, dhamme manasikaroto anuppanno vā kāmāsavo”tiādimāha.

17. Now, wishing to explain those terms in sequence, having posed the question, 'And which, bhikkhus, are the taints to be abandoned by seeing?', He began the discourse founded on a person, in the very manner stated in the Exposition of the Mūlapariyāya: 'Here, bhikkhus, an uninstructed ordinary person.' Therein, 'he does not know the phenomena that should be attended to' means he does not know the phenomena that should be adverted to and brought to mind. 'What should not be attended to' refers to their opposites. This is the method in the remaining terms as well. However, since there is no fixed rule by nature that 'these phenomena should be attended to, and these should not be attended to,' there is, however, a rule by mode. By whatever mode, when attended to, they become a basis for the arising of the unwholesome, by that mode they should not be attended to. By whatever mode they become a basis for the arising of the wholesome, by that mode they should be attended to. Therefore, He said, 'Bhikkhus, for whom, when attending to phenomena, the unarisen taint of sensual desire...' and so on.

Tattha ya’ssāti ye assa assutavato puthujjanassa. Manasikarototi āvajjayato samannāharantassa. Anuppanno vā kāmāsavoti ettha samuccayattho vāsaddo, na vikappattho. Tasmā yathā “yāvatā, bhikkhave, sattā apadā vā dvipadā vā…pe… tathāgato tesaṃ [M 1.0070] aggamakkhāyatī”ti (itivu. 90) vutte apadā ca dvipadā cāti attho, yathā ca “bhūtānaṃ vā sattānaṃ ṭhitiyā sambhavesīnaṃ vā anuggahāyā”ti (ma. ni. 1.402) vutte bhūtānañca sambhavesīnañcāti attho, yathā ca “aggito vā udakato vā mithubhedato vā”ti (udā. 76) vutte aggito ca udakato ca mithubhedato cāti attho, evamidhāpi anuppanno ca kāmāsavo uppajjati, uppanno ca kāmāsavo pavaḍḍhatīti attho daṭṭhabbo. Evaṃ sesesu.

Herein, 'ya’ssa' means 'ye assa,' for that uninstructed ordinary person. 'Manasikaroto' means for one who adverts and brings to mind. In 'anuppanno vā kāmāsavo,' the word 'vā' has a cumulative meaning, not an alternative one. Therefore, just as when it is said, 'Bhikkhus, as far as beings are footless or two-footed... the Tathāgata is declared the foremost among them,' the meaning is 'footless and two-footed beings'; and just as when it is said, 'for the maintenance of beings that have come to be and for the support of those seeking birth,' the meaning is 'for beings that have come to be and for those seeking birth'; and just as when it is said, 'from fire or from water or from dissension,' the meaning is 'from fire and from water and from dissension'—so too here, the meaning should be understood as: the unarisen taint of sensual desire arises, and the arisen taint of sensual desire increases. The same applies to the rest.

Ettha ca kāmāsavoti pañcakāmaguṇiko rāgo. Bhavāsavoti rupārūpabhave chandarāgo, jhānanikanti ca sassatucchedadiṭṭhisahagatā. Evaṃ diṭṭhāsavopi bhavāsave eva samodhānaṃ gacchati. Avijjāsavoti catūsu saccesu aññāṇaṃ. Tattha kāmaguṇe assādato manasikaroto anuppanno ca kāmāsavo uppajjati, uppanno ca pavaḍḍhati. Mahaggatadhamme assādato manasikaroto anuppanno ca bhavāsavo uppajjati, uppanno ca pavaḍḍhati. Tīsu bhūmīsu dhamme catuvipallāsapadaṭṭhānabhāvena manasikaroto anuppanno ca avijjāsavo uppajjati, uppanno ca pavaḍḍhatīti veditabbo. Vuttanayapaccanīkato sukkapakkho vitthāretabbo.

Herein, the taint of sensual desire is lust for the five cords of sensual pleasure. The taint of existence is lustful desire for existence in the form and formless realms, delight in the jhānas, and lust accompanied by eternalist and annihilationist views. Thus, the taint of views is also included within the taint of existence. The taint of ignorance is ignorance concerning the Four Noble Truths. Therein, for one who attends to sensual pleasures by way of gratification, the unarisen taint of sensual desire arises, and the arisen one increases. For one who attends to sublime states by way of gratification, the unarisen taint of existence arises, and the arisen one increases. For one who attends to phenomena in the three planes of existence as a basis for the four perversions, the unarisen taint of ignorance arises, and the arisen one increases—this should be understood. The wholesome side, being the opposite of the method described, should be elaborated.

Kasmā [P 1.0068] pana tayo eva āsavā idha vuttāti. Vimokkhapaṭipakkhato. Appaṇihitavimokkhapaṭipakkho hi kāmāsavo,. Animittasuññatavimokkhapaṭipakkhā itare. Tasmā ime tayo āsave uppādentā tiṇṇaṃ vimokkhānaṃ abhāgino honti, anuppādentā bhāginoti etamatthaṃ dassentena tayo eva vuttāti veditabbā. Diṭṭhāsavopi vā ettha vutto yevāti vaṇṇitametaṃ.

Why then are only three taints mentioned here? Because of their opposition to the liberations. For the taint of sensual desire is the opponent of the desireless liberation, while the others are the opponents of the signless and emptiness liberations. Therefore, those who generate these three taints do not partake of the three liberations, while those who do not generate them do partake. It should be known that only three were taught in order to show this meaning. Alternatively, it has been explained that the taint of views is indeed mentioned here.

Tassa [V 1.0074] amanasikaraṇīyānaṃ dhammānaṃ manasikārāti manasikārahetu, yasmā te dhamme manasi karoti, tasmāti vuttaṃ hoti. Esa nayo dutiyapadepi. “Anuppannā ceva āsavā uppajjanti, uppannā ca āsavā pavaḍḍhantī”ti heṭṭhā vuttaāsavānaṃyeva abhedato nigamanametaṃ.

As for the phrase 'through his attention to phenomena that should not be attended to,' this means 'by reason of attention.' Because he attends to those phenomena, it is therefore said thus. This is the method in the second phrase as well. The statement, 'Unarisen taints arise, and arisen taints increase,' is a conclusion referring without distinction to the taints mentioned before.

18. Ettāvatā yo ayaṃ puggalādhiṭṭhānāya desanāya dassanā pahātabbe āsave niddisituṃ assutavā puthujjano vutto, so yasmā “ayoniso, bhikkhave, manasikaroto anuppannā ceva āsavā uppajjantī”ti evaṃ sāmaññato vuttānaṃ ayoniso manasikārapaccayānaṃ kāmāsavādīnampi [M 1.0071] adhiṭṭhānaṃ, tasmā tepi āsave teneva puggalena dassetvā idāni dassanā pahātabbe āsave dassento so evaṃ ayoniso manasi karoti, ahosiṃ nu kho ahantiādimāha. Vicikicchāsīsena cettha diṭṭhāsavampi dassetuṃ imaṃ desanaṃ ārabhi.

18. Thus far, the uninstructed ordinary person was spoken of in order to point out, by means of a discourse founded on a person, the taints to be abandoned by seeing. Because that person is also the basis for the taints of sensual desire and so on—which have unwise attention as their cause and were mentioned in general terms thus: 'Bhikkhus, for one who attends unwisely, unarisen taints arise'—therefore, having shown those taints through that very person, now, while showing the taints to be abandoned by seeing, He says, 'He attends unwisely thus: "Was I indeed in the past?"' and so on. And here, He began this discourse to show the taint of views as well, with doubt as its head.

Tassattho, yassa te iminā vuttanayena āsavā uppajjanti, so puthujjano, yo cāyaṃ “assutavā”tiādinā nayena vutto, so puthujjano evaṃ ayoniso anupāyena uppathena manasi karoti. Kathaṃ? Ahosiṃ nu kho…pe…so kuhiṃ gāmī bhavissatīti. Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti, so evaṃ ayoniso manasi karoti, yathāssa “ahaṃ ahosiṃ nu kho”tiādinā nayena vuttā soḷasavidhāpi vicikicchā uppajjatīti.

The meaning of this is as follows: That ordinary person for whom those taints arise in the manner described—that is, the ordinary person who was spoken of in the way beginning 'uninstructed'—attends unwisely thus, by an improper means, by a wrong path. How? 'Was I indeed in the past?... Where will he be going?' What is meant by this? He attends unwisely in such a way that the sixteen kinds of doubt, spoken of in the way beginning 'Was I indeed in the past?', arise in him.

Tattha ahosiṃ nu kho nanu khoti sassatākārañca adhiccasamuppattiākārañca nissāya atīte attano vijjamānataṃ avijjamānatañca kaṅkhati. Kiṃ kāraṇanti na vattabbaṃ. Ummattako viya hi bālaputhujjano yathā vā tathā vā pavattati. Apica ayoniso manasikāroyevettha kāraṇaṃ. Evaṃ ayoniso manasikārassa pana kiṃ kāraṇanti. Sveva puthujjanabhāvo ariyānaṃ adassanādīni vā. Nanu ca puthujjanopi yoniso manasi karotīti. Ko vā evamāha na manasi karotīti. Na pana tattha puthujjanabhāvo kāraṇaṃ[P 1.0069], saddhammassavanakalyāṇamittādīni tattha kāraṇāni. Na hi macchamaṃsādīni attano attano pakatiyā sugandhāni, abhisaṅkhārapaccayā pana sugandhānipi honti.

Herein, regarding 'Was I indeed? Was I not indeed?', relying on the mode of eternalism and the mode of fortuitous origination, one doubts one's own existence and non-existence in the past. 'What is the reason for this?' It should not be asked. For the foolish ordinary person, like a madman, acts in any way whatsoever. Moreover, unwise attention is indeed the cause here. But what is the reason for such unwise attention? It is that very state of being an ordinary person, or not seeing the noble ones, and so on. 'But does not an ordinary person also attend wisely?' Who would say they do not attend wisely? However, the state of being an ordinary person is not the cause there; listening to the true Dhamma, good friends, and so on, are the causes there. For fish, meat, and so on, are not fragrant by their own nature, but they can become fragrant due to preparation.

Kiṃ [V 1.0075] nu kho ahosinti jātiliṅgūpapattiyo nissāya khattiyo nu kho ahosiṃ, brāhmaṇavessasuddagahaṭṭhapabbajitadevamanussānaṃ aññataroti kaṅkhati.

Regarding 'What was I indeed?', relying on birth, characteristic, or rebirth, one doubts: 'Was I a noble warrior? Or was I one among brahmins, merchants, laborers, householders, renunciants, gods, or humans?'

Kathaṃ nu khoti saṇṭhānākāraṃ nissāya dīgho nu kho ahosiṃ, rassaodātakaṇhappamāṇikaappamāṇikādīnaṃ aññataroti kaṅkhati. Keci pana issaranimmānādiṃ nissāya kena nu kho kāraṇena ahosinti hetuto kaṅkhatīti vadanti.

Regarding 'How was I indeed?', relying on the mode of physical form, one doubts: 'Was I tall, short, fair, dark, of limited or unlimited measure, or one of these?' Some, however, say that relying on creation by a lord or other such causes, one doubts as to the cause, wondering: 'By what reason, indeed, did I come to be?'

Kiṃ hutvā kiṃ ahosinti jātiādīni nissāya khattiyo hutvā nu kho brāhmaṇo ahosiṃ…pe… devo hutvā manussoti attano paramparaṃ kaṅkhati. Sabbattheva pana addhānanti kālādhivacanametaṃ.

Regarding 'Having been what, what was I?', relying on birth and so on, one doubts about one's own succession: 'Having been a noble warrior, was I a brahmin?... Having been a god, was I a human?' But everywhere, 'duration' is simply a designation for time.

Bhavissāmi [M 1.0072] nu kho nanu khoti sassatākārañca ucchedākārañca nissāya anāgate attano vijjamānataṃ avijjamānatañca kaṅkhati. Sesamettha vuttanayameva.

Regarding 'Will I indeed be? Will I not indeed be?', relying on the mode of eternalism and the mode of annihilationism, one doubts about one's own existence and non-existence in the future. The rest here is according to the method already stated.

Etarahi vā paccuppannamaddhānanti idāni vā paṭisandhiṃ ādiṃ katvā cutipariyantaṃ sabbampi vattamānakālaṃ gahetvā. Ajjhattaṃ kathaṃkathī hotīti attano khandhesu vicikiccho hoti. Ahaṃ nu khosmīti attano atthibhāvaṃ kaṅkhati. Yuttaṃ panetanti? Yuttaṃ ayuttanti kā ettha cintā. Apicettha idaṃ vatthumpi udāharanti. Cūḷamātāya kira putto muṇḍo, mahāmātāya putto amuṇḍo, taṃ puttaṃ muṇḍesuṃ. So uṭṭhāya ahaṃ nu kho cūḷamātāya puttoti cintesi. Evaṃ ahaṃ nu khosmīti kaṅkhā hoti.

Regarding 'Now or the present time': this means taking all the present time, beginning with relinking-consciousness up to the end at death. How is one doubtful internally? One is doubtful about one's own aggregates. Regarding 'Am I indeed?', one doubts one's own existence. But is this fitting? What consideration is there here of 'fitting' or 'unfitting'? Moreover, they also cite this story as an example. It is said that Cūḷamātā's son was shaven-headed, Mahāmātā's son was not shaven-headed, and they shaved that son. He, rising up, thought, 'Am I Cūḷamātā's son?' Thus, the doubt arises: 'Am I indeed?'

No nu khosmīti attano natthibhāvaṃ kaṅkhati. Tatrāpi idaṃ vatthu – eko kira macche gaṇhanto udake ciraṭṭhānena sītibhūtaṃ attano ūruṃ macchoti cintetvā pahari. Aparo susānapasse khettaṃ rakkhanto bhīto saṅkuṭito sayi. So paṭibujjhitvā attano jaṇṇukāni dve yakkhāti cintetvā pahari. Evaṃ no nu khosmīti kaṅkhati.

Regarding 'Am I not indeed?', one doubts one's own non-existence. In this regard, there is this story: It is said that a certain man, while catching fish, stood for a long time in the water, and his thigh became cold; thinking it was a fish, he struck it. Another man, guarding a field near a charnel ground, lay down curled up in fear. Awakening, he thought his own two knees were two yakkhas and struck them. Thus, one doubts, 'Am I not indeed?'

Kiṃ nu khosmīti khattiyova samāno attano khattiyabhāvaṃ kaṅkhati. Esa nayo sesesu. Devo [V 1.0076] pana samāno devabhāvaṃ ajānanto nāma natthi. Sopi pana “ahaṃ rūpī nu kho arūpī nu kho”tiādinā nayena kaṅkhati. Khattiyādayo kasmā na jānantīti ce. Apaccakkhā tesaṃ tattha tattha kule [P 1.0070] uppatti. Gahaṭṭhāpi ca potthalikādayo pabbajitasaññino. Pabbajitāpi “kuppaṃ nu kho me kamma”ntiādinā nayena gahaṭṭhasaññino. Manussāpi ca rājāno viya attani devasaññino honti.

Regarding 'What am I indeed?', even being a noble warrior, one doubts one's own status as a noble warrior. This principle applies to the rest. But there is no such thing as a god who, being a god, is unaware of his divine status. Yet even he may doubt by way of thinking, 'Am I with form or without form?' and so on. If it is asked, 'Why do noble warriors and others not know?' It is because their birth in this or that family is not directly perceived. And householders, like Potthalika and others, perceive themselves as renunciants. And renunciants, by way of thinking, 'Is my monastic act invalid?' and so on, perceive themselves as householders. And humans, like kings, perceive themselves as gods.

Kathaṃ nu khosmīti vuttanayameva. Kevalañcettha abbhantare jīvo nāma atthīti gahetvā tassa saṇṭhānākāraṃ nissāya dīgho nu khosmi, rassacaturaṃsachaḷaṃsaaṭṭhaṃsasoḷasaṃsādīnaṃ aññatarappakāroti kaṅkhanto kathaṃ nu khosmīti kaṅkhatīti veditabbo. Sarīrasaṇṭhānaṃ pana paccuppannaṃ ajānanto nāma natthi.

Regarding 'How am I indeed?', this is as stated before. Here, however, having grasped that 'there is something called a soul inside', and relying on its physical form and appearance, one who doubts 'Am I tall, short, square, hexagonal, octagonal, sixteen-sided, or of some other type?' doubts 'How am I indeed?'. This should be understood. However, there is no one who does not know the present shape of the body.
