Kuto [M 1.0073] āgato, so kuhiṃ gāmī bhavissatīti attabhāvassa āgatigatiṭṭhānaṃ kaṅkhati.

Regarding 'From where has he come? Where will he go?', one doubts the coming, going, and station of one's own existence.

19. Evaṃ soḷasappabhedaṃ vicikicchaṃ dassetvā idāni yaṃ iminā vicikicchāsīsena diṭṭhāsavaṃ dassetuṃ ayaṃ desanā āraddhā. Taṃ dassento tassa evaṃ ayoniso manasikaroto channaṃ diṭṭhīnantiādimāha. Tattha tassa puggalassa yathā ayaṃ vicikicchā uppajjati, evaṃ ayoniso manasikaroto tasseva savicikicchassa ayoniso manasikārassa thāmagatattā channaṃ diṭṭhīnaṃ aññatarā diṭṭhi uppajjatīti vuttaṃ hoti. Tattha sabbapadesu vāsaddo vikappattho, evaṃ vā evaṃ vā diṭṭhi uppajjatīti vuttaṃ hoti. Atthi me attāti cettha sassatadiṭṭhi sabbakālesu attano atthitaṃ gaṇhāti. Saccato thetatoti bhūtato ca thirato ca, “idaṃ sacca”nti bhūtato suṭṭhu daḷhabhāvenāti vuttaṃ hoti. Natthi me attāti ayaṃ pana ucchedadiṭṭhi, sato sattassa tattha tattha vibhavaggahaṇato. Atha vā purimāpi tīsu kālesu atthīti gahaṇato sassatadiṭṭhi, paccuppannameva atthīti gaṇhanto ucchedadiṭṭhi. Pacchimāpi atītānāgatesu natthīti gahaṇato bhasmantāhutiyoti gahitadiṭṭhikānaṃ viya, ucchedadiṭṭhi. Atīte eva natthīti gaṇhanto adhiccasamuppattikasseva sassatadiṭṭhi.

19. Having thus shown doubt with its sixteen divisions, this discourse is now undertaken to show the taint of views, which has this doubt as its basis. In showing that, He said, 'For one who attends unwisely thus, one of six views arises,' and so on. Herein, it is meant that for that person, just as this doubt arises, so for that very person who is possessed of doubt and attends unwisely, due to that unwise attention becoming strong, one of the six views arises. Herein, in all instances, the word 'vā' has the meaning of an alternative; it is meant that a view arises 'either in this way or in that way'. Regarding 'There is a self for me', herein the eternalist view grasps one's own existence in all times. 'As true, as firm' means as real and as stable; it is meant that one grasps 'this is true' as something real and with great firmness. 'There is no self for me', however, is the annihilationist view, from grasping the destruction of an existing being here and there. Alternatively, the former is the eternalist view because of grasping 'it exists' in the three times, while one who grasps 'it exists only in the present' holds the annihilationist view. The latter is also the annihilationist view, because of grasping 'it does not exist' in the past and future, like those who hold the view of being 'consumed in the offering of ashes'. One who grasps 'it did not exist in the past' holds an eternalist view, just like that of a fortuitous-originationist.

Attanāva attānaṃ sañjānāmīti saññākkhandhasīsena khandhe attāti gahetvā saññāya avasesakkhandhe [V 1.0077] sañjānato iminā attanā imaṃ attānaṃ sañjānāmīti hoti. Attanāva anattānanti saññākkhandhaṃyeva attāti gahetvā, itare cattāropi anattāti gahetvā saññāya tesaṃ jānato evaṃ hoti[P 1.0071]. Anattanāva attānanti saññākkhandhaṃ anattāti. Itare cattāro attāti gahetvā saññāya tesaṃ jānato evaṃ hoti, sabbāpi sassatucchedadiṭṭhiyova.

The view 'I perceive self by means of self' is as follows: taking the five aggregates as 'self' with the perception-aggregate as the chief, for one who perceives the remaining aggregates by means of perception, the view arises: 'By means of this self, I perceive this self.' The view 'I perceive not-self by means of self' is as follows: taking only the perception-aggregate as 'self' and taking the other four aggregates as 'not-self', for one who knows them by means of perception, this view arises. The view 'I perceive self by means of not-self' is as follows: taking the perception-aggregate as 'not-self' and taking the other four aggregates as 'self', for one who knows them by means of perception, this view arises. All these are indeed views of eternalism and annihilationism.

Vado vedeyyotiādayo pana sassatadiṭṭhiyā eva abhinivesākārā. Tattha vadatīti vado, vacīkammassa kārakoti vuttaṃ hoti. Vedayatīti vedeyyo, jānāti anubhavati cāti vuttaṃ hoti. Kiṃ vedetīti, tatra tatra kalyāṇapāpakānaṃ kammānaṃ vipākaṃ [M 1.0074] paṭisaṃvedeti. Tatra tatrāti tesu tesu yonigatiṭṭhitinivāsanikāyesu ārammaṇesu vā. Niccoti uppādavayarahito. Dhuvoti thiro sārabhūto. Sassatoti sabbakāliko. Avipariṇāmadhammoti attano pakatibhāvaṃ avijahanadhammo, kakaṇṭako viya nānappakārataṃ nāpajjati. Sassatisamanti candasūriyasamuddamahāpathavīpabbatā lokavohārena sassatiyoti vuccanti. Sassatīhi samaṃ sassatisamaṃ. Yāva sassatiyo tiṭṭhanti, tāva tatheva ṭhassatīti gaṇhato evaṃdiṭṭhi hoti.

As for such terms as 'the speaker' and 'the feeler,' they are expressions of adherence to the eternalist view. Therein, 'speaker' (vado) means one who speaks; this is said to mean the agent of verbal action. 'Feeler' (vedeyyo) means one who feels; this is said to mean one who knows and experiences. What does one feel? One experiences the result of good and bad kamma in various existences. 'In various existences' (tatra tatra) means in those various wombs, destinations, stations of consciousness, abodes, and classes of beings, or in various sense-objects. 'Permanent' (nicco) means devoid of arising and passing away. 'Stable' (dhuvo) means firm, substantial. 'Eternal' (sassato) means existing at all times. 'Unchanging in nature' (avipariṇāmadhammo) means having the nature of not abandoning its own intrinsic state; like a chameleon, it does not undergo various changes. 'Like unto the eternal' (sassatisamaṃ) means: the moon, sun, ocean, great earth, and mountains are, by worldly convention, called 'long-lasting' (sassatiyo). 'Like unto the eternal' means equal to these long-lasting things. For one who holds the view, 'For as long as these long-lasting things stand, so long will it stand in the very same way,' this view arises.

Idaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, diṭṭhigatantiādīsu. Idanti idāni vattabbassa paccakkhanidassanaṃ. Diṭṭhigatasambandhena ca idanti vuttaṃ, na diṭṭhisambandhena. Ettha ca diṭṭhiyeva diṭṭhigataṃ, gūthagataṃ viya. Diṭṭhīsu vā gatamidaṃ dassanaṃ dvāsaṭṭhidiṭṭhiantogadhattātipi diṭṭhigataṃ. Diṭṭhiyā vā gataṃ diṭṭhigataṃ. Idañhi atthi me attātiādi diṭṭhiyā gamanamattameva, natthettha attā vā nicco vā kocīti vuttaṃ hoti. Sā cāyaṃ diṭṭhi dunniggamanaṭṭhena gahanaṃ. Duratikkamaṭṭhena sappaṭibhayaṭṭhena ca kantāro, dubbhikkhakantāravāḷakantārādayo viya. Sammādiṭṭhiyā vinivijjhanaṭṭhena vilomanaṭṭhena vā visūkaṃ. Kadāci sassatassa, kadāci ucchedassa gahaṇato virūpaṃ phanditanti vipphanditaṃ. Bandhanaṭṭhena saṃyojanaṃ. Tenāha “diṭṭhigahanaṃ…pe… diṭṭhisaṃyojana”nti. Idānissa tameva bandhanatthaṃ dassento diṭṭhisaṃyojanasaṃyuttotiādimāha. Tassāyaṃ saṅkhepattho. Iminā diṭṭhisaṃyojanena saṃyutto puthujjano etehi jātiādīhi na parimuccatīti. Kiṃ vā bahunā, sakalavaṭṭadukkhatopi na muccatīti.

In such passages as, 'This, bhikkhus, is called a holding of a view...' Herein, 'this' (idaṃ) is a direct indication of what is now to be spoken of. And it is said as 'this' in connection with what is related to the holding of a view, not in connection with the view itself. And here, the view itself is the 'holding of a view' (diṭṭhigataṃ), like a receptacle of filth (gūthagataṃ). Or, this seeing has 'gone into' (gataṃ) the views, because it is included within the sixty-two views; therefore, it is a 'holding of a view'. Or, 'holding of a view' is the mere process of a view. For this view, such as 'I have a self,' is merely the process of the view; it is meant that herein there is no self or anything permanent. And this view is a 'thicket' (gahanaṃ) in the sense of being hard to escape from. It is a 'wilderness' (kantāro) in the sense of being hard to cross and perilous, like a wilderness of famine or a wilderness of wild beasts. It is a 'contortion' (visūkaṃ) because it must be pierced by right view, or because it is contrary. Because of grasping sometimes at eternalism and sometimes at annihilationism, it is a 'perverse agitation' (virūpaṃ phanditaṃ), hence it is called 'agitation' (vipphanditaṃ). It is a 'fetter' (saṃyojanaṃ) in the sense of binding. Therefore, He said, 'the thicket of views... the fetter of views.' Now, showing that very sense of binding, He said, 'conjoined with the fetter of views,' etc. This is its concise meaning: A worldling conjoined with this fetter of views is not freed from birth and so on. Or, what need is there to say much? One is not freed from the entire suffering of the round of existence.

20. Evaṃ [V 1.0078][P 1.0072] chappabhedaṃ diṭṭhāsavaṃ dassetvā yasmā sīlabbataparāmāso kāmāsavādivacaneneva dassito hoti. Kāmasukhatthañhi bhavasukhabhavavisuddhiatthañca avijjāya abhibhūtā ito bahiddhā samaṇabrāhmaṇā sīlabbatāni parāmasanti, tasmā taṃ adassetvā diṭṭhiggahaṇena vā tassa gahitattāpi taṃ adassetvāva idāni yo puggalo dassanā pahātabbe āsave pajahati, taṃ dassetvā tesaṃ āsavānaṃ pahānaṃ dassetuṃ [M 1.0075] pubbe vā ayoniso manasikaroto puthujjanassa tesaṃ uppattiṃ dassetvā idāni tabbiparītassa pahānaṃ dassetuṃ sutavā ca kho, bhikkhavetiādimāha.

20. Having thus shown the taint of views with its six divisions, the clinging to rites and rituals is not shown separately, because it is already indicated by the terms 'taint of sensual desire,' and so on. For, ascetics and brahmins outside this Dispensation, overwhelmed by ignorance, cling to rites and rituals for the sake of sensual pleasure, and for the sake of pleasure in existence and purification from existence. Therefore, without showing it separately—or because it is also included by the taking up of 'view'—He now speaks. He does so either to show the abandoning of those taints that are to be abandoned by seeing, after having indicated the person who abandons them; or, having previously shown the arising of those taints in a worldling who attends unwisely, to now show their abandoning by one who is the opposite of that. Thus He said: 'And the learned noble disciple, O bhikkhus,' etc.

Tassattho, yāva “so idaṃ dukkha”nti āgacchati, tāva heṭṭhā vuttanayena ca vuttapaccanīkato ca veditabbo. Paccanīkato ca sabbākārena ariyadhammassa akovidāvinītapaccanīkato ayaṃ “sutavā ariyasāvako ariyadhammassa kovido ariyadhamme suvinīto”ti veditabbo. Apica kho sikhāpattavipassanato pabhuti yāva gotrabhu, tāva tadanurūpena atthena ayaṃ ariyasāvakoti veditabbo.

Its meaning, up to the point where the text says, ‘He… this is suffering,’ should be understood by the method stated below and by way of its opposite. By way of its opposite: in contrast to one who is in every way unskilled and undisciplined in the noble Dhamma, this one should be understood as ‘the learned noble disciple, skilled in the noble Dhamma, well-disciplined in the noble Dhamma.’ Moreover, from the insight of equanimity towards formations which has reached its peak, up to the change-of-lineage knowledge, this one should be understood as a ‘noble disciple’ in a sense corresponding to that stage.

21. “So idaṃ dukkhanti yoniso manasi karotī”tiādīsu pana ayaṃ atthavibhāvanā, so catusaccakammaṭṭhāniko ariyasāvako taṇhāvajjā tebhūmakā khandhā dukkhaṃ, taṇhā dukkhasamudayo, ubhinnaṃ appavatti nirodho, nirodhasampāpako maggoti evaṃ pubbeva ācariyasantike uggahitacatusaccakammaṭṭhāno aparena samayena vipassanāmaggaṃ samāruḷho samāno te tebhūmake khandhe idaṃ dukkhanti yoniso manasi karoti, upāyena pathena samannāharati ceva vipassati ca. Ettha hi yāva sotāpattimaggo, tāva manasikārasīseneva vipassanā vuttā. Yā panāyaṃ tasseva dukkhassa samuṭṭhāpikā pabhāvikā taṇhā, ayaṃ samudayoti yoniso manasi karoti. Yasmā pana dukkhañca samudayo ca idaṃ ṭhānaṃ patvā nirujjhanti nappavattanti, tasmā yadidaṃ nibbānaṃ nāma, ayaṃ dukkhanirodhoti yoniso manasi karoti. Nirodhasampāpakaṃ aṭṭhaṅgikaṃ maggaṃ ayaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadāti yoniso manasi karoti, upāyena pathena samannāharati ceva vipassati ca.

21. In such passages as, ‘He wisely attends: “This is suffering,”’ this is the explanation of the meaning: A noble disciple, a practitioner of the meditation on the four truths, having previously learned from a teacher the meditation subject of the four truths thus—‘The aggregates belonging to the three planes, excluding craving, are suffering; craving is the origin of suffering; the non-occurrence of both is cessation; the path is what leads to cessation’—at a later time, having ascended the path of insight, wisely attends to those aggregates belonging to the three planes: ‘This is suffering.’ He reflects and sees with insight by the proper means, by the right path. For herein, up to the path of stream-entry, insight is spoken of with attention as its chief component. And as for that craving which originates and produces that very suffering, he wisely attends: ‘This is the origin.’ And because both suffering and its origin, having reached this state, cease and do not proceed, therefore, as to that which is called Nibbāna, he wisely attends: ‘This is the cessation of suffering.’ Regarding the eightfold path that leads to cessation, he wisely attends: ‘This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.’ He reflects and sees with insight by the proper means, by the right path.

Tatrāyaṃ [P 1.0073] upāyo, abhiniveso nāma vaṭṭe hoti, vivaṭṭe natthi. Tasmā “ayaṃ atthi imasmiṃ [V 1.0079] kāye pathavīdhātu, āpodhātū”tiādinā nayena sakasantatiyaṃ cattāri bhūtāni tadanusārena upādārūpāni ca pariggahetvā ayaṃ rūpakkhandhoti vavatthapeti. Taṃ vavatthāpayato uppanne tadārammaṇe cittacetasike dhamme ime cattāro arūpakkhandhāti vavatthapeti. Tato ime pañcakkhandhā dukkhanti vavatthapeti. Te pana saṅkhepato [M 1.0076] nāmañca rūpañcāti dve bhāgāyeva honti. Idañca nāmarūpaṃ sahetu sappaccayaṃ uppajjati. Tassa ayaṃ hetu ayaṃ paccayoti avijjābhavataṇhākammāhārādike hetupaccaye vavatthapeti. Tato tesaṃ paccayānañca paccayuppannadhammānañca yāthāvasarasalakkhaṇaṃ vavatthapetvā ime dhammā ahutvā hontīti aniccalakkhaṇaṃ āropeti, udayabbayapīḷitattā dukkhāti dukkhalakkhaṇaṃ āropeti. Avasavattanato anattāti anattalakkhaṇaṃ āropeti. Evaṃ tīṇi lakkhaṇāni āropetvā paṭipāṭiyā vipassanaṃ pavattento sotāpattimaggaṃ pāpuṇāti.

Herein, this is the method: this mental application exists in the round of existence; it does not exist in the unbinding from the round. Therefore, by the method beginning with, ‘In this body there is the earth element, the water element,’ having comprehended in his own continuity the four great elements and, in accordance with them, the derived forms, he determines: ‘This is the aggregate of form.’ For him who is determining that, when consciousness and mental factors having that as their object have arisen, he determines: ‘These are the four formless aggregates.’ Then, he determines: ‘These five aggregates are suffering.’ And they, in brief, are just two parts: name and form. And this name-and-form arises with a generative cause and with a supporting condition. He determines the generative and supporting conditions, such as ignorance, becoming, craving, kamma, and nutriment, thus: ‘This is its generative cause; this is its supporting condition.’ Then, having determined the unfailing functional characteristic of those conditions and of the conditionally arisen phenomena, he ascribes the characteristic of impermanence, thus: ‘These phenomena, not having been, come to be.’ Because of being oppressed by arising and passing away, he ascribes the characteristic of suffering, thus: ‘It is suffering.’ Because it does not occur according to one’s will, he ascribes the characteristic of not-self, thus: ‘It is not-self.’ Having thus ascribed the three characteristics, developing insight in due order, he attains the path of stream-entry.

Tasmiṃ khaṇe cattāri saccāni ekapaṭivedheneva paṭivijjhati, ekābhisamayena abhisameti. Dukkhaṃ pariññāpaṭivedhena paṭivijjhati, samudayaṃ pahānapaṭivedhena, nirodhaṃ sacchikiriyāpaṭivedhena, maggaṃ bhāvanāpaṭivedhena. Dukkhañca pariññābhisamayena abhisameti…pe… maggaṃ bhāvanābhisamayena abhisameti, no ca kho aññamaññena ñāṇena. Ekañāṇeneva hi esa nirodhaṃ ārammaṇato, sesāni kiccato paṭivijjhati ceva abhisameti ca. Na hissa tasmiṃ samaye evaṃ hoti – “ahaṃ dukkhaṃ parijānāmī”ti vā…pe… “maggaṃ bhāvemī”ti vā. Apica khvassa ārammaṇaṃ katvā paṭivedhavasena nirodhaṃ sacchikaroto evaṃ taṃ ñāṇaṃ dukkhapariññākiccampi samudayapahānakiccampi maggabhāvanākiccampi karotiyeva. Tassevaṃ upāyena yoniso manasikaroto tīṇi saṃyojanāni pahīyanti, vīsativatthukā sakkāyadiṭṭhi, aṭṭhavatthukā vicikicchā, “sīlena suddhi vatena suddhī”ti sīlabbatānaṃ parāmasanato sīlabbataparāmāsoti. Tattha catūsu āsavesu sakkāyadiṭṭhisīlabbataparāmāsā diṭṭhāsavena saṅgahitattā āsavā ceva saṃyojanā ca. Vicikicchā saṃyojanameva, na āsavo[P 1.0074]. “Dassanā pahātabbā āsavā”ti ettha pariyāpannattā pana āsavāti.

At that moment, he penetrates the four truths with a single penetration and comprehends them with a single comprehension. He penetrates suffering with the penetration of full understanding, the origin with the penetration of abandoning, cessation with the penetration of realization, and the path with the penetration of development. And he comprehends suffering with the comprehension of full understanding… and so on… he comprehends the path with the comprehension of development, but not by different knowledges. For it is by a single knowledge that this yogī penetrates and comprehends cessation by way of object, and the remaining truths by way of function. Indeed, at that time it does not occur to him thus: ‘I am fully understanding suffering’… or ‘I am developing the path.’ Rather, for him who is realizing cessation by making it the object by means of penetration, that very knowledge performs the function of fully understanding suffering, the function of abandoning the origin, and the function of developing the path. For him who thus attends wisely by this method, three fetters are abandoned: the identity-view with its twenty grounds, doubt with its eight grounds, and the grasping of precepts and practices, which arises from misapprehending that ‘purity is through precepts’ or ‘purity is through practices.’ Therein, among the four taints, identity-view and the grasping of precepts and practices, being included in the taint of views, are both taints and fetters. Doubt is only a fetter, not a taint. However, because it is included in the phrase ‘taints to be abandoned by seeing,’ it is also called a taint.

“Ime vuccanti…pe… pahātabbā”ti ime sakkāyadiṭṭhiādayo dassanā pahātabbā nāma [V 1.0080] āsavāti dassento āha. Atha vā yā ayaṃ channaṃ diṭṭhīnaṃ aññatarā diṭṭhi uppajjatīti evaṃ sarūpeneva sakkāyadiṭṭhi vibhattā. Taṃ sandhāyāha “ime vuccanti, bhikkhave”ti. Sā ca yasmā sahajātapahānekaṭṭhehi saddhiṃ pahīyati. Diṭṭhāsave hi pahīyamāne taṃsahajāto catūsu diṭṭhisampayuttacittesu kāmāsavopi avijjāsavopi pahīyati[M 1.0077]. Pahānekaṭṭho pana catūsu diṭṭhivippayuttesu nāgasupaṇṇādisamiddhipatthanāvasena uppajjamāno bhavāsavo. Teneva sampayutto avijjāsavopi, dvīsu domanassacittesu pāṇātipātādinibbattako avijjāsavopi, tathā vicikicchācittasampayutto avijjāsavopīti evaṃ sabbathāpi avasesā tayopi āsavā pahīyanti. Tasmā bahuvacananiddeso katoti evamettha attho veditabbo. Esa porāṇānaṃ adhippāyo.

The Blessed One said, 'These are called... to be abandoned,' showing that these, beginning with identity-view, are called the taints to be abandoned by seeing. Alternatively, identity-view was analyzed simply by its own nature in this way: 'Whichever of the six views arises...' Referring to that, He said, 'These are called, O bhikkhus.' And since that view is abandoned together with what is co-arisen and what is abandoned at the same time: indeed, when the taint of views is being abandoned, the taint of sensual pleasures and the taint of ignorance that are co-arisen with it in the four consciousnesses associated with views are also abandoned. And, abandoned at the same time is the taint of becoming, which arises in the four consciousnesses dissociated from views by way of aspiring for the prosperity of nāgas, supaṇṇas, and so on. The taint of ignorance associated with that is also abandoned; and the taint of ignorance that produces the killing of living beings, etc., in the two consciousnesses accompanied by displeasure; and likewise the taint of ignorance associated with the consciousness of doubt. Thus, in every way, the remaining three taints are also abandoned. Therefore, the designation in the plural was made. Thus should the meaning here be understood. This is the intention of the ancient commentators.

Dassanā pahātabbāti dassanaṃ nāma sotāpattimaggo, tena pahātabbāti attho. Kasmā sotāpattimaggo dassanaṃ? Paṭhamaṃ nibbānadassanato. Nanu gotrabhu paṭhamataraṃ passatīti? No na passati. Disvā kattabbakiccaṃ pana na karoti saṃyojanānaṃ appahānato. Tasmā passatīti na vattabbo. Yattha katthaci rājānaṃ disvāpi paṇṇākāraṃ datvā kiccanipphattiyā adiṭṭhattā “ajjāpi rājānaṃ na passāmī”ti vadanto gāmavāsī puriso cettha nidassanaṃ.

'To be abandoned by seeing': 'seeing' is the name for the path of stream-entry; the meaning is 'to be abandoned by that.' Why is the path of stream-entry called 'seeing'? Because of seeing Nibbāna for the first time. But does not the change-of-lineage consciousness see it even before? Is it that it does not see? No, it does indeed see. However, having seen, it does not perform the task that should be done, because the fetters are not abandoned. Therefore, it should not be said that it 'sees.' Herein, the illustration is a village man who, though he has seen the king somewhere or other and has given a gift, because he was not granted an audience for the accomplishment of his business, says, 'I still have not seen the king.'

Dassanāpahātabbaāsavavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The exposition of the taints to be abandoned by seeing is concluded.

Saṃvarāpahātabbaāsavavaṇṇanā

The Exposition on the Taints to be Abandoned by Restraint.

22. Evaṃ dassanena pahātabbe āsave dassetvā idāni tadanantaruddiṭṭhe saṃvarā pahātabbe dassetuṃ, katame ca, bhikkhave, āsavā saṃvarā pahātabbāti āha. Evaṃ sabbattha sambandho veditabbo. Ito parañhi atthamattameva vaṇṇayissāma.

Thus, having shown the taints to be abandoned by seeing, now, in order to show the taints to be abandoned by restraint which were pointed out immediately after those, He said: 'And which, O bhikkhus, are the taints to be abandoned by restraint?' In this way, the connection should be understood in all instances. From here on, we shall explain only the meaning.

Nanu ca dassanena bhāvanāyāti imehi dvīhi appahātabbo āsavo nāma natthi, atha kasmā visuṃ saṃvarādīhi pahātabbe dassetīti. Saṃvarādīhi pubbabhāge vikkhambhitā āsavā catūhi maggehi samugghātaṃ gacchanti, tasmā tesaṃ maggānaṃ pubbabhāge imehi pañcahākārehi vikkhambhanappahānaṃ [V 1.0081][P 1.0075] dassento evamāha. Tasmā yo cāyaṃ vutto paṭhamo dassanamaggoyeva, idāni bhāvanānāmena vuccissanti tayo maggā, tesaṃ sabbesampi ayaṃ pubbabhāgapaṭipadāti veditabbā.

Is it not so that there is no taint whatsoever that is not to be abandoned by these two, that is, by seeing and by cultivation? If so, why then does He separately show taints to be abandoned by restraint and so on? Because the taints suppressed in the preliminary stage by restraint and so on are eradicated by the four paths, He spoke thus in order to show the abandonment by suppression in these five ways in the preliminary stage of those paths. Therefore, that which was spoken of as the first is the path of seeing itself; now the three paths will be spoken of by the name 'cultivation.' This should be understood as the preliminary practice for all of those paths.

Tattha [M 1.0078] idhāti imasmiṃ sāsane. Paṭisaṅkhāti paṭisaṅkhāya. Tatthāyaṃ saṅkhāsaddo ñāṇakoṭṭhāsapaññattigaṇanāsu dissati. “Saṅkhāyekaṃ paṭisevatī”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 2.168) hi ñāṇe dissati. “Papañcasaññāsaṅkhā samudācarantī”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.201) koṭṭhāse. “Tesaṃ tesaṃ dhammānaṃ saṅkhā samaññā”tiādīsu (dha. sa. 1313) paññattiyaṃ. “Na sukaraṃ saṅkhātu”ntiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 2.128) gaṇanāyaṃ. Idha pana ñāṇe daṭṭhabbo.

22. Therein, 'here' means in this Dispensation. 'Paṭisaṅkhā' means 'having reflected.' Therein, this word 'saṅkhā' is seen in the senses of knowledge, category, designation, and enumeration. For in such phrases as, 'Having reflected, one makes use of a thing,' it is seen in the sense of knowledge. In such phrases as, 'Perceptions and categories of proliferation arise,' it is seen in the sense of category. In such phrases as, 'The category, the designation for these various things,' it is seen in the sense of designation. In such phrases as, 'It is not easy to count,' it is seen in the sense of enumeration. Here, however, it should be understood in the sense of knowledge.

Paṭisaṅkhā yonisoti hi upāyena pathena paṭisaṅkhāya ñatvā paccavekkhitvāti attho. Ettha ca asaṃvare ādīnavapaṭisaṅkhā yoniso paṭisaṅkhāti veditabbā. Sā cāyaṃ “varaṃ, bhikkhave, tattāya ayosalākāya ādittāya sampajjalitāya sajotibhūtāya cakkhundriyaṃ sampalimaṭṭhaṃ, na tveva cakkhuviññeyyesu rūpesu anubyañjanaso nimittaggāho”tiādinā (saṃ. ni. 4.235) ādittapariyāyanayena veditabbā. Cakkhundriyasaṃvarasaṃvuto viharatīti ettha cakkhumeva indriyaṃ cakkhundriyaṃ, saṃvaraṇato saṃvaro, pidahanato thakanatoti vuttaṃ hoti. Satiyā etaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Cakkhundriye saṃvaro cakkhundriyasaṃvaro. Titthakāko āvāṭakacchapo vanamahiṃsotiādayo viya.

Indeed, 'reflecting wisely' means having reflected, known, and reviewed by a proper means, by a path. And here, 'wise reflection' should be understood as the reflection on the danger in non-restraint. And this should be understood by way of the Discourse on Burning, which begins: 'Better it is, O bhikkhus, for the eye faculty to be swept with a heated iron rod, blazing, burning, and glowing, than that there should be the grasping of signs and features in forms cognizable by the eye.' In the phrase 'dwells restrained with the restraint of the eye faculty,' the eye itself is the faculty, hence 'eye faculty.' 'Restraint' (saṃvara) is so-called from 'restraining' (saṃvaraṇa); it means closing or obstructing. This is a synonym for mindfulness. Restraint in the eye faculty is 'eye-faculty-restraint,' similar to compounds like 'a crow on the bank,' 'a turtle in a pit,' or 'a buffalo in the forest.'

Tattha kiñcāpi cakkhundriye saṃvaro vā asaṃvaro vā natthi. Na hi cakkhupasādaṃ nissāya sati vā muṭṭhasaccaṃ vā uppajjati. Apica yadā rūpārammaṇaṃ cakkhussa āpāthaṃ āgacchati, tadā bhavaṅge dvikkhattuṃ uppajjitvā niruddhe kiriyamanodhātu āvajjanakiccaṃ sādhayamānā uppajjitvā nirujjhati, tato cakkhuviññāṇaṃ dassanakiccaṃ, tato vipākamanodhātu sampaṭicchanakiccaṃ, tato vipākāhetukamanoviññāṇadhātu santīraṇakiccaṃ, tato kiriyāhetukamanoviññāṇadhātu voṭṭhabbanakiccaṃ sādhayamānā uppajjitvā nirujjhati. Tadanantaraṃ javanaṃ javati.

Therein, although in the eye faculty itself there is neither restraint nor non-restraint. For neither mindfulness nor unmindfulness arises dependent on the eye-sensitivity. Moreover, when a form-object comes into the range of the eye, then, after the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) has arisen twice and ceased, the functional mind-element, accomplishing the function of adverting, arises and ceases. After that, eye-consciousness accomplishes the function of seeing; then the resultant mind-element accomplishes the function of receiving; then the resultant rootless mind-consciousness-element accomplishes the function of investigating; then the functional rootless mind-consciousness-element, accomplishing the function of determining, arises and ceases. Immediately after that, the impulsion (javana) runs.

Tatthapi [V 1.0082] neva bhavaṅgasamaye, na āvajjanādīnaṃ aññatarasamaye saṃvaro vā asaṃvaro vā atthi. Javanakkhaṇe pana sace dussīlyaṃ [P 1.0076] vā muṭṭhasaccaṃ vā aññāṇaṃ vā akkhanti vā kosajjaṃ vā uppajjati, ayaṃ asaṃvaro hoti. Evaṃ hontopi so cakkhundriye asaṃvaroti vuccati. Kasmā? Tasmiñhi sati dvārampi aguttaṃ hoti, bhavaṅgampi āvajjanādīni vīthicittānipi. Yathā kiṃ[M 1.0079], yathā nagare catūsu dvāresu asaṃvutesu kiñcāpi anto gharakoṭṭhakagabbhādayo susaṃvutā, tathāpi antonagare sabbaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ arakkhitaṃ agopitameva hoti. Nagaradvārena hi pavisitvā corā yadicchanti, taṃ kareyyuṃ, evameva javane dussīlyādīsu uppannesu, tasmiṃ asaṃvare sati dvārampi aguttaṃ hoti, bhavaṅgampi āvajjanādīni vīthicittānipīti.

Therein, there is neither restraint nor non-restraint at the time of the life-continuum, nor at the time of any of the others beginning with adverting. But at the moment of impulsion, if immorality, unmindfulness, ignorance, intolerance, or laziness arises, this is non-restraint. Even though it occurs thus, it is called 'non-restraint in the eye faculty.' Why? Because when that is present, the door is unguarded, as are the life-continuum and the process-consciousnesses beginning with adverting. It is like what? Just as in a city where the four gates are not secured, although the houses, storerooms, and chambers within are well-secured, still all the goods inside the city are unprotected and unguarded. For thieves, having entered by the city gate, could do whatever they wish. In the very same way, when immorality and so on have arisen in the impulsion, when that non-restraint is present, the door is unguarded, as are the life-continuum and the process-consciousnesses beginning with adverting.

Tasmiṃ pana sīlādīsu uppannesu dvārampi guttaṃ hoti, bhavaṅgampi āvajjanādīni vīthicittānipi. Yathā kiṃ? Yathā nagaradvāresu susaṃvutesu kiñcāpi anto gharādayo asaṃvutā, tathāpi antonagare sabbaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ surakkhitaṃ sugopitameva hoti. Nagaradvāresu hi pihitesu corānaṃ paveso natthi, evameva javane sīlādīsu uppannesu dvārampi suguttaṃ hoti, bhavaṅgampi āvajjanādīni vīthicittānipi. Tasmā javanakkhaṇe uppajjamānopi cakkhundriye saṃvaroti vutto. Idha cāyaṃ satisaṃvaro adhippetoti veditabbo. Cakkhundriyasaṃvarena saṃvuto cakkhundriyasaṃvarasaṃvuto, upetoti vuttaṃ hoti. Tathā hi, pātimokkhasaṃvarasaṃvutoti imassa vibhaṅge “iminā pātimokkhasaṃvarena upeto hoti…pe… samannāgato”ti (vibha. 511) vuttaṃ. Taṃ ekajjhaṃ katvā cakkhundriyasaṃvarena saṃvutoti evamattho veditabbo.

But when virtue and so on have arisen in that impulsion, the door is guarded, as are the life-continuum and the process-consciousnesses beginning with adverting. It is like what? Just as when the city gates are well-secured, although the houses and so on within are not secured, still all the goods inside the city are well-protected and secure. For when the city gates are closed, there is no entry for thieves. In the very same way, when virtue and so on have arisen in the impulsion, the door is well-guarded, as are the life-continuum and the process-consciousnesses beginning with adverting. Therefore, although it arises at the moment of impulsion, it is called 'restraint in the eye faculty.' And here, it should be understood that this restraint by mindfulness is intended. 'Restrained by the restraint of the eye faculty' (cakkhundriyasaṃvarasaṃvuto) means one is endowed with it. For so it is said in the analysis of 'restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha': 'He is endowed with this restraint of the Pātimokkha... possessed of it.' Combining these, the meaning should be understood as 'restrained by the restraint of the eye faculty.'

Atha vā saṃvarīti saṃvuto, thakesi pidahīti vuttaṃ hoti. Cakkhundriye saṃvarasaṃvuto cakkhundriyasaṃvarasaṃvuto, cakkhundriyasaṃvarasaññitaṃ satikavāṭaṃ cakkhudvāre, gharadvāre kavāṭaṃ viya saṃvari thakesi pidahīti vuttaṃ hoti. Ayameva cettha attho sundarataro. Tathā hi “cakkhundriyasaṃvaraṃ asaṃvutassa viharato saṃvutassa viharato”ti etesu padesu ayameva attho dissati.

Alternatively, `saṃvuto` means 'restrained' because one has restrained (`saṃvari`); this means 'one has closed, one has shut.' `Cakkhundriyasaṃvarasaṃvuto` means one has restrained the restraint in the eye faculty; this is to say that one has restrained, closed, and shut the door-leaf of mindfulness, known as 'the restraint of the eye faculty,' at the eye-door, just as one closes a door-leaf at a house door. And this very meaning is more excellent here. For indeed, in these passages—'for one dwelling unrestrained in the restraint of the eye faculty' and 'for one dwelling restrained'—this very meaning is seen.

Viharatīti evaṃ cakkhundriyasaṃvarasaṃvuto yena kenaci iriyāpathavihārena viharati. Yañhissātiādimhi [V 1.0083][P 1.0077] yaṃ cakkhundriyasaṃvaraṃ assa bhikkhuno asaṃvutassa athaketvā apidahitvā viharantassāti evamattho veditabbo. Atha vā, ye-kārassa yanti ādeso. Hikāro ca padapūraṇo, ye assāti attho.

'He dwells' means: thus, a monk restrained with the restraint of the eye faculty dwells in any posture whatsoever. In the phrase beginning with `yañhissa`, the meaning should be understood as: 'whatever restraint of the eye faculty for that monk who dwells unrestrained, not having closed it, not having shut it.' Alternatively, `yaṃ` is a substitute for the letter `ye`, and the particle `hi` is merely an expletive; the meaning is `ye assa`.

Uppajjeyyunti [M 1.0080] nibbatteyyuṃ. Āsavā vighātapariḷāhāti cattāro āsavā ca aññe ca vighātakarā kilesapariḷāhā vipākapariḷāhā ca. Cakkhudvāre hi iṭṭhārammaṇaṃ āpāthagataṃ kāmassādavasena assādayato abhinandato kāmāsavo uppajjati, īdisaṃ aññasmimpi sugatibhave labhissāmīti bhavapatthanāya assādayato bhavāsavo uppajjati, sattoti vā sattassāti vā gaṇhantassa diṭṭhāsavo uppajjati, sabbeheva sahajātaṃ aññāṇaṃ avijjāsavoti cattāro āsavā uppajjanti. Tehi sampayuttā apare kilesā vighātapariḷāhā, āyatiṃ vā tesaṃ vipākā. Tepi hi asaṃvutasseva viharato uppajjeyyunti vuccanti.

'They would arise' means they would be produced. 'Taints, distresses, and fevers' refers to the four taints, as well as other fevers that cause distress, namely, the fevers of defilements and the fevers that are their results. For when a pleasant object comes into range at the eye-door, and one savors it with the taste of sensual desire, delighting in it, the taint of sensual desire arises. When one savors it with the thought, 'I will obtain such a thing in another happy existence,' aspiring for continued existence, the taint of existence arises. When one grasps it with the notion of 'a being' or 'belonging to a being,' the taint of views arises. The ignorance co-arisen with all of these is the taint of ignorance—thus, the four taints arise. Associated with them are other defilements that are distresses and fevers, or in the future, their results. These too, it is said, would arise for one who dwells unrestrained.

Evaṃsa teti evaṃ assa te. Evaṃ etena upāyena na honti, no aññathāti vuttaṃ hoti. Esa nayo paṭisaṅkhā yoniso sotindriyasaṃvarasaṃvutotiādīsu.

The phrase `evaṃsa te` is to be divided as `evaṃ assa te`. This means: 'Thus, by this method, they do not arise for him; not otherwise.' This same method applies in the passages beginning with 'reflecting wisely, he is restrained with the restraint of the ear faculty.'

Ime vuccanti, bhikkhave, āsavā saṃvarā pahātabbāti ime chasu dvāresu cattāro cattāro katvā catuvīsati āsavā saṃvarena pahātabbāti vuccanti. Sabbattheva cettha satisaṃvaro eva saṃvaroti veditabbo.

'These, monks, are called the taints to be abandoned by restraint' means: these twenty-four taints, making four for each of the six doors, are said to be 'abandoned by restraint.' And in all these cases, it should be understood that the restraint of mindfulness itself is 'restraint.'

Saṃvarāpahātabbaāsavavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the taints to be abandoned by restraint is concluded.

Paṭisevanāpahātabbaāsavavaṇṇanā

The Exposition on the Taints to be Abandoned by Using

23. Paṭisaṅkhā yoniso cīvarantiādīsu yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ sabbaṃ visuddhimagge sīlakathāyaṃ vuttameva. Yañhissāti yaṃ cīvarapiṇḍapātādīsu vā aññataraṃ assa. Appaṭisevatoti evaṃ yoniso appaṭisevantassa. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva. Kevalaṃ panidha aladdhaṃ cīvarādiṃ patthayato laddhaṃ vā [V 1.0084] assādayato kāmāsavassa uppatti veditabbā. Īdisaṃ aññasmimpi sampattibhave sugatibhave labhissāmīti bhavapatthanāya assādayato bhavāsavassa, ahaṃ labhāmi na labhāmīti vā mayhaṃ vā idanti attasaññaṃ adhiṭṭhahato diṭṭhāsavassa uppatti veditabbā. Sabbeheva pana sahajāto avijjāsavoti evaṃ catunnaṃ āsavānaṃ uppatti vipākapariḷāhā ca navavedanuppādanatopi veditabbā.

23. Regarding passages such as, 'reflecting wisely on the robe,' whatever is to be said, all of that has already been said in the Visuddhimagga, in the discourse on virtue. As for `yañhissa`, it means 'whatever requisite there might be,' whether it is one among robes, alms-food, and so on. As for `appaṭisevato`, it means 'for one who does not use them in this way, with wise reflection.' The remainder is in the manner already stated. However, here in this section on using, for one who longs for requisites such as robes that have not yet been obtained, or for one who savors what has been obtained, the arising of the taint of sensual desire is to be known. For one who savors with a longing for existence, thinking, 'I shall obtain such excellent requisites in another prosperous existence or a good destination,' the arising of the taint of existence is to be known. For one who establishes the perception of self, thinking, 'I obtain,' or 'I do not obtain,' or 'This is my property,' the arising of the taint of views is to be known. However, the ignorance that is co-nascent with all of these is the taint of ignorance. Thus, the arising of the four taints, the fevers of their results, and the production of new feelings are to be known.

Ime [M 1.0081] vuccanti, bhikkhave, āsavā paṭisevanā pahātabbāti ime ekamekasmiṃ paccaye [P 1.0078] cattāro cattāro katvā soḷasa āsavā iminā ñāṇasaṃvarasaṅkhātena paccavekkhaṇapaṭisevanena pahātabbāti vuccanti.

As for the passage, 'These, monks, are called the taints to be abandoned by using': this means that these sixteen taints—making four for each single requisite—are said to be abandoned by this using with reflection, which is called the restraint of knowledge.

Paṭisevanāpahātabbaāsavavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition on the Taints to be Abandoned by Using is concluded.

Adhivāsanāpahātabbaāsavavaṇṇanā

The Exposition on the Taints to be Abandoned by Endurance

24. Paṭisaṅkhā yoniso khamo hoti sītassāti upāyena pathena paccavekkhitvā khamo hoti sītassa sītaṃ khamati sahati, na avīrapuriso viya appamattakenapi sītena calati kampati kammaṭṭhānaṃ vijahati. Apica kho lomasanāgatthero viya anappakenāpi sītena phuṭṭho na calati na kampati, kammaṭṭhānameva manasi karoti. Thero kira cetiyapabbate piyaṅguguhāyaṃ padhānaghare viharanto antaraṭṭhake himapātasamaye lokantarikaniraye paccavekkhitvā kammaṭṭhānaṃ avijahantova abbhokāse vītināmesi. Evaṃ uṇhādīsupi atthayojanā veditabbā.

24. As for 'reflecting wisely, one becomes tolerant of cold': having reflected by means of a suitable method, one becomes tolerant of cold; one endures, one bears the cold. Not like a person without fortitude, one is not shaken, does not tremble, and does not abandon the meditation subject even due to a slight cold. Furthermore, like the Elder Lomasanāga, even when afflicted by considerable cold, one is not shaken, does not tremble, but attends only to the meditation subject. It is said that the Elder, while dwelling in the striving-hall in the Piyaṅgu Cave on Cetiyapabbata during the antaraṭṭhaka period, a time of snowfall, reflected on the Lokantarika hell and, without abandoning his meditation subject, passed the time in the open. In this way, the application of the meaning should be understood for heat and so forth as well.

Kevalañhi yo bhikkhu adhimattampi uṇhaṃ sahati sveva thero viya, ayaṃ “khamo uṇhassā”ti veditabbo. Thero kira gimhasamaye pacchābhattaṃ bahicaṅkame nisīdi. Kammaṭṭhānaṃ manasikaronto sedāpissa kacchehi muccanti. Atha naṃ antevāsiko āha “idha, bhante, nisīdatha, sītalo okāso”ti. Thero “uṇhabhayenevamhi āvuso idha nisinno”ti avīcimahānirayaṃ paccavekkhitvā nisīdiyeva. Uṇhanti cettha aggisantāpova veditabbo. Sūriyasantāpavasena panetaṃ vatthu vuttaṃ.

Indeed, whichever monk endures even excessive heat, just like that same Elder, he is to be known as 'one who is tolerant of heat.' It is said that the Elder, during the hot season, after the meal, sat on the walking path outside. While he was attending to his meditation subject, sweat was released from his armpits. Then his resident pupil said to him, 'Venerable sir, sit here; the place is cool.' The Elder replied, 'Friend, it is precisely because of fear of the heat of hellfire that I am sitting here.' Reflecting on the great Avīci hell, he remained seated. And here, 'heat' should be understood as the heat of fire. However, this story is told with reference to the heat of the sun.

Yo [V 1.0085] ca dve tayo vāre bhattaṃ vā pānīyaṃ vā alabhamānopi anamatagge saṃsāre attano pettivisayūpapattiṃ paccavekkhitvā avedhento kammaṭṭhānaṃ na vijahatiyeva. Adhimattehi ḍaṃsamakasavātātapasamphassehi phuṭṭho cāpi tiracchānūpapattiṃ paccavekkhitvā avedhento kammaṭṭhānaṃ na vijahatiyeva. Sarīsapasamphassena phuṭṭho cāpi anamatagge saṃsāre sīhabyagghādimukhesu anekavāraṃ parivattitapubbabhāvaṃ paccavekkhitvā avedhento kammaṭṭhānaṃ na vijahatiyeva padhāniyatthero viya. Ayaṃ “khamo jighacchāya…pe… sarīsapasamphassāna”nti veditabbo.

And whichever monk, even when not obtaining food or drink for two or three times, reflects on his own birth in the realm of petas in the beginningless saṃsāra and, being unshaken, does not abandon the meditation subject; and even when afflicted by the severe touch of gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, and sun, reflects on birth among animals and, being unshaken, does not abandon the meditation subject; and even when afflicted by the touch of creeping things, reflects on the fact of having been rolled about in the mouths of lions, tigers, and so on many times in the beginningless saṃsāra and, being unshaken, does not abandon the meditation subject, just like the Padhāniya Elder—this monk is to be known as 'one who is tolerant of hunger... (etc.)... and the touch of creeping things'.

Theraṃ [M 1.0082] kira khaṇḍacelavihāre kaṇikārapadhāniyaghare ariyavaṃsaṃ suṇantaṃ ghoraviso sappo ḍaṃsi. Thero jānitvāpi pasannacitto nisinno dhammaṃyeva suṇāti. Visavego thaddho ahosi. Thero upasampadamaṇḍalaṃ ādiṃ katvā sīlaṃ paccavekkhitvā parisuddhasīlohamasmīti pītiṃ uppādesi. Saha pītuppādā visaṃ nivattitvā pathaviṃ pāvisi. Thero [P 1.0079] tattheva cittekaggataṃ labhitvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi.

It is said that a snake with terrible venom bit the Elder on the shoulder while he was listening to the Ariyavaṃsa in the Kaṇikāra striving-hall at the Cetiyavihāra. The Elder, though knowing it, sat with a serene mind and just listened to the Dhamma. The force of the venom became harsh. The Elder, reviewing his virtue beginning from the ordination boundary, generated rapture, thinking, 'I am of pure virtue.' Simultaneously with the arising of rapture, the venom turned back and entered the earth. The Elder, right there, having gained one-pointedness of mind, developed insight and attained Arahantship.

Yo pana akkosavasena durutte duruttattāyeva ca durāgate api antimavatthusaññite vacanapathe sutvā khantiguṇaṃyeva paccavekkhitvā na vedhati dīghabhāṇakaabhayatthero viya. Ayaṃ “khamo duruttānaṃ durāgatānaṃ vacanapathāna”nti veditabbo.

Furthermore, a monk who, having heard verbal paths that are ill-spoken by way of abuse, ill-come because they are ill-spoken, and even designated as the matter of a Pārājika offense, reflects only on the virtue of patience and is not shaken, just like the Elder Dīghabhāṇaka Abhaya—this monk is to be known as 'one who is tolerant of ill-spoken, ill-come verbal paths'.

Thero kira paccayasantosabhāvanārāmatāya mahāariyavaṃsappaṭipadaṃ kathesi, sabbo mahāgāmo āgacchati. Therassa mahāsakkāro uppajjati. Taṃ aññataro mahāthero adhivāsetuṃ asakkonto dīghabhāṇako ariyavaṃsaṃ kathemīti sabbarattiṃ kolāhalaṃ karosītiādīhi akkosi. Ubhopi ca attano attano vihāraṃ gacchantā gāvutamattaṃ ekapathena agamaṃsu. Sakalagāvutampi so taṃ akkosiyeva. Tato yattha dvinnaṃ vihārānaṃ maggo bhijjati, tattha ṭhatvā dīghabhāṇakatthero taṃ vanditvā “esa, bhante, tumhākaṃ maggo”ti āha. So asuṇanto viya agamāsi. Theropi vihāraṃ gantvā pāde pakkhāletvā nisīdi. Tamenaṃ antevāsiko “kiṃ, bhante, sakalagāvutaṃ paribhāsantaṃ na kiñci avocutthā”ti āha. Thero “khantiyeva, āvuso, mayhaṃ bhāro, na akkhanti. Ekapaduddhārepi kammaṭṭhānaviyogaṃ na passāmī”ti āha. Ettha ca vacanameva vacanapathoti veditabbo.

It is said that the Elder, due to his contentment with requisites and delight in development, taught the practice of the Great Ariyavaṃsa. The entire great village came. Great honor arose for the Elder. A certain great elder, unable to endure this, abused him with words such as, 'Dīghabhāṇaka, saying "I will teach the Ariyavaṃsa," makes a clamor all night long!' And both, while going to their respective monasteries, went by a single path for the distance of a gāvuta. For the entire gāvuta, he just abused him. Then, where the path to the two monasteries forked, the Elder Dīghabhāṇaka stood, paid homage to that great elder, and said, 'Venerable sir, this is your path.' He went on as if not hearing. The Elder too, having gone to his monastery, washed his feet and sat down. His resident pupil asked him, 'Venerable sir, why did you not say anything to the great elder who was reviling you for a whole gāvuta?' The Elder said, 'Friend, patience alone is my burden; impatience is not. Even in the lifting of a single footstep, I do not see a separation from my meditation subject.' And here, 'verbal path' should be understood as speech itself.

Yo [V 1.0086] pana uppannā sārīrikā vedanā dukkhamanaṭṭhena dukkhā, bahalaṭṭhena tibbā, pharusaṭṭhena kharā, tikhiṇaṭṭhena kaṭukā, assādavirahato asātā, manaṃ avaḍḍhanato amanāpā, pāṇaharaṇasamatthatāya pāṇaharā adhivāsetiyeva, na vedhati. Evaṃ sabhāvo hoti cittalapabbate padhāniyatthero viya. Ayaṃ “uppannānaṃ…pe… adhivāsanajātiko”ti veditabbo.

Furthermore, whatever monk, when bodily feelings have arisen—which are called suffering (dukkhā) in the sense of causing suffering, intense (tibbā) in the sense of being severe, harsh (kharā) in the sense of being coarse, pungent (kaṭukā) in the sense of being sharp, disagreeable (asātā) due to the absence of what is pleasant, displeasing (amanāpā) because they do not develop the mind, and life-taking (pāṇaharā) due to their capacity to take away life—just endures them and does not tremble. He has such a nature, like the Padhāniya Elder on Cittalapabbata mountain. This monk is to be known as 'one who has the nature of enduring' arisen feelings.

Therassa [M 1.0083] kira rattiṃ padhānena vītināmetvā ṭhitassa udaravāto uppajji. So taṃ adhivāsetuṃ asakkonto āvattati parivattati. Tamenaṃ caṅkamapasse ṭhito piṇḍapātiyatthero āha “āvuso, pabbajito nāma adhivāsanasīlo hotī”ti. So “sādhu, bhante”ti adhivāsetvā niccalo sayi. Vāto nābhito yāva hadayaṃ phāleti. Thero vedanaṃ vikkhambhetvā [P 1.0080] vipassanto muhuttena anāgāmī hutvā parinibbāyīti.

It is said that for the Elder, who was standing after having spent the night striving, a wind in the stomach arose. Unable to endure it, he rolled about this way and that. The Piṇḍapātiya Elder, who was standing near the walking path, said to him: 'Friend, one who is a renunciant has the habit of endurance.' He replied, 'Very well, venerable sir,' and having endured it, he lay down motionless. The wind split him from the navel up to the heart. The Elder, having suppressed the feeling and practicing insight, in a moment became a non-returner and attained final Nibbāna.

Yañhissāti sītādīsu yaṃkiñci ekadhammampi assa. Anadhivāsayatoti anadhivāsentassa akkhamantassa. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva. Āsavuppatti panettha evaṃ veditabbā. Sītena phuṭṭhassa uṇhaṃ patthayantassa kāmāsavo uppajjati, evaṃ sabbattha. Natthi no sampattibhave sugatibhave sītaṃ vā uṇhaṃ vāti bhavaṃ patthayantassa bhavāsavo. Mayhaṃ sītaṃ uṇhanti gāho diṭṭhāsavo. Sabbeheva sampayutto avijjāsavoti.

The phrase 'whatever there might be' (`yañcissā`) means: whatever single thing there might be among cold and so on. The phrase 'by not enduring' (`anadhivāsayato`) means: for one who does not endure, who is impatient. The rest is just as has been stated. Here, the arising of the taints is to be known thus: For one who is touched by cold and longs for heat, the taint of sensual desire arises; it is the same in all cases. For one who longs for existence, thinking, 'For us, in a prosperous existence, in a good destination, there is no cold or heat,' the taint of existence arises. The grasping, 'My cold, my heat,' is the taint of views. Delusion associated with all of these is the taint of ignorance.

“Ime vuccanti…pe… adhivāsanā pahātabbā”ti ime sītādīsu ekamekassa vasena cattāro cattāro katvā aneke āsavā imāya khantisaṃvarasaṅkhātāya adhivāsanāya pahātabbāti vuccantīti attho. Ettha ca yasmā ayaṃ khanti sītādidhamme adhivāseti, attano upari āropetvā vāsetiyeva. Na asahamānā hutvā nirassati, tasmā “adhivāsanā”ti vuccatīti veditabbā.

As for the phrase, 'These are called... to be abandoned by endurance,' the meaning is this: many taints—making them fourfold in connection with each individual case such as cold—are said to be 'abandoned by this endurance,' which is known as restraint through patience. And here, it should be known that because this patience endures phenomena such as cold—it just lets them be, having placed them upon oneself, and does not reject them through intolerance—therefore it is called 'endurance'.

Adhivāsanāpahātabbaāsavavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the taints to be abandoned by endurance is concluded.

Parivajjanāpahātabbaāsavavaṇṇanā

The explanation of the taints to be abandoned by avoidance.

25. Paṭisaṅkhā [V 1.0087] yoniso caṇḍaṃ hatthiṃ parivajjetīti ahaṃ samaṇoti caṇḍassa hatthissa āsanne na ṭhātabbaṃ. Tatonidānañhi maraṇampi siyā maraṇamattampi dukkhanti evaṃ upāyena pathena paccayena paccavekkhitvā caṇḍaṃ hatthiṃ parivajjeti paṭikkamati. Esa nayo sabbattha. Caṇḍanti ca duṭṭhaṃ, vāḷanti vuttaṃ hoti. Khāṇunti khadirakhāṇuādiṃ. Kaṇṭakaṭṭhānanti kaṇṭakānaṃ ṭhānaṃ, yattha kaṇṭakā vijjanti, taṃ okāsanti vuttaṃ hoti. Sobbhanti sabbato paricchinnataṭaṃ. Papātanti ekato chinnataṭaṃ. Candanikanti ucchiṭṭhodakagabbhamalādīnaṃ chaḍḍanaṭṭhānaṃ. Oḷigallanti tesaṃyeva [M 1.0084] sakaddamādīnaṃ sandanokāsaṃ. Taṃ jaṇṇumattampi asucibharitaṃ hoti, dvepi cetāni ṭhānāni amanussaduṭṭhāni honti. Tasmā tāni vajjetabbāni. Anāsaneti ettha pana ayuttaṃ āsanaṃ anāsanaṃ, taṃ atthato aniyatavatthukaṃ rahopaṭicchannāsananti veditabbaṃ. Agocareti etthapi ca ayutto gocaro agocaro, so vesiyādibhedato pañcavidho. Pāpake mitteti lāmake dussīle mittapatirūpake, amitte vā. Bhajantanti sevamānaṃ. Viññū sabrahmacārīti paṇḍitā buddhisampannā sabrahmacārayo, bhikkhūnametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Te hi ekakammaṃ ekuddeso [P 1.0081] samasikkhatāti imaṃ brahmaṃ samānaṃ caranti, tasmā sabrahmacārīti vuccanti. Pāpakesu ṭhānesūti lāmakesu ṭhānesu. Okappeyyunti saddaheyyuṃ, adhimucceyyuṃ “addhā ayamāyasmā akāsi vā karissati vā”ti.

25. Reflecting wisely, one should avoid a fierce elephant: thinking, “I am a monk,” one should not stand near a fierce elephant. For from that cause, death may occur, or suffering amounting to death. Thus, having reflected by way of a suitable method, path, and reason, one avoids a fierce elephant and retreats. This is the method in all cases. 'Fierce' means corrupt; it is said to mean savage. 'Stump' means a stump of acacia wood and so on. 'A place of thorns' means a location of thorns; it is said to mean a place where thorns are found. 'Pit' means a bank cut off on all sides. 'Precipice' means a bank cut off on one side. 'Cesspool' means a dumping ground for things like rinse-water, fetal matter, and filth. 'Sewer' means a channel where those same things flow along with mud and so on. That place, even if only knee-deep, is filled with impurity, and both these places are haunted by non-human beings. Therefore, they should be avoided. Herein, regarding 'in an unsuitable seat': an improper seat is an 'unsuitable seat'; in terms of meaning, it should be known as a seat for an uncertain purpose, a hidden and concealed seat. And herein, regarding 'in an unsuitable resort': an improper resort is an 'unsuitable resort'; it is of five kinds, distinguished as those of prostitutes and so on. 'Evil friends' means base, immoral persons, or counterfeit friends who are non-friends. 'Associating with' means attending upon. 'Wise fellow-practitioners of the holy life' are wise, intelligent fellow-practitioners of the holy life; this is a designation for bhikkhus. For they practice this same holy life, having the same formal acts, the same recitation of the code, and a common training; therefore, they are called 'fellow-practitioners of the holy life'. 'In evil places' means in base places. 'They might suppose' means they would place faith, they would be convinced thus: ‘For sure, this venerable one has done it or will do it.’

Yañhissāti hatthiādīsu yaṃkiñci ekampi assa. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva. Āsavuppatti panettha evaṃ veditabbā. Hatthiādinidānena dukkhena phuṭṭhassa sukhaṃ patthayato kāmāsavo uppajjati. Natthi no sampattibhave sugatibhave īdisaṃ dukkhanti bhavaṃ patthentassa bhavāsavo. Maṃ hatthī maddati, maṃ assoti gāho diṭṭhāsavo. Sabbeheva sampayutto avijjāsavoti.

Regarding 'Whatever there might be for him': whatever single thing among elephants and so on there might be. The rest is just as has been stated. Herein, the arising of the taints should be understood thus: For one who, being afflicted by suffering caused by an elephant and so on, longs for pleasure, the taint of sensual desire arises. For one who longs for existence, thinking, “For us, in a prosperous existence, in a good destination, there is no such suffering,” the taint of existence arises. The grasping, “An elephant tramples me,” “A horse tramples me,” is the taint of views. The delusion associated with all of these is the taint of ignorance.

Ime vuccanti…pe… parivajjanā pahātabbāti ime hatthiādīsu ekekassa vasena cattāro cattāro katvā aneke āsavā iminā sīlasaṃvarasaṅkhātena parivajjanena pahātabbāti vuccantīti veditabbā.

These are called… ‘to be abandoned by avoidance.’ Here, it should be understood that numerous taints, making each of these, such as the elephant, into four, are said to be abandoned by this avoidance, which is called restraint through virtue.

Parivajjanāpahātabbaāsavavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the taints to be abandoned by avoidance is concluded.

Vinodanāpahātabbaāsavavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Taints to be Abandoned by Dispelling.

26. Paṭisaṅkhā [V 1.0088] yoniso uppannaṃ kāmavitakkaṃ nādhivāsetīti “iti pāyaṃ vitakko akusalo, itipi sāvajjo, itipi dukkhavipāko, so ca kho attabyābādhāya saṃvattatī”tiādinā nayena yoniso kāmavitakke ādīnavaṃ paccavekkhitvā tasmiṃ tasmiṃ ārammaṇe uppannaṃ jātamabhinibbattaṃ kāmavitakkaṃ nādhivāseti, cittaṃ āropetvā na vāseti, abbhantare vā na vāsetītipi attho.

26. ‘Reflecting wisely, one does not tolerate an arisen sensual thought’ means: having wisely reflected on the danger in sensual thought by the method beginning with, ‘For this reason, this thought is unwholesome; for this reason, it is blameworthy; for this reason, it has a painful result; and indeed, it leads to one's own affliction,’ one does not tolerate a sensual thought that has arisen, been born, and been produced in this or that object. One does not let it dwell by establishing it in the mind, nor does one let it dwell internally—this is also the meaning.

Anadhivāsento kiṃ karotīti? Pajahati chaḍḍeti.

What does one do when not tolerating? One abandons and discards it.

Kiṃ kacavaraṃ viya piṭakenāti? Na hi, apica kho naṃ vinodeti tudati vijjhati nīharati.

Is it like discarding garbage with a basket? Not so; rather, one dispels it, strikes it, pierces it, and removes it.

Kiṃ [M 1.0085] balibaddaṃ viya patodenāti? Na hi, atha kho naṃ byantīkaroti vigatantaṃ karoti. Yathāssa antopi nāvasissati antamaso bhaṅgamattampi, tathā naṃ karoti.

Is it like striking an ox with a goad? Not so; but rather one eradicates it, makes it vanish. One makes it so that not even a trace remains inside, not even a fragment at the very least.

Kathaṃ pana naṃ tathā karotīti? Anabhāvaṃ gametīti anu anu abhāvaṃ gameti, vikkhambhanappahānena yathā suvikkhambhito hoti, tathā karotīti vuttaṃ hoti. Esa nayo byāpādavihiṃsāvitakkesu.

How then does one do so? One leads it to non-existence—one leads it to non-existence repeatedly. It is said that one does so by abandonment through suppression, so that it is thoroughly suppressed. This is the method for thoughts of ill-will and harmfulness.

Ettha ca kāmavitakkoti “yo kāmapaṭisaṃyutto takko vitakko micchāsaṅkappo”ti vibhaṅge (vibha. 910) vutto. Esa nayo itaresu. Uppannuppanneti uppanne uppanne, uppannamatteyevāti vuttaṃ hoti. Sakiṃ vā uppanne vinodetvā dutiyavāre [P 1.0082] ajjhupekkhitā na hoti, satakkhattumpi uppanne uppanne vinodetiyeva. Pāpake akusaleti lāmakaṭṭhena pāpake, akosallatāya akusale. Dhammeti teyeva kāmavitakkādayo sabbepi vā nava mahāvitakke. Tattha tayo vuttā eva. Avasesā “ñātivitakko janapadavitakko amaravitakko parānuddayatāpaṭisaṃyutto [V 1.0089] vitakko lābhasakkārasilokapaṭisaṃyutto vitakko anavaññattipaṭisaṃyutto vitakko”ti (mahāni. 207) ime cha.

Here, ‘thought of sensual desire’ (kāmavitakka) is as stated in the Vibhaṅga: ‘any thinking, thought, or wrong intention connected with sensual pleasure.’ This is the method for the others. ‘Whenever it arises’ (uppannuppanne) means ‘on each arising, just as it arises.’ It is not that having dispelled it when it has arisen once, one is indifferent the second time; even if it arises a hundred times, one must dispel it each time it arises. ‘Evil and unwholesome’ (pāpake akusale) means ‘evil’ in the sense of being base, and ‘unwholesome’ due to unskillfulness. ‘States’ (dhamme) here refers to those very thoughts of sensual desire, etc., or all nine great thoughts. Among them, three have already been mentioned. The remaining six are: thought of relatives, thought of one's country, thought of immortality, thought connected with sympathy for others, thought connected with gain, honor, and fame, and thought connected with not being despised.

Yañhissāti etesu vitakkesu yaṃkiñci assa, sesaṃ vuttanayameva. Kāmavitakko panettha kāmāsavo eva. Tabbiseso bhavāsavo. Taṃsampayutto diṭṭhāsavo. Sabbavitakkesu avijjāsavoti evaṃ āsavuppattipi veditabbā.

As for ‘whatever there may be for him’ (yañhissa), this means whatever of these thoughts there may be. The rest is by the method already stated. Here, the thought of sensual desire is the taint of sensual desire itself. A specific instance of that is the taint of becoming. That which is associated with them is the taint of views. The delusion associated with all thoughts is the taint of ignorance. In this way, the arising of the taints should also be understood.

Ime vuccanti…pe… vinodanā pahātabbāti ime kāmavitakkādivasena vuttappakārā āsavā iminā tasmiṃ tasmiṃ vitakke ādīnavapaccavekkhaṇasahitena vīriyasaṃvarasaṅkhātena vinodanena pahātabbāti vuccantīti veditabbā.

‘These are called… to be abandoned by dispelling’ means: these taints, described by way of thoughts of sensual desire and so on, are said to be ‘abandoned by this dispelling’—which is reckoned as restraint by energy accompanied by reflection on the danger in each respective thought. This is to be understood.

Vinodanāpahātabbaāsavavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Taints to be Abandoned by Dispelling is concluded.

Bhāvanāpahātabbaāsavavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Taints to be Abandoned by Development.

27. Paṭisaṅkhā yoniso satisambojjhaṅgaṃ bhāvetīti abhāvanāya ādīnavaṃ, bhāvanāya ca ānisaṃsaṃ upāyena pathena paccavekkhitvā satisambojjhaṅgaṃ [M 1.0086] bhāveti, esa nayo sabbattha. Ettha ca kiñcāpi ime uparimaggattayasamayasambhūtā lokuttarabojjhaṅgā eva adhippetā, tathāpi ādikammikānaṃ bojjhaṅgesu asammohatthaṃ lokiyalokuttaramissakena nesaṃ nayena atthavaṇṇanaṃ karissāmi. Idha pana lokiyanayaṃ pahāya lokuttaranayo eva gahetabbo. Tattha satisambojjhaṅgantiādinā nayena vuttānaṃ sattannaṃ ādipadānaṃyeva tāva –

27. “One develops the enlightenment factor of mindfulness with wise reflection” means: having reviewed, by a suitable method, the danger in non-development and the benefit in development, one develops the enlightenment factor of mindfulness. This is the method in all cases. And here, although what is intended are only these supramundane enlightenment factors that arise at the time of the three higher paths, nevertheless, for the sake of non-confusion for beginners regarding the enlightenment factors, I will provide an explanation of their meaning by a method that mixes the mundane and the supramundane. Here, however, the mundane method should be abandoned and only the supramundane method should be adopted. Therein, first, of the seven initial terms spoken by the method beginning with “the enlightenment factor of mindfulness”–

Atthato lakkhaṇādīhi, kamato ca vinicchayo;

Anūnādhikato ceva, viññātabbo vibhāvinā.

The determination should be understood by the discerning one in terms of meaning, characteristics and so on; in terms of sequence; and as being without deficiency or excess.

Tattha satisambojjhaṅge tāva saraṇaṭṭhena sati. Sā panesā upaṭṭhānalakkhaṇā, apilāpanalakkhaṇā vā. Vuttampi hetaṃ “yathā, mahārāja, rañño bhaṇḍāgāriko rañño sāpateyyaṃ [V 1.0090] apilāpeti, ettakaṃ, mahārāja, hiraññaṃ, ettakaṃ suvaṇṇaṃ, ettakaṃ sāpateyyanti, evameva kho, mahārāja[P 1.0083], sati uppajjamānā kusalākusalasāvajjānavajjahīnapaṇītakaṇhasukkasappaṭibhāge dhamme apilāpeti. Ime cattāro satipaṭṭhānā”ti (mi. pa. 2.1.13) vitthāro. Apilāpanarasā. Kiccavaseneva hissa etaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ therena vuttaṃ. Asammosarasā vā. Gocarābhimukhabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānā. Sati eva sambojjhaṅgo satisambojjhaṅgo. Tattha bodhiyā bodhissa vā aṅgoti bojjhaṅgo.

Therein, regarding the enlightenment factor of mindfulness, first, mindfulness (sati) is in the sense of remembering (saraṇa). It has the characteristic of presence, or the characteristic of non-disappearance. For this has been said: 'Just as, great king, a royal treasurer does not let the king's property disappear, [reminding him,] "So much, great king, is the silver, so much is the gold, so much is the property," even so, great king, when mindfulness arises, it does not let wholesome and unwholesome, blameworthy and blameless, inferior and superior, dark and bright states with their counterparts disappear. These are the four establishments of mindfulness' (Milindapañha 2.1.13). It has the function of non-disappearance. Indeed, this characteristic was stated by the Elder in terms of its function. Or, it has the function of non-confusion. Its manifestation is the state of facing the object. Mindfulness itself is an enlightenment factor (sambojjhaṅga), thus it is the mindfulness-enlightenment-factor (satisambojjhaṅga). Therein, it is an 'enlightenment factor' (bojjhaṅga) because it is a factor of enlightenment (bodhi) or a factor of one who awakens (bodhi).

Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti? Yā hi ayaṃ dhammasāmaggī, yāya lokiyalokuttaramaggakkhaṇe uppajjamānāya līnuddhaccapatiṭṭhānāyūhana-kāmasukhattakilamathānuyoga-ucchedasassatābhinivesādīnaṃ anekesaṃ upaddavānaṃ paṭipakkhabhūtāya satidhammavicayavīriyapītipassaddhisamādhiupekkhāsaṅkhātāya dhammasāmaggiyā ariyasāvako bujjhatīti katvā “bodhī”ti vuccati. Bujjhatīti kilesasantānaniddāya uṭṭhahati, cattāri vā ariyasaccāni paṭivijjhati, nibbānameva vā sacchikarotīti vuttaṃ hoti. Yathāha “satta bojjhaṅge bhāvetvā anuttaraṃ sammāsambodhiṃ abhisambuddho”ti. Tassā dhammasāmaggisaṅkhātāya bodhiyā aṅgotipi bojjhaṅgo, jhānaṅgamaggaṅgādayo viya.

What is meant? There is this harmony of dhammas, by which a noble disciple awakens. It arises at the moment of the mundane and supramundane path; it is the opponent of numerous troubles such as the basis for sloth and restlessness, striving, indulgence in sensual pleasures and self-mortification, and adherence to annihilationism and eternalism; and it is designated as mindfulness, investigation-of-dhammas, energy, rapture, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity. Because the noble disciple awakens by it, it is called 'bodhi' (enlightenment). 'To awaken' means: to rise from the sleep that is the continuum of defilements, or to penetrate the four noble truths, or to realize Nibbāna itself. As it is said: 'Having developed the seven factors of enlightenment, one is fully awakened to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.' It is also an 'enlightenment factor' (bojjhaṅga) because it is a factor (aṅga) of that enlightenment (bodhi), which is known as the harmony of dhammas, just like the factors of jhāna, factors of the path, and so on.

Yopesa [M 1.0087] yathāvuttappakārāya etāya dhammasāmaggiyā bujjhatīti katvā ariyasāvako “bodhī”ti vuccati, tassa bodhissa aṅgotipi bojjhaṅgo, senaṅgarathaṅgādayo viya. Tenāhu aṭṭhakathācariyā “bujjhanakassa puggalassa aṅgāti vā bojjhaṅgā”ti. Apica “bojjhaṅgāti kenaṭṭhena bojjhaṅgā? Bodhāya saṃvattantīti bojjhaṅgā, bujjhantīti bojjhaṅgā, anubujjhantīti bojjhaṅgā, paṭibujjhantīti bojjhaṅgā, sambujjhantīti bojjhaṅgā”tiādinā (paṭi. ma. 3.17) paṭisambhidānayenāpi attho veditabbo. Pasattho sundaro vā bojjhaṅgoti sambojjhaṅgo. Evaṃ sati eva sambojjhaṅgo satisambojjhaṅgo. Taṃ satisambojjhaṅgaṃ. Evaṃ tāva ekassa ādipadassa atthato lakkhaṇādīhi ca vinicchayo viññātabbo.

And because that noble disciple awakens by means of this harmony of dhammas of the kind already stated, the noble disciple is called 'bodhi' (one who awakens). It is also an 'enlightenment factor' (bojjhaṅga) because it is a factor (aṅga) of that 'bodhi' (the awakened person), like the constituents of an army, the parts of a chariot, and so on. Therefore the commentary teachers have said: 'They are "enlightenment factors" because they are factors of the person who awakens.' Furthermore, the meaning should also be understood according to the method of the Paṭisambhidāmagga, which begins: 'In what sense are they "enlightenment factors" (bojjhaṅgā)? They conduce to enlightenment (bodhāya), therefore they are bojjhaṅgā. They awaken (bujjhanti), therefore they are bojjhaṅgā. They awaken in accordance (anubujjhanti), therefore they are bojjhaṅgā. They awaken from sleep (paṭibujjhanti), therefore they are bojjhaṅgā. They fully awaken (sambujjhanti), therefore they are bojjhaṅgā' (Paṭisambhidāmagga 3.17). A praised (pasattha) or beautiful (sundara) enlightenment factor (bojjhaṅga) is a 'sambojjhaṅga'. Thus, mindfulness itself being a sambojjhaṅga, it is 'satisambojjhaṅga' (mindfulness-enlightenment-factor). [The text refers to] that mindfulness-enlightenment-factor. In this way, first, the determination of the one initial term should be understood in terms of its meaning, characteristics, and so on.

Dutiyādīsu pana catusaccadhamme vicinātīti dhammavicayo. So pana vicayalakkhaṇo, obhāsanaraso, asammohapaccupaṭṭhāno. Vīrabhāvato vidhinā īrayitabbato ca vīriyaṃ. Taṃ paggahalakkhaṇaṃ[V 1.0091], upatthambhanarasaṃ, anosīdanapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ[P 1.0084]. Pīṇayatīti pīti. Sā pharaṇalakkhaṇā, tuṭṭhilakkhaṇā vā, kāyacittānaṃ pīṇanarasā, tesaṃyeva odagyapaccupaṭṭhānā. Kāyacittadarathapassambhanato passaddhi. Sā upasamalakkhaṇā, kāyacittadarathanimmaddanarasā, āyacittānaṃ aparipphandanabhūtasītibhāvapaccupaṭṭhānā. Samādhānato samādhi. So avikkhepalakkhaṇo, avisāralakkhaṇo vā, cittacetasikānaṃ sampiṇḍanaraso, cittaṭṭhitipaccupaṭṭhāno. Ajjhupekkhanato upekkhā. Sā paṭisaṅkhānalakkhaṇā, samavāhitalakkhaṇā vā, ūnādhikatānivāraṇarasā, pakkhapātupacchedarasā vā, majjhattabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānā. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva. Evaṃ sesapadānampi atthato lakkhaṇādīhi ca vinicchayo viññātabbo.

As for the second and following terms: 'Investigation-of-dhammas' (dhammavicaya) is so called because it investigates (vicināti) the dhammas of the four truths. It has investigation as its characteristic, illumination as its function, and non-confusion as its manifestation. 'Energy' (vīriya) is so called from its nature as heroic (vīra) and because it should be aroused methodically. It has exertion as its characteristic, support as its function, and non-sinking as its manifestation. 'Rapture' (pīti) is so called because it gladdens (pīṇayati). It has suffusion as its characteristic, or delight as its characteristic; gladdening of the mental body and consciousness as its function; and their uplift as its manifestation. 'Tranquility' (passaddhi) is so called because it tranquilizes (passambhanato) the distress of the mental body and consciousness. It has calming as its characteristic, the dispelling of distress of the mental body and consciousness as its function, and the state of being unagitated and cool as its manifestation. 'Concentration' (samādhi) is so called because it concentrates (samādhānato) the mind. It has non-distraction as its characteristic, or non-scattering as its characteristic; the unifying of mind and mental factors as its function; and the stability of mind as its manifestation. 'Equanimity' (upekkhā) is so called because it looks on (ajjhupekkhanato). It has the characteristic of impartial inspection, or the characteristic of even-mindedness; the function of preventing deficiency and excess, or the function of cutting off bias; and the state of neutrality as its manifestation. The rest is as in the method already stated. In this way, the determination of the remaining terms should also be understood in terms of their meaning, characteristics, and so on.

Kamatoti ettha ca “satiñca khvāhaṃ, bhikkhave, sabbatthikaṃ vadāmī”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.234) vacanato sabbesaṃ sesabojjhaṅgānaṃ upakārakattā satisambojjhaṅgova paṭhamaṃ vutto. Tato paraṃ “so tathā sato viharanto taṃ dhammaṃ paññāya pavicinatī”tiādinā (vibha. 469) nayena sesabojjhaṅgānaṃ pubbāpariyavacane payojanaṃ sutteyeva vuttaṃ. Evamettha kamatopi vinicchayo viññātabbo.

Here, regarding 'in terms of sequence' (kamato): because it is said, 'Monks, I declare mindfulness to be of service everywhere,' and because it is helpful to all the remaining enlightenment factors, the enlightenment factor of mindfulness is stated first. After that, the purpose for the sequence of the remaining enlightenment factors is stated in the Sutta itself by the method beginning: 'So, dwelling thus mindful, he investigates that Dhamma with wisdom...' Thus, the determination in terms of sequence should also be understood here.

Anūnādhikatoti kasmā pana bhagavatā satteva bojjhaṅgā vuttā anūnā anadhikāti. Līnuddhaccapaṭipakkhato sabbatthikato ca. Ettha hi tayo [M 1.0088] bojjhaṅgā līnassa paṭipakkhā. Yathāha – “yasmiñca kho, bhikkhave, samaye līnaṃ cittaṃ hoti, kālo tasmiṃ samaye dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgassa bhāvanāya, kālo vīriyasambojjhaṅgassa bhāvanāya, kālo pītisambojjhaṅgassa bhāvanāyā”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.234). Tayo uddhaccassa paṭipakkhā. Yathāha – “yasmiñca kho, bhikkhave, samaye uddhataṃ cittaṃ hoti, kālo tasmiṃ samaye passaddhisambojjhaṅgassa bhāvanāya, kālo samādhisambojjhaṅgassa bhāvanāya, kālo upekkhāsambojjhaṅgassa bhāvanāyā”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.234). Eko panettha sabbatthiko. Yathāha – “satiñca khvāhaṃ, bhikkhave, sabbatthikaṃ vadāmī”ti. “Sabbatthaka”ntipi pāṭho, dvinnampi sabbattha icchitabbanti attho. Evaṃ līnuddhaccapaṭipakkhato sabbatthikato [P 1.0085] ca satteva bojjhaṅgā vuttā anūnā anadhikāti, evamettha anūnādhikatopi vinicchayo viññātabbo.

Regarding 'neither less nor more': Why did the Blessed One teach only seven enlightenment factors, neither less nor more? Because they are the counterpart to dullness and restlessness, and because one is applicable in all circumstances. Herein, three enlightenment factors are the counterpart to dullness. As it is said: 'Monks, at a time when the mind is dull, that is the time to cultivate the enlightenment factor of investigation-of-dhammas, the time to cultivate the enlightenment factor of energy, and the time to cultivate the enlightenment factor of rapture.' Three are the counterpart to restlessness. As it is said: 'Monks, at a time when the mind is restless, that is the time to cultivate the enlightenment factor of tranquility, the time to cultivate the enlightenment factor of concentration, and the time to cultivate the enlightenment factor of equanimity.' One herein is applicable in all circumstances. As it is said: 'Monks, I declare that mindfulness is applicable in all circumstances.' There is also the reading 'sabbatthakaṃ'; the meaning for both is 'desired in all circumstances.' Thus, because they are the counterpart to dullness and restlessness and because one is applicable in all circumstances, only seven enlightenment factors were taught, neither less nor more. In this way, the determination regarding 'neither less nor more' should be understood herein.

Evaṃ [V 1.0092] tāva “satisambojjhaṅga”ntiādinā nayena vuttānaṃ sattannaṃ ādipadānaṃyeva atthavaṇṇanaṃ ñatvā idāni bhāveti vivekanissitantiādīsu evaṃ ñātabbā. Bhāvetīti vaḍḍheti, attano cittasantāne punappunaṃ janeti abhinibbattetīti attho. Vivekanissitanti viveke nissitaṃ. Vivekoti vivittatā. Svāyaṃ tadaṅgaviveko vikkhambhanasamucchedapaṭippassaddhi nissaraṇavivekoti pañcavidho. Tassa nānattaṃ “ariyadhamme avinīto”ti ettha vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Ayameva hi tattha vinayoti vutto. Evaṃ etasmiṃ pañcavidhe viveke.

Thus, having first understood the explanation of the meaning of only the initial terms of the seven factors spoken of in the manner beginning with 'the mindfulness enlightenment factor,' it should now be understood thus regarding the phrases beginning with 'develops, based on seclusion.' 'Develops' (bhāveti) means increases, repeatedly generates and brings into being in one's own mental continuum; this is the meaning. 'Based on seclusion' (vivekanissitaṃ) means based on seclusion. 'Seclusion' (viveka) means secludedness. This seclusion is fivefold: seclusion by substitution, seclusion by suppression, seclusion by cutting off, seclusion by tranquillization, and seclusion by escape. Its variety should be understood in the very manner spoken of in the context of 'untrained in the noble Dhamma,' for this very seclusion is called 'discipline' (vinaya) there. Thus, in this fivefold seclusion.

Vivekanissitanti tadaṅgavivekanissitaṃ samucchedavivekanissitaṃ nissaraṇavivekanissitañca satisambojjhaṅgaṃ bhāvetīti ayamattho veditabbo. Tathā hi ayaṃ bojjhaṅgabhāvanānuyutto yogī vipassanākkhaṇe kiccato tadaṅgavivekanissitaṃ, ajjhāsayato nissaraṇavivekanissitaṃ, maggakāle pana kiccato samucchedavivekanissitaṃ, ārammaṇato nissaraṇavivekanissitaṃ satisambojjhaṅgaṃ bhāveti. Pañcavidhavivekanissitantipi eke, te hi na kevalaṃ balavavipassanāmaggaphalakkhaṇesu eva bojjhaṅge uddharanti, vipassanāpādakakasiṇajjhānaānāpānāsubhabrahmavihārajjhānesupi uddharanti. Na ca paṭisiddhā aṭṭhakathācariyehi. Tasmā tesaṃ matena etesaṃ jhānānaṃ pavattikkhaṇe kiccato eva vikkhambhanavivekanissitaṃ. Yathā [M 1.0089] ca “vipassanākkhaṇe ajjhāsayato nissaraṇavivekanissita”nti vuttaṃ, evaṃ paṭippassaddhivivekanissitampi bhāvetīti vattuṃ vaṭṭati. Esa nayo virāganissitādīsu. Vivekaṭṭhā eva hi virāgādayo.

'Based on seclusion' (vivekanissitaṃ) means this: it should be understood that one develops the mindfulness enlightenment factor based on seclusion by substitution, based on seclusion by cutting off, and based on seclusion by escape. For this yogī devoted to developing the enlightenment factors, at the moment of insight, develops the mindfulness enlightenment factor based on seclusion by substitution in terms of function, and based on seclusion by escape in terms of disposition. At the time of the path, however, one develops it based on seclusion by cutting off in terms of function, and based on seclusion by escape in terms of object. Some teachers also extract the meaning 'based on the fivefold seclusion.' For they do not extract the enlightenment factors only during the moments of powerful insight, path, and fruition, but they also extract them in the jhānas that are the basis for insight: the kasiṇa-jhānas, ānāpāna-jhāna, asubha-jhānas, and brahmavihāra-jhānas. And this is not rejected by the commentary teachers. Therefore, according to their opinion, at the moment of the arising of these jhānas, it is based on seclusion by suppression in terms of function only. And just as it was said, 'at the moment of insight, based on seclusion by escape in terms of disposition,' so too it is fitting to say that one also develops it as 'based on seclusion by tranquillization.' This is the method for 'based on dispassion' and the others. For dispassion and so on indeed have the meaning of seclusion.

Kevalañhettha vossaggo duvidho pariccāgavossaggo ca pakkhandanavossaggo cāti. Tattha pariccāgavossaggoti vipassanākkhaṇe ca tadaṅgavasena, maggakkhaṇe ca samucchedavasena kilesappahānaṃ. Pakkhandanavossaggoti vipassanākkhaṇe tanninnabhāvena, maggakkhaṇe pana ārammaṇakaraṇena nibbānapakkhandanaṃ. Tadubhayampi imasmiṃ lokiyalokuttaramissake atthavaṇṇanānaye vaṭṭati. Tathā hi ayaṃ satisambojjhaṅgo yathāvuttena pakārena kilese pariccajati, nibbānañca pakkhandati. Vossaggapariṇāminti [P 1.0086] iminā pana sakalena vacanena vossaggattaṃ pariṇamantaṃ pariṇatañca paripaccantaṃ paripakkañcāti. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti “ayañhi bojjhaṅgabhāvanānuyutto bhikkhu yathā satisambojjhaṅgo kilesapariccāgavossaggattaṃ nibbānapakkhandanavossaggattañca [V 1.0093] paripaccati, yathā ca paripakko hoti, tathā naṃ bhāvetī”ti. Esa nayo sesabojjhaṅgesu.

Herein, relinquishment is twofold: relinquishment by abandoning and relinquishment by plunging. Therein, relinquishment by abandoning is the abandoning of defilements by way of substitution at the moment of insight, and by way of cutting off at the moment of the path. Relinquishment by plunging is the plunging into Nibbāna by way of inclining towards it at the moment of insight, and by making it the object at the moment of the path. Both of these are applicable in this method of explaining the meaning, which is a mixture of worldly and supramundane. For this mindfulness enlightenment factor abandons defilements in the manner stated and plunges into Nibbāna. And by this whole phrase 'culminating in relinquishment,' what is meant is inclining towards the state of relinquishment, being inclined, ripening, and being ripe. This is what is said: 'This monk devoted to developing the enlightenment factors develops the mindfulness enlightenment factor in such a way that it ripens into the state of relinquishment by abandoning defilements and the state of relinquishment by plunging into Nibbāna, and in such a way that it becomes fully ripe.' This is the method for the remaining enlightenment factors.

Idha pana nibbānaṃyeva sabbasaṅkhatehi vivittattā viveko, sabbesaṃ virāgabhāvato virāgo, nirodhabhāvato nirodhoti vuttaṃ. Maggo eva ca vossaggapariṇāmī, tasmā satisambojjhaṅgaṃ bhāveti vivekaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā pavattiyā vivekanissitaṃ. Tathā virāganissitaṃ nirodhanissitaṃ. Tañca kho ariyamaggakkhaṇuppattiyā kilesānaṃ samucchedato pariccāgabhāvena ca nibbānapakkhandanabhāvena ca pariṇataṃ paripakkanti ayameva attho daṭṭhabbo. Esa nayo sesabojjhaṅgesu.

Here, however, Nibbāna alone is called 'seclusion' because it is secluded from all conditioned things; 'dispassion' because it is the fading away of all conditioned things; and 'cessation' because it is the cessation of all conditioned things. And the path itself culminates in relinquishment. Therefore, one develops the mindfulness enlightenment factor as 'based on seclusion' because it proceeds having made seclusion its object. Similarly, as 'based on dispassion' and 'based on cessation.' And that mindfulness enlightenment factor, through the arising of the noble path, by the cutting off of defilements, becomes inclined and ripe through its nature as abandoning defilements and its nature as plunging into Nibbāna. This very meaning should be understood. This is the method for the remaining enlightenment factors.
