Yañhissāti etesu bojjhaṅgesu yaṃkiñci assa. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva. Āsavuppattiyaṃ panettha imesaṃ uparimaggattayasampayuttānaṃ bojjhaṅgānaṃ abhāvitattā ye uppajjeyyuṃ kāmāsavo bhavāsavo avijjāsavoti tayo āsavā, bhāvayato evaṃsa te āsavā na hontīti ayaṃ nayo veditabbo.

‘Whichever there may be’ means whichever of these enlightenment factors there may be. The rest is in the manner already stated. Here, regarding the arising of taints: because these enlightenment factors associated with the three higher paths have not been developed, whichever three taints might arise—the taint of sensual pleasure, the taint of existence, and the taint of ignorance—for one who develops the enlightenment factors in this way, those taints do not arise. This is the method to be understood.

Ime vuccanti…pe… bhāvanā pahātabbāti ime tayo āsavā imāya maggattayasampayuttāya bojjhaṅgabhāvanāya pahātabbāti vuccantīti veditabbā.

‘These are called… to be abandoned by development’ means: it should be understood that these three taints are called ‘to be abandoned by this development of the enlightenment factors associated with the three higher paths.’

28. Idāni [M 1.0090] imehi sattahākārehi pahīnāsavaṃ bhikkhuṃ thomento āsavappahāne cassa ānisaṃsaṃ dassento eteheva ca kāraṇehi āsavappahāne sattānaṃ ussukkaṃ janento yato kho, bhikkhave…pe… antamakāsi dukkhassāti āha. Tattha yato khoti sāmivacane tokāro, yassa khoti vuttaṃ hoti. Porāṇā pana yasmiṃ kāleti vaṇṇayanti. Ye āsavā dassanā pahātabbāti ye āsavā dassanena pahātabbā, te dassaneneva pahīnā honti, na appahīnesuyeva pahīnasaññī hoti. Evaṃ sabbattha vitthāro.

28. Now, praising the monk who has abandoned the taints by these seven methods, showing the benefit in the abandoning of his taints, and by these very causes causing striving to arise in beings for the abandoning of the taints, He said: 'From when, O monks... He made an end of suffering.' Therein, in the phrase 'yato kho', the particle 'to' is in the sense of the genitive; it means 'of whom'. The ancients, however, explain it as 'at which time'. As for 'the taints to be abandoned by seeing': those taints that are to be abandoned by seeing are abandoned by seeing alone. One does not have the perception 'abandoned' in regard to those that are not yet abandoned. Thus should the detailed explanation be understood in all cases.

Sabbāsavasaṃvarasaṃvutoti sabbehi āsavapidhānehi pihito, sabbesaṃ vā āsavānaṃ pidhānehi pihito. Acchecchi [P 1.0087] taṇhanti sabbampi taṇhaṃ chindi, saṃchindi samucchindi. Vivattayi [V 1.0094] saṃyojananti dasavidhampi saṃyojanaṃ parivattayi nimmalamakāsi. Sammāti hetunā kāraṇena. Mānābhisamayāti mānassa dassanābhisamayā pahānābhisamayā ca. Arahattamaggo hi kiccavasena mānaṃ passati, ayamassa dassanābhisamayo. Tena diṭṭho pana so tāvadeva pahīyati diṭṭhavisena diṭṭhasattānaṃ jīvitaṃ viya. Ayamassa pahānābhisamayo.

'Restrained by the restraint of all taints' means closed off by all coverings of the taints, or, closed off by the coverings of all the taints. 'He cut off craving' means He cut all craving, cut it completely, cut it without remainder. 'He turned away the fetter' means He turned back the tenfold fetter and made it stainless. 'Rightly' means by a suitable cause, by a reason. 'Through the comprehension of conceit' means through the comprehension by seeing conceit and the comprehension by abandoning it. For the path of Arahantship, by way of its function, sees conceit; this is its comprehension through seeing. And that which is seen by it is abandoned at that very moment, like the life of beings seen by a poison-snake. This is its comprehension through abandoning.

Antamakāsi dukkhassāti evaṃ arahattamaggena sammā mānassa diṭṭhattā pahīnattā ca ye ime “kāyabandhanassa anto jīrati (cūḷava. 278). Haritantaṃ vā”ti (ma. ni. 1.304) evaṃ vuttaantimamariyādanto ca, “antamidaṃ, bhikkhave, jīvikāna”nti (itivu. 91; saṃ. ni. 3.80) evaṃ vuttalāmakanto ca, “sakkāyo eko anto”ti (a. ni. 6.61) evaṃ vuttakoṭṭhāsanto ca, “esevanto dukkhassa sabbapaccayasaṅkhayā”ti (saṃ. ni. 2.51) evaṃ vuttakoṭanto cāti evaṃ cattāro antā, tesu sabbasseva vaṭṭadukkhassa antaṃ catutthakoṭisaṅkhātaṃ antimakoṭisaṅkhātaṃ antamakāsi paricchedaṃ parivaṭumaṃ akāsi. Antimasamussayamattāvasesaṃ dukkhaṃ akāsīti vuttaṃ hoti.

As for 'He made an end of suffering': Thus, because conceit was rightly seen and abandoned by the path of Arahantship, of the four kinds of 'end'—(1) the end as an ultimate boundary, as stated in 'the end of the waist-band wears out' and 'the green end'; (2) the end as a base thing, as stated in 'This, monks, is the lowest of livelihoods'; (3) the end as a portion, as stated in 'The existing body is one portion'; and (4) the end as a point, as stated in 'This itself is the end of suffering, with the exhaustion of all conditions'—among these four ends, He made the end of all the suffering of the round of existence, which is reckoned as the fourth point, the final point. He made a demarcation, a place free from the round. This means: He made it so that only the suffering of the final embodiment remains.

Attamanā te bhikkhūti sakamanā tuṭṭhamanā, pītisomanassehi vā sampayuttamanā hutvā. Bhagavato bhāsitaṃ abhinandunti idaṃ dukkhassa antakiriyāpariyosānaṃ [M 1.0091] bhagavato bhāsitaṃ sukathitaṃ sulapitaṃ, evametaṃ bhagavā evametaṃ sugatāti matthakena sampaṭicchantā abbhanumodiṃsūti.

As for 'Delighted were those monks': They had their own minds, satisfied minds; or, having become possessed of minds associated with rapture and gladness. As for 'they rejoiced in the Blessed One's words': Saying, 'This discourse of the Blessed One, which culminates in making an end of suffering, is well-spoken, well-uttered. It is just so, Blessed One! It is just so, Sugata!', and accepting it with their heads, they greatly rejoiced.

Sesamettha yaṃ na vuttaṃ, taṃ pubbe vuttattā ca suviññeyyattā ca na vuttaṃ. Tasmā sabbaṃ vuttānusārena anupadaso paccavekkhitabbaṃ.

Whatever else here has not been commented upon, was not commented upon because it has been stated before and because it is easy to understand. Therefore, everything should be reviewed word by word in accordance with what has been commented upon.

Bhāvanāpahātabbaāsavavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the taints to be abandoned by development is completed.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

In the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya.

Sabbāsavasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Sabbāsava Sutta is completed.

3. Dhammadāyādasuttavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Discourse on Heirs in the Dhamma

29. Evaṃ [V 1.0095] me sutanti dhammadāyādasuttaṃ. Yasmā panassa aṭṭhuppattiko nikkhepo, tasmā taṃ dassetvā vassa apubbapadavaṇṇanaṃ karissāma. Katarāya ca panidaṃ aṭṭhuppattiyā nikkhittanti. Lābhasakkāre. Bhagavato kira mahālābhasakkāro uppajji. Yathā taṃ cattāro asaṅkhyeyye pūritadānapāramīsañcayassa. Sabbadisāsu yamakamahāmegho [P 1.0088] vuṭṭhahitvā mahoghaṃ viya sabbapāramiyo ekasmiṃ attabhāve vipākaṃ dassāmāti sampiṇḍitā viya lābhasakkāramahoghaṃ nibbattayiṃsu. Tato tato annapānayānavatthamālāgandhavilepanādihatthā khattiyabrāhmaṇādayo āgantvā – “kahaṃ buddho, kahaṃ bhagavā, kahaṃ devadevo, narāsabho, purisasīho”ti bhagavantaṃ pariyesanti. Sakaṭasatehipi paccaye āharitvā okāsaṃ alabhamānā samantā gāvutappamāṇampi sakaṭadhurena sakaṭadhuramāhaccatiṭṭhanti ceva anubandhanti ca. Andhakavindabrāhmaṇādayo viya. Sabbaṃ khandhake tesu tesu suttesu ca āgatanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Yathā ca bhagavato, evaṃ bhikkhusaṅghassāpi.

29. Thus have I heard—this is the Dhammadāyāda Sutta. And since this sutta has an introduction concerning the occasion of its arising, therefore, having presented that, I shall provide an explanation of its new words. On what occasion of its arising was this set forth? On the occasion of gain and honor. Indeed, great gain and honor arose for the Blessed One. Due to the perfection of giving fulfilled over four incalculable eons, just as a great twin-cloud, having arisen in all directions, would produce a great flood, so all the perfections, as if gathered together with the thought, 'We shall give our result in this one existence,' produced a great flood of gain and honor. From here and there, khattiyas, brāhmaṇas, and others, with food, drink, vehicles, clothes, garlands, perfumes, and ointments in hand, came searching for the Blessed One, asking, 'Where is the Buddha? Where is the Blessed One? Where is the god of gods, the bull of men, the lion of men?' Bringing requisites even in hundreds of carts, and not getting an opportunity to offer, they stood all around for a distance of even a gāvuta, with cart-yoke touching cart-yoke, and they also followed, like the brāhmaṇas of Andhakavinda and others. All this should be understood in the manner it is presented in the Khandhakas and in those various suttas. And as it was for the Blessed One, so too was it for the community of bhikkhus.

Vuttampi cetaṃ – “tena kho pana samayena bhagavā sakkato hoti garukato mānito pūjito apacito lābhī cīvarapiṇḍapātasenāsanagilānapaccayabhesajjaparikkhārānaṃ, bhikkhusaṅghopi kho sakkato hoti…pe… parikkhārāna”nti (udā. 14). Tathā – “yāvatā [M 1.0092] kho, cunda, etarahi saṅgho vā gaṇo vā loke uppanno, nāhaṃ, cunda, aññaṃ ekasaṅghampi samanupassāmi, evaṃ lābhaggayasaggapattaṃ, yathariva, cunda, bhikkhusaṅgho”ti (dī. ni. 3.176).

And this too has been said: 'At that time, the Blessed One was honored, respected, revered, worshipped, venerated, and a recipient of robes, almsfood, lodging, and medicinal requisites for the sick. The community of bhikkhus was also honored… a recipient of requisites.' (Udā. 14). Similarly: 'Cunda, inasmuch as any saṅgha or group has arisen in the world at present, I do not see, Cunda, any other single saṅgha that has attained such a summit of gain and fame as has the community of bhikkhus.' (Dī. Ni. 3.176).

Svāyaṃ bhagavato ca bhikkhusaṅghassa ca uppanno lābhasakkāro ekato hutvā dvinnaṃ mahānadīnaṃ udakamiva appameyyo ahosi. Kamena bhikkhū paccayagarukā paccayabāhulikā ahesuṃ. Pacchābhattampi telamadhuphāṇitādīsu āhaṭesu gaṇḍiṃyeva paharitvā “amhākaṃ ācariyassa detha, upajjhāyassa dethā”ti uccāsaddamahāsaddaṃ karonti. Sā ca nesaṃ pavatti bhagavatopi [V 1.0096] pākaṭā ahosi. Tato bhagavā ananucchavikanti dhammasaṃvegaṃ uppādetvā cintesi –

This gain and honor that arose for the Blessed One and for the community of bhikkhus, having come together as one, became immeasurable, like the water of two great rivers. Gradually, the bhikkhus came to hold requisites in high esteem and were devoted to an abundance of requisites. Even after the meal, when items like oil, honey, and molasses were brought, they would just strike the gong and make a loud and great noise, saying, 'Give our teacher his share! Give our preceptor his share!' And that conduct of theirs became manifest even to the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One, thinking, 'This is unsuitable,' aroused a sense of spiritual urgency and thought:

“Paccayā akappiyāti na sakkā sikkhāpadaṃ paññapetuṃ. Paccayapaṭibaddhā hi kulaputtānaṃ samaṇadhammavutti. Handāhaṃ dhammadāyādapaṭipadaṃ desemi. Sā sikkhākāmānaṃ kulaputtānaṃ sikkhāpadapaññatti viya bhavissati nagaradvāre ṭhapitasabbakāyikaādāso viya ca, yathā hi nagaradvāre ṭhapite sabbakāyike ādāse cattāro vaṇṇā attano chāyaṃ disvā vajjaṃ pahāya niddosā honti, evameva sikkhākāmā kulaputtā payogamaṇḍanena attānaṃ maṇḍetukāmā imaṃ sabbakāyikādāsūpamaṃ [P 1.0089] desanaṃ āvajjitvā āmisadāyādapaṭipadaṃ vajjetvā dhammadāyādapaṭipadaṃ pūrentā khippameva jātijarāmaraṇassa antaṃ karissantī”ti. Imissā aṭṭhuppattiyā idaṃ suttaṃ abhāsi.

'It is not possible to lay down a training rule [saying], “Requisites are unsuitable.” For the practice of the ascetic life for sons of good family is bound up with requisites. Well now, I shall teach the practice of being heirs to the Dhamma. For sons of good family who desire the training, it will be like the laying down of a training rule, and like a full-length mirror placed at the city gate. For just as when a full-length mirror is placed at the city gate, people of the four castes, seeing their own reflection, abandon any blemish and become flawless, so too, sons of good family who desire the training, wishing to adorn themselves with the ornament of practice, having reflected on this teaching that is like a full-length mirror, avoiding the practice of being heirs to material things and fulfilling the practice of being heirs to the Dhamma, will quickly make an end of birth, aging, and death.' On this occasion of its arising, this sutta was spoken.

Tattha dhammadāyādā me, bhikkhave, bhavatha, mā āmisadāyādāti dhammassa me dāyādā, bhikkhave, bhavatha, mā āmisassa. Yo mayhaṃ dhammo, tassa paṭiggāhakā bhavatha, yañca kho mayhaṃ āmisaṃ, tassa mā paṭiggāhakā bhavathāti vuttaṃ hoti. Tattha dhammopi duvidho – nippariyāyadhammo, pariyāyadhammoti. Āmisampi duvidhaṃ – nippariyāyāmisaṃ, pariyāyāmisanti. Kathaṃ? Maggaphalanibbānabhedo hi navavidhopi lokuttaradhammo nippariyāyadhammo nibbattitadhammo, na yena kenaci pariyāyena kāraṇena vā lesena vā dhammo. Yaṃ panidaṃ vivaṭṭūpanissitaṃ kusalaṃ, seyyathidaṃ, idhekacco [M 1.0093] vivaṭṭaṃ patthento dānaṃ deti, sīlaṃ samādiyati, uposathakammaṃ karoti, gandhamālādīhi vatthupūjaṃ karoti, dhammaṃ suṇāti deseti jhānasamāpattiyo nibbatteti, evaṃ karonto anupubbena nippariyāyadhammaṃ amataṃ nibbānaṃ paṭilabhati, ayaṃ pariyāyadhammo. Tathā cīvarādayo cattāro paccayā nippariyāyāmisameva, na aññena pariyāyena kāraṇena vā lesena vā āmisaṃ. Yaṃ panidaṃ vaṭṭagāmikusalaṃ, seyyathidaṃ, idhekacco vaṭṭaṃ patthento sampattibhavaṃ icchamāno dānaṃ deti…pe… samāpattiyo nibbatteti, evaṃ karonto anupubbena devamanussasampattiṃ paṭilabhati, idaṃ pariyāyāmisaṃ nāma.

Therein, [it was said]: 'Bhikkhus, be my heirs in the Dhamma, not heirs in material things.' This means: 'Bhikkhus, be heirs of my Dhamma, not of material things. Be recipients of my Dhamma, but do not be recipients of my material things.' This is the meaning. Therein, Dhamma is twofold: direct Dhamma and indirect Dhamma. Material things are also twofold: direct material things and indirect material things. How so? The ninefold supramundane Dhamma, divided into path, fruit, and Nibbāna, is the direct Dhamma, a produced Dhamma; it is not a Dhamma that has come about by some indirect means, cause, or pretext. But as to this wholesome action that is supportive of turning away from the round of existence—that is, when someone, aspiring for that turning away, gives gifts, undertakes precepts, observes the Uposatha, performs offerings to the Triple Gem with perfumes, garlands, and so on, listens to and teaches the Dhamma, and produces the jhānas and meditative attainments—by doing so, one gradually attains the deathless Nibbāna, which is the direct Dhamma. This wholesome action is the indirect Dhamma. Similarly, the four requisites—robes and so on—are direct material things; they are not material things by any other indirect means, cause, or pretext. But as to this wholesome action that leads to the round of existence—that is, when someone, aspiring for the round, desiring a fortunate state of existence, gives gifts… produces meditative attainments—by doing so, one gradually attains the prosperity of devas and humans: this is called an indirect material thing.

Tattha nippariyāyadhammopi bhagavatoyeva santako. Bhagavatā hi kathitattā bhikkhū [V 1.0097] maggaphalanibbānāni adhigacchanti. Vuttampi cetaṃ “so hi brāhmaṇa bhagavā anuppannassa maggassa uppādetā, asañjātassa maggassa sañjanetā, anakkhātassa maggassa akkhātā, maggaññū maggavidū maggakovido. Maggānugā ca pana etarahi sāvakā viharanti pacchā samannāgatā”ti (ma. ni. 3.79) ca – “so hāvuso, bhagavā jānaṃ jānāti, passaṃ passati cakkhubhūto ñāṇabhūto dhammabhūto brahmabhūto vattā pavattā atthassa ninnetā amatassa dātā dhammassāmī tathāgato”ti (ma. ni. 1.203) ca. Pariyāyadhammopi bhagavatoyeva santako. Bhagavatā [P 1.0090] hi kathitattā evaṃ jānanti “vivaṭṭaṃ patthetvā dānaṃ dento…pe… samāpattiyo nibbattento anukkamena amataṃ nibbānaṃ paṭilabhatī”ti. Nippariyāyāmisampi ca bhagavatoyeva santakaṃ. Bhagavatā hi anuññātattāyeva bhikkhūhi jīvakavatthuṃ ādiṃ katvā paṇītacīvaraṃ laddhaṃ. Yathāha “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, gahapaticīvaraṃ. Yo icchati, paṃsukūliko hotu, yo icchati, gahapaticīvaraṃ sādiyatu. Itarītarenapāhaṃ, bhikkhave, santuṭṭhiṃyeva vaṇṇemī”ti (mahāva. 337).

Therein, the supramundane Dhamma also belongs to the Blessed One alone. For it is because it has been taught by the Blessed One that monks attain the path, fruition, and Nibbāna. And this has been said: "Indeed, brahmin, the Blessed One is the producer of the unarisen path, the generator of the ungenerated path, the declarer of the undeclared path. He is the knower of the path, the discerner of the path, the one skilled in the path. And now his disciples dwell following the path and afterwards become endowed with it" (MN 3.79); and: "Friends, the Blessed One knows what is to be known, sees what is to be seen. He has become the eye, become knowledge, become the Dhamma, become the supreme. He is the speaker, the proclaimer, the elucidator of the meaning, the giver of the Deathless, the lord of the Dhamma, the Tathāgata" (MN 1.203). The Dhamma of indirect meaning also belongs to the Blessed One alone. For it is because it has been taught by the Blessed One that they know thus: "Aspiring for freedom from the round of existence, one who gives a gift…pe… one who brings about meditative attainments, gradually attains the Deathless, Nibbāna." And the material gain of direct meaning also belongs to the Blessed One alone. For it is only because it has been permitted by the Blessed One that fine robes, beginning with the Jīvaka affair, were obtained by the monks. As he said: "I allow, monks, a robe from a householder. Whoever wishes, let him be a wearer of rag-robes; whoever wishes, let him accept a robe from a householder. Monks, with either this or that, I praise only contentment" (Mahāvagga 337).

Pubbe ca bhikkhū paṇītapiṇḍapātaṃ nālatthuṃ. Sapadānapiṇḍiyālopabhojanā evāhesuṃ. Tehi rājagahe viharantena bhagavatā – “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, saṅghabhattaṃ uddesabhattaṃ nimantanaṃ salākabhattaṃ pakkhikaṃ [M 1.0094] uposathikaṃ pāṭipadika”nti (cūḷava. 325) evaṃ anuññātattāyeva paṇītabhojanaṃ laddhaṃ. Tathā senāsanaṃ. Pubbe hi akatapabbhārarukkhamūlādisenāsanāyeva bhikkhū ahesuṃ. Te “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, pañca leṇānī”ti (cūḷava. 294) evaṃ bhagavatā anuññātattāyeva vihāro aḍḍhayogo pāsādo hammiyaṃ guhāti imāni senāsanāni labhiṃsu. Pubbe ca muttaharītakeneva bhesajjaṃ akaṃsu. Te bhagavatāyeva – “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, pañca bhesajjāni, seyyathidaṃ, sappi, navanītaṃ, telaṃ, madhu, phāṇita”nti (mahāva. 260) evamādinā nayena anuññātattā nānābhesajjāni labhiṃsu.

And previously, monks did not obtain fine almsfood. They were only those who ate morsels of almsfood from an uninterrupted alms-round. It was only because it was permitted by the Blessed One dwelling in Rājagaha—"I allow, monks, a meal for the Sangha, a meal by designation, an invitation, a ticket-meal, a fortnightly meal, an Uposatha-day meal, and a first-day-of-the-fortnight meal" (Cūḷavagga 325)—that fine food was obtained. Likewise, lodgings. For previously, monks only had lodgings such as unprepared mountain clefts and the roots of trees. It was only because it was permitted by the Blessed One—"I allow, monks, five kinds of dwellings" (Cūḷavagga 294)—that they obtained these lodgings: a monastery, a gabled building, a long-house, a storeyed building, and a cave. And previously, they made medicine only with myrobalan fruit pickled in urine. It was because it was permitted by the Blessed One in this way and others—"I allow, monks, five medicines, that is: ghee, fresh butter, oil, honey, and molasses" (Mahāvagga 260)—that they obtained various medicines.

Pariyāyāmisampi bhagavatoyeva santakaṃ. Bhagavatā hi kathitattā yeva jānanti – “sampattibhavaṃ patthento dānaṃ datvā sīlaṃ…pe… samāpattiyo nibbattetvā anukkamena pariyāyāmisaṃ dibbasampattiṃ manussasampattiṃ paṭilabhatī”ti. Tadeva, yasmā nippariyāyadhammopi pariyāyadhammopi [V 1.0098] nippariyāyāmisampi pariyāyāmisampi bhagavatoyeva santakaṃ, tasmā tattha attano sāmibhāvaṃ dassento āha – “dhammadāyādā me, bhikkhave, bhavatha mā āmisadāyādā”ti.

The material gain of indirect meaning also belongs to the Blessed One alone. For it is only because it has been taught by the Blessed One that they know: "Aspiring for a prosperous existence, having given a gift, having undertaken the precepts…pe… having brought about meditative attainments, one gradually obtains the material gain of indirect meaning, that is, divine prosperity and human prosperity." Thus, because the Dhamma of direct meaning, the Dhamma of indirect meaning, the material gain of direct meaning, and the material gain of indirect meaning all belong to the Blessed One alone, therefore, showing his own mastery over them, he said: "Be my heirs in the Dhamma, monks, not heirs in material things."

Yo mayhaṃ santako duvidhopi dhammo, tassa dāyādā bhavatha. Yañca kho etaṃ mayhameva santakaṃ āmisaṃ, tassa [P 1.0091] dāyādā mā bhavatha. Dhammakoṭṭhāsasseva sāmino bhavatha, mā āmisakoṭṭhāsassa. Yo hi jinasāsane pabbajitvā paccayaparamo viharati catūsu taṇhuppādesu sandissamāno nikkhittadhuro dhammānudhammappaṭipattiyaṃ, ayaṃ āmisadāyādo nāma. Tādisā mā bhavatha. Yo pana anuññātapaccayesu appicchatādīni nissāya paṭisaṅkhā sevamāno paṭipattiparamo viharati catūsu ariyavaṃsesu sandissamāno, ayaṃ dhammadāyādo nāma. Tādisā bhavathāti vuttaṃ hoti.

Of whatever twofold Dhamma is my possession, be heirs to that. And of whatever material gain is also my possession, do not be heirs to that. Be masters of the Dhamma-portion only, not of the material-portion. For one who, having gone forth in the Dispensation of the Conqueror, dwells with the requisites as his ultimate concern, being seen in the four sources of craving, having laid down the yoke regarding the practice in conformity with the Dhamma—this one is called an heir in material things. Do not be like that. But one who, wisely reflecting, makes use of the permitted requisites while relying on fewness of wishes and so forth, and dwells with the practice as his ultimate concern, being seen in the four noble traditions—this one is called an heir in the Dhamma. Be like that—this is what was said.

Idāni yesaṃ tattha etadahosi, bhavissati vā anāgatamaddhānaṃ “kiṃ nu kho bhagavā sāvakānaṃ alābhatthiko evamāhā”ti, tesaṃ atipaṇītalābhatthiko ahaṃ evaṃ vadāmīti dassetumāha atthi me tumhesu…pe… no āmisadāyādāti.

Now, for those to whom this thought occurred then, or for those to whom it might occur in the future: 'Could it be that the Blessed One, not desiring gain for his disciples, spoke thus?'—to show them, 'I speak thus because I desire a most excellent gain for you,' he said: 'There is in me for you…pe… not heirs in material things.'

Tassāyamattho [M 1.0095] – atthi me tumhesu anukampā anuddayā hitesitā, kena nu kho kāraṇena kena upāyena sāvakā dhammadāyādā assu dhammakoṭṭhāsasāmino, no āmisadāyādāti. Ayaṃ pana adhippāyo, passati kira bhagavā āmisagarukānaṃ āmise upakkhalitānaṃ atītakāle tāva kapilassa bhikkhuno, “saṅghāṭipi ādittā hotī”tiādinā (pārā. 230; saṃ. ni. 2.218) nayena āgatapāpabhikkhubhikkhunīsikkhamānādīnañca anekasatānaṃ apāyaparipūraṇattaṃ attano sāsane pabbajitānañca devadattādīnaṃ. Dhammagarukānaṃ pana sāriputtamoggallānamahākassapādīnaṃ abhiññāpaṭisambhidādiguṇappaṭilābhaṃ. Tasmā tesaṃ apāyā parimuttiṃ sabbaguṇasampattiñca icchanto āha – “atthi me tumhesu anukampā kinti me sāvakā dhammadāyādā bhaveyyuṃ, no āmisadāyādā”ti. Paccayagaruko ca catuparisantare kūṭakahāpaṇo viya nibbutaṅgāro viya ca nittejo nippabho hoti. Tato vivattitacitto dhammagaruko [V 1.0099] tejavā sīhova abhibhuyyacārī, tasmāpi evamāha – “atthi me…pe… no āmisadāyādā”ti.

This is its meaning: I have compassion for you, sympathy, and a desire for your welfare, thinking: 'By what reason, by what means, might my disciples become heirs to the Dhamma, masters of the Dhamma-portion, and not heirs to material things?' This, however, is the intention: The Blessed One sees, it seems, the filling of the plane of misery for those who value material things and stumble over them—in the past, for instance, for the monk Kapila, as in the passage beginning, "The outer cloak was also ablaze" (Pārājika 230; SN 2.218), and for hundreds of wicked monks, nuns, female probationers, and others; and also for Devadatta and others ordained in his own dispensation. But for those who value the Dhamma, such as Sāriputta, Moggallāna, and Mahākassapa, he sees their attainment of qualities such as the direct knowledges and the analytical insights. Therefore, desiring for them liberation from the plane of misery and the fulfillment of all virtuous qualities, he said: "There is in me for you compassion. How might my disciples become heirs to the Dhamma, and not heirs to material things?" Moreover, one who values the requisites is, amidst the fourfold assembly, like a counterfeit coin and like an extinguished ember, without power and without splendor. Having turned his mind from that, one who values the Dhamma is powerful and, like a lion, moves with mastery. For this reason too, he said: "There is in me…pe… not heirs in material things."

Evaṃ “dhammadāyādā me, bhikkhave, bhavatha, mā āmisadāyādā”ti idaṃ anukampāya paṇītataraṃ lābhaṃ icchantena vuttaṃ, no alābhatthikenāti sāvetvā idāni imassa ovādassa akaraṇe ādīnavaṃ dassento āha “tumhe ca me, bhikkhave…pe… no dhammadāyādā”ti. Tattha tumhepi tena [P 1.0092] ādiyā bhaveyyāthāti tumhepi tena āmisadāyādabhāvena no dhammadāyādabhāvena ādiyā bhaveyyātha. Apadisitabbā visuṃ kātabbā vavatthapetabbā, viññūhi gārayhā bhaveyyāthāti vuttaṃ hoti. Kinti? Āmisadāyādā satthusāvakā viharanti, no dhammadāyādāti.

Thus, 'Be my heirs in the Dhamma, O monks, not heirs in material things.' This was said out of compassion, by one desiring a more excellent gain, not by one who is undesirous of gain. Having declared this, and now showing the danger in not practicing this exhortation, he said: 'And you, O monks... not heirs in the Dhamma.' Therein, 'You too would be censured for that' means: you too, on account of that state of being heirs in material things and not heirs in the Dhamma, would be censured. You should be pointed out for censure, you should be set apart, you should be distinguished; you would be censured by the wise—this is what is meant. How so? 'The Teacher’s disciples dwell as heirs in material things, not as heirs in the Dhamma.'

Ahampi tena ādiyo bhaveyyanti ahampi tena tumhākaṃ āmisadāyādabhāvena no dhammadāyādabhāvena gārayho bhaveyyaṃ. Kinti? Āmisa…pe… dāyādāti. Idaṃ bhagavā tesaṃ atīva mudukaraṇatthamāha. Ayañhi ettha adhippāyo – sace, bhikkhave, tumhe āmisalolā carissatha, tattha viññū maṃ garahissanti “kathañhi nāma sabbaññū samāno attano sāvake [M 1.0096] dhammadāyāde no āmisadāyāde kātuṃ na sakkotī”ti. Seyyathāpi nāma anākappasampanne bhikkhū disvā ācariyupajjhāye garahanti “kassime saddhivihārikā, kassantevāsikā”ti; seyyathā vā pana kulakumārake vā kulakumārikāyo vā dussīle pāpadhamme disvā mātāpitaro garahanti “kassime puttā, kassa dhītaro”ti; evameva maṃ viññū garahissanti “kathañhi nāma sabbaññū samāno attano sāvake dhammadāyāde no āmisadāyāde kātuṃ na sakkotī”ti.

'I too would be reproachable for that' means: I too, on account of your state of being heirs in material things and not heirs in the Dhamma, would be reproachable. How so? 'Material... heirs.' The Blessed One said this to make them exceedingly gentle. For this is the intention here: 'If, O monks, you were to act greedily for material things, in that case the wise would censure me, saying: "How is it that one who is the All-Knowing One is unable to make his disciples become heirs in the Dhamma, not heirs in material things?"' Just as, having seen monks not endowed with proper conduct, they censure the teachers and preceptors, saying: 'Whose co-residents are these? Whose pupils are these?' Or just as, having seen young men or young women who are immoral and of evil nature, they censure their parents, saying: 'Whose sons are these? Whose daughters are these?' In the very same way, the wise will censure me, saying: 'How is it that one who is the All-Knowing One is unable to make his disciples become heirs in the Dhamma, not heirs in material things?'

Evaṃ imassa ovādassa akaraṇe ādīnavaṃ dassetvā karaṇe ānisaṃsaṃ dassento tumhe ca metiādimāha. Tattha ahampi tena na ādiyo bhaveyyanti seyyathāpi nāma vattaparipūrake daharabhikkhū uddesaparipucchāsampanne vassasatikatthere viya ākappasampanne disvā, kassa saddhivihārikā, kassantevāsikāti, asukassāti, “patirūpaṃ therassa, paṭibalo vata ovadituṃ anusāsitu”nti ācariyupajjhāyā na ādiyā na gārayhā bhavanti, evameva ahampi tena tumhākaṃ dhammadāyādabhāvena no āmisadāyādabhāvena kassa sāvakā nālakapaṭipadaṃ [V 1.0100] tuvaṭṭakapaṭipadaṃ candūpamapaṭipadaṃ rathavinītapaṭipadaṃ mahāgosiṅgasālapaṭipadaṃ mahāsuññatapaṭipadaṃ paṭipannā catupaccayasantosabhāvanārāmaariyavaṃsesu sakkhibhūtā paccayagedhato vivattamānasā abbhā muttacandasamā viharantīti; “samaṇassa [P 1.0093] gotamassā”ti vutte “sabbaññū vata bhagavā, asakkhi vata sāvake āmisadāyādapaṭipadaṃ chaḍḍāpetvā dhammadāyādapaṭipattipūrake kātu”nti viññūnaṃ na ādiyo na gārayho bhaveyyanti. Evamimasmiṃ pade adhippāyaṃ ñatvā sesaṃ kaṇhapakkhe vuttanayapaccanīkena veditabbaṃ. Evaṃ imassa ovādassa karaṇe ānisaṃsaṃ dassetvā idāni taṃ ovādaṃ niyyātento āha – “tasmā tiha me, bhikkhave…pe… no āmisadāyādā”ti.

Thus, having shown the danger in not practicing this exhortation, and showing the benefit in practicing it, he said the words beginning with 'And you, O monks...'. Therein, 'I too would not be reproachable for that' means: just as, having seen young monks who fulfill their duties, are accomplished in recitation and questioning, and are endowed with proper conduct like an elder of a hundred rains, people ask, 'Whose co-residents are these? Whose pupils are these?' and when told, 'Of so-and-so,' the teachers and preceptors are not reproachable, not censurable, as people think, 'It is fitting for the elder; indeed, he is capable of exhorting and instructing.' In the very same way, I too, on account of your state of being heirs in the Dhamma and not heirs in material things—when it is said of you, 'Whose disciples are these who dwell, having undertaken the practice of the Nālaka, the Tuvaṭṭaka, the Candūpama, the Rathavinīta, the Mahāgosiṅgasāla, and the Mahāsuññata suttas; having become witnesses to the noble lineages of contentment with the four requisites and delight in development; with minds turned away from greed for requisites; like the moon freed from a cloud?' and the answer is given, 'Of the ascetic Gotama'—I would not be reproachable, not censurable, by the wise, who would think, 'Indeed, the Blessed One is all-knowing! Indeed, he was able to make his disciples abandon the practice of being heirs in material things and become fulfillers of the practice of being heirs in the Dhamma!' Thus, having understood the intention in this passage, the remainder should be understood by the opposite of the method stated in the dark portion. Thus, having shown the benefit in practicing this exhortation, he now, handing over that exhortation, said: 'Therefore, O monks... not heirs in material things.'

30. Evamimaṃ ovādaṃ niyyātetvā idāni tassā dhammadāyādapaṭipattiyā paripūrakāriṃ thometuṃ idhāhaṃ, bhikkhavetiādimāha. Bhagavato hi thomanaṃ sutvāpi hontiyeva tadatthāya paṭipajjitāro.

30. Thus, having handed over this exhortation, now, in order to praise the one who fulfills that practice of being a Dhamma heir, he said the words beginning with 'Here, I, O monks...'. For indeed, even having heard the praise of the Blessed One, there are those who undertake the practice for that purpose.

Tattha [M 1.0097] idhāti nipātapadametaṃ. Bhuttāvīti bhuttavā, katabhattakiccoti vuttaṃ hoti. Pavāritoti yāvadatthapavāraṇāya pavārito, yāvadatthaṃ bhuñjitvā paṭikkhittabhojano tittovāti vuttaṃ hoti. Catubbidhā hi pavāraṇā vassaṃvuṭṭhapavāraṇā paccayapavāraṇā anatirittapavāraṇā yāvadatthapavāraṇāti. Tattha, “anujānāmi bhikkhave, vassaṃvuṭṭhānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ tīhi ṭhānehi pavāretu”nti (mahāva. 209) ayaṃ vassaṃvuṭṭhapavāraṇā. “Icchāmahaṃ, bhante, saṅghaṃ catumāsaṃ bhesajjena pavāretu”nti (pāci. 303) ca “aññatra punapavāraṇāya aññatra niccapavāraṇāyā”ti (pāci. 307) ca ayaṃ paccayapavāraṇā. “Pavārito nāma asanaṃ paññāyati, bhojanaṃ paññāyati, hatthapāse ṭhito abhiharati, paṭikkhepo paññāyati, eso pavārito nāmā”ti (pāci. 239) ayaṃ anatirittapavāraṇā. “Paṇītena khādanīyena bhojanīyena sahatthā santappesi sampavāresī”ti (dī. ni. 1.297, 358) ayaṃ yāvadatthapavāraṇā. Ayamidha adhippetā. Tena vuttaṃ “pavāritoti yāvadatthapavāraṇāya pavārito”ti.

Therein, 'idha' is a particle. 'Bhuttāvī' means 'one who has eaten'; that is to say, 'one who has completed the business of the meal.' 'Pavārito' means one who has been invited with the 'invitation to satisfaction'; that is to say, one who, having eaten to satisfaction, has refused food and is satiated. Indeed, the pavāraṇā is fourfold: the invitation after the rains-residence, the invitation regarding requisites, the invitation regarding non-excess, and the invitation to satisfaction. Therein, 'I allow, O monks, for monks who have completed the rains-residence to be invited on three grounds' is the invitation after the rains-residence. 'I wish, venerable sir, to invite the Sangha with medicine for four months' and 'apart from a renewed invitation, apart from a permanent invitation' is the invitation regarding requisites. 'One is called "invited" when food is apparent, a meal is apparent, one standing within arm's reach offers it, and a refusal is apparent—this is called "invited"' is the invitation regarding non-excess. 'With excellent hard and soft food, he gratified and fully invited them with his own hand' is the invitation to satisfaction. This last one is intended here. Therefore it was said: '“Pavārito” means one who has been invited with the invitation to satisfaction.'

Paripuṇṇoti bhojanena paripuṇṇo. Pariyositoti pariyositabhojano, uttarapadalopo daṭṭhabbo[V 1.0101]. Yāvatakaṃ bhuñjitabbaṃ, tāvatakaṃ bhuttaṃ hoti, avasitā me bhojanakiriyāti attho. Suhitoti dhāto, jighacchādukkhābhāvena vā sukhitoti vuttaṃ hoti. Yāvadatthoti yāvatako [P 1.0094] me bhojanena attho, so sabbo pattoti. Ettha ca purimānaṃ tiṇṇaṃ pacchimāni sādhakāni. Yo hi pariyosito, so bhuttāvī hoti. Yo ca suhito, so yāvadatthapavāraṇāya pavārito. Yo yāvadattho, so paripuṇṇoti. Purimāni vā pacchimānaṃ. Yasmā hi bhuttāvī, tasmā pariyosito. Yasmā pavārito, tasmā suhito. Yasmā paripuṇṇo, tasmā yāvadatthoti. Sabbañcetaṃ parikappetvā vuttanti veditabbaṃ.

“Paripuṇṇo” means “complete with food.” “Pariyosito” means “one whose meal is finished”; the elision of the latter word, bhojano, should be understood. It means that as much as should be eaten, that much has been eaten; “my act of eating is finished”—this is the meaning. “Suhito” means “satiated,” or it is said to mean “happy” due to the absence of the suffering of hunger. “Yāvadattho” means “as much as I need of food, all of that has been obtained.” And here, the latter terms are supportive of the former three. For one who has finished is one who has eaten. And one who is satiated is one who has been invited to take as much as desired. One who has had as much as desired is one who is complete. Alternatively, the former terms are supportive of the latter. For because one has eaten, one has finished. Because one has been invited, one is satiated. Because one is complete, one has had as much as desired. And all this should be understood as having been stated after consideration.

Siyāti ekaṃse ca vikappane ca. “Pathavīdhātu siyā ajjhattikā, siyā bāhirā”ti (ma. ni. 3.349) ekaṃse. “Siyā aññatarassa bhikkhuno āpatti vītikkamo”ti (ma. ni. 3.39) vikappane. Idha ubhayampi vaṭṭati. Atirekova atirekadhammo. Tathā chaḍḍanīya dhammo. Adhiko ca chaḍḍetabbo ca, na aññaṃ kiñci kātabboti [M 1.0098] attho. Athāti tamhi kāle. Jighacchādubbalyaparetāti jighacchāya ca dubbalyena ca paretā phuṭṭhā anugatā ca aṭṭhapi dasapi divasāni. Tattha keci jighacchitāpi na dubbalā honti, sakkonti jighacchaṃ sahituṃ. Ime pana na tādisāti dassetuṃ ubhayamāha. Tyāhanti te ahaṃ. Sace ākaṅkhathāti yadi icchatha.

“Siyā” is used in the sense of “in part” and in the sense of “deliberation.” In “The earth element is partly internal, partly external” (MN 3.349), it is in the sense of “in part.” In “Might there be a transgression of an offense for a certain monk?” (MN 3.39), it is in the sense of “deliberation.” Here, both meanings are suitable. It is an excess, a thing that is in excess. Similarly, it is a thing to be discarded. It is extra and it should be discarded; nothing else is to be done—this is the meaning. “Atha” means “at that time.” “Jighacchādubbalyaparetā” means “overcome, afflicted, and beset by hunger and weakness” for eight or ten days. Among them, some, though hungry, are not weak; they are able to endure hunger. But to show that these two are not like that, he said both. In “tyāhaṃ,” the word division should be made as “te ahaṃ.” “Sace ākaṅkhatha” means “if you wish.”

Appahariteti apparuḷhaharite, yasmiṃ ṭhāne piṇḍapātajjhottharaṇena vinassanadhammāni tiṇāni natthi, tasminti attho. Tena nittiṇañca mahātiṇagahanaṃ ca, yattha sakaṭenapi chaḍḍite piṇḍapāte tiṇāni na vinassanti, tañca ṭhānaṃ pariggahitaṃ hoti. Bhūtagāmasikkhāpadassa hi avikopanatthametaṃ vuttaṃ.

“Appaharite” means “in a place with little green growth”; that is, “in a place where there is no grass liable to be destroyed by the spreading of almsfood”—this is the meaning. By this, both a place without grass and a thicket of mature grass—where, even if almsfood were discarded from a cart, the grass would not be destroyed—that place is included. For this was said for the sake of not violating the training rule concerning living plants.

Appāṇaketi nippāṇake piṇḍapātajjhottharaṇena maritabbapāṇakarahite vā mahāudakakkhandhe. Parittodake eva hi bhattapakkhepena āḷulite sukhumapāṇakā maranti, na mahātaḷākādīsūti. Pāṇakānurakkhaṇatthañhi etaṃ vuttaṃ. Opilāpessāmīti nimujjāpessāmi.

“Appāṇake” means “in water without living beings”; or in a great body of water free from creatures that would be killed by the spreading of almsfood. For it is only in a small amount of water, when stirred by the casting in of food, that minute creatures die, not in large reservoirs and so on. For this was said for the sake of protecting living beings. “Opilāpessāmi” means “I will cause to sink.”

Tatrekassāti tesu dvīsu ekassa. Yo imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ suṭṭhu sutavā punappunaṃ āvajjeti ca[V 1.0102], taṃ sandhāyāha vuttaṃ kho panetanti. Ayaṃ vutta-saddo kesohāraṇepi dissati “kāpaṭiko māṇavo daharo vuttasiro”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 2.426). Ropitepi “yathā sāradikaṃ bījaṃ, khette vuttaṃ virūhatī”tiādīsu [P 1.0095] (jā. 1.3.31). Kathitepi “vuttamidaṃ bhagavatā, vuttamidaṃ arahatā”tiādīsu. Idha pana kathite daṭṭhabbo. Kathitaṃ kho panetanti ayañhissa attho. Āmisaññataranti catunnaṃ paccayāmisānaṃ aññataraṃ, ekanti attho. Yadidanti nipāto, sabbaliṅgavibhattivacanesu tādisova tattha tattha atthato pariṇāmetabbo. Idha panāssa yo esoti attho. Yo eso piṇḍapāto nāma. Idaṃ āmisaññataranti vuttaṃ hoti. Yaṃnūnāhanti sādhu vatāhaṃ. Evanti yathā idāni imaṃ khaṇaṃ vītināmemi, evameva rattindivaṃ. Vītināmeyyanti khepeyyaṃ ativattāpeyyaṃ.

“Tatrekassa” means “of one of those two.” With reference to the one who has heard this Dhamma teaching well and reflects on it again and again, he said, “vuttaṃ kho panetaṃ” (And this was said). This word “vutta” is also seen in the sense of “removing hair,” as in “kāpaṭiko māṇavo daharo vuttasiro” (the young brahmin Kāpaṭika with a shaven head), and so on (MN 2.426). It is also seen in the sense of “sown,” as in “yathā sāradikaṃ bījaṃ, khette vuttaṃ virūhati” (just as an autumn seed, sown in a field, sprouts), and so on (Jā 1.3.31). It is also seen in the sense of “spoken,” as in “vuttamidaṃ bhagavatā, vuttamidaṃ arahatā” (this was spoken by the Blessed One, this was spoken by the Arahant), and so on. But here, it should be understood in the sense of “spoken.” For its meaning is “And this was spoken.” “Āmisaññataraṃ” means “one of the four material requisites”; that is, “one.” “Yadidaṃ” is a particle; in all genders, cases, and numbers, it should be interpreted accordingly by meaning in each context. But here, its meaning is “yo eso” (that which is). “That which is called almsfood, this is one of the material requisites”—this is what is meant. In “yaṃnūnāhaṃ,” the meaning is “sādhu vatāhaṃ” (it would be good indeed for me). “Evaṃ” means “just as I am now passing this moment, in this very way day and night.” “Vītināmeyyaṃ” means “I would spend,” “I would pass.”

So taṃ piṇḍapātanti so taṃ sadevakena lokena sirasā sampaṭicchitabbarūpaṃ sugatātirittampi piṇḍapātaṃ abhuñjitvā dhammadāyādabhāvaṃ ākaṅkhamāno [M 1.0099] ādittasīsūpamaṃ paccavekkhitvā teneva jighacchādubbalyena evaṃ taṃ rattindivaṃ vītināmeyya.

“So taṃ piṇḍapātaṃ” means: that monk, desiring the state of being a Dhamma heir, not having eaten even that almsfood—which was the remainder from the Sugata and fit to be received with the head by the world with its devas—and having reflected on the simile of the head on fire, should thus pass that day and night with that very hunger and weakness.

Atha dutiyassāti imasmiṃ pana vāre esa saṅkhepo, sace so bhikkhu, yaṃnūnāhaṃ…pe… vītināmeyyanti cintento evampi cinteyya, pabbajitena kho vāḷamigākule araññe bhesajjaṃ viya pañcakāmaguṇavāḷākule gāme piṇḍapātopi dukkhaṃ pariyesituṃ. Ayaṃ pana piṇḍapāto iti pariyesanādīnavavimutto ca sugatātiritto cāti ubhato sujātakhattiyakumāro viya hoti, yehi ca pañcahi kāraṇehi piṇḍapāto na paribhuñjitabbo hoti. Seyyathidaṃ, puggalaṃ garahitvā na paribhuñjitabbo hoti “alajjipuggalassa santako”ti. Aparisuddhauppattitāya na paribhuñjitabbo hoti “bhikkhuniparipācanaasantasambhāvanuppanno”ti. Sāmikānukampāya na paribhuñjitabbo hoti “piṇḍapātasāmiko bhikkhu jighacchito”ti. So dhāto tasseva antevāsikādīsu anukampāya na paribhuñjitabbo hoti “antevāsikā aññe vā tappaṭibaddhā jighacchitā”ti, tepi dhātā suhitā, apica kho assaddhatāya na paribhuñjitabbo hoti “piṇḍapātasāmiko bhikkhu assaddho”ti. Tehi ca kāraṇehi ayaṃ vimutto. Bhagavā hi lajjīnaṃ aggo, parisuddhuppattiko piṇḍapāto, bhagavā ca dhāto suhito, paccāsīsakopi añño puggalo natthi, ye loke saddhā, bhagavā tesaṃ aggoti evaṃ cintetvā [V 1.0103] ca so taṃ piṇḍapātaṃ bhuñjitvā…pe… vītināmeyya. Ettāvatā [P 1.0096] yopi abhuñjitvā samaṇadhammaṃ karoti, sopi bhuñjitabbakameva piṇḍapātaṃ na bhutto hoti. Yopi bhuñjitvā samaṇadhammaṃ karoti, sopi bhuñjitabbakameva bhutto hoti. Natthi piṇḍapāte viseso. Puggale pana atthi viseso. Tasmā taṃ dassento kiñcāpi sotiādimāha.

Then, regarding the second instance, this is the summary: If that monk, thinking, 'What if I were to... (etc.)... pass the time?' he might also reflect thus: 'Indeed, for one who has gone forth, it is difficult to seek almsfood in a village teeming with the wild beasts of the five cords of sensual pleasure, just as it is to seek medicine in a wilderness infested with wild beasts.' But this almsfood is both free from the dangers of seeking and is the remainder from the Sugata; thus, it is like a khattiya prince of pure birth on both sides. And there are five reasons for which almsfood is not to be consumed. What are they? It is not to be consumed after censuring the person, [thinking,] 'It is the property of a shameless person.' It is not to be consumed due to its impure origin, [thinking,] 'It arose from a bhikkhunī's arrangement or from speaking of non-existent superhuman states.' It is not to be consumed out of compassion for the owner, [thinking,] 'The monk who owns the almsfood is hungry.' [Even if] he is satisfied, it is not to be consumed out of compassion for his resident pupils and so on, [thinking,] 'His resident pupils or others connected with him are hungry.' (Even if they too are satisfied and content.) Moreover, it is not to be consumed due to faithlessness, [thinking,] 'The monk who owns the almsfood is faithless.' This almsfood is free from those reasons. Indeed, the Blessed One is the foremost of the scrupulous; the almsfood is of pure origin; and the Blessed One is satisfied and content. There is no other person who is an object of expectation. Of those in the world who are faithful, the Blessed One is the foremost. Having reflected thus, that monk, having eaten that almsfood... (etc.)... might pass the time. To this extent, whoever performs the duty of a recluse without eating has not eaten almsfood that should have been eaten. And whoever performs the duty of a recluse after eating has eaten what should have been eaten. There is no difference in the almsfood, but there is a difference in the person. Therefore, to show this, he said, 'Kiñcāpi so...' and so on.

Tattha kiñcāpīti anujānanappasaṃsanatthe nipāto. Kiṃ anujānāti? Tassa bhikkhuno taṃ anavajjaparibhogaṃ. Kiṃ pasaṃsati? Bhutvā samaṇadhammakaraṇaṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti yadipi so bhikkhu evaṃ bhuñjitabbameva bhuñjitvā kātabbameva kareyya. Atha kho asuyeva me purimo bhikkhūti yo purimo bhikkhu tampi piṇḍapātaṃ paṭikkhipitvā samaṇadhammaṃ karoti, soyeva mama dvīsu sūresu sūrataro viya dvīsu paṇḍitesu paṇḍitataro viya ca pujjataro [M 1.0100] ca pāsaṃsataro ca, dutiyabhikkhuto atirekena pūjanīyo ca pasaṃsanīyo cāti vuttaṃ hoti.

Therein, 'kiñcāpi' is a particle in the sense of allowing and praising. What does it allow? That monk's blameless consumption. What does it praise? Performing the duty of a recluse without eating. This is what is said: Even if that monk were to eat what should be eaten and do what should be done, nevertheless, for me he is not brave. The former monk—the one who, having rejected that almsfood, performs the duty of a recluse—that very one is for me like the braver of two brave ones and like the wiser of two wise ones; he is more worthy of honor and more worthy of praise. It is said that, compared to the second monk, he is exceedingly to be honored and to be praised.

Idāni tamatthaṃ kāraṇena sādhento taṃ kissa hetūtiādimāha. Tassattho, tattha siyā tumhākaṃ, kasmā so bhikkhu bhagavato pujjataro ca pāsaṃsataro cāti? Tañhi tassāti yasmā taṃ piṇḍapātapaṭikkhipanaṃ tassa bhikkhuno dīgharattaṃ appicchatāya…pe… vīriyārambhāya saṃvattissati. Kathaṃ? Tassa hi sace aparena samayena paccayesu atricchatā vā pāpicchatā vā mahicchatā vā uppajjissati. Tato naṃ iminā piṇḍapātapaṭikkhepaṅkusena nivāressati “are tvaṃ sugatātirittampi piṇḍapātaṃ paṭikkhipitvā īdisaṃ icchaṃ uppādesī”ti evaṃ paccavekkhamāno. Esa nayo asantuṭṭhiyā asaṃlekhassa cuppannassa nivāraṇe. Evaṃ tāvassa appicchatāya santuṭṭhiyā saṃlekhāya saṃvattissati.

Now, establishing that matter with a reason, he said, 'For what reason?' and so on. Its meaning is: Your thought might be, 'Why is that monk more to be honored and more to be praised by the Blessed One?' Because that rejection of the almsfood will, for a long time, conduce to that monk's fewness of wishes... (etc.)... to the rousing of energy. How so? If, for him, at a later time, in regard to the requisites, there should arise covetousness, or evil wishes, or great wishes, then, reflecting thus, 'Friend, having rejected even the remainder-almsfood from the Sugata, do you give rise to such a wish?', he will restrain himself with this goad of having rejected the almsfood. This is the method for restraining arisen discontent and lack of austerity. Thus, it will conduce to his fewness of wishes, contentment, and austerity.

Subharatāyāti ettha ayaṃ saṃvaṇṇanā – idhekacco attanopi upaṭṭhākānampi dubbharo hoti dupposo. Ekacco attanopi upaṭṭhākānampi subharo hoti suposo. Kathaṃ? Yo hi ambilādīni laddhā anambilādīni pariyesati, aññassa ghare laddhaṃ aññassa ghare chaḍḍento sabbaṃ gāmaṃ vicaritvā rittapattova vihāraṃ pavisitvā nipajjati, ayaṃ attano dubbharo. Yo pana sālimaṃsodanādīnaṃ patte pūretvā dinnepi dummukhabhāvaṃ anattamanabhāvameva ca dasseti, tesaṃ vā sammukhāva taṃ piṇḍapātaṃ “kiṃ tumhehi dinna”nti apasādento [P 1.0097] sāmaṇeragahaṭṭhādīnampi deti[V 1.0104], ayaṃ upaṭṭhākānaṃ dubbharo. Etaṃ disvā manussā dūrato parivajjanti dubbharo bhikkhu na sakkā positunti. Yo pana yaṃkiñci lūkhaṃ vā paṇītaṃ vā laddhā tuṭṭhacittova bhuñjitvā vihāraṃ gantvā attano kammaṃ karoti, ayaṃ attano subharo. Yo ca paresampi appaṃ vā bahuṃ vā lūkhaṃ vā paṇītaṃ vā dānaṃ ahīḷetvā attamano vippasannamukho hutvā tesaṃ sammukhāva paribhuñjitvā yāti, ayaṃ upaṭṭhākānaṃ subharo. Etaṃ disvā manussā ativiya vissatthā honti – “amhākaṃ bhadanto subharo thokenapi tussati, mayameva naṃ posissāmā”ti paṭiññaṃ katvā posenti.

Regarding 'for being easy to support' (subharatāya), this is the explanation: Here, a certain monk is difficult to support and difficult to maintain, both for himself and for his supporters. Another is easy to support and easy to maintain, both for himself and for his supporters. How so? One who, having received sour foods, seeks non-sour foods; or who, discarding in another's house what was received in one house, wanders the entire village and then enters the monastery with an empty bowl and lies down—such a one is difficult to support for himself. Another who, even when given high-quality rice with meat to fill his bowl, shows only a displeased face and a discontented mind; or who, right in their presence, disparages that almsfood by saying, 'What is this you have given?' and then gives it to novices, householders, and so on—such a one is difficult to support for his supporters. Seeing this, people avoid him from afar, thinking, 'This monk is difficult to support; he cannot be maintained.' But one who, having received anything whatsoever, whether coarse or fine, eats it with a contented mind, returns to the monastery, and attends to his own work—such a one is easy to support for himself. And one who, when others give alms, whether little or much, coarse or fine, does not scorn the gift but, being pleased and with a serene face, consumes it in their presence before departing—such a one is easy to support for his supporters. Seeing this, people become exceedingly confident, and having made a pledge, 'Our venerable one is easy to support; he is satisfied even with a little. We ourselves will maintain him,' they maintain him.

Tattha sace aparena samayena assa attano vā upaṭṭhākānaṃ vā dubbharatānayena cittaṃ uppajjissati. Tato naṃ iminā piṇḍapātapaṭikkhepaṅkusena nivāressati – “are tvaṃ sugatātirittampi piṇḍapātaṃ paṭikkhipitvā īdisaṃ [M 1.0101] cittaṃ uppādesī”ti evaṃ paccavekkhamāno, evamassa subharatāya saṃvattissati. Sace panassa kosajjaṃ uppajjissati, tampi etenevaṅkusena nivāressati – “are tvaṃ nāma tadā sugatātirittampi piṇḍapātaṃ paṭikkhipitvā tathā jighacchādubbalyaparetopi samaṇadhammaṃ katvā ajja kosajjamanuyuñjasī”ti evaṃ paccavekkhamāno, evamassa vīriyārambhāya saṃvattissati. Evamassa idaṃ piṇḍapātapaṭikkhipanaṃ dīgharattaṃ appicchatāya…pe… vīriyārambhāya saṃvattissati. Evamassime pañca guṇā paripūrā dasa kathāvatthūni paripūressanti.

In that regard, if at a later time a thought should arise in that monk by way of being difficult to support, either on his own account or on account of his supporters, then this goad of refusing the alms-food will restrain him. Reflecting thus: 'O you! Having refused even the Sugata's leftover alms-food, have you now given rise to such a thought of being difficult to support?' In this way, it will conduce to his being easy to support. If, however, laziness should arise in him, that too will be restrained by this very goad. Reflecting thus: 'O you! At that time, having refused even the Sugata's leftover alms-food and practiced the ascetic's duty even though afflicted by hunger and weakness, do you now indulge in laziness?' In this way, it will conduce to his arousal of energy. Thus, for him, this refusal of alms-food will, for a long time, conduce to fewness of wishes... to the arousal of energy. In this way, for him, these five qualities, being fulfilled, will fulfill the ten topics of discourse.

Kathaṃ? Atra hi pāḷiyaṃyeva appicchatāsantuṭṭhitāvīriyārambhavasena tīṇi āgatāni, sesāni sallekhena saṅgahitāni. Idañhi sabbakathāvatthūnaṃ nāmameva, yadidaṃ sallekho. Yathāha – “yā ca kho ayaṃ, ānanda, kathā abhisallekhikā cetovinīvaraṇasappāyā ekantanibbidāya virāgāya nirodhāya upasamāya abhiññāya sambodhāya nibbānāya saṃvattati. Seyyathidaṃ, appicchakathā”ti (ma. ni. 3.189, 192) vitthāro. Evaṃ ime pañca guṇā paripūrā dasa kathāvatthūni paripūressanti. Dasa kathāvatthūni paripūrāni tisso sikkhā paripūressanti.

How so? For here in the Pāḷi itself, three topics have been mentioned by way of fewness of wishes, contentment, and arousal of energy; the remaining are included by way of effacement. For this is the very name for all topics of discourse, that is, effacement. As it is said: 'And what, Ānanda, is the talk that is for the purpose of effacement, suitable for the opening of the mind from the hindrances, and conduces entirely to disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to full awakening, to Nibbāna? Namely, talk on fewness of wishes.' The full text should be understood. In this way, these five qualities, being fulfilled, will fulfill the ten topics of discourse. The ten topics of discourse, being fulfilled, will fulfill the three trainings.

Kathaṃ? Etesu hi appicchakathā santosakathā asaṃsaggakathā sīlakathāti imā catasso kathā adhisīlasikkhāsaṅgahitāyeva[P 1.0098]. Pavivekakathā vīriyārambhakathā samādhikathāti imā tisso adhicittasikkhasaṅgahitā[V 1.0105]. Paññākathā vimuttikathā vimuttiñāṇadassanakathāti imā tisso adhipaññāsikkhāsaṅgahitāti. Evaṃ dasa kathāvatthūni paripūrāni tisso sikkhā paripūressanti. Tisso sikkhā paripūrā pañca asekkhadhammakkhandhe paripūressanti.

How so? Among these, these four topics—talk on fewness of wishes, talk on contentment, talk on non-association, and talk on virtue—are included in the training in higher virtue. These three—talk on seclusion, talk on arousal of energy, and talk on concentration—are included in the training in higher mind. And these three—talk on wisdom, talk on liberation, and talk on the knowledge and vision of liberation—are included in the training in higher wisdom. Thus, the ten topics of discourse, being fulfilled, will fulfill the three trainings. The three trainings, being fulfilled, will fulfill the five Dhamma-aggregates of one beyond training.

Kathaṃ? Paripūrā hi adhisīlasikkhā asekkho sīlakkhandhoyeva hoti, adhicittasikkhā asekkho samādhikkhandho, adhipaññāsikkhā asekkhā paññā-vimutti-vimuttiñāṇadassanakkhandhā evāti evaṃ tisso sikkhā paripūrā pañca asekkhadhammakkhandhe paripūressanti. Pañca dhammakkhandhā paripūrā amataṃ nibbānaṃ paripūressanti. Seyyathāpi uparipabbate pāvussako mahāmegho abhivuṭṭho [M 1.0102] pabbatakandarasarasākhā paripūreti. Tā paripūrā kusobbhe, kusobbhā mahāsobbhe, mahāsobbhā kunnadiyo, kunnadiyo mahānadiyo, mahānadiyo mahāsamuddasāgaraṃ paripūrenti; evameva tassa bhikkhuno ime pañca guṇā paripūrā dasa kathāvatthuni ādiṃ katvā yāva amataṃ nibbānaṃ paripūressanti. Evamayaṃ bhikkhu dhammadāyādapaṭipadaṃ paṭipanno paramadhammadāyādaṃ labhatīti etamatthaṃ sampassamāno bhagavā “taṃ kissa hetu tañhi tassa, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno”tiādimāha.

How so? For the fulfilled training in higher virtue is indeed the aggregate of virtue of one beyond training; the training in higher mind is the aggregate of concentration of one beyond training; and the training in higher wisdom is indeed the aggregates of wisdom, liberation, and knowledge and vision of liberation of one beyond training. Thus, the three trainings, being fulfilled, will fulfill the five Dhamma-aggregates of one beyond training. The five Dhamma-aggregates, being fulfilled, will fulfill the deathless Nibbāna. Just as when a great seasonal rain cloud, having rained heavily upon a mountaintop, fills the mountain clefts, pools, and streams; when they are full, they fill the small chasms; the small chasms, being full, fill the large chasms; the large chasms, being full, fill the small rivers; the small rivers, being full, fill the great rivers; and the great rivers, being full, fill the great ocean, the sea; in the very same way, for that monk, these five qualities, being fulfilled, starting with the ten topics of discourse, fulfill everything up to the deathless Nibbāna. Thus this monk, who has entered upon the practice of being an heir to the Dhamma, obtains the supreme heritage of the Dhamma. Seeing this meaning, the Blessed One said: 'For what reason? For that monk, O monks...' and so on.

Evaṃ tassa bhikkhuno pujjatarapāsaṃsatarabhāvaṃ kāraṇena sādhetvā idāni te bhikkhū tathattāya sanniyojento tasmā tiha me bhikkhavetiādimāha. Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti, yasmā yo taṃ piṇḍapātaṃ bhuñjitvā samaṇadhammaṃ kareyya, so imehi pañcahi mūlaguṇehi paribāhiro. Yo pana abhuñjitvā kareyya, so imesaṃ bhāgī hoti – “tasmā tiha me, bhikkhave…pe… no āmisadāyādā”ti.

Having thus established, by way of reason, that monk's state of being more worthy of veneration and more worthy of praise, now, urging those monks towards that same state, he said: 'Therefore, O monks...' and so on. What is the meaning? Because whichever monk would practice the ascetic's duty after eating that alms-food, he is excluded from these five root qualities. But whichever monk would practice it without having eaten, he is a partaker of these. Therefore, he said: 'Therefore, O monks... be my heirs in Dhamma, not heirs in material things.'

Idamavoca bhagavāti idaṃ nidānapariyosānato pabhuti yāva no āmisadāyādāti suttappadesaṃ bhagavā avoca. Idaṃ vatvāna sugatoti idañca suttappadesaṃ vatvāva sobhanāya paṭipadāya gatattā sugatoti saṅkhaṃ pattoyeva bhagavā. Uṭṭhāyāsanā vihāraṃ pāvisī paññattavarabuddhāsanato uṭṭhahitvā vihāraṃ attano mahāgandhakuṭiṃ pāvisi asambhinnāya eva parisāya. Kasmā [P 1.0099] dhammathomanatthaṃ.

'The Blessed One said this' means: The Blessed One spoke this portion of the sutta, starting from the end of the introduction up to 'not heirs in material things.' 'Having said this, the Sugata' means: Having spoken this portion of the sutta, the Blessed One, who has attained the designation 'Sugata' because he has gone by the beautiful path... 'Rising from his seat, he entered the dwelling' means: Having risen from the excellent Buddha-seat that had been prepared, he entered his own dwelling, the great fragrant chamber, while the assembly was still gathered. Why? For the purpose of praising the Dhamma.

Buddhā [V 1.0106] kira apariniṭṭhitāya desanāya vihāraṃ pavisantā dvīhi kāraṇehi pavisanti puggalathomanatthaṃ vā dhammathomanatthaṃ vā. Puggalathomanatthaṃ pavisanto evaṃ cintesi – “imaṃ mayā saṃkhittena uddesaṃ uddiṭṭhaṃ, vitthārena avibhattaṃ, dhammapaṭiggāhakā bhikkhū uggahetvā ānandaṃ vā kaccānaṃ vā upasaṅkamitvā pucchissanti, te mayhaṃ ñāṇena saṃsandetvā kathessanti, tato dhammapaṭiggāhakā puna maṃ pucchissanti, tesaṃ ahaṃ sukathitaṃ, bhikkhave, ānandena sukathitaṃ kaccānena, maṃ cepi tumhe etamatthaṃ puccheyyātha, ahampi naṃ evameva byākareyyanti evaṃ te puggale thomessāmi, tato tesu gāravaṃ janetvā bhikkhū upasaṅkamissanti, tepi bhikkhū atthe ca dhamme ca [M 1.0103] niyojessanti, te tehi niyojitā tisso sikkhā paripūrentā dukkhassantaṃ karissantī”ti.

It is said that the Buddhas, when a discourse is not yet finished, enter the dwelling for two reasons: either to praise an individual or to praise the Dhamma. When entering to praise an individual, he thinks thus: 'I have stated this summary in brief, but it has not been analyzed in detail. The monks who are receivers of the Dhamma, having learned it, will approach Ānanda or Kaccāna and ask about it. They will explain it in alignment with my own knowledge. Then the receivers of the Dhamma will ask me again. To them I will say: "It was well spoken by Ānanda, monks! It was well spoken by Kaccāna! If you were to ask me about this meaning, I too would explain it in the very same way." In this way, I will praise those individuals. Then, having generated respect for them, the monks will approach them. They, in turn, will enjoin those monks in the meaning and in the text. Enjoined by them, those monks, fulfilling the three trainings, will make an end of suffering.'

Dhammathomanatthaṃ pavisanto evaṃ cintesi, yathā idheva cintesi – “mayi vihāraṃ paviṭṭhe tameva āmisadāyādaṃ garahanto dhammadāyādañca thomento imissaṃyeva parisati nisinno sāriputto dhammaṃ desessati, evaṃ dvinnampi amhākaṃ ekajjhāsayāya matiyā desitā ayaṃ desanā aggā ca garukā ca bhavissati pāsāṇacchattasadisā. Caturoghanittharaṇaṭṭhena titthe ṭhapitā nāvā viya maggagamanaṭṭhena catuyuttaājaññaratho viya ca bhavissati. Yathā ca ‘evaṃ karontassa ayaṃ daṇḍo’ti parisati āṇaṃ ṭhapetvā uṭṭhāyāsanā pāsādaṃ āruḷhe rājini tattheva nisinno senāpati taṃ raññā ṭhapitaṃ āṇaṃ pavatteti; evampi mayā ṭhapitaṃ desanaṃ imissaṃyeva parisati nisinno sāriputto thometvā desessati, evaṃ dvinnampi amhākaṃ matiyā desitā ayaṃ desanā balavatarā majjhanhikasūriyo viya pajjalissatī”ti. Evamidha dhammathomanatthaṃ uṭṭhāyāsanā vihāraṃ pāvisi.

When entering for the sake of praising the Dhamma, he thought thus, just as he had thought on this very occasion: "When I have entered the monastery, while criticizing those very heirs to material things and praising the heirs to the Dhamma, Sāriputta, seated in this very assembly, will teach the Dhamma. Thus, this discourse, taught with the single intention of both of us, will become foremost and weighty, like a stone umbrella. For the purpose of crossing the four floods, it will be like a boat placed at a ford, and for the purpose of traveling the path, it will be like a chariot yoked with four thoroughbred steeds. Just as when a king, having established a command in the assembly—'This is the penalty for one who does thus'—rises from his seat and ascends to the palace, the commander-in-chief, seated right there, sets in motion the command established by the king; so too, the discourse established by me, Sāriputta, seated in this very assembly, will praise and teach. Thus, this discourse, taught with the intention of both of us, will blaze forth more powerfully, like the midday sun." Thus, here, for the sake of praising the Dhamma, having risen from his seat, he entered the monastery.

Īdisesu ca ṭhānesu bhagavā nisinnāsaneyeva antarahito cittagatiyā vihāraṃ pavisatīti veditabbo. Yadi hi kāyagatiyā gaccheyya, sabbā parisā bhagavantaṃ parivāretvā gaccheyya, sā ekavāraṃ bhinnā puna dussannipātā bhaveyyāti bhagavā cittagatiyā eva pāvisi.

In such instances, it should be understood that the Blessed One, while still on his seat, disappears and enters the monastery by the movement of his mind. For if he were to go by bodily movement, the entire assembly would follow the Blessed One, surrounding him. That assembly, once dispersed, would be difficult to reassemble. Therefore, the Blessed One entered by the movement of his mind alone.

31. Evaṃ [P 1.0100] paviṭṭhe pana bhagavati bhagavato adhippāyānurūpaṃ taṃ dhammaṃ thometukāmo tatra kho [V 1.0107] āyasmā sāriputto…pe…etadavoca. Tattha āyasmāti piyavacanametaṃ. Sāriputtoti tassa therassa nāmaṃ, tañca kho mātito, na pitito. Rūpasāriyā hi brāhmaṇiyā so putto, tasmā sāriputtoti vuccati. Acirapakkantassāti pakkantassa sato nacirena. Āvuso, bhikkhaveti ettha pana buddhā bhagavanto sāvake ālapantā bhikkhaveti ālapanti. Sāvakā pana buddhehi sadisā mā homāti āvusoti paṭhamaṃ vatvā pacchā bhikkhaveti bhaṇanti. Buddhehi ca ālapito bhikkhusaṅgho bhadanteti paṭivacanaṃ deti, sāvakehi āvusoti.

31. When the Blessed One had thus entered, the Venerable Sāriputta, wishing to praise that Dhamma in accordance with the Blessed One’s intention, thereupon said this… Here, "Venerable" (āyasmā) is a term of endearment. "Sāriputta" is the elder’s name, and it is from his mother, not from his father. For he was the son of the brahmin woman Rūpasārī; therefore he is called Sāriputta. "Acirapakkantassa" means 'not long after he had departed.' In "Friends, monks" (āvuso, bhikkhave), the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, when addressing their disciples, address them as 'monks' (bhikkhave). Disciples, however, thinking, "Let us not be like the Buddhas," first say 'friend' (āvuso) and then 'monks' (bhikkhave). And when addressed by the Buddhas, the community of monks responds with 'Venerable Sir' (bhadante); when addressed by disciples, they respond with 'friend' (āvuso).

Kittāvatā [M 1.0104] nu kho, āvusoti ettha kittāvatāti paricchedavacanaṃ, kittakenāti vuttaṃ hoti. Nukāro pucchāyaṃ. Khokāro nipātamattaṃ. Satthu pavivittassa viharatoti, tīhi vivekehi kāyacittaupadhivivekehi satthuno viharantassa. Vivekaṃ nānusikkhantīti tiṇṇaṃ vivekānaṃ aññatarampi nānusikkhanti, āmisadāyādāva hontīti imamatthaṃ āyasmā sāriputto bhikkhū pucchi. Esa nayo sukkapakkhepi.

Here, in 'kittāvatā nu kho, āvuso,' 'kittāvatā' is a word of delimitation; it means 'by how much.' The particle 'nu' is used in a question. The particle 'kho' is a mere particle. 'Satthu pavivittassa viharato' means 'of the Teacher dwelling in seclusion,' that is, of the Teacher dwelling with the three kinds of seclusion: bodily seclusion, mental seclusion, and seclusion from the substrata of existence. 'Vivekaṃ nānusikkhanti' means 'they do not train in seclusion,' that is, they do not train in any of the three kinds of seclusion; they are only heirs to material things. This is the meaning about which the Venerable Sāriputta asked the monks. This is the method in the bright side as well.

Evaṃ vutte tamatthaṃ sotukāmā bhikkhū dūratopi khotiādimāhaṃsu. Tattha dūratopīti tiroraṭṭhatopi tirojanapadatopi anekayojanagaṇanatopīti vuttaṃ hoti. Santiketi samīpe. Aññātunti jānituṃ bujjhituṃ. Āyasmantaṃyeva sāriputtaṃ paṭibhātūti āyasmatoyeva sāriputtassa bhāgo hotu, āyasmā pana sāriputto attano bhāgaṃ katvā vibhajatūti vuttaṃ hoti. Āyasmato hi bhāgo yadidaṃ atthakkhānaṃ, amhākaṃ pana savanaṃ bhāgoti ayamettha adhippāyo, evaṃ saddalakkhaṇena sameti. Keci pana bhaṇanti “paṭibhātūti dissatū”ti. Apare “upaṭṭhātū”ti. Dhāressantīti uggahessanti pariyāpuṇissanti. Tato nesaṃ kathetukāmo thero tena hītiādimāha. Tattha tenāti kāraṇavacanaṃ. Hikāro nipāto. Yasmā sotukāmāttha, yasmā ca mayhaṃ bhāraṃ āropayittha, tasmā suṇāthāti vuttaṃ hoti. Tepi bhikkhū therassa vacanaṃ sampaṭicchiṃsu, tenāha “evamāvusoti…pe…paccassosu”nti.

When this was said, the monks, desiring to hear the meaning, spoke, beginning with 'even from afar.' Here, 'dūratopi' means 'from another country, from another district, from a distance of many leagues'—so it is said. 'Santike' means 'nearby.' 'Aññātuṃ' means 'to know, to understand.' 'Āyasmantaṃyeva sāriputtaṃ paṭibhātu' means 'let it be the Venerable Sāriputta's share; let the Venerable Sāriputta, having made it his own share, expound it'—so it is said. For the explanation of the meaning is the Venerable One's share, while our share is listening—this is the intention here. Thus, it accords with the characteristic of the word. Some, however, say, 'paṭibhātu means "let it be clear".' Others say, 'let it be manifest.' 'Dhāressanti' means 'they will learn it by heart, they will master it by recitation.' Then the elder, wishing to speak to them, said, beginning with 'tena hi.' Here, 'tena' is a word indicating reason. The particle 'hi' is a mere particle. It means: 'Because you desire to hear, and because you have placed the burden on me, therefore, listen.' Those monks accepted the elder’s words, hence it is said, 'Yes, friend' (evaṃ āvuso)... up to '...they responded affirmatively'.

Atha nesaṃ, āmisadāyādaṃ garahantena bhagavatā “tumhepi tena ādiyā bhaveyyāthā”ti ekenevākārena [P 1.0101] vuttamatthaṃ tīhi ākārehi dassento āyasmā sāriputto etadavoca – “idhāvuso[V 1.0108], satthu pavivittassa viharato…pe… ettāvatā kho, āvuso, satthu pavivittassa viharato sāvakā vivekaṃ nānusikkhantī”ti.

Then the Venerable Sāriputta, showing in three ways the meaning that the Blessed One, while disparaging the heirs to material things, had stated in a single way, saying, 'You too would be blameworthy for that,' said this: 'Here, friends, when the Teacher dwells in seclusion... up to... thus far, friends, when the Teacher dwells in seclusion, the disciples do not train in seclusion.'

Ettāvatā yañca bhagavā āmisadāyādapaṭipadaṃ garahanto “tumhepi tena ādiyā bhaveyyāthā”ti āha, yañca attanā pucchaṃ pucchi “kittāvatā nu kho…pe… nānusikkhantī”ti, tassa vitthārato attho suvibhatto hoti. So ca kho bhagavato ādiyabhāvaṃ anāmasitvāva. Bhagavatoyeva hi yuttaṃ sāvake anuggaṇhantassa “ahampi [M 1.0105] tena ādiyo bhavissāmī”ti vattuṃ, na sāvakānaṃ. Esa nayo sukkapakkhepi, ayaṃ tāvettha anusandhikkamayojanā.

Thus far, the meaning of both what the Blessed One said when criticizing the practice of being heirs to material things, saying, 'You too would be blameworthy for that,' and the question he himself asked, 'To what extent... do they not train?' is well distinguished in detail. And that is without touching upon the Blessed One's being blameworthy. For it is appropriate for the Blessed One alone, if he were not to have his disciples follow his example, to say, 'I too will be blameworthy for that,' but not for the disciples. This is the method in the bright side as well. This, for now, is the application of the sequential connection here.

Ayaṃ panatthavaṇṇanā idhāti imasmiṃ sāsane, satthu pavivittassāti satthuno tīhi vivekehi accantapavivittassa. Vivekaṃ nānusikkhantīti kāyavivekaṃ nānusikkhanti, na paripūrentīti vuttaṃ hoti. Yadi pana tividhaṃ vivekaṃ sandhāya vadeyya, pucchāya aviseso siyā. Byākaraṇapakkho hi ayaṃ. Tasmā iminā padena kāyavivekaṃ, “yesañca dhammāna”ntiādinā cittavivekaṃ, “bāhulikā”tiādinā upadhivivekañca dassetīti evamettha saṅkhepato attho veditabbo.

Now, this is the explanation of the meaning. 'Here' (idha) means in this Dispensation. 'Of the secluded Teacher' (satthu pavivittassa) means of the Teacher who is utterly secluded by the three kinds of seclusion. 'They do not train in imitation of seclusion' (vivekaṃ nānusikkhanti) means they do not train in imitation of bodily seclusion, they do not fulfill it; this is the intended meaning. If, however, one were to speak with reference to the threefold seclusion, there would be no distinction in the question. For this is the side of the explanation. Therefore, by this phrase, He shows the non-fulfillment of bodily seclusion; by 'and of which dhammas' (yesañca dhammānaṃ) and so on, He shows the non-fulfillment of mental seclusion; and by 'given to abundance' (bāhulikā) and so on, He shows the non-fulfillment of seclusion from the substrata. Thus, the meaning here should be understood in brief.

Yesañca dhammānanti lobhādayo sandhāyāha, ye parato “tatrāvuso lobho ca pāpako”tiādinā nayena vakkhati. Nappajahantīti na pariccajanti, cittavivekaṃ na paripūrentīti vuttaṃ hoti. Bāhulikāti cīvarādibāhullāya paṭipannā. Sāsanaṃ sithilaṃ gaṇhantīti sāthalikā. Okkamane pubbaṅgamāti ettha okkamanaṃ vuccanti avagamanaṭṭhena pañca nīvaraṇāni, tena pañcanīvaraṇapubbaṅgamāti vuttaṃ hoti. Paviveketi upadhiviveke nibbāne. Nikkhittadhurāti oropitadhurā, tadadhigamāya ārambhampi akurumānāti, ettāvatā upadhivivekaṃ na paripūrentīti vuttaṃ hoti.

'And of which dhammas' (yesañca dhammānaṃ), He spoke with reference to greed and the like, which He will explain later according to the method beginning, 'Herein, friends, greed is an evil thing' (tatrāvuso lobho ca pāpako). 'They do not abandon' (nappajahanti) means they do not relinquish; it is meant that they do not fulfill mental seclusion. 'Given to abundance' (bāhulikā) means they are committed to an abundance of requisites such as robes. Because they take the teaching loosely, they are called 'lax' (sāthalikā). In 'making descending their forerunner' (okkamanepubbaṅgamā), 'descending' (okkamanaṃ), in the sense of going down, refers to the five hindrances. Thus, it is meant that they make the five hindrances their forerunner. 'In seclusion' (paviveke) means in Nibbāna, which is seclusion from the substrata. 'They have cast off the yoke' (nikkhittadhurā) means they have laid down the burden, not making even the initiated effort for its attainment. By this much, it is meant that they do not fulfill seclusion from the substrata.

Ettāvatā aniyameneva vatvā idāni desanaṃ niyamento “tatrāvuso”tiādimāha. Kasmā? Sāvakā “tīhi ṭhānehī”ti evañhi aniyametvāva vuccamāne “kampi maññe bhaṇati[V 1.0109], na amhe”ti udāsināpi honti. “Therā navā majjhimā”ti evaṃ pana niyametvā vuccamāne amhe bhaṇatīti ādaraṃ karonti[P 1.0102]. Yathā raññā “amaccehi nagaravīthiyo sodhetabbā”ti vuttepi “kena nu kho sodhetabbā”ti maññamānā na sodhenti, attano attano gharadvāraṃ sodhetabbanti pana bheriyā nikkhantāya sabbe muhuttena sodhenti ca alaṅkaronti ca, evaṃsampadamidaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Having spoken thus far in an unspecified manner, now, specifying the teaching, he said, 'Herein, friends,' and so on. Why? For when it is spoken without specifying, as 'by three grounds,' the disciples might become indifferent, thinking, 'He speaks of someone else, not of us.' But when it is spoken with specification, as 'elders, new, and middle,' they show respect, thinking, 'He speaks of us.' It is like when a king says, 'The city streets are to be cleaned by the ministers,' they do not clean them, thinking, 'By whom, indeed, are they to be cleaned?' But when the drum is sounded, proclaiming, 'Each is to clean their own doorway,' everyone cleans and decorates it in a moment. This analogy should be understood thus.

Tattha tatrāti tesu sāvakesu. Therāti dasavasse upādāya vuccanti. Tīhi ṭhānehīti tīhi kāraṇehi. Ayañhi ṭhānasaddo issariyaṭṭhitikhaṇakāraṇesu dissati. “Kiṃ panāyasmā devānamindo kammaṃ katvā [M 1.0106] imaṃ ṭhānaṃ patto”tiādīsu hi issariye dissati. “Ṭhānakusalo hoti akkhaṇavedhī”tiādīsu ṭhitiyaṃ. “Ṭhānasovetaṃ tathāgataṃ paṭibhātī”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 2.87) khaṇe. “Ṭhānañca ṭhānato aṭṭhānañca aṭṭhānato”tiādīsu (vibha. 809; ma. ni. 1.148) kāraṇe. Idha pana kāraṇeyeva. Kāraṇañhi yasmā tattha phalaṃ tiṭṭhati tadāyattavuttibhāvena, tasmā ṭhānanti vuccati.

'Therein' (tatrā) means among those disciples. 'Elders' (therā) are so called from those with ten Rains onwards. 'By three grounds' (tīhi ṭhānehi) means by three reasons (kāraṇehi). For this word 'ground' (ṭhāna) is found in the senses of sovereignty, standing, moment, and reason. For instance, in 'By what kamma, venerable lord of devas, did you attain this sovereign state (ṭhāna)?' and so on, it is found in the sense of sovereignty. In 'He is skilled in his stance (ṭhāna), a non-momentary archer' and so on, it is in the sense of standing. In 'At that moment (ṭhāna) this occurred to the Tathāgata' and so on, it is in the sense of moment. In 'He knows a cause (ṭhāna) as a cause and what is not a cause as not a cause' and so on, it is in the sense of reason. Here, however, it is in the sense of reason only. For a reason (kāraṇa) is called a 'ground' (ṭhāna) because the result stands (tiṭṭhati) in it, its occurrence being dependent on that reason.

Iminā paṭhamena ṭhānena therā bhikkhū gārayhāti ettha gārayhāti garahitabbā. Therā nāma samānā araññavanapatthāni pantāni senāsanāni na upenti, gāmantasenāsanaṃ na muñcanti, saṅgaṇikārāmataṃ vaḍḍhentā viharanti, kāyavivekampi na paripūrenti, navamajjhimakāle kīdisā ahesunti evaṃ ninditabbā honti, imaṃ nindaṃ āvuso labhantīti dasseti. Dutiyena ṭhānenāti etthāpi ime nāma āvuso therāpi samānā yesaṃ dhammānaṃ satthā pahānamāha, te lobhādidhamme na jahanti, accharāsaṅghātamattampi ekamantaṃ nisīditvā cittekaggataṃ na labhanti, navamajjhimakāle kīdisā ahesunti evaṃ ninditabbā honti, imaṃ nindaṃ āvuso labhantīti dassetīti evaṃ yojanā kātabbā. Tatiyena ṭhānenāti etthāpi ime nāmāvuso, therāpi samānā itarītarena na yāpenti, cīvarapattasenāsanapūtikāyamaṇḍanānuyogamanuyuttā viharanti upadhivivekaṃ apūrayamānā, navamajjhimakāle kīdisā ahesunti evaṃ ninditabbā honti, imaṃ nindaṃ, āvuso, labhantīti dassetīti evaṃ yojanā veditabbā. Esa nayo majjhimanavavāresu.

In the phrase 'By this first ground, the elder bhikkhus are censurable' (iminā paṭhamena ṭhānena therā bhikkhū gārayhā), 'censurable' (gārayhā) means they are to be censured (garahitabbā). Being so-called elders, they do not resort to remote forest-tract dwellings; they do not relinquish lodgings near a village; they dwell developing delight in company; they do not even fulfill bodily seclusion. They are to be censured thus: 'What must they have been like in their new and middle periods?' It shows that they incur this censure, friends. In 'By the second ground' (dutiyena ṭhānena), the application should be made thus: These so-called elders, friends, though they are elders, do not abandon those dhammas the Teacher said should be abandoned; they do not give up dhammas such as greed. Not even for the duration of a finger-snap can they sit in seclusion and attain one-pointedness of mind. They are to be censured thus: 'What must they have been like in their new and middle periods?' It shows that they incur this censure, friends. In 'By the third ground' (tatiyena ṭhānena), the application should be understood thus: These so-called elders, friends, though they are elders, do not maintain themselves with whatever is at hand. They dwell dedicated to the application of adorning their robes, bowls, lodgings, and this foul body, not fulfilling seclusion from the substrata. They are to be censured thus: 'What must they have been like in their new and middle periods?' It shows that they incur this censure, friends. This is the method for the sections on the middle and new bhikkhus.

Ayaṃ pana viseso. Majjhimāti pañcavasse upādāya yāva nava vassā vuccanti. Navāti [V 1.0110] ūnapañcavassā vuccanti. Yathā ca tattha navamajjhimakāle kīdisā ahesunti vuttaṃ, evamidha [P 1.0103] navakāle kīdisā ahesuṃ, therakāle kīdisā bhavissanti, majjhimatherakāle kīdisā bhavissantīti vatvā yojetabbaṃ.

This, however, is the distinction. 'Middle' (majjhimā) refers to those from five Rains up to nine Rains. 'New' (navā) refers to those with less than five Rains. And just as it was said there, in the case of the elders, 'What must they have been like in their new and middle periods?', so here, in the other cases, the connection should be made by saying: 'What must they have been like in the new period? What will they be like in the elder period?' and 'What will they be like in the middle and elder periods?'

32. Imasmiñca kaṇhapakkhe vuttapaccanīkanayena sukkapakkhe attho veditabbo. Ayaṃ panettha saṅkhepo. Ime vata therāpi samānā yojanaparamparāya araññavanapatthāni pantāni senāsanāni sevanti, gāmantasenāsanaṃ upagantuṃ yuttakālepi na upagacchanti, evaṃ jiṇṇasarīrāpi āraddhavīriyā [M 1.0107] paccayadāyakānaṃ pasādaṃ janenti, navamajjhimakāle kīdisā ahesunti iminā paṭhamena ṭhānena therā pāsaṃsā bhavanti, pasaṃsaṃ labhanti. Lobhādayo pahāya cittavivekaṃ pūrenti, ayampi mahāthero saddhivihārikaantevāsikaparivārito hutvā nisīdituṃ yuttakālepi īdisepi vaye vattamāne bhattakiccaṃ katvā paviṭṭho sāyaṃ nikkhamati, sāyaṃ paviṭṭho pāto nikkhamati, kasiṇaparikammaṃ karoti, samāpattiyo nibbatteti, maggaphalāni adhigacchati, sabbathāpi cittavivekaṃ pūretīti iminā dutiyena ṭhānena therā bhikkhū pāsaṃsā bhavanti, pasaṃsaṃ labhanti. Yasmiṃ kāle therassa paṭṭadukūlakoseyyādīni sukhasamphassāni lahucīvarādīni yuttāni, tasmimpi nāma kāle ayaṃ mahāthero paṃsukūlāni dhāreti, asithilaṃ sāsanaṃ gahetvā vigatanīvaraṇo phalasamāpattiṃ appetvā upadhivivekaṃ paripūrayamāno viharati, navamajjhimakāle kīdiso ahosīti iminā tatiyena ṭhānena therā pāsaṃsā bhavanti, pasaṃsaṃ labhantīti. Esa nayo majjhimanavavāresu.

32. And in this dark fortnight, the meaning should be understood by the method opposite to what was stated for the bright fortnight. This, herein, is the summary.
