Indeed, these elders, although they are elders, frequent remote dwellings that are great forest thickets, one yojana after another. Even at a suitable time, they do not approach a dwelling near a village. Thus, though having aged bodies, they, with aroused energy, generate faith in the donors of requisites. 'In their new and middle periods, what kind of aroused energy must they have had?'—for this first reason, the elders are praiseworthy; they receive praise. Having abandoned greed and so forth, they fulfill mental seclusion. This great elder, too, though surrounded by co-residents and pupils, and though it is a suitable time to sit, and while being at such an age, having performed his meal duties, enters seclusion and comes out in the evening; he enters in the evening and comes out in the morning. He performs the preliminary work for kasiṇa, produces the meditative attainments, and attains the paths and fruits. In every way, he fulfills mental seclusion. For this second reason, the elder bhikkhus are praiseworthy; they receive praise. At a time when robes with a pleasant touch, such as those of fine cloth, fine cotton, and silk, and other light robes are suitable for the elder, even at such a time, this great elder wears rag-robes. Having taken up the teaching without slackness, free from the hindrances, having entered into fruition attainment, he dwells, fulfilling seclusion from the substrates. 'In his new and middle periods, what must he have been like?'—for this third reason, the elders are praiseworthy; they receive praise. This is the method for the middle and new groups.

33. Tatrāvusoti ko anusandhi, evaṃ navahākārehi āmisadāyādapaṭipadaṃ garahanto, navahi dhammadāyādapaṭipadaṃ thomento, aṭṭhārasahākārehi desanaṃ niṭṭhāpetvā, ye te “yesañca dhammānaṃ satthā pahānamāha, te ca dhamme na pajahantī”ti evaṃ pahātabbadhammā vuttā. Te sarūpato “ime te”ti dassetumidaṃ “tatrāvuso, lobho cā”tiādimāha, ayaṃ anusandhi.

33. What is the connection of 'Therein, friends'? Having censured the practice of being heirs to material things in nine aspects and praised the practice of being heirs to the Dhamma in nine aspects, thus concluding the discourse in eighteen aspects, this was said, beginning with 'Therein, friends, is greed...', in order to show in their own nature—as 'these are they'—those dhammas that were spoken of as 'to be abandoned', as in 'And those dhammas which the Teacher said should be abandoned, those dhammas they do not abandon.' This is the connection.

Apica heṭṭhā pariyāyeneva dhammo kathito. Āmisaṃ pana pariyāyenapi nippariyāyenapi kathitaṃ. Idāni nippariyāyadhammaṃ lokuttaramaggaṃ kathetumidamāha. Ayaṃ pettha anusandhi.

Furthermore, previously the Dhamma was taught only by implication. Material things, however, were taught both by implication and directly. Now, to teach the direct Dhamma, the supramundane path, this was said. This, too, is the connection here.

Tattha [V 1.0111] tatrāti atītadesanānidassanaṃ, “satthu pavivittassa viharato sāvakā vivekaṃ nānusikkhantī”tiādinā nayena vuttadesanāyanti vuttaṃ hoti. Lobho ca pāpako, doso ca pāpakoti ime dve dhammā pāpakā lāmakā, ime pahātabbāti [P 1.0104] dasseti. Tattha lubbhanalakkhaṇo lobho. Dussanalakkhaṇo doso. Tesu lobho āmisadāyādassa paccayānaṃ lābhe hoti, doso alābhe. Lobhena [M 1.0108] aladdhaṃ pattheti, dosena alabhanto vighātavā hoti. Lobho ca deyyadhamme hoti, doso adāyake vā amanuññadāyake vā. Lobhena navataṇhāmūlake dhamme paripūreti, dosena pañca macchariyāni.

In that passage, the word 'therein' indicates a past discourse; that is to say, in the discourse spoken with the method beginning, 'When the Teacher dwells in seclusion, the disciples do not train in seclusion.' It shows that 'Greed is evil, and hatred is evil'—these two states are evil; these are to be abandoned. Therein, greed has the characteristic of coveting; hatred has the characteristic of corrupting. Among them, for one who is an heir to material things, greed occurs in the gain of requisites, and hatred in the non-gain. Through greed, one yearns for what has not been gained; through hatred, not gaining it, one becomes distressed. Greed occurs in regard to things to be given; hatred occurs towards a non-giver or a giver of what is not pleasing. Through greed, one fulfills the nine states rooted in craving; through hatred, the five kinds of stinginess.

Idāni tesaṃ pahānūpāyaṃ dassento lobhassa ca pahānāyātiādimāha. Tassattho, tassa pana pāpakassa lobhassa ca dosassa ca pahānāya. Atthi majjhimā paṭipadāti maggaṃ sandhāya idaṃ vuttaṃ. Maggo hi lobho eko anto, doso eko antoti ete dve ante na upeti, na upagacchati, vimutto etehi antehi, tasmā “majjhimā paṭipadā”ti vuccati. Etesaṃ majjhe bhavattā “majjhimā, paṭipajjitabbato ca paṭipadāti. Tathā kāmasukhallikānuyogo eko anto, attakilamathānuyogo eko anto, sassataṃ eko anto, ucchedo eko antoti purimanayeneva vitthāretabbaṃ.

Now, showing the means for their abandonment, he says, 'for the abandoning of greed,' and so forth. The meaning of that is: for the abandoning of that evil greed and hatred. 'There is a middle way'—this was said with reference to the path. For the path does not approach these two extremes—greed is one extreme, hatred is one extreme—it is free from these extremes, therefore it is called 'the middle way.' Because it exists in the middle of these, it is 'middle,' and because it is to be practiced, it is a 'way.' Similarly, the indulgence in sensual pleasures is one extreme, the practice of self-mortification is one extreme; eternalism is one extreme, annihilationism is one extreme—this should be elaborated in the same way as before.

Cakkhukaraṇītiādīhi pana tameva paṭipadaṃ thometi. Sā hi saccānaṃ dassanāya saṃvattati dassanapariṇāyakaṭṭhenāti cakkhukaraṇī. Saccānaṃ ñāṇāya saṃvattati viditakaraṇaṭṭhenāti ñāṇakaraṇī. Rāgādīnañca vūpasamanato upasamāya saṃvattati. Catunnampi saccānaṃ abhiññeyyabhāvadassanato abhiññāya saṃvattati. Sambodhoti maggo, tassatthāya saṃvattanato sambodhāya saṃvattati. Maggoyeva hi maggatthāya saṃvattati maggena kātabbakiccakaraṇato. Nibbānaṃ nāma appaccayaṃ tassa pana sacchikiriyāya paccakkhakammāya saṃvattanato nibbānāya saṃvattatīti vuccati. Ayamettha sāro. Ito aññathā vaṇṇanā papañcā.

With 'vision-making,' and so forth, that very path is praised. For it conduces to the seeing of the truths, hence 'vision-making' in the sense of leading to vision. It conduces to knowledge of the truths, hence 'knowledge-making' in the sense of causing them to be known. And because of the calming of lust and so forth, it conduces to peace. Because it reveals the state of the four truths as 'to be directly known', it conduces to direct knowledge. 'Awakening' is the path; because it conduces to the purpose of that path, it conduces to awakening. For the path itself conduces to the purpose of the path, because by the path the task that should be done is done. Nibbāna is without condition; but because the path conduces to its realization, to its direct experience, it is said to 'conduce to Nibbāna.' This is the essence here. A description other than this is proliferation.

Idāni taṃ majjhimaṃ paṭipadaṃ sarūpato dassetukāmo “katamā ca sā”ti pucchitvā “ayamevā”tiādinā nayena vissajjeti.

Now, wishing to show that middle way in its own nature, he asks, 'And what is that?' and answers by the method beginning: 'It is just this...'

Tattha [V 1.0112] ayamevāti avadhāraṇavacanaṃ, aññamaggappaṭisedhanatthaṃ, buddhapaccekabuddhabuddhasāvakānaṃ sādhāraṇabhāvadassanatthañca. Vuttañcetaṃ “eseva [P 1.0105] maggo natthañño dassanassa visuddhiyā”ti (dha. pa. 274). Svāyaṃ kilesānaṃ ārakattāpi ariyo. Aripahānāya saṃvattatītipi ariyena desitotipi ariyabhāvappaṭilābhāya saṃvattatītipi ariyo. Aṭṭhahi aṅgehi upetattā [M 1.0109] aṭṭhaṅgiko, na ca aṅgavinimutto pañcaṅgikatūriyādīni viya. Kilese mārento gacchati, maggati vā nibbānaṃ, maggīyati vā nibbānatthikehi, gammati vā tehi paṭipajjīyatīti maggo. Seyyathidanti nipāto, tassa katamo so iti ceti attho, katamāni vā tāni aṭṭhaṅgānīti. Ekamekañhi aṅgaṃ maggoyeva. Yathāha “sammādiṭṭhi maggo ceva hetu cā”ti (dha. sa. 1039). Porāṇāpi bhaṇanti – “dassanamaggo sammādiṭṭhi, abhiniropanamaggo sammāsaṅkappo…pe… avikkhepamaggo sammāsamādhī”ti.

Herein, 'ayameva' is a word of emphasis, for the purpose of negating other paths, and for the purpose of showing that it is common to the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and the disciples of the Buddha. And this was stated: 'This very path, there is no other for the purification of vision.' This path is noble (ariya) because it is far from the defilements. It is also noble because it conduces to the abandoning of the enemies (the defilements), because it was taught by the Noble One, and because it conduces to the attainment of the state of a noble one. It is eight-factored (aṭṭhaṅgiko) because it is endowed with eight factors; and a path devoid of factors does not exist, like a five-factored orchestra and so on. It is called a path (magga) because it goes while killing the defilements, or it seeks Nibbāna, or it is sought by those who desire Nibbāna, or it is gone to and practiced by them. 'Seyyathidaṃ' is a particle; its meaning is 'What is that path?' or 'What are those eight factors?' For each single factor is indeed the path. As it is said: 'Right view is both the path and the cause.' The ancients also say: 'The path of seeing is right view, the path of application is right intention... the path of non-distraction is right concentration.'

Sammādiṭṭhādīsu cetesu sammā dassanalakkhaṇā sammādiṭṭhi. Sammā abhiniropanalakkhaṇo sammāsaṅkappo. Sammā pariggahalakkhaṇā sammāvācā. Sammā samuṭṭhānalakkhaṇo sammākammanto. Sammā vodānalakkhaṇo sammāājīvo. Sammā paggahalakkhaṇo sammāvāyāmo. Sammā upaṭṭhānalakkhaṇā sammāsati. Sammā samādhānalakkhaṇo sammāsamādhi. Nibbacanampi nesaṃ sammā passatīti sammādiṭṭhīti eteneva nayena veditabbaṃ.

Among these, beginning with right view: right view has the characteristic of right seeing. Right intention has the characteristic of rightly directing. Right speech has the characteristic of right restraint. Right action has the characteristic of right arousing. Right livelihood has the characteristic of right purification. Right effort has the characteristic of right exertion. Right mindfulness has the characteristic of right establishing. Right concentration has the characteristic of right composure. Their etymology, too, should be understood by this method: 'It sees rightly (sammā passati), therefore it is right view (sammādiṭṭhi).'

Tattha sammādiṭṭhi uppajjamānā micchādiṭṭhiṃ tappaccanīyakilese ca avijjañca pajahati, nibbānañca ārammaṇaṃ karoti, sampayuttadhamme ca passati, te ca kho asammohato, no ārammaṇato, tasmā “sammādiṭṭhī”ti vuccati.

Therein, when right view arises, it abandons wrong view, the defilements opposed to it, and ignorance. It makes Nibbāna its object and sees the associated states. And it sees them by way of non-delusion, not by way of making them an object. Therefore, it is called 'right view.'

Sammāsaṅkappo micchāsaṅkappaṃ tappaccanīyakilese ca pajahati, nibbānañca ārammaṇaṃ karoti, sampayuttadhamme ca sammā abhiniropeti, tasmā “sammāsaṅkappo”ti vuccati.

Right intention abandons wrong intention and the defilements opposed to it, makes Nibbāna its object, and rightly directs the associated states toward it. Therefore, it is called 'right intention.'

Sammāvācā micchāvācaṃ tappaccanīyakilese ca pajahati, nibbānañca ārammaṇaṃ karoti, sampayuttadhamme ca sammā pariggaṇhāti, tasmā “sammāvācā”ti vuccati.

Right speech abandons wrong speech and the defilements opposed to it, makes Nibbāna its object, and rightly restrains the associated states. Therefore, it is called 'right speech.'

Sammākammanto [V 1.0113] micchākammantaṃ tappaccanīyakilese ca pajahati, nibbānañca ārammaṇaṃ karoti, sampayuttadhamme ca sammā [P 1.0106] samuṭṭhāpeti, tasmā “sammākammanto”ti vuccati.

Right action abandons wrong action and the defilements opposed to it, makes Nibbāna its object, and rightly arouses the associated states. Therefore, it is called 'right action.'

Sammāājīvo [M 1.0110] micchāājīvaṃ tappaccanīyakilese ca pajahati, nibbānañca ārammaṇaṃ karoti, sampayuttadhamme ca sammā vodāpeti, tasmā “sammāājīvo”ti vuccati.

Right livelihood abandons wrong livelihood and the defilements opposed to it, makes Nibbāna its object, and rightly purifies the associated states. Therefore, it is called 'right livelihood.'

Sammāvāyāmo micchāvāyāmaṃ tappaccanīyakilese ca kosajjañca pajahati, nibbānañca ārammaṇaṃ karoti, sampayuttadhamme ca sammā paggaṇhāti, tasmā “sammāvāyāmo”ti vuccati.

Right effort abandons wrong effort, the defilements opposed to it, and laziness. It makes Nibbāna its object and rightly exerts the associated states. Therefore, it is called 'right effort.'

Sammāsati micchāsatiṃ tappaccanīyakilese ca pajahati, nibbānañca ārammaṇaṃ karoti, sampayuttadhamme ca sammā upaṭṭhāpeti, tasmā “sammāsatī”ti vuccati.

Right mindfulness abandons wrong mindfulness and the defilements opposed to it, makes Nibbāna its object, and rightly establishes the associated states. Therefore, it is called 'right mindfulness.'

Sammāsamādhi micchāsamādhiṃ tappaccanīyakilese ca uddhaccañca pajahati, nibbānañca ārammaṇaṃ karoti, sampayuttadhamme ca sammā samādhiyati, tasmā “sammāsamādhī”ti vuccati.

Right concentration abandons wrong concentration, the defilements opposed to it, and restlessness. It makes Nibbāna its object and rightly composes the associated states. Therefore, it is called 'right concentration.'

Idāni ayaṃ kho sā, āvusoti tameva paṭipadaṃ nigamento āha. Tassattho, yvāyaṃ cattāropi lokuttaramagge ekato katvā kathito “aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo”, ayaṃ kho sā, āvuso…pe… nibbānāya saṃvattatīti.

Now, bringing that very path to a conclusion, he said: 'This indeed, friends, is that...' The meaning of this is: that which is the eight-factored path spoken of by unifying the four supramundane paths—this indeed, friends... conduces to Nibbāna.

Evaṃ pahātabbadhammesu lobhadose tappahānupāyañca dassetvā idāni aññepi pahātabbadhamme tesaṃ pahānupāyañca dassento tatrāvuso, kodho cātiādimāha. Tattha kujjhanalakkhaṇo kodho, caṇḍikkalakkhaṇo vā, āghātakaraṇaraso, dussanapaccupaṭṭhāno. Upanandhanalakkhaṇo upanāho, vera appaṭinissajjanaraso, kodhānupabandhabhāvapaccupaṭṭhāno. Vuttañcetaṃ – “pubbakāle kodho, aparakāle upanāho”tiādi (vibha. 891).

Thus, having shown greed and hatred among the states to be abandoned and the means for their abandonment, now, showing other states to be abandoned and the means for their abandonment, he said: 'Therein, friends, anger...' and so on. Therein, anger (kodha) has the characteristic of being angry, or the characteristic of fierceness; its function is to cause resentment, and its manifestation is malevolence. A grudge (upanāha) has the characteristic of binding fast; its function is not to relinquish enmity, and its manifestation is the state of being bound to anger. And this was stated: 'In a former time, anger; in a later time, a grudge,' and so on.

Paraguṇamakkhanalakkhaṇo makkho, tesaṃ vināsanaraso, tadavacchādanapaccupaṭṭhāno. Yugaggāhalakkhaṇo [V 1.0114] paḷāso, paraguṇehi attano guṇānaṃ samīkaraṇaraso, paresaṃ guṇappamāṇena upaṭṭhānapaccupaṭṭhāno.

Denigration (makkho) has the characteristic of disparaging others' virtues; its function is to destroy them, and its manifestation is to cover them up. Rivalry (paḷāso) has the characteristic of taking up the yoke; its function is to equate one's own virtues with others' virtues, and its manifestation is presenting oneself by the measure of others' virtues.

Parasampattikhīyanalakkhaṇā issā, tassā akkhamanalakkhaṇā vā, tattha anabhiratirasā, tato vimukhabhāvapaccupaṭṭhānā. Attano sampattinigūhanalakkhaṇaṃ [M 1.0111] maccheraṃ, attano sampattiyā parehi sādhāraṇabhāvaasukhāyanarasaṃ, saṅkocanapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ.

Envy (issā) has the characteristic of being vexed at others' fortune, or the characteristic of intolerance of it; its function is finding no delight in it, and its manifestation is the state of turning one's face away from it. Stinginess (maccheraṃ) has the characteristic of concealing one's own fortune; its function is finding unhappiness in the state of sharing one's own fortune with others, and its manifestation is constriction.

Katapāpapaṭicchādanalakkhaṇā māyā, tassa nigūhanarasā, tadāvaraṇapaccupaṭṭhānā. Attano avijjamānaguṇapakāsanalakkhaṇaṃ sāṭheyyaṃ, tesaṃ samudāharaṇarasaṃ, sarīrākārehipi tesaṃ vibhūtakaraṇapaccupaṭṭhānaṃ.

Deceit (māyā) has the characteristic of concealing evil that has been done; its function is to hide it, and its manifestation is to obstruct it. Fraud (sāṭheyyaṃ) has the characteristic of proclaiming non-existent virtues; its function is to bring them forth, and its manifestation is making them apparent even through bodily gestures.

Cittassa uddhumātabhāvalakkhaṇo [P 1.0107] thambho, appatissayavuttiraso, amaddavatāpaccupaṭṭhāno. Karaṇuttariyalakkhaṇo sārambho, vipaccanīkatāraso, agāravapaccupaṭṭhāno.

Stubbornness (thambho) has the characteristic of the mind's state of being bloated; its function is behavior without deference, and its manifestation is unsuppleness. Presumption (sārambho) has the characteristic of superiority in action; its function is combativeness, and its manifestation is a lack of reverence.

Uṇṇatilakkhaṇo māno, ahaṃkāraraso, uddhumātabhāvapaccupaṭṭhāno. Abbhuṇṇatilakkhaṇo atimāno, ativiya ahaṅkāraraso. Accuddhumātabhāvapaccupaṭṭhāno.

Conceit has the characteristic of elevation, its function is exalting oneself as 'I', and its manifestation is a state of being puffed up. Arrogance has the characteristic of extreme elevation, its function is excessively exalting oneself as 'I', and its manifestation is a state of being extremely puffed up.

Mattabhāvalakkhaṇo mado, madaggāhaṇaraso, ummādapaccupaṭṭhāno. Pañcasu kāmaguṇesu cittavossaggalakkhaṇo pamādo, vossaggānuppadānaraso, sativippavāsapaccupaṭṭhānoti evaṃ imesaṃ dhammānaṃ lakkhaṇādīni veditabbāni. Ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthāro pana “tattha katamo kodho”tiādinā vibhaṅge (vibha. 891) vuttanayeneva veditabbo.

Intoxication has the characteristic of being intoxicated, its function is grasping at intoxication, and its manifestation is derangement. Negligence has the characteristic of letting the mind loose among the five cords of sensual pleasure, its function is reinforcing that letting loose, and its manifestation is the absence of mindfulness. Thus, the characteristics and so forth of these states should be understood. This is the summary here; the detailed explanation, however, should be understood in the manner stated in the Vibhaṅga with 'Therein, what is anger?' and so forth.

Visesato cettha āmisadāyādo attanā alabhanto aññassa lābhino kujjhati, tassa sakiṃ uppanno kodho kodhoyeva, tatuttari upanāho. So evaṃ kuddho upanayhanto ca santepi aññassa lābhino guṇe makkheti, ahampi tādisoti ca yugaggāhaṃ gaṇhāti, ayamassa makkho ca paḷāso ca, evaṃ makkhī paḷāsī tassa lābhasakkārādīsu kiṃ imassa imināti issati padussati, ayamassa issā. Sace panassa kāci sampatti hoti, tassā tena sādhāraṇabhāvaṃ [V 1.0115] na sahati, idamassa maccheraṃ. Lābhahetu kho pana attano santepi dose paṭicchādeti, ayamassa māyā. Asantepi guṇe pakāseti. Idamassa sāṭheyyaṃ. So evaṃ paṭipanno sace yathādhippāyaṃ lābhaṃ labhati, tena thaddho hoti amuducitto, nayidaṃ evaṃ kātabbanti ovadituṃ asakkuṇeyyo, ayamassa thambho. Sace pana naṃ koci kiñci vadati “nayidaṃ evaṃ kātabba”nti, tena sāraddhacitto hoti bhākuṭikamukho “ko me [M 1.0112] tva”nti pasayha bhāṇī, ayamassa sārambho. Tato thambhena “ahameva seyyo”ti attānaṃ maññanto mānī hoti. Sārambhena “ke ime”ti pare atimaññanto atimānī, ayamassa māno ca atimāno ca. So tehi mānātimānehi jātimadādianekarūpaṃ madaṃ janeti. Matto samāno kāmaguṇādibhedesu vatthūsu pamajjati, ayamassa mado ca pamādo cāti.

Here, specifically, a monk who is an heir to material things, not receiving them for himself, becomes angry at another who does receive them. His anger, having arisen once, is just anger; beyond that, it is animosity. Being thus angry and harboring animosity, he disparages even the existing virtues of the one who receives gain. And thinking, 'I too am of such quality,' he takes up rivalry. This is his denigration and competitiveness. Being thus denigrating and competitive, he is envious and corrupts regarding that one's gains, honor, and so on, thinking, 'What is this to him?' This is his envy. If he himself has some possession, he cannot bear for it to be shared with that other. This is his miserliness. For the sake of gain, he conceals his own faults even when they exist. This is his deceit. He proclaims virtues that do not exist. This is his hypocrisy. Having conducted himself thus, if he obtains the gain he desires, he becomes harsh and hard-hearted, unable to be admonished with 'This should not be done thus.' This is his rigidity. If someone says anything to him, such as 'This should not be done thus,' he becomes vexed, with a scowling face, and speaks forcefully, saying, 'Who are you to me?' This is his contentiousness. Then, through rigidity, thinking 'I alone am superior,' he becomes conceited. Through contentiousness, thinking 'Who are these others?' he scorns them and becomes arrogant. This is his conceit and arrogance. Through that conceit and arrogance, he generates various forms of intoxication, such as intoxication with birth. Being intoxicated, he is negligent regarding objects such as the cords of sensual pleasure. This is his intoxication and negligence.

Evaṃ āmisadāyādo aparimutto hoti imehi pāpakehi dhammehi aññehi ca evarūpehi. Evaṃ tāvettha pahātabbadhammā veditabbā. Pahānupāyo [P 1.0108] pāṭhato ca atthato ca sabbattha nibbisesoyeva.

Thus, the heir to material things is not freed from these evil states and from others of a similar nature. In this way, first, the states to be abandoned should be understood herein. The means of abandoning is everywhere without difference, both in the letter and in the meaning.

Ñāṇaparicayapāṭavatthaṃ panettha ayaṃ bhedo ca kamo ca bhāvanānayo ca veditabbo. Tattha bhedo tāva, ayañhi majjhimā paṭipadā kadāci ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo hoti, kadāci sattaṅgiko. Ayañhi lokuttarapaṭhamajjhānavasena uppajjamāno aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo hoti, avasesajjhānavasena sattaṅgiko. Ukkaṭṭhaniddesato panidha aṭṭhaṅgikoti vutto. Ito parañhi maggaṅgaṃ natthi. Evaṃ tāvettha bhedo veditabbo.

For the sake of proficiency through acquaintance with knowledge, this distinction, this sequence, and this method of development should be understood herein. Therein, first, the distinction: for this Middle Practice is sometimes the Noble Eightfold Path, and sometimes the sevenfold. For when arising by way of the first supramundane jhāna, this path is eightfold; by way of the remaining jhānas, it is sevenfold. However, by way of the supreme designation, it is here called 'eightfold'. For there is no path factor beyond this. Thus, first, the distinction should be understood herein.

Yasmā pana sabbakusalānaṃ sammādiṭṭhi seṭṭhā, yathāha “paññā hi seṭṭhā kusalā vadantī”ti (jā. 2.17.81). Kusalavāre ca pubbaṅgamā, yathāha “kathañca, bhikkhave, sammādiṭṭhi pubbaṅgamā hoti, sammādiṭṭhiṃ sammādiṭṭhīti pajānāti, micchādiṭṭhiṃ micchādiṭṭhīti pajānātī”ti (ma. ni. 3.136) vitthāro. Yathā cāha “vijjā ca kho, bhikkhave, pubbaṅgamā kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ samāpattiyā”ti. Tappabhavābhinibbattāni sesaṅgāni, yathāha “sammādiṭṭhissa sammāsaṅkappo pahoti…pe… sammāsatissa sammāsamādhi pahotī”ti (ma. ni. 3.141). Tasmā [V 1.0116] iminā kamena etāni aṅgāni vuttānīti evamettha kamo veditabbo.

Because right view is the best of all wholesome states, as it is said: 'They say wisdom is the best of wholesome things.' And in the context of the wholesome, it is the forerunner, as it is said: 'And how, monks, is right view the forerunner? One understands right view as right view, and wrong view as wrong view'—the detailed explanation should be understood. And as it is said: 'Knowledge, monks, is the forerunner for the attainment of wholesome states.' The remaining factors are produced originating from it, as it is said: 'For one with right view, right intention comes to be… for one with right mindfulness, right concentration comes to be.' Therefore, these factors are stated in this sequence, and thus the sequence should be understood herein.

Bhāvanānayoti koci samathapubbaṅgamaṃ vipassanaṃ bhāveti, koci vipassanāpubbaṅgamaṃ samathaṃ. Kathaṃ? Idhekacco paṭhamaṃ upacārasamādhiṃ vā appanāsamādhiṃ vā uppādeti, ayaṃ samatho; so tañca taṃsampayutte ca dhamme aniccādīhi vipassati, ayaṃ vipassanā. Iti paṭhamaṃ samatho, pacchā vipassanā. Tena vuccati “samathapubbaṅgamaṃ vipassanaṃ bhāvetī”ti. Tassa samathapubbaṅgamaṃ vipassanaṃ bhāvayato maggo sañjāyati, so taṃ maggaṃ āsevati [M 1.0113] bhāveti bahulīkaroti, tassa taṃ maggaṃ āsevato bhāvayato bahulīkaroto saṃyojanāni pahīyanti, anusayā byantīhonti, evaṃ samathapubbaṅgamaṃ vipassanaṃ bhāveti.

Regarding the method of development: someone develops insight preceded by serenity, and someone develops serenity preceded by insight. How? Here, a certain person first produces access concentration or absorption concentration—this is serenity. That person sees that concentration and the states associated with it as impermanent, etc.—this is insight. Thus, first serenity, then insight. Therefore it is said, 'one develops insight preceded by serenity.' For one who develops insight preceded by serenity, the path arises. That person frequents that path, develops it, and makes it abundant. For that person who frequents, develops, and makes the path abundant, the fetters are abandoned, and the underlying tendencies come to an end. Thus one develops insight preceded by serenity.

Idha panekacco vuttappakāraṃ samathaṃ anuppādetvāva pañcupādānakkhandhe aniccādīhi vipassati, ayaṃ [P 1.0109] vipassanā. Tassa vipassanāpāripūriyā tattha jātānaṃ dhammānaṃ vossaggārammaṇato uppajjati cittassa ekaggatā, ayaṃ samatho. Iti paṭhamaṃ vipassanā pacchā samatho. Tena vuccati “vipassanāpubbaṅgamaṃ samathaṃ bhāvetī”ti. Tassa vipassanāpubbaṅgamaṃ samathaṃ bhāvayato maggo sañjāyati, so taṃ maggaṃ āsevati…pe… bahulīkaroti, tassa taṃ maggaṃ āsevato…pe… anusayā byantīhonti (a. ni. 4.170; paṭi. ma. 2.1), evaṃ vipassanāpubbaṅgamaṃ samathaṃ bhāveti.

But here, a certain person, without having produced serenity of the kind described, sees the five aggregates of clinging as impermanent, etc.—this is insight. For that person, upon the completion of insight, singleness of mind arises with relinquishment as its object among the states that have arisen there—this is serenity. Thus, first insight, then serenity. Therefore it is said, 'one develops serenity preceded by insight.' For one who develops serenity preceded by insight, the path arises. That person frequents that path… and makes it abundant. For that person who frequents… the underlying tendencies come to an end. Thus one develops serenity preceded by insight.

Samathapubbaṅgamaṃ pana vipassanaṃ bhāvayatopi vipassanāpubbaṅgamaṃ samathaṃ bhāvayatopi lokuttaramaggakkhaṇe samathavipassanā yuganaddhāva honti. Evamettha bhāvanānayo veditabboti.

However, for one who develops insight with serenity as its forerunner, and for one who develops serenity with insight as its forerunner, at the moment of the supramundane path, serenity and insight are indeed yoked together. Thus, the method of development should be understood here.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

In the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya

Dhammadāyādasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Dhammadāyāda Sutta is concluded.

4. Bhayabheravasuttavaṇṇanā

4. The Exposition of the Bhayabherava Sutta

34. Evaṃ [V 1.0117] me sutanti bhayabheravasuttaṃ. Tatrāyaṃ apubbapadavaṇṇanā – athāti avicchedanatthe nipāto. Khoti avadhāraṇatthe, bhagavato sāvatthiyaṃ vihāre avicchinneyevāti vuttaṃ hoti. Jāṇussoṇīti netaṃ tassa mātāpitūhi katanāmaṃ, apica kho ṭhānantarapaṭilābhaladdhaṃ. Jāṇussoṇiṭṭhānaṃ kira nāmetaṃ purohitaṭṭhānaṃ, taṃ tassa raññā dinnaṃ, tasmā “jānussoṇī”ti vuccati. Brahmaṃ aṇatīti brāhmaṇo, mante sajjhāyatīti attho. Idameva hi jātibrāhmaṇānaṃ niruttivacanaṃ. Ariyā pana bāhitapāpattā brāhmaṇāti vuccanti.

34. “Thus have I heard”—this is the Bhayabherava Sutta. Therein, this is the explanation of words not previously expounded. The word ‘atha’ is a particle in the sense of continuity. The word ‘kho’ is in the sense of emphasis; it is meant that the Blessed One’s dwelling in Sāvatthī was indeed uninterrupted. “Jāṇussoṇi”—this was not a name given to him by his mother and father, but rather one acquired through the attainment of a higher position. It is said that this position of Jāṇussoṇi is the position of royal priest, which was given to him by the king; therefore, he is called “Jāṇussoṇi.” One who recites the Brahman is a ‘brāhmaṇa’; the meaning is that he recites the mantras. This, indeed, is the etymological explanation for brahmins by birth. The noble ones, however, are called ‘brāhmaṇas’ because they have banished evil.

Yena [M 1.0114] bhagavā tenupasaṅkamīti yenāti bhummatthe karaṇavacanaṃ, tasmā yattha bhagavā, tattha upasaṅkamīti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Yena vā kāraṇena bhagavā devamanussehi upasaṅkamitabbo, tena kāraṇena upasaṅkamīti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Kena ca kāraṇena bhagavā upasaṅkamitabbo? Nānappakāraguṇavisesādhigamādhippāyena, sāduphalūpabhogādhippāyena [P 1.0110] dijagaṇehi niccaphalitamahārukkho viya.

Regarding “He approached where the Blessed One was”: here, ‘yena’ is an instrumental word used in the sense of the locative. Therefore, the meaning should be understood here as: “Where the Blessed One was, there he approached.” Or, the meaning should be understood here as: “He approached for the reason that the Blessed One is to be approached by devas and humans.” And for what reason is the Blessed One to be approached? With the intention of attaining various kinds of special qualities; like a great tree constantly bearing fruit is approached by flocks of birds with the intention of enjoying its sweet fruits.

Upasaṅkamīti ca gatoti vuttaṃ hoti. Upasaṅkamitvāti upasaṅkamanapariyosānadīpanaṃ. Atha vā evaṃ gato tato āsannataraṃ ṭhānaṃ bhagavato samīpasaṅkhātaṃ gantvātipi vuttaṃ hoti. Bhagavatā saddhiṃ sammodīti yathā khamanīyādīni pucchanto bhagavā tena, evaṃ sopi bhagavatā saddhiṃ samappavattamodo ahosi, sītodakaṃ viya uṇhodakena sammoditaṃ ekībhāvaṃ agamāsi. Yāya ca “kacci te, bho gotama, khamanīyaṃ, kacci yāpanīyaṃ, kacci bhoto gotamassa gotamasāvakānañca appābādhaṃ appātaṅkaṃ lahuṭṭhānaṃ balaṃ phāsuvihāro”tiādikāya kathāya sammodi, taṃ pītipāmojjasaṅkhātasammodajananato sammodituṃ yuttabhāvato ca sammodanīyaṃ, atthabyañjanamadhuratāya sucirampi kālaṃ sāretuṃ nirantaraṃ pavattetuṃ araharūpato saritabbabhāvato ca sārāṇīyaṃ. Suyyamānasukhato ca sammodanīyaṃ, anussariyamānasukhato ca sāraṇīyaṃ. Tathā byañjanaparisuddhatāya sammodanīyaṃ, atthaparisuddhatāya sāraṇīyanti evaṃ anekehi pariyāyehi sammodanīyaṃ [V 1.0118] kathaṃ sāraṇīyaṃ vītisāretvā pariyosāpetvā niṭṭhāpetvā yenatthena āgato, taṃ pucchitukāmo ekamantaṃ nisīdi.

And “he approached” means “he went.” “Having approached” indicates the completion of the act of approaching. Alternatively, it is also meant that, having gone thus, he went to a place nearer, designated as the Blessed One’s presence. “He exchanged pleasantries with the Blessed One” means that just as the Blessed One, inquiring about his well-being and so on, engaged in mutually agreeable conversation with him, so too did he with the Blessed One, becoming unified, like cool water mixed with hot water becomes one. And that conversation by which he exchanged pleasantries, asking, “Venerable Gotama, are you well? Are you keeping fit? Are you and the disciples of the Venerable Gotama free from illness and affliction, light, strong, and dwelling at ease?”—that conversation is called ‘sammodanīya’ (pleasant) because it generates the pleasure known as joy and delight, and because it is fitting to rejoice in. It is called ‘sāraṇīya’ (memorable) because of the sweetness of its meaning and phrasing, because it is fit to be remembered and continued for a long time without interruption. It is ‘sammodanīya’ because it is pleasant to hear, and ‘sāraṇīya’ because it is pleasant to recollect. Likewise, it is ‘sammodanīya’ for the purity of its phrasing, and ‘sāraṇīya’ for the purity of its meaning. Thus, having conducted, concluded, and finished this pleasant and memorable conversation in many ways, desiring to ask about the purpose for which he had come, he sat down to one side.

Ekamantanti bhāvanapuṃsakaniddeso, “visamaṃ candimasūriyā parivattantī”tiādīsu (a. ni. 4.70) viya. Tasmā yathā nisinno ekamantaṃ nisinno hoti, tathā nisīdīti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Bhummatthe vā etaṃ upayogavacanaṃ. Nisīdīti upāvisi. Paṇḍitā hi purisā garuṭṭhāniyaṃ upasaṅkamitvā āsanakusalatāya ekamantaṃ nisīdanti, ayañca nesaṃ aññataro, tasmā ekamantaṃ nisīdi.

“To one side” (ekamantaṃ) is a neuter noun indicating manner, as in phrases like “the moon and sun revolve unevenly.” Therefore, the meaning here should be understood as: “he sat down in such a way that he was seated to one side.” Alternatively, this is a usage in the locative sense. “He sat down” (nisīdi) means he took a seat. For wise men, having approached a person worthy of reverence, sit down to one side out of skill in seating, and this man was one of them; therefore, he sat down to one side.

Kathaṃ nisinno pana ekamantaṃ nisinno hotīti. Cha nisajjadose vajjetvā. Seyyathidaṃ, atidūraṃ accāsannaṃ uparivātaṃ unnatapadesaṃ atisammukhaṃ atipacchāti. Atidūre nisinno hi sace kathetukāmo hoti, uccāsaddena [M 1.0115] kathetabbaṃ hoti. Accāsanne nisinno saṅghaṭṭanaṃ karoti. Uparivāte nisinno sarīragandhena bādhati. Unnatappadese nisinno agāravaṃ pakāseti. Atisammukhā nisinno sace daṭṭhukāmo [P 1.0111] hoti, cakkhunā cakkhuṃ āhacca daṭṭhabbaṃ hoti. Atipacchā nisinno sace daṭṭhukāmo hoti, gīvaṃ pasāretvā daṭṭhabbaṃ hoti. Tasmā ayampi ete cha nisajjadose vajjetvā nisīdi, tena vuttaṃ “ekamantaṃ nisīdī”ti.

But how is one who is seated, seated “to one side”? By avoiding the six faults of seating. What are they? Being too far, too close, upwind, in a high place, too directly in front, and too far behind. For one who sits too far, if they wish to speak, must speak with a loud voice. One who sits too close causes contact. One who sits upwind offends with body odor. One who sits in a high place displays disrespect. One who sits too directly in front, if they wish to look, must look by meeting eye to eye. One who sits too far behind, if they wish to look, must look by stretching their neck. Therefore, this man also sat down having avoided these six faults of seating. For that reason, it is said, “he sat down to one side.”

Yemeti ye ime. Kulaputtāti duvidhā kulaputtā jātikulaputtā ācārakulaputtā. Tattha “tena kho pana samayena raṭṭhapālo nāma kulaputto tasmiṃyeva thullakoṭṭhike aggakulassa putto”ti (ma. ni. 2.294) evaṃ āgatā uccākulappasutā jātikulaputtā nāma. “Ye te kulaputtā saddhā agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajitā”ti (ma. ni. 3.78) evaṃ āgatā pana yattha katthaci kule pasutāpi ācārasampannā ācārakulaputtā nāma. Idha pana dvīhipi kāraṇehi kulaputtāyeva.

“Yeme” means “ye ime” (these who). “Kulaputtā” (clansmen) are of two kinds: clansmen by birth and clansmen by conduct. Among them, those born into high families, as in the passage, “At that time, a clansman named Raṭṭhapāla was the son of the foremost family in that very Thullakoṭṭhika,” are called clansmen by birth. But those who, though born in any family whatsoever, are endowed with good conduct, as in the passage, “Those clansmen who have gone forth in faith from the household life into homelessness,” are called clansmen by conduct. Here, however, they are indeed clansmen for both reasons.

Saddhāti saddhāya. Agārasmāti agārato. Anagāriyanti pabbajjaṃ bhikkhubhāvañca. Pabbajjāpi hi natthettha agāriyanti anagāriyā, agārassa hitaṃ kasigorakkhādikammamettha natthīti attho. Bhikkhupi natthetassa agāranti anagāro, anagārassa bhāvo anagāriyaṃ. Pabbajitāti [V 1.0119] upagatā, evaṃ sabbathāpi anagāriyasaṅkhātaṃ pabbajjaṃ bhikkhubhāvaṃ vā upagatāti vuttaṃ hoti. Pubbaṅgamoti purato gāmī nāyako. Bahukāroti hitakiriyāya bahūpakāro. Bhavaṃ tesaṃ gotamo samādapetāti te kulaputte bhavaṃ gotamo adhisīlādīni gāhetā sikkhāpetā. Sā janatāti so janasamūho. Diṭṭhānugatiṃ āpajjatīti dassanānugatiṃ paṭipajjati, yandiṭṭhiko bhavaṃ gotamo yaṃkhantiko yaṃruciko, tepi tandiṭṭhikā honti taṃkhantikā taṃrucikāti attho.

Saddhā means by faith. Agārasmā means from the home. Anagāriyaṃ refers to the state of one who has gone forth and the state of a monk. For indeed, in the state of one who has gone forth there is no household affair (agāriyaṃ), hence it is called 'anagāriyā'; the meaning is that herein there is no work for the benefit of a householder, such as ploughing and cattle-rearing. A monk also has no household affair (agāra), hence he is an 'anagāro'; the state of an 'anagāro' is 'anagāriyaṃ'. Pabbajitā means they have approached; thus, it is said that in every way they have approached what is designated as 'anagāriya', whether it be the state of one who has gone forth or the state of a monk. Pubbaṅgamo means one who goes before, a leader. Bahukāro means one who is of great help for their welfare. Bhavaṃ tesaṃ gotamo samādapeti means the Venerable Gotama causes those sons of good family to undertake and to train in the higher virtues and so on. Sā janatā means that group of people. Diṭṭhānugatiṃ āpajjati means they practice in accordance with his view; the meaning is: whatever view the Venerable Gotama holds, whatever he approves of, and whatever he prefers, they too hold that view, approve of that, and prefer that.

Kasmā panāyaṃ evamāhāti? Esa kira pubbe aneke kulaputte agāramajjhe vasante devaputte viya pañcahi kāmaguṇehi paricāriyamāne anto ca bahi ca susaṃvihitārakkhe disvā, te aparena samayena bhagavato madhurarasaṃ dhammadesanaṃ sutvā saddhāya gharā nikkhamma pabbajitvā ghāsacchādanaparamatāya [M 1.0116] santuṭṭhe āraññakesu senāsanesu kenaci arakkhiyamānepi anussaṅkitāparisaṅkite haṭṭhapahaṭṭhe [P 1.0112] udaggudagge addasa, disvā ca imesaṃ kulaputtānaṃ “ayaṃ phāsuvihāro kaṃ nissāya uppanno”ti cintento “samaṇaṃ gotama”nti bhagavati pasādaṃ alattha. So taṃ pasādaṃ nivedetuṃ bhagavato santikaṃ āgato, tasmā evamāha.

But why did he say this? It is said that previously he saw many sons of good family dwelling in the midst of households, being served by the five strands of sensual pleasure like divine sons, with well-arranged protection both inside and outside. Later, having heard the Blessed One’s sweet-tasting Dhamma teaching, they went forth from their homes out of faith. He saw them content with the minimum of food and clothing, dwelling in forest lodgings, and although unprotected by anyone, they were without alarm or trepidation, joyful and elated, exultant and jubilant. Having seen them, he reflected, “This comfortable abiding—on what does it depend for its arising?” and gained confidence in the Blessed One, thinking, “It depends on the ascetic Gotama.” To declare that confidence, he came into the presence of the Blessed One, and thus he spoke.

Athassa bhagavā taṃ vacanaṃ sampaṭicchanto abbhanumodanto ca evametaṃ brāhmaṇātiādimāha. Vacanasampaṭicchanānumodanatthoyeva hi ettha ayaṃ evanti nipāto. Mamaṃ uddissāti maṃ uddissa. Saddhāti saddhāyeva. Na iṇaṭṭhā na bhayaṭṭātiādīni sandhāyāha. Īdisānaṃyeva hi bhagavā pubbaṅgamo, na itaresaṃ. Durabhisambhavāni hīti sambhavituṃ dukkhāni dussahāni, na sakkā appesakkhehi ajjhogāhitunti vuttaṃ hoti. Araññavanapatthānīti araññāni ca vanapatthāni ca. Tattha kiñcāpi abhidhamme nippariyāyena, “nikkhamitvā bahi indakhilā sabbametaṃ arañña”nti vuttaṃ, tathāpi yantaṃ “pañcadhanusatikaṃ pacchima”nti āraññikaṅganipphādakaṃ senāsanaṃ vuttaṃ, tadeva adhippetanti veditabbaṃ.

Then the Blessed One, accepting and greatly rejoicing in those words, said, “So it is, brahmin,” and so forth. Herein, this particle 'evaṃ' has only the meaning of accepting and rejoicing in the speech. 'Mamaṃ uddissa' means 'having me as the object'. 'Saddhā' means 'by faith alone'. He spoke with reference to such things as 'not because of debt, not because of fear'. For the Blessed One is indeed the forerunner of such persons, not of others. 'Durabhisambhavāni' means they are difficult to accomplish, hard to endure; it is said that they cannot be entered into by those of little power. 'Araññavanapatthāni' means both forests and jungle wildernesses. Therein, although in the Abhidhamma it is stated without alternative explanation, “Having gone out beyond the threshold-post, all that is ‘forest’,” nevertheless, it should be understood that what is intended here is the dwelling that fulfills the ascetic practice of a forest-dweller, which is stated as, “a minimum of five hundred bow-lengths.”

Vanapatthanti gāmantaṃ atikkamitvā manussānaṃ anupacāraṭṭhānaṃ, yattha na kasīyati na vapīyati. Vuttampi cetaṃ “vanapatthanti dūrānametaṃ senāsanānaṃ adhivacanaṃ, vanapatthanti vanasaṇḍānametaṃ senāsanānaṃ, vanapatthanti bhiṃsanakānametaṃ, vanapatthanti salomahaṃsānametaṃ, vanapatthanti [V 1.0120] pariyantānametaṃ, vanapatthanti na manussūpacārānametaṃ senāsanānaṃ adhivacana”nti. Ettha ca pariyantānanti imamekaṃ pariyāyaṃ ṭhapetvā sesapariyāyehi vanapatthāni veditabbānī. Pantānīti pariyantāni atidūrāni. Dukkaraṃ pavivekanti kāyavivekaṃ dukkaraṃ. Durabhiramanti abhiramituṃ na sukhaṃ. Ekatteti ekībhāve. Kiṃ dasseti? Kāyaviveke katepi tattha cittaṃ abhiramāpetuṃ dukkaraṃ. Dvayaṃdvayārāmo hi ayaṃ lokoti. Haranti [P 1.0113] maññeti haranti viya ghasanti viya. Manoti manaṃ. Samādhiṃ alabhamānassāti upacārasamādhiṃ vā appanāsamādhiṃ vā alabhantassa. Kiṃ dasseti? Īdisassa bhikkhuno tiṇapaṇṇamigādisaddehi vividhehi ca bhiṃsanakehi vanāni cittaṃ vikkhipanti maññeti, sabbaṃ brāhmaṇo saddhāpabbajitānaṃ kulaputtānaṃ araññavāse (vibha. 529) vimhito āha.

Vanapattha is a place beyond the village boundary, a place not frequented by humans, where there is no ploughing or sowing. And this has been said: 'Vanapattha is a designation for remote dwellings; Vanapattha is a designation for dwellings in forest groves; Vanapattha is a designation for terrifying places; Vanapattha is a designation for places that make one's hair stand on end; Vanapattha is a designation for frontier dwellings; Vanapattha is a designation for dwellings not frequented by humans.' Herein, setting aside this one term 'frontier dwellings', 'vanapatthāni' should be understood by the remaining terms. Pantāni means frontier, extremely far. Dukkaraṃ pavivekaṃ means physical seclusion is difficult. Durabhiramaṃ means it is not easy to delight in. Ekatteti means in the state of being alone. What does this show? Even when physical seclusion is accomplished, it is difficult to make the mind delight therein, for this world delights in pairs. Haranti maññe means they seem to carry away, as if to devour. Mano means the mind. Samādhiṃ alabhamānassa means 'of one not attaining either access concentration or absorption concentration'. What does this show? For such a monk, the forests seem to scatter the mind with the sounds of grass, leaves, deer, and so on, and with various terrifying things. The brahmin, amazed at the forest-dwelling of the sons of good family who had gone forth out of faith, said all this.

Kāyakammantavārakathā

The Discourse on the Section of Bodily Work

35. Athassa [M 1.0117] bhagavā purimanayeneva “evametaṃ brāhmaṇā”tiādīhi taṃ taṃ vacanaṃ sampaṭicchitvā abbhanumoditvā ca yasmā soḷasasu ṭhānesu ārammaṇapariggaharahitānaṃyeva tādisāni senāsanāni durabhisambhavāni, na tesu ārammaṇapariggāhayuttānaṃ, attanā ca bodhisatto samāno tādiso ahosi, tasmā attano tādisānaṃ senāsanānaṃ durabhisambhavataṃ dassetuṃ, mayhampi khotiādimāha.

35. Then the Blessed One, with the same method as before, accepted and greatly rejoiced in those statements of that brahmin, saying, “So it is, brahmin,” and so on. And because in the sixteen instances such dwellings are difficult to delight in only for those devoid of grasping a meditation object, not for those endowed with it, and because he himself, being a Bodhisatta, was such, therefore, to show how such dwellings were difficult for him to delight in, he spoke the words beginning with, “For me too, indeed…”

Tattha pubbeva sambodhāti sambodhato pubbeva, ariyamaggappattito aparabhāgeyevāti vuttaṃ hoti. Anabhisambuddhassāti appaṭividdhacatusaccassa. Bodhisattasseva satoti bujjhanakasattasseva sammāsambodhiṃ adhigantuṃ arahasattasseva sato, bodhiyā vā sattasseva laggasseva sato. Dīpaṅkarassa hi bhagavato pādamūle aṭṭhadhammasamodhānena abhinīhārasamiddhito pabhuti tathāgato bodhiyā satto laggo “pattabbā mayā esā”ti tadadhigamāya parakkamaṃ amuñcantoyeva āgato, tasmā bodhisattoti vuccati. Tassa mayhanti tassa evaṃ bodhisattasseva sato mayhaṃ. Ye kho keci samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vāti ye keci pabbajjūpagatā vā bhovādino vā.

Herein, 'before awakening' means even before awakening; it is said to be in the period subsequent to having attained the noble path. 'Not fully awakened' means not having penetrated the four truths. 'Only as a Bodhisatta' means only as a being destined for awakening, only as a being worthy to attain perfect enlightenment, or only as a being attached to awakening. For from the time of the successful fulfillment of the aspiration at the feet of the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara through the eightfold concurrence of qualities, the Tathāgata was attached to awakening, thinking, 'This is to be attained by me,' never relaxing effort for its realization until he arrived. Therefore, he is called a Bodhisatta. 'For me then' means for me, who was thus only a Bodhisatta. 'Whatever ascetics or brahmins' means whatever those who have gone forth or those who address others as 'bho'.

Aparisuddhakāyakammantāti aparisuddhena pāṇātipātādinā kāyakammantena samannāgatā. Aparisuddhakāyakammantasandosahetūti [V 1.0121] aparisuddhassa kāyakammantasaṅkhātassa attano dosassa hetu, aparisuddhakāyakammantakāraṇāti vuttaṃ hoti. Haveti ekaṃsavacane nipāto. Akusalanti sāvajjaṃ akkhemañca. Bhayabheravanti bhayañca bheravañca. Cittutrāsassa ca bhayānakārammaṇassa cetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Tatra [P 1.0114] bhayaṃ sāvajjaṭṭhena akusalaṃ, bheravaṃ akkhemaṭṭhenāti veditabbaṃ. Avhāyantīti pakkosanti. Kathaṃ? Te hi pāṇātipātādīni katvā “mayaṃ ayuttamakamhā, sace no te jāneyyuṃ, yesaṃ aparajjhimhā, idāni anubandhitvā anayabyasanaṃ āpādeyyu”nti araññaṃ pavisitvā gacchantare vā gumbantare vā nisīdanti. Te “appamattakampi tiṇasaddaṃ vā paṇṇasaddaṃ vā sutvā, idānimhā naṭṭhā”ti tasanti vittasanti, āgantvā parehi parivāritā viya baddhā vadhitā viya ca honti. Evaṃ taṃ bhayabheravaṃ attani samāropanaṭṭhena avhāyanti pakkosanti.

'Impure bodily action' means being endowed with impure bodily action, such as killing living beings. 'The cause of defilement due to impure bodily action' means the cause of one's own fault, which is termed impure bodily action; it is said to be the reason for impure bodily action. 'Indeed' is a particle used in the sense of certainty. 'Unwholesome' means blameworthy and insecure. 'Fear and terror' means both fear and terror. This is a designation for mental agitation and for a frightening object. Herein, 'fear' should be understood as the unwholesome in the sense of being blameworthy, and 'terror' as the insecure in the sense of being unsafe. 'They summon' means they call forth. How? Having committed acts such as killing living beings, they think, 'We have done what is improper. If those whom we have wronged were to find out, they would now pursue us and bring us to ruin.' So they enter the forest and sit in a thicket or inside a bush. Hearing even a slight sound of grass or leaves, they tremble and panic, thinking, 'Now we are lost!' They become as if they are surrounded, bound, and slain by others who have come. Thus, by imposing it upon themselves, they summon that fear and terror.

Na [M 1.0118] kho panāhaṃ…pe… paṭisevāmīti ahaṃ kho pana aparisuddhakāyakammanto hutvā araññavanapatthāni pantāni senāsanāni na paṭisevāmi. Ye hi voti ettha voti nipātamattaṃ. Ariyā vuccanti buddhā ca buddhasāvakā ca. Parisuddhakāyakammantāti īdisā hutvā. Tesamahaṃ aññataroti tesaṃ ahampi eko aññataro. Bodhisatto hi gahaṭṭhopi pabbajitopi parisuddhakāyakammantova hoti. Bhiyyoti atirekatthe nipāto. Pallomanti pannalomataṃ, khemaṃ sotthibhāvanti attho. Āpādinti āpajjiṃ, atirekaṃ sotthibhāvaṃ atirekena vā sotthibhāvamāpajjinti vuttaṃ hoti. Araññe vihārāyāti araññe vihāratthāya.

'But I, indeed, do not... resort' means: I do not resort to remote forest-wilderness dwellings and lodgings as one who is of impure bodily action. In the phrase 'Ye hi vo', the word 'vo' is merely a particle. The noble ones are said to be the Buddhas and the disciples of the Buddhas. 'Of purified bodily conduct' means being such as these. 'I am one of them' means I too am one among them. For the Bodhisatta, whether a householder or one who has gone forth, is indeed of purified bodily conduct. 'Bhiyyo' is a particle in the sense of 'more' or 'excess'. 'Pallomaṃ' means the state of having settled hair; the meaning is security, a state of well-being. 'Āpādiṃ' means 'I attained'; it is said, 'I attained an excess of well-being,' or 'I attained well-being in excess.' 'For dwelling in the forest' means for the purpose of dwelling in the forest.

Kāyakammantavārakathā niṭṭhitā.

The discussion on the section of bodily action is concluded.

Vacīkammantavārādivaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Section on Verbal Action and So Forth

36. Esa nayo sabbattha. Ayaṃ pana viseso, vacīkammantavāre tāva aparisuddhavacīkammantāti aparisuddhena musāvādādinā vacīkammantena samannāgatā. Te kathaṃ bhayabheravaṃ avhāyanti? Te musāvādena parassa atthaṃ bhañjitvā, pisuṇavācāya mittabhedaṃ katvā pharusavācāya paresaṃ parisamajjhe mammāni tuditvā niratthakavācāya parasattānaṃ kammante nāsetvā [V 1.0122] “mayaṃ ayuttamakamhā, sace no te jāneyyuṃ, yesaṃ aparajjhimhā, idāni anubandhitvā anayabyasanaṃ pāpeyyu”nti araññaṃ pavisitvā gacchantare vā gumbantare vā nisīdanti. Te “appamattakampi tiṇasaddaṃ vā paṇṇasaddaṃ vā sutvā idānimhā naṭṭhā”ti tasanti vittasanti āgantvā parehi parivāritā viya baddhā vadhitā viya ca honti. Evaṃ taṃ bhayabheravaṃ [P 1.0115] attani samāropanaṭṭhena avhāyanti, pakkosanti.

36. This is the method in all cases. Here, however, is the distinction: first, in the section on verbal action, 'those with impure verbal action' means those endowed with impure verbal action such as lying and so forth. How do they summon fear and terror? By lying, they ruin the welfare of others; by divisive speech, they cause friendships to be broken; by harsh speech, they pierce the vital spots of others in the midst of an assembly; by useless chatter, they ruin the work of other beings. Thinking, 'We have acted wrongly; if those we have wronged knew, they would now pursue us and bring us misfortune and ruin,' they enter the forest and sit in a thicket or in a bush. Hearing even the slightest sound of grass or leaves, they tremble and are terrified, thinking, 'Now we are ruined!' They become as if they are surrounded, bound, and slain by others who have come. Thus, by imposing it upon themselves, they summon that fear and terror.

Manokammantavāre aparisuddhamanokammantāti aparisuddhena abhijjhādinā manokammantena samannāgatā. Te kathaṃ bhayabheravaṃ avhāyanti? Te paresaṃ rakkhitagopitesu bhaṇḍesu abhijjhāvisamalobhaṃ uppādetvā parassa kujjhitvā parasatte micchādassanaṃ gāhāpetvā mayaṃ ayuttamakamhā…pe… attani samāropanaṭṭhena avhāyanti pakkosanti.

In the section on mental action, 'those with impure mental action' means being endowed with impure mental action such as covetousness and so forth. How do they summon fear and terror? They arouse covetousness and unrighteous greed for others’ guarded and protected possessions, become angry at another, and cause other beings to adopt wrong views. Thinking, 'We have acted wrongly'...pe... by imposing it upon themselves, they summon that fear and terror.

Ājīvavāre [M 1.0119] aparisuddhājīvāti aparisuddhena vejjakammadūtakammavaḍḍhipayogādinā ekavīsatianesanabhedena ājīvena samannāgatā. Te kathaṃ bhayabheravaṃ avhāyanti? Te evaṃ jīvikaṃ kappetvā suṇanti – “sāsanasodhakā kira tepiṭakā bhikkhū sāsanaṃ sodhetuṃ nikkhantā, ajja vā sve vā idhāgamissantī”ti araññaṃ pavisitvā gacchantare vā…pe… tasanti vittasanti. Te hi āgantvā parivāretvā gahitā viya odātavatthanivāsitā viya ca hontīti. Sesaṃ tādisameva.

In the section on livelihood, 'those with impure livelihood' means being endowed with an impure livelihood of twenty-one kinds of improper seeking, such as practicing medicine, acting as a messenger, lending on interest, and so forth. How do they summon fear and terror? Having made a living in such ways, they hear: 'Indeed, the monks, masters of the three Piṭakas, purifiers of the Teaching, have set out to purify the Teaching; they will arrive here today or tomorrow.' Entering the forest...pe... they tremble and are terrified. For they become as if, those monks having come and surrounded them, they are captured, or as if they are made to wear white clothes. The rest is just the same.

37. Ito paraṃ abhijjhālūtiādīsu kiñcāpi abhijjhābyāpādā manokammantena saṅgahitā tathāpi nīvaraṇavasena puna vuttāti veditabbā. Tattha abhijjhālūti parabhaṇḍādiabhijjhāyanasīlā. Kāmesu tibbasārāgāti vatthukāmesu bahalakilesarāgā, te kathaṃ bhayabheravaṃ avhāyanti? Te avavatthitārammaṇā honti, tesaṃ avavatthitārammaṇānaṃ araññe viharantānaṃ divā diṭṭhaṃ rattiṃ bhayabheravaṃ hutvā upaṭṭhāti – “te ākulacittā appamattakenapi tasanti vittasanti, rajjuṃ vā lataṃ vā disvā sappasaññino honti, khāṇuṃ disvā yakkhasaññino, thalaṃ vā pabbataṃ vā disvā hatthisaññino sappādīhi anayabyasanaṃ āpāditā viya hontī”ti. Sesaṃ tādisameva.

37. From here onward, in the sections beginning with 'covetous,' although covetousness and ill-will are included under mental action, it should be understood that they are nevertheless mentioned again by way of the hindrances. Herein, 'covetous' refers to those whose nature is to covet others' possessions and so forth. 'Intensely lustful for sensual pleasures' means those with thick defilement and lust for the objects of sensual pleasure. How do they summon fear and terror? They have an undemarcated object of mind. For those with an undemarcated object dwelling in the forest, what was seen during the day appears at night, having become a cause for fear and terror—their minds are agitated, and they tremble and are terrified even at the slightest thing; seeing a rope or a creeper, they perceive a snake; seeing a stump, they perceive a yakkha; seeing high ground or a mountain, they perceive an elephant; they become as if brought to misfortune and ruin by snakes and so forth. The rest is just the same.

38. Byāpannacittāti [V 1.0123] pakatibhāvavijahanena vipannacittā. Kilesānugatañhi cittaṃ pakatibhāvaṃ vijahati, purāṇabhattabyañjanaṃ viya pūtikaṃ hoti. Paduṭṭhamanasaṅkappāti paduṭṭhacittasaṅkappā, abhadrakena paresaṃ anatthajanakena cittasaṅkappena samannāgatāti vuttaṃ hoti. Te kathaṃ bhayabheravaṃ avhāyanti? Bhayabheravāvhāyanaṃ [P 1.0116] ito pabhuti abhijjhāluvāre vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Yattha pana viseso bhavissati, tattha vakkhāma. Na kho panāhaṃ byāpannacittoti ettha pana mettacitto ahaṃ hitacittoti dasseti, īdisā hi bodhisattā honti. Evaṃ sabbattha vuttadosapaṭipakkhavasena bodhisattassa guṇā vaṇṇetabbā.

38. 'Hostile-minded' means having a corrupted mind due to abandoning its natural state. For a mind accompanied by defilements abandons its natural state, becoming putrid like stale food. 'With corrupt thoughts' means having corrupt mental intentions; that is to say, being endowed with unwholesome mental intentions that bring harm to others. How do they summon fear and terror? From this point onward, the summoning of fear and terror should be understood in the same way as explained in the section on the covetous. But where there is a distinction, we shall state it. As for the passage, 'But I am not hostile-minded,' here it shows, 'I am one with a mind of loving-kindness, a mind for the welfare of others.' Indeed, such are the bodhisattas. Thus, in all cases, the virtues of the Bodhisatta should be praised by way of the opposite of the faults mentioned.

39. Thinamiddhapariyuṭṭhitāti cittagelaññabhūtena thinena sesanāmakāyagelaññabhūtena middhena ca pariyuṭṭhitā, abhibhūtā gahitāti vuttaṃ hoti. Te niddābahulā honti.

39. 'Overcome by sloth and torpor' means assailed, overwhelmed, and seized by sloth, which is the sickness of the mind, and by torpor, which is the sickness of the remaining mental aggregates. That is what is meant. They are given to much sleep.

40. Uddhatāti [M 1.0120] uddhaccapakatikā vipphandamānacittā, uddhaccena hi ekārammaṇe cittaṃ vipphandati dhajayaṭṭhiyaṃ vātena paṭākā viya. Avūpasantacittāti anibbutacittā, idha kukkuccaṃ gahetuṃ vaṭṭati.

40. 'Restless' means those whose nature is agitation, having a fluttering mind. For by agitation, the mind flutters regarding a single object, like a banner on a flagpole in the wind. 'With an unpacified mind' means with a mind that is not stilled; here, remorse is to be included.

41. Kaṅkhī vicikicchīti ettha ekamevidaṃ pañcamaṃ nīvaraṇaṃ. Kiṃ nu kho idanti ārammaṇaṃ kaṅkhanato kaṅkhā, idamevidanti nicchetuṃ asamatthabhāvato vicikicchāti vuccati, tena samannāgatā samaṇabrāhmaṇā “kaṅkhī vicikicchī”ti vuttā.

41. 'Doubtful, wavering'—here, this fifth hindrance is one and the same. Because of doubting the object, thinking, 'What indeed is this?', it is called doubt (kaṅkhā). Because of the inability to determine with certainty, 'This is just so,' it is called wavering (vicikicchā). Ascetics and brahmins who are endowed with this are called 'doubtful and wavering.'

42. Attukkaṃsanakā paravambhīti ye attānaṃ ukkaṃsenti ukkhipanti, ucce ṭhāne ṭhapenti, parañca vambhenti garahanti nindanti, nīce ṭhāne ṭhapenti, tesametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Te kathaṃ bhayabheravaṃ avhāyanti? Te parehi “asuko ca kira asuko ca attānaṃ ukkaṃsenti, amhe garahanti, dāse viya karonti, gaṇhatha ne”ti anubaddhā palāyitvā araññaṃ pavisitvā gacchantare vā gumbantare vāti kāyakammantasadisaṃ vitthāretabbaṃ.

42. 'Self-praising and disparaging others' is a designation for those who exalt and elevate themselves, placing themselves in a high position, while disparaging, blaming, and censuring others, placing them in a low position. How do they summon fear and terror? When pursued by others who say, 'It is said that so-and-so and so-and-so exalt themselves and disparage us, treating us like slaves—seize them!', they flee, enter the forest, and go among the trees or bushes. This should be elaborated similarly to the section on bodily action.

43. Chambhīti kāyathambhanalomahaṃsanakarena thambhena samannāgatā. Bhīrukajātikāti bhīrukapakatikā, gāmadārakā viya bhayabahulā asūrā kātarāti vuttaṃ hoti.

43. 'Stupefied' means endowed with a stiffness that causes the body to become rigid and the hair to stand on end. 'Timid by nature' means those whose nature is fearful; that is to say, like village children, they are full of fear, not brave, and cowardly. That is what is meant.

44. Lābhasakkārasilokanti [V 1.0124] ettha labbhatīti lābho, catunnaṃ paccayānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Sakkāroti sundarakāro, paccayā eva hi paṇītapaṇītā sundarasundarā ca abhisaṅkharitvā katā sakkārāti vuccanti. Yā ca parehi attano gāravakiriyā pupphādīhi vā pūjā. Silokoti vaṇṇabhaṇanaṃ etaṃ[P 1.0117], lābhañca sakkārañca silokañca lābhasakkārasilokaṃ. Nikāmayamānāti patthayamānā. Bhayabheravāvhāyanaṃ abhijjhāluvārasadisameva. Tadatthadīpakaṃ panettha piyagāmikavatthuṃ kathenti –

44. Regarding 'gain, honor, and praise': here, because it is obtained (labbhati), it is called 'gain' (lābha); this is a designation for the four requisites. 'Honor' (sakkāra) means a fine preparation (sundarakāra). Indeed, requisites that are prepared and made to be most excellent and most beautiful are called 'honor.' Also, the act of reverence shown by others to oneself, or worship with flowers and so on, is called 'honor.' 'Praise' (siloka) is the speaking of praise. This gain, honor, and praise is 'gain, honor, and praise.' 'Longing for' means desiring. The summoning of fear and terror is just the same as in the section on the covetous. To illustrate this meaning, they relate here the story of Piyagāmika:

Eko kira piyagāmiko nāma bhikkhu samādinnadhutaṅgānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ lābhaṃ disvā “ahampi dhutaṅgaṃ samādiyitvā lābhaṃ uppādemī”ti cintetvā sosānikaṅgaṃ samādāya susāne vasati. Athekadivasaṃ eko kammamutto jaraggavo divā gocare caritvā rattiṃ tasmiṃ susāne pupphagumbe sīsaṃ katvā romanthayamāno aṭṭhāsi. Piyagāmiko rattiṃ caṅkamanā nikkhanto [M 1.0121] tassa hanusaddaṃ sutvā cintesi “addhā maṃ lābhagiddho esa susāne vasatīti ñatvā devarājā viheṭhetuṃ āgato”ti, so jaraggavassa purato añjaliṃ paggahetvā “sappurisa devarāja ajja me ekarattiṃ khama, sve paṭṭhāya na evaṃ karissāmī”ti namassamāno sabbarattiṃ yācanto aṭṭhāsi. Tato sūriye uṭṭhite taṃ disvā kattarayaṭṭhiyā paharitvā palāpesi “sabbarattiṃ maṃ bhiṃsāpesī”ti.

It is said that a certain monk named Piyagāmika, seeing the gains of monks who had undertaken the ascetic practices, thought, 'I too, having undertaken an ascetic practice, will generate gain.' Having undertaken the charnel-ground practice, he dwelt in a charnel ground. Then one day, an old ox, freed from work, having grazed in the pasture by day, at night stood in that charnel ground, placing its head on a flowering bush while chewing the cud. Piyagāmika, having gone out from his walking meditation path at night, heard the sound of its jaw and thought, 'Surely, knowing that I dwell in the charnel ground out of greed for gain, the king of the gods has come to harass me.' He stood for the entire night before the old ox, raising his joined hands, pleading, 'Good sir, king of the gods, forgive me for this one night. Starting from tomorrow, I will not do so,' and paying homage. Then, when the sun had risen, seeing it, he struck it with a bamboo staff and drove it away, saying, 'It made me afraid the whole night!'

45. Kusītāti kosajjānugatā. Hīnavīriyāti hīnā vīriyena virahitā viyuttā, nibbīriyāti vuttaṃ hoti. Tattha kusītā kāyikavīriyārambhavirahitā honti, hīnavīriyā cetasikavīriyārambhavirahitā. Te ārammaṇavavatthānamattampi kātuṃ na sakkonti. Tesaṃ avavatthitārammaṇānanti sabbaṃ pubbasadisameva.

45. 'Lazy' means given to indolence. 'Of inferior energy' means inferior, devoid of energy, dissociated from it; that is to say, without energy. Herein, the lazy are devoid of the undertaking of bodily energy, while those of inferior energy are devoid of the undertaking of mental energy. They are unable even to merely determine an object. The passage beginning 'For them, whose objects are undetermined...' and all that follows is just as before.

46. Muṭṭhassatīti naṭṭhassatī. Asampajānāti paññārahitā, imassa ca paṭipakkhe “upaṭṭhitassatīhamasmī”ti vacanato satibhājaniyamevetaṃ. Paññā panettha satidubbalyadīpanatthaṃ vuttā. Duvidhā hi sati paññāsampayuttā paññāvippayuttā ca. Tattha paññāsampayuttā balavatī, vippayuttā dubbalā, tasmā yadāpi tesaṃ sati hoti, tadāpi asampajānantā muṭṭhassatīyeva te, dubbalāya satiyā satikiccābhāvatoti etamatthaṃ dīpetuṃ “asampajānā”ti vuttaṃ. Te evaṃ [V 1.0125] muṭṭhassatī asampajānā ārammaṇavavatthānamattampi kātuṃ na sakkontīti sabbaṃ pubbasadisameva.

46. “Of confused mindfulness” means of lost mindfulness. “Not clearly comprehending” means devoid of wisdom. And because in the opposite case it is said, “I am of established mindfulness,” this is indeed a matter pertaining to mindfulness. Herein, wisdom is mentioned to show the weakness of mindfulness. For mindfulness is twofold: that associated with wisdom and that dissociated from wisdom. Among these, that associated with wisdom is strong; that dissociated from it is weak. Therefore, even when they have mindfulness, they are still of confused mindfulness, not clearly comprehending, due to the absence of the function of mindfulness on account of its weakness. To show this meaning, “not clearly comprehending” is said. They, being thus of confused mindfulness and not clearly comprehending, are unable even to merely determine an object—all is just as before.

47. Asamāhitāti upacārappanāsamādhivirahitā. Vibbhantacittāti ubbhantacittā. Samādhivirahena laddhokāsena uddhaccena tesaṃ samādhivirahānaṃ cittaṃ nānārammaṇesu [P 1.0118] paribbhamati, vanamakkaṭo viya vanasākhāsu uddhaccena ekārammaṇe vipphandati. Pubbe vuttanayenena te evaṃ asamāhitā vibbhantacittā ārammaṇavavatthānamattampi kātuṃ na sakkontīti sabbaṃ pubbasadisameva.

47. “Unconcentrated” means devoid of access and absorption concentration. “Of agitated mind” means of a wandering mind. Through restlessness that has found an opportunity due to the absence of concentration, the minds of those who are devoid of concentration wander among various objects, like a forest monkey among the branches of the forest; through restlessness, the mind trembles even on a single object. By the method previously stated, they, being thus unconcentrated and of agitated mind, are unable even to merely determine an object—all is just as before.

48. Duppaññāti nippaññānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Paññā pana duṭṭhā nāma natthi. Eḷamūgāti elamukhā, kha-kārassa ga-kāro kato. Lālamukhāti vuttaṃ hoti. Duppaññānañhi kathentānaṃ lālā mukhato galati, lālā ca elāti [M 1.0122] vuccati. Yathāha “passelamūgaṃ uragaṃ dujjivha”nti. Tasmā te “eḷamūgā”ti vuccanti. “Elamukhā”tipi pāṭho. “Elamugā”ti keci paṭhanti, apare “elamukā”tipi, sabbattha “elamukhā”ti attho. Te kathaṃ bhayabheravaṃ avhāyanti? Te duppaññā eḷamūgā ārammaṇavavatthānamattampi kātuṃ na sakkonti. Tesaṃ avavatthitārammaṇānaṃ araññe viharantānaṃ divā diṭṭhaṃ rattiṃ bhayabheravaṃ hutvā upaṭṭhāti “te ākulacittā appamattakenapi tasanti vittasanti, rajjuṃ vā lataṃ vā disvā sappasaññino honti, khāṇuṃ disvā yakkhasaññino, thalaṃ vā pabbataṃ vā disvā hatthisaññino sappādīhi anayavyasanaṃ āpāditā viya hontī”ti. Evaṃ taṃ bhayabheravaṃ attani samāropanaṭṭhena avhāyanti pakkosanti. Paññāsampannohamasmīti ettha paññāsampannoti paññāya sampanno samannāgato, no ca kho vipassanāpaññāya, na maggapaññāya, apica kho pana imesu soḷasasu ṭhānesu ārammaṇavavatthānapaññāyāti attho. Sesaṃ sabbattha vuttanayamevāti.

48. “Of poor wisdom” is a designation for those without wisdom. For there is no such thing as “corrupt” wisdom. “Slobbering” (eḷamūgā) means having a faulty mouth (elamukhā); the letter ‘kh’ is made into the letter ‘g’. This means having a drooling mouth (lālamukhā). For when those of poor wisdom speak, saliva (lālā) drips from their mouth, and saliva is also called elā. As it is said: “See the slobbering, two-tongued serpent.” Therefore they are called “slobbering.” There is also the reading “elamukhā.” Some read it as “elamugā,” others as “elamukā,” but in all cases the meaning is “elamukhā” (having a faulty mouth). How do they summon fear and terror? They, being of poor wisdom and slobbering, are unable even to merely determine an object. For them, dwelling in the forest with an undetermined object, what is seen by day appears at night, having become fear and terror. “Their minds are agitated; they tremble and are terrified at the slightest thing. Seeing a rope or a vine, they perceive a snake; seeing a stump, they perceive a yakkha; seeing high ground or a mountain, they perceive an elephant, as if brought to ruin and disaster by snakes and so on.” Thus they summon and call forth that fear and terror by superimposing it upon themselves. Here, regarding “I am endowed with wisdom,” “endowed with wisdom” means endowed or furnished with wisdom; however, not with insight wisdom, nor with path wisdom, but rather, it is the wisdom of determining the object in these sixteen instances. The remainder is by the method stated everywhere else.

Vacīkammantavārādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the section on verbal conduct and so on is concluded.

Soḷasaṭṭhānārammaṇapariggaho niṭṭhito.

The comprehension of the object in the sixteen instances is concluded.

Bhayabheravasenāsanādivaṇṇanā

The Description of Fear, Terror, Dwellings, and so forth

49. Tassa [V 1.0126] mayhanti ko anusandhi? Bodhisatto kira imāni soḷasārammaṇāni pariggaṇhanto ca bhayabheravaṃ adisvā bhayabheravaṃ nāma evarūpāsu rattīsu evarūpe senāsane ca paññāyati, handa naṃ tatthāpi gavesissāmīti bhayabheravagavesanamakāsi, etamatthaṃ bhagavā idāni brāhmaṇassa dassento tassa mayhantiādimāha.

49. What is the connection with “To me…” (tassa mayhaṃ)? The Bodhisatta, it is said, while comprehending these sixteen objects, did not see that which causes fear and terror. He thought, ‘That which is called fear and terror appears on such nights and in such a dwelling. Come now, I shall seek it there as well.’ Thinking thus, he undertook a search for that which causes fear and terror. To show this meaning, the Blessed One, now wishing to teach the brahmin, said, “To me…” (tassa mayhaṃ), and so forth.

Tattha yā tāti ubhayametaṃ rattīnaṃyeva uddesaniddesavacanaṃ. Abhiññātāti [P 1.0119] ettha abhīti lakkhaṇatthe upasaggo. Tasmā abhiññātāti candapāripūriyā candaparikkhayenāti evamādīhi lakkhaṇehi ñātāti veditabbā. Abhilakkhitāti ettha upasaggamattameva, tasmā abhilakkhitāti lakkhaṇīyā icceva attho, uposathasamādānadhammassavanapūjāsakkārādikaraṇatthaṃ lakkhetabbā sallakkhetabbā upalakkhetabbāti vuttaṃ hoti.

Therein, the pair of words ‘yā’ and ‘tā’ is a term of general indication and specific designation for the nights. In the word ‘abhiññātā’ (well-known), ‘abhi’ is a prefix in the sense of a characteristic mark. Therefore, ‘abhiññātā’ should be understood as ‘known by such characteristic marks as the fullness of the moon and the waning of the moon.’ In ‘abhilakkhitā’ (marked), ‘abhi’ is merely a prefix; therefore, the meaning of ‘abhilakkhitā’ is simply ‘to be marked.’ It is meant that they are to be marked, to be well-marked, and to be noted for the purpose of undertaking the Uposatha, listening to the Dhamma, making offerings, showing respect, and so forth.

Cātuddasīti [M 1.0123] pakkhassa paṭhamadivasato pabhuti catuddasannaṃ pūraṇī ekā ratti. Evaṃ pañcadasī aṭṭhamī ca. Pakkhassāti sukkapakkhassa kaṇhapakkhassa ca. Etā tisso tisso katvā cha rattiyo, tasmā sabbattha pakkhavacanaṃ yojetabbaṃ “pakkhassa cātuddasī pakkhassa pañcadasī pakkhassa aṭṭhamī”ti. Atha pañcamī kasmā na gahitāti? Asabbakālikattā. Buddhe kira bhagavati anuppannepi uppajjitvā aparinibbutepi pañcamī anabhilakkhitāyeva, parinibbute pana dhammasaṅgāhakattherā cintesuṃ “dhammassavanaṃ cirena hotī”ti. Tato sammannitvā pañcamīti dhammassavanadivasaṃ ṭhapesuṃ, tato pabhuti sā abhilakkhitā jātā, evaṃ asabbakālikattā ettha na gahitāti.

“The fourteenth” (cātuddasī) is the one night that is the completion of the fourteen days, starting from the first day of the fortnight. It is similar for “the fifteenth” (pañcadasī) and “the eighth” (aṭṭhamī). “Of the fortnight” (pakkhassa) refers to both the bright fortnight and the dark fortnight. As there are three such nights in each, making six nights in total, the word ‘pakkhassa’ should be connected everywhere, as in “the fourteenth of the fortnight, the fifteenth of the fortnight, the eighth of the fortnight.” Then why is the fifth not included? Because it was not always so. It is said that before the Blessed One, the Buddha, had arisen, and also after he had arisen but before he had attained Parinibbāna, the fifth was unmarked. But after he had attained Parinibbāna, the Elder Monks who were compilers of the Dhamma considered, “Listening to the Dhamma occurs only after a long interval.” Then, having designated it as “the fifth,” they established it as a day for listening to the Dhamma. From that time onwards, that day became marked. Thus, because it was not always so, it is not included here.

Tathārūpāsūti tathāvidhāsu. Ārāmacetiyānīti pupphārāmaphalārāmādayo ārāmā eva ārāmacetiyāni. Cittīkataṭṭhena hi cetiyānīti vuccanti, pūjanīyaṭṭhenāti vuttaṃ hoti. Vanacetiyānīti baliharaṇavanasaṇḍasubhagavanadevasālavanādīni vanāniyeva vanacetiyāni. Rukkhacetiyānīti gāmanigamādidvāresu pūjanīyarukkhāyeva rukkhacetiyāni. Lokiyā hi dibbādhivatthāti vā maññamānā tesuyeva vā dibbasaññino hutvā ārāmavanarukkhe cittīkaronti[V 1.0127], pūjenti, tena te sabbepi cetiyānīti vuccanti. Bhiṃsanakānīti bhayajanakāni, passatopi suṇatopi bhayaṃ janenti. Salomahaṃsānīti saheva lomahaṃsena vattanti, pavisamānasseva lomahaṃsajananato. Appeva nāma passeyyanti api nāma taṃ bhayabheravaṃ passeyyameva. Aparena samayenāti, “etadahosi yaṃnūnāha”nti evaṃ cintitakālato paṭṭhāya aññena kālena.

'Tathārūpāsu' means of such kinds. 'Ārāmacetiyāni' means parks such as flower parks, fruit parks, and so forth; the parks themselves are 'ārāmacetiyāni'. For they are called 'cetiyāni' because they are places for veneration; this is to say, because they are worthy of worship. 'Vanacetiyānīti' means forests such as the Baliharaṇa forest, forest groves, the Subhagavana, the Devasālavana, and so forth; the forests themselves are 'vanacetiyāni'. 'Rukkhacetiyānīti' means venerable trees at the gates of villages, towns, and so forth; the trees themselves are 'rukkhacetiyāni'. For worldly people, thinking 'they are inhabited by deities,' or having the perception of deities in those very places, venerate and worship the parks, forests, and trees. Therefore, all of them are called 'cetiyāni'. 'Bhiṃsanakāni' means fear-inspiring; they inspire fear in one who sees or hears. 'Salomahaṃsāni' means they exist together with hair-raising, because they cause the hair to stand on end for one who is just entering. 'Appeva nāma passeyyaṃ' means 'Perhaps I might indeed see that object that causes fear and terror.' 'Aparena samayena' means at another time, starting from the time of thinking thus, 'It occurred to me, "What if I..."'.

Tattha ca me brāhmaṇa viharatoti [P 1.0120] tathārūpesu senāsanesu yaṃ yaṃ manussānaṃ āyācanaupahārakaraṇārahaṃ yakkhaṭṭhānaṃ pupphadhūpamaṃsaruhiravasāmedapihakapapphāsasurāmerayādīhi okiṇṇakilinnadharaṇitalaṃ ekanipātaṃ viya yakkharakkhasapisācānaṃ, yaṃ divāpi passantānaṃ hadayaṃ maññe phalati, taṃ ṭhānaṃ sandhāyāha “tattha ca me, brāhmaṇa, viharato”ti. Mago vā āgacchatīti siṅgāni vā khurāni vā koṭṭento gokaṇṇakhaggadīpivarāhādibhedo mago vā āgacchati, sabbacatuppadānañhi idha magoti nāmaṃ. Katthaci pana kāḷasiṅgālopi vuccati. Yathāha –

'And there, brahmin, as I was dwelling': referring to such dwelling places—whatever place of yakkhas is suitable for human requests and offerings, the ground of which is strewn and wet with flowers, incense, flesh, blood, fat, marrow, spleen, lungs, liquor, spirits, and so forth, like a single gathering place of yakkhas, rakkhasas, and pisācas; a place which, when seen even by day, would make the heart of those who see it, I think, burst—referring to such a place, he said, 'And there, brahmin, as I was dwelling.' 'Or a beast might come' means a beast of such kinds as a gokaṇṇa, rhinoceros, leopard, or boar might come, butting with its horns or striking with its hooves. For here, 'beast' (maga) is a name for all four-footed creatures. In some places, however, even a black jackal is meant. As it is said:

“Usabhasseva [M 1.0124] te khandho, sīhasseva vijambhitaṃ;

Magarāja namo tyatthu, api kiñci labhāmase”ti. (jā. 1.3.133);

'Your shoulder is like a bull's, your yawn is like a lion's. O King of Beasts, homage be to you! Perhaps we might obtain something.'

Moro vā kaṭṭhaṃ pātetīti moro vā sukkhakaṭṭhaṃ rukkhato cāletvā pāteti. Moraggahaṇena ca idha sabbapakkhiggahaṇaṃ adhippetaṃ, tena yo koci pakkhīti vuttaṃ hoti. Atha vā moro vāti vā saddena añño vā koci pakkhīti. Esa nayo purime magaggahaṇepi. Vāto vā paṇṇakasaṭaṃ eretīti vāto vā paṇṇakacavaraṃ ghaṭṭeti. Etaṃ nūna taṃ bhayabheravaṃ āgacchatīti yametaṃ āgacchati, taṃ bhayabheravaṃ nūnāti. Ito pabhuti ca ārammaṇameva bhayabheravanti veditabbaṃ. Parittassa ca adhimattassa ca bhayassa ārammaṇattā sukhārammaṇaṃ rūpaṃ sukhamiva. Kiṃ nu kho ahaṃ aññadatthu bhayapaṭikaṅkhī viharāmīti ahaṃ kho kiṃ kāraṇaṃ ekaṃseneva bhayaṃ ākaṅkhamāno icchamāno hutvā viharāmi.

'Or a peacock might make a piece of wood fall' means a peacock might shake a dry piece of wood from a tree and make it fall. And by the taking of 'peacock' here, the inclusion of all birds is intended; thus it is said, 'any bird whatsoever.' Alternatively, in 'or a peacock' (moro vā), by the word 'or' (vā), any other bird is intended to be included. This is the same method as in the previous inclusion of 'beast' (maga). 'Or the wind might stir a heap of leaves' means the wind might strike the leaf-litter. 'Surely this that is coming is that fear and terror' means: 'This which is coming, is it not indeed that object that causes fear and terror?' From this point on, it should be understood that the object itself is 'fear and terror'. Because it is the object of both slight and intense fear, just as a pleasant object, a visible form, is like pleasure itself. 'Why indeed do I dwell expecting only fear?' means: 'For what reason do I dwell, expecting and desiring only fear?'

Yathābhūtaṃ yathābhūtassāti yena yena iriyāpathena bhūtassa bhavitassa sato vattamānassa samaṅgībhūtassa [V 1.0128] vā. Meti mama santike. Tathābhūtaṃ tathābhūto vāti tena teneva iriyāpathena bhūto bhavito santo vattamāno samaṅgībhūto vāti attho. So kho ahaṃ…pe… paṭivinemīti bodhisattassa kira caṅkamantassa tasmiṃ magasiṅgakhurasaddādibhede bhayabheravārammaṇe āgate neva mahāsatto tiṭṭhati, na [P 1.0121] nisīdati na sayati, atha kho caṅkamantova parivīmaṃsanto parivicinanto bhayabheravaṃ na passati, magasiṅgakhurasaddādimattameva cetaṃ hoti, so taṃ ñatvā idaṃ nāmetaṃ, na bhayabheravanti tato tiṭṭhati vā nisīdati vā sayati vā. Etamatthaṃ dassento “so kho aha”ntiādimāha. Esa nayo sabbapeyyālesu. Ito parañca iriyāpathapaṭipāṭiyā avatvā āsannapaṭipāṭiyā iriyāpathā vuttāti veditabbā, caṅkamantassa hi bhayabherave āgate na ṭhito na nisinno na nipanno ṭhitassāpi āgate na caṅkamīti evaṃ tassa āsannapaṭipāṭiyā vuttāti.

'In whatever state, for one who is in that state' means: by whatever posture, for one who has become, is existing, is present, or is endowed. 'Meti' means in my presence. 'In that very state, as one who is in that state' means: by that very posture, one has become, is becoming, is present, or is endowed. This is the meaning. 'That I… indeed… dispel' means: It is said that for the Bodhisatta, while he was walking, when an object of fear and terror arose—distinguished by sounds such as those of a deer's horns or hooves—the Great Being did not stand, did not sit, and did not lie down. Rather, while still walking, investigating and examining, he did not see the object of fear and terror. It was merely the sound of a deer's horns, hooves, and so forth. Having understood this, he thought, “This is just that sound by name; it is not an object of fear and terror.” Then he would stand, sit, or lie down. To show this meaning, he said, “That I…” and so on. This is the method in all elided passages. Furthermore, it should be understood that from this point on, the postures are not stated in their usual sequence, but are stated in the sequence of proximity. For when an object of fear and terror arose for him while walking, he did not stand, did not sit, did not lie down. And when it arose for him while standing, he did not walk. Thus, for him, it is spoken in terms of the sequence of proximity.

Bhayabheravasenāsanādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Description of Fear and Terror, Lodgings, and so forth, is concluded.

Asammohavihāravaṇṇanā

The Description of Abiding without Delusion

50. Evaṃ [M 1.0125] bhiṃsanakesupi ṭhānesu attano bhayabheravābhāvaṃ dassetvā idāni jhāyīnaṃ sammohaṭṭhānesu attano asammohavihāraṃ dassetuṃ santi kho pana, brāhmaṇātiādimāha.
