50. Having thus shown his own absence of fear and terror even in frightening places, now, in order to demonstrate his own abiding without delusion in situations where jhāna-practitioners become deluded, he said, “But there are, brahmin…” and so on.

Tattha santīti atthi saṃvijjanti upalabbhanti. Rattiṃyeva samānanti rattiṃyeva santaṃ, divāti sañjānantīti “divaso aya”nti sañjānanti. Divāyeva samānanti divasaṃyeva santaṃ. Rattīti sañjānantīti “ratti aya”nti sañjānanti. Kasmā panete evaṃsaññino hontīti. Vuṭṭhānakosallābhāvato vā sakuṇarutato vā. Kathaṃ? Idhekacco odātakasiṇalābhī divā parikammaṃ katvā divā samāpanno divāyeva vuṭṭhahāmīti manasikāraṃ uppādeti, no ca kho addhānaparicchede kusalo hoti. So divasaṃ atikkamitvā rattibhāge vuṭṭhāti. Odātakasiṇapharaṇavasena cassa visadaṃ hoti vibhūtaṃ suvibhūtaṃ. So, divā vuṭṭhahāmīti uppāditamanasikāratāya odātakasiṇapharaṇavisadavibhūtatāya ca rattiṃyeva samānaṃ divāti sañjānāti. Idha panekacco nīlakasiṇalābhī rattiṃ parikammaṃ katvā rattiṃ samāpanno rattiṃyeva vuṭṭhahāmīti [V 1.0129] manasikāraṃ uppādeti, no ca kho addhānaparicchede kusalo hoti. So rattiṃ atikkamitvā divasabhāge vuṭṭhāti. Nīlakasiṇapharaṇavasena cassa avisadaṃ hoti avibhūtaṃ. So rattiṃ vuṭṭhahāmīti uppāditamanasikāratāya nīlakasiṇapharaṇāvisadāvibhūtatāya ca divāyeva samānaṃ rattīti sañjānāti. Evaṃ tāva vuṭṭhānakosallābhāvato evaṃsaññino honti.

Therein, “santi” means they exist, they are found, they are obtained. “Rattiṃyeva samānaṃ” means it being only night. “divāti sañjānanti” means they perceive, “This is day.” “Divāyeva samānaṃ” means it being only day. “Rattīti sañjānanti” means they perceive, “This is night.” Why then do they have such perceptions? Due to a lack of skill in emerging from jhāna or due to the sound of birds calling. How so? Here, a certain person who has attained the white kasiṇa, having done the preliminary work during the day and entered absorption during the day, produces the thought, “I will emerge during the day,” but is not skilled in discerning the passage of time. He passes the day and emerges in the nighttime. And for him, by the pervasion of the white kasiṇa, it is clear, manifest, and very manifest. So, because of the thought produced, “I will emerge during the day,” and because of the clear and manifest pervasion of the white kasiṇa, though it is only night, he perceives it as day. Here, on the other hand, a certain person who has attained the blue kasiṇa, having done the preliminary work at night and entered absorption at night, produces the thought, “I will emerge at night,” but is not skilled in discerning the passage of time. He passes the night and emerges in the daytime. And for him, by the pervasion of the blue kasiṇa, it is not clear and not manifest. So, because of the thought produced, “I will emerge at night,” and because of the unclear and unmanifest pervasion of the blue kasiṇa, though it is only day, he perceives it as night. Thus, firstly, due to a lack of skill in emerging, they have such perceptions.

Sakuṇarutato pana idhekacco antosenāsane nisinno hoti. Atha divā ravanakasakuṇā kākādayo candālokena divāti [P 1.0122] maññamānā rattiṃ ravanti, aññehi vā kāraṇehi. So tesaṃ saddaṃ sutvā rattiṃyeva samānaṃ divāti sañjānāti. Idha panekacco pabbatantare gambhīrāya ghanavanappaṭicchannāya giriguhāya sattāhavaddalikāya vattamānāya antarahitasūriyāloke kāle nisinno hoti. Atha rattiṃ ravanakasakuṇā ulūkādayo majjhanhikasamayepi tattha tattha samandhakāre nilīnā rattisaññāya vā aññehi vā kāraṇehi ravanti. So tesaṃ saddaṃ sutvā divāyeva samānaṃ rattīti sañjānāti. Evaṃ sakuṇarutato evaṃsaññino hontīti. Idamahanti idaṃ ahaṃ evaṃ sañjānanaṃ[M 1.0126]. Sammohavihārasmiṃ vadāmīti sammohavihārapariyāpannaṃ antogadhaṃ, sammohavihārānaṃ aññataraṃ vadāmīti vuttaṃ hoti.

Furthermore, regarding the sound of birds calling: here, a certain person is seated inside a dwelling. Then birds that call during the day, such as crows, thinking it is day because of the moonlight, call out at night, or they call for other reasons. Hearing their sound, though it is only night, he perceives it as day. Here, on the other hand, a certain person is seated in a mountain cave—deep, covered by a dense forest canopy—at a time when the sunlight is blocked during a seven-day continuous rain. Then birds that call at night, such as owls, hidden in the deep darkness here and there even at midday, call out, either from the perception of it being night or for other reasons. Hearing their sound, though it is only day, he perceives it as night. Thus, due to the sound of birds calling, they have such perceptions. Regarding “idamahaṃ”: this is the word division “idaṃ ahaṃ,” meaning such a perception. “Sammohavihārasmiṃ vadāmi” means: I say it is included in and has entered into the dwelling in delusion; that is to say, I declare it to be one of the dwellings in delusion.

Ahaṃ kho pana brāhmaṇa…pe… sañjānāmīti pākaṭo bodhisattassa rattindivaparicchedo sattāhavaddalepi candimasūriyesu adissamānesupi jānātiyeva “ettakaṃ purebhattakālo gato, ettakaṃ pacchābhattakālo, ettakaṃ paṭhamayāmo, ettakaṃ majjhimayāmo, ettakaṃ pacchimayāmo”ti, tasmā evamāha. Anacchariyañcetaṃ yaṃ pūritapāramī bodhisatto evaṃ jānāti. Padesañāṇe ṭhitānaṃ sāvakānampi hi rattindivaparicchedo pākaṭo hoti.

“But I, brahmin… perceive” means: For the Bodhisatta, the distinction between night and day is clear. Even during a seven-day continuous rain, when the moon and sun are not visible, he still knows, “This much of the forenoon has passed, this much of the afternoon; this much of the first watch, this much of the middle watch, this much of the last watch has passed.” Therefore, he spoke thus. And it is no wonder that the Bodhisatta, who had fulfilled the perfections, knows this. For even for disciples who are established in partial knowledge, the distinction between night and day is clear.

Kalyāṇiyamahāvihāre kira godattatthero dvaṅgulakāle bhattaṃ gahetvā aṅgulakāle bhuñjati. Sūriye adissamānepi pātoyeva senāsanaṃ pavisitvā tāya velāya nikkhamati. Ekadivasaṃ ārāmikā “sve therassa nikkhamanakāle passāmā”ti bhattaṃ sampādetvā kālatthambhamūle nisīdiṃsu. Thero dvaṅgulakāleyeva nikkhamati. Tato pabhuti kira sūriye adissamānepi therassa nikkhamanasaññāya eva bheriṃ ākoṭenti.

It is said that at the Kalyāṇiya Mahāvihāra, the Elder Godatta would take his almsfood at the time of the two-finger shadow and eat at the time of the one-finger shadow. Even when the sun was not visible, he would enter his lodging early in the morning and emerge at that exact time. One day, the monastery attendants, thinking, “Tomorrow we will see the elder at the time of his emergence,” prepared the meal and sat at the base of the time-post. The elder emerged at the exact time of the two-finger shadow. From then on, it is said, even when the sun was not visible, they would beat the drum simply by the sign of the elder’s emergence.

Ajagaravihārepi [V 1.0130] kāḷadevatthero antovasse yāmagaṇḍikaṃ paharati, āciṇṇametaṃ therassa. Na ca yāmayantanāḷikaṃ payojeti, aññe bhikkhū payojenti. Atha nikkhante paṭhame yāme there muggaraṃ gahetvā ṭhitamatteyeva ekaṃ dve vāre paharanteyeva vā yāmayantaṃ patati, evaṃ tīsu yāmesu samaṇadhammaṃ katvā thero pātoyeva gāmaṃ pavisitvā piṇḍapātaṃ ādāya vihāraṃ āgantvā bhojanavelāya [P 1.0123] pattaṃ gahetvā divā vihāraṭṭhānaṃ gantvā samaṇadhammaṃ karoti. Bhikkhū kālatthambhaṃ disvā therassa adisvā āgamanatthāya pesenti. So bhikkhu theraṃ divā vihāraṭṭhānā nikkhamantameva vā antarāmagge vā passati. Evaṃ padesañāṇe ṭhitānaṃ sāvakānampi rattindivaparicchedo pākaṭo hoti, kimaṅgaṃ pana bodhisattānanti.

Also, at the Ajagaravihāra, the Elder Kāḷadeva would strike the watch-gong during the rains-retreat—this was the elder’s regular practice. He did not use a water-clock, but other monks did. Then, when the first watch had passed, as soon as the elder stood holding the mallet, or after striking it once or twice, the time-marker of the water-clock would fall. Thus, having performed the duties of an ascetic during the three watches, the elder would enter the village very early in the morning, collect alms-food, return to the monastery, take his bowl at mealtime, and go to his place for daytime abiding to perform his ascetic duties. The monks, seeing the time-post but not seeing the elder, would send someone to fetch him. That monk would see the elder either leaving his place for daytime abiding or along the path. In this way, even for disciples established in partial knowledge, the distinction between night and day becomes clear—what then to say of the Bodhisattas?

Yaṃ kho taṃ brāhmaṇa…pe… vadeyyāti ettha pana “yaṃ kho taṃ, brāhmaṇa, asammohadhammo satto loke uppanno…pe… sukhāya devamanussāna”nti vacanaṃ [M 1.0127] vadamāno koci sammā vadeyya, sammā vadamāno siyā, na vitathavādī assa. Mameva taṃ vacanaṃ vadamāno sammā vadeyya, sammā vadamāno siyā, na vitathavādī assāti evaṃ padasambandho veditabbo.

Regarding the text “Whatever, brahmin… he might say.” Here, if someone were to say, “Whatever, brahmin, a being whose nature is non-delusion has arisen in the world… for the happiness of gods and humans,” that person would be speaking rightly, would be one who speaks rightly, and would not be one who speaks falsely. Speaking that statement with reference to me alone, one would be speaking rightly, would be one who speaks rightly, and would not be one who speaks falsely. This is how the connection of the words should be understood.

Tattha asammohadhammoti asammohasabhāvo. Loketi manussaloke. Bahujanahitāyāti bahujanassa hitatthāya, paññāsampattiyā diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikahitūpadesakoti. Bahujanasukhāyāti bahujanassa sukhatthāya, cāgasampattiyā upakaraṇasukhassa dāyakoti. Lokānukampāyāti lokassa anukampatthāya, mettākaruṇāsampattiyā mātāpitaro viya lokassa rakkhitā gopayitāti. Atthāya hitāya sukhāya devamanussānanti idha devamanussaggahaṇena ca bhabbapuggalaveneyyasatteyeva gahetvā tesaṃ nibbānamaggaphalādhigamāya attano uppattiṃ dassetīti veditabbo. Atthāyāti hi vutte paramatthatthāya nibbānāyāti vuttaṃ hoti. Hitāyāti vutte taṃ sampāpakamaggatthāyāti vuttaṃ hoti, nibbānasampāpakamaggato hi uttari hitaṃ nāma natthi. Sukhāyāti vutte phalasamāpattisukhatthāyāti vuttaṃ hoti, tato uttari sukhābhāvato. Vuttañcetaṃ “ayaṃ samādhi paccuppannasukho ceva āyatiñca sukhavipāko”ti (dī. ni. 3.355; a. ni. 5.27; vibha. 804).

Herein, 'one whose nature is non-delusion' means having a nature of non-delusion. 'In the world' means in the human world. 'For the welfare of the many' means for the welfare of the many people; because of the accomplishment in wisdom, he is an instructor of welfare in the present life and in future lives. 'For the happiness of the many' means for the happiness of the many people; because of the accomplishment in generosity, he is a giver of the happiness of requisites. 'Out of compassion for the world' means for the sake of compassion for the world; because of the accomplishment in loving-kindness and compassion, he is a protector and guardian of the world, like parents. Regarding 'For the goal, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans,' here, by the inclusion of 'gods and humans,' it should be understood that taking only those beings to be trained who are capable individuals, he shows his own arising for their attainment of the path and fruit of Nibbāna. For when 'for the goal' is said, it is meant 'for the sake of the ultimate goal, for Nibbāna.' When 'for the welfare' is said, it is meant 'for the sake of the path that leads to it,' for indeed, there is no welfare higher than the path that leads to Nibbāna. When 'for the happiness' is said, it is meant 'for the sake of the happiness of the attainment of fruition,' because there is no happiness higher than that. And this was said: “This concentration is happiness in the present and has a happy result in the future” (Dī. Ni. 3.355; A. Ni. 5.27; Vibh. 804).

Asammohavihāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The exposition on abiding without confusion is concluded.

Pubbabhāgapaṭipadādivaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Preliminary Practice, etc.

51. Evaṃ [V 1.0131] bhagavā buddhaguṇapaṭilābhāvasānaṃ attano asammohavihāraṃ brāhmaṇassa dassetvā idāni yāya paṭipadāya taṃ koṭippattaṃ asammohavihāraṃ adhigato, taṃ pubbabhāgato pabhuti dassetuṃ āraddhaṃ kho pana me brāhmaṇātiādimāha.

51. Thus, the Blessed One, having shown the brahmin His own state of non-delusion which culminates in the attainment of the virtues of a Buddha, now, in order to show the practice by which He attained that state of non-delusion that has reached the pinnacle, beginning from the preliminary part, spoke the words beginning with, 'But, brahmin, my energy was aroused...'

Keci panāhu “imaṃ asammohavihāraṃ sutvā brāhmaṇassa cittamevaṃ uppannaṃ ‘kāya nu kho paṭipadāya imaṃ patto’ti, tassa cittamaññāya imāyāhaṃ paṭipadāya imaṃ uttamaṃ asammohavihāraṃ pattoti dassento evamāhā”ti.

Some, however, say: 'Having heard of this state of non-delusion, a thought arose in the brahmin’s mind thus: “By what practice, indeed, was this attained?” Knowing his thought, the Blessed One, showing, “I attained this supreme state of non-delusion by this practice,” spoke thus.'

Tattha [M 1.0128][P 1.0124] āraddhaṃ kho pana me, brāhmaṇa, vīriyaṃ ahosīti, brāhmaṇa, na mayā ayaṃ uttamo asammohavihāro kusītena muṭṭhassatinā sāraddhakāyena vikkhittacittena vā adhigato, apica kho tadadhigamāya āraddhaṃ kho pana me vīriyaṃ ahosi, bodhimaṇḍe nisinnena mayā caturaṅgavīriyaṃ āraddhaṃ ahosi, paggahitaṃ asithilappavattitanti vuttaṃ hoti. Āraddhattāyeva ca metaṃ asallīnaṃ ahosi.

Therein, the words 'But, brahmin, my energy was aroused' mean this: Brahmin, this supreme state of non-delusion was not attained by me through laziness, with lapsed mindfulness, with an agitated body, or with a distracted mind. But rather, for its attainment, my energy was indeed aroused. Seated at the Bodhi-seat, four-factored energy was aroused by me; it was exerted and unremittingly applied—this is the meaning. And precisely because it was aroused, it was not sluggish.

Upaṭṭhitā sati asammuṭṭhāti na kevalañca vīriyameva, satipi me ārammaṇābhimukhībhāvena upaṭṭhitā ahosi. Upaṭṭhitattāyeva ca asammuṭṭhā. Passaddho kāyoti kāyacittappassaddhisambhavena kāyopi me passaddho ahosi. Tattha yasmā nāmakāye passaddhe rūpakāyopi passaddhoyeva hoti, tasmā nāmakāyo rūpakāyoti avisesetvāva passaddho kāyoti vuttaṃ. Asāraddhoti so ca kho passaddhattāyeva asāraddho, vigatadarathoti vuttaṃ hoti. Samāhitaṃ cittaṃ ekagganti cittampi me sammā āhitaṃ suṭṭhu ṭhapitaṃ appitaṃ viya ahosi. Samāhitattā eva ca ekaggaṃ acalaṃ nipphandananti, ettāvatā jhānassa pubbabhāgapaṭipadā kathitā hoti.

As to 'Mindfulness was established and unconfused': Not only was there energy, but my mindfulness, too, was established by way of facing the object. And precisely because it was established, it was unconfused. As to 'The body was tranquil': Due to the arising of bodily and mental tranquility, my body, too, was tranquil. Therein, because when the mental body is tranquil the physical body is also tranquil, it was therefore said, 'the body was tranquil,' without making a distinction between the mental body and the physical body. As to 'unagitated': And that body, precisely because of being tranquil, was unagitated; this means it was free from distress. As to 'The mind was concentrated and one-pointed': My mind, too, was rightly placed, well established, as if it had reached absorption. And precisely because it was concentrated, it was one-pointed, unshaken, and still. By this much, the preliminary-part practice for jhāna has been explained.

Idāni imāya paṭipadāya adhigataṃ paṭhamajjhānaṃ ādiṃ katvā vijjāttayapariyosānaṃ visesaṃ dassento so kho ahantiādimāha. Tattha vivicceva kāmehi…pe… catutthajjhānaṃ upasampajja [V 1.0132] vihāsinti ettha tāva yaṃ vattabbaṃ siyā, taṃ sabbaṃ visuddhimagge pathavīkasiṇakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ. Kevalañhi tattha “upasampajja viharatī”ti āgataṃ, idha “vihāsi”nti, ayameva viseso. Kiṃ katvā pana bhagavā imāni jhānāni upasampajja vihāsīti, kammaṭṭhānaṃ bhāvetvā. Kataraṃ? Ānāpānassatikammaṭṭhānaṃ.

Now, wishing to show the special attainment which begins with the first jhāna attained by this practice and culminates in the three true knowledges, He spoke the words beginning with, 'Then I...' Therein, regarding the passage 'Quite secluded from sensual pleasures... I entered and abode in the fourth jhāna,' whatever should be said about this has all been said in the Visuddhimagga in the section on the earth kasiṇa. It is only that there it appears as 'enters and abides' (viharati), whereas here it appears as 'I abode' (vihāsiṃ); this alone is the difference. But having done what did the Blessed One enter and abide in these jhānas? Having developed a meditation subject. Which one? The meditation subject of mindfulness of breathing.

Imāni ca pana cattāri jhānāni kesañci cittekaggatatthāni honti, kesañci vipassanāpādakāni, kesañci abhiññāpādakāni, kesañci nirodhapādakāni, kesañci bhavokkamanatthāni. Tattha khīṇāsavānaṃ cittekaggatatthāni honti. Te hi samāpajjitvā [P 1.0125] ekaggacittā sukhaṃ divasaṃ viharissāmāti iccevaṃ kasiṇaparikammaṃ katvā aṭṭha samāpattiyo nibbattenti. Sekkhaputhujjanānaṃ samāpattito vuṭṭhāya samāhitena cittena vipassissāmāti nibbattentānaṃ vipassanāpādakāni honti. Ye pana aṭṭha samāpattiyo nibbattetvā abhiññāpādakajjhānaṃ samāpajjitvā samāpattito vuṭṭhāya “ekopi [M 1.0129] hutvā bahudhā hotī”ti (dī. ni. 1.238; paṭi. ma. 1.102) vuttanayā abhiññāyo patthentā nibbattenti, tesaṃ abhiññāpādakāni honti. Ye pana aṭṭha samāpattiyo nibbattetvā nirodhasamāpattiṃ samāpajjitvā sattāhaṃ acittā hutvā diṭṭheva dhamme nirodhaṃ nibbānaṃ patvā sukhaṃ viharissāmāti nibbattenti, tesaṃ nirodhapādakāni honti. Ye pana aṭṭha samāpattiyo nibbattetvā aparihīnajjhānā brahmaloke uppajjissāmāti nibbattenti, tesaṃ bhavokkamanatthāni honti.

Furthermore, these four jhānas are for some for the purpose of concentration of mind; for some, they are the basis for insight; for some, they are the basis for the direct knowledges; for some, they are the basis for the attainment of cessation; and for some, they are for the purpose of passing on to a new existence. Therein, for the destroyers of the cankers, they are for the purpose of concentration of mind. For they, having entered into jhāna and with a concentrated mind, thinking, 'We will abide happily for the day,' perform the preliminary work for the kasiṇa and produce the eight attainments. For learners and worldlings who produce them thinking, 'Having emerged from the attainment, with a concentrated mind, we will practice insight,' they are the basis for insight. For those who, having produced the eight attainments, enter the jhāna that is the basis for the direct knowledges, emerge from the attainment, and produce them while aspiring for the direct knowledges in the manner stated, 'Having been one, he becomes many,' for them, they are the basis for the direct knowledges. For those who, having produced the eight attainments, thinking, 'Having entered the attainment of cessation and having been without a mind for seven days, having reached cessation—Nibbāna—in this very life, we will abide happily,' produce them, for them, they are the basis for the attainment of cessation. For those who, having produced the eight attainments, produce them thinking, 'Not having fallen away from jhāna, we will be reborn in the Brahma world,' for them, they are for the purpose of passing on to a new existence.

Bhagavatā panidaṃ catutthajjhānaṃ bodhirukkhamūle nibbattitaṃ, taṃ tassa vipassanāpādakañceva ahosi abhiññāpādakañca sabbakiccasādhakañca, sabbalokiyalokuttaraguṇadāyakanti veditabbaṃ.

But by the Blessed One, this fourth jhāna was produced at the root of the Bodhi tree. For Him, it was both the basis for insight and the basis for the direct knowledges, and the accomplisher of all duties; it should be known as the giver of all worldly and supramundane qualities.

Pubbabhāgapaṭipadādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Preliminary-Part Practice, etc., is finished.

Pubbenivāsakathāvaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Discourse of Previous Abodes

52. Yesañca [V 1.0133] guṇānaṃ dāyakaṃ ahosi, tesaṃ ekadesaṃ dassento so evaṃ samāhite cittetiādimāha. Tattha dvinnaṃ vijjānaṃ anupadavaṇṇanā ceva bhāvanānayo ca visuddhimagge vitthārito. Kevalañhi tattha “so evaṃ samāhite citte…pe… abhininnāmetī”ti vuttaṃ, idha “abhininnāmesi”nti. Ayaṃ kho me brāhmaṇāti ayañca appanāvāro tattha anāgatoti ayameva viseso. Tattha soti so ahaṃ. Abhininnāmesinti abhinīhariṃ. Abhininnāmesinti ca vacanato soti ettha so ahanti evamattho veditabbo.

52. And of which virtues it was the giver, wishing to show a portion of them, He spoke the words beginning with 'so evaṃ samāhite citte...'. Therein, the sequential word-explanation of the two knowledges and the method of development are elaborated in the Visuddhimagga. For only there it is said, 'so evaṃ samāhite citte...pe... abhininnāmeti' (with his mind thus concentrated... he directs it), whereas here it is said, 'abhininnāmesiṃ' (I directed it). And this section on absorption, 'Ayaṃ kho me brāhmaṇa...', does not appear there; this alone is the difference. Therein, 'so' (he) is 'so ahaṃ' (that I). 'Abhininnāmesiṃ' (I directed it) means 'abhinīhariṃ' (I brought it to bear). And because it is said 'abhininnāmesiṃ', the meaning of 'so' here should be understood as 'so ahaṃ' (that I).

Yasmā cidaṃ bhagavato vasena pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇaṃ āgataṃ, tasmā “so tato cuto idhūpapanno”ti ettha evaṃ yojanā veditabbā. Ettha hi so tato cutoti paṭinivattantassa paccavekkhaṇaṃ. Tasmā idhūpapannoti imissā idhūpapattiyā anantaraṃ. Amutra udapādinti tusitabhavanaṃ sandhāyāhāti veditabbo. Tatrāpāsiṃ evaṃnāmoti tatrāpi tusitabhavane setaketu nāma devaputto ahosiṃ. Evaṃgottoti tāhi devatāhi saddhiṃ ekagotto. Evaṃvaṇṇoti suvaṇṇavaṇṇo. Evamāhāroti dibbasudhāhāro. Evaṃsukhadukkhappaṭisaṃvedīti evaṃ dibbasukhapaṭisaṃvedī. Dukkhaṃ pana saṅkhāradukkhamattameva[P 1.0126]. Evamāyupariyantoti evaṃ sattapaññāsavassakoṭisaṭṭhivassasatasahassāyupariyanto. So [M 1.0130] tato cutoti so ahaṃ tato tusitabhavanato cuto. Idhūpapannoti idha mahāmāyāya deviyā kucchimhi nibbatto.

And because this knowledge of recollecting previous abodes came by way of the Blessed One, the construction here in the phrase 'He, having passed away from there, reappeared here' should be understood thus. Herein, 'He, having passed away from there' is the reviewing of the one recollecting in reverse order. Therefore, 'reappeared here' is immediately after this rebirth here. It should be understood that 'I arose there' is said in reference to the Tusita heaven. 'There I was of such a name' means: in that Tusita heaven, I was a devaputta named Setaketu. 'Of such a clan' means: of the same clan as those devas. 'Of such a complexion' means: of a golden complexion. 'Having such food' means: having divine ambrosial food. 'Experiencing such pleasure and pain' means: thus experiencing divine pleasure. Pain, however, was merely the suffering of formations. 'Having such a lifespan' means: thus having a lifespan of fifty-seven koṭis and sixty hundred-thousands of years. 'He, having passed away from there' means: I, having passed away from that Tusita heaven. 'Reappeared here' means: I was born here in the womb of Queen Mahāmāyā.

Ayaṃ kho me brāhmaṇātiādīsu meti mayā. Vijjāti viditakaraṇaṭṭhena vijjā. Kiṃ viditaṃ karoti? Pubbenivāsaṃ. Avijjāti tasseva pubbenivāsassa aviditakaraṇaṭṭhena tappaṭicchādako moho vuccati. Tamoti sveva moho paṭicchādakaṭṭhena “tamo”ti vuccati. Ālokoti sāyeva vijjā obhāsakaraṇaṭṭhena “āloko”ti vuccati. Ettha ca vijjā adhigatāti ayaṃ attho, sesaṃ pasaṃsāvacanaṃ. Yojanā panettha ayaṃ kho me vijjā adhigatā, tassa me adhigatavijjassa avijjā vihatā, vinaṭṭhāti attho. Kasmā? Yasmā vijjā uppannā. Esa nayo itarasmimpi padadvaye.

In 'Ayaṃ kho me brāhmaṇa...' and so on, 'me' means 'by me'. 'Vijjā' (knowledge) is so called in the sense of making known. What does it make known? Previous abodes. 'Avijjā' (ignorance) is said to be the delusion that conceals that very previous abode, in the sense of making it unknown. 'Tamo' (darkness) is that very delusion, so called in the sense of concealing. 'Āloko' (light) is that very knowledge, so called in the sense of illuminating. And herein, 'knowledge is attained' is the meaning; the rest is a word of praise. The construction here is: 'This knowledge was attained by me. For me, who has attained knowledge, ignorance is struck down, destroyed.' Why? Because knowledge has arisen. This same method should be seen in the other pair of terms as well.

Yathā [V 1.0134] tanti ettha yathāti opamme. Tanti nipāto. Satiyā avippavāsena appamattassa. Vīriyātāpena ātāpino. Kāye ca jīvite ca anapekkhatāya pahitattassa, pesitattassāti attho. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti “yathā appamattassa ātāpino pahitattassa viharato avijjā vihaññeyya, vijjā uppajjeyya. Tamo vihaññeyya, āloko uppajjeyya. Evameva mama avijjā vihatā, vijjā uppannā. Tamo vihato, āloko uppanno. Etassa me padhānānuyogassa anurūpameva phalaṃ laddha”nti.

Herein, in 'yathā taṃ', 'yathā' is a particle in the sense of a simile; 'taṃ' is just a particle. 'Appamattassa' (of one who is diligent) means: through the non-absence of mindfulness. 'Ātāpino' (of one who is ardent) means: through the heat of energy. 'Pahitattassa' (of one who is resolute) means: through non-concern for body and life; the meaning is 'of one with a dispatched self'. This is what is meant: 'Just as for one dwelling diligent, ardent, and resolute, ignorance would be struck down and knowledge would arise; darkness would be struck down and light would arise, in this very way, for me, ignorance has been struck down and knowledge has arisen; darkness has been struck down and light has arisen. For me, engaged in this striving, a befitting fruit has been obtained.'

Pubbenivāsakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Discourse of Previous Abodes is concluded.

Dibbacakkhuñāṇakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse on the Knowledge of the Divine Eye

53. Cutūpapātakathāyaṃ yasmā idha bhagavato vasena pāḷi āgatā, tasmā “passāmi pajānāmī”ti vuttaṃ, ayaṃ viseso. Sesaṃ visuddhimagge vuttasadisameva.

53. In the discourse on passing away and reappearing, since the Pāḷi text here has come by way of the Blessed One, therefore it is said, 'I see, I know'—this is the distinction. The rest is just as stated in the Visuddhimagga.

Ettha pana vijjāti dibbacakkhuñāṇavijjā. Avijjāti sattānaṃ cutipaṭisandhipaṭicchādikā avijjā. Sesaṃ vuttanayamevāti. Yasmā ca pūritapāramīnaṃ mahāsattānaṃ parikammakiccaṃ nāma natthi. Te hi citte abhininnāmitamatteyeva anekavihitaṃ [M 1.0131] pubbenivāsaṃ anussaranti, dibbena cakkhunā satte passanti. Tasmā yo tattha parikammaṃ ādiṃ katvā bhāvanānayo vutto, na tena idha atthoti.

Here, 'knowledge' means the knowledge of the divine eye. 'Ignorance' means the ignorance that obscures the passing away and rebirth of beings. The rest is just as explained previously. Furthermore, for great beings who have fulfilled the perfections, there is no such thing as preliminary work. For they, merely by inclining their minds, recall manifold past lives and see beings with the divine eye. Therefore, the method of development, beginning with preliminary work, that was mentioned there has no purpose here.

Dibbacakkhuñāṇakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Discourse on the Knowledge of the Divine Eye is concluded.

Āsavakkhayañāṇakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse on the Knowledge of the Destruction of the Taints

54. Tatiyavijjāya so evaṃ samāhite citteti vipassanāpādakaṃ catutthajjhānacittaṃ veditabbaṃ. Āsavānaṃ khayañāṇāyāti [P 1.0127] arahattamaggañāṇatthāya. Arahattamaggo hi āsavavināsanato āsavānaṃ khayoti vuccati, tatra cetaṃ ñāṇaṃ, tappariyāpannattāti. Cittaṃ abhininnāmesinti [V 1.0135] vipassanācittaṃ abhinīhariṃ. So idaṃ dukkhanti evamādīsu “ettakaṃ dukkhaṃ, na ito bhiyyo”ti sabbampi dukkhasaccaṃ sarasalakkhaṇapaṭivedhena yathābhūtaṃ abbhaññāsiṃ jāniṃ paṭivijjhiṃ. Tassa ca dukkhassa nibbattikaṃ taṇhaṃ ayaṃ dukkhasamudayoti. Tadubhayampi yaṃ ṭhānaṃ patvā nirujjhati, taṃ tesaṃ appavattiṃ nibbānaṃ ayaṃ dukkhanirodhoti. Tassa sampāpakaṃ ariyamaggaṃ ayaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadāti sarasalakkhaṇapaṭivedhena yathābhūtaṃ abbhaññāsiṃ jāniṃ paṭivijjhinti evamattho veditabbo.

54. Regarding the third knowledge, by 'when the mind was thus concentrated,' the fourth jhāna consciousness, which is the basis for insight, should be understood. 'For the knowledge of the destruction of the taints' means for the sake of the knowledge of the path of Arahantship. Indeed, the path of Arahantship is called 'the destruction of the taints' because it destroys the taints, and this knowledge is meant by that, because it is included therein. 'I inclined my mind' means I directed the insight-mind. Regarding 'This is suffering,' and so on, I directly knew the entire truth of suffering as it actually is by penetrating its intrinsic characteristic, thinking: 'This much is suffering; there is no more than this.' And I directly knew as it actually is the craving that produces that suffering, thinking: 'This is the origin of suffering.' And I directly knew as it actually is Nibbāna—that state which is the non-occurrence of those two, the place they reach and cease—thinking: 'This is the cessation of suffering.' And I directly knew as it actually is, by penetrating its intrinsic characteristic, the Noble Path that leads to its attainment, thinking: 'This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering.' In this way the meaning should be understood.

Evaṃ sarūpato saccāni dassetvā idāni kilesavasena pariyāyato dassento ime āsavātiādimāha. Tassa me evaṃ jānato evaṃ passatoti tassa mayhaṃ evaṃ jānantassa evaṃ passantassa. Saha vipassanāya koṭippattaṃ maggaṃ katheti. Kāmāsavāti kāmāsavato. Vimuccitthāti iminā phalakkhaṇaṃ dasseti, maggakkhaṇe hi cittaṃ vimuccati, phalakkhaṇe vimuttaṃ hoti. Vimuttasmiṃ vimuttamiti ñāṇanti iminā paccavekkhaṇañāṇaṃ dasseti. Khīṇā jātītiādīhi tassa bhūmiṃ, tena hi ñāṇena bhagavā paccavekkhanto “khīṇā jātī”tiādīni abbhaññāsi. Katamā pana bhagavato jāti khīṇā, kathañca naṃ abbhaññāsīti? Na tāvassa atītā jāti khīṇā, pubbeva khīṇattā, na anāgatā, anāgate vāyāmābhāvato, na paccuppannā, vijjamānattā. Yā pana maggassa abhāvitattā uppajjeyya ekacatupañcavokārabhavesu ekacatupañcakkhandhabhedā jāti, sā maggassa bhāvitattā anuppādadhammataṃ āpajjanena khīṇā, taṃ so maggabhāvanāya pahīnakilese paccavekkhitvā “kilesābhāve vijjamānampi kammaṃ āyatiṃ appaṭisandhikaṃ hotī”ti jānanto abbhaññāsi.

Having thus shown the truths in their essential nature, now, showing them indirectly by way of the defilements, he said the words beginning with, 'These are the taints.' 'Of me, thus knowing, thus seeing' means 'of me who knows thus and sees thus.' He speaks of the path that, together with insight, has reached its culmination. The phrase `kāmāsavā` is an ablative, meaning `kāmāsavato` (from the taint of sensual desire). By the words 'my mind was liberated,' he shows the moment of fruition. For at the moment of the path, the mind is becoming free; at the moment of fruition, it is freed. By the phrase 'the knowledge, "It is liberated in the liberated,"' he shows the reviewing knowledge. By the phrases beginning with 'Birth is destroyed,' he shows its basis. For it was with that knowledge that the Blessed One, while reviewing, directly knew 'Birth is destroyed,' and so on. But which birth of the Blessed One was destroyed, and how did he directly know it? His past birth was not destroyed, for it was already destroyed before. The future one was not destroyed, because there is no effort concerning the future. The present one was not destroyed, because it is currently existing. But that birth—differentiated as having one, four, or five aggregates in the one-, four-, or five-constituent planes of existence—which would have arisen because the path had not been developed, that birth is destroyed by its attainment of the state of non-arising due to the path having been developed. He directly knew this, having reviewed the defilements abandoned through the development of the path and knowing, 'In the absence of defilements, even existing karma does not lead to future rebirth.'

Vusitanti [M 1.0132] vutthaṃ parivutthaṃ, kataṃ caritaṃ niṭṭhitanti attho. Brahmacariyanti maggabrahmacariyaṃ, puthujjanakalyāṇakena hi saddhiṃ sattasekkhā brahmacariyavāsaṃ vasanti nāma, khīṇāsavo vutthavāso. Tasmā bhagavā attano brahmacariyavāsaṃ paccavekkhanto “vusitaṃ brahmacariya”nti abbhaññāsi. Kataṃ karaṇīyanti catūsu [P 1.0128] saccesu catūhi maggehi pariññāpahānasacchikiriyābhāvanāvasena soḷasavidhampi kiccaṃ niṭṭhāpitanti attho. Puthujjanakalyāṇakādayo hi taṃ kiccaṃ karonti, khīṇāsavo katakaraṇīyo. Tasmā bhagavā attano karaṇīyaṃ paccavekkhanto “kataṃ karaṇīya”nti abbhaññāsi.

'Lived' means lived, dwelt, done, practiced, completed. 'The holy life' means the holy life of the path. For the seven learners, together with the virtuous worldling, are said to be living the holy life, whereas the one whose taints are destroyed has lived the life. Therefore the Blessed One, reviewing his own living of the holy life, directly knew: 'The holy life has been lived.' 'What had to be done is done' means that the sixteenfold task regarding the four truths—by way of full understanding, abandoning, realizing, and developing through the four paths—has been completed. For the virtuous worldling and others are doing that task, whereas the one whose taints are destroyed has done what was to be done. Therefore the Blessed One, reviewing what he had to do, directly knew: 'What had to be done is done.'

Nāparaṃ [V 1.0136] itthattāyāti idāni puna itthabhāvāya evaṃsoḷasakiccabhāvāya, kilesakkhayāya vā maggabhāvanākiccaṃ me natthīti abbhaññāsi. Atha vā itthattāyāti itthabhāvato imasmā evaṃpakārā idāni vattamānakkhandhasantānā aparaṃ khandhasantānaṃ mayhaṃ natthi. Ime pana pañcakkhandhā pariññātā tiṭṭhanti chinnamūlakā rukkhā viya. Te carimakaviññāṇanirodhena anupādāno viya jātavedo nibbāyissantīti abbhaññāsi.

'There is no more for this state' means: 'Now, for me there is no further task of developing the path for this state—that is, for the state of the sixteenfold task, or for the destruction of defilements'—thus he directly knew. Or, 'for this state' means: 'From this state of being, from this present continuum of aggregates of such a kind, there is no other continuum of aggregates for me. These five aggregates, however, having been fully understood, remain like trees with their roots cut off. With the cessation of the final consciousness, they will be extinguished like a fire without fuel'—thus he directly knew.

Idāni evaṃ paccavekkhaṇañāṇapariggahitaṃ āsavānaṃ khayañāṇādhigamaṃ brāhmaṇassa dassento, ayaṃ kho me brāhmaṇātiādimāha. Tattha vijjāti arahattamaggañāṇavijjā. Avijjāti catusaccapaṭicchādikā avijjā. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva. Ettāvatā ca pubbenivāsañāṇena atītaṃsañāṇaṃ, dibbacakkhunā paccuppannānāgataṃsañāṇaṃ, āsavakkhayena sakalalokiyalokuttaraguṇanti evaṃ tīhi vijjāhi sabbepi sabbaññuguṇe saṅgahetvā pakāsento attano asammohavihāraṃ brāhmaṇassa dassesi.

Now, showing the brahmin the attainment of the knowledge of the destruction of the taints, which is comprehended by the reviewing knowledge, he said the words beginning with, 'This, O brahmin...'. Herein, 'knowledge' is the knowledge of the path of Arahantship. 'Ignorance' is the ignorance that obscures the four truths. The rest is just as previously explained. And thus, by means of the three knowledges—with the knowledge of past lives, comprehending the past; with the divine eye, the present and the future; and with the destruction of the taints, all worldly and supramundane qualities—having gathered and shown all the qualities of an omniscient one, he revealed to the brahmin his own state of non-delusion.

Āsavakkhayañāṇakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Discourse on the Knowledge of the Destruction of the Taints is concluded.

Araññavāsakāraṇavaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Reasons for Dwelling in the Forest

55. Evaṃ vutte kira brāhmaṇo cintesi – “samaṇo gotamo sabbaññutaṃ paṭijānāti, ajjāpi ca araññavāsaṃ na vijahati, atthi nu khvassa aññampi kiñci karaṇīya”nti. Athassa bhagavā ajjhāsayaṃ viditvā iminā ajjhāsayānusandhinā, siyā kho pana tetiādimāha. Tattha siyā kho pana te, brāhmaṇa, evamassāti, brāhmaṇa, kadāci tuyhaṃ evaṃ bhaveyya. Na kho panetaṃ brāhmaṇa evaṃ daṭṭhabbanti etaṃ kho pana, brāhmaṇa, tayā mayhaṃ pantasenāsanapaṭisevanaṃ [M 1.0133] avītarāgāditāyāti evaṃ na daṭṭhabbaṃ. Evaṃ pantasenāsanapaṭisevane akāraṇaṃ paṭikkhipitvā kāraṇaṃ dassento dve kho ahantiādimāha. Tattha atthoyeva atthavaso. Tasmā dve kho ahaṃ, brāhmaṇa, atthavaseti ahaṃ kho, brāhmaṇa, dve atthe dve kāraṇāni sampassamānoti vuttaṃ hoti. Attano ca diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāranti ettha diṭṭhadhammo nāma ayaṃ paccakkho attabhāvo. Sukhavihāro nāma catunnampi iriyāpathavihārānaṃ phāsutā, ekakassa hi [V 1.0137][P 1.0129] araññe antamaso uccārapassāvakiccaṃ upādāya sabbeva iriyāpathā phāsukā honti, tasmā diṭṭhadhammassa sukhavihāranti ayamattho veditabbo. Pacchimañca janataṃ anukampamānoti kathaṃ araññavāsena pacchimā janatā anukampitā hoti? Saddhāpabbajitā hi kulaputtā bhagavato araññavāsaṃ disvā bhagavāpi nāma araññasenāsanāni na muñcati, yassa nevatthi pariññātabbaṃ na pahātabbaṃ na bhāvetabbaṃ na sacchikātabbaṃ, kimaṅgaṃ pana mayanti cintetvā tattha vasitabbameva maññissanti. Evaṃ khippameva dukkhassantakarā bhavissanti. Evaṃ pacchimā janatā anukampitā hoti. Etamatthaṃ dassento āha “pacchimañca janataṃ anukampamāno”ti.

55. When this was said, it is said, the brahmin thought: "The ascetic Gotama claims omniscience, yet even today he does not abandon forest dwelling. Could there be some other duty for him?" Then the Blessed One, knowing his inclination, spoke in connection with this line of thought, saying: "It might be, brahmin, that you think thus." Herein, "It might be, brahmin, that you think thus" means: "Brahmin, sometimes such a thought might occur to you." "But this, brahmin, should not be seen in that way" means: "This frequenting of remote dwellings by me, brahmin, should not be seen by you as being due to not being free from lust, and so on." Having thus rejected the non-reason for frequenting remote dwellings, and in order to show the reason, he said: "There are two reasons, brahmin..." and so on. Herein, `atthavasa` is `attha` itself. Therefore, "For two `atthavasa`, brahmin..." means: "I, brahmin, seeing two purposes, two reasons..." so it is said. In the phrase "And for a pleasant dwelling in this very life," "this very life" refers to this directly perceived existence. "A pleasant dwelling" means the comfort of dwelling in all four postures. For one dwelling alone in the forest, all postures, even down to the act of urination and defecation, are comfortable. Therefore, the meaning should be understood as "a pleasant dwelling for this very life." Regarding "And out of compassion for future generations": how is the future generation shown compassion through forest dwelling? When sons of good families who have gone forth in faith see the Blessed One's forest dwelling, they will think: "Even the Blessed One, for whom there is nothing to be fully understood, nothing to be abandoned, nothing to be developed, and nothing to be realized, does not abandon forest dwellings. What then of us?" Thinking thus, they will consider that it is indeed to be dwelt in there. In this way, they will quickly make an end of suffering. Thus, the future generation is shown compassion. To show this meaning, he said: "And out of compassion for future generations."

Araññavāsakāraṇavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Reasons for Dwelling in the Forest is concluded.

Desanānumodanāvaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Approval of the Teaching

56. Taṃ sutvā attamano brāhmaṇo anukampitarūpātiādimāha. Tattha anukampitarūpāti anukampitajātikā anukampitasabhāvā. Janatāti janasamūho. Yathā taṃ arahatā sammāsambuddhenāti yathā arahaṃ sammāsambuddho anukampeyya, tatheva anukampitarūpāti.

56. Hearing this, the delighted brahmin said, beginning with 'anukampitarūpā.' Herein, 'anukampitarūpā' means of a compassionate nature, of a compassionate disposition. 'Janatā' means a multitude of people. 'Yathā taṃ arahatā sammāsambuddhena' means: just as the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, would show compassion, in that very way are they of a compassionate nature.

Evañca pana vatvā puna taṃ bhagavato dhammadesanaṃ abbhanumodamāno bhagavantaṃ etadavoca abhikkantaṃ, bho gotama, abhikkantaṃ, bho gotamāti. Tatthāyaṃ abhikkantasaddo khayasundarābhirūpaabbhanumodanesu dissati. “Abhikkantā, bhante, ratti, nikkhanto paṭhamo yāmo, ciranisinno bhikkhusaṅgho”tiādīsu (cūḷava. 383; a. ni. 8.20) hi khaye dissati. “Ayaṃ imesaṃ catunnaṃ puggalānaṃ abhikkantataro ca paṇītataro cā”tiādīsu (a. ni. 4.100) sundare.

Having said this, and further approving of the Blessed One's teaching, he said this to the Blessed One: "Excellent, Venerable Gotama, excellent, Venerable Gotama." Herein, this word 'abhikkanta' is seen in the senses of passing, beauty, handsomeness, and approval. For instance, in passages such as, "The night is advanced, Venerable Sir, the first watch has passed, the Saṅgha of monks has sat for a long time," it is seen in the sense of passing. In passages such as, "This one is more excellent and more sublime among these four persons," it is seen in the sense of beauty.

“Ko [M 1.0134] me vandati pādāni, iddhiyā yasasā jalaṃ;

Abhikkantena vaṇṇena, sabbā obhāsayaṃ disā”ti. –

"Who is it that venerates my feet, blazing with power and glory, with surpassing beauty, illuminating all directions?"

Ādīsu (vi. va. 857) abhirūpe. “Abhikkantaṃ, bhante”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 1.250; pārā. 15) abbhanumodane[V 1.0138]. Idhāpi abbhanumodaneyeva. Yasmā ca abbhanumodane, tasmā sādhu sādhu bho, gotamāti vuttaṃ hotīti veditabbaṃ.

In such passages, it is in the sense of handsomeness. In passages such as 'Excellent, venerable sir,' it is in the sense of approval. Here too, it is in the sense of approval. And because it is in the sense of approval, it should be understood to mean, 'Good, good, Venerable Gotama.'

“Bhaye kodhe pasaṃsāyaṃ, turite kotūhalacchare;

Hāse soke pasāde ca, kare āmeḍitaṃ budho”ti. –

"In fear, anger, praise, haste, excitement, astonishment, mirth, sorrow, and confidence, a wise person makes a repetition."

Iminā ca lakkhaṇena idha pasādavasena pasaṃsāvasena cāyaṃ dvikkhattuṃ vuttoti veditabbo. Atha [P 1.0130] vā abhikkantanti abhikantaṃ. Atiiṭṭhaṃ atimanāpaṃ, atisundaranti vuttaṃ hoti.

And by this rule, it should be understood that here it was said twice out of confidence and praise. Alternatively, 'abhikkantaṃ' means 'abhikantaṃ'; that is to say, exceedingly desired, exceedingly pleasing, exceedingly beautiful.

Tattha ekena abhikkantasaddena desanaṃ thometi, ekena attano pasādaṃ. Ayañhettha adhippāyo – abhikkantaṃ, bho gotama, yadidaṃ bhoto gotamassa dhammadesanā, abhikkantaṃ yadidaṃ bhoto gotamassa dhammadesanaṃ āgamma mama pasādoti. Bhagavatoyeva vā vacanaṃ dve dve atthe sandhāya thometi – bhoto gotamassa vacanaṃ abhikkantaṃ dosanāsanato, abhikkantaṃ guṇādhigamanato, tathā saddhājananato, paññājananato, sātthato, sabyañjanato, uttānapadato, gambhīratthato, kaṇṇasukhato, hadayaṅgamato, anattukkaṃsanato, aparavambhanato, karuṇāsītalato, paññāvadātato, āpātharamaṇīyato, vimaddakkhamato, suyyamānasukhato, vīmaṃsīyamānahitatoti evamādīhi yojetabbaṃ.

Herein, with one word 'abhikkanta', he praises the teaching, and with the other, his own confidence. This is the intended meaning: "Excellent, Venerable Gotama, is this teaching of the Venerable Gotama; excellent is the confidence that has arisen in me based on the Venerable Gotama's teaching." Alternatively, he praises the Blessed One's word by referring to pairs of meanings: the Venerable Gotama's word is excellent for its removal of faults, excellent for its attainment of virtues; likewise, for generating faith, for generating wisdom; for being meaningful, for being well-phrased; for having clear terms, for having profound meaning; for being pleasant to the ear, for entering the heart; for not exalting oneself, for not disparaging others; for being cool with compassion, for being purified by wisdom; for being delightful on first hearing, for enduring scrutiny; for being pleasant while being heard, for being beneficial when investigated—it should be connected in these and other similar ways.

Tato parampi catūhi upamāhi desanaṃyeva thometi. Tattha nikkujjitanti adhomukhaṭhapitaṃ, heṭṭhāmukhajātaṃ vā. Ukkujjeyyāti upari mukhaṃ kareyya. Paṭicchannanti tiṇapaṇṇādicchāditaṃ. Vivareyyāti ugghāṭeyya. Mūḷhassāti disāmūḷhassa. Maggaṃ ācikkheyyāti hatthe gahetvā “esa maggo”ti vadeyya. Andhakāreti kāḷapakkhacātuddasīaḍḍharattaghanavanasaṇḍameghapaṭalehi caturaṅge tame, ayaṃ tāva anuttānapadattho.

After that, he praises the teaching with four similes. Herein, 'nikkujjitaṃ' means placed face-down, or naturally facing downwards. 'Ukkujjeyya' means to turn it face-up. 'Paṭicchannaṃ' means concealed by grass, leaves, and so on. 'Vivareyya' means to uncover. 'Mūḷhassa' means for one who is lost as to the directions. 'Maggaṃ ācikkheyya' means to take one by the hand and say, "This is the path." 'Andhakāre' refers to the fourfold darkness of the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, midnight, a dense forest thicket, and a layer of clouds. This, for a start, is the meaning of the non-obvious terms.

Ayaṃ pana adhippāyayojanā – yathā koci nikkujjitaṃ ukkujjeyya, evaṃ saddhammavimukhaṃ asaddhamme patitaṃ maṃ asaddhammā vuṭṭhāpentena, yathā paṭicchannaṃ vivareyya[M 1.0135]. Evaṃ kassapassa bhagavato sāsanantaradhānato pabhuti micchādiṭṭhigahanapaṭicchannaṃ sāsanaṃ vivarantena, yathā [V 1.0139] mūḷhassa maggaṃ ācikkheyya, evaṃ kummaggamicchāmaggappaṭipannassa me saggamokkhamaggaṃ ācikkhantena, yathā andhakāre telapajjotaṃ dhāreyya, evaṃ mohandhakāre nimuggassa me buddhādiratanarūpāni apassato tappaṭicchādakamohandhakāraviddhaṃsakadesanāpajjotadhāraṇena mayhaṃ bhotā gotamena etehi pariyāyehi pakāsitattā anekapariyāyena dhammo pakāsitoti.

This is the explanation of the intended meaning: Just as one might set upright what was overturned, so the venerable Gotama has raised me—who had turned away from the true Dhamma and fallen into the false Dhamma—from that false Dhamma. Just as one might uncover what is covered, so he has revealed the Dispensation, which had been covered by the thicket of wrong views since the disappearance of the Dispensation of the Blessed One Kassapa. Just as one might point out the way to one who is lost, so he has shown me the path to heaven and liberation, who had entered upon the wrong path, the false path. Just as one might hold up an oil lamp in the darkness, so he has held up the lamp of the teaching that destroys the darkness of delusion which conceals the forms of the Buddha and the other jewels for me, who was plunged in the darkness of delusion and unable to see them. Because the Dhamma has been declared to me by the venerable Gotama in these ways, the Dhamma has been declared in many ways.

Desanānumodanāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Description of Rejoicing in the Teaching is concluded.

Pasannākāravaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Expression of Faith

Evaṃ desanaṃ thometvā imāya desanāya ratanattayapasannacitto pasannākāraṃ karonto esāhantiādimāha. Tattha esāhanti eso ahaṃ. Bhavantaṃ gotamaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmīti bhavaṃ me gotamo saraṇaṃ parāyaṇaṃ, aghassa tātā[P 1.0131], hitassa ca vidhātāti iminā adhippāyena bhavantaṃ gotamaṃ gacchāmi, bhajāmi, sevāmi, payirupāsāmi, evaṃ vā jānāmi, bujjhāmīti. Yesañhi dhātūnaṃ gatiattho, buddhipi tesaṃ attho. Tasmā gacchāmīti imassa jānāmi, bujjhāmīti ayamattho vutto. Dhammañca bhikkhusaṅghañcāti ettha pana adhigatamagge sacchikatanirodhe yathānusiṭṭhaṃ paṭipajjamāne ca apāyesu apatamāne dhāretīti dhammo, so atthato ariyamaggo ceva nibbānañca. Vuttañhetaṃ – “yāvatā, bhikkhave, dhammā saṅkhatā, ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo tesaṃ aggamakkhāyatī”ti (a. ni. 4.34) vitthāro. Na kevalañca ariyamaggo ceva nibbānañca, apica kho ariyaphalehi saddhiṃ pariyattidhammopi. Vuttañhetaṃ chattamāṇavakavimāne –

Thus having praised the teaching, with a mind of faith in the Three Jewels through this discourse, and making an expression of his faith, he spoke the words beginning with 'Esāhaṃ'. Therein, 'Esāhaṃ' is 'eso ahaṃ' (this I am). 'I go to the venerable Gotama for refuge' means: 'The venerable Gotama is my refuge and my ultimate resort, a protector from evil and a provider of welfare.' With this intention, 'I go to the venerable Gotama for refuge, I associate with him, I serve him, I attend upon him'; or, 'I know, I understand it thus.' For those verbal roots that have the meaning of 'going' also have the meaning of 'understanding.' Therefore, for 'gacchāmi' (I go), the meaning 'jānāmi, bujjhāmi' (I know, I understand) is stated. As for 'and the Dhamma and the Saṅgha of monks': herein, it is called 'Dhamma' because it supports those who have attained the path, realized cessation, and practice as instructed, preventing them from falling into the woeful states. In terms of its meaning, that is the Noble Path and Nibbāna. For it is said: 'Bhikkhus, of all conditioned things, the Noble Eightfold Path is declared the foremost,' and so on in detail. And not only are the Noble Path and Nibbāna the Dhamma, but also the scriptural Dhamma along with the Noble Fruits. For it is said in the Chattamāṇavaka-vimāna:

“Rāgavirāgamanejamasokaṃ, dhammamasaṅkhatamappaṭikūlaṃ;

Madhuramimaṃ paguṇaṃ suvibhattaṃ, dhammamimaṃ saraṇatthamupehī”ti. (vi. va. 887);

“The Dhamma which is the fading away of passion, unshakable, sorrowless, unconditioned, and not repulsive; this sweet, proficient, well-analyzed Dhamma—approach this Dhamma for refuge.”

Ettha rāgavirāgoti maggo kathito. Anejamasokanti phalaṃ. Dhammamasaṅkhatanti nibbānaṃ. Appaṭikūlaṃ madhuramimaṃ paguṇaṃ suvibhattanti piṭakattayena vibhattā sabbadhammakkhandhāti. Diṭṭhisīlasaṅghātena [V 1.0140] saṃhatoti saṅgho, so atthato aṭṭha ariyapuggalasamūho. Vuttañhetaṃ tasmiṃyeva vimāne.

Herein, by 'the fading away of passion,' the Path is spoken of. By 'unshakable and sorrowless,' the Fruit is spoken of. By 'the unconditioned Dhamma,' Nibbāna is spoken of. By 'not repulsive, sweet, this proficient, well-analyzed,' all the aggregates of the Dhamma, as analyzed in the three Piṭakas, are spoken of. Because it is assembled by the commonality of view and virtue, it is the Saṅgha; in terms of its meaning, that is the community of the eight noble individuals. This has been stated in that very same celestial mansion.

“Yattha [M 1.0136] ca dinnamahapphalamāhu, catūsu sucīsu purisayugesu;

Aṭṭha ca puggala dhammadasā te, saṅghamimaṃ saraṇatthamupehī”ti. (vi. va. 888);

“That wherein a gift is said to be of great fruit—among the four pure pairs of persons; and those eight individuals are seers of the Dhamma. Approach this Saṅgha for refuge.”

Bhikkhūnaṃ saṅgho bhikkhusaṅgho. Ettāvatā brāhmaṇo tīṇi saraṇagamanāni paṭivedesi.

The community of monks is the Bhikkhusaṅgha. With this, the brahmin declared his going to the three refuges.

Pasannākāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Expression of Faith is concluded.

Saraṇagamanakathāvaṇṇanā

The Exposition on Going for Refuge

Idāni tesu saraṇagamanesu kosallatthaṃ saraṇaṃ, saraṇagamanaṃ. Yo ca saraṇaṃ gacchati, saraṇagamanappabhedo[P 1.0132], saraṇagamanassa phalaṃ, saṃkileso, bhedoti ayaṃ vidhi veditabbo. Seyyathidaṃ – padatthato tāva hiṃsatīti saraṇaṃ, saraṇagatānaṃ teneva saraṇagamanena bhayaṃ santāsaṃ dukkhaṃ duggatiparikilesaṃ hanati vināsetīti attho, ratanattayassevetaṃ adhivacanaṃ.

Now, regarding those goings for refuge, for the sake of proficiency, this method should be known: refuge, the going for refuge, the one who goes for refuge, the classification of going for refuge, the fruit of going for refuge, its defilement, and its breach. As follows: firstly, in terms of word-meaning, because it destroys (hiṃsati), it is a 'refuge' (saraṇa). The meaning is that for those who have gone for refuge, by that very going for refuge, it strikes down and destroys fear, terror, suffering, and the defilements of a woeful destination. This is a designation for the Triple Gem alone.

Atha vā hite pavattanena ahitā ca nivattanena sattānaṃ bhayaṃ hiṃsati buddho. Bhavakantārā uttāraṇena assāsadānena ca dhammo. Appakānampi kārānaṃ vipulaphalapaṭilābhakaraṇena saṅgho. Tasmā imināpi pariyāyena ratanattayaṃ saraṇaṃ. Tappasādataggarutāhi vihatakileso tapparāyaṇatākārappavatto cittuppādo saraṇagamanaṃ. Taṃsamaṅgisatto saraṇaṃ gacchati, vuttappakārena cittuppādena etāni me tīṇi saraṇāni saraṇaṃ, etāni parāyaṇanti evaṃ upetīti attho. Evaṃ tāva saraṇaṃ saraṇagamanaṃ yo ca saraṇaṃ gacchatīti idaṃ tayaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Alternatively, the Buddha destroys the fear of beings by promoting what is beneficial and warding off what is not. The Dhamma does so by leading them across the wilderness of existence and by giving assurance. The Saṅgha does so by causing the attainment of abundant fruit even from small offerings. Therefore, by this method also, the Triple Gem is a refuge. The going for refuge is a thought-arising with defilements destroyed through faith and reverence for them, occurring in the manner of having them as the final resort. A being endowed with that goes for refuge, approaching with a thought-arising of the kind described, thus: 'These three are my refuges, these are my final resort.' This is the meaning.

Saraṇagamanappabhede pana duvidhaṃ saraṇagamanaṃ lokuttaraṃ lokiyañca. Tattha lokuttaraṃ diṭṭhasaccānaṃ [V 1.0141] maggakkhaṇe saraṇagamanupakkilesasamucchedena ārammaṇato nibbānārammaṇaṃ hutvā kiccato sakalepi ratanattaye ijjhati. Lokiyaṃ puthujjanānaṃ saraṇagamanupakkilesavikkhambhanena ārammaṇato buddhādiguṇārammaṇaṃ hutvā ijjhati, taṃ atthato buddhādīsu vatthūsu saddhāpaṭilābho, saddhāmūlikā ca sammādiṭṭhi dasasu puññakiriyavatthūsu diṭṭhijukammanti vuccati.

Now, in the classification of going for refuge, the going for refuge is twofold: supramundane and mundane. Therein, the supramundane going for refuge, for those who have seen the truths, is accomplished at the moment of the path by eradicating the defilements of going for refuge, having Nibbāna as its object, and functioning in respect to the entire Triple Gem. The mundane going for refuge, for worldlings, is accomplished by suppressing the defilements of going for refuge and having the qualities of the Buddha and so on as its object. In meaning, it is the attainment of faith in the objects such as the Buddha. And right view that has faith as its root, in the context of the ten bases of meritorious action, is called 'the straightening of views'.

Tayidaṃ catudhā pavattati attasanniyyātanena tapparāyaṇatāya sissabhāvūpagamanena paṇipātenāti. Tattha attasanniyyātanaṃ nāma “ajja [M 1.0137] ādiṃ katvā ahaṃ attānaṃ buddhassa niyyātemi, dhammassa, saṅghassā”ti evaṃ buddhādīnaṃ attapariccajanaṃ. Tapparāyaṇatā nāma “ajja ādiṃ katvā ahaṃ buddhaparāyaṇo, dhammaparāyaṇo, saṅghaparāyaṇo iti maṃ dhārethā”ti evaṃ tapparāyaṇabhāvo. Sissabhāvūpagamanaṃ nāma “ajja ādiṃ katvā ahaṃ buddhassa antevāsiko, dhammassa, saṅghassāti maṃ dhārethā”ti evaṃ sissabhāvūpagamo. Paṇipāto nāma “ajja ādiṃ katvā ahaṃ abhivādanapaccuṭṭhānaañjalikammasāmīcikammaṃ buddhādīnaṃyeva tiṇṇaṃ vatthūnaṃ karomi, iti maṃ dhārethā”ti evaṃ buddhādīsu [P 1.0133] paramanipaccakāro. Imesañhi catunnaṃ ākārānaṃ aññatarampi karontena gahitaṃyeva hoti saraṇagamanaṃ.

This occurs in four ways: by self-dedication, by taking them as the final resort, by entering into discipleship, and by paying homage. Therein, self-dedication is: 'From today onward, I dedicate myself to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha'—thus it is the relinquishing of oneself to the Buddha and so on. Taking them as the final resort is: 'From today onward, I have the Buddha as my final resort, the Dhamma as my final resort, the Saṅgha as my final resort—may you remember me thus'—thus it is the state of having them as the final resort. Entering into discipleship is: 'From today onward, I am a disciple of the Buddha, of the Dhamma, of the Saṅgha—may you remember me thus'—thus it is entering into the state of a disciple. Paying homage is: 'From today onward, I perform acts of salutation, rising up, joining the palms, and proper service only towards the three objects, the Buddha and so on—may you remember me thus'—thus it is the supreme reverence towards the Buddha and so on. For by performing even one of these four modes, the going for refuge is indeed taken.

Apica bhagavato attānaṃ pariccajāmi, dhammassa, saṅghassa attānaṃ pariccajāmi. Jīvitaṃ pariccajāmi, pariccattoyeva me attā, pariccattaṃyeva me jīvitaṃ, jīvitapariyantikaṃ buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi, buddho me saraṇaṃ leṇaṃ tāṇanti evampi attasanniyyātanaṃ veditabbaṃ. “Satthārañca vatāhaṃ passeyyaṃ bhagavantameva passeyyaṃ, sugatañca vatāhaṃ passeyyaṃ bhagavantameva passeyyaṃ, sammāsambuddhañca vatāhaṃ passeyyaṃ bhagavantameva passeyya”nti (saṃ. ni. 2.154) evampi mahākassapassa saraṇagamanaṃ viya sissabhāvūpagamanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Furthermore: “I relinquish myself to the Blessed One, I relinquish myself to the Dhamma, I relinquish myself to the Saṅgha. I relinquish my life; my self is indeed relinquished, my life is indeed relinquished. For as long as life lasts, I go to the Buddha for refuge; the Buddha is my refuge, shelter, and protection”—this too should be understood as self-dedication. “Indeed, may I see the Teacher, may I see the Blessed One; indeed, may I see the Sugata, may I see the Blessed One; indeed, may I see the Perfectly Enlightened One, may I see the Blessed One”—thus, like Mahākassapa’s going for refuge, it should be seen as entering into discipleship.

“So ahaṃ vicarissāmi, gāmā gāmaṃ purā puraṃ;

Namassamāno sambuddhaṃ, dhammassa ca sudhammata”nti. (su. ni. 194; saṃ. ni. 1.246) –

“I shall wander from village to village, from town to town, paying homage to the Fully Enlightened One and the good nature of the Dhamma.”

Evampi āḷavakādīnaṃ saraṇagamanaṃ viya tapparāyaṇatā veditabbā. “Atha kho brahmāyu brāhmaṇo [V 1.0142] uṭṭhāyāsanā ekaṃsaṃ uttarāsaṅgaṃ karitvā bhagavato pādesu sirasā nipatitvā bhagavato pādāni mukhena ca paricumbati, pāṇīhi ca parisambāhati, nāmañca sāveti brahmāyu ahaṃ, bho gotama, brāhmaṇo, brahmāyu ahaṃ, bho gotama, brāhmaṇo”ti (ma. ni. 2.394) evampi paṇipāto daṭṭhabbo.

Thus, like the going for refuge of Āḷavaka and others, taking them as the final resort should be understood. ‘Then the brahmin Brahmāyu rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, kissed the Blessed One’s feet with his mouth, stroked them with his hands, and announced his name: “I, Venerable Gotama, am the brahmin Brahmāyu; I, Venerable Gotama, am the brahmin Brahmāyu”’—thus, homage should be regarded.

So panesa ñātibhayācariyadakkhiṇeyyavasena catubbidho hoti. Tattha dakkhiṇeyyapaṇipātena saraṇagamanaṃ hoti, na itarehi. Seṭṭhavaseneva hi saraṇaṃ gayhati, seṭṭhavasena bhijjati, tasmā yo sākiyo [M 1.0138] vā koliyo vā “buddho amhākaṃ ñātako”ti vandati, aggahitameva hoti saraṇaṃ. Yo vā “samaṇo gotamo rājapūjito mahānubhāvo, avandiyamāno anatthampi kareyyā”ti bhayena vandati, aggahitameva hoti saraṇaṃ. Yo vā bodhisattakāle bhagavato santike kiñci uggahitaṃ saramāno buddhakāle vā –

This going for refuge by homage, however, is fourfold: by way of relatives, fear, teachers, and those worthy of offerings. Therein, going for refuge occurs by homage to those worthy of offerings, not by the others. For refuge is taken only by way of what is supreme, and is broken by way of what is supreme. Therefore, if a Sākiyan or Koliyan pays homage thinking, “The Buddha is our relative,” the refuge is not taken. Or if one pays homage out of fear, thinking, “The ascetic Gotama is honored by kings and possesses great power; if I do not pay respect, he may bring me harm,” the refuge is not taken. Or if one recalls something learned in the presence of the Blessed One during his time as a Bodhisatta or during his time as a Buddha—

“Ekena bhoge bhuñjeyya, dvīhi kammaṃ payojaye;

Catutthañca nidhāpeyya, āpadāsu bhavissatī”ti. (dī. ni. 3.265) –

“With one portion, one should enjoy wealth; with two, one should apply it to work; and the fourth, one should set aside, thinking: ‘It will be for times of adversity.’”

Evarūpaṃ anusāsaniṃ uggahetvā “ācariyo me”ti vandati, aggahitameva [P 1.0134] hoti saraṇaṃ. Yo pana “ayaṃ loke aggadakkhiṇeyyo”ti vandati, teneva gahitaṃ hoti saraṇaṃ.

—and having learned such an instruction, pays homage thinking, “He is my teacher,” the refuge is not taken. But if one pays homage thinking, “This one is the foremost worthy of offerings in the world,” then the refuge is taken.

Evaṃ gahitasaraṇassa ca upāsakassa vā upāsikāya vā aññatitthiyesu pabbajitampi ñātiṃ “ñātako me aya”nti vandato saraṇagamanaṃ na bhijjati, pageva apabbajitaṃ. Tathā rājānaṃ bhayavasena vandato, so hi raṭṭhapūjitattā avandiyamāno anatthampi kareyyāti. Tathā yaṃkiñci sippaṃ sikkhāpakaṃ titthiyaṃ “ācariyo me aya”nti vandatopi na bhijjatīti evaṃ saraṇagamanappabhedo veditabbo.

For a male or female lay follower who has thus taken refuge, their going for refuge is not broken even when paying homage to a relative who has gone forth among other sectarians, thinking, “This is my relative”—how much more so if paying homage to one who has not gone forth. Similarly, for one who pays homage to a king out of fear, it is not broken; for that king, being honored by the country, might bring harm if not paid homage to. Likewise, even for one who pays homage to a sectarian who teaches some craft, thinking, “This is my teacher,” it is not broken. In this way, the distinctions of the going for refuge should be understood.

Ettha ca lokuttarassa saraṇagamanassa cattāri sāmaññaphalāni vipākaphalaṃ, sabbadukkhakkhayo ānisaṃsaphalaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ –

Herein, for the supramundane going for refuge, the four fruits of recluseship are the resultant fruit, and the destruction of all suffering is the benefit-fruit. For this was stated:

“Yo [V 1.0143] ca buddhañca dhammañca, saṅghañca saraṇaṃ gato;

Cattāri ariyasaccāni, sammappaññāya passati.

“Whoever has gone to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Sangha for refuge, sees with right wisdom the Four Noble Truths:

Dukkhaṃ dukkhasamuppādaṃ, dukkhassa ca atikkamaṃ;

Ariyañcaṭṭhaṅgikaṃ maggaṃ, dukkhūpasamagāminaṃ.

Suffering, the origin of suffering, the overcoming of suffering, and the Noble Eightfold Path leading to the stilling of suffering.

Etaṃ kho saraṇaṃ khemaṃ, etaṃ saraṇamuttamaṃ;

Etaṃ saraṇamāgamma, sabbadukkhā pamuccatī”ti. (dha. pa. 190-192);

This indeed is the secure refuge, this is the supreme refuge; having come to this refuge, one is released from all suffering.”

Apica niccato anupagamanādivasena petassa ānisaṃsaphalaṃ veditabbaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ, “aṭṭhānametaṃ, bhikkhave, anavakāso, yaṃ diṭṭhisampanno puggalo kañci saṅkhāraṃ niccato upagaccheyya, sukhato upagaccheyya, kañci dhammaṃ attato upagaccheyya, mātaraṃ jīvitā voropeyya, pitaraṃ arahantaṃ [M 1.0139] jīvitā voropeyya, duṭṭhacitto tathāgatassa lohitaṃ uppādeyya, saṅghaṃ bhindeyya, aññaṃ satthāraṃ uddiseyya, netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjatī”ti (ma. ni. 3.128; a. ni. 1.268-276).

Furthermore, the benefit-fruit of this supramundane refuge should be understood by way of not approaching any formation as permanent, and so on. For this was stated: “This is impossible, monks, it cannot be, that a person accomplished in view would approach any formation as permanent, would approach it as pleasant, would approach any phenomenon as self; that they would deprive their mother of life, their father, or an Arahant of life; that with a mind of hate they would cause the blood of a Tathāgata to flow; that they would cause a schism in the Sangha; or that they would point to another as teacher. That possibility does not exist.”

Lokiyassa pana saraṇagamanassa bhavasampadāpi bhogasampadāpi phalameva. Vuttañhetaṃ –

But for the worldly going for refuge, the accomplishment of good existence and the accomplishment of wealth are indeed the fruit. For this was stated:

“Yekeci buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gatāse,

Na te gamissanti apāyabhūmiṃ;

Pahāya mānusaṃ dehaṃ,

Devakāyaṃ paripūressantī”ti. (saṃ. ni. 1.37);

“Whoever has gone to the Buddha for refuge, they will not go to a plane of misery; having abandoned the human body, they will fill the host of devas.”

Aparampi [P 1.0135] vuttaṃ “atha kho sakko devānamindo asītiyā devatāsahassehi saddhiṃ yenāyasmā mahāmoggallāno, tenupasaṅkami…pe… ekamantaṃ ṭhitaṃ kho sakkaṃ devānamindaṃ āyasmā mahāmoggallāno etadavoca ‘sādhu kho devānaminda buddhaṃ saraṇagamanaṃ hoti, buddhaṃ saraṇagamanahetu kho devānaminda evamidhekacce sattā kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ [V 1.0144] upapajjantī’ti. Te aññe deve dasahi ṭhānehi adhigaṇhanti dibbena āyunā dibbena vaṇṇena sukhena yasena ādhipateyyena dibbehi rūpehi saddehi gandhehi rasehi phoṭṭhabbehī”ti (saṃ. ni. 4.341). Esa nayo dhamme saṅghe ca. Apica velāmasuttādivasenāpi (a. ni. 9.20) saraṇagamanassa phalaviseso veditabbo. Evaṃ saraṇagamanaphalaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Furthermore, it was stated: “Then Sakka, the lord of the devas, with eighty thousand devas, approached the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna… Having stood to one side, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna said this to Sakka, the lord of the devas: ‘It is indeed good, lord of the devas, to go for refuge to the Buddha. Because of going for refuge to the Buddha, lord of the devas, some beings here, with the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world.’ They surpass other devas in ten respects: in divine lifespan, divine beauty, happiness, fame, sovereignty, and in divine forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tactile objects.” This is the method for the Dhamma and the Sangha as well. Furthermore, the special fruit of going for refuge should be understood by way of the Velāma Sutta and others. Thus, the fruit of going for refuge should be understood.

Tattha lokiyasaraṇagamanaṃ tīsu vatthūsu aññāṇasaṃsayamicchāñāṇādīhi saṃkilissati, na mahājutikaṃ hoti, na mahāvipphāraṃ. Lokuttarassa natthi saṃkileso. Lokiyassa ca saraṇagamanassa duvidho bhedo sāvajjo anavajjo ca. Tattha sāvajjo aññasatthārādīsu attasanniyyātanādīhi hoti, so aniṭṭhaphalo. Anavajjo kālaṃ kiriyāya, so avipākattā aphalo. Lokuttarassa pana nevatthi bhedo. Bhavantarepi hi ariyasāvako aññasatthāraṃ na uddisatīti evaṃ saraṇagamanassa saṃkileso ca bhedo ca veditabboti. Upāsakaṃ maṃ bhavaṃ gotamo dhāretūti maṃ bhavaṃ gotamo “upāsako aya”nti evaṃ dhāretu, jānātūti attho.

Herein, the worldly going for refuge is defiled by ignorance, doubt, wrong knowledge, and so on, concerning the three objects; it is not of great radiance, nor of great pervasiveness. The supramundane has no defilement. And for the worldly going for refuge, its breaking is of two kinds: blameworthy and blameless. The blameworthy breaking occurs through self-dedication to other teachers and the like, and it has an undesirable fruit. The blameless breaking occurs at the time of death, and since it is without result, it is fruitless. But for the supramundane, there is no breaking whatsoever. For even in another existence, a noble disciple does not point to another as teacher. Thus, the defilement and the breaking of the going for refuge should be understood. “May the venerable Gotama hold me as a lay follower” means, “May the venerable Gotama hold and know me thus: ‘This is a lay follower.’”

Saraṇagamanakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Discourse on Going for Refuge is concluded.

Upāsakavidhikathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse on the Conduct of a Lay Follower

Upāsakavidhikosallatthaṃ [M 1.0140] panettha ko upāsako, kasmā upāsakoti vuccati, kimassa sīlaṃ, ko ājīvo, kā vipatti, kā sampattīti idaṃ pakiṇṇakaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Herein, for the purpose of becoming skilled in the conduct of a lay follower, this miscellaneous section should be understood: Who is a lay follower? Why is one called a lay follower? What is his virtue? What is his livelihood? What is his failure? What is his accomplishment?

Tattha ko upāsakoti yo koci tisaraṇagato gahaṭṭho. Vuttañhetaṃ – “yato kho mahānāma upāsako buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gato hoti, dhammaṃ saraṇaṃ gato hoti, saṅghaṃ saraṇaṃ gato hoti. Ettāvatā kho mahānāma upāsako hotī”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.1033).

Therein, as to “Who is a lay follower?”: any householder who has gone for refuge to the Three Refuges. For this was stated: “Mahānāma, when a lay follower has gone for refuge to the Buddha, has gone for refuge to the Dhamma, and has gone for refuge to the Saṅgha, to that extent, Mahānāma, he is a lay follower.”

Kasmā upāsakoti ratanattayassa upāsanato. So hi buddhaṃ upāsatīti upāsako. Dhammaṃ, saṅghaṃ upāsatīti upāsako.

As to “Why is one called a lay follower?”: because of attending upon the Triple Gem. For he attends upon the Buddha, thus he is a lay follower. He attends upon the Dhamma and the Saṅgha, thus he is a lay follower.

Kimassa [V 1.0145] sīlanti pañca veramaṇiyo. Yathāha “yato kho mahānāma upāsako pāṇātipātā paṭivirato hoti adinnādānā[P 1.0136], kāmesu micchācārā, musāvādā, surāmerayamajjapamādaṭṭhānā paṭivirato hoti. Ettāvatā kho mahānāma upāsako sīlavā hotī”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.1033).

As to “What is his virtue?”: the five abstinences. As it is said: “Mahānāma, when a lay follower is abstinent from the destruction of life, from taking what is not given, from misconduct in sensual pleasures, from false speech, and from the partaking of liquor, wine, and intoxicants which are the basis for heedlessness, to that extent, Mahānāma, a lay follower is virtuous.”

Ko ājīvoti pañca micchāvaṇijjā pahāya dhammena samena jīvitakappanaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ “pañcimā, bhikkhave, vaṇijjā upāsakena akaraṇīyā. Katamā pañca? Satthavaṇijjā, sattavaṇijjā, maṃsavaṇijjā, majjavaṇijjā, visavaṇijjā. Imā kho, bhikkhave, pañca vaṇijjā upāsakena akaraṇīyā”ti (a. ni. 5.177).

As to “What is his livelihood?”: it is making a living righteously and justly, having abandoned the five wrong trades. For this was stated: “Monks, there are these five trades that should not be engaged in by a lay follower. Which five? Trade in weapons, trade in living beings, trade in meat, trade in intoxicants, and trade in poisons. These, monks, are the five trades that should not be engaged in by a lay follower.”

Kā vipattīti yā tasseva sīlassa ca ājīvassa ca vipatti, ayamassa vipatti. Apica yāya esa caṇḍālo ceva hoti malañca patikuṭṭho ca. Sāpissa vipattīti veditabbā. Te ca atthato assaddhiyādayo pañca dhammā honti. Yathāha “pañcahi, bhikkhave, dhammehi samannāgato upāsako upāsakacaṇḍālo ca hoti upāsakamalañca upāsakapatikuṭṭho ca. Katamehi pañcahi? Assaddho hoti, dussīlo hoti, kotūhalamaṅgaliko hoti, maṅgalaṃ pacceti no kammaṃ, ito ca bahiddhā dakkhiṇeyyaṃ pariyesati tattha ca pubbakāraṃ karotī”ti (a. ni. 5.175).

As to “What is his failure?”: whatever is the failure of that very virtue and livelihood, this is his failure. Furthermore, that by which he becomes an outcast, a stain, and despicable—that too should be understood as his failure. And in meaning, these are the five qualities beginning with lack of faith. As it is said: “Monks, a lay follower endowed with five qualities is an outcast among lay followers, a stain among lay followers, and despicable among lay followers. With which five? He is without faith, he is without virtue, he is given to omens and auspicious signs, he believes in auspicious signs and not in kamma, and he seeks a recipient worthy of offerings outside of this Dispensation and makes his first offerings there.”

Kā [M 1.0141] sampattīti yā cassa sīlasampadā ca ājīvasampadā ca, sā sampatti. Ye cassa ratanabhāvādikarā saddhādayo pañca dhammā. Yathāha “pañcahi, bhikkhave, dhammehi samannāgato upāsako upāsakaratanañca hoti upāsakapadumañca upāsakapuṇḍarīkañca. Katamehi pañcahi? Saddho hoti, sīlavā hoti, na kotūhalamaṅgaliko hoti, kammaṃ pacceti no maṅgalaṃ, na ito bahiddhā dakkhiṇeyyaṃ gavesati, idha ca pubbakāraṃ karotī”ti (a. ni. 5.175).

As to “What is his accomplishment?”: the accomplishment of his virtue and the accomplishment of his livelihood, that is his accomplishment. And also the five qualities beginning with faith, which make him a jewel among lay followers, and so on. As it is said: “Monks, a lay follower endowed with five qualities is a jewel among lay followers, a paduma lotus among lay followers, and a puṇḍarīka lotus among lay followers. With which five? He has faith, he is virtuous, he is not given to omens and auspicious signs, he believes in kamma and not in auspicious signs, he does not seek a recipient worthy of offerings outside of this Dispensation, and he makes his first offerings here.”

Ajjataggeti ettha ayaṃ aggasaddo ādikoṭikoṭṭhāsaseṭṭhesu dissati. “Ajjatagge, samma dovārika, āvarāmi dvāraṃ nigaṇṭhānaṃ nigaṇṭhīna”ntiādīsu (ma. ni. 2.70) hi ādimhi [V 1.0146] dissati. “Teneva aṅgulaggena taṃ aṅgulaggaṃ parāmaseyya, (kathā. 441) ucchaggaṃ veḷagga”ntiādīsu koṭiyaṃ. “Ambilaggaṃ vā madhuraggaṃ vā tittakaggaṃ vā (saṃ. ni. 5.374), anujānāmi, bhikkhave, vihāraggena vā pariveṇaggena vā bhājetu”ntiādīsu (cūḷava. 318) koṭṭhāse. “Yāvatā, bhikkhave, sattā apadā vā…pe… tathāgato tesaṃ aggamakkhāyatī”tiādīsu (a. ni. 4.34) seṭṭhe. Idha panāyaṃ [P 1.0137] ādimhi daṭṭhabbo. Tasmā ajjataggeti ajjataṃ ādiṃ katvā, evamettha attho veditabbo. Ajjatanti ajjabhāvaṃ. Ajjadaggeti vā pāṭho, da-kāro padasandhikaro, ajja aggaṃ katvāti attho.

Regarding “ajjatagge”: here the word ‘agga’ is seen in the senses of beginning, end, portion, and excellence. In such phrases as, “From today onwards, good gatekeeper, I close the door to the Nigaṇṭha men and Nigaṇṭha women,” it is seen in the sense of beginning. In such phrases as, “With that very fingertip, one should touch that fingertip,” and “the tip of the sugarcane, the tip of the bamboo,” it is seen in the sense of end. In such phrases as, “a sour portion, a sweet portion, or a bitter portion,” and “I allow, monks, that you divide it by the monastery's portion or by the monastic cell's portion,” it is seen in the sense of portion. In such phrases as, “Monks, of all beings, whether footless… the Tathāgata is declared the chief among them,” it is seen in the sense of excellence. Here, however, it should be understood in the sense of beginning. Therefore, in ‘ajjatagge,’ the meaning should be understood as “making today the beginning.” ‘Ajjataṃ’ means the state of being today. Alternatively, there is the reading ‘ajjadagge,’ where the letter ‘da’ is for euphonic conjunction, and the meaning is “making today the beginning.”

Pāṇupetanti pāṇehi upetaṃ, yāva me jīvitaṃ pavattati, tāva upetaṃ. Anaññasatthukaṃ tīhi saraṇagamanehi saraṇaṃ gataṃ upāsakaṃ kappiyakārakaṃ maṃ bhavaṃ gotamo dhāretu jānātu. Ahañhi sacepi me tikhiṇena asinā sīsaṃ chindeyya, neva buddhaṃ “na buddho”ti vā dhammaṃ “na dhammo”ti vā, saṅghaṃ “na saṅgho”ti vā vadeyyanti. Evaṃ attasanniyyātanena saraṇaṃ gantvā catūhi ca paccayehi pavāretvā uṭṭhāyāsanā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā tikkhattuṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā pakkāmīti.

“Endowed with life” means endowed with life-breath; as long as my life-faculty continues, for that long I am endowed. May the venerable Gotama know me as a lay follower and a servitor who has gone for refuge with the three goings for refuge, having no other teacher. For even if my head were to be cut off with a sharp sword, I would never say of the Buddha, “He is not the Buddha,” or of the Dhamma, “It is not the Dhamma,” or of the Saṅgha, “It is not the Saṅgha.” Thus, having gone for refuge by means of this self-dedication, and having invited the Blessed One with the four requisites, he rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him three times, and departed.

Upāsakavidhikathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Discourse on the Conduct of a Lay Follower is finished.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

The Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya.

Bhayabheravasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Bhayabherava Sutta is finished.

5. Anaṅgaṇasuttavaṇṇanā

5. The Commentary on the Anaṅgaṇa Sutta

57. Evaṃ [M 1.0142][V 1.0147] me sutaṃ…pe… āyasmā sāriputtoti anaṅgaṇasuttaṃ. Tatrāyaṃ anuttānapadavaṇṇanā – yathā cettha, evaṃ sabbasuttesu. Tasmā ito paraṃ ettakampi avatvā apubbapadavaṇṇanaṃyeva karissāma.

57. “Thus have I heard… (etc.) …the Venerable Sāriputta”—this is the Anaṅgaṇa Sutta. Therein, this is the explanation of obscure words. As it is here, so it is in all suttas. Therefore, from here onwards, without saying even this much, we will only provide the explanation of new words.

Cattāroti gaṇanaparicchedo. Puggalāti sattā narā posā. Ettāvatā ca puggalavādī mahātheroti na gahetabbaṃ, ayañhi āyasmā buddhaputtānaṃ seṭṭho, so buddhassa bhagavato desanaṃ avilomentoyeva deseti.

“Four” is a delimitation of number. “Persons” means beings, humans, individuals. And by this much, it should not be taken that the Great Elder is a proponent of the personalist view; for this venerable one is the foremost among the Buddha's sons, and he teaches the teaching of the Buddha, the Blessed One, only without contradicting it.

Sammutiparamatthadesanākathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Discourse on Conventional and Ultimate Teachings

Buddhassa bhagavato duvidhā desanā sammutidesanā, paramatthadesanā cāti. Tattha puggalo satto itthī puriso khattiyo brāhmaṇo devo māroti evarūpā sammutidesanā. Aniccaṃ dukkhaṃ anattā, khandhā dhātū āyatanāni satipaṭṭhānāti evarūpā paramatthadesanā.

The teaching of the Buddha, the Blessed One, is twofold: conventional teaching and ultimate teaching. Therein, “person,” “being,” “woman,” “man,” “noble,” “brahmin,” “deva,” “Māra”—such is the conventional teaching. “Impermanent,” “suffering,” “non-self,” “aggregates,” “elements,” “sense bases,” “foundations of mindfulness”—such is the ultimate teaching.

Tattha bhagavā ye sammutivasena desanaṃ sutvā atthaṃ paṭivijjhitvā mohaṃ pahāya visesaṃ adhigantuṃ samatthā, tesaṃ sammutidesanaṃ deseti. Ye pana paramatthavasena desanaṃ sutvā atthaṃ paṭivijjhitvā mohaṃ pahāya visesamadhigantuṃ samatthā, tesaṃ paramatthadesanaṃ deseti. Tatthāyaṃ upamā, yathā hi desabhāsākusalo tiṇṇaṃ vedānaṃ atthasaṃvaṇṇanako ācariyo ye damiḷabhāsāya vutte [P 1.0138] atthaṃ jānanti, tesaṃ damiḷabhāsāya ācikkhati. Ye andhakabhāsādīsu aññatarāya, tesaṃ tāya tāya bhāsāya. Evaṃ te māṇavakā chekaṃ byattaṃ ācariyamāgamma khippameva sippaṃ uggaṇhanti. Tattha ācariyo viya buddho bhagavā. Tayo vedā viya kathetabbabhāvena ṭhitāni tīṇi piṭakāni. Desabhāsākosallamiva sammutiparamatthakosallaṃ. Nānādesabhāsā māṇavakā viya sammutiparamatthadesanāpaṭivijjhanasamatthā veneyyasattā. Ācariyassa [V 1.0148] damiḷabhāsādiācikkhanaṃ viya bhagavato sammutiparamatthavasena desanā veditabbā. Āha cettha –

Therein, the Blessed One teaches the conventional teaching to those who, having heard the teaching by means of convention, are capable of penetrating the meaning, abandoning delusion, and attaining a special state. But to those who, having heard the teaching by means of the ultimate, are capable of penetrating the meaning, abandoning delusion, and attaining a special state, he teaches the ultimate teaching. Herein, there is this simile: just as a teacher skilled in regional languages, an explainer of the meaning of the three Vedas, explains in the Damiḷa language to those who understand the meaning when it is spoken in the Damiḷa language. To those who understand it in another language, such as the Andhaka language, he explains in that respective language. In this way, those young men, relying on a skilled and proficient teacher, quickly learn the craft. Therein, the Buddha, the Blessed One, is like the teacher.
