The three Piṭakas, standing in the state of needing to be taught, are like the three Vedas. Skill in conventional and ultimate truths is like skill in regional languages. The teachable beings capable of penetrating the conventional and ultimate teachings are like the young men of various regional languages. The Blessed One’s teaching by means of conventional and ultimate truths should be understood as being like the teacher’s instruction in the Damiḷa and other languages. And it is said herein:

“Duve saccāni akkhāsi, sambuddho vadataṃ varo;

Sammutiṃ paramatthañca, tatiyaṃ nūpalabbhati.

“The Perfectly Enlightened One, the best of speakers, declared two truths: the conventional and the ultimate; a third is not found.

Saṅketavacanaṃ [M 1.0143] saccaṃ, lokasammutikāraṇā;

Paramatthavacanaṃ saccaṃ, dhammānaṃ bhūtakāraṇā.

Speech by designation is true, for the reason of worldly convention; speech in the ultimate sense is true, for the reason of the real nature of phenomena.

Tasmā vohārakusalassa, lokanāthassa satthuno;

Sammutiṃ voharantassa, musāvādo na jāyatī”ti.

Therefore, for the Teacher, the Lord of the World, skilled in conventional usage, no falsehood arises when speaking in terms of convention.”

Apica aṭṭhahi kāraṇehi bhagavā puggalakathaṃ katheti – hirottappadīpanatthaṃ, kammassakatādīpanatthaṃ, paccattapurisakāradīpanatthaṃ, ānantariyadīpanatthaṃ, brahmavihāradīpanatthaṃ, pubbenivāsadīpanatthaṃ, dakkhiṇāvisuddhidīpanatthaṃ, lokasammutiyā appahānatthañcāti. “Khandhadhātuāyatanāni hirīyanti ottappantī”ti hi vutte mahājano na jānāti, sammohamāpajjati, paṭisattu hoti “kimidaṃ khandhadhātuāyatanāni hirīyanti ottappanti nāmā”ti. “Itthī hirīyati ottappati puriso khattiyo brāhmaṇo devo māro”ti vutte pana jānāti, na sammohamāpajjati, na paṭisattu hoti. Tasmā bhagavā hirottappadīpanatthaṃ puggalakathaṃ katheti.

Furthermore, the Blessed One gives a discourse on the person for eight reasons: to illuminate moral shame and moral dread, to illuminate the ownership of kamma, to illuminate individual action, to illuminate the actions with immediate result, to illuminate the divine abodes, to illuminate past lives, to illuminate the purity of offerings, and in order not to abandon worldly conventions. For if it were said, “The aggregates, elements, and sense bases feel moral shame and moral dread,” the great populace would not understand, would become confused, and would become hostile, thinking, “What is this, that aggregates, elements, and sense bases feel moral shame and moral dread?” But when it is said, “A woman feels moral shame and moral dread, a man, a noble, a brahmin, a deva, Māra,” they understand, do not become confused, and are not hostile. Therefore, the Blessed One gives a discourse on the person to illuminate moral shame and moral dread.

“Khandhā kammassakā dhātuyo āyatanānī”ti vuttepi eseva nayo. Tasmā bhagavā kammassakatādīpanatthaṃ puggalakathaṃ katheti.

Even when it is said, “The aggregates are the owners of their kamma, as are the elements and the sense bases,” the same principle applies. Therefore, the Blessed One gives a discourse on the person to illuminate the ownership of kamma.

“Veḷuvanādayo mahāvihārā khandhehi kārāpitā dhātūhi āyatanehī”ti vuttepi eseva nayo. Tasmā bhagavā paccattapurisakāradīpanatthaṃ puggalakathaṃ katheti.

Even when it is said, “Great monasteries like the Veḷuvana were caused to be built by aggregates, elements, and sense bases,” the same principle applies. Therefore, the Blessed One gives a discourse on the person in order to illuminate individual action.

“Khandhā [V 1.0149] mātaraṃ jīvitā voropenti pitaraṃ arahantaṃ ruhiruppādakammaṃ [P 1.0139] karonti, saṅghabhedakammaṃ karonti, dhātuyo āyatanānī”ti vuttepi eseva nayo. Tasmā bhagavā ānantariyadīpanatthaṃ puggalakathaṃ katheti. “Khandhā mettāyanti dhātuyo āyatanānī”ti vuttepi eseva nayo. Tasmā bhagavā brahmavihāradīpanatthaṃ puggalakathaṃ katheti.

Even when it is said, “The aggregates deprive their mother of life, their father of life, and an arahant of life; they perform the act of shedding the Buddha's blood and the act of causing a schism in the Sangha, as do the elements and sense bases,” the same principle applies. Therefore, the Blessed One gives a discourse on the person to illuminate the actions with immediate result. Even when it is said, “The aggregates practice loving-kindness, as do the elements and sense bases,” the same principle applies. Therefore, the Blessed One gives a discourse on the person to illuminate the divine abodes.

“Khandhā pubbenivāsamanussaranti dhātuyo āyatanānī”ti vuttepi eseva nayo. Tasmā bhagavā pubbenivāsadīpanatthaṃ puggalakathaṃ katheti. “Khandhā dānaṃ paṭiggaṇhanti dhātuyo āyatanānī”ti vuttepi mahājano na jānāti, sammohamāpajjati, paṭisattu hoti “kimidaṃ khandhadhātuāyatanāni paṭiggaṇhanti nāmā”ti. “Puggalā paṭiggaṇhanti sīlavanto kalyāṇadhammā”ti vutte pana jānāti, na sammohamāpajjati, na paṭisattu hoti. Tasmā bhagavā dakkhiṇāvisuddhidīpanatthaṃ puggalakathaṃ katheti.

Even when it is said, “The aggregates, elements, and sense bases recollect past lives,” the same principle applies. Therefore, the Blessed One gives a discourse on the person to illuminate past lives. Even when it is said, “The aggregates, elements, and sense bases receive a gift,” the great populace does not understand, becomes confused, and becomes hostile, thinking, “What is this, that aggregates, elements, and sense bases receive a gift?” But when it is said, “Persons who are virtuous and of good character receive a gift,” they understand, do not become confused, and are not hostile. Therefore, the Blessed One gives a discourse on the person to illuminate the purity of offerings.

Lokasammutiñca [M 1.0144] buddhā bhagavanto nappajahanti, lokasamaññāya lokaniruttiyaṃ lokābhilāpe ṭhitāyeva dhammaṃ desenti. Tasmā bhagavā lokasammutiyā appahānatthampi puggalakathaṃ katheti. Tasmā ayampi āyasmā lokavohārakusalatāya buddhassa bhagavato desanaṃ avilomento lokasammutiyaṃ ṭhatvāva cattārome, āvuso, puggalāti āha. Tasmā ettha paramatthavasena aggahetvā sammutivaseneva puggalo veditabbo.

And the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, do not abandon worldly convention. They teach the Dhamma while remaining established in the world's common usage, the world's expressions, and the world's speech. Therefore, the Blessed One also gives a discourse on the person in order not to abandon worldly convention. Thus, this venerable one, being skilled in worldly usage and not contradicting the teaching of the Buddha, the Blessed One, speaks while standing within worldly convention: “Friends, there are these four kinds of persons.” Therefore, herein, a person should be understood only in terms of convention, without being grasped in terms of ultimate reality.

Santo saṃvijjamānāti lokasaṅketavasena atthi upalabbhamānā. Lokasminti sattaloke. Sāṅgaṇova samānotiādīsu pana aṅgaṇanti katthaci kilesā vuccanti. Yathāha “tattha katamāni tīṇi aṅgaṇāni? Rāgo aṅgaṇaṃ, doso aṅgaṇaṃ, moho aṅgaṇa”nti (vibha. 924). Katthaci yaṃkiñci malaṃ vā paṅko vā, yathāha “tasseva rajassa vā aṅgaṇassa vā pahānāya vāyamatī”ti. Katthaci tathārūpo bhūmibhāgo, so bodhiyaṅgaṇaṃ cetiyaṅgaṇantiādīnaṃ vasena veditabbo. Idha pana nānappakārā tibbakilesā “aṅgaṇa”nti adhippetā. Tathā hi vakkhati “pāpakānaṃ kho etaṃ, āvuso, akusalānaṃ icchāvacarānaṃ adhivacanaṃ, yadidaṃ aṅgaṇa”nti (ma. ni. 1.60). Saha aṅgaṇena sāṅgaṇo.

The term 'existing and being found' (santo saṃvijjamānā) means, by worldly convention, 'they exist, they are found.' 'In the world' (lokasmiṃ) means in the world of beings. In passages such as 'one with a blemish, while dwelling' (sāṅgaṇova samāno), however, in some places defilements are called a 'blemish' (aṅgaṇa). As it is said: 'Therein, what are the three blemishes? Greed is a blemish, aversion is a blemish, delusion is a blemish.' In some places, it means any kind of stain or mud, as it is said: 'He strives for the abandonment of that very dust or mud.' In some places, it means a certain type of ground, which should be understood by way of terms such as 'the Bodhi-precinct' and 'the Cetiya-precinct.' Here, however, by 'blemish' is meant various kinds of intense defilements. For indeed, it will be said: 'Friend, this is a designation for evil, unwholesome states that move in the sphere of desire, that is, a blemish.' One who is together with a blemish is 'one with a blemish' (sāṅgaṇo).

Sāṅgaṇova [V 1.0150] samānoti sakilesoyeva santo[P 1.0140]. Atthi me ajjhattaṃ aṅgaṇanti yathābhūtaṃ nappajānātīti mayhaṃ attano cittasantāne kileso atthītipi na jānāti. “Ime kilesā nāma kakkhaḷā vāḷā jahitabbā na gahitabbā visaduṭṭhasallasadisā”ti evaṃ yāthāvasarasatopi na jānāti. Yo atthīti ca jānāti, evañca jānāti. So “atthi me ajjhattaṃ aṅgaṇanti yathābhūtaṃ pajānātī”ti vuccati. Yassa pana na ca maggena samūhatā kilesā, na ca uppajjanti yena vā tena vā vāritattā, ayamidha anaṅgaṇoti adhippeto. Natthi me ajjhattaṃ aṅgaṇanti yathābhūtaṃ nappajānātīti “mayhaṃ kilesā yena vā tena vā vāritattā natthi, na maggena samūhatattā”ti na jānāti, “te uppajjamānā mahāanatthaṃ karissanti kakkhaḷā vāḷā visaduṭṭhasallasadisā”ti evaṃ yāthāvasarasatopi na jānāti. Yo pana “iminā kāraṇena natthī”ti ca jānāti, evañca jānāti, so “natthi me ajjhattaṃ aṅgaṇanti yathābhūtaṃ pajānātī”ti vuccati[M 1.0145]. Tatrāti tesu catūsu puggalesu, tesu vā dvīsu sāṅgaṇesu, yvāyanti yo ayaṃ, yāyantipi pāṭho.

`Sāṅgaṇova samāno` means: being one who indeed has defilements. 'He does not know as it really is, "There is a blemish within me"' means: he does not know, "There is a defilement in my own mental continuum." He also does not know according to their true nature: "These things called defilements are rough, fierce, to be abandoned, not to be grasped, like a poisoned, corrupted arrow." But one who knows "it exists" and also knows it in this way, is said to 'know as it really is, "There is a blemish within me."' However, one for whom defilements do not arise, either because they have been eradicated by the path or because they are prevented by some means or other, this one is here intended as 'one without a blemish' (anaṅgaṇa). 'He does not know as it really is, "There is no blemish within me"' means: he does not know, "For me, defilements do not exist because they are prevented by some means or other, not because they have been eradicated by the path." And he does not know according to their true nature: "Those defilements, should they arise, will cause great harm, being rough, fierce, like a poisoned, corrupted arrow." But one who knows "they do not exist for this reason" and also knows them in this way, is said to 'know as it really is, "There is no blemish within me."' 'Therein' (tatra) means: among those four persons, or among those two with blemishes. Yvāyaṃ is to be parsed as yo ayaṃ. There is also the reading yāyaṃ.

58. Ko nu kho, āvuso, sāriputta, hetu ko paccayoti ubhayenāpi kāraṇameva pucchati. Yenimesanti yena hetunā yena paccayena imesaṃ dvinnaṃ eko seṭṭhapuriso eko hīnapurisoti akkhāyati, so ko hetu ko paccayoti evamettha sambandho veditabbo. Tattha kiñcāpi “nappajānāti pajānātī”ti evaṃ vuttaṃ, pajānanā nappajānanāti idameva ubhayaṃ hetu ceva paccayo ca.

58. 'What, friend Sāriputta, is the cause, what is the condition?'—with both terms, he asks for the very same reason. The connection here should be understood thus: By what cause, by what condition, among these two persons, is one called a superior person and the other an inferior person? What is that cause, and what is that condition? Therein, although it is said, 'he does not know' and 'he knows,' this very pair—knowing and not knowing—is both the cause and the condition.

59. Thero pana attano vicitrapaṭibhānatāya taṃ pākaṭataraṃ katvā dassetuṃ puna tatrāvusotiādimāha. Tattha tassetaṃ pāṭikaṅkhanti tassa puggalassa etaṃ pāṭikaṅkhitabbaṃ. Idameva esa pāpuṇissati, na aññanti icchitabbaṃ, avassaṃ bhāvīti vuttaṃ hoti. “Na chandaṃ janessatī”tiādinā nayena vuttaṃ achandajananādiṃ sandhāyāha.

59. The Elder, however, on account of his varied brilliance, in order to present the matter more clearly, spoke again, beginning with, 'Therein, friend...' Therein, 'this is to be expected of him' (tassetaṃ pāṭikaṅkhaṃ) means: for that person, this non-abandonment of the blemish is to be expected. It is to be intended thus: 'This person will attain only this state of being together with the unwholesome; he will not attain another.' This means it is said to be inevitable. He said this referring to the non-generation of desire and so on—spoken in the manner beginning, 'He will not generate desire.'

Tattha ca na chandaṃ janessatīti appajānanto tassa aṅgaṇassa pahānatthaṃ kattukamyatāchandaṃ na janessati. Na vāyamissatīti tato balavataraṃ vāyāmaṃ na karissati, na vīriyaṃ ārabhissatīti thāmagatavīriyaṃ pana neva ārabhissati, na pavattessatīti vuttaṃ hoti. Sāṅgaṇoti imehi rāgādīhi aṅgaṇehi [V 1.0151] sāṅgaṇo. Saṃkiliṭṭhacittoti tehiyeva suṭṭhutaraṃ [P 1.0141] kiliṭṭhacitto malīnacitto vibādhitacitto upatāpitacitto ca hutvā. Kālaṃ karissatīti marissati.

And therein, 'he will not generate desire' means: not knowing, he will not generate the desire-to-act for the sake of abandoning that blemish. 'He will not strive' means he will not make an effort stronger than that. 'He will not arouse energy' means he will certainly not arouse resolute energy; he will not set it in motion. This is the meaning. 'With a blemish' (sāṅgaṇa) means: one with a blemish on account of these blemishes such as greed. 'With a defiled mind' (saṃkiliṭṭhacitto) means: having a mind that is, on account of those very things, exceedingly defiled, stained, oppressed, and tormented. 'He will make his time' (kālaṃ karissati) means: he will die.

Seyyathāpīti yathā nāma. Kaṃsapātīti kaṃsalohabhājanaṃ. Ābhatāti ānītā. Āpaṇā vā kammārakulā vāti āpaṇato vā kaṃsapātikārakānaṃ kammārānaṃ gharato vā. Rajenāti āgantukarajena paṃsuādinā. Malenāti tattheva uṭṭhitena lohamalena. Pariyonaddhāti sañchannā. Na ceva paribhuñjeyyunti udakakhādanīyapakkhipanādīhi paribhogaṃ na kareyyuṃ. Na ca pariyodapeyyunti dhovanaghaṃsanādīhi na parisuddhaṃ kārāpeyyuṃ. Rajāpatheti rajapathe. Ayameva vā pāṭho, rajassa āgamanaṭṭhāne vā vuṭṭhānuṭṭhāne vā heṭṭhāmañce vā thusakoṭṭhake vā bhājanantare vā, yattha rajena okirīyatīti attho. Saṃkiliṭṭhatarā assa malaggahitāti ettha rajāpathe nikkhipanena saṃkiliṭṭhatarā, aparibhogāpariyodapanehi [M 1.0146] malaggahitatarāti vuttaṃ hoti, paṭipucchāvacanañcetaṃ. Tenassa evamattho veditabbo, āvuso, sā kaṃsapāti evaṃ karīyamānā aparena kālena saṃkiliṭṭhatarā ca malaggahitatarā ca mattikapātīti vā kaṃsapātīti vā itipi dujjānā bhaveyya nu kho noti, thero taṃ paṭijānanto āha “evamāvuso”ti. Puna dhammasenāpati opammaṃ sampaṭipādento, evameva khotiādimāha. Tatthevaṃ opammasaṃsandanā veditabbā – kiliṭṭhakaṃsapātisadiso sāṅgaṇo puggalo. Saṃkiliṭṭhakaṃsapātiyā naparibhuñjanamādiṃ katvā rajāpathanikkhepo viya tassa puggalassa pabbajjaṃ labhamānassa vejjakammādīsu pasutapuggalasantike pabbajjāpaṭilābho. Saṃkiliṭṭhakaṃsapātiyā puna saṃkiliṭṭhatarabhāvo viya tassa puggalassa anukkamena ācariyupajjhāyānaṃ anusikkhato vejjakammādikaraṇaṃ, ettha ṭhitassa sāṅgaṇakālakiriyā. Atha vā anukkamena dukkaṭadubbhāsitavītikkamanaṃ, ettha ṭhitassa sāṅgaṇakālakiriyā. Atha vā anukkamena pācittiyathullaccayavītikkamanaṃ, saṅghādisesavītikkamanaṃ, pārājikavītikkamanaṃ, mātughātādiānantariyakaraṇaṃ, ettha ṭhitassa sāṅgaṇakālakiriyāti.

Seyyathāpi means: just as. Kaṃsapāti means: a bronze vessel. Ābhatā means: brought. Āpaṇā vā kammārakulā vā means: from a shop or from the house of smiths who make bronze bowls. Rajena means: with adventitious dust, such as dirt. Malena means: with the metal tarnish that arises right there. Pariyonaddhā means: covered over. Na ceva paribhuñjeyyuṃ means: they would not use it for things such as putting in water or food. Na ca pariyodapeyyuṃ means: they would not have it made pure by washing, scrubbing, and so on. Rajāpathe means: on a dusty path. Or this is the reading: in a place where dust comes from, or where it arises and settles, or under a bed, or in a husk-bin, or between vessels; the meaning is, where it gets strewn with dust. Regarding saṃkiliṭṭhatarā assa malaggahitā, it is said: by being placed on a dusty path, it becomes more defiled; by not being used and not being cleaned, it becomes more stained. And this is a question posed in return. Therefore, its meaning should be understood thus: ‘Friend, that bronze bowl, being treated in this way, would in time become more defiled and more stained. Would it not then be difficult to recognize whether it is an earthen bowl or a bronze bowl? Or would it not?’ The elder, assenting to this, said, ‘So it is, friend.’ Then the General of the Dhamma, connecting the simile, said, ‘Even so...’ and so on. Therein, the application of the simile should be understood thus: a person with defilements is like the defiled bronze bowl. Just as the defiled bronze bowl, starting with not being used, is placed on a dusty path, so too for that person who is obtaining ordination, is the gaining of ordination in the presence of a person given to medical practice and so on. Just as the defiled bronze bowl becomes even more defiled, so too for that person who is sequentially following his teachers and preceptors, is the practice of medicine and so on; for one established therein, there is dying with defilements. Or, sequentially, there is the transgression of wrong-doing and wrong-speech; for one established therein, there is dying with defilements. Or, sequentially, there is the transgression of pācittiya and thullaccaya offenses, the transgression of saṅghādisesa offenses, the transgression of pārājika offenses, the committing of matricide and other fixed-consequence karma; for one established therein, there is dying with defilements.

Saṃkiliṭṭhacitto kālaṃ karissatīti ettha ca akusalacittena kālaṃ karissatīti na evamattho daṭṭhabbo. Sabbasattā hi pakaticittena bhavaṅgacitteneva kālaṃ karonti. Ayaṃ [P 1.0142] pana avisodhetvā cittasantānaṃ kālaṃ karissatīti etamatthaṃ sandhāya evaṃ vuttoti veditabbo.

Herein, regarding the phrase 'he will die with a defiled mind' (saṃkiliṭṭhacitto kālaṃ karissati), the meaning should not be taken as, ‘he will die with an unwholesome mind.’ For indeed, all beings die with the natural mind, that is, with the life-continuum consciousness (bhavaṅga-citta). Rather, it should be understood that this was said in reference to this meaning: ‘This person, however, will die without having purified the continuum of his mind.’

Dutiyavāre [V 1.0152] pariyodapeyyunti dhovanaghaṃsanasaṇhachārikāparimajjanādīhi parisuddhaṃ ādāsamaṇḍalasadisaṃ kareyyuṃ. Na ca naṃ rajāpatheti pubbe vuttappakāre ṭhāne anikkhipitvā karaṇḍamañjūsādīsu vā ṭhapeyyuṃ, paliveṭhetvā vā nāgadante lageyyuṃ. Sesaṃ vuttanayānusāreneva gahetabbaṃ.

In the second case, 'they would make it pure' (pariyodapeyyuṃ) means: they would make it pure, like the disk of a mirror, by washing, scrubbing, polishing with fine ash, and so on. 'And not on a dusty path' (na ca naṃ rajāpathe) means: not placing it in the kind of place mentioned before, they would place it in caskets, chests, and so on, or having wrapped it, they would hang it on an ivory peg. The remainder should be understood according to the method already explained.

Upamāsaṃsandanā cettha evaṃ veditabbā – kiliṭṭhakaṃsapātisadiso sāṅgaṇo bhabbapuggalo. Kiliṭṭhakaṃsapātiyā paribhuñjanamādiṃ katvā suddhaṭṭhāne ṭhapanaṃ viya tassa puggalassa pabbajjaṃ labhamānassa pesalabhikkhūnaṃ santike pabbajjāpaṭilābho. Ye ovadanti anusāsanti appamattakampi pamādaṃ disvā daṇḍakammaṃ katvā punappunaṃ sikkhāpenti, saṃkiliṭṭhakaṃsapātiyā aparakāle [M 1.0147] parisuddhapariyodātabhāvo viya tassa puggalassa ācariyupajjhāyānaṃ anusikkhato anukkamena sammāvattapaṭipatti, ettha ṭhitassa anaṅgaṇakālakiriyā. Atha vā anukkamena parisuddhe sīle patiṭṭhāya attano anurūpaṃ buddhavacanaṃ uggaṇhitvā dhutaṅgāni samādāya attano anukūlakammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā gāmantasenāsanavāsaṃ muñcitvā pantasenāsanavāso, ettha ṭhitassa anaṅgaṇakālakiriyā. Atha vā anukkamena kasiṇaparikammaṃ katvā aṭṭhasamāpattinibbattanena kilesavikkhambhanaṃ, vipassanāpādakajjhānā vuṭṭhāya vipassanāya kilesānaṃ tadaṅganivāraṇaṃ, sotāpattiphalādhigamo…pe… arahattasacchikiriyāti ettha ṭhitassa accantaṃ anaṅgaṇakālakiriyā eva.

And here, the application of the simile should be understood thus: a person with defilements who is capable of being trained is like a tarnished bronze bowl. Just as the tarnished bronze bowl, starting with being used, is placed in a clean place, so too for that person who is obtaining ordination, is the gaining of ordination in the presence of virtuous monks. They are the ones who admonish, instruct, and upon seeing even the slightest negligence, apply a corrective measure and train him again and again. Just as the tarnished bronze bowl in a later time becomes pure and radiant, so too for that person who is sequentially following his teachers and preceptors, there comes to be the right practice and conduct. For one established therein, there is a dying without defilements. Or, sequentially, having become established in pure virtue, having learned the word of the Buddha that is suitable for oneself, having undertaken the ascetic practices, having taken up a meditation subject suitable for oneself, and having given up dwelling in a monastery near a village, one dwells in a secluded lodging. For one established therein, there is a dying without defilements. Or, sequentially, having done the preliminary work for the kasiṇas, there is the suppression of the defilements by producing the eight attainments. Having emerged from the jhāna that is the basis for insight, there is the removal of defilements for the moment by means of insight. There is the attainment of the fruit of stream-entry... (and so on)... there is the realization of the fruit of Arahantship. For one established in this, there is indeed a dying utterly without defilements.

Tatiyavāre subhanimittanti rāgaṭṭhāniyaṃ iṭṭhārammaṇaṃ. Manasi karissatīti tasmiṃ vipannassati taṃ nimittaṃ āvajjissati. Tassa subhanimittassa manasikārāti tassa puggalassa subhanimittamanasikārakāraṇā. Anuddhaṃsessatīti hiṃsissati adhibhavissati. Rāgo hi uppajjanto kusalavāraṃ pacchinditvā sayameva akusalajavanaṃ hutvā tiṭṭhanto kusalacittaṃ anuddhaṃsetīti veditabbo. Sesaṃ vuttanayānusāreneva gahetabbaṃ.

In the third case, 'a beautiful sign' (subhanimittaṃ) means a desirable object that is a basis for lust. 'He will attend to' (manasi karissati) means: when that object is present, he will advert to that sign. 'Because of attending to that beautiful sign' (tassa subhanimittassa manasikārā) means: because of the cause, which is that person’s attending to the beautiful sign. 'It will corrupt' (anuddhaṃsessati) means: it will harm, it will overwhelm. For it should be understood that lust, when arising, cuts off the occasion for the wholesome and, standing as an unwholesome impulsion itself, it corrupts the wholesome mind. The remainder should be understood according to the method already explained.

Opammasaṃsandanā panettha evaṃ veditabbā – parisuddhakaṃsapātisadiso pakatiyā [P 1.0143] appakileso anaṅgaṇapuggalo. Parisuddhakaṃsapātiyā naparibhuñjanaṃ ādiṃ katvā rajāpathe nikkhepo viya tassa puggalassa pabbajjaṃ labhamānassāti ito paraṃ sabbaṃ paṭhamavārasadisameva.

Here, the application of the simile should be understood thus: a person without defilements, who is naturally of few defilements, is like a pure bronze bowl. Just as the pure bronze bowl, starting with not being used, is placed on a dusty path, so too for that person who is obtaining ordination... From this point onward, everything is the same as in the first case.

Catutthavāre [V 1.0153] subhanimittaṃ na manasi karissatīti tasmiṃ sativirahābhāvato taṃ nimittaṃ nāvajjissati, sesaṃ dutiyavārānusārena veditabbaṃ. “Ayaṃ kho, āvuso”tiādi “ko nu kho, āvuso”tiādimhi vuttanayameva.

In the fourth case, regarding the phrase 'he will not attend to the beautiful sign' (subhanimittaṃ na manasi karissati): this is because, due to the absence of a lack of mindfulness in that instance, he will not advert to that sign. The remainder should be understood according to the second case. The phrase beginning with 'Indeed, friend, this...' is of the very same method as that stated in the phrase beginning with 'What then, friend...'

60. Idāni taṃ aṅgaṇaṃ nānappakārato pākaṭaṃ kārāpetukāmenāyasmatā mahāmoggallānena “aṅgaṇaṃ aṅgaṇa”ntiādinā nayena puṭṭho taṃ byākaronto pāpakānaṃ kho etaṃ, āvusotiādimāha. Tattha icchāvacarānanti icchāya avacarānaṃ, icchāvasena otiṇṇānaṃ pavattānaṃ nānappakārānaṃ kopaappaccayānanti attho. Yaṃ idhekaccassāti yena idhekaccassa evaṃ icchā uppajjeyya, taṃ ṭhānaṃ taṃ kāraṇaṃ vijjati atthi, upalabbhatīti [M 1.0148] vuttaṃ hoti. Āpanno assanti āpanno bhaveyyaṃ. Na ca maṃ bhikkhū jāneyyunti bhikkhū ca maṃ na jāneyyuṃ. Kiṃ panettha ṭhānaṃ, lābhatthikatā. Lābhatthiko hi bhikkhu pakatiyāpi ca katapuñño manussehi sakkato garukato evaṃ cinteti “āpattiṃ āpannaṃ bhikkhuṃ therā ñatvā majjhimānaṃ ārocenti, te navakānaṃ, navakā vihāre vighāsādādīnaṃ, te ovādaṃ āgatānaṃ bhikkhunīnaṃ, evaṃ kamena catasso parisā jānanti. Evamassa lābhantarāyo hoti. Aho vatāhaṃ āpattiñca vata āpanno assaṃ, na ca maṃ bhikkhū jāneyyu”nti.

60. Now, the Venerable Sāriputta, wishing to explain the matter when asked by the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna—who desired to make that stain manifest in various ways—in the manner of 'a stain, a stain...', spoke the words beginning with, 'Indeed, friend, this is a term for evil things...'. Therein, 'of those who are moved by desire' (icchāvacarānaṃ) means: of those who follow after desire, of those who have descended into and are proceeding by the power of desire; this is a name for the various kinds of anger and discontent. This is the meaning. 'That for some here' (yaṃ idhekaccassa) means: the condition or cause by which such a desire might arise for a certain one here exists, is present, is found—this is what is meant. 'I might be one who has fallen into an offense' (āpanno assaṃ) means 'I might be one who has fallen into an offense.' 'And may the monks not know me' (na ca maṃ bhikkhū jāneyyuṃ) means 'And may the monks not know me.' What is the condition here? The desire for gain. For a monk who desires gain, and who by nature has made merit and is honored and respected by people, thinks thus: 'The elder monks, upon knowing a monk who has fallen into an offense, inform the middle-ranking monks; they inform the junior monks; the junior monks inform the eaters of leftovers and others in the monastery; they inform the nuns who have come for an exhortation. In this way, the fourfold assembly gradually comes to know. Thus, his gain is endangered. Oh, that I might indeed fall into an offense, and that the monks might not know me!'

Yaṃ taṃ bhikkhuṃ bhikkhū jāneyyunti yena kāraṇena taṃ bhikkhuṃ aññe bhikkhū jāneyyuṃ, taṃ kāraṇaṃ vijjati kho pana atthiyeva, no natthi. Therā hi ñatvā majjhimānaṃ ārocenti. Evaṃ so pubbe vuttanayena catūsu parisāsu pākaṭo hoti. Evaṃ pākaṭo ca ayasābhibhūto gāmasatampi pavisitvā ummārasatesu ṭhānesu uñchitvā yathādhotena pattena nikkhamati. Tato jānanti maṃ bhikkhū āpattiṃ āpannoti tehi camhi evaṃ nāsitoti cintetvā, iti so kupito hoti appatīto so iminā kāraṇena kupito ceva hoti kodhābhibhūto appatīto ca domanassābhibhūto.

The phrase 'That the monks would know that monk' (yaṃ taṃ bhikkhuṃ bhikkhū jāneyyuṃ) means: the cause by which other monks would know that monk. That cause indeed exists; it is not that it does not exist. For the elders, knowing, inform the middle-ranking monks. Thus, in the manner previously stated, he becomes well-known in the four assemblies. Being thus well-known and overcome by ill-repute, even after entering a hundred villages and gleaning at a hundred door-sills, he departs with his bowl just as it was washed. Then, thinking, 'The monks know of me that I have fallen into an offense, and I have been thus destroyed by them,' he becomes angry and displeased. For this reason, that monk is both angry and overcome by anger, and displeased and overcome by dejection.

Yo ceva kho[P 1.0144], āvuso, kopo yo ca appaccayo ubhayametaṃ aṅgaṇanti, āvuso, yo cāyaṃ saṅkhārakkhandhasaṅgahito kopo, yo ca vedanākkhandhasaṅgahito appaccayo, etaṃ ubhayaṃ aṅgaṇanti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Idañca tādisānaṃ puggalānaṃ vasena vuttaṃ. Lobho pana imassa aṅgaṇassa pubbabhāgavasena, moho sampayogavasenāpi gahitoyeva hoti.

Regarding the phrase 'Friend, both anger and displeasure, these two are a stain': Friend, whatever anger is included in the aggregate of formations, and whatever displeasure is included in the aggregate of feeling, both these are called a stain. Thus should the meaning be understood here. This, too, was spoken with reference to such persons. Greed, however, is included by way of being in the preceding stage of this stain, and delusion is also included by way of association.

Anuraho [V 1.0154] manti purimasadisameva bhikkhuṃ gahetvā vihārapaccante senāsanaṃ pavesetvā dvāraṃ thaketvā codente icchati. Ṭhānaṃ kho panetanti etaṃ kāraṇaṃ vijjati, yaṃ taṃ bhikkhuṃ catuparisamajjhe ānetvā byattā vinītā “tayā asukamhi nāma ṭhāne vejjakammaṃ kata”ntiādinā nayena codeyyuṃ. So catūsu parisāsu pākaṭo hoti. Evaṃ pākaṭo ca ayasābhibhūtoti sabbaṃ purimasadisameva.

He wishes to admonish in private: he wishes to accuse a monk just as in the previous case, having taken him, led him into a dwelling in a remote part of the monastery, and shut the door. 'However, this condition exists': this cause exists, that expert and disciplined monks, having brought that monk into the midst of the fourfold assembly, might accuse him in the manner of, 'You performed a medical practice at such-and-such a place,' and so on. He becomes notorious in the four assemblies. Being thus notorious and overcome by ill-repute—all this is just the same as the previous case.

Sappaṭipuggaloti [M 1.0149] samāno puggalo. Samānoti sāpattiko. Paṭipuggaloti codako. Ayaṃ sāpattikeneva codanaṃ icchati, tvampi imañcimañca āpattiṃ āpanno, taṃ tāva paṭikarohi pacchā maṃ codessasīti vattuṃ sakkāti maññamāno. Apica jātiādīhipi samāno puggalo sappaṭipuggalo. Ayañhi attano jātiyā kulena bāhusaccena byattatāya dhutaṅgenāti evamādīhipi samāneneva codanaṃ icchati, tādisena vuttaṃ nātidukkhaṃ hotīti maññamāno. Appaṭipuggaloti ettha ayutto paṭipuggalo appaṭipuggalo. Imehi āpattādīhi asadisattā paṭisattu paṭisallo codako bhavituṃ ayuttoti vuttaṃ hoti. Iti so kupitoti iti so imāya appaṭipuggalacodanāya evaṃ kupito hoti.

'With a counterpart' means an equal person. 'Equal' means one who has committed an offense. 'Counterpart' means the accuser. This monk desires accusation only by one who has also committed an offense, thinking, 'It is possible to say: “You too have fallen into this and that offense. First, atone for that; afterwards, you may accuse me.”' Furthermore, a person who is equal in birth and other such things is 'with a counterpart.' For this monk desires accusation only by one who is his equal in birth, family, great learning, cleverness, ascetic practices, and so on, thinking, 'Words spoken by such a one are not too painful.' In the term 'without a counterpart,' an unsuitable counterpart is a 'non-counterpart.' It is meant that because of being dissimilar in these things, such as having committed an offense, he is unsuitable to be an accuser, being an adversary, a thorn. 'Thus he is angered' means: that monk becomes angered precisely because of this accusation by a non-counterpart.

Catutthavāre aho vatāti “aho vata re amhākaṃ paṇḍitakā, aho vata re amhākaṃ bahussutakā tevijjakā”ti (dī. ni. 1.291) garahāyaṃ dissati. “Aho vata maṃ daharaṃyeva samānaṃ rajje abhisiñceyyu”nti (mahāva. 57) patthanāyaṃ. Idha patthanāyameva. Paṭipucchitvā paṭipucchitvāti punappunaṃ pucchitvā. Ayaṃ bhikkhu lābhatthiko bhagavato attānaṃ paṭipucchitabbaṃ icchati, tañca kho anumatipucchāya, no maggaṃ vā phalaṃ vā vipassanaṃ vā antaraṃ katvā. Ayañhi passati bhagavantaṃ sāriputtādayo mahāthere “taṃ kiṃ maññasi, sāriputta, moggallāna, kassapa[P 1.0145], rāhula cakkhuṃ niccaṃ vā aniccaṃ vā”ti evaṃ parisamajjhe paṭipucchitvā paṭipucchitvā dhammaṃ desentaṃ, manusse ca “tesa paṇḍitā therā satthu cittaṃ ārādhentī”ti vaṇṇaṃ bhaṇante, lābhasakkārañca upaharante. Tasmā taṃ lābhasakkāraṃ icchanto evaṃ cintetvā nikhaṇitvā ṭhapitakhāṇu viya bhagavato puratova hoti.

In the fourth instance, the expression 'aho vata' is seen in the sense of censure, as in: 'Alas, friends, for our wise ones! Alas, friends, for our learned ones, masters of the three Vedas!' It is also seen in the sense of aspiration, as in: 'Oh, that they would anoint me king while I am still young!' Here, it is used only in the sense of aspiration. 'Having questioned and questioned' means having asked again and again. This gain-desiring monk wishes that the Blessed One would question him, and he wishes to be questioned with a question seeking approval, not one that makes a distinction regarding the path, the fruit, or insight. For he sees the Blessed One teaching the Dhamma by repeatedly questioning the great elders such as Sāriputta and others in the midst of the assembly, saying, 'What do you think, Sāriputta, Moggallāna, Kassapa, Rāhula, is the eye permanent or impermanent?' And he sees people praising their virtues, saying, 'Those elders are wise; they delight the Teacher’s mind,' and bringing offerings of gain and honor. Therefore, desiring that gain and honor, he thinks thus and stands right before the Blessed One like a post that has been dug in and set up.

Iti so kupitoti atha bhagavā taṃ amanasikaritvāva aññaṃ theraṃ paṭipucchitvā dhammaṃ deseti[V 1.0155], tena so kupito hoti bhagavato ca therassa ca. Kathaṃ bhagavato kuppati? “Ahaṃ pabbajitakālato pabhuti gandhakuṭipariveṇato bahinikkhamanaṃ na jānāmi, sabbakālaṃ chāyāva na vijahāmi, maṃ nāma pucchitvā dhammadesanāmattampi natthi. Taṃmuhuttaṃ diṭṭhamattakameva theraṃ pucchitvā dhammaṃ desetī”ti evaṃ bhagavato kuppati. Kathaṃ therassa kuppati? “Ayaṃ mahallakatthero bhagavato purato khāṇu [M 1.0150] viya nisīdati, kadā nu kho imaṃ dhammakammikā abhabbaṭṭhānaṃ pāpetvā nīharissanti, ayañhi yadi imasmiṃ vihāre na bhaveyya, avassaṃ bhagavā mayā saddhiṃ sallapeyyā”ti evaṃ therassa kuppati.

'Thus he is angered' means: Then the Blessed One, disregarding him, questions another elder and teaches the Dhamma. Because of this, he becomes angry with both the Blessed One and the elder. How is he angry with the Blessed One? 'From the time of my going forth, I have not known of leaving the precinct of the Perfumed Chamber. At all times, I do not leave him, like a shadow. Yet there is not even the mere teaching of the Dhamma after questioning me by name. He questions and teaches the Dhamma to an elder who has only just been seen for a moment!' Thus he is angry with the Blessed One. How is he angry with the elder? 'This old elder sits before the Blessed One like a tree stump. When, I wonder, will the monks who perform the Dhamma-act make him reach an unsuitable state and expel him? Indeed, if this old elder were not in this monastery, the Blessed One would surely converse with me!' Thus he is angry with the elder.

Purakkhatvā purakkhatvāti purato purato katvā, samparivāretvāti vuttaṃ hoti. Ayampi lābhatthikoyeva, ayañhi passati bahussute bhikkhū mahāparivārena gāmaṃ pavisante, cetiyaṃ vandante, tesañca taṃ sampattiṃ disvā upāsake pasanne pasannākāraṃ karonte. Tasmā evaṃ icchati. Kupitoti ayampi dvīsu ṭhānesu kuppati bhikkhūnaṃ therassa ca. Kathaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ? “Ime yadeva mayhaṃ uppajjati cīvaraṃ vā piṇḍapāto vā, taṃ gahetvā paribhuñjanti, mayhaṃ pana pattacīvaraṃ gahetvā piṭṭhito āgacchantopi natthī”ti evaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ kuppati. Kathaṃ therassa? “Eso mahallakatthero tesu tesu ṭhānesu sayameva paññāyati, kudāssu nāma naṃ dhammakammikā nikkaḍḍhissanti, imasmiṃ asati avassaṃ maṃyeva parivāressantī”ti.

'Having placed in front, having placed in front' means having placed them at the very front; it means 'having surrounded.' This monk, too, is one who desires gain. For this monk sees learned monks entering a village with a large retinue and paying homage at a cetiya, and seeing their success and the pleased lay devotees making gestures of faith, he therefore desires the same. 'He is angry' means this monk also becomes angry on two accounts: with the monks and with the elder. How with the monks? 'These monks take and consume whatever robe or alms-food arises for me, but for me, there is not even a single person who follows behind carrying my bowl and robe.' Thus he is angry with the monks. How with the elder? 'That old elder is prominent by himself in those various places. When, I wonder, will the monks who perform the Dhamma-act expel him? When he is not present, they will surely attend upon me!' Thus he is angry.

Bhattaggeti bhojanaṭṭhāne. Aggāsananti saṅghattherāsanaṃ. Aggodakanti dakkhiṇodakaṃ. Aggapiṇḍanti saṅghattherapiṇḍaṃ. Sabbattha vā agganti paṇītādhivacanametaṃ. Tattha ahameva labheyyanti icchā nātimahāsāvajjā. Na añño bhikkhu labheyyāti pana atimahāsāvajjā[P 1.0146]. Ayampi lābhatthiko pāsādiko hoti cīvaradhāraṇādīhi, kadāci pabbajati, kadāci vibbhamati. Tena so pubbe laddhapubbaṃ āsanādiṃ pacchā alabhanto evaṃ cintesi. Na so bhikkhu labheyyāti na so bhikkhu therānaṃ aggāsanādīsu tadanusārena majjhimānaṃ aññesañca navānaṃ kadāci yaṃ vā taṃ vā sabbanihīnaṃ āsanādiṃ labhati. Kupitoti ayampi dvīsu ṭhānesu kuppati manussānañca therānañca. Kathaṃ manussānaṃ? “Ime maṅgalādīsu maṃ nissāya bhikkhū labhanti, ete, ‘bhante, ettake bhikkhū gahetvā amhākaṃ anukampaṃ karothā’ti vadanti, idāni taṃmuhuttaṃ diṭṭhamattakaṃ mahallakattheraṃ gahetvā gatā, hotu idāni, nesaṃ kicce uppanne jānissāmī”ti evaṃ [V 1.0156] manussānaṃ kuppati. Kathaṃ therānaṃ? “Ime nāma yadi na bhaveyyuṃ, maṃyeva manussā nimanteyyu”nti evaṃ therānaṃ kuppati.

'At the meal-hall' means at the place for eating. 'The chief seat' means the seat of the Saṅgha elder. 'The chief water' means the dedicatory water. 'The chief alms-food' means the alms-food for the Saṅgha elder. Alternatively, in all instances, 'agga' is a term for what is excellent. Therein, the desire 'May I myself receive it' is not very blameworthy. But the desire 'May no other monk receive it' is extremely blameworthy. This monk who desires gain is also of pleasing appearance through his wearing of robes and so on; sometimes he goes forth, sometimes he leaves the monkhood. Because of this, that monk, having previously received the chief seat and so on, but not receiving it later, thought thus. The phrase 'May that monk not receive it' is explained: that monk does not receive the chief seats of the elders, nor, following them, those of the middle and new monks; sometimes he receives only whatever most inferior seat there is. 'He is angry' means this one also becomes angry in two instances: with the laypeople and with the elders. How with the laypeople? 'On auspicious occasions and so on, these people get monks because of me. They say, "Venerable sir, please show compassion to us by bringing this many monks." Now they have approached the old elder who was only seen for a moment, and have gone. Let it be. When a need arises for them, I will know!' Thus, he is angry with the laypeople. How with the elders? 'If these elders did not exist, the laypeople would surely invite me!' Thus, he is angry with the elders.

Anumodeyyanti [M 1.0151] anumodanaṃ kareyyaṃ. Ayampi lābhatthiko yaṃ vā taṃ vā khaṇḍānumodanaṃ jānāti, “so anumodanaṭṭhāne bahū mātugāmā āgacchanti, tā maṃ sañjānitvā tato pabhuti thālakabhikkhaṃ dassantī”ti patthento evaṃ cintesi. Ṭhānanti bahussutānaṃ anumodanā bhāro, tena bahussuto anumodeyyāti vuttaṃ hoti. Kupitoti ayampi tīsu ṭhānesu kuppati manussānaṃ therassa dhammakathikassa ca. Kathaṃ manussānaṃ? “Ime pubbe maṃyeva upasaṅkamitvā yācanti ‘amhākaṃ nāgatthero amhākaṃ sumanatthero anumodatū’ti, ajja pana nāvocu”nti evaṃ manussānaṃ kuppati. Kathaṃ therassa? “Ayaṃ saṅghatthero ‘tumhākaṃ kulupakaṃ nāgattheraṃ sumanattheraṃ upasaṅkamatha, ayaṃ anumodissatī’ti na bhaṇatī”ti evaṃ therassa kuppati. Kathaṃ dhammakathikassa? “Therena vuttamatteyeva pahāraṃ laddhakukkuṭo viya turitaturitaṃ vassati, imaṃ nāma nikkaḍḍhantā natthi, imasmiñhi asati ahameva anumodeyya”nti evaṃ dhammakathikassa kuppati.

'They should give thanks' means they should perform the giving of thanks. This monk who desires gain knows some or other fragmentary giving of thanks. Aspiring, he thought thus: 'Many women come to the place for the giving of thanks. Recognizing me, from then on they will give me alms cooked in a pot.' 'It is the responsibility' means that for the learned, the giving of thanks is a responsibility; therefore, it is said, 'A learned one should give thanks.' 'He is angry' means this one also becomes angry in three instances: with the laypeople, with the elder, and with the Dhamma-preacher. How with the laypeople? 'Previously, these people would approach me and request, "Let our Elder Nāga, our Elder Sumana, give thanks." But today, they did not say so.' Thus, he is angry with the laypeople. How with the elder? 'This Saṅgha elder does not say, "Approach your family's preceptor, Elder Nāga or Elder Sumana; he will give thanks."' Thus, he is angry with the elder. How with the Dhamma-preacher? 'As soon as he is spoken to by the elder, he preaches very hastily, like a rooster that has been struck. There is no one to expel this one. Indeed, if he were not present, I myself would surely give thanks.' Thus, he is angry with the Dhamma-preacher.

Ārāmagatānanti vihāre sannipatitānaṃ. Ayampi lābhatthiko yaṃ vā taṃ vā khaṇḍadhammakathaṃ jānāti, so passati tādisesu ṭhānesu dviyojanatiyojanato sannipatitvā bhikkhū sabbarattikāni dhammassavanāni suṇante, tuṭṭhacitte [P 1.0147] ca dahare vā sāmaṇere vā sādhu sādhūti mahāsaddena sādhukāraṃ dente, tato dutiyadivase antogāmagate bhikkhū upāsakā pucchanti “ke, bhante, dhammaṃ kathesu”nti. Te bhaṇanti “asuko ca asuko cā”ti. Taṃ sutvā pasannā manussā dhammakathikānaṃ mahāsakkāraṃ karonti. So taṃ icchamāno evaṃ cintesi. Ṭhānanti bahussutānaṃ vinicchayakusalānaṃ dhammadesanā bhāro, tena bahussuto deseyyāti vuttaṃ hoti. Kupitoti catuppadikaṃ gāthampi vattuṃ okāsaṃ alabhamāno kupito hoti attano mandabhāvassa “ahañhi mando duppañño kuto labhissāmi desetu”nti.

‘Of those gone to the monastery’ means of the monks gathered in the monastery. This gain-seeker, too, knows some fragmentary Dhamma talk or other. He sees that in such places, monks, having gathered from two or three yojanas away, listen to Dhamma hearings throughout the night; and with delighted minds, young monks or novices give a great shout of approval, saying, ‘Excellent, excellent!’ Then, on the following day, when the monks have gone into the village, lay followers ask, ‘Venerable sirs, who preached the Dhamma?’ They reply, ‘So-and-so and so-and-so.’ Hearing this, the faithful people make great offerings to the Dhamma-preachers. Desiring that, he thinks thus. ‘The occasion’ means: the preaching of the Dhamma is the burden of the very learned who are skilled in resolving questions; therefore, it is meant that a learned one should preach. ‘He is angry’ means: being unable to get an opportunity to speak even a four-lined verse, he becomes angry because of his own dullness, thinking, ‘I am dull and unwise; how will I get to preach?’

Bhikkhunīnanti ovādatthaṃ vā uddesatthaṃ vā paripucchatthaṃ vā pūjākaraṇatthaṃ vā ārāmaṃ āgantvā sannipatitabhikkhunīnaṃ. Ayampi lābhatthiko, tassevaṃ hoti imā mahākulā pabbajitā bhikkhuniyo, tāsu kulesu pavisetvā nisinnāsu manussā pucchissanti “kassa santike [V 1.0157] ovādaṃ vā uddesaṃ vā paripucchaṃ vā gaṇhathā”ti. Tato vakkhanti “asuko nāma ayyo [M 1.0152] bahussuto, tassa detha karothā”ti, tenassa evaṃ icchā uppajjati. Ṭhānanti ovādādayo nāma bahussutānaṃ bhāro, tena bahussuto deseyyāti vuttaṃ hoti. Kupitoti ayampi dvīsu ṭhānesu kuppati, tāsañca bhikkhunīnaṃ “imā pubbe maṃ nissāya uposathappavāraṇādīni labhanti, tā idāni taṃmuhuttaṃ diṭṭhamattakamahallakattherassa santikaṃ gatā”ti. Dhammakathikassa ca “esa imāsaṃ sahasā ovādaṃ adāsiyevā”ti.

‘Of the nuns’ means of the assembled nuns who have come to the monastery for the purpose of receiving admonition, or learning the Pāḷi, or learning the commentary, or making offerings. This monk, too, is a gain-seeker. A thought like this occurs to him: ‘These nuns have gone forth from great families. When they have entered those families and are seated, people will ask, “From whom do you receive admonition, or learn the Pāḷi, or learn the commentary?” Then they will say, “The venerable one named so-and-so is very learned; give to him, pay respect to him.”’ Thus, such a desire arises in him. ‘The occasion’ means: giving admonition and so forth is the burden of the very learned. Therefore, it is meant that a very learned one should preach. ‘He is angry’ means: this monk becomes angry on two grounds. He is angry at those nuns, thinking: ‘Previously, these nuns, relying on me, received the observances of Uposatha, Pavāraṇā, and so on. Now they have gone to an elder whom they have only just seen for a moment.’ And he is angry at the Dhamma-preacher, thinking: ‘This one hastily gave admonition to them.’

Upāsakānanti, ārāmagatānaṃ upāsakānaṃ. Nissaṭṭhakammantā nāma mahāupāsakā honti, te puttabhātukānaṃ kammaṃ niyyātetvā dhammaṃ suṇantā vicaranti, ayaṃ tesaṃ desetuṃ icchati, kiṃ kāraṇā? Ime pasīditvā upāsikānampi ārocessanti, tato saddhiṃ upāsikāhi mayhameva lābhasakkāraṃ upaharissantīti. Ṭhānaṃ bahussuteneva yojetabbaṃ. Kupitoti ayampi dvīsu ṭhānesu kuppati, upāsakānañca “ime aññattha suṇanti, amhākaṃ kulupakassa santike suṇāmāti nāgacchanti, hotu idāni, tesaṃ uppanne kicce jānissāmī”ti dhammakathikassa ca, “ayametesaṃ desetī”ti.

‘Of the laymen’ means of the laymen who have come to the monastery. There are great laymen called ‘those who have relinquished their work’; having entrusted their work to their sons and brothers, they wander about listening to the Dhamma. This monk desires to preach to them. For what reason? ‘These men, being pleased, will also inform the laywomen, and then, together with the laywomen, they will surely bring gain and honor to me alone.’ ‘The occasion’ should be connected only with a very learned one. ‘He is angry’ means: this monk also becomes angry on two grounds. At the laymen, thinking: ‘These men listen elsewhere; they do not come thinking, “Let us listen in the presence of our family’s preceptor.” Let it be for now; when some business arises for them, I shall know.’ And at the Dhamma-preacher, thinking: ‘This one is preaching to them.’

Upāsikānanti [P 1.0148] ārāmagatānaṃ. Upāsikā nāma āsanapūjādikaraṇatthaṃ vā uposathadivase vā dhammassavanatthaṃ sannipatitā. Sesaṃ upāsakavāre vuttanayameva.

‘Of the laywomen’ means of those who have gone to the monastery. Laywomen are those who have assembled either for the purpose of making offerings of seats and so on, or on an Uposatha day to hear the Dhamma. The remainder is just according to the method already stated in the section on laymen.

Sakkareyyunti sakkaccañca kareyyuṃ, sundarañca kareyyuṃ. Iminā attani kāraṃ karīyamānaṃ sakkaccaṃ katañca sundarañca pattheti. Garuṃ kareyyunti bhāriyaṃ kareyyuṃ. Iminā bhikkhūhi attānaṃ garuṭṭhāne ṭhapīyamānaṃ pattheti. Māneyyunti piyāyeyyuṃ. Pūjeyyunti evaṃ sakkarontā garuṃ karontā mānentā paccayehi pūjeyyunti paccayapūjaṃ pattheti. Ṭhānanti “piyo garu bhāvaniyo”ti vuttappakāro bahussuto ca sīlavā ca etaṃ vidhiṃ arahati tena bhikkhū evarūpaṃ evaṃ kareyyunti vuttaṃ hoti. Kupitoti ayampi dvīsu ṭhānesu kuppati bhikkhūnañca “ime etaṃ sakkarontī”ti therassa ca “imasmiṃ asati maṃyeva sakkareyyu”nti. Esa nayo ito paresu tīsu vāresu.

‘They should honor’ means they should act respectfully and they should act excellently. By this, he desires the honor rendered to himself to be done respectfully and excellently. ‘They should respect’ means they should treat him as important. By this, he desires to be placed in a position of respect by the monks. ‘They should esteem’ means they should hold him dear. ‘They should venerate’ means: ‘While thus honoring, respecting, and esteeming, may they venerate with requisites’—thus he desires veneration with requisites. ‘The occasion’ means: a very learned and virtuous monk of the type described as ‘dear, respected, and to be developed’ is worthy of this treatment. Therefore, it is meant that monks should treat such a one in this way. ‘He is angry’ means: this monk also becomes angry on two grounds. At the monks, thinking: ‘These monks honor him.’ And at the elder, thinking: ‘If this one were not present, they would surely honor me.’ This same method should be understood in the three sections that follow.

Paṇītānaṃ [M 1.0153][V 1.0158] cīvarānanti paṭṭadukūlapaṭṭuṇṇakoseyyādīnaṃ mahagghasukhumasukhasamphassānaṃ cīvarānaṃ. Idhāpi ahameva lābhī assanti icchā nātimahāsāvajjā. Na añño bhikkhu lābhī assāti pana mahāsāvajjā.

‘Of exquisite robes’ means of robes such as those made of silk, fine linen, woollen cloth, or silk cloth, which are of great value, delicate, and pleasant to the touch. Here too, the desire, ‘May I alone be the recipient,’ is not very blameworthy. But the desire, ‘May no other monk be the recipient,’ is very blameworthy.

Paṇītānaṃ piṇḍapātānanti sappitelamadhusakkarādipūritānaṃ seṭṭhapiṇḍapātānaṃ. Paṇītānaṃ senāsanānanti anekasatasahassagghanakānaṃ mañcapīṭhādīnaṃ paṇītānaṃ. Gilānappaccayabhesajjaparikkhārānanti sappitelamadhuphāṇitādīnaṃ uttamabhesajjānaṃ. Sabbatthāpi ṭhānaṃ bahussutehi puññavantehi ca yojetabbaṃ. Kupitoti sabbatthāpi dvīsu ṭhānesu kuppati, manussānañca “imesaṃ nāma paricitabhāvopi natthi, dīgharattaṃ ekato vasantassa paṃsukūlatthāya vā piṇḍapātatthāya vā sappitelādikāraṇā vā gharapaṭipāṭiyā carantassāpi me ekadivasampi kiñci paṇītaṃ paccayaṃ na denti. Āgantukaṃ mahallakaṃ pana disvāva yaṃ icchati, taṃ dentī”ti, therassa ca “ayampi mahallako imesaṃ attānaṃ dassentoyeva carati, kudāssu nāma naṃ dhammakammikā nikkaḍḍheyyuṃ, evaṃ imasmiṃ asati ahameva lābhī assa”nti.

‘Of exquisite almsfood’ means of the best almsfood, filled with ghee, oil, honey, sugar, and so on. ‘Of exquisite lodgings’ means of beds, chairs, and so on, worth many hundreds of thousands. ‘Of exquisite medicinal requisites for the sick’ means of the best medicines, such as ghee, oil, honey, and molasses. In all these cases, ‘the occasion’ should be connected with those who are very learned and those who are meritorious. ‘He is angry’ means: in all these cases, he becomes angry on two grounds. At the people, thinking: ‘These people have no sense of familiarity. Though I have lived together with them for a long time, going from house to house for the sake of rag-robes, or for almsfood, or for reasons of ghee, oil, and so on, they do not give me any exquisite requisite, not even for a single day. But as soon as they see a visiting elder, they give whatever requisite he desires.’ And at the elder, thinking: ‘This elder, too, goes about only showing himself to these people. When on earth will the monks who perform legal acts expel him? It would be good! Thus, if this elder were not present, I alone would surely be the recipient.’”

Imesaṃ kho, etaṃ āvusoti imesaṃ heṭṭhā ekūnavīsativārehi vuttānaṃ icchāvacarānaṃ.

‘Indeed, friends, this is of these’ refers to these spheres of evil desire spoken of in the nineteen sections above.

61. Dissanti ceva sūyanti cāti [P 1.0149] na icchāvacarā cakkhunā dissanti, na sotena sūyanti, manoviññāṇavisayattā. Appahīnaicchāvacarassa pana puggalassa icchāvacaravasena pavattakāyakammaṃ disvā diṭṭhā viya vacīkammaṃ sutvā sutā viya ca honti, tena vuttaṃ “dissanti ceva sūyanti cā”ti. Paccakkhakāle dissanti, “asuko kira bhikkhu īdiso”ti tirokkhakāle sūyanti. Kiñcāpīti anuggahagarahavacanaṃ. Tena āraññikattaṃ anuggaṇhāti, icchāvacarānaṃ appahānaṃ garahati.

61. “They are seen and they are heard”: It is not that evil desires are seen with the eye or heard with the ear, for they are objects of mind-consciousness. However, for a person whose evil desires are unabandoned, upon seeing the bodily actions and hearing the verbal actions that arise from those evil desires, it is as if the desires themselves are seen and heard. Therefore, it is said, “They are seen and they are heard.” They are seen in the present moment, at the time of direct perception; they are heard of when out of sight, as when it is said, “That monk is said to be of such a nature.” The word “kiñcāpi” (even though) is a statement of both commendation and censure. By it, the Buddha commends the state of being a forest-dweller and censures the non-abandonment of evil desires.

Tatrāyaṃ yojanā, kiñcāpi so bhikkhu gāmantasenāsanaṃ paṭikkhipitvā āraññiko hoti, ante pantasenāsane vasati, ime cassa ettakā icchāvacarā appahīnā. Kiñcāpi so atirekalābhaṃ paṭikkhipitvā piṇḍapātiko [M 1.0154] hoti. Kiñcāpi so loluppacāraṃ vajjetvā sapadānacārī hoti. Kiñcāpi so gahapaticīvaraṃ paṭikkhipitvā paṃsukūliko hoti.

Herein, this is the application: Even though that monk, having rejected a dwelling near a village, becomes a forest-dweller and lives in a remote, secluded lodging, still for him these many evil desires remain unabandoned. Even though that monk, having rejected extra gains, becomes one who eats only alms-food. Even though that monk, having avoided greedy wandering, becomes one who goes on an uninterrupted alms-round. Even though that monk, having rejected robes given by householders, becomes a wearer of rag-robes.

Lūkhacīvaradharoti [V 1.0159] ettha pana lūkhanti satthalūkhaṃ suttalūkhaṃ rajanalūkhanti tīhi kāraṇehi lūkhaṃ veditabbaṃ. Tattha satthena khaṇḍākhaṇḍikaṃ chinnaṃ satthalūkhaṃ nāma, taṃ agghena parihāyati, thūladīghasuttakena sibbitaṃ suttalūkhaṃ nāma, taṃ phassena parihāyati kharasamphassaṃ hoti. Rajanena rattaṃ rajanalūkhaṃ nāma, taṃ vaṇṇena parihāyati dubbaṇṇaṃ hoti. Kiñcāpi so bhikkhu evaṃ satthalūkhasuttalūkharajanalūkhacīvaradharo hoti, ime cassa ettakā icchāvacarā appahīnā dissanti ceva sūyanti ca, atha kho naṃ viññū sabrahmacārī neva sakkaronti…pe… na pūjentīti. Taṃ kissa hetūti ettha tanti nipātamattaṃ, kissa hetūti kiṃ kāraṇā. Te hi tassa…pe… sūyanti ca yasmā tassa te pāpakā sūyanti cāti vuttaṃ hoti. Imesaṃ icchāvacarānaṃ appahīnattāti ayamettha adhippāyo.

Regarding the phrase “wearer of rough robes,” “rough” should be understood as being so for three reasons: rough due to a knife, rough due to thread, and rough due to dye. Therein, a robe cut into pieces with a knife is called “rough due to a knife”; it is diminished in value. A robe sewn with coarse, long thread is called “rough due to thread”; it is diminished in its feel, becoming harsh to the touch. A robe dyed with dye is called “rough due to dye”; it is diminished in its appearance, becoming unattractive in color. Even though that monk is a wearer of robes that are rough due to a knife, rough due to thread, and rough due to dye, for him these many unabandoned evil desires are seen and heard. Therefore, his wise fellows in the holy life neither honor him… nor revere him. Regarding “For what reason?”: here, “taṃ” is a mere particle. “Kissa hetu” means “for what reason?” For it is said, “Because for him, those evil desires are heard of.” The intention here is: “due to the non-abandonment of these evil desires.”

Idāni tamatthaṃ upamāya pākaṭaṃ karonto seyyathāpītiādimāha. Tattha kuṇapanti matakaḷevaraṃ. Ahissa kuṇapaṃ ahikuṇapaṃ. Evaṃ itarāni. Atipaṭikūlajigucchanīyabhāvato cettha imāneva tīṇi vuttānīti veditabbāni. Aññesañhi sasasūkarādīnaṃ kuṇapaṃ manussā kaṭukabhaṇḍādīhi abhisaṅkharitvā paribhuñjantipi. Imesaṃ pana kuṇapaṃ abhinavampi jigucchantiyeva, ko pana vādo kālātikkamena pūtibhūte. Racayitvāti vaḍḍhetvā, paripūretvāti attho, kuṇapaṃ gahetvā kaṃsapātiyaṃ pakkhipitvāti vuttaṃ hoti. Aññissāti aparāya. Paṭikujjitvāti pidahitvā[P 1.0150]. Antarāpaṇanti āpaṇānamantare mahājanasaṃkiṇṇaṃ racchāmukhaṃ. Paṭipajjeyyunti gaccheyyuṃ. Jaññajaññaṃ viyāti cokkhacokkhaṃ viya manāpamanāpaṃ viya. Apica vadhukāpaṇṇākāraṃ viyāti vuttaṃ hoti. Vadhukāti janetti vuccati, tassā nīyamānaṃ paṇṇākāraṃ jaññaṃ, ubhayatthāpi ādaravasena vā pasaṃsāvasena vā punaruttaṃ. “Jaññajaññaṃ byā”tipi pāṭho.

Now, making that meaning clear with a simile, the Buddha said, “Just as…” and so on. Therein, “carrion” means a dead body. “A snake’s carrion” is the carcass of a snake. Likewise for the others. It should be understood that these three in particular are mentioned here because of their extremely repulsive and disgusting nature. For people prepare and even consume the carrion of other creatures, such as hares and pigs, by seasoning them with spices and so on. But the carrion of these three is disgusting even when fresh; what then needs to be said of it when it has become putrid over time? “Having placed it” means having piled it up, having filled it; that is the meaning. It means: having taken the carrion and placed it in a bronze bowl. “With another” means with a second one. “Having covered it” means having closed it. “In the market street” means on a road between the market stalls, crowded with many people. “They might proceed” means they might go. “Like a fine treasure” means like something very fine, like something very pleasing. Furthermore, it is said to be like a gift for a new bride. A new bride is called a “vadhukā”; a gift brought for her is called a “jañña.” In both interpretations, the repetition is used out of respect or praise. There is also the reading, “jaññaṃ jaññaṃ byā.”

Apāpuritvāti vivaritvā. Tassa saha dassanena amanāpatā ca saṇṭhaheyyāti tassa kuṇapassa dassanena saheva tassa janassa amanāpatā [M 1.0155] tiṭṭheyya. Amanāpatāti ca “amanāpamida”nti uppannacittacetasikānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Esa nayo paṭikulyajegucchatāsu. Jighacchitānampīti chātānampi. Na bhottukamyatā assāti bhuñjitukāmatā na bhaveyya. Pageva suhitānanti dhātānaṃ pana paṭhamatarameva bhuñjitukāmatā na bhaveyyāti vuttaṃ hoti.

“Having uncovered it” means having opened it. “And upon seeing it, displeasure would be established” means that simultaneously with seeing that carrion, displeasure would be established for that person. “Displeasure” is a designation for the mind and mental factors that have arisen with the thought, “This is unpleasant.” This same method applies to revulsion and disgust. “Even for the hungry” means even for those afflicted by hunger. “There would be no desire to eat” means the desire to eat would not arise. “How much more so for the satiated” means that for those who are not hungry, the desire to eat would not arise in the first place.

Tatrāyaṃ [V 1.0160] upamāsaṃsandanā – parisuddhakaṃsapātisadisaṃ imassa pabbajjāliṅgaṃ, kuṇaparacanaṃ viya icchāvacarānaṃ appahānaṃ, aparakaṃsapātiyā paṭikujjhanaṃ viya āraññikaṅgādīhi icchāvacarappaṭicchādanaṃ, kaṃsapātiṃ vivaritvā kuṇapadassanena janassa amanāpatā viya āraññikaṅgādīni anādiyitvā icchāvacaradassanena sabrahmacārīnaṃ asakkārakaraṇāditāti.

Herein, this is the application of the simile: The sign of this monk’s going forth should be seen as being like a pure bronze bowl. The non-abandonment of evil desires should be seen as being like the stench of carrion. The concealing of evil desires by means of the forest-dweller’s ascetic practices and so on should be seen as being like covering the bowl with another bronze bowl. Just as opening the bowl and seeing the carrion causes displeasure among the people, so the lack of respect shown by his fellows in the holy life should be seen as being caused by their disregarding his forest-dweller’s practices and seeing his evil desires.

62. Sukkapakkhe pana, kiñcāpīti anuggahapasaṃsāvacanaṃ, tena āraññikattaṃ anuggaṇhāti, icchāvacarappahānaṃ pasaṃsati. Nemantanikoti nimantanapaṭiggāhako. Vicitakāḷakanti vicinitvā apanītakāḷakaṃ. Anekasūpaṃ anekabyañjananti ettha sūpo nāma hatthahāriyo vuccati. Byañjananti uttaribhaṅgaṃ, tena macchamaṃsamuggasūpādīhi anekasūpaṃ, nānappakāramaṃsādibyañjanehi anekabyañjananti vuttaṃ hoti. Sesaṃ vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ.

62. In the bright portion, however, “kiñcāpi” is a word of commendation and praise. By it, the Buddha commends the state of being a forest-dweller and praises the abandonment of evil desires. “One who accepts invitations” is one who accepts what is offered by invitation. “From which impurities have been picked out” means from which black grains and other impurities have been picked out and removed. Regarding “with many curries and many side dishes”: herein, “curry” (sūpa) refers to what is portable by hand. “Side dish” (byañjana) refers to an additional item. By these two terms, it is meant: “with many curries” such as those made of fish, meat, and beans; and “with many side dishes” such as various kinds of meat dishes. The rest should be understood in the way already explained.

Upamāsaṃsandane ca sālivarabhattaracanaṃ viya icchāvacarappahānaṃ, aparakaṃsapātiyā paṭikujjhanaṃ viya appicchatāsamuṭṭhānehi gāmantavihārādīhi icchāvacarappahānappaṭicchādakaṃ, kaṃsapātiṃ vivaritvā sālivarabhattadassanena janassa manāpatā [P 1.0151] viya gāmantavihārādīni anādiyitvā icchāvacarappahānadassanena sabrahmacārīnaṃ sakkārakaraṇāditā veditabbā.

And in the application of the simile: The abandonment of evil desires should be seen as being like the fragrance of excellent Sāli rice. The concealing of the abandonment of evil desires by means of practices that arise from fewness of wishes, such as dwelling near a village, should be seen as being like covering the bowl with another bronze bowl. Just as opening the bowl and seeing the excellent Sāli rice is pleasing to the people, so the respect shown by his fellows in the holy life should be understood as being caused by their disregarding his practice of dwelling near a village and seeing his abandonment of evil desires.

63. Upamā maṃ, āvuso sāriputta, paṭibhātīti mayhaṃ, āvuso sāriputta, upamā upaṭṭhāti. Ekaṃ upamaṃ vattukāmo ahanti adhippāyo. Paṭibhātu tanti tuyhaṃ paṭibhātu upaṭṭhātu, vada tvanti adhippāyo. Ekamidāhanti ettha idāti nipātamattaṃ, ekasmiṃ samaye ahanti vuttaṃ hoti, bhummatthe upayogavacanaṃ. Rājagahe viharāmi giribbajeti, rājagahanti tassa nagarassa nāmaṃ. Samantato pana giriparikkhepena vajo viya saṇṭhitattā giribbajanti vuccati. Tasmiṃ nagare viharāmi, taṃ nissāya ahaṃ [M 1.0156] viharāmīti vuttaṃ hoti. Atha khvāhanti atha kho ahaṃ. Ettha ca athāti aññādhikāravacanārambhe nipāto. Khoti padapūraṇamatte. Pubbaṇhasamayanti divasassa pubbabhāgasamayaṃ. Pubbaṇhasamayeti attho, pubbaṇhe vā samayaṃ pubbaṇhasamayaṃ, pubbaṇhe ekaṃ khaṇanti vuttaṃ hoti, evaṃ accantasaṃyoge upayogavacanaṃ labbhati. Nivāsetvāti paridahitvā, vihāranivāsanaparivattanavasenetaṃ veditabbaṃ. Gāmappavesanatthāya vā saṇṭhapetvā nivāsanavasena, na hi so tato pubbe anivattho ahosi.

63. “Upamā maṃ, āvuso sāriputta, paṭibhātīti” means: “Friend Sāriputta, a simile occurs to me.” The meaning is: I wish to state a simile. “Paṭibhātu tan ti” means: “Let it occur to you, let it arise; speak.” In “Ekamidāhanti,” “idaṃ” is merely a particle; it means: “I, on one occasion.” The accusative case is used in the sense of the locative. “Rājagahe viharāmi giribbajeti”: “Rājagaha” is the name of that city. Because it is established on all sides with a mountain enclosure like a cattle pen, it is called “Giribbaja.” It means: “I dwell in that city; I dwell relying on it.” “Atha khvāhanti” is “atha kho ahaṃ.” Here, “atha” is a particle for beginning a new topic, and “kho” is merely for filling out the line. “Pubbaṇhasamayaṃ” means the time of the early part of the day. The meaning is the morning time, or “pubbaṇhasamayaṃ” is the time in the morning; it means a certain period in the morning. Thus, the accusative case is found in the sense of continuous connection. “Nivāsetvā” means having put on the lower robe. This should be understood in the sense of changing from the robe worn in the monastery, or in the sense of adjusting and wearing the robe for the purpose of entering a village; for indeed, he was not unclothed before that.

Pattacīvaramādāyāti [V 1.0161] pattaṃ hatthena cīvaraṃ kāyena ādiyitvā. Piṇḍāyāti piṇḍapātatthāya. Samītīti tassa nāmaṃ. Yānakāraputtoti rathakāraputto. Paṇḍuputtoti paṇḍussa putto. Ājīvakoti naggasamaṇako. Purāṇayānakāraputtoti porāṇayānakārakulassa putto. Paccupaṭṭhitoti upagantvā ṭhito. Vaṅkaṃ nāma ekato kuṭilaṃ. Jimhaṃ nāma sappagatamaggasadisaṃ. Dosanti phegguvisamagaṇṭhikādi. Yathā yathāti kālatthe nipāto, yadā yadā yasmiṃ tasmiṃ kāleti vuttaṃ hoti. Tathā tathāti ayampi kālatthoyeva, tasmiṃ tasmiṃ kāleti vuttaṃ hoti. So attano suttānulomena cintesi, itaro tena cintitakkhaṇe cintitaṭṭhānameva tacchati. Attamanoti sakamano tuṭṭhamano pītisomanassehi gahitamano. Attamanavācaṃ nicchāresīti attamanatāya vācaṃ[P 1.0152], attamanabhāvassa vā yuttaṃ vācaṃ nicchāresi udīrayi, pabyāharīti vuttaṃ hoti. Hadayā hadayaṃ maññe aññāyāti cittena cittaṃ jānitvā viya.

“Pattacīvaramādāya” means having taken the bowl with the hand and the robe with the body. “Piṇḍāya” means for the purpose of alms-food. “Samīti” is his name. “Yānakāraputto” means a chariot-maker’s son. “Paṇḍuputto” means the son of Paṇḍu. “Ājīvako” means a naked ascetic. “Purāṇayānakāraputto” means the son of his former chariot-maker family. “Paccupaṭṭhito” means having gone near, he stood. “Vaṅkaṃ” means crooked on one side. “Jimhaṃ” means like the track of a snake’s movement. “Dosaṃ” means sapwood, uneven places, knots, and so on. “Yathā yathā” is a particle in the sense of time; it means: whenever, at whatever time. “Tathā tathā” also has the sense of time; it means: at that very time. He planned in accordance with his chalk line; the other, at the very moment he planned, adzed the very spot he had planned. “Attamano” means one whose mind is his own, a satisfied mind, a mind seized by rapture and gladness. “Attamanavācaṃ nicchāresi” means: because of his delight, he uttered speech, or he uttered speech suitable to his state of delight; it means he uttered, he spoke, he declared. “Hadayā hadayaṃ maññe aññāya” means as if knowing mind with mind.

Assaddhāti buddhadhammasaṅghesu saddhāvirahitā. Jīvikatthāti iṇabhayādīhi pīḷitā bahi jīvituṃ asakkontā idha jīvikatthikā hutvā. Na saddhāti na saddhāya. Saṭhā māyāvinoti māyāsāṭheyyehi yuttā. Ketabinoti sikkhitakerāṭikā, nipphannathāmagatasāṭheyyāti vuttaṃ hoti. Sāṭheyyañhi abhūtaguṇadassanato abhūtabhaṇḍaguṇadassanasamaṃ katvā “kerāṭiya”nti vuccati. Unnaḷāti uggatanaḷā, uṭṭhitatucchamānāti vuttaṃ hoti[M 1.0157]. Capalāti pattacīvaramaṇḍanādinā cāpallena yuttā. Mukharāti mukhakharā, kharavacanāti vuttaṃ hoti, vikiṇṇavācāti asaṃyatavacanā, divasampi niratthakavacanappalāpino. Indriyesu aguttadvārāti chasu indriyesu asaṃvutakammadvārā. Bhojane amattaññunoti bhojane yā mattā jānitabbā pariyesanapaṭiggahaṇaparibhogesu yuttatā, tassā ajānanakā. Jāgariyaṃ ananuyuttāti jāgare ananuyuttā. Sāmaññe anapekkhavantoti samaṇadhamme nirapekkhā, dhammānudhammappaṭipattirahitāti attho. Sikkhāya na tibbagāravāti sikkhāpadesu bahulagāravā na honti, āpattivītikkamabahulā vā. Bāhulikātiādi dhammadāyāde vuttaṃ, kusītātiādi bhayabherave. Dhammapariyāyenāti dhammadesanāya.

“Assaddhā” means those devoid of faith in the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Sangha. “Jīvikatthā” means: being oppressed by debt, fear, and so on, and being unable to make a living outside the Dispensation, they become seekers of a livelihood here. “Na saddhā” means not through faith. “Saṭhā māyāvino” means those endowed with deceit and craftiness. “Keṭubino” means those who have learned craftiness, whose craftiness has reached a state of perfected power. Indeed, because craftiness shows non-existent qualities, it is like showing the qualities of non-existent goods, and for this reason it is called “kerāṭiya.” “Unnaḷā” means having a raised reed of conceit; it means having arisen, empty conceit. “Capalā” means those endowed with fickleness through the adornment of bowl and robes, and so on. “Mukharā” means those with a harsh mouth; it means those with harsh speech. “Vikiṇṇavācā” means those with unrestrained speech, those who are accustomed to speaking useless words all day. “Indriyesu aguttadvārā” means those whose doors of action are unrestrained in the six sense faculties. “Bhojane amattaññuno” means those who do not know the measure that should be known in food—the proper amount for sustenance in seeking, receiving, and consuming. “Jāgariyaṃ ananuyuttā” means those not devoted to the effort of wakefulness. “Sāmaññe anapekkhavanto” means those who have no regard for the duties of a recluse, those devoid of the practice in conformity with the Dhamma; this is the meaning. “Sikkhāya na tibbagāravā” means they do not have much reverence for the training rules, or they are abundant in transgressing offenses. “Bāhulikā,” and so on, is stated in the Dhammadāyāda Sutta; “kusītā,” and so on, in the Bhayabherava Sutta. “Dhammapariyāyena” means by the teaching of the Dhamma.

Saddhā agārasmāti pakatiyāpi saddhā, pabbajitāpi saddhāya agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajitā. Pivanti maññe ghasanti maññeti pivanti viya ghasanti viya. Attamanavācaṃ nicchārentā vacasā pivanti viya, abbhanumodantā manasā ghasanti viya. Sādhu vatāti sundaraṃ vata[V 1.0162]. Sabrahmacārīti rassampi vaṭṭati dīghampi. Rasse sati sāriputtassa upari hoti, dīghe sati sabrahmacārīnaṃ. Yadā sāriputtassa upari hoti, tadā sabrahmacārī sāriputto amhe akusalā vuṭṭhāpetvāti attho. Yadā sabrahmacārīnaṃ, tadā sabrahmacārayo akusalā vuṭṭhāpetvāti attho. Daharoti taruṇo. Yuvāti yobbanabhāve ṭhito. Maṇḍanakajātikoti [P 1.0153] alaṅkārakasabhāvo. Tattha koci taruṇopi yuvā na hoti yathā atitaruṇo, koci yuvāpi maṇḍanakajātiko na hoti yathā upasantasabhāvo, ālasiyabyasanādīhi vā abhibhūto, idha pana daharo ceva yuvā ca maṇḍanakajātiko ca adhippeto, tasmā evamāha. Uppalādīni lokasammatattā vuttāni. Itiha teti evaṃ te. Ubho mahānāgāti dvepi mahānāgā, dvepi hi ete aggasāvakā “mahānāgā”ti vuccanti. Tatrāyaṃ vacanattho, chandādīhi na gacchantīti nāgā, tena tena maggena pahīne kilese na āgacchantīti nāgā, nānappakārakaṃ āguṃ na karontīti nāgā, ayamettha saṅkhepo. Vitthāro pana mahāniddese (mahāni. 80) vuttanayeneva veditabbo. Apica –

“Saddhā agārasmā”: Even those who are faithful by nature, having gone forth, are “those who have gone forth from the household life into homelessness through faith.” “Pivanti maññe ghasanti maññe”: It means “as if they drink, as if they eat.” By uttering words of delight, they are as if drinking with speech; by greatly rejoicing, they are as if eating with the mind. “Sādhu vata”: It means “How wonderful!” “Sabrahmacārī”: Both the short and long vowels are acceptable. When it is short, it modifies Sāriputta; when it is long, it modifies “sabrahmacārīnaṃ.” When it modifies Sāriputta, the meaning is “the fellow practitioner Sāriputta, having raised us from unwholesome states...” When it modifies “sabrahmacārīnaṃ,” the meaning is “having raised the fellow practitioners from unwholesome states...” “Daharo” means young. “Yuvā” means one established in the state of youth. “Maṇḍanakajātiko” means having a nature for adornment. In this context, someone may be young but not youthful, such as one who is very young; someone may be youthful but not of a nature for adornment, such as one with a peaceful disposition or one overcome by laziness, misfortune, and so on. Here, however, one who is young, youthful, and of a nature for adornment is intended; therefore, it is said thus. Lotuses and so on are mentioned because they are considered auspicious by the world. “Itiha te” means “thus those two.” “Ubho mahānāgā” means “both are great nāgas”; indeed, both these chief disciples are called “great nāgas.” Herein, this is the etymological explanation: because they do not go (na gacchanti) by way of desire and so on, they are nāgas; because they do not come back (na āgacchanti) to the defilements abandoned by this or that path, they are nāgas; because they do no (na karonti) wrong (āguṃ) of any kind, they are nāgas. This is the summary here. The detailed explanation, however, should be understood according to the method stated in the Mahāniddesa. Furthermore—

“Āguṃ [M 1.0158] na karoti kiñci loke,

Sabbasaṃyoge visajja bandhanāni;

Sabbattha na sajjatī vimutto,

Nāgo tādi pavuccate tathattā”ti. (su. ni. 527; mahāni. 80);

“He who does no wrong whatsoever in the world, having cast off the bonds of all fetters; liberated, he is not attached anywhere, such a one, due to that state, is called a ‘Nāga’.”

Evamettha attho veditabbo. Mahantā nāgā mahānāgā, aññehi khīṇāsavanāgehi pujjatarā ca pāsaṃsatarā cāti attho. Aññamaññassāti añño aññassa. Samanumodiṃsūti samaṃ anumodiṃsu. Tattha imāya upamāya mahāmoggallāno anumodi, paṭibhātu taṃ āvusoti dhammasenāpati. Tena vuttaṃ “aññamaññassa subhāsitaṃ samanumodiṃsū”ti.

Thus the meaning here should be understood. “Mahānāgā” means great nāgas; the meaning is that they are more worthy of veneration and more worthy of praise than other nāgas who are destroyers of the taints. “Aññamaññassa” means “of one, of another.” “Samanumodiṃsu” means they rejoiced together. Therein, Mahāmoggallāna rejoiced with this simile, and the General of the Dhamma rejoiced with the words beginning, “May it be clear to you, friend...” Therefore, it was said, “They rejoiced in each other’s well-spoken words.”

Sammutiparamatthadesanākathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Discourse on the Teaching of Conventional and Ultimate Truths is concluded.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

Of the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya.

Anaṅgaṇasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Anaṅgaṇa Sutta is concluded.

6. Ākaṅkheyyasuttavaṇṇanā

6. Commentary on the Ākaṅkheyya Sutta

64. Evaṃ [V 1.0163] me sutanti ākaṅkheyyasuttaṃ. Tattha sampannasīlāti tividhaṃ sampannaṃ paripuṇṇasamaṅgimadhuravasena. Tattha –

64. This sutta, beginning with “Thus have I heard,” is the Ākaṅkheyya Sutta. Therein, regarding the term “sampannasīlā,” “sampanna” (accomplishment) is threefold: by way of being complete (paripuṇṇa), being endowed (samaṅgi), and being sweet (madhura). Among these three:

“Sampannaṃ sālikedāraṃ, suvā bhuñjanti kosiya;

Paṭivedemi te brahme, na naṃ vāretumussahe”ti. (jā. 1.14.1);

“The perfected rice-field, O Kosiya, the parrots are eating; I inform you, Brahmin, I am unable to prevent them.”

Idaṃ paripuṇṇasampannaṃ nāma. “Iminā pātimokkhasaṃvarena upeto hoti samupeto upāgato samupāgato upapanno sampanno samannāgato”ti (vibha. 511) idaṃ samaṅgisampannaṃ [P 1.0154] nāma. “Imissā, bhante, mahāpathaviyā heṭṭhimatalaṃ sampannaṃ, seyyathāpi khuddamadhuṃ aneḷakaṃ, evamassāda”nti (pārā. 17) idaṃ madhurasampannaṃ nāma. Idha pana paripuṇṇasampannampi samaṅgisampannampi vaṭṭati. Tasmā sampannasīlāti paripuṇṇasīlā hutvātipi sīlasamaṅgino hutvātipi evamettha attho vedibbo. Sīlanti kenaṭṭhena sīlaṃ? Sīlanaṭṭhena sīlaṃ. Tassa vitthārakathā visuddhimagge vuttā.

This is called `paripuṇṇasampanna` (complete accomplishment). 'With this Pātimokkha restraint one is endowed, well-endowed, arrived, well-arrived, possessed, accomplished, furnished' (Vibh 511)—this is called `samaṅgisampanna` (endowment-accomplishment). 'Venerable sir, the lower surface of this great earth is perfect in flavor, just like honey from small bees, free from impurities; such is its taste' (Pārā 17)—this is called `madhurasampanna` (sweet accomplishment). Here, however, both `paripuṇṇasampanna` and `samaṅgisampanna` are suitable. Therefore, in this context, the meaning of `sampannasīlā` should be understood as both 'having become perfected in virtue' and 'having become endowed with virtue.' In what sense is it `sīla` (virtue)? It is `sīla` in the sense of `sīlana` (composing). The detailed discourse on this has been stated in the Visuddhimagga.

Tattha [M 1.0159] “paripuṇṇasīlā”ti iminā atthena khettadosavigamena khettapāripūrī viya sīladosavigamena sīlapāripūrī vuttā hoti. Yathā hi khettaṃ bījakhaṇḍaṃ vappakhaṇḍaṃ udakakhaṇḍaṃ ūsakhaṇḍanti catudosasamannāgataṃ aparipūraṃ hoti.

Therein, by the meaning 'perfected in virtue' (`paripuṇṇasīlā`), the perfection of virtue through the removal of its defects is spoken of, just like the perfection of a field through the removal of its defects. For a field endowed with four defects—the defect of seed (`bījakhaṇḍa`), the defect of sowing (`vappakhaṇḍa`), the defect of water (`udakakhaṇḍa`), and the defect of saline soil (`ūsakhaṇḍa`)—is incomplete.

Tattha bījakhaṇḍaṃ nāma yattha antarantarā bījāni khaṇḍāni vā pūtīni vā honti, tāni yattha vapanti, tattha sassaṃ na uṭṭheti, khettaṃ khaṇḍaṃ hoti. Vappakhaṇḍaṃ nāma yattha akusalo bījāni vapanto antarantarā nipāteti. Evañhi sabbattha sassaṃ na uṭṭheti, khettaṃ khaṇḍaṃ hoti. Udakakhaṇḍaṃ nāma yattha katthaci udakaṃ atibahu vā na vā hoti, tatrāpi hi sassāni na uṭṭhenti, khettaṃ khaṇḍaṃ hoti. Ūsakhaṇḍaṃ nāma yattha kassako kismiñci padese naṅgalena [V 1.0164] bhūmiṃ cattāro pañca vāre kasanto atigambhīraṃ karoti, tato ūsaṃ uppajjati, tatrāpi hi sassaṃ na uṭṭheti, khettaṃ khaṇḍaṃ hoti, tādisañca khettaṃ na mahapphalaṃ hoti na mahānisaṃsaṃ, tatrāpi hi bahumpi vapitvā appaṃ labhati. Imesaṃ pana catunnaṃ dosānaṃ vigamā khettaṃ paripuṇṇaṃ hoti. Tādisañca khettaṃ mahapphalaṃ hoti mahānisaṃsaṃ. Evameva khaṇḍaṃ chiddaṃ sabalaṃ kammāsanti catudosasamannāgataṃ sīlaṃ aparipūraṃ hoti. Tādisañca sīlaṃ na mahapphalaṃ hoti, na mahānisaṃsaṃ. Imesaṃ pana catunnaṃ dosānaṃ vigamā sīlakhettaṃ paripuṇṇaṃ hoti, tādisañca sīlaṃ mahapphalaṃ hoti mahānisaṃsaṃ.

Therein, `bījakhaṇḍa` (defect of seed) is when, here and there, the seeds are broken or rotten; where they are sown, the crop does not grow, and the field is deficient. `Vappakhaṇḍa` (defect of sowing) is when an unskillful person, sowing seeds, drops them intermittently; thus the crop does not grow everywhere, and the field is deficient. `Udakakhaṇḍa` (defect of water) is when in some place there is either too much water or none at all; there too the crops do not grow, and the field is deficient. `Ūsakhaṇḍa` (defect of saline soil) is when a farmer, plowing the earth in some area with a plough four or five times, makes it too deep, from which saline soil arises; there too the crop does not grow, and the field is deficient. Such a field is not of great fruit, nor of great benefit; even having sown much there, one obtains little. But with the removal of these four defects, the field becomes complete. Such a field is of great fruit and of great benefit. In the very same way, virtue endowed with the four defects—being broken (`khaṇḍa`), perforated (`chidda`), spotted (`sabala`), and mottled (`kammāsa`)—is incomplete. Such virtue is not of great fruit, nor of great benefit. But with the removal of these four defects, the field of virtue becomes complete. Such virtue is of great fruit and of great benefit.

“Sīlasamaṅgino”ti iminā panatthena sīlena samaṅgibhūtā samodhānaṃ gatā samannāgatā hutvā viharathāti idameva vuttaṃ hoti. Tattha dvīhi kāraṇehi sampannasīlatā hoti sīlavipattiyā ca ādīnavadassanena sīlasampattiyā [P 1.0155] ca ānisaṃsadassanena. Tadubhayampi visuddhimagge vitthāritaṃ.

Now, by this meaning 'endowed with virtue' (`sīlasamaṅgino`), this is what is said: 'Dwell, having become endowed with virtue, having come to unification, having become possessed of it.' Therein, accomplishment in virtue comes about for two reasons: by seeing the danger in the corruption of virtue and by seeing the benefit in the accomplishment of virtue. Both of these are elaborated upon in the Visuddhimagga.

Tattha “sampannasīlā”ti ettāvatā kira bhagavā catupārisuddhisīlaṃ uddisitvā “pātimokkhasaṃvarasaṃvutā”ti iminā tattha jeṭṭhakasīlaṃ vitthāretvā dassesīti dīpavihāravāsī sumanatthero āha. Antevāsiko panassa tepiṭakacūḷanāgatthero āha – ubhayatthāpi pātimokkhasaṃvaro bhagavatā vutto, pātimokkhasaṃvaroyeva hi sīlaṃ.
