Itarāni pana tīṇi sīlanti vuttaṭṭhānaṃ nāma atthīti ananujānanto vatvā āha [M 1.0160] – “indriyasaṃvaro nāma chadvārarakkhāmattakameva, ājīvapārisuddhi dhammena samena paccayuppattimattakaṃ, paccayanissitaṃ paṭiladdhapaccaye idamatthanti paccavekkhitvā paribhuñjanamattakaṃ. Nippariyāyena pātimokkhasaṃvarova sīlaṃ. Yassa so bhinno, ayaṃ chinnasīso viya puriso hatthapāde sesāni rakkhissatīti na vattabbo. Yassa pana so arogo, ayaṃ acchinnasīso viya puriso jīvitaṃ sesāni puna pākatikāni katvā rakkhituṃ sakkoti. Tasmā ‘sampannasīlā’ti iminā pātimokkhasaṃvaraṃ uddisitvā ‘sampannapātimokkhā’ti tasseva vevacanaṃ vatvā taṃ vitthāretvā dassento ‘pātimokkhasaṃvarasaṃvutā’tiādimāhā”ti.

Therein, the elder Sumana, a resident of Dīpavihāra, said: 'It seems the Blessed One, having indicated the fourfold purification virtue with the phrase `sampannasīlā`, then elaborated on the principal virtue among them with the phrase `pātimokkhasaṃvarasaṃvutā`.' But his disciple, the elder Tepiṭaka Cūḷanāga, said: 'In both instances, the Pātimokkha restraint was taught by the Blessed One, for the Pātimokkha restraint itself is virtue. As for the other three, while admitting that there is a context where they are called "virtue," he said: "Restraint of the senses (`indriyasaṃvara`) is merely the guarding of the six doors. Purification of livelihood (`ājīvapārisuddhi`) is merely the arising of requisites righteously and equitably. That which is dependent on requisites (`paccayanissita`) is merely using requisites after reflecting, ‘This is for this purpose.’ In the primary sense, only the Pātimokkha restraint is virtue. For whom that is broken, it cannot be said of this person, like one whose head is cut off, that he will protect his hands and feet and other parts. But for whom that is unimpaired, this person, like one whose head is not cut off, is able to restore his life and other parts to their natural state and protect them. Therefore, having indicated the Pātimokkha restraint with `sampannasīlā`, and having stated its synonym `sampannapātimokkhā`, the Blessed One, wishing to elaborate on it, said `pātimokkhasaṃvarasaṃvutā`, and so on.''

Tattha pātimokkhasaṃvarasaṃvutāti pātimokkhasaṃvarena samannāgatā. Ācāragocarasampannāti ācārena [V 1.0165] ca gocarena ca sampannā. Aṇumattesūti appamattakesu. Vajjesūti akusaladhammesu. Bhayadassāvīti bhayadassino. Samādāyāti sammā ādiyitvā. Sikkhatha sikkhāpadesūti sikkhāpadesu taṃ taṃ sikkhāpadaṃ samādiyitvā sikkhatha. Apica samādāya sikkhatha sikkhāpadesūti yaṃkiñci sikkhākoṭṭhāsesu sikkhitabbaṃ kāyikaṃ vācasikañca, taṃ sabbaṃ samādāya sikkhathāti ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthārato pana sabbānetāni pātimokkhasaṃvarādīni padāni visuddhimagge vuttāni.

Therein, `pātimokkhasaṃvarasaṃvutā` means endowed with the Pātimokkha restraint. `Ācāragocarasampannā` means accomplished in both conduct and resort. `Aṇumattesu` means in minute things. `Vajjesu` means in faults, in unwholesome states. `Bhayadassāvī` means seeing danger. `Samādāya` means having rightly undertaken. `Sikkhatha sikkhāpadesu` means: having undertaken each and every training rule among the training rules, you should train. Alternatively, `samādāya sikkhatha sikkhāpadesu` means: whatever is to be trained in among the sections of training, whether bodily or verbal, having undertaken all of it, you should train. This is the summary here. In detail, however, all these terms beginning with `pātimokkhasaṃvara` have been stated in the Visuddhimagga.

65. Ākaṅkheyya ceti idaṃ kasmā āraddhaṃ? Sīlānisaṃsadassanatthaṃ. Sacepi acirapabbajitānaṃ vā duppaññānaṃ [P 1.0156] vā evamassa “bhagavā sīlaṃ pūrethāti vadati, ko nu kho sīlapūraṇe ānisaṃso, ko viseso, kā vaḍḍhī”ti? Tesaṃ sattarasa ānisaṃse dassetuṃ evamāha. Appeva nāma etaṃ sabrahmacārīnaṃ piyamanāpatādiāsavakkhayapariyosānaṃ ānisaṃsaṃ sutvāpi sīlaṃ paripūreyyunti. Visakaṇṭakavāṇijo viya. Visakaṇṭakavāṇijo nāma guḷavāṇijo vuccati.

65. Why was this discourse begun with 'Ākaṅkheyya ce'? To show the benefits of virtue. If for those recently gone forth or of weak wisdom, it might occur thus: 'The Blessed One says, "Fulfill virtue"—but what is the benefit, what is the distinction, what is the growth in fulfilling virtue?' To show them these seventeen benefits, he spoke thus. Perhaps, hearing of these benefits—beginning with being dear and agreeable to their fellows in the holy life and ending in the destruction of the taints—they might perfect their virtue. Like the Visakaṇṭaka merchant. A Visakaṇṭaka merchant is said to be a jaggery merchant.

So kira guḷaphāṇitakhaṇḍasakkharādīni sakaṭenādāya paccantagāmaṃ gantvā “visakaṇṭakaṃ gaṇhatha, visakaṇṭakaṃ gaṇhathā”ti ugghosesi. Taṃ sutvā gāmikā “visaṃ nāma kakkhaḷaṃ, yo naṃ khādati, so marati, kaṇṭakampi vijjhitvā māreti, ubhopete kakkhaḷā, ko ettha ānisaṃso”ti gehadvārāni thakesuṃ, dārake ca palāpesuṃ. Taṃ disvā vāṇijo [M 1.0161] “avohārakusalā ime gāmikā, handa ne upāyena gaṇhāpemī”ti “atimadhuraṃ gaṇhatha, atisāduṃ gaṇhatha, guḷaṃ phāṇitaṃ sakkharaṃ samagghaṃ labbhati, kūṭamāsakakūṭakahāpaṇādīhipi labbhatī”ti ugghosesi. Taṃ sutvā gāmikā haṭṭhatuṭṭhā āgantvā bahumpi mūlaṃ datvā gahesuṃ. Tattha vāṇijassa “visakaṇṭakaṃ gaṇhathā”ti ugghosanaṃ viya bhagavato “sampannasīlā, bhikkhave, viharatha…pe… samādāya sikkhatha sikkhāpadesū”ti vacanaṃ. “Ubhopete kakkhaḷā, ko ettha ānisaṃso”ti gāmikānaṃ cintanaṃ viya bhagavā “sampannasīlā viharathā”ti āha, “sīlañca nāmetaṃ kakkhaḷaṃ pharusaṃ khiḍḍādipaccanīkaṃ, ko nu kho sampannasīlānaṃ ānisaṃso”ti bhikkhūnaṃ cintanaṃ. Atha tassa vāṇijassa “atimadhuraṃ gaṇhathā”tiādivacanaṃ viya [V 1.0166] bhagavato piyamanāpatādiāsavakkhayapariyosānaṃ sattarasaānisaṃsappakāsanatthaṃ “ākaṅkheyya ce”tiādivacanaṃ veditabbaṃ.

It is said that a merchant loaded a cart with jaggery, molasses, lumps of sugar, and other goods, then went to a border village and shouted, 'Buy poison-thorns! Buy poison-thorns!' Hearing this, the villagers thought, 'Poison is harsh—whoever eats it, dies. Thorns, too, pierce and kill. Both of these are harsh—what benefit is there in them?' So they barred their doors and sent their children away. Seeing this, the merchant thought, 'These villagers are unskilled in commerce. Now, I will get them to buy by means of a stratagem.' So he shouted, 'Buy the sweetest! Buy the most delicious! Jaggery, molasses, sugar—it is obtained for a small price! It can even be had with counterfeit māsakas and counterfeit kahāpaṇas!' Hearing this, the villagers, joyful and delighted, came and bought much, giving a high price. Here, the merchant’s cry of 'Buy poison-thorns!' is to be understood as like the Blessed One’s statement: 'Dwell, monks, endowed with virtue… train yourselves by undertaking the training rules.' The villagers’ thought, 'Both of these are harsh—what benefit is there in them?' is to be understood as like the monks’ thought when the Blessed One said, 'Dwell endowed with virtue': 'This virtue is harsh, rough, and contrary to playfulness and the like. What, indeed, is the benefit for those endowed with virtue?' Then, that merchant’s statement beginning with 'Buy the sweetest!' is to be understood as like the Blessed One’s statement beginning with 'Ākaṅkheyya ce,' for the purpose of explaining the seventeen benefits, beginning with being dear and agreeable and culminating in the destruction of the taints.

Tattha ākaṅkheyya ceti yadi ākaṅkheyya yadi iccheyya. Piyo ca assanti piyacakkhūhi sampassitabbo, sinehuppattiyā padaṭṭhānabhūto bhaveyyanti vuttaṃ hoti. Manāpoti tesaṃ manavaḍḍhanako, tesaṃ vā manena pattabbo, mettacittena pharitabboti vuttaṃ hoti. Garūti tesaṃ garuṭṭhāniyo pāsāṇacchattasadiso. Bhāvanīyoti “addhā ayamāyasmā jānaṃ jānāti passaṃ passatī”ti evaṃ sambhāvanīyo. Sīlesvevassa paripūrakārīti catupārisuddhisīlesuyeva paripūrakārī assa, anūnena paripūritākārena samannāgato [P 1.0157] bhaveyyāti vuttaṃ hoti. Ajjhattaṃ cetosamathamanuyuttoti attano cittasamathe yutto, ettha hi ajjhattanti vā attanoti vā etaṃ ekatthaṃ, byañjanameva nānaṃ. Bhummatthe panetaṃ samathanti upayogavacanaṃ. Anūti iminā upasaggena yoge siddhaṃ. Anirākatajjhānoti bahi anīhaṭajjhāno, avināsitajjhāno vā, nīharaṇavināsatthañhi idaṃ nirākaraṇaṃ nāma. Thambhaṃ niraṃkatvā nivātavuttītiādīsu cassa payogo daṭṭhabbo.

Therein, 'should wish' means if one should wish, if one should desire. 'Dear' means one who should be looked upon with loving eyes, who would be a foundation for the arising of affection—this is the meaning. 'Agreeable' means one who increases their joy, or one who is to be attained by their mind, or one who is to be pervaded with a mind of loving-kindness—this is the meaning. 'Respected' means a basis for their respect, like a stone umbrella. 'To be esteemed' means one who is to be praised thus: 'Surely this venerable one knows what is to be known and sees what is to be seen.' 'One who is a fulfiller of the virtues' means one who would be a fulfiller in the fourfold purification virtue, who would be endowed with the quality of having fulfilled it without deficiency—this is the meaning. 'Devoted to the internal calming of the mind' means devoted to the calming of one's own mind; here, 'internal' and 'one's own' have the same meaning, only the expression is different. This word 'calming' (samathaṃ) is an accusative used in the sense of the locative, accomplished in connection with the prefix 'anu'. 'One whose jhāna is not rejected' means one whose jhāna is not brought outside, or whose jhāna is not destroyed; for this word 'nirākaraṇa' has the meaning of bringing out and destruction. Its usage should be seen in examples such as 'thambhaṃ niraṃkatvā nivātavuttī' (having erected a pillar, one is of steady conduct).

Vipassanāya samannāgatoti sattavidhāya anupassanāya yutto, sattavidhā anupassanā nāma aniccānupassanā dukkhānupassanā anattānupassanā nibbidānupassanā virāgānupassanā nirodhānupassanā paṭinissaggānupassanāti. Tā visuddhimagge vitthāritā. Brūhetā suññāgārānanti vaḍḍhetā [M 1.0162] suññāgārānaṃ, ettha ca samathavipassanāvasena kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā rattindivaṃ suññāgāraṃ pavisitvā nisīdamāno bhikkhu “brūhetā suññāgārāna”nti veditabbo. Ekabhūmakādipāsāde kurumānopi pana neva suññāgārānaṃ brūhetāti daṭṭhabboti.

‘Endowed with insight’ means possessed of the sevenfold contemplation. The sevenfold contemplation is: contemplation of impermanence, contemplation of suffering, contemplation of non-self, contemplation of disenchantment, contemplation of dispassion, contemplation of cessation, and contemplation of relinquishment. These are explained in detail in the Visuddhimagga. ‘A cultivator of empty dwellings’ means an augmenter of empty dwellings. And here, a monk who, by way of serenity and insight, takes up a meditation subject and, entering a secluded place, sits down night and day, is to be understood as ‘a cultivator of empty dwellings.’ But it should be understood that one dwelling in a palace of one or more stories is not a cultivator of empty dwellings.

Ettāvatā ca yathā taṇhāvicaritadesanā paṭhamaṃ taṇhāvasena āraddhāpi taṇhāpadaṭṭhānattā mānadiṭṭhīnaṃ mānadiṭṭhiyo osaritvā kamena papañcattayadesanā jātā, evamayaṃ desanā paṭhamaṃ adhisīlasikkhāvasena āraddhāpi sīlapadaṭṭhānattā samathavipassanānaṃ samathavipassanāyo osaritvā kamena sikkhattayadesanā jātāti veditabbā.

And by this much, it should be understood thus: Just as the discourse on the wandering of craving, though at first begun by way of craving, descended to conceit and views because craving is the foundation for them, and in sequence became a discourse on the threefold training; so too this discourse, though at first begun by way of the higher training in virtue, descended to serenity and insight because virtue is the foundation for them, and in sequence became a discourse on the threefold training.

Ettha [V 1.0167] hi “sīlesvevassa paripūrakārī”ti ettāvatā adhisīlasikkhā vuttā. “Ajjhattaṃ cetosamathamanuyutto anirākatajjhāno”ti ettāvatā adhicittasikkhā, “vipassanāya samannāgato”ti ettāvatā adhipaññāsikkhā, “brūhetā suññāgārāna”nti iminā pana samathavasena suññāgāravaḍḍhane adhicittasikkhā, vipassanāvasena adhipaññāsikkhāti evaṃ dvepi sikkhā saṅgahetvā vuttā. Ettha ca “ajjhattaṃ cetosamathamanuyutto anirākatajjhāno”ti imehi padehi sīlānurakkhikā eva cittekaggatā kathitā. “Vipassanāyā”ti iminā padena sīlānurakkhiko saṅkhārapariggaho.

Here, indeed, 'one who is a perfecter in virtue'—to this extent, the higher training in virtue is stated. 'Devoted to internal serenity of mind, not rejecting meditative absorption'—to this extent, the higher training in mind is stated. 'Endowed with insight'—to this extent, the higher training in wisdom is stated. 'One who cultivates empty dwellings'—by this, through the aspect of serenity, the higher training in mind is meant as the development of empty dwellings; through the aspect of insight, the higher training in wisdom is meant. Thus, both trainings are included and stated. And in this context, the phrases 'devoted to internal serenity of mind, not rejecting meditative absorption' refer to one-pointedness of mind that protects virtue. The phrase 'with insight' refers to the comprehension of formations that protects virtue.

Kathaṃ [P 1.0158] cittekaggatā sīlamanurakkhati? Yassa hi cittekaggatā natthi, so byādhimhi uppanne vihaññati, so byādhivihato vikkhittacitto sīlaṃ vināsetvāpi byādhivūpasamaṃ kattā hoti. Yassa pana cittekaggatā atthi, so taṃ byādhidukkhaṃ vikkhambhetvā samāpattiṃ samāpajjati, samāpannakkhaṇe dukkhaṃ dūrāpakataṃ hoti, balavatarasukhamuppajjati. Evaṃ cittekaggatā sīlaṃ anurakkhati.

How does one-pointedness of mind protect virtue? For one who lacks one-pointedness of mind, when illness arises, he is afflicted. Being afflicted by illness, with a distracted mind, he might even destroy virtue to make the illness subside. But for one who possesses one-pointedness of mind, he withstands that suffering of illness and enters into meditative attainment. At the moment of attainment, suffering is far removed, and a stronger happiness arises. Thus, one-pointedness of mind protects virtue.

Kathaṃ saṅkhārapariggaho sīlamanurakkhati? Yassa hi saṅkhārapariggaho natthi, tassa “mama rūpaṃ mama viññāṇa”nti attabhāve balavamamattaṃ hoti, so tathārūpesu dubbhikkhabyādhibhayādīsu sampattesu sīlaṃ vināsetvāpi attabhāvaṃ posetā hoti. Yassa pana saṅkhārapariggaho atthi, tassa attabhāve balavamamattaṃ vā sineho vā na hoti, so tathārūpesu dubbhikkhabyādhibhayādīsu sampattesu sacepissa antāni bahi nikkhamanti, sacepi [M 1.0163] ussussati visussati, khaṇḍākhaṇḍiko vā hoti satadhāpi sahassadhāpi, neva sīlaṃ vināsetvā attabhāvaṃ posetā hoti. Evaṃ saṅkhārapariggaho sīlamanurakkhati. “Brūhetā suññāgārāna”nti iminā pana tasseva ubhayassa brūhanā vaḍḍhanā sātaccakiriyā dassitā.

How does the comprehension of formations protect virtue? For one who lacks comprehension of formations, there arises a strong cherishing of his personal existence in terms of 'my form, my consciousness.' Such a person, when faced with hardships like famine, disease, and fear, is one who would sustain his personal existence even by destroying virtue. But for one who has comprehension of formations, there is no strong cherishing or affection for his personal existence. Such a person, when faced with such hardships—even if his entrails were to protrude, even if he were to dry up and wither away, or be cut into a hundred or a thousand pieces—is never one who would sustain his personal existence by destroying virtue. Thus, the comprehension of formations protects virtue. By the phrase 'developer of empty dwellings,' the developing, increasing, and continuous practice of that very pair is shown.

Evaṃ bhagavā yasmā “sabrahmacārīnaṃ piyo cassaṃ manāpo ca garu ca bhāvanīyo cā”ti ime cattāro dhamme ākaṅkhantena natthaññaṃ kiñci kātabbaṃ, aññadatthu sīlādiguṇasamannāgatena bhavitabbaṃ, idiso hi sabrahmacārīnaṃ piyo hoti manāpo garu bhāvanīyo. Vuttampi hetaṃ –

Thus, the Blessed One shows that since for a monk who aspires for these four qualities—'May I be dear to my fellow practitioners, pleasing, respected, and venerable'—there is nothing else whatsoever to be done, except that he must be endowed with the qualities beginning with virtue. For such a one is dear to his fellow practitioners, pleasing, respected, and venerable. And this has been said:

“Sīladassanasampannaṃ[V 1.0168], dhammaṭṭhaṃ saccavādinaṃ;

Attano kamma kubbānaṃ, taṃ jano kurute piya”nti. (dha. pa. 217);

“One endowed with virtue and vision, established in the Dhamma, a speaker of truth, doing one's own work—such a person the people hold dear.”

Tasmā “ākaṅkheyya ce, bhikkhave, bhikkhu sabrahmacārīnaṃ piyo cassaṃ manāpo ca garu ca bhāvanīyo cāti sīlesvevassa paripūrakārī…pe… suññāgārāna”nti vatvā idāni yasmā paccayalābhādiṃ patthayantenāpi idameva karaṇīyaṃ, na aññaṃ kiñci, tasmā “ākaṅkheyya ce, bhikkhave, bhikkhu lābhī assa”ntiādimāha. Na cettha bhagavā lābhanimittaṃ sīlādiparipūraṇaṃ kathetīti veditabbo. Bhagavā hi ghāsesanaṃ [P 1.0159] chinnakatho na vācaṃ payuttaṃ bhaṇeti, evaṃ sāvake ovadati, so kathaṃ lābhanimittaṃ sīlādiparipūraṇaṃ kathessati, puggalajjhāsayavasena panetaṃ vuttaṃ. Yesañhi evaṃ ajjhāsayo bhaveyya “sace mayaṃ catūhi paccayehi na kilameyyāma, sīlādiṃ pūretuṃ sakkuṇeyyāmā”ti, tesaṃ ajjhāsayavasena bhagavā evamāha. Apica rasānisaṃso esa sīlassa, yadidaṃ cattāro paccayā nāma. Tathā hi paṇḍitamanussā koṭṭhādīsu ṭhapitaṃ nīharitvā puttādīnampi adatvā attanāpi aparibhuñjitvā sīlavantānaṃ dentīti sīlassa sarasānisaṃsadassanatthaṃ petaṃ vuttaṃ.

Therefore, having said, 'If, monks, a monk should wish: “May I be dear to my fellow practitioners, pleasing, respected, and venerable,” he should be one who fulfills the virtues… (etc.)… developer of empty dwellings,' now, since even by one who desires the gain of requisites and so on this very thing must be done and nothing else, the Blessed One therefore said, 'If, monks, a monk should wish: “May I be a gainer...”' and so on. And here it should be understood that the Blessed One does not teach the fulfillment of virtue and so on as a sign for gain. For the Blessed One, having cut off talk concerning the pursuit of food, does not speak speech employed for gain; thus he instructs his disciples. How then would he teach the fulfillment of virtue and so on as a sign for gain? Rather, this was said according to the disposition of the individual. For those whose disposition might be, 'If we were not troubled by the four requisites, we would be able to fulfill virtue and so on,' the Blessed One spoke thus according to their disposition. Moreover, this is a sweet benefit of virtue, that is to say, the four requisites. For wise people, taking what is stored in granaries and so on, not giving it even to their sons and others, and not consuming it themselves, give it to the virtuous. Thus, this was said for the purpose of showing the sweet benefit of virtue.

Tatiyavāre yesāhanti yesaṃ ahaṃ. Tesaṃ te kārāti tesaṃ devānaṃ vā manussānaṃ vā te mayi katā paccayadānakārā. Devāpi hi sīlādiguṇayuttānaṃ paccaye denti, na kevalaṃ manussāyeva, sakko viya āyasmato mahākassapassa. Mahapphalā mahānisaṃsāti ubhayametaṃ atthato ekaṃ, byañjanameva nānaṃ. Mahantaṃ vā lokiyasukhaṃ phalantīti mahapphalā[M 1.0164]. Mahato lokuttarasukhassa ca paccayā hontīti mahānisaṃsā. Sīlādiguṇayuttassa hi kaṭacchubhikkhāpi pañcaratanamattāya bhūmiyā paṇṇasālāpi katvā dinnā anekāni kappasahassāni duggativinipātato rakkhati, pariyosāne ca amatāya parinibbānadhātuyāpaccayo hoti. “Khīrodanaṃ ahamadāsi”ntiādīni (vi. va. 413) cettha vatthūni, sakalameva vā petavatthu vimānavatthu ca sādhakaṃ. Tasmā paccayadāyakehi attani katānaṃ kārānaṃ mahapphalataṃ icchantenāpi sīlādiguṇayutteneva bhavitabbanti dasseti.

In the third section, `yesāhaṃ` is `yesaṃ ahaṃ` (of whom I). `Tesaṃ te kārā` means: for them, whether devas or humans, those deeds of giving requisites done to me. For devas too give requisites to those endowed with the qualities beginning with virtue, not only humans—just as Sakka did for the Venerable Mahākassapa. `Mahapphalā mahānisaṃsā` (of great fruit, of great benefit)—these two are one in meaning, only the expression is different. They are 'of great fruit' because they result in great worldly happiness. They are 'of great benefit' because they are conditions for great supramundane happiness. Indeed, for one endowed with the qualities beginning with virtue, even a ladleful of almsfood, or a leaf-hut built and given on a piece of land measuring five ratanas, protects one from a bad destination and ruin for many thousands of eons, and at the end becomes a condition for the deathless, the element of final Nibbāna. The stories beginning with 'I gave milk-rice' are illustrations here, or the entire Petavatthu and Vimanavatthu serve as proof. Therefore, this shows that even a monk who wishes for the great fruitfulness of the deeds done for him by the donors of requisites must himself be endowed with the qualities beginning with virtue.

Catutthavāre ñātīti sassusasurapakkhikā. Sālohitāti ekalohitasambaddhā pītipitāmahādayo[V 1.0169]. Petāti peccabhāvaṃ gatā. Kālaṅkatāti matā. Tesaṃ tanti tesaṃ taṃ mayi pasannacittataṃ vā pasannena cittena anussaraṇaṃ vā. Yassa hi bhikkhuno kālaṅkato pitā vā mātā vā “amhākaṃ ñātako thero sīlavā kalyāṇadhammo”ti pasannacitto hutvā taṃ bhikkhuṃ anussarati, tassa so cittappasādopi taṃ anussaraṇamattampi mahapphalaṃ mahānisaṃsameva hoti, anekāni kappasatasahassāni [P 1.0160] duggatito vāretuṃ ante ca amataṃ pāpetuṃ samatthameva hoti. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā “ye te, bhikkhave, bhikkhū sīlasampannā samādhisampannā paññā, vimutti, vimuttiñāṇadassanasampannā, dassanaṃpāhaṃ, bhikkhave, tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ bahukāraṃ vadāmi. Savanaṃ, anussatiṃ, anupabbajjaṃ, upasaṅkamanaṃ, payirupāsanaṃpāhaṃ, bhikkhave, tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ bahukāraṃ vadāmī”ti (itivu. 104). Tasmā ñātisālohitānaṃ attani cittappasādassa anussatiyā ca mahapphalataṃ icchantenāpi sīlādiguṇayutteneva, bhavitabbanti dasseti.

In the fourth instance, `ñāti` (relatives) refers to mothers-in-law, fathers-in-law, and those on their side. `Sālohitā` (blood relations) means those connected by the same bloodline, such as fathers, grandfathers, and great-grandfathers. `Petā` (departed ones) are those who have gone to the subsequent existence. `Kālaṅkatā` (those who have passed away) refers to the deceased. Regarding `tesaṃ taṃ` [that of theirs]: it refers to their state of having a confident mind in me, or their recollection of me with a confident mind. For when a monk’s deceased father or mother, with a confident mind, thinks, "Our relative, the elder, is virtuous and has good qualities," and recollects that monk, even that confidence of mind and mere recollection bear great fruit and immense benefit. Indeed, it is capable of preventing them from states of deprivation for many hundreds of thousands of eons and ultimately leading them to the deathless. This was spoken by the Blessed One: "Monks, I say that seeing those monks who are accomplished in virtue, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation is of great benefit. Listening, recollecting, following after, approaching, and attending upon them—I say these too are of great benefit" (Itivuttaka 104). Therefore, this shows that one who wishes for the great fruit of the confidence and recollection of one's relatives and blood relations in oneself must be endowed with virtues such as morality.

66. Pañcamavāre aratiratisaho assanti aratiyā ratiyā ca saho abhibhavitā ajjhottharitā bhaveyyaṃ. Ettha ca aratīti adhikusalesu dhammesu pantasenāsanesu ca ukkaṇṭhā. Ratīti pañcakāmaguṇarati. Na ca maṃ arati saheyyāti mañca arati na abhibhaveyya na maddeyya na ajjhotthareyya. Uppannanti jātaṃ nibbattaṃ. Sīlādiguṇayutto hi aratiñca ratiñca sahati ajjhottharati madditvā tiṭṭhati. Tasmā īdisaṃ attānaṃ icchantenāpi sīlādiguṇayutteneva bhavitabbanti dasseti.

66. In the fifth instance, `aratiratisaho assaṃ` means "may I be one who overcomes and overwhelms discontent and delight." Here, `arati` (discontent) refers to restlessness in regard to higher wholesome states and secluded abodes. `Rati` (delight) means delight in the five strands of sensual pleasure. `Na ca maṃ arati saheyya` (May discontent not overcome me) means may discontent not overpower, crush, or overwhelm me. `Uppannaṃ` (arisen) means born or produced. One endowed with virtues such as morality overcomes and overwhelms discontent and delight, standing firm after crushing them. Therefore, this shows that even one wishing to be such a person must be endowed with virtues such as morality.

Chaṭṭhavāre [M 1.0165] bhayaṃ cittutrāsopi ārammaṇampi. Bheravaṃ ārammaṇameva. Sesaṃ pañcamavāre vuttanayameva. Sīlādiguṇayutto hi bhayabheravaṃ sahati ajjhottharati madditvā tiṭṭhati ariyakoṭiyavāsīmahādattatthero viya.

In the sixth instance, fear (`bhaya`) is both mental terror (`cittutrāsa`) and its object (`ārammaṇa`). The dreadful (`bherava`) is only the object. The rest follows the same method as stated in the fifth instance. One endowed with virtues such as morality overcomes fear and the dreadful, standing firm after crushing them, like the great elder Mahādatta, resident of Pāṭiyakoṭiya.

Thero kira maggaṃ paṭipanno aññataraṃ pāsādikaṃ araññaṃ disvā “idhevajja samaṇadhammaṃ katvā gamissāmī”ti maggā okkamma aññatarasmiṃ rukkhamūle saṅghāṭiṃ paññapetvā pallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvā nisīdi. Rukkhadevatāya dārakā therassa sīlatejena sakabhāvena saṇṭhātuṃ asakkontā vissaramakaṃsu. Devatāpi rukkhaṃ cālesi. Thero acalova nisīdi. Sā devatā dhūmāyi, pajjali, neva sakkhi theraṃ cāletuṃ, tato upāsakavaṇṇenāgantvā vanditvā aṭṭhāsi. “Ko [V 1.0170] eso”ti vuttā “ahaṃ, bhante, etasmiṃ rukkhe adhivatthā devatā”ti avoca. Tvaṃ ete vikāre akāsīti. Āma bhanteti. Kasmāti ca vuttā āha – “tumhākaṃ, bhante[P 1.0161], sīlatejena dārakā sakabhāvena saṇṭhātuṃ asakkontā vissaramakaṃsu, sāhaṃ tumhe palāpetuṃ evamakāsi”nti. Thero āha – “atha kasmā idha, bhante, mā vasatha, mayhaṃ aphāsūti paṭikacceva nāvacāsi. Idāni pana mā kiñci avaca, ariyakoṭiyamahādatto amanussabhayena gatoti vacanato lajjāmi, tenāhaṃ idheva vasissaṃ, tvaṃ pana ajjekadivasaṃ yattha katthaci vasāhī”ti. Evaṃ sīlādiguṇayutto bhayabheravasaho hoti. Tasmā īdisamattānaṃ icchantenāpi sīlādiguṇayutteneva bhavitabbanti dasseti.

The elder, it is said, while walking along the road, saw a delightful forest grove and thought, "Right here today, having practiced the recluse's duty, I will then proceed." Stepping off the path, he spread his outer robe at the foot of a tree, folded his legs, and sat down. The tree-deity's children, unable to remain in their own state due to the elder's power of virtue, cried out loudly. The deity herself shook the tree. The elder remained unmoved. The deity then produced smoke and burst into flames, yet still could not make the elder stir. Then, she approached in the guise of a female lay devotee, paid homage, and stood there. When asked, "Who are you?" she replied, "Venerable sir, I am the deity dwelling in this tree." "Did you cause these disturbances?" "Yes, venerable sir." "Why?" When asked, she said, "Venerable sir, unable to remain in their own state due to your power of virtue, my children cried out. So I did this to make you leave." The elder said, "Then why did you not say from the start, 'Venerable sir, do not stay here; it is uncomfortable for me'? Now say nothing more. I would be ashamed if it were said, 'Mahādatta of Pāṭiyakoṭiya left due to fear of non-humans.' Therefore, I will stay right here. You, however, may dwell wherever you like for today." Thus, one endowed with virtues like morality is able to withstand fear and the dreadful. Therefore, this shows that even those who desire such a state must be endowed with virtues like morality.

Sattamavāre ābhicetasikānanti abhicetoti abhikkantaṃ visuddhacittaṃ vuccati, adhicittaṃ vā, abhicetasi jātāni ābhicetasikāni, abhiceto sannissitānīti vā ābhicetasikāni. Diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārānanti diṭṭhadhamme sukhavihārānaṃ. Diṭṭhadhammoti paccakkho attabhāvo vuccati, tattha sukhavihārabhūtānanti attho, rūpāvacarajjhānānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Tāni hi appetvā nisinnā jhāyino imasmiṃyeva attabhāve asaṃkiliṭṭhaṃ nekkhammasukhaṃ vindanti, tasmā “diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārānī”ti vuccanti. Nikāmalābhīti nikāmena lābhī attano icchāvasena lābhī, icchiticchitakkhaṇe [M 1.0166] samāpajjituṃ samatthoti vuttaṃ hoti. Akicchalābhīti sukheneva paccanīkadhamme vikkhambhetvā samāpajjituṃ samatthoti vuttaṃ hoti. Akasiralābhīti akasirānaṃ vipulānaṃ lābhī, yathāparicchedeyeva vuṭṭhātuṃ samatthoti vuttaṃ hoti. Ekacco hi lābhīyeva hoti, na pana sakkoti icchiticchitakkhaṇe samāpajjituṃ. Ekacco sakkoti tathā samāpajjituṃ, pāribandhike pana kicchena vikkhambheti. Ekacco tathā samāpajjati, pāribandhike ca akiccheneva vikkhambheti, na sakkoti nāḷikāyantaṃ viya yathāparicchedeyeva ca vuṭṭhātuṃ. Yo pana imaṃ tividhampi sampadaṃ icchati, sopi sīlesvevassa paripūrakārīti.

In the seventh instance, regarding `ābhicetasikānaṃ`: `abhiceto` is said to be the exalted, purified mind (`abhikkantaṃ visuddhacittaṃ`), or the higher mind (`adhicitta`). States born from `abhiceto` are `ābhicetasikāni`, or states dependent on `abhiceto` are `ābhicetasikāni`. `Diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārānaṃ` means 'of blissful abidings in this very life.' `Diṭṭhadhamma` refers to the directly visible existence; here, the meaning is 'those that have become blissful abidings.' This is a designation for the jhānas of the form realm. For those meditators who attain them and sit, they experience undefiled bliss of renunciation right in this very existence. Therefore, they are called "blissful abidings in this very life." `Nikāmalābhī` means "one who gains at will"; this means one is able to enter absorption at any desired moment. `Akicchalābhī` means "one who gains without difficulty"; this means one is able to enter absorption, having suppressed the opposing states with ease. `Akasiralābhī` means "one who gains the unconstricted and extensive"; this means one is able to emerge at the precisely determined time. For one person may be a gainer, but is not able to enter absorption at any desired moment. Another is able to enter in that way, but suppresses the opposing factors with difficulty. Another enters in that way and suppresses the opposing factors with ease, but is not able to emerge at a precisely determined time like a water-clock. Whoever desires this threefold accomplishment must be one who fulfills the virtues.

Evaṃ abhiññāpādake jhāne vutte kiñcāpi abhiññānaṃ vāro āgato, atha kho naṃ bhagavā aggahetvāva yasmā na kevalaṃ abhiññāpādakajjhānāni ca abhiññāyoyeva ca sīlānaṃ [V 1.0171] ānisaṃso, apica kho cattāri āruppajhānānipi [P 1.0162] tayo ca heṭṭhimā ariyamaggā, tasmā taṃ sabbaṃ pariyādiyitvā dassetuṃ ākaṅkheyya ce…pe… ye te santāti evamādimāha.

Thus, although after speaking on the jhāna that is the basis for direct knowledge it was the turn for the direct knowledges, the Blessed One did not take that up. This is because not only the jhānas that are the basis for direct knowledge and the direct knowledges themselves are the benefit of virtue; but indeed, the four formless jhānas and the three lower noble paths are also the benefit of virtue. Therefore, to show all of that benefit comprehensively, He spoke the words beginning with, 'If he should wish... (etc.)... those which are peaceful...'

Tattha santāti aṅgasantatāya ceva ārammaṇasantatāya ca. Vimokkhāti paccanīkadhammehi vimuttattā ārammaṇe ca adhimuttattā. Atikkamma rūpeti rūpāvacarajjhāne atikkamitvā, ye te vimokkhā atikkamma rūpe santāti padasambandho, itarathā hi atikkamma rūpe kiṃ karotīti na paññāyeyyuṃ. Āruppāti ārammaṇato ca vipākato ca rūpavirahitā. Kāyena phusitvāti nāmakāyena phusitvā pāpuṇitvā, adhigantvāti vuttaṃ hoti. Sesaṃ vuttānameva. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti “yopi bhikkhu ime vimokkhe phusitvā viharitukāmo, sopi sīlesvevassa paripūrakārī”ti.

Therein, 'santā' (peaceful) is so called because of the peacefulness of its factors and the peacefulness of its object. 'Vimokkhā' (liberations) is so called because of being liberated from opposing states and because of being intent upon the object. 'Atikkamma rūpe' (having transcended form) means having transcended the fine-material sphere jhānas. The connection of the words should be made thus: 'those liberations which, having transcended form, are peaceful.' Indeed, otherwise, it would not be clear what is done 'having transcended form.' 'Āruppā' (formless) means devoid of form both in terms of object and in terms of result. 'Kāyena phusitvā' (having touched with the body) means having touched, reached, and attained with the mental body. The rest is self-evident. This is what is meant: 'Whatever bhikkhu wishes to dwell having attained these liberations, he too should be one who completely fulfills the virtues.'

67. Navamavāre tiṇṇaṃ saṃyojanānanti sakkāyadiṭṭhivicikicchāsīlabbataparāmāsasaṅkhātānaṃ tiṇṇaṃ bandhanānaṃ. Tāni hi saṃyojenti khandhagatibhavādīhi khandhagatibhavādayo, kammaṃ vā phalena, tasmā saṃyojanānīti vuccanti, bandhanānīti attho. Parikkhayāti parikkhayena. Sotāpannoti sotaṃ [M 1.0167] āpanno. Sototi ca maggassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Sotāpannoti taṃsamaṅgipuggalassa. Yathāha “soto sototi hidaṃ, sāriputta, vuccati. Katamo nu kho, sāriputta, sototi? Ayameva hi, bhante, ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo. Seyyathidaṃ, sammādiṭṭhi…pe… sammāsamādhīti. Sotāpanno sotāpannoti hidaṃ, sāriputta, vuccati. Katamo nu kho, sāriputta, sotāpannoti? Yo hi, bhante, iminā aṭṭhaṅgikena maggena samannāgato, ayaṃ vuccati sotāpanno, yoyaṃ āyasmā evaṃnāmo evaṃgotto”ti. Idha pana maggena phalassa nāmaṃ dinnaṃ, tasmā phalaṭṭho “sotāpanno”ti veditabbo. Avinipātadhammoti vinipātetīti vinipāto, nāssa vinipāto dhammoti avinipātadhammo, na attānaṃ apāye vinipātasabhāvoti vuttaṃ hoti. Kasmā? Ye dhammā apāyagamaniyā, tesaṃ pahīnattā. Sambodhi paraṃ ayanaṃ gati assāti sambodhiparāyaṇo, uparimaggattayaṃ avassaṃ sampāpakoti [P 1.0163] attho. Kasmā? Paṭiladdhapaṭhamamaggattā. Sīlesvevāti īdiso hotukāmopi sīlesvevassa paripūraṇārīti.

67. In the ninth section, 'tiṇṇaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ' (of the three fetters) refers to the three bonds designated as identity-view, doubt, and adherence to rites and rituals. Indeed, they connect the aggregates, destinations, and states of existence with the aggregates, destinations, states of existence, and so on; or they connect kamma with its fruit. Therefore, they are called 'saṃyojanāni' (fetters); the meaning is 'bonds.' 'Parikkhayā' (through the destruction) means because of their destruction. 'Sotāpanna' (stream-enterer) means one who has entered the stream ('sota'). And 'sota' is a designation for the path. 'Sotāpanna' is a designation for the person endowed with it. As it is said: '“Stream, stream,” Sāriputta, is what is said. Now what, Sāriputta, is the stream? It is this very Noble Eightfold Path, venerable sir, that is: right view... (etc.)... right concentration. “Stream-enterer, stream-enterer,” Sāriputta, is what is said. Now what, Sāriputta, is a stream-enterer? Whoever, venerable sir, is endowed with this Noble Eightfold Path is called a stream-enterer, that is, the venerable one of such a name and such a clan.' Here, however, the path gives the name to the fruit; therefore, one established in the fruit should be understood as a 'stream-enterer.' 'Avinipātadhammo' (one not subject to fall) means: that which causes one to fall is a 'vinipāta'. For him, there is no state that causes falling; therefore, he is 'avinipātadhammo'. It means he does not have a nature that causes himself to fall into the plane of misery. Why? Because those states that lead to the plane of misery have been abandoned. 'Sambodhiparāyaṇo' (one whose final destination is enlightenment) means that for him, enlightenment is the ultimate destination; the meaning is that he will unerringly attain the three higher paths. Why? Because he has attained the first path. 'Sīlesveva' (in the virtues alone) means: even one who wishes to become like this should be one who completely fulfills the virtues.

Dasamavāre [V 1.0172] paṭhamamaggena parikkhīṇānipi tīṇi saṃyojanāni sakadāgāmimaggassa vaṇṇabhaṇanatthaṃ vuttāni. Rāgadosamohānaṃ tanuttāti etesaṃ tanubhāvena, tanuttakaraṇenāti vuttaṃ hoti. Tattha dvīhi kāraṇehi tanuttaṃ veditabbaṃ adhiccuppattiyā ca pariyuṭṭhānamandatāya ca. Sakadāgāmissa hi vaṭṭānusārimahājanasseva kilesā abhiṇhaṃ na uppajjanti, kadāci karahaci uppajjanti viraḷākārā hutvā, viraḷavāpite khette aṅkurā viya. Uppajjamānāpi ca vaṭṭānusārimahājanasseva maddantā pharantā chādentā andhakāraṃ karontā na uppajjanti, mandamandā uppajjanti tanukākārā hutvā, abbhapaṭalamiva makkhikāpattamiva ca.

In the tenth section, the three fetters, although already destroyed by the first path, are mentioned for the purpose of extolling the once-returner's path. 'Rāgadosamohānaṃ tanuttā' (the attenuation of lust, hatred, and delusion) means because of their state of being attenuated, because of the act of making them attenuated. Therein, this attenuation should be understood through two reasons: infrequent arising and the weakness of the mental obsession's arising. Indeed, for a once-returner, defilements do not arise constantly as they do for the multitude of beings who follow the round of existence; they arise only sometimes, occasionally, becoming sparse in nature, like sprouts in a sparsely sown field. And even when they do arise, they do not arise crushing, pervading, enveloping, and creating darkness as they do for the multitude of people who follow the round; they arise very weakly, having become thin in nature, like a thin layer of cloud or a fly's wing.

Tattha keci therā bhaṇanti “sakadāgāmissa kilesā kiñcāpi cirena uppajjanti, bahalāva uppajjanti, tathā hissa puttā ca dhītaro ca dissantī”ti, etaṃ pana appamāṇaṃ. Puttadhītaro hi aṅgapaccaṅgaparāmasanamattenapi hontīti. Dvīhiyeva kāraṇehissa kilesānaṃ tanuttaṃ veditabbaṃ adhiccuppattiyā ca pariyuṭṭhānamandatāya cāti.

In that regard, some elders say: 'For a once-returner, although defilements arise after a long time, they arise intensely; indeed, it is for this reason that sons and daughters are seen for him.' But this statement is not a valid measure. Indeed, sons and daughters can come to be merely by the touching of limbs. The attenuation of his defilements should be understood for only two reasons: infrequent arising and the weakness of the mental obsession's arising.

Sakadāgāmīti [M 1.0168] sakiṃ āgamanadhammo. Sakideva imaṃ lokaṃ āgantvāti ekavāraṃyeva imaṃ manussalokaṃ paṭisandhivasena āgantvā. Yopi hi idha sakadāgāmimaggaṃ bhāvetvā idheva parinibbāti, sopi idha na gahito. Yopi idha maggaṃ bhāvetvā devesu upapajjitvā tattheva parinibbāti. Yopi devaloke maggaṃ bhāvetvā tattheva parinibbāti. Yopi devaloke maggaṃ bhāvetvā idheva manussaloke nibbattitvā parinibbāti. Yo pana idha maggaṃ bhāvetvā devaloke nibbatto, tattha yāvatāyukaṃ ṭhatvā puna idheva upapajjitvā parinibbāti, ayamidha gahitoti veditabbo. Dukkhassantaṃ kareyyanti vaṭṭadukkhassa paricchedaṃ kareyyaṃ. Sīlesvevāti īdiso hotukāmopi sīlesvevassa paripūrakārīti.

'Sakadāgāmī' (once-returner) means one who has the nature of returning once. 'Sakideva imaṃ lokaṃ āgantvā' (having come to this world only once) means having come to this human world by way of rebirth only one time. Indeed, the person who, having developed the once-returner's path here, attains parinibbāna right here, is not the one taken here. Nor is the one who, having developed the path here, is reborn among the devas and attains parinibbāna right there. Nor is the one who, having developed the path in the deva world, attains parinibbāna right there. Nor is the one who, having developed the path in the deva world, is reborn right here in the human world and attains parinibbāna. But the person who, having developed the path here, is reborn in the deva world, and having remained there for the extent of his lifespan, is reborn again right here and attains parinibbāna—this is the one who should be understood as taken here. 'Dukkhassantaṃ kareyya' (they would make an end of suffering) means they would make a limit to the suffering of the round of existence. 'Sīlesveva' (in the virtues alone) means: even one who wishes to become like this should be one who completely fulfills the virtues.

Ekādasamavāre pañcannanti gaṇanaparicchedo. Orambhāgiyānanti oraṃ vuccati heṭṭhā, heṭṭhābhāgiyānanti attho, kāmāvacaraloke uppattipaccayānanti adhippāyo. Saṃyojanānanti bandhanānaṃ, tāni kāmarāgabyāpādasaṃyojanehi [P 1.0164] saddhiṃ pubbe vuttasaṃyojanāneva veditabbāni. Yassa hi etāni appahīnāni, so kiñcāpi bhavagge uppanno hoti, atha kho āyuparikkhayā kāmāvacare nibbattatiyeva, gilitabalisamacchūpamo svāyaṃ puggalo dīghasuttakena pāde [V 1.0173] baddhavihaṅgūpamo cāti veditabbo. Pubbe vuttānampi cettha vacanaṃ vaṇṇabhaṇanatthamevāti veditabbaṃ. Opapātikoti sesayonipaṭikkhepavacanametaṃ. Tatthaparinibbāyīti tattheva brahmaloke parinibbāyī. Anāvattidhammo tasmā lokāti tato brahmalokā paṭisandhivasena puna anāvattisabhāvo. Sīlesvevāti īdiso hotukāmopi sīlesvevassa paripūrakārīti.

In the eleventh section, 'of the five' (pañcannaṃ) is a specification of number. 'Of the lower fetters' (orambhāgiyānaṃ) means: 'oraṃ' is said to mean 'lower'; the meaning is 'of those pertaining to the lower part,' and the purport is 'of those that are conditions for rebirth in the desire-sphere world.' 'Of the fetters' (saṃyojanānaṃ) means 'of the bonds'; these should be understood as the very same fetters mentioned previously, together with the fetters of sensual lust and ill will. For one by whom these have not been abandoned, even if they are born at the peak of existence, they are nevertheless reborn in the desire-sphere world upon the exhaustion of their lifespan. That person should be understood as being like a fish that has swallowed a baited hook, and like a bird bound by the foot with a long string. And the mention here of what was said before should be understood as being for the purpose of extolling the path of the non-returner. 'One of spontaneous birth' (opapātiko) is a term rejecting the other kinds of birth. 'Attaining parinibbāna there' (tatthaparinibbāyī) means attaining parinibbāna right there in that Brahma-world. 'Of the nature of not returning from that world' (anāvattidhammo tasmā lokā) means having the nature of not returning again from that Brahma-world by way of rebirth. 'In virtue alone' (sīlesveva) shows the meaning that one who wishes to be such should be a fulfiller of virtue.

68. Evaṃ anāgāmimagge vutte kiñcāpi catutthamaggassa vāro āgato, atha kho naṃ bhagavā aggahetvāva yasmā na kevalā āsavakkhayābhiññā eva sīlānaṃ ānisaṃso, apica kho lokiyapañcābhiññāyopi, tasmā tāpi dassetuṃ, yasmā ca āsavakkhaye kathite desanā niṭṭhitā hoti, evañca sati imesaṃ guṇānaṃ akathitattā ayaṃ kathā muṇḍābhiññākathā nāma bhaveyya, tasmā ca abhiññāpāripūriṃ katvā dassetumpi, yasmā ca anāgāmimagge ṭhitassa sukhena iddhivikuppanā [M 1.0169] ijjhati, samādhiparibandhānaṃ kāmarāgabyāpādānaṃ samūhatattā, anāgāmī hi sīlesu ca samādhimhi ca paripūrakārī, tasmā yuttaṭṭhāneyeva lokiyābhiññāyo dassetumpi “ākaṅkheyya ce…pe… anekavihita”nti evamādimāhāti ayamanusandhi.

68. Thus, when the path of the non-returner was spoken of, although the turn for the fourth path had come, the Blessed One did not take it up. This is because the direct knowledge of the destruction of the taints is not the only benefit of virtue; on the contrary, the five mundane direct knowledges are also a benefit. Therefore, in order to show them also; and because when the destruction of the taints is spoken of, the discourse is concluded, and this being so, due to these qualities not being mentioned, this discourse would be called 'a discourse shorn of the direct knowledges'; therefore, also to show it after making the direct knowledges complete; and because for one established on the path of the non-returner, the transformation of psychic power succeeds easily, due to the eradication of sensual lust and ill will, which are obstacles to concentration, for a non-returner is a fulfiller in virtue and in concentration; therefore, also to show the mundane direct knowledges in their proper place, he said, 'If he should wish... various kinds,' and so on. This is the connection.

Tattha “anekavihitaṃ iddhividha”ntiādinā nayena āgatānaṃ pañcannampi lokiyābhiññānaṃ pāḷivaṇṇanā saddhiṃ bhāvanānayena visuddhimagge vuttā.

Therein, the explanation of the Pāḷi for all five mundane direct knowledges, which are presented by the method beginning with 'various kinds of psychic power,' is stated in the Visuddhimagga together with the method of development.

69. Chaṭṭhābhiññāya āsavānaṃ khayāti arahattamaggena sabbakilesānaṃ khayā. Anāsavanti āsavavirahitaṃ. Cetovimuttiṃ paññāvimuttinti ettha cetovacanena arahattaphalasampayuttova samādhi, paññāvacanena taṃsampayuttā paññāva vuttā. Tattha ca samādhi rāgato vimuttattā cetovimutti, paññā avijjāya vimuttattā paññāvimuttīti veditabbā. Vuttañcetaṃ bhagavatā “yo hissa, bhikkhave, samādhi, tadassa samādhindriyaṃ. Yā hissa, bhikkhave, paññā, tadassa paññindriyaṃ. Iti kho, bhikkhave[P 1.0165], rāgavirāgā cetovimutti, avijjāvirāgā paññāvimuttī”ti, apicettha samathaphalaṃ cetovimutti, vipassanāphalaṃ paññāvimuttīti veditabbā.

69. In the section on the sixth direct knowledge, 'the destruction of the taints' means the destruction of all defilements by means of the path of arahantship. 'Taintless' means free from the taints. As to 'mind-liberation and wisdom-liberation,' here by the word 'mind' is meant the concentration associated with the fruit of arahantship, and by the word 'wisdom' is meant the wisdom associated with it. And therein, concentration, because it is liberated from lust, is to be known as mind-liberation; and wisdom, because it is liberated from ignorance, is to be known as wisdom-liberation. And this was said by the Blessed One: 'For, monks, whatever his concentration is, that is his faculty of concentration. Whatever his wisdom is, that is his faculty of wisdom. Thus, monks, from dispassion for lust comes mind-liberation; from dispassion for ignorance comes wisdom-liberation.' Moreover, herein, the fruit of serenity is to be known as mind-liberation, and the fruit of insight as wisdom-liberation.

Diṭṭheva dhammeti imasmiṃyeva attabhāve. Sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvāti attanoyeva paññāya paccakkhaṃ [V 1.0174] katvā, aparapaccayena ñatvāti attho. Upasampajja vihareyyanti pāpuṇitvā sampādetvā vihareyyaṃ. Sīlesvevāti evaṃ sabbāsave niddhunitvā cetovimuttiṃ paññāvimuttiṃ adhigantukāmopi sīlesvevassa paripūrakārīti.

'In this very life' means in this very existence. 'Having realized it oneself by direct knowledge' means having realized it directly with one's own wisdom, having known it without reliance on another. 'Having attained, I would dwell' means: having reached, having accomplished, I would dwell. 'In virtue alone' shows this meaning: even one who wishes to attain mind-liberation and wisdom-liberation by thus shaking off all the taints should be a fulfiller in virtue alone.

Evaṃ bhagavā sīlānisaṃsakathaṃ yāva arahattā kathetvā idāni sabbampi taṃ sīlānisaṃsaṃ sampiṇḍetvā dassento nigamanaṃ āha “sampannasīlā, bhikkhave…pe… idametaṃ paṭicca vutta”nti. Tassāyaṃ saṅkhepattho, “sampannasīlā, bhikkhave, viharatha…pe… samādāya sikkhatha sikkhāpadesū”ti iti yaṃ taṃ mayā pubbe evaṃ vuttaṃ, idaṃ sabbampi sampannasīlo bhikkhu sabrahmacārīnaṃ piyo hoti manāpo, garu bhāvanīyo paccayānaṃ lābhī, paccayadāyakānaṃ mahapphalakaro, pubbañātīnaṃ anussaraṇacetanāya phalamahattakaro, aratiratisaho, bhayabheravasaho, rūpāvacarajjhānānaṃ arūpāvacarajjhānānañca lābhī, heṭṭhimāni tīṇi sāmaññaphalāni pañca lokiyābhiññā āsavakkhayañāṇanti ca ime ca guṇe sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikattā [M 1.0170] hoti, etaṃ paṭicca idaṃ sandhāya vuttanti. Idamavoca bhagavā, attamanā te bhikkhu bhagavato bhāsitaṃ abhinandunti.

Thus the Blessed One, having spoken on the benefits of virtue up to arahantship, now, showing all those benefits of virtue in summary, spoke the conclusion: 'Endowed with virtue, monks... This was said in reference to that.' The concise meaning of this is: That which was spoken by me previously, 'Endowed with virtue, monks, dwell... Undertake and train in the training rules,' was said in reference to and because of all this: a monk endowed with virtue is dear and agreeable to his companions in the holy life, respected and revered; he is a recipient of the requisites; he brings great fruit to the donors of requisites; he brings great fruit to the volition of recollecting departed relatives; he is able to endure discontent and delight; he is able to endure fear and terror; he is a recipient of the form-sphere and formless-sphere absorptions; and he has directly known and realized for himself these qualities: the three lower fruits of recluseship, the five mundane direct knowledges, and the knowledge of the destruction of the taints. This the Blessed One said. Delighted, those monks rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

From the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya.

Ākaṅkheyyasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Ākaṅkheyyasutta is concluded.

7. Vatthasuttavaṇṇanā

7. The Commentary on the Discourse on the Cloth

70. Evaṃ [V 1.0175] me sutanti vatthasuttaṃ. Tattha seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, vatthanti upamāvacanamevetaṃ. Upamaṃ karonto ca bhagavā katthaci paṭhamaṃyeva upamaṃ dassetvā pacchā atthaṃ dasseti, katthaci [P 1.0166] paṭhamamatthaṃ dassetvā pacchā upamaṃ, katthaci upamāya atthaṃ parivāretvā dasseti, katthaci atthena upamaṃ.

70. “Thus have I heard” begins the Discourse on the Cloth. Therein, the phrase “Just as, monks, a cloth” is simply an expression of simile. And when making a comparison, the Blessed One sometimes first presents the simile and then shows the meaning; sometimes he first shows the meaning and then the simile; sometimes he surrounds the meaning with a simile; and sometimes he surrounds the simile with the meaning.

Tathā hesa – “seyyathāpissu, bhikkhave, dve agārā sadvārā, tattha cakkhumā puriso majjhe ṭhito passeyyā”ti (ma. ni. 3.261) sakalampi devadūtasuttaṃ upamaṃ paṭhamaṃ dassetvā pacchā atthaṃ dassento āha. “Tirokuṭṭaṃ tiropākāraṃ tiropabbataṃ asajjamāno gacchati, seyyathāpi ākāse”tiādinā (dī. ni. 1.238; paṭi. ma. 1.102) pana nayena sakalampi iddhividhamatthaṃ paṭhamaṃ dassetvā pacchā upamaṃ dassento āha. “Seyyathāpi brāhmaṇapuriso sāratthiko sāragavesī”tiādināva (ma. ni. 1.318) nayena sakalampi cūḷasāropamasuttaṃ upamāya atthaṃ parivāretvā dassento āha. “Idha pana, bhikkhave, ekacce kulaputtā dhammaṃ pariyāpuṇanti suttaṃ…pe… seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, puriso alagaddatthiko”tiādinā (ma. ni. 1.238) nayena sakalampi alagaddasuttaṃ mahāsāropamasuttanti evamādīni suttāni atthena upamaṃ parivāretvā dassento āha.

For so it is. In the entire Devadūta Sutta, he said: “Just as, monks, there might be two houses with facing doors, and a man with good eyesight standing in between them could see…”, thus showing the simile first and then showing the meaning. By the method beginning, “He goes unhindered through a wall, through a rampart, through a mountain, as if through space,” he taught the entire section on the spiritual power, showing the meaning first and then showing the simile. By the method beginning, “Just as, a brahmin man who was in need of heartwood, seeking heartwood…”, he taught the entire Cūḷasāropama Sutta, surrounding the meaning with the simile. By the method beginning, “Here, monks, some clansmen master the Dhamma—the discourses… and so on… Just as, monks, a man in need of a water snake…”, he taught the entire Alagadda Sutta, the Mahāsāropama Sutta, and other such suttas, surrounding the simile with the meaning.

Svāyaṃ idha paṭhamaṃ upamaṃ dassetvā pacchā atthaṃ dasseti. Kasmā panevaṃ bhagavā dassetīti? Puggalajjhāsayena vā desanāvilāsena vā. Ye hi puggalā paṭhamaṃ upamaṃ dassetvā vuccamānamatthaṃ sukhena paṭivijjhanti, tesaṃ [M 1.0171] paṭhamaṃ upamaṃ dasseti. Esa nayo sabbattha. Yassā ca dhammadhātuyā suppaṭividdhattā desanāvilāsaṃ patto hoti, tassā suppaṭividdhā. Tasmā esa desanāvilāsampatto dhammissaro dhammarājā, so yathā yathā icchati, tathā tathā dhammaṃ desetīti evaṃ iminā puggalajjhāsayena vā desanāvilāsena vā evaṃ dassetīti veditabbo.

Here, this Blessed One first presents the simile and then shows the meaning. But why does the Blessed One teach in this way? Either due to the disposition of individuals or due to the elegance of the discourse. For those individuals who easily penetrate the meaning when it is spoken after a simile has first been shown, he shows the simile first. This is the method in all cases. And because of his thorough penetration of the Dhamma-element, he has attained elegance in teaching; that Dhamma-element is thoroughly penetrated by him. Therefore, this one who has attained elegance in teaching, the Lord of the Dhamma, the King of the Dhamma, teaches the Dhamma in whatever way he wishes. Thus, it should be understood that he teaches in this way either due to this disposition of individuals or this elegance of the teaching.

Tattha [V 1.0176] vatthanti pakatiparisuddhaṃ vatthaṃ. Saṃkiliṭṭhaṃ malaggahitanti āgantukena paṃsurajādinā saṃkilesena saṃkiliṭṭhaṃ, sedajallikādinā malena gahitattā malaggahitaṃ. Raṅgajāteti ettha raṅgameva raṅgajātaṃ. Upasaṃhareyyāti upanāmeyya. Yadi nīlakāyāti nīlakāya vā, nīlakatthāya vāti vuttaṃ hoti. Evaṃ sabbattha. Rajako hi nīlakatthāya upasaṃharanto kaṃsanīlapalāsanīlādike nīlaraṅge upasaṃharati. Pītakatthāya upasaṃharanto kaṇikārapupphasadise pītakaraṅge. Lohitakatthāya upasaṃharanto bandhujīvakapupphasadise [P 1.0167] lohitakaraṅge. Mañjiṭṭhakatthāya upasaṃharanto kaṇavīrapupphasadise mandarattaraṅge. Tena vuttaṃ “yadi nīlakāya…pe… yadi mañjiṭṭhakāyā”ti.

Therein, “cloth” means a naturally pure cloth. “Soiled and stained” means it is soiled by adventitious defilements such as dust and dirt, and stained because it is seized by filth such as sweat and grime. Herein, in “type of dye,” the dye itself is the type of dye. “Would dip it in” means would apply it. “If for blue” means “for the purpose of making it blue” or “for a blue color.” This is so in all cases. For a dyer, when applying dye for the purpose of making something blue, applies blue dyes such as bronze-blue and palāsa-leaf-blue. When applying dye for the purpose of making something yellow, he applies yellow dyes like the color of kaṇikāra flowers. When applying dye for the purpose of making something red, he applies red dyes like the color of bandhujīvaka flowers. When applying dye for the purpose of making something madder-colored, he would apply a slightly red dye like the color of kaṇavīra flowers. Therefore it was said: “if for blue… and so on… if for madder.”

Durattavaṇṇamevassāti duṭṭhu rañjitavaṇṇameva assa. Aparisuddhavaṇṇamevassāti nīlavaṇṇopissa parisuddho na bhaveyya, sesavaṇṇopi. Tādisañhi vatthaṃ nīlakumbhiyā pakkhittampi sunīlaṃ na hoti, sesakumbhīsu pakkhittampi pītakādivaṇṇaṃ na hoti, milātanīla kuraṇḍa-kaṇikāra-bandhujīvaka-kaṇavīrapupphavaṇṇameva hoti. Taṃ kissa hetūti taṃ vatthaṃ kissa hetu kiṃ kāraṇā īdisaṃ hoti, tasmiṃ vā vatthe raṅgajātaṃ kissa hetu īdisaṃ durattavaṇṇaṃ aparisuddhavaṇṇaṃ hotīti? Yasmā panassa vatthassa saṃkiliṭṭhabhāvoyevettha kāraṇaṃ, na aññaṃ kiñci, tasmā “aparisuddhattā, bhikkhave, vatthassā”ti āha.

“It would be of a bad color” means it would have a badly dyed color. “It would be of an impure color” means its blue color would not be pure, nor would the other colors. For such a cloth, even when put into a blue vat, does not become a good blue; and when put into other vats, it does not become yellow or other colors. It only becomes the color of a faded blue kuraṇḍa flower, a kaṇikāra flower, a bandhujīvaka flower, or a kaṇavīra flower. “What is the reason for that?” means: For what reason, for what cause, is that cloth like this? Or, on that cloth, for what reason does the type of dye become such a badly-dyed, impure color? Because the state of being soiled of that cloth is the only reason here, and nothing else, therefore he said, “Because of the impurity of the cloth, monks.”

Evameva khoti upamāsampaṭipādanaṃ. Citte saṃkiliṭṭheti cittamhi saṃkiliṭṭhamhi. Kasmā pana bhagavā saṃkiliṭṭhavatthena opammaṃ akāsīti ce, vāyāmamahapphaladassanatthaṃ. Yathā hi āgantukehi malehi saṃkiliṭṭhaṃ vatthaṃ pakatiyā paṇḍarattā puna dhovīyamānaṃ paṇḍaraṃ hoti, na tattha jātikāḷake viya eḷakalome vāyāmo nipphalo hoti, evaṃ cittampi āgantukehi kilesehi saṃkiliṭṭhaṃ. Pakatiyā pana taṃ sakalepi paṭisandhibhavaṅgavāre paṇḍarameva. Yathāha – “pabhassaramidaṃ, bhikkhave, cittaṃ, tañca [M 1.0172] kho āgantukehi upakkilesehi upakkiliṭṭha”nti (a. ni. 1.51). Taṃ visodhīyamānaṃ sakkā pabhassarataraṃ kātuṃ, na tattha vāyāmo nipphaloti evaṃ vāyāmamahapphaladassanatthaṃ saṃkiliṭṭhavatthena opammaṃ akāsīti veditabbo.

“Just so” is for the purpose of connecting the simile. “When the mind is defiled” means when the mind is defiled. If it is asked, “But why did the Blessed One make a simile with a soiled cloth?” it was for the purpose of showing the great fruit of effort. Just as a cloth soiled by adventitious impurities, because it is naturally white, becomes white again when washed—effort is not fruitless there, as it would be with naturally black sheep’s wool—so too the mind is soiled by adventitious defilements. But naturally, that mind, in all instances of rebirth-linking and the life-continuum, is pure. As it was said: “This mind, monks, is luminous, but it is defiled by adventitious defilements.” When it is being purified, it is possible to make it more luminous; effort is not fruitless there. Thus, it should be understood that he made the simile with a soiled cloth to show the great fruit of effort.

Duggati pāṭikaṅkhāti īdise citte duggati pāṭikaṅkhitabbā, duggatiṃ eva esa pāpuṇissati[V 1.0177], nāññanti evaṃ duggati icchitabbā, avassaṃ bhāvīti vuttaṃ hoti. Sā cāyaṃ duggati nāma paṭipattiduggati, gatiduggatīti duvidhā hoti. Paṭipattiduggatipi agāriyapaṭipattiduggati, anagāriyapaṭipattiduggatīti duvidhā hoti.

“A bad destination is to be expected” means: when such a mind arises, a bad destination is to be expected. This person will reach only a bad destination, not another. Thus, a bad destination is to be expected; it is said to be inevitable. And this so-called “bad destination” is of two kinds: a bad destination of practice and a bad destination of rebirth. The bad destination of practice is also of two kinds: the bad destination of a householder’s practice and the bad destination of a homeless one’s practice.

Agāriyo hi saṃkiliṭṭhacitto pāṇampi [P 1.0168] hanati, adinnampi ādiyati, sakalepi dasa akusalakammapathe pūreti, ayamassa agāriyapaṭipattiduggati. So tattha ṭhito kāyassa bhedā nirayampi gacchati, tiracchānayonimpi, pettivisayampi gacchati, ayamassa gatiduggati.

For a householder with a defiled mind kills living beings, takes what is not given, and fulfills all ten unwholesome courses of action—this is his bad destination of practice as a householder. Established in that, with the breakup of the body, he goes to hell, the animal realm, or the sphere of the petas—this is his bad destination of rebirth.

Anagāriyopi imasmiṃ sāsane pabbajito saṃkiliṭṭhacitto dūteyyapahiṇagamanaṃ gacchati, vejjakammaṃ karoti, saṅghabhedāya cetiyabhedāya parakkamati, veḷudānādīhi jīvikaṃ kappeti, sakalampi anācāraṃ agocarañca paripūreti, ayamassa anagāriyapaṭipattiduggati.So tattha ṭhito kāyassa bhedā nirayampi gacchati, tiracchānayonimpi, pettivisayampi gacchati samaṇayakkho nāma hoti samaṇapeto, ādittehi saṅghāṭiādīhi sampajjalitakāyo aṭṭassaraṃ karonto vicarati, ayamassa gatiduggati.

A renunciant also, ordained in this Dispensation, with a defiled mind, goes on errands as a messenger, practices medicine, strives to split the Sangha or destroy a shrine, makes a living by means of giving bamboo and the like, and completely fulfills all improper conduct and unsuitable resort—this is his bad destination of practice as a renunciant. Established in that, with the breakup of the body, he goes to hell, the animal realm, or the sphere of the petas. He becomes what is called a “monk-yakkha” or a “monk-peta,” his body blazing with burning robes and so on, wandering while uttering cries of distress—this is his bad destination of rebirth.

Seyyathāpīti sukkapakkhaṃ dassetumāraddho, tassattho kaṇhapakkhe vuttapaccanīkeneva veditabbo. Etthāpi ca sugati nāma paṭipattisugati gatisugatīti duvidhā hoti. Paṭipattisugatipi agāriyapaṭipattisugati anagāriyapaṭipattisugatīti duvidhā hoti. Agāriyo hi parisuddhacitto pāṇātipātāpi viramati, adinnādānāpi, sakalepi dasa kusalakammapathe paripūreti, ayamassa agāriyapaṭipattisugati. So tattha ṭhito kāyassa bhedā manussamahantatampi devamahantatampi upapajjati, ayamassa gatisugati.

The passage beginning with 'Just as...' is started in order to show the bright side. Its meaning should be understood by way of the opposite of what was said in the dark side. Here, too, a good destination is of two kinds: a good destination of practice and a good destination of rebirth. The good destination of practice is also of two kinds: the good destination of practice for a householder and the good destination of practice for a renunciant. For a householder with a purified mind refrains from killing living beings, from taking what is not given, and fulfills all ten wholesome courses of action—this is his good destination of practice as a householder. Established in this, with the breakup of the body, he is reborn in a great state as a human or in a great state as a deva—this is his good destination of rebirth.

Anagāriyopi [M 1.0173] imasmiṃ sāsane pabbajitvā parisuddhacitto catupārisuddhisīlaṃ sodheti, terasa dhutaṅgāni samādiyati, aṭṭhatiṃsārammaṇesu attano anukūlakammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā pantasenāsane paṭisevamāno kasiṇaparikammaṃ katvā jhānasamāpattiyo nibbatteti, sotāpattimaggaṃ bhāveti…pe… anāgāmimaggaṃ bhāveti, ayamassa anagāriyapaṭipattisugati. So tattha ṭhito kāyassa bhedā manussaloke vā tīsu mahākulesu, chasu vā kāmāvacaradevesu, dasasu vā brahmabhavanesu[V 1.0178], pañcasu vā suddhāvāsesu, catūsu vā āruppesu upapajjati, ayamassa gatisugatīti.

A renunciant also, having gone forth in this Dispensation, with a purified mind, purifies the fourfold purity of virtue, undertakes the thirteen ascetic practices, takes up a meditation subject suitable for oneself among the thirty-eight objects, and while resorting to a secluded dwelling, having done the preliminary work on a kasina, produces the jhāna attainments, develops the path of stream-entry... up to... develops the path of non-returning—this is his good destination of practice as a renunciant. Established therein, with the breakup of the body, he is reborn in the human world in one of the three great families, or among the six sense-sphere devas, or in the ten brahma realms, or in the five Pure Abodes, or in the four formless realms—this is his good destination of rebirth.

71. Evaṃ saṃkiliṭṭhe citte duggati pāṭikaṅkhā, asaṃkiliṭṭhe ca sugatīti vatvā idāni yehi upakkilesehi cittaṃ saṃkiliṭṭhaṃ hoti, te dassento katame ca, bhikkhave, cittassa upakkilesā[P 1.0169]? Abhijjhā visamalobhotiādimāha.

71. Thus, having said, “When the mind is defiled, a bad destination is to be expected, and when it is undefiled, a good destination,” now, wishing to show by which defilements the mind becomes defiled, he said, “And what, bhikkhus, are the defilements of the mind? Covetousness and unrighteous greed,” and so on.

Tattha sakabhaṇḍe chandarāgo abhijjhā, parabhaṇḍe visamalobho. Atha vā sakabhaṇḍe vā parabhaṇḍe vā hotu, yuttapattaṭṭhāne chandarāgo abhijjhā, ayuttāpattaṭṭhāne visamalobho. Thero panāha “kissa vinibbhogaṃ karotha, yutte vā ayutte vā hotu, ‘rāgo visamaṃ doso visamaṃ moho visama’nti (vibha. 924) vacanato na koci lobho avisamo nāma, tasmā lobhoyeva abhijjhāyanaṭṭhena abhijjhā, visamaṭṭhena visamaṃ, ekatthametaṃ byañjanameva nāna”nti. So panesa abhijjhāvisamalobho uppajjitvā cittaṃ dūseti, obhāsituṃ na deti. Tasmā “cittassa upakkileso”ti vuccati.

Therein, strong passion for one’s own property is covetousness; for another’s property, it is unrighteous greed. Alternatively, whether it be for one’s own property or another’s, strong passion in a suitable case is covetousness; in an unsuitable case, it is unrighteous greed. But the Elder said: “Why do you make a distinction? Whether in a suitable case or an unsuitable one, as it is said, ‘Greed is unrighteous, hatred is unrighteous, delusion is unrighteous,’ there is no greed whatsoever that is not unrighteous. Therefore, greed itself is covetousness in the sense of coveting, and unrighteous in the sense of being uneven. This is one meaning; only the expression is different.” And this covetousness and unrighteous greed, when it has arisen, corrupts the mind and does not allow it to shine. Therefore, it is called “a defilement of the mind.”

Yathā cesa, evaṃ navavidhaāghātavatthusambhavo byāpādo. Dasavidhaāghātavatthusambhavo kodho. Punappunaṃ cittapariyonandhano upanāho. Agāriyassa vā anagāriyassa vā sukatakaraṇavināsano makkho. Agāriyopi hi kenaci anukampakena daliddo samāno ucce ṭhāne ṭhapito, aparena samayena “kiṃ tayā mayhaṃ kata”nti tassa sukatakaraṇaṃ vināseti. Anagāriyopi sāmaṇerakālato pabhuti [M 1.0174] ācariyena vā upajjhāyena vā catūhi paccayehi uddesaparipucchāhi ca anuggahetvā dhammakathānayapakaraṇakosallādīni sikkhāpito, aparena samayena rājarājamahāmattādīhi sakkato garukato ācariyupajjhāyesu acittīkato caramāno “ayaṃ amhehi daharakāle evaṃ anuggahito saṃvaḍḍhito ca, atha panidāni nissineho jāto”ti vuccamāno “kiṃ mayhaṃ tumhehi kata”nti tesaṃ sukatakaraṇaṃ vināseti, tassa so sukatakaraṇavināsano makkho uppajjitvā cittaṃ dūseti, obhāsituṃ na deti. Tasmā “cittassa upakkileso”ti vuccati.

Just as this is, so too, aversion arising from the nine grounds of resentment is ill will. Aversion arising from the ten grounds of resentment is anger. Aversion that repeatedly binds the mind is hostility. The wiping away of a good deed done for one, whether a householder or a renunciant, is denigration. Indeed, a householder, though poor, may be placed in a high position by some compassionate person; at a later time, saying, “What have you done for me?” he destroys the good deed done by that person. A renunciant, too, from the time of being a novice, may have been supported by a teacher or preceptor with the four requisites and with instruction and questioning, and taught skills in the method of Dhamma talks, exposition, and so on. At a later time, when honored and respected by kings, royal ministers, and others, while behaving without respect towards his teachers and preceptors, and when it is said, “This person was supported and raised by us when he was young, and yet now he has become unaffectionate,” he destroys the good deed done by them, saying, “What have you done for me?” For him, that denigration, which is the destruction of a good deed done, arises and corrupts the mind; it does not allow it to shine. Therefore, it is called “a defilement of the mind.”

Yathā [V 1.0179] cāyaṃ, evaṃ bahussutepi puggale ajjhottharitvā “īdisassa ceva bahussutassa aniyatā gati, tava vā mama vā ko viseso”tiādinā nayena uppajjamāno yugaggāhagāhī paḷāso. Paresaṃ sakkārādīni khīyanā issā. Attano sampattiyā parehi sādhāraṇabhāvaṃ asahamānaṃ macchariyaṃ. Vañcanikacariyabhūtā māyā. Kerāṭikabhāvena uppajjamānaṃ sāṭheyyaṃ. Kerāṭiko hi āyatanamaccho viya hoti. Āyatanamaccho nāma kira macchānaṃ naṅguṭṭhaṃ dasseti sappānaṃ sīsaṃ[P 1.0170], “tumhehi sadiso aha”nti jānāpetuṃ. Evameva kerāṭiko puggalo yaṃ yaṃ suttantikaṃ vā ābhidhammikaṃ vā upasaṅkamati, taṃ taṃ evaṃ vadati “ahaṃ tumhākaṃ baddhacaro, tumhe mayhaṃ anukampakā, nāhaṃ tumhe muñcāmī”ti “evamete ‘sagāravo ayaṃ amhesu sappatisso’ti maññissantī”ti. Tassetaṃ kerāṭikabhāvena uppajjamānaṃ sāṭheyyaṃ uppajjitvā cittaṃ dūseti, obhāsituṃ na deti. Tasmā “cittassa upakkileso”ti vuccati.

Just as this is so, likewise, overwhelming a very learned person, there arises, by way of thinking, 'For such a very learned one, the future state is uncertain; what difference is there between you and me?', the contempt that grasps with rivalry. Disparaging the honor and so forth of others is envy. Not being able to bear the sharing of one's own possessions with others is stinginess. Conduct that is fraudulent is deceit. That which arises in the manner of a trickster is hypocrisy. For a trickster is like the āyatanamaccha fish. It is said that the āyatanamaccha shows its tail to fish and its head to snakes to make them know, 'I am like you.' In the same way, a trickster, on approaching any expert in the Suttanta or the Abhidhamma, speaks thus: 'I am your devoted follower, you are compassionate toward me, I will not leave you,' thinking, 'In this way they will think, "This one is respectful and reverential towards us."' This hypocrisy of his, arising in the manner of a trickster, having arisen, corrupts the mind; it does not allow it to shine. Therefore, it is called 'a defilement of the mind.'

Yathā cetaṃ, evaṃ vātabharitabhastasadisathaddhabhāvapaggahitasiraanivātavuttikārakaraṇo thambho. Taduttarikaraṇo sārambho. So duvidhena labbhati akusalavasena ceva kusalavasena ca. Tattha agāriyassa parena kataṃ alaṅkārādiṃ disvā taddiguṇakaraṇena uppajjamāno, anagāriyassa ca yattakaṃ yattakaṃ paro pariyāpuṇāti vā katheti vā, mānavasena taddiguṇataddiguṇakaraṇena uppajjamāno akusalo. Agāriyassa pana paraṃ ekaṃ salākabhattaṃ dentaṃ disvā attanā dve vā tīṇi vā dātukāmatāya uppajjamāno, anagāriyassa ca parena ekanikāye [M 1.0175] gahite mānaṃ anissāya kevalaṃ taṃ disvā attanā ālasiyaṃ abhibhuyya dve nikāye gahetukāmatāya uppajjamāno kusalo. Idha pana akusalo adhippeto. Ayañhi uppajjitvā cittaṃ dūseti, obhāsituṃ na deti. Tasmā “cittassa upakkileso”ti vuccati.

Just as this is so, likewise, stubbornness (thambha) is that which causes one to act without humility, with one's head held high and with a stiff nature like a leather bag filled with wind. Contention (sārambha) is the act of trying to surpass that. It is obtained in two ways: by way of the unwholesome and by way of the wholesome. Therein, for a householder, seeing the decorations and so forth made by another, the contention that arises from doing twice as much is unwholesome. And for one who has gone forth, however many Nikāyas another learns or teaches, the contention that arises through the power of conceit by doing twice as much in return is unwholesome. On the other hand, for a householder, seeing another giving one ticket-meal, the contention that arises from the desire to give two or three oneself is wholesome. And for one who has gone forth, seeing that another has mastered one Nikāya, not based on conceit but merely seeing that person and overcoming one's own laziness, the contention that arises from the desire to master two Nikāyas is wholesome. Here, however, the unwholesome is intended. For this, having arisen, corrupts the mind; it does not allow it to shine. Therefore, it is called 'a defilement of the mind.'

Yathā cāyaṃ, evaṃ jātiādīni nissāya cittassa uṇṇativasena pavattamāno māno, accuṇṇativasena atimāno, madaggahaṇākāro mado, kāmaguṇesu cittavossaggavasena uppajjamāno pamādo uppajjitvā cittaṃ dūseti, obhāsituṃ na deti. Tasmā “cittassa upakkileso”ti vuccati.

Just as this is so, likewise, conceit (māna), which arises dependent on birth and so forth, proceeds by way of elevating the mind; excessive conceit (atimāna) proceeds by way of extreme elevation; intoxication (mada) has the characteristic of being in the grip of pride; and heedlessness (pamāda) arises by way of letting the mind loose amidst the strands of sensual pleasure. Having arisen, these corrupt the mind; they do not allow it to shine. Therefore, they are called 'defilements of the mind.'

Kasmā [V 1.0180] pana bhagavā upakkilesaṃ dassento lobhamādiṃ katvā dassetīti? Tassa paṭhamuppattito. Sabbasattānañhi yattha katthaci upapannānaṃ antamaso suddhāvāsabhūmiyampi sabbapaṭhamaṃ bhavanikantivasena lobho uppajjati, tato attano attano anurūpapaccayaṃ paṭicca yathāsambhavaṃ itare, na ca ete soḷaseva cittassa upakkilesā, etena pana nayena sabbepi kilesā gahitāyeva hontīti veditabbā.

Why then does the Blessed One, when showing the defilements, present greed first? Because of its primary arising. For of all beings, wherever they are reborn, even down to the Pure Abodes, greed arises first of all by way of delight in existence. Then, depending on their respective appropriate conditions, the others arise as is possible. And it is not that only these sixteen are the defilements of the mind; rather, it should be understood that by this method all defilements are indeed included.

72. Ettāvatā [P 1.0171] saṃkilesaṃ dassetvā idāni vodānaṃ dassento sa kho so, bhikkhavetiādimāha. Tattha iti viditvāti evaṃ jānitvā. Pajahatīti samucchedappahānavasena ariyamaggena pajahati. Tattha kilesapaṭipāṭiyā maggapaṭipāṭiyāti dvidhā pahānaṃ veditabbaṃ. Kilesapaṭipāṭiyā tāva abhijjhāvisamalobho thambho sārambho māno atimāno madoti ime cha kilesā arahattamaggena pahīyanti. Byāpādo kodho upanāho pamādoti ime cattāro kilesā anāgāmimaggena pahīyanti. Makkho paḷāso issā macchariyaṃ māyā sāṭheyyanti ime cha sotāpattimaggena pahīyantīti. Maggapaṭipāṭiyā pana, sotāpattimaggena makkho paḷāso issā macchariyaṃ māyā sāṭheyyanti ime cha pahīyanti. Anāgāmimaggena byāpādo kodho upanāho pamādoti ime cattāro. Arahattamaggena abhijjhāvisamalobho thambho sārambho māno atimāno madoti ime cha pahīyantīti.

72. Having shown the side of defilement to this extent, now, showing the side of purification, he said, 'So indeed, monks...' and so on. Therein, 'having known thus' means having understood thus. 'Abandons' means one abandons by the noble path by way of eradication. Therein, abandonment should be understood in two ways: by the sequence of the defilements and by the sequence of the path. First, by the sequence of the defilements: covetousness and unrighteous greed, stubbornness, contention, conceit, excessive conceit, and intoxication—these six defilements are abandoned by the path of arahantship. Ill will, anger, resentment, and heedlessness—these four defilements are abandoned by the path of non-returning. Disparagement, contempt, envy, stinginess, deceit, and hypocrisy—these six are abandoned by the path of stream-entry. Then, by the sequence of the path: by the path of stream-entry, disparagement, contempt, envy, stinginess, deceit, and hypocrisy—these six are abandoned. By the path of non-returning: ill will, anger, resentment, and heedlessness—these four. By the path of arahantship: covetousness and unrighteous greed, stubbornness, contention, conceit, excessive conceit, and intoxication—these six are abandoned.

Imasmiṃ [M 1.0176] pana ṭhāne ime kilesā sotāpattimaggavajjhā vā hontu, sesamaggavajjhā vā, atha kho anāgāmimaggeneva pahānaṃ sandhāya “abhijjhāvisamalobhaṃ cittassa upakkilesaṃ pajahatī”tiādimāhāti veditabbā. Ayamettha paveṇimaggāgato sambhavo, so ca upari catutthamaggasseva niddiṭṭhattā yujjati, tatiyamaggena pahīnāvasesānañhi visamalobhādīnaṃ tena pahānaṃ hoti, sesānaṃ imināva. Yepi hi sotāpattimaggena pahīyanti, tepi taṃsamuṭṭhāpakacittānaṃ appahīnattā anāgāmimaggeneva suppahīnā hontīti. Keci pana paṭhamamaggena cettha pahānaṃ vaṇṇayanti, taṃ pubbāparena na sandhiyati. Keci vikkhambhanappahānampi, taṃ tesaṃ icchāmattameva.

But in this place, whether these defilements are to be abandoned by the path of stream-entry or by the remaining paths, it should be understood that he spoke, 'he abandons the defilement of the mind, covetousness and unrighteous greed,' and so on, with reference to their abandonment by the path of non-returning alone. This here is the explanation that has come down through the traditional lineage, and it is fitting because above, only the fourth path was indicated. For the abandonment of the remnants of unrighteous greed and so forth, left over from what is abandoned by the third path, occurs by that fourth path; and the abandonment of the rest is by this same method. For even those defilements that are abandoned by the path of stream-entry are only truly well-abandoned by the path of non-returning, because the minds that give rise to them have not yet been completely abandoned. Some, however, explain the abandonment here as being by the first path, but that does not connect with what precedes and follows. Some explain it as abandonment by suppression, but that is merely their own opinion.

73. Yato [V 1.0181] kho, bhikkhaveti ettha yatoti yamhi kāle. Pahīno hotīti anāgāmimaggakkhaṇe pahānaṃ sandhāyevāha.

73. In the phrase 'When, monks...,' yato means 'at which time.' The phrase 'is abandoned' was spoken with reference only to the abandonment at the moment of the path of non-returning.

74. So buddhe aveccappasādenāti etaṃ “yato kho, bhikkhave, abhijjhāvisamalobho pahīno hoti, so buddhe aveccappasādena samannāgato hotī”ti evaṃ ekamekena padena yojetabbaṃ. Imassa hi bhikkhuno anāgāmimaggena lokuttarappasādo āgato, athassa aparena samayena buddhaguṇe dhammaguṇe saṅghaguṇe ca anussarato lokiyo uppajjati, tamassa sabbampi lokiyalokuttaramissakaṃ [P 1.0172] pasādaṃ dassento bhagavā “buddhe aveccappasādenā”tiādimāha.

74. As for 'He is endowed with unwavering confidence in the Buddha,' this should be connected with each and every phrase, thus: 'When, bhikkhus, covetousness and unrighteous greed have been abandoned, he is endowed with unwavering confidence in the Buddha.' Indeed, for this bhikkhu, supramundane confidence has arisen by means of the path of non-returning. Then, at a later time, as he recollects the virtues of the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha, mundane confidence arises. The Blessed One, wishing to show all of this bhikkhu's confidence, which is a mixture of the mundane and the supramundane, spoke the words beginning with 'with unwavering confidence in the Buddha.'

Tattha aveccappasādenāti buddhadhammasaṅghaguṇānaṃ yāthāvato ñātattā acalena accutena pasādena. Idāni yathā tassa bhikkhuno anussarato so aveccappasādo uppanno, taṃ vidhiṃ dassento “itipi so bhagavā”tiādinā nayena tīṇi anussatiṭṭhānāni vitthāresi. Tesaṃ atthavaṇṇanā sabbākārena visuddhimagge anussatikathāyaṃ vuttā.

Therein, 'with unwavering confidence' means with confidence that is unshakeable and immovable, due to having known the virtues of the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha as they truly are. Now, wishing to show the method by which that unwavering confidence arose for that bhikkhu as he was recollecting, He elaborated on the three grounds for recollection by the method beginning with, 'Thus indeed is the Blessed One…' The explanation of their meaning has been stated in every respect in the Visuddhimagga, in the discourse on recollection.

75. Evamassa lokiyalokuttaramissakaṃ pasādaṃ dassetvā idāni kilesappahānaṃ aveccappasādasamannāgatañca paccavekkhato uppajjamānaṃ somanassādiānisaṃsaṃ [M 1.0177] dassento yathodhi kho panassātiādimāha. Anāgāmissa hi paccante vuṭṭhitaṃ corupaddavaṃ vūpasametvā taṃ paccavekkhato mahānagare vasantassa rañño viya ime cime ca mama kilesā pahīnāti attano kilesappahānaṃ paccavekkhato balavasomanassaṃ uppajjati. Taṃ dassento bhagavā “yathodhi kho panassā”tiādimāha.

75. Having thus shown his confidence, which is a mixture of the mundane and the supramundane, and now wishing to show the benefits, beginning with gladness, that arise for one who reflects upon the abandonment of defilements and upon being endowed with unwavering confidence, the Blessed One spoke the words beginning with 'yathodhi kho panassa…' Indeed, for a non-returner who reflects, 'These and those defilements of mine have been abandoned,' strong gladness arises, just as strong gladness arises for a king dwelling in a great city who reflects upon having pacified the danger from thieves that had arisen in a border region. Wishing to show this, the Blessed One spoke the words beginning with 'yathodhi kho panassa…'
