Their opposites are “those easy to admonish.” “Those with evil friends” are those whose friends are like Devadatta and others. “Those with virtuous friends” are those whose friends are like the Buddha or Sāriputta and others. “The heedless” are those who are negligent in bodily misconduct and so on, due to the mind's abandonment of wholesome states. Their opposites are to be understood as “the heedful.” These three pairs are stated in a miscellaneous way. The seven beginning with “the faithless” are in terms of the qualities of an unworthy person. Among them, “the faithless” are those in whom faith is absent regarding the three objects. On the bright side, “the faithful” are those who have faith, or they are so called because faith is present in them. “The shameless” are those in whom there is no shame; this is a designation for those who feel no disgust at unwholesome attainments. “Those with a mind of shame” are those in whose mind shame is present, or whose minds are endowed with shame. “Those without moral dread” are so called because they do not have moral dread; this means they do not fear unwholesome attainments. Their opposites are “those with moral dread.” “Those of little learning” are those who have little learning; and “little” here should not be taken to mean a small amount, but rather “none.” For “those of little learning” are said to be without learning, lacking in learning. “The learned” are those who have much learning; this is a designation for those who, having known even a single verse spoken by the Tathāgata as it truly is, practice accordingly. “The lazy” are those who sink down blameworthily; this is a designation for those of inferior energy. “Those with aroused energy” are those who have aroused energy; this is a designation for those engaged in the right strivings. “Those with lapsed mindfulness” are those whose mindfulness is lost; this means they have lost mindfulness. “Those with established mindfulness” are those whose mindfulness is established; this is a designation for those whose mindfulness is constantly directed toward the object. “The unwise” are those whose wisdom is corrupted; this means they have lost wisdom. “Those endowed with wisdom” are so called because they are endowed with wisdom. Here, “wisdom” should be understood as insight-wisdom. For in this context, the foundation for insight is fully present; therefore, this is insight-wisdom—this is the ruling of the ancients.

Idāni ekameva lokuttaraguṇānaṃ antarāyakaraṃ aniyyānikadiṭṭhiṃ tīhākārehi dassento sandiṭṭhiparāmāsītiādimāha. Tattha sandiṭṭhiṃ parāmasantīti sandiṭṭhiparāmāsī. Ādhānaṃ gaṇhantīti ādhānaggāhī, ādhānanti daḷhaṃ vuccati, daḷhaggāhīti attho. Yuttakāraṇaṃ disvāva laddhiṃ paṭinissajjantīti paṭinissaggī, dukkhena kicchena kasirena bahumpi kāraṇaṃ dassetvā na sakkā paṭinissaggaṃ kātunti duppaṭinissaggī, ye attano uppannaṃ diṭṭhiṃ idameva saccanti daḷhaṃ gaṇhitvā api buddhādīhi kāraṇaṃ dassetvā vuccamānā na paṭinissajjanti, tesametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Tādisā hi puggalā yaṃ yadeva dhammaṃ vā adhammaṃ vā gaṇhanti, taṃ sabbaṃ “evaṃ amhākaṃ ācariyehi kathitaṃ, evaṃ amhehi [P 1.0191] suta”nti kummova aṅgāni sake kapāle antoyeva samodahanti, kumbhīlaggāhaṃ gaṇhanti na vissajjanti. Vuttavipariyāyena sukkapakkho veditabbo.

Now, wishing to show in three ways the wrong view that is not a cause for release, which is the one and only obstacle to the attainment of the supramundane qualities, He spoke the words beginning with 'one who wrongly clings to their own view.' Therein, 'they wrongly cling to their own view' (sandiṭṭhiṃ parāmasanti), thus they are called 'those who wrongly cling to their own view' (sandiṭṭhiparāmāsī). 'They take up a firm grasp' (ādhānaṃ gaṇhanti), thus they are called 'those who take up a firm grasp' (ādhānaggāhī). 'Ādhāna' is said to mean a firm grasp; the meaning is 'one who grasps firmly.' 'They relinquish their doctrine only after seeing a suitable reason' (yuttakāraṇaṃ disvāva laddhiṃ paṭinissajjanti), thus they are called 'those who relinquish' (paṭinissaggī). 'It is not possible to make them relinquish it even after showing many reasons with difficulty, trouble, and hardship' (dukkhena kicchena kasirena bahumpi kāraṇaṃ dassetvā na sakkā paṭinissaggaṃ kātuṃ), thus they are called 'those who are difficult to make relinquish' (duppaṭinissaggī). This is a designation for those who, having firmly grasped a view that has arisen in themselves, thinking, 'This alone is the truth,' do not relinquish it even when spoken to and shown the reason by the Buddha and others. Indeed, such individuals, whatever Dhamma or non-Dhamma they grasp, grasp it thinking, 'Thus it was said by our teachers, thus we have heard,' just as a tortoise draws its limbs into its own shell; they grasp with a crocodile's grip and do not let go. The bright side should be understood in the opposite way of what has been said.

84. Evaṃ catucattālīsāya ākārehi sallekhaṃ dassetvā idāni tasmiṃ sallekhe cittuppādassāpi bahūpakārataṃ dassetuṃ cittuppādampi kho ahantiādimāha.

84. Thus, having shown effacement in forty-four ways, now, in order to show the great benefit of even the arising of a thought in that effacement, He spoke the words beginning with 'cittuppādampi kho ahaṃ'.

Tassattho[V 1.0199], ahaṃ, cunda, kusalesu dhammesu cittuppādampi bahūpakāraṃ vadāmi, yā panetā kāyena ca vācāya ca anuvidhiyanā, yathā paṭhamaṃ cittaṃ uppannaṃ, tatheva tesaṃ dhammānaṃ kāyena karaṇaṃ, vācāya ca “karothā”ti āṇāpanaṃ vā, uggahaparipucchādīni vā, tattha vādoyeva ko, ekantabahūpakārāyeva hi tā anuvidhiyanāti dasseti. Kasmā panettha cittuppādopi bahūpakāroti? Ekantahitasukhāvahattā anuvidhiyanānaṃ hetuttā ca.

Its meaning is: I, Cunda, declare that even the arising of a thought in wholesome qualities is of great benefit. What then is there to say of the subsequent practice by body and speech? He shows that just as the thought first arose, so too the performance of those wholesome qualities with the body, and with the speech—whether it be giving the command, 'Do this,' or the learning of the Pāḷi, the questioning of the commentary, and so on—what is there to say of that? Indeed, those subsequent practices are certainly of great benefit. Why, then, is even the arising of a thought in this context of great benefit? It is of great benefit because it certainly brings welfare and happiness, and because it is the cause of the subsequent practices.

“Dānaṃ [M 1.0195] dassāmī”ti hi cittuppādo sayampi ekantahitasukhāvaho anuvidhiyanānampi hetu, evañhi uppannacittattāyeva dutiyadivase mahāvīthiṃ pidahitvā mahāmaṇḍapaṃ katvā bhikkhusatassa vā bhikkhusahassassa vā dānaṃ deti, “bhikkhusaṅghaṃ nimantetha pūjetha parivisathā”ti parijane āṇāpeti. Evaṃ “saṅghassa cīvaraṃ senāsanaṃ bhesajjaṃ dassāmī”ti cittuppādo sayampi ekantahitasukhāvaho anuvidhiyanānampi hetu, evaṃ uppannacittattāyeva hi cīvarādīni abhisaṅkharoti deti dāpeti ca. Esa nayo saraṇagamanādīsu.

Indeed, the arising of the thought, 'I will give a gift,' is itself certainly a bringer of welfare and happiness and is also a cause for subsequent practices. For it is precisely because of having that arisen thought that on the second day, having blocked off the main road and constructed a great pavilion, one gives a gift to a hundred bhikkhus or to a thousand bhikkhus, and commands one's attendants, saying, 'Invite the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, honor them, serve them.' Similarly, the arising of the thought, 'I will give robes, lodging, and medicine to the Saṅgha,' is itself certainly a bringer of welfare and happiness and is also a cause for subsequent practices. Indeed, it is precisely because of having that arisen thought that one prepares robes and so on, gives them, and causes them to be given. This is the method in the case of going for refuge and so on.

“Saraṇaṃ gacchāmī”ti hi cittaṃ uppādetvāva pacchā kāyena vā vācāya vā saraṇaṃ gaṇhāti. Tathā “pañcaṅgaṃ aṭṭhaṅgaṃ dasaṅgaṃ vā sīlaṃ samādiyissāmī”ti cittaṃ uppādetvā kāyena vā vācāya vā samādiyati, “pabbajitvā catūsu sīlesu patiṭṭhahissāmī”ti ca cittaṃ uppādetvā kāyena vācāya ca pūretabbaṃ sīlaṃ pūreti. “Buddhavacanaṃ uggahessāmī”ti cittaṃ uppādetvāva ekaṃ vā nikāyaṃ dve vā tayo vā cattāro vā pañca vā nikāye vācāya uggaṇhāti. Evaṃ dhutaṅgasamādāna-kammaṭṭhānuggaha-kasiṇaparikamma-jhānasamāpattivipassanāmaggaphala- paccekabodhi-sammāsambodhivasena netabbaṃ.

Indeed, only after having aroused the thought, 'I will go for refuge,' does one afterwards take refuge with the body or with speech. Likewise, having aroused the thought, 'I will undertake the five-precept virtue, the eight-precept virtue, or the ten-precept virtue,' one undertakes it with the body or with speech. And having aroused the thought, 'Having gone forth, I will establish myself in the fourfold purification of virtue,' one fulfills with body and speech the virtue that is to be fulfilled. Only after having aroused the thought, 'I will learn the word of the Buddha,' does one learn with speech one Nikāya, or two, three, four, or the five Nikāyas. In this way, it should be applied by way of the undertaking of ascetic practices, the learning of a meditation subject, the preliminary development of a kasiṇa, jhāna and its attainment, insight, path, fruition, the knowledge of a Paccekabuddha, and the knowledge of Perfect Self-Enlightenment.

“Buddho bhavissāmī”ti hi cittuppādo sayampi ekantahitasukhāvaho anuvidhiyanānampi hetu, evañhi uppannacittattāyeva [P 1.0192] aparena samayena kappasatasahassādhikāni cattāri asaṅkheyyāni kāyena vācāya ca pāramiyo pūretvā sadevakaṃ lokaṃ tārento vicarati. Evaṃ sabbattha cittuppādopi bahūpakāro. Kāyavācāhi pana anuvidhiyanā atibahūpakārāyevāti veditabbā.

Indeed, the arising of the thought, 'I will become a Buddha,' is itself certainly a bringer of welfare and happiness and is also a cause for subsequent practices. For it is precisely because of having that arisen thought that at a later time, having fulfilled the perfections with body and speech for four incalculable aeons and more than one hundred thousand kappas, he wanders liberating the world with its devas. Thus, in every case, the arising of a thought is of great benefit. But the subsequent practices by body and speech should be understood as being exceedingly beneficial.

Evaṃ [V 1.0200] kusalesu dhammesu cittuppādassāpi bahūpakārataṃ dassetvā idāni tattha niyojento “tasmā tiha cundā”tiādimāha. Taṃ atthato pākaṭameva.

Thus, having shown the great benefit of even the arising of a thought in wholesome qualities, now, wishing to encourage engagement therein, He spoke the words beginning with 'tasmā tiha cunda.' That is clear in its meaning.

85. Evaṃ catucattālīsāya ākārehi dassite sallekhe cittuppādassāpi bahūpakārataṃ dassetvā idāni tasseva sallekhassa hitādhigamāya maggabhāvaṃ dassento seyyathāpītiādimāha.

85. Thus, in the effacement shown in forty-four ways, having shown the great benefit of even the arising of a thought, now, wishing to show that that very effacement is the path for the attainment of welfare, He spoke the words beginning with 'seyyathāpi'.

Tassattho[M 1.0196], yathā nāma, cunda, khāṇukaṇṭakapāsāṇādīhi visamo maggo bhaveyya, tassa parikkamanāya parivajjanatthāya añño suparikammakato viya bhūmibhāgo samo maggo bhaveyya, yathā ca rukkhamūlapāsāṇapapātakumbhīlamakarādi paribyākulaṃ visamaṃ titthamassa, tassa parikkamanāya parivajjanatthāya aññaṃ avisamaṃ anupubbagambhīraṃ sopānaphalakasadisaṃ titthaṃ bhaveyya, yaṃ paṭipanno sukheneva taṃ nadiṃ vā taḷākaṃ vā ajjhogāhetvā nhāyeyya vā uttareyya vā, evameva kho, cunda, visamamaggavisamatitthasadisāya vihiṃsāya samannāgatassa vihiṃsakapuggalassa samamaggasamatitthasadisā avihiṃsā hoti parikkamanāya. Yatheva hi visamamaggatitthaparivajjanatthāya samo maggo ca titthañca paṭiyattaṃ, evaṃ vihiṃsāparivajjanatthāya avihiṃsā paṭiyattā, yaṃ paṭipanno sukheneva manussagatiṃ vā devagatiṃ vā ajjhogāhetvā sampattiṃ vā anubhaveyya uttareyya vā lokā. Eteneva upāyena sabbapadāni yojetabbāni.

Its meaning is: Just as, Cunda, there might be an uneven path with stumps, thorns, stones, and so on, and for the purpose of bypassing and avoiding it, there might be another even path, like a well-prepared stretch of ground; and just as there might be an uneven ford, troubled by tree roots, stones, cliffs, crocodiles, sea-monsters, and so on, and for the purpose of bypassing and avoiding it, there might be another, even ford, gradually deepening, like a flight of stairs or a plank, by which one who has entered could easily plunge into that river or pond and either bathe or cross over; even so, Cunda, for a harmful person who is endowed with harmfulness—which is like an uneven path and an uneven ford—non-harming is for the purpose of avoidance, like an even path and an even ford. To make it clear: just as an even path and an even ford are prepared for the purpose of avoiding an uneven path and an uneven ford, so too is non-harming prepared for the purpose of avoiding harmfulness. One who has entered upon it can easily plunge into a human destination or a divine destination and experience prosperity, or one may transcend the world. By this method, all the terms should be connected.

86. Evaṃ tasseva hitādhigamāya maggabhāvaṃ dassetvā idāni uparibhāgaṅgamanīyataṃ dassento, seyyathāpītiādimāha.

86. Thus, having shown that that very effacement is the path for the attainment of welfare, now, wishing to show its quality of leading to the higher states, he spoke the words beginning with 'Just as...'

Tassattho, yathā nāma, cunda, ye keci akusalā dhammā paṭisandhiyā janakā vā ajanakā vā, dinnāyapi paṭisandhiyā vipākajanakā vā ajanakā vā, sabbe te jātivasena adhobhāgaṅgamanīyāti evaṃnāmāva honti, vipākakāle aniṭṭhākantavipākattā. Yathā ca ye keci kusalā dhammā [P 1.0193] paṭisandhiyā janakā vā ajanakā vā dinnāyapi paṭisandhiyā vipākajanakā vā ajanakā vā, sabbe te jātivasena uparibhāgaṅgamanīyāti evaṃnāmāva honti, vipākakāle iṭṭhakantavipākattā, evameva kho, cunda, vihiṃsakassa…pe… uparibhāgāyāti. Tatrāyaṃ opammasaṃsandanā – yathā sabbe akusalā adhobhāgaṅgamanīyā, evaṃ vihiṃsakassa [V 1.0201] ekā vihiṃsāpi. Yathā ca sabbe kusalā uparibhāgaṅgamanīyā, evaṃ avihiṃsakassa ekā avihiṃsāpi. Eteneva upāyena akusalaṃ akusalena kusalañca kusalena upametabbaṃ, ayaṃ kirettha adhippāyoti.

Its meaning is this: Cunda, just as whatever unwholesome states there are—whether they are generative of rebirth or not, or whether, in a given rebirth, they are productive of results or not—all of them, by their nature, are named 'downward-leading' because at the time of fruition they result in what is undesirable and unpleasant; and just as whatever wholesome states there are—whether they are generative of rebirth or not, or whether, in a given rebirth, they are productive of results or not—all of them, by their nature, are named 'upward-leading' because at the time of fruition they result in what is desirable and pleasant; even so, Cunda, for a harmful person it is downward-leading, and for a non-harming person it is upward-leading. Herein, this is the application of the simile: just as all unwholesome states are downward-leading, so too for a harmful person is even a single act of harmfulness. And just as all wholesome states are upward-leading, so too for a non-harming person is even a single act of non-harming. By this method, the unwholesome should be compared with the unwholesome, and the wholesome with the wholesome. This, it is said, is the intended meaning here.

87. Evaṃ tasseva sallekhassa uparibhāgaṅgamanīyataṃ dassetvā idāni parinibbāpane samatthabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ so vata cundātiādimāha. Tattha [M 1.0197] soti vuttappakārapuggalaniddeso. Tassa yoti imaṃ uddesavacanaṃ āharitvā yo attanā palipapalipanno, so vata, cunda, paraṃ palipapalipannaṃ uddharissatīti evaṃ sabbapadesu sambandho veditabbo. Palipapalipannoti gambhīrakaddame nimuggo vuccati, no ca kho ariyassa vinaye. Ariyassa pana vinaye palipanti pañca kāmaguṇā vuccanti. Palipannoti tattha nimuggo bālaputhujjano, tasmā evamettha atthayojanā veditabbā. Yathā, cunda, koci puriso yāva nāsikaggā gambhīre kaddame nimuggo aparaṃ tattheva nimuggaṃ hatthe vā sīse vā gahetvā uddharissatīti netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati, na hi taṃ kāraṇamatthi, yena so taṃ uddharitvā thale patiṭṭhapeyya, evameva yo attanā pañcakāmaguṇapalipe palipanno, so vata paraṃ tatheva palipapalipannaṃ uddharissatīti netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati.

87. Thus, having shown the quality of that very effacement to lead to the higher states, now, to show its capability for causing final extinguishment, he spoke the words beginning with 'So indeed, Cunda...'. Therein, 'so' is an indication of a person of the type already mentioned. For that ('so'), having supplied this introductory word 'yo', the connection in all phrases should be understood thus: 'Whatever person is oneself sunk in the swamp, that person, Cunda, could indeed pull out another sunk in the swamp'—that case does not exist. 'Sunk in the swamp' (palipapalipanno) refers to one submerged in deep mud, but this is not so in the Noble One's Discipline. In the Noble One's Discipline, 'swamp' (palipa) refers to the five strands of sensual pleasure. 'Sunk' (palipanno) refers to a foolish ordinary person submerged therein. Therefore, the application of the meaning here should be understood thus: Just as, Cunda, it is not possible that a person submerged in deep mud up to the tip of their nose could pull out another person also submerged therein by grasping their hand or head—for that reason by which he could pull that person out and establish them on dry land does not exist—even so, it is not possible that a person who is oneself sunk in the swamp of the five strands of sensual pleasure could indeed pull out another person similarly sunk.

Tattha siyā ayuttametaṃ, puthujjanānampi bhikkhubhikkhunīupāsakaupāsikānaṃ dhammadesanaṃ sutvā hontiyeva dhammaṃ abhisametāro, tasmā palipapalipanno uddharatīti, taṃ na tathā daṭṭhabbaṃ. Bhagavāyeva hi tattha uddharati, pasaṃsāmattameva pana dhammakathikā labhanti raññā pahitalekhavācako viya. Yathā hi rañño paccantajanapade pahitaṃ lekhaṃ tattha manussā lekhaṃ vācetuṃ ajānantā yo vācetuṃ jānāti, tena vācāpetvā tamatthaṃ sutvā “rañño āṇā”ti ādarena sampādenti, na ca nesaṃ [P 1.0194] hoti “lekhavācakassa ayaṃ āṇā”ti. Lekhavācako pana “vissaṭṭhāya vācāya vācesi anelagaḷāyā”ti pasaṃsāmattameva labhati, evameva kiñcāpi sāriputtapabhutayo dhammakathikā dhammaṃ desenti, atha kho likhitapaṇṇavācako viya te honti. Bhagavatoyeva pana sā dhammadesanā rañño āṇā viya. Ye ca taṃ sutvā dhammaṃ abhisamenti, te bhagavāyeva uddharatīti veditabbā. Dhammakathikā pana “vissaṭṭhāya vācāya dhammaṃ desenti anelagaḷāyā”ti pasaṃsāmattameva labhantīti. Tasmā yuttamevetanti. Vuttavipariyāyena sukkapakkho veditabbo.

Herein, one might say: 'This is unreasonable, for there are indeed those who comprehend the Dhamma after hearing a Dhamma-discourse from ordinary monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen; therefore, one sunk in the swamp does pull another out.' That should not be seen in that way. For it is the Blessed One who pulls them out in that case; the Dhamma-teachers, however, only receive praise, like a reader of a letter sent by the king. For just as when a king sends a letter to a border region, the people there, not knowing how to read the letter, have it read by one who knows how, and having heard its meaning, they carry it out with respect, thinking, 'This is the king's command,' and it does not occur to them, 'This is the letter-reader's command.' The letter-reader, however, receives only praise, as in: 'He read it with a clear and fluent voice.' Even so, although Dhamma-teachers like Sāriputta teach the Dhamma, they are like the reader of the written leaf. But that Dhamma-discourse is the Blessed One's, like the king's command. And those who comprehend the Dhamma after hearing it, it should be understood that the Blessed One pulls them out. The Dhamma-teachers, however, receive only praise, as in: 'They teach the Dhamma with a clear and fluent voice.' Therefore, that statement is indeed reasonable. The bright side should be understood by way of the reverse of what has been said.

Adanto [V 1.0202] avinīto aparinibbutoti ettha pana anibbisatāya adanto. Asikkhitavinayatāya avinīto. Anibbutakilesatāya aparinibbutoti veditabbo. So tādiso paraṃ damessati, nibbisaṃ karissati[M 1.0198], vinessati vā tisso sikkhā sikkhāpessati, parinibbāpessati vā tassa kilese nibbāpessatīti netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati. Vuttavipariyāyena sukkapakkho veditabbo.

As for 'untamed, undisciplined, unquenched': herein, 'untamed' is due to not having expelled the poison of the defilements; 'undisciplined' is due to not having been trained in the discipline; 'unquenched' is due to having unquenched defilements—thus it should be understood. That such a person could tame another, make them poisonless; or discipline them, train them in the three trainings; or cause them to be fully quenched, extinguish their defilements—this is not possible. The bright side should be understood by way of the reverse of what has been said.

Evameva kho, cunda, vihiṃsakassa…pe… parinibbānāyāti ettha pana evamattho veditabbo – yathā hi attanā apalipapalipanno paraṃ palipapalipannaṃ uddharissati, danto damessati, vinīto vinessati, parinibbuto parinibbāpessatīti ṭhānametaṃ vijjatīti. Kiṃ pana tanti? Apalipapalipannattaṃ, dantattaṃ vinītattaṃ parinibbutattañca, evameva kho, cunda, vihiṃsakassa purisapuggalassa avihiṃsā hoti parinibbānāya. Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti? Yo attanā avihiṃsako, tassa yā avihiṃsā, ayaṃ yā esā vihiṃsakassa parassa vihiṃsā, tassā parinibbānāya hoti, attanā hi avihiṃsako parassa vihiṃsācetanaṃ nibbāpessatīti ṭhānametaṃ vijjati. Kiṃ pana tanti? Avihiṃsakattameva. Yañhi yena attanā adhigataṃ hoti, so paraṃ tadatthāya samādapetuṃ sakkotīti.

As for 'Even so, Cunda, for a harmful person... for final extinguishment,' the meaning here should be understood thus: Just as one who is not oneself sunk in the swamp will pull out another who is sunk in the swamp; one who is tamed will tame another; one who is disciplined will discipline another; one who is fully quenched will cause another to be fully quenched—this is possible. And what is the reason for that? The state of not being sunk in the swamp, the state of being tamed, the state of being disciplined, and the state of being fully quenched. Even so, Cunda, for a non-harming individual, non-harming leads to final extinguishment. What is meant by this? A person who is oneself non-harming—their non-harming leads to the final extinguishment of the harming of another who is a harmful person. For it is possible that one who is oneself non-harming will extinguish the harmful intention of another. And what is the reason for that? The state of being non-harming itself. For whatever Dhamma has been attained by a person themselves, they are able to cause another to undertake it for the sake of that attainment.

Atha vā yathā attanā apalipanno danto vinīto parinibbuto paraṃ palipapalipannaṃ adantaṃ avinītaṃ aparinibbutañca uddharissati damessati vinessati parinibbāpessatīti ṭhānametaṃ vijjati, evameva vihiṃsakassa purisapuggalassa vihiṃsāpahānāya maggaṃ bhāvayato uppannā avihiṃsā hoti parinibbānāya. Parinibbuto viya hi aparinibbutaṃ avihiṃsācetanāva vihiṃsācetanaṃ parinibbāpetuṃ [P 1.0195] samatthā. Etamatthaṃ dassento “evameva kho, cundā”tiādimāhāti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Yathā cettha, evaṃ sabbapadesu. Ativitthārabhayena pana anupadayojanā na katāti.

Or else, just as one who is not sunk in the mire, who is tamed, disciplined, and extinguished, can lift up, tame, discipline, and lead to extinguishment another who is sunk in the mire, untamed, undisciplined, and unextinguished—such a possibility exists. So too, for a violent individual, when they develop the path for abandoning violence, the non-violence that arises is for the sake of extinguishment. Indeed, just as one who is extinguished is capable of extinguishing one who is not, so non-violent intention is capable of extinguishing violent intention. To show this meaning, He said, ‘Just so, Cunda…’ and so on. Thus, the meaning should be understood here. And as it is here, so the meaning should be understood in all passages. However, for fear of excessive elaboration, a word-by-word explanation is not given.

88. Evaṃ tassa parinibbāpane samatthabhāvaṃ dassetvā idāni taṃ desanaṃ nigametvā dhammapaṭipattiyaṃ niyojetuṃ iti kho, cundātiādimāha. Tattha sallekhapariyāyoti sallekhakāraṇaṃ. Esa nayo sabbattha ettha avihiṃsādayo eva vihiṃsādīnaṃ sallekhanato sallekhakāraṇaṃ[V 1.0203]. Tesaṃ vasena cittassa uppādetabbato cittupādakāraṇaṃ, vihiṃsādi, parikkamanassa hetuto parikkamanakāraṇaṃ, uparibhāganipphādanato uparibhāgakāraṇaṃ[M 1.0199], vihiṃsādīnaṃ parinibbāpanato parinibbānakāraṇanti veditabbā. Hitesināti hitaṃ esantena. Anukampakenāti anukampamānena. Anukampaṃ upādāyāti anukampaṃ cittena pariggahetvā, pariccātipi vuttaṃ hoti. Kataṃ vo taṃ mayāti taṃ mayā ime pañca pariyāye dassentena tumhākaṃ kataṃ. Ettakameva hi anukampakassa satthu kiccaṃ, yadidaṃ aviparītadhammadesanā. Ito paraṃ pana paṭipatti nāma sāvakānaṃ kiccaṃ. Tenāha etāni, cunda, rukkhamūlāni…pe… amhākaṃ anusāsanīti.

88. Having thus shown its capability for causing extinguishment, now, concluding that teaching and in order to urge one to the practice of the Dhamma, He said, ‘So it is, Cunda…’ and so on. Therein, ‘the discourse on effacement’ is the cause of effacement. This is the method in all cases. Here, non-violence and so on are the cause of effacement because they efface violence and so on. Because the mind is to be aroused by means of them, it is the cause for arousing the mind. Because it is the cause for turning away from violence and so on, it is the cause for turning away. Because it accomplishes the higher portion, it is the cause for the higher portion. Because it extinguishes violence and so on, it is the cause of extinguishment—thus it should be known. ‘Seeking welfare’ means one who seeks welfare. ‘Compassionate’ means one who is compassionate. ‘Having taken up compassion’ means having embraced it with a compassionate mind, based on it. ‘What was to be done for you by me has been done’ means: ‘By me, showing these five methods, that teaching has been given to you.’ For this much is the duty of a compassionate Teacher: the teaching of the Dhamma without distortion. Beyond this, however, the practice is the duty of the disciples. Therefore, He said, ‘These, Cunda, are the roots of trees… this is our instruction.’

Tattha ca rukkhamūlānīti iminā rukkhamūlasenāsanaṃ dasseti. Suññāgārānīti iminā janavivittaṭṭhānaṃ. Ubhayenāpi ca yogānurūpasenāsanamācikkhati, dāyajjaṃ niyyāteti. Jhāyathāti ārammaṇūpanijjhānena aṭṭhatiṃsārammaṇāni, lakkhaṇūpanijjhānena ca aniccādito khandhāyatanādīni upanijjhāyatha, samathañca vipassanañca vaḍḍhethāti vuttaṃ hoti. Mā pamādatthāti mā pamajjittha. Mā pacchā vippaṭisārino ahuvatthāti ye hi pubbe daharakāle, ārogyakāle, sattasappāyādisampattikāle, satthu sammukhībhāvakāle ca yonisomanasikāravirahitā rattindivaṃ maṅgulabhattā hutvā seyyasukhaṃ middhasukhamanubhontā pamajjanti, te pacchā jarākāle, rogakāle, maraṇakāle, vipattikāle, satthu parinibbutakāle ca taṃ pubbe pamādavihāraṃ anussarantā, sappaṭisandhikālakiriyañca bhāriyaṃ sampassamānā vippaṭisārino honti, tumhe pana tādisā mā ahuvatthāti etamatthaṃ dassento āha “mā [P 1.0196] pacchā vippaṭisārino ahuvatthā”ti. Ayaṃ vo amhākaṃ anusāsanīti ayaṃ amhākaṃ santikā “jhāyatha mā pamādatthā”ti tumhākaṃ anusāsanī, ovādoti vuttaṃ hoti.

And therein, by ‘roots of trees,’ He indicates the dwelling at the root of a tree. By ‘empty dwellings,’ He indicates a place secluded from people. And by both, He points out a dwelling suitable for meditative practice; He bestows it as an inheritance. ‘Meditate’ means: contemplate the thirty-eight meditation subjects by means of absorption upon the object, and contemplate the aggregates, sense bases, and so on, beginning with impermanence, by means of absorption upon the characteristics; develop both serenity and insight—thus it is said. ‘Do not be negligent’ means do not be heedless. ‘Do not be ones who have remorse later’ means: for those who previously, in their youth, in time of health, in time of the fulfillment of the seven kinds of suitability, and in the time of being in the Teacher's presence, being devoid of wise attention, day and night become like those fed on festive food, and being negligent, experience the pleasure of lying down and the pleasure of drowsiness; they later, in time of old age, in time of sickness, in time of death, in time of misfortune, and in the time after the Teacher's complete extinguishment, repeatedly recollecting that former negligent abiding, and clearly seeing the weighty act of dying with a linking-consciousness, become remorseful. But you, do not be like that—to show this meaning, He said, ‘Do not be ones who have remorse later.’ ‘This is our instruction to you’ means: from us, this instruction to you, ‘Meditate, do not be negligent,’ is our admonition—thus it is said.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

Of the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya

Sallekhasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Sallekha Sutta is concluded.

9. Sammādiṭṭhisuttavaṇṇanā

9. Commentary on the Discourse on Right View

89. Evaṃ [V 1.0204] me sutanti sammādiṭṭhisuttaṃ. Tattha “sammādiṭṭhi sammādiṭṭhīti, āvuso, vuccati, kittāvatā nu kho, āvuso”ti vā “katamaṃ panāvuso[M 1.0200], akusala”nti vā evaṃ yattakā therena pucchā vuttā, sabbā kathetukamyatā pucchā eva.

89. Thus have I heard—the Discourse on Right View. Therein, “Friend, ‘right view, right view’ is said; now to what extent, friend?” or “But what, friend, is the unwholesome?”—all such questions as were spoken by the Elder were indeed questions from a desire to explain.

Tattha yasmā jānantāpi sammādiṭṭhīti vadanti ajānantāpi bāhirakāpi sāsanikāpi anussavādivasenāpi attapaccakkhenāpi, tasmā taṃ bahūnaṃ vacanaṃ upādāya dvikkhattuṃ āmasanto “sammādiṭṭhi sammādiṭṭhīti, āvuso, vuccatī”ti āha. Ayañhi ettha adhippāyo, aparehipi sammādiṭṭhīti vuccati, athāparehipi sammādiṭṭhīti vuccati, svāyaṃ evaṃ vuccamāno atthañca lakkhaṇañca upādāya kittāvatā nu kho, āvuso, ariyasāvako sammādiṭṭhi hotīti. Tattha sammādiṭṭhīti sobhanāya pasatthāya ca diṭṭhiyā samannāgato. Yadā pana dhammeyeva ayaṃ sammādiṭṭhisaddo vattati, tadāssa sobhanā pasatthā ca diṭṭhi sammādiṭṭhīti evamattho veditabbo.

Herein, because those who know say 'right view,' and those who do not know—both outsiders and those within the Dispensation, both by way of hearsay and by personal realization—also say it, therefore, taking up that word of the many, wishing to touch upon it twice, he said, 'Friend, "right view, right view" is said.' Indeed, this is the intention here: since 'right view' is spoken of by some, and 'right view' is also spoken of by others, the question, 'To what extent, friend, is a noble disciple one of right view?' is raised concerning this term so spoken, taking up its meaning and characteristic. Therein, 'one of right view' is one endowed with a view that is beautiful and praiseworthy. But when this word 'sammādiṭṭhi' is used in reference to the Dhamma itself, then its meaning should be understood thus: a view that is beautiful and praiseworthy is right view.

Sā cāyaṃ sammādiṭṭhi duvidhā hoti lokiyā lokuttarāti. Tattha kammassakatāñāṇaṃ saccānulomikañāṇañca lokiyā sammādiṭṭhi, saṅkhepato vā sabbāpi sāsavā paññā. Ariyamaggaphalasampayuttā paññā lokuttarā sammādiṭṭhi. Puggalo pana tividho hoti puthujjano sekkho asekkho ca. Tattha puthujjano duvidho hoti bāhirako sāsaniko ca. Tattha bāhirako kammavādī kammassakatādiṭṭhiyā sammādiṭṭhi hoti, no saccānulomikāya attadiṭṭhiparāmāsakattā. Sāsaniko dvīhipi. Sekkho niyatāya sammādiṭṭhiyā sammādiṭṭhi. Asekkho asekkhāya. Idha pana niyatāya niyyānikāya lokuttarakusalasammādiṭṭhiyā samannāgato “sammādiṭṭhī”ti adhippeto. Tenevāha “ujugatāssa diṭṭhi dhamme aveccappasādena samannāgato āgato imaṃ saddhamma”nti, lokuttarakusalasammādiṭṭhiyeva hi antadvayamanupagamma ujubhāvena gatattā[P 1.0197], kāyavaṅkādīni ca sabbavaṅkāni samucchinditvā gatattā ujugatā hoti, tāyeva [V 1.0205] ca diṭṭhiyā samannāgato navappakārepi lokuttaradhamme aveccappasādena acalappasādena samannāgato hoti, sabbadiṭṭhigahanāni ca vinibbeṭhento sabbakilese pajahanto jātisaṃsārā nikkhamanto paṭipattiṃ pariniṭṭhapento ariyena maggena āgato imaṃ sambuddhappaveditaṃ amatogadhaṃ nibbānasaṅkhātaṃ saddhammanti vuccati.

And this right view is twofold: mundane and supramundane. Therein, the knowledge of the ownership of kamma and the knowledge conforming to the truths constitute mundane right view—or, in brief, all wisdom associated with taints. The wisdom associated with the noble path and fruition is supramundane right view. A person, however, is threefold: an ordinary person, a trainee, and one beyond training. Among them, the ordinary person is twofold: an outsider and one within the Dispensation. Therein, the outsider who is a proponent of kamma is of right view through the view of kamma-ownership, but not through the knowledge conforming to the truths, because of grasping at the self-view. One within the Dispensation is of right view by both. The trainee is of right view through the assured right view. The one beyond training is of right view through the right view of one beyond training. Here, however, it is intended that one endowed with the assured, liberating, supramundane wholesome right view is called 'one of right view.' For that reason, it is said: “His view is straight, endowed with unwavering confidence in the Dhamma, he has come to this true Dhamma.” For the supramundane wholesome right view alone, by not approaching either of the two extremes, proceeds straightly; and because it proceeds having eradicated all crookedness, such as bodily crookedness, it is straight. Endowed with that very view, one is endowed with unwavering, unshakable confidence in the nine kinds of supramundane states. And untangling all thickets of views, abandoning all defilements, emerging from the round of birth, bringing the practice to completion, one has come by the noble path to this true Dhamma proclaimed by the Fully Enlightened Ones—the deathless state, known as Nibbāna; thus it is said.

Yato khoti kālaparicchedavacanametaṃ, yasmiṃ kāleti vuttaṃ hoti. Akusalañca pajānātīti dasākusalakammapathasaṅkhātaṃ akusalañca [M 1.0201] pajānāti, nirodhārammaṇāya pajānanāya kiccavasena “idaṃ dukkha”nti paṭivijjhanto akusalaṃ pajānāti. Akusalamūlañca pajānātīti tassa mūlapaccayabhūtaṃ akusalamūlañca pajānāti, teneva pakārena “ayaṃ dukkhasamudayo”ti paṭivijjhanto. Esa nayo kusalañca kusalamūlañcāti etthāpi. Yathā cettha, evaṃ ito paresu sabbavāresu kiccavaseneva vatthupajānanā veditabbā. Ettāvatāpīti ettakena iminā akusalādippajānanenāpi. Sammādiṭṭhi hotīti vuttappakārāya lokuttarasammādiṭṭhiyā samannāgato hoti. Ujugatāssa…pe… imaṃ saddhammanti ettāvatā saṃkhittadesanā niṭṭhitā hoti. Desanāyeva cesā saṃkhittā, tesaṃ pana bhikkhūnaṃ vitthāravaseneva sammāmanasikārappaṭivedho veditabbo.

The word 'when indeed' (yato kho) indicates a division of time; it means 'at which time.' 'And one understands the unwholesome' means one understands the unwholesome, which is designated as the ten unwholesome courses of action. By means of understanding that has cessation as its object, by way of function, by penetrating, “This is suffering,” one understands the unwholesome. 'And one understands the root of the unwholesome' means one understands the root of the unwholesome, which is its root-condition, by penetrating in that very way: “This is the origin of suffering.” This same method applies to 'the wholesome and the root of the wholesome.' And as it is here, so in all subsequent sections, the understanding of the subject matter should be known by way of its function. 'To this extent' means even with this much understanding of the unwholesome and so forth. 'One is of right view' means one is endowed with the supramundane right view of the kind described. 'His view is straight...' up to '...this true Dhamma'—to this extent, the brief exposition is concluded. And this exposition itself is brief, but for those monks, the penetration through right attention should be understood as being in detail.

Dutiyavāre pana desanāpi vitthārena manasikārappaṭivedhopi vitthāreneva vuttoti veditabbo. Tattha “saṃkhittadesanāya dve heṭṭhimamaggā, vitthāradesanāya dve uparimamaggā kathitā”ti bhikkhū āhaṃsu vitthāradesanāvasāne “sabbaso rāgānusayaṃ pahāyā”tiādivacanaṃ sampassamānā. Thero panāha “saṃkhittadesanāyapi cattāro maggā rāsito kathitā, vitthāradesanāyapī”ti. Yā cāyaṃ [P 1.0198] idha saṃkhittavitthāradesanāsu vicāraṇā āvikatā, sā sabbavāresu idha vuttanayeneva veditabbā. Apubbānuttānapadavaṇṇanāmattameva hi ito paraṃ karissāma.

In the second section, however, it should be understood that both the teaching and the penetration through attention are spoken of in detail. Therein, seeing the words 'having completely abandoned the underlying tendency to lust,' and so on, at the end of the detailed teaching, the monks said: 'In the brief teaching, the two lower paths are spoken of; in the detailed teaching, the two higher paths are spoken of.' But the Elder said: 'In the brief teaching too, the four paths are spoken of collectively, and in the detailed teaching too.' And this investigation that has been made evident here into the brief and detailed teachings should be understood in all sections according to the method stated here. For from here on, we will provide only the explanation of words that are new and not obvious.

Akusalakammapathavaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Unwholesome Courses of Action

Tattha paṭhamavārassa tāva vitthāradesanāya “pāṇātipāto kho, āvuso, akusala”ntiādīsu akosallappavattiyā akusalaṃ veditabbaṃ, parato vattabbakusalappaṭipakkhato [V 1.0206] vā. Taṃ lakkhaṇato sāvajjadukkhavipākaṃ saṃkiliṭṭhaṃ vā. Ayaṃ tāvettha sādhāraṇapadavaṇṇanā.

Herein, firstly, in the detailed exposition of the first section, regarding passages such as, “The destruction of life, friend, is unwholesome,” the unwholesome should be understood as arising from unskillfulness, or as being the opposite of the wholesome which is to be spoken of later. By its characteristic, it is blameworthy and has a painful result, or it is defiled. This, for now, is the explanation of the common terms herein.

Asādhāraṇesu pana pāṇassa atipāto pāṇātipāto, pāṇavadho pāṇaghātoti vuttaṃ hoti. Pāṇoti cettha vohārato satto, paramatthato jīvitindriyaṃ. Tasmiṃ pana pāṇe pāṇasaññino jīvitindriyupacchedakaupakkamasamuṭṭhāpikā kāyavacīdvārānaṃ aññataradvārappavattā vadhakacetanā pāṇātipāto. So guṇavirahitesu tiracchānagatādīsu pāṇesu khuddake pāṇe appasāvajjo, mahāsarīre [M 1.0202] mahāsāvajjo. Kasmā? Payogamahantatāya. Payogasamattepi vatthumahantatāya. Guṇavantesu manussādīsu appaguṇe pāṇe appasāvajjo, mahāguṇe mahāsāvajjo. Sarīraguṇānaṃ pana samabhāve sati kilesānaṃ upakkamānañca mudutāya appasāvajjo, tibbatāya mahāsāvajjoti veditabbo. Tassa pañca sambhārā honti pāṇo, pāṇasaññitā, vadhakacittaṃ, upakkamo, tena maraṇanti. Cha payogā sāhatthiko, āṇattiko, nissaggiyo, thāvaro, vijjāmayo, iddhimayoti. Imasmiṃ panettha vitthārīyamāne atipapañco hoti, tasmā naṃ na vitthārayāma, aññañca evarūpaṃ. Atthikehi pana samantapāsādikaṃ vinayaṭṭhakathaṃ (pārā. aṭṭha. 2.172) oloketvā gahetabbo.

Now, regarding the specific terms: the destruction of a living being is the destruction of life; this is what is meant by the slaying of a being or the killing of a being. Herein, a ‘living being’ is, by convention, a being; in the ultimate sense, it is the life faculty. With regard to that living being, the volition to kill of one who perceives it as a living being—a volition which gives rise to an effort that severs the life faculty and which occurs through either the body-door or the speech-door—is the destruction of life. This act, when directed towards beings devoid of virtue such as animals, is of little blame in the case of a small being, but of great blame in the case of a large-bodied being. Why? Because of the greatness of the effort. Even when the effort is the same, it is of great blame because of the greatness of the object. Among virtuous beings such as humans, it is of little blame in the case of a being with little virtue, but of great blame in the case of one with great virtue. However, when the physical and virtuous qualities are equal, it should be understood that the act is of little blame due to the mildness of the defilements and the effort, and of great blame due to their intensity. It has five components: a living being, the perception of it as a living being, the thought of killing, the effort, and the death resulting therefrom. There are six modes of application: by one's own hand, by command, by missile, by a fixed contrivance, by magical knowledge, and by psychic power. If this were to be elaborated upon here, it would become excessively prolix; therefore, we shall not elaborate on it, nor on other similar matters. Those who are interested, however, should look into the Samantapāsādikā, the commentary on the Vinaya, and grasp it from there.

Adinnassa ādānaṃ adinnādānaṃ, parassa haraṇaṃ theyyaṃ, corikāti vuttaṃ hoti. Tattha adinnanti parapariggahitaṃ, yattha paro yathākāmakāritaṃ āpajjanto adaṇḍāraho anupavajjo ca hoti. Tasmiṃ pana parapariggahite parapariggahitasaññino tadādāyakaupakkamasamuṭṭhāpikā theyyacetanā adinnādānaṃ. Taṃ hīne parasantake appasāvajjaṃ[P 1.0199], paṇīte mahāsāvajjaṃ. Kasmā? Vatthupaṇītatāya. Vatthusamatte sati guṇādhikānaṃ santake vatthusmiṃ mahāsāvajjaṃ. Taṃ taṃ guṇādhikaṃ upādāya tato tato hīnaguṇassa santake vatthusmiṃ appasāvajjaṃ. Tassa pañca sambhārā honti parapariggahitaṃ, parapariggahitasaññitā, theyyacittaṃ, upakkamo, tena haraṇanti. Cha payogā sāhatthikādayova. Te ca kho yathānurūpaṃ theyyāvahāro, pasayhāvahāro, paṭicchannāvahāro, parikappāvahāro, kusāvahāroti imesaṃ avahārānaṃ vasena pavattāti ayamettha saṅkhepo. Vitthāro pana samantapāsādikāyaṃ (pārā. aṭṭha. 1.92) vutto.

The taking of what is not given is adinnādāna; this is what is meant by the carrying away of another's property, theft, or stealing. Herein, 'what is not given' means what is possessed by another, property over which the owner, in acting as they please, is not liable to punishment or censure. With regard to that which is possessed by another, the volition to steal of one who perceives it as possessed by another—a volition which gives rise to an effort to take it—is adinnādāna. This act is of little blame in the case of an inferior possession belonging to another, but of great blame in the case of a superior one. Why? Because of the superiority of the object. When the objects are of equal value, the blame is great in the case of an object belonging to those of superior virtue. In dependence on this or that superior virtue, the blame is less in the case of an object belonging to one of inferior virtue. It has five components: what is possessed by another, the perception of it as possessed by another, the thought of stealing, the effort, and the taking by that effort. There are six modes of application, beginning with that done by one's own hand. And these, as is appropriate, proceed by way of these types of theft: theft by fraudulent means, theft by force, theft by concealment, theft by demarcation, and theft by manipulating lots. This is the summary here. The detailed explanation, however, is given in the Samantapāsādikā.

Kāmesumicchācāroti [V 1.0207] ettha pana kāmesūti methunasamācāresu. Micchācāroti ekantanindito lāmakācāro. Lakkhaṇato pana asaddhammādhippāyena kāyadvārappavattā agamanīyaṭṭhānavītikkamacetanā kāmesumicchācāro.

Now, regarding sexual misconduct (kāmesumicchācāra): herein, the term 'in sensual pleasures' (kāmesu) refers to matters of sexual intercourse. 'Misconduct' (micchācāra) means base conduct that is entirely censurable. By characteristic, however, sexual misconduct is the volition to transgress with a forbidden partner, arising through the body-door with an unrighteous intention.

Tattha agamanīyaṭṭhānaṃ nāma purisānaṃ tāva māturakkhitā, piturakkhitā, mātāpiturakkhitā, bhāturakkhitā, bhaginirakkhitā, ñātirakkhitā, gottarakkhitā, dhammarakkhitā, sārakkhā, saparidaṇḍāti māturakkhitādayo dasa[M 1.0203]; dhanakkītā, chandavāsinī, bhogavāsinī, paṭavāsinī, odapattakinī, obhaṭacumbaṭā, dāsī ca bhariyā ca, kammakārī ca bhariyā ca, dhajāhatā, muhuttikāti etā ca dhanakkītādayo dasāti vīsati itthiyo. Itthīsu pana dvinnaṃ sārakkhāsaparidaṇḍānaṃ, dasannañca dhanakkītādīnanti dvādasannaṃ itthīnaṃ aññe purisā, idaṃ agamanīyaṭṭhānaṃ nāma. So panesa micchācāro sīlādiguṇarahite agamanīyaṭṭhāne appasāvajjo, sīlādiguṇasampanne mahāsāvajjo. Tassa cattāro sambhārā agamanīyavatthu, tasmiṃ sevanacittaṃ, sevanapayogo, maggenamaggappaṭipattiadhivāsananti. Eko payogo sāhatthiko eva.

Herein, for men, what is called a forbidden partner are, first, these twenty types of women: the ten beginning with one protected by her mother (namely, one protected by her mother, by her father, by both mother and father, by a brother, by a sister, by relatives, by her clan, or by the Dhamma; one who has a guardian; and one subject to penalty); and these ten beginning with one bought with wealth (namely, one bought with wealth, one who lives together by consent, one who lives for the sake of wealth, one who lives for the sake of clothing, a wife taken by the water ceremony, a wife who was a porter, one who is both a slave and a wife, one who is both a worker and a wife, one captured in war, and a temporary wife). Among these women, for other men, the two types—she who has a guardian and she who is subject to penalty—and the ten types beginning with she who is bought with wealth, these twelve women are what is called a forbidden partner. This misconduct is of little blame when the forbidden partner is devoid of virtues such as morality, but of great blame when she is endowed with virtues such as morality. It has four components: the forbidden object, the thought of engaging with it, the effort to engage, and the consent to the union of the paths. There is only one mode of application: that done by one's own hand.

Musāti [P 1.0200] visaṃvādanapurekkhārassa atthabhañjako vacīpayogo kāyapayogo vā. Visaṃvādanādhippāyena panassa paravisaṃvādanakakāyavacīpayogasamuṭṭhāpikā cetanā musāvādo. Aparo nayo musāti abhūtaṃ atacchaṃ vatthu. Vādoti tassa bhūtato tacchato viññāpanaṃ. Lakkhaṇato pana atathaṃ vatthuṃ tathato paraṃ viññāpetukāmassa tathāviññattisamuṭṭhāpikā cetanā musāvādo. So yamatthaṃ bhañjati, tassa appatāya appasāvajjo, mahantatāya mahāsāvajjo. Apica gahaṭṭhānaṃ attano santakaṃ adātukāmatāya natthītiādinayappavatto appasāvajjo, sakkhinā hutvā atthabhañjanatthaṃ vutto mahāsāvajjo. Pabbajitānaṃ appakampi telaṃ vā sappiṃ vā labhitvā hasādhippāyena “ajja gāme telaṃ nadīmaññe sandatī”ti purāṇakathānayena pavatto appasāvajjo, adiṭṭhaṃyeva pana diṭṭhantiādinā nayena vadantānaṃ mahāsāvajjo. Tassa cattāro sambhārā honti atathaṃ vatthu, visaṃvādanacittaṃ, tajjo vāyāmo, parassa tadatthavijānananti. Eko payogo sāhatthikova. So kāyena vā kāyappaṭibaddhena vā vācāya vā visaṃvādakakiriyākaraṇe [V 1.0208] daṭṭhabbo. Tāya ce kiriyāya paro tamatthaṃ jānāti, ayaṃ kiriyāsamuṭṭhāpikacetanākkhaṇeyeva musāvādakammunā bajjhati.

Falsehood (musā) is a verbal or bodily application that destroys another's benefit, with deception as its precursor. The volition, however, that arises with the intention to deceive and gives rise to a bodily or verbal application that deceives others, is false speech (musāvāda). Another method: 'False' (musā) is an unreal, untrue matter. 'Speech' (vāda) is making that known as real and true. By characteristic, however, false speech is the volition of one who, desiring to make another know an untrue matter as true, gives rise to such a communication. It is of little blame when the benefit it destroys is minor, and of great blame when it is major. Furthermore, for householders, false speech that proceeds from the unwillingness to give what belongs to oneself, such as saying, 'There is none,' is of little blame; spoken when acting as a witness for the purpose of destroying another's benefit, it is of great blame. For monastics, false speech that proceeds in the manner of an old tale, such as, having received even a little oil or ghee, saying with humorous intent, 'Today in the village, oil flows like a river,' is of little blame; but for those who speak in the manner of saying, 'I saw,' regarding what was not seen, it is of great blame. It has four components: an untrue matter, a mind desiring to deceive, the corresponding effort, and the other's understanding of that meaning. There is one mode of application, that done by oneself. It should be understood as the performance of a deceptive action by body, by what is connected to the body, or by speech. And if by that action the other person comes to know that meaning, at the very moment of the volition that gives rise to the action, one is bound by the kamma of false speech.

Pisuṇā vācātiādīsu yāya vācāya yassa taṃ vācaṃ bhāsati, tassa hadaye attano piyabhāvaṃ parassa ca suññabhāvaṃ karoti, sā pisuṇā vācā. Yāya pana attānampi parampi pharusampi karoti, sā vācā sayampi pharusā neva kaṇṇasukhā na hadayasukhā vā, ayaṃ pharusā vācā. Yena [M 1.0204] samphaṃ palapati niratthakaṃ, so samphappalāpo. Tesaṃ mūlabhūtā cetanāpi pisuṇāvācādināmameva labhati, sā eva ca idha adhippetāti. Tattha saṃkiliṭṭhacittassa paresaṃ vā bhedāya attano piyakamyatāya vā kāyavacīpayogasamuṭṭhāpikā cetanā pisuṇā vācā. Sā yassa bhedaṃ karoti, tassa appaguṇatāya appasāvajjā, mahāguṇatāya mahāsāvajjā. Tassā cattāro sambhārā bhinditabbo paro, “iti ime nānā bhavissanti vinā bhavissantī”ti bhedapurekkhāratā vā, “ahaṃ [P 1.0201] piyo bhavissāmi vissāsiko”ti piyakamyatā vā, tajjo vāyāmo, tassa tadatthavijānananti.

Regarding 'divisive speech' (pisuṇā vācā) and so forth: that speech by which, when one speaks it to someone, one creates in that person's heart a state of dearness towards oneself and a state of estrangement from another, is divisive speech. That speech, however, which makes both oneself and the other harsh, and that speech which is itself harsh—neither pleasant to the ear nor pleasant to the heart—is harsh speech (pharusā vācā). That by which one babbles what is useless is idle chatter (samphappalāpa). The root volition of these also obtains the name 'divisive speech,' and so forth; and it is that volition itself that is intended here. Therein, divisive speech is the volition of one with a defiled mind that gives rise to bodily or verbal application, either for the purpose of dividing others or for the sake of desiring to be dear to them. Insofar as it creates division, it is of little blame due to the few virtues of the person being divided, and of great blame due to their great virtues. It has four components: the other person to be divided; either having division as the aim, thinking, 'Thus they will become separate, they will be apart,' or the desire to be dear, thinking, 'I will be dear and trusted'; the corresponding effort; and that person's understanding of that meaning.

Parassa mammacchedakakāyavacīpayogasamuṭṭhāpikā ekantapharusā cetanā pharusā vācā. Tassa āvibhāvatthamidaṃ vatthu – eko kira dārako mātuvacanaṃ anādiyitvā araññaṃ gacchati, taṃ mātā nivattetuṃ asakkontī “caṇḍā taṃ mahiṃsī anubandhatū”ti akkosi. Athassa tattheva araññe mahiṃsī uṭṭhāsi. Dārako “yaṃ mama mātā mukhena kathesi taṃ mā hotu, yaṃ cittena cintesi taṃ hotū”ti saccakiriyamakāsi. Mahiṃsī tattheva baddhā viya aṭṭhāsi. Evaṃ mammacchedakopi payogo cittasaṇhatāya pharusā vācā na hoti. Mātāpitaro hi kadāci puttake evampi vadanti “corā vo khaṇḍākhaṇḍikaṃ karontū”ti, uppalapattampi ca nesaṃ upari patantaṃ na icchanti. Ācariyupajjhāyā ca kadāci nissitake evaṃ vadanti “kiṃ ime ahirikā anottappino caranti niddhamatha ne”ti. Atha kho nesaṃ āgamādhigamasampattiṃ icchanti. Yathā ca cittasaṇhatāya pharusā vācā na hoti, evaṃ vacanasaṇhatāya apharusā vācāpi na hoti. Na hi mārāpetukāmassa “imaṃ sukhaṃ sayāpethā”ti vacanaṃ apharusā vācā hoti. Cittapharusatāya panesā pharusā vācāva. Sā yaṃ [V 1.0209] sandhāya pavattitā, tassa appaguṇatāya appasāvajjā, mahāguṇatāya mahāsāvajjā. Tassā tayo sambhārā akkositabbo paro, kupitacittaṃ, akkosanāti.

Harsh speech is the entirely harsh volition that gives rise to bodily and verbal application that cuts to another's heart. To make this clear, there is this story: A certain boy, not heeding his mother's word, went into the forest. His mother, unable to make him return, cursed him, saying, “May a fierce buffalo chase you!” Then a buffalo arose for him right there in the forest. The boy made an act of truth, saying, “May what my mother spoke with her mouth not come to be, but may what she thought with her mind come to be.” The buffalo stood right there as if bound. Thus, even a heart-cutting application, due to the gentleness of the mind, is not harsh speech. For parents sometimes say even this to their children: “May thieves cut you to pieces!” yet they do not wish even a lotus petal to fall upon them. And teachers and preceptors sometimes say this of their dependents: “Why do these shameless and reckless ones wander about? Expel them!” And yet, they desire for them accomplishment in learning and attainment. And just as, due to the gentleness of the mind, it is not harsh speech, so too, due to the gentleness of the words, it does not become non-harsh speech. For the words of one who desires to have someone killed, “Let him sleep comfortably,” are not non-harsh speech. Due to the harshness of the mind, this is indeed harsh speech. Insofar as it is directed toward someone, it is of small fault due to that person's few virtues, and of great fault due to their great virtues. It has three components: the other person to be reviled, an angry mind, and the act of reviling.

Anatthaviññāpakakāyavacīpayogasamuṭṭhāpikā akusalacetanā samphappalāpo. So āsevanamandatāya appasāvajjo, āsevanamahantatāya mahāsāvajjo. Tassa dve sambhārā bhāratayuddhasītāharaṇādiniratthakakathāpurekkhāratā, tathārūpīkathākathananti.

Idle chatter is the unwholesome volition that gives rise to bodily and verbal application that makes known what is unbeneficial. Due to the weakness of its cultivation, it is of small fault; due to the greatness of its cultivation, it is of great fault. It has two components: having as a precursor meaningless talk such as the Bhārata war, the abduction of Sītā, and so forth; and the speaking of such talk.

Abhijjhāyatīti [M 1.0205] abhijjhā, parabhaṇḍābhimukhī hutvā tanninnatāya pavattatīti attho. Sā “aho vata idaṃ mamassā”ti evaṃ parabhaṇḍābhijjhāyanalakkhaṇā. Adinnādānaṃ viya appasāvajjā ca mahāsāvajjā ca. Tassā dve sambhārā parabhaṇḍaṃ, attano pariṇāmanañca. Parabhaṇḍavatthuke hi lobhe uppannepi na tāva kammapathabhedo hoti, yāva “aho vatīdaṃ mamassā”ti attano na pariṇāmeti.

It is called 'covetousness' (abhijjhā) because it covets (abhijjhāyati); the meaning is that, having become directed towards another's goods, it proceeds with an inclination towards them. It is characterized by coveting another's goods thus: 'Oh, that this were mine!' Like taking what is not given, it is of small fault and of great fault. It has two components: another's goods, and turning them towards oneself. For even when greed arises regarding another's goods, there is no breach of the course of action so long as one does not turn it towards oneself, thinking, 'Oh, that this were mine!'

Hitasukhaṃ byāpādayatīti byāpādo. So paravināsāya manopadosalakkhaṇo[P 1.0202], pharusā vācā viya appasāvajjo mahāsāvajjo ca. Tassa dve sambhārā parasatto ca, tassa ca vināsacintā. Parasattavatthuke hi kodhe uppannepi na tāva kammapathabhedo hoti, yāva “aho vatāyaṃ ucchijjeyya vinasseyyā”ti tassa vināsaṃ na cinteti.

It is called 'ill will' (byāpāda) because it destroys (byāpādayati) welfare and happiness. It is characterized by corruption of mind for the destruction of others. Like harsh speech, it is of small fault and of great fault. It has two components: another being, and the thought of that being's destruction. For even when anger arises based on another being, there is no breach of the course of action so long as one does not think of their destruction, thus: 'Oh, that this one might be annihilated, might perish!'

Yathābhuccagahaṇābhāvena micchā passatīti micchādiṭṭhi. Sā “natthi dinna”ntiādinā nayena viparītadassanalakkhaṇā. Samphappalāpo viya appasāvajjā mahāsāvajjā ca. Apica aniyatā appasāvajjā, niyatā mahāsāvajjā. Tassā dve sambhārā vatthuno ca gahitākāraviparītatā, yathā ca taṃ gaṇhāti, tathābhāvena tassupaṭṭhānanti.

Because it sees wrongly due to the absence of grasping things as they truly are, it is wrong view. It has the characteristic of perverse seeing, in the manner of 'There is nothing given,' and so on. Like frivolous speech, it is of slight fault and of great fault. Moreover, the unfixed wrong view is of slight fault; the fixed wrong view is of great fault. Its two constituents are: the perversion of the mode in which the object is grasped, and the appearance of that object in accordance with how it is grasped.

Imesaṃ pana dasannaṃ akusalakammapathānaṃ dhammato koṭṭhāsato ārammaṇato vedanāto mūlatoti pañcahākārehi vinicchayo veditabbo.

The determination of these ten unwholesome courses of action should be known in five ways: by way of nature, by way of category, by way of object, by way of feeling, and by way of root.

Tattha [V 1.0210] dhammatoti etesu hi paṭipāṭiyā satta, cetanādhammāva honti, abhijjhādayo tayo cetanāsampayuttā.

Therein, as for 'by way of nature': among these, seven in sequence are only volitional states; the three beginning with covetousness are associated with volition.

Koṭṭhāsatoti paṭipāṭiyā satta, micchādiṭṭhi cāti ime aṭṭha kammapathā eva honti, no mūlāni. Abhijjhābyāpādā kammapathā ceva mūlāni ca. Abhijjhā hi mūlaṃ patvā lobho akusalamūlaṃ hoti. Byāpādo doso akusalamūlaṃ.

As for 'by way of category': the seven in sequence and wrong view—these eight are only courses of action, not roots. Covetousness and ill will are both courses of action and roots. For covetousness, having reached the state of a root, becomes greed, an unwholesome root. Ill will is hatred, an unwholesome root.

Ārammaṇatoti pāṇātipāto jīvitindriyārammaṇato saṅkhārārammaṇo hoti. Adinnādānaṃ sattārammaṇaṃ vā saṅkhārārammaṇaṃ vā. Micchācāro phoṭṭhabbavasena saṅkhārārammaṇo. Sattārammaṇotipi eke. Musāvādo sattārammaṇo vā saṅkhārārammaṇo vā. Tathā pisuṇā vācā. Pharusā vācā sattārammaṇāva. Samphappalāpo diṭṭhasutamutaviññātavasena sattārammaṇo [M 1.0206] vā saṅkhārārammaṇo vā, tathā abhijjhā. Byāpādo sattārammaṇova. Micchādiṭṭhi tebhūmakadhammavasena saṅkhārārammaṇā.

As for 'by way of object': Killing, because it has the life faculty as its object, has formations as its object. Stealing has a being as its object or formations as its object. Sexual misconduct, by way of the tangible, has formations as its object; some say it also has a being as its object. False speech has a being as its object or formations as its object; likewise for divisive speech. Harsh speech has only a being as its object. Frivolous speech, by way of what is seen, heard, sensed, or cognized, has a being as its object or formations as its object; likewise for covetousness. Ill will has only a being as its object. Wrong view, by way of phenomena of the three planes, has formations as its object.

Vedanātoti pāṇātipāto dukkhavedano hoti. Kiñcāpi hi rājāno coraṃ disvā hasamānāpi “gacchatha naṃ ghātethā”ti vadanti, sanniṭṭhāpakacetanā pana nesaṃ dukkhasampayuttāva hoti. Adinnādānaṃ tivedanaṃ. Micchācāro sukhamajjhattavasena dvivedano, sanniṭṭhāpakacitte pana majjhattavedano na hoti. Musāvādo tivedano, tathā pisuṇā vācā. Pharusā vācā dukkhavedanāva. Samphappalāpo tivedano[P 1.0203]. Abhijjhā sukhamajjhattavasena dvivedanā, tathā micchādiṭṭhi. Byāpādo dukkhavedano.

As for 'by way of feeling': Killing has painful feeling. For although kings, upon seeing a thief, might say even while laughing, 'Go and kill him,' their decisive volition is only associated with pain. Stealing has three feelings. Sexual misconduct, by way of pleasure and neutrality, has two feelings; but in the decisive consciousness, it does not have neutral feeling. False speech has three feelings; likewise for divisive speech. Harsh speech has only painful feeling. Frivolous speech has three feelings. Covetousness, by way of pleasure and neutrality, has two feelings; likewise for wrong view. Ill will has painful feeling.

Mūlatoti pāṇātipāto dosamohavasena dvimūlako hoti. Adinnādānaṃ dosamohavasena vā lobhamohavasena vā. Micchācāro lobhamohavasena. Musāvādo dosamohavasena vā lobhamohavasena vā, tathā pisuṇā vācā samphappalāpo ca. Pharusā vācā dosamohavasena. Abhijjhā mohavasena ekamūlā, tathā byāpādo. Micchādiṭṭhi lobhamohavasena dvimūlāti.

As for 'by way of root': Killing, by way of hatred and delusion, is two-rooted. Stealing is two-rooted either by way of hatred and delusion or by way of greed and delusion. Sexual misconduct is two-rooted by way of greed and delusion. False speech is two-rooted either by way of hatred and delusion or by way of greed and delusion; likewise for divisive speech and frivolous speech. Harsh speech is two-rooted by way of hatred and delusion. Covetousness is one-rooted by way of delusion; likewise for ill will. Wrong view is two-rooted by way of greed and delusion.

Lobho akusalamūlantiādīsu lubbhatīti lobho. Dussatīti doso. Muyhatīti moho. Tesu lobho sayañca akusalo sāvajjadukkhavipākaṭṭhena, imesañca pāṇātipātādīnaṃ akusalānaṃ [V 1.0211] kesañci sampayuttappabhāvakaṭṭhena kesañci upanissayapaccayaṭṭhena mūlanti akusalamūlaṃ. Vuttampi cetaṃ “ratto kho āvuso rāgena abhibhūto pariyādinnacitto pāṇampi hanatī”tiādi. Dosamohānaṃ akusalamūlabhāvepi eseva nayo.

In the phrase 'Greed is an unwholesome root,' and so on: it clings, thus it is greed (lobha). It is hostile, thus it is hatred (dosa). It is deluded, thus it is delusion (moha). Among these, greed is itself unwholesome because it is blameworthy and has a painful result; and it is the root of these unwholesome states, such as killing, because for some it is an influential associated state, and for others it is a decisive support condition. Thus, it is an unwholesome root. And this has been said: 'Friend, one who is impassioned by lust, overwhelmed, with mind obsessed, even kills a living being,' and so on. This same method applies to hatred and delusion being unwholesome roots.

Akusalakammapathavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The exposition of the unwholesome courses of action is concluded.

Kusalakammapathavaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Wholesome Courses of Action

Pāṇātipātā veramaṇī kusalantiādīsu pāṇātipātādayo vuttatthā eva. Veraṃ maṇatīti veramaṇī, veraṃ pajahatīti attho. Viramati vā etāya karaṇabhūtāya, vikārassa vekāraṃ katvāpi veramaṇī. Ayaṃ tāvettha byañjanato vaṇṇanā. Atthato pana veramaṇīti kusalacittasampayuttā virati. Yā “pāṇātipātā viramantassa, yā tasmiṃ samaye [M 1.0207] pāṇātipātā ārati viratī”ti evaṃ vuttā kusalacittasampayuttā virati, sā bhedato tividho hoti sampattavirati samādānavirati samucchedaviratīti. Tattha asamādinnasikkhāpadānaṃ attano jātivayabāhusaccādīni paccavekkhitvā “ayuttaṃ amhākaṃ evarūpaṃ kātu”nti sampattavatthuṃ avītikkamantānaṃ uppajjamānā virati sampattaviratīti veditabbā sīhaḷadīpe cakkanaupāsakassa viya.

In such passages as 'Abstinence from the destruction of life is wholesome,' the meanings of 'destruction of life' and so on have already been stated. It is veramaṇi because it abandons (maṇati) enmity (veraṃ); the meaning is that it forsakes enmity. Or, one abstains (viramati) by means of it (etāya) which is the instrument; it is also veramaṇi by changing the 'vi' of virati to 've'. This, for now, is the explanation by way of wording. In terms of meaning, however, veramaṇi is the abstinence associated with a wholesome mind. That abstinence associated with a wholesome mind, which is spoken of thus: 'For one abstaining from the destruction of life, that which at that time is the refraining, the abstaining from the destruction of life'—this, by way of division, is threefold: abstinence on the occasion (sampattavirati), abstinence by undertaking (samādānavirati), and abstinence by eradication (samucchedavirati). Therein, for those who have not undertaken the training precepts, the abstinence that arises when, having reflected on their own birth, age, learning, and so on, they do not transgress the object that has presented itself, thinking, 'It is not proper for us to do such a thing'—this should be known as abstinence on the occasion, like that of the lay devotee Cakkana on the island of Sīhaḷa.

Tassa kira daharakāleyeva mātuyā rogo uppajji. Vejjena ca “allasasamaṃsaṃ laddhuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vuttaṃ. Tato cakkanassa bhātā “gaccha tāta khettaṃ āhiṇḍāhī”ti cakkanaṃ pesesi. So tattha gato. Tasmiñca samaye eko saso taruṇasassaṃ khādituṃ āgato hoti, so taṃ disvā vegena dhāvento valliyā baddho “kiri kirī”ti saddamakāsi. Cakkano tena saddena gantvā taṃ gahetvā cintesi “mātu [P 1.0204] bhesajjaṃ karomī”ti. Puna cintesi “na metaṃ patirūpaṃ, yvāhaṃ mātu jīvitakāraṇā paraṃ jīvitā voropeyya”nti. Atha naṃ “gaccha araññe sasehi saddhiṃ tiṇodakaṃ paribhuñjā”ti muñci. Bhātarā ca “kiṃ tāta saso laddho”ti pucchito taṃ pavattiṃ ācikkhi. Tato naṃ bhātā paribhāsi. So mātusantikaṃ gantvā “yatohaṃ [V 1.0212] jāto, nābhijānāmi sañcicca pāṇaṃ jīvitā voropetā”ti saccaṃ vatvā adhiṭṭhāsi. Tāvadevassa mātā arogā ahosi.

It is said that when he was just a young boy, his mother's illness arose. And the physician said, 'It is proper to get fresh hare's meat.' Then Cakkana's brother sent Cakkana, saying, 'Go, dear boy, wander in the field.' He went there. And at that time, a certain hare had come to eat the young grain. Seeing him, that hare, while running with speed, became bound by a vine and made the sound 'kiri kiri.' Cakkana, going by that sound, caught it and thought, 'I will make medicine for my mother.' Again he thought, 'This is not proper for me, that I, for the sake of my mother's life, should deprive another of life.' Then he released it, saying, 'Go, consume grass and water in the forest together with the hares.' And being asked by his brother, 'What, dear boy, was a hare obtained?' he related that event. Then his brother reviled him. He went to his mother and made a formal declaration of truth, saying, 'From when I became a person of understanding, I do not recall ever having intentionally deprived a living being of life.' At that very moment, his mother became free from illness.

Samādinnasikkhāpadānaṃ pana sikkhāpadasamādāne ca tatuttari ca attano jīvitampi pariccajitvā vatthuṃ avītikkamantānaṃ uppajjamānā virati samādānaviratīti veditabbā uttaravaḍḍhamānapabbatavāsīupāsakassa viya.

Furthermore, for those who have undertaken the training precepts, the abstinence that arises when, both in the undertaking of the training precept and thereafter, they do not transgress the object of transgression even while giving up their own life—this should be known as abstinence by undertaking, like that of the lay devotee dwelling on Mount Uttaravaḍḍhamāna.

So kira ambariyavihāravāsīpiṅgalabuddharakkhitattherassa santike sikkhāpadāni gahetvā khettaṃ kassati. Athassa goṇo naṭṭho, so taṃ gavesanto uttaravaḍḍhamānapabbataṃ āruhi, tatra naṃ mahāsappo aggahesi. So cintesi “imāyassa tikhiṇavāsiyā sīsaṃ chindāmī”ti. Puna cintesi “na metaṃ patirūpaṃ, yvāhaṃ bhāvanīyassa garuno santike sikkhāpadaṃ gahetvā bhindeyya”nti. Evaṃ yāvatatiyaṃ cintetvā “jīvitaṃ [M 1.0208] pariccajāmi, na sikkhāpada”nti aṃse ṭhapitaṃ tikhiṇadaṇḍavāsiṃ araññe chaḍḍesi. Tāvadeva naṃ mahāvāḷo muñcitvā agamāsīti.

It is said that he, having taken the training precepts in the presence of the Elder Piṅgalabuddharakkhita, a resident of Ambariyavihāra, was ploughing a field. Then his ox was lost. Searching for it, he climbed Mount Uttaravaḍḍhamāna, where a great serpent seized him. He thought, 'I will cut off its head with this sharp adze.' Again he thought, 'This is not proper for me, that I, having taken the training precept in the presence of the Elder Buddharakkhita, should break it.' Having thought thus up to the third time, he resolved, 'I will give up my life, but not the training precept,' and cast the sharp-handled adze that was on his shoulder into the forest. At that very moment, the great serpent released him and went away.

Ariyamaggasampayuttā pana virati samucchedaviratīti veditabbā. Yassā uppattito pabhuti “pāṇaṃ ghātessāmī”ti ariyapuggalānaṃ cittampi na uppajjatīti. Sā panāyaṃ virati kosallappavattiyā kusalanti vuttā. Kucchitasayanato vā kusanti laddhavohāraṃ dussīlyaṃ lunātītipi kusalaṃ. Katamañcāvuso kusalanti imassa pana pañhassa ananurūpattā kusalāti na vuttā.

Furthermore, the abstinence associated with the noble path should be known as abstinence by eradication. From the arising of which, not even the thought 'I will kill a living being' arises for noble individuals. This abstinence is called 'wholesome' because of its proceeding from skill. Or, because of the inactivity of what is contemptible (kucchita-sayana), it is called 'kusa'; that which cuts off (lunāti) immoral conduct (dussīlyaṃ), which has received this designation, is also 'wholesome' (kusalaṃ). However, to this question, 'And what, friend, is the wholesome?', the answer is not given as kusalā [feminine] because it would be inappropriate in gender.

Yathā ca akusalānaṃ, evaṃ imesampi kusalakammapathānaṃ dhammato koṭṭhāsato ārammaṇato vedanāto mūlatoti pañcahākārehi vinicchayo veditabbo.

And just as for the unwholesome, so too for these wholesome courses of action, the analysis should be understood in five ways: by way of nature (dhammato), by way of category (koṭṭhāsato), by way of object (ārammaṇato), by way of feeling (vedanāto), and by way of root (mūlato).

Tattha dhammatoti etesu hi paṭipāṭiyā satta cetanāpi vaṭṭanti, viratiyopi. Ante tayo cetanāsampayuttāva.

Therein, by way of nature: in sequence, the first seven are applicable as volitions and also as abstinences. The last three are only factors associated with volition.

Koṭṭhāsatoti [P 1.0205] paṭipāṭiyā satta kammapathā eva, no mūlāni. Ante tayo kammapathā ceva [V 1.0213] mūlāni ca. Anabhijjhā hi mūlaṃ patvā alobho kusalamūlaṃ hoti. Abyāpādo adoso kusalamūlaṃ. Sammādiṭṭhi amoho kusalamūlaṃ.

By way of category: in sequence, the seven are only courses of action, not roots. The last three are both courses of action and roots. Indeed, non-covetousness, when it functions as a root, is non-greed, a wholesome root. Non-ill will is non-hatred, a wholesome root. Right view is non-delusion, a wholesome root.

Ārammaṇatoti pāṇātipātādīnaṃ ārammaṇāneva etesaṃ ārammaṇāni, vītikkamitabbatoyeva hi veramaṇī nāma hoti. Yathā pana nibbānārammaṇo ariyamaggo kilese pajahati, evaṃ jīvitindriyādiārammaṇāpete kammapathā pāṇātipātādīni dussīlyāni pajahantīti veditabbā.

By way of object: the objects of these are the very same objects as those of the destruction of life, etc. Indeed, abstinence is so-called from the very thing to be transgressed. And it should be known that just as the noble path, having Nibbāna as its object, abandons the defilements, so too these courses of action, having the life faculty, etc., as their objects, abandon immoral conduct such as the destruction of life, etc.

Vedanātoti sabbe sukhavedanā vā honti, majjhattavedanā vā. Kusalaṃ patvā hi dukkhavedanā nāma natthi.

By way of feeling: all are accompanied by either pleasant feeling or by neutral feeling. Indeed, in the sphere of the wholesome, there is no such thing as painful feeling.

Mūlatoti paṭipāṭiyā satta kammapathā ñāṇasampayuttacittena viramantassa alobhaadosaamohavasena timūlā honti. Ñāṇavippayuttacittena viramantassa dvimūlā. Anabhijjhā ñāṇasampayuttacittena viramantassa [M 1.0209] dvimūlā. Ñāṇavippayuttacittena ekamūlā. Alobho pana attanāva attano mūlaṃ na hoti, abyāpādepi eseva nayo. Sammādiṭṭhi alobhādosavasena dvimūlāvāti.

By way of root: in sequence, the seven courses of action, for one who abstains with a mind associated with knowledge, are three-rooted by way of non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion. For one who abstains with a mind dissociated from knowledge, they are two-rooted. Non-covetousness, for one who abstains with a mind associated with knowledge, is two-rooted. For one who abstains with a mind dissociated from knowledge, it is one-rooted. Non-greed, however, is not its own root; for non-ill will, too, this same method applies. Right view has only two roots, by way of non-greed and non-hatred.

Alobho kusalamūlantiādīsu na lobhoti alobho, lobhapaṭipakkhassa dhammassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Adosāmohesupi eseva nayo. Tesu alobho sayañca kusalaṃ, imesañca pāṇātipātā veramaṇīādīnaṃ kusalānaṃ kesañci sampayuttappabhāvakaṭṭhena kesañci upanissayapaccayaṭṭhena mūlanti kusalamūlaṃ. Adosāmohānampi kusalamūlabhāve eseva nayo.

In such passages as 'Non-greed is a wholesome root,' it is 'non-greed' because it is 'not greed'; this is a designation for the state that is the opposite of greed. This same method applies also to non-hatred and non-delusion. Among them, non-greed is itself wholesome, and it is a 'wholesome root' because for some of these wholesome states, such as abstaining from killing living beings, it is a root by way of its associated nature, and for others, by way of being a decisive support condition. This same method applies to non-hatred and non-delusion also being wholesome roots.

Idāni sabbampi taṃ saṅkhepena ca vitthārena ca desitamatthaṃ nigamento yato kho āvusotiādiappanāvāramāha. Tattha evaṃ akusalaṃ pajānātīti evaṃ yathāniddiṭṭhadasākusalakammapathavasena akusalaṃ pajānāti. Evaṃ akusalamūlantiādīsupi eseva nayo. Ettāvatā ekena nayena catusaccakammaṭṭhānikassa yāva arahattā niyyānaṃ kathitaṃ hoti. Kathaṃ? Ettha hi ṭhapetvā abhijjhaṃ dasa akusalakammapathā ca kusalakammapathā ca dukkhasaccaṃ. Abhijjhā ca lobho akusalamūlañcāti ime dve dhammā nippariyāyena samudayasaccaṃ. Pariyāyena pana sabbepi kammapathā dukkhasaccaṃ. Sabbāni kusalākusalamūlāni samudayasaccaṃ. Ubhinnaṃ appavatti nirodhasaccaṃ[V 1.0214]. Dukkhaṃ parijānanto samudayaṃ pajahamāno nirodhaṃ [P 1.0206] pajānanto ariyamaggo maggasaccanti iti dve saccāni sarūpena vuttāni, dve āvattahāravasena veditabbāni.

Now, wishing to conclude the meaning that has been taught both briefly and in detail, he states the section on absorption beginning with 'When, friend...' and so on. Therein, 'he understands the unwholesome thus' means he understands the unwholesome by way of the ten unwholesome courses of action as they have been pointed out. This same method applies also to such passages as 'the unwholesome root thus.' By this much, through this one method, the deliverance up to Arahantship for one who practices the meditation subject of the Four Truths is explained. How? Here, setting aside covetousness, the remaining unwholesome courses of action and the ten wholesome courses of action are the truth of suffering. Covetousness and greed, which is an unwholesome root—these two states are, unequivocally, the truth of the origin. By way of implication, however, all courses of action are the truth of suffering. All wholesome and unwholesome roots are the truth of the origin. The non-occurrence of both is the truth of cessation. The Noble Path—which fully understands suffering, abandons the origin, and realizes cessation—is the truth of the path. Thus, two truths are stated in their own nature, and two are to be understood by way of transference.

So sabbaso rāgānusayaṃ pahāyāti so evaṃ akusalādīni pajānanto sabbākārena rāgānusayaṃ pajahitvā. Paṭighānusayaṃ paṭivinodetvāti paṭighānusayañca sabbākāreneva nīharitvāti vuttaṃ hoti. Ettāvatā anāgāmimaggo kathito. Asmīti diṭṭhimānānusayaṃ samūhanitvāti pañcasu khandhesu kañci dhammaṃ anavakārīkaritvā “asmī”ti iminā samūhaggahaṇākārena pavattaṃ diṭṭhimānānusayaṃ samugghāṭetvā.

Regarding 'He, having completely abandoned the underlying tendency to lust,' this means: he, thus understanding the unwholesome and so on, has abandoned the underlying tendency to lust in all its aspects. Regarding 'having dispelled the underlying tendency to aversion,' this means one has removed the underlying tendency to aversion in all its aspects. By this much, the path of the non-returner is explained. Regarding 'having uprooted the underlying tendency to the conceit “I am” and to views,' this means having eradicated the underlying tendency to conceit that is similar to a view, which occurs with respect to the five aggregates in the manner of grasping them as a group.

Tattha diṭṭhimānānusayanti diṭṭhisadisaṃ mānānusayanti vuttaṃ hoti. Ayañhi mānānusayo asmīti pavattattā diṭṭhisadiso hoti, tasmā evaṃ vutto[M 1.0210]. Imañca asmimānaṃ vitthārato viññātukāmena khandhiyavagge khemakasuttaṃ (saṃ. ni. 3.89) oloketabbanti.

Therein, 'the underlying tendency to views and conceit' is said to mean the underlying tendency to conceit that is similar to a view. For this underlying tendency to conceit is similar to a view because it occurs as 'I am'; therefore, it is stated thus. One who wishes to understand this conceit of 'I am' in detail should look at the Khemaka Sutta in the Khandha Vagga.

Avijjaṃ pahāyāti vaṭṭamūlaṃ avijjaṃ pajahitvā. Vijjaṃ uppādetvāti tassā avijjāya samugghāṭikaṃ arahattamaggavijjaṃ uppādetvā. Ettāvatā arahattamaggo kathito. Diṭṭheva dhamme dukkhassantakaro hotīti asmiṃyeva attabhāve vaṭṭadukkhassa paricchedakaro hoti. Ettāvatāpi kho, āvusoti desanaṃ niyyāteti, imāya kammapathadesanāya vuttamanasikārappaṭivedhavasenapīti vuttaṃ hoti. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva. Evaṃ anāgāmimaggaarahattamaggehi desanaṃ niṭṭhapesīti.

Regarding 'having abandoned ignorance,' this means having abandoned ignorance, the root of the round of suffering. Regarding 'having generated knowledge,' this means having generated the knowledge of the path of Arahantship, which eradicates that ignorance. By this much, the path of Arahantship is explained. Regarding 'in this very life, he becomes an ender of suffering,' this means in this very existence he becomes one who makes an end to the suffering of the round. With 'Thus far also, friend,' he delivers the teaching. This means: also by means of the penetration through appropriate attention as taught in this discourse on the courses of action. The remainder is just as has been stated. Thus, he concludes the teaching with the paths of the non-returner and Arahantship.

Kusalakammapathavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the section on the wholesome courses of action is concluded.

Āhāravāravaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Section on Nutriment.

90. Sādhāvusoti kho…pe… āgato imaṃ saddhammanti evaṃ āyasmato sāriputtassa kusalākusalamukhena catusaccadesanaṃ sutvā taṃ āyasmato sāriputtassa bhāsitaṃ “sādhāvuso”ti iminā vacanena te bhikkhū abhinanditvā imasseva vacanassa samuṭṭhāpakena cittena anumoditvā vacasā sampaṭicchitvā cetasā sampiyāyitvāti vuttaṃ hoti. Idāni yasmā thero nānappakārena [V 1.0215] catusaccadesanaṃ desetuṃ paṭibalo, yathāha “sāriputto, bhikkhave, pahoti cattāri ariyasaccāni vitthārena ācikkhituṃ desetu”nti yasmā vā uttarimpi desetukāmova hutvā “ettāvatāpi kho”ti [P 1.0207] avaca, tasmā aparenapi nayena saccadesanaṃ sotukāmā te bhikkhū āyasmantaṃ sāriputtaṃ uttariṃ pañhaṃ apucchiṃsu. Tena sayameva pucchitvā vissajjitapañhato uttariṃ siyā kho panāvuso, aññopi pariyāyo bhaveyya aññampi kāraṇanti iminā nayena aññaṃ atirekaṃ pañhaṃ pucchiṃsu, purimapañhassa vā uparibhāge pucchiṃsūti vuttaṃ hoti. Atha nesaṃ byākaramāno thero siyā, āvusotiādimāha. Tatthāyaṃ anuttānapadavaṇṇanā, āhāranti paccayaṃ. Paccayo hi āharati attano phalaṃ, tasmā “āhāro”ti vuccati.
