“Good, friend,” so it is said… having come to this true Dhamma—thus, having heard the Venerable Sāriputta's exposition of the Four Truths by way of the wholesome and unwholesome, those monks greatly delighted in that statement of the Venerable Sāriputta with the words “Good, friend.” It is meant that they rejoiced with a mind aroused by this very statement, accepted it with speech, and cherished it with the mind. Now, because the Elder was capable of teaching the exposition of the Four Truths in various ways—as it is said, “Monks, Sāriputta is able to announce and teach the Four Noble Truths in detail”—or because, wishing to teach even further, he said, “Even this much…,” therefore, those monks, desiring to hear the exposition of the truths by another method, asked the Venerable Sāriputta a further question. Thus, beyond the question that he himself had asked and answered, they asked another, additional question by the method of, “Friend, might there be another way, another reason?” Or, it is meant that they asked about the upper part of the previous question. Then, while explaining to them, the Elder said, “It might be, friend,” and so on. Here is the explanation of the non-obvious terms: “Nutriment” means condition. Because a condition brings forth its own fruit, therefore, it is called “nutriment.”

Bhūtānaṃ [M 1.0211] vā sattānantiādīsu bhūtāti sañjātā, nibbattā. Sambhavesīnanti ye sambhavaṃ jātiṃ nibbattiṃ esanti gavesanti. Tattha catūsu yonīsu aṇḍajajalābujā sattā yāva aṇḍakosaṃ vatthikosañca na bhindanti, tāva sambhavesino nāma. Aṇḍakosaṃ vatthikosañca bhinditvā bahi nikkhantā bhūtā nāma. Saṃsedajā opapātikā ca paṭhamacittakkhaṇe sambhavesino nāma. Dutiyacittakkhaṇato pabhuti bhūtā nāma. Yena yena vā iriyāpathena jāyanti, yāva te tato aññaṃ na pāpuṇanti, tāva sambhavesino nāma. Tato paraṃ bhūtā nāma.

In the phrase "for beings or creatures" and so on, `bhūtā` means those who have been born, who have come into existence. `Sambhavesīnaṃ` means those who seek and search for becoming, birth, and arising. In this context, among the four kinds of birth, egg-born and womb-born beings are called `sambhavesino` as long as they have not broken the eggshell and the womb-sac. Having broken the eggshell and the womb-sac and emerged outside, they are called `bhūtā`. Moisture-born and spontaneously-born beings are called `sambhavesino` at the first moment of consciousness. From the second moment of consciousness onward, they are called `bhūtā`. Or, by whatever posture they are born, as long as they have not attained another posture from that one, they are called `sambhavesino`. After that, they are called `bhūtā`.

Atha vā bhūtāti jātā abhinibbattā, ye bhūtāyeva na puna bhavissantīti saṅkhyaṃ gacchanti, tesaṃ khīṇāsavānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Sambhavamesantīti sambhavesino. Appahīnabhavasaṃyojanattā āyatimpi sambhavaṃ esantānaṃ sekkhaputhujjanānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Evaṃ sabbathāpi imehi dvīhi padehi sabbasatte pariyādiyati. Vāsaddo cettha sampiṇḍanattho, tasmā bhūtānañca sambhavesīnañcāti ayamattho veditabbo.

Alternatively, `bhūtā` means those who are born, who have fully arisen; those who, having truly come into being, are not reckoned as those who 'will become again'—this is a designation for those whose taints are destroyed. Because they seek becoming, they are called `sambhavesino`. Because the fetter of becoming is not yet abandoned, this is a designation for learners and worldlings who also seek becoming in the future. Thus, in every way, all beings are encompassed by these two terms. Here, the word `vā` has the meaning of grouping together. Therefore, this meaning should be understood as "of both those who have become and those who are seeking to become."

Ṭhitiyāti ṭhitatthaṃ. Anuggahāyāti anuggahatthaṃ upakāratthaṃ. Vacanabhedo cesa, attho pana dvinnampi padānaṃ ekoyeva. Atha vā ṭhitiyāti tassa tassa sattassa uppannadhammānaṃ anuppabandhavasena avicchedāya. Anuggahāyāti anuppannānaṃ uppādāya. Ubhopi cetāni bhūtānaṃ ṭhitiyā ceva anuggahāya ca. Sambhavesīnaṃ vā ṭhitiyā ceva anuggahāya cāti evaṃ ubhayattha [V 1.0216] daṭṭhabbāni. Kabaḷīkāro āhāroti kabaḷaṃ katvā ajjhoharitabbato [P 1.0208] kabaḷīkāro āhāro, odanakummāsādivatthukāya ojāyetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Oḷāriko vā sukhumo vāti vatthuoḷārikatāya oḷāriko, vatthusukhumatāya sukhumo. Sabhāvena pana sukhumarūpapariyāpannattā kabaḷīkāro āhāro sukhumova hoti. Sāpi cassa vatthuto oḷārikatā sukhumatā ca upādāyupādāya veditabbā.

`Ṭhitiyā` means for the purpose of duration. `Anuggahāya` means for the purpose of support, for the purpose of assistance. This is a difference of terms, but the meaning of both terms is one and the same. Alternatively, `ṭhitiyā` means for the non-interruption, by way of continuity, of the arisen states of each and every being. `Anuggahāya` means for the arising of unarisen states. Both of these are for the duration and support of Arahants. Or, they should be seen in both cases as for the duration and support of those seeking to become. Edible food (`kabaḷīkāro āhāro`) is so called because it is to be swallowed after making it into a morsel; this is a designation for the nutritive essence that has rice, gruel, and so on as its physical basis. "Coarse or subtle" means: it is coarse due to the coarseness of its physical basis; it is subtle due to the subtlety of its physical basis. However, by its intrinsic nature, because it is included in subtle matter, edible food is indeed subtle. And that coarseness and subtlety of it should be known by considering its physical basis in each case.

Kumbhīlānañhi āhāraṃ upādāya morānaṃ āhāro sukhumo. Kumbhīlā kira pāsāṇe gilanti. Te ca nesaṃ kucchippattāva vilīyanti. Morā sappavicchikādipāṇe khādanti. Morānaṃ pana āhāraṃ upādāya taracchānaṃ āhāro sukhumo. Te kira tivassachaḍḍitāni visāṇāni ceva aṭṭhīni ca khādanti. Tāni ca nesaṃ kheḷena temitamatteneva kandamūlaṃ viya [M 1.0212] mudukāni honti. Taracchānampi āhāraṃ upādāya hatthīnaṃ āhāro sukhumo. Tepi nānārukkhasākhāyo khādanti. Hatthīnaṃ āhārato gavayagokaṇṇamigādīnaṃ āhāro sukhumo. Te kira nissārāni nānārukkhapaṇṇādīni khādanti. Tesampi āhārato gunnaṃ āhāro sukhumo. Te allasukkhatiṇāni khādanti. Tesaṃ āhārato sasānaṃ āhāro sukhumo. Sasānaṃ āhārato sakuṇānaṃ āhāro sukhumo. Sakuṇānaṃ āhārato paccantavāsīnaṃ āhāro sukhumo. Paccantavāsīnaṃ āhārato gāmabhojakānaṃ āhāro sukhumo. Gāmabhojakānaṃ āhārato rājarājamahāmattānaṃ āhāro sukhumo. Tesampi āhārato cakkavattino āhāro sukhumo. Cakkavattino āhārato bhummadevānaṃ āhāro sukhumo. Bhummadevānaṃ āhārato cātumahārājikānaṃ āhāro sukhumo. Evaṃ yāva paranimmitavasavattīnaṃ āhāro vitthāretabbo, tesaṃ āhāro sukhumotveva niṭṭhaṃ patto.

In relation to the food of crocodiles, the food of peacocks is subtle. It is said that crocodiles swallow stones, and these dissolve upon reaching their stomachs. Peacocks eat creatures such as snakes and scorpions. In relation to the food of peacocks, the food of hyenas is subtle. It is said that they eat horns and bones that have been discarded for three years, and these, merely by being moistened with their saliva, become soft like a tuberous root. In relation to the food of hyenas, the food of elephants is subtle. They eat the branches of various trees. In relation to the food of elephants, the food of gayals, gokannas, deer, and other such animals is subtle. It is said that they eat the sapless leaves of various trees. In relation to their food, the food of cattle is subtle. They eat fresh and dry grass. In relation to their food, the food of hares is subtle. In relation to the food of hares, the food of birds is subtle. In relation to the food of birds, the food of frontier-dwellers is subtle. In relation to the food of frontier-dwellers, the food of village headmen is subtle. In relation to the food of village headmen, the food of kings and great ministers is subtle. In relation to their food, the food of a wheel-turning monarch is subtle. In relation to the food of a wheel-turning monarch, the food of earth-deities is subtle. In relation to the food of earth-deities, the food of the devas of the realm of the Four Great Kings is subtle. In this way, it should be elaborated up to the food of the Paranimmitavasavattī devas. Their food reaches the conclusion of being subtle indeed.

Ettha ca oḷārike vatthusmiṃ ojā parittā hoti dubbalā, sukhume balavatī. Tathā hi ekapattapūrampi yāguṃ pīvato muhutteneva jighacchito hoti, yaṃkañcideva khāditukāmo. Sappiṃ pana pasaṭamattaṃ pivitvā divasaṃ abhottukāmo hoti. Tattha vatthu parissamaṃ vinodeti, na pana sakkoti pāletuṃ. Ojā pāleti, na sakkoti parissamaṃ vinodetuṃ. Dve pana ekato hutvā parissamañceva vinodenti pālenti cāti.

And here, in a coarse physical substance, the nutritive essence is meager and weak; in a subtle one, it is strong. Indeed, one who drinks even a bowlful of gruel becomes hungry in just a moment, desiring to eat just anything. But having drunk just a spoonful of ghee, one desires not to eat for the whole day. Therein, the physical substance dispels fatigue but is not able to sustain. The nutritive essence sustains but is not able to dispel fatigue. The two, however, having come together, both dispel fatigue and sustain.

Phasso [V 1.0217][P 1.0209] dutiyoti cakkhusamphassādi chabbidhopi phasso. Etesu catūsu āhāresu dutiyo āhāroti veditabbo. Desanānayo eva cesa. Tasmā iminā nāma kāraṇena dutiyo vā tatiyo vāti idamettha na gavesitabbaṃ. Manosañcetanāti cetanā eva vuccati. Viññāṇanti yaṃkiñci cittaṃ.

‘Contact is the second’: this means the sixfold contact, beginning with eye-contact. Among these four nutriments, it should be understood as the second nutriment. And this is merely the method of exposition. Therefore, one should not investigate here for some reason why this is the second or that the third. ‘Mental volition’: this is just called volition. ‘Consciousness’: this means any mind whatsoever.

Etthāha, yadi paccayaṭṭho āhāraṭṭho, atha kasmā aññesupi sattānaṃ paccayesu vijjamānesu imeyeva cattāro vuttāti? Vuccate, ajjhattikasantatiyā [M 1.0213] visesapaccayattā. Visesapaccayo hi kabaḷīkārāhārabhakkhānaṃ sattānaṃ rūpakāyassa kabaḷīkāro āhāro. Nāmakāye vedanāya phasso, viññāṇassa manosañcetanā, nāmarūpassa viññāṇaṃ. Yathāha –

Here a questioner asks: If the meaning of ‘nutriment’ is ‘condition,’ then why, when other conditions for beings also exist, were only these four spoken of? The answer is given: Because they are special conditions for the internal continuity. For, edible food is a special condition for the physical body of beings who consume edible food. In the mental body, contact is a special condition for feeling, mental volition is a special condition for consciousness, and consciousness is a special condition for mentality-materiality. As it was said:

“Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, ayaṃ kāyo āhāraṭṭhitiko, āhāraṃ paṭicca tiṭṭhati, anāhāro no tiṭṭhati. Tathā phassapaccayā vedanā, saṅkhārapaccayā viññāṇaṃ, viññāṇapaccayā nāmarūpa”nti.

‘Just as, monks, this body is established by nutriment, stands in dependence on nutriment, and does not stand without nutriment; so too, conditioned by contact there is feeling, conditioned by formations there is consciousness, and conditioned by consciousness there is mentality-materiality.’

Ko panettha āhāro, kiṃ āharatīti? Kabaḷīkārāhāro ojaṭṭhamakarūpāni āharati. Phassāhāro tisso vedanā, manosañcetanāhāro tayo bhave, viññāṇāhāro paṭisandhināmarūpanti.

What here is nutriment, and what does it bring? The nutriment of physical food brings material phenomena which have nutritive essence as their eighth factor. The nutriment of contact brings the three feelings. The nutriment of mental volition brings the three kinds of existence. The nutriment of consciousness brings mentality-materiality at rebirth-linking.

Kathaṃ? Kabaḷīkārāhāro tāva mukhe ṭhapitamattoyeva aṭṭha rūpāni samuṭṭhāpeti. Dantavicuṇṇitaṃ pana ajjhohariyamānaṃ ekekaṃ sitthaṃ aṭṭhaṭṭha rūpāni samuṭṭhāpetiyeva. Evaṃ ojaṭṭhamakarūpāni āharati.

How so? Firstly, the nutriment of physical food, merely upon being placed in the mouth, gives rise to eight material phenomena. Then, being ground by the teeth and swallowed, each single morsel gives rise to eight material phenomena each. Thus it brings material phenomena which have nutritive essence as their eighth factor.

Phassāhāro pana sukhavedaniyo phasso uppajjamāno sukhavedanaṃ āharati, tathā dukkhavedaniyo dukkhaṃ, adukkhamasukhavedaniyo adukkhamasukhanti evaṃ sabbathāpi phassāhāro tisso vedanā āharati.

As for the nutriment of contact: when contact associated with pleasant feeling arises, it brings pleasant feeling. Similarly, contact associated with painful feeling brings painful feeling, and contact associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling brings neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. Thus, in every way, the nutriment of contact brings the three feelings.

Manosañcetanāhāro [V 1.0218] kāmabhavūpagaṃ kammaṃ kāmabhavaṃ āharati, rūpārūpabhavūpagāni taṃ taṃ bhavaṃ. Evaṃ sabbathāpi manosañcetanāhāro tayo bhave āharati.

The nutriment of mental volition, as kamma leading to the sense-sphere existence, brings the sense-sphere existence. As kamma leading to the fine-material and immaterial sphere existences, it brings those respective existences. Thus, in every way, the nutriment of mental volition brings the three kinds of existence.

Viññāṇāhāro pana ye ca paṭisandhikkhaṇe taṃsampayuttakā tayo khandhā, yāni ca tisantativasena tiṃsarūpāni uppajjanti, sahajātādipaccayanayena tāni āharatīti vuccati. Evaṃ viññāṇāhāro paṭisandhināmarūpaṃ āharatīti.

As for the nutriment of consciousness, it is said that it brings the three aggregates associated with it at the moment of rebirth-linking, and the thirty material phenomena that arise by way of the three continuities, through the method of the co-nascence condition and so on. Thus, the nutriment of consciousness brings mentality-materiality at rebirth-linking.

Ettha ca manosañcetanāhāro tayo bhave āharatīti sāsavā kusalākusalacetanāva vuttā. Viññāṇaṃ paṭisandhināmarūpaṃ āharatīti paṭisandhiviññāṇameva vuttaṃ[P 1.0210]. Avisesena pana taṃsampayuttataṃsamuṭṭhānadhammānaṃ āharaṇato pete āhārāti veditabbā.

And here, by ‘the nutriment of mental volition brings the three kinds of existence,’ wholesome and unwholesome volitions connected with the taints are meant. By ‘consciousness brings mentality-materiality at rebirth-linking,’ only rebirth-linking consciousness is meant. However, in a general sense, these should also be known as ‘nutriments’ because they bring their associated and co-arisen phenomena.

Etesu [M 1.0214] catūsu āhāresu kabaḷīkārāhāro upatthambhento āhārakiccaṃ sādheti. Phasso phusantoyeva, manosañcetanā āyūhamānāva. Viññāṇaṃ vijānantameva.

Among these four nutriments, the nutriment of physical food accomplishes its function as nutriment by supporting. Contact accomplishes it just by contacting; mental volition, just by accumulating; consciousness, just by cognizing.

Kathaṃ? Kabaḷīkārāhāro hi upatthambhentoyeva kāyaṭṭhapanena sattānaṃ ṭhitiyā hoti. Kammajanitopi hi ayaṃ kāyo kabaḷīkārāhārena upatthambhito dasapi vassāni vassasatampi yāva āyuparimāṇaṃ tiṭṭhati. Yathā kiṃ? Yathā mātuyā janitopi dārako dhātiyā thaññādīni pāyetvā posiyamānova ciraṃ tiṭṭhati, yathā cupatthambhena upatthambhitagehaṃ. Vuttampi cetaṃ –

How so? The nutriment of physical food, by the very act of supporting, becomes a condition for the continuity of beings by establishing the body. Indeed, this body, though born of kamma, when supported by physical food, stands for ten years, a hundred years, for as long as the lifespan extends. What is the simile? Just as a child, though born of its mother, stands for a long time when nourished by a wet-nurse who gives it milk and so on to drink; and just as a house supported by a prop stands for a long time. And this was also said:

“Yathā mahārāja gehe patante aññena dārunā upatthambhenti, aññena dārunā upatthambhitaṃ santaṃ evaṃ taṃ gehaṃ na patati, evameva kho mahārāja ayaṃ kāyo āhāraṭṭhitiko, āhāraṃ paṭicca tiṭṭhatī”ti.

Just as, great king, when a house is collapsing, it is supported by another piece of wood, and being supported by another piece of wood, that house does not collapse, just so, great king, this body is maintained by food; it exists dependent on food.

Evaṃ kabaḷīkāro āhāro upatthambhento āhārakiccaṃ sādheti. Evaṃ sādhentopi ca kabaḷīkāro āhāro dvinnaṃ rūpasantatīnaṃ paccayo hoti āhārasamuṭṭhānassa ca upādinnassa ca. Kammajānaṃ anupālako hutvā paccayo hoti. Āhārasamuṭṭhānānaṃ janako hutvā paccayo hoti.

Thus, edible food, by supporting, accomplishes the function of nutriment. Even while accomplishing this, edible food becomes a condition for two continuities of form, namely, that which is nutriment-originated and that which is clung-to. It acts as a condition by maintaining the kamma-born. It acts as a condition by generating the nutriment-originated.

Phasso [V 1.0219] pana sukhādivatthubhūtaṃ ārammaṇaṃ phusantoyeva sukhādivedanāpavattanena sattānaṃ ṭhitiyā hoti. Manosañcetanā kusalākusalakammavasena āyūhamānāyeva bhavamūlanipphādanato sattānaṃ ṭhitiyā hoti. Viññāṇaṃ vijānantameva nāmarūpappavattanena sattānaṃ ṭhitiyā hoti.

Contact, however, by touching an object that is the basis for pleasure and so on, contributes to the continuation of beings through the arising of feelings of pleasure and the like. Mental volition, by accumulating wholesome and unwholesome kamma, contributes to the continuation of beings by producing the root of existence. Consciousness, by cognizing, contributes to the continuation of beings through the arising of mentality-materiality.

Evaṃ upatthambhanādivasena āhārakiccaṃ sādhayamānesu panetesu cattāri bhayāni daṭṭhabbāni. Seyyathidaṃ, kabaḷīkārāhāre nikantiyeva bhayaṃ, phasse upagamanameva, manosañcetanāya āyūhanameva, viññāṇe abhinipātoyeva bhayanti. Kiṃ kāraṇā? Kabaḷīkārāhāre hi nikantiṃ katvā sītādīnaṃ purekkhatā sattā āhāratthāya muddāgaṇanādikammāni karontā anappakaṃ dukkhaṃ nigacchanti. Ekacce ca imasmiṃ sāsane [M 1.0215] pabbajitvāpi vejjakammādikāya anesanāya āhāraṃ pariyesantā diṭṭhepi dhamme gārayhā honti. Samparāyepi tassa saṅghāṭipi ādittā sampajjalitātiādinā lakkhaṇasaṃyutte vuttanayena samaṇapetā honti. Imināva tāva kāraṇena kabaḷīkārāhāre nikantiyeva bhayanti veditabbā.

Thus, in these nutriments which accomplish the function of nutriment by way of support and so on, four dangers should be seen. They are as follows: in the nutriment of physical food, craving itself is a danger; in contact, approaching itself is a danger; in mental volition, exertion itself is a danger; in consciousness, descent itself is a danger. For what reason? Because beings, having formed a craving for the nutriment of physical food and being beset by cold and so forth, undergo immense suffering while performing actions such as finger-reckoning and calculation for the sake of nutriment. And some, even after going forth in this Dispensation, are blameworthy in this very life while seeking nutriment through wrong livelihood such as the practice of medicine. And in the next life, they become ascetic-petas, their outer robe ignited and blazing, according to the method stated in the Lakkhaṇa Saṃyutta. For this very reason, it should be understood that in the nutriment of physical food, craving itself is a danger.

Phassaṃ upagacchantāpi [P 1.0211] phassassādino paresaṃ rakkhitagopitesu dārādīsu bhaṇḍesu aparajjhanti. Te saha bhaṇḍena bhaṇḍasāmikā gahetvā khaṇḍākhaṇḍikaṃ vā chinditvā saṅkārakūṭesu chaḍḍenti. Rañño vā niyyātenti. Tato ne rājā vividhā kammakāraṇā kārāpeti. Kāyassa ca bhedā duggati nesaṃ pāṭikaṅkhā hoti. Iti phassassādamūlakaṃ diṭṭhadhammikampi samparāyikampi bhayaṃ sabbamāgatameva hoti. Iminā kāraṇena phassāhāre upagamanameva bhayanti veditabbaṃ.

Those who delight in contact, even while approaching contact, transgress with regard to the guarded and protected goods of others, such as their wives and so on. The owners, seizing them along with the goods, either cut them into pieces or discard them on rubbish heaps. Or they hand them over to the king. Then the king has various punishments inflicted upon them. And after the breakup of the body, a woeful destination is to be expected for them. Thus, all danger rooted in delight in contact, both that in the present life and that in the next, has indeed come to be. For this reason, it should be understood that in the nutriment of contact, approaching itself is a danger.

Kusalākusalakammāyūhaneneva pana tammūlakaṃ tīsu bhavesu bhayaṃ sabbamāgataṃyeva hoti. Iminā kāraṇena manosañcetanāhāre āyūhanameva bhayanti veditabbaṃ.

Furthermore, through the very exertion of wholesome and unwholesome kamma, all danger rooted therein comes to be in the three forms of existence. For this reason, it should be understood that in the nutriment of mental volition, exertion itself is a danger.

Paṭisandhiviññāṇañca yasmiṃ yasmiṃ ṭhāne abhinipatati, tasmiṃ tasmiṃ ṭhāne paṭisandhināmarūpaṃ gahetvāva nibbattati, tasmiñca nibbatte sabbabhayāni nibbattāniyeva honti, tammūlakattāti, iminā kāraṇena viññāṇāhāre abhinipātoyeva bhayanti veditabbo.

And in whatever place relinking-consciousness descends, in that very place it arises only after having taken up mentality-materiality at rebirth-linking. And when that has arisen, all dangers indeed arise, because that is their root. For this reason, it should be known that in the nutriment of consciousness, descent itself is a danger.

Evaṃ [V 1.0220] sabhayesu pana imesu āhāresu sammāsambuddho kabaḷīkārāhāre nikantipariyādānatthaṃ “seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, dve jāyampatikā”tiādinā (saṃ. ni. 2.63) nayena puttamaṃsūpamaṃ desesi. Phassāhāre nikantipariyādānatthaṃ “seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, gāvī niccammā”tiādinā nayena niccammagāvūpamaṃ desesi. Manosañcetanāhāre nikantipariyādānatthaṃ “seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, aṅgārakāsū”tiādinā nayena aṅgārakāsūpamaṃ desesi. Viññāṇāhāre nikantipariyādānatthaṃ “seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, coraṃ āgucāri”ntiādinā nayena sattisatāhatūpamaṃ desesi.

Thus, with regard to these dangerous nutriments, the Fully Enlightened One, for the purpose of destroying craving for physical nutriment, taught the simile of the son's flesh by the method beginning, 'Suppose, monks, a husband and wife...' For the purpose of destroying craving for the nutriment of contact, he taught the simile of the flayed cow by the method beginning, 'Suppose, monks, a flayed cow...' For the purpose of destroying craving for the nutriment of mental volition, he taught the simile of the charcoal pit by the method beginning, 'Suppose, monks, a charcoal pit...' For the purpose of destroying craving for the nutriment of consciousness, he taught the simile of the man struck by a hundred spears by the method beginning, 'Suppose, monks, a criminal caught in the act...'

Tatrāyaṃ bhūtamatthaṃ katvā saṅkhepato atthayojanā, dve kira jāyampatikā puttaṃ gahetvā parittena pātheyyena yojanasatikaṃ kantāramaggaṃ [M 1.0216] paṭipajjiṃsu. Tesaṃ paññāsa yojanāni gantvā pātheyyaṃ niṭṭhāsi. Te khuppipāsāturā viraḷacchāyāyaṃ nisīdiṃsu. Tato puriso bhariyaṃ āha “bhadde ito samantā paññāsa yojanāni gāmo vā nigamo vā natthi, tasmā yaṃ taṃ purisena kātabbaṃ bahumpi kasigorakkhādikammaṃ, na dāni sakkā taṃ mayā kātuṃ, ehi maṃ māretvā upaḍḍhamaṃsaṃ khāditvā upaḍḍhaṃ pātheyyaṃ [P 1.0212] katvā puttena saddhiṃ kantāraṃ nittharāhī”ti. Sāpi āha “sāmi mayā dāni yaṃ taṃ itthiyā kātabbaṃ bahumpi suttakantanādikammaṃ, taṃ kātuṃ na sakkā, ehi maṃ māretvā upaḍḍhamaṃsaṃ khāditvā upaḍḍhaṃ pātheyyaṃ katvā puttena saddhiṃ kantāraṃ nittharāhī”ti. Tato so taṃ āha “bhadde mātugāmamaraṇena dvinnaṃ maraṇaṃ paññāyati. Na hi mando kumāro mātaraṃ vinā jīvituṃ sakkoti. Yadi pana mayaṃ jīvāma, puna dārakaṃ labheyyāma, handa dāni puttakaṃ māretvā maṃsaṃ gahetvā kantāraṃ nittharāmā”ti.

Herein, taking the true meaning, is a brief explanation: A certain husband and wife, taking their son, set out on a hundred-yojana wilderness path with meager provisions. Having gone fifty yojanas, their provisions were exhausted. Afflicted by hunger and thirst, they sat down in a sparse shade. Then the husband said to his wife, 'Good lady, for fifty yojanas all around from here there is no village or town. Therefore, the many tasks a man must do, such as farming and herding, I cannot do now. Come, kill me, eat half my flesh, make the other half into provisions, and cross the wilderness with our son.' She too said, 'Husband, the many tasks a woman must do, such as spinning thread, I cannot do now. Come, kill me, eat half my flesh, make the other half into provisions, and cross the wilderness with our son.' Then he said to her, 'Good lady, with the death of a woman, the death of two is evident. For a tender young boy cannot live without his mother. But if we live, we might get another child. Come now, let us kill our little son, take his flesh, and cross the wilderness.'

Tato mātā puttamāha “tāta pitu santikaṃ gacchāhī”ti. So agamāsi. Athassa pitā “mayā puttakaṃ posessāmīti kasigorakkhādīhi anappakaṃ dukkhamanubhūtaṃ, na sakkomi puttaṃ māretuṃ, tvaṃyeva tava puttakaṃ mārehī”ti vatvā “tāta mātusantikameva gacchāhī”ti āha. So agamāsi. Athassa mātāpi “mayā puttaṃ patthentiyā govatakukkuravatadevatāyācanādīhipi tāva anappakaṃ dukkhaṃ anubhūtaṃ, ko pana vādo kucchinā pariharantiyā? Na sakkāhaṃ puttaṃ māretu”nti vatvā “tāta pitusantikaṃyeva gacchāhī”ti āha. Evaṃ so dvinnaṃ antarā gacchantoyeva mato. Te taṃ disvā paridevitvā pubbe [V 1.0221] vuttanayeneva maṃsāni gahetvā khādantā pakkamiṃsu. Tesaṃ so puttamaṃsāhāro navahi kāraṇehi paṭikulattā neva davāya hoti, na madāya na maṇḍanāya na vibhūsanāya, kevalaṃ kantāranittharaṇatthāyeva hoti.

Then the mother said to her son, 'Dear son, go to your father.' He went. Then his father, saying, 'Thinking, "I will raise my little son," I have experienced immense suffering through farming, herding, and so on. I cannot kill my son. You yourself kill your son,' told him, 'Dear son, go to your mother.' He went. Then his mother also, saying, 'While longing for a son, I experienced immense suffering through such things as the cow-vow, the dog-vow, and supplications to deities—what then needs to be said of carrying him in my womb? I cannot kill my son,' told him, 'Dear son, go to your father.' Thus, just while going between the two of them, he died. Seeing him, they lamented, and in the way previously described, they took his flesh and, while eating it, departed. For them, that nutriment of their son's flesh, being repulsive for nine reasons, was not for sport, not for intoxication, not for beautification, not for adornment, but was solely for the purpose of crossing the wilderness.

Katamehi navahi kāraṇehi paṭikūloti ce? Sajātimaṃsatāya ñātimaṃsatāya puttamaṃsatāya piyaputtamaṃsatāya taruṇamaṃsatāya āmakamaṃsatāya agorasamaṃsatāya aloṇatāya adhūpitatāyāti. Tasmā yo bhikkhu kabaḷīkārāhāraṃ evaṃ puttamaṃsasadisaṃ passati[M 1.0217], so tattha nikantiṃ pariyādiyati. Ayaṃ tāva puttamaṃsūpamāyaṃ atthayojanā.

By what nine reasons is it repulsive? If one were to ask, it is because it is the flesh of one's own kind, because it is the flesh of a relative, because it is the flesh of a son, because it is the flesh of a beloved son, because it is tender flesh, because it is raw flesh, because it is flesh without a rich taste, because it is unsalted, and because it is unsmoked. Therefore, whichever monk regards physical food as being thus similar to a son's flesh, he exhausts delight in it. This, firstly, is the explanation of the meaning in the simile of the son's flesh.

Niccammagāvūpamāyaṃ pana yathā sā gāvī gīvato yāva khurā, tāva cammaṃ uddāletvā muttā yaṃ yadeva nissāya tiṭṭhati, tattha pāṇakehi khajjamānā dukkhassevādhikaraṇaṃ hoti, evaṃ phassopi yaṃ yadeva vatthuṃ ārammaṇaṃ vā nissāya tiṭṭhati, taṃtaṃvatthārammaṇasambhavassa vedayitadukkhassa adhikaraṇameva hoti. Tasmā yo bhikkhu phassāhāraṃ evaṃ niccammagāvisadisaṃ passati[P 1.0213], so tattha nikantiṃ pariyādiyati, ayaṃ niccammagāvūpamāyaṃ atthayojanā.

Furthermore, in the simile of the skinless cow: just as that cow, having had its skin flayed from the neck down to the hooves and been released, wherever it stands relying on something, there, being eaten by creatures, it becomes a basis for suffering alone; in the same way, contact also, whatever physical basis or whatever object it stands relying on, becomes only a basis for the experienced suffering that arises from that very physical basis and object. Therefore, whichever monk sees the nutriment of contact as being thus similar to a skinless cow, he exhausts delight in it. This is the explanation of the meaning in the simile of the skinless cow.

Aṅgārakāsūpamāyaṃ pana yathā sā aṅgārakāsu, evaṃ mahāpariḷāhaṭṭhena tayo bhavā. Yathā nānābāhāsu gahetvā tattha upakaḍḍhakā dve purisā, evaṃ bhavesu upakaḍḍhanaṭṭhena manosañcetanā. Tasmā yo bhikkhu manosañcetanāhāraṃ evaṃ aṅgārakāsūpakaḍḍhakapurisasadisaṃ passati, so tattha nikantiṃ pariyādiyati, ayaṃ aṅgārakāsūpamāyaṃ atthayojanā.

In the simile of the charcoal pit, however: just as the charcoal pit, so too are the three kinds of existence to be understood in the sense of causing great torment. Just as two men, having seized a person by their various arms, drag them towards it, so too is mental volition to be understood in the sense of dragging one towards the kinds of existence. Therefore, whichever monk sees the nutriment of mental volition as being thus similar to the men dragging a person towards the charcoal pit, he exhausts delight in it. This is the explanation of the meaning in the simile of the charcoal pit.

Sattisatāhatūpamāyaṃ pana yena so puriso pubbaṇhasamaye sattisatena haññati, tamassa sarīre vaṇamukhasataṃ katvā antarā aṭṭhatvā vinivijjhitvā aparabhāgeyeva patati, evaṃ itarāni dve sattisatāni, evamassa patitokāse apatitvā apatitvā gatāhi sattīhi sabbasarīraṃ chiddāvachiddameva hoti, tassa ekavaṇamukhepi uppannassa dukkhassa pamāṇaṃ natthi, ko pana vādo tīsu vaṇamukhasatesu? Tattha sattinipātakālo viya paṭisandhiviññāṇanibbattakālo. Vaṇamukhajananaṃ viya khandhajananaṃ. Vaṇamukhesu dukkhavedanuppādo viya [V 1.0222] jātesu khandhesu vaṭṭamūlakanānāvidhadukkhuppādo. Aparo nayo, āgucārī puriso viya paṭisandhiviññāṇaṃ. Tassa sattighātehi uppannavaṇamukhāni viya viññāṇapaccayā nāmarūpaṃ. Vaṇamukhapaccayā tassa purisassa kakkhaḷadukkhuppādo viya nāmarūpapaccayā viññāṇassa dvattiṃsakammakāraṇaaṭṭhanavutirogādivasena nānappakārakadukkhuppādo daṭṭhabbo. Tasmā yo bhikkhu viññāṇāhāraṃ evaṃ sattisatāhatasadisaṃ passati. So tattha nikantiṃ pariyādiyati, ayaṃ sattisatāhatūpamāyaṃ atthayojanā.

In the simile of being struck by a hundred spears, however: a man is struck by a hundred spears in the morning. Having made a hundred wound-mouths in his body, they pierce through without stopping in between and fall only on the other side. Similarly with the other two hundred spears. Thus, his entire body becomes riddled with holes from the spears that have gone, falling again and again in the places where they have already fallen. For him, the measure of suffering that has arisen even in a single wound-mouth is immeasurable; what then is to be said of the suffering in three hundred wound-mouths? Here, the time of the arising of rebirth-linking consciousness is to be understood as being like the time of the spears' impact. The generation of the aggregates is to be understood as being like the generation of wound-mouths. The arising of various kinds of suffering rooted in the cycle of existence in the arisen aggregates is to be understood as being like the arising of painful feeling in the wound-mouths. Another method: rebirth-linking consciousness is to be understood as being like a transgressor. Name-and-form, which arises conditioned by consciousness, is to be understood as being like the wound-mouths that have arisen for that man from the spear strikes. Just as for that man, conditioned by the wound-mouths, there is the arising of coarse suffering, so too, conditioned by name-and-form, the arising of various kinds of suffering for consciousness—by way of the thirty-two kinds of tortures, ninety-eight diseases, and so on—is to be understood. Therefore, whichever monk sees the nutriment of consciousness as being thus similar to being struck by a hundred spears, he exhausts delight in it. This is the explanation of the meaning in the simile of being struck by a hundred spears.

So [M 1.0218] evaṃ imesu āhāresu nikantiṃ pariyādiyanto cattāropi āhāre parijānāti, yesu pariññātesu sabbampi pariññātaṃ vatthu pariññātameva hoti. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā –

Thus, while exhausting delight in these nutriments, he fully understands the four nutriments as well. When these have been fully understood, the entire matter to be fully understood becomes fully understood indeed. For this was said by the Blessed One:

“Kabaḷīkāre, bhikkhave, āhāre pariññāte pañcakāmaguṇiko rāgo pariññāto hoti. Pañcakāmaguṇike rāge pariññāte natthi taṃ saṃyojanaṃ, yena saṃyojanena saṃyutto ariyasāvako puna imaṃ lokaṃ āgaccheyya. Phasse, bhikkhave, āhāre pariññāte tisso vedanā pariññātā honti. Tīsu [P 1.0214] vedanāsu pariññātāsu ariyasāvakassa natthi kiñci uttarikaraṇīyanti vadāmi. Manosañcetanāya, bhikkhave, āhāre pariññāte tisso taṇhā pariññātā honti. Tīsu taṇhāsu pariññātāsu ariyasāvakassa natthi kiñci uttarikaraṇīyanti vadāmi. Viññāṇe, bhikkhave, āhāre pariññāte nāmarūpaṃ pariññātaṃ hoti. Nāmarūpe pariññāte ariyasāvakassa natthi kiñci uttarikaraṇīyanti vadāmī”ti (saṃ. ni. 2.63).

‘Monks, when the nutriment of physical food is fully understood, passion for the five strands of sensual pleasure is fully understood. When passion for the five strands of sensual pleasure is fully understood, there is no fetter, bound by which fetter a noble disciple would come again to this world. Monks, when the nutriment of contact is fully understood, the three feelings are fully understood. When the three feelings have been fully understood, I say there is nothing further for a noble disciple to do. Monks, when the nutriment of mental volition is fully understood, the three kinds of craving are fully understood. When the three kinds of craving have been fully understood, I say there is nothing further for a noble disciple to do. Monks, when the nutriment of consciousness is fully understood, name-and-form is fully understood. When name-and-form has been fully understood, I say there is nothing further for a noble disciple to do.’

Taṇhāsamudayā āhārasamudayoti purimataṇhāsamudayā paṭisandhikānaṃ āhārānaṃ samudayo nibbatto hotīti attho. Kathaṃ? Paṭisandhikkhaṇe hi tisantativasena uppannasamatiṃsarūpabbhantare jātā ojā atthi. Ayaṃ taṇhāpaccayā nibbatto upādinnakakabaḷīkārāhāro. Paṭisandhicittasampayuttā pana phassacetanā sayañca cittaṃ viññāṇanti ime taṇhāpaccayā nibbattā upādinnakaphassamanosañcetanā viññāṇāhārāti. Evaṃ tāva purimataṇhāsamudayā paṭisandhikānaṃ āhārānaṃ samudayo veditabbo. Yasmā panidha upādinnakāpi anupādinnakāpi āhārā missetvā kathitā, tasmā anupādinnakānampi evaṃ taṇhāsamudayā āhārasamudayo veditabbo[V 1.0223]. Aṭṭhalobhasahagatacittasamuṭṭhitesu hi rūpesu ojā atthi, ayaṃ sahajātataṇhāpaccayā nibbatto anupādinnakakabaḷīkārāhāro. Lobhasahagatacittasampayuttā pana phassacetanā sayañca cittaṃ viññāṇanti ime taṇhāpaccayā nibbattā anupādinnakaphassamanosañcetanā viññāṇāhārāti.

‘From the arising of craving, there is the arising of nutriment’ means that from the arising of craving in a previous existence, there is the production and arising of nutriments at the time of rebirth-linking. How so? At the moment of rebirth-linking, there is nutritive essence born within the thirty material phenomena that have arisen by way of the three continuities. This is the clung-to physical nutriment, produced conditioned by craving. Furthermore, the contact and volition associated with the rebirth-linking consciousness, and that consciousness itself, are the clung-to nutriments of contact, mental volition, and consciousness, produced conditioned by craving. Thus, firstly, the arising of nutriments at the time of rebirth-linking is to be understood as being from the arising of craving in a previous existence. However, since here both clung-to and non-clung-to nutriments are spoken of mixed together, the arising of nutriment from the arising of craving is to be understood in this way for non-clung-to nutriments as well. For in material phenomena arisen from the eight types of consciousness accompanied by greed, there is nutritive essence. This is the non-clung-to physical nutriment, produced conditioned by co-nascent craving. Furthermore, the contact and volition associated with consciousness accompanied by greed, and that consciousness itself, are the non-clung-to nutriments of contact, mental volition, and consciousness, produced conditioned by craving.

Taṇhānirodhā [M 1.0219] āhāranirodhoti imissā upādinnakānañca anupādinnakānañca āhārānaṃ paccayabhūtāya taṇhāya nirodhena āhāranirodho paññāyati. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva. Ayaṃ pana viseso, idha cattāripi saccāni sarūpeneva vuttāni. Yathā ca idha, evaṃ ito uttarimpi sabbavāresūti. Tasmā sabbattha asammuyhantena saccāni uddharitabbāni. Sabbavāresu ca “ettāvatāpi kho āvuso”ti idaṃ desanāniyyātanaṃ tattha tattha desitadhammavasena yojetabbaṃ. Tassa idha tāva ayaṃ yojanā ettāvatāpīti imāya āhāradesanāya vuttamanasikārappaṭivedhavasenāpīti vuttaṃ hoti. Esa nayo sabbatthāpi.

Regarding 'With the cessation of craving, there is the cessation of nutriment': the cessation of nutriment is known through the cessation of this craving, which has become the condition for both clung-to and non-clung-to nutriments. The remainder is just as has been stated. This, however, is the distinction: here, the four truths are stated only by their intrinsic nature. And as it is here, so also hereafter in all sections. Therefore, the truths should be extracted in all instances without confusion. And in all sections, this handing over of the teaching, 'To this extent, friend,' should be connected according to the Dhamma taught in each respective context. Of that, firstly here, this is the connection: 'To this extent' means 'by the power of the penetration through attention stated in this teaching on nutriment.' Thus it is said. This is the method in all instances.

Āhāravāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The exposition of the section on nutriment is concluded.

Saccavāravaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Section on the Truths.

91. Idāni [P 1.0215] “sādhāvuso”ti purimanayeneva therassa bhāsitaṃ abhinanditvā anumoditvā te bhikkhū uttarimpi pañhaṃ pucchiṃsu. Thero ca nesaṃ aññenapi pariyāyena byākāsi. Esa nayo ito paresupi sabbavāresu. Tasmā ito paraṃ evarūpāni vacanāni anāmasitvā yena yena pariyāyena byākaroti, tassa tasseva atthaṃ vaṇṇayissāma. Imassa pana vārassa saṅkhepadesanāyaṃ dukkhañca pajānātīti ettha dukkhanti dukkhasaccaṃ. Vitthāradesanāyaṃ pana yaṃ vattabbaṃ siyā, taṃ sabbaṃ visuddhimagge saccaniddese vuttamevāti.

Now, having delighted in and rejoiced at the Elder's speech in the same way as before, saying, 'Good, friend,' those monks asked a further question. And the Elder explained to them by another method. This is the method in all subsequent sections as well. Therefore, from now on, without touching upon such words, by whichever method he explains, we shall explain the meaning of that very method. In the concise teaching of this section, however, in the phrase 'and he understands suffering,' 'suffering' is the truth of suffering. But in the detailed teaching, whatever should be said, all of that has already been said in the Visuddhimagga, in the Exposition of the Truths.

Saccavāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

91. The exposition of the section on the truths is concluded.

Jarāmaraṇavāravaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Section on Aging and Death

92. Ito [V 1.0224] paraṃ paṭiccasamuppādavasena desanā hoti. Tattha jarāmaraṇavāre tāva tesaṃ tesanti ayaṃ saṅkhepato anekesaṃ sattānaṃ sādhāraṇaniddesoti ñātabbo. Yā devadattassa jarā, yā somadattassa jarāti evañhi divasampi kathentassa neva sattā pariyādānaṃ [M 1.0220] gacchanti. Imehi pana dvīhi padehi na koci satto apariyādinno hoti. Tasmā vuttaṃ “ayaṃ saṅkhepato anekesaṃ sattānaṃ sādhāraṇaniddeso”ti.

92. From here on, the teaching proceeds by way of dependent origination. Therein, firstly in the section on aging and death, it should be known that 'of those, of those' (tesaṃ tesaṃ) is, in brief, a common designation for many beings. For if one were to speak thus even for a whole day, of 'the aging of Devadatta, the aging of Somadatta,' beings would not come to an end. But by these two words, no being whatsoever is not included. Therefore, it was said, 'this is, in brief, a common designation for many beings.'

Tamhi tamhīti ayaṃ gatijātivasena anekesaṃ nikāyānaṃ sādhāraṇaniddeso. Sattanikāyeti sādhāraṇaniddesena niddiṭṭhassa sarūpanidassanaṃ. Jarā jīraṇatātiādīsu pana jarāti sabhāvaniddeso. Jīraṇatāti ākāraniddeso. Khaṇḍiccantiādayo kālātikkame kiccaniddesā. Pacchimā dve pakatiniddesā. Ayañhi jarāti iminā padena sabhāvato dīpitā, tenassāyaṃ sabhāvaniddeso. Jīraṇatāti iminā ākārato. Tenassāyaṃ ākāraniddeso. Khaṇḍiccanti iminā kālātikkame dantanakhānaṃ khaṇḍitabhāvakaraṇakiccato. Pāliccanti iminā kesalomānaṃ palitabhāvakaraṇakiccato. Valittacatāti iminā maṃsaṃ milāpetvā tace valittabhāvakaraṇakiccato dīpitā. Tenassā ime khaṇḍiccantiādayo tayo kālātikkame kiccaniddesā. Tehi imesaṃ vikārānaṃ dassanavasena pākaṭībhūtā pākaṭajarā dassitā. Yatheva hi udakassa vā aggino vā vātassa vā tiṇarukkhādīnaṃ sambhaggapalibhaggatāya vā jhāmatāya vā gatamaggo pākaṭo hoti, na ca so gatamaggo [P 1.0216] tāneva udakādīni, evameva jarāya dantādīsu khaṇḍiccādivasena gatamaggo pākaṭo, cakkhuṃ ummīletvāpi gayhati. Na ca khaṇḍiccādīneva jarā, na hi jarā cakkhuviññeyyā hoti.

'In this, in that' (tamhi tamhi) is a common designation for many classes of beings by way of destination and birth. 'In the classes of beings' (sattanikāye) is a demonstration of the intrinsic nature of what was indicated by the common designation. But in 'aging, decrepitude,' etc., 'aging' (jarā) is a designation of its nature. 'Decrepitude' (jīraṇatā) is a designation of its mode. 'Brokenness (of teeth)' (khaṇḍiccaṃ), etc., are designations of its function in the passing of time. The last two are designations of its natural state. For this aging is shown by the word 'jarā' in terms of its nature; hence, this is a designation of its nature. It is shown by 'jīraṇatā' in terms of its mode; hence, this is a designation of its mode. It is shown by 'khaṇḍiccaṃ' due to its function in the passing of time of causing the state of being broken in teeth and nails; by 'pāliccaṃ' (graying) due to its function of causing the state of being gray in head-hair and body-hair; and by 'valittacatā' (wrinkled skin) due to its function of causing the state of being wrinkled in the skin after having caused the flesh to wither. Therefore, these three—'khaṇḍiccaṃ,' etc.—are designations of its function in the passing of time. By them, manifest aging, which has become evident through the seeing of these alterations, is shown. For just as the path taken by water, fire, or wind becomes evident through the breaking and shattering or the burning of grass, trees, etc., but that path taken is not the water, etc., itself; even so, the path taken by aging becomes evident by way of brokenness, etc., in the teeth, etc., and is grasped even by opening the eye. And aging is not just brokenness, etc., for aging is not cognizable by eye-consciousness.

Āyuno saṃhāni indriyānaṃ paripākoti imehi pana padehi kālātikkameyeva abhibyattatāya āyukkhayacakkhādiindriyaparipākasaññitāya pakatiyā dīpitā. Tenassime pacchimā dve pakatiniddesāti veditabbā.

But by these words, 'diminution of life, ripening of the faculties' (āyuno saṃhāni indriyānaṃ paripāko), its natural state, which is designated as the exhaustion of the life-span and the ripening of the faculties such as the eye, is shown because of its manifestation in the passing of time. Therefore, these last two should be known as designations of its natural state.

Tattha yasmā jaraṃ pattassa āyu hāyati, tasmā jarā “āyuno saṃhānī”ti phalūpacārena vuttā[V 1.0225]. Yasmā ca daharakāle suppasannāni sukhumampi attano visayaṃ sukheneva gaṇhanasamatthāni cakkhādīni indriyāni jaraṃ pattassa paripakkāni āluḷitāni avisadāni oḷārikampi attano visayaṃ gahetuṃ asamatthāni honti, tasmā “indriyānaṃ paripāko”tipi phalūpacāreneva [M 1.0221] vuttā. Sā panāyaṃ evaṃ niddiṭṭhā sabbāpi jarā pākaṭā paṭicchannāti duvidhā hoti.

Therein, because for one who has reached aging the life-span diminishes, aging is called 'the diminution of life' by a metaphor of the effect. And because the faculties, such as the eye—which in youth are very clear and capable of easily grasping even a subtle object in their own range—become, for one who has reached aging, ripened, confused, unclear, and incapable of grasping even a coarse object in their own range, it is also called 'the ripening of the faculties' by a metaphor of the effect. But all this aging, thus pointed out, is twofold: manifest and concealed.

Tattha dantādīsu khaṇḍabhāvādidassanato rūpadhammesu jarā pākaṭajarā nāma. Arūpadhammesu pana tādisassa vikārassa adassanato paṭicchannajarā nāma. Tattha yvāyaṃ khaṇḍādibhāvo dissati, so tādisānaṃ dantādīnaṃ suviññeyyattā vaṇṇoyeva, taṃ cakkhunā disvā manodvārena cintetvā “ime dantā jarāya pahaṭā”ti jaraṃ jānāti udakaṭṭhāne baddhāni gosīsādīni oloketvā heṭṭhā udakassa atthibhāvaṃ jānanaṃ viya. Puna avīci savīcīti evampi duvidhā hoti. Tattha maṇikanakarajatapavāḷasūriyādīnaṃ mandadasakādīsu pāṇīnaṃ viya pupphaphalapallavādīsu ca apāṇīnaṃ viya antarantarā vaṇṇavisesādīnaṃ duviññeyyattā jarā avīcijarā nāma, nirantarajarāti attho. Tato aññesu pana yathāvuttesu antarantarā vaṇṇavisesādīnaṃ suviññeyyattā jarā savīcijarā nāmāti veditabbā.

Therein, because of showing the state of being broken, etc., in the teeth, etc., aging in material phenomena is called manifest aging. But in immaterial phenomena, because such an alteration is not seen, it is called concealed aging. Therein, this state of being broken, etc., that is seen is merely the color of such teeth, etc., because they are easily cognizable. Seeing that with the eye and reflecting with the mind-door, one knows aging thus: 'These teeth have been struck by aging,' just like knowing the presence of water below by observing ox-skulls, etc., found in a watery place. Again, it is also twofold: non-intermittent and intermittent. Therein, in things like gems, gold, and silver, and in inanimate things like flowers, fruits, and shoots, because the distinctions of color, etc., are difficult to discern in the intervals, aging is called non-intermittent aging; the meaning is continuous aging. But in other things than those mentioned, because the distinctions of color, etc., are easy to discern in the intervals, aging should be known as intermittent aging.

Ito paraṃ, tesaṃ tesantiādi vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Cuti cavanatātiādīsu pana cutīti cavanakavasena vuccati, ekacatupañcakkhandhānaṃ sāmaññavacanametaṃ. Cavanatāti bhāvavacanena lakkhaṇanidassanaṃ. Bhedoti cutikkhandhānaṃ bhaṅguppattiparidīpanaṃ. Antaradhānanti ghaṭasseva bhinnassa bhinnānaṃ cutikkhandhānaṃ yena kenaci pariyāyena ṭhānābhāvaparidīpanaṃ. Maccu maraṇanti maccusaṅkhātaṃ maraṇaṃ. Tena samucchedamaraṇādīni nisedheti. Kālo nāma antako, tassa kiriyāti kālakiriyā. Etena lokasammutiyā maraṇaṃ dīpeti.

From here on, the passage beginning with 'of those, of those,' etc., should be understood in the manner already stated. As for the terms 'passing away, deceasing,' etc., 'passing away' (cuti) is so called in the sense of deceasing; this is a general term for the one, four, or five aggregates. The term 'deceasing' (cavanatā), being an abstract noun, indicates the characteristic of perishing. 'Dissolution' (bhedo) is a term that indicates the attainment of the breaking up of the aggregates that are passing away. 'Disappearance' (antaradhānaṃ) is a term that indicates, by any means whatsoever, the non-existence of a state for the aggregates that have passed away and broken up, just as for a broken pot there is no existing again. 'Death, dying' (maccu maraṇaṃ) indicates the death designated as maccu. By this, it excludes annihilation-death and so on. Time (kālo) is the end-maker (antako); its action (kiriyā) is 'the action of time' (kālakiriyā). By this, it reveals death according to worldly convention.

Idāni paramatthena [P 1.0217] dīpetuṃ, khandhānaṃ bhedotiādimāha. Paramatthena hi khandhāyeva bhijjanti, na satto nāma koci marati. Khandhesu pana bhijjamānesu satto marati, bhinnesu matoti vohāro hoti.

Now, to explain in the ultimate sense, he said the passage beginning with 'the dissolution of the aggregates.' For, in the ultimate sense, only the aggregates dissolve; no being whatsoever dies. But when the aggregates are dissolving, it is said that 'a being dies'; when they have dissolved, the convention 'is dead' arises.

Ettha [V 1.0226] ca catuvokāravasena khandhānaṃ bhedo, ekavokāravasena kaḷevarassa nikkhepo. Catuvokāravasena vā khandhānaṃ bhedo, sesadvayavasena kaḷevarassa nikkhepo veditabbo. Kasmā? Bhavadvayepi rūpakāyasaṅkhātassa kaḷevarassa sambhavato. Atha vā yasmā ca cātumahārājikādīsu khandhā bhijjanteva, na kiñci nikkhipanti, tasmā tesaṃ vasena [M 1.0222] khandhānaṃ bhedo, manussādīsu kaḷevarassa nikkhepo. Ettha ca kaḷevarassa nikkhepakāraṇato maraṇaṃ kaḷevarassa nikkhepoti vuttanti evamattho daṭṭhabbo.

And herein, in terms of the four-constituent existence, there is the dissolution of the aggregates; in terms of the one-constituent existence, there is the laying down of the body. Or, in terms of the four-constituent existence, there is the dissolution of the aggregates, and in terms of the remaining two types of existence, the laying down of the body is to be understood. Why? Because in both types of existence, the body, designated as the form-body, can exist. Or else, since in the realm of the Four Great Kings and so on the aggregates just dissolve and they do not lay down anything, therefore, in terms of them, there is the dissolution of the aggregates; among humans and so on, there is the laying down of the body. And herein, the meaning should be understood thus: death is called 'the laying down of the body' because the laying down of the body is its cause.

Iti ayañca jarā idañca maraṇaṃ. Idaṃ vuccatāvusoti idaṃ ubhayampi ekato katvā jarāmaraṇanti kathīyati. Sesaṃ vuttanayamevāti.

Thus: this is aging, and this is death. As to the phrase 'This is said, friend,' it means that these two, having been combined, are called 'aging-and-death.' The remainder is in the manner already stated.

Jarāmaraṇavāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The exposition of the section on aging-and-death is concluded.

Jātivāravaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Section on Birth

93. Jātivāre jāti sañjātītiādīsu jāyanaṭṭhena jāti, sā aparipuṇṇāyatanavasena yuttā. Sañjāyanaṭṭhena sañjāti, sā paripuṇṇāyatanavasena yuttā. Okkamanaṭṭhena okkanti, sā aṇḍajajalābujavasena yuttā. Te hi aṇḍakosañca vatthikosañca okkamantā pavisantā viya paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhanti. Abhinibbattanaṭṭhena abhinibbatti, sā saṃsedajaopapātikavasena yuttā, te hi pākaṭāyeva hutvā nibbattanti. Ayaṃ tāva vohāradesanā.

93. In the section on birth, regarding 'birth, coming-into-existence,' and so forth: 'birth' (jāti) is so called in the sense of being born; it is associated with incomplete sense-bases. 'Coming-into-existence' (sañjāti) is so called in the sense of being born completely; it is associated with complete sense-bases. 'Descent' (okkanti) is so called in the sense of descending; it is associated with the egg-born and the womb-born. For they take rebirth-linking as if descending and entering into an eggshell and a womb-sac. 'Full manifestation' (abhinibbatti) is so called in the sense of manifesting clearly; it is associated with the moisture-born and the spontaneously born, for they arise having already become manifest. This, for now, is the conventional teaching.

Idāni paramatthadesanā hoti. Khandhāyeva hi paramatthato pātubhavanti, na satto. Tattha ca khandhānanti ekavokārabhave ekassa catuvokārabhave catunnaṃ pañcavokārabhave pañcannampi gahaṇaṃ veditabbaṃ. Pātubhāvoti uppatti. Āyatanānanti ettha tatra tatra uppajjamānāyatanavaseneva saṅgaho veditabbo. Paṭilābhoti santatiyaṃ pātubhāvoyeva. Pātubhavantāneva hi tāni paṭiladdhāni nāma honti. Ayaṃ vuccatāvuso jātīti iminā padena vohārato paramatthato ca desitāya jātiyā nigamanaṃ karotīti. Bhavasamudayāti ettha pana jātiyā paccayabhūto kammabhavo veditabbo. Sesaṃ vuttanayamevāti.

Now there is the ultimate teaching. For, in the ultimate sense, only the aggregates appear, not a being. And therein, by 'of the aggregates,' the inclusion of one in the one-constituent existence, of four in the four-constituent existence, and of all five in the five-constituent existence should be understood. 'Appearance' is arising. Herein, regarding 'of the sense-bases,' the inclusion should be understood solely in terms of the sense-bases that are arising in each respective case. 'Acquisition' is simply the appearance in the continuity. For it is only when they appear that they are called 'acquired.' By this phrase, 'This, friend, is called birth,' he makes a conclusion about the birth that has been taught both conventionally and in the ultimate sense—thus it should be understood. But here, in 'from the arising of existence,' the kamma-becoming that is the condition for birth should be understood. The remainder is in the manner already stated.

Jātivāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The exposition of the section on birth is concluded.

Bhavavāravaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Section on Becoming

94. Bhavavāre [M 1.0223][V 1.0227][P 1.0218] kāmabhavoti kammabhavo ca upapattibhavo ca. Tattha kammabhavo nāma kāmabhavūpagaṃ kammameva. Tañhi upapattibhavassa kāraṇattā “sukho buddhānamuppādo (dha. pa. 194) dukkho pāpassa uccayo”tiādīni (dha. pa. 117) viya phalavohārena bhavoti vuttaṃ. Upapattibhavo nāma tena kammena nibbattaṃ upādinnakhandhapañcakaṃ. Tañhi tattha bhavatīti katvā bhavoti vuttaṃ. Evaṃ sabbathāpi idaṃ kammañca upapatti ca ubhayampetamidha “kāmabhavo”ti vuttaṃ. Esa nayo rūpārūpabhavesu. Upādānasamudayāti ettha pana upādānaṃ kusalakammabhavassa upanissayavaseneva paccayo hoti. Akusalakammabhavassa upanissayavasenapi sahajātādivasenapi. Upapattibhavassa pana sabbassāpi upanissayavaseneva. Sesaṃ vuttanayamevāti.

94. In the section on becoming, sensual becoming is both kamma-becoming and rebirth-becoming. Therein, kamma-becoming is the very kamma that is the cause for rebirth in the sensual plane. For, being the cause of rebirth-becoming, it is called 'becoming' by the figurative use of the effect's name, as in such passages as, 'Happy is the arising of Buddhas' and 'Painful is the accumulation of evil.' Rebirth-becoming is the five clung-to aggregates produced by that kamma. For, it is called 'becoming' because it 'comes to be' (bhavati) there. Thus, in every way, both this kamma and this rebirth are here called 'sensual becoming.' This is the method in the form and formless becomings. But in the phrase 'from the arising of clinging,' clinging is a condition for wholesome kamma-becoming only by way of decisive support. For unwholesome kamma-becoming, it is a condition by way of decisive support and also by way of co-nascence and so forth. But for all rebirth-becoming, it is a condition only by way of decisive support. The remainder is in the manner already stated.

Bhavavāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The exposition of the section on becoming is concluded.

Upādānavāravaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Section on Clinging

95. Upādānavāre kāmupādānantiādīsu vatthukāmaṃ upādiyati etena, sayaṃ vā taṃ upādiyatīti kāmupādānaṃ. Kāmo ca so upādānañcāti vā kāmupādānaṃ. Upādānanti daḷhaggahaṇaṃ vuccati. Daḷhattho hi ettha upasaddo, “upāyāsa upakaṭṭhā”tiādīsu viya pañcakāmaguṇikarāgassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Ayamettha saṅkhepo. Vitthārato panetaṃ “tattha katamaṃ kāmupādānaṃ, yo kāmesu kāmacchando”ti (dha. sa. 1220; vibha. 938) vuttanayena veditabbaṃ.

95. In the section on clinging, regarding 'sensual clinging' and so forth: one clings to an object of sensual pleasure by means of it, or it itself clings to that object; thus it is 'sensual clinging.' Or, it is 'sensual clinging' because it is both sensual pleasure and clinging. 'Clinging' is said to be firm grasping. For here the prefix 'upa-' has the meaning of firmness, as in 'upāyāsa' (distress) and 'upakaṭṭhā' (close at hand). This is a designation for the passion for the five strands of sensual pleasure. This is the summary here. But in detail, it should be understood according to the method stated: 'Therein, what is sensual clinging? It is the desire for sensual pleasures...'

Tathā diṭṭhi ca sā upādānañcāti diṭṭhupādānaṃ. Atha vā diṭṭhiṃ upādiyati, upādiyanti vā etena diṭṭhinti diṭṭhupādānaṃ. Upādiyati hi purimadiṭṭhiṃ uttaradiṭṭhi. Upādiyanti ca tāya diṭṭhiṃ. Yathāha “sassato attā ca loko ca, idameva saccaṃ moghamañña”ntiādi (ma. ni. 3.27), sīlabbatupādānaattavādupādānavajjassa sabbadiṭṭhigatassetaṃ [V 1.0228] adhivacanaṃ. Ayamettha saṅkhepo. Vitthārato panetaṃ “tattha katamaṃ diṭṭhupādānaṃ natthi dinna”nti (dha. sa. 1220; vibha. 938) vuttanayena veditabbaṃ.

Similarly, 'clinging to views' is so called because it is both a view and clinging. Alternatively, one clings to a view, or by means of it they cling to a view; thus it is 'clinging to views.' For a later view clings to a former view, and by means of that view, they cling to the view. As it is said: 'The self and the world are eternal; this alone is true, anything else is foolish,' and so forth. This is a designation for all wrong views, excluding clinging to rites and rituals and clinging to the doctrine of self. This is the summary here. In detail, however, it should be understood according to the method stated: 'Therein, what is clinging to views? "There is nothing given..."'

Tathā [M 1.0224] sīlabbataṃ upādiyanti etena, sayaṃ vā taṃ upādiyati, sīlabbatañca taṃ upādānañcāti vā sīlabbatupādānaṃ. Gosīlagovatādīni hi evaṃ suddhīti abhinivesato sayameva upādānāni ayamettha saṅkhepo. Vitthārato panetaṃ “tattha katamaṃ sīlabbatupādānaṃ, ito bahiddhā samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ sīlena [P 1.0219] suddhī”ti vuttanayena veditabbaṃ.

Similarly, 'clinging to rites and rituals' is so called because they cling to rites and rituals by means of it, or it itself clings to them, or because it is both rites and rituals and clinging. For cow-observance, dog-observance, and so forth, are themselves clingings due to the conviction that 'purity is thus.' This is the summary here. In detail, however, it should be understood according to the method stated: 'Therein, what is clinging to rites and rituals? It is the view of ascetics and brahmins outside of this teaching that "purity is by means of virtue..."'

Idāni vadanti etenāti vādo. Upādiyanti etenāti upādānaṃ. Kiṃ vadanti, upādiyanti vā? Attānaṃ. Attano vādupādānaṃ attavādupādānaṃ. Attavādamattameva vā attāti upādiyati etenāti attavādupādānaṃ, vīsativatthukāya sakkāyadiṭṭhiyā etaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Ayamettha saṅkhepo. Vitthārato panetaṃ “tattha katamaṃ attavādupādānaṃ, idha assutavā puthujjano ariyānaṃ adassāvī”ti (dha. sa. 1223) vuttanayena veditabbaṃ.

Now, 'doctrine' is so called because they assert by means of it. 'Clinging' is so called because they cling by means of it. What do they assert, or cling to? The self. The clinging to the doctrine of self is 'clinging to the doctrine of self.' Or, it is 'clinging to the doctrine of self' because by means of it one clings to the mere doctrine of self as 'self.' This is a designation for the twenty-factored personality view. This is the summary here. In detail, however, it should be understood according to the method stated: 'Therein, what is clinging to the doctrine of self? Here, an uninstructed worldling, who has not seen the noble ones...'

Taṇhāsamudayāti ettha taṇhā kāmupādānassa upanissayavasena anantarasamanantaranatthivigatāsevanavasena vā paccayo. Avasesānaṃ pana sahajātādivasenāpi. Sesaṃ vuttanayamevāti.

Herein, regarding 'from the arising of craving': craving is a condition for sensual clinging by way of decisive support, or by way of contiguity, immediate contiguity, absence, disappearance, and repetition. For the remaining types of clinging, however, it is also a condition by way of co-nascence and so forth. The remainder is in the manner already stated.

Upādānavāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The exposition of the section on clinging is concluded.

Taṇhāvāravaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Section on Craving

96. Taṇhāvāre rūpataṇhā…pe… dhammataṇhāti evaṃ cakkhudvārādīsu javanavīthiyaṃ pavattāya taṇhāya “seṭṭhiputto brāhmaṇaputto”ti evamādīsu pitito nāmaṃ viya pitisadisārammaṇato nāmaṃ. Ettha ca rūpārammaṇā taṇhā, rūpe taṇhāti rūpataṇhā. Sā kāmarāgabhāvena rūpaṃ assādentī pavattamānā kāmataṇhā. Sassatadiṭṭhisahagatarāgabhāvena rūpaṃ niccaṃ dhuvaṃ sassatanti evaṃ assādentī pavattamānā bhavataṇhā. Ucchedadiṭṭhisahagatarāgabhāvena rūpaṃ [V 1.0229] ucchijjati vinassati pecca na bhavissatīti evaṃ assādentī pavattamānā vibhavataṇhāti evaṃ tividhā hoti. Yathā ca rūpataṇhā, tathā saddataṇhādayopīti etāni aṭṭhārasa taṇhāvicaritāni honti. Tāni ajjhattarūpādīsu aṭṭhārasa, bahiddhārūpādīsu aṭṭhārasāti chattiṃsa. Iti atītāni chattiṃsa, anāgatāni chattiṃsa, paccuppannāni chattiṃsāti aṭṭhasataṃ. “Ajjhattikassupādāya ‘asmī’ti hoti[M 1.0225], ‘itthasmī’ti [P 1.0220] hotī”ti (vibha. 973-974) vā evamādīnā ajjhattikarūpādinissitāni aṭṭhārasa, “bāhirassupādāya ‘iminā asmī’ti hoti, ‘iminā itthasmī’ti hotī”ti vā (vibha. 975) evamādinā bāhirarūpādinissitāni aṭṭhārasāti chattiṃsa. Iti atītāni chattiṃsa, anāgatāni chattiṃsa, paccuppannāni chattiṃsāti evampi aṭṭhasatataṇhāvicaritāni honti. Puna saṅgahe karīyamāne rūpādīsu ārammaṇesu chaḷeva taṇhākāyā tissoyeva kāmataṇhādayo hontīti evaṃ –

96. In the Section on Craving, 'craving for forms' (rūpataṇhā), and so forth, up to 'craving for mental phenomena' (dhammataṇhā): the craving that arises in the javana-process in the sense-door courses, beginning with the eye-door, is named from an object similar to a father, just as a name is derived from a father, as in 'the merchant’s son' or 'the brahmin’s son'. Here, craving that has form as its object, or craving for form, is 'craving for forms'. When it arises relishing form by way of sensual passion, it is 'sensual craving' (kāmataṇhā). When it arises relishing form by way of passion accompanied by eternalist view, thinking 'form is permanent, stable, eternal,' it is 'craving for existence' (bhavataṇhā). When it arises relishing form by way of passion accompanied by annihilationist view, thinking 'form is annihilated, destroyed, and will not exist after death,' it is 'craving for non-existence' (vibhavataṇhā). Thus, it is threefold. Just as with craving for forms, so too with craving for sounds, and so forth; thus there are eighteen courses of craving. These are eighteen in relation to internal forms and so forth, and eighteen in relation to external forms and so forth, making thirty-six. Thus, thirty-six pertain to the past, thirty-six to the future, and thirty-six to the present, totaling one hundred and eight. Or, as stated: 'Due to clinging to the internal, one thinks, "I am," or "I am thus,"' (Vibh. 973–974)—in this way, there are eighteen dependent on internal forms and so forth. And as stated: 'Due to clinging to the external, one thinks, "By this, I am," or "By this, I am thus,"' (Vibh. 975)—in this way, there are eighteen dependent on external forms and so forth, making thirty-six. Thus, thirty-six pertain to the past, thirty-six to the future, and thirty-six to the present—in this way too, there are one hundred and eight courses of craving. Again, when a summary is made, regarding the objects such as forms, there are just six groups of craving, and these are only the three: sensual craving, and so forth. Thus—

Niddesatthena niddesa-vitthārā vitthārassa ca;

Puna saṅgahato taṇhā, viññātabbā vibhāvināti.

Craving is to be understood by the discerning one through the meaning of the Niddesa, through its detailed exposition, and through the elaboration of that exposition; and again, through the summary.

Vedanāsamudayāti ettha pana vedanāti vipākavedanā adhippetā. Sā kathaṃ chasu dvāresu taṇhāya paccayo hotīti ce? Assādanīyato. Sukhāya hi vedanāya assādanena sattā vedanaṃ mamāyantā vedanāya taṇhaṃ uppādetvā vedanārāgarattā hutvā cakkhudvāre iṭṭhameva rūpaṃ patthenti, laddhā ca naṃ assādenti, ārammaṇadāyakānañca cittakārādīnaṃ sakkāraṃ karonti. Tathā sotadvārādīsu iṭṭhe ca saddādayo patthenti, laddhā ca ne assādenti, ārammaṇadāyakānañca vīṇāvādaka-gandhikasūda-tantavāya-nānāvidhasippasandassakādīnaṃ sakkāraṃ karonti. Yathā kiṃ? Yathā puttasinehena puttaṃ mamāyantā dhātiyā sakkāraṃ karonti, sappāyasappikhīrādīniyeva naṃ pāyenti ceva bhojenti ca. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva.

Regarding 'the arising of feeling' (vedanāsamudaya): Here, 'feeling' (vedanā) is intended as resultant feeling. If it is asked, 'How does it become a condition for craving in the six doors?' The answer is: Through its being an object to be relished. Indeed, beings, by relishing pleasant feeling, cherish feeling as 'mine,' give rise to craving for feeling, and, being impassioned with passion for feeling, at the eye-door, they long only for desirable forms, and having obtained them, they relish them. They also make offerings to those who provide such objects, like painters and so forth. Similarly, at the ear-door and other sense-doors, they long for desirable sounds and so forth, and having obtained them, they relish them. They also make offerings to those who provide such objects, like lute players, perfumers, cooks, weavers, and those who make and display various kinds of crafts. Like what? Just as those who, with affection for a child, cherish the child as 'mine,' make offerings to the wet-nurse, and give the child only suitable ghee, milk, and so forth to drink and eat. The rest is as previously explained.

Taṇhāvāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Section on Craving is concluded.

Vedanāvāravaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Section on Feeling

97. Vedanāvāre [V 1.0230] vedanākāyāti vedanāsamūhā. Cakkhusamphassajā vedanā…pe… manosamphassajā vedanāti etaṃ “cakkhusamphassajā vedanā atthi kusalā, atthi akusalā, atthi abyākatā”ti (vibha. 34) evaṃ vibhaṅge āgatattā cakkhudvārādīsu pavattānaṃ kusalākusalābyākatavedanānaṃ “sāriputto, mantāṇiputto”ti evamādīsu mātito nāmaṃ viya mātisadisavatthuto nāmaṃ. Vacanattho panettha cakkhusamphassahetu [P 1.0221] jātā vedanā cakkhusamphassajā vedanāti. Esa nayo sabbattha. Ayaṃ tāvettha sabbasaṅgāhikakathā[M 1.0226]. Vipākavasena pana cakkhudvāre dve cakkhuviññāṇāni, dve manodhātuyo, tisso manoviññāṇadhātuyoti etāhi sampayuttavasena vedanā veditabbā. Esa nayo sotadvārādīsu. Manodvāre manoviññāṇadhātusampayuttāva.

97. In the Section on Feeling, 'a body of feeling' means a collection of feelings. 'Feeling born of eye-contact… (and so on)... feeling born of mind-contact'—regarding this, because it is stated in the Vibhaṅga thus: 'There is feeling born of eye-contact that is wholesome, there is that which is unwholesome, there is that which is indeterminate' (Vibh. 34), it is a name for the wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate feelings that arise at the eye-door and so on, derived from its basis which is like a mother, just as in such cases as 'Sāriputta, son of Mantāṇī,' the name is derived from the mother. Here, the meaning of the term should be known thus: 'feeling born of eye-contact' is the feeling born because of eye-contact. This is the method in all cases. This, to begin with, is the all-inclusive discourse here. But by way of result, at the eye-door, feelings should be known by way of association with these: two eye-consciousnesses, two mind-elements, and three mind-consciousness-elements. This is the method at the ear-door and so on. At the mind-door, they are associated only with the mind-consciousness-element.

Phassasamudayāti ettha pana pañcadvāre pañcavatthukavedanānaṃ sahajātacakkhusamphassādisamudayā samudayo hoti. Avasesānaṃ cakkhusamphassādayo upanissayādivasena paccayā. Manodvāre tadārammaṇavedanānaṃ advārikānañca paṭisandhibhavaṅgacutivedanānaṃ sahajātamanosamphassasamudayā samudayo hotīti veditabbo. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva.

But here, in the phrase 'from the arising of contact': at the five doors, for the feelings based on the five physical bases, arising occurs from the conascent arising of eye-contact and so on. For the remaining feelings, eye-contact and so on are conditions by way of decisive support condition and so on. At the mind-door, it should be known that for the feelings of registration and for the door-freed feelings of rebirth-linking, life-continuum, and death, arising occurs from the conascent arising of mind-contact. The rest is just as has been explained.

Vedanāvāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Section on Feeling is concluded.

Phassavāravaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Section on Contact

98. Phassavāre cakkhusamphassoti cakkhumhi samphasso. Esa nayo sabbattha. Cakkhusamphasso…pe… kāyasamphassoti ettāvatā ca kusalākusalavipākā pañcavatthukā dasa samphassā vuttā honti. Manosamphassoti iminā sesā bāvīsati lokiyavipākamanasampayuttaphassā. Saḷāyatanasamudayāti channaṃ cakkhādīnaṃ āyatanānaṃ samudayena imassa chabbidhassāpi samphassassa samudayo hotīti veditabbo. Sesaṃ vuttanayamevāti.

98. In the Section on Contact, 'eye-contact' means contact depending on the eye-base. This is the method in all cases. By the passage 'Eye-contact… (and so on)... body-contact,' the ten contacts based on the five physical bases, which are wholesome-resultant and unwholesome-resultant, are stated. By this term 'mind-contact,' the remaining twenty-two contacts associated with mundane resultant mind-consciousness are stated. As for 'from the arising of the six sense bases,' it should be known that through the arising of the six sense bases, the eye and so on, there is the arising of this sixfold contact. The rest is just as has been explained.

Phassavāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Section on Contact is concluded.

Saḷāyatanavāravaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Section on the Six Sense Bases

99. Saḷāyatanavāre [V 1.0231] cakkhāyatanantiādīsu yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ sabbaṃ visuddhimagge khandhaniddese ceva āyatananiddese ca vuttanayameva. Nāmarūpasamudayāti ettha pana yaṃ nāmaṃ yañca rūpaṃ, yañca nāmarūpaṃ yassa āyatanassa paccayo hoti, tassa vasena visuddhimagge paṭiccasamuppādaniddese vuttanayena nāmarūpasamudayā saḷāyatanasamudayo veditabbo. Sesaṃ vuttappakāramevāti.

99. In the Section on the Six Sense Bases, whatever is to be said regarding 'the eye-base' and so on, all of that is of the same method as that stated in the Visuddhimagga, in both the exposition of the aggregates and the exposition of the sense bases. Here, however, regarding 'from the arising of name-and-form': by means of whichever name, whichever form, or whichever name-and-form is a condition for whichever sense base, the arising of the six sense bases from the arising of name-and-form is to be understood according to the method stated in the Visuddhimagga in the exposition of dependent origination. The remainder is of the same kind as that already stated.

Saḷāyatanavāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Section on the Six Sense Bases is concluded.

Nāmarūpavāravaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Section on Name-and-Form

100. Nāmarūpavāre namanalakkhaṇaṃ nāmaṃ. Ruppanalakkhaṇaṃ rūpaṃ. Vitthāravāre panassa vedanāti vedanākkhandho. Saññāti saññākkhandho. Cetanā phasso manasikāroti saṅkhārakkhandho veditabbo. Kāmañca aññepi saṅkhārakkhandhasaṅgahitā [M 1.0227] dhammā santi, ime pana tayo sabbadubbalesupi cittesu santi. Tasmā etesaṃyeva vasenettha saṅkhārakkhandhopi dassito. Cattāri ca mahābhūtānīti [P 1.0222] ettha cattārīti gaṇanaparicchedo. Mahābhūtānīti pathavīāpatejavāyānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Yena pana kāraṇena tāni mahābhūtānīti vuccanti, yo cettha añño vinicchayanayo, so sabbo visuddhimagge rūpakkhandhaniddese vutto.

100. In the section on name-and-form, name has the characteristic of inclining towards an object. Form has the characteristic of being afflicted. But in its detailed section, 'feeling' is to be understood as the feeling aggregate; 'perception' is to be understood as the perception aggregate; volition, contact, and attention are to be understood as the formations aggregate. And although there are other mental factors included in the formations aggregate, these three are present even in all the weakest minds. Therefore, by means of these very three, the formations aggregate is also shown here. And here, in 'the four great elements,' 'four' is a numerical determination. 'Great elements' is a designation for earth, water, fire, and air. And for what reason they are called 'great elements,' and whatever other method of determination there is here, all of that is stated in the Visuddhimagga in the exposition of the form aggregate.

Catunnañca mahābhūtānaṃ upādāyāti ettha pana catunnanti upayogatthe sāmivacanaṃ, cattāri ca mahābhūtānīti vuttaṃ hoti. Upādāyāti upādiyitvā, gahetvāti attho. Nissāyātipi eke. Vattamānanti ayañcettha pāṭhaseso. Samūhatthe vā etaṃ sāmivacanaṃ. Tena catunnañca mahābhūtānaṃ samūhaṃ upādāya pavattamānaṃ rūpanti ayamattho veditabbo. Evaṃ sabbatthāpi yāni cattāri pathavīādīni mahābhūtāni, yañca catunnaṃ mahābhūtānaṃ upādāya vattamānaṃ cakkhāyatanādibhedena abhidhammapāḷiyameva vuttaṃ tevīsatividhaṃ rūpaṃ, taṃ sabbampi “rūpa”nti veditabbaṃ. Viññāṇasamudayāti ettha pana yaṃ viññāṇaṃ yassa nāmassa yassa ca rūpassa yassa ca [V 1.0232] nāmarūpassa paccayo hoti, tassa vasena visuddhimagge paṭiccasamuppādaniddese vuttanayeneva viññāṇasamudayā nāmarūpasamudayo veditabbo. Sesaṃ vuttanayamevāti.

But here, in 'and depending on the four great elements': 'of the four' is the genitive case in the sense of the accusative; it means 'the four great elements.' 'Upādāya' (depending) means 'having taken up,' 'having grasped.' Some also say it means 'nissāya' (relying on). And here the remainder of the text, 'vattamānaṃ' (occurring), should be supplied. Or, this is the genitive case in the sense of a collection. By that, this meaning is to be understood: 'form that occurs depending on the collection of the four great elements.' Thus, in all cases, whatever are the four great elements beginning with earth, and whatever twenty-threefold form there is—stated only in the Abhidhamma Pāḷi, differentiated as the eye-base and so on, occurring in dependence on the four great elements—all of that is to be understood as 'form.' But here, in 'from the arising of consciousness': by means of whichever consciousness is a condition for whichever name, whichever form, or whichever name-and-form, in the very same way as stated in the Visuddhimagga in the exposition of dependent origination, the arising of name-and-form from the arising of consciousness is to be understood. The remainder is of the same method as that already stated.

Nāmarūpavāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Section on Name-and-Form is completed.

Viññāṇavāravaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Section on Consciousness

101. Viññāṇavāre cakkhuviññāṇanti cakkhumhi viññāṇaṃ, cakkhuto vā jātaṃ viññāṇanti cakkhuviññāṇaṃ. Evaṃ sotaghānajivhākāyaviññāṇāni. Itaraṃ pana manoyeva viññāṇanti manoviññāṇaṃ. Dvipañcaviññāṇavajjassa tebhūmakavipākacittassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Saṅkhārasamudayāti ettha pana yo saṅkhāro yassa viññāṇassa paccayo hoti, tassa vasena saṅkhārasamudayā viññāṇasamudayo veditabbo. Sesaṃ vuttanayamevāti.

101. In the section on consciousness, as for 'eye-consciousness,' it is consciousness depending on the eye, or consciousness born from the eye; therefore, it is called eye-consciousness. The same applies to ear-, nose-, tongue-, and body-consciousness. The remaining, however, is that the mind itself is consciousness; therefore, it is called mind-consciousness. This is a designation for the resultant consciousness of the three planes, excluding the ten instances of the fivefold sense-consciousness. As for 'from the arising of formations,' herein, by means of that formation which is a condition for a particular consciousness, the arising of consciousness from the arising of formations is to be understood. The rest is just as has been explained.

Viññāṇavāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Section on Consciousness is completed.

Saṅkhāravāravaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Section on Formations

102. Saṅkhāravāre abhisaṅkharaṇalakkhaṇo saṅkhāro. Vitthāravāre panassa kāyasaṅkhāroti kāyato pavattasaṅkhāro, kāyadvāre copanavasena [M 1.0228] pavattānaṃ kāmāvacarakusalato aṭṭhannaṃ, akusalato dvādasannanti vīsatiyā kāyasañcetanānametaṃ [P 1.0223] adhivacanaṃ. Vacīsaṅkhāroti vacito pavattasaṅkhāro, vacīdvāre vacanabhedavasena pavattānaṃ vīsatiyā eva vacīsañcetanānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Cittasaṅkhāroti cittato pavattasaṅkhāro, kāyavacīdvāre copanaṃ akatvā raho nisīditvā cintayantassa pavattānaṃ lokiyakusalākusalavasena ekūnatiṃsamanosañcetanānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Avijjāsamudayāti ettha pana kusalānaṃ upanissayavasena akusalānaṃ sahajātādivasenāpi avijjāpaccayo hotīti veditabbā. Sesaṃ vuttanayamevāti.

102. In the section on formations, a formation has the characteristic of forming. In its detailed exposition, however, 'bodily formation' is the formation arising from the body; this is a designation for the twenty bodily volitions that arise through the body-door by way of instigation: eight wholesome volitions of the sense-sphere and twelve unwholesome volitions. 'Verbal formation' is the formation arising from speech; this is a designation for the twenty verbal volitions that arise through the speech-door in various forms of speech. 'Mental formation' is the formation arising from the mind; this is a designation for the twenty-nine mental volitions that arise by way of mundane wholesome and unwholesome states for one who sits in seclusion and thinks without instigating action through the body-door or speech-door. As for 'from the arising of ignorance,' herein it should be understood that ignorance is a condition for wholesome states by way of decisive support, and for unwholesome states by way of co-nascence, and so on. The rest is just as has been explained.

Saṅkhāravāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Section on Formations is completed.

Avijjāvāravaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Section on Ignorance

103. Avijjāvāre [V 1.0233] dukkhe aññāṇanti dukkhasacce aññāṇaṃ, mohassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Esa nayo samudaye aññāṇantiādīsu. Tattha catūhi kāraṇehi dukkhe aññāṇaṃ veditabbaṃ antogadhato vatthuto ārammaṇato paṭicchādanato ca. Tathā hi taṃ dukkhasaccapariyāpannattā dukkhe antogadhaṃ, dukkhasaccañcassa nissayapaccayabhāvena vatthu, ārammaṇapaccayabhāvena ārammaṇaṃ, dukkhasaccañca etaṃ paṭicchādeti, tassa yāthāvalakkhaṇappaṭivedhanivāraṇena, ñāṇappavattiyā cettha appadānena.

103. In the section on ignorance, 'not-knowing suffering' means not-knowing the truth of suffering; this is a designation for delusion. The same principle applies to 'not-knowing the origin,' and so forth. Here, not-knowing suffering should be understood for four reasons: by way of inclusion, by way of basis, by way of object, and by way of concealment. For it is included in suffering, being comprised within the truth of suffering. And the truth of suffering is its basis by way of being a support condition, and its object by way of being an object condition. And it conceals the truth of suffering by preventing the penetration of its true characteristics and by not allowing the arising of knowledge concerning it.

Samudaye aññāṇaṃ tīhi kāraṇehi veditabbaṃ vatthuto ārammaṇato paṭicchādanato ca. Nirodhe paṭipadāyañca aññāṇaṃ ekeneva kāraṇena veditabbaṃ paṭicchādanato. Nirodhapaṭipadāya hi paṭicchādakameva aññāṇaṃ tesaṃ yāthāvalakkhaṇappaṭivedhanivāraṇena, tesu ca ñāṇappavattiyā appadānena. Na pana tattha antogadhaṃ, tasmiṃ saccadvaye apariyāpannattā.
