Na tassa taṃ saccadvayaṃ vatthu, asahajātattā. Nārammaṇaṃ, tadārabbha appavattanato. Pacchimañhi saccadvayaṃ gambhīrattā duddasaṃ, na cettha andhabhūtaṃ aññāṇaṃ pavattati. Purimaṃ pana vañcaniyaṭṭhena sabhāvalakkhaṇassa duddasattā gambhīraṃ, tattha vipallāsaggāhavasena pavattati.

Not-knowing regarding the origin should be understood through three reasons: by way of basis, by way of object, and by way of concealment. And not-knowing regarding cessation and the path should be understood through one reason only: by way of concealment. For regarding cessation and the path, not-knowing is merely a concealer, preventing the penetration of their true characteristics and not allowing the arising of knowledge concerning them. But it is not included within, since it is not comprised in that pair of truths. Nor is that pair of truths its basis, since they are not co-nascent. Nor are they its object, since it does not arise in relation to them. For the latter pair of truths is profound and hard to see; not-knowing, having become blinding, does not operate here. The former pair of truths, however, is profound because its own characteristic is hard to see in the sense of being deceptive; there, it operates by way of perverse grasping.

Apica dukkheti ettāvatā saṅgahato vatthuto ārammaṇato kiccato ca avijjā dīpitā. Dukkhasamudayeti ettāvatā vatthuto ārammaṇato [M 1.0229] kiccato ca. Dukkhanirodhe dukkhanirodhagāminiyā paṭipadāyāti ettāvatā kiccato. Avisesato pana aññāṇanti etena sabhāvato niddiṭṭhāti ñātabbā. Āsavasamudayāti ettha pana kāmāsavabhavāsavā sahajātādivasena avijjāya paccayā honti. Avijjāsavo upanissayavaseneva. Pubbuppannā cettha avijjā avijjāsavoti [P 1.0224] veditabbā. Sā aparāparuppannāya avijjāya upanissayapaccayo hoti. Sesaṃ vuttanayamevāti.

Furthermore, by the phrase 'in suffering,' ignorance is shown to this extent by way of inclusion, basis, object, and function. By the phrase 'in the origin of suffering,' to this extent by way of basis, object, and function. By the phrases 'in the cessation of suffering' and 'in the path leading to the cessation of suffering,' to this extent by way of function. Generally, however, it should be known that by this term 'not-knowing,' ignorance is pointed out by way of its intrinsic nature. Regarding the phrase 'from the arising of the taints,' herein the taints of sensual pleasure and existence are conditions for ignorance by way of co-nascence, and so on. The taint of ignorance is a condition only by way of decisive support. Herein, previously arisen ignorance should be understood as the taint of ignorance. It is a decisive support condition for ignorance that arises subsequently. The rest is just as has been explained.

Avijjāvāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Section on Ignorance is completed.

Āsavavāravaṇṇanā

Elucidation of the Section on Taints

104. Āsavavāre [V 1.0234] avijjāsamudayāti ettha avijjā kāmāsavabhavāsavānaṃ sahajātādivasena paccayo hoti. Avijjāsavassa upanissayavaseneva. Aparāparuppannā cettha avijjā avijjāsavoti veditabbā. Pubbuppannā avijjāyevassa aparāparuppannassa avijjāsavassa upanissayapaccayo hoti. Sesaṃ vuttanayamevāti. Ayaṃ vāro yā esā paṭiccasamuppādapadesu jeṭṭhikā avijjā, tassāpi paccayadassanavasena vutto. Evaṃ vuttena vārena saṃsārassa anamataggatā sādhitā hoti. Kathaṃ? Āsavasamudayena hi avijjāsamudayo. Avijjāsamudayenāpi āsavasamudayo. Evaṃ āsavā avijjāya avijjāpi āsavānaṃ paccayoti katvā pubbakoṭi na paññāyati avijjāya, tassā apaññāyanato saṃsārassa anamataggatā siddhā hotīti.

104. In the section on the taints, regarding the phrase 'from the arising of ignorance,' here ignorance is a condition for the taints of sensual pleasure and existence by way of co-nascence and so on. For the taint of ignorance, it is a condition only by way of natural decisive support. And here, subsequently arisen ignorance should be understood as the taint of ignorance. Presently arisen ignorance is simply ignorance; it is a natural decisive support condition for the subsequently arisen taint of ignorance. The rest is in the manner already stated. This section is stated by way of showing the condition even for that ignorance which is the chief among the sections on dependent origination. By this section thus stated, the beginninglessness of saṃsāra is established. How? Through the arising of the taints, there is the arising of ignorance. And through the arising of ignorance, there is the arising of the taints. Thus, the taints are conditions for ignorance, and ignorance is also a condition for the taints. For this reason, a first point of ignorance is not discerned. Due to its not being discerned, the beginninglessness of saṃsāra is established.

Evaṃ sabbepime imasmiṃ sutte kammapathavāro āhāravāro dukkhavāro jarā-maraṇa-jāti-bhava-upādāna-taṇhā-vedanā-phassa-saḷāyatana-nāmarūpa- viññāṇa-saṅkhāra-avijjā-āsavavāroti soḷasavārā vuttā.

Thus, in this Sutta, all these sixteen sections are stated: the section on the path of action, the section on nutriment, the section on suffering, the sections on aging-and-death, birth, existence, clinging, craving, feeling, contact, the six sense bases, name-and-form, consciousness, formations, ignorance, and the taints.

Tesu ekekassa vārassa saṅkhepavitthāravasena dvidhā vibhattā dvattiṃsaṭṭhānāni honti. Iti imasmiṃ sutte imesu dvattiṃsaṭṭhānesu cattāri saccāni kathitāni. Etesaṃyeva vitthāravasena vuttesu soḷasasu ṭhānesu arahattaṃ kathitaṃ. Therassa pana matena dvattiṃsāyapi ṭhānesu cattāri saccāni cattāro ca maggā kathitāti. Iti sakalepi pañcamahānikāyasaṅgahite buddhavacane natthi taṃ suttaṃ, yattha dvattiṃsakkhattuṃ cattāri saccāni dvattiṃsakkhattuñca arahattaṃ pakāsitaṃ aññatra imamhā sammādiṭṭhisuttāti.

Among these, for each section, being divided in two ways by means of the concise and the detailed, there are thirty-two instances. Thus, in this Sutta, the Four Truths are stated in these thirty-two instances. In the sixteen instances that are stated in detail, arahantship is explained. However, according to the Elder's view, in all thirty-two instances the Four Truths and the Four Paths are stated. Thus, in the entire word of the Buddha collected in the five great Nikāyas, there is no other sutta wherein the Four Truths are expounded thirty-two times and arahantship is expounded thirty-two times, apart from this Sammādiṭṭhi Sutta.

Idamavocāyasmā [M 1.0230] sāriputtoti idaṃ dvattiṃsāya catusaccapariyāyehi dvattiṃsāya arahattapariyāyehīti catusaṭṭhiyā kāraṇehi alaṅkaritvā sammādiṭṭhisuttaṃ āyasmā sāriputto avoca, attamanā te bhikkhū āyasmato sāriputtassa bhāsitaṃ abhinandunti.

The Venerable Sāriputta spoke this Sammādiṭṭhi Sutta, adorning it with sixty-four reasons: thirty-two expositions on the Four Noble Truths and thirty-two expositions on arahantship. Delighted, those bhikkhus rejoiced in the Venerable Sāriputta's words.

Āsavavāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Elucidation of the Section on Taints is concluded.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

From the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Middle Length Discourses.

Sammādiṭṭhisuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Elucidation of the Sammādiṭṭhi Sutta is concluded.

10. Satipaṭṭhānasuttavaṇṇanā

10. Commentary on the Discourse on the Establishment of Mindfulness

105. Evaṃ [V 1.0235][P 1.0225] me sutanti satipaṭṭhānasuttaṃ. Tattha kurūsu viharatīti kurunāmakā jānapadino rājakumārā, tesaṃ nivāso ekopi janapado ruḷhīsaddena kurūti vuccati, tasmiṃ kurūsu janapade. Aṭṭhakathācariyā panāhu – mandhātukāle tīsu dīpesu manussā jambudīpo nāma buddhapaccekabuddhamahāsāvakacakkavattipabhutīnaṃ uttamapurisānaṃ uppattibhūmi uttamadīpo atiramaṇīyoti sutvā raññā mandhātucakkavattinā cakkaratanaṃ purakkhatvā cattāro dīpe anusaṃyāyantena saddhiṃ āgamaṃsu. Tato rājā pariṇāyakaratanaṃ pucchi –

105. 'Thus have I heard.' This is the Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta. Therein, 'dwelling among the Kurus' refers to the princes of the country named Kuru. Their domain, even a single country, is by convention called 'Kuru'; thus, in that Kuru country. The commentators, however, say: During the time of King Mandhātu, people from the three continents, having heard that Jambudīpa—the birthplace of supreme beings such as Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, great disciples, and wheel-turning monarchs—was the most excellent and extremely delightful continent, came along with King Mandhātu, the wheel-turning monarch, who, placing the wheel-treasure before him, was journeying through the four continents. Then the king asked his counsellor-treasure:

“Atthi nu kho manussalokato ramaṇīyataraṃ ṭhāna”nti?

“Is there any place more delightful than the human world?”

“Kasmā deva evaṃ bhaṇasi?

“Why, Your Majesty, do you say so?”

“Kiṃ na passasi candimasūriyānaṃ ānubhāvaṃ?

“Do you not see the power of the moon and the sun?”

“Nanu etesaṃ ṭhānaṃ ito ramaṇīyatara”nti?

“Is not their abode surely more delightful than this?”

Rājā cakkaratanaṃ purakkhatvā tattha agamāsi. Cattāro mahārājāno “mandhātumahārājā āgato”ti sutvāva “mahiddhiko mahānubhāvo rājā na sakkā yuddhena paṭibāhitu”nti sakarajjaṃ niyyātesuṃ. So taṃ gahetvā puna pucchi – “atthi nu kho ito ramaṇīyataraṃ ṭhāna”nti. Athassa tāvatiṃsabhavanaṃ kathayiṃsu – “tāvatiṃsabhavanaṃ, deva, ramaṇīyataraṃ, tattha sakkassa devarañño ime cattāro mahārājāno paricārakā dovārikabhūmiyaṃ tiṭṭhanti. Sakko devarājā mahiddhiko mahānubhāvo. Tassimāni pana upabhogaṭṭhānāni, yojanasahassubbedho vejayantapāsādo, pañcayojanasatubbedhā sudhammā devasabhā, diyaḍḍhayojanasatiko vejayantaratho, tathā erāvaṇo hatthī, dibbarukkhasahassapaṭimaṇḍitaṃ [M 1.0231] nandanavanaṃ cittalatāvanaṃ phārusakavanaṃ missakavanaṃ[V 1.0236]. Yojanasatubbedho pāricchattako koviḷāro, tassa heṭṭhā saṭṭhiyojanāyāmā paṇṇāsayojanavitthatā pañcadasayojanubbedhā jayasumanapupphavaṇṇā paṇḍukambalasilā, yassā mudutāya sakkassa nisīdato upaḍḍhakāyo anupavisatī”ti.

The king, placing the wheel-treasure before him, went there. The four great kings, upon hearing, “King Mandhātu has arrived,” thinking, “The king is of great psychic power and great majesty; he cannot be repelled by battle,” surrendered their own kingdoms. Having taken them, he asked again, “Is there any place more delightful than this?” Then they told him about the Tāvatiṃsa heaven: “The Tāvatiṃsa heaven, Your Majesty, is more delightful. There, these four great kings stand as attendants in the position of gatekeepers for Sakka, the king of the gods. Sakka, the king of the gods, is of great psychic power and great majesty. And these are his places of enjoyment: the Vejayanta palace, a thousand yojanas in height; the Sudhammā assembly hall of the gods, five hundred yojanas in height; the Vejayanta chariot, one hundred and fifty yojanas in size; likewise the elephant Erāvaṇa; the Nandana grove, the Cittalatā grove, the Phārusaka grove, and the Missaka grove, all adorned with a thousand celestial trees. The Pāricchattaka coral tree is a hundred yojanas in height, and beneath it lies the Paṇḍukambala stone—sixty yojanas in length, fifty yojanas in width, and fifteen yojanas in thickness, the color of the jayasumana flower—of which the softness is such that when Sakka sits upon it, half his body sinks in.”

Taṃ sutvā rājā tattha gantukāmo cakkaratanaṃ abbhukkiri[P 1.0226]. Taṃ ākāse patiṭṭhāsi saddhiṃ caturaṅginiyā senāya. Atha dvinnaṃ devalokānaṃ vemajjhato cakkaratanaṃ otaritvā pathaviyaṃ patiṭṭhāsi saddhiṃ pariṇāyakaratanappamukhāya caturaṅginiyā senāya. Rājā ekakova tāvatiṃsabhavanaṃ agamāsi. Sakko “mandhātā āgato”ti sutvāva tassa paccuggamanaṃ katvā – “svāgataṃ te, mahārāja, sakaṃ te, mahārāja. Anusāsa, mahārājā”ti vatvā saddhiṃ nāṭakehi rajjaṃ dvebhāge katvā ekaṃ bhāgamadāsi. Rañño tāvatiṃsabhavane patiṭṭhitamattasseva manussabhāvo vigacchi, devabhāvo pāturahosi.

Hearing this, the king, desiring to go there, sent forth the wheel-treasure. It stood in the sky together with the fourfold army. Then, descending from between the two divine worlds, the wheel-treasure established itself on the earth together with the fourfold army led by the counsellor-treasure. The king went alone to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. Sakka, upon hearing, “Mandhātu has come,” went out to meet him and, saying, “Welcome to you, great king! It is yours, great king! Rule, great king!” he, together with the celestial musicians, divided the kingdom into two parts and gave one part to him. As soon as the king was established in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, his human state vanished, and a divine state arose.

Tassa kira sakkena saddhiṃ paṇḍukambalasilāyaṃ nisinnassa akkhinimisamattena nānattaṃ paññāyati. Taṃ asallakkhentā devā sakkassa ca tassa ca nānatte muyhanti. So tattha dibbasampattiṃ anubhavamāno yāva chattiṃsa sakkā uppajjitvā cutā, tāva rajjaṃ kāretvā atittoyeva kāmehi tato cavitvā attano uyyāne patiṭṭhito vātātapena phuṭṭhagatto kālamakāsi.

It is said that when he was seated with Sakka on the Paṇḍukambala stone, the difference between them was perceptible in the mere blinking of an eye. Not noticing this, the gods were confused about the difference between Sakka and him. Enjoying divine fortune there, he reigned for as long as thirty-six Sakkas arose and passed away. Still insatiate with sensual pleasures, he passed away from there and, having established himself in his own park, his body touched by wind and sun, he died.

Cakkaratane pana pathaviyaṃ patiṭṭhite pariṇāyakaratanaṃ suvaṇṇapaṭṭe mandhātuupāhanaṃ likhāpetvā idaṃ mandhāturajjanti rajjamanusāsi. Tepi tīhi dīpehi āgatamanussā puna gantuṃ asakkontā pariṇāyakaratanaṃ upasaṅkamitvā “deva mayaṃ rañño ānubhāvena āgatā, idāni gantuṃ na sakkoma, vasanaṭṭhānaṃ no dehī”ti yāciṃsu. So tesaṃ ekekaṃ janapadamadāsi. Tattha pubbavidehato āgatamanussehi āvasitapadeso tāyeva purimasaññāya videharaṭṭhanti nāmaṃ labhi. Aparagoyānato āgatamanussehi āvasitapadeso aparantajanapadoti nāmaṃ labhi. Uttarakuruto āgatamanussehi āvasitapadeso kururaṭṭhanti nāmaṃ labhīti[M 1.0232]. Bahuke pana gāmanigamādayo upādāya bahuvacanena voharīyati. Tena vuttaṃ “kurūsu viharatī”ti.

When the wheel-treasure, however, had established itself on the earth, the counsellor-treasure, having had Mandhātu’s sandals depicted on a golden plate, administered the kingdom, proclaiming, “This is Mandhātu’s kingdom.” Those people who had come from the three continents, being unable to return, approached the counsellor-treasure and pleaded, “Your Majesty, we came by the power of the king; now we are unable to go back. Grant us a place to live.” He gave each of them a country. Therein, the region inhabited by the people who came from Pubbavideha received the name Videha country, by that same former designation. The region inhabited by the people who came from Aparagoyāna received the name Aparanta country. The region inhabited by the people who came from Uttarakuru received the name Kuru country. But on account of the many villages, towns, and so forth, it is referred to in the plural. Therefore, it was said, “dwelling among the Kurus.”

Kammāsadhammaṃ [V 1.0237] nāma kurūnaṃ nigamoti. Kammāsadhammanti ettha keci dha-kārassa da-kārena atthaṃ vaṇṇayanti. Kammāso ettha damitoti kammāsadammo. Kammāsoti kammāsapādo porisādo vuccati. Tassa kira pāde khāṇukena viddhaṭṭhāne vaṇo ruhanto cittadārusadiso hutvā ruhi, tasmā kammāsapādoti paññāyittha[P 1.0227]. So ca tasmiṃ okāse damito porisādabhāvato paṭisedhito. Kena? Mahāsattena. Katarasmiṃ jātaketi? Mahāsutasomajātaketi eke. Ime pana therā jayaddisajātaketi vadanti. Tadā hi mahāsattena kammāsapādo damito. Yathāha –

Kammāsadhamma is the name of a market town of the Kurus. Herein, regarding “Kammāsadhamma,” some explain the meaning by means of the letter ‘da’ for the letter ‘dha’: Kammāsa was tamed (damito) here (ettha), thus Kammāsadamma. “Kammāsa” refers to the man-eater Kammāsapāda. It is said that on his foot, in the place pierced by a stump, a wound, as it healed, became like variegated wood; therefore, he became known as Kammāsapāda. And in that place, he was tamed, restrained from his state as a man-eater. By whom? By the Great Being. In which Jātaka? Some say in the Mahāsutasoma Jātaka. These elders, however, say it was in the Jayaddisa Jātaka. For it was then that the Great Being tamed Kammāsapāda. As it is said:

“Putto yadā homi jayaddisassa,

Pañcālaraṭṭhādhipatissa atrajo;

Cajitvāna pāṇaṃ pitaraṃ pamocayiṃ,

Kammāsapādampi cahaṃ pasādayi”nti.

“When I was the son of Jayaddisa, the own son of the ruler of the Pañcāla country, having given up my life, I freed my father, and I also won the confidence of Kammāsapāda.”

Keci pana dha-kāreneva atthaṃ vaṇṇayanti. Kururaṭṭhavāsīnaṃ kira kuruvattadhammo tasmiṃ kammāso jāto, tasmā taṃ ṭhānaṃ kammāso ettha dhammo jātoti kammāsadhammanti vuccati. Tattha niviṭṭhanigamassāpi etadeva nāmaṃ. Bhummavacanena kasmā na vuttanti? Avasanokāsato. Bhagavato kira tasmiṃ nigame vasanokāso koci vihāro nāhosi. Nigamato pana apakkamma aññatarasmiṃ udakasampanne ramaṇīye bhūmibhāge mahāvanasaṇḍo ahosi. Tattha bhagavā vihāsi. Taṃ nigamaṃ gocaragāmaṃ katvā, tasmā evamettha attho veditabbo “kurūsu viharati kammāsadhammaṃ nāma kurūnaṃ nigamo, taṃ gocaragāmaṃ katvā”ti.

Some, however, explain the meaning with the 'dha' intact. It is said that the Kuru observance of the inhabitants of the Kuru country became stained there. Therefore, that place is called Kammāsadhamma, meaning 'Here, the Dhamma became stained.' The market town established there also has the same name. Why is it not mentioned in the locative case? Because of the absence of a dwelling place. It is said that the Blessed One had no dwelling place, no monastery, in that market town. Instead, having departed from the market town, there was a large forest grove in a delightful region endowed with water. The Blessed One resided there, having made that market town his alms-resort village. Therefore, the meaning here should be understood thus: 'He dwells among the Kurus, having made Kammāsadhamma, a market town of the Kurus, his alms-resort village.'

Uddesavārakathāvaṇṇanā

Exposition of the Summary Section

106. Ekāyano ayaṃ, bhikkhave, maggoti. Kasmā bhagavā idaṃ suttamabhāsi? Kururaṭṭhavāsīnaṃ gambhīradesanāpaṭiggahaṇasamatthatāya. Kururaṭṭhavāsino kira bhikkhū bhikkhuniyo upāsakā upāsikāyo utupaccayādisampannattā tassa raṭṭhassa sappāyautupaccayasevanena niccaṃ [M 1.0233] kallasarīrā kallacittā ca honti. Te cittasarīrakallatāya anuggahitapaññābalā gambhīrakathaṃ pariggahetuṃ samatthā honti. Tena tesaṃ bhagavā imaṃ gambhīradesanāpaṭiggahaṇasamatthataṃ sampassanto ekavīsatiyā [V 1.0238] ṭhānesu kammaṭṭhānaṃ arahatte pakkhipitvā idaṃ gambhīratthaṃ satipaṭṭhānasuttaṃ abhāsi. Yathā hi puriso suvaṇṇacaṅkoṭakaṃ labhitvā tattha nānāpupphāni pakkhipeyya, suvaṇṇamañjūsaṃ [P 1.0228] vā pana labhitvā sattaratanāni pakkhipeyya, evaṃ bhagavā kururaṭṭhavāsiparisaṃ labhitvā gambhīradesanaṃ desesi. Tenevettha aññānipi gambhīratthāni dīghanikāye mahānidānaṃ mahāsatipaṭṭhānaṃ imasmiṃ majjhimanikāye sāropamaṃ rukkhūpamaṃ raṭṭhapālaṃ māgaṇḍiyaṃ āneñjasappāyanti aññānipi suttāni desesi.

106. “Bhikkhus, this is the one way.” Why did the Blessed One speak this discourse? Because the residents of the Kuru country were capable of receiving profound teachings. It is said that the bhikkhus, bhikkhunīs, male lay followers, and female lay followers of the Kuru country, due to the favorable climate and other conducive conditions of that region, always had healthy bodies and calm minds. Supported by their physical and mental well-being, their power of wisdom was aided, and they were capable of grasping profound teachings. Therefore, seeing their capability to receive profound instruction, the Blessed One, having established the meditation subjects in twenty-one sections culminating in arahantship, delivered this Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta of profound meaning. Just as a person who obtains a golden basket might fill it with various flowers, or one who obtains a golden chest might fill it with the seven treasures, so too the Blessed One, having obtained the assembly of the Kuru country, taught them this profound discourse. For this reason, he also taught other profound discourses there: in the Dīgha Nikāya, the Mahānidāna and Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Suttas; and in this Majjhima Nikāya, the Sāropama, Rukkhūpama, Raṭṭhapāla, Māgaṇḍiya, and Āneñjasappāya Suttas, as well as other suttas.

Apica tasmiṃ janapade catasso parisā pakatiyāva satipaṭṭhānabhāvanānuyogamanuyuttā viharanti, antamaso dāsakammakaraparijanāpi satipaṭṭhānappaṭisaṃyuttameva kathaṃ kathenti. Udakatitthasuttakantanaṭṭhānādīsupi niratthakakathā nāma na pavattati. Sace kāci itthī “amma tvaṃ kataraṃ satipaṭṭhānabhāvanaṃ manasikarosī”ti pucchitā “na kiñcī”ti vadati. Taṃ garahanti “dhiratthu tava jīvitaṃ, jīvamānāpi tvaṃ matasadisā”ti. Atha naṃ “mā dāni puna evamakāsī”ti ovaditvā aññataraṃ satipaṭṭhānaṃ uggaṇhāpenti. Yā pana “ahaṃ asukaṃ satipaṭṭhānaṃ manasikaromī”ti vadati. Tassā “sādhu sādhū”ti sādhukāraṃ datvā “tava jīvitaṃ sujīvitaṃ, tvaṃ nāma manussattaṃ pattā, tavatthāya sammāsambuddho uppanno”tiādīhi pasaṃsanti. Na kevalañcettha manussajātiyāyeva satipaṭṭhānamanasikārayuttā, te nissāya viharantā tiracchānagatāpi. Tatridaṃ vatthu – eko kira naṭako suvapotakaṃ gahetvā sikkhāpento vicarati. So bhikkhunupassayaṃ upanissāya vasitvā gamanakāle suvapotakaṃ pamussitvā gato. Taṃ sāmaṇeriyo gahetvā paṭijaggiṃsu. Buddharakkhitotissa nāmaṃ akaṃsu. Taṃ ekadivasaṃ purato nisinnaṃ disvā mahātherī āha – “buddharakkhitā”ti?

Moreover, in that country, the four assemblies naturally dwell engaged in the practice of developing the establishments of mindfulness. Even servants, laborers, and attendants converse only on topics related to the establishments of mindfulness. At places like water-fords and spinning-places, meaningless talk does not occur. If any woman is asked, “Mother, which development of the establishments of mindfulness do you apply your mind to?” and she replies, “None,” they rebuke her, saying, “Shame on your life! Though alive, you are like the dead.” Then they advise her, “Do not act like this again,” and teach her one of the establishments of mindfulness. But if she says, “I apply my mind to such-and-such an establishment of mindfulness,” they praise her, saying, “Good, good!” and applaud her, declaring, “Your life is well-lived! You have attained human existence, and for your sake, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One has arisen.” Not only human beings there are devoted to the application of mindfulness, but also the animals living in dependence on them. Here is an account: A certain entertainer, while training a young parrot, wandered about. He stayed near a nunnery and, when leaving, forgot the young parrot. The novice nuns took it in and cared for it, naming it Buddharakkhita. One day, seeing it seated in front of her, the elder nun asked, “Buddharakkhita?”

Kiṃ ayyeti.

“What is it, venerable lady?”

Atthi koci tava manasikāroti?

“Do you practice any mental application?”

Natthi ayyeti.

“No, venerable lady.”

Āvuso[V 1.0239], pabbajitānaṃ santike vasantena nāma vissaṭṭhaattabhāvena bhavituṃ na vaṭṭati, kocideva [P 1.0229] manasikāro icchitabbo, tvaṃ pana aññaṃ na sakkhissasi “aṭṭhi aṭṭhī”ti [M 1.0234] sajjhāyaṃ karohīti. So theriyā ovāde ṭhatvā “aṭṭhi aṭṭhī”ti sajjhāyanto carati.

“Friend, for one living near those who have gone forth, it is not proper to be of a negligent nature. Some mental application should be undertaken. But you will be unable to do anything else—recite ‘bone, bone.’” So, abiding by the elder nun’s advice, he went about reciting, “bone, bone.”

Taṃ ekadivasaṃ pātova toraṇagge nisīditvā bālātapaṃ tapamānaṃ eko sakuṇo nakhapañjarena aggahesi. So “kiri kirī”ti saddamakāsi. Sāmaṇeriyo sutvā “ayye buddharakkhito sakuṇena gahito, mocema na”nti leḍḍuādīni gahetvā anubandhitvā mocesuṃ. Taṃ ānetvā purato ṭhapitaṃ therī āha –

One day, early in the morning, as he was sitting at the top of the gateway basking in the mild sunlight, a bird seized him with its talons. He cried out, “Kiri, kirī!” Hearing this, the novice nuns said, “Venerable lady, Buddharakkhita has been caught by a bird! Let us free him.” Taking clods of earth and other things, they pursued it and freed him. They brought him back and placed him before the elder nun, who asked:

“Buddharakkhita, sakuṇena gahitakāle kiṃ cintesī”ti?

“Buddharakkhita, what were you thinking at the time you were seized by the bird?”

Na ayye aññaṃ cintesiṃ, “aṭṭhipuñjova aṭṭhipuñjaṃ gahetvā gacchati, katarasmimpi ṭhāne vippakirissatī”ti evaṃ ayye aṭṭhipuñjameva cintesinti.

“Venerable lady, I thought of nothing else. I only thought, ‘A heap of bones is carrying away a heap of bones. In what place will it be scattered?’ Thus, venerable lady, I thought only of the heap of bones.”

Sādhu sādhu, buddharakkhita, anāgate bhavakkhayassa te paccayo bhavissatīti. Evaṃ tattha tiracchānagatāpi satipaṭṭhānamanasikārayuttā, tasmā nesaṃ bhagavā satipaṭṭhānabuddhimeva janento idaṃ suttaṃ abhāsi.

“Good, good, Buddharakkhita. In the future, this will be a condition for the destruction of your existence.” Thus, even beings born in the animal realm there are devoted to the application of mindfulness. Therefore, generating in them the very understanding of the establishments of mindfulness, the Blessed One spoke this sutta.

Tattha ekāyanoti ekamaggo. Maggassa hi –

Therein, ‘ekāyana’ means ‘one path.’ For of the path:

“Maggo pantho patho pajjo, añjasaṃ vaṭumāyanaṃ;

Nāvā uttarasetū ca, kullo ca bhisisaṅkamo”ti. (cūḷani. 101) –

“Path, road, way, track, straight path, road, and way; boat and high bridge, raft and causeway.”

Bahūni nāmāni. Svāyaṃ idha ayananāmena vutto. Tasmā ekāyano ayaṃ, bhikkhave, maggoti ettha ekamaggo ayaṃ, bhikkhave, maggo, na dvedhāpathabhūtoti evamattho daṭṭhabbo. Atha vā ekena ayitabboti ekāyano. Ekenāti gaṇasaṅgaṇikaṃ pahāya vūpakaṭṭhena pavivittacittena. Ayitabboti paṭipajjitabbo. Ayanti vā etenāti ayano, saṃsārato nibbānaṃ gacchantīti attho[V 1.0240]. Ekassa ayano ekāyano, ekassāti seṭṭhassa. Sabbasattānaṃ seṭṭho ca bhagavā, tasmā bhagavatoti vuttaṃ hoti. Kiñcāpi hi tena aññepi ayanti, evaṃ santepi bhagavatova so ayano tena uppāditattā. Yathāha “so hi, brāhmaṇa, bhagavā anuppannassa maggassa uppādetā”tiādi (ma. ni. 3.79). Ayatīti vā ayano, gacchati pavattatīti attho. Ekasmiṃ ayanoti ekāyano, imasmiṃyeva dhammavinaye pavattati, na aññatrāti vuttaṃ hoti. Yathāha [P 1.0230] “imasmiṃ kho, subhadda, dhammavinaye ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo upalabbhatī”ti (dī. ni. 2.214). Desanābhedoyeva heso, attho paneko. Apica [M 1.0235] ekaṃ ayatīti ekāyano. Pubbabhāge nānāmukhabhāvanānayappavattopi aparabhāge ekaṃ nibbānameva gacchatīti vuttaṃ hoti. Yathāha brahmā sahampati –

Many are the names. Here, this is referred to by the name 'ayana' (path). Thus, concerning 'This is the one-way path, bhikkhus,' the meaning should be understood as 'This is the one path, bhikkhus, not a forked path.' Alternatively, 'to be traveled by one' (ekāyano) means by one who has abandoned association with crowds, with a secluded and withdrawn mind. 'To be traveled' means to be followed. Or, 'that by which one travels' (ayano) means that by which they go from saṃsāra to Nibbāna. 'The path of the one' (ekāyano) means the path of the supreme one. The Blessed One is the supreme among all beings, hence it is said 'of the Blessed One.' Although others may also travel by it, still, it is the Blessed One’s path because he originated it. As it is said: "For, brahmin, the Blessed One is the originator of the unarisen path," etc. Or, 'that which goes' (ayano) means that which proceeds or continues. 'Going in one' (ekāyano) means it continues only in this Dhamma and Discipline, not elsewhere. As it is said: "In this Dhamma and Discipline, Subhadda, the noble eightfold path is found." This is merely a difference in teaching, but the meaning is one. Furthermore, 'going to one' (ekāyano) means that though in the preliminary stage the development may proceed through various methods, in the final stage it goes only to the one Nibbāna. As Brahmā Sahampati said:

“Ekāyanaṃ jātikhayantadassī,

Maggaṃ pajānāti hitānukampī;

Etena maggena tariṃsu pubbe,

Tarissanti ye ca taranti ogha”nti. (saṃ. ni. 5.409);

"The one who sees the destruction of birth, compassionate for the welfare of others, knows the one-way path. By this path, they crossed over in the past, and will cross, and are crossing the flood."

Keci pana “na pāraṃ diguṇaṃ yantī”ti gāthānayena yasmā ekavāraṃ nibbānaṃ gacchati. Tasmā “ekāyano”ti vadanti, taṃ na yujjati. Imassa hi atthassa sakiṃ ayanoti iminā byañjanena bhavitabbaṃ. Yadi pana ekaṃ ayanamassa ekā gati pavattīti evamatthaṃ yojetvā vucceyya, byañjanaṃ yujjeyya, attho pana ubhayathāpi na yujjati. Kasmā? Idha pubbabhāgamaggassa adhippetattā. Kāyādicatuārammaṇappavatto hi pubbabhāgasatipaṭṭhānamaggo idha adhippeto, na lokuttaro. So ca anekavārampi ayati, anekañcassa ayanaṃ hoti.

However, some, following the verse, "They do not go to the far shore twice," say that because one goes to Nibbāna only once, it is therefore called the 'one-way path.' But this is not correct. For this meaning, the expression should be 'sakiṃ ayano' (going once). If, however, the meaning were construed as 'it has one going, one course, one proceeding,' the expression would be suitable, but the meaning would not be correct in either case. Why? Because here the preliminary path is intended. For here, the preliminary path of the establishments of mindfulness, which proceeds with the four objects beginning with the body, is intended, not the supramundane path. And that path is traveled many times, and its going occurs many times.

Pubbepi ca imasmiṃ pade mahātherānaṃ sākacchā ahosiyeva. Tipiṭakacūḷanāgatthero “pubbabhāgasatipaṭṭhānamaggo”ti āha. Ācariyo panassa tipiṭakacūḷasumatthero “missakamaggo”ti āha. Pubbabhāgo bhanteti. Missako āvusoti. Ācariye punappunaṃ bhaṇante appaṭibāhitvā tuṇhī ahosi. Pañhaṃ avinicchinitvāva uṭṭhahiṃsu. Athācariyatthero nhānakoṭṭhakaṃ gacchanto “mayā missakamaggo kathito, cūḷanāgo pubbabhāgoti ādāya voharati[V 1.0241], ko nu kho ettha nicchayo”ti suttantaṃ ādito paṭṭhāya parivattento “yo hi koci, bhikkhave, ime cattāro satipaṭṭhāne evaṃ bhāveyya satta vassānī”ti imasmiṃ ṭhāne sallakkhesi, lokuttaramaggo uppajjitvā satta vassāni tiṭṭhamāno nāma natthi, mayā vutto missakamaggo na labbhati, cūḷanāgena diṭṭho pubbabhāgamaggova labbhatīti ñatvā aṭṭhamiyaṃ dhammassavane saṅghuṭṭhe agamāsi.

In the past, there was a discussion among the great elders on this very point. The Elder Tipiṭaka Cūḷanāga said, "It is the preliminary path of the foundations of mindfulness." But his teacher, the Elder Tipiṭaka Cūḷasumana, said, "It is the mixed path." "The preliminary part, venerable sir?" "The mixed, friend." When the teacher repeatedly said this, Cūḷanāga, not contradicting him, remained silent. They rose without having resolved the question. Then, as the teacher, the elder, was going to the bathing chamber, he reflected, "I have said it is the mixed path, while Cūḷanāga holds that it is the preliminary part. What is the correct conclusion here?" Reviewing the discourse from the beginning, he noted the passage: "Bhikkhus, whoever should develop these four foundations of mindfulness in this way for seven years..." Realizing that there is no such thing as a supramundane path that arises and persists for seven years, he knew, "The mixed path I spoke of is not found; the preliminary path seen by Cūḷanāga is indeed found." On the eighth day, when the hearing of the Dhamma was announced, he went.

Porāṇakattherā [M 1.0236][P 1.0231] kira piyadhammassavanā honti. Saddaṃ sutvāva “ahaṃ paṭhamaṃ, ahaṃ paṭhama”nti ekappahāreneva osaranti. Tasmiñca divase cūḷanāgattherassa vāro. Tena dhammāsane nisīditvā vījaniṃ gahetvā pubbagāthāsu vuttāsu therassa āsanapiṭṭhiyaṃ ṭhitassa etadahosi “raho nisīditvā na vakkhāmī”ti. Porāṇakattherā hi anusūyakā honti, na attano rucimeva ucchubhāraṃ viya evaṃ ukkhipitvā vicaranti, kāraṇameva gaṇhanti, akāraṇaṃ vissajjenti. Tasmā thero “āvuso cūḷanāgā”ti āha. So ācariyassa viya saddoti dhammaṃ ṭhapetvā “kiṃ bhante”ti āha. Āvuso cūḷanāga mayā vutto missakamaggo na labbhati, tayā vutto pubbabhāgasatipaṭṭhānamaggova labbhatīti.

The ancient elders, it is said, were fond of hearing the Dhamma. As soon as they heard the sound, they would rush forward at once, saying, "I first, I first!" On that day, it was Elder Cūḷanāga’s turn. After he had sat on the Dhamma seat, taken the fan, and the introductory verses had been recited, it occurred to the Elder (his teacher), who was standing behind the seat, 'I will not speak in private.' For the ancient elders were without envy; they did not go about holding up their own preferences like a load of sugarcane, but accepted what was reasonable and rejected what was unreasonable. Therefore, the elder said, "Friend Cūḷanāga." Recognizing the voice as his teacher's, he set aside the Dhamma talk and said, "What is it, venerable sir?" "Friend Cūḷanāga, the mixed path I spoke of is not found; the preliminary path of the foundations of mindfulness that you spoke of is indeed found."

Thero cintesi “amhākaṃ ācariyo sabbapariyattiko tepiṭako sutabuddho, evarūpassapi nāma bhikkhuno ayaṃ pañho āluḷeti, anāgate mama bhātikā imaṃ pañhaṃ āluḷessantīti suttaṃ gahetvā imaṃ pañhaṃ niccalaṃ karissāmī”ti paṭisambhidāmaggato “ekāyanamaggo vuccati pubbabhāgasatipaṭṭhānamaggo –

The elder reflected, "Our teacher is a master of all the scriptures, an expert in the Tipiṭaka, one awakened through learning. Yet even for such a bhikkhu this question causes confusion. In the future, my brethren will be confused by this question. Therefore, I will take a discourse and make this question unshakable." From the Paṭisambhidāmagga, he cited: "The one-way path is said to be the preliminary path of the foundations of mindfulness—

“Maggānaṭṭhaṅgiko seṭṭho, saccānaṃ caturo padā;

Virāgo seṭṭho dhammānaṃ, dvipadānañca cakkhumā.

"Of paths, the eightfold is the best; of truths, the four statements; of dhammas, dispassion is the best; and of bipeds, the one with vision."

Eseva maggo natthañño, dassanassa visuddhiyā;

Etañhi tumhe paṭipajjatha, mārasenappamaddanaṃ;

Etañhi tumhe paṭipannā, dukkhassantaṃ karissathā”ti. (dha. pa. 273-275) –

"This is the only path, there is no other for the purification of vision. You should follow this, which confounds the army of Māra. Having followed this, you will make an end of suffering."

Suttaṃ [V 1.0242] āharitvā ṭhapesi.

Having brought forth the discourse, he established it.

Maggoti kenaṭṭhena maggo? Nibbānagamanaṭṭhena nibbānatthikehi magganiyaṭṭhena ca. Sattānaṃ visuddhiyāti rāgādīhi malehi abhijjhāvisamalobhādīhi ca upakkilesehi kiliṭṭhacittānaṃ sattānaṃ visuddhatthāya. Tathā hi imināva maggena ito satasahassakappādhikānaṃ catunnaṃ [P 1.0232] asaṅkhyeyyānaṃ upari ekasmiññeva kappe nibbatte taṇhaṅkaramedhaṅkarasaraṇaṅkaradīpaṅkaranāmake buddhe ādiṃ katvā sakyamunipariyosānā aneke sammāsambuddhā anekasatā paccekabuddhā gaṇanapathaṃ vītivattā ariyasāvakā cāti ime [M 1.0237] sattā sabbe cittamalaṃ pavāhetvā paramavisuddhiṃ pattā. Rūpamalavasena pana saṃkilesavodānapaññattiyeva natthi. Tathā hi –

In what sense is it a 'path' (magga)? It is a path in the sense that it goes to Nibbāna and in the sense that it should be sought by those who desire Nibbāna. 'For the purification of beings' means for the purification of beings whose minds are defiled by stains such as lust, and by corruptions such as covetousness and unrighteous greed. Indeed, by this very path, beginning with the Buddhas named Taṇhaṅkara, Medhaṅkara, Saraṇaṅkara, and Dīpaṅkara, who arose in a single aeon more than four incalculable and one hundred thousand aeons ago, up to the Sage of the Sakyans at the end—many Perfectly Enlightened Buddhas, many hundreds of Paccekabuddhas, and noble disciples beyond reckoning—all these beings, having washed away the defilements of the mind, attained supreme purity. In terms of the defilement of form, however, there is no designation of defilement and purification. For it is said:

Rūpena saṃkiliṭṭhena, saṃkilissanti māṇavā;

Rūpe suddhe visujjhanti, anakkhātaṃ mahesinā.

That beings are defiled by defiled form, or that they are purified by pure form—this was not declared by the Great Seer.

Cittena saṃkiliṭṭhena, saṃkilissanti māṇavā;

Citte suddhe visujjhanti, iti vuttaṃ mahesinā.

That beings are defiled by a defiled mind, and that they are purified by a pure mind—this was declared by the Great Seer.

Yathāha “cittasaṃkilesā, bhikkhave, sattā saṃkilissanti, cittavodānā visujjhantī”ti (saṃ. ni. 3.100). Tañca cittavodānaṃ iminā satipaṭṭhānamaggena hoti. Tenāha “sattānaṃ visuddhiyā”ti.

As it is said: "Monks, beings are defiled through the defilement of the mind; beings are purified through the cleansing of the mind" (SN 22.101). And that cleansing of the mind occurs through this path of the establishments of mindfulness. Therefore, He said, 'for the purification of beings.'

Sokaparidevānaṃ samatikkamāyāti sokassa ca paridevassa ca samatikkamāya, pahānāyāti attho. Ayañhi maggo bhāvito santatimahāmattādīnaṃ viya sokasamatikkamāya, paṭācārādīnaṃ viya ca paridevasamatikkamāya ca saṃvattati. Tenāha “sokaparidevānaṃ samatikkamāyā”ti. Kiñcāpi hi santatimahāmatto –

'For the overcoming of sorrow and lamentation' means for the overcoming, that is, for the abandonment, of sorrow and lamentation. For this path, when developed, leads to the overcoming of sorrow, as in the case of the great minister Santati and others, and to the overcoming of lamentation, as in the case of Paṭācārā and others. Therefore, He said, 'for the overcoming of sorrow and lamentation.' Although the great minister Santati—

“Yaṃ [V 1.0243] pubbe taṃ visodhehi, pacchā te māhu kiñcanaṃ;

Majjhe ce no gahessasi, upasanto carissasī”ti. (su. ni. 955);

“Purify that which is past; let there be nothing for you in the future. If you will not grasp at what is in the middle, you will fare on in peace.” (Snp 4.15)

Imaṃ gāthaṃ sutvā saha paṭisambhidāhi arahattaṃ patto.

—having heard this verse, attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges.

Paṭācārā –

And Paṭācārā—

“Na santi puttā tāṇāya, na pitā nāpi bandhavā;

Antakenādhipannassa, natthi ñātīsu tāṇatā”ti. (dha. pa. 288);

“Sons are no protection, nor father, nor relatives; for one overcome by the Ender, there is no protection among kinsmen.” (Dhp 288)

Imaṃ gāthaṃ sutvā sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhitā. Yasmā pana kāyavedanācittadhammesu kañci dhammaṃ anāmasitvā bhāvanā nāma natthi, tasmā tepi imināva maggena sokaparideve samatikkantāti veditabbā.

—having heard this verse, was established in the fruit of stream-entry. But since there is no such thing as development of meditation without attending to some phenomenon among body, feelings, mind, and mental objects, it should be understood that they too overcame sorrow and lamentation by this very path.

Dukkhadomanassānaṃ atthaṅgamāyāti kāyikadukkhassa [P 1.0233] ca cetasikadomanassassa cāti imesaṃ dvinnaṃ atthaṅgamāya, nirodhāyāti attho. Ayañhi maggo bhāvito tissattherādīnaṃ viya dukkhassa, sakkādīnaṃ viya ca domanassassa atthaṅgamāya saṃvattati.

'For the disappearance of pain and displeasure' means for the disappearance, that is, for the cessation, of these two: bodily pain and mental displeasure. For this path, when developed, leads to the disappearance of pain, as in the case of the Elder Tissa and others, and to the disappearance of displeasure, as in the case of Sakka and others.

Tatrāyaṃ [M 1.0238] atthadīpanā – sāvatthiyaṃ kira tisso nāma kuṭumbikaputto cattālīsa hiraññakoṭiyo pahāya pabbajitvā agāmake araññe viharati. Tassa kaniṭṭhabhātubhariyā “gacchatha naṃ jīvitā voropethā”ti pañcasate core pesesi. Te gantvā theraṃ parivāretvā nisīdiṃsu. Thero āha “kasmā āgatattha upāsakā”ti? Taṃ jīvitā voropessāmāti. Pāṭibhogaṃ me upāsakā gahetvā ajjekarattiṃ jīvitaṃ dethāti. Ko te, samaṇa, imasmiṃ ṭhāne pāṭibhogo bhavissatīti? Thero mahantaṃ pāsāṇaṃ gahetvā dve ūruṭṭhīni bhinditvā “vaṭṭati upāsakā pāṭibhogo”ti āha. Te apakkamitvā caṅkamanasīse aggiṃ katvā nipajjiṃsu. Therassa vedanaṃ vikkhambhetvā sīlaṃ paccavekkhato parisuddhaṃ sīlaṃ nissāya pītipāmojjaṃ uppajji[V 1.0244]. Tato anukkamena vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhento tiyāmarattiṃ samaṇadhammaṃ katvā aruṇuggamane arahattaṃ patto imaṃ udānaṃ udānesi –

Here is the explanation of the meaning: In Sāvatthī, it is said, a householder’s son named Tissa renounced forty crores of gold, went forth, and lived in a forest far from any village. His younger brother’s wife sent five hundred robbers, saying, "Go and deprive him of his life." They went, surrounded the elder, and sat down. The elder asked, "Why have you come, lay followers?" "To deprive you of your life," they replied. "Lay followers, take a pledge from me and grant me my life for just this one night." "What pledge can you give us in this place, recluse?" The elder took a large stone, broke both his thigh bones, and said, "Is this pledge sufficient, lay followers?" They withdrew, made a fire at the head of the walking path, and lay down. As the elder suppressed his pain and reflected on his virtue, rapture and joy arose in him on account of his pure virtue. Then, gradually developing insight, he practiced the duties of a recluse throughout the three watches of the night. At the break of dawn, he attained Arahantship and uttered this inspired utterance:

“Ubho pādāni bhinditvā, saññapessāmi vo ahaṃ;

Aṭṭiyāmi harāyāmi, sarāgamaraṇaṃ ahaṃ.

“Having broken both my legs, I will appease you; I am troubled and ashamed of a death with lust.

Evāhaṃ cintayitvāna, yathābhūtaṃ vipassisaṃ;

Sampatte aruṇuggamhi, arahattamapāpuṇi”nti.

Having reflected thus, I saw things as they really are; when the dawn broke, I attained Arahantship.”

Aparepi tiṃsa bhikkhū bhagavato santike kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā araññavihāre vassaṃ upagantvā “āvuso, tiyāmarattiṃ samaṇadhammova kātabbo, na aññamaññassa santikaṃ āgantabba”nti vatvā vihariṃsu. Tesaṃ samaṇadhammaṃ katvā paccūsasamaye pacalāyantānaṃ eko byaggho āgantvā ekekaṃ bhikkhuṃ gahetvā gacchati. Na koci “maṃ byaggho gaṇhī”ti vācampi nicchāresi. Evaṃ pañcasu dasasu bhikkhūsu khāditesu uposathadivase “itare, āvuso, kuhi”nti pucchitvā ñatvā ca “idāni gahitena, gahitomhīti vattabba”nti vatvā vihariṃsu.

Furthermore, thirty monks received a meditation subject from the Blessed One, went to a forest dwelling for the rains retreat, and lived there after agreeing, "Friends, for the three watches of the night, only the duties of a recluse should be performed; we should not visit one another." As they were practicing the duties of a recluse, a tiger came at dawn while they were dozing and carried them off one by one. Not one of them uttered even a word, such as, "A tiger has seized me!" In this way, after five or ten monks had been eaten, on the Uposatha day, they asked, "Friends, where are the others?" Upon learning what had happened, they resolved, "From now on, if one is seized, one must say, 'I have been seized!'" and they continued to dwell there.

Atha aññataraṃ daharabhikkhuṃ purimanayeneva byaggho gaṇhi. So “byaggho, bhante”ti āha. Bhikkhū kattaradaṇḍe ca ukkāyo ca gahetvā mocessāmāti anubandhiṃsu. Byaggho bhikkhūnaṃ agatiṃ chinnataṭaṭṭhānaṃ [P 1.0234] āruyha taṃ bhikkhuṃ pādaṅguṭṭhakato paṭṭhāya khādituṃ ārabhi. Itarepi “idāni[M 1.0239], sappurisa, amhehi kattabbaṃ natthi, bhikkhūnaṃ viseso nāma evarūpe ṭhāne paññāyatī”ti āhaṃsu. So byagghamukhe nipannova taṃ vedanaṃ vikkhambhetvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhento yāva gopphakā khāditasamaye sotāpanno hutvā, yāva jaṇṇukā khāditasamaye sakadāgāmī, yāva nābhiyā khāditasamaye anāgāmī hutvā, hadayarūpe akhāditeyeva saha paṭisambhidāhi arahattaṃ patvā imaṃ udānaṃ udānesi –

Then a certain young monk was seized by a tiger in the same manner as before. He cried out, "A tiger, venerable sirs!" The monks, taking bladed staffs and torches, pursued it, intending to free him. The tiger climbed onto a steep embankment, a place inaccessible to the monks, and began to devour the monk starting from his big toe. The other monks said, "Now, good man, there is nothing more we can do. The distinction of monks is indeed made known in such a situation." As he lay in the tiger's mouth, he suppressed that feeling, developed insight, and became a stream-enterer by the time the tiger had eaten up to his ankle. By the time it reached his knee, he became a once-returner. When it reached his navel, he became a non-returner. Before his heart-basis was eaten, he attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges and uttered this inspired utterance:

“Sīlavā [V 1.0245] vatasampanno, paññavā susamāhito;

Muhuttaṃ pamādamanvāya, byagghenoruddhamānaso.

“Virtuous, accomplished in observances, wise, and well-composed; yet through a moment of heedlessness, my mind was seized by a tiger.

Pañjarasmiṃ gahetvāna, silāya uparīkato;

Kāmaṃ khādatu maṃ byaggho, bhakkho kāyo amittānaṃ;

Paṭiladdhe kammaṭṭhāne, maraṇaṃ hehiti bhaddaka”nti.

Caught in its clutches and placed upon a stone, let the tiger eat me as it wishes. This body is food for enemies; having regained the meditation subject, death will be auspicious indeed.”

Aparopi pītamallatthero nāma gihikāle tīsu rajjesu paṭākaṃ gahetvā tambapaṇṇidīpaṃ āgamma rājānaṃ disvā raññā katānuggaho ekadivasaṃ kilañjakāpaṇasāladvārena gacchanto “rūpaṃ, bhikkhave, na tumhākaṃ, taṃ pajahatha, taṃ vo pahīnaṃ dīgharattaṃ hitāya sukhāya bhavissatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 3.33-34) natumhākavaggaṃ sutvā cintesi “neva kira rūpaṃ attano, na vedanā”ti. So taṃyeva aṅkusaṃ katvā nikkhamitvā mahāvihāraṃ gantvā pabbajjaṃ yācitvā pabbajito upasampanno dvemātikā paguṇaṃ katvā tiṃsa bhikkhū gahetvā gabalavāliyaaṅgaṇaṃ gantvā samaṇadhammamakāsi. Pādesu avahantesu jaṇṇukehi caṅkamati. Tamenaṃ rattiṃ eko migaluddako migoti maññamāno sattiyā pahari. Satti vinivijjhitvā gatā. So taṃ sattiṃ harāpetvā pahāramukhāni tiṇavaṭṭiyā pūrāpetvā pāsāṇapiṭṭhiyaṃ attānaṃ nisīdāpetvā okāsaṃ kāretvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā saha paṭisambhidāhi arahattaṃ patvā ukkāsitasaddena āgatānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ byākaritvā imaṃ udānaṃ udānesi –

Another elder named Pītamalla, in his householder days, was the champion in three kingdoms. Coming to the island of Tambapaṇṇi and seeing the king, he received the king's favor. One day, while passing by the door of a mat shop, he heard the section on 'Not Yours': 'Bhikkhus, form is not yours; abandon it. That abandonment will be for your long-term welfare and happiness.' Reflecting, he thought, 'Indeed, neither form nor feeling belongs to oneself.' Taking that as a goad, he left home, went to the Great Monastery, requested ordination, and was ordained. Having mastered the two matrices, he took thirty bhikkhus and went to the Gabalavāli courtyard, where he practiced the recluse's duty. When his feet were worn away, he continued his walking meditation on his knees. One night, a deer hunter, mistaking him for a deer, struck him with a spear. The spear passed right through him. The elder had the spear removed, plugged the wound openings with wads of grass, and seated himself on a stone slab. Having made an opportunity, he developed insight and, together with the analytical knowledges, attained Arahantship. When bhikkhus arrived at the sound of his throat-clearing, he declared his attainment and uttered this inspired utterance:

“Bhāsitaṃ [P 1.0235] buddhaseṭṭhassa, sabbalokaggavādino;

Na tumhākamidaṃ rūpaṃ, taṃ jaheyyātha bhikkhavo.

“This was spoken by the Buddha, the best of beings, the foremost speaker in all the world: ‘This form is not yours, bhikkhus; you should abandon it.’

Aniccā [M 1.0240] vata saṅkhārā, uppādavayadhammino;

Uppajjitvā nirujjhanti, tesaṃ vūpasamo sukho”ti.

Impermanent, alas, are conditioned formations, subject to arising and passing away. Having arisen, they cease; their stilling is bliss.”

Atha naṃ bhikkhū āhaṃsu “sace, bhante, sammāsambuddho arogo abhavissā, addhā te muddhamatthake [V 1.0246] hatthaṃ pasāretvā sīsaṃ parāmaseyyā”ti. Ettāvatā ayaṃ maggo tissattherādīnaṃ viya dukkhassa atthaṅgamāya saṃvattati.

Then the bhikkhus said to him, 'Venerable sir, if the Perfectly Enlightened One were still alive and well, surely he would have stretched out his hand and stroked your head.' Thus, this path leads to the cessation of suffering, just as it did for the Elder Tissa and others.

Sakko pana devānamindo attano pañcavidhaṃ pubbanimittaṃ disvā maraṇabhayasantajjito domanassajāto bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamitvā pañhaṃ pucchi. So upekkhāpañhavissajjanāvasāne asītisahassāhi devatāhi saddhiṃ sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhāsi. Sā cassa upapatti puna pākatikāva ahosi.

Sakka, the lord of the gods, seeing his own fivefold portents and terrified by the fear of death, became distressed in mind. He approached the Blessed One and asked a question. At the conclusion of the answer to the question concerning equanimity, along with eighty thousand deities, he was established in the fruit of stream-entry. And his existence was restored to its normal state.

Subrahmāpi devaputto accharāsahassaparivāro saggasampattiṃ anubhoti, tattha pañcasatā accharāyo rukkhato pupphāni ocinantiyo cavitvā niraye upapannā. So “kiṃ imā cirāyantī”ti upadhārento tāsaṃ niraye nibbattabhāvaṃ disvā “kittakaṃ nu kho mama āyū”ti upaparikkhanto attanopi āyuparikkhayaṃ viditvā tattheva niraye nibbattanabhāvaṃ disvā bhīto ativiya domanassajāto hutvā “imaṃ me domanassaṃ satthā vinayissati na añño”ti avasesā pañcasatā accharāyo gahetvā bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamitvā pañhaṃ pucchi –

The devaputta Subrahmā, surrounded by a thousand celestial nymphs, was enjoying heavenly prosperity. There, five hundred nymphs, while picking flowers from trees, passed away and were reborn in hell. Noticing, 'Why are they delayed?' he investigated and saw that they had been reborn in hell. Reflecting, 'How much longer is my own lifespan?' he perceived the exhaustion of his own life and saw that he too would be reborn in that same hell. Terrified and exceedingly distressed, he thought, 'The Teacher will dispel this sorrow of mine, no one else.' Taking the remaining five hundred nymphs, he approached the Blessed One and asked a question:

“Niccaṃ utrastamidaṃ cittaṃ, niccaṃ ubbiggidaṃ mano;

Anuppannesu kicchesu, atho uppatitesu ca;

Sace atthi anutrastaṃ, taṃ me akkhāhi pucchito”ti. (saṃ. ni. 1.98);

“This heart is ever terrified, this mind is ever agitated, concerning troubles that have not yet arisen and also those that have. If there is a state free from terror, I ask you to explain it to me.”

Tato naṃ bhagavā āha –

Then the Blessed One said to him:

“Nāññatra bojjhā tapasā, nāññatrindriyasaṃvarā;

Nāññatra sabbanissaggā, sotthiṃ passāmi pāṇina”nti. (saṃ. ni. 1.98);

“Not apart from enlightenment and austerity, not apart from restraint of the sense faculties, not apart from the relinquishing of all, do I see safety for living beings.”

So [P 1.0236] desanāpariyosāne pañcahi accharāsatehi saddhiṃ sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhāya taṃ sampattiṃ [V 1.0247] thāvaraṃ katvā devalokameva agamāsīti[M 1.0241]. Evamayaṃ maggo bhāvito sakkādīnaṃ viya domanassassa atthaṅgamāya saṃvattatīti veditabbo.

At the conclusion of the teaching, he, along with the five hundred nymphs, was established in the fruit of stream-entry. Having made that attainment stable, he went to the devaloka. Thus, it should be understood that this path, when developed, leads to the subsiding of sorrow, just as it did for Sakka and others.

Ñāyassa adhigamāyāti ñāyo vuccati ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo, tassa adhigamāya, pattiyāti vuttaṃ hoti. Ayañhi pubbabhāge lokiyo satipaṭṭhānamaggo bhāvito lokuttarassa maggassa adhigamāya saṃvattati. Tenāha “ñāyassa adhigamāyā”ti. Nibbānassa sacchikiriyāyāti taṇhāvānavirahitattā nibbānanti laddhanāmassa amatassa sacchikiriyāya, attapaccakkhatāyāti vuttaṃ hoti. Ayañhi maggo bhāvito anupubbena nibbānasacchikiriyaṃ sādheti. Tenāha “nibbānassa sacchikiriyāyā”ti.

'For the attainment of the right method'—the right method is the Noble Eightfold Path. 'For its attainment' means for its achievement. For this mundane path of the foundations of mindfulness, when developed in its preliminary stage, conduces to the attainment of the supramundane path. Hence it is said, 'for the attainment of the right method.' 'For the realization of Nibbāna' means for the realization, the direct experience, of the Deathless, which is named Nibbāna because it is devoid of the 'stitching' of craving. For this path, when developed, gradually accomplishes the realization of Nibbāna. Hence it is said, 'for the realization of Nibbāna.'

Tattha kiñcāpi “sattānaṃ visuddhiyā”ti vutte sokasamatikkamādīni atthato siddhāneva honti, ṭhapetvā pana sāsanayuttikovide aññesaṃ na pākaṭāni, na ca bhagavā paṭhamaṃ sāsanayuttikovidaṃ janaṃ katvā pacchā dhammaṃ deseti. Tena teneva pana suttena taṃ taṃ atthaṃ ñāpeti. Tasmā idha yaṃ yaṃ atthaṃ ekāyanamaggo sādheti, taṃ taṃ pākaṭaṃ katvā dassento “sokaparidevānaṃ samatikkamāyā”tiādimāha. Yasmā vā yā sattānaṃ visuddhi ekāyanamaggena saṃvattati, sā sokaparidevānaṃ samatikkamena hoti, sokaparidevānaṃ samatikkamo dukkhadomanassānaṃ atthaṅgamena, dukkhadomanassānaṃ atthaṅgamo ñāyassādhigamena, ñāyassādhigamo nibbānassa sacchikiriyāya. Tasmā imampi kamaṃ dassento “sattānaṃ visuddhiyā”ti vatvā “sokaparidevānaṃ samatikkamāyā”tiādimāha.

Here, although when it is said 'for the purification of beings,' the overcoming of sorrow and the like are indeed established in meaning, they are not evident to others apart from those skilled in the proper application of the Teaching. The Blessed One does not first make people skilled in the proper application of the Teaching and afterwards teach the Dhamma. Rather, by that very discourse, he makes each respective meaning known. Therefore, here, making evident and showing each purpose that the direct path accomplishes, he says, 'for the overcoming of sorrow and lamentation,' and so on. Or, because the purification of beings that comes about through the direct path is through the overcoming of sorrow and lamentation; the overcoming of sorrow and lamentation is through the disappearance of pain and grief; the disappearance of pain and grief is through the attainment of the right method; and the attainment of the right method is for the realization of Nibbāna. Therefore, showing this sequence as well, after saying 'for the purification of beings,' he says, 'for the overcoming of sorrow and lamentation,' and so on.

Apica vaṇṇabhaṇanametaṃ ekāyanamaggassa. Yatheva hi bhagavā “dhammaṃ vo, bhikkhave, desessāmi ādikalyāṇaṃ majjhekalyāṇaṃ pariyosānakalyāṇaṃ sātthaṃ sabyañjanaṃ kevalaparipuṇṇaṃ parisuddhaṃ brahmacariyaṃ pakāsessāmi, yadidaṃ chachakkānī”ti (ma. ni. 3.420) chachakkadesanāya aṭṭhahi padehi vaṇṇaṃ abhāsi, yathā ca ariyavaṃsadesanāya “cattārome, bhikkhave, ariyavaṃsā aggaññā rattaññā vaṃsaññā porāṇā asaṃkiṇṇā asaṃkiṇṇapubbā na [P 1.0237] saṃkīyanti, na saṃkīyissanti, appaṭikuṭṭhā samaṇehi brāhmaṇehi viññūhī”ti [M 1.0242] (a. ni. 4.28) navahi [V 1.0248] padehi vaṇṇaṃ abhāsi, evaṃ imassapi ekāyanamaggassa sattānaṃ visuddhiyātiādīhi sattahi padehi vaṇṇaṃ abhāsi.

Moreover, this is a praise of the direct path. Just as the Blessed One praised the teaching of the six sixes with eight phrases—'Bhikkhus, I will teach you the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with its meaning and its phrasing; I will proclaim the holy life that is utterly complete and pure, namely, the six sixes'—and as he praised the teaching of the noble lineages with nine phrases—'Bhikkhus, these four noble lineages are foremost, of long standing, traditional, ancient, unadulterated, not adulterated in the past, not being adulterated, and not to be adulterated in the future, unrejected by wise ascetics and brahmins'—so too, he extolled this direct path with seven phrases, beginning with 'for the purification of beings.'

Kasmā iti ce? Tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ ussāhajananatthaṃ. Vaṇṇabhāsanañhi sutvā te bhikkhū “ayaṃ kira maggo hadayasantāpabhūtaṃ sokaṃ, vācāvippalāpabhūtaṃ paridevaṃ, kāyikaasātabhūtaṃ dukkhaṃ, cetasikaasātabhūtaṃ domanassanti cattāro upaddave hanati, visuddhiṃ ñāyaṃ nibbānanti tayo visese āvahatī”ti ussāhajātā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ uggahetabbaṃ pariyāpuṇitabbaṃ dhāretabbaṃ vācetabbaṃ, imañca maggaṃ bhāvetabbaṃ maññissanti. Iti tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ ussāhajananatthaṃ vaṇṇaṃ abhāsi, kambalavāṇijādayo kambalādīnaṃ vaṇṇaṃ viya.

Why is that? To inspire enthusiasm in those bhikkhus. For upon hearing this praise, those bhikkhus will think, 'This path, it seems, destroys the four calamities—sorrow, which is a burning of the heart; lamentation, which is verbal wailing; pain, which is bodily displeasure; and grief, which is mental displeasure—and brings the three special attainments: purity, the right method, and Nibbāna.' Inspired, they will think, 'This Dhamma teaching should be learned, mastered, remembered, and recited, and this path should be developed.' Thus, the praise was spoken to inspire enthusiasm in those bhikkhus, just as blanket merchants praise their blankets and other goods.

Yathā hi satasahassagghanikapaṇḍukambalavāṇijena kambalaṃ gaṇhathāti ugghositepi asukakambaloti na tāva manussā jānanti. Kesakambalavālakambalādayopi hi duggandhā kharasamphassā kambalātveva vuccanti. Yadā pana tena gandhārako rattakambalo sukhumo ujjalo sukhasamphassoti ugghositaṃ hoti, tadā ye pahonti, te gaṇhanti. Ye na pahonti, tepi dassanakāmā honti, evamevaṃ “ekāyano ayaṃ, bhikkhave, maggo”ti vuttepi asukamaggoti na tāva pākaṭo hoti. Nānappakārakā hi aniyyānamaggāpi maggātveva vuccanti. “Sattānaṃ visuddhiyā”tiādimhi pana vutte “ayaṃ kira maggo cattāro upaddave hanati, tayo visese āvahatī”ti ussāhajātā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ uggahetabbaṃ pariyāpuṇitabbaṃ dhāretabbaṃ vācetabbaṃ, imañca maggaṃ bhāvetabbaṃ maññissantīti vaṇṇaṃ bhāsanto “sattānaṃ visuddhiyā”tiādimāha. Yathā ca satasahassagghanikapaṇḍukambalavāṇijopamā, evaṃ rattajambunadasuvaṇṇaudakappasādakamaṇiratanasuvisuddhamuttāratanadhotapavāḷādivāṇijūpamādayopettha āharitabbā.

Just as when a merchant selling a valuable blanket worth a hundred thousand announces, 'Buy a blanket!' people do not yet know which blanket he means. For blankets made of hair, tail-hair, and so forth, though foul-smelling and rough to the touch, are still called blankets. But when he announces, 'A red blanket from Gandhāra, fine, bright, and pleasant to the touch,' then those who can afford it buy it. Even those who cannot afford it still desire to see it. In the same way, when it is said, 'Bhikkhus, this is the direct path,' the specific path is not yet clear. For various kinds of paths that do not lead to liberation are also called paths. But when it is said, 'For the purification of beings,' and so on, then people become inspired, thinking, 'This path, it is said, destroys four calamities and brings three special attainments.' They resolve to learn this teaching, master it, memorize it, recite it, and develop this path. Thus, extolling its virtues, he says, 'For the purification of beings,' and so on. And just as there is the simile of the merchant selling the valuable blanket worth a hundred thousand, so too should the similes of merchants selling red Jambu River gold, water-purifying jewel-gems, perfectly pure pearl-gems, washed coral, and other such goods be brought in here.

Yadidanti nipāto, ye imeti ayamassa attho. Cattāroti gaṇanaparicchedo, tena na tato heṭṭhā na uddhanti satipaṭṭhānaparicchedaṃ dīpeti. Satipaṭṭhānāti tayo satipaṭṭhānā satigocaropi, tidhā paṭipannesu sāvakesu [P 1.0238] satthuno paṭighānunayavītivattatāpi, satipi. “Catunnaṃ[M 1.0243], bhikkhave, satipaṭṭhānānaṃ samudayañca atthaṅgamañca desessāmi, taṃ suṇātha…pe…. Ko ca, bhikkhave, kāyassa samudayo? Āhārasamudayā kāyasamudayo”tiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 3.408) hi [V 1.0249] satigocaro satipaṭṭhānanti vuccati. Tathā “kāyo paṭṭhānaṃ, no sati. Sati paṭṭhānañceva sati cā”tiādīsupi (paṭi. ma. 3.35). Tassattho – patiṭṭhāti asminti paṭṭhānaṃ. Kā patiṭṭhāti? Sati. Satiyā paṭṭhānaṃ satipaṭṭhānaṃ. Padhānaṭṭhānanti vā paṭṭhānaṃ. Satiyā paṭṭhānaṃ satipaṭṭhānaṃ, hatthiṭṭhānaassaṭṭhānādīni viya. “Tayo satipaṭṭhānā, yadariyo sevati, yadariyo sevamāno satthā gaṇamanusāsitumarahatī”ti (ma. ni. 3.311) etthāpi tidhā paṭipannesu sāvakesu satthuno paṭighānunayavītivattatā “satipaṭṭhāna”nti vuttā. Tassattho – paṭṭhapetabbato paṭṭhānaṃ, pavattayitabbatoti attho. Kena paṭṭhapetabbatoti? Satiyā. Satiyā paṭṭhānaṃ satipaṭṭhānanti. “Cattāro satipaṭṭhānā bhāvitā bahulīkatā satta bojjhaṅge paripūrentī”tiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 5.989) pana satiyeva “satipaṭṭhāna”nti vuccati. Tassattho – patiṭṭhātīti paṭṭhānaṃ, upaṭṭhāti okkantitvā pakkhanditvā pavattatīti attho. Satiyeva paṭṭhānaṃ satipaṭṭhānaṃ. Atha vā saraṇaṭṭhena sati, upaṭṭhānaṭṭhena paṭṭhānaṃ. Iti sati ca sā paṭṭhānañcātipi satipaṭṭhānaṃ. Idamidha adhippetaṃ.

The word 'yadidaṃ' is a particle, and its meaning is 'which are these'. 'Cattāro' is a numerical definition, indicating that there are neither fewer nor more than four, thus defining the scope of the foundations of mindfulness. The term 'satipaṭṭhāna' refers to three things: the domain of mindfulness (satigocara), the Teacher's transcendence of aversion and affection towards disciples who practice in three ways, and mindfulness itself (sati). For in passages such as, "Bhikkhus, I will teach the arising and passing away of the four foundations of mindfulness. Listen... And what, bhikkhus, is the arising of the body? With the arising of nutriment there is the arising of the body," the domain of mindfulness is called 'satipaṭṭhāna'. Likewise in passages such as, "The body is the foundation, not mindfulness. Mindfulness is both the foundation and mindfulness itself." Its meaning is: 'paṭṭhāna' is that in which it is established. What is established? Mindfulness. The establishment of mindfulness is 'satipaṭṭhāna'. Or 'paṭṭhāna' means a principal station. The principal station of mindfulness is 'satipaṭṭhāna', just like an elephant’s station or a horse’s station. In the passage, "There are three foundations of mindfulness that the noble one cultivates, and by cultivating which the Teacher is worthy to instruct the order," here too, the Teacher’s transcendence of aversion and affection towards disciples who practice in three ways is called 'satipaṭṭhāna'. Its meaning is: 'paṭṭhāna' because it is to be established, meaning it is to be set in motion. By what is it to be established? By mindfulness. The establishing by mindfulness is 'satipaṭṭhāna'. But in passages such as, "When the four foundations of mindfulness are developed and cultivated, they fulfill the seven factors of enlightenment," mindfulness itself is called 'satipaṭṭhāna'. Its meaning is: 'paṭṭhāna' because it stands firm, meaning it is present, proceeding by entering and plunging into the object. Mindfulness itself is the foundation, 'satipaṭṭhāna'. Alternatively, 'sati' is in the sense of remembering, and 'paṭṭhāna' is in the sense of presence. Thus, 'satipaṭṭhāna' is both that which is mindfulness and that which is presence. This is what is intended here.

Yadi evaṃ, kasmā “satipaṭṭhānā”ti bahuvacanaṃ? Satibahuttā. Ārammaṇabhedena hi bahukā etā satiyo. Atha maggoti kasmā ekavacanaṃ? Maggaṭṭhena ekattā. Catassopi hi etā satiyo maggaṭṭhena ekattaṃ gacchanti. Vuttañhetaṃ “maggoti kenaṭṭhena maggo? Nibbānagamanaṭṭhena, nibbānatthikehi magganīyaṭṭhena cā”ti. Catassopi cetā aparabhāge kāyādīsu ārammaṇesu kiccaṃ sādhayamānā nibbānaṃ gacchanti. Ādito paṭṭhāya ca nibbānatthikehi maggīyanti, tasmā catassopi eko maggoti vuccanti[P 1.0239]. Evañca sati vacanānusandhinā sānusandhikāva desanā hoti, “mārasenappamaddanaṃ vo, bhikkhave, maggaṃ desessāmi, taṃ suṇātha…pe… katamo ca, bhikkhave, mārasenappamaddano maggo? Yadidaṃ sattabojjhaṅgā”tiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 5.224) viya hi yathā mārasenappamaddanoti ca sattabojjhaṅgāti ca atthato [M 1.0244] ekaṃ, byañjanamevettha nānaṃ. Evaṃ ekāyanamaggoti ca cattāro satipaṭṭhānāti ca atthato ekaṃ, byañjanamevettha nānaṃ. Tasmā maggaṭṭhena ekattā ekavacanaṃ, ārammaṇabhedena satibahuttā bahuvacanaṃ veditabbaṃ.

If so, why is 'foundations of mindfulness' in the plural? Because of the multiplicity of mindfulness. Indeed, due to the diversity of objects, these instances of mindfulness are many. But why is 'path' in the singular? Because of its unity in the sense of path. For these four kinds of mindfulness become one in the sense of path. As it has been said: "In what sense is it a path? In the sense of going to Nibbāna, and in the sense of being sought by those who desire Nibbāna." These four, subsequently accomplishing their task regarding objects such as the body and so forth, go to Nibbāna. And from the beginning they are sought by those who desire Nibbāna. Therefore, all four are called one path. And so, through the connection of the wording, the teaching is indeed connected, just as in passages like, "Bhikkhus, I will teach you the path for crushing Māra’s army; listen… And what, bhikkhus, is the path for crushing Māra’s army? It is these seven factors of enlightenment," where 'crushing Māra’s army' and 'seven factors of enlightenment' are one in meaning, only the phrasing here is different. So too, 'the direct path' and 'the four foundations of mindfulness' are one in meaning, only the phrasing here is different. Therefore, it should be understood that the singular is used because of the unity in the sense of path, and the plural is used because of the multiplicity of mindfulness due to the diversity of objects.

Kasmā pana bhagavatā cattārova satipaṭṭhānā vuttā anūnā anadhikāti? Veneyyahitattā[V 1.0250]. Taṇhācaritadiṭṭhicaritasamathayānikavipassanāyānikesu hi mandatikkhavasena dvedhā dvedhā pavattesu veneyyesu mandassa taṇhācaritassa oḷārikaṃ kāyānupassanāsatipaṭṭhānaṃ visuddhimaggo, tikkhassa sukhumaṃ vedanānupassanaṃ satipaṭṭhānaṃ. Diṭṭhicaritassāpi mandassa nātippabhedagataṃ cittānupassanāsatipaṭṭhānaṃ visuddhimaggo, tikkhassa atippabhedagataṃ dhammānupassanāsatipaṭṭhānaṃ. Samathayānikassa ca mandassa akicchena adhigantabbanimittaṃ paṭhamaṃ satipaṭṭhānaṃ visuddhimaggo, tikkhassa oḷārikārammaṇe asaṇṭhahanato dutiyaṃ. Vipassanāyānikassapi mandassa nātippabhedagatārammaṇaṃ tatiyaṃ, tikkhassa atippabhedagatārammaṇaṃ catutthaṃ. Iti cattārova vuttā anūnā anadhikāti.

Why then did the Blessed One teach exactly four foundations of mindfulness, neither fewer nor more? For the welfare of the trainees. For among trainees—those of craving temperament and speculative temperament, and those who have serenity as their vehicle and insight as their vehicle, each proceeding in two ways as dull or sharp—the path of purification for the dull one of craving temperament is the coarse foundation of mindfulness, the contemplation of the body, while for the sharp one it is the subtle foundation of mindfulness, the contemplation of feelings. For the dull one of speculative temperament, the path of purification is the foundation of mindfulness, the contemplation of the mind, which is not overly differentiated, while for the sharp one it is the foundation of mindfulness, the contemplation of phenomena, which is highly differentiated. For the dull one who has serenity as their vehicle, the first foundation of mindfulness is the path of purification, as its sign is to be attained without difficulty; for the sharp one, the second is, due to their inability to become established in a coarse object. For the dull one who has insight as their vehicle, the third is the path of purification, as its object is not overly differentiated, while for the sharp one, the fourth is, as its object is highly differentiated. Thus, exactly four were taught—neither fewer nor more.

Subhasukhaniccaattabhāvavipallāsapahānatthaṃ vā. Kāyo hi asubho, tattha ca subhavipallāsavipallatthā sattā, tesaṃ tattha asubhabhāvadassanena tassa vipallāsassa pahānatthaṃ paṭhamaṃ satipaṭṭhānaṃ vuttaṃ. Sukhaṃ niccaṃ attāti gahitesupi ca vedanādīsu vedanā dukkhā, cittaṃ aniccaṃ, dhammā anattā, tesu ca sukhaniccaattavipallāsavipallatthā sattā, tesaṃ tattha dukkhādibhāvadassanena tesaṃ vipallāsānaṃ pahānatthaṃ sesāni tīṇi vuttānīti evaṃ subhasukhaniccaattabhāvavipallāsapahānatthaṃ vā cattārova vuttā anūnā anadhikāti veditabbā.

Or, for the purpose of abandoning the perversions regarding the beautiful, the pleasant, the permanent, and the self. The body is indeed impure, yet beings are perverted by the perversion of beauty. To abandon this perversion by seeing its impure nature, the first foundation of mindfulness was taught. And although feelings and so on are grasped as pleasant, permanent, and self, feelings are actually suffering, the mind is impermanent, and phenomena are not-self. Yet beings are perverted by the perversions of pleasure, permanence, and self. To abandon these perversions by seeing their nature as suffering, impermanence, and not-self, the remaining three were taught. Thus, it should be understood that the four were taught—neither fewer nor more—for the purpose of abandoning the perversions regarding the beautiful, the pleasant, the permanent, and the self.

Na kevalañca vipallāsapahānatthameva, atha kho caturoghayogāsavaganthaupādānaagatipahānatthampi [P 1.0240] catubbidhāhārapariññatthañca cattārova vuttāti veditabbā. Ayaṃ tāva pakaraṇanayo.

And it should be understood that exactly four were taught not only for the purpose of abandoning the perversions, but also for abandoning the four floods, yokes, cankers, bodily ties, forms of clinging, and wrong courses, and for the full understanding of the four kinds of nutriment. This, for now, is the textual method.

Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana saraṇavasena ceva ekattasamosaraṇavasena ca ekameva satipaṭṭhānaṃ ārammaṇavasena cattāroti etadeva vuttaṃ. Yathā hi catudvāre nagare pācīnato āgacchantā pācīnadisāya uṭṭhānakaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ gahetvā pācīnadvārena nagarameva pavisanti, dakkhiṇato pacchimato uttarato āgacchantā uttaradisāya uṭṭhānakaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ gahetvā uttaradvārena nagarameva pavisanti, evaṃsampadamidaṃ veditabbaṃ. Nagaraṃ viya hi nibbānamahānagaraṃ[M 1.0245]. Dvāraṃ viya aṭṭhaṅgiko lokuttaramaggo. Pācīnadisādayo viya kāyādayo.

In the commentary, however, it is stated that, in terms of its destination and in terms of its convergence into unity, there is only one foundation of mindfulness, but in terms of its objects, there are four. Just as, in a city with four gates, those coming from the east, taking goods originating in the eastern region, enter the city through the eastern gate, and those coming from the south, west, or north, taking goods originating in the northern region, enter the city through the northern gate—this should be understood in the same way. For the city is like the great city of Nibbāna. The gate is like the supramundane Noble Eightfold Path. The directions, such as the east, are like the body and so on.

Yathā [V 1.0251] pācīnato āgacchantā pācīnadisāya uṭṭhānakaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ gahetvā pācīnadvārena nagarameva pavisanti, evaṃ kāyānupassanāmukhena āgacchantā cuddasavidhena kāyānupassanaṃ bhāvetvā kāyānupassanābhāvanānubhāvanibbattena ariyamaggena ekaṃ nibbānameva osaranti.

Just as those coming from the east, taking merchandise originating in the eastern region, enter the city through the eastern gate, so too, those approaching through the gateway of contemplation of the body, having cultivated the fourteen kinds of contemplation of the body, converge upon the one Nibbāna through the noble path produced by the power of cultivating the contemplation of the body.

Yathā dakkhiṇato āgacchantā dakkhiṇadisāya uṭṭhānakaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ gahetvā dakkhiṇadvārena nagarameva pavisanti, evaṃ vedanānupassanāmukhena āgacchantā navavidhena vedanānupassanaṃ bhāvetvā vedanānupassanābhāvanānubhāvanibbattena ariyamaggena ekaṃ nibbānameva osaranti.

Just as those coming from the south, taking merchandise originating in the southern region, enter the city through the southern gate, so too, those approaching through the gateway of contemplation of feelings, having cultivated the nine kinds of contemplation of feelings, converge upon the one Nibbāna through the noble path produced by the power of cultivating the contemplation of feelings.

Yathā pacchimato āgacchantā pacchimadisāya uṭṭhānakaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ gahetvā pacchimadvārena nagarameva pavisanti, evaṃ cittānupassanāmukhena āgacchantā soḷasavidhena cittānupassanaṃ bhāvetvā cittānupassanābhāvanānubhāvanibbattena ariyamaggena ekaṃ nibbānameva osaranti.

Just as those coming from the west, taking merchandise originating in the western region, enter the city through the western gate, so too, those approaching through the gateway of contemplation of mind, having cultivated the sixteen kinds of contemplation of mind, converge upon the one Nibbāna through the noble path produced by the power of cultivating the contemplation of mind.

Yathā uttarato āgacchantā uttaradisāya uṭṭhānakaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ gahetvā uttaradvārena nagarameva pavisanti, evaṃ dhammānupassanāmukhena āgacchantā pañcavidhena dhammānupassanaṃ bhāvetvā dhammānupassanābhāvanānubhāvanibbattena ariyamaggena ekaṃ nibbānameva osaranti.

Just as those coming from the north, taking merchandise originating in the northern region, enter the city through the northern gate, so too, those approaching through the gateway of contemplation of phenomena, having cultivated the five kinds of contemplation of phenomena, converge upon the one Nibbāna through the noble path produced by the power of cultivating the contemplation of phenomena.

Evaṃ saraṇavasena ceva ekattasamosaraṇavasena ca ekameva satipaṭṭhānaṃ ārammaṇavasena cattārova vuttāti veditabbā.

Thus, it should be understood that in terms of its destination and in terms of its convergence into unity, there is only one foundation of mindfulness, but in terms of its objects, four are spoken of.

Katame [P 1.0241] cattāroti kathetukamyatā pucchā. Idhāti imasmiṃ sāsane. Bhikkhaveti dhammapaṭiggāhakapuggalālapanametaṃ. Bhikkhūti paṭipattisampādakapuggalanidassanametaṃ. Aññepi ca devamanussā paṭipattiṃ sampādentiyeva, seṭṭhattā pana paṭipattiyā bhikkhubhāvadassanato ca, “bhikkhū”ti āha. Bhagavato hi anusāsaniṃ sampaṭicchantesu bhikkhu seṭṭho, sabbappakārāya anusāsaniyā bhājanabhāvato, tasmā seṭṭhattā “bhikkhū”ti āha. Tasmiṃ gahite pana sesā gahitāva honti rājagamanādīsu rājaggahaṇena sesaparisā viya. Yo ca imaṃ paṭipattiṃ paṭipajjati, so bhikkhu nāma hotīti [M 1.0246] paṭipattiyā bhikkhubhāvadassanatopi “bhikkhū”ti āha[V 1.0252]. Paṭipannako hi devo vā hotu manusso vā, “bhikkhū”ti saṅkhaṃ gacchatiyeva. Yathāha –

“What are the four?” This is a question asked out of a desire to explain. “Here” means in this Dispensation. “O monks” is an address to the individuals who are recipients of the Dhamma. “A monk” is an indication of the individual who accomplishes the practice. Indeed, other deities and humans also accomplish the practice, but it is said “a monk” on account of the excellence of the practice and to show the state of a monk. For among those who accept the Blessed One’s instruction, a monk is supreme, being a vessel for all kinds of instruction; therefore, on account of this excellence, it is said “a monk.” When the monk is mentioned, the rest are included as well, just as in a royal procession, the mention of the king includes the rest of the retinue. And whoever undertakes this practice is called a monk; thus, it is also said “a monk” to show that the practice itself confers the state of a monk. For whether a deity or a human is a practitioner, they are indeed reckoned as “a monk.” As it is said:

“Alaṅkato cepi samaṃ careyya,

Santo danto niyato brahmacārī;

Sabbesu bhūtesu nidhāya daṇḍaṃ,

So brāhmaṇo so samaṇo sa bhikkhū”ti. (dha. pa. 142);

“Though he be adorned, if he lives in peace, is calm, controlled, established in the holy life, and has laid aside the rod towards all beings—he is a brahmin, he is an ascetic, he is a monk.”

Kāyeti rūpakāye. Rūpakāyo hi idha aṅgapaccaṅgānaṃ kesādīnañca dhammānaṃ samūhaṭṭhena hatthikāyarathakāyādayo viya kāyoti adhippeto. Yathā ca samūhaṭṭhena, evaṃ kucchitānaṃ āyaṭṭhena. Kucchitānañhi paramajegucchānaṃ so āyotipi kāyo. Āyoti uppattideso. Tatrāyaṃ vacanattho, āyanti tatoti āyo. Ke āyanti? Kucchitā kesādayo. Iti kucchitānaṃ āyoti kāyo. Kāyānupassīti kāyamanupassanasīlo, kāyaṃ vā anupassamāno.

“In the body” means in the physical body. Here, the physical body is intended as a “body” in the sense of a collection of constituent parts, such as hair and so on, like an elephant’s body, a chariot’s body, and so on. And just as it is a body in the sense of a collection, so too is it in the sense of being a source of despicable things. For it is a source of the utterly disgusting, hence it is a “body” (kāya). “Source” (āya) means place of origin. Here, the etymology is: “they arise (āyanti) from it (tato), thus it is a source (āyo).” What arises? Despicable things like hair, etc. Thus, it is a “body” (kāya) because it is a source (āya) of despicable things (kucchita). “Contemplating the body” means one who is by nature a contemplator of the body, or one who is contemplating the body.

“Kāye”ti ca vatvāpi puna “kāyānupassī”ti dutiyaṃ kāyaggahaṇaṃ asammissato vavatthānaghanavinibbhogādidassanatthaṃ katanti veditabbaṃ. Tena na kāye vedanānupassī vā, cittadhammānupassī vā, atha kho kāyānupassīyevāti kāyasaṅkhāte vatthusmiṃ kāyānupassanākārasseva dassanena asammissato vavatthānaṃ dassitaṃ hoti. Tathā na kāye aṅgapaccaṅgavimuttaekadhammānupassī, nāpi kesalomādivinimuttaitthipurisānupassī. Yopi cettha kesalomādiko bhūtupādāyasamūhasaṅkhāto kāyo[P 1.0242], tatthapi na bhūtupādāyavinimuttaekadhammānupassī, atha kho rathasambhārānupassako viya aṅgapaccaṅgasamūhānupassī, nagarāvayavānupassako viya kesalomādisamūhānupassī, kadalikkhandhapattavaṭṭivinibbhujanako viya rittamuṭṭhiviniveṭhako viya ca bhūtupādāyasamūhānupassīyevāti nānappakārato samūhavaseneva kāyasaṅkhātassa vatthuno dassanena ghanavinibbhogo dassito hoti. Na hettha yathāvuttasamūhavinimutto kāyo vā itthī vā puriso vā añño vā koci dhammo dissati[M 1.0247], yathāvuttadhammasamūhamatteyeva pana tathā tathā sattā micchābhinivesaṃ karonti. Tenāhu porāṇā –

It should be understood that having said “in the body,” the second mention of “body” in “contemplating the body” is made to show, without confusion, the demarcation, the breaking up of the solid mass, and so on. By this, it is not contemplating feelings in the body, or contemplating mind or phenomena in the body, but solely contemplating the body. Thus, the demarcation without confusion is shown by seeing only the mode of contemplating the body in the object designated as “body.” Similarly, it is not contemplating a single phenomenon detached from the limbs and parts of the body, nor contemplating a man or woman detached from hair, body hair, and so on. Even in this body, which is designated as a collection of primary elements and derived matter, it is not contemplating a single phenomenon detached from the primary elements and derived matter. Rather, just as one who observes the components of a chariot contemplates the collection of its parts, as one who observes the sections of a city contemplates the collection of hair, body hair, and so on, as one who peels apart the layers of a plantain trunk, or as one who unwraps an empty fist, one contemplates the collection of primary elements and derived matter. In these various ways, the breaking up of the solid mass is shown by seeing the object designated as the body solely as a collection. For here, no body, woman, man, or any other such thing is seen apart from the aforementioned collection of phenomena. It is only to this mere collection of phenomena that beings, in various ways, form a wrong adherence. Therefore, the ancients have said:

“Yaṃ [V 1.0253] passati na taṃ diṭṭhaṃ, yaṃ diṭṭhaṃ taṃ na passati;

Apassaṃ bajjhate mūḷho, bajjhamāno na muccatī”ti. –

“What one sees is not what is truly seen; what is truly seen, one does not see. Not seeing, the fool is bound; being bound, he is not liberated.”
