Ghanavinibbhogādidassanatthanti vuttaṃ. Ādisaddena cettha ayampi attho veditabbo – ayañhi ekasmiṃ kāye kāyānupassīyeva, na aññadhammānupassī. Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti? Yathā anudakabhūtāyapi marīciyā udakānupassino honti, na evaṃ aniccadukkhānattaasubhabhūteyeva imasmiṃ kāye niccasukhaattasubhabhāvānupassī, atha kho kāyānupassī aniccadukkhānattaasubhākārasamūhānupassīyevāti. Atha vā yvāyaṃ parato “idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu araññagato vā…pe… so satova assasatī”tiādinā nayena assāsapassāsādicuṇṇikajātaaṭṭhikapariyosāno kāyo vutto, yo ca “idhekacco pathavikāyaṃ aniccato anupassati āpokāyaṃ tejokāyaṃ vāyokāyaṃ kesakāyaṃ lomakāyaṃ chavikāyaṃ cammakāyaṃ maṃsakāyaṃ ruhirakāyaṃ nahārukāyaṃ aṭṭhikāyaṃ aṭṭhimiñjakāya”nti paṭisambhidāyaṃ (paṭi. ma. 3.35) kāyo vutto, tassa sabbassa imasmiṃyeva kāye anupassanato “kāye kāyānupassī”ti evampi attho daṭṭhabbo.

It is said to be for the purpose of showing the breaking up of the solid mass, etc. And here, by the word “etc.,” this meaning should also be understood: for this is indeed one who contemplates the body in the body alone, not one who contemplates other phenomena. What is meant by this? Just as there are those who perceive water in a mirage that is actually waterless, so one is not a contemplator of the state of permanence, pleasure, self, or beauty in this body—which is actually impermanent, suffering, non-self, and foul—but rather, one who contemplates the body is a contemplator of it as a collection of aspects of impermanence, suffering, non-self, and foulness. Alternatively, the body that is described later by way of “Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu gone to the forest… he breathes in mindfully,” etc., ending with bones reduced to powder, and the body that is described in the Paṭisambhidāmagga (Paṭi. Ma. 3.35) as “Here, someone contemplates the earth element as impermanent, the water element, the fire element, the air element, hair, body hair, skin, hide, flesh, blood, sinews, bones, bone marrow”—because of contemplating all of that in this very body, the meaning of “contemplating the body in the body” is also to be understood in this way.

Atha vā kāye ahanti vā mamanti vā evaṃ gahetabbassa yassa kassaci ananupassanato tassa tasseva pana kesālomādikassa nānādhammasamūhassa anupassanato kāye kesādidhammasamūhasaṅkhātakāyānupassīti evamattho daṭṭhabbo. Apica “imasmiṃ kāye aniccato anupassati, no niccato”tiādinā nayena [P 1.0243] paṭisambhidāyaṃ āgatanayassa sabbasseva aniccalakkhaṇādino ākārasamūhasaṅkhātassa kāyassānupassanatopi “kāye kāyānupassī”ti evampi attho daṭṭhabbo.

Alternatively, because one does not contemplate in the body anything that can be grasped as 'I' or 'mine,' but rather contemplates that very diverse collection of phenomena such as hair, body hair, etc., the meaning should be understood thus: one is a contemplator of the body—designated as a collection of phenomena such as hair—in the body. Moreover, the meaning 'one is a contemplator of the body in the body' should also be understood from the contemplation of the body designated as a collection of all aspects, beginning with the characteristic of impermanence, according to the method given in the Paṭisambhidāmagga, by way of “He contemplates in this body impermanence, not permanence,” and so on.

Tathā hi ayaṃ kāye kāyānupassanāpaṭipadaṃ paṭipanno bhikkhu imaṃ kāyaṃ aniccānupassanādīnaṃ sattannaṃ anupassanānaṃ vasena aniccato anupassati, no niccato. Dukkhato anupassati, no sukhato. Anattato [M 1.0248] anupassati, no attato. Nibbindati, no nandati. Virajjati, no rajjati. Nirodheti, no samudeti. Paṭinissajjati, no ādiyati. So taṃ aniccato anupassanto niccasaññaṃ pajahati, dukkhato anupassanto sukhasaññaṃ [V 1.0254] pajahati, anattato anupassanto attasaññaṃ pajahati, nibbindanto nandiṃ pajahati, virajjanto rāgaṃ pajahati, nirodhento samudayaṃ pajahati, paṭinissajjanto ādānaṃ pajahatīti veditabbo.

For indeed, this bhikkhu, practicing the path of contemplation of the body in the body, contemplates this body as impermanent, not as permanent, by way of the seven contemplations beginning with the contemplation of impermanence; as suffering, not as pleasure; as non-self, not as self. He becomes disenchanted, he does not delight. He becomes dispassionate, he is not impassioned. He brings to cessation, he does not bring to origination. He relinquishes, he does not grasp. It should be understood that by contemplating it as impermanent, he abandons the perception of permanence; by contemplating it as suffering, he abandons the perception of pleasure; by contemplating it as non-self, he abandons the perception of self; by becoming disenchanted, he abandons delight; by becoming dispassionate, he abandons passion; by bringing to cessation, he abandons origination; by relinquishing, he abandons grasping.

Viharatīti iriyati. Ātāpīti tīsu bhavesu kilese ātāpetīti ātāpo, vīriyassetaṃ nāmaṃ. Ātāpo assa atthīti ātāpī. Sampajānoti sampajaññasaṅkhātena ñāṇena samannāgato. Satimāti kāyapariggāhikāya satiyā samannāgato. Ayaṃ pana yasmā satiyā ārammaṇaṃ pariggahetvā paññāya anupassati, na hi sativirahitassa anupassanā nāma atthi. Tenevāha “satiñca khvāhaṃ, bhikkhave, sabbatthikaṃ vadāmī”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.234). Tasmā ettha “kāye kāyānupassī viharatī”ti ettāvatā kāyānupassanāsatipaṭṭhānakammaṭṭhānaṃ vuttaṃ hoti. Atha vā yasmā anātāpino antosaṅkhepo antarāyakaro hoti, asampajāno upāyapariggahe anupāyaparivajjane ca sammuyhati, muṭṭhassati upāyāpariccāge anupāyāpariggahe ca asamattho hoti, tenassa taṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ na sampajjati, tasmā yesaṃ dhammānaṃ ānubhāvena taṃ sampajjati. Tesaṃ dassanatthaṃ “ātāpī sampajāno satimāti idaṃ vutta”nti veditabbaṃ.

He dwells: he moves about. Ardent: he burns up defilements in the three existences, thus there is ardor; this is a name for energy. He has ardor, thus he is ardent. Clearly comprehending: endowed with the knowledge designated as clear comprehension. Mindful: endowed with mindfulness that encompasses the body. Moreover, since he grasps the object with mindfulness and contemplates with wisdom—for there is no contemplation without mindfulness—therefore it is said, “Indeed, bhikkhus, I say that mindfulness is useful everywhere” (Saṃ. Ni. 5.234). Therefore, by the phrase “he dwells contemplating the body in the body,” the meditation subject of the establishment of mindfulness through body contemplation is stated. Alternatively, because for one who is not ardent, inward listlessness creates an obstacle; one who is not clearly comprehending is confused in adopting the right means and avoiding the wrong means; one who is unmindful is incapable of not abandoning the right means and of not adopting the wrong means—therefore, that meditation subject does not succeed. Hence, to show the qualities by whose power it succeeds, it is to be understood that “ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful” is said here.

Iti kāyānupassanāsatipaṭṭhānaṃ sampayogaṅgañcassa dassetvā idāni pahānaṅgaṃ dassetuṃ vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassanti vuttaṃ. Tattha vineyyāti tadaṅgavinayena vā vikkhambhanavinayena vā vinayitvā. Loketi tasmiṃyeva [P 1.0244] kāye. Kāyo hi idha lujjanapalujjanaṭṭhena lokoti adhippeto. Yasmā panassa na kāyamatteyeva abhijjhādomanassaṃ pahīyati, vedanādīsupi pahīyatiyeva, tasmā “pañcapi upādānakkhandhā loko”ti vibhaṅge (vibha. 362) vuttaṃ. Lokasaṅkhātattā vā tesaṃ dhammānaṃ atthuddhāranayenetaṃ vuttaṃ. Yaṃ panāha “tattha katamo loko? Sveva kāyo loko”ti. Ayamevettha attho, tasmiṃ loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ vineyyāti evaṃ sambandho daṭṭhabbo. Yasmā panettha abhijjhāgahaṇena kāmacchando[M 1.0249], domanassaggahaṇena byāpādo saṅgahaṃ gacchati, tasmā nīvaraṇapariyāpannabalavadhammadvayadassanena nīvaraṇappahānaṃ vuttaṃ hotīti veditabbaṃ.

Having thus shown the establishment of mindfulness through body contemplation and its factor of application, now, to show the factor of abandoning, it is said: “having subdued covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world.” Herein, “having subdued” means having subdued either by removal by substitution or by removal by suppression. “The world” means in this very body. For here, the body is intended as the world in the sense of disintegrating and crumbling. And since covetousness and displeasure are not abandoned merely in regard to the body but are also abandoned in regard to feelings, etc., therefore it is said in the Vibhaṅga (Vibh. 362): “The five aggregates subject to clinging are the world.” Or, because those phenomena are designated as the world, this is said by way of extracting the meaning. But when it is said, “Herein, what is the world? Just this body is the world,” this is the meaning here. The connection should be seen thus: “having subdued covetousness and displeasure in regard to that world.” And since here, by the term 'covetousness,' sensual desire is included, and by the term 'displeasure,' ill will is included, it should be understood that by showing these two powerful states included among the hindrances, the abandoning of the hindrances is stated.

Visesena [V 1.0255] cettha abhijjhāvinayena kāyasampattimūlakassa anurodhassa, domanassavinayena pana kāyavipattimūlakassa virodhassa, abhijjhāvinayena ca kāye abhiratiyā, domanassavinayena kāyabhāvanāya anabhiratiyā, abhijjhāvinayena kāye abhūtānaṃ subhasukhabhāvādīnaṃ pakkhepassa, domanassavinayena ca kāye bhūtānaṃ asubhāsukhabhāvādīnaṃ apanayanassa ca pahānaṃ vuttaṃ. Tena yogāvacarassa yogānubhāvo yogasamatthatā ca dīpitā hoti. Yogānubhāvo hi esa, yadidaṃ anurodhavirodhavippamutto aratiratisaho abhūtapakkhepabhūtāpanayanavirahito ca hoti. Anurodhavirodhavippamutto cesa aratiratisaho abhūtaṃ apakkhipanto bhūtañca anapanento yogasamattho hotīti.

Here, in particular, through the removal of covetousness, the abandoning of attachment rooted in bodily success is spoken of, and through the removal of displeasure, the abandoning of aversion rooted in bodily failure. And through the removal of covetousness, the abandoning of delight in the body is spoken of, and through the removal of displeasure, the abandoning of non-delight in the development of the body. And through the removal of covetousness, the abandoning of projecting unreal states such as beauty and pleasure onto the body is spoken of, and through the removal of displeasure, the abandoning of removing real states such as ugliness and displeasure from the body. Thus, the meditator's meditative power and fitness for meditation are revealed. For this is meditative power: being free from attachment and aversion, being able to endure discontent and delight, and being without the projection of the unreal and the removal of the real. And being free from attachment and aversion, being able to endure discontent and delight, neither projecting the unreal nor removing the real—this is fitness for meditation.

Aparo nayo “kāye kāyānupassī”ti ettha anupassanāya kammaṭṭhānaṃ vuttaṃ. “Viharatī”ti ettha vuttavihārena kammaṭṭhānikassa kāyapariharaṇaṃ. “Ātāpī”tiādīsu ātāpena sammappadhānaṃ, satisampajaññena sabbatthikakammaṭṭhānaṃ, kammaṭṭhānapariharaṇūpāyo vā, satiyā vā kāyānupassanāvasena paṭiladdhasamatho, sampajaññena vipassanā, abhijjhādomanassavinayena bhāvanāphalaṃ vuttanti veditabbaṃ.

Another method: In “contemplating the body in the body,” the meditation subject is stated by way of contemplation. In “he dwells,” the proper conduct of one devoted to the meditation subject is stated by way of the dwelling mentioned. In “ardent,” etc., right effort is stated by way of ardor; the universal meditation subject by way of mindfulness and clear comprehension, or the means of maintaining the meditation subject; or, tranquility attained by mindfulness in dependence on the contemplation of the body, insight by clear comprehension, and the fruit of development by the removal of covetousness and displeasure, are stated—this should be understood.

Vibhaṅge pana “anupassī”ti tattha katamā anupassanā? Yā paññā pajānanā…pe… sammādiṭṭhi. Ayaṃ vuccati anupassanā. Imāya anupassanāya upeto hoti samupeto upāgato samupāgato upapanno sampanno samannāgato. Tena vuccati anupassīti.

In the Vibhaṅga, however, regarding “one who contemplates”: therein, what is contemplation? It is wisdom, understanding... right view. This is called contemplation. One who is endowed with this contemplation, fully endowed, has attained it, fully attained, is possessed of it, accomplished, and fully equipped. Therefore, he is called “one who contemplates.”

Viharatīti iriyati [P 1.0245] vattati pāleti yapeti yāpeti carati viharati. Tena vuccati viharatīti.

He dwells: he moves, proceeds, maintains, keeps up, continues, lives, dwells. Therefore, it is said, “he dwells.”

Ātāpīti tattha katamo ātāpo? Yo cetasiko vīriyārambho…pe… sammāvāyāmo. Ayaṃ vuccati ātāpo. Iminā ātāpena upeto hoti…pe… samannāgato. Tena vuccati ātāpīti.

Ardent: what is ardor here? Whatever mental exertion of energy… right effort. This is called ardor. One is endowed with this ardor… possessed of it. Therefore, one is called “ardent.”

Sampajānoti [M 1.0250] tattha katamaṃ sampajaññaṃ? Yā paññā pajānanā…pe… sammādiṭṭhi. Idaṃ vuccati [V 1.0256] sampajaññaṃ. Iminā sampajaññena upeto hoti…pe… samannāgato. Tena vuccati sampajānoti.

Clearly comprehending: what is clear comprehension here? Whatever wisdom, understanding… right view. This is called clear comprehension. One is endowed with this clear comprehension… possessed of it. Therefore, one is called “clearly comprehending.”

Satimāti tattha katamā sati? Yā sati anussati…pe… sammāsati. Ayaṃ vuccati sati. Imāya satiyā upeto hoti…pe… samannāgato. Tena vuccati satimāti.

Mindful: what is mindfulness here? Whatever mindfulness, recollection… right mindfulness. This is called mindfulness. One is endowed with this mindfulness… possessed of it. Therefore, one is called “mindful.”

Vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassanti tattha katamo loko? Sveva kāyo loko, pañcapi upādānakkhandhā loko. Ayaṃ vuccati loko. Tattha katamā abhijjhā? Yo rāgo sārāgo anunayo anurodho nandī nandīrāgo cittassa sārāgo, ayaṃ vuccati abhijjhā. Tattha katamaṃ domanassaṃ? Yaṃ cetasikaṃ asātaṃ, cetasikaṃ dukkhaṃ, cetosamphassajaṃ asātaṃ…pe… dukkhā vedanā. Idaṃ vuccati domanassaṃ. Iti ayañca abhijjhā idañca domanassaṃ imamhi loke vinītā honti paṭivinītā santā vūpasantā samitā vūpasamitā atthaṅgatā abbhatthaṅgatā appitā byappitā sositā visositā byantīkatā, tena vuccati vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassanti (vibha. 356) evametesaṃ padānamattho vutto. Tena saha ayaṃ aṭṭhakathānayo yathā saṃsandati, evaṃ veditabbo. Ayaṃ tāva kāyānupassanāsatipaṭṭhānuddesassa atthavaṇṇanā.

“Having removed covetousness and displeasure in the world”—herein, what is the world? This very body is the world; the five aggregates of clinging are the world. This is called the world. Herein, what is covetousness? That which is lust, intense lust, affection, fondness, delight, delight with lust, the mind’s intense lust—this is called covetousness. Herein, what is displeasure? Whatever is mental unpleasantness, mental pain, unpleasant feeling born of mental contact… painful feeling. This is called displeasure. Thus, this covetousness and this displeasure are removed in this world, dispelled, calmed, stilled, quieted, ceased, set, vanished, given up, relinquished, dried up, thoroughly dried up, brought to an end. Therefore, it is said, “having removed covetousness and displeasure in the world.” (Vibhanga 356) Thus, the meaning of these terms has been stated. This commentarial method should be understood in line with that. This, for now, is the explanation of the meaning of the summary section on the Contemplation of the Body.

Vedanāsu… citte… dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati…pe… vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassanti ettha pana vedanānupassīti evamādīsu vedanādīnaṃ puna vacane payojanaṃ kāyānupassanāyaṃ vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Vedanāsu vedanānupassī, citte cittānupassī, dhammesu dhammānupassīti ettha pana vedanāti tisso vedanā, tā ca lokiyā eva. Cittampi lokiyaṃ, tathā dhammā. Tesaṃ vibhāgo niddesavāre pākaṭo bhavissati. Kevalaṃ panidha yathā vedanā anupassitabbā, tathā anupassanto vedanāsu vedanānupassīti veditabbo. Esa nayo cittadhammesupi. Kathañca vedanā anupassitabbāti? Sukhā tāva vedanā [P 1.0246] dukkhato, dukkhā sallato, adukkhamasukhā aniccato. Yathāha –

“Contemplating feelings in feelings… mind in mind… phenomena in phenomena, he dwells… having removed covetousness and displeasure in the world”—here, regarding “contemplating feelings,” etc., the purpose of repeating “feelings,” etc., should be understood in the same way as explained in the section on the contemplation of the body. Moreover, regarding “Contemplating feelings in feelings, mind in mind, phenomena in phenomena”—here, “feelings” refers to the three kinds of feelings, and these are exclusively mundane. The mind too is mundane, and so are phenomena. Their classification will be clear in the exposition section. However, here it should simply be understood that one who contemplates feelings as they should be contemplated is called “one who contemplates feelings in feelings.” The same principle applies to mind and phenomena. And how should feelings be contemplated? Pleasant feeling as suffering, painful feeling as a dart, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling as impermanent. As it is said:

“Yo [V 1.0257][M 1.0251] sukhaṃ dukkhato adda, dukkhamaddakkhi sallato;

Adukkhamasukhaṃ santaṃ, adakkhi naṃ aniccato;

Sa ve sammaddaso bhikkhu, upasanto carissatī”ti. (saṃ. ni. 4.253);

“He who saw pleasure as suffering, saw suffering as a dart, and saw the peaceful neither-painful-nor-pleasant as impermanent—that monk, having right view, will fare on tranquilly.” (Saṃyutta Nikāya 4.253)

Sabbā eva cetā dukkhātipi anupassitabbā. Vuttañhetaṃ “yaṃkiñci vedayitaṃ, sabbaṃ taṃ dukkhasminti vadāmī”ti (saṃ. ni. 4.259). Sukhadukkhatopi ca anupassitabbā. Yathāha “sukhā vedanā ṭhitisukhā vipariṇāmadukkhā”ti (ma. ni. 1.464) sabbaṃ vitthāretabbaṃ. Apica aniccādisattānupassanāvasenapi anupassitabbā. Sesaṃ niddesavāreyeva pākaṭaṃ bhavissati. Cittadhammesupi cittaṃ tāva ārammaṇādhipatisahajātabhūmikammavipākakiriyādinānattabhedānaṃ aniccādisattānupassanānaṃ niddesavāre āgatasarāgādibhedānañca vasena anupassitabbaṃ. Dhammā salakkhaṇasāmaññalakkhaṇānaṃ suññatadhammassa aniccādisattānupassanānaṃ niddesavāre āgatasantāsantādibhedānañca vasena anupassitabbā. Sesaṃ vuttanayameva. Kāmañcettha yassa kāyasaṅkhāte loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ pahīnaṃ, tassa vedanādilokesupi taṃ pahīnameva. Nānāpuggalavasena pana nānācittakkhaṇikasatipaṭṭhānabhāvanāvasena ca sabbattha vuttaṃ. Yato vā ekattha pahīnaṃ sesesupi pahīnaṃ hoti. Tenevassa tattha pahānadassanatthampi evaṃ vuttanti veditabbanti.

All these feelings should also be contemplated as suffering. As it is said: “Whatever is felt, all that I declare as suffering” (Saṃyutta Nikāya 4.259). They should also be contemplated as pleasant and painful. As it is stated: “Pleasant feeling is pleasant while it lasts, but painful when it changes” (Majjhima Nikāya 1.464); all this should be elaborated. Furthermore, they should also be contemplated by way of the seven contemplations on impermanence, etc. The rest will become clear in the section on exposition. Regarding the contemplation of mind and phenomena, the mind should first be contemplated by way of the various distinctions such as object, predominance, co-arising, basis, kamma, result, and function, etc., by means of the seven contemplations on impermanence, etc., and also by way of the distinctions of being with lust, etc., which are mentioned in the section on exposition. Phenomena should be contemplated by way of their individual and general characteristics, the state of emptiness, and the seven contemplations on impermanence, etc., and also by way of the distinctions of being present and absent, etc., which are mentioned in the section on exposition. The rest is as has been explained. Indeed, for one for whom covetousness and displeasure are abandoned in the world designated as the body, for them, they are also abandoned in the worlds of feelings, etc. However, this is stated in all cases with reference to different individuals and to the development of the establishments of mindfulness in various moments of consciousness. Or, since when it is abandoned in one, it is also abandoned in the others, it should be understood that this is stated thus to show its abandonment in those cases as well.

Uddesavārakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Summary Section is concluded.

Kāyānupassanāānāpānapabbavaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Section on Mindfulness of Breathing in the Contemplation of the Body

107. Idāni seyyathāpi nāma cheko vilīvakārako thūlakilañjasaṇhakilañjacaṅkoṭakapeḷāpuṭādīni upakaraṇāni kattukāmo ekaṃ mahāveṇuṃ labhitvā catudhā bhinditvā tato ekekaṃ veṇukhaṇḍaṃ gahetvā phāletvā taṃ taṃ upakaraṇaṃ kareyya, evameva bhagavā satipaṭṭhānadesanāya sattānaṃ anekappakāravisesādhigamaṃ kattukāmo ekameva sammāsatiṃ “cattāro satipaṭṭhānā. Katame cattāro? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu kāye kāyānupassī viharatī”tiādinā [V 1.0258] nayena ārammaṇavasena [P 1.0247] catudhā bhinditvā tato ekekaṃ satipaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā vibhajanto “kathañca bhikkhave”tiādinā nayena niddesavāraṃ vattumāraddho.

107. Now, just as a skilled basket-maker, wishing to make various implements such as a large winnowing basket, a small winnowing basket, a hamper, or a container, would take a single large bamboo, split it into four parts, and then take each piece of bamboo, split it further, and make each respective implement—in the same way, the Blessed One, wishing to enable beings to achieve various kinds of distinctions through the teaching of the establishments of mindfulness, took the single right mindfulness and divided it into four parts based on the objects: "The four establishments of mindfulness. What are the four? Here, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body..." and so on. Then, taking each establishment of mindfulness separately and analyzing it, he began to set forth the section of exposition: "And how, monks..." and so on.

Tattha [M 1.0252] kathañcātiādi vitthāretukamyatā pucchā. Ayaṃ panettha saṅkhepattho – bhikkhave, kena ca pakārena bhikkhu kāye kāyānupassī viharatīti? Esa nayo sabbapucchāvāresu. Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhūti, bhikkhave, imasmiṃ sāsane bhikkhu. Ayañhettha idha-saddo sabbappakārakāyānupassanānibbattakassa puggalassa sannissayabhūtasāsanaparidīpano aññasāsanassa tathābhāvapaṭisedhano ca. Vuttañhetaṃ “idheva, bhikkhave, samaṇo…pe… suññā parappavādā samaṇebhi aññehī”ti (ma. ni. 1.139). Tena vuttaṃ “imasmiṃ sāsane bhikkhū”ti.

Herein, 'And how, etc.' is a question indicating the desire to elaborate. The concise meaning is this: 'Monks, in what way does a bhikkhu dwell contemplating the body in the body?' This is the method in all passages of questioning. 'Here, monks, a bhikkhu' means a bhikkhu in this Dispensation. For here the word 'here' illuminates this Dispensation as the foundation for the person who develops all kinds of contemplation of the body, and it refutes that this is so in other dispensations. For it is said: “It is only here, monks, that there is a recluse... empty are the doctrines of other recluses” (Majjhima Nikāya 1.139). Therefore it was said, 'a bhikkhu in this Dispensation.'

“Araññagato vā…pe… suññāgāragato vā”ti idamassa satipaṭṭhānabhāvanānurūpasenāsanapariggahaparidīpanaṃ. Imassa hi bhikkhuno dīgharattaṃ rūpādīsu ārammaṇesu anuvisaṭaṃ cittaṃ kammaṭṭhānavīthiṃ otarituṃ na icchati, kūṭagoṇayuttaratho viya uppathameva dhāvati, tasmā seyyathāpi nāma gopo kūṭadhenuyā sabbaṃ khīraṃ pivitvā vaḍḍhitaṃ kūṭavacchaṃ dametukāmo dhenuto apanetvā ekamante mahantaṃ thambhaṃ nikhaṇitvā tattha yottena bandheyya. Athassa so vaccho ito cito ca vipphanditvā palāyituṃ asakkonto tameva thambhaṃ upanisīdeyya vā upanipajjeyya vā, evameva imināpi bhikkhunā dīgharattaṃ rūpārammaṇādirasapānavaḍḍhitaṃ duṭṭhacittaṃ dametukāmena rūpādiārammaṇato apanetvā araññaṃ vā rukkhamūlaṃ vā suññāgāraṃ vā pavesetvā tattha satipaṭṭhānārammaṇatthambhe satiyottena bandhitabbaṃ. Evamassa taṃ cittaṃ ito cito ca vipphanditvāpi pubbe āciṇṇārammaṇaṃ alabhamānaṃ satiyottaṃ chinditvā palāyituṃ asakkontaṃ tamevārammaṇaṃ upacārappanāvasena upanisīdati ceva upanipajjati ca. Tenāhu porāṇā –

“‘Having gone to the forest… or to an empty dwelling,’ this illuminates the taking up of a dwelling suitable for the development of the establishments of mindfulness. For this bhikkhu’s mind, which has for a long time been immersed in objects such as forms, does not wish to enter the path of the meditation subject; like a cart yoked to an untamed bull, it runs only off the path. Therefore, just as a cowherd, wishing to tame a wild calf that has grown up by drinking all the milk of a wild cow, would take it away from the cow, dig a large post in a secluded spot, and tie the calf to it with a rope; then that calf, after struggling this way and that, being unable to escape, would sit down or lie down by that very post. In the same way, this bhikkhu, wishing to tame his corrupted mind, which has for a long time been nourished by drinking the flavour of objects such as forms, should take it away from objects such as forms, lead it into the forest, or to the foot of a tree, or to an empty dwelling, and there bind it with the rope of mindfulness to the post of the object of the establishment of mindfulness. Thus his mind, though struggling this way and that, not finding its formerly accustomed object and being unable to break the rope of mindfulness and escape, sits down and lies down by that very object by way of access and absorption concentration. Therefore the ancients said:

“Yathā thambhe nibandheyya, vacchaṃ damaṃ naro idha;

Bandheyyevaṃ sakaṃ cittaṃ, satiyārammaṇe daḷha”nti.

“Just as a person here would tie a calf to be tamed to a post; so too should one bind one’s own mind firmly to the object of mindfulness.”

Evamassa taṃ senāsanaṃ bhāvanānurūpaṃ hoti. Tena vuttaṃ “idamassa satipaṭṭhānabhāvanānurūpasenāsanapariggahaparidīpana”nti.

Thus, that dwelling is suitable for his cultivation. Therefore, it is said, “This is an explanation of the selection of a dwelling suitable for the development of the establishments of mindfulness.”

Apica [V 1.0259][M 1.0253][P 1.0248] yasmā idaṃ kāyānupassanāya muddhabhūtaṃ sabbabuddhapaccekabuddhabuddhasāvakānaṃ visesādhigamadiṭṭhadhammasukhavihārapadaṭṭhānaṃ ānāpānassatikammaṭṭhānaṃ itthipurisahatthiassādisaddasamākulaṃ gāmantaṃ apariccajitvā na sukaraṃ sampādetuṃ, saddakaṇṭakattā jhānassa. Agāmake pana araññe sukaraṃ yogāvacarena idaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ pariggahetvā ānāpānacatutthajjhānaṃ nibbattetvā tadeva jhānaṃ pādakaṃ katvā saṅkhāre sammasitvā aggaphalaṃ arahattaṃ pāpuṇituṃ. Tasmāssa anurūpasenāsanaṃ dassento bhagavā “araññagato vā”tiādimāha.

Moreover, since this meditation subject of mindfulness of breathing—which is the pinnacle of the contemplation of the body, and the foundation for the attainment of special qualities and for a pleasant abiding in this very life for all Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and the disciples of the Buddha—is not easy to accomplish without having left the vicinity of a village, which is crowded with the sounds of men, women, elephants, horses, and so on, because sound is a thorn to jhāna; whereas in a forest without a village, it is easy for a yogī to undertake this meditation subject, produce the fourth jhāna of mindfulness of breathing, and, having made that very jhāna the basis, to comprehend the formations and attain the supreme fruit, arahantship; therefore the Blessed One, showing a suitable dwelling for him, said, “Having gone to the forest…” and so on.

Vatthuvijjācariyo viya hi bhagavā. So yathā vatthuvijjācariyo nagarabhūmiṃ passitvā suṭṭhu upaparikkhitvā “ettha nagaraṃ māpethā”ti upadisati, sotthinā ca nagare niṭṭhite rājakulato mahāsakkāraṃ labhati, evameva yogāvacarassa anurūpaṃ senāsanaṃ upaparikkhitvā “ettha kammaṭṭhānaṃ anuyuñjitabba”nti upadisati. Tato tattha kammaṭṭhānaṃ anuyuñjantena yoginā anukkamena arahatte patte “sammāsambuddho vata so bhagavā”ti mahantaṃ sakkāraṃ labhati.

For the Blessed One is like an expert in site-lore. Just as an expert in site-lore, having seen and thoroughly examined a city site, instructs, “Build the city here,” and when the city is safely completed, he receives great honour from the royal family, so too, having examined a suitable dwelling for the meditator, he instructs, “Here one should apply oneself to the meditation subject.” Then, when the yogī who applies himself to the meditation subject there has gradually attained arahantship, the Blessed One receives great honour, with the thought, “Truly, that Blessed One is the Fully Enlightened One.”

Ayaṃ pana bhikkhu dīpisadisoti vuccati. Yathā hi mahādīpirājā araññe tiṇagahanaṃ vā vanagahanaṃ vā pabbatagahanaṃ vā nissāya nilīyitvā vanamahiṃsagokaṇṇasūkarādayo mige gaṇhāti, evameva ayaṃ araññādīsu kammaṭṭhānaṃ anuyuñjanto bhikkhu yathākkamena cattāro magge ceva cattāri ariyaphalāni ca gaṇhāti. Tenāhu porāṇā –

This bhikkhu, however, is said to be like a leopard. Just as a great leopard king, relying on a thicket of grass, a forest thicket, or a mountain thicket, lies hidden and captures wild animals such as forest buffalo, gokaṇṇa-deer, and boars, so too this bhikkhu, applying himself to the meditation subject in the forest and other such places, gradually attains the four paths and the four noble fruits. Therefore, the ancients have said:

“Yathāpi dīpiko nāma, nilīyitvā gaṇhatī mige;

Tathevāyaṃ buddhaputto, yuttayogo vipassako;

Araññaṃ pavisitvāna, gaṇhāti phalamuttama”nti.

“Just as a leopard, lying in wait, captures its prey; so too this son of the Buddha, devoted to the practice, an insight practitioner, having entered the forest, attains the supreme fruit.”

Tenassa parakkamajavayoggabhūmiṃ araññasenāsanaṃ dassento bhagavā “araññagato vā”tiādimāha. Ito paraṃ imasmiṃ tāva ānāpānapabbe yaṃ vattabbaṃ siyā, taṃ visuddhimagge vuttameva.

Therefore, showing the forest dwelling as the ground suitable for his striving and exertion, the Blessed One said, “Gone to the forest,” and so on. From this point on, whatever should be said in this section on mindfulness of breathing has already been stated in the Visuddhimagga.

Tassa [V 1.0260] pana imesaṃ “dīghaṃ vā assasanto dīghaṃ assasāmīti pajānāti…pe… passambhayaṃ kāyasaṅkhāraṃ passasissāmīti sikkhatī”ti evaṃ vuttānaṃ [M 1.0254] assāsapassāsānaṃ vasena sikkhato assāsapassāsanimitte [P 1.0249] cattāri jhānāni uppajjanti. So jhānā vuṭṭhahitvā assāsapassāse vā pariggaṇhāti jhānaṅgāni vā. Tattha assāsapassāsakammiko “ime assāsapassāsā kiṃ nissitā, vatthuṃ nissitā, vatthu nāma karajakāyo, karajakāyo nāma cattāri mahābhūtāni upādārūpañcā”ti evaṃ rūpaṃ pariggaṇhāti, tato tadārammaṇe phassapañcamake nāmanti evaṃ nāmarūpaṃ pariggahetvā tassa paccayaṃ pariyesanto avijjādipaṭiccasamuppādaṃ disvā “paccayapaccayuppannadhammamattamevetaṃ, añño satto vā puggalo vā natthī”ti vitiṇṇakaṅkho sappaccayanāmarūpe tilakkhaṇaṃ āropetvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhento anukkamena arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti. Idaṃ ekassa bhikkhuno yāva arahattā niyyānamukhaṃ.

For one who is training by means of these in-breaths and out-breaths, as it is said, “Breathing in long, he knows, ‘I breathe in long’… he trains himself, ‘I shall breathe out calming the bodily formation,’” the four jhānas arise with the sign of the in-and-out breaths as their object. Emerging from those jhānas, he discerns either the in-breaths and out-breaths or the jhāna factors. In this case, the practitioner of in-and-out breathing reflects: “On what do these in-breaths and out-breaths depend? They depend on a basis. The basis is the physical body. The physical body is the four great elements and derived form.” In this way he discerns material form. Then, with that as the object, he discerns mentality with contact as the fifth factor. Having thus discerned mentality-and-materiality, he investigates its cause and sees the dependent origination beginning with ignorance. Having overcome doubt, he sees: “This is merely a phenomenon arisen from its cause and condition; there is no other being or person.” Applying the three characteristics to mentality-and-materiality together with its cause, he develops insight and gradually attains arahantship. This is one bhikkhu’s path of deliverance up to arahantship.

Jhānakammikopi “imāni jhānaṅgāni kiṃ nissitāni, vatthuṃ nissitāni. Vatthu nāma karajakāyoti jhānaṅgāni nāmaṃ, karajakāyo rūpa”nti nāmarūpaṃ vavatthapetvā tassa paccayaṃ pariyesanto avijjādipaccayākāraṃ disvā “paccayapaccayuppannadhammamattamevetaṃ, añño satto vā puggalo vā natthī”ti vitiṇṇakaṅkho sappaccayanāmarūpe tilakkhaṇaṃ āropetvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhento anukkamena arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti, idaṃ ekassa bhikkhuno yāva arahattā niyyānamukhaṃ.

The practitioner of jhāna also reflects: 'On what do these jhāna factors depend? They depend on a basis. The basis is the physical body.' He defines mentality-and-materiality thus: 'The jhāna factors are mentality, the physical body is materiality.' Having investigated its cause and seen the pattern of conditions beginning with ignorance, he overcomes doubt, thinking: 'This is merely a phenomenon arisen from its cause and condition; there is no other being or person.' Applying the three characteristics to mentality-and-materiality together with its cause, he develops insight and gradually attains arahantship. This is one monk's path of deliverance up to arahantship.

Iti ajjhattaṃ vāti evaṃ attano vā assāsapassāsakāye kāyānupassī viharati. Bahiddhā vāti parassa vā assāsapassāsakāye. Ajjhattabahiddhā vāti kālena attano, kālena parassa assāsapassāsakāye. Etenassa paguṇakammaṭṭhānaṃ aṭṭhapetvā aparāparaṃ sañcaraṇakālo kathito. Ekasmiṃ kāle panidaṃ ubhayaṃ na labbhati.

Thus, 'internally' means he dwells contemplating the body in his own body of in-and-out breaths. 'Externally' means in another's body of in-and-out breaths. 'Internally and externally' means at times in his own, and at times in another's body of in-and-out breaths. By this is described the time for alternating back and forth, after having established a proficient meditation subject. But at any single moment, both are not possible.

Samudayadhammānupassī vāti yathā nāma kammārabhastañca gaggaranāḷiñca tajjañca vāyāmaṃ paṭicca vāto aparāparaṃ sañcarati, evaṃ bhikkhuno karajakāyañca nāsāpuṭañca cittañca paṭicca assāsapassāsakāyo aparāparaṃ sañcarati. Kāyādayo dhammā samudayadhammā, te passanto “samudayadhammānupassī vā kāyasmiṃ viharatī”ti vuccati. Vayadhammānupassī vāti yathā bhastāya apanītāya gaggaranāḷiyā bhinnāya tajje ca vāyāme asati so vāto nappavattati[M 1.0255], evameva kāye bhinne nāsāpuṭe viddhaste citte [V 1.0261] ca niruddhe assāsapassāsakāyo nāma nappavattatīti kāyādinirodhā assāsapassāsanirodhoti evaṃ passanto “vayadhammānupassī [P 1.0250] vā kāyasmiṃ viharatī”ti vuccati. Samudayavayadhammānupassī vāti kālena samudayaṃ, kālena vayaṃ anupassanto. Atthi kāyoti vā panassāti kāyova atthi, na satto, na puggalo, na itthī, na puriso, na attā, na attaniyaṃ, nāhaṃ, na mama, na koci, na kassacīti evamassa sati paccupaṭṭhitā hoti.

'He dwells contemplating the nature of arising in the body': Just as wind moves back and forth dependent on a blacksmith's bellows, the bellows' pipe, and the appropriate effort, so too, the body of in-and-out breaths moves back and forth dependent on the physical body, the nostrils, and the mind. The body and the other conditions are phenomena subject to arising; one who sees them as such is said to 'dwell contemplating the nature of arising in the body.' 'He dwells contemplating the nature of passing away in the body': Just as that wind does not proceed when the bellows is taken away, the pipe is broken, and the appropriate effort is absent, so too, the body of in-and-out breaths does not proceed when the physical body is broken, the nostrils are destroyed, and the mind has ceased. Thus, seeing that 'with the cessation of the body and the other conditions, there is the cessation of the in-and-out breaths,' one is said to 'dwell contemplating the nature of passing away in the body.' 'He dwells contemplating both the nature of arising and passing away in the body' means contemplating arising at one time and passing away at another. 'Or his mindfulness is established that “There is a body”': For him, there is only the body, not a being, not a person, not a woman, not a man, not a self, not what belongs to a self, not 'I,' not 'mine,' not anyone, not belonging to anyone. In this way his mindfulness is established.

Yāvadevāti payojanaparicchedavavatthāpanametaṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yā sati paccupaṭṭhitā hoti, sā na aññatthāya. Atha kho yāvadeva ñāṇamattāya aparāparaṃ uttaruttari ñāṇapamāṇatthāya ceva satipamāṇatthāya ca, satisampajaññānaṃ vuḍḍhatthāyāti attho. Anissito ca viharatīti taṇhānissayadiṭṭhinissayānaṃ vasena anissito viharati. Na ca kiñci loke upādiyatīti lokasmiṃ kiñci rūpaṃ vā…pe… viññāṇaṃ vā “ayaṃ me attā vā attaniyaṃ vā”ti na gaṇhāti. Evampīti upariatthaṃ upādāya sampiṇḍanattho pikāro. Iminā pana padena bhagavā ānāpānapabbadesanaṃ niyyātetvā dasseti.

'As far as' is for the purpose of defining the scope of application. This is said to mean: the mindfulness that is established does not serve any other purpose; rather, it is solely for the sake of mere knowledge, for the gradual increase of higher knowledge and mindfulness, and for the growth of mindfulness and clear comprehension—this is the meaning. 'And he dwells independent'—he dwells independent, free from dependence on craving and wrong views. 'And he does not cling to anything in the world'—he does not cling to anything in the world, whether form... or consciousness, thinking, "This is my self" or "This belongs to my self." 'Thus also'—the particle 'pi' here serves to consolidate the foregoing meaning. By this passage, the Blessed One demonstrates, having concluded the teaching on the section of mindfulness of breathing.

Tattha assāsapassāsapariggāhikā sati dukkhasaccaṃ, tassā samuṭṭhāpikā purimataṇhā samudayasaccaṃ, ubhinnaṃ appavatti nirodhasaccaṃ, dukkhaparijānano samudayapajahano nirodhārammaṇo ariyamaggo maggasaccaṃ. Evaṃ catusaccavasena ussakkitvā nibbutiṃ pāpuṇātīti idamekassa assāsapassāsavasena abhiniviṭṭhassa bhikkhuno yāva arahattā niyyānamukhanti.

Therein, the mindfulness that comprehends the in-breaths and out-breaths is the truth of suffering. The prior craving that gives rise to it is the truth of the origin. The non-occurrence of both is the truth of cessation. The noble path that fully understands suffering, abandons the origin, and has cessation as its object is the truth of the path. Thus, having striven by way of the Four Noble Truths, one attains Nibbāna. For a monk devoted to the in-breaths and out-breaths, this is the means of deliverance up to Arahantship.

Ānāpānapabbavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the section on mindfulness of breathing is concluded.

Iriyāpathapabbavaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Section on Postures

108. Evaṃ assāsapassāsavasena kāyānupassanaṃ vibhajitvā idāni iriyāpathavasena vibhajituṃ puna caparantiādimāha. Tattha kāmaṃ soṇasiṅgālādayopi gacchantā “gacchāmā”ti jānanti. Na panetaṃ evarūpaṃ jānanaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Evarūpañhi jānanaṃ sattūpaladdhiṃ na pajahati[V 1.0262][P 1.0251], attasaññaṃ na ugghāṭeti[M 1.0256], kammaṭṭhānaṃ vā satipaṭṭhānabhāvanā vā na hoti. Imassa pana bhikkhuno jānanaṃ sattūpaladdhiṃ pajahati, attasaññaṃ ugghāṭeti, kammaṭṭhānañceva satipaṭṭhānabhāvanā ca hoti. Idañhi “ko gacchati, kassa gamanaṃ, kiṃ kāraṇā gacchatī”ti evaṃ sampajānanaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Ṭhānādīsupi eseva nayo.

108. Having thus analyzed the contemplation of the body by way of in-breaths and out-breaths, now, to analyze it by way of postures, he said, 'Furthermore,' and so on. In this context, even animals like dogs and jackals, while walking, know, 'We are walking.' But this was not said with reference to that kind of knowing. For such knowing does not abandon the perception of a being, does not eradicate the notion of a self, and is neither a meditation subject nor the development of the foundations of mindfulness. This monk's knowing, however, abandons the perception of a being, eradicates the notion of a self, and is both a meditation subject and the development of the foundations of mindfulness. For this was said with reference to clearly comprehending in this way: 'Who is walking? Whose is the walking? For what reason does one walk?' The same method applies to standing and the other postures.

Tattha ko gacchatīti na koci satto vā puggalo vā gacchati. Kassa gamananti na kassaci sattassa vā puggalassa vā gamanaṃ. Kiṃ kāraṇā gacchatīti cittakiriyavāyodhātuvipphārena gacchati. Tasmā esa evaṃ pajānāti “gacchāmī”ti cittaṃ uppajjati, taṃ vāyaṃ janeti, vāyo viññattiṃ janeti, cittakiriyavāyodhātuvipphārena sakalakāyassa purato abhinīhāro gamananti vuccati. Ṭhānādīsupi eseva nayo.

Therein, 'Who walks?'—no being or person walks. 'Whose walking is it?'—it is not the walking of any being or person. 'For what reason does one walk?'—one walks due to the impulse of the air element produced by mental activity. Therefore, one understands thus: the thought 'I am walking' arises, that generates air, the air generates bodily intimation, and the forward movement of the entire body due to the impulse of the air element produced by mental activity is called 'walking.' The same method applies to standing and the other postures.

Tatrāpi hi “tiṭṭhāmī”ti cittaṃ uppajjati, taṃ vāyaṃ janeti, vāyo viññattiṃ janeti, cittakiriyavāyodhātuvipphārena sakalakāyassa koṭito paṭṭhāya ussitabhāvo ṭhānanti vuccati. “Nisīdāmī”ti cittaṃ uppajjati, taṃ vāyaṃ janeti, vāyo viññattiṃ janeti, cittakiriyavāyodhātuvipphārena heṭṭhimakāyassa samiñjanaṃ uparimakāyassa ussitabhāvo nisajjāti vuccati. “Sayāmī”ti cittaṃ uppajjati, taṃ vāyaṃ janeti, vāyo viññattiṃ janeti, cittakiriyavāyodhātuvipphārena sakalasarīrassa tiriyato pasāraṇaṃ sayananti vuccatīti.

In those cases too, the thought 'I am standing' arises; that generates the air element, the air element generates bodily intimation, and the upright state of the entire body, from the extremities upwards, due to the impulse of the air element produced by mental activity, is called 'standing.' The thought 'I am sitting' arises; that generates the air element, the air element generates bodily intimation, and the bending of the lower body and the upright state of the upper body, due to the impulse of the air element produced by mental activity, is called 'sitting.' The thought 'I am lying down' arises; that generates the air element, the air element generates bodily intimation, and the horizontal extension of the entire body, due to the impulse of the air element produced by mental activity, is called 'lying down.'

Tassa evaṃ pajānato evaṃ hoti “satto gacchati satto tiṭṭhatī”ti vuccati. Atthi pana koci satto gacchanto vā ṭhito vā natthi. Yathā pana “sakaṭaṃ gacchati sakaṭaṃ tiṭṭhatī”ti vuccati, na ca kiñci sakaṭaṃ nāma gacchantaṃ vā tiṭṭhantaṃ vā atthi. Cattāro pana goṇe yojetvā chekamhi sārathimhi pājente “sakaṭaṃ gacchati sakaṭaṃ tiṭṭhatī”ti vohāramattameva hoti, evameva ajānanaṭṭhena sakaṭaṃ viya kāyo. Goṇā viya cittajavātā. Sārathi viya cittaṃ. Gacchāmi tiṭṭhāmīti citte uppanne vāyodhātu viññattiṃ janayamānā uppajjati, cittakiriyavāyodhātuvipphārena gamanādīni pavattanti. Tato “satto gacchati, satto [M 1.0257] tiṭṭhati, ahaṃ gacchāmi, ahaṃ tiṭṭhāmī”ti vohāramattaṃ hotīti. Tenāha –

For one who understands thus, it occurs to him: it is said, 'A being goes, a being stands.' But is there any being that goes or stands? There is not. Just as it is said, 'The cart goes, the cart stands,' yet there is no thing called a cart that goes or stands. But when four oxen are yoked and a skilled driver urges them on, 'the cart goes, the cart stands' is merely a convention. In the same way, the body is like the cart in the sense of being insentient; the mind-generated winds are like the oxen; the mind is like the driver. When the thought 'I go' or 'I stand' arises, the air element arises generating bodily intimation, and through the impulse of the air element produced by mental activity, movements such as going occur. Therefore, 'a being goes,' 'a being stands,' 'I go,' 'I stand' is merely convention. Thus it is said:

“Nāvā [V 1.0263][P 1.0252] mālutavegena, jiyāvegena tejanaṃ;

Yathā yāti tathā kāyo, yāti vātāhato ayaṃ.

Just as a boat by the force of the wind, and an arrow by the force of the bowstring, so this body goes, impelled by the air element.

Yantaṃ suttavaseneva, cittasuttavasenidaṃ;

Payuttaṃ kāyayantampi, yāti ṭhāti nisīdati.

As a machine by the power of its strings, so this body-machine, yoked by the power of the mind's strings, goes, stands, and sits.

Ko nāma ettha so satto, yo vinā hetupaccaye;

Attano ānubhāvena, tiṭṭhe vā yadi vā vaje”ti.

What being is there here, who, without causes and conditions, could by his own power stand or go?

Tasmā evaṃ hetupaccayavaseneva pavattāni gamanādīni sallakkhento esa gacchanto vā gacchāmīti pajānāti, ṭhito vā, nisinno vā, sayāno vā sayānomhīti pajānātīti veditabbo.

Therefore, it should be understood that one who thus discerns that movements such as going occur solely by the power of causes and conditions, when going, knows, 'I am going'; when standing, knows, 'I am standing'; when sitting, knows, 'I am sitting'; or when lying down, knows, 'I am lying down.'

Yathā yathā vā panassa kāyo paṇihito hoti, tathā tathā naṃ pajānātīti sabbasaṅgāhikavacanametaṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yena yena vā ākārena tassa kāyo ṭhito hoti, tena tena naṃ pajānāti. Gamanākārena ṭhitaṃ gacchatīti pajānāti. Ṭhānanisajjāsayanākārena ṭhitaṃ sayānoti pajānātīti.

'And however his body is disposed, he knows it accordingly'—this is an all-inclusive statement. This is what is meant: in whatever manner his body is positioned, in that manner he knows it. When it is positioned in the manner of going, he knows, 'It is going.' When it is positioned in the manner of standing, sitting, or lying down, he knows accordingly.

Iti ajjhattaṃ vāti evaṃ attano vā catuiriyāpathapariggaṇhanena kāye kāyānupassī viharati. Bahiddhā vāti parassa vā catuiriyāpathapariggaṇhanena. Ajjhattabahiddhā vāti kālena attano, kālena parassa catuiriyāpathapariggaṇhanena kāye kāyānupassī viharati. Samudayadhammānupassī vātiādīsu pana “avijjāsamudayā rūpasamudayo”tiādinā (paṭi. ma. 1.49) nayena pañcahākārehi rūpakkhandhassa samudayo ca vayo ca nīharitabbo. Tañhi sandhāya idha “samudayadhammānupassī vā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Atthi kāyoti vā panassātiādi vuttasadisameva.

Thus, 'internally' means one dwells contemplating the body in the body by comprehending the four postures of oneself. 'Externally' means by comprehending the four postures of another. 'Both internally and externally' means one dwells contemplating the body in the body, at one time by comprehending the four postures of oneself, and at another time those of another. Regarding 'observing the nature of arising,' the arising and passing away of the form aggregate should be ascertained in five ways, according to the method shown in the phrase 'with the arising of ignorance, there is the arising of form' (Paṭisambhidāmagga 1.49). It is with reference to this that it is said here, 'observing the nature of arising,' and so on. The phrase 'there is a body' and so on is just as was stated previously.

Idha pana catuiriyāpathapariggāhikā sati dukkhasaccaṃ, tassā samuṭṭhāpikā purimataṇhā samudayasaccaṃ[V 1.0264], ubhinnaṃ appavatti nirodhasaccaṃ, dukkhaparijānano samudayapajahano nirodhārammaṇo ariyamaggo maggasaccaṃ. Evaṃ [M 1.0258] catusaccavasena ussakkitvā nibbutiṃ pāpuṇātīti idamekassa catūiriyāpathapariggāhakassa bhikkhuno yāva arahattā niyyānamukhanti.

Here, mindfulness that comprehends the four postures is the truth of suffering. The prior craving that gives rise to it is the truth of the origin of suffering. The non-arising of both is the truth of the cessation of suffering. The noble path that fully knows suffering, abandons its origin, and has cessation as its object is the truth of the path. Thus, having striven by means of the four truths, one attains Nibbāna. This is the door to deliverance, up to Arahantship, for a monk who comprehends the four postures.

Iriyāpathapabbavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the section on the postures is concluded.

Catusampajaññapabbavaṇṇanā

The Commentary on the Section on the Four Kinds of Clear Comprehension

109. Evaṃ [P 1.0253] iriyāpathavasena kāyānupassanaṃ vibhajitvā idāni catusampajaññavasena vibhajituṃ puna caparantiādimāha. Tattha abhikkante paṭikkanteti ettha tāva abhikkantaṃ vuccati gamanaṃ. Paṭikkantaṃ nivattanaṃ. Tadubhayampi catūsu iriyāpathesu labbhati. Gamane tāva purato kāyaṃ abhiharanto abhikkamati nāma. Paṭinivattento paṭikkamati nāma. Ṭhānepi ṭhitakova kāyaṃ purato onāmento abhikkamati nāma. Pacchato apanāmento paṭikkamati nāma. Nisajjāyapi nisinnakova āsanassa purimaaṅgābhimukho saṃsaranto abhikkamati nāma. Pacchimaaṅgappadesaṃ pacchā saṃsaranto paṭikkamati nāma. Nipajjāyapi eseva nayo.

109. Having thus analyzed the contemplation of the body in terms of postures, now, in order to analyze it in terms of the four kinds of clear comprehension, the text begins again with the phrase 'furthermore' (puna ca paraṃ) and so on. Here, regarding 'in going forward and returning' (abhikkante paṭikkante), 'going forward' (abhikkanta) is said to be advancing, and 'returning' (paṭikkanta) is turning back. Both are found in the four postures. In walking, moving the body forward is called 'going forward' (abhikkamati). Turning back is called 'returning' (paṭikkamati). Even while standing, bending the body forward is called 'going forward' (abhikkamati). Drawing it backward is called 'returning' (paṭikkamati). In sitting, though seated, moving forward toward the front part of the seat is called 'going forward' (abhikkamati). Moving backward toward the rear part of the seat is called 'returning' (paṭikkamati). The same principle applies to lying down.

Sampajānakārī hotīti sampajaññena sabbakiccakārī, sampajaññameva vā kārī. So hi abhikkantādīsu sampajaññaṃ karoteva, na katthaci sampajaññavirahito hoti. Tattha sātthakasampajaññaṃ sappāyasampajaññaṃ gocarasampajaññaṃ asammohasampajaññanti catubbidhaṃ sampajaññaṃ. Tattha abhikkamanacitte uppanne cittavaseneva agantvā “kiṃ nu me ettha gatena attho atthi natthī”ti atthānatthaṃ pariggaṇhitvā atthapariggahaṇaṃ sātthakasampajaññaṃ. Tattha ca atthoti cetiyadassanabodhidassanasaṅghadassanatheradassanaasubhadassanādivasena dhammato vaḍḍhi. Cetiyaṃ vā bodhiṃ vā disvāpi hi buddhārammaṇaṃ saṅghadassanena saṅghārammaṇaṃ pītiṃ uppādetvā tadeva khayavayato sammasanto arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti. There disvā tesaṃ ovāde patiṭṭhāya asubhaṃ disvā tattha paṭhamajjhānaṃ uppādetvā tadeva khayavayato sammasanto arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti. Tasmā etesaṃ dassanaṃ sātthakaṃ. Keci pana “āmisatopi vaḍḍhi atthoyeva, taṃ nissāya brahmacariyānuggahāya paṭipannattā”ti vadanti.

He acts with clear comprehension means he performs all activities with clear comprehension, or he acts solely with clear comprehension. For he indeed practices clear comprehension in going forward and so on, and is never devoid of clear comprehension in any situation. Herein, clear comprehension is fourfold: clear comprehension of purpose, clear comprehension of suitability, clear comprehension of resort, and clear comprehension of non-delusion. Here, when the thought of going arises, instead of going simply because of the mind's impulse, one considers, "Is there any benefit for me in going there, or not?" and discerns benefit or non-benefit. This discernment of benefit is clear comprehension of purpose. Herein, "benefit" refers to growth in the Dhamma through seeing shrines, seeing the Bodhi tree, seeing the Saṅgha, seeing elders, seeing the unattractive, and so on. For even after seeing a shrine or the Bodhi tree, one can arouse joy with the Buddha as the object; through seeing the Saṅgha, one can arouse joy with the Saṅgha as the object, and then, by contemplating that very joy as subject to destruction and vanishing, one attains arahantship. Having seen elders and establishing oneself in their advice, or seeing the unattractive and arousing the first jhāna based on that, and by contemplating that very jhāna as subject to destruction and vanishing, one attains arahantship. Therefore, seeing these things is purposeful. Some, however, say, "Growth in material gains is also a benefit, for one practices the holy life, supported by that."

Tasmiṃ [V 1.0265] pana gamane sappāyāsappāyaṃ pariggaṇhitvā sappāyapariggahaṇaṃ sappāyasampajaññaṃ. Seyyathidaṃ, cetiyadassanaṃ tāva sātthakaṃ. Sace pana cetiyassa [M 1.0259] mahāpūjāya dasadvādasayojanantare parisā sannipatanti. Attano vibhavānurūpaṃ itthiyopi purisāpi alaṅkatappaṭiyattā cittakammarūpakāni viya sañcaranti. Tatra cassa iṭṭhe ārammaṇe [P 1.0254] lobho, aniṭṭhe paṭigho, asamapekkhane moho uppajjati, kāyasaṃsaggāpattiṃ vā āpajjati, jīvitabrahmacariyānaṃ vā antarāyo hoti, evaṃ taṃ ṭhānaṃ asappāyaṃ hoti. Vuttappakāraantarāyābhāve sappāyaṃ. Bodhidassanepi eseva nayo. Saṅghadassanampi sātthaṃ. Sace pana antogāme mahāmaṇḍapaṃ kāretvā sabbarattiṃ dhammassavanaṃ kārentesu manussesu vuttappakāreneva janasannipāto ceva antarāyo ca hoti, evaṃ taṃ ṭhānaṃ asappāyaṃ. Antarāyābhāve sappāyaṃ. Mahāparisaparivārānaṃ therānaṃ dassanepi eseva nayo.

In that journey, having discerned what is suitable and unsuitable, the discernment of what is suitable is clear comprehension of suitability. For example, visiting a shrine is indeed purposeful. However, if a large crowd gathers for a major shrine festival within ten or twelve yojanas, and men and women, adorned and prepared according to their wealth, move about like painted figures, then desire may arise in him towards a pleasing object, aversion towards an unpleasing one, and delusion towards what is indifferent; or he may commit an offense involving physical contact, or there may be an obstacle to his life or his holy life. Thus, that place is unsuitable. In the absence of obstacles of the type mentioned, it is suitable. The same principle applies to seeing the Bodhi tree. Seeing the Saṅgha is also purposeful. However, if people construct a great pavilion within the village and have people listen to the Dhamma all night, there will be a gathering of crowds and the same obstacles as described before. Thus, that place is unsuitable. In the absence of obstacles, it is suitable. The same principle applies to seeing elders surrounded by large assemblies.

Asubhadassanampi sātthaṃ. Tadatthadīpanatthañca idaṃ vatthu – eko kira daharabhikkhu sāmaṇeraṃ gahetvā dantakaṭṭhatthāya gato. Sāmaṇero maggā okkamitvā purato gacchanto asubhaṃ disvā paṭhamajjhānaṃ nibbattetvā tadeva pādakaṃ katvā saṅkhāre sammasanto tīṇi phalāni sacchikatvā uparimaggatthāya kammaṭṭhānaṃ pariggahetvā aṭṭhāsi. Daharo taṃ apassanto “sāmaṇerā”ti pakkosi. So “mayā pabbajitadivasato paṭṭhāya bhikkhunā saddhiṃ dve kathā nāma na kathitapubbā. Aññasmimpi divase uparivisesaṃ nibbattessāmī”ti cintetvā “kiṃ, bhante”ti paṭivacanaṃ adāsi. Ehīti ca vutte ekavacaneneva āgantvā “bhante, iminā tāva maggena gantvā mayā ṭhitokāse muhuttaṃ puratthābhimukho ṭhatvā olokethā”ti āha. So tathā katvā tena pattavisesameva pāpuṇi. Evaṃ ekaṃ asubhaṃ dvinnaṃ janānaṃ atthāya jāyati. Evaṃ sātthampi panetaṃ purisassa mātugāmāsubhaṃ asappāyaṃ. Mātugāmassa ca purisāsubhaṃ sabhāgameva sappāyanti evaṃ sappāyapariggahaṇaṃ sappāyasampajaññaṃ nāma.

The perception of foulness is also purposeful. To illustrate this meaning, here is a story: A certain young monk, taking a novice, went to get a tooth-stick. The novice, stepping off the path and walking ahead, saw a foul object and produced the first jhāna. Making that his foundation, he contemplated the formations and realized the three fruits. Then, for the sake of the higher path, he took up a meditation subject and stood still. The young monk, not seeing him, called out, “Novice!” He thought, “Since the day I went forth, I have never spoken even two words with the monk. I will produce a higher distinction on another day,” and replied, “What is it, venerable sir?” And when told, “Come,” he approached at that single word and said, “Venerable sir, please go along this path for a moment, stand in the place where I stood, face east, and look.” He did so and attained the very same special attainment as the novice. Thus, one foul object arises for the benefit of two people. In this way, although it is purposeful, the foulness of a woman is unsuitable for a man, while for a woman, the foulness of a man is suitable by its very nature. Thus, the discernment of what is suitable is called the clear comprehension of suitability.

Evaṃ pariggahitasātthasappāyassa pana aṭṭhatiṃsāya kammaṭṭhānesu attano cittarucitakammaṭṭhānasaṅkhātaṃ gocaraṃ uggahetvā bhikkhācāragocare taṃ gahetvā gamanaṃ gocarasampajaññaṃ nāma. Tassāvibhāvatthaṃ idaṃ catukkaṃ veditabbaṃ. Idhekacco bhikkhu harati na paccāharati[V 1.0266], ekacco na harati paccāharati[M 1.0260], ekacco neva [P 1.0255] harati na paccāharati, ekacco harati ca paccāharati ca.

Now, for one who has thus discerned what is purposeful and suitable, the taking up of a meditation subject agreeable to one's own mind from among the thirty-eight meditation subjects—which is known as one's 'resort'—and going on the alms-round while holding to it, is called the clear comprehension of the resort. To make this clear, this tetrad should be understood: Here, a certain monk takes it but does not bring it back; a certain monk does not take it but brings it back; a certain monk neither takes it nor brings it back; and a certain monk both takes it and brings it back.

Tattha yo bhikkhu divasaṃ caṅkamena nisajjāya āvaraṇīyehi dhammehi cittaṃ parisodhetvā tathā rattiyā paṭhamaṃ yāmaṃ majjhime yāme seyyaṃ kappetvā pacchimayāmepi nisajjācaṅkamehi vītināmetvā pageva cetiyaṅgaṇabodhiyaṅgaṇavattaṃ katvā bodhirukkhe udakaṃ abhisiñcitvā pānīyaṃ paribhojanīyaṃ paccupaṭṭhapetvā ācariyupajjhāyavattādīni sabbāni khandhakavattāni samādāya vattati. So sarīraparikammaṃ katvā senāsanaṃ pavisitvā dve tayo pallaṅke usumaṃ gāhāpento kammaṭṭhānaṃ anuyuñjitvā bhikkhācāravelāya uṭṭhahitvā kammaṭṭhānasīseneva pattacīvaramādāya senāsanato nikkhamitvā kammaṭṭhānaṃ manasikarontova cetiyaṅgaṇaṃ gantvā sace buddhānussatikammaṭṭhānaṃ hoti, taṃ avissajjetvāva cetiyaṅgaṇaṃ pavisati. Aññaṃ ce kammaṭṭhānaṃ hoti, sopānapādamūle ṭhatvā hatthena gahitabhaṇḍaṃ viya taṃ ṭhapetvā buddhārammaṇaṃ pītiṃ gahetvā cetiyaṅgaṇaṃ āruyha mahantaṃ cetiyaṃ ce, tikkhattuṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā catūsu ṭhānesu vanditabbaṃ. Khuddakaṃ cetiyaṃ ce, tatheva padakkhiṇaṃ katvā aṭṭhasu ṭhānesu vanditabbaṃ. Cetiyaṃ vanditvā bodhiyaṅgaṇaṃ pattenāpi buddhassa bhagavato sammukhā viya nipaccakāraṃ dassetvā bodhi vanditabbo. So evaṃ cetiyañca bodhiñca vanditvā paṭisāmitaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā paṭisāmitabhaṇḍakaṃ hatthena gaṇhanto viya nikkhittakammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā gāmasamīpe kammaṭṭhānasīseneva cīvaraṃ pārupitvā gāmaṃ piṇḍāya pavisati.

In this case, there is a monk who, having purified his mind from the hindering states by walking and sitting during the day, likewise spends the first watch of the night, prepares his bed in the middle watch, and passes the last watch in sitting and walking. Early in the morning, having performed his duties in the cetiya-courtyard and the Bodhi-courtyard, sprinkled water on the Bodhi tree, set out drinking water and water for use, and undertaken all the duties from the Khandhakas, such as the duties towards teachers and preceptors, he attends to his bodily needs and enters his dwelling. Having generated warmth in his body over two or three cross-legged sittings, he applies himself to his meditation subject. When it is time for the alms-round, he rises and, taking his bowl and robe with his meditation subject at the forefront, he leaves his dwelling. Continuing to attend to his meditation subject, he goes to the cetiya-courtyard. If his meditation subject is the recollection of the Buddha, he enters the cetiya-courtyard without abandoning it. If it is another meditation subject, he stands at the foot of the stairs and sets it aside like an object held in the hand. Then, taking up joy with the Buddha as his object, he ascends to the cetiya-courtyard. If it is a large cetiya, he should circumambulate it three times and pay homage at four places. If it is a small cetiya, he should likewise circumambulate it and pay homage at eight places. Having paid homage to the cetiya, upon reaching the Bodhi-courtyard, he should pay homage to the Bodhi tree, showing reverence as if in the presence of the Blessed One. Having thus paid homage to the cetiya and the Bodhi tree, he goes to the place where he set it aside and takes up his meditation subject again, as if picking up a stored item with his hand. Keeping his meditation subject at the forefront, he puts on his robe near the village and enters the village for alms-food.

Atha naṃ manussā disvā “ayyo no āgato”ti paccuggantvā pattaṃ gahetvā āsanasālāyaṃ vā gehe vā nisīdāpetvā yāguṃ datvā yāva bhattaṃ na niṭṭhāti, tāva pāde dhovitvā telena makkhetvā purato nisīditvā pañhaṃ vā pucchanti, dhammaṃ vā sotukāmā honti. Sacepi na kathāpenti, janasaṅgahatthaṃ dhammakathā nāma kātabbāyevāti aṭṭhakathācariyā vadanti. Dhammakathā hi kammaṭṭhānavinimuttā nāma natthi[P 1.0256]. Tasmā kammaṭṭhānasīseneva dhammaṃ kathetvā kammaṭṭhānasīseneva āhāraṃ paribhuñjitvā anumodanaṃ katvā nivattiyamānehipi manussehi anugatova gāmato nikkhamitvā tattheva nivattetvā maggaṃ paṭipajjati. Atha naṃ puretaraṃ [V 1.0267] nikkhamitvā bahigāme [M 1.0261] katabhattakiccā sāmaṇeradaharabhikkhū disvā paccuggantvā pattacīvaramassa gaṇhanti.

Then, seeing him, the people say, “Our noble one has come!” and going out to meet him, they take his bowl and have him seated in an assembly hall or in a house. They give him rice-gruel, and while the meal is being prepared, they wash his feet, anoint them with oil, and sit before him, either asking questions or desiring to hear the Dhamma. The commentators say that even if they do not start a conversation, a Dhamma talk should be given for the sake of the people's welfare. For there is no Dhamma talk that is separate from a meditation subject. Therefore, having given a Dhamma talk with his meditation subject at the forefront, having eaten his meal with his meditation subject at the forefront, and having given the blessing, he leaves the village, followed by the people whom he is sending back. Having turned them back right there, he proceeds on his way. Then, the novices and young monks who had left earlier and finished their meal outside the village see him, go out to meet him, and take his bowl and robe.

Porāṇā bhikkhū kira “na amhākaṃ upajjhāyo ācariyo”ti mukhaṃ ulloketvā vattaṃ karonti. Sampattaparicchedeneva karonti. Te taṃ pucchanti “bhante, ete manussā tumhākaṃ kiṃ honti mātupakkhato sambandhā pitipakkhato”ti. Kiṃ disvā pucchathāti. Tumhesu etesaṃ pemaṃ bahumānanti. Āvuso, yaṃ mātāpitūhipi dukkaraṃ, taṃ ete amhākaṃ karonti, pattacīvarampi no etesaṃ santakameva, etesaṃ ānubhāvena neva bhaye bhayaṃ, na chātake chātakaṃ jānāma, edisā nāma amhākaṃ upakārino natthīti tesaṃ guṇe kathento gacchati, ayaṃ vuccati harati na paccāharatīti.

It is said that the monks of old perform their duties not by looking at the face to see if it is 'our preceptor' or 'our teacher'; they perform them simply by determining who has arrived. They ask him, “Venerable sir, what are these people to you? Are they related on your mother's side or your father's side?” He asks, “Having seen what, do you ask?” They reply, “The love and great respect these people have for you.” He says, “Friends, what is difficult even for mothers and fathers to do, these people do for us. Even our bowl and robes are theirs. Through their power, we know no fear when there is cause for fear, no hunger when there is cause for hunger. We have no benefactors such as these.” Thus he goes along, speaking of their virtues. This one is called: 'he carries away but does not bring back.'

Yassa pana pageva vuttappakāraṃ vattapaṭipattiṃ karontassa kammajatejo pajjalati, anupādinnakaṃ muñcitvā upādinnakaṃ gaṇhāti, sarīrato sedā muccanti, kammaṭṭhānavīthiṃ nārohati, so pageva pattacīvaramādāya vegasāva cetiyaṃ vanditvā gorūpānaṃ nikkhamanavelāyameva gāmaṃ yāgubhikkhāya pavisitvā yāguṃ labhitvā āsanasālaṃ gantvā pivati. Athassa dvattikkhattuṃ ajjhoharaṇamatteneva kammajatejo upādinnakaṃ muñcitvā anupādinnakaṃ gaṇhāti. Ghaṭasatena nhāto viya tejodhātupariḷāhanibbāpanaṃ patvā kammaṭṭhānasīsena yāguṃ paribhuñjitvā pattañca mukhañca dhovitvā antarābhatte kammaṭṭhānaṃ manasikatvā avasesaṭṭhāne piṇḍāya caritvā kammaṭṭhānasīsena āhāraṃ paribhuñjitvā tato paṭṭhāya poṅkhānupoṅkhaṃ upaṭṭhahamānaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvāva āgacchati, ayaṃ vuccati na harati paccāharatīti. Edisā ca bhikkhū yāguṃ pivitvā vipassanaṃ ārabhitvā buddhasāsane arahattaṃ pattā [P 1.0257] nāma gaṇanapathaṃ vītivattā, sīhaḷadīpeyeva tesu tesu gāmesu āsanasālāyaṃ na taṃ āsanaṃ atthi, yattha yāguṃ pivitvā arahattappattabhikkhū natthīti.

But for one who, while performing his duties in the manner described, has the bodily heat born of kamma blazing, releasing the unappropriated and seizing the appropriated, from whose body sweat pours, and for whom the path of the meditation subject does not arise—such a one, taking his bowl and robes, quickly pays homage at the cetiya and, at the very moment the cattle are driven out, enters the village for gruel. Having received gruel, he goes to the assembly hall and drinks it. Then, after swallowing just two or three mouthfuls, the bodily heat born of kamma releases the appropriated and grasps the unappropriated. Like one bathed with a hundred pots of water, he attains the quenching of the burning of the heat element. With the meditation subject as the focus, he partakes of the gruel, washes his bowl and mouth, and during the interval before the meal, he attends to his meditation subject. Afterwards, he goes for alms in the remaining places, partakes of his meal with the meditation subject as the focus, and from then on, he returns with the meditation subject continuously present, like an unbroken stream. This is called, 'He does not carry away, but he brings back.' Such monks, having drunk the gruel, begun insight meditation, and attained arahantship in the Buddha’s Dispensation—they are beyond reckoning. In the island of Sri Lanka itself, in those various villages, there is no seat in an assembly hall where monks have not attained arahantship after drinking gruel.

Yo pana pamādavihārī hoti nikkhittadhuro, sabbavattāni bhinditvā pañcavidhacetokhilavinibandhacitto viharanto “kammaṭṭhānaṃ nāma atthī”tipi saññaṃ akatvā gāmaṃ [V 1.0268] piṇḍāya pavisitvā ananulomikena gihisaṃsaggena saṃsaṭṭho caritvā ca bhuñjitvā ca tuccho nikkhamati, ayaṃ vuccati neva harati na paccāharatīti.

But whoever lives heedlessly, having laid down his burden, breaking all observances, dwelling with a mind bound by the five kinds of mental barrenness—without even the perception, 'There is such a thing as a meditation subject'—enters the village for alms, mingles with householders in an unsuitable manner, wanders and eats, and then leaves empty. This is called, 'He neither carries away nor brings back.'

Yo [M 1.0262] panāyaṃ harati ca paccāharati cāti vutto, so gatapaccāgatikavattavasena veditabbo. Attakāmā hi kulaputtā sāsane pabbajitvā dasapi vīsampi tiṃsampi cattālīsampi paññāsampi satampi ekato vasantā katikavattaṃ katvā viharanti, āvuso, tumhe na iṇaṭṭhā na bhayaṭṭā na jīvikāpakatā pabbajitā, dukkhā muccitukāmā panettha pabbajitā, tasmā gamane uppannakilesaṃ gamaneyeva niggaṇhatha, ṭhāne, nisajjāyaṃ, sayane uppannakilesaṃ sayaneyeva niggaṇhathāti. Te evaṃ katikavattaṃ katvā bhikkhācāraṃ gacchantā aḍḍhausabhausabhaaḍḍhagāvutagāvutantaresu pāsāṇā honti. Tāya saññāya kammaṭṭhānaṃ manasikarontāva gacchanti. Sace kassaci gamane kileso uppajjati, tattheva naṃ niggaṇhāti. Tathā asakkonto tiṭṭhati. Athassa pacchato āgacchantopi tiṭṭhati. So “ayaṃ bhikkhu tuyhaṃ uppannavitakkaṃ jānāti, ananucchavikaṃ te eta”nti attānaṃ paṭicodetvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā tattheva ariyabhūmiṃ okkamati. Tathā asakkonto nisīdati. Athassa pacchato āgacchantopi nisīdatīti soyeva nayo. Ariyabhūmiṃ okkamituṃ asakkontopi taṃ kilesaṃ vikkhambhetvā kammaṭṭhānaṃ manasikarontova gacchati. Na kammaṭṭhānavippayuttena cittena pādaṃ uddharati. Uddharati ce, paṭinivattetvā purimapadesaṃ yeva eti āḷindakavāsī mahāphussadevatthero viya.

And this one who is said to 'carry away and bring back,' he should be understood by way of the practice of going and returning. For sons of good families, desiring their own welfare, having gone forth into the Dispensation, living together in groups of ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, or a hundred, make a formal agreement and dwell thus: "Venerable sirs, you have not gone forth because of debt, or fear, or for a livelihood, but desiring liberation from suffering you have gone forth here. Therefore, when a defilement arises while walking, restrain it right there while walking; when one arises while standing, sitting, or lying down, restrain it right there while standing, sitting, or lying down." Having made such a formal agreement, when going for alms they become as steadfast as stones at intervals of half an usabha, an usabha, half a gāvuta, or a gāvuta. With that perception, they go along attending to their meditation subject. If a defilement arises in anyone while walking, he restrains it right there. If unable to do so, he stands still. Then, the one coming up behind him also stands still. Thinking, "This monk knows of your arisen thought; this is not appropriate for you," he reproaches himself, develops insight, and right there enters the noble stage. If unable to do so, he sits down. Then, the one coming up behind him also sits down—the same method applies. Even if unable to enter the noble stage, he suppresses that defilement and continues with his meditation subject, attending to it. He does not lift his foot with a mind disjoined from the meditation subject. If he does lift it, he turns back and returns to the original spot, like the Elder Mahāphussadeva, the Verandah-dweller.

So kira ekūnavīsativassāni gatapaccāgatikavattaṃ pūrento eva vihāsi. Manussāpi [P 1.0258] sudaṃ antarāmagge kasantā ca vapantā ca maddantā ca kammāni ca karontā theraṃ tathāgacchantaṃ disvā “ayaṃ thero punappunaṃ nivattitvā gacchati. Kiṃ nu kho maggamūḷho udāhu kiñci pamuṭṭho”ti samullapanti. So taṃ anādiyitvā kammaṭṭhānayuttacitteneva samaṇadhammaṃ karonto vīsativassabbhantare arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Arahattappattadivaseyevassa caṅkamanakoṭiyaṃ adhivatthā devatā aṅgulīhi dīpaṃ ujjāletvā aṭṭhāsi. Cattāropi mahārājāno sakko ca devānamindo brahmā ca sahampati upaṭṭhānaṃ agamaṃsu. Tañca obhāsaṃ disvā vanavāsīmahātissatthero taṃ dutiyadivase pucchi “rattibhāge āyasmato santike obhāso ahosi, kiṃ so obhāso”ti[V 1.0269]. Thero vikkhepaṃ karonto “obhāso nāma dīpobhāsopi hoti maṇiobhāsopī”ti evamādimāha. Tato [M 1.0263] paṭicchādetha tumheti nibaddho āmāti paṭijānitvā ārocesi kālavallimaṇḍapavāsī mahānāgatthero viya ca.

It is said that he lived for nineteen years fulfilling just this practice of going and returning. People too, while plowing, sowing, threshing, and doing other work along the road, seeing the Elder going thus, would say, "This Elder keeps turning back as he goes. Is he confused about the path, or has he forgotten something?" Ignoring them, with his mind yoked to the meditation subject, he performed the duties of a recluse and, within twenty years, attained arahantship. On the very day he attained arahantship, the deity dwelling at the end of his walking path lit a lamp with her fingers and stood there. The Four Great Kings, Sakka, king of the devas, and Brahmā Sahampati also came to attend upon him. Seeing that radiance, the Elder Mahātissa, the forest-dweller, asked him the next day: "Venerable sir, there was a radiance near you during the night. What was that radiance?" The Elder, wishing to be evasive, said: "Radiance can be the light of a lamp or the light of a gem," and so on. Then, being pressed with, "You are concealing it!" he admitted, "Yes," and related the matter, just like the Elder Mahānāga, the dweller of the Kālavallimaṇḍapa.

Sopi kira gatapaccāgatikavattaṃ pūrento paṭhamaṃ tāva bhagavato mahāpadhānaṃ pūjessāmīti satta vassāni ṭhānacaṅkamanameva adhiṭṭhāsi. Puna soḷasa vassāni gatapaccāgatikavattaṃ pūretvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. So kammaṭṭhānayutteneva cittena pādaṃ uddharanto viyuttena uddhate paṭinivattanto gāmassa samīpaṃ gantvā “gāvī nu pabbajito nū”ti āsaṅkanīyapadese ṭhatvā cīvaraṃ pārupitvā kacchakantarato udakena pattaṃ dhovitvā udakagaṇḍūsaṃ karoti. Kiṃ kāraṇā? Mā me bhikkhaṃ dātuṃ vandituṃ vā āgate manusse dīghāyukā hothāti vacanamattenāpi kammaṭṭhānavikkhepo ahosīti. Ajja, bhante, katimīti divasaṃ vā bhikkhugaṇanaṃ vā pañhe vā pucchito pana udakaṃ gilitvā ārocesi. Sace divasādipucchakā na honti, nikkhamanavelāya gāmadvāre niṭṭhubhitvāva yāti kalambatitthavihāre vassūpagatapaññāsabhikkhū viya.

It is said that he too, while fulfilling the practice of going and returning, first resolved, "I will honor the Great Striving of the Blessed One," and for seven years undertook only standing and walking meditation. After fulfilling the practice of going and returning for another sixteen years, he attained arahantship. With his mind yoked to the meditation subject, he would lift his foot; and when it was lifted with a disjoined mind, he would turn back. Approaching the village, he would stand in a place where one might wonder, "Is it a cow or a renunciate?" Then he would put on his robe, wash his alms bowl with water from a water-skin, and take a mouthful of water. For what reason? Lest there be a distraction from his meditation subject even by the mere utterance, "May you be long-lived," to people who came to offer alms or pay respects. If asked, "Venerable sir, what day is it today?" or about the number of monks, or other questions, he would swallow the water and then inform them. If there were no questioners about the day and so forth, upon leaving, he would spit at the village gate and go, just like the fifty monks who had entered the rains retreat at Kalambatittha Monastery.

Te kira āsāḷhīpuṇṇamāyaṃ katikavattaṃ akaṃsu “arahattaṃ appatvā aññamaññaṃ na ālapissāmā”ti. Gāmañca piṇḍāya pavisantā udakagaṇḍūsaṃ katvā pavisiṃsu. Divasādīsu [P 1.0259] pucchitesu vuttanayeneva paṭipajjiṃsu. Tattha manussā niṭṭhubhanaṃ disvā jāniṃsu, “ajjeko āgato, ajja dve”ti. Evañca cintesuṃ “kiṃ nu kho ete amhehiyeva saddhiṃ na sallapanti, udāhu aññamaññampi, yadi aññamaññaṃ na sallapanti, addhā vivādajātā bhavissanti, etha ne aññamaññaṃ khamāpessāmā”ti sabbe vihāraṃ gantvā paññāsāya bhikkhusu dvepi bhikkhū ekokāse nāddasaṃsu. Tato yo tesu cakkhumā puriso, so āha “na bho kalahakārakānaṃ okāso īdiso hoti, susammaṭṭhaṃ cetiyaṅgaṇaṃ bodhiyaṅgaṇaṃ, sunikkhittā sammajjaniyo, sūpaṭṭhapitaṃ pānīyaṃ paribhojanīya”nti. Te tatova nivattā, tepi bhikkhū antotemāseyeva arahattaṃ patvā mahāpavāraṇāya visuddhipavāraṇaṃ pavāresuṃ.

It is said that on the full moon day of Āsāḷhī, they made an agreement: "Until we attain arahantship, we will not speak to one another." Entering the village for alms, they took a mouthful of water and then entered. When questioned about the day and so forth, they proceeded in the manner stated. Seeing the spitting, the people knew: "Today one has come, today two." And they thought, "Why do they not converse with us, or indeed with each other? If they do not converse with each other, surely they must have fallen into a dispute. Come, let us make them ask forgiveness of each other." All went to the monastery, but among the fifty monks, they did not see even two monks in one place. Then a discerning man among them said, "Sirs, the dwelling of quarrelsome people is not like this. The courtyard of the shrine and the Bodhi tree is well-swept, the brooms are neatly placed, and drinking water and water for use are well-provided." They turned back from there. Within those three months, those monks attained arahantship, and on the great Pavāraṇā day, they performed the Pavāraṇā of purity.

Evaṃ kālavallimaṇḍapavāsī mahānāgatthero viya kalambatitthavihāre vassūpagatabhikkhū viya [V 1.0270] ca kammaṭṭhānayutteneva cittena pādaṃ uddharanto gāmasamīpaṃ [M 1.0264] patvā udakagaṇḍūsaṃ katvā vīthiyo sallakkhetvā yattha surāsoṇḍadhuttādayo kalahakārakā caṇḍahatthiassādayo vā natthi, taṃ vīthiṃ paṭipajjati. Tattha ca piṇḍāya caramāno na turitaturito viya javena gacchati. Na hi javena piṇḍapātiyadhutaṅgaṃ nāma kiñci atthi. Visamabhūmibhāgappattaṃ pana udakasakaṭaṃ viya niccalo hutvā gacchati. Anugharaṃ paviṭṭho ca taṃ dātukāmaṃ vā adātukāmaṃ vā sallakkhetuṃ tadanurūpaṃ kālaṃ āgamento bhikkhaṃ gahetvā antogāme vā bahigāme vā vihārameva vā āgantvā yathāphāsuke patirūpe okāse nisīditvā kammaṭṭhānaṃ manasikaronto āhāre paṭikūlasaññaṃ upaṭṭhāpetvā akkhabbhañjanavaṇalepanaputtamaṃsūpamāvasena naṃ paccavekkhanto aṭṭhaṅgasamannāgataṃ āhāraṃ āhāreti, neva davāya na madāya na maṇḍanāya na vibhūsanāya. Bhuttāvī ca udakakiccaṃ katvā muhuttaṃ bhattakilamathaṃ paṭippassambhetvā yathā purebhattaṃ, evaṃ pacchābhattaṃ. Yathā purimayāmaṃ, evaṃ pacchimayāmañca kammaṭṭhānameva manasi karoti, ayaṃ vuccati harati ca paccāharati cāti.

Thus, like the great elder Mahānāga who lived in the Kālavallimaṇḍapa, and like the monks who had entered the rains retreat at Kalambatittha Monastery, he lifts his foot with his mind yoked to the meditation subject. Upon reaching the vicinity of the village, he takes a mouthful of water, observes the streets, and proceeds along a path where there are no drunkards, rogues, troublemakers, or fierce elephants and horses. While walking for alms there, he does not go in a great hurry or with speed. For there is no ascetic practice whatsoever called 'speedy alms-gathering.' But when he reaches an uneven part of the ground, he goes steadily, like a water cart. Having entered a house, he discerns whether the people wish to give or not and waits for a suitable time. After receiving alms, whether inside the village, outside the village, or back at the monastery, he sits in a suitable and comfortable spot, attends to his meditation subject, and establishes the perception of the repulsiveness of food. Reflecting on it as lubricating an axle, dressing a wound, or like the flesh of one's own son, he partakes of the food endowed with eight factors—not for sport, nor for intoxication, nor for adornment, nor for beautification. Having eaten, he performs his water duties, and having allayed the fatigue of the meal for a moment, then, just as before the meal, so too after the meal; just as in the first watch of the night, so too in the last watch, he attends to his meditation subject. This is called 'he takes away and brings back.'

Idaṃ [P 1.0260] pana haraṇapaccāharaṇasaṅkhātaṃ gatapaccāgatikavattaṃ pūrento yadi upanissayasampanno hoti. Paṭhamavaye eva arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti. No ce paṭhamavaye pāpuṇāti, atha majjhimavaye. No ce majjhimavaye pāpuṇāti, atha pacchimavaye. No ce pacchimavaye pāpuṇāti, atha maraṇasamaye. No ce maraṇasamaye pāpuṇāti, atha devaputto hutvā. No ce devaputto hutvā pāpuṇāti, anuppanne buddhe nibbatto paccekabodhiṃ sacchikaroti. No ce paccekabodhiṃ sacchikaroti, atha buddhānaṃ sammukhībhāve khippābhiñño vā hoti seyyathāpi thero bāhiyo dārucīriyo, mahāpañño vā seyyathāpi thero sāriputto, mahiddhiko vā seyyathāpi thero mahāmoggallāno, dhutaṅgadharo vā seyyathāpi thero mahākassapo, dibbacakkhuko vā seyyathāpi thero anuruddho, vinayadharo vā seyyathāpi thero upāli, dhammakathiko vā seyyathāpi thero puṇṇo mantāṇiputto, āraññiko vā seyyathāpi thero revato, bahussuto vā seyyathāpi thero ānando, sikkhākāmo vā seyyathāpi thero rāhulo buddhaputtoti. Iti imasmiṃ catukke yvāyaṃ harati ca paccāharati ca, tassa gocarasampajaññaṃ sikhāpattaṃ hoti.
