While fulfilling this practice of going and returning, known as 'taking away and bringing back,' if one is endowed with supporting conditions, one attains arahantship in the first period of life. If one does not attain it in the first period, then in the middle period. If one does not attain it in the middle period, then in the last period. If one does not attain it in the last period, then at the moment of death. If one does not attain it at the moment of death, then after becoming a deva. If one does not attain it even after becoming a deva, then being reborn when no Buddha has arisen, one realizes the enlightenment of a Paccekabuddha. If one does not realize the enlightenment of a Paccekabuddha, then in the presence of Buddhas, one is either quick in higher knowledge, like the Elder Bāhiya Dārucīriya; or of great wisdom, like the Elder Sāriputta; or of great psychic power, like the Elder Mahāmoggallāna; or a holder of the ascetic practices, like the Elder Mahākassapa; or with the divine eye, like the Elder Anuruddha; or a holder of the Vinaya, like the Elder Upāli; or a Dhamma speaker, like the Elder Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta; or a forest dweller, like the Elder Revata; or greatly learned, like the Elder Ānanda; or desirous of training, like the Elder Rāhula, the Buddha's own son. Thus, for one who 'takes away and brings back,' the clear comprehension of the proper domain within this tetrad reaches its culmination.

Abhikkamādīsu [M 1.0265] pana asammuyhanaṃ asammohasampajaññaṃ. Taṃ evaṃ veditabbaṃ – idha bhikkhu abhikkamanto [V 1.0271] vā paṭikkamanto vā yathā andhaputhujjanā abhikkamādīsu “attā abhikkamati, attanā abhikkamo nibbattito”ti vā “ahaṃ abhikkamāmi, mayā abhikkamo nibbattito”ti vā sammuyhanti. Tathā asammuyhanto “abhikkamāmī”ti citte uppajjamāne teneva cittena saddhiṃ cittasamuṭṭhānā vāyodhātu viññattiṃ janayamānā uppajjati, iti cittakiriyavāyodhātuvipphāravasena ayaṃ kāyasammato aṭṭhisaṅghāto abhikkamati, tassevaṃ abhikkamato ekekapāduddharaṇe pathavīdhātu āpodhātūti dve dhātuyo omattā honti mandā, itarā dve adhimattā honti balavatiyo, tathā atiharaṇavītiharaṇesu. Vossajjane tejovāyodhātuyo omattā honti mandā, itarā dve adhimattā honti balavatiyo. Tathā sannikkhepanasannirumbhanesu. Tattha uddharaṇe pavattā [P 1.0261] rūpārūpadhammā atiharaṇaṃ na pāpuṇanti. Tathā atiharaṇe pavattā vītiharaṇaṃ, vītiharaṇe pavattā vossajjanaṃ, vossajjane pavattā sannikkhepanaṃ, sannikkhepane pavattā sannirumbhanaṃ na pāpuṇanti. Tattha tattheva pabbaṃ pabbaṃ sandhi sandhi odhi odhi hutvā tattakapāle pakkhittatilāni viya paṭapaṭāyantā bhijjanti. Tattha ko eko abhikkamati? Kassa vā ekassa abhikkamanaṃ? Paramatthato hi dhātūnaṃyeva gamanaṃ, dhātūnaṃ ṭhānaṃ, dhātūnaṃ nisajjanaṃ, dhātūnaṃ sayanaṃ, tasmiṃ tasmiñhi koṭṭhāse saddhiṃ rūpena –

But in going forward and so forth, non-confusion is the clear comprehension of non-delusion. This should be understood as follows: Here, a bhikkhu, when going forward or backward, does not become deluded in the way that blind ordinary people become deluded in going forward and so forth, thinking: 'A self goes forward, going forward is produced by a self,' or 'I go forward, going forward is produced by me.' Not being deluded thus, when the thought 'I am going forward' arises, the mind-originated air element, generating bodily intimation, arises together with that very mind. Thus, this heap of bones, conventionally called a body, goes forward by means of the activity of the mind and the expansion of the air element. As it thus goes forward, with each lifting of a foot, the earth element and the water element, these two elements, become diminished and weak, while the other two become augmented and strong; the same applies to carrying forward and carrying back. In putting down, the fire element and the air element become diminished and weak, while the other two become augmented and strong. The same applies to placing down and pressing down. Herein, the material and immaterial phenomena that occur during lifting do not reach carrying forward. Similarly, those that occur during carrying forward do not reach carrying back; those during carrying back do not reach putting down; those during putting down do not reach placing down; and those during placing down do not reach pressing down. At each and every point, joint by joint, connection by connection, limit by limit, they break apart, crackling like sesame seeds thrown into a hot pan. Here, who is the one who goes forward? Or whose going forward is it? In the ultimate sense, it is merely the elements that go, the elements that stand, the elements that sit, the elements that lie down. For in each of those divisions, together with form—

Aññaṃ uppajjate cittaṃ, aññaṃ cittaṃ nirujjhati;

Avīcimanusambandho, nadīsotova vattatīti.

One mind arises, another mind ceases; like the current of a river, it flows on in uninterrupted succession.

Evaṃ abhikkamādīsu asammuyhanaṃ asammohasampajaññaṃ nāmāti;

Niṭṭhito abhikkante paṭikkante sampajānakārī hotīti padassa attho;

Thus, non-delusion in going forward and so forth is called the clear comprehension of non-delusion. Here concludes the meaning of the phrase 'he acts with clear comprehension when going forward and returning.'

Ālokite vilokiteti ettha pana ālokitaṃ nāma purato pekkhanaṃ. Vilokitaṃ nāma anudisāpekkhanaṃ. Aññānipi heṭṭhā upari pacchato pekkhanavasena olokitaullokitāpalokitāni nāma [M 1.0266] honti, tāni idha na gahitāni. Sāruppavasena pana imāneva dve gahitāni, iminā vā mukhena sabbānipi tāni gahitānevāti.

Here, in 'in looking forward, in looking around,' 'looking forward' (ālokita) means looking ahead. 'Looking around' (vilokita) means looking in the intermediate directions. There are also other terms such as 'looking down' (olokita), 'looking up' (ullokita), and 'looking behind' (apalokita), which are ways of looking below, above, and behind, but they are not included here. However, for the sake of suitability, only these two are included. Or, by this very expression, all of them are to be understood as included.

Tattha [V 1.0272] “ālokessāmī”ti citte uppanne cittavaseneva anoloketvā atthapariggahaṇaṃ sātthakasampajaññaṃ. Taṃ āyasmantaṃ nandaṃ kāyasakkhiṃ katvā veditabbaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā – “sace, bhikkhave, nandassa puratthimā disā āloketabbā hoti, sabbaṃ cetasā samannāharitvā nando puratthimaṃ disaṃ āloketi, evaṃ me puratthimaṃ disaṃ ālokayato na abhijjhādomanassā pāpakā akusalā dhammā anvāssaveyyunti iti so tattha sampajāno hoti, sace, bhikkhave, nandassa pacchimā disā, uttarā disā, dakkhiṇā disā, uddhaṃ, adho, anudisā āloketabbā hoti, sabbaṃ cetaso samannāharitvā nando anudisaṃ āloketi. Evaṃ me anudisaṃ ālokayato…pe… sampajāno hotī”ti (a. ni. 8.9).

Therein, when the thought 'I will look' arises, grasping the purpose by means of the mind alone before looking is the clear comprehension of purposefulness. This should be understood by taking the Venerable Nanda, a body-witness, as an example. For this was said by the Blessed One: 'Monks, if Nanda wishes to look towards the eastern direction, having fully applied his mind, Nanda looks towards the eastern direction, thinking: "While I look towards the eastern direction, may no covetousness or displeasure, no evil unwholesome states, overwhelm me." Thus he acts with clear comprehension in that situation. If, monks, Nanda wishes to look towards the western direction, the northern direction, the southern direction, upwards, downwards, or the intermediate directions, having fully applied his mind, Nanda looks towards the intermediate direction, thinking: "While I look towards the intermediate directions… may no covetousness or displeasure, no evil unwholesome states, overwhelm me." Thus he acts with clear comprehension in that situation.' (A. Ni. 8.9)

Apica idhāpi pubbe vuttacetiyadassanādivaseneva sātthakatā ca sappāyatā ca veditabbā. Kammaṭṭhānassa pana avijahanameva gocarasampajaññaṃ. Tasmā khandhadhātuāyatanakammaṭṭhānikehi attano kammaṭṭhānavaseneva, kasiṇādikammaṭṭhānikehi [P 1.0262] vā pana kammaṭṭhānasīseneva ālokanavilokanaṃ kātabbaṃ. Abbhantare attā nāma āloketā vā viloketā vā natthi, ālokessāmīti pana citte uppajjamāne teneva cittena saddhiṃ cittasamuṭṭhānā vāyodhātu viññattiṃ janayamānā uppajjati. Iti cittakiriyavāyodhātuvipphāravaseneva heṭṭhimaṃ akkhidalaṃ adho sīdati, uparimaṃ uddhaṃ laṅgheti, koci yantakena vivaranto nāma natthi, tato cakkhuviññāṇaṃ dassanakiccaṃ sādhentaṃ uppajjatīti. Evaṃ sampajānanaṃ panettha asammohasampajaññaṃ nāma.

Moreover, here too, purposefulness and suitability should be understood in the same way as previously stated regarding seeing shrines and so on. Not abandoning the meditation subject, however, is the clear comprehension of the domain. Therefore, those whose meditation subject is the aggregates, elements, or sense bases should look and look around only in accordance with their own meditation subject. And those whose meditation subject is a kasiṇa or the like should look and look around only with the meditation subject as their main focus. Inside, there is no self that is a looker or a glancer. Yet, when the thought 'I will look' arises, the air element originated by that very mind, generating bodily intimation, arises together with the mind. Thus, through the force of the expansion of mental activity and the air element, the lower eyelid sinks down, and the upper eyelid lifts up—there is no one opening them with a mechanism. Then eye-consciousness arises, accomplishing the function of seeing. To clearly comprehend in this way is, herein, the clear comprehension of non-delusion.

Apica mūlapariññāāgantukatāvakālikabhāvavasenapettha asammohasampajaññaṃ veditabbaṃ. Mūlapariññāvasena tāva –

Furthermore, herein, the clear comprehension of non-delusion should be understood in terms of root-comprehension, adventitiousness, and temporariness. First, in terms of root-comprehension—

Bhavaṅgāvajjanañceva, dassanaṃ sampaṭicchanaṃ;

Santīraṇaṃ voṭṭhabbanaṃ, javanaṃ bhavati sattamaṃ.

Life-continuum and adverting, seeing and receiving; investigating, determining, and impulsion becomes the seventh.

Tattha bhavaṅgaṃ upapattibhavassa aṅgakiccaṃ sādhayamānaṃ pavattati, taṃ āvaṭṭetvā kiriyamanodhātu āvajjanakiccaṃ sādhayamānā, tannirodhā cakkhuviññāṇaṃ [M 1.0267] dassanakiccaṃ sādhayamānaṃ[V 1.0273], tannirodhā vipākamanodhātu sampaṭicchanakiccaṃ sādhayamānā, tannirodhā vipākamanoviññāṇadhātu santīraṇakiccaṃ sādhayamānā, tannirodhā kiriyamanoviññāṇadhātu voṭṭhabbapanakiccaṃ sādhayamānā, tannirodhā sattakkhattuṃ javanaṃ javati. Tattha paṭhamajavanepi “ayaṃ itthī, ayaṃ puriso”ti rajjanadussanamuyhanavasena ālokitavilokitaṃ na hoti. Dutiyajavanepi…pe… sattamajavanepi. Etesu pana yuddhamaṇḍale yodhesu viya heṭṭhupariyavasena bhijjitvā patitesu “ayaṃ itthī, ayaṃ puriso”ti rajjanādivasena ālokitavilokitaṃ hoti. Evaṃ tāvettha mūlapariññāvasena asammohasampajaññaṃ veditabbaṃ.

There, the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), performing the function of a factor of renewed existence, flows on. Having turned away from that, the functional mind-element (kiriyamanodhātu) performs the function of adverting; on its cessation, eye-consciousness performs the function of seeing; on its cessation, the resultant mind-element (vipākamanodhātu) performs the function of receiving; on its cessation, the resultant mind-consciousness-element (vipākamanoviññāṇadhātu) performs the function of investigating; on its cessation, the functional mind-consciousness-element (kiriyamanoviññāṇadhātu) performs the function of determining; on its cessation, impulsion (javana) occurs seven times. Here, even in the first impulsion, there is no looking or glancing with lust, aversion, or delusion, thinking, 'This is a woman, this is a man.' Similarly, in the second impulsion... and so on... even in the seventh impulsion. But when these have broken up and fallen in disarray, like warriors on a battlefield, then looking or glancing occurs with lust and so on, thinking, 'This is a woman, this is a man.' Thus, here, comprehension without delusion should be understood by way of root-comprehension.

Cakkhudvāre pana rūpe āpāthagate bhavaṅgacalanato uddhaṃ sakakiccaṃ nipphādanavasena āvajjanādīsu uppajjitvā niruddhesu avasāne javanaṃ uppajjati. Taṃ pubbe uppannānaṃ āvajjanādīnaṃ gehabhūte cakkhudvāre āgantukapuriso viya hoti. Tassa yathā paragehe kiñci yācituṃ paviṭṭhassa āgantukapurisassa gehasāmikesu tuṇhīmāsinesu āṇākaraṇaṃ na yuttaṃ. Evaṃ āvajjanādīnaṃ gehabhūte cakkhudvāre [P 1.0263] āvajjanādīsupi arajjantesu adussantesu amuyhantesu ca rajjanadussanamuyhanaṃ ayuttanti evaṃ āgantukabhāvavasena asammohasampajaññaṃ veditabbaṃ.

When a visible form comes into the range of the eye-door, after the disturbance of the life-continuum, the adverting and other processes, arising in succession to perform their respective functions, cease. At the end of these, the impulsion arises. This is like a visitor in the eye-door, which is the home of the previously arisen adverting and other processes. Just as it is not proper for a visitor who has entered another's house to issue commands while the householders are sitting silently, so too, in the eye-door—their home—when the adverting and other processes are without attachment, aversion, or delusion, it is improper for impulsion to arise with attachment, aversion, or delusion. Thus, comprehension without delusion should be understood by way of its adventitious nature.

Yāni pana tāni cakkhudvāre voṭṭhabbapanapariyosānāni cittāni uppajjanti, tāni saddhiṃ sampayuttadhammehi tattha tattheva bhijjanti, aññamaññaṃ na passantīti ittarāni tāvakālikāni honti. Tattha yathā ekasmiṃ ghare sabbesu mānusakesu matesu avasesassa ekassa taṅkhaṇeññeva maraṇadhammassa na yuttā naccagītādīsu abhirati nāma, evameva ekadvāre sasampayuttesu āvajjanādīsu tattha tattheva matesu avasesassa taṅkhaṇeññeva maraṇadhammassa javanassāpi rajjanadussanamuyhanavasena abhirati nāma na yuttāti evaṃ tāvakālikabhāvavasena asammohasampajaññaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Those consciousnesses that arise at the eye-door, ending in determination, break apart right there along with their associated mental factors, not seeing each other—thus they are transient and temporary. Here, just as in a house where all the people have died, it is not fitting for the remaining one, being subject to death at that very moment, to delight in dancing, singing, and so on, so too at a single sense door, when the associated factors such as adverting have ceased right there, it is not fitting for the remaining impulsion, also being subject to death at that very moment, to delight in terms of lust, aversion, or delusion. Thus, comprehension without delusion should be understood by way of its temporary nature.

Apica khandhāyatanadhātupaccayapaccavekkhaṇavasenapetaṃ veditabbaṃ. Ettha hi cakkhu ceva rūpañca rūpakkhandho, dassanaṃ viññāṇakkhandho, taṃsampayuttā vedanā vedanākkhandho, saññā saññākkhandho, phassādikā saṅkhārakkhandho. Evametesaṃ [M 1.0268] pañcannaṃ khandhānaṃ samavāye ālokanavilokanaṃ [V 1.0274] paññāyati. Tattha ko eko āloketi, ko viloketi? Tathā cakkhu cakkhāyatanaṃ, rūpaṃ rūpāyatanaṃ, dassanaṃ manāyatanaṃ, vedanādayo sampayuttadhammā dhammāyatanaṃ. Evametesaṃ catunnaṃ āyatanānaṃ samavāye ālokanavilokanaṃ paññāyati. Tattha ko eko āloketi, ko viloketi? Tathā cakkhu cakkhudhātu, rūpaṃ rūpadhātu, dassanaṃ cakkhuviññāṇadhātu, taṃsampayuttā vedanādayo dhammadhātu. Evametāsaṃ catunnaṃ dhātūnaṃ samavāye ālokanavilokanaṃ paññāyati. Tattha ko eko āloketi, ko viloketi? Tathā cakkhu nissayapaccayo, rūpaṃ ārammaṇapaccayo, āvajjanaṃ anantarasamanantarūpanissayanatthivigatapaccayo, āloko upanissayapaccayo vedanādayo sahajātapaccayo. Evametesaṃ paccayānaṃ samavāye ālokanavilokanaṃ paññāyati. Tattha ko eko āloketi, ko viloketīti? Evamettha khandhāyatanadhātupaccayapaccavekkhaṇavasenapi [P 1.0264] asammohasampajaññaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Furthermore, this should be understood through the contemplation in terms of aggregates, sense bases, elements, and conditions. Here, the eye and form constitute the form aggregate; seeing is the consciousness aggregate; the associated feeling is the feeling aggregate; perception is the perception aggregate; contact and the rest are the volitional formations aggregate. Thus, at the convergence of these five aggregates, looking and glancing are discerned. Here, who is it that looks? Who is it that glances? Similarly, the eye is the eye base, form is the form base, seeing is the mind base, and feeling and other associated factors are the mental phenomena base. Thus, at the convergence of these four bases, looking and glancing are discerned. Here, who is it that looks? Who is it that glances? Likewise, the eye is the eye element, form is the form element, seeing is the eye-consciousness element, and feeling and other associated factors are the mental phenomena element. Thus, at the convergence of these four elements, looking and glancing are discerned. Here, who is it that looks? Who is it that glances? Further, the eye is the dependence condition, form is the object condition, adverting is the immediately contiguous, immediately preceding, strong dependence, absence, and disappearance condition, light is the strong dependence condition, and feeling and the rest are the co-nascence condition. Thus, at the convergence of these conditions, looking and glancing are discerned. Here, who is it that looks? Who is it that glances? In this way, comprehension without delusion should also be understood through the contemplation in terms of aggregates, sense bases, elements, and conditions.

Samiñjite pasāriteti pabbānaṃ samiñjanapasāraṇe. Tattha cittavaseneva samiñjanapasāraṇaṃ akatvā hatthapādānaṃ samiñjanapasāraṇapaccayā atthānatthaṃ pariggahetvā atthapariggahaṇaṃ sātthakasampajaññaṃ. Tattha hatthapāde aticiraṃ samiñjetvā pasāretvā eva vā ṭhitassa khaṇe khaṇe vedanā uppajjanti, cittaṃ ekaggaṃ na labhati, kammaṭṭhānaṃ paripatati, visesaṃ nādhigacchati. Kāle samiñjentassa kāle pasārentassa pana tā vedanā na uppajjanti, cittaṃ ekaggaṃ hoti, kammaṭṭhānaṃ phātiṃ gacchati, visesamadhigacchatīti evaṃ atthānatthapariggahaṇaṃ veditabbaṃ.

In drawing in and stretching out—this refers to the bending and stretching of the limbs. Here, without merely bending and stretching by the power of mind, one should discern what is beneficial and what is not through the bending and stretching of the hands and feet, and thus the grasping of what is beneficial is clear comprehension of purpose. If one bends and stretches the hands and feet for too long, or having done so, remains still, sensations arise moment by moment, the mind does not gain concentration, the meditation subject deteriorates, and no special attainment is reached. But when bending and stretching at the proper time, those sensations do not arise, the mind becomes concentrated, the meditation subject flourishes, and special attainment is reached. Thus, the discernment of what is beneficial and what is not should be understood.

Atthe pana satipi sappāyāsappāyaṃ pariggaṇhitvā sappāyapariggahaṇaṃ sappāyasampajaññaṃ. Tatrāyaṃ nayo – mahācetiyaṅgaṇe kira daharabhikkhū sajjhāyaṃ gaṇhanti. Tesaṃ piṭṭhipasse daharabhikkhuniyo dhammaṃ suṇanti. Tatreko daharo hatthaṃ pasārento kāyasaṃsaggaṃ patvā teneva kāraṇena gihī jāto. Aparopi bhikkhu pādaṃ pasārento aggimhi pasāresi, aṭṭhiṃ āhacca pādo jhāyi. Aparo vammike pasāresi, so āsīvisena daṭṭho. Aparo cīvarakuṭidaṇḍake pasāresi, taṃ maṇisappo [M 1.0269] ḍaṃsi. Tasmā evarūpe asappāye apasāretvā sappāye pasāretabbaṃ. Idamettha sappāyasampajaññaṃ.

Moreover, even when there is a purpose, discerning what is suitable and unsuitable and then grasping what is suitable is clear comprehension of suitability. Herein is this method: In the great cetiya courtyard, it is said that young monks were reciting. Behind them, young nuns were listening to the Dhamma. There, one young monk, stretching out his hand, made physical contact and for that very reason became a layman. Another monk, stretching out his foot, stretched it into a fire; having struck a bone, his foot was burnt. Another stretched it into an anthill and was bitten by a venomous snake. Another stretched it towards the pole of a robe-hut, and a jeweled serpent bit him. Therefore, having refrained from stretching out in such an unsuitable place, one should stretch out in a suitable place. This, herein, is clear comprehension of suitability.

Gocarasampajaññaṃ [V 1.0275] pana mahātheravatthunā dīpetabbaṃ – mahāthero kira divāṭṭhāne nisinno antevāsikehi saddhiṃ kathayamāno sahasā hatthaṃ samiñjetvā puna yathāṭhāne ṭhapetvā saṇikaṃ samiñjesi. Taṃ antevāsikā pucchiṃsu “kasmā bhante sahasā hatthaṃ samiñjetvā puna yathāṭhāne ṭhapetvā saṇikaṃ samiñjayitthā”ti. Yato paṭṭhāyāhaṃ, āvuso, kammaṭṭhānaṃ manasikātuṃ āraddho, na me kammaṭṭhānaṃ muñcitvā hattho samiñjitapubbo, idāni pana tumhehi saddhiṃ kathayamānena kammaṭṭhānaṃ muñcitvā samiñjito, tasmā puna yathāṭhāne ṭhapetvā samiñjesinti. Sādhu, bhante, bhikkhunā nāma evarūpena [P 1.0265] bhavitabbanti. Evametthāpi kammaṭṭhānāvijahanameva gocarasampajaññanti veditabbaṃ.

Now, clear comprehension of the resort should be illustrated by the story of the great elder. It is said that a great elder, sitting in his day-abode and conversing with his resident pupils, suddenly bent his hand, then placed it back in its original position and bent it slowly. His resident pupils asked him, 'Venerable sir, why did you suddenly bend your hand, then place it back in its original position and bend it slowly?' 'Friends, from the time I began to attend to my meditation subject, my hand has never before been bent having abandoned the meditation subject. But just now, while conversing with you, it was bent having abandoned the meditation subject. Therefore, I placed it back in its original position and bent it again.' 'Excellent, venerable sir! A bhikkhu should indeed be of such a nature.' Thus, herein also, the non-abandonment of the meditation subject itself should be understood as clear comprehension of the resort.

Abbhantare attā nāma koci samiñjento vā pasārento vā natthi. Vuttappakāracittakiriyavāyodhātuvipphārena pana suttakaḍḍhanavasena dāruyantassa hatthapādalaḷanaṃ viya samiñjanapasāraṇaṃ hotīti evaṃ parijānanaṃ panettha asammohasampajaññanti veditabbaṃ.

Internally, there is no self whatsoever that contracts or extends. Rather, it is by the diffusion of the wind element, produced by the action of the mind in the aforesaid manner, that this contracting and extending occurs, just like the movement of the hands and feet of a wooden puppet by means of the pulling of strings. Thoroughly knowing it thus should be understood as the clear comprehension of non-delusion herein.

Saṅghāṭipattacīvaradhāraṇeti ettha saṅghāṭicīvarānaṃ nivāsanapārupanavasena pattassa bhikkhāpaṭiggahaṇādivasena paribhogo dhāraṇaṃ nāma. Tattha saṅghāṭicīvaradhāraṇe tāva nivāsetvā pārupitvā ca piṇḍāya carato āmisalābho “sītassa paṭighātāyā”tiādinā nayena bhagavatā vuttappakāroyeva ca attho attho nāma. Tassa vasena sātthakasampajaññaṃ veditabbaṃ.

In the phrase 'the wearing of the outer robe, bowl, and robes,' 'wearing' is the name for the use of the outer robe and robes by way of wearing the lower garment and putting on the upper garment, and of the bowl by way of receiving almsfood and so forth. Therein, firstly, with regard to wearing the outer robe and robes: for one who wanders for alms having worn the lower garment and put on the upper garment, the gain of material things has a purpose. The purpose is indeed of the very kind stated by the Blessed One in the passage beginning, 'For the warding off of cold...' By means of that, clear comprehension of purpose should be understood.

Uṇhapakatikassa pana dubbalassa ca cīvaraṃ sukhumaṃ sappāyaṃ. Sītālukassa ghanaṃ dupaṭṭaṃ. Viparītaṃ asappāyaṃ. Yassa kassaci jiṇṇaṃ asappāyameva. Aggaḷādidāne hissa taṃ palibodhakaraṃ hoti. Tathā paṭṭuṇṇadukūlādibhedaṃ lobhanīyacīvaraṃ. Tādisañhi araññe ekakassa nivāsantarāyakaraṃ jīvitantarāyakaraṃ vāpi hoti. Nippariyāyena pana yaṃ nimittakammādimicchājīvavasena uppannaṃ, yañcassa sevamānassa akusalā dhammā abhivaḍḍhanti, kusalā dhammā parihāyanti, taṃ asappāyaṃ. Viparītaṃ sappāyaṃ[M 1.0270]. Tassa vasenettha sappāyasampajaññaṃ, kammaṭṭhānāvijahanavaseneva ca gocarasampajaññaṃ veditabbaṃ.

However, for one of a hot temperament and for one who is weak, a thin robe is suitable. For one who is sensitive to cold, a thick, double-layered one is suitable. The opposite is unsuitable. For anyone, a worn-out robe is indeed unsuitable. For him, it becomes an impediment in matters such as giving a door-bolt. Likewise, a desirable robe, such as one of silk, wool, or fine linen, is unsuitable. Indeed, for one dwelling alone in the forest, such a thing can become a danger to his dwelling or even a danger to his life. But unconditionally, that which is produced by means of wrong livelihood such as hinting, and that which, when used by him, causes unwholesome states to increase and wholesome states to decline, is unsuitable. The opposite is suitable. By means of that, clear comprehension of suitability should be understood herein, and by means of not abandoning the meditation subject, clear comprehension of the resort.

Abbhantare attā nāma koci cīvaraṃ pārupanto natthi. Vuttappakāracittakiriyavāyodhātuvipphāreneva [V 1.0276] pana cīvarapārupanaṃ hoti. Tattha cīvarampi acetanaṃ, kāyopi acetano. Cīvaraṃ na jānāti “mayā kāyo pāruto”ti. Kāyopi na jānāti “ahaṃ cīvarena pāruto”ti, dhātuyova dhātusamūhaṃ paṭicchādenti paṭapilotikāya potthakarūpapaṭicchādane viya. Tasmā neva sundaraṃ cīvaraṃ labhitvā somanassaṃ kātabbaṃ, na asundaraṃ labhitvā domanassaṃ. Nāgavammikacetiyarukkhādīsu [P 1.0266] hi keci mālāgandhadhūmavatthādīhi sakkāraṃ karonti, keci gūthamuttakaddamadaṇḍasatthappahārādīhi asakkāraṃ, na te nāgavammikarukkhādayo somanassaṃ vā domanassaṃ vā karonti; evameva neva sundaraṃ cīvaraṃ labhitvā somanassaṃ kātabbaṃ, na asundaraṃ labhitvā domanassanti evaṃ pavattapaṭisaṅkhānavasena panettha asammohasampajaññaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Internally, there is no self whatsoever that puts on the robe. Rather, it is solely by the diffusion of the wind element, produced by the action of the mind in the aforesaid manner, that the putting on of the robe occurs. Therein, the robe is insentient, and the body is also insentient. The robe does not know, 'The body is covered by me.' The body also does not know, 'I am covered by the robe.' It is just elements covering a collection of elements, like the covering of a plaster figure with a strip of cloth. Therefore, one should not create gladness upon receiving a beautiful robe, nor dejection upon receiving an unattractive one. For some make offerings to Nāga-anthills, shrines, trees, and so on with garlands, perfumes, incense, and cloth, while others show disrespect with excrement, urine, mud, sticks, and blows from weapons; yet those Nāga-anthills, trees, and so on create neither gladness nor dejection. In the very same way, one should not create gladness upon receiving a beautiful robe, nor dejection upon receiving an unattractive one. Thus, by means of reflection on this process, clear comprehension of non-delusion should be understood herein.

Pattadhāraṇepi pattaṃ sahasāva aggahetvā imaṃ gahetvā piṇḍāya caramāno bhikkhaṃ labhissāmīti evaṃ pattagahaṇapaccayā paṭilabhitabbaatthavasena sātthakasampajaññaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Also in the case of carrying the bowl, not taking the bowl hastily, but reflecting, 'Having taken this and wandering for alms, I will obtain almsfood'—thus, by means of the purpose to be obtained which is conditioned by the taking of the bowl, clear comprehension of purpose should be understood.

Kisadubbalasarīrassa pana garu patto asappāyo. Yassa kassaci catupañcagaṇḍikāhato dubbisodhanīyo asappāyova. Duddhotapatto hi na vaṭṭati, taṃ dhovantasseva cassa palibodho hoti. Maṇivaṇṇapatto pana lobhanīyo cīvare vuttanayeneva asappāyo. Nimittakammādivasena laddho pana yañcassa sevamānassa akusalā dhammā abhivaḍḍhanti, kusalā dhammā parihāyanti, ayaṃ ekantaasappāyova. Viparīto sappāyo. Tassa vasenettha sappāyasampajaññaṃ, kammaṭṭhānāvijahanavaseneva ca gocarasampajaññaṃ veditabbaṃ.

However, for one with an emaciated and weak body, a heavy bowl is unsuitable. For anyone, a bowl that is patched in four or five places and is difficult to clean is indeed unsuitable. For a bowl that is difficult to wash is not allowable, and for him, the washing of it becomes an impediment. Furthermore, a desirable bowl of a jewel-like color is unsuitable, in the same way as was stated concerning the robe. But that which is obtained by means of hinting and so on, and that which, when used by him, causes unwholesome states to increase and wholesome states to decline—this is absolutely unsuitable. The opposite is suitable. By means of that, clear comprehension of suitability should be understood herein, and by means of not abandoning the meditation subject, clear comprehension of the resort.

Abbhantare attā nāma koci pattaṃ gaṇhanto natthi. Vuttappakāracittakiriyavāyodhātuvipphāreneva pana pattaggahaṇaṃ nāma hoti. Tattha pattopi acetano, hatthāpi acetanā. Patto na jānāti “ahaṃ hatthehi gahito”ti. Hatthāpi na jānanti “patto amhehi gahito”ti. Dhātuyova [M 1.0271] dhātusamūhaṃ gaṇhanti saṇḍāsena aggivaṇṇapattaggahaṇe viyāti evaṃ pavattapaṭisaṅkhānavasenettha asammohasampajaññaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Internally, there is no self whatsoever who takes the bowl. Rather, it is solely by the diffusion of the wind element, produced by the action of the mind in the aforesaid manner, that the taking of the bowl occurs. Therein, the bowl is insentient, and the hands are also insentient. The bowl does not know, 'I am taken by the hands.' The hands also do not know, 'The bowl is taken by us.' It is merely elements grasping a group of elements, like grasping a burning-hot bowl with tongs. Thus, by means of reflection on this process, clear comprehension of non-delusion should be understood herein.

Apica yathā chinnahatthapāde vaṇamukhehi paggharitapubbalohitakimikule nīlamakkhikasamparikiṇṇe anāthasālāyaṃ nipanne anāthamanusse disvā dayālukā purisā tesaṃ vaṇapaṭṭacoḷakāni [V 1.0277] ceva kapālādīhi ca bhesajjāni upanāmenti. Tattha coḷakānipi kesañci saṇhāni, kesañci thūlāni pāpuṇanti. Bhesajjakapālakānipi kesañci susaṇṭhānāni, kesañci dussaṇṭhānāni pāpuṇanti, na te tattha sumanā vā dummanā vā honti. Vaṇappaṭicchādanamatteneva hi coḷakena bhesajjapaṭiggahaṇamatteneva ca kapālakena [P 1.0267] tesamattho, evameva yo bhikkhu vaṇacoḷakaṃ viya cīvaraṃ, bhesajjakapālakaṃ viya pattaṃ, kapāle bhesajjamiva ca patte laddhaṃ bhikkhaṃ sallakkheti. Ayaṃ saṅghāṭipattacīvaradhāraṇe asammohasampajaññena uttamasampajānakārīti veditabbo.

Moreover, just as when compassionate men, seeing helpless people with severed hands and feet, lying in a charity hospital, their wound openings oozing pus and blood, swarming with maggots and blue flies, bring them wound-bandages and medicines in bowls and so forth—there some receive fine cloths, others coarse; some receive well-shaped medicinal bowls, others ill-shaped—yet they are neither pleased nor displeased there. Indeed, their purpose is merely to cover the wounds with the cloth and to receive medicine with the bowl. In the same way, a bhikkhu regards his robe as a wound-bandage, his bowl as a medicinal bowl, and the almsfood received in the bowl as medicine in a bowl. Such a bhikkhu, who wears the triple robe and carries the bowl with clear comprehension of non-delusion, is to be known as one who acts with the highest clear comprehension.

Asitādīsu asiteti piṇḍapātabhojane. Pīteti yāguādipāne. Khāyiteti piṭṭhakhajjakādikhādane. Sāyiteti madhuphāṇitādisāyane. Tattha “neva davāyā”tiādinā nayena vutto aṭṭhavidhopi attho attho nāma. Tassa vasena sātthakasampajaññaṃ veditabbaṃ. Lūkhapaṇītatittamadhurādīsu pana yena bhojanena yassa aphāsu hoti, taṃ tassa asappāyaṃ. Yaṃ pana nimittakammādivasena paṭiladdhaṃ, yañcassa bhuñjato akusalā dhammā abhivaḍḍhanti, kusalā dhammā parihāyanti, taṃ ekantaasappāyameva. Viparītaṃ sappāyaṃ. Tassa vasenettha sappāyasampajaññaṃ, kammaṭṭhānāvijahanavaseneva ca gocarasampajaññaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Among 'eating, drinking, chewing, and tasting,' 'eating' refers to consuming solid food. 'Drinking' refers to drinking beverages like gruel. 'Chewing' refers to chewing things like flour-based snacks. 'Tasting' refers to tasting things like honey and molasses. Here, the eightfold purpose stated in the manner beginning with 'not for amusement' is indeed the purpose. In accordance with that, purposeful clear comprehension should be understood. However, among coarse, refined, bitter, sweet, and so forth, whatever food causes discomfort to someone is unsuitable for him. But that which is obtained through hinting and the like, and that which, when consumed, increases unwholesome states and decreases wholesome states, that is entirely unsuitable. The opposite is suitable. In accordance with that, suitable clear comprehension should be understood here, and also clear comprehension of the domain, by way of not abandoning the meditation subject.

Abbhantare attā nāma koci bhuñjako natthi, vuttappakāracittakiriyavāyodhātuvipphāravaseneva pana pattapaṭiggahaṇaṃ nāma hoti. Cittakiriyavāyodhātuvipphāreneva hatthassa patte otāraṇaṃ nāma hoti. Cittakiriyavāyodhātuvipphāreneva ālopakaraṇaṃ ālopauddharaṇaṃ mukhavivaraṇañca hoti. Na koci kuñcikāya yantakena ca hanukaṭṭhīni vivarati, cittakiriyavāyodhātuvipphāreneva ālopassa mukhe ṭhapanaṃ, uparidantānaṃ musalakiccasādhanaṃ, heṭṭhādantānaṃ udukkhalakiccasādhanaṃ, jivhāya hatthakiccasādhanañca hoti.

Inside, there is no eater called a self. However, the receiving of the bowl occurs simply by means of the agitation of the wind element born of mental activity, as previously described. The lowering of the hand into the bowl occurs simply by means of the agitation of the wind element born of mental activity. The making of a morsel, the lifting of the morsel, and the opening of the mouth also occur simply by means of the agitation of the wind element born of mental activity. No one opens the jawbones with a key or a mechanism. The placing of the morsel in the mouth, the upper teeth performing the function of a pestle, the lower teeth performing the function of a mortar, and the tongue performing the function of a hand—all occur simply by means of the agitation of the wind element born of mental activity.

Iti [M 1.0272] taṃ tattha aggajivhāya tanukakheḷo mūlajivhāya bahalakheḷo makkheti. Taṃ heṭṭhādantaudukkhale jivhāhatthaparivattitaṃ kheḷaudakatemitaṃ uparidantamusalasañcuṇṇitaṃ koci kaṭacchunā vā dabbiyā vā antopavesento nāma natthi, vāyodhātuyāva pavisati. Paviṭṭhaṃ paviṭṭhaṃ koci palālasantharaṃ katvā dhārento nāma natthi, vāyodhātuvaseneva tiṭṭhati. Ṭhitaṃ ṭhitaṃ [V 1.0278] koci uddhanaṃ katvā aggiṃ jāletvā pacanto nāma natthi, tejodhātuyāva paccati. Pakkaṃ pakkaṃ [P 1.0268] koci daṇḍena vā yaṭṭhiyā vā bahi nīhārako nāma natthi, vāyodhātuyeva nīharati.

Thus, there, thin saliva from the tip of the tongue and thick saliva from the base of the tongue smear it. That food, turned over by the tongue-hand in the lower-teeth-mortar, moistened with saliva-water, and crushed by the upper-teeth-pestle—no one inserts it inside with a spoon or ladle; it enters by means of the wind element alone. What has entered, no one holds by making a straw-bed; it remains by means of the wind element alone. What has remained, no one cooks by making a hearth and kindling a fire; it is cooked by means of the fire element alone. What has been cooked, no one takes it out with a stick or rod; the wind element alone takes it out.

Iti vāyodhātu atiharati ca vītiharati ca dhāreti ca parivatteti ca sañcuṇṇeti visoseti ca nīharati ca. Pathavīdhātu dhāreti ca parivatteti ca sañcuṇṇeti ca visoseti ca. Āpodhātu sineheti ca allattañca anupāleti. Tejodhātu antopaviṭṭhaṃ paripāceti. Ākāsadhātu añjaso hoti. Viññāṇadhātu tattha tattha sammāpayogamanvāya ābhujatīti evaṃpavattapaṭisaṅkhānavasenettha asammohasampajaññaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Thus, the wind element propels, distributes, maintains, revolves, pulverizes, dries up, and eliminates. The earth element maintains, revolves, pulverizes, and dries up. The water element causes cohesion and maintains moisture. The fire element digests what has entered within. The space element provides a path. The consciousness element inclines towards this or that in accordance with proper application. In this way, undeluded clear comprehension should be understood here through reflection on this ongoing process.

Apica gamanato pariyesanato paribhogato āsayato nidhānato aparipakkato paripakkato phalato nissandato sammakkhaṇatoti evaṃ dasavidhapaṭikūlabhāvapaccavekkhaṇatopettha asammohasampajaññaṃ veditabbaṃ. Vitthārakathā panettha visuddhimagge āhārapaṭikūlasaññāniddesato gahetabbā.

Furthermore, undeluded clear comprehension should be understood here through reflection on the ten aspects of repulsiveness: by way of going, seeking, consuming, the receptacle, the repository, the undigested, the digested, the result, the outflow, and the smearing. The detailed explanation on this should be taken from the Visuddhimagga’s section on the exposition of the perception of repulsiveness in food.

Uccārapassāvakammeti uccārassa ca passāvassa ca karaṇe. Tattha pattakāle uccārapassāvaṃ akarontassa sakalasarīrato sedā muccanti, akkhīni bhamanti, cittaṃ na ekaggaṃ hoti, aññe ca rogā uppajjanti. Karontassa pana sabbaṃ taṃ na hotīti ayamettha attho. Tassa vasena sātthakasampajaññaṃ veditabbaṃ. Aṭṭhāne uccārapassāvaṃ karontassa pana āpatti hoti, ayaso vaḍḍhati, jīvitantarāyo hoti. Patirūpe ṭhāne karontassa sabbaṃ taṃ na hotīti idamettha sappāyaṃ. Tassa vasena sappāyasampajaññaṃ, kammaṭṭhānāvijahanavaseneva ca gocarasampajaññaṃ veditabbaṃ.

‘In the act of defecating and urinating’ refers to the doing of defecation and urination. Here, if one does not defecate and urinate at the proper time, sweat oozes from the entire body, the eyes spin, the mind is not concentrated, and other illnesses arise. But for one who does so, none of that occurs—this is the purpose here. In accordance with this, purposeful clear comprehension should be understood. However, for one who defecates and uricates in an improper place, an offense is incurred, disrepute grows, and there is danger to life. But for one who does so in a suitable place, none of that occurs—this is the suitability here. In accordance with this, suitable clear comprehension, and clear comprehension of the proper resort, should be understood by way of not abandoning the meditation subject.

Abbhantare [M 1.0273] attā nāma koci uccārapassāvaṃ karonto natthi. Cittakiriyavāyodhātuvipphāreneva pana uccārapassāvakammaṃ hoti. Yathā pana pakke gaṇḍe gaṇḍabhedena pubbalohitaṃ akāmatāya nikkhamati, yathā ca atibharitā udakabhājanā udakaṃ akāmatāya nikkhamati, evaṃ pakkāsayamuttavatthīsu sannicitā uccārapassāvā vāyuvegasamuppīḷitā [V 1.0279] akāmatāyapi nikkhamanti. So panāyaṃ evaṃ nikkhamanto uccārapassāvo neva tassa bhikkhuno attano hoti, na parassa. Kevalaṃ sarīranissandova [P 1.0269] hoti. Yathā kiṃ? Yathā udakakumbhato purāṇaudakaṃ chaḍḍentassa neva taṃ attano hoti, na paresaṃ. Kevalaṃ paṭijagganamattameva hoti. Evaṃpavattapaṭisaṅkhānavasenettha asammohasampajaññaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Within, there is no being called a self that defecates or uricates. Rather, the act of defecation and urination occurs simply by means of the agitation of the wind element born of mental activity. Just as pus and blood are discharged without volition when a ripe abscess bursts, or just as water flows out without volition from an overfilled water vessel, so too, the feces and urine accumulated in the stomach and bladder, when pressed by the force of the wind, are expelled even without volition. And this feces and urine thus expelled belong neither to that monk himself, nor to another. It is simply a bodily discharge. What is it like? It is like old water that one throws out of a water pot, which belongs neither to oneself nor to others. It is merely a matter of maintenance. Herein, through reflection on this ongoing process, the clear comprehension that is non-delusion should be understood.

Gatādīsu gateti gamane. Ṭhiteti ṭhāne. Nisinneti nisajjāya. Sutteti sayane. Jāgariteti jāgaraṇe. Bhāsiteti kathane. Tuṇhībhāveti akathane. “Gacchanto vā gacchāmīti pajānāti, ṭhito vā ṭhitomhīti pajānāti, nisinno vā nisinnomhīti pajānāti, sayāno vā sayānomhīti pajānātī”ti imasmiñhi ṭhāne addhānairiyāpathā kathitā. “Abhikkante paṭikkante ālokite vilokite samiñjite pasārite”ti imasmiṃ majjhimā. “Gate ṭhite nisinne sutte jāgarite”ti idha pana khuddakacuṇṇikairiyāpathā kathitā. Tasmā etesupi vuttanayeneva sampajānakāritā veditabbā.

Regarding ‘going,’ etc.: ‘going’ refers to walking; ‘standing’ refers to being stationary; ‘sitting’ refers to the posture of sitting; ‘lying down’ refers to reclining; ‘being awake’ refers to wakefulness; ‘speaking’ refers to talking; ‘being silent’ refers to not talking. In the passage, “When walking, one knows, ‘I am walking’; when standing, one knows, ‘I am standing’; when sitting, one knows, ‘I am sitting’; when lying down, one knows, ‘I am lying down,’” the long-course postures are discussed. In the passage, “When going forward, when returning, when looking ahead, when looking around, when bending, when stretching,” the intermediate postures are discussed. Here, in the passage, “When going, standing, sitting, lying down, being awake,” the minor and momentary postures are discussed. Therefore, in these cases too, the practice of acting with clear comprehension should be understood in the manner explained.

Tipiṭakamahāsīvatthero panāha – yo ciraṃ gantvā vā caṅkamitvā vā aparabhāge ṭhito iti paṭisañcikkhati “caṅkamanakāle pavattā rūpārūpadhammā ettheva niruddhā”ti, ayaṃ gate sampajānakārī nāma. Yo sajjhāyaṃ vā karonto pañhaṃ vā vissajjento kammaṭṭhānaṃ vā manasikaronto ciraṃ ṭhatvā aparabhāge nisinno iti paṭisañcikkhati “ṭhitakāle pavattā rūpārūpadhammā ettheva niruddhā”ti, ayaṃ ṭhite sampajānakārī nāma. Yo sajjhāyādikaraṇavaseneva ciraṃ nisīditvā aparabhāge nipanno iti paṭisañcikkhati “nisinnakāle pavattā rūpārūpadhammā ettheva niruddhā”ti, ayaṃ nisinne sampajānakārī nāma. Yo pana nipannako sajjhāyaṃ vā karonto kammaṭṭhānaṃ vā manasikaronto niddaṃ okkamitvā aparabhāge vuṭṭhāya [M 1.0274] iti paṭisañcikkhati “sayanakāle pavattā rūpārūpadhammā ettheva niruddhā”ti, ayaṃ sutte jāgarite ca sampajānakārī nāma. Kiriyamayacittānañhi appavattaṃ suttaṃ nāma, pavattaṃ jāgaritaṃ nāmāti. Yo pana bhāsamāno “ayaṃ saddo nāma oṭṭhe ca paṭicca dante ca jivhañca tāluñca paṭicca cittassa tadanurūpaṃ payogaṃ paṭicca jāyatī”ti sato sampajāno bhāsati, ciraṃ vā pana kālaṃ sajjhāyaṃ vā katvā dhammaṃ vā kathetvā kammaṭṭhānaṃ [V 1.0280] vā parivattetvā pañhaṃ vā vissajjetvā aparabhāge tuṇhībhūto [P 1.0270] iti paṭisañcikkhati “bhāsitakāle uppannā rūpārūpadhammā ettheva niruddhā”ti, ayaṃ bhāsite sampajānakārī nāma. Yo tuṇhībhūto ciraṃ dhammaṃ vā kammaṭṭhānaṃ vā manasikatvā aparabhāge iti paṭisañcikkhati “tuṇhībhūtakāle pavattā rūpārūpadhammā ettheva niruddhā, upādārūpapavattiyā sati bhāsati nāma, asati tuṇhī bhavati nāmā”ti, ayaṃ tuṇhībhāve sampajānakārī nāmāti.

The Elder Mahāsīva, master of the Tipiṭaka, however, said: One who, after walking or pacing for a long time, later reflects while standing, “The material and immaterial phenomena that occurred during the time of walking have ceased right here”—this is called one who acts with clear comprehension in going. One who, while reciting, answering a question, or attending to a meditation subject, stands for a long time and later reflects while sitting, “The material and immaterial phenomena that occurred during the time of standing have ceased right here”—this is called one who acts with clear comprehension in standing. One who, by means of reciting and so on, sits for a long time and later reflects while lying down, “The material and immaterial phenomena that occurred during the time of sitting have ceased right here”—this is called one who acts with clear comprehension in sitting. One who, while lying down, reciting, or attending to a meditation subject, falls asleep, and later reflects upon waking, “The material and immaterial phenomena that occurred during the time of lying down have ceased right here”—this is called one who acts with clear comprehension in sleeping and in being awake. For the non-occurrence of functional consciousness is called 'sleep'; its occurrence is called 'being awake.' One who, while speaking, mindfully and with clear comprehension understands, “This sound arises in dependence on the lips, the teeth, the tongue, and the palate, and in dependence on the mind’s corresponding effort,” or who, after reciting for a long time, or teaching the Dhamma, or reviewing a meditation subject, or answering a question, later reflects while silent, “The material and immaterial phenomena that arose during the time of speaking have ceased right here”—this is called one who acts with clear comprehension in speaking. One who, having been silent for a long time while attending to the Dhamma or a meditation subject, later reflects, “The material and immaterial phenomena that occurred during the time of silence have ceased right here; when there is an occurrence of derived materiality, one is said to be speaking; when there is not, one is said to be silent”—this is called one who acts with clear comprehension in being silent.

Tayidaṃ mahāsīvattherena vuttaṃ asammohadhuraṃ imasmiṃ satipaṭṭhānasutte adhippetaṃ. Sāmaññaphale pana sabbampi catubbidhaṃ sampajaññaṃ labbhati. Tasmā visesato ettha asammohasampajaññasseva vasena sampajānakāritā veditabbā. Sampajānakārī sampajānakārīti ca sabbapadesu satisampayuttasseva sampajaññassa vasenattho veditabbo. Vibhaṅgappakaraṇe pana, “sato sampajāno abhikkamati, sato sampajāno paṭikkamatī”ti (vibha. 523) evametāni padāni vibhattāneva.

This which was stated by the Elder Mahāsīva is the primary aspect of non-delusion intended in this Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta. In the Sāmaññaphala Sutta, however, all four kinds of clear comprehension are found. Therefore, here, acting with clear comprehension should be understood specifically on the basis of the clear comprehension that is non-delusion. And in all instances, the phrase “acting with clear comprehension” should be understood in the sense of clear comprehension associated with mindfulness. In the Vibhaṅga, however, these phrases are analyzed thus: “Mindful and with clear comprehension he goes forward; mindful and with clear comprehension he returns.”

Iti ajjhattaṃ vāti evaṃ catusampajaññapariggahaṇena attano vā kāye, parassa vā kāye, kālena vā attano, kālena vā parassa kāye kāyānupassī viharati. Idha samudayavayadhammānupassītiādīsu rūpakkhandhasseva samudayo ca vayo ca nīharitabbo. Sesaṃ vuttasadisameva.

Thus, 'internally,' etc.: in this way, by grasping the four kinds of clear comprehension, one dwells contemplating the body in the body—whether in one’s own body, or in another’s body, or at times in one’s own body and at times in another’s body. Here, in the phrases “contemplating the nature of arising and passing away,” etc., the arising and passing away of the material aggregate alone should be drawn out. The rest is just as has been stated.

Idha catusampajaññapariggāhikā sati dukkhasaccaṃ, tassā samuṭṭhāpikā purimataṇhā samudayasaccaṃ, ubhinnaṃ appavatti nirodhasaccaṃ, vuttappakāro ariyamaggo maggasaccaṃ. Evaṃ catusaccavasena ussakkitvā nibbutiṃ pāpuṇātīti idamekassa [M 1.0275] catusampajaññapariggāhakassa bhikkhuno vasena yāva arahattā niyyānamukhanti.

Here, the mindfulness that grasps the fourfold clear comprehension is the truth of suffering. The preceding craving that originates it is the truth of the origin. The non-occurrence of both is the truth of cessation. The noble path of the kind described is the truth of the path. Thus, by striving by way of the Four Truths, one attains Nibbāna. This, for a single monk who grasps the fourfold clear comprehension, is the entrance to deliverance, leading up to Arahantship.

Catusampajaññapabbavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The exposition of the section on the fourfold clear comprehension is concluded.

Paṭikūlamanasikārapabbavaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Section on Reflection on Repulsiveness

110. Evaṃ [V 1.0281] catusampajaññavasena kāyānupassanaṃ vibhajitvā idāni paṭikūlamanasikāravasena vibhajituṃ puna caparantiādimāha. Tattha imameva kāyantiādīsu yaṃ vattabbaṃ siyā, taṃ sabbaṃ sabbākārena vitthārato visuddhimagge kāyagatāsatikammaṭṭhāne vuttaṃ. Ubhatomukhāti heṭṭhā ca upari cāti dvīhi mukhehi yuttā. Nānāvihitassāti [P 1.0271] nānāvidhassa.

110. Having thus analyzed the contemplation of the body by way of the four kinds of clear comprehension, now, in order to analyze it by way of reflection on repulsiveness, he begins with 'furthermore' and so on. Here, whatever should be said concerning 'this very body' and so on, all that has been fully explained in every way in the Visuddhimagga, in the meditation subject of mindfulness of the body. 'Open at both ends' (ubhatomukhā) means furnished with two openings, below and above. 'Of various kinds' (nānāvihitassa) means of diverse types.

Idaṃ panettha opammasaṃsandanaṃ – ubhatomukhā putoḷi viya hi cātumahābhūtiko kāyo, tattha missetvā pakkhittanānāvidhadhaññaṃ viya kesādayo dvattiṃsākārā, cakkhumā puriso viya yogāvacaro, tassa taṃ putoḷiṃ muñcitvā paccavekkhato nānāvidhadhaññassa pākaṭakālo viya yogino dvattiṃsākārassa vibhūtākāro veditabbo.

Herein is the comparison to be understood: This body, composed of the four great elements, is like a double-mouthed sack. The thirty-two aspects, beginning with hair of the head, are like various kinds of grain mixed and put into it. The meditator is like a man with eyes. Just as when that man, having untied that sack, examines it, the time when the various kinds of grain become distinct, so too should the yogi understand the distinct appearance of the thirty-two aspects.

Iti ajjhattaṃ vāti evaṃ kesādipariggahaṇena attano vā kāye, parassa vā kāye, kālena vā attano, kālena vā parassa kāye kāyānupassī viharati, ito paraṃ vuttanayameva. Kevalañhi idha dvattiṃsākārapariggāhikā sati dukkhasaccanti evaṃ yojanaṃ katvā niyyānamukhaṃ veditabbaṃ. Sesaṃ purimasadisamevāti.

Thus, 'internally,' etc.: in this way, by discerning hair of the head and so forth, one dwells contemplating the body in the body—whether in one’s own body, or in another’s body, or at times in one’s own body and at times in another’s body. Beyond this, the method is as previously stated. Here, however, mindfulness that apprehends the thirty-two aspects is the truth of suffering; having made this connection, the entrance to deliverance should be known. The rest is similar to what was said before.

Paṭikūlamanasikārapabbavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The exposition of the section on reflection on repulsiveness is concluded.

Dhātumanasikārapabbavaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Section on Reflection on the Elements

111. Evaṃ paṭikūlamanasikāravasena kāyānupassanaṃ vibhajitvā idāni dhātumanasikāravasena vibhajituṃ puna caparantiādimāha. Tatrāyaṃ opammasaṃsandanena [M 1.0276] saddhiṃ atthavaṇṇanā – yathā koci goghātako vā tasseva vā bhattavetanabhato antevāsiko gāviṃ vadhitvā vinivijjhitvā catasso disā gatānaṃ mahāpathānaṃ vemajjhaṭṭhānasaṅkhāte catumahāpathe koṭṭhāsaṃ koṭṭhāsaṃ katvā nisinno assa, evameva bhikkhu catunnaṃ iriyāpathānaṃ yena kenaci ākārena [V 1.0282] ṭhitattā yathāṭhitaṃ, yathāṭhitattā ca yathāpaṇihitaṃ kāyaṃ – “atthi imasmiṃ kāye pathavīdhātu…pe… vāyodhātū”ti evaṃ paccavekkhati.

111. Having thus analyzed the contemplation of the body by way of reflection on repulsiveness, now, in order to analyze it by way of reflection on the elements, he begins with 'furthermore' and so on. Herein is the explanation of the meaning together with the comparison: Just as a butcher or his apprentice, supported by food and wages, having slaughtered a cow and cut it up, would sit at the four great crossroads, a place known as the central point of the four great highways, having made portion after portion; so too a monk, because the body is placed in any of the four postures, examines the body as it is placed, and because it is placed, as it is arranged, thus: 'In this body there is the earth element... the air element.' Thus he reflects.

Kiṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yathā goghātakassa gāviṃ posentassāpi āghātanaṃ āharantassāpi āharitvā tattha bandhitvā ṭhapentassāpi vadhentassāpi vadhitaṃ mataṃ passantassāpi tāvadeva gāvīti saññā na antaradhāyati, yāva naṃ padāletvā bīlaso na vibhajati. Vibhajitvā nisinnassa pana [P 1.0272] gāvīti saññā antaradhāyati, maṃsasaññā pavattati, nāssa evaṃ hoti “ahaṃ gāviṃ vikkiṇāmi, ime gāviṃ harantī”ti. Atha khvassa “ahaṃ maṃsaṃ vikkiṇāmi, ime maṃsaṃ haranti”cceva hoti, evameva imassāpi bhikkhuno pubbe bālaputhujjanakāle gihibhūtassāpi pabbajitassāpi tāvadeva sattoti vā puggaloti vā saññā na antaradhāyati, yāva imameva kāyaṃ yathāṭhitaṃ yathāpaṇihitaṃ ghanavinibbhogaṃ katvā dhātuso na paccavekkhati. Dhātuso paccavekkhato panassa sattasaññā antaradhāyati, dhātuvaseneva cittaṃ santiṭṭhati. Tenāha bhagavā – “imameva kāyaṃ yathāṭhitaṃ yathāpaṇihitaṃ dhātuso paccavekkhati, atthi imasmiṃ kāye pathavīdhātu āpodhātu tejodhātu vāyodhātūti. Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, dakkho goghātako vā…pe… vāyodhātū”ti.

What is meant by this? Just as for a butcher, even while raising a cow, or bringing it to the slaughterhouse, or having brought it there and tied it up, or striking it, or seeing it struck and dead, the perception 'cow' does not disappear until he cuts it up and divides it into pieces. But when he has divided it and sits down, the perception 'cow' disappears, and the perception 'meat' arises. He does not think, 'I am selling a cow, these people are taking a cow.' Rather, he thinks, 'I am selling meat, these people are taking meat.' In the same way, for this monk, even when he was previously an ordinary person, whether as a householder or a renunciant, the perception 'being' or 'person' does not disappear until he breaks up this very body, just as it is placed and arranged, by making a breaking up of its compactness, and reviews it by way of the elements. But when he reviews it by way of the elements, the perception 'being' disappears, and his mind settles on the elements. Therefore the Blessed One said: 'He reviews this very body, however it is placed or arranged, by way of the elements: "In this body there is the earth element, the water element, the fire element, the air element." Just as, monks, a skilled butcher or his apprentice... the air element.'

Goghātako viya hi yogī, gāvīti saññā viya sattasaññā, catumahāpatho viya catuiriyāpatho, bīlaso vibhajitvā nisinnabhāvo viya dhātuso paccavekkhaṇanti ayamettha pāḷivaṇṇanā, kammaṭṭhānakathā pana visuddhimagge vitthāritā.

Indeed, the yogi is like a butcher; the perception 'being' is like the perception 'cow'; the four postures are like the four great crossroads; and the contemplation by way of elements is like the state of sitting having divided it into pieces. This is the explanation of the Pali here, but the exposition on the meditation subject is extensively given in the Visuddhimagga.

Iti ajjhattaṃ vāti evaṃ catudhātupariggahaṇena attano vā kāye, parassa vā kāye, kālena vā attano, kālena vā parassa kāye kāyānupassī [M 1.0277] viharati. Ito paraṃ vuttanayameva. Kevalañhi idha catudhātupariggāhikā sati dukkhasaccanti evaṃ yojanaṃ katvā niyyānamukhaṃ veditabbaṃ. Sesaṃ purimasadisamevāti.

Thus, 'internally' and so on, means that by apprehending the four elements, one dwells contemplating the body in one's own body, or in another's body, or at one time in one's own body, at another time in another's body. Beyond this, the method is as previously stated. Here, however, mindfulness that apprehends the four elements should be understood as the truth of suffering; having made this connection, the gateway to liberation should be known. The rest is similar to what was said before.

Dhātumanasikārapabbavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the section on reflection on the elements is completed.

Navasivathikapabbavaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Section on the Nine Charnel Grounds

112. Evaṃ [V 1.0283] dhātumanasikāravasena kāyānupassanaṃ vibhajitvā idāni navahi sivathikapabbehi vibhajituṃ, puna caparantiādimāha. Tattha seyyathāpi passeyyāti yathā passeyya. Sarīranti matasarīraṃ. Sivathikāya chaḍḍītanti susāne apaviddhaṃ. Ekāhaṃ matassa assāti ekāhamataṃ. Dvīhaṃ matassa assāti dvīhamataṃ. Tīhaṃ matassa assāti tīhamataṃ. Bhastā viya vāyunā uddhaṃ jīvitapariyādānā yathānukkamaṃ samuggatena sūnabhāvena uddhumātattā uddhumātakaṃ. Vinīlaṃ [P 1.0273] vuccati viparibhinnavaṇṇaṃ. Vilīnameva vinīlakaṃ. Paṭikūlattā vā kucchitaṃ vinīlanti vinīlakaṃ. Maṃsussadaṭṭhānesu rattavaṇṇassa pubbasannicayaṭṭhānesu setavaṇṇassa yebhuyyena ca nīlavaṇṇassa nīlaṭṭhānesu nīlasāṭakapārutasseva chavasarīrassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Paribhinnaṭṭhānehi navahi vā vaṇamukhehi visandamānaṃ pubbaṃ vipubbaṃ. Vipubbameva vipubbakaṃ, paṭikūlattā vā kucchitaṃ vipubbanti vipubbakaṃ. Vipubbakaṃ jātaṃ tathābhāvaṃ gatanti vipubbakajātaṃ.

112. Having thus analyzed the contemplation of the body by way of reflection on the elements, now, in order to analyze it by means of the nine charnel ground sections, the text begins with 'again, moreover.' Herein, 'just as one might see' means 'as one would see.' 'A corpse' refers to a dead body. 'Discarded in the charnel ground' means thrown away in the cemetery. 'One day dead' means dead for one day. 'Two days dead' means dead for two days. 'Three days dead' means dead for three days. 'Bloated' (uddhumātakaṃ) refers to being distended by a state of swelling that has arisen successively, like a bellows filled with wind, due to the cessation of life. 'Discolored' (vinīlakaṃ) is said to be of a changed color. That which is discolored is a discolored thing. Or, because it is repulsive, a repulsive discolored thing is called a discolored thing. This is a designation for a corpse that is like one wrapped in a blue cloth, being red in places where flesh is prominent, white in places where pus has accumulated, and mostly blue in the blue areas. 'Festering' (vipubbakaṃ) is pus oozing from broken places or from the nine wound-openings. A festering thing is simply that which is festering. Or, because it is repulsive, a repulsive festering thing is called a festering thing. 'Become festering' (vipubbakajātaṃ) means having become festering, having reached that state.

So imameva kāyanti so bhikkhu imaṃ attano kāyaṃ tena kāyena saddhiṃ ñāṇena upasaṃharati upaneti. Kathaṃ? Ayampi kho kāyo evaṃdhammo evaṃbhāvī evaṃanatītoti. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – āyu, usmā, viññāṇanti imesaṃ tiṇṇaṃ dhammānaṃ atthitāya ayaṃ kāyo ṭhānagamanādikhamo hoti imesaṃ pana vigamā ayampi evaṃdhammo evaṃpūtikasabhāvoyeva, evaṃbhāvī evaṃuddhumātādibhedo bhavissati, evaṃanatīto evaṃuddhumātādibhāvaṃ anatikkantoti.

That monk compares this very body of his with that corpse, applying wisdom. How? 'This body, too, has such a nature, is bound to become so, and has not gone beyond this.' This is what is said: Because of the existence of these three things—life-faculty, heat, and consciousness—this body is capable of standing, going, and so on. But with their passing away, this body too is of such a nature, that is, it has a putrid nature; it is bound to become so, that is, it will become bloated and so on; and it has not gone beyond this, that is, it has not transcended the state of becoming bloated and so on.

Iti ajjhattaṃ vāti evaṃ uddhumātādipariggahaṇena attano vā kāye, parassa vā kāye, kālena vā attano, kālena vā parassa kāye kāyānupassī viharati.

Thus, 'internally,' and so on. By grasping the bloated state and so on, he dwells contemplating the body in his own body, or in another's body; at times in his own body, and at times in another's body.

Khajjamānanti [M 1.0278] udarādīsu nisīditvā udaramaṃsaoṭṭhamaṃsaakkhikūṭādīni luñcitvā luñcitvā khādiyamānaṃ. Samaṃsalohitanti sesāvasesamaṃsalohitayuttaṃ. Nimaṃsalohitamakkhitanti maṃse khīṇepi lohitaṃ na sussati, taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “nimaṃsalohitamakkhita”nti. Aññenāti aññena disābhāgena. Hatthaṭṭhikanti catusaṭṭhibhedampi hatthaṭṭhikaṃ pāṭiyekkaṃ vippakiṇṇaṃ. Pādaṭṭhikādīsupi eseva nayo. Terovassikānīti atikkantasaṃvaccharāni. Pūtīnīti abbhokāse ṭhitāni [V 1.0284] vātātapavuṭṭhisamphassena terovassikāneva pūtīni honti. Antobhūmigatāni pana cirataraṃ tiṭṭhanti. Cuṇṇakajātānīti cuṇṇaṃ cuṇṇaṃ hutvā vippakiṇṇāni. Sabbattha so imamevāti vuttanayena khajjamānādīnaṃ vasena yojanā kātabbā.

'Being devoured' means being eaten after creatures have settled on the belly and so on, and have repeatedly torn out the flesh of the belly, the flesh of the lips, the eye-sockets, and so on. 'With flesh and blood' means endowed with the remaining flesh and blood. 'Without flesh but smeared with blood' means that even when the flesh is gone, the blood does not dry up; with reference to this it is said 'without flesh but smeared with blood.' 'Elsewhere' means in another direction. 'Hand bones' means the hand bones, of sixty-four kinds, scattered individually. The same method applies also to foot bones and so on. 'Over a year old' means that a year has passed. 'Rotten' means that those lying in the open become rotten in the course of a year, through contact with wind, sun, and rain. But those that are underground last much longer. 'Become powdered' means having become powder and scattered. Everywhere, the application should be made by way of 'being devoured,' etc., in the manner stated concerning 'this very body'.

Iti ajjhattaṃ vāti evaṃ khajjamānādipariggahaṇena yāva cuṇṇakabhāvā attano [P 1.0274] vā kāye, parassa vā kāye, kālena vā attano, kālena vā parassa kāye kāyānupassī viharati.

Thus, 'internally,' etc. By grasping the state of 'being devoured' and so on, up to the state of being powder, he dwells contemplating the body in his own body, or in another's body; at times in his own body, and at times in another's body.

Idha pana ṭhatvā navasivathikā samodhānetabbā. “Ekāhamataṃ vā”tiādinā nayena vuttā sabbāpi ekā, “kākehi vā khajjamāna”ntiādikā ekā, “aṭṭhikasaṅkhalikaṃ samaṃsalohitaṃ nhārusambandha”nti ekā, “nimaṃsalohitamakkhitaṃ nhārusambandha”nti ekā, “apagatamaṃsalohitaṃ nhārusambandha”nti ekā, “aṭṭhikāni apagatasambandhānī”tiādikā ekā, “aṭṭhikāni setāni saṅkhavaṇṇapaṭibhāgānī”ti ekā, “puñjakitāni terovassikānī”ti ekā, “pūtīni cuṇṇakajātānī”ti ekā.

Here, at this point, the nine charnel ground sections should be combined. All that is stated in the manner of 'one day dead,' etc., is one section. 'Being devoured by crows,' etc., is one. 'A skeleton with flesh and blood, held together by sinews' is one. 'Without flesh but smeared with blood, held together by sinews' is one. 'Without flesh and blood, held together by sinews' is one. 'Bones disconnected,' etc., is one. 'Bones white, like the color of conch shells' is one. 'Heaped up, more than a year old' is one. 'Rotten, crumbled to dust' is one.

Evaṃ kho, bhikkhaveti idaṃ navasivathikā dassetvā kāyānupassanaṃ niṭṭhapento āha. Tattha navasivathikapariggāhikā sati dukkhasaccaṃ, tassā samuṭṭhāpikā purimataṇhā samudayasaccaṃ, ubhinnaṃ appavatti nirodhasaccaṃ, dukkhaparijānano samudayapajahano nirodhārammaṇo ariyamaggo maggasaccaṃ. Evaṃ catusaccavaseneva ussakkitvā nibbutiṃ pāpuṇātīti idaṃ navasivathikapariggāhakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ yāva arahattā niyyānamukhanti.

'Thus, monks'—having shown the nine charnel ground sections, he said this, concluding the contemplation of the body. Herein, the mindfulness that grasps the nine charnel ground sections is the truth of suffering. The prior craving that gives rise to it is the truth of the origin. The non-occurrence of both is the truth of cessation. The Noble Path—which fully knows suffering, abandons the origin, and has cessation as its object—is the truth of the path. Thus, by means of the Four Truths, having striven, one attains Nibbāna. This is the means of deliverance up to Arahantship for the monks who grasp the nine charnel ground sections.

Navasivathikapabbavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Section on the Nine Charnel Grounds is concluded.

Ettāvatā ca ānāpānapabbaṃ iriyāpathapabbaṃ catusampajaññapabbaṃ paṭikūlamanasikārapabbaṃ dhātumanasikārapabbaṃ navasivathikapabbānīti cuddasapabbā kāyānupassanā niṭṭhitā hoti.

And with this, the contemplation of the body, consisting of fourteen sections—the section on mindfulness of breathing, the section on postures, the section on fourfold clear comprehension, the section on attention to repulsiveness, the section on attention to the elements, and the nine charnel ground sections—is completed.

Tattha [V 1.0285][M 1.0279] ānāpānapabbaṃ paṭikūlamanasikārapabbanti imāneva dve appanākammaṭṭhānāni. Sivathikānaṃ pana ādīnavānupassanāvasena vuttattā sesāni dvādasāpi upacārakammaṭṭhānānevāti.

Herein, the section on mindfulness of breathing and the section on attention to repulsiveness—these two alone are meditation subjects for absorption. But because the charnel ground sections are taught by way of contemplating their drawbacks, the remaining twelve are only meditation subjects for access concentration.

Kāyānupassanā niṭṭhitā.

The Contemplation of the Body is concluded.

Vedanānupassanāvaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Contemplation of Feeling

113. Evaṃ bhagavā cuddasavidhena kāyānupassanāsatipaṭṭhānaṃ kathetvā idāni navavidhena vedanānupassanaṃ kathetuṃ kathañca, bhikkhavetiādimāha. Tattha sukhaṃ vedananti kāyikaṃ vā cetasikaṃ vā sukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedayamāno “ahaṃ sukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedayāmī”ti pajānātīti attho. Tattha kāmaṃ uttānaseyyakāpi dārakā thaññapivanādikāle sukhaṃ vedayamānā “sukhaṃ vedayāmā”ti pajānanti, na panetaṃ evarūpaṃ jānanaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Evarūpaṃ jānanaṃ hi sattūpaladdhiṃ na jahati, sattasaññaṃ na ugghāṭeti, kammaṭṭhānaṃ vā satipaṭṭhānabhāvanā vā na hoti. Imassa pana bhikkhuno jānanaṃ sattūpaladdhiṃ jahati[P 1.0275], sattasaññaṃ ugghāṭeti, kammaṭṭhānaṃ ceva satipaṭṭhānabhāvanā ca hoti. Idañhi “ko vedayati, kassa vedanā, kiṃ kāraṇā vedanā”ti evaṃ sampajānavediyanaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ.

113. Having thus explained the establishment of mindfulness on the body in fourteen ways, the Blessed One, in order to now explain the contemplation of feeling in nine ways, spoke the words beginning, 'And how, monks…' Herein, feeling a pleasant feeling means that when experiencing a pleasant feeling, whether bodily or mental, one understands, 'I am feeling a pleasant feeling.' In this regard, even infants lying on their backs, at the time of suckling milk and so on, know they are feeling pleasure, but this is not the kind of knowing being referred to here. Such knowing does not abandon the apprehension of a being, does not uproot the perception of a being, and is neither a meditation subject nor the development of mindfulness. But this monk’s knowing abandons the apprehension of a being, uproots the perception of a being, and is both a meditation subject and the development of mindfulness. This is said with reference to experiencing with clear comprehension, as in the questions: 'Who feels? Whose is the feeling? What is the cause of the feeling?'

Tattha ko vedayatīti na koci satto vā puggalo vā vedayati. Kassa vedanāti na kassaci sattassa vā puggalassa vā vedanā. Kiṃ kāraṇā vedanāti vatthuārammaṇāva panassa vedanā. Tasmā esa evaṃ pajānāti – “taṃ taṃ sukhādīnaṃ vatthuṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā vedanāva vedayati. Taṃ pana vedanāpavattiṃ upādāya ‘ahaṃ vedayāmī’ti vohāramattaṃ hotī”ti. Evaṃ vedanāva vatthuṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā vedanāva vedayatīti sallakkhento esa “sukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedayāmī”ti pajānātīti veditabbo. Cittalapabbate aññataro thero viya. Thero kira aphāsukakāle balavavedanāya nitthunanto aparāparaṃ parivattati. Tameko daharo āha “kataraṃ vo, bhante, ṭhānaṃ rujjatī”ti. Āvuso, pāṭiyekkaṃ rujjanaṭṭhānaṃ nāma natthi, vatthuṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā vedanāva vedayatīti. Evaṃ jānanakālato [M 1.0280] paṭṭhāya adhivāsetuṃ vaṭṭati no, bhanteti. Adhivāsemi āvusoti. Adhivāsanā, bhante, seyyāti. Thero adhivāsesi. Tato vāto [V 1.0286] yāva hadayā phālesi, mañcake antāni rāsikatāni ahesuṃ. Thero daharassa dassesi “vaṭṭatāvuso, ettakā adhivāsanā”ti. Daharo tuṇhī ahosi. Thero vīriyasamataṃ yojetvā saha paṭisambhidāhi arahattaṃ pāpuṇitvā samasīsī hutvā parinibbāyi.

Herein, 'Who feels?' No being or person feels. 'Whose is the feeling?' The feeling belongs to no being or person. 'What is the cause of the feeling?' The feeling has a basis and an object as its cause. Therefore, one understands thus: 'It is feeling itself that feels, having taken such and such a basis and object as its object. The expression "I feel" is merely a convention based on the occurrence of feeling.' One who thus discerns that it is feeling itself that feels, having taken a basis and an object as its object, should be understood as one who understands, 'I am feeling a pleasant feeling.' This is like the elder on Cittalapabbata. It is said that the elder, during a time of illness, was groaning due to severe pain and was tossing and turning. A young monk asked him, 'Venerable sir, what part of you is in pain?' 'Friend, there is no particular place that is in pain; it is simply feeling that feels, having taken a basis and an object as its object.' The young monk then asked, 'Venerable sir, from the time of knowing thus, is it not possible to endure?' 'I am enduring, friend.' 'Endurance is excellent, venerable sir.' The elder endured. Then, sharp pains tore through him up to his heart, and his intestines were piled upon the bed. The elder showed the young monk, saying, 'Friend, this much endurance is possible.' The young monk remained silent. The elder, establishing a balance of energy, attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges and attained final Nibbāna with his head held level.

Yathā ca sukhaṃ, evaṃ dukkhaṃ…pe… nirāmisaṃ adukkhamasukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedayamāno “nirāmisaṃ adukkhamasukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedayāmī”ti pajānāti. Iti bhagavā rūpakammaṭṭhānaṃ kathetvā arūpakammaṭṭhānaṃ kathento vedanāvasena kathesi. Duvidhañhi kammaṭṭhānaṃ rūpakammaṭṭhānañca arūpakammaṭṭhānañca. Rūpapariggaho arūpapariggahotipi etadeva vuccati. Tattha bhagavā rūpakammaṭṭhānaṃ kathento saṅkhepamanasikāravasena vā vitthāramanasikāravasena vā catudhātuvavatthānaṃ kathesi. Tadubhayampi sabbākārato visuddhimagge dassitameva.

And as with pleasant feeling, so it is with painful feeling… [and so on, down to]… when experiencing an unworldly neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, one understands, 'I am experiencing an unworldly neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.' Thus, the Blessed One, having taught the meditation subject of form, taught the meditation subject of the formless by way of feeling. For the meditation subject is twofold: the meditation subject of form and the meditation subject of the formless. This is also called the comprehension of form and the comprehension of the formless. Therein, the Blessed One, when teaching the meditation subject of form, taught the analysis of the four elements either by way of brief attention or by way of detailed attention. Both of these are shown in the Visuddhimagga in every respect.

Arūpakammaṭṭhānaṃ [P 1.0276] pana kathento yebhuyyena vedanāvasena katheti. Tividho hi arūpakammaṭṭhāne abhiniveso phassavasena vedanāvasena cittavasenāti. Kathaṃ? Ekaccassa hi saṃkhittena vā vitthārena vā pariggahite rūpakammaṭṭhāne tasmiṃ ārammaṇe cittacetasikānaṃ paṭhamābhinipāto taṃ ārammaṇaṃ phusanto uppajjamāno phasso pākaṭo hoti. Ekaccassa taṃ ārammaṇaṃ anubhavantī uppajjamānā vedanā pākaṭā hoti. Ekaccassa taṃ ārammaṇaṃ pariggahetvā vijānantaṃ uppajjamānaṃ viññāṇaṃ pākaṭaṃ hoti. Tattha yassa phasso pākaṭo hoti, sopi “na kevalaṃ phassova uppajjati, tena saddhiṃ tadeva ārammaṇaṃ anubhavamānā vedanāpi uppajjati, sañjānanamānā saññāpi, cetayamānā cetanāpi, vijānanamānaṃ viññāṇampi uppajjatī”ti phassapañcamakeyeva pariggaṇhāti. Yassa vedanā pākaṭā hoti. So “na kevalaṃ vedanāva uppajjati, tāya saddhiṃ tadevārammaṇaṃ phusamāno phassopi uppajjati, sañjānanamānā saññāpi, cetayamānā cetanāpi, vijānanamānaṃ viññāṇampi uppajjatī”ti phassapañcamakeyeva pariggaṇhāti. Yassa viññāṇaṃ pākaṭaṃ hoti, so “na kevalaṃ viññāṇameva uppajjati, tena saddhiṃ tadevārammaṇaṃ phusamāno phassopi [M 1.0281] uppajjati, anubhavamānā vedanāpi, sañjānanamānā saññāpi, cetayamānā cetanāpi uppajjatī”ti phassapañcamakeyeva pariggaṇhāti.

However, when teaching the formless meditation subject, he teaches it for the most part by way of feeling. For in the formless meditation subject, there are three kinds of approach: by way of contact, by way of feeling, and by way of consciousness. How so? For a certain person, when the form meditation subject has been comprehended either briefly or in detail, the first impact of mind and mental factors on that object—the contact arising while touching that object—becomes evident. For another, the feeling arising while experiencing that object becomes evident. For yet another, the consciousness arising while cognizing that object becomes evident. Therein, for one to whom contact is evident, one comprehends not only that contact arises, but that along with it, feeling also arises experiencing that same object, perception arises perceiving it, volition arises intending it, and consciousness arises cognizing it—thus one comprehends the pentad with contact as the fifth. For one to whom feeling is evident, one comprehends not only that feeling arises, but that along with it, contact also arises touching that same object, perception arises perceiving it, volition arises intending it, and consciousness arises cognizing it—thus one comprehends the pentad with contact as the fifth. For one to whom consciousness is evident, one comprehends not only that consciousness arises, but that along with it, contact also arises touching that same object, feeling arises experiencing it, perception arises perceiving it, and volition arises intending it—thus one comprehends the pentad with contact as the fifth.

So [V 1.0287] “ime phassapañcamakā dhammā kiṃ nissitā”ti upadhārento “vatthuṃ nissitā”ti pajānāti. Vatthu nāma karajakāyo, yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “idañca me viññāṇaṃ ettha sitaṃ ettha paṭibaddha”nti (dī. ni. 1.234,235; ma. ni. 2.252). So atthato bhūtāni ceva upādārūpāni ca. Evamettha “vatthu rūpaṃ, phassapañcamakā nāma”nti nāmarūpamattameva passati. Rūpaṃ cettha rūpakkhandho, nāmaṃ cattāro arūpino khandhāti pañcakkhandhamattaṃ hoti. Nāmarūpavinimuttā hi pañcakkhandhā, pañcakkhandhavinimuttañca nāmarūpaṃ natthi.

When considering, 'On what do these phenomena, the pentad with contact as the fifth, depend?' one understands that they depend on a basis. The basis is the physical body, regarding which it was said: 'And this consciousness of mine is established here, bound here.' In essence, it is both the primary elements and derived material form. Thus, here one sees merely name-and-form: 'The basis is form, and the phenomena of the pentad with contact as the fifth are name.' In this context, form is the form aggregate, while name is the four immaterial aggregates—thus, it is merely the five aggregates. For the five aggregates are not separate from name-and-form, and there is no name-and-form separate from the five aggregates.

So “ime pañcakkhandhā kiṃ hetukā”ti upaparikkhanto “avijjādihetukā”ti passati. Tato paccayo ceva paccayuppannañca idaṃ, añño satto vā puggalo vā natthi, suddhasaṅkhārapuñjamattamevāti sappaccayanāmarūpavasena tilakkhaṇaṃ āropetvā vipassanāpaṭipāṭiyā “aniccaṃ dukkhaṃ anattā”ti sammasanto vicarati.

When examining, 'What is the cause of these five aggregates?', one sees that they are caused by ignorance and so on. Then, one understands: 'This is merely condition and conditioned; there is no other being or person, only a mere heap of formations.' By applying the three characteristics to name-and-form together with its conditions, one proceeds, contemplating in the order of insight: 'impermanent, suffering, not-self.'

So [P 1.0277] “ajja ajjā”ti paṭivedhaṃ ākaṅkhamāno tathārūpe divase utusappāya puggalasappāya bhojanasappāya dhammassavanasappāyaṃ labhitvā ekapallaṅkena nisinno vipassanaṃ matthakaṃ pāpetvā arahatte patiṭṭhāti. Evaṃ imesampi tiṇṇaṃ janānaṃ yāva arahattā kammaṭṭhānaṃ kathitaṃ hoti.

Desiring penetration 'Today! Today!', having found a day with such favorable conditions—favorable season, person, food, and hearing of the Dhamma—one sits down in a single cross-legged posture, brings insight to its culmination, and is established in arahantship. Thus, the meditation subject for these three individuals has been taught up to arahantship.

Idha pana bhagavā arūpakammaṭṭhānaṃ kathento vedanāvasena kathesi. Phassavasena vā hi viññāṇavasena vā kathīyamānaṃ na pākaṭaṃ hoti, andhakāraṃ viya khāyati. Vedanāvasena pana pākaṭaṃ hoti. Kasmā? Vedanānaṃ uppattipākaṭatāya. Sukhadukkhavedanānañhi uppatti pākaṭā. Yadā sukhaṃ uppajjati, sakalasarīraṃ khobhentaṃ maddantaṃ pharamānaṃ abhisandayamānaṃ satadhotaṃ sappiṃ khādāpayantaṃ viya satapākatelaṃ makkhayamānaṃ viya ghaṭasahassena pariḷāhaṃ nibbāpayamānaṃ viya “aho sukhaṃ aho sukha”nti vācaṃ nicchārayamānameva uppajjati. Yadā dukkhaṃ uppajjati, sakalasarīraṃ khobhentaṃ maddantaṃ pharamānaṃ abhisandayamānaṃ tattaphālaṃ pavesentaṃ viya vilīnatambalohena āsiñcantaṃ viya sukkhatiṇavanappatimhi araññe dāruukkākalāpaṃ khipamānaṃ viya [M 1.0282] “aho dukkhaṃ aho dukkha”nti vippalāpayamānameva uppajjati. Iti sukhadukkhavedanānaṃ uppatti pākaṭā hoti.

Here, however, the Blessed One, when teaching the formless meditation subject, taught it by way of feeling. For if it were taught by way of contact or consciousness, it would not be manifest—it would appear like darkness. But when taught by way of feeling, it becomes manifest. Why? Because the arising of feelings is manifest. Indeed, the arising of pleasant and painful feelings is manifest. When a pleasant feeling arises, it arises agitating, massaging, pervading, and suffusing the entire body, as if making one eat ghee washed a hundred times, as if anointing one with oil refined a hundred times, as if extinguishing a burning fever with a thousand pots of water, while causing one to exclaim, 'Ah, pleasure! Ah, pleasure!' When a painful feeling arises, it arises agitating, massaging, pervading, and suffusing the entire body, as if inserting a hot ploughshare, as if pouring molten copper over one, as if throwing a bundle of firebrands into a forest of dry grass and trees, while causing one to lament, 'Ah, pain! Ah, pain!' Thus, the arising of pleasant and painful feelings is manifest.

Adukkhamasukhā [V 1.0288] pana duddīpanā andhakārāva avibhūtā. Sā sukhadukkhānaṃ apagame sātāsātappaṭikkhepavasena majjhattākārabhūtā adukkhamasukhā vedanāti nayato gaṇhantassa pākaṭā hoti. Yathā kiṃ? Yathā antarā piṭṭhipāsāṇaṃ ārohitvā palātassa migassa anupathaṃ gacchanto migaluddako piṭṭhipāsāṇassa orabhāgepi parabhāgepi padaṃ disvā majjhe apassantopi “ito āruḷho, ito oruḷho, majjhe piṭṭhipāsāṇe iminā padesena gato bhavissatī”ti nayato jānāti, evaṃ āruḷhaṭṭhāne padaṃ viya hi sukhavedanāya uppatti pākaṭā hoti. Oruḷhaṭṭhāne padaṃ viya dukkhavedanāya uppatti pākaṭā hoti. “Ito āruyha ito oruyha majjhe evaṃ gato”ti nayato gahaṇaṃ viya sukhadukkhānaṃ apagame sātāsātappaṭikkhepavasena majjhattākārabhūtā adukkhamasukhā vedanāti nayato [P 1.0278] gaṇhantassa pākaṭā hoti. Evaṃ bhagavā paṭhamaṃ rūpakammaṭṭhānaṃ kathetvā pacchā arūpakammaṭṭhānaṃ vedanāvasena nibbattetvāva dassesi.

But neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is hard to illuminate, like darkness, and unmanifest. It becomes manifest to one who grasps it by inference as the neutral feeling that is the state of neutrality through the rejection of the agreeable and disagreeable upon the cessation of pleasure and pain. How so? It is like a deer hunter who, following the track of a fleeing deer that has climbed onto a flat rock, sees its footprint on the near side and on the far side, but not in the middle.
