Even without seeing it, he knows by inference, 'It must have gone by this region in the middle of the flat rock, having ascended from here and descended from there.' In the same way, the arising of pleasant feeling is manifest like the footprint at the place of ascent. The arising of painful feeling is manifest like the footprint at the place of descent. Just as there is the grasping by inference, 'Having ascended from here and descended from there, it went through the middle thus,' so too, it becomes manifest to one who grasps by inference the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling as the state of neutrality through the rejection of the agreeable and disagreeable upon the cessation of pleasure and pain. Thus, the Blessed One first taught the meditation subject of form and afterwards, having brought forth the formless meditation subject by way of feeling, he showed it.

Na kevalañca idheva evaṃ dassesi, cūḷataṇhāsaṅkhaye, mahātaṇhāsaṅkhaye, cūḷavedalle, mahāvedalle, raṭṭhapālasutte, māgaṇḍiyasutte, dhātuvibhaṅge, āneñjasappāye, dīghanikāyamhi mahānidāne, sakkapañhe, mahāsatipaṭṭhāne, saṃyuttamhi cūḷanidānasutte, rukkhopame, parivīmaṃsanasutte, sakale vedanāsaṃyutteti evaṃ anekesu suttesu paṭhamaṃ rūpakammaṭṭhānaṃ kathetvā pacchā arūpakammaṭṭhānaṃ vedanāvasena nibbattetvā dassesi. Yathā ca tesu, evaṃ imasmimpi satipaṭṭhānasutte paṭhamaṃ rūpakammaṭṭhānaṃ kathetvā pacchā arūpakammaṭṭhānaṃ vedanāvasena nibbattetvā dassesi.

And not only here did he show it thus, but also in the Cūḷataṇhāsaṅkhaya, Mahātaṇhāsaṅkhaya, Cūḷavedalla, Mahāvedalla, Raṭṭhapālasutta, Māgaṇḍiyasutta, Dhātuvibhaṅga, Āneñjasappāya, the Mahānidāna in the Dīgha Nikāya, the Sakkapañha, the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna, the Cūḷanidānasutta in the Saṃyutta Nikāya, the Rukkhopama, the Parivīmaṃsanasutta, and in the entire Vedanāsaṃyutta—in these many suttas, having first taught the meditation subject of form, he afterwards brought forth and showed the formless meditation subject by way of feeling. And as in those, so too in this Satipaṭṭhānasutta, having first taught the meditation subject of form, he afterwards brought forth and showed the formless meditation subject by way of feeling.

Tattha sukhaṃ vedanantiādīsu ayaṃ aparopi pajānanapariyāyo – sukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedayāmīti pajānātīti sukhavedanākkhaṇe dukkhāya vedanāya abhāvato sukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedayamāno “sukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedayāmī”ti pajānāti. Tena yā pubbe anubhūtapubbā dukkhā vedanā, tassā idāni abhāvato imissā ca sukhāya vedanāya ito paṭhamaṃ abhāvato [M 1.0283] vedanā nāma aniccā adhuvā vipariṇāmadhammā, itiha tattha sampajāno hoti.

Therein, regarding the words 'experiencing a pleasant feeling...', this is another method of knowing: 'He understands, "I am experiencing a pleasant feeling."' At the moment of a pleasant feeling, due to the absence of a painful feeling, one who is experiencing a pleasant feeling understands, 'I am experiencing a pleasant feeling.' By that, because the painful feeling experienced before is now absent, and because this pleasant feeling was absent before this, one understands that feelings are by nature impermanent, unstable, and subject to change. Thus, one is clearly comprehending in that respect.

Vuttampi cetaṃ bhagavatā –

And this was said by the Blessed One:

“Yasmiṃ [V 1.0289] aggivessana samaye sukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedeti, neva tasmiṃ samaye dukkhaṃ vedanaṃ vedeti, na adukkhamasukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedeti, sukhaṃyeva tasmiṃ samaye vedanaṃ vedeti, yasmiṃ aggivessana samaye dukkhaṃ…pe… adukkhamasukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedeti, neva tasmiṃ samaye sukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedeti, na dukkhaṃ vedanaṃ vedeti, adukkhamasukhaññeva tasmiṃ samaye vedanaṃ vedeti. Sukhāpi kho aggivessana vedanā aniccā saṅkhatā paṭiccasamuppannā khayadhammā vayadhammā virāgadhammā nirodhadhammā. Dukkhāpi kho…pe… adukkhamasukhāpi kho aggivessana vedanā aniccā…pe… nirodhadhammā. Evaṃ passaṃ aggivessana sutavā ariyasāvako sukhāyapi vedanāya dukkhāyapi vedanāya adukkhamasukhāyapi [P 1.0279] vedanāya nibbindati, nibbindaṃ virajjati, virāgā vimuccati, vimuttasmiṃ vimuttamiti ñāṇaṃ hoti. ‘Khīṇā jāti, vusitaṃ brahmacariyaṃ, kataṃ karaṇīyaṃ, nāparaṃ itthattāyā’ti pajānātī”ti (ma. ni. 2.205).

"Aggivessana, at a time when one experiences a pleasant feeling, one does not at that time experience a painful feeling or a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling; one experiences only a pleasant feeling at that time. Aggivessana, at a time when one experiences a painful feeling... or a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, one does not at that time experience a pleasant feeling or a painful feeling; one experiences only a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling at that time. Aggivessana, pleasant feeling is also impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to destruction, subject to vanishing, subject to fading away, subject to cessation. Painful feeling also... and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling also, Aggivessana, is impermanent... subject to cessation. Seeing thus, Aggivessana, the instructed noble disciple becomes disenchanted with pleasant feeling, with painful feeling, and with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. Being disenchanted, one becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion, one is liberated. When one is liberated, the knowledge arises, 'Liberated.' One understands: 'Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.'" (M. II. 205).

Sāmisaṃ vā sukhantiādīsu sāmisā sukhā nāma pañcakāmaguṇāmisanissitā cha gehasitasomanassavedanā. Nirāmisā sukhā nāma cha nekkhammasitasomanassavedanā. Sāmisā dukkhā nāma cha gehasitadomanassavedanā. Nirāmisā dukkhā nāma cha nekkhammasitadomanassavedanā. Sāmisā adukkhamasukhā nāma cha gehasitaupekkhā vedanā. Nirāmisā adukkhamasukhā nāma cha nekkhammasitaupekkhā vedanā. Tāsaṃ vibhāgo uparipaṇṇāsake pāḷiyaṃ āgatoyeva.

In the passage beginning 'Worldly pleasant feeling,' worldly pleasant feeling refers to the six types of joy-based feeling connected to household life, dependent on the five strands of sensual pleasure. Spiritual pleasant feeling refers to the six types of joy-based feeling connected to renunciation. Worldly painful feeling refers to the six types of grief-based feeling connected to household life. Spiritual painful feeling refers to the six types of grief-based feeling connected to renunciation. Worldly neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling refers to the six types of equanimity-based feeling connected to household life. Spiritual neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling refers to the six types of equanimity-based feeling connected to renunciation. Their analysis is given in the Pāḷi of the Uparipaṇṇāsaka.

Iti ajjhattaṃ vāti evaṃ sukhavedanādipariggahaṇena attano vā vedanāsu, parassa vā vedanāsu, kālena vā attano, kālena vā parassa vedanāsu vedanānupassī viharati. Samudayavayadhammānupassī vāti ettha pana “avijjāsamudayā vedanāsamudayo”tiādīhi (paṭi. ma. 1.50) pañcahi pañcahi ākārehi vedanānaṃ samudayañca vayañca passanto samudayadhammānupassī vā [M 1.0284] vedanāsu viharati, vayadhammānupassī vā vedanāsu viharati, kālena samudayadhammānupassī vā, kālena vayadhammānupassī vā vedanāsu viharatīti veditabbo. Ito paraṃ kāyānupassanāyaṃ vuttanayameva.

Thus, 'internally,' etc.—in this way, by comprehending feelings such as pleasant feeling, one dwells contemplating feelings in one's own feelings, or in others' feelings, or at times in one's own feelings and at times in others' feelings. As to 'contemplating the nature of arising and passing away': here, seeing the arising and passing away of feelings in five ways each, such as 'with the arising of ignorance, there is the arising of feeling' (Paṭis.M. I, 50), one dwells contemplating the nature of arising in feelings, or one dwells contemplating the nature of passing away in feelings, or at times one dwells contemplating the nature of arising and at times contemplating the nature of passing away in feelings—this should be understood. From here on, the method is just as stated in the contemplation of the body.

Kevalañhi [V 1.0290] idha vedanāpariggāhikā sati dukkhasaccanti evaṃ yojanaṃ katvā vedanāpariggāhakassa bhikkhuno niyyānamukhaṃ veditabbaṃ. Sesaṃ tādisamevāti.

For here, indeed, by construing that mindfulness which comprehends feeling is the truth of suffering, the gateway to deliverance for the monk who comprehends feeling should be understood. The rest is just the same.

Vedanānupassanā niṭṭhitā.

The Contemplation of Feeling is concluded.

Cittānupassanāvaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Contemplation of Mind

114. Evaṃ navavidhena vedanānupassanāsatipaṭṭhānaṃ kathetvā idāni soḷasavidhena cittānupassanaṃ kathetuṃ kathañca, bhikkhavetiādimāha. Tattha sarāganti aṭṭhavidhaṃ lobhasahagataṃ. Vītarāganti lokiyakusalābyākataṃ. Idaṃ pana yasmā sammasanaṃ na dhammasamodhānaṃ, tasmā idha ekapadepi lokuttaraṃ na labbhati. Sesāni cattāri akusalacittāni neva purimapadaṃ, na pacchimapadaṃ bhajanti. Sadosanti duvidhaṃ dosasahagataṃ[P 1.0280]. Vītadosanti lokiyakusalābyākataṃ. Sesāni dasākusalacittāni neva purimaṃ padaṃ, na pacchimaṃ padaṃ bhajanti. Samohanti vicikicchāsahagatañceva uddhaccasahagatañcāti duvidhaṃ. Yasmā pana moho sabbākusalesu uppajjati, tasmā tānipi idha vaṭṭantiyeva. Imasmiṃyeva hi duke dvādasākusalacittāni pariyādiṇṇānīti. Vītamohanti lokiyakusalābyākataṃ. Saṃkhittanti thinamiddhānupatitaṃ, etañhi saṃkuṭitacittaṃ nāma. Vikkhittanti uddhaccasahagataṃ, etañhi pasaṭacittaṃ nāma.

114. Having thus explained the establishment of mindfulness through the contemplation of feelings in nine ways, now, to explain the contemplation of mind in sixteen ways, he said, 'And how, O monks?' and so on. Herein, 'with lust' refers to the eight types of consciousness accompanied by greed. 'Without lust' refers to worldly wholesome and indeterminate states. However, since this is an analysis and not a synthesis of phenomena, not even a single supramundane state is obtained here. The remaining four unwholesome consciousnesses belong neither to the former term nor to the latter. 'With hate' refers to the two types of consciousness accompanied by aversion. 'Without hate' refers to worldly wholesome and indeterminate states. The remaining ten unwholesome consciousnesses belong neither to the former term nor to the latter. 'With delusion' refers to the two types, namely that accompanied by doubt and that accompanied by restlessness. And since delusion arises in all unwholesome states, they too are applicable here. Indeed, in this very pair, the twelve unwholesome consciousnesses are encompassed. 'Without delusion' refers to worldly wholesome and indeterminate states. 'Contracted' refers to that which is overcome by sloth and torpor, for this is called a contracted mind. 'Distracted' refers to that which is accompanied by restlessness, for this is called a scattered mind.

Mahaggatanti rūpārūpāvacaraṃ. Amahaggatanti kāmāvacaraṃ. Sauttaranti kāmāvacaraṃ. Anuttaranti rūpāvacarañca arūpāvacarañca. Tatrāpi sauttaraṃ rūpāvacaraṃ, anuttaraṃ arūpāvacarameva. Samāhitanti yassa appanāsamādhi upacārasamādhi vā atthi. Asamāhitanti ubhayasamādhivirahitaṃ. Vimuttanti tadaṅgavikkhambhanavimuttīhi vimuttaṃ. Avimuttanti ubhayavimuttivirahitaṃ, samucchedapaṭippassaddhinissaraṇavimuttīnaṃ pana idha okāsova natthi.

'Exalted' refers to the form and formless spheres. 'Unexalted' refers to the sense-sphere. 'With a superior' refers to the sense-sphere. 'Without a superior' refers to the form-sphere and the formless-sphere. Yet even there, the form-sphere is 'with a superior', while the formless-sphere alone is 'without a superior'. 'Concentrated' refers to that which has either attainment concentration or access concentration. 'Unconcentrated' refers to that which is devoid of both concentrations. 'Liberated' refers to that which is liberated by liberation by substitution and liberation by suppression. 'Unliberated' refers to that which is devoid of both these liberations; however, for the liberations of cutting off, tranquilization, and escape, there is no opportunity here.

Iti [M 1.0285] ajjhattaṃ vāti evaṃ sarāgādipariggahaṇena yasmiṃ yasmiṃ khaṇe yaṃ yaṃ cittaṃ pavattati, taṃ taṃ sallakkhento attano vā citte, parassa vā citte, kālena vā attano, kālena vā parassa citte cittānupassī viharati. Samudayavayadhammānupassīti ettha pana “avijjāsamudayā [V 1.0291] viññāṇasamudayo”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.50) evaṃ pañcahi pañcahi ākārehi viññāṇassa samudayo ca vayo ca nīharitabbo. Ito paraṃ vuttanayameva.

Thus, regarding the phrase beginning 'internally,' it means that in this way, by comprehending 'with lust' and so on, at whatever moment whatever mind is occurring, one dwells contemplating mind in the mind—observing that very mind, whether in one’s own mind or in the mind of another, or at one time in one’s own mind and at another time in the mind of another. As for 'contemplating the phenomena of arising and passing away,' here the arising and passing away of consciousness should be deduced in five ways each, as in the text: 'With the arising of ignorance, there is the arising of consciousness' (Paṭisambhidāmagga 1.50). From here on, the method is as has been stated.

Kevalañhi idha cittapariggāhikā sati dukkhasaccanti evaṃ yojanaṃ katvā cittapariggāhakassa bhikkhuno niyyānamukhaṃ veditabbaṃ. Sesaṃ tādisamevāti.

Indeed, here, having made the connection that mindfulness which comprehends the mind is the truth of suffering, the entrance to deliverance for the monk who comprehends the mind is to be understood. The rest is just the same.

Cittānupassanāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Contemplation of Mind is finished.

Dhammānupassanā nīvaraṇapabbavaṇṇanā

Contemplation of Phenomena: The Section on the Hindrances

115. Evaṃ soḷasavidhena cittānupassanāsatipaṭṭhānaṃ kathetvā idāni pañcavidhena dhammānupassanaṃ kathetuṃ kathañca, bhikkhavetiādimāha. Apica bhagavatā kāyānupassanāya suddharūpapariggaho kathito, vedanācittānupassanāhi suddhaarūpapariggaho. Idāni rūpārūpamissakapariggahaṃ kathetuṃ “kathañca, bhikkhave”tiādimāha[P 1.0281]. Kāyānupassanāya vā rūpakkhandhapariggahova kathito, vedanānupassanāya vedanākkhandhapariggahova, cittānupassanāya viññāṇakkhandhapariggahovāti idāni saññāsaṅkhārakkhandhapariggahampi kathetuṃ “kathañca, bhikkhave”tiādimāha.

115. Having thus explained the establishment of mindfulness of the mind in sixteen ways, now, to explain the contemplation of phenomena in five ways, he began by saying, “And how, O bhikkhus?” Furthermore, the Blessed One has explained the comprehension of pure form in the contemplation of the body, and the comprehension of pure formlessness in the contemplations of feeling and mind. Now, to explain the comprehension of a mixture of form and formlessness, he began by saying, “And how, O bhikkhus?” Or, in the contemplation of the body, only the comprehension of the form aggregate was explained; in the contemplation of feeling, only the comprehension of the feeling aggregate; and in the contemplation of the mind, only the comprehension of the consciousness aggregate. Now, to also explain the comprehension of the perception and mental formations aggregates, he began by saying, “And how, O bhikkhus?”

Tattha santanti abhiṇhasamudācāravasena saṃvijjamānaṃ. Asantanti asamudācāravasena vā pahīnattā vā avijjamānaṃ. Yathā cāti yena kāraṇena kāmacchandassa uppādo hoti. Tañca pajānātīti tañca kāraṇaṃ pajānāti. Iminā nayena sabbapadesu attho veditabbo.

Herein, 'present' means existing by way of frequent occurrence. 'Absent' means not existing, either by way of non-occurrence or because it has been abandoned. And 'how' means the cause by which the arising of sensual desire occurs. 'And he understands that' means he understands that cause. In this way, the meaning should be understood in all passages.

Tattha subhanimitte ayonisomanasikārena kāmacchandassa uppādo hoti. Subhanimittaṃ nāma subhampi subhanimittaṃ, subhārammaṇampi subhanimittaṃ. Ayonisomanasikāro nāma anupāyamanasikāro uppathamanasikāro anicce niccanti vā dukkhe sukhanti vā anattani attāti vā asubhe [M 1.0286] subhanti vā manasikāro, taṃ tattha bahulaṃ pavattayato kāmacchando uppajjati. Tenāha bhagavā – “atthi, bhikkhave, subhanimittaṃ, tattha ayonisomanasikārabahulīkāro[V 1.0292], ayamāhāro anuppannassa vā kāmacchandassa uppādāya uppannassa vā kāmacchandassa bhiyyobhāvāya vepullāyā”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.232).

Herein, sensual desire arises through unwise attention to an attractive sign. An 'attractive sign' means both the beautiful itself is an attractive sign and a beautiful object is an attractive sign. 'Unwise attention' means attention that is not the proper means, attention that is the wrong path—attention to the impermanent as permanent, to the painful as pleasant, to non-self as self, or to the foul as beautiful. For one who frequently applies such attention to that sign, sensual desire arises. Therefore, the Blessed One said: “O bhikkhus, there is the attractive sign. Frequent unwise attention to it is the nutriment for the arising of unarisen sensual desire and for the increase and expansion of arisen sensual desire.” (Saṃyutta Nikāya 5.232).

Asubhanimitte pana yonisomanasikārenassa pahānaṃ hoti. Asubhanimittaṃ nāma asubhampi asubhārammaṇampi. Yonisomanasikāro nāma upāyamanasikāro pathamanasikāro anicce aniccanti vā dukkhe dukkhanti vā anattani anattāti vā asubhe asubhanti vā manasikāro, taṃ tattha bahulaṃ pavattayato kāmacchando pahīyati. Tenāha bhagavā – “atthi, bhikkhave, asubhanimittaṃ, tattha yonisomanasikārabahulīkāro, ayamanāhāro anuppannassa vā kāmacchandassa anuppādāya uppannassa vā kāmacchandassa pahānāyā”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.232).

But through wise attention to the sign of unattractiveness, its abandoning occurs. A 'sign of unattractiveness' means both the unattractive itself and an unattractive object. 'Wise attention' means attention that is the proper means, attention that is the path—attention to the impermanent as impermanent, to the painful as painful, to non-self as non-self, or to the unattractive as unattractive. For one who frequently applies such attention to that sign, sensual desire is abandoned. Therefore, the Blessed One said: “O bhikkhus, there is the sign of unattractiveness. Frequent wise attention to it is the non-nutriment for the non-arising of unarisen sensual desire and for the abandoning of arisen sensual desire.” (Saṃyutta Nikāya 5.232).

Apica cha dhammā kāmacchandassa pahānāya saṃvattanti asubhanimittassa uggaho asubhabhāvanānuyogo indriyesu [P 1.0282] guttadvāratā bhojane mattaññutā kalyāṇamittatā sappāyakathāti. Dasavidhañhi asubhanimittaṃ uggaṇhantassāpi kāmacchando pahīyati, bhāventassāpi, indriyesu pihitadvārassāpi, catunnaṃ pañcannaṃ ālopānaṃ okāse sati udakaṃ pivitvā yāpanasīlatāya bhojane mattaññunopi. Tenetaṃ vuttaṃ –

Furthermore, six things conduce to the abandoning of sensual desire: learning the sign of unattractiveness, devotion to the development of unattractiveness, guarding the doors of the sense faculties, moderation in eating, good friendship, and suitable talk. Indeed, for one who learns the ten kinds of signs of unattractiveness, sensual desire is abandoned; it is also abandoned for one who develops them, for one who has guarded the sense doors, and for one who is moderate in eating, having the habit of sustaining oneself by drinking water when there is still room for four or five morsels. Hence it was said:

“Cattāro pañca ālope, abhutvā udakaṃ pive;

Alaṃ phāsuvihārāya, pahitattassa bhikkhuno”ti. (theragā. 983);

“Leaving four or five morsels uneaten, one should drink water; this is sufficient for the comfortable abiding of a bhikkhu with a resolute mind.” (Theragā. 983);

Asubhakammikatissattherasadise asubhabhāvanārate kalyāṇamitte sevantassāpi kāmacchando pahīyati, ṭhānanisajjādīsu dasaasubhanissitasappāyakathāyapi pahīyati. Tena vuttaṃ “cha dhammā kāmacchandassa pahānāya saṃvattantī”ti. Imehi pana chahi dhammehi pahīnassa kāmacchandassa arahattamaggena āyatiṃ anuppādo hotīti pajānāti.

For one who associates with a good friend who delights in the development of unattractiveness, such as the Elder Tissa the Meditator on Foulness, sensual desire is abandoned. It is also abandoned through suitable talk connected with the ten kinds of unattractiveness while in the postures of standing, sitting, and so on. Therefore, it was said: 'Six things conduce to the abandoning of sensual desire.' And one understands that for sensual desire abandoned by these six things, its future non-arising occurs through the path of Arahantship.

Paṭighanimitte ayonisomanasikārena pana byāpādassa uppādo hoti. Tattha paṭighampi paṭighanimittaṃ, paṭighārammaṇampi paṭighanimittaṃ. Ayonisomanasikāro sabbattha ekalakkhaṇova. Taṃ [V 1.0293] tasmiṃ nimitte bahulaṃ pavattayato [M 1.0287] byāpādo uppajjati. Tenāha bhagavā – “atthi, bhikkhave, paṭighanimittaṃ, tattha ayonisomanasikārabahulīkāro, ayamāhāro anuppannassa vā byāpādassa uppādāya uppannassa vā byāpādassa bhiyyobhāvāya vepullāyā”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.232).

But through unwise attention to a sign of aversion, the arising of ill will occurs. Herein, aversion itself is a sign of aversion, and an object of aversion is also a sign of aversion. Unwise attention is of a single characteristic everywhere. For one who frequently applies it to that sign, ill will arises. Therefore, the Blessed One said: “O bhikkhus, there is the sign of aversion. Frequent unwise attention to it is the nutriment for the arising of unarisen ill will and for the increase and expansion of arisen ill will.” (Saṃ. Ni. 5.232).

Mettāya pana cetovimuttiyā yonisomanasikārenassa pahānaṃ hoti. Tattha tattha “mettā”ti vutte appanāpi upacāropi vaṭṭati. “Cetovimuttī”ti appanāva. Yonisomanasikāro vuttalakkhaṇova. Taṃ tattha bahulaṃ pavattayato byāpādo pahīyati. Tenāha bhagavā – “atthi, bhikkhave, mettā cetovimutti, tattha yonisomanasikārabahulīkāro, ayamanāhāro anuppannassa vā byāpādassa anuppādāya uppannassa vā byāpādassa pahānāyā”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.232).

But its abandoning occurs through wise attention applied to the mind-deliverance of loving-kindness. Herein, when 'loving-kindness' is said, both absorption and access concentration are appropriate. 'Mind-deliverance' means absorption only. Wise attention is of the characteristic already stated. For one who frequently applies it, ill will is abandoned. Therefore, the Blessed One said: “O bhikkhus, there is the mind-deliverance of loving-kindness. Frequent wise attention to it is the non-nutriment for the non-arising of unarisen ill will and for the abandoning of arisen ill will.” (Saṃ. Ni. 5.232).

Apica cha dhammā byāpādassa pahānāya saṃvattanti [P 1.0283] mettānimittassa uggaho mettābhāvanānuyogo kammassakatāpaccavekkhaṇā paṭisaṅkhānabahutā kalyāṇamittatā sappāyakathāti. Odhisakaanodhisakadisāpharaṇānañhi aññataravasena mettaṃ uggaṇhantassāpi byāpādo pahīyati, odhiso anodhiso disāpharaṇavasena mettaṃ bhāventassāpi. “Tvaṃ etassa kuddho kiṃ karissasi, kimassa sīlādīni nāsetuṃ sakkhissasi, nanu tvaṃ attano kammena āgantvā attano kammeneva gamissasi, parassa kujjhanaṃ nāma vītaccitaṅgāra-tattaayasalāka-gūthādīni gahetvā paraṃ paharitukāmatāsadisaṃ hoti. Esopi tava kuddho kiṃ karissati, kiṃ te sīlādīni vināsetuṃ sakkhissati, esa attano kammeneva āgantvā attano kammena gamissati, appaṭicchitapaheṇakaṃ viya paṭivātaṃ khittarajomuṭṭhi viya ca etassevesa kodho matthake patissatī”ti evaṃ attano ca parassa ca kammassakataṃ paccavekkhatopi, ubhayakammassakataṃ paccavekkhitvā paṭisaṅkhāne ṭhitassāpi, assaguttattherasadise mettābhāvanārate kalyāṇamitte sevantassāpi byāpādo pahīyati. Ṭhānanisajjādīsu mettānissitasappāyakathāyapi pahīyati. Tena vuttaṃ “cha dhammā byāpādassa pahānāya saṃvattantī”ti. Imehi pana chahi dhammehi pahīnassa byāpādassa anāgāmimaggena āyatiṃ anuppādo hotīti pajānāti.

Furthermore, six things conduce to the abandonment of ill will: taking up the sign of loving-kindness, engaging in the cultivation of loving-kindness, reflecting on the ownership of one's actions, frequent reflection, good friendship, and suitable talk. For one who takes up loving-kindness in any way—whether by way of specific or non-specific pervasion in all directions—ill will is abandoned. Similarly, for one who develops loving-kindness by way of specific or non-specific pervasion in all directions. "If you are angry with this person, what will you do? Can you destroy their virtue and so forth? Are you not one who has come by your own actions and will depart by your own actions? To be angry with another is like picking up glowing embers, a red-hot iron rod, or filth, wishing to strike another with it. If this person is angry with you, what will they do? Can they destroy your virtue and so forth? They too have come by their own actions and will depart by their own actions. Like a gift that is not accepted, like a handful of dust thrown against the wind, that anger of theirs will fall back on their own head." Thus, for one who reflects on the ownership of actions for oneself and others, for one who stands firm in reflection after considering the ownership of actions for both, and for one who associates with good friends like the Elder Assagutta who delight in the cultivation of loving-kindness—ill will is abandoned. It is also abandoned through suitable talk based on loving-kindness during standing, sitting, and so forth. Therefore, it is said: "Six things conduce to the abandonment of ill will." Moreover, one understands that for ill will abandoned by these six things, its non-arising in the future occurs through the path of the non-returner.

Aratiādīsu [V 1.0294][M 1.0288] ayonisomanasikārena thinamiddhassa uppādo hoti. Arati nāma ukkaṇṭhitā. Tandī nāma kāyālasiyatā. Vijambhitā nāma kāyavināmanā. Bhattasammado nāma bhattamucchā bhattapariḷāho. Cetaso līnattaṃ nāma cittassa līnākāro. Imesu aratiādīsu ayonisomanasikāraṃ bahulaṃ pavattayato thinamiddhaṃ uppajjati. Tenāha – “atthi, bhikkhave, arati tandī vijambhitā bhattasammado cetaso līnattaṃ, tattha ayonisomanasikārabahulīkāro, ayamāhāro anuppannassa vā thinamiddhassa uppādāya uppannassa vā thinamiddhassa bhiyyobhāvāya vepullāyā”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.232).

Sloth and torpor arise through unwise attention to discontent and so on. Discontent means dissatisfaction. Lethargy means bodily sluggishness. Yawning means stretching the body. Drowsiness after a meal means faintness from food or weariness from food. Mental sluggishness means the sluggish state of the mind. When one frequently applies unwise attention to these things—discontent and so on—sloth and torpor arise. Therefore, he said: "There is, O bhikkhus, discontent, lethargy, yawning, drowsiness after a meal, and mental sluggishness. The frequent application of unwise attention to that is the nutriment for the arising of unarisen sloth and torpor or for the increase and abundance of arisen sloth and torpor." (Saṃ. Ni. 5.232).

Ārambhadhātuādīsu pana yonisomanasikārenassa pahānaṃ hoti. Ārambhadhātu nāma paṭhamārambhavīriyaṃ. Nikkamadhātu nāma kosajjato nikkhantatāya [P 1.0284] tato balavataraṃ. Parakkamadhātu nāma paraṃ paraṃ ṭhānaṃ akkamanato tatopi balavataraṃ. Imasmiṃ tippabhede vīriye yonisomanasikāraṃ bahulaṃ pavattayato thinamiddhaṃ pahīyati. Tenāha – “atthi, bhikkhave, ārambhadhātu nikkamadhātu parakkamadhātu, tattha yonisomanasikārabahulīkāro, ayamāhāro anuppannassa vā thinamiddhassa anuppādāya uppannassa vā thinamiddhassa pahānāyā”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.232).

However, through wise attention to the element of initiative and so on, its abandonment occurs. The element of initiative means initial effort. The element of exertion means that which is stronger because of having emerged from laziness. The element of striving means that which is even stronger because it advances to higher and higher states. When one frequently applies wise attention to this threefold effort, sloth and torpor are abandoned. Therefore, he said: "O bhikkhus, there is the element of initiative, the element of exertion, and the element of striving. The frequent application of wise attention to that is the non-nutriment for the non-arising of sloth and torpor that has not yet arisen, and for the abandoning of that which has arisen." (Saṃ. Ni. 5.232).

Apica cha dhammā thinamiddhassa pahānāya saṃvattanti, atibhojane nimittaggāho iriyāpathasamparivattanatā ālokasaññāmanasikāro abbhokāsavāso kalyāṇamittatā sappāyakathāti. Āharahatthakatatravaṭṭakaalaṃsāṭakakākamāsakabhuttavamitakabhojanaṃ bhuñjitvā rattiṭṭhāne divāṭṭhāne nisinnassa hi samaṇadhammaṃ karoto thinamiddhaṃ mahāhatthī viya ottharantaṃ āgacchati. Catupañcaālopaokāsaṃ pana ṭhapetvā pānīyaṃ pivitvā yāpanasīlassa bhikkhuno taṃ na hotīti evaṃ atibhojane nimittaṃ gaṇhantassāpi thinamiddhaṃ pahīyati. Yasmiṃ iriyāpathe thinamiddhaṃ okkamati, tato aññaṃ parivattentassāpi, rattiṃ candālokadīpālokaukkāloke divā sūriyālokaṃ manasikarontassāpi, abbhokāse vasantassāpi, mahākassapattherasadise pahīnathinamiddhe kalyāṇamitte sevantassāpi thinamiddhaṃ pahīyati. Ṭhānanisajjādīsu dhutaṅganissitasappāyakathāyapi pahīyati. Tena vuttaṃ “cha dhammā thinamiddhassa pahānāya [M 1.0289] saṃvattantī”ti[V 1.0295]. Imehi pana chahi dhammehi pahīnassa thinamiddhassa arahattamaggena āyatiṃ anuppādo hotīti pajānāti.

Furthermore, six things conduce to the abandonment of sloth and torpor: grasping the sign of moderation in eating, changing one's posture, attending to the perception of light, dwelling in the open, good friendship, and suitable talk. For one who eats an excessive meal—the size of a carrying-pole basket, a hand-basket, a pot, a cloth bag, a crow's portion, or food that has been eaten and vomited—and then sits in the day quarters or night quarters practicing the ascetic's duty, sloth and torpor come upon them, overwhelming them like a great elephant. But for a monk who lives by moderation, leaving a space of four or five mouthfuls and drinking water, this does not happen. Thus, for one who grasps the sign of moderation in eating, sloth and torpor are abandoned. For one in whom sloth and torpor arise in a particular posture, by changing to another, it is abandoned. For one who attends to the light of the moon, lamps, or a torch at night, or the sunlight by day, it is abandoned. For one dwelling in the open, it is abandoned. For one associating with good friends like the great Elder Kassapa, who has abandoned sloth and torpor, it is abandoned. Through suitable talk connected with the ascetic practices while standing, sitting, and so on, it is also abandoned. Therefore, it is said: “Six things conduce to the abandonment of sloth and torpor.” Moreover, one understands that for sloth and torpor abandoned by these six things, its non-arising in the future occurs through the path of Arahantship.

Cetaso avūpasame ayonisomanasikārena uddhaccakukkuccassa uppādo hoti. Avūpasamo nāma avūpasantākāro. Uddhaccakukkuccamevetaṃ atthato. Tattha ayonisomanasikāraṃ bahulaṃ pavattayato uddhaccakukkuccaṃ uppajjati. Tenāha “atthi, bhikkhave, cetaso avūpasamo, tattha ayonisomanasikārabahulīkāro, ayamāhāro anuppannassa vā uddhaccakukkuccassa uppādāya uppannassa [P 1.0285] vā uddhaccakukkuccassa bhiyyobhāvāya vepullāyā”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.232).

Restlessness and remorse arise through unwise attention to the mind's lack of calm. Lack of calm means the state of being unpacified. In essence, this is just restlessness and remorse. When one frequently applies unwise attention to that, restlessness and remorse arise. Therefore, he said: "There is, monks, a lack of calm in the mind; the frequent application of unwise attention to that is the nutriment for the arising of unarisen restlessness and remorse, or for the increase and abundance of arisen restlessness and remorse" (Saṃ. Ni. 5.232).

Samādhisaṅkhāte pana cetaso vūpasame yonisomanasikārenassa pahānaṃ hoti. Tenāha – “atthi, bhikkhave, cetaso vūpasamo, tattha yonisomanasikārabahulīkāro, ayamāhāro anuppannassa vā uddhaccakukkuccassa anuppādāya uppannassa vā uddhaccakukkuccassa pahānāyā”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.232).

However, through wise attention to the pacification of the mind, which is designated as concentration, its abandonment occurs. Therefore, he said: "Monks, there is pacification of the mind. The frequent application of wise attention to that is the nutriment for the non-arising of restlessness and remorse that has not yet arisen, and for the abandoning of that which has arisen" (Saṃ. Ni. 5.232).

Apica cha dhammā uddhaccakukkuccassa pahānāya saṃvattanti bahussutatā paripucchakatā vinaye pakataññutā vuddhasevitā kalyāṇamittatā sappāyakathāti. Bāhusaccenapi hi ekaṃ vā dve vā tayo vā cattāro vā pañca vā nikāye pāḷivasena ca atthavasena ca uggaṇhantassāpi uddhaccakukkuccaṃ pahīyati. Kappiyākappiyaparipucchābahulassāpi, vinayapaññattiyaṃ ciṇṇavasibhāvatāya pakataññunopi, vuddhe mahallakatthere upasaṅkamantassāpi, upālittherasadise vinayadhare kalyāṇamitte sevantassāpi uddhaccakukkuccaṃ pahīyati. Ṭhānanisajjādīsu kappiyākappiyanissitasappāyakathāyapi pahīyati. Tena vuttaṃ – “cha dhammā uddhaccakukkuccassa pahānāya saṃvattantī”ti. Imehi pana chahi dhammehi pahīne uddhaccakukkucce uddhaccassa arahattamaggena kukkuccassa anāgāmimaggena āyatiṃ anuppādo hotīti pajānāti.

Moreover, six things conduce to the abandoning of restlessness and remorse: being very learned, questioning, being skilled in the Discipline, association with elders, good friendship, and suitable talk. For even in one who learns one, two, three, four, or five Nikāyas thoroughly, both in text and meaning, restlessness and remorse are abandoned. Also in one who frequently questions what is allowable and what is not, who is skilled and practiced in the rules of the Discipline, in one who approaches elder and senior monks, in one who associates with good friends like the Elder Upāli, a master of the Vinaya, restlessness and remorse are abandoned. They are also abandoned through suitable talk concerning what is allowable and what is not regarding standing, sitting, and so on. Therefore, it is said: "Six things conduce to the abandonment of restlessness and remorse." When restlessness and remorse have been abandoned by these six things, one understands that restlessness is prevented from arising in the future by the path of Arahantship, and remorse by the path of non-returning.

Vicikicchāṭṭhānīyesu dhammesu ayonisomanasikārena vicikicchāya uppādo hoti. Vicikicchāṭṭhānīyā [V 1.0296] dhammā nāma punappunaṃ vicikicchāya kāraṇattā vicikicchāva. Tattha ayonisomanasikāraṃ bahulaṃ pavattayato vicikicchā uppajjati. Tenāha – “atthi, bhikkhave, vicikicchāṭṭhānīyā dhammā[M 1.0290], tattha ayonisomanasikārabahulīkāro, ayamāhāro anuppannāya vā vicikicchāya uppādāya uppannāya vā vicikicchāya bhiyyobhāvāya vepullāyā”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.232).

Doubt arises due to unwise attention to things that are grounds for doubt. Things that are grounds for doubt are so called because they repeatedly cause doubt; they are themselves doubt. In this case, doubt arises in one who frequently practices unwise attention. Therefore, he said: "There are, monks, things that are grounds for doubt. Frequently giving unwise attention to them is a nutriment for the arising of doubt that has not yet arisen, and for the increase and abundance of doubt that has already arisen" (Saṃ. Ni. 5.232).

Kusalādīsu dhammesu yonisomanasikārena panassā pahānaṃ hoti. Tenāha – “atthi, bhikkhave, kusalākusalā dhammā sāvajjānavajjā dhammā sevitabbāsevitabbā dhammā hīnappaṇītā dhammā kaṇhasukkasappaṭibhāgā dhammā, tattha yonisomanasikārabahulīkāro[P 1.0286], ayamāhāro anuppannāya vā vicikicchāya anuppādāya uppannāya vā vicikicchāya pahānāyā”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.232).

However, its abandonment occurs through wise attention to wholesome states and so on. Therefore, he said: "There are, monks, wholesome and unwholesome states, blameworthy and blameless states, states to be cultivated and not to be cultivated, inferior and superior states, dark and bright states with their counterparts. Frequent engagement in wise attention regarding these is the nutriment for the non-arising of unarisen doubt and for the abandoning of arisen doubt" (Saṃ. Ni. 5.232).

Apica cha dhammā vicikicchāya pahānāya saṃvattanti bahussutatā paripucchakatā vinaye pakataññutā adhimokkhabahulatā kalyāṇamittatā sappāyakathāti. Bāhusaccenapi hi ekaṃ vā…pe… pañca vā nikāye pāḷivasena atthavasena ca uggaṇhantassāpi vicikicchā pahīyati. Tīṇi ratanāni ārabbha paripucchābahulassāpi, vinaye ciṇṇavasibhāvassāpi, tīsu ratanesu okappaniyasaddhāsaṅkhātaadhimokkhabahulassāpi, saddhādhimutte vakkalittherasadise kalyāṇamitte sevantassāpi vicikicchā pahīyati. Ṭhānanisajjādīsu tiṇṇaṃ ratanānaṃ guṇanissitasappāyakathāyapi pahīyati. Tena vuttaṃ – “cha dhammā vicikicchāya pahānāya saṃvattantī”ti. Imehi pana chahi dhammehi pahīnāya vicikicchāya sotāpattimaggena āyatiṃ anuppādo hotīti pajānāti.

Furthermore, six things conduce to the abandonment of doubt: being well-learned, being given to questioning, proficiency in the discipline, abundance of conviction, good friendship, and suitable talk. For even in one who learns one or... up to five Nikāyas by way of the text and the meaning, doubt is abandoned. Also in one who frequently asks questions concerning the Three Jewels, in one who is of established mastery in the discipline, in one who abounds in conviction, that is, confident faith in the Three Jewels, in one who cultivates good friends like the venerable Vakkali who is liberated by faith—doubt is abandoned. It is also abandoned through suitable talk based on the qualities of the Three Jewels in situations like standing and sitting. Therefore, it was said: "Six things conduce to the abandonment of doubt." When doubt has been abandoned through these six things, one understands that doubt is prevented from arising in the future by the path of stream-entry.

Iti ajjhattaṃ vāti evaṃ pañcanīvaraṇapariggahaṇena attano vā dhammesu, parassa vā dhammesu, kālena vā attano, kālena vā parassa dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati. Samudayavayā panettha subhanimitta asubhanimittādīsu ayonisomanasikārayonisomanasikāravasena pañcasu nīvaraṇesu vuttanayena nīharitabbā. Ito paraṃ vuttanayameva.

Thus, 'internally,' and so on. In this way, by comprehending the five hindrances, one dwells contemplating phenomena in one's own phenomena, or in another's phenomena, at times in one's own, or at times in another's phenomena. Here, the arising and passing away in the five hindrances should be drawn out in the manner described, by way of unwise and wise attention to the sign of beauty, the sign of ugliness, and so on. From here on, the method is as has been stated.

Kevalañhi [V 1.0297] idha nīvaraṇapariggāhikā sati dukkhasaccanti evaṃ yojanaṃ katvā nīvaraṇapariggāhakassa bhikkhuno niyyānamukhaṃ veditabbaṃ. Sesaṃ tādisamevāti.

For here, having made the connection thus: 'Mindfulness that comprehends the hindrances is the truth of suffering,' the gateway to liberation for a monk who comprehends the hindrances should be understood. The rest is similar.

Nīvaraṇapabbavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the section on the hindrances is concluded.

Khandhapabbavaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Chapter on the Aggregates

116. Evaṃ [M 1.0291] pañcanīvaraṇavasena dhammānupassanaṃ vibhajitvā idāni pañcakkhandhavasena vibhajituṃ puna caparantiādimāha. Tattha pañcasu upādānakkhandhesūti upādānassa khandhā upādānakkhandhā, upādānassa paccayabhūtā dhammapuñjā dhammarāsayoti attho. Ayamettha saṅkhepo[P 1.0287]. Vitthārato pana khandhakathā visuddhimagge vuttā. Iti rūpanti “idaṃ rūpaṃ, ettakaṃ rūpaṃ, na ito paraṃ rūpaṃ atthī”ti sabhāvato rūpaṃ pajānāti. Vedanādīsupi eseva nayo. Ayamettha saṅkhepo. Vitthārena pana rūpādīni visuddhimagge khandhakathāyameva vuttāni. Iti rūpassa samudayoti evaṃ avijjāsamudayādivasena pañcahākārehi rūpassa samudayo. Iti rūpassa atthaṅgamoti evaṃ avijjānirodhādivasena pañcahākārehi rūpassa atthaṅgamo, vedanādīsupi eseva nayo. Ayamettha saṅkhepo. Vitthāro pana visuddhimagge udayabbayañāṇakathāyaṃ vutto.

116. Having thus analyzed the contemplation of phenomena in terms of the five hindrances, now, in order to analyze it in terms of the five aggregates, he says, beginning with 'furthermore.' Herein, 'in the five aggregates of clinging' means that the aggregates of clinging are aggregates for clinging, meaning heaps or collections of phenomena that are conditions for clinging. This is the brief explanation here. The detailed explanation, however, is given in the Visuddhimagga in the discussion on the aggregates. Thus, 'form': one understands form in terms of its intrinsic nature, thinking, 'This is form, this much is form, there is no form beyond this.' The same method applies to feeling and so forth. This is the brief explanation here. The detailed explanation of form and the others is given in the Visuddhimagga in the discussion on the aggregates itself. Thus, 'the arising of form': in this way, the arising of form is in five aspects, such as through the arising of ignorance. Thus, 'the passing away of form': in this way, the passing away of form is in five aspects, such as through the cessation of ignorance. The same method applies to feeling and so forth. This is the brief explanation here. The detailed explanation, however, is given in the Visuddhimagga in the discussion on the knowledge of arising and passing away.

Iti ajjhattaṃ vāti evaṃ pañcakkhandhapariggahaṇena attano vā dhammesu, parassa vā dhammesu, kālena vā attano, kālena vā parassa dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati. Samudayavayā panettha “avijjāsamudayā rūpasamudayo”tiādīnaṃ (paṭi. ma. 1.50) pañcasu khandhesu vuttānaṃ paññāsāya lakkhaṇānaṃ vasena nīharitabbā. Ito paraṃ vuttanayameva.

Thus, 'internally,' and so on. In this way, by comprehending the five aggregates, one dwells contemplating phenomena in one's own phenomena, or in others' phenomena, at times in one's own, or at times in another's phenomena. Here, the arising and passing away should be drawn out in terms of the fifty characteristics mentioned for the five aggregates, such as 'with the arising of ignorance, there is the arising of form,' and so on (Patisambhidamagga 1.50). From here onward, the method is as has been stated.

Kevalañhi idha khandhapariggāhikā sati dukkhasaccanti evaṃ yojanaṃ katvā khandhapariggāhakassa bhikkhuno niyyānamukhaṃ veditabbaṃ. Sesaṃ tādisamevāti.

For here, having made the connection thus: 'Mindfulness that comprehends the aggregates is the truth of suffering,' the gateway to liberation for a monk who comprehends the aggregates should be understood. The rest is similar.

Khandhapabbavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Chapter on the Aggregates is concluded.

Āyatanapabbavaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Chapter on the Sense Bases

117. Evaṃ [V 1.0298] pañcakkhandhavasena dhammānupassanaṃ vibhajitvā idāni āyatanavasena vibhajituṃ puna caparantiādimāha. Tattha chasu ajjhattikabāhiresu āyatanesūti cakkhu sotaṃ ghānaṃ jivhā kāyo manoti imesu chasu ajjhattikesu rūpaṃ saddo gandho raso phoṭṭhabbo dhammāti imesu chasu [M 1.0292] bāhiresu. Cakkhuṃ ca pajānātīti cakkhupasādaṃ yāthāvasarasalakkhaṇavasena pajānāti. Rūpe ca pajānātīti bahiddhā catusamuṭṭhānikarūpañca yāthāvasarasalakkhaṇavasena pajānāti. Yañca tadubhayaṃ paṭicca uppajjati saṃyojananti yañca taṃ cakkhuṃ ceva rūpe cāti ubhayaṃ paṭicca kāmarāgasaṃyojanaṃ paṭigha-māna-diṭṭhi-vicikicchā-sīlabbataparāmāsa-bhavarāga-issā-macchariyāvijjāsaṃyojananti dasavidhaṃ saṃyojanaṃ uppajjati, tañca yāthāvasarasalakkhaṇavasena pajānāti.

117. Having thus analyzed the contemplation of phenomena in terms of the five aggregates, now, in order to analyze it in terms of the sense bases, he says, beginning with 'furthermore.' Herein, 'in the six internal and external sense bases' refers to these six internal ones: the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; and these six external ones: forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangible objects, and mental phenomena. And 'he understands the eye' means he understands the eye-sensitivity according to its true nature and characteristic. And 'he understands forms' means he understands external materiality arisen from the four causes according to its true nature and characteristic. And 'whatever fetter arises dependent on both' means that whatever ten kinds of fetter—namely, the fetter of sensual lust, aversion, conceit, wrong view, doubt, attachment to rites and rituals, craving for existence, envy, stinginess, and ignorance—arises dependent on both the eye and forms, he understands that according to its true nature and characteristic.

Kathaṃ [P 1.0288] panetaṃ uppajjatīti? Cakkhudvāre tāva āpāthagataṃ iṭṭhārammaṇaṃ kāmassādavasena assādayato abhinandato kāmarāgasaṃyojanaṃ uppajjati. Aniṭṭhārammaṇe kujjhato paṭighasaṃyojanaṃ uppajjati. “Ṭhapetvā maṃ na koci añño etaṃ ārammaṇaṃ vibhāvetuṃ samattho atthī”ti maññato mānasaṃyojanaṃ uppajjati. “Etaṃ rūpārammaṇaṃ niccaṃ dhuva”nti gaṇhato diṭṭhisaṃyojanaṃ uppajjati. “Etaṃ rūpārammaṇaṃ satto nu kho, sattassa nu kho”ti vicikicchato vicikicchāsaṃyojanaṃ uppajjati. “Sampattibhave vata no idaṃ sulabhaṃ jāta”nti bhavaṃ patthentassa bhavarāgasaṃyojanaṃ uppajjati. “Āyatimpi evarūpaṃ sīlabbataṃ samādiyitvā sakkā laddhu”nti sīlabbataṃ samādiyantassa sīlabbataparāmāsasaṃyojanaṃ uppajjati. “Aho vata etaṃ rūpārammaṇaṃ aññe na labheyyu”nti usūyato issāsaṃyojanaṃ uppajjati. Attanā laddhaṃ rūpārammaṇaṃ aññassa maccharāyato macchariyasaṃyojanaṃ uppajjati. Sabbeheva sahajātaaññāṇavasena avijjāsaṃyojanaṃ uppajjati.

How, then, does this arise? First, at the eye-door, for one who delights in and savors a desirable object that has come within range, in terms of the enjoyment of sensual pleasure, the fetter of sensual lust arises. For one who gets angry at an undesirable object, the fetter of aversion arises. For one who thinks, 'No one else is capable of discerning this object apart from me,' the fetter of conceit arises. For one who grasps, 'This form-object is permanent and lasting,' the fetter of wrong view arises. For one who doubts, 'Is this form-object a being, or does it belong to a being?' the fetter of doubt arises. For one who longs for existence, thinking, 'Oh, may this be easily obtained for us in a fortunate existence,' the fetter of craving for existence arises. For one who undertakes virtuous practices, thinking, 'It is possible to obtain this even in the future by undertaking such virtuous practices,' the fetter of attachment to rites and rituals arises. For one who envies, thinking, 'Oh, may others not obtain this form-object,' the fetter of envy arises. For one who is stingy towards others regarding a form-object one has obtained, the fetter of stinginess arises. And due to the ignorance co-arisen with all of these, the fetter of ignorance arises.

Yathā ca anuppannassāti yena kāraṇena asamudācāravasena anuppannassa tassa dasavidhassāpi saṃyojanassa uppādo hoti, tañca kāraṇaṃ pajānāti. Yathā ca uppannassāti appahīnaṭṭhena pana samudācāravasena vā uppannassa tassa dasavidhassāpi saṃyojanassa yena kāraṇena pahānaṃ hoti, tañca kāraṇaṃ pajānāti. Yathā ca pahīnassāti tadaṅgavikkhambhanappahānavasena [V 1.0299] pahīnassāpi tassa dasavidhassa saṃyojanassa yena kāraṇena āyatiṃ anuppādo hoti, tañca pajānāti. Kena kāraṇena panassa āyatiṃ anuppādo hoti? Diṭṭhivicikicchāsīlabbataparāmāsaissāmacchariyabhedassa tāva pañcavidhassa saṃyojanassa sotāpattimaggena [M 1.0293] āyatiṃ anuppādo hoti. Kāmarāgapaṭighasaṃyojanadvayassa oḷārikassa sakadāgāmimaggena, aṇusahagatassa anāgāmimaggena, mānabhavarāgāvijjāsaṃyojanattayassa arahattamaggena āyatiṃ anuppādo hoti.

And 'as for the unarisen' (yathā ca anuppannassa): one understands the cause by which the arising of those ten kinds of fetters, which are unarisen due to non-occurrence, comes to be. And 'as for the arisen' (yathā ca uppannassa): one understands the cause by which the abandonment of those ten kinds of fetters, which are arisen either through occurrence or because of not being abandoned, comes to be. And 'as for the abandoned' (yathā ca pahīnassa): one understands the cause by which there is no future arising of those ten kinds of fetters, even when abandoned by way of abandonment by substitution of opposites and by suppression. By what cause, then, is there no future arising of them? First, for the fivefold fetter—namely, wrong view, doubt, attachment to rites and rituals, envy, and stinginess—there is no future arising through the path of stream-entry. For the two gross fetters of sensual lust and aversion, there is no future arising through the path of once-returning; for the subtle ones associated with them, there is no future arising through the path of non-returning. For the three fetters of conceit, craving for existence, and ignorance, there is no future arising through the path of arahantship.

Sotañca pajānāti sadde cā tiādīsupi eseva nayo. Apicettha āyatanakathā vitthārato [P 1.0289] visuddhimagge āyatananiddese vuttanayeneva veditabbā.

The same method applies to 'one understands the ear and sounds' (sotañca pajānāti sadde ca) and so forth. Moreover, here the discussion on the sense bases should be understood in detail in the manner stated in the Visuddhimagga's exposition on the sense bases.

Iti ajjhattaṃ vāti evaṃ ajjhattikāyatanapariggahaṇena attano vā dhammesu, bāhirāyatanapariggahaṇena parassa vā dhammesu, kālena vā attano, kālena vā parassa dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati. Samudayavayā panettha “avijjāsamudayā cakkhusamudayo”ti rūpāyatanassa rūpakkhandhe, arūpāyatanesu manāyatanassa viññāṇakkhandhe, dhammāyatanassa sesakkhandhesu vuttanayena nīharitabbā. Lokuttaradhammā na gahetabbā. Ito paraṃ vuttanayameva.

Thus, 'internally' (iti ajjhattaṃ vā): in this way, by comprehending the internal sense bases, one dwells contemplating phenomena in one's own phenomena; or by comprehending the external sense bases, in others' phenomena; or at times in one's own phenomena, and at times in others' phenomena. Here, the arising and passing away should be extracted in the manner stated in 'with the arising of ignorance, there is the arising of the eye': for the form-base, in the form aggregate; for the mind-base among the formless bases, in the consciousness aggregate; and for the mental-phenomena-base, in the remaining aggregates. Supramundane phenomena are not to be taken. From here onward, it is by the method already stated.

Kevalañhi idha āyatanapariggāhikā sati dukkhasaccanti evaṃ yojanaṃ katvā āyatanapariggāhakassa bhikkhuno niyyānamukhaṃ veditabbaṃ. Sesaṃ tādisamevāti.

For here, the monk who comprehends the sense bases should understand the entrance to deliverance by making the connection thus: 'Mindfulness, which merely comprehends the sense bases, is the truth of suffering.' The remainder is just the same.

Āyatanapabbavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Chapter on the Sense Bases is concluded.

Bojjhaṅgapabbavaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Chapter on the Factors of Enlightenment

118. Evaṃ cha ajjhattikabāhirāyatanavasena dhammānupassanaṃ vibhajitvā idāni bojjhaṅgavasena vibhajituṃ puna caparanti ādimāha. Tattha bojjhaṅgesūti bujjhanakasattassa aṅgesu. Santanti paṭilābhavasena saṃvijjamānaṃ. Satisambojjhaṅganti satisaṅkhātaṃ sambojjhaṅgaṃ. Ettha hi sambujjhati āraddhavipassakato paṭṭhāya yogāvacaroti sambodhi, yāya vā so satiādikāya sattadhammasāmaggiyā [V 1.0300] sambujjhati kilesaniddāto uṭṭhāti, saccāni vā paṭivijjhati, sā dhammasāmaggī sambodhi. Tassa sambodhissa, tassā vā sambodhiyā aṅganti sambojjhaṅgaṃ. Tena vuttaṃ “satisaṅkhātaṃ sambojjhaṅga”nti. Sesasambojjhaṅgesupi imināva nayena vacanattho veditabbo.

118. Having thus analyzed the contemplation of phenomena by way of the six internal and external sense bases, now, to analyze it by way of the factors of enlightenment, the text begins with 'Furthermore...' (puna caparaṃ). Herein, 'in the factors of enlightenment' (bojjhaṅgesu) means in the factors of a being who awakens. 'Present' (santaṃ) means existing by way of attainment. 'The mindfulness factor of enlightenment' (satisambojjhaṅgaṃ) is the factor of enlightenment reckoned as mindfulness. Here, enlightenment (sambodhi) is that by which the yogi, from the time of beginning insight practice, awakens; or, it is that harmony of seven factors, beginning with mindfulness, by which one awakens from the slumber of the defilements, or penetrates the truths—that harmony of factors is enlightenment. A factor (aṅga) of that enlightenment is a factor of enlightenment (sambojjhaṅga). Therefore it is said, 'the factor of enlightenment reckoned as mindfulness.' The meaning of the terms for the remaining factors of enlightenment should also be understood in this same way.

Asantanti [M 1.0294] appaṭilābhavasena avijjamānaṃ. Yathā ca anuppannassātiādīsu pana satisambojjhaṅgassa tāva – “atthi, bhikkhave, satisambojjhaṅgaṭṭhānīyā dhammā, tattha yonisomanasikārabahulīkāro, ayamāhāro anuppannassa vā satisambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya, uppannassa vā satisambojjhaṅgassa bhiyyobhāvāya vepullāya bhāvanāya pāripūriyā saṃvattatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.183) evaṃ uppādo hoti[P 1.0290]. Tattha satiyeva satisambojjhaṅgaṭṭhānīyā dhammā. Yonisomanasikāro vuttalakkhaṇoyeva, taṃ tattha bahulaṃ pavattayato satisambojjhaṅgo uppajjati.

'Absent' (asantaṃ) means non-existent by way of non-attainment. Now, as for 'of the unarisen,' etc., regarding the mindfulness factor of enlightenment first: 'There are, monks, states that are a foundation for the mindfulness factor of enlightenment. Therein, the frequent practice of wise attention is the nutriment for the arising of the unarisen mindfulness factor of enlightenment, or for the increase, growth, development, and culmination of the arisen mindfulness factor of enlightenment' (SN 46.2). Thus its arising occurs. Here, mindfulness itself constitutes the states that are a foundation for the mindfulness factor of enlightenment. Wise attention is of the characteristic already stated; for one who frequently applies it therein, the mindfulness factor of enlightenment arises.

Apica cattāro dhammā satisambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya saṃvattanti satisampajaññaṃ muṭṭhassatipuggalaparivajjanatā upaṭṭhitassatipuggalasevanatā tadadhimuttatāti. Abhikkantādīsu hi sattasu ṭhānesu satisampajaññena bhattanikkhittakākasadise muṭṭhassatipuggale parivajjanena tissadattattheraabhayattherasadise upaṭṭhitassatipuggale sevanena ṭhānanisajjādīsu satisamuṭṭhāpanatthaṃ ninnapoṇapabbhāracittatāya ca satisambojjhaṅgo uppajjati. Evaṃ catūhi kāraṇehi uppannassa panassa arahattamaggena bhāvanāpāripūrī hotīti pajānāti.

Furthermore, four things conduce to the arising of the mindfulness factor of enlightenment: mindfulness and clear comprehension, avoiding persons of lapsed mindfulness, associating with persons of established mindfulness, and inclination toward that. For the mindfulness factor of enlightenment arises through mindfulness and clear comprehension in the seven activities beginning with going forward; by avoiding persons of lapsed mindfulness, who are like a crow that has dropped its food; by associating with persons of established mindfulness, like the elders Tissadatta and Abhaya; and through a mind that is inclined, sloping, and tending toward arousing mindfulness in postures such as standing and sitting. Thus, one understands that for this factor, having arisen from these four causes, the culmination of its development occurs with the path of Arahantship.

Dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgassa pana – “atthi, bhikkhave, kusalākusalā dhammā…pe… kaṇhasukkasappaṭibhāgā dhammā, tattha yonisomanasikārabahulīkāro, ayamāhāro anuppannassa vā dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya, uppannassa vā dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgassa bhiyyobhāvāya vepullāya bhāvanāya pāripūriyā saṃvattatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.232) evaṃ uppādo hoti.

As for the investigation-of-states factor of enlightenment: 'There are, monks, skillful and unskillful states... states with dark and bright counterparts. Therein, the frequent practice of wise attention is the nutriment for the arising of the unarisen investigation-of-states factor of enlightenment, or for the increase, growth, development, and culmination of the arisen investigation-of-states factor of enlightenment' (SN 46.2). Thus its arising occurs.

Apica satta dhammā dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya saṃvattanti paripucchakatā vatthuvisadakiriyā indriyasamattapaṭipādanā duppaññapuggalaparivajjanā paññavantapuggalasevanā gambhīrañāṇacariyapaccavekkhaṇā tadadhimuttatāti. Tattha paripucchakatāti khandhadhātuāyatanaindriyabalabojjhaṅgamaggaṅgajhānaṅgasamathavipassanānaṃ atthasannissitaparipucchābahulatā.

Furthermore, seven things conduce to the arising of the investigation-of-states factor of enlightenment: being inquisitive, making the basis clear, balancing the faculties, avoiding persons of poor wisdom, associating with persons of wisdom, reflecting on the sphere of profound knowledge, and being inclined toward that. Herein, 'being inquisitive' means frequently asking questions related to the meaning of the aggregates, elements, sense bases, faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, path factors, jhāna factors, serenity, and insight.

Vatthuvisadakiriyāti [V 1.0301] ajjhattikabāhirānaṃ vatthūnaṃ visadabhāvakaraṇaṃ. Yadā hissa kesanakhalomā atidīghā honti, sarīraṃ vā ussannadosañceva sedamalamakkhitañca, tadā ajjhattikaṃ vatthu avisadaṃ hoti aparisuddhaṃ[M 1.0295]. Yadā pana cīvaraṃ jiṇṇaṃ kiliṭṭhaṃ duggandhaṃ hoti, senāsanaṃ vā uklāpaṃ, tadā bāhiraṃ vatthu avisadaṃ hoti aparisuddhaṃ. Tasmā kesādicchedāpanena uddhaṃvirecanaadhovirecanādīhi sarīrasallahukabhāvakaraṇena [P 1.0291] ucchādananhāpanena ca ajjhattikaṃ vatthu visadaṃ kātabbaṃ.

'Making the basis clear' means making the internal and external bases clear. For when one's hair, nails, or body hair are too long, or the body is afflicted with an excess of bodily humors and smeared with sweat and dirt, then the internal basis is unclear and impure. And when one's robe is old, soiled, and foul-smelling, or one's lodging is filthy, then the external basis is unclear and impure. Therefore, the internal basis should be made clear by having hair and so on cut, by making the body light through means such as emetics and purgatives, and by anointing and bathing.

Sūcikammadhovanarajanaparibhaṇḍakaraṇādīhi bāhiraṃ vatthu visadaṃ kātabbaṃ. Etasmiñhi ajjhattikabāhire vatthusmiṃ avisade uppannesu cittacetasikesu ñāṇampi aparisuddhaṃ hoti, aparisuddhāni dīpakapallakavaṭṭitelāni nissāya uppannadīpasikhāya obhāso viya. Visade pana ajjhattikabāhire vatthumhi uppannesu cittacetasikesu ñāṇampi visadaṃ hoti, parisuddhāni dīpakapallakavaṭṭitelāni nissāya uppannadīpasikhāya obhāso viya. Tena vuttaṃ – “vatthuvisadakiriyā dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya saṃvattatī”ti.

The external basis should be made clear by such activities as needlework, washing, dyeing, and mending. For when this internal and external basis is unclear, the knowledge in the arisen consciousness and mental factors is also impure, like the light from a lamp flame that has arisen depending on an unclean lamp bowl, wick, and oil. But when the internal and external basis is clear, the knowledge in the arisen consciousness and mental factors is also clear, like the light from a lamp flame that has arisen depending on a clean lamp bowl, wick, and oil. Therefore it was said: 'Making the basis clear conduces to the arising of the investigation-of-states factor of enlightenment.'

Indriyasamattapaṭipādanā nāma saddhādīnaṃ indriyānaṃ samabhāvakaraṇaṃ. Sace hissa saddhindriyaṃ balavaṃ hoti, itarāni mandāni. Tato vīriyindriyaṃ paggahakiccaṃ, satindriyaṃ upaṭṭhānakiccaṃ, samādhindriyaṃ avikkhepakiccaṃ, paññindriyaṃ dassanakiccaṃ kātuṃ na sakkoti. Tasmā taṃ dhammasabhāvapaccavekkhaṇena vā yathā vā manasikaroto balavaṃ jātaṃ, tathā amanasikārena hāpetabbaṃ. Vakkalittherassa vatthu cettha nidassanaṃ. Sace pana vīriyindriyaṃ balavaṃ hoti, atha neva saddhindriyaṃ adhimokkhakiccaṃ kātuṃ sakkoti, na itarāni itarakiccabhedaṃ. Tasmā taṃ passaddhādibhāvanāya hāpetabbaṃ. Tatrāpi soṇattherassa vatthu dassetabbaṃ. Evaṃ sesesupi ekassa balavabhāve sati itaresaṃ attano kiccesu asamatthatā veditabbā.

Balancing the faculties means making the faculties of faith and the others equal. If one's faculty of faith is strong while the others are weak, then the faculty of energy cannot perform its function of exertion, the faculty of mindfulness its function of establishment, the faculty of concentration its function of non-distraction, nor the faculty of wisdom its function of seeing. Therefore, that which has become strong should be diminished by reflecting on the nature of phenomena or by not attending to it in the way that it became strong. The story of the Elder Vakkali is an example here. If, however, the faculty of energy is strong, then neither can the faculty of faith perform its function of resolution, nor the others their respective functions. Thus, it should be diminished by cultivating tranquility and so on. The story of the Elder Soṇa should be cited in that case. Similarly, when one faculty is strong, the inability of the others to perform their own functions should be understood.

Visesato panettha saddhāpaññānaṃ samādhivīriyānaṃ ca samataṃ pasaṃsanti. Balavasaddho hi mandapañño mudhāpasanno hoti, avatthusmiṃ pasīdati. Balavapañño mandasaddho kerāṭikapakkhaṃ bhajati. Bhesajjasamuṭṭhito viya rogo atekiccho hoti. Cittuppādamatteneva kusalaṃ hotīti atidhāvitvā dānādīni akaronto niraye uppajjati. Ubhinnaṃ samatāya vatthusmiṃyeva pasīdati[V 1.0302]. Balavasamādhiṃ pana mandavīriyaṃ samādhissa kosajjapakkhattā kosajjaṃ adhibhavati. Balavavīriyaṃ mandasamādhiṃ vīriyassa uddhaccapakkhattā [M 1.0296] uddhaccaṃ adhibhavati[P 1.0292]. Samādhi pana vīriyena saṃyojito kosajje patituṃ na labhati. Vīriyaṃ samādhinā saṃyojitaṃ uddhacce patituṃ na labhati. Tasmā tadubhayaṃ samaṃ kātabbaṃ. Ubhayasamatāya hi appanā hoti.

Here, in particular, they praise the balancing of faith with wisdom, and of concentration with energy. For one strong in faith but weak in wisdom has misplaced confidence and places faith in an unworthy object. One strong in wisdom but weak in faith inclines towards craftiness; like a disease caused by the medicine itself, he is incurable. Thinking, 'Merit is made by the mere arising of a thought,' he overshoots the mark and, by not performing acts of generosity and so on, is reborn in hell. Through the balance of both, however, one places faith only in a worthy object. One strong in concentration but weak in energy is overcome by laziness, since concentration sides with sloth. One strong in energy but weak in concentration is overcome by restlessness, since energy sides with agitation. But concentration yoked with energy does not fall into sloth. Energy yoked with concentration does not fall into agitation. Therefore, those two should be made equal, for it is through their equality that absorption is attained.

Apica samādhikammikassa balavatīpi saddhā vaṭṭati. Evaṃ saddahanto okappento appanaṃ pāpuṇissati. Samādhipaññāsu pana samādhikammikassa ekaggatā balavatī vaṭṭati, evañhi so appanaṃ pāpuṇāti. Vipassanākammikassa paññā balavatī vaṭṭati, evañhi so lakkhaṇappaṭivedhaṃ pāpuṇāti. Ubhinnaṃ pana samatāyapi appanā hotiyeva. Sati pana sabbattha balavatī vaṭṭati. Sati hi cittaṃ uddhaccapakkhikānaṃ saddhāvīriyapaññānaṃ vasena uddhaccapātato, kosajjapakkhikena ca samādhinā kosajjapātato rakkhati. Tasmā sā loṇadhūpanaṃ viya sabbabyañjanesu sabbakammikaamacco viya ca sabbarājakiccesu sabbattha icchitabbā. Tenāha – “sati ca pana sabbatthikā vuttā bhagavatā. Kiṃ kāraṇā? Cittañhi sati paṭisaraṇaṃ, ārakkhapaccupaṭṭhānā ca sati, na ca vinā satiyā cittassa paggahaniggaho hotī”ti.

Moreover, for one undertaking the work of concentration, strong faith is suitable. By thus having faith and conviction, one will attain absorption. But between concentration and wisdom, for one undertaking the work of concentration, strong one-pointedness is suitable, for in that way one attains absorption. For one undertaking the work of insight, strong wisdom is suitable, for in that way one attains penetration of the characteristics. However, absorption also occurs through the balance of both. But strong mindfulness is suitable everywhere. For mindfulness protects the mind from falling into agitation through faith, energy, and wisdom, which side with agitation, and from falling into laziness through concentration, which sides with sloth. Therefore, it is to be desired in all circumstances, like salt in all sauces, and like a prime minister in all the king's affairs. Thus it was said: 'Mindfulness, it is said by the Blessed One, is always needed. For what reason? The mind has mindfulness as its refuge, mindfulness manifests as protection, and without mindfulness there is no exerting and restraining of the mind.'

Duppaññapuggalaparivajjanā nāma khandhādibhede anogāḷhapaññānaṃ dummedhapuggalānaṃ ārakāva parivajjanaṃ. Paññavantapuggalasevanā nāma samapaññāsalakkhaṇapariggāhikāya udayabbayapaññāya samannāgatapuggalasevanā. Gambhīrañāṇacariyapaccavekkhaṇā nāma gambhīresu khandhādīsu pavattāya gambhīrapaññāya pabhedapaccavekkhaṇā. Tadadhimuttatā nāma ṭhānanisajjādīsu dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgasamuṭṭhāpanatthaṃ ninnapoṇapabbhāracittatā. Evaṃ uppannassa panassa arahattamaggena bhāvanāpāripūrī hotīti pajānāti.

Avoiding unwise persons means keeping far away from foolish people whose wisdom has not penetrated the analysis of the aggregates and so on. Associating with wise persons means associating with persons endowed with the wisdom of arising and passing away that grasps the characteristics of the fifty-three mental formations. Reflecting on the domain of profound knowledge means reflecting on the various kinds of profound wisdom that proceeds in regard to the profound aggregates and so on. Being resolved on that means, in all postures such as standing and sitting, having a mind that is inclined, sloping, and tending towards the arousal of the investigation-of-states enlightenment factor. One understands that for one for whom it has thus arisen, the fulfillment of its development occurs with the path of Arahantship.

Vīriyasambojjhaṅgassa – “atthi, bhikkhave, ārabbhadhātu nikkamadhātu parakkamadhātu, tattha yoniso manasikārabahulīkāro, ayamāhāro anuppannassa vā vīriyasambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya, uppannassa vā vīriyasambojjhaṅgassa bhiyyobhāvāya vepullāya bhāvanāya pāripūriyā saṃvattatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.232) evaṃ uppādo hoti.

Regarding the enlightenment factor of energy: "Bhikkhus, there is the element of initiative, the element of exertion, the element of striving. The frequent practice of wise attention to these is the nutriment for the arising of the unarisen enlightenment factor of energy, and for the increase, growth, development, and fulfillment of the arisen enlightenment factor of energy." (SN 5.232) Thus does it arise.

Apica [V 1.0303][M 1.0297] ekādasa dhammā vīriyasambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya [P 1.0293] saṃvattanti apāyabhayapaccavekkhaṇatā ānisaṃsadassāvitā gamanavīthipaccavekkhaṇatā piṇḍapātāpacāyanatā dāyajjamahattapaccavekkhaṇatā satthumahattapaccavekkhaṇatā jātimahattapaccavekkhaṇatā sabrahmacārimahattapaccavekkhaṇatā kusītapuggalaparivajjanatā āraddhavīriyapuggalasevanatā tadadhimuttatāti.

Furthermore, eleven things lead to the arising of the energy enlightenment factor: reflecting on the fear of the woeful states, seeing the advantages, reflecting on the path to be traversed, honoring the almsfood, reflecting on the greatness of the inheritance, reflecting on the greatness of the Teacher, reflecting on the greatness of one's birth, reflecting on the greatness of one's spiritual companions, avoiding lazy individuals, associating with energetic individuals, and being resolved on that.

Tattha nirayesu pañcavidhabandhanakammakāraṇato paṭṭhāya mahādukkhaṃ anubhavanakālepi, tiracchānayoniyaṃ jālakkhipakumīnādīhi gahitakālepi, pājanakaṇṭakādippahāratunnassa pana sakaṭavāhanādikālepi, pettivisaye anekānipi vassasahassāni ekaṃ buddhantarampi khuppipāsāhi āturitakālepi, kālakañjikaasuresu saṭṭhihatthaasītihatthappamāṇena aṭṭhicammamatteneva attabhāvena vātātapādidukkhānubhavanakālepi na sakkā vīriyasambojjhaṅgaṃ uppādetuṃ. Ayameva te bhikkhu kālo vīriyakaraṇāyāti evaṃ apāyabhayaṃ paccavekkhantassāpi vīriyasambojjhaṅgo uppajjati.

Therein, it is impossible to arouse the enlightenment factor of energy: even while experiencing great suffering in the hells, beginning with the fivefold bondage and the 'deed-doing' torture; even when, in the animal realm, one is caught by nets, snares, fish-traps, and so on; even when pierced by the blows of goads, thorns, and the like, while pulling carts and other vehicles; even when, in the realm of afflicted spirits, one is tormented by hunger and thirst for many thousands of years or for an entire Buddha-interval; even when, among the Kālakañjika asuras, with a body of mere skin and bone sixty or eighty cubits high, one experiences the suffering of wind, sun, and so on. The enlightenment factor of energy arises for one who reflects on the fear of the woeful states in this way: 'Bhikkhu, this is the very time for you to make an effort!'

“Na sakkā kusītena navalokuttaradhammaṃ laddhuṃ, āraddhavīriyeneva sakkā ayamānisaṃso vīriyassā”ti evaṃ ānisaṃsadassāvinopi uppajjati. “Sabbabuddhapaccekabuddhamahāsāvakehi te gatamaggo gantabbo, so ca na sakkā kusītena gantu”nti evaṃ gamanavīthiṃ paccavekkhantassāpi uppajjati. “Ye taṃ piṇḍapātādīhi upaṭṭhahanti, ime te manussā neva ñātakā, na dāsakammakarā, nāpi ‘taṃ nissāya jīvissāmā’ti te paṇītāni piṇḍapātādīni denti, atha kho attano kārānaṃ mahapphalataṃ paccāsīsamānā denti, satthārāpi ‘ayaṃ ime paccaye paribhuñjitvā kāyadaḷhībahulo sukhaṃ viharissatī’ti na evaṃ sampassatā tuyhaṃ paccayā anuññātā, atha kho ‘ayaṃ ime paribhuñjamāno samaṇadhammaṃ katvā vaṭṭadukkhato muccissatī’ti te paccayā anuññātā, so dāni tvaṃ kusīto viharanto na taṃ piṇḍaṃ apacāyissasi, āraddhavīriyasseva hi piṇḍapātāpacāyanaṃ nāma hotī”ti evaṃ piṇḍapātāpacāyanaṃ paccavekkhantassāpi uppajjati mahāmittattherassa [P 1.0294] viya.

"It is not possible for a lazy person to attain the nine supramundane Dhammas; only one with aroused energy can. This is the benefit of energy." Thus, the energy enlightenment factor arises even for one who sees its advantages. "The path trodden by all Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and great disciples must be trodden by you, and it cannot be trodden by a lazy person." Thus, the energy enlightenment factor arises even for one who reflects on the course of the journey. "Those who support you with almsfood and other requisites—these people are neither your relatives, nor your slaves or workers, nor do they give you fine almsfood thinking, 'We will live by depending on him.' Rather, they give, hoping for the great fruitfulness of their own actions. The Teacher, too, did not permit you these requisites with the thought, 'Having used these requisites, he will live happily with a strong body.' Rather, he permitted them with the thought, 'Using these, he will fulfill the duties of a recluse and be freed from the suffering of the round of rebirth.' Now, if you live lazily, you will not be honoring that almsfood. For honoring almsfood is only for one with aroused energy." Thus, the energy enlightenment factor arises even for one who reflects on honoring the almsfood, as in the case of the Elder Mahāmitta.

Thero [M 1.0298] kira kassakaleṇe nāma paṭivasati. Tassa ca gocaragāme ekā mahāupāsikā theraṃ [V 1.0304] puttaṃ katvā paṭijaggati. Sā ekadivasaṃ araññaṃ gacchantī dhītaraṃ āha – “amma asukasmiṃ ṭhāne purāṇataṇḍulā, asukasmiṃ khīraṃ, asukasmiṃ sappi, asukasmiṃ phāṇitaṃ, tava bhātikassa ayyamittassa āgatakāle bhattaṃ pacitvā khīrasappiphāṇitehi saddhiṃ dehi, tvaṃ ca bhuñjeyyāsi, ahaṃ pana hiyyo pakkaṃ pārivāsikabhattaṃ kañjikena bhuttāmhī”ti. Divā kiṃ bhuñjissasi ammāti? Sākapaṇṇaṃ pakkhipitvā kaṇataṇḍulehi ambilayāguṃ pacitvā ṭhapehi ammāti.

The elder, it is said, was residing in a place called the Farmer's Cave. In his alms-round village, a great female lay devotee looked after the elder as her own son. One day, as she was going to the forest, she said to her daughter: "My dear, in such-and-such a place there is aged rice, in such-and-such a place milk, in such-and-such a place ghee, and in such-and-such a place molasses. When your brother, the venerable Mitta, comes, cook a meal and give it to him with the milk, ghee, and molasses. You should eat as well. As for me, I ate yesterday's leftover food with rice gruel." "What will you eat during the day, mother?" "Cook some sour gruel with broken rice, add some vegetable leaves, and set it aside, my dear."

Thero cīvaraṃ pārupitvā pattaṃ nīharantova taṃ saddaṃ sutvā attānaṃ ovadi – “mahāupāsikā kira kañjiyena pārivāsikabhattaṃ bhuñji, divāpi kaṇapaṇṇambilayāguṃ bhuñjissati, tuyhaṃ atthāya pana purāṇataṇḍulādīni ācikkhati, taṃ nissāya kho panesā neva khettaṃ na vatthuṃ na bhattaṃ na vatthaṃ paccāsīsati, tisso pana sampattiyo patthayamānā deti, tvaṃ etissā tā sampattiyo dātuṃ sakkhissasi na sakkhissasīti, ayaṃ kho pana piṇḍapāto tayā sarāgena sadosena samohena na sakkā gaṇhitunti pattaṃ thavikāya pakkhipitvā gaṇṭhikaṃ muñcitvā nivattitvā kassakaleṇameva gantvā pattaṃ heṭṭhāmañce cīvaraṃ cīvaravaṃse ṭhapetvā arahattaṃ apāpuṇitvā na nikkhamissāmī”ti vīriyaṃ adhiṭṭhahitvā nisīdi. Dīgharattaṃ appamatto hutvā nivutthabhikkhu vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā purebhattameva arahattaṃ patvā vikasitaṃ viya padumaṃ mahākhīṇāsavo sitaṃ karontova nikkhami. Leṇadvāre rukkhamhi adhivatthā devatā –

The elder, while putting on his robe and taking out his alms bowl, heard that conversation and admonished himself: "The great female lay devotee, it seems, ate leftover food with gruel. During the day, she will also eat sour gruel with broken rice and vegetable leaves. Yet, for your sake, she points out the aged rice and other fine things. In supporting you, she does not expect a field, property, food, or cloth. Instead, she gives, wishing for the three kinds of attainment. Will you be able to give her those attainments or not? This almsfood cannot be accepted by you while you have greed, hatred, and delusion." Putting the bowl back in its bag and untying his belt, he turned back and went to the Farmer's Cave. There, he placed the bowl under his couch and the robe on the robe-rack, and sat down, making a resolution: "I will not leave until I have attained Arahantship." As a monk who had lived diligently for a long time, he developed insight and attained Arahantship right before the forenoon meal. Like a fully blossomed lotus, the great Arahant, whose cankers were destroyed, came out smiling. At the entrance of the cave, a deity dwelling in a tree uttered this verse:

“Namo te purisājañña, namo te purisuttama;

Yassa te āsavā khīṇā, dakkhiṇeyyosi mārisā”ti. –

"Homage to you, O thoroughbred of men, homage to you, O supreme among men; your cankers are destroyed, you are worthy of offerings, O venerable sir!"

Evaṃ udānaṃ udānetvā “bhante, piṇḍāya paviṭṭhānaṃ tumhādisānaṃ arahantānaṃ bhikkhaṃ datvā mahallakitthiyo dukkhā muccissantī”ti āha.

Having uttered this inspired utterance, the deity said, "Venerable sir, by giving alms to Arahants like you who have entered for alms, that elderly woman will be freed from suffering."

Thero [P 1.0295] uṭṭhahitvā dvāraṃ vivaritvā kālaṃ olokento pātoyevāti ñatvā pattacīvaramādāya gāmaṃ pāvisi. Dārikāpi bhattaṃ sampādetvā “idāni me bhātā āgamissati[V 1.0305], idāni āgamissatī”ti dvāraṃ olokayamānā nisīdi. Sā there gharadvāraṃ sampatte pattaṃ gahetvā sappiphāṇitayojitassa khīrapiṇḍapātassa pūretvā hatthe ṭhapesi. Thero “sukhaṃ hotū”ti anumodanaṃ katvā pakkāmi. Sāpi taṃ olokayamānāva [M 1.0299] aṭṭhāsi. Therassa hi tadā ativiya parisuddho chavivaṇṇo ahosi, vippasannāni indriyāni, mukhaṃ bandhanā pamuttatālapakkaṃ viya ativiya virocittha. Mahāupāsikā araññā āgantvā “kiṃ amma, bhātiko te āgato”ti pucchi. Sā sabbaṃ taṃ pavattiṃ ārocesi. Sā upāsikā “ajja me puttassa pabbajitakiccaṃ matthakaṃ patta”nti ñatvā “abhiramati te amma bhātā buddhasāsane na ukkaṇṭhatī”ti āha.

The elder, having risen, opened the door, and observing the time, knew it was early morning. Taking his bowl and robe, he entered the village. The young girl, having prepared the meal, sat watching the door, thinking, "Now my brother will come, now he will come." When the elder reached the door of the house, she took his bowl, filled it with milk-rice mixed with ghee and molasses, and placed it in his hands. The elder gave his blessing, saying, "May you be happy," and departed. She stood watching him as he left. At that moment, the elder's complexion was exceedingly pure, his spiritual faculties were serene, and his face shone brilliantly, like a ripe palm fruit freed from its stalk. The great female lay devotee, returning from the forest, asked, "My dear, did your brother come?" The daughter related the whole event. The lay devotee, understanding, said, "Today my son's purpose for going forth has reached its culmination. My dear, your brother delights in the Buddha's Dispensation; he is not discontented."

“Mahantaṃ kho panetaṃ satthu dāyajjaṃ, yadidaṃ sattaariyadhanaṃ nāma, taṃ na sakkā kusītena gahetuṃ. Yathā hi vippaṭipannaṃ puttaṃ mātāpitaro ‘ayaṃ amhākaṃ aputto’ti paribāhiraṃ karonti, so tesaṃ accayena dāyajjaṃ na labhati, evaṃ kusītopi idaṃ ariyadhanadāyajjaṃ na labhati, āraddhavīriyova labhatī”ti dāyajjamahattataṃ paccavekkhatopi uppajjati. “Mahā kho pana te satthā, satthuno hi mātukucchismiṃ paṭisandhiggahaṇakālepi abhinikkhamanepi abhisambodhiyampi dhammacakkappavattanayamakapāṭihāriyadevorohaṇa-āyusaṅkhāravossajjanesupi parinibbānakālepi dasasahassilokadhātu kampittha, yuttaṃ nu te evarūpassa satthuno sāsane ‘pabbajitvā kusītena bhavitu’”nti evaṃ satthumahattaṃ paccavekkhatopi uppajjati.

‘Great indeed is the Teacher’s inheritance, namely the seven noble treasures, which cannot be obtained by the indolent. Just as parents disown a wayward child, saying, “This is no child of ours,” and after their death, he does not receive the inheritance, so too the indolent do not obtain this inheritance of the noble treasures—only the energetic do.’ It also arises for one reflecting on the greatness of the inheritance. ‘Great indeed is your Teacher, for at the time of his conception in his mother’s womb, his renunciation, his enlightenment, the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma, the twin miracle, the descent from the world of the devas, the relinquishing of the life-principle, and his final passing away—the ten-thousandfold world system shook. Is it fitting for you, having gone forth in the dispensation of such a Teacher, to be indolent?’ It also arises for one reflecting on the greatness of the Teacher.

Jātiyāpi – “tvaṃ idāni na lāmakajātiko, asambhinnāya mahāsammatapaveṇiyā āgato, ukkākarājavaṃse jātosi, suddhodhanamahārājassa mahāmāyādeviyā ca nattā, rāhulabhaddassa kaniṭṭho, tayā nāma evarūpena jinaputtena hutvā na yuttaṃ kusītena viharitu”nti evaṃ jātimahattaṃ paccavekkhatopi uppajjati. “Sāriputtamoggallānā ceva asīti ca mahāsāvakā vīriyeneva lokuttaradhammaṃ paṭivijjhiṃsu, tvaṃ etesaṃ sabrahmacārīnaṃ [P 1.0296] maggaṃ paṭipajjissasi na paṭipajjissasī”ti evaṃ sabrahmacārimahattaṃ paccavekkhatopi uppajjati. Kucchiṃ pūretvā ṭhitaajagarasadise vissaṭṭhakāyikacetasikavīriye kusītapuggale parivajjantassāpi, āraddhavīriye pahitatte puggale sevantassāpi, ṭhānanisajjādīsu vīriyuppādanatthaṃ [V 1.0306] ninnapoṇapabbhāracittassāpi uppajjati. Evaṃ uppannassa panassa arahattamaggena bhāvanāpāripūrī hotīti pajānāti.

Also by way of birth: ‘You are now not of low birth; you have come from the unbroken lineage of the Great Elect, born in the line of the Okkāka kings, a grandson of the great King Suddhodana and Queen Mahāmāyā, a junior to Rāhulabhadra. It is not fitting for one like you, a son of the Victor, to live idly.’ Thus, it also arises for one reflecting on the greatness of one's birth. ‘Sāriputta and Moggallāna, along with the eighty great disciples, penetrated the supramundane Dhamma through energy alone. Will you follow the path of these fellow practitioners or not?’ Thus, it also arises for one reflecting on the greatness of one's fellow practitioners.
