It also arises for one who avoids lazy persons, whose physical and mental energy is slack like a python with a full belly; for one who associates with persons of aroused energy and resolute effort; and for one whose mind is inclined, bent, and sloped toward arousing energy in postures such as standing and sitting. One understands that for one for whom this has thus arisen, the perfection of development is achieved through the path to arahantship.

Pītisambojjhaṅgassa – “atthi, bhikkhave, pītisambojjhaṅgaṭṭhānīyā dhammā, tattha yonisomanasikārabahulīkāro, ayamāhāro anuppannassa vā pītisambojjhaṅgassa [M 1.0300] uppādāya, uppannassa vā pītisambojjhaṅgassa bhiyyobhāvāya vepullāya bhāvanāya pāripūriyā saṃvattatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.232) evaṃ uppādo hoti. Tattha pītiyeva pītisambojjhaṅgaṭṭhānīyā dhammā nāma, tassa uppādakamanasikāro yonisomanasikāro nāma.

Regarding the enlightenment factor of joy: “There are, bhikkhus, qualities that are a basis for the enlightenment factor of joy. Frequent, wise attention to them is the nourishment for the arising of the unarisen enlightenment factor of joy, and for the increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment of the arisen enlightenment factor of joy.” (SN 5.232) Thus is its arising. Here, joy itself is what is meant by ‘qualities that are a basis for the enlightenment factor of joy.’ The attention that produces it is what is meant by ‘wise attention.’

Apica ekādasa dhammā pītisambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya saṃvattanti buddhānussati dhammasaṅghasīlacāgadevatānussati upasamānussati lūkhapuggalaparivajjanatā siniddhapuggalasevanatā pasādanīyasuttantapaccavekkhaṇatā tadadhimuttatāti.

Furthermore, eleven things conduce to the arising of the enlightenment factor of joy: recollection of the Buddha, recollection of the Dhamma, recollection of the Sangha, recollection of virtue, recollection of generosity, recollection of deities, recollection of peace, avoiding coarse individuals, associating with refined individuals, reflecting on inspiring discourses, and being inclined thereto.

Buddhaguṇe anussarantassāpi hi yāva upacārā sakalasarīraṃ pharamāno pītisambojjhaṅgo uppajjati. Dhammasaṅghaguṇe anussarantassāpi, dīgharattaṃ akhaṇḍaṃ katvā rakkhitaṃ catupārisuddhisīlaṃ paccavekkhantassāpi, gihino dasasīlapañcasīlaṃ paccavekkhantassāpi, dubbhikkhabhayādīsu paṇītaṃ bhojanaṃ sabrahmacārīnaṃ datvā “evaṃ nāma adamhā”ti cāgaṃ paccavekkhantassāpi, gihinopi evarūpe kāle sīlavantānaṃ dinnadānaṃ paccavekkhantassāpi, yehi guṇehi samannāgatā devatā devattaṃ pattā, tathārūpānaṃ guṇānaṃ attani atthitaṃ paccavekkhantassāpi, “samāpattiyā vikkhambhitā kilesā saṭṭhipi, sattatipi vassāni na samudācarantī”ti paccavekkhantassāpi, cetiyadassanabodhidassanatheradassanesu asakkaccakiriyāya saṃsūcitalūkhabhāve buddhādīsu [P 1.0297] pasādasinehābhāvena gadrabhapiṭṭhe rajasadise lūkhapuggale parivajjantassāpi, buddhādīsu pasādabahule muducitte siniddhapuggale sevantassāpi, ratanattayaguṇaparidīpake pasādanīye suttante paccavekkhantassāpi, ṭhānanisajjādīsu pītiuppādanatthaṃ ninnapoṇapabbhāracittassāpi uppajjati. Evaṃ uppannassa panassa arahattamaggena bhāvanāpāripūrī hotīti pajānāti.

For one recollecting the virtues of the Buddha, the enlightenment factor of joy arises, suffusing the entire body up to the level of access concentration. It also arises for one recollecting the virtues of the Dhamma and Sangha; for one reflecting on virtue long maintained unbroken and guarded by the fourfold purity; for a layperson reflecting on the five or ten precepts; for one who gives fine food to fellow practitioners in times of famine and reflects, ‘Thus have I given’; for a layperson reflecting on gifts given to virtuous persons on such occasions; for one reflecting on the presence in oneself of the same virtues possessed by deities who have attained divine status; for one reflecting, ‘The defilements suppressed by attainment do not arise even for sixty or seventy years’; for one who avoids coarse persons—like dust on a donkey's back—whose coarseness is indicated by their careless behavior when visiting shrines, bodhi trees, and elders, and by their lack of faith and affection for the Buddha and others; for one associating with refined persons, whose minds are soft and full of faith in the Buddha and others; for one reflecting on inspiring discourses that illuminate the virtues of the Triple Gem; and for one whose mind is inclined, bent, and sloped toward arousing joy in postures such as standing and sitting. One understands that for one for whom this has thus arisen, its perfection of development comes through the path of arahantship.

Passaddhisambojjhaṅgassa [V 1.0307] – “atthi, bhikkhave, kāyapassaddhi cittapassaddhi, tattha yonisomanasikārabahulīkāro, ayamāhāro anuppannassa vā passaddhisambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya, uppannassa vā passaddhisambojjhaṅgassa bhiyyobhāvāya vepullāya bhāvanāya pāripūriyā saṃvattatī”ti evaṃ uppādo hoti.

Regarding the enlightenment factor of tranquility: “There are, O monks, tranquility of body and tranquility of mind. Frequent, appropriate attention to them is the food for the arising of the unarisen enlightenment factor of tranquility, and for the increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment of the arisen enlightenment factor of tranquility.” Thus is its arising.

Apica satta dhammā passaddhisambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya saṃvattanti paṇītabhojanasevanatā utusukhasevanatā iriyāpathasukhasevanatā majjhattapayogatā [M 1.0301] sāraddhakāyapuggalaparivajjanatā passaddhakāyapuggalasevanatā tadadhimuttatāti.

Furthermore, seven things conduce to the arising of the enlightenment factor of tranquility: partaking of fine food, partaking of agreeable weather, partaking of agreeable postures, application of neutrality, avoiding persons with agitated bodies, associating with persons with tranquil bodies, and being inclined thereto.

Paṇītañhi siniddhaṃ sappāyabhojanaṃ bhuñjantassāpi, sītuṇhesu utūsu ṭhānādīsu iriyāpathesu sappāyaṃ utuṃ ca iriyāpathaṃ ca sevantassāpi passaddhi uppajjati. Yo pana mahāpurisajātiko sabbautuiriyāpathakkhamova hoti, na taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Yassa sabhāgavisabhāgatā atthi, tasseva visabhāge utuiriyāpathe vajjetvā sabhāge sevantassāpi uppajjati. Majjhattapayogo vuccati attano ca parassa ca kammassakatāpaccavekkhaṇā, iminā majjhattapayogena uppajjati. Yo leḍḍudaṇḍādīhi paraṃ viheṭhayamānova vicarati. Evarūpaṃ sāraddhakāyaṃ puggalaṃ parivajjantassāpi, saṃyatapādapāṇiṃ passaddhakāyaṃ puggalaṃ sevantassāpi, ṭhānanisajjādīsu passaddhiuppādanatthāya ninnapoṇapabbhāracittassāpi uppajjati. Evaṃ uppannassa panassa arahattamaggena bhāvanāpāripūrī hotīti pajānāti.

For tranquility arises even for one who eats delicious, rich, and agreeable food, or for one who cultivates agreeable seasons and postures in cold and hot seasons. However, this is not said with reference to a great being who is capable of enduring all seasons and postures. For one for whom there is agreeableness and disagreeableness, tranquility arises by avoiding disagreeable seasons and postures and cultivating the agreeable ones. The application of equanimity is called the reflection on one's own and others' ownership of kamma; through this application of equanimity, it arises. It also arises when one avoids a person who wanders about harming others with clods of earth, sticks, and the like—a person with an agitated body; when one associates with a person who is restrained in feet and hands, tranquil in body; and when one's mind is inclined toward the arising of tranquility in standing, sitting, and so on. When it has thus arisen, one understands that its perfection of development is by means of the path to arahantship.

Samādhisambojjhaṅgassa – “atthi, bhikkhave, samathanimittaṃ abyagganimittaṃ, tattha yonisomanasikārabahulīkāro, ayamāhāro anuppannassa vā samādhisambojjhaṅgassa [P 1.0298] uppādāya, uppannassa vā samādhisambojjhaṅgassa bhiyyobhāvāya vepullāya bhāvanāya pāripūriyā saṃvattatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.232) evaṃ uppādo hoti. Tattha samathova samathanimittaṃ, avikkhepaṭṭhena ca abyagganimittanti.

Regarding the enlightenment factor of concentration: “There are, O monks, the sign of serenity and the sign of non-agitation. Frequent wise attention to that is a nutriment for the arising of the unarisen enlightenment factor of concentration, and for the increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment of the arisen enlightenment factor of concentration.” (SN 5.232) Thus it arises. Herein, serenity itself is the sign of serenity, and in the sense of non-distraction, it is the sign of non-agitation.

Apica ekādasa dhammā samādhisambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya saṃvattanti vatthuvisadakiriyatā indriyasamattapaṭipādanatā nimittakusalatā samaye cittassa paggahaṇatā samaye cittassa niggahaṇatā [V 1.0308] samaye sampahaṃsanatā samaye ajjhupekkhanatā asamāhitapuggalaparivajjanatā samāhitapuggalasevanatā jhānavimokkhapaccavekkhaṇatā tadadhimuttatāti. Tattha vatthuvisadakiriyatā ca indriyasamattapaṭipādanatā ca vuttanayeneva veditabbā.

Moreover, eleven things lead to the arising of the enlightenment factor of concentration: clarity of the basis, balancing the faculties, skill in the sign, uplifting the mind at the proper time, restraining the mind at the proper time, gladdening the mind at the proper time, regarding the mind with equanimity at the proper time, avoiding unconcentrated persons, associating with concentrated persons, reviewing the jhānas and liberations, and inclination towards that. Herein, clarity of the basis and balancing the faculties should be understood in the way already stated.

Nimittakusalatā nāma kasiṇanimittassa uggahaṇakusalatā. Samaye cittassa paggahaṇatāti yasmiṃ samaye atisithilavīriyatādīhi līnaṃ cittaṃ hoti, tasmiṃ samaye dhammavicayavīriyasambojjhaṅgasamuṭṭhāpanena tassa paggahaṇaṃ. Samaye cittassa niggahaṇatāti yasmiṃ samaye accāraddhavīriyatādīhi [M 1.0302] uddhataṃ cittaṃ hoti, tasmiṃ samaye passaddhisamādhiupekkhāsambojjhaṅgasamuṭṭhāpanena tassa niggahaṇaṃ. Samaye sampahaṃsanatāti yasmiṃ samaye cittaṃ paññāpayogamandatāya vā upasamasukhānadhigamena vā nirassādaṃ hoti, tasmiṃ samaye aṭṭhasaṃvegavatthupaccavekkhaṇena saṃvejeti. Aṭṭha saṃvegavatthūni nāma jātijarābyādhimaraṇāni cattāri, apāyadukkhaṃ pañcamaṃ, atīte vaṭṭamūlakaṃ dukkhaṃ, anāgate vaṭṭamūlakaṃ dukkhaṃ, paccuppanne āhārapariyeṭṭhimūlakaṃ dukkhanti. Ratanattayaguṇānussaraṇena ca pasādaṃ janeti. Ayaṃ vuccati “samaye sampahaṃsanatā”ti.

Skill in the sign means skill in grasping the sign of a kasiṇa. Uplifting the mind at the proper time: that is, at the time when the mind is sluggish due to excessive slackness of energy and so on, at that time uplifting it by arousing the enlightenment factors of investigation-of-dhamma and energy. Restraining the mind at the proper time: that is, at the time when the mind is agitated due to excessive energy and so on, at that time restraining it by arousing the enlightenment factors of tranquility, concentration, and equanimity. Gladdening the mind at the proper time: that is, at the time when the mind is without zest due to sluggishness in the application of wisdom or failure to attain the bliss of serenity, at that time arousing a sense of spiritual urgency by reflecting on the eight grounds for such urgency. The eight grounds for spiritual urgency are: birth, aging, sickness, and death (four); suffering in the lower realms (the fifth); suffering rooted in the past round of existence; suffering rooted in the future round of existence; and suffering rooted in the present search for nourishment. And by recollecting the qualities of the Triple Gem, one generates serene faith. This is called 'gladdening the mind at the proper time'.

Samaye ajjhupekkhanatā nāma yasmiṃ samaye sammāpaṭipattiṃ āgamma alīnaṃ anuddhataṃ anirassādaṃ ārammaṇe samappavattaṃ samathavīthipaṭipannaṃ cittaṃ hoti, tadāssa paggahaniggahasampahaṃsanesu na byāpāraṃ āpajjati sārathi viya samappavattesu. Assesu. Ayaṃ vuccati “samaye ajjhupekkhanatā”ti. Asamāhitapuggalaparivajjanatā nāma upacāraṃ vā appanaṃ vā appattānaṃ vikkhittacittānaṃ puggalānaṃ ārakā parivajjanaṃ. Samāhitapuggalasevanatā nāma upacārena vā appanāya vā samāhitacittānaṃ [P 1.0299] sevanā bhajanā payirupāsanā. Tadadhimuttatā nāma ṭhānanisajjādīsu samādhiuppādanatthaṃyeva ninnapoṇapabbhāracittatā. Evañhi paṭipajjato esa uppajjati. Evaṃ uppannassa panassa arahattamaggena bhāvanāpāripūrī hotīti pajānāti.

Regarding the mind with equanimity at the proper time: that is, when the mind, having arrived at the right practice, is neither sluggish nor agitated, is not without zest, and proceeds evenly with its object, having entered upon the path of serenity—then, like a charioteer with evenly-proceeding horses, one does not engage in the effort of uplifting, restraining, or gladdening. This is called 'regarding the mind with equanimity at the proper time'. Avoiding unconcentrated persons means avoiding from afar individuals whose minds are distracted, who have not attained access concentration or absorption. Associating with concentrated persons means associating with, frequenting, and attending upon those whose minds are concentrated through access concentration or absorption. Inclination towards that means having a mind inclined, bent, and sloped towards arousing concentration only, in postures such as standing and sitting. For one who practices thus, this arises. And when this has arisen, one understands that its perfection of development is by the path of arahantship.

Upekkhāsambojjhaṅgassa – “atthi, bhikkhave, upekkhāsambojjhaṅgaṭṭhānīyā dhammā, tattha yonisomanasikārabahulīkāro, ayamāhāro anuppannassa vā upekkhāsambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya, uppannassa vā upekkhāsambojjhaṅgassa bhiyyobhāvāya vepullāya bhāvanāya pāripūriyā saṃvattatī”ti [V 1.0309] (saṃ. ni. 5.232) evaṃ uppādo hoti. Tattha upekkhāyeva upekkhāsambojjhaṅgaṭṭhānīyā dhammā nāma.

Regarding the enlightenment factor of equanimity: “There are, O monks, things that are a basis for the enlightenment factor of equanimity. Frequent wise attention to them is a nutriment for the arising of the unarisen enlightenment factor of equanimity, and for the increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment of the arisen enlightenment factor of equanimity.” (SN 5.232) Thus it arises. Here, equanimity itself is what is meant by 'things that are a basis for the enlightenment factor of equanimity'.

Apica pañca dhammā upekkhāsambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya saṃvattanti sattamajjhattatā saṅkhāramajjhattatā sattasaṅkhārakelāyanapuggalaparivajjanatā sattasaṅkhāramajjhattapuggalasevanatā tadadhimuttatāti.

Moreover, five things lead to the arising of the equanimity enlightenment factor: equanimity towards beings, equanimity towards formations, avoiding persons who are attached to beings and formations, associating with persons who are equanimous towards beings and formations, and inclination towards that.

Tattha dvīhākārehi sattamajjhattataṃ samuṭṭhāpeti – “tvaṃ attano kammena āgantvā attano kammena gamissasi, esopi attano kammena āgantvā [M 1.0303] attano kammena gamissati, tvaṃ kaṃ kelāyasī”ti evaṃ kammassakatāpaccavekkhaṇena ca, “paramatthato sattoyeva natthi, so tvaṃ kaṃ kelāyasī”ti evaṃ nissattapaccavekkhaṇena ca. Dvīhevākārehi saṅkhāramajjhattataṃ samuṭṭhāpeti – “idaṃ cīvaraṃ anupubbena vaṇṇavikāraṃ ceva jiṇṇabhāvaṃ ca upagantvā pādapuñchanacoḷakaṃ hutvā yaṭṭhikoṭiyā chaḍḍanīyaṃ bhavissati, sace panassa sāmiko bhaveyya, nāssa evaṃ vinassituṃ dadeyyā”ti evaṃ asāmikabhāvaṃ paccavekkhaṇena, “anaddhaniyaṃ idaṃ tāvakālika”nti evaṃ tāvakālikatāpaccavekkhaṇena ca. Yathā ca cīvare, evaṃ pattādīsupi yojanā kātabbā.

Herein, one arouses equanimity towards beings in two ways: by reflecting on kamma as one's own property—'You have come by your own kamma and will go by your own kamma; this one too has come by their own kamma and will go by their own kamma. For whom are you concerned?'—and by reflecting on the absence of a being—'In the ultimate sense, there is no being. For whom are you concerned?' One arouses equanimity towards formations in two ways: by reflecting on ownerlessness—'This robe, having gradually undergone change of color and decay, will become a foot-wiping cloth and be fit to be discarded with the tip of a stick. If it had an owner, they would not allow it to be destroyed like this'—and by reflecting on its temporariness—'This is not long-lasting; it is temporary.' And as with the robe, so the application should be made to the bowl and other things.

Sattasaṅkhārakelāyanapuggalaparivajjanatāti ettha yo puggalo gihi vā attano puttadhītādike, pabbajito vā attano antevāsikasamānupajjhāyakādike mamāyati, sahattheneva nesaṃ kesacchedanasūcikammacīvaradhovanarajanapattapacanādīni karoti, muhuttampi apassanto “asuko sāmaṇero kuhiṃ, asuko daharo kuhi”nti bhantamigo viya ito cito ca āloketi[P 1.0300], aññena kesacchedanādīnaṃ atthāya “muhuttaṃ tāva asukaṃ pesethā”ti yācīyamānopi “amhepi taṃ attano kammaṃ na kārema, tumhe taṃ gahetvā kilamessathā”ti na deti. Ayaṃ sattakelāyano nāma. Yo pana pattacīvarathālakakattarayaṭṭhiādīni mamāyati, aññassa hatthena parāmasitumpi na deti, tāvakālikaṃ yācito “mayampi idaṃ mamāyantā na paribhuñjāma, tumhākaṃ kiṃ dassāmā”ti vadati. Ayaṃ saṅkhārakelāyano nāma. Yo pana tesu dvīsupi vatthūsu majjhatto udāsino. Ayaṃ sattasaṅkhāramajjhatto nāma. Iti ayaṃ upekkhāsambojjhaṅgo evarūpaṃ sattasaṅkhārakelāyanaṃ puggalaṃ ārakā parivajjantassāpi, sattasaṅkhāramajjhattapuggalaṃ sevantassāpi, ṭhānanisajjādīsu [V 1.0310] taduppādanatthaṃ ninnapoṇapabbhāracittassāpi uppajjati. Evaṃ uppannassa panassa arahattamaggena bhāvanāpāripūrī hotīti pajānāti.

Regarding 'the avoidance of a person with fondness for beings and formations': Herein, a person—whether a householder who is attached to his own sons, daughters, and so on, or one gone forth who is attached to his own pupils, fellow monks, preceptors, and so on—personally performs for them tasks such as cutting hair, needlework, washing and dyeing robes, cooking in the bowl, and so on. Not seeing them even for a moment, he looks here and there like a bewildered deer, thinking, 'Where is that novice? Where is that young one?' Even when requested by another, 'Please send so-and-so for a moment for the purpose of cutting hair,' he does not give him, saying, 'We ourselves would not make him do our own work; you would take him and make him weary.' This is called 'one with fondness for beings.' One who, on the other hand, is attached to his bowl, robe, plate, small knife, staff, and so on, does not allow another to even touch them with their hand. When asked for a temporary loan, he says, 'Even we, being attached to this, do not use it; what could we give to you?' This is called 'one with fondness for formations.' But one who is neutral and indifferent towards these two things is called 'one who is equanimous towards beings and formations.' Thus, this equanimity enlightenment factor arises for one who avoids from afar such a person with fondness for beings and formations, for one who associates with a person who is equanimous towards beings and formations, and for one whose mind is inclined, sloping, and tending towards its production in postures such as standing and sitting. He understands that for one in whom it has thus arisen, the perfection of its development comes about through the path of Arahantship.

Iti ajjhattaṃ vāti evaṃ attano vā satta sambojjhaṅge pariggaṇhitvā, parassa vā, kālena vā attano, kālena vā parassa bojjhaṅge pariggaṇhitvā [M 1.0304] dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati. Samudayavayā panettha bojjhaṅgānaṃ nibbattinirodhavasena veditabbā. Ito paraṃ vuttanayameva.

Thus, 'internally,' and so on: having comprehended the seven enlightenment factors either in oneself, or in another, or at times in oneself and at times in another, one dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena. Herein, the arising and passing away of the enlightenment factors should be understood by way of their production and cessation. From here on, the method is as has been stated.

Kevalañhi idha bojjhaṅgapariggāhikā sati dukkhasaccanti evaṃ yojanaṃ katvā bojjhaṅgapariggāhakassa bhikkhuno niyyānamukhaṃ veditabbaṃ. Sesaṃ tādisamevāti.

For here, having made the application thus: 'Mindfulness that comprehends the enlightenment factors is the truth of suffering,' the outlet for the monk who comprehends the enlightenment factors should be understood. The rest is just the same.

Bojjhaṅgapabbavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Section on the Enlightenment Factors is concluded.

Catusaccapabbavaṇṇanā

The Exposition on the Section of the Four Truths

119. Evaṃ sattabojjhaṅgavasena dhammānupassanaṃ vibhajitvā idāni catusaccavasena vibhajituṃ puna caparantiādimāha.

119. Having thus analyzed the contemplation of phenomena by way of the seven factors of enlightenment, now, in order to analyze it by way of the four truths, he says, 'And further…' and so on.

Tattha idaṃ dukkhanti yathābhūtaṃ pajānātīti ṭhapetvā taṇhaṃ tebhūmake dhamme “idaṃ dukkha”nti yathāsabhāvato pajānāti, tasseva kho pana dukkhassa janikaṃ samuṭṭhāpikaṃ purimataṇhaṃ “ayaṃ dukkhasamudayo”ti, ubhinnaṃ appavattiṃ nibbānaṃ “ayaṃ dukkhanirodho”ti, dukkhaparijānanaṃ samudayapajahanaṃ nirodhasacchikaraṇaṃ ariyamaggaṃ “ayaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā”ti yathāsabhāvato pajānātīti attho. Avasesā ariyasaccakathā visuddhimagge vitthāritāyeva.

Here, regarding 'one comprehends “this is suffering” as it truly is': excluding craving, one comprehends the phenomena in the three realms of existence as 'this is suffering' according to their own nature. Furthermore, one comprehends the prior craving that generates and gives rise to this very suffering as 'this is the origin of suffering'; one comprehends Nibbāna, the non-occurrence of both, as 'this is the cessation of suffering'; and one comprehends the Noble Path—which is the full understanding of suffering, the abandoning of its origin, and the realization of cessation—as 'this is the path leading to the cessation of suffering' according to its own nature. This is the meaning. The remaining discourse on the Noble Truths is explained in detail in the Visuddhimagga.

Iti ajjhattaṃ vāti evaṃ attano vā cattāri saccāni [P 1.0301] pariggaṇhitvā, parassa vā, kālena vā attano, kālena vā parassa cattāri saccāni pariggaṇhitvā dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati. Samudayavayā panettha catunnaṃ saccānaṃ yathāsambhavato uppattinivattivasena veditabbā. Ito paraṃ vuttanayameva.

Thus, 'internally' and so on means that having grasped the four truths concerning oneself, or concerning another, or at times concerning oneself and at times concerning another, one dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena. Here, the arising and passing away with respect to these four truths should be understood according to their possibility, in terms of their coming into being and ceasing. From here on, the method is as previously stated.

Kevalañhi [V 1.0311] idha catusaccapariggāhikā sati dukkhasaccanti evaṃ yojanaṃ katvā saccapariggāhakassa bhikkhuno niyyānamukhaṃ veditabbaṃ. Sesaṃ tādisamevāti.

Here, indeed, having made the application thus: 'Mindfulness that grasps the four truths is the truth of suffering,' the gateway to liberation for the bhikkhu who grasps the truths should be understood. The rest is just the same.

Catusaccapabbavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition on the Section of the Four Truths is concluded.

Ettāvatā [M 1.0305] ānāpānaṃ catuiriyāpathaṃ catusampajaññaṃ dvattiṃsākāraṃ catudhātuvavatthānaṃ navasivathikā vedanānupassanā cittānupassanā nīvaraṇapariggaho khandhapariggaho āyatanapariggaho bojjhaṅgapariggaho saccapariggahoti ekavīsati kammaṭṭhānāni vuttāni. Tesu ānāpānaṃ dvattiṃsākāro navasivathikāti ekādasa appanākammaṭṭhānāni honti. Dīghabhāṇakamahāsīvatthero pana “navasivathikā ādīnavānupassanāvasena vuttā”ti āha. Tasmā tassa matena dveyeva appanākammaṭṭhānāni, sesāni upacārakammaṭṭhānāni. Kiṃ panetesu sabbesu abhiniveso jāyatīti? Na jāyati. Iriyāpathasampajaññanīvaraṇabojjhaṅgesu hi abhiniveso na jāyati, sesesu jāyatīti. Mahāsīvatthero panāha – “etesupi abhiniveso jāyati, ayañhi atthi nu kho me cattāro iriyāpathā, udāhu natthi, atthi nu kho me catusampajaññaṃ, udāhu natthi, atthi nu kho me pañcanīvaraṇā, udāhu natthi, atthi nu kho me sattabojjhaṅgā, udāhu natthīti evaṃ pariggaṇhāti, tasmā sabbattha abhiniveso jāyatī”ti.

Thus far, twenty-one meditation subjects have been stated: mindfulness of breathing, the four postures, the four kinds of clear comprehension, the thirty-two parts of the body, the analysis of the four elements, the nine charnel ground contemplations, contemplation of feelings, contemplation of mind, comprehension of the hindrances, comprehension of the aggregates, comprehension of the sense bases, comprehension of the factors of enlightenment, and comprehension of the truths. Among these, mindfulness of breathing, the thirty-two parts of the body, and the nine charnel ground contemplations are eleven absorption meditation subjects. However, the Elder Mahāsīva, the Dīgha-reciter, says, 'The nine charnel ground contemplations are stated by way of contemplation of disadvantage.' Therefore, according to his view, there are only two absorption meditation subjects, and the rest are access meditation subjects. But does adherence arise in all these? It does not arise. For adherence does not arise in the case of the postures, clear comprehension, the hindrances, and the factors of enlightenment; it arises in the rest. But the Elder Mahāsīva says, 'Adherence arises even in these, for one comprehends thus: “Do I have the four postures or not? Do I have the four kinds of clear comprehension or not? Do I have the five hindrances or not? Do I have the seven factors of enlightenment or not?” Thus one comprehends; therefore, adherence arises in all cases.'

137. Yo hi koci, bhikkhaveti yo hi koci bhikkhu vā bhikkhunī vā upāsako vā upāsikā vā. Evaṃ bhāveyyāti ādito paṭṭhāya vuttena bhāvanānukkamena bhāveyya. Pāṭikaṅkhanti paṭikaṅkhitabbaṃ, avassaṃ bhāvīti attho. Aññāti arahattaṃ. Sati vā upādiseseti upādānasese vā sati [P 1.0302] aparikkhīṇe. Anāgāmitāti anāgāmibhāvo.

137. 'Whoever, O bhikkhus' means any bhikkhu or bhikkhunī, male lay follower or female lay follower. 'Should develop thus' means one should develop from the beginning according to the stated sequence of development. 'One should expect' means it is to be expected, it will certainly come to be—this is the meaning. 'Final knowledge' means Arahantship. 'Or if there is a residue of clinging' means while a residue of appropriation remains unexhausted. 'Non-returning' means the state of a non-returner.

Evaṃ sattannaṃ vassānaṃ vasena sāsanassa niyyānikabhāvaṃ dassetvā puna tato appatarepi kāle dassento “tiṭṭhantu, bhikkhave”tiādimāha. Sabbampi cetaṃ majjhimasseva neyyapuggalassa vasena vuttaṃ. Tikkhapaññaṃ pana sandhāya – “pāto anusiṭṭho sāyaṃ visesaṃ adhigamissati, sāyaṃ anusiṭṭho pāto visesaṃ adhigamissatī”ti (ma. ni. 2.345) vuttaṃ.

Having thus shown the teaching's quality of leading to liberation by way of seven years, then demonstrating it again in an even shorter time, he said, 'Let be, bhikkhus…' and so on. All this was said with reference to a person of average intellect who is amenable to guidance. But regarding one of keen wisdom, it was said: 'If instructed in the morning, one will attain distinction by evening; if instructed in the evening, one will attain distinction by morning' (MN 2.345).

Iti [V 1.0312][M 1.0306] bhagavā “evaṃniyyānikaṃ, bhikkhave, mama sāsana”nti dassetvā ekavīsatiyāpi ṭhānesu arahattanikūṭena desitaṃ desanaṃ niyyātento “ekāyano ayaṃ, bhikkhave, maggo…pe… iti yaṃ taṃ vuttaṃ, idametaṃ paṭicca vutta”nti āha. Sesaṃ uttānatthamevāti.

Thus the Blessed One, having shown that 'My teaching, bhikkhus, leads to liberation in this way,' and having brought to a conclusion the teaching that was taught in twenty-one instances culminating in Arahantship, said, 'This is the direct path, bhikkhus… and so on… Thus what was said, was said in reference to this.' The rest is of clear meaning.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

From the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya

Satipaṭṭhānasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta is concluded.

Paṭhamavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the First Chapter is concluded.

2. Sīhanādavaggo

2. The Chapter on the Lion's Roar

1. Cūḷasīhanādasuttavaṇṇanā

1. The Commentary on the Shorter Discourse on the Lion’s Roar

139. Evaṃ [V 1.0313][M 1.0307][P 2.0001] me sutanti cūḷasīhanādasuttaṃ. Yasmā panassa atthuppattiko nikkhepo, tasmā taṃ dassetvā cassa anupubbapadavaṇṇanaṃ karissāma. Katarāya panidaṃ atthuppattiyā nikkhittanti? Lābhasakkārapaccayā titthiyaparidevite. Bhagavato kira dhammadāyādasutte vuttanayena mahālābhasakkāro uppajji. Catuppamāṇiko hi ayaṃ lokasannivāso, rūpappamāṇo rūpappasanno, ghosappamāṇo ghosappasanno, lūkhappamāṇo lūkhappasanno, dhammappamāṇo dhammappasannoti imesaṃ puggalānaṃ vasena catudhā ṭhito.

139. Thus have I heard—the Cūḷasīhanāda Sutta. Since its exposition is based on the occasion of its arising, we will first present that and then provide a sequential word-by-word commentary. On what occasion was it set forth? On account of the lamentation of the sectarians due to gain and honour. It is said that great gain and honour arose for the Blessed One in the manner described in the Discourse on the Heirs of the Dhamma. For this world of beings is established in four ways, according to these types of individuals: those who are measured by form and are pleased by form; those who are measured by sound and are pleased by sound; those who are measured by austerity and are pleased by austerity; and those who are measured by the Dhamma and are pleased by the Dhamma.

Tesaṃ idaṃ nānākaraṇaṃ – katamo ca puggalo rūpappamāṇo rūpappasanno? Idhekacco puggalo ārohaṃ vā passitvā pariṇāhaṃ vā passitvā saṇṭhānaṃ vā passitvā pāripūriṃ vā passitvā tattha pamāṇaṃ gahetvā pasādaṃ janeti, ayaṃ vuccati puggalo rūpappamāṇo rūpappasanno.

This is their distinction. And what sort of person is measured by form and pleased by form? Here, some person, having seen height, or breadth, or shape, or completeness, takes that as a measure and generates confidence. This is called a person who is measured by form and pleased by form.

Katamo ca puggalo ghosappamāṇo ghosappasanno? Idhekacco puggalo paravaṇṇanāya parathomanāya parapasaṃsanāya paravaṇṇahārikāya, tattha pamāṇaṃ gahetvā pasādaṃ janeti, ayaṃ vuccati puggalo ghosappamāṇo ghosappasanno.

And what sort of person is measured by sound and pleased by sound? Here, some person, through the praise, commendation, approval, or conveying of praise by others, takes that as a measure and generates confidence. This is called a person who is measured by sound and pleased by sound.

Katamo ca puggalo lūkhappamāṇo lūkhappasanno? Idhekacco puggalo cīvaralūkhaṃ vā passitvā pattalūkhaṃ vā passitvā, senāsanalūkhaṃ vā passitvā vividhaṃ vā dukkarakārikaṃ passitvā [V 1.0314] tattha pamāṇaṃ gahetvā pasādaṃ janeti, ayaṃ [P 2.0002] vuccati puggalo lūkhappamāṇo lūkhappasanno.

And what sort of person is measured by austerity and pleased by austerity? Here, some person, having seen a coarse robe, or a coarse almsbowl, or a coarse dwelling, or various difficult practices, takes that as a measure and generates confidence. This is called a person who is measured by austerity and pleased by austerity.

Katamo ca puggalo dhammappamāṇo dhammappasanno? Idhekacco puggalo sīlaṃ vā passitvā samādhiṃ vā passitvā paññaṃ vā passitvā tattha pamāṇaṃ gahetvā pasādaṃ janeti, ayaṃ vuccati puggalo dhammappamāṇo dhammappasannoti.

And what sort of person is measured by the Dhamma and pleased by the Dhamma? Here, some person, having seen virtue, or concentration, or wisdom, takes that as a measure and generates confidence. This is called a person who is measured by the Dhamma and pleased by the Dhamma.

Imesu [M 1.0308] catūsu puggalesu rūpappamāṇopi bhagavato ārohapariṇāhasaṇṭhānapāripūrivaṇṇapokkharataṃ, asītianubyañjanappaṭimaṇḍitattā nānāratanavicittamiva suvaṇṇamahāpaṭaṃ, dvattiṃsamahāpurisalakkhaṇasamākiṇṇatāya tārāgaṇasamujjalaṃ viya gaganatalaṃ sabbaphāliphullaṃ viya ca yojanasatubbedhaṃ pāricchattakaṃ aṭṭhārasaratanubbedhaṃ byāmappabhāparikkhepaṃ sassirikaṃ anopamasarīraṃ disvā sammāsambuddheyeva pasīdati.

Among these four types of individuals, even one who is measured by form, seeing the Blessed One’s perfect height, proportion, well-formed figure, and completeness of complexion, adorned with the eighty minor characteristics, like a great golden cloth embellished with various precious gems; adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great man, like the sky illuminated by stars; or like the fully bloomed Pāricchattaka tree, a hundred yojanas high, with an aura eighteen cubits high and a fathom in circumference, his glorious and incomparable body—seeing this, one gains confidence in the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One alone.

Ghosappamāṇopi, bhagavatā kappasatasahassādhikāni cattāri asaṅkhyeyyāni dasa pāramiyo dasa upapāramiyo dasa paramatthapāramiyo pūritā aṅgapariccāgo puttadārapariccāgo, rajjapariccāgo attapariccāgo nayanapariccāgo ca katotiādinā nayena pavattaṃ ghosaṃ sutvā sammāsambuddheyeva pasīdati.

Even one who is measured by sound, hearing the report that arose in this manner—that the Blessed One fulfilled the ten perfections, the ten intermediate perfections, and the ten supreme perfections over four incalculable periods and a hundred thousand eons, through acts such as giving away limbs, giving up children and spouse, relinquishing kingdoms, sacrificing his own life, and offering his eyes, and so forth—gains confidence in the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One alone.

Lūkhappamāṇopi bhagavato cīvaralūkhaṃ disvā “sace bhagavā agāraṃ ajjhāvasissa, kāsikavatthameva adhārayissa. Pabbajitvā panānena sāṇapaṃsukūlacīvarena santussamānena bhāriyaṃ kata”nti sammāsambuddheyeva pasīdati. Pattalūkhampi disvā – “iminā agāraṃ ajjhāvasantena rattavarasuvaṇṇabhājanesu cakkavattibhojanārahaṃ sugandhasālibhojanaṃ paribhuttaṃ, pabbajitvā pana pāsāṇamayaṃ pattaṃ ādāya uccanīcakuladvāresu sapadānaṃ piṇḍāya caritvā laddhapiṇḍiyālopena santussamāno bhāriyaṃ karotī”ti sammāsambuddheyeva pasīdati. Senāsanalūkhaṃ disvāpi – “ayaṃ agāraṃ ajjhāvasanto tiṇṇaṃ utūnaṃ anucchavikesu tīsu pāsādesu tividhanāṭakaparivāro dibbasampattiṃ viya rajjasiriṃ anubhavitvā idāni pabbajjūpagato rukkhamūlasenāsanādīsu dāruphalakasilāpaṭṭapīṭhamañcakādīhi santussamāno bhāriyaṃ karotī”ti sammāsambuddheyeva [V 1.0315] pasīdati. Dukkarakārikamassa disvāpi – “chabbassāni nāma muggayūsakulatthayūsahareṇuyūsādīnaṃ pasaṭamattena yāpessati, appāṇakaṃ [P 2.0003] jhānaṃ jhāyissati, sarīre ca jīvite ca anapekkho viharissati, aho dukkarakārako bhagavā”ti sammāsambuddheyeva pasīdati.

Even one who is measured by austerity, seeing the Blessed One’s coarse robe, thinks: “If the Blessed One were living the household life, he would wear only Kāsi cloth. But having gone forth, being content with robes of hemp and rags, he does what is weighty.” Thus, they gain confidence in the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One alone. Seeing his coarse almsbowl, they think: “While living the household life, this one would have eaten fragrant rice worthy of a wheel-turning monarch from excellent golden vessels. But having gone forth, he takes a stone bowl and walks for alms from house to house in regular order, content with the morsels he receives, doing what is weighty.” Thus, they gain confidence in the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One alone. Seeing his coarse dwelling, they think: “While living the household life, this one would have enjoyed royal splendour like divine luxury in three palaces suited to the three seasons, surrounded by various theatrical performances. But now, having gone forth, he is content with lodgings such as the foot of a tree, and with wooden planks, stone slabs, benches, and couches, doing what is weighty.” Thus, they gain confidence in the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One alone. Seeing his difficult practices, they think: “For six years, he sustained himself on a mere handful of mung bean soup, horse gram soup, or chickpea soup. He meditated with suspended breath, dwelling without regard for body and life. Ah, the Blessed One does what is difficult!” Thus, they gain confidence in the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One alone.

Dhammappamāṇopi [M 1.0309] bhagavato sīlaguṇaṃ samādhiguṇaṃ paññāguṇaṃ jhānavimokkhasamādhisamāpattisampadaṃ abhiññāpāripūriṃ yamakapāṭihāriyaṃ devorohaṇaṃ pāthikaputtadamanādīni ca anekāni acchariyāni disvā sammāsambuddheyeva pasīdati, te evaṃ pasannā bhagavato mahantaṃ lābhasakkāraṃ abhiharanti. Titthiyānaṃ pana bāverujātake kākassa viya lābhasakkāro parihāyittha. Yathāha –

Even one who is measured by the Dhamma, seeing the Blessed One’s virtues of morality, concentration, and wisdom, his attainment of jhāna, liberation, concentration, and meditative accomplishments, the fulfillment of higher knowledge, the twin miracle, the descent from the heavens, the taming of Pāthikaputta, and many other marvels, gains confidence in the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One alone. Those thus confident bring great gain and honour to the Blessed One. But for the sectarians, like the crow in the Bāveru Jātaka, gain and honour dwindled away. As it is said:

“Adassanena morassa, sikhino mañjubhāṇino;

Kākaṃ tattha apūjesuṃ, maṃsena ca phalena ca.

“Not seeing the peacock, crested, sweet-voiced, they honoured the crow there with meat and fruit.

Yadā ca sarasampanno, moro bāverumāgamā;

Atha lābho ca sakkāro, vāyasassa ahāyatha.

When the peacock, endowed with a beautiful voice, came to Bāveru, then the crow's gain and honour declined.

Yāva nuppajjati buddho, dhammarājā pabhaṅkaro;

Tāva aññe apūjesuṃ, puthū samaṇabrāhmaṇe.

As long as the Buddha, the radiant King of Dhamma, did not arise, so long did they honour the many other ascetics and brahmins.

Yadā ca sarasampanno, buddho dhammamadesayi;

Atha lābho ca sakkāro, titthiyānaṃ ahāyathā”ti. (jā. 1.4.153-156);

When the Buddha, endowed with a beautiful voice, taught the Dhamma, then gain and honour declined for the sectarians.”

Te evaṃ pahīnalābhasakkārā rattiṃ ekadvaṅgulamattaṃ obhāsetvāpi sūriyuggamane khajjopanakā viya hatappabhā ahesuṃ.

Thus deprived of gain and honour, even when shining a mere one or two fingers' breadth at night, they became like fireflies at sunrise, their radiance destroyed.

Yathā [V 1.0316] hi khajjopanakā, kāḷapakkhamhi rattiyā;

Nidassayanti obhāsaṃ, etesaṃ visayo hi so.

Just as fireflies, on a night of the dark fortnight, display their radiance, for that is their domain.

Yadā ca rasmisampanno, abbhudeti pabhaṅkaro;

Atha khajjupasaṅghānaṃ, pabhā antaradhāyati.

But when the light-maker, endowed with rays, arises, then the radiance of the host of fireflies disappears.

Evaṃ khajjupasadisā, titthiyāpi puthū idha;

Kāḷapakkhūpame loke, dīpayanti sakaṃ guṇaṃ.

Thus, like fireflies, the various sectarians here, in a world comparable to the dark fortnight, illuminate their own qualities.

Yadā ca buddho lokasmiṃ, udeti amitappabho;

Nippabhā titthiyā honti, sūriye khajjupakā yathāti.

And when the Buddha of boundless radiance arises in the world, the sectarians become devoid of radiance, just as fireflies do in the sun.

Te evaṃ nippabhā hutvā kacchupiḷakādīhi kiṇṇasarīrā paramapārijuññapattā yena buddho yena dhammo yena saṅgho yena ca mahājanassa sannipāto, tena [M 1.0310] tena gantvā antaravīthiyampi [P 2.0004] siṅghāṭakepi catukkepi sabhāyampi ṭhatvā paridevanti –

Thus, having become devoid of radiance, their bodies covered with scabies, boils, and the like, and having reached a state of extreme affliction, they went to where the Buddha was, where the Dhamma was, where the Sangha was, and where a large gathering of people was. Standing in the inner streets, at crossroads, in squares, and in assembly halls, they lamented:

“Kiṃ bho samaṇoyeva gotamo samaṇo, mayaṃ assamaṇā; samaṇasseva gotamassa sāvakā samaṇā, amhākaṃ sāvakā assamaṇā? Samaṇasseva gotamassa sāvakānañcassa dinnaṃ mahapphalaṃ, na amhākaṃ, sāvakānañca no dinnaṃ mahapphalaṃ? Nanu samaṇopi gotamo samaṇo, mayampi samaṇā. Samaṇassapi gotamassa sāvakā samaṇā, amhākampi sāvakā samaṇā. Samaṇassapi gotamassa sāvakānañcassa dinnaṃ mahapphalaṃ, amhākampi sāvakānañca no dinnaṃ mahapphalañceva? Samaṇassapi gotamassa sāvakānañcassa detha karotha, amhākampi sāvakānañca no detha sakkarotha? Nanu samaṇo gotamo purimāni divasāni uppanno, mayaṃ pana loke uppajjamāneyeva uppannā”ti.

“Sirs, is only the ascetic Gotama an ascetic, and we are not ascetics? Are only the disciples of the ascetic Gotama ascetics, and our disciples not ascetics? Does only what is given to the ascetic Gotama and his disciples bring great fruit, and not what is given to us and our disciples? Is it not so that the ascetic Gotama is an ascetic, and we too are ascetics? That the disciples of the ascetic Gotama are ascetics, and our disciples too are ascetics? That what is given to the ascetic Gotama and his disciples brings great fruit, and what is given to us and our disciples also brings great fruit? You should give and pay respect to the ascetic Gotama and his disciples, and you should also give and pay respect to us and our disciples! Is it not so that the ascetic Gotama has arisen only in recent days, whereas we arose when the world itself was arising?”

Evaṃ nānappakāraṃ viravanti. Atha bhikkhū bhikkhuniyo upāsakā upāsikāyoti catasso parisā tesaṃ saddaṃ sutvā bhagavato ārocesuṃ “titthiyā bhante idañcidañca kathentī”ti[V 1.0317]. Taṃ sutvā bhagavā – “mā tumhe, bhikkhave, titthiyānaṃ vacanena ‘aññatra samaṇo atthī’ti saññino ahuvatthā”ti vatvā aññatitthiyesu samaṇabhāvaṃ paṭisedhento idheva ca anujānanto imissā atthuppattiyā idheva, bhikkhave, samaṇoti idaṃ suttaṃ abhāsi.

Thus, they wailed in various ways. Then the fourfold assembly—monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen—heard their cries and reported to the Blessed One, saying: “Venerable sir, the sectarians are saying this and that.” Hearing this, the Blessed One said, “Monks, on account of the words of the sectarians, you should not hold the perception that ‘there is an ascetic elsewhere.’” Then, refuting the state of being an ascetic among other sectarians and sanctioning it only here, on this occasion, he spoke this discourse: “Here, monks, is the ascetic.”

Tattha idhevāti imasmiṃyeva sāsane. Ayaṃ pana niyamo sesapadesupi veditabbo. Dutiyādayopi hi samaṇā idheva, na aññattha. Samaṇoti sotāpanno. Tenevāha – “katamo ca, bhikkhave, paṭhamo samaṇo? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu tiṇṇaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ parikkhayā sotāpanno hoti avinipātadhammo niyato sambodhiparāyaṇo, ayaṃ, bhikkhave, paṭhamo samaṇo”ti (a. ni. 4.241).

Therein, ‘here’ means in this very dispensation. This principle should be understood to apply to the remaining phrases as well. For the second and other ascetics are also ‘here,’ not elsewhere. ‘Ascetic’ means a stream-enterer. Therefore, he said: “And what, monks, is the first ascetic? Here, monks, a monk, through the destruction of the three fetters, becomes a stream-enterer, not subject to downfall, assured, and bound for enlightenment. This, monks, is the first ascetic.” (AN 4.241)

Dutiyoti sakadāgāmī. Tenevāha – “katamo ca? Bhikkhave, dutiyo samaṇo. Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu tiṇṇaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ parikkhayā rāgadosamohānaṃ [M 1.0311] tanuttā sakadāgāmī hoti, sakideva imaṃ lokaṃ āgantvā dukkhassantaṃ karoti. Ayaṃ, bhikkhave, dutiyo samaṇo”ti.

‘The second’ means the once-returner. Therefore, he said: “And what, monks, is the second ascetic? Here, monks, a monk, through the destruction of the three fetters and the attenuation of greed, hatred, and delusion, becomes a once-returner who, after returning to this world just once, makes an end of suffering. This, monks, is the second ascetic.”

Tatiyoti anāgāmī. Tenevāha – “katamo ca, bhikkhave, tatiyo samaṇo? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu pañcannaṃ orambhāgiyānaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ parikkhayā opapātiko hoti tattha parinibbāyī anāvattidhammo tasmā [P 2.0005] lokā. Ayaṃ, bhikkhave, tatiyo samaṇo”ti.

‘The third’ means the non-returner. Therefore, he said: “And what, monks, is the third ascetic? Here, monks, a monk, through the destruction of the five lower fetters, is spontaneously reborn and attains final Nibbāna there, being of the nature of not returning from that world. This, monks, is the third ascetic.”

Catutthoti arahā. Tenevāha – “katamo ca, bhikkhave, catuttho samaṇo? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu āsavānaṃ khayā anāsavaṃ cetovimuttiṃ paññāvimuttiṃ diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharati. Ayaṃ, bhikkhave, catuttho samaṇo”ti (a. ni. 4.241). Iti imasmiṃ ṭhāne cattāro phalaṭṭhakasamaṇāva adhippetā.

‘The fourth’ means the Arahant. Therefore, he said: “And what, monks, is the fourth ascetic? Here, monks, a monk, through the destruction of the taints, having realized for himself with direct knowledge, enters and abides in the taintless liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom, in this very life. This, monks, is the fourth ascetic.” (AN 4.241) Thus, in this context, it is the four ascetics established in the fruits who are intended.

Suññāti rittā tucchā. Parappavādāti cattāro sassatavādā, cattāro ekaccasassatikā, cattāro antānantikā, cattāro amarāvikkhepikā, dve adhiccasamuppannikā, soḷasa saññīvādā, aṭṭha asaññīvādā, aṭṭha nevasaññīnāsaññīvādā, satta ucchedavādā, pañca diṭṭhadhammanibbānavādāti ime sabbepi brahmajāle āgatā dvāsaṭṭhi diṭṭhiyo. Ito bāhirānaṃ paresaṃ [V 1.0318] vādā parappavādā nāma. Te sabbepi imehi catūhi phalaṭṭhakasamaṇehi suññā, na hi te ettha santi. Na kevalañca eteheva suññā, catūhi pana maggaṭṭhakasamaṇehipi catunnaṃ maggānaṃ atthāya āraddhavipassakehipīti dvādasahipi samaṇehi suññā eva. Imameva atthaṃ sandhāya bhagavatā mahāparinibbāne vuttaṃ –

‘Empty’ means devoid, hollow. ‘The doctrines of others’ refers to all these sixty-two views found in the Brahmajāla Sutta: the four eternalist views, the four partial-eternalist views, the four views on the finitude and infinitude of the world, the four evasive wrigglers, the two doctrines of fortuitous origination, the sixteen doctrines of perception, the eight doctrines of non-perception, the eight doctrines of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, the seven annihilationist views, and the five doctrines of Nibbāna in this very life. The doctrines of others external to this are called ‘the doctrines of others.’ All of these are empty of these four ascetics established in the fruits; for they are not found therein. And they are not only empty of these, but also of the four ascetics established in the path and of those who have undertaken insight meditation for the sake of the four paths—thus, they are empty of all twelve kinds of ascetics. It is with reference to this very meaning that the Blessed One spoke in the Mahāparinibbāna Sutta:

“Ekūnatiṃso vayasā subhadda,

Yaṃ pabbajiṃ kiṃ kusalānuesī;

Vassāni paññāsa samādhikāni,

Yato ahaṃ pabbajito subhadda;

Ñāyassa dhammassa padesavattī,

Ito bahiddhā samaṇopi natthi.

“At twenty-nine years of age, Subhadda, I went forth in search of the wholesome. More than fifty years have passed, Subhadda, since I went forth as one who fares in the domain of the true Dhamma. Outside of this, there is no ascetic.

“Dutiyopi samaṇo natthi, tatiyopi samaṇo natthi, catutthopi samaṇo natthi. Suññā parappavādā samaṇebhi aññehī”ti (dī. ni. 2.214).

There is also no second ascetic, no third ascetic, and no fourth ascetic. The doctrines of others are empty of ascetics.” (DN 2.214).

Ettha [M 1.0312] hi padesavattīti āraddhavipassako adhippeto. Tasmā sotāpattimaggassa āraddhavipassakaṃ maggaṭṭhaṃ phalaṭṭhanti tayopi ekato katvā samaṇopi natthīti āha. Sakadāgāmimaggassa āraddhavipassakaṃ maggaṭṭhaṃ phalaṭṭhanti tayopi ekato katvā dutiyopi samaṇo natthīti āha. Itaresupi dvīsu eseva nayo.

Here, by ‘one who dwells in a portion,’ one who has initiated insight is meant. Therefore, concerning the path of stream-entry, it is said there is no ascetic, by grouping together these three: one who has initiated insight, one who is on the path, and one who is in the fruition. Similarly, concerning the path of the once-returner, it is said there is no second ascetic, by grouping together these three: one who has initiated insight, one who is on the path, and one who is in the fruition. The same method applies to the remaining two.

Kasmā panete aññattha natthīti? Akhettatāya. Yathā hi na āragge sāsapo tiṭṭhati, na udakapiṭṭhe aggi jalati, na piṭṭhipāsāṇe bījāni ruhanti, evameva bāhiresu titthāyatanesu [P 2.0006] na ime samaṇā uppajjanti, imasmiṃyeva pana sāsane uppajjanti. Kasmā? Khettatāya. Tesaṃ akhettatā ca khettatā ca ariyamaggassa abhāvato ca bhāvato ca veditabbā. Tenāha bhagavā –

But why are these not found elsewhere? Because of being an unsuitable field. For just as a mustard seed does not remain on the point of an awl, fire does not burn on the surface of water, and seeds do not sprout on a rock slab, so too these ascetics do not arise in external sectarian systems—they arise only in this Dispensation. Why? Because of being a suitable field. Their unsuitability and suitability should be understood as due to the absence and presence of the Noble Path. Therefore, the Blessed One said:

“Yasmiṃ kho, subhadda, dhammavinaye ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo na upalabbhati, samaṇopi tattha [V 1.0319] na upalabbhati, dutiyopi tattha samaṇo na upalabbhati, tatiyopi tattha samaṇo na upalabbhati, catutthopi tattha samaṇo na upalabbhati. Yasmiñca kho, subhadda, dhammavinaye ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo upalabbhati, samaṇopi tattha upalabbhati, dutiyopi tattha…pe…. Catutthopi tattha samaṇo upalabbhati. Imasmiṃ kho, subhadda, dhammavinaye ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo upalabbhati, idheva, subhadda, samaṇo, idha dutiyo samaṇo, idha tatiyo samaṇo, idha catuttho samaṇo, suññā parappavādā samaṇebhi aññehī”ti (dī. ni. 2.214).

“Subhadda, in whatever Teaching and Discipline the Noble Eightfold Path is not found, an ascetic is not found there, nor a second ascetic, nor a third ascetic, nor a fourth ascetic. But in whatever Teaching and Discipline, Subhadda, the Noble Eightfold Path is found, an ascetic is found there, a second ascetic… a fourth ascetic is found there. In this Teaching and Discipline, Subhadda, the Noble Eightfold Path is found. Here, Subhadda, is the ascetic; here, the second ascetic; here, the third ascetic; here, the fourth ascetic. The doctrines of others are empty of ascetics.” (DN 2.214).

Evaṃ yasmā titthāyatanaṃ akhettaṃ, sāsanaṃ khettaṃ, tasmā yathā surattahatthapādo sūrakesarako sīho migarājā na susāne vā saṅkārakūṭe vā paṭivasati, tiyojanasahassavitthataṃ pana himavantaṃ ajjhogāhetvā maṇiguhāyaṃyeva paṭivasati. Yathā ca chaddanto nāgarājā na gocariyahatthikulādīsu navasu nāgakulesu uppajjati, chaddantakuleyeva uppajjati. Yathā ca valāhako assarājā na gadrabhakule vā ghoṭakakule vā uppajjati, sindhuyā tīre pana sindhavakuleyeva uppajjati. Yathā ca sabbakāmadadaṃ manoharaṃ maṇiratanaṃ na saṅkārakūṭe [M 1.0313] vā paṃsupabbatādīsu vā uppajjati, vepullapabbatabbhantareyeva uppajjati. Yathā ca timirapiṅgalo maccharājā na khuddakapokkharaṇīsu uppajjati, caturāsītiyojanasahassagambhīre mahāsamuddeyeva uppajjati. Yathā ca diyaḍḍhayojanasatiko supaṇṇarājā na gāmadvāre eraṇḍavanādīsu paṭivasati, mahāsamuddaṃ pana ajjhogāhetvā simbalidahavaneyeva paṭivasati. Yathā ca dhataraṭṭho suvaṇṇahaṃso na gāmadvāre āvāṭakādīsu paṭivasati, navutihaṃsasahassaparivāro hutvā cittakūṭapabbateyeva paṭivasati. Yathā ca catuddīpissaro cakkavattirājā [P 2.0007] na nīcakule uppajjati, asambhinnajātikhattiyakuleyeva pana uppajjati. Evameva imesu samaṇesu ekasamaṇopi na aññatitthāyatane uppajjati, ariyamaggaparikkhitte pana buddhasāsaneyeva uppajjati. Tenāha bhagavā “idheva, bhikkhave, samaṇo…pe… suññā parappavādā samaṇehi samaṇebhi aññehī”ti.

Thus, since sectarian systems are an unsuitable field while the Buddha's Dispensation is a suitable field, it is like this: Just as the lion, king of beasts, with deep-red paws and a tawny mane, does not dwell in a charnel ground or on a rubbish heap, but having entered the Himalayas, three thousand leagues in extent, dwells only in a jeweled cave; and just as Chaddanta, the nāga-king, is not born among the nine nāga-clans, such as the common elephant herds, but is born only in the Chaddanta clan; and just as Valāhaka, the horse-king, is not born in a donkey-clan or a common horse-clan, but is born only in the Sindhava clan on the bank of the river Sindhu; and just as the delightful, wish-fulfilling gem that grants all desires does not arise on a rubbish heap or on dust-hills, but arises only within Mount Vepulla; and just as Timirapiṅgala, the fish-king, is not born in small ponds, but is born only in the great ocean, eighty-four thousand leagues deep; and just as the supaṇṇa-king, one hundred and fifty leagues in size, does not dwell at a village gate or in a castor-oil grove, but having entered the great ocean, dwells only in the silk-cotton tree forest; and just as the golden goose Dhataraṭṭha does not dwell at a village gate or in pits, but, surrounded by ninety thousand geese, dwells only on Mount Cittakūṭa; and just as the wheel-turning king, lord of the four great continents, is not born in a low-class family, but is born only in a khattiya family of unmixed lineage; in the very same way, not one of these ascetics arises in another sectarian system, but arises only in the Buddha's Dispensation, which is circumscribed by the Noble Path. Therefore, the Blessed One said: 'Here, monks, is the ascetic… the doctrines of others are empty of other ascetics.'

Sammā sīhanādaṃ nadathāti ettha sammāti hetunā nayena kāraṇena. Sīhanādanti seṭṭhanādaṃ abhītanādaṃ appaṭinādaṃ. Imesañhi catunnaṃ samaṇānaṃ idheva atthitāya ayaṃ nādo seṭṭhanādo nāma hoti uttamanādo. “Ime samaṇā idheva atthī”ti vadantassa aññato bhayaṃ vā āsaṅkā [V 1.0320] vā natthīti abhītanādo nāma hoti. “Amhākampi sāsane ime samaṇā atthī”ti pūraṇādīsu ekassāpi uṭṭhahitvā vattuṃ asamatthatāya ayaṃ nādo appaṭinādo nāma hoti. Tena vuttaṃ “sīhanādanti seṭṭhanādaṃ abhītanādaṃ appaṭināda”nti.

Regarding the phrase 'Roar the right lion's roar,' here 'rightly' means with reason, with method, with cause. 'Lion's roar' means the best roar, the fearless roar, the unanswerable roar. Indeed, because these four ascetics exist right here, this roar is called the best roar, the supreme roar. Because for one who says, 'These ascetics exist right here,' there is no fear or doubt from any other quarter, it is called the fearless roar. Because not even one among Pūraṇa and the others is able to stand up and say, 'In our dispensation too, these ascetics exist,' this roar is called the unanswerable roar. Therefore it is said: ''Lion's roar' means the best roar, the fearless roar, the unanswerable roar.'

140. Ṭhānaṃ kho panetaṃ vijjatīti idaṃ kho pana kāraṇaṃ vijjati. Yaṃ aññatitthiyāti yena kāraṇena aññatitthiyā. Ettha ca titthaṃ jānitabbaṃ, titthakaro jānitabbo titthiyā jānitabbā, titthiyasāvakā jānitabbā. Titthaṃnāma dvāsaṭṭhi diṭṭhiyo. Ettha hi sattā taranti uppalavanti ummujjanimujjaṃ karonti, tasmā titthanti vuccanti. Tāsaṃ diṭṭhīnaṃ uppādetā titthakaro nāma. Tassa laddhiṃ gahetvā pabbajitā titthiyā nāma. Tesaṃ paccayadāyakā titthiyasāvakāti veditabbā. Paribbājakāti gihibandhanaṃ pahāya pabbajjūpagatā. Assāsoti avassayo patiṭṭhā upatthambho. Balanti thāmo. Yena tumheti yena assāsena vā balena vā evaṃ vadetha.

140. The phrase 'This possibility exists' means: this reason exists. The phrase 'That other sectarians...' means: for which reason other sectarians... Herein, a 'sect' should be known, a 'sect-founder' should be known, 'sectarians' should be known, and 'disciples of sectarians' should be known. A 'sect' means the sixty-two views. Herein beings cross over, float up, and sink and emerge; therefore, these are called 'fords' (tittha). The originator of these views is called a 'sect-founder.' Those who have gone forth having accepted his doctrine are called 'sectarians.' Those who provide them with support should be known as 'disciples of sectarians.' 'Wanderers' means those who have abandoned the bonds of the household life and have undertaken the going-forth. 'Assurance' means reliance, foundation, support. 'Strength' means might. 'By which you...' means: by what assurance or strength you might speak thus.

Atthi [M 1.0314] kho no, āvuso, tena bhagavatā jānatā passatā arahatā sammāsambuddhenāti ettha ayaṃ saṅkhepattho – yo so bhagavā samatiṃsa pāramiyo pūretvā sabbakilese bhañjitvā anuttaraṃ sammāsambodhiṃ abhisambuddho, tena bhagavatā tesaṃ tesaṃ sattānaṃ āsayānusayaṃ jānatā, hatthatale ṭhapitaṃ āmalakaṃ viya sabbaṃ ñeyyadhammaṃ passatā. Apica pubbenivāsādīhi jānatā, dibbena cakkhunā passatā. Tīhi vijjāhi [P 2.0008] chahi vā pana abhiññāhi jānatā, sabbattha appaṭihatena samantacakkhunā passatā. Sabbadhammajānanasamatthāya paññāya jānatā, sabbasattānaṃ cakkhuvisayātītāni tirokuṭṭādigatāni vāpi rūpāni ativisuddhena maṃsacakkhunā passatā. Attahitasādhikāya samādhipadaṭṭhānāya paṭivedhapaññāya jānatā, parahitasādhikāya karuṇāpadaṭṭhānāya desanāpaññāya passatā. Arīnaṃ hatattā paccayādīnaṃ arahattā ca arahatā, sammā sāmañca saccānaṃ buddhattā sammāsambuddhena. Antarāyikadhamme vā jānatā, niyyānikadhamme passatā. Kilesārīnaṃ hatattā arahatā, sammā sāmaṃ sabbadhammānaṃ buddhattā sammāsambuddhenāti, evaṃ catuvesārajjavasena catūhi ākārehi thomitena cattāro dhammā akkhātā, ye mayaṃ attani sampassamānā evaṃ vadema, na rājarājamahāmattādīnaṃ upatthambhaṃ kāyabalanti.

‘Friends, it is indeed by the Blessed One, who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One.’ Here is the concise meaning: That Blessed One, having fulfilled the thirty perfections, having destroyed all defilements, and having fully awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment; by that Blessed One who knows the inclinations and latent tendencies of those various beings, and who sees all knowable phenomena as clearly as a myrobalan fruit placed on the palm of the hand. Moreover, he knows through the recollection of past lives and so forth, and sees with the divine eye. He knows through the three kinds of knowledge or the six direct knowledges, and sees with the unobstructed all-seeing eye. He knows with the wisdom capable of knowing all phenomena, and sees with his supremely purified physical eye forms that are beyond the range of vision of all beings, whether they are behind walls or elsewhere. He knows through the wisdom of penetration, which has concentration as its proximate cause and accomplishes his own welfare, and sees through the wisdom of teaching, which has compassion as its proximate cause and accomplishes the welfare of others. He is an ‘Arahant’ because of having destroyed the enemies (the defilements) and because of being worthy of requisites and so on; and he is a ‘Perfectly Enlightened One’ because of having rightly and by himself awakened to the truths. Alternatively, he knows obstructive phenomena and sees liberating phenomena. He is an ‘Arahant’ because of having destroyed the enemies that are the defilements, and a ‘Perfectly Enlightened One’ because of having rightly and by himself awakened to all phenomena. Thus, by him who is praised in four ways through the four kinds of fearlessness, four things have been declared, which we, seeing in ourselves, speak of thus, not because of the support of kings, royal ministers, and so on as our backing.

Satthari [V 1.0321] pasādoti “itipi so bhagavā”tiādinā nayena buddhaguṇe anussarantānaṃ uppannappasādo. Dhamme pasādoti “svākkhāto bhagavatā dhammo”tiādinā nayena dhammaguṇe anussarantānaṃ uppannappasādo. Sīlesu paripūrakāritāti ariyakantesu sīlesu paripūrakāritā. Ariyakantasīlāni nāma pañcasīlāni. Tāni hi bhavantaragatopi ariyasāvako attano ariyasāvakabhāvaṃ ajānantopi na vītikkamati. Sacepi hi naṃ koci vadeyya – “imaṃ sakalaṃ cakkavattirajjaṃ sampaṭicchitvā khuddakamakkhikaṃ jīvitā voropehī”ti, aṭṭhānametaṃ, yaṃ so tassa vacanaṃ kareyya. Evaṃ ariyānaṃ sīlāni kantāni piyāni manāpāni. Tāni sandhāya vuttaṃ “sīlesu paripūrakāritā”ti.

‘Faith in the Teacher’ is the faith that arises in those who recollect the qualities of the Buddha, beginning with ‘Thus indeed is the Blessed One...’ ‘Faith in the Dhamma’ is the faith that arises in those who recollect the qualities of the Dhamma, beginning with ‘The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One...’ ‘Fulfillment in virtues’ means complete fulfillment in the virtues cherished by the noble ones. The virtues cherished by the noble ones are the five precepts. Even if a noble disciple is reborn elsewhere and unaware of their noble disciple status, they would not transgress these. Even if someone were to say, ‘Accept this entire universal kingship and then take the life of a tiny fly,’ it is impossible that they would comply. Thus, the virtues of the noble ones are cherished, dear, and agreeable. This is what is meant by ‘fulfillment in virtues.’

Sahadhammikā kho panāti bhikkhu bhikkhunī sikkhamānā sāmaṇero sāmaṇerī upāsako upāsikāti ete satta sahadhammacārino. Etesu hi bhikkhu bhikkhūhi saddhiṃ sahadhammaṃ carati samānasikkhatāya. Tathā [M 1.0315] bhikkhunī bhikkhunīhi…pe… upāsikā upāsikāhi, sotāpanno sotāpannehi, sakadāgāmī…pe… anāgāmīhi sahadhammaṃ carati. Tasmā sabbepete sahadhammikāti vuccanti. Apicettha ariyasāvakāyeva adhippetā. Tesañhi [P 2.0009] bhavantarepi maggadassanamhi vivādo natthi, tasmā te accantaṃ ekadhammacāritāya sahadhammikā. Iminā, “suppaṭipanno bhagavato sāvakasaṅgho”tiādinā nayena saṅghaṃ anussarantānaṃ uppannappasādo kathito. Ettāvatā cattāri sotāpannassa aṅgāni kathitāni honti.

‘Companions in the Dhamma’ refers to monks, nuns, female probationers, male novices, female novices, laymen, and laywomen; these seven are companions in the Dhamma. Among these, a monk lives in harmony with fellow monks through shared training. Similarly, a nun with nuns... up to a laywoman with laywomen; a stream-enterer with stream-enterers, a once-returner... up to a non-returner, live in harmony in the Dhamma. Therefore, all these are called ‘companions in the Dhamma.’ Moreover, in this context, noble disciples are especially intended, for even in future lives, they have no disagreement regarding the vision of the path. Thus, they are ultimately united in the practice of the Dhamma, and are companions in the Dhamma. Through this, the faith that arises in those who recollect the Sangha, beginning with ‘The Sangha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing well...’ is spoken of. Thus far, the four factors of a stream-enterer have been spoken of.

Ime kho no, āvusoti, āvuso, ime cattāro dhammā tena bhagavatā amhākaṃ assāso ceva balañcāti akkhātā, ye mayaṃ attani sampassamānā evaṃ vadema.

‘These, friends, are the four qualities declared by the Blessed One as our comfort and strength, which we, seeing in ourselves, thus speak.’

141. Yo amhākaṃ satthāti iminā pūraṇakassapādike cha satthāro apadissanti. Yathā pana idāni sāsane ācariyupajjhāyādīsu “amhākaṃ ācariyo, amhākaṃ upajjhāyo”ti gehasitapemaṃ hoti. Evarūpaṃ pemaṃ sandhāya “satthari pasādo”ti vadanti. Thero panāha – “yasmā satthā nāma na ekassa, na dvinnaṃ hoti, sadevakassa lokassa ekova satthā, tasmā titthiyā ‘amhākaṃ satthā’ ti ekapadeneva satthāraṃ visuṃ katvā imināva padena viruddhā parājitā”ti. Dhamme pasādoti idaṃ pana yathā idāni sāsane “amhākaṃ dīghanikāyo amhākaṃ [V 1.0322] majjhimanikāyo”ti mamāyanti, evaṃ attano attano pariyattidhamme gehasitapemaṃ sandhāya vadanti. Sīlesūti ajasīlagosīlameṇḍakasīlakukkurasīlādīsu. Idha no āvusoti ettha idhāti pasādaṃ sandhāya vadanti. Ko adhippayāsoti ko adhikappayogo. Yadidanti yamidaṃ tumhākañceva amhākañca nānākaraṇaṃ vadeyyātha. Taṃ kiṃ nāma? Tumhākampi hi catūsu ṭhānesu pasādo, amhākampi. Nanu etasmiṃ pasāde tumhe ca amhe ca dvedhā bhinnasuvaṇṇaṃ viya ekasadisāti vācāya samadhurā hutvā aṭṭhaṃsu.

141. ‘Our teacher’—by this, the six teachers such as Pūraṇa Kassapa are disparaged. Just as now in the Dispensation, regarding teachers and preceptors, there is an affection rooted in household life, as when one says, ‘Our teacher, our preceptor.’ It is with reference to such affection that they speak of ‘faith in the Teacher.’ But the Elder said: ‘Because a teacher is not for one or two, but the Teacher is one for the entire world, including the devas, therefore the sectarians, by saying “our teacher” and thus setting the Teacher apart with this very phrase, are contradicted and defeated by this word itself.’ ‘Faith in the Dhamma’—this refers to how now in the Dispensation, one makes a claim of ownership, saying, ‘Our Dīghanikāya, our Majjhimanikāya,’ thus speaking with reference to an affection rooted in household life for their own respective scriptural collections. ‘In virtues’—this refers to the goat-practice, cow-practice, sheep-practice, dog-practice, and so on. ‘Here, friends’—here, by ‘here,’ they speak with reference to faith. ‘What is the intention?’ means ‘What is the further application?’ ‘Yadidaṃ’ means: that which you might state as a difference between you and us. What is it? For you too have faith in these four things, and so do we. Is it not that in this matter of faith, you and we are exactly alike, like a piece of gold split in two? Thus, having become sweet in speech, they stood in accord.

Atha nesaṃ taṃ samadhurataṃ bhindanto bhagavā evaṃ vādinotiādimāha. Tattha ekā niṭṭhāti yā tassa pasādassa pariyosānabhūtā [M 1.0316] niṭṭhā, kiṃ sā ekā, udāhu puthūti evaṃ pucchathāti vadati. Yasmā pana tasmiṃ tasmiṃ samaye niṭṭhaṃ apaññapento nāma natthi, brāhmaṇānañhi brahmaloko niṭṭhā, mahātāpasānaṃ ābhassarā, paribbājakānaṃ subhakiṇhā, ājīvakānaṃ “anantamānaso”ti evaṃ parikappito asaññībhavo[P 2.0010]. Imasmiṃ sāsane pana arahattaṃ niṭṭhā. Sabbeva cete arahattameva niṭṭhāti vadanti. Diṭṭhivasena pana brahmalokādīni paññapenti. Tasmā attano attano laddhivasena ekameva niṭṭhaṃ paññapenti, taṃ dassetuṃ bhagavā sammā byākaramānātiādimāha.

Then, breaking their harmonious agreement, the Blessed One spoke, beginning with the words ‘evaṃ vādi’. Here, ‘one culmination’ refers to that culmination which is the final end of that faith. He is saying they should ask thus: ‘Is it one, or is it many?’ For indeed, there is no one who, at any given time, does not declare a culmination. For brahmins, the Brahma-world is the culmination; for great ascetics, the Ābhassara realm; for wanderers, the Subhakiṇha realm; for Ājīvakas, the realm of non-perception, which is conceived by them as the ‘boundless mind’. But in this Dispensation, Arahantship is the culmination. And all of them, in fact, declare Arahantship itself to be the culmination. However, according to their own views, they proclaim the Brahma-world and other such states. Therefore, each declares just one culmination according to their own doctrine. To show this, the Blessed One, explaining rightly, spoke, beginning with the words ‘sammā byākaramāna’.

Idāni bhikkhūnampi ekā niṭṭhā, titthiyānampi ekā niṭṭhāti dvīsu aṭṭakārakesu viya ṭhitesu bhagavā anuyogavattaṃ dassento sā panāvuso, niṭṭhā sarāgassa, udāhu vītarāgassātiādimāha. Tattha yasmā rāgarattādīnaṃ niṭṭhā nāma natthi. Yadi siyā, soṇasiṅgālādīnampi siyāti imaṃ dosaṃ passantānaṃ titthiyānaṃ “vītarāgassa āvuso sā niṭṭhā”tiādinā nayena byākaraṇaṃ dassitaṃ.

Now, with there being one culmination for the bhikkhus and one culmination for the sectarians, as they stood like two litigants, the Blessed One, showing the method of inquiry, spoke, beginning with: ‘But, friends, is that culmination for one with lust, or for one free from lust?’ Here, because there is no such thing as a culmination for those impassioned with lust and so on—for if there were, even dogs and jackals would have it—it is shown that the sectarians, seeing this fault, gave their answer in this way: ‘That culmination, friend, is for one free from lust,’ and so on.

Tattha viddasunoti paṇḍitassa. Anuruddhapaṭiviruddhassāti rāgena anuruddhassa kodhena paṭiviruddhassa. Papañcārāmassa papañcaratinoti ettha āramanti etthāti ārāmo. Papañco ārāmo assāti papañcārāmo. Papañce rati assāti papañcarati. Papañcoti ca mattapamattākārabhāvena pavattānaṃ taṇhādiṭṭhimānānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Idha pana taṇhādiṭṭhiyova adhippetā. Sarāgassātiādīsu pañcasu ṭhānesu ekova kileso āgato. Tassa ākārato nānattaṃ [V 1.0323] veditabbaṃ. Sarāgassāti hi vuttaṭṭhāne pañcakāmaguṇikarāgavasena gahito. Sataṇhassāti bhavataṇhāvasena. Saupādānassāti gahaṇavasena. Anuruddhapaṭiviruddhassāti yugaḷavasena. Papañcārāmassāti papañcuppattidassanavasena. Sarāgassāti vā ettha akusalamūlavasena gahito. Sataṇhassāti ettha taṇhāpaccayā upādānadassanavasena. Sesaṃ purimasadisameva. Thero panāha “kasmā evaṃ viddhaṃsetha? Ekoyeva hi ayaṃ lobho rajjanavasena rāgoti vutto. Taṇhākaraṇavasena taṇhā. Gahaṇaṭṭhena upādānaṃ. Yugaḷavasena anurodhapaṭivirodho. Papañcuppattidassanaṭṭhena papañco”ti.

Here, ‘viddasuno’ means of the wise. ‘Anuruddhapaṭiviruddhassa’ refers to one who is attracted through lust and repelled through anger. Regarding ‘papañcārāmassa papañcaratino’, here, ‘ārāma’ means that in which one delights; thus, ‘papañcārāmo’ is one whose resort is proliferation. ‘Papañcarati’ means one whose pleasure is in proliferation. And ‘papañca’ is a term for craving, views, and conceit that proceed by way of intoxication and heedlessness. Here, however, only craving and views are intended. In the five instances—‘sarāgassa’ (for one with lust) and so on—only one defilement is mentioned, but its diversity of aspect should be understood. For where ‘sarāgassa’ is stated, it is taken as lust related to the five strands of sensual pleasure. ‘Sataṇhassa’ is taken as craving for existence. ‘Saupādānassa’ is taken as grasping. ‘Anuruddhapaṭiviruddhassa’ is taken as a pair. ‘Papañcārāmassa’ is taken as the manifestation of the arising of proliferation. Alternatively, ‘sarāgassa’ here is taken as being based on an unwholesome root. ‘Sataṇhassa’ here is taken as the manifestation of clinging conditioned by craving. The rest is the same as before. The Elder, however, said: “Why do you analyze it this way? This is just one and the same greed, which is called ‘lust’ (rāga) because it attaches, ‘craving’ (taṇhā) because it creates thirst, ‘clinging’ (upādāna) because it grasps, ‘attraction and repulsion’ (anurodhapaṭivirodha) because it is a pair, and ‘proliferation’ (papañca) because it manifests the arising of proliferation.”

142. Idāni [M 1.0317] imesaṃ kilesānaṃ mūlabhūtaṃ diṭṭhivādaṃ dassento dvemā, bhikkhave, diṭṭhiyotiādimāha.

142. Now, to show the doctrine of views that is the root of these defilements, he spoke, beginning with: “Bhikkhus, there are these two views.”

Tattha bhavadiṭṭhīti sassatadiṭṭhi. Vibhavadiṭṭhīti ucchedadiṭṭhi. Bhavadiṭṭhiṃ allīnāti taṇhādiṭṭhivasena sassatadiṭṭhiṃ allīnā. Upagatāti [P 2.0011] taṇhādiṭṭhivaseneva upagatā. Ajjhositāti taṇhādiṭṭhivaseneva anupaviṭṭhā. Vibhavadiṭṭhiyā te paṭiviruddhāti te sabbe ucchedavādīhi saddhiṃ – “tumhe andhabālā na jānātha, sassato ayaṃ loko, nāyaṃ loko ucchijjatī”ti paṭiviruddhā niccaṃ kalahabhaṇḍanapasutā viharanti. Dutiyavārepi eseva nayo.

Here, the view of existence is the eternalist view. The view of non-existence is the annihilationist view. ‘Clinging to the view of existence’ means they cling to the eternalist view by way of craving and wrong view. ‘Approaching’ means they approach by way of craving and wrong view. ‘Being obsessed’ means they have entered into it by way of craving and wrong view. ‘Being opposed to the view of non-existence’ means that all of them are opposed to the annihilationists, and constantly dwell intent on quarrels and disputes, saying: “You blind fools do not know; this world is eternal, this world is not annihilated.” The same method applies in the second instance as well.

Samudayañcātiādīsu dve diṭṭhīnaṃ samudayā khaṇikasamudayo paccayasamudayo ca. Khaṇikasamudayo diṭṭhīnaṃ nibbatti. Paccayasamudayo aṭṭha ṭhānāni. Seyyathidaṃ, khandhāpi diṭṭhiṭṭhānaṃ, avijjāpi, phassopi, saññāpi, vitakkopi, ayonisomanasikāropi, pāpamittopi, paratoghosopi diṭṭhiṭṭhānaṃ. “Khandhā hetu khandhā paccayo diṭṭhīnaṃ upādāya samuṭṭhānaṭṭhena. Evaṃ khandhāpi diṭṭhiṭṭhānaṃ. Avijjā… phasso… saññā… vitakko… ayonisomanasikāro… pāpamitto… paratoghoso hetu, paratoghoso paccayo diṭṭhīnaṃ upādāya samuṭṭhānaṭṭhena. Evaṃ paratoghosopi diṭṭhiṭṭhānaṃ” (paṭi. ma. 1.124). Atthaṅgamāpi dveyeva khaṇikatthaṅgamo paccayatthaṅgamo ca. Khaṇikatthaṅgamo nāma khayo vayo bhedo paribhedo aniccatā antaradhānaṃ. Paccayatthaṅgamo nāma sotāpattimaggo. Sotāpattimaggo hi diṭṭhiṭṭhānasamugghātoti vutto.

In the section beginning ‘samudayañca’, there are two origins of views: momentary origin and causal origin. Momentary origin is the arising of views. Causal origin comprises eight bases. That is to say: the aggregates are a basis for views, as are ignorance, contact, perception, thought, unwise attention, a bad friend, and the voice of another. “The aggregates are a cause, the aggregates are a condition for the dependent arising of views. Thus, the aggregates are a basis for views. Ignorance… contact… perception… thought… unwise attention… a bad friend… the voice of another is a cause, the voice of another is a condition for the dependent arising of views. Thus, the voice of another is also a basis for views” (Paṭisambhidāmagga 1.124). Cessation is also twofold: momentary cessation and causal cessation. Momentary cessation is defined as decay, passing away, breaking up, dissolution, impermanence, and disappearance. Causal cessation is the path of stream-entry. For the path of stream-entry is said to be the eradication of the bases for views.

Assādanti [V 1.0324] diṭṭhimūlakaṃ ānisaṃsaṃ. Yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ – “yaṃdiṭṭhiko satthā hoti, taṃdiṭṭhikā sāvakā honti. Yaṃdiṭṭhikā satthāraṃ sāvakā sakkaronti, garuṃ karonti, mānenti, pūjenti, labhanti tatonidānaṃ cīvarapiṇḍapātasenāsanagilānapaccayabhesajjaparikkhāraṃ. Ayaṃ, bhikkhave, diṭṭhiyā diṭṭhadhammiko ānisaṃso”ti. Ādīnavanti diṭṭhiggahaṇamūlakaṃ upaddavaṃ. So vaggulivataṃ ukkuṭikappadhānaṃ kaṇṭakāpassayatā pañcātapatappanaṃ sānupapātapatanaṃ kesamassuluñcanaṃ appoṇakaṃ jhānantiādīnaṃ vasenaṃ veditabbo. Nissaraṇanti diṭṭhīnaṃ nissaraṇaṃ nāma nibbānaṃ. Yathābhūtaṃ [M 1.0318] nappajānantīti ye etaṃ sabbaṃ yathāsabhāvaṃ na jānanti. Na parimuccanti dukkhasmāti sakalavaṭṭadukkhato [P 2.0012] na parimuccanti. Iminā etesaṃ niṭṭhā nāma natthīti dasseti. Parimuccanti dukkhasmāti sakalavaṭṭadukkhato parimuccanti. Iminā etesaṃ niṭṭhā nāma atthīti dvinnaṃ aṭṭakārakānaṃ aṭṭaṃ chindanto viya sāsanasmiṃyeva niṭṭhāya atthitaṃ patiṭṭhapeti.

The gratification is the benefit rooted in views. Regarding this, it is said: “When the teacher holds a certain view, the disciples hold the same view. When the disciples honor, respect, revere, and venerate the teacher for that view, they receive robes, almsfood, lodging, and medicinal requisites because of it. This, bhikkhus, is the immediate benefit of holding a view.” The danger is the harm rooted in clinging to views. This should be understood in terms of practices like the bat-vow, the squatting practice, reliance on thorn-beds, the fivefold scorching, plunging downwards from a precipice, tearing out hair and beard, meditation with meager sustenance, and so on. The escape is the liberation from views, namely Nibbāna. ‘Not comprehending as it truly is’ means those who do not understand all this according to its true nature. ‘They are not freed from suffering’ means they are not liberated from all the suffering of the cycle of existence. Through this, it is shown that for them, there is no culmination. ‘They are freed from suffering’ means they are liberated from all the suffering of the cycle of existence. Through this, it is established that in the teaching itself, there indeed exists a culmination—just as one cutting off the arguments of the two disputants, establishes the existence of the culmination.

143. Idāni diṭṭhicchedanaṃ dassento cattārimāni, bhikkhave, upādānānītiādimāha. Tesaṃ vitthārakathā visuddhimagge vuttāyeva.

143. Now, to show the cutting off of views, he said, beginning with: “Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of clinging.” The detailed explanation of these is as stated in the Visuddhimagga.

Sabbupādānapariññāvādā paṭijānamānāti mayaṃ sabbesaṃ upādānānaṃ pariññaṃ samatikkamaṃ vadāmāti evaṃ paṭijānamānā. Na sammā sabbupādānapariññanti sabbesaṃ upādānānaṃ samatikkamaṃ sammā na paññapenti. Keci kāmupādānamattassa pariññaṃ paññapenti. Keci diṭṭhupādānamattassa paññapenti, keci sīlabbatupādānassāpi. Attavādupādānassa pana pariññaṃ paññapento nāma natthi. Tesaṃ pana bhedaṃ dassento kāmupādānassa pariññaṃ paññapentītiādimāha. Tattha sabbepi kāmupādānassa pariññaṃ paññapentiyeva, channavuti pāsaṇḍāpi hi “kāmā kho pabbajitena na sevitabbā”ti vatthupaṭisevanaṃ kāmaṃ kappatīti na paññapenti, akappiyameva katvā paññapenti. Ye pana sevanti, te theyyena sevanti. Tena vuttaṃ “kāmupādānassa pariññaṃ paññapentī”ti.

Claiming to advocate the complete comprehension of all clingings, they declare, "We proclaim the complete comprehension and overcoming of all clingings." But they do not rightly teach the complete comprehension and overcoming of all clingings. Some teach only the comprehension of sensual clinging. Some teach only the comprehension of view clinging; some, also the clinging to habits and observances. But there is no one who teaches the comprehension of self-doctrine clinging. To show their distinctions, it is said, "Some teach the comprehension of sensual clinging," and so on. In this regard, all of them indeed teach the comprehension of sensual clinging. For even the ninety-six sectarians do not teach that indulgence in sensual objects is permissible, saying, "sensual pleasures are not to be indulged in by one who has gone forth"; they teach them as entirely impermissible. Those who do indulge in them do so stealthily. Therefore, it is said, "They teach the comprehension of sensual clinging."

Yasmā “natthi dinna”ntiādīni gahetvā caranti. “Sīlena suddhi vatena suddhi, bhāvanāya suddhī”ti gaṇhanti, attupaladdhiṃ na pajahanti, tasmā na diṭṭhupādānassa, na sīlabbatupādānassa[V 1.0325], na attavādupādānassa pariññaṃ paññapenti. Taṃ kissa hetūti taṃ apaññāpanaṃ etesaṃ kissa hetu, kiṃ kāraṇā? Imāni hi te bhontoti yasmā te bhonto imāni tīṇi kāraṇāni yathāsabhāvato na jānantīti attho. Ye panettha dvinnaṃ pariññānaṃ paññāpanakāraṇaṃ diṭṭhiñceva sīlabbatañca “etaṃ pahātabba”nti yathāsabhāvato jānanti. Te sandhāya parato dve vārā vuttā. Tattha ye “atthi dinna”ntiādīni gaṇhanti, te diṭṭhupādānassa pariññaṃ paññapenti. Ye pana “na sīlena suddhi, na vatena suddhi, na [P 2.0013] bhāvanāya suddhī”ti gaṇhanti, te sīlabbatupādānassa pariññaṃ paññapenti. Attavādupādānassa pariññaṃ pana ekopi paññapetuṃ na sakkoti. Aṭṭhasamāpattilābhinopi hi candimasūriye pāṇinā [M 1.0319] parimajjitvā caramānāpi ca titthiyā tisso pariññā paññapenti. Attavādaṃ muñcituṃ na sakkonti. Tasmā punappunaṃ vaṭṭasmiṃyeva patanti. Pathavijigucchanasasako viya hi ete.

Because they take up views such as "there is no giving" and so forth. They hold that "purity comes by virtue, purity comes by vows, purity comes by meditation," yet they do not abandon self-identification. Therefore, they do not make known the full understanding of clinging to views, clinging to rites and rituals, or clinging to the doctrine of self. Why is that? What is the reason for this non-declaration? It is because these venerable ones do not truly understand these three things as they really are—that is the meaning. But here, those who know the reason for declaring the full understanding of the two—views and rites and rituals—know as it really is that "this should be abandoned." Concerning them, two statements are made in what follows. Among them, those who take up views such as "there is giving" and so forth declare the full understanding of clinging to views.
