Those, however, who take up the view that "purity does not come by virtue, purity does not come by vows, purity does not come by meditation" declare the full understanding of clinging to rites and rituals. Yet, not even one can declare the full understanding of clinging to the doctrine of self. For even sectarians who attain the eight meditative attainments and go about stroking the sun and moon with their hands teach the full understanding of three types of clinging, yet they cannot relinquish the doctrine of self. Therefore, they fall back again and again into the cycle. Truly, they are like the hare disgusted with the earth.

Tatthāyaṃ atthasallāpikā upamā – pathavī kira sasakaṃ āha – “bho sasakā”ti. Sasako āha – “ko eso”ti. “Kasmā mameva upari sabbairiyāpathe kappento uccārapassāvaṃ karonto maṃ na jānāsī”ti. “Suṭṭhu tayā ahaṃ diṭṭho, mayā akkantaṭṭhānampi aṅgulaggehi phuṭṭhaṭṭhānaṃ viya hoti, vissaṭṭhaudakaṃ appamattakaṃ, karīsaṃ katakaphalamattaṃ. Hatthiassādīhi pana akkantaṭṭhānampi mahantaṃ, passāvopi nesaṃ ghaṭamatto hoti, uccāropi pacchimatto hoti, alaṃ mayhaṃ tayā”ti uppatitvā aññasmiṃ ṭhāne patito. Tato naṃ pathavī āha – “are dūraṃ gatopi nanu mayhaṃ upariyeva patitosī”ti. So puna taṃ jigucchanto uppatitvā aññattha patito, evaṃ vassasahassampi uppatitvā patamāno sasako pathaviṃ muñcituṃ na sakkoti. Evamevaṃ titthiyā sabbūpādānapariññaṃ paññapentopi kāmupādānādīnaṃ tiṇṇaṃyeva samatikkamaṃ paññapenti. Attavādaṃ pana muñcituṃ na sakkonti, asakkontā punappunaṃ vaṭṭasmiṃyeva patantīti.

Here is an illustrative story: The earth once said to a hare, "Hey, hare!" The hare replied, "Who is that?" The earth said, "Why do you not recognize me, when you conduct all your activities upon me, defecating and urinating on me?" The hare answered, "You have seen me well indeed, but the places I tread upon are as if touched by the tips of my toes, the water I release is but a tiny drop, and my dung is the size of a kataka fruit. However, the places trodden by elephants and horses are vast, their urine is a potful, and their dung is the size of a cooking pot. Enough of you for me!" So saying, the hare leaped away and landed elsewhere. Then the earth said, "Hey, even if you go far, have you not still landed upon me?" Disgusted, the hare leaped again and landed somewhere else. Even if the hare were to leap and land for a thousand years, he could not escape the earth. In the same way, though sectarians claim full understanding of all clinging, they only teach the overcoming of the three kinds of clinging—such as clinging to sensual pleasures—but they cannot free themselves from the doctrine of self. Unable to do so, they keep falling back into the cycle of existence.

Evaṃ yaṃ titthiyā samatikkamituṃ na sakkonti, tassa vasena diṭṭhicchedavādaṃ vatvā idāni pasādapacchedavādaṃ dassento evarūpe kho, bhikkhave, dhammavinayetiādimāha. Tattha dhammavinayeti dhamme ceva vinaye ca, ubhayenapi aniyyānikasāsanaṃ dasseti. “Yo satthari pasādo [V 1.0326] so na sammaggato”ti aniyyānikasāsanamhi hi satthā kālaṃ katvā sīhopi hoti, byagghopi hoti, dīpipi acchopi taracchopi. Sāvakā panassa migāpi sūkarāpi pasadāpi honti, so “ime mayhaṃ pubbe upaṭṭhākā paccayadāyakā”ti khantiṃ vā mettaṃ vā anuddayaṃ vā akatvā tesaṃ upari patitvā lohitaṃ pivati, thūlathūlamaṃsānipi khādati. Satthā vā pana biḷāro hoti, sāvakā [P 2.0014] kukkuṭā vā mūsikā vā. Atha ne vuttanayeneva anukampaṃ akatvā khādati. Atha vā satthā nirayapālo hoti, sāvakā nerayikasattā. So “ime mayhaṃ pubbe upaṭṭhākā paccayadāyakā”ti anukampaṃ akatvā vividhā kammakāraṇā karoti, ādittepi rathe yojeti, aṅgārapabbatampi āropeti, lohakumbhiyampi khipati[M 1.0320], anekehipi dukkhadhammehi sampayojeti. Sāvakā vā pana kālaṃ katvā sīhādayo honti, satthā migādīsu aññataro. Te “imaṃ mayaṃ pubbe catūhi paccayehi upaṭṭhahimhā, satthā no aya”nti tasmiṃ khantiṃ vā mettaṃ vā anuddayaṃ vā akatvā vuttanayeneva anayabyasanaṃ pāpenti. Evaṃ aniyyānikasāsane yo satthari pasādo, so na sammaggato hoti, kañci kālaṃ gantvāpi pacchā vinassatiyeva.

Thus, having stated the doctrine of severing views by means of that which the sectarians are unable to transcend, he now, to show the doctrine of severing confidence, says: 'Such, O monks, is this Dhamma and Discipline,' and so on. Herein, 'Dhamma and Discipline' refers to both the Dhamma and the Discipline; by both, he indicates a teaching that does not lead to deliverance. 'For confidence in the teacher is not well-directed'—for in a teaching that does not lead to deliverance, the teacher, after death, may become a lion, a tiger, a leopard, a bear, or a hyena. His disciples, however, may become deer, boars, or spotted deer. Then, without showing patience, loving-kindness, or compassion, thinking, 'These were formerly my attendants and providers of requisites,' he pounces upon them, drinks their blood, and devours their coarse flesh. Or the teacher may become a cat, and his disciples may become chickens or mice. Then, without showing compassion as described above, he devours them. Or the teacher may become a hell-warden, and his disciples may become beings in hell. Without compassion, thinking, 'These were formerly my attendants and providers of requisites,' he inflicts various forms of torture—yoking them to a flaming chariot, making them ascend a mountain of embers, casting them into a metal cauldron, and subjecting them to many states of suffering. Or the disciples, after death, may become lions and the like, while the teacher becomes one of the deer and such. Without showing patience, loving-kindness, or compassion, thinking, 'We formerly supported this one with the four requisites; he was our teacher,' they bring about his ruin and downfall in the way described above. Thus, in a teaching that does not lead to deliverance, confidence in the teacher is not well-directed. Even after some time has passed, it will surely perish.

Yo dhamme pasādoti aniyyānikasāsanasmiñhi dhamme pasādo nāma, uggahitapariyāpuṭa – dhāritavācittamattake tantidhamme pasādo hoti, vaṭṭamokkho panettha natthi. Tasmā yo ettha pasādo, so punappunaṃ vaṭṭameva gambhīraṃ karotīti sāsanasmiṃ asammaggato asabhāvato akkhāyati.

As for confidence in the Dhamma: in a teaching that does not lead to deliverance, confidence in the Dhamma is merely confidence in the textual Dhamma that has been learned, mastered, retained, and recited. In this, there is no release from the round of existence. Therefore, whatever confidence there is here only makes the round of existence deeper and deeper. Thus, in this teaching, it is said to be not well-directed and not in accordance with its true nature.

Yā sīlesu paripūrakāritāti yāpi ca aniyyānikasāsane ajasīlādīnaṃ vasena paripūrakāritā, sāpi yasmā vaṭṭamokkhaṃ bhavanissaraṇaṃ na sampāpeti, sampajjamānā pana tiracchānayoniṃ āvahati, vipaccamānā nirayaṃ, tasmā sā na sammaggatā akkhāyati. Yā sahadhammikesūti aniyyānikasāsanasmiñhi ye sahadhammikā, tesu yasmā ekacce kālaṃ katvā sīhādayopi honti, ekacce migādayo, tattha sīhādibhūtā “ime amhākaṃ sahadhammikā ahesu”nti migādibhūtesu khantiādīni akatvā pubbe vuttanayeneva nesaṃ mahādukkhaṃ uppādenti. Tasmā ettha sahadhammikesu piyamanāpatāpi asammaggatā akkhāyati.

As for the complete fulfillment in virtues: since the complete fulfillment of virtues in a non-liberating teaching, such as the practice of goat-virtue and so on, does not lead to release from the round of existence or escape from becoming—but rather, when undertaken leads to the animal realm, and when it ripens leads to hell—it is therefore said to be not well-directed. As for those who are companions in the Dhamma: in a non-liberating teaching, among those who are companions in the Dhamma, some, after death, become lions and the like, while others become deer and the like. Because of this, those who have become lions and so on, thinking, 'These were our companions in the Dhamma,' do not show patience and so on toward those who have become deer and the like, but cause them great suffering in the way previously described. Therefore, in this case, affection and fondness for companions in the Dhamma are also said to be not well-directed.

Idaṃ pana sabbampi kāraṇabhedaṃ ekato katvā dassento bhagavā taṃ kissa hetu? Evañhetaṃ[V 1.0327], bhikkhave, hotītiādimāha. Tatrāyaṃ saṃkhepattho – evañhetaṃ, bhikkhave, hoti, yaṃ mayā vuttaṃ “yo satthari pasādo so na sammaggato akkhāyatī”tiādi, taṃ evameva hoti. Kasmā? Yasmā te pasādādayo durakkhāte dhammavinaye [P 2.0015]…pe… asammāsambuddhappavediteti, ettha hi yathā tanti kāraṇatthe nipāto. Tattha durakkhāteti dukkathite, dukkhathitattāyeva duppavedite. So panesa yasmā maggaphalatthāya na niyyāti, tasmā aniyyāniko. Rāgādīnaṃ upasamāya asaṃvattanato anupasamasaṃvattaniko. Na sammāsambuddhena sabbaññunā [M 1.0321] paveditoti asammāsambuddhappavedito. Tasmiṃ aniyyānike anupasamasaṃvattanike asammāsambuddhappavedite. Ettāvatā bhagavā titthiyesu pasādo surāpītasiṅgāle pasādo viya niratthakoti dasseti.

Now, presenting all these different reasons together, the Blessed One said: 'For what reason? It is so, monks,' and so on. Here is the brief meaning: 'It is so, monks'—what I have said, namely, 'Confidence in the teacher is not said to be well-directed,' and so on, is just so. Why? Because that confidence and so on are in a Dhamma and Discipline that is badly expounded... not proclaimed by a Perfectly Enlightened One. Herein, the particle yasmā is used in the sense of a reason. Therein, 'badly expounded' means badly taught; and because it is badly taught, it is badly proclaimed. Furthermore, because it does not lead to the attainment of the path and its fruit, it is 'not leading to deliverance.' Because it does not conduce to the calming of lust and so on, it is 'not conducive to calming.' It is not proclaimed by a Perfectly Enlightened One, an All-Knowing One, thus it is 'proclaimed by one who is not a Perfectly Enlightened One.' In that which is not leading to deliverance, not conducive to calming, and proclaimed by one who is not a Perfectly Enlightened One. To this extent, the Blessed One shows that confidence in the sectarians is as useless as confidence in a drunken jackal.

Eko kira kāḷasiṅgālo rattiṃ nagaraṃ paviṭṭho surājallikaṃ khāditvā punnāgavane nipajjitvā niddāyanto sūriyuggamane pabujjhitvā cintesi “imasmiṃ kāle na sakkā gantuṃ, bahū amhākaṃ verino, ekaṃ vañcetuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. So ekaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ gacchantaṃ disvā imaṃ vañcessāmīti “ayya brāhmaṇā”ti āha. Ko eso brāhmaṇaṃ pakkosatīti. “Ahaṃ, sāmī, ito tāva ehīti. Kiṃ bhoti? Maṃ bahigāmaṃ nehi, ahaṃ te dve kahāpaṇasatāni dassāmīti. Sopi nayissāmīti taṃ pādesu gaṇhi. Are bāla brāhmaṇa, na mayhaṃ kahāpaṇā chaḍḍitakā atthi, dullabhā kahāpaṇā, sādhukaṃ maṃ gaṇhāhīti. Kathaṃ bho gaṇhāmīti? Uttarāsaṅgena gaṇṭhikaṃ katvā aṃse laggetvā gaṇhāhīti. Brāhmaṇo taṃ tathā gahetvā dakkhiṇadvārasamīpaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā ettha otāremīti pucchi. Kataraṭṭhānaṃ nāma etanti? Mahādvāraṃ etanti. Are bāla, brāhmaṇa, kiṃ tava ñātakā antaradvāre kahāpaṇaṃ ṭhapenti, parato maṃ harā”ti. So punappunaṃ thokaṃ thokaṃ gantvā “ettha otāremi ettha otāremī”ti pucchitvā tena tajjito khemaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā tattha otārehīti vutto otāretvā sāṭakaṃ gaṇhi. Kāḷasiṅgālo āha “ahaṃ te dve kahāpaṇasatāni dassāmīti avocaṃ. Mayhaṃ pana kahāpaṇā bahū, na dve kahāpaṇasatāneva, yāva ahaṃ kahāpaṇe āharāmi, tāva tvaṃ sūriyaṃ olokento tiṭṭhā”ti vatvā thokaṃ gantvā nivattetvā puna brāhmaṇaṃ āha “ayya brāhmaṇa mā ito olokehi, sūriyameva olokento tiṭṭhā”ti. Evañca pana vatvā ketakavanaṃ pavisitvā yathāruciṃ pakkanto. Brāhmaṇassapi sūriyaṃ [P 2.0016] olokentasseva nalāṭato ceva kacchehi ca sedā mucciṃsu. Atha naṃ rukkhadevatā āha –

Once, it is said, a black jackal entered the city at night, ate some dregs of liquor, lay down in a Punnāga grove, and fell asleep. Waking at sunrise, he thought, 'At this time, it is not possible to go. We have many enemies. It is fitting to deceive someone.' Seeing a brahmin passing by, he thought, 'I will deceive him,' and called out, 'Sir brahmin!' The brahmin wondered, 'Who is this calling a brahmin?' 'It is I, sir,' said the jackal, 'come here.' 'What is it, sir?' 'Take me outside the city, and I will give you two hundred kahapanas.' The brahmin, agreeing to take him, took hold of him by the feet. The jackal said, 'You foolish brahmin, I do not have kahapanas to be thrown away; kahapanas are hard to come by. Hold me carefully!' 'How should I hold you, sir?' 'Making a bundle with your upper robe, carry me on your shoulder.' The brahmin did so and, reaching a place near the southern gate, asked, 'Shall I set you down here?' 'What place is this?' 'This is the great gate.' 'You foolish brahmin, do your relatives keep kahapanas inside the gate? Carry me further!' Repeatedly, after going a little further, the brahmin would ask, 'Shall I set you down here? Shall I set you down here?' Being threatened by him, he reached a safe place and was told, 'Set me down here.' After setting him down, the brahmin took his cloth. The black jackal said, 'I said I would give you two hundred kahapanas. But I have many kahapanas, not just two hundred. Until I bring the kahapanas, you stand here watching the sun.' Having said this, he went a short distance, turned back, and again said to the brahmin, 'Sir brahmin, do not look this way; just stand watching the sun.' And having said this, he entered a Ketaka grove and departed as he pleased. As for the brahmin, while he stood watching the sun, sweat poured from his forehead and armpits. Then a tree deity said to him:

“Saddahāsi [V 1.0328] siṅgālassa, surāpītassa brāhmaṇa;

Sippikānaṃ sataṃ natthi, kuto kaṃsasatā duve”ti. (jā. 1.1.113);

“You trust the jackal, O brahmin, who has drunk liquor; he does not possess even a hundred cowrie shells, so whence two hundred bronze coins?”

Evaṃ yathā kāḷasiṅgāle pasādo niratthako, evaṃ titthiyesupīti.

Thus, just as confidence in a black jackal is fruitless, so too is it in the sectarians.

144. Aniyyānikasāsane [M 1.0322] pasādassa niratthakabhāvaṃ dassetvā niyyānikasāsane tassa sātthakataṃ dassetuṃ tathāgato ca kho, bhikkhavetiādimāha. Tattha kāmupādānassa pariññaṃ paññapetīti arahattamaggena kāmupādānassa pahānapariññaṃ samatikkamaṃ paññapeti, itaresaṃ tiṇṇaṃ upādānānaṃ sotāpattimaggena pariññaṃ paññapeti. Evarūpe kho, bhikkhave, dhammavinayeti, bhikkhave, evarūpe dhamme ca vinaye ca. Ubhayenapi niyyānikasāsanaṃ dasseti. Satthari pasādoti evarūpe sāsane yo satthari pasādo, so sammaggato akkhāyati, bhavadukkhanissaraṇāya saṃvattati.

144. Having shown the uselessness of faith in a teaching that does not lead to liberation, to demonstrate its meaningfulness in a teaching that does lead to liberation, the Tathāgata said, 'But, bhikkhus,' and so on. Herein, 'he declares the full understanding of clinging to sensual pleasures' means he declares the full understanding as abandoning and the transcending of clinging to sensual pleasures through the path of arahantship. For the other three kinds of clinging, he declares their full understanding through the path of stream-entry. 'In such a Dhamma and Discipline, bhikkhus...' means, bhikkhus, in such a Dhamma and in such a Discipline. By both, he indicates the teaching that leads to liberation. 'Faith in the Teacher' means that in such a teaching, faith in the Teacher is said to be rightly directed; it conduces to the escape from the suffering of existence.

Tatrimāni vatthūni – bhagavā kira vediyakapabbate indasālaguhāyaṃ paṭivasati. Atheko ulūkasakuṇo bhagavati gāmaṃ piṇḍāya pavisante upaḍḍhamaggaṃ anugacchati, nikkhamante upaḍḍhamaggaṃ paccuggamanaṃ karoti. So ekadivasaṃ sammāsambuddhaṃ sāyanhasamaye bhikkhusaṅghaparivutaṃ nisinnaṃ pabbatā oruyha vanditvā pakkhe paṇāmetvā añjaliṃ paggayha sīsaṃ heṭṭhā katvā dasabalaṃ namassamāno aṭṭhāsi. Bhagavā taṃ oloketvā sitaṃ pātvākāsi. Ānandatthero “ko nu kho, bhante, hetu ko paccayo sitassa pātukammāyā”ti pucchi. “Passānanda, imaṃ ulūkasakuṇaṃ, ayaṃ mayi ca bhikkhusaṅghe ca cittaṃ pasādetvā satasahassakappe devesu ca manussesu ca saṃsaritvā somanasso nāma paccekabuddho bhavissatī”ti āha –

Herein are these stories: It is said that the Blessed One was dwelling in the Indasāla Cave on Vediyaka Mountain. Now, a certain owl would follow the Blessed One halfway when he entered the village for alms and would come halfway to meet him when he left. One day, in the evening, that owl descended from the mountain, paid homage to the Perfectly Enlightened One as he sat surrounded by the Sangha of bhikkhus, lowered its wings, made a gesture of reverence, bowed its head, and stood there worshipping the One of Ten Powers. The Blessed One looked at it and manifested a smile. The Elder Ānanda asked, 'What, venerable sir, is the cause, what is the reason for the manifestation of a smile?' The Blessed One replied, 'Ānanda, do you see this owl? Having generated confidence in its mind toward me and the Sangha of bhikkhus, after wandering among devas and humans for a hundred thousand aeons, it will become a Paccekabuddha named Somanassa.'

Ulūkamaṇḍalakkhika, vediyake ciradīghavāsika;

Sukhitosi tvaṃ ayya kosiya, kāluṭṭhitaṃ passasi buddhavaraṃ.

“O owl with circular eyes, long-time dweller on Vediyaka; happy are you, noble Kosiya, you see the excellent Buddha, arisen at the proper time.

Mayi [V 1.0329][P 2.0017] cittaṃ pasādetvā, bhikkhusaṅghe anuttare;

Kappānaṃ satasahassāni, duggateso na gacchati.

Having placed confidence in me, and in the unsurpassed Sangha of bhikkhus, for a hundred thousand aeons, he will not go to a state of woe.

Devalokā cavitvāna, kusalamūlena codito;

Bhavissati anantañāṇo, somanassoti vissutoti.

Having departed from the deva world, impelled by wholesome roots, he will be of infinite wisdom, renowned as Somanassa.”

Aññānipi cettha rājagahanagare sumanamālākāravatthu mahābherivādakavatthu morajikavatthu vīṇāvādakavatthu saṅkhadhamakavatthūti evamādīni vatthūni [M 1.0323] vitthāretabbāni. Evaṃ niyyānikasāsane satthari pasādo sammaggato hoti.

Here in the city of Rājagaha, other stories are also to be elaborated, such as the story of Sumana the garland-maker, the story of the great drum player, the story of the peacock-keeper, the story of the lute player, and the story of the conch blower. Thus, in the teaching that leads to liberation, faith in the Teacher is rightly directed.

Dhamme pasādoti niyyānikasāsanamhi dhamme pasādo sammaggato hoti. Saramatte nimittaṃ gahetvā suṇantānaṃ tiracchānagatānampi sampattidāyako hoti, paramatthe kiṃ pana vattabbaṃ. Ayamattho maṇḍūkadevaputtādīnaṃ vatthuvasena veditabbo.

Faith in the Dhamma means that in the teaching that leads to liberation, faith in the Dhamma is rightly directed. Even for animals who listen, grasping a sign in the mere sound, it becomes a giver of attainment; what then need be said of the ultimate goal? This meaning should be understood by way of the story of the frog devaputta and others.

Sīlesu paripūrakāritāti niyyānikasāsanamhi sīlesu paripūrakāritāpi sammaggatā hoti, saggamokkhasampattiṃ āvahati. Tattha chattamāṇavakavatthusāmaṇeravatthuādīni dīpetabbāni.

The practice of fulfilling the precepts means that in the teaching that leads to liberation, the practice of fulfilling the precepts is also rightly directed; it brings about the attainment of heaven and liberation. Here, the stories of Chatta the young man, the novice monk, and others should be explained.

Sahadhammikesūti niyyānikasāsane sahadhammikesu piyamanāpatāpi sammaggatā hoti, mahāsampattiṃ āvahati. Ayamattho vimānapetavatthūhi dīpetabbo. Vuttañhetaṃ –

'Among fellow practitioners' means that in the teaching that leads to liberation, being dear and agreeable among fellow practitioners is also rightly directed; it brings about great attainment. This meaning should be illustrated with stories from the Vimanavatthu and Petavatthu. For it has been said:

“Khīrodanamahamadāsiṃ, bhikkhuno piṇḍāya carantassa…pe…

“I gave milk-rice to a bhikkhu wandering for alms… and so on…

Phāṇitaṃ…pe… ucchukhaṇḍikaṃ… timbarusakaṃ… kakkārikaṃ…

Molasses... sugarcane pieces... timbaru fruit... kakkārika fruit...

Eḷālukaṃ… vallipakkaṃ… phārusakaṃ… hatthapatākaṃ…

A type of cucumber... ripe melon... Grewia asiatica fruit... Hatthapataka plant...

Sākamuṭṭhiṃ [V 1.0330] … pupphakamuṭṭhiṃ… mūlakaṃ… nimbamuṭṭhiṃ…

A handful of greens... a handful of flowers... a root... a handful of neem leaves...

Ambikañjikaṃ… doṇinimmajjaniṃ… kāyabandhanaṃ…

Sour gruel... a water-dipper... a waistband...

Aṃsabaddhakaṃ… āyogapaṭṭaṃ… vidhūpanaṃ… tālavaṇṭaṃ…

A shoulder-strap... a belt... a whisk... a palm-leaf fan...

Morahatthaṃ… chattaṃ… upāhanaṃ… pūvaṃ modakaṃ…

A peacock-feather fan... an umbrella... sandals... a cake... a dumpling...

Sakkhalikaṃ [P 2.0018] ahamadāsiṃ, bhikkhuno piṇḍāya carantassa…pe…

I gave a piece of crystal sugar to a bhikkhu wandering for alms...

Tassā me passa vimānaṃ, accharā kāmavaṇṇinīhamasmī”ti (vi. va. 406).

See my celestial mansion; I am a nymph of delightful beauty,” (Vv. 406).

Taṃ kissa hetūtiādi vuttanayānusāreneva yojetvā veditabbaṃ.

The phrase 'For what reason?' and so on should be understood by connecting it according to the method already stated.

145. Idāni [M 1.0324] yesaṃ upādānānaṃ titthiyā na sammā pariññaṃ paññapenti, tathāgato paññapeti, tesaṃ paccayaṃ dassetuṃ ime ca, bhikkhavetiādimāha. Tattha kiṃnidānātiādīsu nidānādīni sabbāneva kāraṇavevacanāni. Kāraṇañhi yasmā phalaṃ nideti handa, naṃ gaṇhathāti appeti viya, tasmā nidānanti vuccati. Yasmā taṃ tato jāyati samudeti pabhavati, tasmā samudayo, jāti, pabhavoti vuccati. Ayaṃ panettha padattho – kiṃ nidānaṃ etesanti kiṃnidānā. Ko samudayo etesanti kiṃsamudayā. Kā jāti etesanti kiṃjātikā. Ko pabhavo etesanti kiṃpabhavā. Yasmā pana tesaṃ taṇhā yathāvuttena atthena nidānañceva samudayo ca jāti ca pabhavo ca, tasmā “taṇhānidānā”tiādimāha. Evaṃ sabbapadesu attho veditabbo. Yasmā pana bhagavā na kevalaṃ upādānasseva paccayaṃ jānāti, upādānassa paccayabhūtāya taṇhāyapi, taṇhādipaccayānaṃ vedanādīnampi paccayaṃ jānātiyeva, tasmā taṇhā cāyaṃ, bhikkhavetiādimāha.

145. Now, regarding those clingings for which other teachers do not declare a full understanding, the Tathāgata does declare it. To show the cause for these, he said, “And these, bhikkhus,” and so on. Herein, in “What is the cause?” and so on, all the terms “cause,” and so on, are synonyms for “reason.” For a reason, since it ‘lays down’ (nideti) a result as if saying, “Here, take it! Grasp it!”, therefore it is called ‘cause’ (nidāna). Since from it a thing arises, originates, and comes into being, therefore it is called ‘origin’ (samudaya), ‘birth’ (jāti), and ‘source’ (pabhava). Herein, the meaning of the words is this: “What is the cause of these?”—thus “of what cause are these?” “What is the origin of these?”—thus “of what origin are these?” “What is the birth of these?”—thus “of what birth are these?” “What is the source of these?”—thus “of what source are these?” But because craving, in the manner stated, is the cause, origin, birth, and source of these, therefore he said, “Craving-caused,” and so on. In this way, the meaning should be understood in all passages. Moreover, since the Blessed One knows not only the cause of clinging, but also of craving, which is the cause of clinging, and further knows the causes of feeling and so on, which are causes of craving and so on, therefore he said, “And this craving, bhikkhus,” and so on.

Yato [V 1.0331] ca khoti yasmiṃ kāle. Avijjā pahīnā hotīti vaṭṭamūlikā avijjā anuppādanirodhena pahīnā hoti. Vijjā uppannāti arahattamaggavijjā uppannā. So avijjāvirāgā vijjuppādāti. So bhikkhu avijjāya ca pahīnattā vijjāya ca uppannattā. Neva kāmupādānaṃ upādiyatīti neva kāmupādānaṃ gaṇhāti na upeti, na sesāni upādānāni. Anupādiyaṃ na paritassatīti evaṃ kiñci upādānaṃ aggaṇhanto taṇhāparitassanāya na paritassati. Aparitassanti aparitassanto taṇhaṃ anuppādento. Paccattaṃyeva parinibbāyatīti sayameva kilesaparinibbānena parinibbāyati. Evamassa āsavakkhayaṃ dassetvā idāni khīṇāsavassa bhikkhuno paccavekkhaṇaṃ dassento khīṇā jātītiādimāha. Taṃ vuttatthamevāti.

`Yato ca kho` means: at which time. `Ignorance is abandoned` means: the ignorance that is the root of the round of existence is abandoned through cessation by non-arising. `Knowledge has arisen` means: the knowledge of the path to arahantship has arisen. `So avijjāvirāgā vijjuppādā`: That bhikkhu, due to the fading away of ignorance and the arising of knowledge—that is, due to the abandoning of ignorance and the arising of knowledge—does not cling to sensual clinging, nor to the remaining clingings. `Anupādiyaṃ na paritassati`: Not clinging, he does not tremble: thus not grasping any clinging, he does not tremble with the agitation of craving. `Aparitassaṃ`: Not trembling: not trembling, not producing craving. `Paccattaṃyeva parinibbāyati`: He attains final Nibbāna within himself: he himself is fully extinguished through the extinguishment of defilements. Having thus shown the destruction of the taints, now, to show the reflection of the bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed, he said, “Destroyed is birth,” and so on. The meaning is just as has been stated.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Middle Length Discourses.

Cūḷasīhanādasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Cūḷasīhanāda Sutta is concluded.

2. Mahāsīhanādasuttavaṇṇanā

2. The Commentary on the Mahāsīhanāda Sutta.

Vesālinagaravaṇṇanā

Description of the City of Vesālī.

146. Evaṃ [V 1.0332][M 1.0325][P 2.0019] me sutanti mahāsīhanādasuttaṃ. Tattha vesāliyanti evaṃnāmake nagare. Taṃ kira aparāparaṃ visālībhūtatāya “vesālī”ti saṅkhaṃ gataṃ. Tatrāyaṃ anupubbakathā – bārāṇasirañño kira aggamahesiyā kucchimhi gabbho saṇṭhāsi. Sā ñatvā rañño nivedesi. Rājā gabbhaparihāraṃ adāsi. Sā sammā pariharīyamānā gabbhaparipākakāle vijāyanagharaṃ pāvisi. Puññavantīnaṃ paccūsasamaye gabbhavuṭṭhānaṃ hoti, sā ca tāsaṃ aññatarā, tena paccūsasamaye alattakapaṭalabandhujīvakapupphasadisaṃ maṃsapesiṃ vijāyi. Tato “aññā deviyo suvaṇṇabimbasadise putte vijāyanti, aggamahesī maṃsapesinti rañño purato mama avaṇṇo uppajjeyyā”ti cintetvā tena avaṇṇabhayena taṃ maṃsapesiṃ ekasmiṃ bhājane pakkhipitvā paṭikujjitvā rājamuddikāya lañchetvā gaṅgāya sote pakkhipāpesi. Manussehi chaḍḍitamatte devatā ārakkhaṃ saṃvidahiṃsu. Suvaṇṇapaṭṭakañcettha jātihiṅgulakena “bārāṇasirañño aggamahesiyā pajā”ti likhitvā bandhiṃsu. Tato taṃ bhājanaṃ ūmibhayādīhi anupaddutaṃ gaṅgāsotena pāyāsi.

146. Thus have I heard: the Mahāsīhanāda Sutta. Therein, 'in Vesālī' means in the city of that name. It is said that because it was repeatedly made spacious, it came to be known as ‘Vesālī’. Herein is the story in sequence: It is said that a fetus was conceived in the womb of the chief queen of the king of Bārāṇasī. Knowing this, she informed the king. The king provided care for the pregnancy. Being well cared for, when the time came for the fetus to mature, she entered the delivery chamber. For women of great merit, the delivery occurs at dawn, and she was one of them. Therefore, at dawn, she gave birth to a lump of flesh resembling a patch of lac, vermilion, or a bandhujīvaka flower. Then she thought, “Other queens give birth to sons like golden images, but the chief queen gives birth to a lump of flesh; disparagement might arise for me before the king.” Fearing that disgrace, she placed that lump of flesh in a vessel, covered it, sealed it with the royal seal, and had it cast into the current of the Ganges. As soon as it was discarded by humans, deities arranged for its protection. And on it, they attached a golden plaque inscribed with “Offspring of the chief queen of the king of Bārāṇasī” in cinnabar. Then that vessel, undisturbed by fear of waves and so on, floated down the current of the Ganges.

Tena ca samayena aññataro tāpaso gopālakakulaṃ nissāya gaṅgātīre viharati. So pātova gaṅgaṃ otiṇṇo taṃ bhājanaṃ āgacchantaṃ disvā paṃsukūlasaññāya aggahesi. Athettha taṃ akkharapaṭṭikaṃ rājamuddikālañchanaṃ ca disvā muñcitvā taṃ maṃsapesiṃ addasa, disvānassa etadahosi “siyā gabbho, tathā hissa duggandhapūtikabhāvo natthī”ti. Assamaṃ netvā suddhe okāse ṭhapesi. Atha aḍḍhamāsaccayena dve maṃsapesiyo ahesuṃ. Tāpaso disvā sādhutaraṃ ṭhapesi. Tato puna aḍḍhamāsaccayena ekamekissā maṃsapesiyā hatthapādasīsānamatthāya pañca pañca piḷakā uṭṭhahiṃsu. Atha tato aḍḍhamāsaccayena ekā maṃsapesi suvaṇṇabimbasadiso dārako, ekā dārikā ahosi.

At that time, a certain ascetic was dwelling on the bank of the Ganges, relying on a cowherd family. Early in the morning, having descended into the Ganges and seeing that vessel approaching, he took it, perceiving it to be a dust-heap rag. Then, having seen the inscribed plaque and the royal seal on it, he opened it and saw that lump of flesh. Having seen it, this thought occurred to him: “It might be a fetus, for it does not have a foul or putrid smell.” He took it to his hermitage and placed it in a clean place. Then, after half a month, there were two lumps of flesh. The ascetic, having seen this, placed them more carefully. Then, after another half a month, from each lump of flesh, five protuberances arose for the purpose of hands, feet, and head. Then, after another half a month, one lump of flesh became a boy resembling a golden image, and the other became a girl.

Tesu [V 1.0333] tāpasassa puttasineho uppajji, aṅguṭṭhakato cassa khīraṃ nibbatti. Tato pabhuti ca [P 2.0020] khīrabhattaṃ alabhittha, so bhattaṃ bhuñjitvā khīraṃ dārakānaṃ mukhe [M 1.0326] āsiñcati. Tesaṃ udaraṃ yaṃ yaṃ pavisati, taṃ taṃ sabbaṃ maṇibhājanagataṃ viya dissati, evaṃ nicchavī ahesuṃ. Apare āhu “sibbetvā ṭhapitā viya nesaṃ aññamaññaṃ līnā chavi ahosī”ti. Evaṃ te nicchavitāya vā līnacchavitāya vā licchavīti paññāyiṃsu.

Paternal affection for them arose in the ascetic, and milk issued from his thumb. From then on, he obtained rice with milk. Having eaten his meal, he would pour the milk into the children’s mouths. Whatever entered their stomachs was visible as if contained in a jeweled vessel; thus, they were ‘skinless’ (nicchavī). Others said, “Their skin was joined to each other as if sewn and placed together.” Thus, due to their being ‘skinless’ (nicchavī) or having ‘joined skin’ (līnacchavī), they came to be known as the Licchavis.

Tāpaso dārake posento ussūre gāmaṃ sikkhāya pavisati, atidivā paṭikkamati. Tassa taṃ byāpāraṃ ñatvā gopālakā āhaṃsu – “bhante, pabbajitānaṃ dārakaposanaṃ palibodho, amhākaṃ dārake detha, mayaṃ posessāma, tumhe attano kammaṃ karothā”ti. Tāpaso sādhūti paṭissuṇi. Gopālakā dutiyadivase maggaṃ samaṃ katvā pupphehi okiritvā dhajapaṭākā ussāpetvā tūriyehi vajjamānehi assamaṃ āgatā. Tāpaso – “mahāpuññā dārakā appamādena vaḍḍhetha, vaḍḍhetvā ca aññamaññaṃ āvāhavivāhaṃ karotha, pañcagorasena rājānaṃ tosetvā bhūmibhāgaṃ gahetvā nagaraṃ māpetha, tattha kumāraṃ abhisiñcathā”ti vatvā dārake adāsi. Te sādhūti paṭissuṇitvā dārake netvā posesuṃ.

While fostering the children, the ascetic would enter the village for alms at dawn and return late in the day. Knowing of his activity, the cowherds said to him, “Venerable sir, fostering children is an impediment for one who has gone forth. Give us the children; we will foster them. You may attend to your own duties.” The ascetic assented, saying, “Good.” On the next day, the cowherds, having leveled the path, scattered flowers, raised banners and flags, and with musical instruments playing, came to the hermitage. The ascetic said, “The children are of great merit. Raise them with diligence, and when they are grown, arrange marriages among them. Please the king with the five products of the cow, receive a portion of land, build a city, and there consecrate the prince.” Having said this, he gave the children to them. They assented, saying, “Good,” took the children away, and fostered them.

Dārakā vuddhimanvāya kīḷantā vivādaṭṭhānesu aññe gopālakadārake hatthenapi pādenapi paharanti. Te rodanti. “Kissa rodathā”ti ca mātāpitūhi vuttā “ime nimmātāpitikā tāpasapositā amhe atipaharantī”ti vadanti. Tato tesaṃ mātāpitaro “ime dārakā aññe dārake vināsenti dukkhāpenti, na ime saṅgahetabbā, vajjetabbā ime”ti āhaṃsu. Tato pabhuti kira so padeso vajjīti vuccati yojanasatiko parimāṇena. Atha taṃ padesaṃ gopālakā rājānaṃ tosetvā aggahesuṃ. Tattha ca nagaraṃ māpetvā soḷasavassuddesikaṃ kumāraṃ abhisiñcitvā rājānaṃ akaṃsu. Tāya cassa dārikāya saddhiṃ vivāhaṃ katvā katikaṃ akaṃsu “bāhirakadārikā na ānetabbā, ito dārikā na kassaci dātabbā”ti. Tesaṃ paṭhamasaṃvāsena dve dārakā jātā dhītā ca putto ca. Evaṃ soḷasakkhattuṃ dve dve jātā. Tato tesaṃ dārakānaṃ yathākkamaṃ vaḍḍhantānaṃ ārāmuyyānanivāsaṭṭhānaparivārasampattiṃ gahetuṃ appahontā nagaraṃ tikkhattuṃ gāvutantarena gāvutantarena [P 2.0021] parikkhipiṃsu[M 1.0327]. Tassa punappunaṃ visālīkatattā vesālītveva nāmaṃ jātaṃ. Tena vuttaṃ “vesāliyanti evaṃ nāmake nagare”ti.

The children, having grown up, would strike other cowherd boys with their hands and feet in places of dispute while playing. They would cry. And when asked by their parents, “Why are you crying?”, they would say, “These motherless and fatherless ones, raised by the ascetic, strike us excessively.” Then their parents said, “These children harm and distress other children; they should not be associated with; they should be avoided (vajjetabbā).” From then on, it is said, that region came to be called ‘Vajji,’ being a hundred yojanas in measure. Then the cowherds, having pleased the king, took possession of that region. And there they built a city and consecrated the prince, who was sixteen years old, as king. And they arranged a marriage for him with that girl and made an agreement: “No girl from outside should be brought in, and no girl from here should be given to anyone.” From their first union, two children were born: a daughter and a son. Thus, sixteen times, two children were born each time. Then, as their children grew up in succession, being unable to accommodate the abundance of residences, gardens, parks, and retinues, they expanded the city three times, each time by an interval of a gāvuta. Due to its being repeatedly made spacious, it came to be known by the name ‘Vesālī.’ Therefore, it is said, ‘in the city named Vesālī.’

01 Bahinagareti [V 1.0334] nagarassa bahi, na ambapālivanaṃ viya antonagarasmiṃ. Ayaṃ pana jīvakambavanaṃ viya nagarassa bahiddhā vanasaṇḍo. Tena vuttaṃ “bahinagare”ti. Aparapureti purassa apare, pacchimadisāyanti attho. Vanasaṇḍeti so kira vanasaṇḍo nagarassa pacchimadisāyaṃ gāvutamatte ṭhāne. Tattha manussā bhagavato gandhakuṭiṃ katvā taṃ parivāretvā bhikkhūnaṃ rattiṭṭhānadivāṭṭhānacaṅkamaleṇakuṭimaṇḍapādīni patiṭṭhapesuṃ, bhagavā tattha viharati. Tena vuttaṃ “aparapure vanasaṇḍe”ti. Sunakkhattoti tassa nāmaṃ. Licchavīnaṃ pana puttattā licchaviputtoti vutto. Acirapakkantoti vibbhamitvā gihibhāvūpagamanena adhunāpakkanto. Parisatīti parisamajjhe. Uttarimanussadhammāti ettha manussadhammā nāma dasakusalakammapathā. Te paṭisedhetuṃ na sakkoti. Kasmā? Upārambhabhayā. Vesāliyañhi bahū manussā ratanattaye pasannā buddhamāmakā dhammamāmakā saṅghamāmakā. Te dasakusalakammapathamattampi natthi samaṇassa gotamassāti vutte tvaṃ kattha bhagavantaṃ pāṇaṃ hanantaṃ addasa, kattha adinnaṃ ādiyantantiādīni vatvā attano pamāṇaṃ na jānāsi? Kiṃ dantā me atthīti pāsāṇasakkharā khādasi, ahinaṅguṭṭhe gaṇhituṃ vāyamasi, kakacadantesu pupphāvaḷikaṃ kīḷituṃ icchasi? Mukhato te dante pātessāmāti vadeyyuṃ. So tesaṃ upārambhabhayā evaṃ vattuṃ na sakkoti.

Outside the city means outside the city, not like the Ambapālī grove which is within the city. This, however, is a woodland outside the city, like Jīvaka's mango grove. Therefore, it is said, "outside the city." Beyond the city means to the west of the city, that is, in the western direction. That woodland, it is said, was a woodland about a gāvuta away in the western direction of the city. There, people built a perfumed chamber for the Blessed One, surrounded it, and established for the monks places to stay at night, places to dwell during the day, walking paths, shelters, huts, and pavilions. The Blessed One dwelled there. Therefore, it is said, "in the woodland beyond the city." Sunakkhatta is his name. But because he was a son of the Licchavis, he is called Licchaviputta. Recently departed means recently departed by having disrobed and returned to the householder's life. In the assembly means in the midst of the assembly. Regarding superhuman states, here, human states are the ten wholesome courses of action. He is unable to deny them. Why? Out of fear of reproach. For in Vesālī, many people have confidence in the Triple Gem and are followers of the Buddha, followers of the Dhamma, and followers of the Sangha. If he were to say, "The ascetic Gotama does not even possess the ten wholesome courses of action," they would say, "Where did you see the Blessed One killing a living being? Where did you see him taking what was not given?" and so on, adding, "Do you not know your own measure? What, because you have teeth, do you chew stones and gravel? Do you try to grasp a snake by its tail? Do you wish to play with a garland of flowers in the teeth of a saw? We will knock the teeth out of your mouth!" Out of fear of their reproach, he is unable to speak thus.

Vesālinagaravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The description of the city of Vesālī is finished.

Uttarimanussadhammādivaṇṇanā

The Explanation of Superhuman States, etc.

Tato uttariṃ pana visesādhigamaṃ paṭisedhento uttari manussadhammā alamariyañāṇadassanavisesoti āha.

Furthermore, denying any superior attainment beyond that, he spoke of a 'superhuman state, a special knowledge and vision suitable for the noble ones'.

Tattha alamariyaṃ ñātunti alamariyo, ariyabhāvāya samatthoti vuttaṃ hoti. Ñāṇadassanameva ñāṇadassanaviseso. Alamariyo ca so ñāṇadassanaviseso cāti alamariyañāṇadassanaviseso. Ñāṇadassananti dibbacakkhupi vipassanāpi maggopi phalampi paccavekkhaṇañāṇampi [P 2.0022] sabbaññutaññāṇampi vuccati. “Appamatto samāno ñāṇadassanaṃ ārādhetī”ti (ma. ni. 1.311) hi ettha dibbacakkhu ñāṇadassanaṃ nāma. “Ñāṇadassanāya [V 1.0335] cittaṃ abhinīharati [M 1.0328] abhininnāmetī”ti (dī. ni. 1.235) ettha vipassanāñāṇaṃ. “Abhabbā te ñāṇadassanāya anuttarāya sambodhāyā”ti (a. ni. 4.196) ettha maggo. “Ayamañño uttari manussadhammā alamariyañāṇadassanaviseso adhigato phāsu vihāro”ti (ma. ni. 1.328) ettha phalaṃ. “Ñāṇañca pana me dassanaṃ udapādi, akuppā me cetovimutti, ayamantimā jāti, natthi dāni punabbhavo”ti (mahāva. 16) ettha paccavekkhaṇañāṇaṃ. “Ñāṇañca pana me dassanaṃ udapādi sattāhakālaṅkato āḷāro kāḷāmo”ti (ma. ni. 2.340) ettha sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ. Idha pana lokuttaramaggo adhippeto. Tañhi so bhagavato paṭisedheti.

Therein, 'alamariya' means suitable for the state of being noble. A special knowledge and vision is simply knowledge and vision. That which is 'alamariya' and that special knowledge and vision together form 'alamariyañāṇadassanaviseso' (a special knowledge and vision suitable for the noble ones). 'Knowledge and vision' (ñāṇadassana) can refer to the divine eye, insight, the path, fruition, reviewing knowledge, and omniscient knowledge. For instance, in the passage, "Being diligent, one attains knowledge and vision" (MN 1.311), 'knowledge and vision' refers to the divine eye. In, "He directs and inclines his mind toward knowledge and vision" (DN 1.235), it refers to insight knowledge. In, "They are incapable of that knowledge and vision, of the unsurpassed supreme awakening" (AN 4.196), it refers to the path. In, "This other superhuman state, a special knowledge and vision suitable for the noble ones, has been attained, a pleasant abiding" (MN 1.328), it refers to fruition. In, "Knowledge and vision arose in me: 'Unshakable is my liberation of mind, this is my last birth, now there is no more renewed existence'" (Mahāva. 16), it refers to reviewing knowledge. In, "Knowledge and vision arose in me: 'Āḷāra Kālāma passed away seven days ago'" (MN 2.340), it refers to omniscient knowledge. Here, however, the supramundane path is intended, for it is that which he denies of the Blessed One.

Takkapariyāhatanti iminā ācariyaṃ paṭibāhati. Evaṃ kirassa ahosi – samaṇena gotamena ācariye upasaṅkamitvā sukhumaṃ dhammantaraṃ gahitaṃ nāma natthi, takkapariyāhataṃ pana takketvā evaṃ bhavissati evaṃ bhavissatīti takkapariyāhataṃ dhammaṃ desetīti. Vīmaṃsānucaritanti iminā cassa lokiyapaññaṃ anujānāti. Samaṇo gotamo paññavā, so taṃ paññāsaṅkhātaṃ indavajirūpamaṃ vīmaṃsaṃ evaṃ vaṭṭissati, evaṃ vaṭṭissatīti ito cito ca anucarāpetvā vīmaṃsāya anucaritaṃ dhammaṃ deseti. Sayaṃpaṭibhānanti imināssa dhammesu paccakkhabhāvaṃ paṭibāhati. Evaṃ hissa ahosi – samaṇassa gotamassa sukhumaṃ dhammantaraṃ vipassanā vā maggo vā phalaṃ vā paccavekkhaṇā vā natthi, ayaṃ pana laddhapariso, rājānaṃ cakkavattiṃ viya naṃ cattāro vaṇṇā parivārenti, suphusitaṃ panassa dantāvaraṇaṃ, mudukā jivhā, madhuro saro, anelagaḷā vācā, so yaṃ yadevassa upaṭṭhāti, taṃ taṃ gahetvā sayaṃpaṭibhānaṃ kathento mahājanaṃ rañjetīti.

By 'hammered out by reasoning,' he denies that the teaching came from a teacher. For this is what he thought: "The ascetic Gotama has not grasped any subtle, distinct Dhamma by approaching a teacher. Rather, having reasoned it out, he teaches a Dhamma that is hammered out by reasoning, thinking, 'It will be thus, it will be thus.'" By 'following investigation,' he concedes the Buddha's worldly wisdom. He thought: "The ascetic Gotama is wise; he directs that investigation—which is like Indra's thunderbolt and is called wisdom—this way and that, thinking 'it will turn out thus, it will turn out thus,' and so teaches a Dhamma that follows investigation." By 'of his own invention,' he denies the Buddha's direct experience of the Dhammas. For this is what he thought: "The ascetic Gotama has no subtle, distinct Dhamma—no insight, path, fruition, or reviewing. But he has gained a following; the four castes surround him as they would a wheel-turning monarch. His lips are well-formed, his tongue is soft, his voice is sweet, and his speech is fluent. Whatever occurs to him, he takes it up and, speaking from his own invention, delights the great assembly."

Yassa ca khvāssa atthāya dhammo desitoti yassa ca kho atthāya assa dhammo desito. Seyyathidaṃ, rāgapaṭighātatthāya asubhakammaṭṭhānaṃ, dosappaṭighātatthāya mettābhāvanā, mohapaṭighātatthāya pañca dhammā, vitakkūpacchedāya [P 2.0023] ānāpānassati.

The phrase 'And for the sake of which this Dhamma was taught' means for the purpose for which this Dhamma was taught. Namely: the meditation on foulness is for the sake of overcoming lust; the development of loving-kindness is for the sake of overcoming hatred; the five qualities are for the sake of overcoming delusion; mindfulness of breathing is for the sake of cutting off discursive thoughts.

So niyyāti takkarassa sammā dukkhakkhayāyāti so dhammo yo taṃ yathādesitaṃ karoti, tassa takkarassa sammā hetunā nayena kāraṇena vaṭṭadukkhakkhayāya niyyāti gacchati tamatthaṃ sādhetīti [V 1.0336] dīpeti[M 1.0329]. Idaṃ panesa na attano ajjhāsayena vadati. Buddhānañhi dhammo aniyyānikoti evamevaṃ pavedeyya, na pana sakkoti vattuṃ. Kasmā? Upārambhabhayā. Vesāliyañhi bahū sotāpanna-sakadāgāmi-anāgāmiupāsakā. Te evaṃ vadeyyuṃ “sunakkhatta tvaṃ bhagavatā desitadhammo aniyyānikoti vadasi, yadi ayaṃ dhammo aniyyāniko, imasmiṃ nagare ime kasmā ettakā sotāpannā jātā, ettakā sakadāgāmī, ettakā anāgāmīti pubbe vuttanayena upārambhaṃ kareyyu”nti. So iminā upārambhabhayena aniyyānikoti vattuṃ asakkonto ajjunena vissaṭṭhakaṇḍaṃ viya assa dhammo amogho niyyāti, abbhantare panassa kiñci natthīti vadati.

The phrase 'it leads to the complete cessation of suffering for one who practices it' means that the Dhamma, for one who practices it as taught, leads that practitioner, by the right cause, method, and reason, to the cessation of the suffering of the cycle of existence; it accomplishes that goal—this is what is explained. However, he does not speak this out of his own inclination. For he would have declared, 'The Dhamma of the Buddhas is not liberating,' but he is unable to say so. Why? Out of fear of reproach. In Vesālī, there were many lay followers who were stream-enterers, once-returners, and non-returners. They might say: 'Sunakkhatta, you claim that the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One is not liberating. If this Dhamma were not liberating, how is it that so many stream-enterers, so many once-returners, and so many non-returners have arisen in this city?' Thus, they would reproach him in the manner previously stated. Fearing this reproach, he is unable to declare that it is not liberating. Instead, like an arrow released by Arjuna, he says that the Dhamma is not in vain, it leads forth, but within it, there is nothing.

Assosi khoti vesāliyaṃ brāhmaṇakulaseṭṭhikulādīsu tattha tattha parisamajjhe evaṃ bhāsamānassa taṃ vacanaṃ suṇi, na pana paṭisedhesi. Kasmā? Kāruññatāya. Evaṃ kirassa ahosi ayaṃ kuddho jhāyamānaṃ veḷuvanaṃ viya pakkhittaloṇaṃ uddhanaṃ viya ca kodhavasena paṭapaṭāyati, mayā paṭibāhito pana mayipi āghātaṃ bandhissati, evamassa tathāgate ca mayi cāti dvīsu janesu āghāto atibhāriyo bhavissatīti kāruññatāya na paṭisedhesi. Api cassa evaṃ ahosi, buddhānaṃ avaṇṇakathanaṃ nāma puṇṇacande dosāropanasadisaṃ, ko imassa kathaṃ gaṇhissati? Sayameva kheḷe pacchinne mukhe sukkhe oramissatīti iminā kāraṇena na paṭisedhesi. Piṇḍapātapaṭikkantoti piṇḍapātapariyesanato apagato.

He heard that speech of his as he was speaking thus in Vesālī, in the midst of gatherings here and there among brahmin families, wealthy families, and the like, but he did not refute it. Why? Out of compassion. For it occurred to him thus: 'This angry man crackles with rage like a burning bamboo grove and like a fireplace into which salt has been thrown. If rebuked by me, he would harbor resentment towards me as well. Thus, his resentment towards two people, the Tathāgata and me, would become extremely heavy.' Out of compassion, he did not refute him. Furthermore, it occurred to him thus: 'Speaking ill of the Buddhas is like casting blame on the full moon; who will take his word? He himself will fall silent when the spittle in his mouth has run out and his mouth is dry.' For this reason, he did not refute him. 'Having returned from the alms-round' means having departed from the seeking of alms.

147. Kodhanoti caṇḍo pharuso. Moghapurisoti tucchapuriso. Yassa hi tasmiṃ attabhāve maggaphalānaṃ upanissayo natthi, taṃ buddhā “moghapuriso”ti vadanti. Upanissaye satipi tasmiṃ khaṇe magge vā phale vā asati “moghapuriso”ti vadantiyeva. Imassa pana tasmiṃ attabhāve maggaphalānaṃ [P 2.0024] upanissayo samucchinnoyeva, tena taṃ “moghapuriso”ti āha. Kodhā ca panassa esā vācā bhāsitāti esā ca panassa vācā kodhena bhāsitā.

147. 'Kodhano' means fierce and harsh. 'Moghapuriso' means an empty man. Indeed, the Buddhas call one in whom there is no supporting condition for the path and its fruits in that very existence an 'empty man.' Even when there is a supporting condition, if the path or fruit is absent at that moment, they still call him an 'empty man.' But for this one, the supporting condition for the path and its fruits in that very existence is completely cut off; therefore, he was called an 'empty man.' The phrase 'Moreover, this speech of his was spoken out of anger' means that this speech of his was indeed spoken in anger.

Kasmā [M 1.0330] panesa bhagavato kuddhoti? Ayañhi pubbe bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamitvā dibbacakkhuparikammaṃ pucchi. Athassa bhagavā kathesi. So dibbacakkhuṃ nibbattetvā ālokaṃ vaḍḍhetvā devaloke olokento nandanavanacittalatāvanaphārusakavanamissakavanesu dibbasampattiṃ anubhavamāne [V 1.0337] devaputte ca devadhītaro ca disvā etesaṃ evarūpāya attabhāvasampattiyā ṭhitānaṃ kīvamadhuro nu kho saddo bhavissatīti saddaṃ sotukāmo hutvā dasabalaṃ upasaṅkamitvā dibbasotadhātuparikammaṃ pucchi. Bhagavā panassa dibbasotadhātuyā upanissayo natthīti ñatvā parikammaṃ na kathesi. Na hi buddhā upanissayavirahita tassa parikammaṃ kathenti. So bhagavati āghātaṃ bandhitvā cintesi “ahaṃ samaṇaṃ gotamaṃ paṭhamaṃ dibbacakkhuparikammaṃ pucchiṃ, so ‘mayhaṃ taṃ sampajjatu vā mā vā sampajjatū’ti kathesi. Ahaṃ pana paccattapurisakārena taṃ nibbattetvā dibbasotadhātuparikammaṃ pucchiṃ, taṃ me na kathesi. Addhāssa evaṃ hoti ‘ayaṃ rājapabbajito dibbacakkhuñāṇaṃ nibbattetvā dibbasotadhātuñāṇaṃ nibbattetvā cetopariyañāṇaṃ nibbattetvā āsavānaṃ khayañāṇaṃ nibbattetvā mayā samasamo bhavissatī’ti issāmacchariyavasena mayhaṃ na kathetī”ti. Bhiyyoso āghātaṃ bandhitvā kāsāyāni chaḍḍetvā gihibhāvaṃ patvāpi na tuṇhībhūto vicarati. Dasabalaṃ pana asatā tucchena abbhācikkhanto vicarati. Tenāha bhagavā “kodhā ca panassa esā vācā bhāsitā”ti.

But why is this one angry with the Blessed One? Previously, he approached the Blessed One and asked about the preliminary practice for the divine eye. Then the Blessed One taught it to him. Having developed the divine eye and increased his vision, while gazing upon the celestial realm, he saw gods and goddesses enjoying divine pleasures in the Nandana Grove, the Cittalatā Grove, the Phārusaka Grove, and the Missaka Grove. Wishing to hear how sweet the sound of those beings established in such a state of existence would be, he approached the Ten-Powered One and asked about the preliminary practice for the divine ear element. But the Blessed One, knowing that he lacked the supporting condition for the divine ear element, did not teach him the preliminary practice. For the Buddhas do not teach the preliminary practice to one who lacks the supporting condition. Harboring a grudge against the Blessed One, he thought: 'First, I asked the ascetic Gotama about the preliminary practice for the divine eye, and he taught it to me without concern for whether it would succeed for me or not. But when I, through my own personal effort, developed it and then asked about the preliminary practice for the divine ear element, he did not teach it to me. Surely, he must think: "This one, who has gone forth from kingship, will develop the knowledge of the divine eye, then the knowledge of the divine ear element, then the knowledge of penetrating minds, and finally the knowledge of the destruction of the taints—and thus become my equal." Out of envy and stinginess, he does not teach me.' Harboring even more resentment, he discarded his saffron robes and returned to the household life, yet he did not remain silent. Instead, he went about falsely accusing the Ten-Powered One with what is untrue and empty. Therefore, the Blessed One said, 'And this speech of his was spoken out of anger.'

Vaṇṇo heso, sāriputtāti, sāriputta, tathāgatena satasahassakappādhikāni cattāri asaṅkhyeyyāni pāramiyo pūrentena etadatthameva vāyāmo kato “desanādhammo me niyyāniko bhavissatī”ti. Tasmā yo evaṃ vadeyya, so vaṇṇaṃyeva tathāgatassa bhāsati. Vaṇṇo heso, sāriputta, tathāgatassa guṇo eso tathāgatassa, na aguṇoti dasseti.

'This is indeed praise, Sāriputta.' Sāriputta, the Tathāgata, while fulfilling the perfections for four incalculable periods and a hundred thousand aeons, made this very effort for this purpose: 'May the Dhamma I teach be one that leads out.' Therefore, whoever speaks thus speaks only in praise of the Tathāgata. This shows that this is indeed praise, Sāriputta, a quality of the Tathāgata, not a demerit.

Ayampi [P 2.0025] hi nāma sāriputtātiādinā kiṃ dasseti? Sunakkhattena paṭisiddhassa uttarimanussadhammassa attani atthitaṃ dasseti. Bhagavā kira ayaṃ, sāriputta, sunakkhatto moghapuriso natthi tathāgatassa uttarimanussadhammoti vadati. Mayhañca sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ nāma atthi, iddhividhañāṇaṃ nāma atthi, dibbasotadhātuñāṇaṃ nāma atthi, cetopariyañāṇaṃ nāma atthi, dasabalañāṇaṃ [M 1.0331] nāma atthi, catuvesārajjañāṇaṃ nāma atthi, aṭṭhasu parisāsu akampanañāṇaṃ nāma atthi, catuyoniparicchedakañāṇaṃ nāma atthi, pañcagatiparicchedakañāṇaṃ nāma atthi, sabbepi cete uttarimanussadhammāyeva. Evarūpesu uttarimanussadhammesu ekassāpi vijānanasamatthaṃ dhammanvayamattampi nāma etassa moghapurisassa na bhavissatīti etamatthaṃ dassetuṃ ayampi hi nāma sāriputtātiādinā nayena imaṃ desanaṃ ārabhi. Tattha anvetīti anvayo, jānāti[V 1.0338], anubujjhatīti attho. Dhammassa anvayo dhammanvayo, taṃ taṃ sabbaññutaññāṇādidhammaṃ jānanapaññāyetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. “Itipi so bhagavā”tiādīhi evarūpampi nāma mayhaṃ sabbaññutaññāṇasaṅkhātaṃ uttarimanussadhammaṃ vijjamānameva atthīti jānituṃ tassa moghapurisassa dhammanvayopi na bhavissatīti dasseti. Iddhividhañāṇādīsupi evaṃ yojanā veditabbā.

What does the Blessed One indicate by the phrase 'This too, Sāriputta, indeed' and so forth? He shows the existence within Himself of the superhuman qualities that Sunakkhatta has denied. For the Blessed One thought: 'Sāriputta, this foolish man Sunakkhatta says, “The Tathāgata has no superhuman qualities.” But I do possess the knowledge of omniscience, the knowledge of psychic powers, the knowledge of the divine ear element, the knowledge of penetrating minds, the knowledge of the ten powers, the knowledge of the four kinds of intrepidity, the knowledge of unshakability in the eight assemblies, the knowledge of discerning the four kinds of birth, and the knowledge of discerning the five destinies—all these are indeed superhuman qualities. For this foolish man, there will not be even a mere consequential understanding of the Dhamma capable of knowing even one of these superhuman qualities.' To convey this meaning, the Blessed One began this teaching with the method beginning, 'This too, Sāriputta, indeed'. Herein, 'anvayo' (consequence) is from 'anveti' (it follows); the meaning is 'it knows', 'it understands'. The consequence of the Dhamma is 'dhammanvayo'; this is a designation for the wisdom that knows that particular Dhamma, such as the knowledge of omniscience. By phrases such as 'Thus indeed is the Blessed One', He shows that for that foolish man, not even a consequential understanding of the Dhamma will arise to know that such a superhuman quality, called the knowledge of omniscience, actually exists in me. The application should be understood in the same way for the knowledge of psychic powers and the rest.

Uttarimanussadhammādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of superhuman qualities and so forth is concluded.

Dasabalañāṇādivaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Knowledge of the Ten Powers and So Forth

148. Ettha ca kiñcāpi cetopariyañāṇānantaraṃ tisso vijjā vattabbā siyuṃ, yasmā pana tāsu vuttāsu upari dasabalañāṇaṃ na paripūrati, tasmā tā avatvā tathāgatassa dasabalañāṇaṃ paripūraṃ katvā dassento dasa kho panimāni sāriputtātiādimāha. Tattha tathāgatabalānīti aññehi asādhāraṇāni tathāgatasseva balāni. Yathā vā pubbabuddhānaṃ balāni puññussayasampattiyā āgatāni, tathā āgatabalānītipi attho. Tattha duvidhaṃ tathāgatabalaṃ kāyabalañca ñāṇabalañca. Tesu kāyabalaṃ hatthikulānusārena veditabbaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ porāṇehi –

148. Here, although the three knowledges might have been stated immediately after the knowledge of penetrating minds, because if they were stated, the knowledge of the ten powers further on would not be complete, therefore, without stating them, the Blessed One, showing the Tathāgata’s knowledge of the ten powers as complete, said, 'Sāriputta, there are these ten...' and so on. Herein, 'the powers of the Tathāgata' are the Tathāgata's own powers, not shared by others. Or, the meaning is 'powers that have come in such a way', just as the powers of former Buddhas came about through the accomplishment of an abundance of merit. Therein, the Tathāgata's power is twofold: bodily power and the power of knowledge. Of these, bodily power should be understood in accordance with the elephant clans. For this was said by the ancients:

“Kālāvakañca gaṅgeyyaṃ, paṇḍaraṃ tambapiṅgalaṃ;

Gandhamaṅgalahemañca, uposathachaddantime dasā”ti.

“Kālāvaka and Gaṅgeyya, Paṇḍara, Tamba, Piṅgala; Gandha, Maṅgala, and Hema, Uposatha, Chaddanta—these are the ten.”

Imāni [P 2.0026] hi dasa hatthikulāni. Tattha kālāvakanti pakatihatthikulaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Yaṃ dasannaṃ purisānaṃ kāyabalaṃ, taṃ ekassa kālāvakahatthino. Yaṃ dasannaṃ kālāvakānaṃ balaṃ, taṃ ekassa gaṅgeyyassa. Yaṃ dasannaṃ gaṅgeyyānaṃ, taṃ ekassa paṇḍarassa. Yaṃ dasannaṃ paṇḍarānaṃ, taṃ ekassa tambassa. Yaṃ dasannaṃ tambānaṃ, taṃ ekassa piṅgalassa. Yaṃ dasannaṃ piṅgalānaṃ, taṃ ekassa gandhahatthino. Yaṃ dasannaṃ gandhahatthīnaṃ, taṃ ekassa maṅgalassa. Yaṃ dasannaṃ maṅgalānaṃ, taṃ ekassa hemavatassa. Yaṃ dasannaṃ hemavatānaṃ, taṃ ekassa uposathassa. Yaṃ [M 1.0332] dasannaṃ uposathānaṃ, taṃ ekassa chaddantassa. Yaṃ dasannaṃ chaddantānaṃ taṃ ekassa tathāgatassa. Nārāyanasaṅghātabalantipi idameva vuccati[V 1.0339]. Tadetaṃ pakatihatthigaṇanāya hatthīnaṃ koṭisahassānaṃ purisagaṇanāya dasannaṃ purisakoṭisahassānaṃ balaṃ hoti. Idaṃ tāva tathāgatassa kāyabalaṃ.

Indeed, these are the ten elephant clans. Among them, the Kālāvaka should be seen as the ordinary elephant clan. The bodily strength of ten men is that of one Kālāvaka elephant. The strength of ten Kālāvaka elephants is that of one Gaṅgeyya. The strength of ten Gaṅgeyyas is that of one Paṇḍara. The strength of ten Paṇḍaras is that of one Tamba. The strength of ten Tambas is that of one Piṅgala. The strength of ten Piṅgalas is that of one Gandha elephant. The strength of ten Gandha elephants is that of one Maṅgala. The strength of ten Maṅgalas is that of one Hemavata. The strength of ten Hemavatas is that of one Uposatha. The strength of ten Uposathas is that of one Chaddanta. The strength of ten Chaddantas is that of one Tathāgata. This is also called the strength of Nārāyaṇa’s combined power. By the reckoning of ordinary elephants, this is the strength of a thousand koṭis of elephants; by the reckoning of men, it is the strength of ten thousand koṭis of men. This, then, is the Tathāgata's bodily strength.

Ñāṇabalaṃ pana pāḷiyaṃ tāva āgatameva. Dasabalañāṇaṃ, catuvesārajjañāṇaṃ, aṭṭhasu parisāsu akampanañāṇaṃ, catuyoniparicchedakañāṇaṃ, pañcagatiparicchedakañāṇaṃ. Saṃyuttake (saṃ. ni. 2.34) āgatāni tesattati ñāṇāni sattasattati ñāṇānīti evaṃ aññānipi anekāni ñāṇasahassāni, etaṃ ñāṇabalaṃ nāma. Idhāpi ñāṇabalameva adhippetaṃ. Ñāṇañhi akampiyaṭṭhena upatthambhanaṭṭhena ca balanti vuttaṃ.

As for the power of knowledge, it is indeed found in the Pāḷi text. The knowledge of the ten powers, the knowledge of the four kinds of intrepidity, the knowledge of unshakeability in the eight assemblies, the knowledge that discerns the four kinds of generation, the knowledge that discerns the five destinations. In the Saṃyutta Nikāya (SN 12.34) are mentioned the seventy-three kinds of knowledge and the seventy-seven kinds of knowledge, and thus many other thousands of knowledges—this is called the power of knowledge. Here too, it is the power of knowledge that is intended. For knowledge is called 'power' because of its quality of being unshakeable and its quality of supporting.

Yehi balehi samannāgatoti yehi dasahi ñāṇabalehi upeto samupeto. Āsabhaṃ ṭhānanti seṭṭhaṭṭhānaṃ uttamaṭṭhānaṃ. Āsabhā vā pubbabuddhā, tesaṃ ṭhānanti attho. Apica gavasatajeṭṭhako usabho, gavasahassajeṭṭhako vasabho. Vajasatajeṭṭhako vā usabho, vajasahassajeṭṭhako vasabho. Sabbagavaseṭṭho sabbaparissayasaho seto pāsādiko mahābhāravaho asanisatasaddehipi akampaniyo nisabho, so idha usabhoti adhippeto. Idampi hi tassa pariyāyavacanaṃ. Usabhassa idanti āsabhaṃ. Ṭhānanti catūhi pādehi pathaviṃ uppīḷetvā acalaṭṭhānaṃ. Idaṃ pana āsabhaṃ viyāti āsabhaṃ. Yatheva hi nisabhasaṅkhāto usabho usabhabalena samannāgato catūhi pādehi pathaviṃ uppīḷetvā [P 2.0027] acalaṭṭhānena tiṭṭhati, evaṃ tathāgatopi dasahi tathāgatabalehi samannāgato catūhi vesārajjapādehi aṭṭhaparisapathaviṃ uppīḷetvā sadevake loke kenaci paccatthikena paccāmittena akampiyo acalaṭṭhānena tiṭṭhati. Evaṃ tiṭṭhamānova taṃ āsabhaṃ ṭhānaṃ paṭijānāti, upagacchati na paccakkhāti attani āropeti. Tena vuttaṃ “āsabhaṃ ṭhānaṃ paṭijānātī”ti.

Endowed with those powers—that is, equipped and fully endowed with the ten powers of knowledge. The foremost place—the supreme place, the excellent place. Or, the former Buddhas are bulls; their place—this is the meaning. Furthermore, among a hundred cattle, the eldest is an ox (usabha); among a thousand cattle, the eldest is a bull (vasabha). Or, among a hundred in a pen, the eldest is an ox (usabha); among a thousand in a pen, the eldest is a bull (vasabha). The chief of all cattle, tolerant of all adversity, white, inspiring confidence, bearing great burdens, unmoved even by the sound of a hundred thunderbolts—that incomparable bull (nisabha) is what is intended here by 'usabha'. This too is a synonym for it. 'Āsabhaṃ' means 'belonging to the bull'. The 'stance' (ṭhānaṃ) is an unshakeable position, pressing the earth with four feet. Or, it is 'āsabhaṃ' because it is like a bull. Just as a bull called nisabha, endowed with a bull's strength, stands unshaken, pressing the earth with four feet, so too the Tathāgata, endowed with the ten powers of a Tathāgata, stands unshaken, pressing the earth of the eightfold assembly with the four feet of confidence, unmoved by any adversary or enemy in the world with its gods. Standing thus, he acknowledges that foremost place, approaches it, does not reject it, and attributes it to himself. Therefore, it is said: “He acknowledges the foremost place.”

Parisāsūti aṭṭhasu parisāsu. Sīhanādaṃ nadatīti seṭṭhanādaṃ abhītanādaṃ nadati, sīhanādasadisaṃ vā nādaṃ nadati. Ayamattho sīhanādasuttena [M 1.0333] dīpetabbo. Yathā vā sīho sahanato hananato ca sīhoti vuccati, evaṃ tathāgato lokadhammānaṃ sahanato parappavādānañca hananato sīhoti vuccati. Evaṃ vuttassa sīhassa nādaṃ sīhanādaṃ. Tattha yathā sīho sīhabalena samannāgato sabbattha visārado vigatalomahaṃso sīhanādaṃ nadati, evaṃ tathāgatasīhopi tathāgatabalehi samannāgato aṭṭhasu [V 1.0340] parisāsu visārado vigatalomahaṃso iti rūpantiādinā nayena nānāvidhadesanāvilāsasampannaṃ sīhanādaṃ nadati. Tena vuttaṃ “parisāsu sīhanādaṃ nadatī”ti. Brahmacakkaṃ pavattetīti ettha brahmanti seṭṭhaṃ uttamaṃ visiṭṭhaṃ. Cakka-saddo panāyaṃ –

‘In the assemblies’ means in the eight assemblies. ‘Roaring the lion's roar’ means he roars the supreme roar, the fearless roar, or a roar comparable to a lion's roar. This meaning should be elucidated by the Sīhanāda Sutta. Just as a lion is called a 'sīha' because it endures (sahanato) and strikes down (hananato), so too the Tathāgata is called a 'sīha' because he endures worldly phenomena and strikes down the doctrines of others. The roar of such a lion is called the 'lion's roar.' Here, just as a lion, endowed with a lion's strength, roars the lion's roar everywhere with confidence and with hair not bristling, so too the lion that is the Tathāgata, endowed with the powers of a Tathāgata, roars in the eight assemblies with confidence and with hair not bristling the lion's roar that is possessed of the elegance of various teachings, in the manner of “This is form,” and so on. Thus it is said, “He roars the lion's roar in the assemblies.” ‘Sets rolling the Brahma-wheel’: Here, 'Brahma' means supreme, excellent, distinguished. The word 'cakka' (wheel), however—

Sampattiyaṃ lakkhaṇe ca, rathaṅge iriyāpathe;

Dāne ratanadhammūra-cakkādīsu ca dissati;

Dhammacakke idha mato, tañca dvedhā vibhāvaye.

In prosperity and in characteristics, in a chariot-wheel and in deportment; in giving, in the jewel-wheel, the Dhamma-wheel, the breast-wheel, and so on, it is seen; here, the Dhamma-wheel is intended, and that should be analyzed in two ways.

“Cattārimāni, bhikkhave, cakkāni, yehi samannāgatānaṃ devamanussāna”ntiādīsu (a. ni. 4.31) hi ayaṃ sampattiyaṃ dissati. “Pādatalesu cakkāni jātānī”ti (dī. ni. 2.35) ettha lakkhaṇe. “Cakkaṃva vahato pada”nti (dha. pa. 1) ettha rathaṅge. “Catucakkaṃ navadvāra”nti (saṃ. ni. 1.29) ettha iriyāpathe. “Dadaṃ bhuñja mā ca pamādo, cakkaṃ pavattaya sabbapāṇina”nti (jā. 1.7.149) ettha dāne. “Dibbaṃ cakkaratanaṃ pāturahosī”ti (dī. ni. 2.243) ettha ratanacakke. “Mayā pavattitaṃ cakka”nti (su. ni. 562) ettha dhammacakke. “Icchāhatassa posassa, cakkaṃ bhamati matthake”ti (jā. 1.1.104; 1.5.103) ettha uracakke. “Khurapariyantena cepi cakkenā”ti (dī. ni. 1.166) ettha [P 2.0028] paharaṇacakke. “Asanivicakka”nti (dī. ni. 3.61; saṃ. ni. 2.162) ettha asanimaṇḍale. Idha panāyaṃ dhammacakke adhippeto.

Indeed, in passages like “Monks, these four wheels, by which gods and humans are endowed” (AN 4.31), this word is seen in the sense of accomplishment. In “Wheels are born on the soles of the feet” (DN 14.1.35), it is in the sense of a characteristic mark. In “Like the wheel following the foot of the ox” (Dhp 1), it is in the sense of a chariot-wheel. In “Four-wheeled, nine-gated” (SN 1.29), it is in the sense of deportment. In “Give, enjoy, and do not be heedless; turn the wheel for all beings” (Ja 424), it is in the sense of giving. In “The divine jewel-wheel appeared” (DN 26.6), it is in the sense of the jewel-wheel. In “The wheel set in motion by me” (Snp 3.11), it is in the sense of the Dhamma-wheel. In “For a man consumed by desire, the wheel turns on his head” (Ja 75), it is in the sense of the breast-wheel. In “Even if with a wheel rimmed with razors” (DN 1.2.27), it is in the sense of a weapon-wheel. In “Thunderbolt-wheel” (DN 27.15; SN 2.21), it is in the sense of a thunderbolt-circle. Here, however, the Dhamma-wheel is intended.

Taṃ pana dhammacakkaṃ duvidhaṃ hoti paṭivedhañāṇañceva desanāñāṇañca. Tattha paññāpabhāvitaṃ attano ariyabalāvahaṃ paṭivedhañāṇaṃ. Karuṇāpabhāvitaṃ sāvakānaṃ ariyabalāvahaṃ desanāñāṇaṃ. Tattha paṭivedhañāṇaṃ uppajjamānaṃ uppannanti duvidhaṃ. Tañhi abhinikkhamanato yāva arahattamaggā uppajjamānaṃ, phalakkhaṇe uppannaṃ nāma. Tusitabhavanato vā yāva mahābodhipallaṅke [M 1.0334] arahattamaggā uppajjamānaṃ, phalakkhaṇe uppannaṃ nāma. Dīpaṅkaradasabalato paṭṭhāya vā yāva arahattamaggā uppajjamānaṃ, phalakkhaṇe uppannaṃ nāma. Desanāñāṇampi pavattamānaṃ pavattanti duvidhaṃ. Tañhi yāva aññātakoṇḍaññassa sotāpattimaggā pavattamānaṃ, phalakkhaṇe pavattaṃ nāma. Tesu paṭivedhañāṇaṃ [V 1.0341] lokuttaraṃ, desanāñāṇaṃ lokiyaṃ. Ubhayampi panetaṃ aññehi asādhāraṇaṃ, buddhānaṃyeva orasañāṇaṃ.

That Dhamma-wheel is twofold: the knowledge of penetration and the knowledge of teaching. Here, the knowledge of penetration, developed by wisdom, brings the noble power to oneself. The knowledge of teaching, developed by compassion, brings the noble power to disciples. Herein, the knowledge of penetration is twofold: that which is arising and that which has arisen. For it is called 'arising' from the time of the great renunciation up to the Arahant path, and at the moment of fruition, it is called 'arisen.' Or it is called 'arising' from the Tusita realm up to the Arahant path at the great Bodhi-seat, and at the moment of fruition, it is called 'arisen.' Or starting from the time of Dīpaṅkara, the Ten-Powered One, up to the Arahant path, it is called 'arising,' and at the moment of fruition, it is called 'arisen.' The knowledge of teaching is also twofold: that which is occurring and that which has occurred. For it is called 'occurring' up to the stream-entry path of Aññāta Koṇḍañña, and at the moment of that path's fruition, it is called 'occurred.' Among these, the knowledge of penetration is supramundane, while the knowledge of teaching is mundane. Yet both are unique to the Buddhas; they are the Buddhas' very own innate knowledge.

Idāni yehi balehi samannāgato tathāgato āsabhaṃ ṭhānaṃ paṭijānāti, yāni āditova “dasa kho panimāni, sāriputta, tathāgatassa tathāgatabalānī”ti nikkhittāni, tāni vitthārato dassetuṃ katamāni dasa? Idha, sāriputta, tathāgato ṭhānañca ṭhānatotiādimāha. Tattha ṭhānañca ṭhānatoti kāraṇañca kāraṇato. Kāraṇañhi yasmā tattha phalaṃ tiṭṭhati tadāyattavuttiyāya uppajjati ceva pavattati ca, tasmā ṭhānanti vuccati. Taṃ bhagavā “ye ye dhammā yesaṃ yesaṃ dhammānaṃ hetū paccayā uppādāya, taṃ taṃ ṭhānaṃ. Ye ye dhammā yesaṃ yesaṃ dhammānaṃ na hetū na paccayā uppādāya, taṃ taṃ aṭṭhāna”nti pajānanto ṭhānañca ṭhānato aṭṭhānañca aṭṭhānato yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti. Abhidhamme panetaṃ, “tattha katamaṃ tathāgatassa ṭhānañca ṭhānato aṭṭhānañca aṭṭhānato yathābhūtaṃ ñāṇa”ntiādinā (vibha. 809) nayena vitthāritameva. Yampīti yena ñāṇena. Idampi, sāriputta, tathāgatassāti idampi ṭhānāṭṭhānañāṇaṃ tathāgatassa tathāgatabalaṃ nāma hotīti attho. Evaṃ sabbapadesu yojanā veditabbā.

Now, with what powers endowed does the Tathāgata claim the foremost place? Those very powers which from the outset were declared as, “These, Sāriputta, are the ten powers of the Tathāgata.” To show them in detail, what are those ten? Here, Sāriputta, the Tathāgata says, “the possible as possible,” and so forth. Herein, “the possible as possible” (ṭhānañca ṭhānato) means “cause as cause” (kāraṇañca kāraṇato). For, because the result stands there, arising and continuing in dependence on it, it is therefore called a basis (ṭhāna). The Blessed One, knowing, “Those phenomena which are the cause and condition for the arising of certain phenomena, that is the basis. Those phenomena which are not the cause and condition for the arising of certain phenomena, that is the non-basis,” knows the possible as possible and the impossible as impossible as they truly are. In the Abhidhamma, this is elaborated in detail in the way beginning with: “Herein, what is the Tathāgata’s knowledge of the possible as possible and the impossible as impossible as it truly is?” (Vibhaṅga 809). The word `yampi` is explained as `yena ñāṇena` (by which knowledge). The phrase `idampi, sāriputta, tathāgatassa` means: this knowledge of the possible and impossible is called a power of the Tathāgata. This method of application should be understood in all passages.

Kammasamādānānanti [P 2.0029] samādiyitvā katānaṃ kusalākusalakammānaṃ, kammameva vā kammasamādānaṃ. Ṭhānaso hetusoti paccayato ceva hetuto ca. Tattha gatiupadhikālapayogā vipākassa ṭhānaṃ. Kammaṃ hetu. Imassa pana ñāṇassa vitthārakathā “atthekaccāni pāpakāni kammasamādānāni gatisampattipaṭibāḷhāni na vipaccantī”tiādinā (vibha. 810) nayena abhidhamme āgatāyeva.

“The undertaking of kamma” (kammasamādānānaṃ) means the wholesome and unwholesome kamma performed after undertaking them, or simply the kamma itself. “As to place and cause” (ṭhānaso hetuso) means as to condition and cause. Here, destination, substratum, time, and means are the place for the result. The kamma is the cause. The detailed explanation of this knowledge is already found in the Abhidhamma in the passage beginning, “There are some evil undertakings of kamma which, obstructing a good destination, do not ripen,” and so forth (Vibhaṅga 810).

Sabbatthagāmininti sabbagatigāminiṃ agatigāminiñca. Paṭipadanti maggaṃ. Yathābhūtaṃ pajānātīti bahūsupi manussesu ekameva pāṇaṃ ghātentesu imassa [M 1.0335] cetanā nirayagāminī bhavissati, imassa cetanā tiracchānayonigāminīti iminā nayena ekavatthusmimpi kusalākusalacetanāsaṅkhātānaṃ paṭipattīnaṃ aviparītato sabhāvaṃ jānāti. Imassa ca ñāṇassa vitthārakathā “tattha katamaṃ tathāgatassa sabbatthagāminiṃ paṭipadaṃ yathābhūtaṃ ñāṇaṃ? Idha tathāgato ayaṃ [V 1.0342] maggo ayaṃ paṭipadā nirayagāmīti pajānātī”tiādinā (vibha. 811) nayena abhidhamme āgatāyeva.

“The path leading to all destinations” (sabbatthagāminiṃ) means leading to all destinies and to a destiny-less state. “The path” (paṭipadanti) means the way. “He knows as it truly is” (yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti)—even when many people kill a single living being, he knows the nature of the various courses of conduct consisting of wholesome and unwholesome volitions related to even a single object, without error: “This person’s volition will lead to hell, this one’s to the animal realm,” and so forth. The detailed explanation of this knowledge is found in the Abhidhamma in the way beginning: “Herein, what is the Tathāgata’s knowledge of the path leading to all destinations as it truly is? Here, the Tathāgata understands, ‘This path, this course of conduct leads to hell,’” and so forth (Vibhaṅga 811).

Anekadhātunti cakkhudhātuādīhi kāmadhātuādīhi vā dhātūhi bahudhātuṃ. Nānādhātunti tāsaṃyeva dhātūnaṃ vilakkhaṇatāya nānappakāradhātuṃ. Lokanti khandhāyatanadhātulokaṃ. Yathābhūtaṃ pajānātīti tāsaṃ tāsaṃ dhātūnaṃ aviparītato sabhāvaṃ paṭivijjhati. Idampi ñāṇaṃ “tattha katamaṃ tathāgatassa anekadhātunānādhātulokaṃ yathābhūtaṃ ñāṇaṃ, idha tathāgato khandhanānattaṃ pajānātī”tiādinā nayena abhidhamme vitthāritameva.

“The world with its many elements” (anekadhātuṃ) means a world of many elements through elements such as the eye-element, etc., or the elements of the desire realm, etc. “With its diverse elements” (nānādhātuṃ) means a world of diverse kinds of elements due to the distinct characteristics of those very elements. “World” (lokaṃ) means the world of aggregates, sense bases, and elements. “He knows as it truly is” (yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti) means he penetrates the own-nature of those respective elements without perversion. This knowledge too is elaborated in the Abhidhamma in the way beginning: “Herein, what is the Tathāgata’s knowledge of the world with its many and diverse elements as it truly is? Here, the Tathāgata understands the diversity of the aggregates,” and so forth.

Nānādhimuttikatanti hīnādīhi adhimuttīhi nānādhimuttikabhāvaṃ. Idampi ñāṇaṃ, “tattha katamaṃ tathāgatassa sattānaṃ nānādhimuttikataṃ yathābhūtaṃ ñāṇaṃ, idha tathāgato pajānāti santi sattā hīnādhimuttikā”ti ādinā nayena abhidhamme vitthāritameva.

“The diversity of inclinations” (nānādhimuttikataṃ) means the state of having diverse inclinations, that is, inclinations that are inferior and so forth. This knowledge is elaborated in detail in the Abhidhamma in the way beginning: “Herein, what is the Tathāgata’s knowledge of the diversity of beings’ inclinations as it truly is? Here, the Tathāgata understands that there are beings with inferior inclinations,” and so forth.

Parasattānanti padhānasattānaṃ. Parapuggalānanti tato paresaṃ hīnasattānaṃ. Ekatthameva vā etaṃ [P 2.0030] padadvayaṃ. Veneyyavasena pana dvedhā vuttaṃ. Indriyaparopariyattanti saddhādīnaṃ indriyānaṃ parabhāvaṃ aparabhāvañca, vuddhiñca hāniñcāti attho. Imassapi ñāṇassa vitthārakathā – “tattha katamaṃ tathāgatassa parasattānaṃ parapuggalānaṃ indriyaparopariyattaṃ yathābhūtaṃ ñāṇaṃ, idha tathāgato sattānaṃ āsayaṃ pajānāti anusayaṃ pajānātī”tiādinā (vibha. 814) nayena abhidhamme āgatāyeva.

“Other beings” (parasattānaṃ) refers to beings who are energetic or striving. “Other individuals” (parapuggalānaṃ) refers to beings who are inferior to those. Alternatively, these two terms have just one meaning. But, they are stated in two ways according to those to be guided. “The superiority and inferiority of the faculties” (indriyaparopariyattaṃ) refers to the superiority and inferiority, growth and decline, of the faculties such as faith. The detailed explanation of this knowledge is found in the Abhidhamma in the way beginning: “Herein, what is the Tathāgata’s knowledge of the superiority and inferiority of the faculties of other beings and other individuals as it truly is? Here, the Tathāgata knows the inclinations of beings, knows the underlying tendencies,” and so forth (Vibhaṅga 814).

Jhānavimokkhasamādhisamāpattīnanti paṭhamādīnaṃ catunnaṃ jhānānaṃ rūpī rūpāni passatītiādīnaṃ aṭṭhannaṃ vimokkhānaṃ savitakkasavicārādīnaṃ tiṇṇaṃ samādhīnaṃ paṭhamajjhānasamāpattiādīnañca navannaṃ anupubbasamāpattīnaṃ. Saṃkilesanti hānabhāgiyadhammaṃ. Vodānanti visesabhāgiyadhammaṃ. Vuṭṭhānanti “vodānampi vuṭṭhānaṃ. Tamhā [M 1.0336] tamhā samādhimhā vuṭṭhānampi vuṭṭhāna”nti (vibha. 828) evaṃ vuttapaguṇajjhānañceva bhavaṅgaphalasamāpattiyo ca. Heṭṭhimaṃ heṭṭhimañhi paguṇajjhānaṃ uparimassa uparimassa padaṭṭhānaṃ hoti. Tasmā “vodānampi vuṭṭhāna”nti vuttaṃ. Bhavaṅgena pana sabbajjhānehi vuṭṭhānaṃ hoti. Phalasamāpattiyā nirodhasamāpattito [V 1.0343] vuṭṭhānaṃ hoti. Taṃ sandhāya “tamhā tamhā samādhimhā vuṭṭhānampi vuṭṭhāna”nti vuttaṃ. Idampi ñāṇaṃ “tattha katamaṃ tathāgatassa jhānavimokkhasamādhisamāpattīnaṃ saṃkilesaṃ vodānaṃ vuṭṭhānaṃ yathābhūtaṃ ñāṇaṃ, jhāyīti cattāro jhāyī, atthekacco jhāyī sampattiṃyeva samānaṃ vipattīti paccetī”tiādinā (vibha. 828) nayena abhidhamme vitthāritaṃ. Sattannaṃ ñāṇānaṃ vitthārakathāvinicchayo sammohavinodaniyaṃ vibhaṅgaṭṭhakathāyaṃ vutto. Pubbenivāsānussatidibbacakkhuñāṇakathā visuddhimagge vitthāritā. Āsavakkhayakathā bhayabherave.

“Of the absorptions, liberations, concentrations, and attainments” refers to the four absorptions beginning with the first, the eight liberations such as ‘one with form sees forms,’ the three concentrations such as that with applied and sustained thought, and the nine successive attainments beginning with the first absorption attainment. “Defilement” refers to qualities that lead to decline. “Purification” refers to qualities that lead to distinction. “Emergence” refers to proficient absorption, the life-continuum, and fruition attainments, which are spoken of thus: “Purification is also emergence. Emergence from this or that concentration is also emergence” (Vibhaṅga 828). For the lower proficient absorption serves as the foundation for the higher one; hence it is said, “Purification is also emergence.” Moreover, emergence from all absorptions occurs through the life-continuum, while emergence from the attainment of cessation occurs by means of the attainment of fruition. Referring to that, it is stated, “Emergence from this or that concentration is also emergence.” This knowledge is also elaborated in the Abhidhamma in the way beginning: “Herein, what is the Tathāgata’s knowledge of the defilement, purification, and emergence of the absorptions, liberations, concentrations, and attainments as it truly is? ‘A meditator’ means the four kinds of meditators; some meditator regards success itself as failure,” and so on (Vibhaṅga 828). The detailed analysis of the seven knowledges is stated in the Sammohavinodanī, the commentary to the Vibhaṅga. The explanation of the recollection of past lives and the divine eye is detailed in the Visuddhimagga. The explanation of the destruction of the taints is in the Bhayabherava Sutta.

149. Imāni kho sāriputtāti yāni pubbe “dasa kho panimāni, sāriputta, tathāgatassa tathāgatabalānī”ti avocaṃ, imāni tānīti appanaṃ karoti. Tattha [P 2.0031] paravādīkathā hoti – dasabalañāṇaṃ nāma pāṭiyekkaṃ natthi, sabbaññutaññāṇassevāyaṃ pabhedoti. Taṃ na tathā daṭṭhabbaṃ. Aññameva hi dasabalañāṇaṃ, aññaṃ sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ. Dasabalañāṇañhi sakasakakiccameva jānāti. Sabbaññutañāṇaṃ tampi tato avasesampi pajānāti. Dasabalañāṇesu hi paṭhamaṃ kāraṇākāraṇameva jānāti. Dutiyaṃ kammantaravipākantarameva. Tatiyaṃ kammaparicchedameva. Catutthaṃ dhātunānattakāraṇameva. Pañcamaṃ sattānaṃ ajjhāsayādhimuttimeva. Chaṭṭhaṃ indriyānaṃ tikkhamudubhāvameva. Sattamaṃ jhānādīhi saddhiṃ tesaṃ saṃkilesādimeva. Aṭṭhamaṃ pubbenivutthakhandhasantatimeva. Navamaṃ sattānaṃ cutipaṭisandhimeva. Dasamaṃ saccaparicchedameva. Sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ pana etehi jānitabbañca tato uttariñca pajānāti. Etesaṃ pana kiccaṃ na sabbaṃ karoti. Tañhi jhānaṃ hutvā appetuṃ na sakkoti, iddhi hutvā vikubbituṃ na sakkoti, maggo hutvā kilese khepetuṃ na sakkoti. Apica paravādī evaṃ pucchitabbo – “dasabalañāṇaṃ nāma etaṃ savitakkasavicāraṃ avitakkavicāramattaṃ avitakkaavicāraṃ kāmāvacaraṃ rūpāvacaraṃ arūpāvacaraṃ lokiyaṃ lokuttara”nti? Jānanto paṭipāṭiyā satta ñāṇāni savitakkasavicārānīti vakkhati. Tato parāni dve [M 1.0337] avitakkaavicārānīti vakkhati. Āsavakkhayañāṇaṃ siyā savitakkasavicāraṃ, siyā avitakkavicāramattaṃ, siyā avitakkaavicāranti vakkhati. Tathā paṭipāṭiyā satta kāmāvacarāni, tato parāni dve rūpāvacarāni, avasāne ekaṃ lokuttaranti vakkhati, sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ pana savitakkasavicārameva kāmāvacarameva lokiyamevāti vakkhati.

149. “These, Sāriputta,” signifies: “What I previously referred to as ‘these ten powers of the Tathāgata, Sāriputta,’ these are they,” thus he affirms. Here, a disputant might argue: “There is no separate knowledge called the ten powers; it is merely a division of omniscient knowledge.” But this should not be seen as so.
