For the knowledge of the ten powers is one thing, and omniscient knowledge is another. The knowledge of the ten powers knows only its own specific function, whereas omniscient knowledge knows both that and what remains beyond it. For, among the ten powers: the first knows only what is possible and impossible; the second, only the diversity of actions and their results; the third, only the delimitation of actions; the fourth, only the cause of the diversity of elements; the fifth, only the inclinations and dispositions of beings; the sixth, only the sharpness and dullness of the faculties of beings; the seventh, only their defilement and so on, along with the absorptions and so on; the eighth, only the continuity of aggregates in past lives; the ninth, only the passing away and rebirth of beings; the tenth, only the discernment of the truths. Omniscient knowledge, however, knows what is to be known by these and also what is beyond them. But it does not perform all of their functions. For it cannot, having become an absorption, enter absorption; having become a psychic power, perform transformations; or having become the path, eradicate defilements. Furthermore, the disputant should be asked: “Is this knowledge of the ten powers accompanied by applied and sustained thought, without applied thought but with sustained thought only, or without applied and sustained thought? Is it of the sense sphere, the form sphere, or the formless sphere? Is it mundane or supramundane?” One who knows would say in sequence: the seven knowledges are accompanied by applied and sustained thought. The next two are without applied and sustained thought. The knowledge of the destruction of the taints may be accompanied by applied and sustained thought, or without applied thought but with sustained thought only, or without applied and sustained thought. Similarly, in sequence, he would say: seven are of the sense sphere, the next two are of the form sphere, and the one at the end is supramundane. But omniscient knowledge, he would say, is only accompanied by applied and sustained thought, only of the sense sphere, and only mundane.

Evamettha [V 1.0344] anupadavaṇṇanaṃ katvā idāni yasmā tathāgato paṭhamaṃyeva ṭhānāṭṭhānañāṇena veneyyasattānaṃ āsavakkhayādhigamassa ceva anadhigamassa ca ṭhānāṭṭhānabhūtaṃ kilesāvaraṇābhāvaṃ passati, lokiyasammādiṭṭhiṭṭhānadassanato niyatamicchādiṭṭhiṭṭhānābhāvadassanato ca. Atha nesaṃ kammavipākañāṇena vipākāvaraṇābhāvaṃ passati, tihetukapaṭisandhidassanato. Sabbatthagāminīpaṭipadāñāṇena [P 2.0032] kammāvaraṇābhāvaṃ passati, anantariyakammābhāvadassanato. Evaṃ anāvaraṇānaṃ anekadhātunānādhātuñāṇena anukūladhammadesanatthaṃ cariyavisesaṃ passati, dhātuvemattadassanato. Atha nesaṃ nānādhimuttikatāñāṇena adhimuttiṃ passati, payogaṃ anādiyitvāpi adhimuttivasena dhammadesanatthaṃ. Athevaṃ diṭṭhādhimuttīnaṃ yathāsatti yathābalaṃ dhammaṃ desetuṃ indriyaparopariyattañāṇena indriyaparopariyattaṃ passati, saddhādīnaṃ tikkhamudubhāvadassanato. Evaṃ pariññātindriyaparopariyattā pana te sace dūre honti, paṭhamajjhānādīsu vasībhūtattā iddhivisesena te khippaṃ upagacchati. Upagantvā ca nesaṃ pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇena pubbajātibhāvanaṃ, dibbacakkhuñāṇānubhāvato pattabbena cetopariyañāṇena sampati cittavisesaṃ passanto āsavakkhayañāṇānubhāvena āsavakkhayagāminiyā paṭipadāya vigatasammohattā āsavakkhayāya dhammaṃ deseti. Tasmā iminā anukkamena imāni dasabalāni vuttānīti veditabbāni.

Having thus made a word-by-word exposition, now, because the Tathāgata first discerns, through the knowledge of possible and impossible states, the absence of the obstacle of defilements—which is the condition for the attainment or non-attainment of the destruction of the taints in beings capable of being trained—by seeing the ground for mundane right view and the absence of the ground for fixed wrong view; then, through the knowledge of kamma and its results, he sees the absence of the obstacle of results in them, by discerning three-rooted rebirth-linking; through the knowledge of the path leading everywhere, he sees the absence of the obstacle of kamma in them, by discerning the absence of kamma with immediate result; thus, for those free from obstacles, through the knowledge of the diverse and various elements, he discerns their particular conduct for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma suited to them, by seeing the diversity of elements; then, through the knowledge of their diverse inclinations, he discerns their dispositions, for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma according to their dispositions, even without their making an effort; then, for those whose views and dispositions have been thus seen, in order to teach the Dhamma according to their capacity and strength, he discerns the superiority and inferiority of their faculties through the knowledge of the superiority and inferiority of faculties, by seeing the sharpness and dullness of their faith and other faculties; having thus fully understood the superiority and inferiority of their faculties, if they are far away, he quickly approaches them by a special psychic power, due to his mastery of the first jhāna and so on; upon approaching, through the knowledge of recollecting past lives, he discerns the condition of their past births, and by the power of the divine eye, through the knowledge of penetrating others' minds which is to be attained thereby, he sees their present specific state of mind; then, by the power of the knowledge of the destruction of the taints, being free from delusion regarding the path leading to the destruction of the taints, he teaches the Dhamma for the destruction of the taints. Therefore, it should be understood that these ten powers are stated in this sequence.

Taṃ, sāriputta, vācaṃ appahāyātiādīsu puna evarūpiṃ vācaṃ na vakkhāmīti vadanto taṃ vācaṃ pajahati nāma. Puna evarūpaṃ cittaṃ na uppādessāmīti cintento cittaṃ pajahati nāma. Puna evarūpaṃ diṭṭhiṃ na gaṇhissāmīti pajahanto diṭṭhiṃ paṭinissajjati nāma, tathā akaronto neva pajahati, na paṭinissajjati. So yathābhataṃ nikkhitto evaṃ nirayeti yathā nirayapālehi āharitvā niraye ṭhapito, evaṃ niraye ṭhapitoyevāti veditabbo.

Regarding the phrase 'having not abandoned that speech, Sāriputta,' and so on: one who says, 'I will not speak such words again,' is said to abandon that speech. One who thinks, 'I will not arouse such a thought again,' is said to abandon that thought. One who abandons by resolving, 'I will not grasp such a view again,' is said to relinquish that view. One who does not act thus neither abandons nor relinquishes. The phrase 'he is cast into hell just as he was carried there' means: just as one is brought by the hell-wardens and placed in hell, so it should be understood that he is indeed placed in hell.

Idānissa [M 1.0338] atthasādhakaṃ upamaṃ dassento seyyathāpītiādimāha. Tattha sīlasampannotiādīsu lokiyalokuttarā sīlasamādhipaññā veditabbā. Lokuttaravaseneva vinivattetumpi vaṭṭati. Ayañhi sammāvācākammantājīvehi sīlasampanno, sammāvāyāmasatisamādhīhi samādhisampanno, sammādiṭṭhisaṅkappehi paññāsampanno, so evaṃ sīlādisampanno bhikkhu yathā diṭṭheva dhamme imasmiṃyeva attabhāve aññaṃ ārādheti arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti, evaṃsampadamidaṃ, sāriputta, vadāmi imampi [V 1.0345] kāraṇaṃ evarūpameva[P 2.0033]. Yathā hi maggānantaraṃ avirajjhitvāva phalaṃ nibbattati, evameva imassāpi puggalassa cutianantaraṃ avirajjhitvāva niraye paṭisandhi hotīti dasseti. Sakalasmiñhi buddhavacane imāya upamāya gāḷhataraṃ katvā vuttaupamā nāma natthi.

Now, to present a simile that establishes the meaning, he speaks the words beginning with 'just as.' Here, in the phrases 'endowed with virtue,' and so on, mundane and supramundane virtue, concentration, and wisdom should be understood. It is also proper to apply this in terms of the supramundane alone. For this monk is 'endowed with virtue' through right speech, right action, and right livelihood; 'endowed with concentration' through right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration; and 'endowed with wisdom' through right view and right intention. He shows that just as a monk so endowed with virtue and so on attains final knowledge, that is, reaches arahatship, in this very life, in this very existence, so too is this matter: 'This case, Sāriputta, I declare to be of such a kind,' meaning this reason is also of such a nature. Just as the fruit arises immediately after the path without any gap, so too for this individual, rebirth-linking in hell occurs immediately after death without any gap. Indeed, in the entire teaching of the Buddha, there is no simile spoken more forcefully than this one.

150. Vesārajjānīti ettha sārajjapaṭipakkho vesārajjaṃ, catūsu ṭhānesu sārajjābhāvaṃ paccavekkhantassa uppannasomanassamayañāṇassetaṃ nāmaṃ. Sammāsambuddhassa te paṭijānatoti ahaṃ sammāsambuddho, sabbe dhammā mayā abhisambuddhāti evaṃ paṭijānato tava. Anabhisambuddhāti ime nāma dhammā tayā anabhisambuddhā. Tatra vatāti tesu vata anabhisambuddhāti evaṃ dassitadhammesu. Sahadhammenāti sahetunā sakāraṇena vacanena sunakkhatto viya vippalapanto appamāṇaṃ. Nimittametanti ettha puggalopi dhammopi nimittanti adhippeto. Taṃ puggalaṃ na passāmi, yo maṃ paṭicodessati, taṃ dhammaṃ na passāmi, yaṃ dassetvā ayaṃ nāma dhammo tayā anabhisambuddhoti maṃ paṭicodessatīti ayamettha attho. Khemappattoti khemaṃ patto, sesapadadvayaṃ imasseva vevacanaṃ. Sabbañhetaṃ vesārajjañāṇameva sandhāya vuttaṃ. Dasabalassa hi ayaṃ nāma dhammo tayā anabhisambuddhoti codakaṃ puggalaṃ vā codanākāraṇaṃ anabhisambuddhadhammaṃ vā apassato sabhāvabuddhoyeva vā samāno ahaṃ buddhosmīti vadāmīti paccavekkhantassa balavataraṃ somanassaṃ uppajjati. Tena sampayuttaṃ ñāṇaṃ vesārajjaṃ nāma. Taṃ sandhāya “khemappatto”tiādimāha. Evaṃ sabbattha attho veditabbo.

150. Regarding 'fearlessnesses' (vesārajjāni): here, fearlessness (vesārajja) is the opposite of timidity (sārajja). It is the name for the knowledge accompanied by joy that arises in one who reflects on the absence of timidity in four situations. Regarding the phrase 'when you claim to be a Perfectly Enlightened One': this refers to you claiming, 'I am a Perfectly Enlightened One; all phenomena have been fully awakened to by me.' 'Are not fully awakened to' refers to someone saying, 'These particular phenomena have not been fully awakened to by you.' 'In that regard' refers to those phenomena thus pointed out as not being fully awakened to. 'Rightfully' (sahadhammena) means with a statement that has a basis and a reason, not like Sunakkhatta, who prattled on without limit. Regarding 'I do not see this ground' (nimittametaṃ): here, by 'ground' (nimitta), both a person and a teaching are intended. The meaning is this: 'I do not see that person who could reproach me; I do not see that teaching which, having been pointed out, would be the basis for someone to reproach me, saying, "This particular teaching has not been fully awakened to by you."' 'Having attained security' (khemappatto) means having reached security; the other two phrases are synonyms for this. All this is said with reference to the knowledge of fearlessness. For when the Possessor of the Ten Powers reflects, 'I do not see a person who could reproach me, nor an unawakened-to teaching that could be the reason for reproach, and being one who is enlightened by his very nature, I declare, "I am a Buddha,"' a very powerful joy arises. The knowledge associated with that is called fearlessness. It is with reference to this that he said, 'Having attained security,' and so on. The meaning should be understood in this way in all instances.

Antarāyikā dhammāti ettha pana antarāyaṃ karontīti antarāyikā, te atthato sañcicca vītikkantā satta āpattikkhandhā. Sañcicca vītikkantañhi antamaso dukkaṭa-dubbhāsitampi maggaphalānaṃ antarāyaṃ karoti. Idha pana methunadhammo [M 1.0339] adhippeto. Methunaṃ sevato hi yassa kassaci nissaṃsayameva maggaphalānaṃ antarāyo hoti. Yassa kho pana tesu atthāyāti rāgakkhayādīsu yassa atthāya. Dhammo desitoti asubhabhāvanādidhammo kathito[P 2.0034]. Tatra vata manti tasmiṃ aniyyānikadhamme maṃ. Sesaṃ vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ.

Herein, obstructive states are so called because they create an obstruction. In essence, they are the seven classes of offenses that are intentionally transgressed. For even a wrongdoing or improper speech, if done deliberately, obstructs the path and its fruits. Here, however, sexual intercourse is specifically intended. For one who engages in sexual intercourse, there is undoubtedly an obstruction to the path and its fruits. Regarding the phrase 'for whose purpose among these,' it refers to the purpose of destroying lust and so on. And regarding 'the Dhamma is taught,' it refers to the Dhamma such as the development of foulness being taught. 'In that case, indeed, me' means 'me in that state that does not lead to liberation.' The rest should be understood in the same way as previously stated.

Dasabalañāṇādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The exposition on the knowledge of the ten powers and so forth is concluded.

Aṭṭhaparisavaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Eight Assemblies

151. “Aṭṭha [V 1.0346] kho imā sāriputtā”ti idaṃ kasmā āraddhaṃ? Vesārajjañāṇassa baladassanatthaṃ. Yathā hi byattaṃ parisaṃ ajjhogāhetvā viññūnaṃ cittaṃ ārādhanasamatthāya kathāya dhammakathikassa chekabhāvo paññāyati, evaṃ imā aṭṭha parisā patvā vesārajjañāṇassa vesārajjabhāvo sakkā ñātunti vesārajjañāṇassa balaṃ dassento, aṭṭha kho imā sāriputtātiādimāha.

151. “Sāriputta, there are these eight…” Why was this discourse begun? To show the power of the knowledge of fearlessness. Just as, having entered an expert assembly, the skill of a Dhamma-speaker becomes apparent through a talk capable of pleasing the minds of the wise, so too, having reached these eight assemblies, the fearlessness of the knowledge of fearlessness can be known. Thus, to show the power of the knowledge of fearlessness, he began, “Sāriputta, there are these eight…”

Tattha khattiyaparisāti khattiyānaṃ sannipatitvā nisinnaṭṭhānaṃ, esa nayo sabbattha. Mārakāyikānaṃ pana sannipatitvā nisinnaṭṭhānaṃ māraparisā veditabbā, na mārānaṃ. Sabbāpi cetā parisā uggaṭṭhānadassanavasena gahitā. Manussā hi “ettha rājā nisinno”ti pakativacanampi vattuṃ na sakkonti, kacchehi sedā muccanti. Evaṃ uggā khattiyaparisā. Brāhmaṇā tīsu vedesu kusalā honti, gahapatayo nānāvohāresu ceva akkharacintāya ca. Samaṇā sakavādaparavādesu kusalā honti. Tesaṃ majjhe dhammakathākathanaṃ nāma ativiya bhāro. Amanussāpi uggā honti. Amanussoti hi vuttamattepi manussānaṃ sakalasarīraṃ saṅkampati, tesaṃ rūpaṃ vā disvā saddaṃ vā sutvā sattā visaññino honti. Evaṃ amanussaparisā uggā. Tāsupi dhammakathākathanaṃ nāma ativiya bhāro. Iti uggaṭṭhānadassanavasena tā gahitāti veditabbā.

Therein, the assembly of nobles is the place where nobles gather and sit; this is the principle in all cases. However, the place where the hosts of Māra assemble and sit should be understood as the assembly of Māra’s retinue, not of Māras themselves. All these assemblies are considered formidable due to their awe-inspiring nature. For people cannot even utter the ordinary phrase, 'Here sits the king,' without sweat breaking out from their armpits. Thus formidable is the assembly of nobles. Brahmins are skilled in the three Vedas; householders in various transactions and in the study of letters. Ascetics are skilled in their own doctrines and the doctrines of others. To deliver a discourse on the Dhamma in their midst is an exceedingly heavy burden. Non-human beings are also formidable. Merely at the mention of 'non-human beings,' the entire bodies of humans tremble; upon seeing their forms or hearing their voices, beings become unconscious. Thus formidable is the assembly of non-humans. To deliver a discourse on the Dhamma among them is also an exceedingly heavy burden. Therefore, it should be understood that these are considered formidable assemblies due to their awe-inspiring nature.

Ajjhogāhatīti anupavisati. Anekasataṃ khattiyaparisanti bimbisārasamāgama ñātisamāgama licchavīsamāgamasadisaṃ. Aññesupi cakkavāḷesu labbhatiyeva. Kiṃ pana bhagavā aññāni cakkavāḷānipi gacchatīti? Āma gacchati. Kīdiso hutvā? Yādisā te, tādisoyeva. Tenevāha “abhijānāmi [M 1.0340] kho panāhaṃ, ānanda, anekasataṃ khattiyaparisaṃ upasaṅkamitā, tattha yādisako tesaṃ [P 2.0035] vaṇṇo hoti, tādisako mayhaṃ vaṇṇo hoti. Yādisako tesaṃ saro hoti, tādisako mayhaṃ saro hoti. Dhammiyā kathāya sandassemi samādapemi samuttejemi sampahaṃsemi. Bhāsamānañca maṃ na jānanti ‘ko nu kho ayaṃ bhāsati devo vā manusso vā’ti. Dhammiyā kathāya sandassetvā samādapetvā samuttejetvā sampahaṃsetvā antaradhāyāmi[V 1.0347]. Antarahitañca maṃ na jānanti ‘ko nu kho ayaṃ antarahito devo vā manusso vā’”ti (dī. ni. 2.172).

‘He plunges into’ means he enters. An assembly of many hundreds of nobles is like the meeting with Bimbisāra, a gathering of relatives, or an assembly of the Licchavis. Such assemblies can also be found in other world-systems. But does the Blessed One also go to other world-systems? Yes, he does. In what form? Just as they are, so is he. Therefore, he said: “I recall, Ānanda, having approached many hundreds of assemblies of nobles. There, whatever their complexion was, such was my complexion. Whatever their voice was, such was my voice. I instructed, urged, roused, and delighted them with a Dhamma talk. And while I was speaking, they did not know me, thinking: ‘Who is this who speaks—a god or a human?’ Having instructed, urged, roused, and delighted them with a Dhamma talk, I vanished. And when I had vanished, they did not know me, thinking: ‘Who was this who vanished—a god or a human?’” (DN 16).

Khattiyā keyūraṅgadamālāgandhādivibhūsitā nānāvirāgavasanā āmukkamaṇikuṇḍalā moḷidharā honti. Kiṃ bhagavāpi evaṃ attānaṃ maṇḍeti? Te ca odātāpi honti kāḷāpi maṃgulacchavīpi. Kiṃ satthāpi evarūpo hotīti? Satthā attano pabbajitavaseneva gacchati, tesaṃ pana tādiso hutvā upaṭṭhāti, gantvā rājāsane nisinnaṃ attānaṃ dasseti, tesaṃ “ajja amhākaṃ rājā ativiya virocatī”ti hoti. Te ca bhinnassarāpi honti gaggassarāpi kākassarāpi. Satthā brahmassareneva dhammaṃ katheti. Tādisako mayhaṃ saro hotīti idaṃ pana bhāsantaraṃ sandhāya kathitaṃ. Manussānaṃ pana taṃ sutvā “ajja rājā madhurena sarena kathetī”ti hoti. Kathetvā pakkante ca bhagavati puna rājānaṃ āgataṃ disvā “ko nu kho aya”nti vīmaṃsā uppajjati.

Nobles are adorned with armlets, bracelets, garlands, perfumes, and so on; they wear various colorful garments, jeweled earrings, and turbans. Does the Blessed One also adorn himself in this way? And they may be fair, dark, or golden-skinned. Is the Teacher also of such appearance? The Teacher goes simply in the garb of a renunciate, yet he appears before them in such a form. Having gone and seated himself on the royal throne, he reveals himself to them, and they think, 'Today our king shines exceedingly.' They may also have voices that are discordant, guttural, or croaking. The Teacher, however, speaks the Dhamma with a Brahmā-like voice. The statement, 'such was my voice,' however, was said with reference to a different language. But when people hear it, they think, 'Today the king speaks with a sweet voice.' After the Blessed One has spoken and departed, when they see the king return, the question arises: 'Who could this be?'

Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – ko nu kho ayaṃ imasmiṃ ṭhāne idāneva māgadhabhāsāya sīhaḷabhāsāya madhurena sarena kathento antarahito, kiṃ devo, udāhu manussoti? Kimatthaṃ panevaṃ ajānantānaṃ dhammaṃ desetīti? Vāsanatthāya. Evaṃ sutopi hi dhammo anāgate paccayo hotiyevāti anāgataṃ paṭicca desetīti.

This is what is meant: 'Who was it that just now, in this place, speaking in the Māgadhan language or the Sinhala language with a sweet voice, disappeared? Was it a god, or a human?' But why does he teach the Dhamma to those who do not recognize him? For the sake of implanting a latent tendency. For the Dhamma heard in this way indeed becomes a condition in the future; thus, he teaches with regard to the future.

Sannisinnapubbanti saṅgamma nisinnapubbaṃ. Sallapitapubbanti ālāpasallāpo katapubbo. Sākacchāti dhammasākacchāpi samāpajjitapubbā. Anekasataṃ brāhmaṇaparisantiādīnampi soṇadaṇḍasamāgamādivasena ceva aññacakkavāḷavasena ca sambhavo veditabbo.

‘Previously seated together’ means having gathered and sat together before. ‘Previously conversed’ means having had talk and conversation before. ‘Discussion’ means having also engaged in discussions on the Dhamma before. The occurrence of “many hundreds of brahmin assemblies” and so forth should be understood as happening both on occasions like the assembly with Soṇadaṇḍa and in other world-systems as well.

Aṭṭhaparisavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The exposition of the eight assemblies is concluded.

Catuyonivaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Four Kinds of Birth

152. Catasso [M 1.0341] kho imā, sāriputta, yoniyoti ettha yonīti khandhakoṭṭhāsassapi kāraṇassapi passāvamaggassapi nāmaṃ. “Catasso nāgayoniyo catasso supaṇṇayoniyo”ti (saṃ. ni. 3.342, 392) ettha [V 1.0348] hi khandhakoṭṭhāso yoni nāma. “Yoni hesā [P 2.0036] bhūmija phalassa adhigamāyā”ti (ma. ni. 2.227) ettha kāraṇaṃ. “Na cāhaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ brūmi, yonijaṃ mattisambhava”nti (ma. ni. 2.457; dha. pa. 396) ettha passāvamaggo. Idha pana khandhakoṭṭhāso yonīti adhippeto. Tattha aṇḍe jātā aṇḍajā. Jalābumhi jātā jalābujā. Saṃsede jātā saṃsedajā. Vinā etehi kāraṇehi uppatitvā viya nibbattā abhinibbattāti opapātikā. Abhinibbhijja jāyantīti bhinditvā nikkhamanavasena jāyanti. Pūtikuṇape vātiādīhi aniṭṭhaṭṭhānāneva dassitāni. Iṭṭhesupi sappitelamadhuphāṇitādīsu sattā jāyanti eva. Devātiādīsu cātumahārājikato paṭṭhāya uparidevā opapātikāva honti. Bhūmadevā pana catuyonikā. Ekacce ca manussāti manussesu keci devā viya opapātikā ca honti. Yebhuyyena panete jalābujāva, aṇḍajāpi ettha kontaputtā dvebhātiyattherā viya, saṃsedajāpi padumagabbhe nibbattapokkharasātibrāhmaṇapadumavatidevīādayo viya, evaṃ vinipātikesu nijjhāmataṇhikapetā nerayikā viya opapātikāyeva, avasesā catuyonikāpi honti. Yathā te evaṃ yakkhāpi sabbacatuppadapakkhijātidīghajātiādayopi sabbe catuyonikāyeva.

152. “Sāriputta, there are these four kinds of birth.” Here, the term “yoni” refers to a constituent of the aggregates, a cause, or a birth passage. In the phrase, “There are four kinds of birth for nāgas, four kinds of birth for supaṇṇas” (Saṃ. Ni. 3.342, 392), here “yoni” means a constituent of the aggregates. In the phrase, “This, Bhūmija, is the cause for the attainment of the fruit” (Ma. Ni. 2.227), here it means a cause. In the phrase, “I do not call one a brahmin merely because of birth from a womb, from a mother” (Ma. Ni. 2.457; Dhp. 396), here it refers to the birth passage. But here, “yoni” is intended to mean a constituent of the aggregates. Among these: Those born from eggs are egg-born. Those born from a womb are womb-born. Those born from moisture are moisture-born. Those who arise without these causes, as if appearing spontaneously, are spontaneously-born. They are born by bursting forth, meaning they are born by breaking out and emerging. Through phrases like “in a putrid corpse” and so forth, only undesirable places are indicated. But beings are also born in desirable places such as ghee, oil, honey, and molasses. As for devas, starting from the Four Great Kings upwards, the higher devas are all spontaneously-born. Earth-dwelling devas, however, belong to all four kinds of birth. And some humans, like certain devas, are also spontaneously-born. But for the most part, they are womb-born; there are also egg-born ones here, like Kontaputta and the two Bhātiya elders, and moisture-born ones, like the Brahmin Pokkharasāti who was born in a lotus womb, Queen Padumavatī, and others. Similarly, among those in the realms of loss, the hungry ghosts tormented by thirst and the hell-beings are spontaneously-born. The rest also belong to all four kinds of birth. Just as with them, so too yakkhas, all four-footed creatures, birds, long-bodied creatures, and others—all belong to the four kinds of birth.

Catuyonivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Four Kinds of Birth is concluded.

Pañcagativaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Five Destinies

153. Pañca kho imā, sāriputta, gatiyoti ettha sukatadukkaṭakammavasena gantabbāti gatiyo. Apica gatigati nibbattigati ajjhāsayagati vibhavagati nipphattigatīti bahuvidhā gati nāma. Tattha “taṃ gatiṃ pecca gacchāmī”ti (a. ni. 4.184) ca, “yassa gatiṃ na jānanti, devā gandhabbamānusā”ti (dha. pa. 420) ca ayaṃ gatigati nāma. “Imesaṃ kho ahaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ sīlavantānaṃ neva jānāmi gatiṃ vā agatiṃ vā”ti (ma. ni. 1.508) ayaṃ nibbattigati nāma. “Evampi kho te ahaṃ brahme [M 1.0342] gatiṃ ca pajānāmi jutiñca pajānāmī”ti (ma. ni. 1.503) ayaṃ ajjhāsayagati nāma. “Vibhavo gati dhammānaṃ, nibbānaṃ arahato gatī”ti (pari. 339) ayaṃ vibhavagati nāma. “Dveyeva gatiyo bhavanti [V 1.0349] anaññā”ti (dī. ni. 1.258; 2.34) ayaṃ nipphattigati nāma. Tāsu idha gatigati adhippetā.

153. “Sāriputta, these five are destinies (gati),” so called because they are to be gone to (gantabbā) by way of well-done and ill-done kamma. Moreover, the term “gati” is of many kinds: destination-gati, rebirth-gati, inclination-gati, cessation-gati, and accomplishment-gati. Here, “After passing away, I will go to that destiny” (A.N. 4.184) and “Whose destiny neither devas, gandhabbas, nor humans know” (Dhp. 420)—this is called destination-gati. “Of these virtuous bhikkhus, I do not know their rebirth or non-rebirth” (M.N. 1.508)—this is called rebirth-gati. “Thus, O Brahmā, I understand your inclination and your radiance” (M.N. 1.503)—this is called inclination-gati. “Cessation is the destiny of phenomena, Nibbāna is the destiny of the arahant” (Pari. 339)—this is called cessation-gati. “There are only two destinies, no others” (D.N. 1.258; 2.34)—this is called accomplishment-gati. Among these, here, destination-gati is intended.

Nirayotiādīsu [P 2.0037] niratiatthena nirassādaṭṭhena nirayo. Tiriyaṃ añchitāti tiracchānā. Tesaṃ yoni tiracchānayoni. Peccabhāvaṃ pattānaṃ visayoti pettivisayo. Manaso ussannattā manussā. Pañcahi kāmaguṇehi attano attano ānubhāvehi ca dibbantīti devā. Nirayañcāhaṃ, sāriputtātiādīsu nirayoti saddhiṃ okāsena khandhā. Tiracchānayoniṃ cātiādīsupi eseva nayo. Maggaṃ paṭipadanti ubhayenāpi vuttagatisaṃvattanika kammameva dasseti. Yathā ca paṭipannoti yena maggena yāya paṭipadāya paṭipannoti ubhayampi ekato katvā niddisati. Apāyantiādīsu vaḍḍhisaṅkhātā sukhasaṅkhātā vā ayā apetattā apāyo. Dukkhassa gati paṭisaraṇanti duggati. Dukkaṭakārino ettha vinipatantīti vinipāto. Nibbānañcāhanti idaṃ pana na kevalaṃ gatigatimeva, gatinissaraṇaṃ nibbānampi jānāmīti dassanatthamāha. Idha maggo paṭipadāti ubhayenāpi ariyamaggova vutto.

In the case of “niraya” and so forth, it is called “niraya” because it is without delight (nirati) and without satisfaction (nirassāda). Those who move horizontally are called “tiracchānā.” Their kind of birth is the animal kind of birth. The sphere of those who have attained the state of departed spirits is “pettivisayo.” Humans are called “manussā” because of the elevation of mind. Devas are called “devā” because they delight (dibbanti) in the five strands of sensual pleasure and their own respective powers. In passages such as “And I, Sāriputta, know hell” and so forth, “niraya” refers to the aggregates together with the space they occupy. The same applies to phrases like “and the animal kind of birth” and so forth. By both 'path' and 'practice', it indicates the very kamma that leads to the said destiny. And 'how one has practiced' indicates, by taking both together, the path and the practice by which one has practiced. In terms like “apāya” and so forth, it is called “apāya” because growth (vaḍḍhi) or happiness (sukha), which are called “aya” (gain), are absent (apeta). “Duggati” is the destiny, the resort of suffering. “Vinipāto” is where wrongdoers fall down. As for “And I know Nibbāna,” this is stated not merely to show the destination-destiny, but also to show that I know Nibbāna, the escape from destinies. Here, 'path' and 'practice' both refer to the Noble Path.

Pañcagativaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Five Destinies is concluded.

Ñāṇappavattākāravaṇṇanā

The Exposition on the Mode of Operation of Knowledge

154. Idāni yathāvuttesu sattasu ṭhānesu aṭṭhasu ṭhānesu attano ñāṇappavattākāraṃ dassento idhāhaṃ, sāriputtātiādimāha.

154. Now, to show the manner in which his own knowledge operates in the seven or eight places previously mentioned, he says: 'Here, I, O Sāriputta,' and so forth.

Tattha ekantadukkhāti niccadukkhā nirantaradukkhā. Tibbāti bahalā. Kaṭukāti kharā. Seyyathāpītiādīni opammadassanatthaṃ vuttāni. Tattha kāsūti āvāṭopi vuccati rāsipi.

There, 'ekantadukkhā' means constant suffering, uninterrupted suffering. 'Tibbā' means intense. 'Kaṭukā' means harsh. 'Seyyathāpi' and so forth are stated for the purpose of showing a simile. There, 'kāsu' is called both a pit and a heap.

“Kinnu santaramānova, kāsuṃ khaṇasi sārathi;

Puṭṭho me samma akkhāhi, kiṃ kāsuyā karissasī”ti. (jā. 2.22.3) –

“Why do you dig the pit so hastily, charioteer? When asked, dear friend, tell me, what will you do with this pit?” (Jā 2.22.3)

Ettha [V 1.0350] hi āvāṭo kāsu nāma.

Here, indeed, 'kāsu' means a pit.

“Aṅgārakāsuṃ [M 1.0343] apare phunanti, narā rudantā paridaḍḍhagattā”ti. (jā. 2.22.462) –

“Some leap into a pit of embers, people wailing, their bodies scorched.” (Jā 2.22.462)

Ettha rāsi. Idha pana āvāṭo adhippeto. Tenevāha “sādhikaporisā”ti. Tattha sādhikaṃ porisaṃ pamāṇaṃ assāti sādhikaporisā, atirekapañcaratanāti attho. Vītaccikānaṃ vītadhūmānanti etaṃ pariḷāhassa balavabhāvadīpanatthaṃ vuttaṃ, acciyā vā sati dhūme vā sati, vāto samuṭṭhāti, tena pariḷāho na balavā hoti. Ghammaparetoti ghammānugato[P 2.0038]. Tasitoti jātataṇho. Pipāsitoti udakaṃ pātukāmo. Ekāyanena maggenāti ekapatheneva maggena, anukkamaniyena ubhosu passesu nirantarakaṇṭakarukkhagahanena. Paṇidhāyāti aṅgārakāsuyaṃ patthanā nāma natthi, aṅgārakāsuṃ ārabbha pana iriyāpathassa ṭhapitattā evaṃ vuttaṃ.

Here, a heap. Here, however, a pit is intended. Hence it is said, 'more than a man's height.' There, 'sādhikaporisā' means its measure exceeds a man's height; the meaning is, exceeding five cubits. 'Without flames, without smoke' – this is said to indicate the intensity of the burning. If there were flames or smoke, wind would arise, and thereby the burning would not be so intense. 'Overcome by heat' means afflicted by heat. 'Thirsty' means with thirst arisen. 'Parched with thirst' means wishing to drink water. 'By a single path' means by a single-track path only, a path from which one cannot step aside, with a continuous thicket of thorny trees on both sides. 'Having resolved' means there is no aspiration towards the pit of embers; however, because the posture is established with reference to the pit of embers, it is said thus.

Evameva khoti ettha idaṃ opammasaṃsandanaṃ – aṅgārakāsu viya hi nirayo daṭṭhabbo. Aṅgārakāsumaggo viya nirayūpagaṃ kammaṃ. Maggāruḷho viya kammasamaṅgī puggalo. Cakkhumā puriso viya dibbacakkhuko bhagavā. Yathā so puriso maggāruḷhaṃ disvā vijānāti “ayaṃ iminā maggena gantvā aṅgārakāsuyaṃ patissatī”ti, evamevaṃ bhagavā pāṇātipātādīsu yaṃkiñci kammaṃ āyūhantaṃ evaṃ jānāti “ayaṃ imaṃ kammaṃ katvā niraye nibbattissattī”ti. Yathā so puriso aparabhāge taṃ aṅgārakāsuyā patitaṃ passati, evameva bhagavā aparabhāge “so puriso taṃ kammaṃ katvā kuhiṃ nibbatto”ti ālokaṃ vaḍḍhetvā dibbacakkhunā olokento niraye nibbattaṃ passati pañcavidhabandhanādimahādukkhaṃ anubhavantaṃ. Tattha kiñcāpi tassa kammāyūhanakāle añño vaṇṇo, niraye nibbattassa añño. Athāpi “so satto taṃ kammaṃ katvā kattha nibbatto”ti olokentassa anekasahassānaṃ sattānaṃ majjhe ṭhitopi “ayaṃ so”ti soyeva satto āpāthaṃ āgacchati, “dibbacakkhubalaṃ nāma eta”nti vadanti.

In the same way, here is the connection of the simile: the hell realm should be seen as like a pit of glowing coals. The path leading to a pit of glowing coals is like the action leading to hell. The person walking along that path is like the individual engaged in that action. The clear-sighted man is like the Blessed One, who possesses the divine eye. Just as that man, seeing the person on the path, understands, 'This one, having gone by this path, will fall into the pit of glowing coals,' so too the Blessed One knows of any being accumulating any action—such as killing living beings—'This one, having done this deed, will be reborn in hell.' Just as that man later sees the one fallen into the pit of glowing coals, so too the Blessed One, later expanding his light and surveying with the divine eye, sees that being reborn in hell, experiencing the great suffering of the fivefold bondage and so on. Though at the time of accumulating the action, that being had one appearance, and in hell another, still, when the Blessed One looks to see, 'That being, having done that deed—where was he reborn?' even amidst thousands of other beings, 'this is the one,' that very being comes into focus. They say, 'This is the power of the divine eye.'

Dutiyaupamāyaṃ yasmā aṅgārakāsuyaṃ viya gūthakūpe pariḷāho natthi, tasmā “ekantadukkhā”ti avatvā “dukkhā”tiādimāha. Etthāpi purimanayeneva opammasaṃsandanaṃ veditabbaṃ[V 1.0351]. Imampi hi puggalaṃ bhagavā hatthiyoniādīsu [M 1.0344] yattha katthaci nibbattaṃ vadhabandhanaākaḍḍhanavikaḍḍhanādīhi mahādukkhaṃ anubhavamānaṃ passatiyeva.

In the second simile, because in a cesspool there is no burning as there is in a pit of embers, it is not called 'exclusively painful,' but simply 'painful,' and so on. Here too, the connection with the simile should be understood in the same way as before. For the Blessed One indeed sees this person, reborn anywhere such as in an elephant's womb, experiencing great suffering through slaughter, imprisonment, being dragged to and fro, and so on.

Tatiyaupamāyaṃ tanupattapalāsoti na abbhapaṭalaṃ viya tanupaṇṇo, viraḷapaṇṇattaṃ panassa sandhāya idaṃ vuttaṃ. Kabaracchāyoti viraḷacchāyo. Dukkhabahulāti pettivisayasmiñhi [P 2.0039] dukkhameva bahulaṃ, sukhaṃ parittaṃ kadāci anubhavitabbaṃ hoti, tasmā evamāha. Etthāpi purimanayeneva opammasaṃsandanaṃ veditabbaṃ.

In the third simile, 'tanupattapalāso' does not mean thin-leaved like a layer of cloud, but this is said referring to its sparse foliage. 'Kabaracchāyo' means sparse shade. 'Full of suffering'—for in the realm of ghosts, suffering is indeed abundant, while happiness is meager and only occasionally experienced; thus it is said. Here too, the connection to the simile should be understood in the same way as before.

Catutthaupamāyaṃ bahalapattapalāsoti nirantarapaṇṇo pattasañchanno. Santacchāyoti pāsāṇacchattaṃ viya ghanacchāyo. Sukhabahulā vedanāti manussaloke khattiyakulādīsu sukhabahulā vedanā vedayitabbā hoti, tā vedayamānaṃ nipannaṃ vā nisinnaṃ vā passāmīti dasseti. Idhāpi opammasaṃsandanaṃ purimanayeneva veditabbaṃ.

In the fourth simile, 'bahalapattapalāso' means with continuous leaves, covered with foliage. 'Santacchāyo' means with thick shade, like a stone umbrella. 'Abundant pleasant feelings' refers to the abundant pleasant feelings to be experienced in the human world, in families of nobles, and so on. It shows that he sees a person lying down or sitting while experiencing these feelings. Here too, the connection of the simile should be understood in the same way as before.

Pañcamaupamāyaṃ pāsādoti dīghapāsādo. Ullittāvalittanti anto ceva ullittaṃ bahi ca avalittaṃ. Phusitaggaḷanti dvārabāhāhi saddhiṃ supihitakavāṭaṃ. Gonakatthatoti caturaṅgulādhikalomena kāḷakojavena atthato. Paṭikatthatoti uṇṇāmayena setaattharaṇena atthato. Paṭalikatthatoti ghanapupphakena uṇṇāmayaattharaṇena atthato. Kadalimigapavarapaccattharaṇoti kadalimigacammamayena uttamapaccattharaṇena atthato. Taṃ kira paccattharaṇaṃ setavatthassa upari kadalimigacammaṃ attharitvā sibbetvā karonti. Sauttaracchadoti saha uttaracchadena, uttaribaddhena rattavitānena saddhinti attho. Ubhatolohitakūpadhānoti sīsūpadhānañca pādūpadhānañcāti pallaṅkassa ubhato ṭhapitalohitakūpadhāno. Idhāpi upamāsaṃsandanaṃ purimanayeneva veditabbaṃ.

In the fifth simile, 'pāsādo' means a long palace. 'Ullittāvalittaṃ' means plastered inside and out. 'Phusitaggaḷaṃ' means with its door panels well-closed against the doorposts. 'Gonakatthatoti' refers to a spread made of black goat-hair with a fleece more than four finger-breadths long. 'Paṭikatthatoti' refers to a spread made of a white woolen covering. 'Paṭalikatthatoti' refers to a spread made of a woolen covering with dense floral patterns. 'Kadalimigapavarapaccattharaṇaṃ' refers to the finest spread made of kadali deer hide. It is said that this spread is made by spreading kadali deer hide over white cloth and sewing it. 'Sauttaracchado' means together with an upper cover; the meaning is, with a red canopy fastened above. 'Ubhatolohitakūpadhāno' means with a head cushion and a foot cushion, that is, with red cushions placed at both ends of the couch. Here too, the connection of the simile should be understood in the same way as before.

Ayaṃ panettha aparabhāgayojanā, yathā so puriso maggāruḷhameva jānāti “ayaṃ etena maggena gantvā pāsādaṃ āruyha kūṭāgāraṃ pavisitvā pallaṅke nisīdissati vā nipajjissati vā”ti, evamevaṃ bhagavā dānādīsu puññakiriyavatthūsu yaṃkiñci kusalakammaṃ āyūhantaṃyeva puggalaṃ disvā “ayaṃ imaṃ katvā devaloke nibbattissatī”ti jānāti. Yathā so puriso aparabhāge [M 1.0345][V 1.0352] taṃ pāsādaṃ āruyha kūṭāgāraṃ pavisitvā pallaṅke nisinnaṃ vā nipannaṃ vā ekantasukhaṃ nirantarasukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedayamānaṃ passati, evamevaṃ bhagavā aparabhāge “so taṃ kalyāṇaṃ katvā kuhiṃ nibbatto”ti ālokaṃ vaḍḍhetvā dibbacakkhunā olokento devaloke [P 2.0040] nibbattaṃ passati, nandanavanādīsu accharāsaṅghaparivutaṃ dibbasampattiṃ anubhavamānaṃ.

Herein, this is the application of the latter part. Just as that man knows of one who has embarked on the path, 'This person, having gone by this path, will ascend the palace, enter the gabled chamber, and sit or lie down on the couch,' so too the Blessed One, upon seeing a person undertaking any wholesome action whatsoever among the grounds for meritorious action, such as giving, knows, 'This person, having done this, will be reborn in the world of devas.' And just as that man, in the latter part, having ascended that palace and entered the gabled chamber, sees him sitting or lying on the couch, experiencing a feeling of exclusive and uninterrupted bliss, so too the Blessed One, in the latter part—having extended his light to see, 'Where has this person been reborn after doing that good deed?'—looking with the divine eye, sees him reborn in the world of devas, surrounded by a host of celestial nymphs in the Nandana Grove and other such places, enjoying divine fortune.

Ñāṇappavattākāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Mode of the Proceeding of Knowledge is concluded.

Āsavakkhayavāravaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Section on the Destruction of the Taints

Āsavakkhayavāre “dibbena cakkhunā”ti avatvā “tamenaṃ passāmī”ti vuttaṃ. Taṃ kasmāti ce? Niyamābhāvā. Imañhi puggalaṃ dibbacakkhunāpi passissati, cetopariyañāṇenāpi jānissati, sabbaññutaññāṇenapi jānissatiyeva. Ekantasukhā vedanāti idaṃ kiñcāpi devalokasukhena saddhiṃ byañjanato ekaṃ, atthato pana nānā hoti. Devalokasukhañhi rāgapariḷāhādīnaṃ atthitāya na ekanteneva sukhaṃ. Nibbānasukhaṃ pana sabbapariḷāhānaṃ vūpasamāya sabbākārena ekantasukhaṃ. Upamāyampi “yathā pāsāde ekantasukhā”ti vuttaṃ. Taṃ maggapariḷāhassa avūpasantatāya chātajjhattatāya pipāsābhibhūtatāya ca na ekantameva sukhaṃ. Vanasaṇḍe pana pokkharaṇiyaṃ oruyha rajojallassa pavāhitattā maggadarathassa vūpasantatāya bhisamūlakhādanena ceva madhurodakapānena ca khuppipāsānaṃ vinītatāya udakasāṭakaṃ parivattetvā maṭṭhadukūlaṃ nivāsetvā taṇḍulatthavikaṃ ussīsake katvā udakasāṭakaṃ pīḷetvā hadaye ṭhapetvā mandamandena ca vātena bījayamānassa nipannattā sabbākārena ekantasukhaṃ hoti.

In the section on the destruction of the taints, it is said, 'I see him,' without saying 'with the divine eye.' If it is asked why, it is because there is no fixed rule. For one will see this person with the divine eye, or know him with the knowledge of others' minds, or indeed know him with omniscient knowledge. The phrase 'a feeling of exclusive bliss'—though it is one in expression with the bliss of the world of devas, in meaning it is different. For the bliss of the world of devas, due to the presence of the fever of lust and so forth, is not exclusively bliss. But the bliss of Nibbāna, because of the calming of all fevers, is in every way exclusively bliss. Even in the simile, it is said, 'as in the palace, exclusive bliss.' But that, due to the uncalmed fever of the journey, being afflicted by hunger, and being overcome by thirst, is not exclusively bliss. In the forest grove, however, for one who has descended into a lotus pond, with dust and dirt washed away, with the weariness of the journey calmed, with hunger and thirst subdued by eating lotus roots and drinking sweet water, having changed the wet cloth and put on a clean, fine cloth, having made a bag of rice-grains into a pillow, having wrung out the wet cloth and placed it on his chest, and lying down while being fanned by a gentle breeze—it is in every way exclusively bliss.

Evameva khoti ettha idaṃ opammasaṃsandanaṃ – pokkharaṇī viya hi ariyamaggo daṭṭhabbo. Pokkharaṇimaggo viya pubbabhāgapaṭipadā. Maggāruḷho viya paṭipadāsamaṅgīpuggalo. Cakkhumā puriso viya dibbacakkhu bhagavā. Vanasaṇḍo viya nibbānaṃ. Yathā so puriso maggāruḷhaṃ disvāva jānāti “ayaṃ iminā maggena gantvā pokkharaṇiyaṃ nhatvā ramaṇīye vanasaṇḍe rukkhamūle nisīdissati vā nipajjissati vā”ti, evamevaṃ bhagavā paṭipadaṃ pūrentameva nāmarūpaṃ [V 1.0353] paricchindantameva paccayapariggahaṃ karontameva lakkhaṇārammaṇāya vipassanāya kammaṃ karontameva jānāti “ayaṃ imaṃ paṭipadaṃ pūretvā sabbaāsave khepetvā anāsavaṃ cetovimuttiṃ paññāvimuttinti evaṃ vuttaṃ phalasamāpattiṃ upasampajja [M 1.0346] viharissatī”ti. Yathā [P 2.0041] so puriso aparabhāge tāyaṃ pokkharaṇiyaṃ nhatvā vanasaṇḍaṃ pavisitvā nisinnaṃ vā nipannaṃ vā ekantasukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedayamānaṃ passati, evameva bhagavā aparabhāge taṃ puggalaṃ paṭipadaṃ pūretvā maggaṃ bhāvetvā phalaṃ sacchikatvā nirodhasayanavaragataṃ nibbānārammaṇaṃ phalasamāpattiṃ appetvā ekantasukhaṃ vedanaṃ vedayamānaṃ passati.

'Just so, indeed,' herein is the connection of the simile: the noble path is to be seen as like a lotus pond. The preliminary practice is like the path to the lotus pond. The person endowed with the practice is like one who has embarked on the path. The Blessed One, possessing the divine eye, is like the man with vision. Nibbāna is like the forest grove. Just as that man, upon seeing one who has embarked on the path, knows, 'This person, having gone by this path, will bathe in the lotus pond and then sit or lie down at the foot of a tree in the delightful forest grove,' so too the Blessed One—seeing one who is fulfilling the practice, defining name-and-form, undertaking the comprehension of conditions, and undertaking the practice of insight meditation with characteristics as its object—knows, 'This person, having fulfilled this practice and exhausted all the taints, will enter and dwell in the fruition attainment called the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom.' And just as that man, in the latter part, sees that person—having bathed in that lotus pond and entered the forest grove—sitting or lying down experiencing a feeling of exclusive bliss, so too the Blessed One, in the latter part, sees that person—having fulfilled the practice, developed the path, realized the fruit, and entered the fruition attainment which has Nibbāna as its object and is the excellent resting place of cessation—experiencing a feeling of exclusive bliss.

Āsavakkhayavāravaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Section on the Destruction of the Taints is concluded.

Dukkarakārikādisuddhivaṇṇanā

The Explanation of Purification through Difficult Practices and so forth

155. “Abhijānāmi kho panāhaṃ, sāriputta, caturaṅgasamannāgata”nti idaṃ kasmā āraddhaṃ? Pāṭiyekkaṃ anusandhivasena āraddhaṃ. Ayaṃ kira sunakkhatto dukkarakārikāya suddhi hotīti evaṃ laddhiko. Athassa bhagavā mayā ekasmiṃ attabhāve ṭhatvā caturaṅgasamannāgataṃ dukkaraṃ kataṃ, dukkarakārako nāma mayā sadiso natthi. Dukkarakārena suddhiyā sati ahameva suddho bhaveyyanti dassetuṃ imaṃ desanaṃ ārabhi. Apica ayaṃ sunakkhatto dukkarakārikāya pasanno, so cassa pasannabhāvo, “addasā kho, bhaggava, sunakkhatto licchaviputto acelaṃ korakkhattiyaṃ catukkuṇḍikaṃ chamānikiṇṇaṃ bhakkhasaṃ mukhena khādantaṃ mukhena bhuñjantaṃ. Disvānassa etadahosi ‘sādhu rūpo vata, bho, ayaṃ samaṇo catukkuṇḍiko chamānikiṇṇaṃ bhakkhasaṃ mukheneva khādati, mukheneva bhuñjatī’”ti evamādinā pāthikasutte (dī. ni. 3.7) āgatanayena veditabbo.

155. “I recall, Sāriputta, being endowed with four factors”—why was this begun? It was begun by way of individual connection. This Sunakkhatta, it is said, held the view that purity is attained through difficult practices. Then the Blessed One, to show that “Having been in one existence, I performed a difficult task endowed with four factors; there is none like me who performs difficult tasks. If purity were attained through performing difficult tasks, then I alone would be pure,” began this teaching. Moreover, this Sunakkhatta was impressed by difficult practices, and his state of being impressed is to be understood by the method stated in the Pāṭika Sutta (Dī. Ni. 3.7), beginning with: “Sunakkhatta the Licchavi prince saw the naked ascetic Korakkhattiya, crawling on all fours, eating food scattered on the ground, consuming it with his mouth. Seeing him, he thought, ‘How admirable, good sir, is this ascetic! Crawling on all fours, he eats food scattered on the ground, consuming it with his mouth!’”

Atha bhagavā ayaṃ dukkarakārikāya pasanno, mayā ca etasmiṃ attabhāve ṭhatvā caturaṅgasamannāgataṃ dukkaraṃ kataṃ, dukkarakāre pasīdantenāpi anena mayi pasīditabbaṃ siyā, sopissa pasādo mayi natthīti dassento imaṃ desanaṃ ārabhi.

Then the Blessed One, showing that this Sunakkhatta was impressed by difficult practices, and that “I, having been in this existence, performed a difficult task endowed with four factors; therefore, even he who is impressed by a performer of difficult tasks should have been impressed with me, but that impression of his is not in me,” began this teaching.

Tatra [V 1.0354] brahmacariyanti dānampi veyyāvaccampi sikkhāpadampi brahmavihārāpi dhammadesanāpi methunaviratipi sadārasantosopi uposathopi ariyamaggopi sakalasāsanampi ajjhāsayopi vīriyampi vuccati.

Herein, “the holy life” is said to refer to generosity, service, the precepts, the divine abidings, teaching the Dhamma, abstinence from sexual intercourse, contentment with one's own wife, the Uposatha, the Noble Path, the entire Dispensation, inclination, and energy.

“Kiṃ [M 1.0347] te vataṃ kiṃ pana brahmacariyaṃ,

Kissa suciṇṇassa ayaṃ vipāko;

Iddhī jutī balavīriyūpapatti,

Idañca te nāga mahāvimānaṃ.

“What is your observance? What is your holy life? Of what well-practiced deed is this the result: the manifestation of psychic power, splendor, strength, and energy, and this great mansion of yours, O Nāga?”

Ahañca [P 2.0042] bhariyā ca manussaloke,

Saddhā ubho dānapatī ahumhā;

Opānabhūtaṃ me gharaṃ tadāsi,

Santappitā samaṇabrāhmaṇā ca.

“In the human world, both my wife and I were faithful, generous donors. My home was then like a public well, and ascetics and brahmins were satisfied.”

Taṃ me vataṃ taṃ pana brahmacariyaṃ,

Tassa suciṇṇassa ayaṃ vipāko;

Iddhī jutī balavīriyūpapatti,

Idañca me dhīra mahāvimāna”nti. (jā. 2.22.1592, 1593, 1595) –

“That was my observance, that was my holy life. This is the result of that well-practiced deed: the manifestation of psychic power, splendor, strength, and energy, and this great mansion of mine, O wise one.”

Imasmiñhi puṇṇakajātake dānaṃ brahmacariyanti vuttaṃ.

In this Puṇṇaka Jātaka, giving is called the holy life.

“Kena pāṇi kāmadado, kena pāṇi madhussavo;

Kena te brahmacariyena, puññaṃ pāṇimhi ijjhati.

“By what is your hand a giver of wishes, by what is your hand a flow of honey? By what holy life of yours does merit prosper in your hand?”

Tena pāṇi kāmadado, tena pāṇi madhussavo;

Tena me brahmacariyena, puññaṃ pāṇimhi ijjhatī”ti. (pe. va. 275) –

“By that is my hand a giver of wishes, by that is my hand a flow of honey. By that holy life of mine, merit prospers in my hand.”

Imasmiṃ [V 1.0355] aṅkurapetavatthusmiṃ veyyāvaccaṃ brahmacariyanti vuttaṃ. “Evaṃ kho taṃ, bhikkhave, tittiriyaṃ nāma brahmacariyaṃ ahosī”ti (cūḷava. 311) imasmiṃ tittirajātake pañcasikkhāpadaṃ brahmacariyanti vuttaṃ. “Taṃ kho pana me pañcasikha brahmacariyaṃ neva nibbidāya na virāgāya na nirodhāya, yāvadeva brahmalokūpapattiyā”ti (dī. ni. 2.329) imasmiṃ mahāgovindasutte brahmavihārā brahmacariyanti vuttaṃ. “Ekasmiṃ brahmacariyasmiṃ, sahassaṃ maccuhāyina”nti (saṃ. ni. 1.184) ettha dhammadesanā brahmacariyanti vuttā. “Pare abrahmacārī bhavissanti, mayamettha brahmacārī bhavissāmā”ti (ma. ni. 1.83) sallekhasutte methunavirati brahmacariyanti vuttā.

In this Aṅkura Petavatthu, service is called the holy life. In this Tittira Jātaka, where it is said, “Thus indeed, monks, that was the partridge's holy life” (Cūḷava. 311), the five precepts are called the holy life. In this Mahāgovinda Sutta, where it is said, “But that holy life of mine, O Pañcasikha, led neither to disenchantment, nor to dispassion, nor to cessation—only to rebirth in the Brahma-world” (Dī. Ni. 2.329), the divine abidings are called the holy life. Here, where it is said, “In one holy life, a thousand abandon death” (Saṃ. Ni. 1.184), the teaching of the Dhamma is called the holy life. In the Sallekha Sutta, where it is said, “Others will be unchaste, but we here will be chaste” (Ma. Ni. 1.83), abstinence from sexual intercourse is called the holy life.

“Mayañca [M 1.0348] bhariyā nātikkamāma,

Amhe ca bhariyā nātikkamanti;

Aññatra tāhi brahmacariyaṃ carāma,

Tasmā hi amhaṃ daharā na mīyare”ti. (jā. 1.10.97) –

“We do not transgress against our wives, nor do our wives transgress against us. Except with them, we practice the holy life. Therefore, our young ones do not die.”

Mahādhammapālajātake sadārasantoso brahmacariyanti vutto.

In the Mahādhammapāla Jātaka, contentment with one's own wife is called the holy life.

“Hīnena brahmacariyena, khattiye upapajjati;

Majjhimena ca devattaṃ, uttamena visujjhatī”ti. (jā. 1.8.75) –

“By an inferior holy life, one is reborn among the warrior caste; by a middling one, among the gods; by the highest, one is purified.”

Evaṃ [P 2.0043] nimijātake attadamanavasena kato aṭṭhaṅgiko uposatho brahmacariyanti vutto. “Idaṃ kho pana me, pañcasikha, brahmacariyaṃ ekantanibbidāya virāgāya…pe… ayameva ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo”ti (dī. ni. 2.329) mahāgovindasuttasmiññeva ariyamaggo brahmacariyanti vutto. “Tayidaṃ brahmacariyaṃ iddhañceva phītañca vitthārikaṃ bāhujaññaṃ puthubhūtaṃ yāva devamanussehi suppakāsita”nti (dī. ni. 3.174) pāsādikasutte sikkhattayasaṅgahaṃ sāsanaṃ brahmacariyanti vuttaṃ.

Thus, in the Nimi Jātaka, the eight-factored Uposatha undertaken by way of self-taming is called the holy life. In the Mahāgovinda Sutta, where it is said, “And this holy life of mine, O Pañcasikha, leads solely to disenchantment, to dispassion… this very Noble Eightfold Path” (Dī. Ni. 2.329), the Noble Path itself is called the holy life. In the Pāsādika Sutta, where it is said, “And this holy life is successful and prosperous, widespread, known to many, and has become vast, well-proclaimed among gods and humans” (Dī. Ni. 3.174), the Dispensation comprising the threefold training is called the holy life.

“Api [V 1.0356] ataramānānaṃ, phalāsāva samijjhati;

Vipakkabrahmacariyosmi, evaṃ jānāhi gāmaṇī”ti. (jā. 1.1.8) –

“Even for those not hurrying, the hope for the fruit is accomplished. I am one whose holy life has ripened; thus know, O village headman.”

Ettha ajjhāsayo brahmacariyanti vutto. Idha pana vīriyaṃ brahmacariyanti adhippetaṃ. Vīriyabrahmacariyassa hi idameva suttaṃ. Tadetaṃ ekasmiṃ attabhāve catubbidhassa dukkarassa katattā caturaṅgasamannāgatanti vuttaṃ.

Here, inclination is called the holy life. But in this context, energy is intended as the holy life. For this very discourse is about the holy life of energy. Therefore, because of having performed four kinds of difficult tasks in a single existence, it is said to be “endowed with four factors.”

Tapassī sudaṃ homīti sudanti nipātamattaṃ, tapanissitako homīti attho. Paramatapassīti paramo tapassī, tapanissitakānaṃ uttamo. Lūkho sudaṃ homīti lūkho homi. Jegucchīti pāpajegucchiko. Pavivitto sudaṃ homīti pavivitto ahaṃ homi. Tatrāssu me idaṃ, sāriputtāti tatra caturaṅge brahmacariye idaṃ mama tapassitāya hoti, tapanissitakabhāve mayhaṃ idaṃ acelakāditapassitakattaṃ hotīti dasseti.

I was an ascetic—'sudaṃ' is merely a particle; the meaning is: I was one who relied on austerity. A supreme ascetic—the supreme ascetic, the highest among those who rely on austerity. I was rough—I was rough indeed. One who is disgusted—one who is disgusted by evil. I was solitary—I was solitary indeed. Herein, Sāriputta, this was my practice of austerity in that four-factored holy life; in my state of relying on austerity, this practice of austerity, such as nakedness, was mine—thus he shows.

Tattha [M 1.0349] acelakoti niccelo naggo. Muttācāroti visaṭṭhācāro, uccārakammādīsu lokiyakulaputtācārena virahito, ṭhitakova uccāraṃ karomi, passāvaṃ karomi, khādāmi bhuñjāmi ca. Hatthāpalekhanoti hatthe piṇḍamhi ṭhite jivhāya hatthaṃ apalikhāmi, uccāraṃ vā katvā hatthasmiññeva daṇḍakasaññī hutvā hatthena apalikhāmīti dasseti. Te kira daṇḍakaṃ sattoti paññapenti, tasmā tesaṃ paṭipadaṃ pūrento evamakāsi. Bhikkhāgahaṇatthaṃ ehi bhaddanteti vutto na etīti na ehibhaddantiko. Tena hi tiṭṭha bhaddanteti vuttopi na tiṭṭhatīti na tiṭṭhabhaddantiko. Tadubhayampi [P 2.0044] titthiyā evaṃ etassa vacanaṃ kataṃ bhavissatīti na karonti. Ahampi evaṃ akāsinti dasseti. Abhihaṭanti puretaraṃ gahetvā āhaṭaṃ bhikkhaṃ. Uddissakatanti idaṃ tumhe uddissa katanti evaṃ ārocitabhikkhaṃ. Na nimantananti asukaṃ nāma kulaṃ vā vīthiṃ vā gāmaṃ vā paviseyyāthāti evaṃ nimantitabhikkhampi na sādiyāmi na gaṇhāmi.

Herein, 'naked' means unclothed, bare. 'Of unrestrained conduct' means of abandoned conduct, devoid of the conduct of worldly sons of good family in matters such as excretion; I defecate, urinate, eat, and drink while standing. 'Licking the hand' means: when almsfood is in my hand, I lick my hand with my tongue; or, after defecating, perceiving my hand to be a cleansing stick, I lick my hand—thus he shows. It is said that they declare a stick to be a living being; therefore, fulfilling their practice, he acted thus. When, for the purpose of receiving alms, he is told, 'Come, venerable sir,' he does not come—thus he is not one who comes when told 'Come, venerable sir.' Then, when told, 'Stay, venerable sir,' he also does not stay—thus he is not one who stays when told 'Stay, venerable sir.' The sectarians do not do either of these, thinking, 'In this way, his word will have been followed.' 'I too acted thus'—thus he shows. 'Brought forward' means alms brought from a distance. 'Specifically prepared' means alms announced thus: 'This was prepared for you.' 'Not an invitation' means: I do not consent to nor accept alms offered with an invitation, such as, 'May you enter such-and-such a family, street, or village.'

Na kumbhimukhāti kumbhito uddharitvā diyyamānaṃ bhikkhaṃ na gaṇhāmi. Na kaḷopimukhāti kaḷopīti ukkhali vā pacchi vā. Tatopi na gaṇhāmi. Kasmā? Kumbhikaḷopiyo [V 1.0357] maṃ nissāya kaṭacchunā pahāraṃ labhantīti. Na eḷakamantaranti ummāraṃ antaraṃ katvā diyyamānaṃ na gaṇhāmi. Kasmā? Ayaṃ maṃ nissāya antarakaraṇaṃ labhatīti. Daṇḍamusalesupi eseva nayo. Na dvinnanti dvīsu bhuñjamānesu ekasmiṃ uṭṭhāya dente na gaṇhāmi. Kasmā? Kabaḷantarāyo hotīti. Na gabbhiniyātiādīsu pana gabbhiniyā kucchiyaṃ dārako kilamati, pāyantiyā dārakassa khīrantarāyo hoti, purisantaragatāya ratiantarāyo hotīti na gaṇhāmi. Na saṃkittīsūti saṃkittetvā katabhattesu. Dubbhikkhasamaye kira acelakasāvakā acelakānaṃ atthāya tato tato taṇḍulādīni samādapetvā bhattaṃ pacanti. Ukkaṭṭhācelako tatopi na paṭiggaṇhāti.

Not from the mouth of a pot means: I do not accept alms being given after being drawn from a pot. Not from the mouth of a basket means: a 'kaḷopī' is a cooking pot or a basket. From that too, I do not accept. Why? Because on my account, the pots and baskets might receive a blow from a ladle. Not placed across a threshold means: I do not accept what is given by placing it across a threshold. Why? Because on my account, it becomes an intervening object. The same principle applies to a stick or a pestle. Not from two people means: when two are eating, if one gets up and gives, I do not accept. Why? Because it would be an interruption to their mouthful. Regarding 'not from a pregnant woman' and so on: in the case of a pregnant woman, the child in the womb is troubled; for a nursing woman, it is an interruption to the child's milk; for a woman who has gone to a man, it is an interruption to their love-making—therefore, I do not accept. Not from collected alms means: from meals made by collection. It is said that in a time of famine, the disciples of naked ascetics have rice and other things collected from here and there and cook a meal for the naked ascetics. A naked ascetic of the highest order does not accept even from that.

Na yattha sāti yattha sunakho piṇḍaṃ labhissāmīti upaṭṭhito hoti, tattha tassa adatvā āhaṭaṃ na gaṇhāmi. Kasmā? Etassa piṇḍantarāyo hotīti. Saṇḍasaṇḍacārinīti samūhasamūhacārinī, sace hi acelakaṃ disvā imassa bhikkhaṃ dassāmāti mānusakā bhattagehaṃ pavisanti. Tesu ca pavisantesu kaḷopimukhādīsu nilīnā makkhikā uppatitvā saṇḍasaṇḍā caranti. Tato [M 1.0350] āhaṭaṃ bhikkhaṃ na gaṇhāmi. Kasmā? Maṃ nissāya makkhikānaṃ gocarantarāyo jātoti, ahampi tathā akāsiṃ. Na thusodakanti sabbasassasambhārehi kataṃ loṇasovīrakaṃ. Ettha ca surāpānameva sāvajjaṃ, ayaṃ pana sabbesupi sāvajjasaññī.

Not where a dog is present means: where a dog is present, thinking, 'I will get some alms,' I do not accept what is brought without first giving to it. Why? Because it would be an interruption to its alms. Not where flies move in swarms means: moving in group after group. For if people, upon seeing a naked ascetic, think, 'We will give alms to him,' they enter the dining hall. And as they enter, flies hiding in the mouths of pots and so on fly up and move about in swarms. I do not accept the alms brought from there. Why? Because on my account, an interruption to the flies' feeding ground has occurred. I too acted in that way. Not sour gruel means: a salty and sour gruel made from the ingredients of all kinds of grain. And in this teaching, only the drinking of intoxicants is at fault, but this one perceives fault in all of them.

Ekāgārikoti yo ekasmiññeva gehe bhikkhaṃ labhitvā nivattati. Ekālopikoti yo ekeneva ālopena yāpeti. Dvāgārikādīsupi eseva nayo. Ekissāpi dattiyāti ekāya [P 2.0045] dattiyā. Datti nāma ekā khuddakapāti hoti, yattha aggabhikkhaṃ pakkhipitvā ṭhapenti. Ekāhikanti ekadivasantarikaṃ. Addhamāsikanti addhamāsantarikaṃ. Pariyāyabhattabhojananti vārabhattabhojanaṃ. Ekāhavārena dvīhavārena sattāhavārena aḍḍhamāsavārenāti evaṃ divasavārena ābhataṃ bhattabhojanaṃ.

A one-houser is one who, having received alms at a single house, returns. A one-morseler is one who subsists on a single morsel. The same principle applies to a two-houser and so on. With a single serving means: with one serving. A 'datti' is a small bowl where the first portion of alms is placed and kept. At one-day intervals means: with an interval of one day. At half-month intervals means: with an interval of a half-month. Eating meals by turns means: eating a meal in rotation. This is eating a meal brought in rotation by days, that is, by a turn of one day, two days, seven days, or a half-month.

Sākabhakkhoti allasākabhakkho. Sāmākabhakkhoti sāmākataṇḍulabhakkho. Nīvārādīsu nīvārā nāma tāva araññe sayaṃjātavīhijāti. Daddulanti cammakārehi cammaṃ likhitvā chaḍḍitakasaṭaṃ. Haṭaṃ vuccati silesopi sevālopi kaṇikārādirukkhaniyyāsopi. Kaṇanti kuṇḍakaṃ[V 1.0358]. Ācāmoti bhattaukkhalikāya laggo jhāmaodano, taṃ chaḍḍitaṭṭhāne gahetvā khādati. “Odanakañjiya”ntipi vadanti. Piññākādayo pākaṭā eva. Pavattaphalabhojīti patitaphalabhojī.

An eater of greens is an eater of fresh greens. An eater of sāmāka-millet is an eater of sāmāka-millet grains. Among nīvāra-rice and so on, nīvāra is a species of paddy that grows wild in the forest. Leather-parings are the refuse discarded by leatherworkers after scraping a hide. Slime is said to be both moss and algae, and also the resin of trees such as the kaṇikāra. Rice-powder is fine bran. Scum is the burnt rice stuck to the cooking pot; he takes it from where it has been discarded and eats it. Some also call it 'rice-gruel.' Oil-cake and so on are well-known. An eater of what has fallen is an eater of fallen fruit.

Sāṇānīti sāṇavākacoḷāni. Masāṇānīti missakacoḷāni. Chavadussānīti matasarīrato chaḍḍitavatthāni. Erakatiṇādīni vā ganthetvā katanivāsanāni. Paṃsukūlānīti pathaviyaṃ chaḍḍitanantakāni. Tiritānīti rukkhattacavatthāni. Ajinanti ajinamigacammaṃ. Ajinakkhipanti tadeva majjhe phālitaṃ. Sakhurakantipi vadanti. Kusacīranti kusatiṇaṃ ganthetvā katacīraṃ. Vākacīraphalakacīresupi eseva nayo. Kesakambalanti manussakesehi katakambalaṃ. Yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “yāni kānici, bhikkhave, tantāvutānaṃ vatthānaṃ, kesakambalo tesaṃ paṭikuṭṭho akkhāyati. Kesakambalo, bhikkhave, sīte sīto, uṇhe uṇho, dubbaṇṇo duggandho dukkhasamphaso”ti (a. ni. 3.138). Vālakambalanti assavālādīhi katakambalaṃ. Ulūkapakkhakanti ulūkapattāni ganthetvā katanivāsanaṃ. Ubbhaṭṭhakoti uddhaṃ ṭhitako. Ukkuṭikappadhānamanuyuttoti ukkuṭikavīriyaṃ anuyutto, gacchantopi ukkuṭikova hutvā uppatitvā [M 1.0351] uppatitvā gacchati. Kaṇṭakāpassayikoti [P 2.0046] ayakaṇṭake vā pakatikaṇṭake vā bhūmiyaṃ koṭṭetvā tattha cammaṃ attharitvā ṭhānacaṅkamādīni karomīti dasseti. Seyyanti sayantopi tattheva seyyaṃ kappemi. Sāyaṃ tatiyamassāti sāyatatiyakaṃ. Pāto majjhanhike sāyanti divasassa tikkhattuṃ pāpaṃ pavāhessāmīti udakorohanānuyogaṃ anuyutto viharāmīti dasseti.

Sāṇa garments are robes made of hemp. Masāṇa garments are mixed cloths. Chavadussa garments are clothes discarded from a corpse. Erakatiṇa garments are lower garments made by binding eraka grass or other materials. Paṃsukūla garments are rags discarded on the ground. Tirita garments are clothes made from tree bark. Ajina is the hide of an antelope. Ajinakkhipa is the same hide split in the middle; some also call it sakhuraka. Kusacīra is a robe made by binding kusa grass. The same method applies to bark-fiber robes and wood-fiber robes. Kesakambala is a blanket made of human hair. Regarding this, it is said: 'Whatever woven fabrics exist, bhikkhus, the hair blanket is considered the worst among them. The hair blanket, bhikkhus, is cold in the cold, hot in the heat, ugly, foul-smelling, and uncomfortable to the touch' (Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.138). Vālakambala is a blanket made from horsehair and so on. Ulūkapakkhaka is a lower garment made by binding owl feathers. Ubbhaṭṭhaka means one who stands upright. Ukkuṭikappadhānamanuyutto means one devoted to the exertion of squatting; even while walking, one moves by hopping up and down in a squatting position. Kaṇṭakāpassayika indicates one who, having driven iron spikes or natural thorns into the ground and spread a hide over them, performs practices such as standing and walking meditation there. Seyyaṃ means that even when lying down, one makes one's bed in that very place. Sāyatatiyakaṃ means having the third time in the evening. Pāto majjhanhike sāyanti means morning, noon, and evening. This indicates one who lives devoted to the practice of entering the water, thinking: 'I will wash away evil three times a day.'

156. Nekavassagaṇikanti nekavassagaṇasañjātaṃ. Rajojallanti rajamalaṃ, idaṃ attano rajojallakavatasamādānakālaṃ sandhāya vadati. Jegucchisminti pāpajigucchanabhāve. Yāva udakabindumhipīti yāva udakathevakepi mama dayā paccupaṭṭhitā hoti, ko pana vādo aññesu sakkharakaṭhaladaṇḍakavālikādīsu. Te kira udakabinduṃ ca ete ca sakkharakaṭhalādayo khuddakapāṇāti paññapenti. Tenāha “yāva udakabindumhipi me dayā paccupaṭṭhitā hotī”ti. Udakabindumpi na hanāmi na vināsemi, kiṃ kāraṇā. Māhaṃ khuddake pāṇe visamagate saṅghātaṃ āpādesinti. Ninnathalatiṇaggarukkhasākhādīsu visamaṭṭhāne gate udakabindusaṅkhāte khuddakapāṇe saṅghātaṃ [V 1.0359] vadhaṃ mā āpādesinti. Etamatthaṃ “satova abhikkamāmī”ti dasseti. Acelakesu kira bhūmiṃ akkantakālato pabhuti sīlavā nāma natthi. Bhikkhācāraṃ gacchantāpi dussīlāva hutvā gacchanti, upaṭṭhākānaṃ gehe bhuñjantāpi dussīlāva hutvā bhuñjanti. Āgacchantāpi dussīlāva hutvā āgacchanti. Yadā pana morapiñchena phalakaṃ sammajjitvā sīlaṃ adhiṭṭhāya nisīdanti, tadā sīlavantā nāma honti.

156. Nekavassagaṇika means originating from a group of many rains. Rajojalla means dust and dirt; this is said with reference to the time of undertaking one's own vow of dust and dirt. Jegucchī refers to the state of abhorring evil. 'Even for a drop of water' means that my compassion is present even for a single drop of water, how much more so for other things like gravel, hard lumps, sticks, and sand. They indeed declare a drop of water and these gravel, hard lumps, and so on, to be small living beings. Therefore, it is said: 'Even for a drop of water, my compassion is present.' 'I do not kill or destroy even a drop of water—why? Lest I should cause the slaughter of small beings who have gone to an uneven place.' Lest I should cause the slaughter and death of small beings, designated as a drop of water, who have gone to uneven places like low-lying areas, high ground, grass tips, tree branches, and so on. This meaning is shown by 'mindfully I proceed.' It is said that among the naked ascetics, from the time they step on the ground, there is no one called virtuous. Even when going for alms, they go having become unvirtuous. Even when eating in the homes of supporters, they eat having become unvirtuous. Even when returning, they return having become unvirtuous. But when they sweep a plank with a peacock feather and sit down, having resolved on the moral precepts, then they are called virtuous.

Vanakammikanti kandamūlaphalāphalādīnaṃ atthāya vane vicarantaṃ. Vanena vananti vanato vanaṃ, esa nayo sabbattha. Saṃpatāmīti gacchāmi. Āraññakoti araññe jātavuddho, idaṃ attano ājīvakakālaṃ sandhāya vadati. Bodhisatto kira pāsaṇḍapariggaṇhaṇatthāya taṃ pabbajjaṃ pabbaji, niratthakabhāvaṃ pana ñatvāpi na uppabbajjito, bodhisattā hi yaṃ yaṃ ṭhānaṃ upenti, tato anivattitadhammā honti, pabbajitvā pana mā maṃ koci addasāti tatova araññaṃ paviṭṭho. Tenevāha “mā maṃ te addasaṃsu ahañca mā te addasa”nti.

Vanakammika means one who wanders in the forest for the sake of roots, tubers, fruits, and other such things. Vanena vanaṃ means from forest to forest; this is the method everywhere. Saṃpatāmi means I go. Āraññaka means one born and grown up in the wilderness; this is said with reference to the time when he was an Ājīvaka ascetic. The Bodhisatta, it is said, undertook that going forth in order to investigate the various sects, but even after realizing its futility, he did not disrobe. For Bodhisattas are of a nature not to turn back from whatever state they have entered. Having gone forth, he entered that very wilderness, thinking, 'May no one see me.' Therefore he said: 'May they not see me, and may I not see them.'

Goṭṭhāti [P 2.0047] govajā. Paṭṭhitagāvoti nikkhantagāvo. Tattha catukkuṇḍikoti vananteyeva ṭhito gopālakānaṃ gāvīhi saddhiṃ apagatabhāvaṃ disvā [M 1.0352] dve hatthe dve ca jaṇṇukāni bhūmiyaṃ ṭhapetvā evaṃ catukkuṇḍiko upasaṅkamitvāti attho. Tāni sudaṃ āhāremīti mahallakavacchakānaṃ gomayāni kasaṭāni nirojāni honti, tasmā tāni vajjetvā yāni taruṇavacchakānaṃ khīrapāneneva vaḍḍhantānaṃ saojāni gomayāni tāni kucchipūraṃ khāditvā puna vanasaṇḍameva pavisati. Taṃ sandhāyāha “tāni sudaṃ āhāremī”ti. Yāvakīvañca meti yattakaṃ kālaṃ mama sakaṃ muttakarīsaṃ aparikkhīṇaṃ hoti. Yāva me dvāravaḷañjo pavattittha, tāva tadeva āhāremīti attho. Kāle pana gacchante gacchante parikkhīṇamaṃsalohito upacchinnadvāravaḷañjo vacchakānaṃ gomayāni āhāremi. Mahāvikaṭabhojanasminti mahante vikaṭabhojane, apakatibhojaneti attho.

Goṭṭhā means cattle herds. Paṭṭhitagāvo means the cows have gone out. There, catukkuṇḍiko means this: standing at the edge of the forest and seeing that the cowherds have departed with the cows, one places two hands and two knees on the ground and thus approaches on all fours. 'I feed on them' refers to this: the dung of older calves is coarse and without nutrients. Therefore, avoiding that, he eats his fill of the nutritious dung of young calves who grow by drinking milk alone, and then re-enters the thicket. This is the meaning of 'I feed on them.' 'As long as' means for as long as my own urine and feces were not exhausted. The meaning is, as long as my excretory passage remained functional, I continued to feed on that alone. But as time passed, my flesh and blood wasted away, my excretory passage ceased to function, and I fed on the dung of calves. Mahāvikaṭabhojanasmiṃ means in greatly repulsive food, that is, unnatural food.

157. Tatrāssudaṃ, sāriputta, bhiṃsanakassa vanasaṇḍassa bhiṃsanakatasmiṃ hotīti. Tatrāti purimavacanāpekkhanaṃ. Sudanti padapūraṇamatte nipāto. Sāriputtāti ālapanaṃ. Ayaṃ panettha atthayojanā – tatrāti yaṃ vuttaṃ aññataraṃ bhiṃsanakaṃ vanasaṇḍanti, tatra yo so bhiṃsanako vanasaṇḍo [V 1.0360] vutto, tassa bhiṃsanakassa vanasaṇḍassa bhiṃsanakatasmiṃ hoti, bhiṃsanakakiriyāya hotīti attho. Kiṃ hoti? Idaṃ hoti, yo koci avītarāgo…pe… lomāni haṃsantīti.

157. "There, Sāriputta, in that frightening forest thicket, it is frightening." Tatra refers back to the previous statement. Sudaṃ is a particle used merely to fill out the phrase. Sāriputta is a vocative. Here, the application of the meaning is this: Tatra refers to that frightening forest thicket that was mentioned. In that frightening forest thicket, it is frightening—meaning it exists in a state of being frightening, by means of frightening action. What is it? It is this: any being not free from lust... (and so on) ... their hairs stand on end.

Atha vā tatrāti sāmiatthe bhummaṃ. Su iti nipāto. Kiṃ su nāma te bhonto samaṇabrāhmaṇātiādīsu viya. Idanti adhippetamatthaṃ paccakkhaṃ viya katvā dassanavacanaṃ. Sudanti su idaṃ, sandhivasena ikāralopo veditabbo. Cakkhundriyaṃ itthindriyaṃ anaññātaññassāmītindriyaṃ kiṃ sūdhavittantiādīsu viya. Ayaṃ panettha atthayojanā, tassa, sāriputta, bhiṃsanakassa vanasaṇḍassa bhiṃsanakatasmiṃ idaṃsu hotīti. Bhiṃsanakatasminti bhiṃsanakabhāveti attho. Ekassa takārassa lopo daṭṭhabbo. “Bhiṃsanakattasmi”ntiyeva vā pāṭho[P 2.0048], bhiṃsanakatāya iti vā vattabbe liṅgavipallāso kato, nimittatthe cetaṃ bhummavacanaṃ. Tasmā evaṃ sambandho veditabbo, bhiṃsanakabhāve idaṃsu hoti, bhiṃsanakabhāvanimittaṃ bhiṃsanakabhāvahetu, bhiṃsanakabhāvapaccayā idaṃsu hoti. Yo koci avītarāgo taṃ vanasaṇḍaṃ pavisati. Yebhuyyena lomāni haṃsanti [M 1.0353] bahutarāni lomāni haṃsanti, uddhaṃ mukhāni sūcisadisāni kaṇṭakasadisāni ca hutvā tiṭṭhanti, appāni na haṃsanti, bahutarānaṃ vā sattānaṃ haṃsanti, appakānaṃ atisūrapurisānaṃ na haṃsantīti.

Alternatively, tatra is a locative in the sense of proximity. Su is a particle, as in, 'What, sirs, is the name of those venerable ascetics and brahmins?' and so on. Idaṃ is a demonstrative word, showing the intended meaning as if directly perceived. Sudaṃ is su idaṃ; the elision of the vowel i due to sandhi should be understood, as in 'the faculty of the eye, the faculty of femininity, the faculty of “I shall know the unknown,” and “what wealth is here?”' and so on. Herein, this is the application of the meaning: 'Sāriputta, in that terrifying forest grove, this indeed happens.' Bhiṃsanakatasmiṃ means 'in the state of being terrifying.' The elision of one t should be noted. Alternatively, the reading could be bhiṃsanakattasmiṃ, or, where bhiṃsanakatāya should be said, a change of gender has been made, and this is a locative in the sense of a cause. Therefore, the connection should be understood thus: 'In the state of being terrifying, this indeed happens'; it happens as a sign of the terrifying state, as a cause of the terrifying state, conditioned by the terrifying state. Any being not free from passion who enters that forest grove—for the most part, their hairs stand on end. Most of their hairs stand on end, rising straight up like needles or thorns. Few do not stand on end; or, the hairs of most beings stand on end, but not those of a few exceptionally courageous men.

Antaraṭṭhakāti māghamāsassa avasāne catasso, phagguṇamāsassa ādimhi catassoti evaṃ ubhinnaṃ antare aṭṭharatti. Abbhokāseti mahāsatto himapātasamaye rattiṃ abbhokāse viharati, athassa lomakūpesu āvutamuttā viya himabindūni tiṭṭhanti, sarīraṃ setadukūlapārutaṃ viya hoti. Divā vanasaṇḍeti divā himabindūsu sūriyātapasamphassena vigatesu assāsopi bhaveyya, ayaṃ pana sūriye uggacchanteyeva vanasaṇḍaṃ pavisati, tatrāpissa sūriyātapena paggharantaṃ himaṃ sarīreyeva patati. Divā abbhokāse viharāmi rattiṃ vanasaṇḍeti gimhakāle kiresa divā abbhokāse vihāsi, tenassa kacchehi sedadhārā mucciṃsu, rattiṃ assāso bhaveyya, ayaṃ pana sūriye atthaṃ gacchanteyeva vanasaṇḍaṃ pavisati. Athassa divā gahitausme vanasaṇḍe aṅgārakāsuyaṃ pakkhitto viya attabhāvo paridayhittha. Anacchariyāti anuacchariyā. Paṭibhāsīti upaṭṭhāsi.

Antaraṭṭhakā means the eight nights in between: four at the end of the month of Māgha and four at the beginning of the month of Phagguṇa. Abbhokāse (in the open): The Great Being dwells in the open air at night during the time of frost-fall. Then, drops of frost settle in his hair-pores like covered pearls, and his body appears as if wrapped in white linen. Divā vanasaṇḍe (by day in a forest grove): By day, when the drops of frost have vanished through contact with the sun's heat, there might be some relief. But he enters the forest grove just as the sun is rising, and there the melting frost, due to the sun's heat, falls right onto his body. Divā abbhokāse viharāmi rattiṃ vanasaṇḍe (I dwell by day in the open and at night in a forest grove): It is said that in the hot season he dwelt by day in the open air. Because of this, streams of sweat poured from his armpits. At night, there might be some relief, but he enters the forest grove just as the sun is setting. Then, in the forest grove which had absorbed the day's heat, his body was scorched as if thrown into a pit of embers. Anacchariyā means 'not wonderful.' Paṭibhāsi means 'it occurred to me,' 'it appeared.'

Sotattoti [V 1.0361] divā ātapena rattiṃ vanausmāya sutatto. Sosinnoti rattiṃ himena divā himodakena suṭṭhu tinto. Bhiṃsanaketi bhayajanake. Naggoti niccelo. Nivāsanapārupane hi sati sītaṃ vā uṇhaṃ vā na atibādheyya, tampi me natthīti dasseti. Na caggimāsinoti aggimpi na upagato. Esanāpasutoti suddhiesanatthāya pasuto, payutto. Munīti, tadā attānaṃ munīti katvā katheti.

Sotatto means 'well-heated,' scorched by the sun's heat during the day and by the forest's heat at night. Sosinno means 'well-soaked,' thoroughly drenched by frost at night and by frost-water during the day. Bhiṃsanake means 'fear-inducing,' terrifying. Naggo means 'naked,' without clothes. For if one had lower and upper garments, one would not be excessively troubled by cold or heat, but 'even that I do not have'—this is what he shows. Na caggimāsi means 'not even having approached a fire.' Esanāpasuto means 'intent on the quest,' engaged in the quest for purity. Munī: At that time, considering himself a sage, he speaks thus.

Chavaṭṭhikānīti upaḍḍhadaḍḍhāni aṭṭhīni. Upadhāyāti yathā sīsūpadhānañca pādūpadhānañca paññāyati, evaṃ santharitvā tattha seyyaṃ kappemīti dasseti. Gāmaṇḍalāti [P 2.0049] gopāladārakā. Te kira bodhisattassa santikaṃ gantvā, sumedha, tvaṃ imasmiṃ ṭhāne kasmā nisinno, kathehīti vadanti. Bodhisatto adhomukho nisīdati, na katheti. Atha naṃ te akathetuṃ na dassāmāti parivāretvā oṭṭhubhanti sarīre kheḷaṃ pātenti. Bodhisatto [M 1.0354] evampi na katheti. Atha naṃ tvaṃ na kathesīti omuttenti passāvamassa upari vissajjenti. Bodhisatto evampi na kathetiyeva. Tato naṃ kathehi kathehīti paṃsukena okiranti. Bodhisatto evampi na kathetiyeva. Athassa na kathesīti daṇḍakasalākā gahetvā kaṇṇasotesu pavesenti. Bodhisatto dukkhā tibbā kaṭukā vedanā adhivāsento kassaci kiñci na karissāmīti matako viya acchati. Tenāha “na kho panāhaṃ, sāriputta, abhijānāmi tesu pāpakaṃ cittaṃ uppādetā”ti. Na mayā tesu pāpakaṃ cittampi uppāditanti attho. Upekkhāvihārasmiṃ hotīti upekkhāvihāro hoti. Vihāro eva hi vihārasminti vutto. Teneva ca “idaṃsu me”ti etthāpi ayaṃsu meti evaṃ attho veditabbo. Iminā nayena aññānipi evarūpāni padāni veditabbāni. Iminā ito ekanavutikappe pūritaṃ upekkhāvihāraṃ dasseti. Yaṃ sandhāyāha –

`Chavaṭṭhikāni` means 'half-burnt bones.' `Upadhāya` means 'having placed as a support,' indicating, 'I will arrange them as one would a headrest and footrest, and make my bed there.' `Gāmaṇḍalā` means 'cowherd lads.' It is said that they approached the Bodhisatta and said, 'Sumedha, why are you sitting in this place? Speak!' The Bodhisatta sat with his head down and did not speak. Then they said, 'We will not let you not speak,' and surrounding him, they spat, letting saliva fall on his body. Still, the Bodhisatta did not speak. Then they said, 'You will not speak?' and urinated, releasing it upon him. Even then, the Bodhisatta did not speak. Next, they said, 'Speak, speak!' and scattered dust over him. Still, the Bodhisatta did not speak. Then they said, 'You will not speak?' and, taking sticks and twigs, thrust them into his ear canals. The Bodhisatta endured the painful, sharp, and bitter feelings, remaining still as if dead, thinking, 'I will not do anything to anyone.' Therefore, he said, 'But, Sāriputta, I do not recall having aroused any evil thought toward them.' The meaning is, 'I did not even arouse an evil thought toward them.' `Upekkhāvihārasmiṃ hoti` means 'he abides in equanimity.' For `vihāro` (abiding) is indeed expressed as `vihārasmiṃ.` And by this same token, in the phrase `idaṃsu me,` the meaning should be understood as `ayaṃsu me` (this is to me). In this way, other similar phrases should be understood. By this, he shows the abiding in equanimity that was fulfilled ninety-one eons ago. Referring to this, he says:

“Sukhapatto na rajjāmi, dukkhe na homi dummano;

Sabbattha tulito homi, esā me upekkhāpāramī”ti.

When encountering happiness, I am not impassioned; when encountering suffering, I am not dismayed. I am balanced in all circumstances; this is my perfection of equanimity.

Dukkarakārikādisuddhivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of purification by means of difficult practices and so forth is completed.

Āhārasuddhivaṇṇanā

The Exposition of the Purity of Food

158. Āhārena [V 1.0362] suddhīti kolādinā ekaccena parittakaāhārena sakkā sujjhitunti evaṃdiṭṭhino honti. Evamāhaṃsūti evaṃ vadanti. Kolehīti padarehi. Kolodakanti kolāni madditvā katapānakaṃ. Kolavikatinti kolasāḷavakolapūvakolaguḷādikolavikāraṃ. Etaparamoti etaṃ pamāṇaṃ paramaṃ assāti etaparamo. Tadā ekanavutikappamatthake pana na beluvapakkatālapakkapamāṇo kolo hoti, yaṃ etarahi kolassa pamāṇaṃ, ettakova hotīti attho.

158. “By food there is purity”—some hold the view that it is possible to be purified by a minimal amount of food, such as jujube fruits and so on. Thus they speak. “Kolehī” means with jujube fruits. “Kolodaka” is a drink made by crushing kola fruits. “Kolavikati” means various preparations made with kola, such as kola relish, kola cakes, kola sweets, and other kola derivatives. “Etaparamo” means this is the highest limit—this is the ultimate extent.
