But at that time, at the head of the ninety-first eon, the kola fruit was not the size of a ripe beluva or tala fruit; it was only this size, the size of a kola fruit now—that is the meaning.

159. Adhimattakasimānanti ativiya kisabhāvaṃ. Āsītikapabbāni vā kāḷapabbāni vāti yathā āsītikavalliyā vā kāḷavalliyā vā sandhiṭṭhānesu milāyitvā majjhe unnatunnatāni honti, evaṃ mayhaṃ aṅgapaccaṅgāni hontīti dasseti. Oṭṭhapadanti [P 2.0050] yathā oṭṭhassa padaṃ majjhe gambhīraṃ hoti, evamevaṃ bodhisattassa milāte maṃsalohite vaccadvārassa antopaviṭṭhattā ānisadaṃ majjhe gambhīraṃ hoti. Athassa bhūmiyaṃ nisinnaṭṭhānaṃ sarapoṅkhena [M 1.0355] akkantaṃ viya majjhe unnataṃ hoti. Vaṭṭanāvaḷīti yathā rajjuyā āvunitvā katā vaṭṭanāvaḷī vaṭṭanānaṃ antarantarā ninnā hoti, vaṭṭanaṭṭhānesu unnatā, evaṃ piṭṭhikaṇṭako unnatāvanato hoti, jarasālāya gopānasiyoti jiṇṇasālāya gopānasiyo, tā vaṃsato muccitvā maṇḍale patiṭṭhahanti, maṇḍalato muccitvā bhūmiyanti; evaṃ ekā upari hoti, ekā heṭṭhāti oluggaviluggā bhavanti. Bodhisattassa pana na evaṃ phāsuḷiyo, tassa hi lohite chinne maṃse milāte phāsuḷantarehi cammāni heṭṭhā otiṇṇāni, taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ.

159. “Exceedingly emaciated” means excessively thin. “Like the joints of a withered vine or a black vine”—just as the joints of a withered vine or a black vine shrivel at the points of connection and become raised in the middle, so my limbs became like that—this is what is being shown. “Like a camel's hoof”—just as a camel’s footprint is deeply hollowed in the middle, so too, due to the Bodhisatta’s shriveled flesh and blood, his buttocks became deeply hollowed. Moreover, the place where he sat on the ground became raised in the middle, as if pressed by the butt of an arrow. “Like the coils of a rope”—just as when a rope is coiled, the spaces between the coils are sunken while the coils themselves are raised, so the spine became raised and bent. “Like the rafters of an old barn”—the rafters of an old barn, having come loose from the ridge-pole, fall apart; thus, one is above, another below, hanging loosely. The Bodhisatta's ribs, however, were not exactly like that; for him, when the flesh and blood had withered, the skin sank down between the ribs. This is what is meant by this.

Okkhāyikāti heṭṭhā anupaviṭṭhā. Tassa kira lohite chinne maṃse milāte akkhiāvāṭakā matthaluṅgaṃ āhacca aṭṭhaṃsu, tenassa evarūpā akkhitārakā ahesuṃ. Āmakacchinnoti atitaruṇakāle chinno, so hi vātātapena saṃphusati ceva milāyati ca. Yāvassu me, sāriputtāti, sāriputta, mayhaṃ udaracchavi yāva piṭṭhikaṇṭakaṃ allīnā hoti. Atha vā yāvassu me, sāriputta, bhāriyabhāriyā ahosi dukkarakārikā, mayhaṃ udaracchavi yāva piṭṭhikaṇṭakaṃ allīnā ahosīti evamettha sambandho veditabbo. Piṭṭhikaṇṭakaṃyeva pariggaṇhāmīti [V 1.0363] sahaudaracchaviṃ gaṇhāmi. Udaracchaviṃyeva pariggaṇhāmīti sahapiṭṭhikaṇṭakaṃ gaṇhāmi. Avakujjo papatāmīti tassa hi uccārapassāvatthāya nisinnassa passāvo neva nikkhamati, vaccaṃ pana ekaṃ dve kaṭakaṭṭhimattaṃ nikkhamati. Balavadukkhaṃ uppādeti. Sarīrato sedā muccanti, tattheva avakujjo bhūmiyaṃ patati. Tenāha “avakujjo papatāmī”ti. Tameva kāyanti taṃ ekanavutikappamatthake kāyaṃ. Mahāsaccakasutte pana pacchimabhavikakāyaṃ sandhāya imameva kāyanti āha. Pūtimūlānīti maṃse vā lohite vā sati tiṭṭhanti. Tassa pana abhāve cammakhaṇḍe lomāni viya hattheyeva lagganti, taṃ sandhāyāha “pūtimūlāni lomāni kāyasmā patantī”ti.

“Sunken” means deeply recessed. It is said that as his blood diminished and his flesh withered, the sockets of his eyes reached his brain, and thus his eyeballs appeared as they did. “Like a bitter gourd cut while raw” means cut at a very young age, so it was exposed to wind and heat, causing it to shrivel. “So much so, Sāriputta”—Sāriputta, the skin of my belly clung to my spine. Or alternatively, “So much so, Sāriputta, was my arduous striving, that the skin of my belly clung to my spine”—this is how the connection should be understood. “I grasp only the spine”—I grasp it together with the belly skin. “I grasp only the belly skin”—I grasp it together with the spine. “I fall flat on my face”—for him, when sitting down to defecate and urinate, urine would not come out, and only one or two pellets of feces, the size of a clearing-nut seed, would pass. This caused intense pain. Sweat poured from his body, and right there, he fell flat on his face on the ground. Hence it is said, “I fall flat on my face.” “That very body”—that body at the head of the ninety-first eon. But in the Mahāsaccaka Sutta, referring to the body of his last existence, he says, “this very body.” “With rotten roots”—they remain when there is flesh or blood. But in their absence, the hairs come away in the hand as if from a piece of hide. This is what is meant by “the hairs, with rotten roots, fall from my body.”

Alamariyañāṇadassanavisesanti [P 2.0051] ariyabhāvaṃ kātuṃ samatthaṃ lokuttaramaggaṃ. Imissāyeva ariyāya paññāyāti vipassanāpaññāya anadhigamā. Yāyaṃ ariyāti yā ayaṃ maggapaññā adhigatā. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yathā etarahi vipassanāpaññāya adhigatattā maggapaññā adhigatā, evaṃ ekanavutikappamatthake [M 1.0356] vipassanāpaññāya anadhigatattā lokuttaramaggapaññaṃ nādhigatosmīti, majjhimabhāṇakattherā panāhu, imissāyevāti vuttapaññāpi yāyaṃ ariyāti vuttapaññāpi maggapaññāyeva. Atha ne bhikkhū āhaṃsu “evaṃ sante maggassa anadhigatattā maggaṃ nādhigatosmīti idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti, bhante”ti. Āvuso, kiñcāpi dīpetuṃ na sakkomi, dvepi pana maggapaññāyevāti, etadeva cettha yuttaṃ. Itarathā hi yā ayanti niddeso ananurūpo siyā.

“Sufficient for the distinction of noble knowledge and vision” means the supramundane path, which is capable of producing the noble state. “By this very noble wisdom” means: due to the non-attainment of insight wisdom. “Which is noble” means this path wisdom that has been attained. This is what is said: just as at present, because insight wisdom has been attained, path wisdom is attained, so too, at the head of the ninety-first aeon, because insight wisdom was not attained, I did not attain the supramundane path wisdom. The elders who are reciters of the Middle-Length Discourses, however, said: both the wisdom referred to as “by this very” and the wisdom referred to as “which is noble” are path wisdom itself. Then the monks said to them, “Venerable sirs, if that is so, then this is what is said: ‘Because the path was not attained, I did not attain the path.’” They replied, “Friends, although I cannot explain it, both are indeed path wisdom.” This alone is proper here. Otherwise, the exposition beginning with “which is” would be unsuitable.

Āhārasuddhivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition of the Purity of Food is completed.

Saṃsārasuddhiādivaṇṇanā

An Exposition on Purification through the Cycle of Existence and So Forth

160. Saṃsārena suddhīti bahukaṃ saṃsaritvā sujjhantīti vadanti. Upapattiyā suddhīti bahukaṃ upapajjitvā sujjhantīti vadanti. Āvāsena suddhīti bahūsu ṭhānesu vasitvā sujjhantīti vadanti. Tīsupi ṭhānesu saṃsaraṇakavasena saṃsāro. Upapajjanakavasena upapatti. Vasanakavasena āvāsoti khandhāyeva vuttā. Yaññenāti bahuyāge yajitvā sujjhantīti vadanti. Muddhāvasittenāti [V 1.0364] tīhi saṅkhehi khattiyābhisekena muddhani abhisittena. Aggipāricariyāyāti bahuaggiparicaraṇena sujjhantīti vadanti.

160. 'By wandering, purity,' they say, meaning one is purified by wandering much. 'By rebirth, purity,' they say, meaning one is purified by being reborn much. 'By dwelling, purity,' they say, meaning one is purified by dwelling in many places. In all three cases, 'wandering' (saṃsāra) is in the sense of wandering on; 'rebirth' (upapatti) is in the sense of being reborn; and 'dwelling' (āvāsa) is in the sense of residing—it is just the aggregates that are spoken of. 'By sacrifice,' they say, meaning one is purified by performing many sacrifices. 'By one anointed on the head' means by one anointed on the head with the royal consecration by means of three conch shells. 'By fire-worship,' they say, meaning one is purified by much tending of the fire.

161. Daharoti taruṇo. Yuvāti yobbanena samannāgato. Susukāḷakesoti suṭṭhu kāḷakeso. Bhadrena yobbanena samannāgatoti imināssa yena yobbanena samannāgato yuvā, taṃ yobbanaṃ bhaddaṃ laddhakanti dasseti. Paṭhamena vayasāti paṭhamavayo nāma tettiṃsa vassāni, tena samannāgatoti attho, paññāveyyattiyenāti paññāveyyattibhāvena. Jiṇṇoti jarājiṇṇo. Vuddhoti vaḍḍhitvā ṭhitaaṅgapaccaṅgo. Mahallakoti jātimahallako. Addhagatoti bahuaddhānaṃ gato cirakālātikkanto. Vayo anuppattoti vassasatassa tatiyakoṭṭhāsaṃ pacchimavayaṃ anuppatto. Āsītiko me vayo vattatīti imaṃ kira suttaṃ bhagavā parinibbānasaṃvacchare kathesi. Tasmā evamāha. Paramāyāti uttamāya. Satiyātiādīsu padasatampi padasahassampi vadantasseva gahaṇasamatthatā [P 2.0052] sati nāma. Tadeva ādhāraṇaupanibandhanasamatthatā gati nāma. Evaṃ gahitaṃ dhāritaṃ sajjhāyaṃ kātuṃ [M 1.0357] samatthavīriyaṃ dhiti nāma. Tassa atthañca kāraṇañca dassanasamatthatā paññāveyyattiyaṃ nāma.

161. 'Dahara' means young. 'Yuvā' means endowed with youth. 'Susukāḷakesa' means having very black hair. 'Bhadrena yobbanena samannāgata' (endowed with fine youth) indicates that the youth with which he is endowed is a fine, acquired youth. 'Paṭhamena vayasā' (in the first stage of life) means endowed with the first stage of life, which is thirty-three years. 'Paññāveyyattiyena' means with the distinction of wisdom. 'Jiṇṇa' means aged by old age. 'Vuddha' means one whose limbs and appendages have grown and are established. 'Mahallaka' means old by birth. 'Addhagata' means one who has gone a long way, who has passed a long time. 'Vayo anuppatta' means having reached the final stage of life, the last third of a hundred years. 'My age is eighty years'—it is said the Blessed One spoke this discourse in the year of his final passing away; hence he spoke thus. 'Paramāya' means supreme. In 'satiyā' (with mindfulness) and so on: the ability to grasp even a hundred or a thousand phrases as they are being spoken is called mindfulness (sati). That very ability to retain and connect is called understanding (gati). The energy capable of reciting what has been thus grasped and retained is called perseverance (dhiti). The ability to see its meaning and reason is called the distinction of wisdom (paññāveyyattiya).

Daḷhadhammā dhanuggahoti daḷhaṃ dhanuṃ gahetvā ṭhito issāso. Daḷhadhanu nāma dvisahassathāmaṃ vuccati, dvisahassathāmaṃ nāma yassa āropitassa jiyābaddho lohasīsādīnaṃ bhāro daṇḍe gahetvā yāva kaṇḍappamāṇā ukkhittassa pathavito muccati. Sikkhitoti dasa dvādasa vassāni ācariyakule uggahitasippo. Katahatthoti koci sippameva uggaṇhāti. Katahattho na hoti, ayaṃ pana katahattho ciṇṇavasībhāvo. Katūpāsanoti rājakulādīsu dassitasippo. Lahukena asanenāti anto susiraṃ katvā tūlādīni pūretvā katalākhāparikammena sallahukakaṇḍena. Evaṃ katañhi ekausabhagāmī dve usabhāni gacchati, aṭṭhausabhagāmī soḷasausabhāni gacchati. Appakasirenāti nidukkhena. Atipāteyyāti atikkameyya. Evaṃ adhimattasatimantoti yathā so dhanuggaho taṃ vidatthicaturaṅgulachāyaṃ sīghaṃ eva atikkameti, evaṃ padasatampi padasahassampi uggahetuṃ upadhāretuṃ sajjhāyituṃ atthakāraṇāni ca upaparikkhituṃ samatthāti attho. Aññatra asitapītakhāyitasāyitāti asitapītādīni hi bhagavatāpi kātabbāni honti, bhikkhūhipi. Tasmā tesaṃ karaṇamattakālaṃ ṭhapetvāti dasseti.

'Daḷhadhammā dhanuggaho' means an archer standing holding a strong bow. A 'strong bow' is said to have a strength of two thousand. A strength of two thousand means that when the bow is strung, a weight of iron heads and so on attached to the bowstring, when held on the bow stave and lifted to the height of an arrow, is released from the ground. 'Sikkhita' means one who has learned the craft in a teacher's family for ten or twelve years. 'Katahattha' (skilled-handed): someone may learn the craft but not be skilled-handed; this one, however, is skilled-handed, his practice having reached a state of mastery. 'Katūpāsana' means one who has demonstrated his craft in royal families and so on. 'Lahukena asanena' (with a light arrow) means with a very light shaft, made by hollowing it out, filling it with cotton and the like, and finishing it with lacquer. An arrow made thus, which would normally travel one usabha, travels two usabhas; one that would travel eight usabhas, travels sixteen usabhas. 'Appakasirena' means without difficulty. 'Atipāteyya' means it would surpass. 'Evaṃ adhimattasatimanto' (thus with exceedingly intense mindfulness) means: just as that archer swiftly surpasses the shadow of a span and four fingers, so too is one capable of learning, retaining, reciting a hundred or a thousand phrases, and examining their meanings and reasons. 'Aññatra asitapītakhāyitasāyitā' (except for eating, drinking, chewing, and tasting)—for eating, drinking, and so on must be done by the Blessed One and also by the monks. Therefore, this shows that only the time for performing these actions is set aside.

Apariyādinnāyevāti [V 1.0365] aparikkhīṇāyeva. Sace hi eko bhikkhu kāyānupassanaṃ pucchati, añño vedanānupassanaṃ, añño cittānupassanaṃ, ayyo dhammānupassanaṃ. Iminā puṭṭhaṃ ahaṃ pucchissāmīti eko ekaṃ na oloketi. Evaṃ santepi tesaṃ vāro paññāyati. Evaṃ buddhānaṃ pana vāro na paññāyati, vidatthicaturaṅgulachāyaṃ atikkamato puretaraṃyeva bhagavā cuddasavidhena kāyānupassanaṃ, navavidhena vedanānupassanaṃ, soḷasavidhena cittānupassanaṃ, pañcavidhena dhammānupassanaṃ katheti. Tiṭṭhantu vā tāva ete cattāro. Sace hi aññe cattāro sammappadhānesu, aññe iddhipādesu, aññe pañca indriyesu, aññe pañca balesu, aññe satta bojjhaṅgesu, aññe aṭṭha maggaṅgesu pañhaṃ puccheyyuṃ, tampi bhagavā [P 2.0053] katheyya. Tiṭṭhantu vā ete aṭṭha. Sace aññe sattatiṃsa janā bodhipakkhiyesu pañhaṃ [M 1.0358] puccheyyuṃ, tampi bhagavā tāvadeva katheyya. Kasmā? Yāvatā hi lokiyamahājanā ekaṃ padaṃ kathenti. Tāva ānandatthero aṭṭha padāni katheti. Ānandatthere pana ekaṃ padaṃ kathenteyeva bhagavā soḷasapadāni katheti. Kasmā? Bhagavato hi jivhā mudukā dantāvaraṇaṃ suphusitaṃ vacanaṃ agalitaṃ bhavaṅgaparivāso lahuko. Tenāha “apariyādinnāyevassa, sāriputta, tathāgatassa dhammadesanā”ti.

'Apariyādinnāyeva' means not at all depleted. For if one monk asks about the contemplation of the body, another about the contemplation of feelings, another about the contemplation of the mind, and another about the contemplation of phenomena, no one looks at another thinking, 'I will ask what this one has asked.' Even so, their turn is apparent. But for the Buddhas, no such turn is apparent. Even before the shadow of a span and four fingers has passed, the Blessed One can speak on the contemplation of the body in fourteen ways, the contemplation of feelings in nine ways, the contemplation of the mind in sixteen ways, and the contemplation of phenomena in five ways. Let these four stand. If four others were to ask questions on the right strivings, others on the bases of psychic power, others on the five faculties, others on the five powers, others on the seven factors of enlightenment, and others on the eight path factors, the Blessed One could speak on that too. Let these eight stand. If thirty-seven other people were to ask questions on the factors of enlightenment, the Blessed One could speak on that at that very moment. Why? Because in the time it takes the great mass of worldly people to speak one phrase, the Venerable Ānanda speaks eight phrases. But in the time it takes the Venerable Ānanda to speak one phrase, the Blessed One speaks sixteen phrases. Why? Because the Blessed One’s tongue is soft, his teeth are well-covered, his speech is fluent, and his life-continuum is swift. Therefore, he said: 'The Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dhamma, Sāriputta, is not at all depleted.'

Tattha dhammadasenāti tantiṭhapanā. Dhammapadabyañjananti pāḷiyā padabyañjanaṃ, tassa tassa atthassa byañjanakaṃ akkharaṃ. Pañhapaṭibhānanti pañhabyākaraṇaṃ. Iminā kiṃ dasseti? Tathāgato pubbe daharakāle akkharāni sampiṇḍetvā padaṃ vattuṃ sakkoti, padāni sampiṇḍetvā gāthaṃ vattuṃ sakkoti, catuakkharehi vā aṭṭhaakkharehi vā soḷasaakkharehi vā padehi yuttāya gāthāya atthaṃ vattuṃ sakkoti. Idāni pana mahallakakāle akkharāni sampiṇḍetvā padaṃ vā, padāni sampiṇḍetvā gāthaṃ vā, gāthāya atthaṃ vā vattuṃ na sakkotīti evaṃ natthi. Daharakāle ca mahallakakāle ca sabbametaṃ tathāgatassa apariyādinnamevāti imaṃ dasseti. Mañcakena cepi manti idaṃ buddhabaladīpanatthameva parikappetvā āha. Dasabalaṃ pana mañcake āropetvā gāmanigamarājadhāniyo pariharaṇakālo nāma natthi. Tathāgatā hi pañcame āyukoṭṭhāse khaṇḍiccādīhi anabhibhūtā suvaṇṇavaṇṇasarīrassa vevaṇṇiye ananuppatte devamanussānaṃ piyamanāpakāleyeva parinibbāyanti.

Here, 'dhammadesanā' means the establishment of the text. 'Dhammapadabyañjana' refers to the words and syllables of the Pāli text, the letters indicating the meaning of each. 'Pañhapaṭibhāna' means answering questions. What does this indicate? In his early youth, the Tathāgata could combine syllables to form words, combine words to form verses, and explain meanings with verses composed of four, eight, or sixteen syllables. But now, in his old age, it is not the case that he cannot combine syllables to form words, words to form verses, or explain the meaning of verses. This shows that whether in youth or old age, all this remains undiminished for the Tathāgata. The statement about being carried on a couch was devised and spoken solely to illuminate the Buddha's power. However, there is no occasion for carrying the Ten-Powered One on a palanquin through villages, towns, and royal capitals. For the Tathāgatas, in the fifth stage of life, not overcome by decay and so forth, their golden-hued bodies not having faded, pass into final Nibbāna precisely when they are most beloved and agreeable to gods and humans.

162. Nāgasamāloti tassa therassa nāmaṃ. Paṭhamabodhiyañhi vīsativassabbhantare upavānanāgitameghiyattherā [V 1.0366] viya ayampi bhagavato upaṭṭhāko ahosi. Bījayamānoti mandamandena tālavaṇṭavātena bhagavato utusukhaṃ samuṭṭhāpayamāno. Etadavocāti sakalasuttantaṃ sutvā bhagavato pubbacaritaṃ dukkarakārakaṃ āgamma pasanno etaṃ “acchariyaṃ bhante”tiādivacanaṃ avoca. Tattha accharaṃ paharituṃ yuttanti acchariyaṃ. Abhūtapubbaṃ bhūtanti abbhutaṃ. Ubhayenapi attano vimhayameva [P 2.0054] dīpeti. Ko nāmo ayaṃ bhanteti idaṃ bhaddako vatāyaṃ dhammapariyāyo, handassa bhagavantaṃ āyācitvā nāmaṃ gaṇhāpemīti adhippāyena āha. Athassa bhagavā nāmaṃ gaṇhanto tasmā tiha tvantiādimāha. Tassattho, yasmā idaṃ suttaṃ sutvā tava lomāni haṭṭhāni, tasmā tiha tvaṃ[M 1.0359], nāgasamāla, imaṃ dhammapariyāyaṃ “lomahaṃsana pariyāyo”tveva naṃ dhārehīti.

162. 'Nāgasamāla' was the name of that elder. For within twenty years of the first enlightenment, just like the Elders Upavāna, Nāgita, and Meghiya, he too was an attendant of the Blessed One. 'Bījayāmāna' means slowly creating physical comfort for the Blessed One with a mild breeze from a palm-leaf fan. 'Etadavoca' means that after hearing the entire discourse, being inspired by the Blessed One's former conduct involving hardship, he uttered these words beginning with 'It is wonderful, venerable sir.' Here, 'acchariya' (wonderful) means that which is worthy of a finger-snap. 'Abbhuta' means unprecedented. With both, he reveals his own astonishment. 'What is this called, venerable sir?'—this was said with the intention: 'This teaching is truly excellent; let me approach the Blessed One and have him give it a name.' Then the Blessed One, assigning a name to it, spoke thus: 'Therefore, you...' Its meaning is: 'Because upon hearing this discourse your hairs stood on end, therefore, Nāgasamāla, you should remember this teaching as "The Discourse on the Bristling of Hairs."

Saṃsārasuddhiādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Description of the Purification of the Cycle of Existence and So Forth is Concluded.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

The Papañcasūdanī, Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya.

Mahāsīhanādasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Great Lion's Roar Discourse is Concluded.

3. Mahādukkhakkhandhasuttavaṇṇanā

3. The Commentary on the Great Mass of Suffering Sutta

163. Evaṃ [V 1.0367] me sutanti mahādukkhakkhandhasuttaṃ. Tattha vinayapariyāyena tayo janā sambahulāti vuccanti, tato paraṃ saṅgho. Suttantapariyāyena tayo tayo eva, tato uddhaṃ sambahulāti vuccanti. Idha suttantapariyāyena sambahulāti veditabbā. Piṇḍāya pāvisiṃsūti paviṭṭhā, te pana na tāva paviṭṭhā, pavisissāmāti nikkhantattā pana pavisiṃsūti vuttā. Yathā gāmaṃ gamissāmīti nikkhantapuriso taṃ gāmaṃ appattopi “kuhiṃ itthannāmo”ti vutte “gāmaṃ gato”ti vuccati, evaṃ. Paribbājakānaṃ ārāmoti jetavanato avidūre aññatitthiyānaṃ paribbājakānaṃ ārāmo atthi, taṃ sandhāya evamāhaṃsu. Samaṇo, āvusoti, āvuso, tumhākaṃ satthā samaṇo gotamo. Kāmānaṃ pariññanti kāmānaṃ pahānaṃ samatikkamaṃ paññapeti. Rūpavedanāsupi eseva nayo.

163. Thus have I heard—the Great Mass of Suffering Sutta. There, in the disciplinary context, three people are called ‘several’; beyond that, the Sangha. In the Sutta context, three are just three; beyond that, they are called ‘several’. Here, in the Sutta context, ‘several’ should be understood. ‘They entered for alms’ means they had entered. But they had not yet actually entered; because they had set out intending to enter, they are said to have entered. Just as a person who has set out thinking, ‘I will go to the village,’ even before reaching that village, when asked, ‘Where is so-and-so?’ is said to have ‘gone to the village,’ so it is here. ‘The wanderers’ park’ means that not far from Jeta’s Grove, there was a park belonging to wanderers of other sects; referring to that, they said this. ‘Ascetic, friend’—meaning, ‘Friend, your teacher is the ascetic Gotama.’ ‘The full understanding of sensual pleasures’ means he teaches the abandoning and transcending of sensual pleasures. The same principle applies to form and feeling.

Tattha titthiyā sakasamayaṃ jānantā kāmānaṃ pariññaṃ paññapeyyuṃ paṭhamajjhānaṃ vadamānā, rūpānaṃ pariññaṃ paññapeyyuṃ arūpabhavaṃ vadamānā, vedanānaṃ pariññaṃ paññapeyyuṃ asaññabhavaṃ vadamānā. Te pana “idaṃ nāma paṭhamajjhānaṃ ayaṃ rūpabhavo ayaṃ arūpabhavo”tipi na jānanti. Te paññapetuṃ asakkontāpi kevalaṃ “paññapema paññapemā”ti vadanti. Tathāgato kāmānaṃ pariññaṃ anāgāmimaggena paññapeti, rūpavedanānaṃ arahattamaggena[P 2.0055]. Te evaṃ mahante visese vijjamānepi idha no, āvuso, ko vivesotiādimāhaṃsu.

There, sectarians, knowing their own doctrines, would teach the full understanding of sensual pleasures while speaking of the first jhāna, would teach the full understanding of forms while speaking of the formless realm, and would teach the full understanding of feelings while speaking of the non-percipient realm. Yet they do not know, ‘This is what is called the first jhāna; this, the realm of form; this, the formless realm.’ Though unable to teach, they merely say, ‘We teach, we teach.’ The Tathāgata teaches the full understanding of sensual pleasures by the path of non-returning, and of forms and feelings by the path of arahantship. Though such a great difference exists, they said, ‘Friend, what difference is there here for us?’ and so on.

Tattha idhāti imasmiṃ paññāpane. Dhammadesanāya vā dhammadesananti yadidaṃ samaṇassa vā gotamassa dhammadesanāya saddhiṃ amhākaṃ dhammadesanaṃ, amhākaṃ vā dhammadesanāya saddhiṃ samaṇassa gotamassa dhammadesanaṃ ārabbha nānākaraṇaṃ vuccetha, taṃ kinnāmāti vadanti. Dutiyapadepi eseva nayo[M 1.0360]. Iti vemajjhe bhinnasuvaṇṇaṃ viya sāsanena saddhiṃ attano laddhivacanamattena samadhuraṃ ṭhapayiṃsu. Neva abhinandiṃsūti evametanti na sampaṭicchiṃsu. Nappaṭikkosiṃsūti nayidaṃ evanti nappaṭisedhesuṃ. Kasmā? Te kira titthiyā nāma andhasadisā, jānitvā vā ajānitvā vā katheyyunti [V 1.0368] nābhinandiṃsu, pariññanti vacanena īsakaṃ sāsanagandho atthīti nappaṭikkosiṃsu. Janapadavāsino vā te sakasamayaparasamayesu na suṭṭhu kusalātipi ubhayaṃ nākaṃsu.

Here, ‘idha’ means in this teaching. Regarding the teaching of the Dhamma or the Dhamma discourse—whether it is the Dhamma discourse of the ascetic Gotama along with our Dhamma discourse, or our Dhamma discourse along with the Dhamma discourse of the ascetic Gotama—if a differentiation were to be made, what would be its name? This is what they say. The same method applies to the second term. Thus, in the middle, like a split piece of gold, they placed their own doctrinal statements on an equal footing with the teaching. They neither approved—meaning they did not accept it as ‘thus it is’—nor did they disapprove—meaning they did not deny it as ‘this is not so.’ Why? Because those sectarians, being like the blind, spoke whether knowing or not knowing; thus they did not approve. And since there was a slight fragrance of the teaching in the statement, implied by the word ‘full understanding,’ they did not disapprove. Or perhaps the inhabitants of the region were not very skilled in their own doctrines or others’, and so they did neither.

165. Na ceva sampāyissantīti sampādetvā kathetuṃ na sakkhissanti. Uttariñca vighātanti asampāyanato uttarimpi dukkhaṃ āpajjissanti. Sampādetvā kathetuṃ asakkontānaṃ nāma hi dukkhaṃ uppajjati. Yathā taṃ, bhikkhave, avisayasminti ettha yathāti kāraṇavacanaṃ, tanti nipātamattaṃ. Yasmā avisaye pañho pucchito hotīti attho. Sadevaketi saha devehi sadevake. Samārakādīsupi eseva nayo. Evaṃ tīṇi ṭhānāni loke pakkhipitvā dve pajāyāti pañcahipi sattalokameva pariyādiyitvā etasmiṃ sadevakādibhede loke taṃ devaṃ vā manussaṃ vā na passāmīti dīpeti. Ito vā pana sutvāti ito vā pana mama sāsanato sutvā atathāgatopi atathāgatasāvakopi ārādheyya paritoseyya. Aññathā ārādhanaṃ nāma natthīti dasseti.

165. ‘They will not be able to furnish an answer,’ meaning they will not be able to speak successfully. ‘And further, they will come to ruin,’ meaning that from being unable to furnish an answer, they will fall into further suffering. For suffering indeed arises for those who are unable to speak successfully. Regarding the phrase, ‘Just as, monks, in an improper sphere,’ here ‘just as’ is a term indicating reason, and ‘that’ is merely a particle. The meaning is: because the question was asked in an improper sphere. ‘With the devas’ means together with the devas. The same principle applies to Māra and others. Thus, having included three stations and two generations in the world, thereby encompassing all five realms of sentient beings, he shows that in this world, with its division into devas and the like, he does not see that deva or human. Or else, ‘having heard this from here’ means having heard this from my dispensation, even one who is not a Tathāgata or a disciple of a non-Tathāgata could propitiate and satisfy. Otherwise, there is no such thing as propitiation—this is shown.

166. Idāni attano tesaṃ pañhānaṃ veyyākaraṇena cittārādhanaṃ dassento ko ca, bhikkhavetiādimāha. Kāmaguṇāti kāmayitabbaṭṭhena kāmā. Bandhanaṭṭhena guṇā. “Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, ahatānaṃ vatthānaṃ dviguṇaṃ saṅghāṭi”nti (mahāva. 348) ettha hi paṭalaṭṭho guṇaṭṭho. “Accenti [P 2.0056] kālā tarayanti rattiyo, vayoguṇā anupubbaṃ jahantī”ti (saṃ. ni. 1.4) ettha rāsaṭṭho guṇaṭṭho. “Sataguṇā dakkhiṇā pāṭikaṅkhitabbā”ti (ma. ni. 3.379) ettha ānisaṃsaṭṭho guṇaṭṭho. “Antaṃ antaguṇaṃ (khu. pā. 3 dvattiṃsākāre; dī. ni. 2.377) kayirā mālāguṇe bahū”ti (dha. pa. 53) ettha bandhanaṭṭho guṇaṭṭho. Idhāpi eseva adhippeto, tena vuttaṃ “bandhanaṭṭhena guṇā”ti. Cakkhuviññeyyāti [M 1.0361] cakkhuviññāṇena passitabbā. Etenupāyena sotaviññeyyādīsupi attho veditabbo. Iṭṭhāti pariyiṭṭhā vā hontu mā vā, iṭṭhārammaṇabhūtāti attho. Kantāti kamanīyā. Manāpāti manavaḍḍhanakā. Piyarūpāti piyajātikā. Kāmūpasaṃhitāti ārammaṇaṃ katvā uppajjamānena kāmena upasaṃhitā. Rajanīyāti rajjaniyā, rāguppattikāraṇabhūtāti attho.

166. Now, showing how to win their hearts by answering their questions, he said, ‘What then, monks?’ and so on. ‘Cords of sensual pleasure’ (kāmaguṇā): ‘sensual pleasures’ (kāmā) in the sense of what is to be desired; ‘cords’ (guṇā) in the sense of bonds. For example, in ‘I allow, monks, a double-layered outer robe,’ here ‘guṇa’ means layer. In ‘Times pass, nights fly by, the collections of age-stages are successively left behind,’ here ‘guṇa’ means collection. In ‘A gift a hundredfold should be expected,’ here ‘guṇa’ means benefit. In ‘One should make many garlands from a string of flowers,’ here ‘guṇa’ means bond. Here too, the same is intended, hence it is said, ‘cords in the sense of bonds.’ ‘Cognizable by the eye’ (cakkhuviññeyya) means to be seen by eye-consciousness. By this method, the meaning in ‘cognizable by the ear’ and so on should be understood. ‘Pleasing’ (iṭṭhā) means whether sought after or not, the meaning is that they serve as agreeable objects. ‘Lovely’ (kantā) means delightful. ‘Charming’ (manāpā) means heart-gladdening. ‘Of a dear form’ (piyarūpā) means having a dear nature. ‘Connected with sensual pleasure’ (kāmūpasaṃhitā) means connected with the sensual pleasure that arises by making it an object. ‘Enticing’ (rajanīyā) means arousing passion, that is, being a cause for the arising of lust.

167. Yadi muddāyātiādīsu muddāti aṅgulipabbesu saññaṃ ṭhapetvā hatthamuddā. Gaṇanāti acchiddagaṇanā. Saṅkhānanti piṇḍagaṇanā. Yāya khettaṃ oloketvā idha ettakā vīhī bhavissanti[V 1.0369], rukkhaṃ oloketvā idha ettakāni phalāni bhavissanti, ākāsaṃ oloketvā ime ākāse sakuṇā ettakā nāma bhavissantīti jānanti.

167. In ‘if by a seal’ and so on, ‘seal’ (muddā) refers to a hand seal made by placing a mark on the finger joints. ‘Counting’ (gaṇanā) means unbroken counting. ‘Calculation’ (saṅkhāna) means aggregate counting. By this, having surveyed a field, they know, ‘Here, this much rice will be’; having surveyed a tree, they know, ‘Here, this many fruits will be’; having surveyed the sky, they know, ‘These birds in the sky will be this many.’

Kasīti kasikammaṃ. Vaṇijjāti jaṅghavaṇijjathalavaṇijjādivaṇippatho. Gorakkhanti attano vā paresaṃ vā gāvo rakkhitvā pañcagorasavikkayena jīvanakammaṃ. Issattho vuccati āvudhaṃ gahetvā upaṭṭhānakammaṃ. Rājaporisanti āvudhena rājakammaṃ katvā upaṭṭhānaṃ. Sippaññataranti gahitāvasesaṃ hatthiassasippādi. Sītassa purakkhatoti lakkhaṃ viya sarassa sītassa purato, sītena bādhīyamānoti attho. Uṇhepi eseva nayo. Ḍaṃsādīsu ḍaṃsāti piṅgalamakkhikā. Makasāti sabbamakkhikā, sarīsapāti ye keci saritvā gacchanti. Rissamānoti ruppamāno, ghaṭṭiyamāno. Mīyamānoti maramāno. Ayaṃ, bhikkhaveti, bhikkhave, ayaṃ muddādīhi jīvikakappanaṃ āgamma sītādipaccayo ābādho. Kāmānaṃ ādīnavoti kāmesu upaddavo, upassaggoti attho. Sandiṭṭhikoti paccakkho [P 2.0057] sāmaṃ passitabbo. Dukkhakkhandhoti dukkharāsi. Kāmahetūtiādīsu paccayaṭṭhena kāmā assa hetūti kāmahetu. Mūlaṭṭhena kāmā nidānamassāti kāmanidāno. Liṅgavipallāsena pana kāmanidānanti vutto. Kāraṇaṭṭhena kāmā adhikaraṇaṃ assāti kāmādhikaraṇo. Liṅgavipallāseneva pana kāmādhikaraṇanti vutto. Kāmānameva hetūti idaṃ niyamavacanaṃ, kāmapaccayā uppajjatiyevāti attho.

Plowing (kasī) means the work of plowing. Trading (vaṇijjā) means the path of trade such as travelling trade, overland trade, and so on. Cattle-keeping (gorakkha) is the livelihood of guarding one’s own or others’ cattle and living by selling the five products of the cow. The profession of arms (issattha) is called the work of attendance by taking up weapons. Royal service (rājaporisa) is attendance by performing royal duties with weapons. Some other craft (sippaññatara) refers to the remaining crafts like elephant training, horse training, and so on. “Exposed to cold” (sītassa purakkhato) means like a target for an arrow, in front of the cold; the meaning is being afflicted by the cold. The same principle applies to heat. Among gadflies and so on, “gadflies” (ḍaṃsa) refer to the reddish-brown fly. “Mosquitoes” (makasa) means all flies. “Creeping creatures” (sarīsapa) are whatever moves by creeping. “Afflicted” (rissamāna) means being tormented, being harassed. “Dying” (mīyamāna) means perishing. “This, monks”—meaning, monks, this is the affliction that arises from causes like cold, through resorting to livelihoods such as computation and the like. “The danger of sensual pleasures” (kāmānaṃ ādīnava) means trouble in sensual pleasures; the meaning is affliction. “Visible” (sandiṭṭhika) means directly seen, to be witnessed oneself. “A mass of suffering” (dukkhakkhandha) means a heap of suffering. In “because of sensual pleasures” and so on, “sensual pleasures are the cause” (kāmahetu) means in the sense of condition. “Sensual pleasures are the origin” (kāmanidāna) means in the sense of root. But it is said to be “originating in sensual pleasures” due to a change of gender. “Sensual pleasures are the basis” (kāmādhikaraṇa) means in the sense of reason. But it is said to be “based on sensual pleasures” due to a change of gender. “Sensual pleasures themselves are the cause”—this is a definitive statement, meaning it arises solely dependent on sensual pleasures.

Uṭṭhahatoti [M 1.0362] ājīvasamuṭṭhāpakavīriyena uṭṭhahantassa. Ghaṭatoti taṃ vīriyaṃ pubbenāparaṃ ghaṭentassa. Vāyamatoti vāyāmaṃ parakkamaṃ payogaṃ karontassa. Nābhinipphajjantīti na nipphajjanti, hatthaṃ nābhiruhanti. Socatīti citte uppannabalavasokena socati. Kilamatīti kāye uppannadukkhena kilamati. Paridevatīti vācāya paridevati. Urattāḷinti uraṃ tāḷetvā. Kandatīti rodati. Sammohaṃ āpajjatīti visaññī viya sammūḷho hoti. Moghanti tucchaṃ. Aphaloti nipphalo. Ārakkhādhikaraṇanti ārakkhakāraṇā. Kintīti kena nu kho upāyena. Yampi meti yampi mayhaṃ kasikammādīni katvā uppāditaṃ dhanaṃ ahosi. Tampi no natthīti tampi amhākaṃ idāni natthi.

“Striving” (uṭṭhahato) means of one who strives with the energy that generates a livelihood. “Making an effort” (ghaṭato) means of one who connects that energy continuously from one moment to the next. “Exerting oneself” (vāyamato) means of one who makes effort, exertion, and endeavor. “They do not succeed” (nābhinipphajjanti) means they are not accomplished, they do not come to hand. “One grieves” (socati) means one grieves with strong grief that has arisen in the mind. “One is exhausted” (kilamati) means one is exhausted with suffering that has arisen in the body. “One laments” (paridevati) means one laments with speech. “Beating the breast” (urattāḷiṃ) means having struck the breast. “One wails” (kandati) means one weeps. “One falls into confusion” (sammohaṃ āpajjati) means one becomes bewildered as if senseless. “Futile” (moghaṃ) means empty. “Fruitless” (aphala) means without result. “On account of protection” (ārakkhādhikaraṇaṃ) means for the reason of protection. “By what means?” (kinti) means by what means indeed. “Whatever of mine” (yampi me) means whatever wealth was generated by me by doing farming and so on. “That too we do not have” (tampi no natthi) means that too is not ours now.

168. Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, kāmahetūtiādināpi kāraṇaṃ dassetvāva ādīnavaṃ dīpeti. Tattha [V 1.0370] kāmahetūti kāmapaccayā rājānopi rājūhi vivadanti. Kāmanidānanti bhāvanapuṃsakaṃ, kāme nidānaṃ katvā vivadantīti attho. Kāmādhikaraṇantipi bhāvanapuṃsakameva, kāme adhikaraṇaṃ katvā vivadantīti attho. Kāmānameva hetūti gāmanigamanagarasenāpatipurohitaṭṭhānantarādīnaṃ kāmānameva hetu vivadantīti attho. Upakkamantīti paharanti. Asicammanti asiñceva kheṭakaphalakādīni ca. Dhanukalāpaṃ sannayhitvāti dhanuṃ gahetvā sarakalāpaṃ sannayhitvā. Ubhatobyūḷanti ubhato rāsibhūtaṃ. Pakkhandantīti pavisanti. Usūsūti kaṇḍesu. Vijjotalantesūti viparivattantesu. Te tatthāti te tasmiṃ saṅgāme.

168. Furthermore, monks, by showing the reason through 'because of sensual pleasures' and so on, he illuminates the danger. Herein, “because of sensual pleasures” (kāmahetu) means kings quarrel with kings with sensual pleasures as the condition. “Originating in sensual pleasures” (kāmanidānaṃ) is a neuter abstract noun, meaning they quarrel having made sensual pleasures the root. “Based on sensual pleasures” (kāmādhikaraṇaṃ) is also a neuter abstract noun, meaning they quarrel having made sensual pleasures the ground. “For the sake of sensual pleasures alone” (kāmānameva hetu) means they quarrel for the sake of sensual pleasures alone, for things such as villages, market towns, cities, and positions like commander, priest, and other offices. “They attack” (upakkamanti) means they strike. “Sword and shield” (asicammaṃ) means a sword and also a shield, buckler, and so on. “Having equipped a bow and quiver” (dhanukalāpaṃ sannayhitvā) means having taken up a bow and having equipped a quiver of arrows. “Massed on both sides” (ubhatobyūḷaṃ) means formed into masses on both sides. “They charge” (pakkhandanti) means they enter. “With arrows” (usūsu) means with shafts. “Whirling about” (vijjotalantesu) means turning about. “They there” (te tattha) means they in that battle.

Addāvalepanā [P 2.0058] upakāriyoti cettha manussā pākārapādaṃ assakhurasaṇṭhānena iṭṭhakāhi cinitvā upari sudhāya limpanti. Evaṃ katā pākārapādā upakāriyoti vuccanti. Tā tintena kalalena sittā addāvalepanā nāma honti. Pakkhandantīti tāsaṃ heṭṭhā tikhiṇaayasūlādīhi vijjhīyamānāpi pākārassa picchilabhāvena ārohituṃ asakkontāpi upadhāvantiyeva. Chakaṇakāyāti kuthitagomayena. Abhivaggenāti satadantena. Taṃ aṭṭhadantākārena katvā “nagaradvāraṃ bhinditvā [M 1.0363] pavisissāmā”ti āgate uparidvāre ṭhitā tassa bandhanayottāni chinditvā tena abhivaggena omaddanti.

“Supporting structures with wet plaster” (addāvalepanā upakāriyo): Here, people build the base of the city wall with bricks shaped like horse hooves and coat the top with lime. Wall bases prepared in this way are called “supporting structures” (upakāriyo). When sprinkled with wet mortar, they are called “having wet plaster” (addāvalepanā). “They charge” (pakkhandanti): Though they are pierced from below by sharp iron spikes and so on, and though they are unable to climb due to the wall's slippery nature, they still rush forward. “With cow dung” (chakaṇakāya): With rotten cow dung. “With a hundred-toothed device” (abhivaggena): With a `satadanta`. When the attackers come with a device made in the shape of eight teeth, thinking, 'We will break the city gate and enter,' those standing at the upper gate cut the binding ropes of that device and crush them with that hundred-toothed device.

169. Sandhimpi chindantīti gharasandhimpi chindanti. Nillopanti gāme paharitvā mahāvilopaṃ karonti. Ekāgārikanti paṇṇāsamattāpi saṭṭhimattāpi parivāretvā jīvaggāhaṃ gahetvā āharāpenti. Paripanthepi tiṭṭhantīti panthadūhanakammaṃ karonti. Aḍḍhadaṇḍakehīti muggarehi pahārasādhanatthaṃ vā catuhatthadaṇḍaṃ dvedhā chetvā gahitadaṇḍakehi. Bilaṅgathālikanti kañjiyaukkhalikammakāraṇaṃ, taṃ karontā sīsakapālaṃ uppāṭetvā tattaṃ ayoguḷaṃ saṇḍāsena gahetvā tattha pakkhipanti, tena matthaluṅgaṃ pakkuthitvā upari uttarati. Saṅkhamuṇḍikanti saṅkhamuṇḍakammakāraṇaṃ, taṃ karontā uttaroṭṭhaubhatokaṇṇacūḷikagaḷavāṭaparicchedena cammaṃ chinditvā sabbakese ekato gaṇṭhiṃ katvā daṇḍakena vallitvā uppāṭenti, saha kesehi cammaṃ uṭṭhahati. Tato sīsakaṭāhaṃ thūlasakkharāhi ghaṃsitvā dhovantā saṅkhavaṇṇaṃ karonti.

169. “They break in” (sandhimpi chindanti) means they even break into a house. “They plunder” (nillopanti) means they attack a village and commit great plunder. “Robbing a single house” (ekāgārikaṃ): About fifty or sixty of them surround a house, take the inhabitants alive, and make them bring out their valuables. “They lie in wait on the highway” (paripanthepi tiṭṭhanti) means they perform the act of highway robbery. “With half-staffs” (aḍḍhadaṇḍakehi): With mallets, or with sticks obtained by cutting a four-cubit staff in two for the purpose of striking. “The gruel-pot torture” (bilaṅgathālikaṃ): This is the act of the `kañjiyaukkhalika`; in performing this, they tear off the scalp, take a red-hot iron ball with tongs, and drop it inside, causing the brain to boil and rise to the top. “The conch-shell head torture” (saṅkhamuṇḍikaṃ): This is the act of the `saṅkhamuṇḍaka`; in performing this, they cut the skin around the upper lip, the tips of both ears, and the nape of the neck, gather all the hair into a single knot, twist it with a stick, and pull it off—the scalp comes away with the hair. Then they scrub the skull with coarse gravel, wash it, and make it the color of a conch shell.

Rāhumukhanti rāhumukhakammakāraṇaṃ, taṃ karontā saṅkunā mukhaṃ vivaritvā antomukhe dīpaṃ jālenti[V 1.0371][P 2.0059]. Kaṇṇacūḷikāhi vā paṭṭhāya mukhaṃ nikhādanena khaṇanti. Lohitaṃ paggharitvā mukhaṃ pūreti. Jotimālikanti sakalasarīraṃ telapilotikāya veṭhetvā ālimpanti. Hatthapajjotikanti hatthe telapilotikāya veṭhetvā dīpaṃ viya jālenti. Erakavattikanti erakavattakammakāraṇaṃ, taṃ karontā gīvato paṭṭhāya cammabaddhe kantitvā gopphake ṭhapenti. Atha naṃ yottehi bandhitvā kaḍḍhanti. So attano cammabaddhe akkamitvā akkamitvā patati. Cīrakavāsikanti cīrakavāsikakammakāraṇaṃ, taṃ karontā tatheva cammabaddhe kantitvā kaṭiyaṃ ṭhapenti. Kaṭito paṭṭhāya kantitvā gopphakesu ṭhapenti. Uparimehi heṭṭhimasarīraṃ cīrakanivāsananivatthaṃ viya hoti. Eṇeyyakanti eṇeyyakakammakāraṇaṃ. Taṃ karontā ubhosu kapparesu ca jāṇūsu ca ayavalayāni datvā ayasūlāni koṭṭenti. So catūhi ayasūlehi bhūmiyaṃ patiṭṭhahati. Atha naṃ parivāretvā aggiṃ karonti. “Eṇeyyako jotipariggaho yathā”ti [M 1.0364] āgataṭṭhānepi idameva vuttaṃ. Taṃ kālena kālaṃ sūlāni apanetvā catūhi aṭṭhikoṭīhiyeva ṭhapenti. Evarūpā kāraṇā nāma natthi.

Rāhumukhaṃ means the act of making Rāhu's mouth. Those who perform it open the mouth with a hook and light a lamp inside the mouth. Or they dig the mouth with a digging tool, starting from the earlobes. Blood flows and fills the mouth. Jotimālikaṃ means the garland of flames: wrapping the entire body with oil-soaked cloth and setting it alight. Hatthapajjotikaṃ means the hand-lamp: wrapping the hands with oil-soaked cloth and lighting them like a lamp. Erakavattikaṃ means the act of making a grass wick. Those who perform it cut strips of skin from the neck downwards and place them at the ankles. Then, they bind him with cords and pull. Stepping on his own strips of skin, he repeatedly falls. Cīrakavāsikaṃ means the act of making a bark-cloth garment. Those who perform it similarly cut strips of skin and place them at the waist. Cutting from the waist downwards, they place them at the ankles. The lower body appears as if clothed in a garment of bark-cloth by the upper strips. Eṇeyyakaṃ means the act of making an antelope. Those who perform it place iron rings on both elbows and knees and hammer in iron spikes. He stands fixed to the ground with four iron spikes. Then, they surround him and light a fire. The phrase 'like an antelope encircled by flame' is explained in the same way even in the place where it appears. From time to time, they remove the spikes and leave him supported on just the four bone-ends. Such tortures do not exist.

Baḷisamaṃsikanti ubhatomukhehi baḷisehi paharitvā cammamaṃsanhārūni uppāṭenti. Kahāpaṇikanti sakalasarīraṃ tiṇhāhi vāsīhi koṭito paṭṭhāya kahāpaṇamattaṃ kahāpaṇamattaṃ pātentā koṭṭenti. Khārāpatacchikanti sarīraṃ tattha tattha āvudhehi paharitvā kocchehi khāraṃ ghaṃsanti. Cammasaṃsanhārūni paggharitvā savanti. Aṭṭhikasaṅkhalikāva tiṭṭhati. Palighaparivattikanti ekena passena nipajjāpetvā kaṇṇacchidde ayasūlaṃ koṭṭetvā pathaviyā ekābaddhaṃ karonti. Atha naṃ pāde gahetvā āvijjhanti. Palālapīṭhakanti cheko kāraṇiko chavicammaṃ acchinditvā nisadapotehi aṭṭhīni bhinditvā kesesu gahetvā ukkhipanti. Maṃsarāsiyeva hoti, atha naṃ keseheva pariyonandhitvā gaṇhanti. Palālavaṭṭiṃ viya katvā pana veṭhenti. Sunakhehipīti [P 2.0060] katipayāni divasāni āhāraṃ adatvā chātakehi sunakhehi khādāpenti. Te muhuttena aṭṭhisaṅkhalikameva karonti. Samparāyikoti samparāye dutiyattabhāve vipākoti attho.

Baḷisamaṃsikaṃ means striking with double-headed hooks, they tear off skin, flesh, and sinews. Kahāpaṇikaṃ means chopping the entire body with sharp adzes, starting from the top, causing coin-sized pieces to fall. Khārāpatacchikaṃ means striking the body here and there with weapons, they rub a caustic substance on it with brushes. Skin, flesh, and sinews dissolve and flow away. Only a chain of bones remains. Palighaparivattikaṃ means making him lie on one side, they drive an iron stake through his ear-hole and fix it to the ground. Then they grab his feet and swing him around. Palālapīṭhakaṃ means a skilled torturer strips off his outer and inner skin and breaks his bones with grinding stones, then lifts him up by his hair. He becomes a mere heap of flesh. Then they seize him, having wrapped him up completely in his own hair. They roll him up like a bundle of straw. Sunakhehipi means not giving food for several days, they have him eaten by famished dogs. In a moment, they reduce him to a mere skeleton. Samparāyika means the result in the future, in a second existence.

170. Chandarāgavinayo chandarāgappahānanti nibbānaṃ. Nibbānañhi āgamma kāmesu chandarāgo vinīyati ceva pahīyati ca, tasmā nibbānaṃ chandarāgavinayo chandarāgappahānanti ca vuttaṃ. Sāmaṃ vā kāme parijānissantīti sayaṃ vā te kāme tīhi pariññāhi parijānissanti. Tathattāyāti tathabhāvāya. Yathāpaṭipannoti yāya paṭipadāya paṭipanno.

170. The removal of sensual desire, the abandoning of sensual desire: this is Nibbāna. For, based on Nibbāna, sensual desire for sensual pleasures is both removed and abandoned. Therefore, Nibbāna is called 'the removal of sensual desire' and 'the abandoning of sensual desire'. 'Or they will fully understand sensual pleasures for themselves' means they will fully understand those sensual pleasures by themselves with the three kinds of full understanding. 'For suchness' means for such a state. 'One who has practiced accordingly' means one who has practiced according to that practice.

171. Khattiyakaññā [V 1.0372] vātiādi aparittena vipulena kusalena gahitapaṭisandhikaṃ vatthālaṅkārādīni labhanaṭṭhāne nibbattaṃ dassetuṃ vuttaṃ. Pannarasavassuddesikāti pannarasavassavayā. Dutiyapadepi eseva nayo. Vayapadesaṃ kasmā gaṇhāti? Vaṇṇasampattidassanatthaṃ. Mātugāmassa hi duggatakule nibbattassāpi etasmiṃ kāle thokaṃ thokaṃ vaṇṇāyatanaṃ pasīdati. Purisānaṃ pana vīsativassakāle pañcavīsativassakāle pasannaṃ hoti. Nātidīghātiādīhi chadosavirahitaṃ sarīrasampattiṃ dīpeti. Vaṇṇanibhāti vaṇṇoyeva.

171. 'A khattiya maiden, etc.' is said to show that she, having taken rebirth with merit that was not insignificant but extensive, was born in a place where she would obtain clothing, ornaments, and so on. 'Of fifteen years' means of fifteen years of age. The same method applies to the second phrase as well. Why is the age mentioned? To show the accomplishment of beauty. For even a woman born in a poor family, at this time her sphere of beauty gradually brightens. But for men, it becomes bright at the age of twenty or twenty-five. By 'not too tall', etc., it indicates the accomplishment of the body, devoid of the six faults. 'Radiance of beauty' means simply beauty.

Jiṇṇanti [M 1.0365] jarājiṇṇaṃ. Gopānasivaṅkanti gopānasī viya vaṅkaṃ. Bhogganti bhaggaṃ, imināpissa vaṅkabhāvameva dīpeti. Daṇḍaparāyaṇanti daṇḍapaṭisaraṇaṃ daṇḍadutiyaṃ. Pavedhamānanti kampamānaṃ. Āturanti jarāturaṃ. Khaṇḍadantanti jiṇṇabhāvena khaṇḍitadantaṃ. Palitakesanti paṇḍarakesaṃ. Vilūnanti luñcitvā gahitakesaṃ viya khallāṭaṃ. Khalitasiranti mahākhallāṭasīsaṃ. Valinanti sañjātavaliṃ. Tilakāhatagattanti setakāḷatilakehi vikiṇṇasarīraṃ. Ābādhikanti byādhikaṃ. Dukkhitanti dukkhapattaṃ.

'Worn out' means worn out by old age. 'Bent like a gable-rafter' means crooked like a gable-rafter. 'Bent' means broken; by this, it also indicates his crooked state. 'Dependent on a stick' means taking a stick as refuge, having a stick as a companion. 'Trembling' means shaking. 'Afflicted' means afflicted by old age. 'With broken teeth' means having teeth broken due to old age. 'With gray hair' means having white hair. 'Sparse-haired' means bald as if the hair has been plucked out. 'A bald head' means a very bald head. 'Wrinkled' means having developed wrinkles. 'A body covered with spots' means a body scattered with white and black spots. 'Sickly' means diseased. 'Suffering' means having encountered suffering.

Bāḷhagilānanti adhimattagilānaṃ. Sivathikāya chaḍḍitanti āmakasusāne pātitaṃ. Sesamettha satipaṭṭhāne vuttameva. Idhāpi nibbānaṃyeva chandarāgavinayo.

'Severely ill' means extremely ill. 'Abandoned in a charnel ground' means thrown into a charnel ground for uncremated bodies. The rest here is as stated in the Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta. Here too, the removal of sensual desire is Nibbāna itself.

173. Neva tasmiṃ samaye attabyābādhāyāti tasmiṃ samaye attanopi dukkhatthāya na ceteti. Abyābajjhaṃyevāti niddukkhameva[P 2.0061].

173. 'At that time, he does not intend for his own affliction' means at that time he does not intend for his own suffering. 'Only non-affliction' means only without suffering.

174. Yaṃ, bhikkhave, vedanā aniccāti, bhikkhave, yasmā vedanā aniccā, tasmā ayaṃ aniccādiākārova vedanāya ādīnavoti attho, nissaraṇaṃ vuttappakāramevāti.

174. ‘Bhikkhus, whatever feeling is impermanent’ means, bhikkhus, since feeling is impermanent, therefore this very aspect of impermanence, etc., is the danger in feeling; and the escape is as previously stated.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

From the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Middle Length Discourses.

Mahādukkhakkhandhasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Mahādukkhakkhandha Sutta is concluded.

4. Cūḷadukkhakkhandhasuttavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Cūḷadukkhakkhandha Sutta.

175. Evaṃ [V 1.0373] me sutanti cūḷadukkhakkhandhasuttaṃ. Tattha sakkesūti evaṃnāmake janapade. So hi janapado sakyānaṃ rājakumārānaṃ vasanaṭṭhānattā sakyātveva saṅkhyaṃ gato. Sakyānaṃ pana uppatti ambaṭṭhasutte āgatāva. Kapilavatthusminti evaṃnāmake nagare. Tañhi kapilassa isino nivāsaṭṭhāne katattā kapilavatthūti vuttaṃ, taṃ gocaragāmaṃ katvā. Nigrodhārāmeti nigrodho nāma sakko, so ñātisamāgamakāle kapilavatthuṃ āgate bhagavati attano ārāme vihāraṃ kāretvā bhagavato niyyātesi, tasmiṃ viharatīti attho. Mahānāmoti anuruddhattherassa bhātā bhagavato cuḷapituputto. Suddhodano [M 1.0366] sukkodano sakkodano dhotodano amitodanoti ime pañca janā bhātaro. Amitā nāma devī tesaṃ bhaginī. Tissatthero tassā putto. Tathāgato ca nandatthero ca suddhodanassa puttā, mahānāmo ca anuruddhatthero ca sukkodanassa. Ānandatthero amitodanassa, so bhagavato kaniṭṭho. Mahānāmo mahallakataro sakadāgāmī ariyasāvako.

175. ‘Thus have I heard’ is the Cūḷadukkhakkhandha Sutta. Therein, ‘among the Sakyans’ means in a region so named. For that region, being the dwelling place of the Sakyan princes, came to be reckoned as Sakya. The origin of the Sakyans, however, is already given in the Ambaṭṭha Sutta. ‘In Kapilavatthu’ means in a city so named. For it was called Kapilavatthu because it was built on the dwelling place of the sage Kapila, having made it his alms-resort village. ‘In the Nigrodha Park’ means that Nigrodha, a Sakyan, when the Blessed One came to Kapilavatthu for a gathering of relatives, had a monastery built in his park and presented it to the Blessed One; the meaning is that the Blessed One dwelt there. ‘Mahānāma’ means the brother of the Elder Anuruddha, the son of the Blessed One’s paternal uncle. Suddhodana, Sukkodana, Sakkodana, Dhotodana, and Amitodana—these five persons were brothers. Their sister was the lady Amitā by name. The Elder Tissa was her son. The Tathāgata and the Elder Nanda were sons of Suddhodana; Mahānāma and the Elder Anuruddha were sons of Sukkodana; the Elder Ānanda was the son of Amitodana, and he was the Blessed One’s younger cousin. Mahānāma, the elder, was a once-returner, a noble disciple.

Dīgharattanti mayhaṃ sakadāgāmiphaluppattito paṭṭhāya cirarattaṃ jānāmīti dasseti. Lobhadhammāti lobhasaṅkhātā dhammā, nānappakārakaṃ lobhaṃyeva sandhāya vadati. Itaresupi dvīsu eseva nayo. Pariyādāya tiṭṭhantīti khepetvā tiṭṭhanti. Idañhi pariyādānaṃ nāma “sabbaṃ hatthikāyaṃ pariyādiyitvā sabbaṃ assakāyaṃ sabbaṃ rathakāyaṃ sabbaṃ pattikāyaṃ pariyādiyitvā jīvantaṃyeva naṃ osajjeyya”nti (saṃ. ni. 1.126) ettha gahaṇe āgataṃ. “Aniccasaññā, bhikkhave, bhāvitā bahulīkatā sabbaṃ [P 2.0062] kāmarāgaṃ pariyādiyatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 3.102) ettha khepane. Idhāpi khepane adhippetaṃ. Tena vuttaṃ “pariyādiyitvāti khepetvā”ti.

‘For a long time’ shows that from the arising of my once-returner’s fruit onwards, I have known it for a long time. ‘States of greed’ means phenomena designated as greed; it speaks with reference to greed of various kinds. The same method applies to the other two. ‘They stand consuming’ means they exhaust and remain. For here, the term ‘consuming’ (pariyādāna) occurs in the sense of ‘taking’ in the passage: ‘Having taken possession of the entire elephant division, the entire horse division, the entire chariot division, the entire infantry division, he would abandon him while still alive.’ And in the sense of ‘exhausting’ in the passage: ‘The perception of impermanence, bhikkhus, when developed and cultivated, consumes all sensual lust.’ Here too, ‘exhausting’ is intended. Therefore it is said: ‘“Having consumed” means having exhausted.’”

Yena me ekadā lobhadhammāpīti yena mayhaṃ ekekasmiṃ kāle lobhadhammāpi cittaṃ pariyādāya tiṭṭhantīti pucchati. Ayaṃ kira rājā “sakadāgāmimaggena lobhadosamohā niravasesā pahīyantī”ti saññī ahosi, ayaṃ “appahīnaṃ me atthī”tipi jānāti, appahīnakaṃ [V 1.0374] upādāya pahīnakampi puna pacchatovāvattatīti saññī hoti. Ariyasāvakassa evaṃ sandeho uppajjatīti? Āma uppajjati. Kasmā? Paṇṇattiyā akovidattā. “Ayaṃ kileso asukamaggavajjho”ti imissā paṇṇattiyā akovidassa hi ariyasāvakassapi evaṃ hoti. Kiṃ tassa paccavekkhaṇā natthīti? Atthi. Sā pana na sabbesaṃ paripuṇṇā hoti. Eko hi pahīnakilesameva paccavekkhati. Eko avasiṭṭhakilesameva, eko maggameva, eko phalameva, eko nibbānameva. Imāsu pana pañcasu paccavekkhaṇāsu ekaṃ vā dve vā no laddhuṃ na vaṭṭati. Iti yassa paccavekkhaṇā na paripuṇṇā, tassa maggavajjhakilesapaṇṇattiyaṃ akovidattā evaṃ hoti.

Regarding the phrase 'Whereby at one time states of greed also overcame my mind,' he asks, 'Whereby at a certain time do states of greed also overcome my mind?' This king, it seems, had the perception that ‘by the path of the once-returner, greed, hatred, and delusion are completely abandoned.’ Yet he also knows, ‘Something in me remains unabandoned,’ and clinging to what is unabandoned, he perceives that what has been abandoned returns again later. Does such doubt arise in a noble disciple? Yes, it arises. Why? Due to lack of skill in terminology. For a noble disciple lacking skill with the terminology ‘This defilement is to be abandoned by such-and-such path,’ this happens. Does he lack reflection? No, it exists. But that reflection is not complete for everyone. One reflects only on abandoned defilements. Another reflects only on remaining defilements. Another reflects only on the path. Another reflects only on the fruit. Another reflects only on Nibbāna. Among these five reflections, it is not proper to lack even one or two. Thus, for one whose reflection is incomplete, due to lack of skill with the terminology of defilements to be abandoned by the path, this happens.

176. So [M 1.0367] eva kho teti soyeva lobho doso moho ca tava santāne appahīno, tvaṃ pana pahīnasaññī ahosīti dasseti. So ca hi teti so tuyhaṃ lobhadosamohadhammo. Kāmeti duvidhe kāme. Na paribhuñjeyyāsīti mayaṃ viya pabbajeyyāsīti dasseti.

176. ‘That very thing of yours’ means that same greed, hatred, and delusion remain unabandoned in your being, yet you had the perception that they were abandoned—this is what is shown. ‘For that, indeed, is yours’ means that state of greed, hatred, and delusion is yours. ‘Desires’ refers to the two kinds of desires. ‘You should not indulge in them’ shows that you should go forth as we have.

177. Appassādāti parittasukhā. Bahudukkhāti diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikadukkhamevettha bahukaṃ. Bahupāyāsāti diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyiko upāyāsakilesoyevettha bahu. Ādīnavoti diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyiko upaddavo. Ettha bhiyyoti etesu kāmesu ayaṃ ādīnavoyeva bahu. Assādo pana himavantaṃ upanidhāya sāsapo viya appo, parittako. Iti cepi mahānāmāti mahānāma evaṃ cepi ariyasāvakassa. Yathābhūtanti yathāsabhāvaṃ. Sammā nayena kāraṇena paññāya suṭṭhu diṭṭhaṃ hotīti dasseti. Tattha paññāyāti vipassanāpaññāya, heṭṭhāmaggadvayañāṇenāti attho. So [P 2.0063] cāti so eva maggadvayena diṭṭhakāmādīnavo ariyasāvako. Pītisukhanti iminā sappītikāni dve jhānāni dasseti. Aññaṃ vā tato santataranti tato jhānadvayato santataraṃ aññaṃ uparijhānadvayañceva maggadvayañca. Neva tāva anāvaṭṭī kāmesu hotīti atha kho so dve magge paṭivijjhitvā ṭhitopi ariyasāvako upari jhānānaṃ vā maggānaṃ vā anadhigatattā neva tāva kāmesu anāvaṭṭī hoti, anāvaṭṭino anābhogo na hoti. Āvaṭṭino sābhogoyeva hoti. Kasmā? Catūhi jhānehi vikkhambhanappahānassa, dvīhi maggehi samucchedappahānassa abhāvā.

177. ‘Of little pleasure’ means happiness is limited. ‘Full of suffering’ means that here, suffering, both in this life and the next, is abundant. ‘Full of despair’ means that here, distress and defilements, both in this life and the next, are abundant. ‘Danger’ means peril, both in this life and the next. ‘Even more’ here means that among these sensual pleasures, this danger is indeed abundant. The pleasure, however, is as insignificant as a mustard seed compared to the Himalayas—small and limited. ‘Even so, Mahānāma’ means even so for a noble disciple. ‘As it truly is’ means according to its true nature. ‘Properly seen with wisdom’ indicates that it is well seen through the right method, reason, and wisdom. Here, ‘with wisdom’ refers to insight wisdom, meaning the knowledge of the two lower paths. ‘And that’ refers to that same noble disciple who has seen the danger of sensual pleasures through the two paths. ‘Joy and happiness’ indicates the two jhānas accompanied by joy. ‘Or something more peaceful than that’ means something even more tranquil than those two jhānas—namely, the two higher jhānas and the two higher paths. ‘He is not yet a non-returner to sensual pleasures’ means that even though that noble disciple has penetrated the two paths and remains established, because of not yet attaining the higher jhānas or paths, he is not yet a non-returner to sensual pleasures. A non-returner is not without mental application; a returner is indeed with mental application. Why? Because of the absence of suppression of defilements by the four jhānas, and the absence of eradication by the two paths.

Mayhampi [V 1.0375] khoti na kevalaṃ tuyheva, atha kho mayhampi. Pubbeva sambodhāti maggasambodhito paṭhamatarameva. Paññāya sudiṭṭhaṃ hotīti ettha orodhanāṭakā pajahanapaññā adhippetā. Pītisukhaṃ nājjhagamanti sappītikāni dve jhānāni na paṭilabhiṃ. Aññaṃ vā tato santataranti idha upari jhānadvayaṃ ceva cattāro ca maggā adhippetā. Paccaññāsinti paṭiaññāsiṃ.

‘For me too’ means not only for you, but for me too. ‘Even before enlightenment’ means even before the enlightenment of the path. ‘Clearly seen with wisdom’—here, the wisdom of abandoning, which obstructs and destroys, is intended. ‘I did not attain joy and happiness’ means I did not attain the two jhānas accompanied by joy. ‘Or something even more peaceful than that’—here, the two higher jhānas and the four paths are intended. ‘I realized’ means I fully knew.

179. Ekamidāhaṃ mahānāma samayanti kasmā āraddhaṃ? Ayaṃ pāṭiyekko anusandhi. Heṭṭhā kāmānaṃ assādopi ādīnavopi kathito[M 1.0368], nissaraṇaṃ na kathitaṃ, taṃ kathetuṃ ayaṃ desanā āraddhā. Kāmasukhallikānuyogo hi eko anto attakilamathānuyogo ekoti imehi antehi muttaṃ mama sāsananti upari phalasamāpattisīsena sakalasāsanaṃ dassetumpi ayaṃ desanā āraddhā.

179. ‘Mahānāma, at one time’—why was this begun? This is a separate connection. Below, the gratification and danger of sensual pleasures have been discussed, but the escape has not been discussed; to explain that, this discourse has been begun. For indulgence in sensual pleasures is one extreme, and self-mortification is the other extreme; to show that my teaching is free from these two extremes, and to show the entire teaching with the attainment of fruition as its apex, this discourse has also been begun.

Gijjhakūṭe pabbateti tassa pabbatassa gijjhasadisaṃ kūṭaṃ atthi, tasmā gijjhakūṭoti vuccati. Gijjhā vā tassa kūṭesu nivasantītipi gijjhakūṭoti vuccati. Isigilipasseti isigilipabbatassa passe. Kāḷasilāyanti kāḷavaṇṇe piṭṭhipāsāṇe. Ubbhaṭṭhakā hontīti uddhaṃyeva ṭhitakā honti anisinnā. Opakkamikāti ubbhaṭṭhakādinā attano upakkamena nibbattitā. Nigaṇṭho, āvusoti aññaṃ kāraṇaṃ vattuṃ asakkontā nigaṇṭhassa upari pakkhipiṃsu. Sabbaññū sabbadassāvīti [P 2.0064] so amhākaṃ satthā atītānāgatapaccuppannaṃ sabbaṃ jānāti passatīti dasseti. Aparisesaṃ ñāṇadassanaṃ paṭijānātīti so amhākaṃ satthā aparisesaṃ dhammaṃ jānanto aparisesasaṅkhātaṃ ñāṇadassanaṃ paṭijānāti, paṭijānanto ca evaṃ paṭijānāti “carato ca me tiṭṭhato ca…pe… paccupaṭṭhita”nti. Tattha satatanti niccaṃ. Samitanti tasseva vevacanaṃ.

“On Vulture Peak Mountain”—that mountain has a peak resembling a vulture, hence it is called Vulture Peak; or because vultures dwell on its peaks, it is called Vulture Peak. “On the slope of Isigili”—on the slope of Isigili Mountain. “On the Black Rock”—on a black flat stone. “Standing upright”—they remained standing; they were not sitting. “Brought about by effort”—brought about by their own effort through standing upright, etc. “Nigaṇṭha, friend”—unable to say anything else, they cast the blame upon the Nigaṇṭha. “All-knowing, all-seeing”—this shows that “Our Teacher knows and sees all, past, future, and present.” “He claims to have complete knowledge and vision”—this means that “Our Teacher, knowing the Dhamma without remainder, claims to have knowledge and vision reckoned as without remainder, and in claiming, he claims thus: ‘Whether walking or standing...it is ever present.’” Here, `satataṃ` means constantly. `Samitaṃ` is a synonym for that.

180. Kiṃ pana tumhe, āvuso, nigaṇṭhā jānātha ettakaṃ vā dukkhaṃ nijjiṇṇanti idaṃ bhagavā puriso nāma yaṃ karoti, taṃ jānāti. Vīsatikahāpaṇe iṇaṃ gahetvā dasa datvā “dasa me dinnā dasa avasiṭṭhā”ti jānāti, tepi datvā “sabbaṃ dinna”nti jānāti. Khettassa tatiyabhāgaṃ lāyitvā “eko bhāgo lāyito, dve avasiṭṭhā”ti jānāti. Puna ekaṃ lāyitvā [V 1.0376] “dve lāyitā, eko avasiṭṭho”ti jānāti. Tasmimpi lāyite “sabbaṃ niṭṭhita”nti jānāti, evaṃ sabbakiccesu katañca akatañca jānāti, tumhehipi tathā ñātabbaṃ siyāti dasseti. Akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ pahānanti iminā akusalaṃ pahāya kusalaṃ bhāvetvā suddhantaṃ patto nigaṇṭho nāma tumhākaṃ sāsane atthīti pucchati.

180. “But do you, friends, Nigaṇṭhas, know this much: ‘So much suffering has been exhausted’?” By this, the Blessed One shows that a person knows what he does. For example, if one borrows twenty kahāpaṇas and repays ten, he knows, “Ten have been repaid, ten remain.” If he repays those ten, he knows, “All has been repaid.” If a third of a field is reaped, he knows, “One part is reaped, two remain.” If another part is reaped, he knows, “Two parts are reaped, one remains.” When that too is reaped, he knows, “All is finished.” Similarly, in all tasks, one knows what has been done and what has not been done. He shows that you too should know thus. “The abandoning of unwholesome states”—with this, he asks whether in your teaching there is a Nigaṇṭha who, having abandoned the unwholesome and developed the wholesome, has reached purity.

Evaṃ santeti tumhākaṃ evaṃ ajānanabhāve sati. Luddāti luddācārā. Lohitapāṇinoti pāṇe jīvitā voropentā lohitena makkhitapāṇino. Pāṇaṃ hi hanantassapi yassa lohitena pāṇi na makkhiyati[M 1.0369], sopi lohitapāṇītveva vuccati. Kurūrakammantāti dāruṇakammā. Mātari pitari dhammikasamaṇabrāhmaṇādīsu ca katāparādhā. Māgavikādayo vā kakkhaḷakammā.

“Being thus”—this means when you are in such a state of unknowing. “Cruel”—meaning of cruel conduct. “Bloodstained hands”—meaning those who deprive living beings of life, their hands stained with blood. For even if one kills a living being and his hands are not stained with blood, he is still called “bloodstained-handed.” “Ruthless in action”—meaning those of fierce action, who have committed offenses against mother, father, righteous ascetics, brahmins, and so on; or those of harsh action, such as hunters and the like.

Na kho, āvuso, gotamāti idaṃ nigaṇṭhā “ayaṃ amhākaṃ vāde dosaṃ deti, mayampissa dosaṃ āropemā”ti maññamānā ārabhiṃsu. Tassattho, “āvuso, gotama yathā tumhe paṇītacīvarāni dhārentā sālimaṃsodanaṃ bhuñjantā devavimānavaṇṇāya gandhakuṭiyā vasamānā sukhena sukhaṃ adhigacchatha, na evaṃ sukhena sukhaṃ adhigantabbaṃ. Yathā pana mayaṃ ukkuṭikappadhānādīhi nānappakāraṇaṃ dukkhaṃ anubhavāma, evaṃ dukkhena sukhaṃ adhigantabba”nti. Sukhena ca hāvusoti idaṃ sace sukhena ca sukhaṃ adhigantabbaṃ siyā. Rājā adhigaccheyyāti dassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ[P 2.0065]. Tattha māgadhoti magadharaṭṭhassa issaro. Seniyoti tassa nāmaṃ. Bimbīti attabhāvassa nāmaṃ. So tassa sārabhūto dassanīyo pāsādiko attabhāvasamiddhiyā bimbisāroti vuccati. Sukhavihāritaroti idaṃ te nigaṇṭhā rañño tīsu pāsādesu tividhavayehi nāṭakehi saddhiṃ sampattianubhavanaṃ sandhāya vadanti. Addhāti ekaṃsena. Sahasā appaṭisaṅkhāti sāhasaṃ katvā, appaccavekkhitvāva yathā ratto rāgavasena duṭṭho dosavasena mūḷho mohavasena bhāsati, evamevaṃ vācā bhāsitāti dasseti.

“Not so, friend Gotama”—this the Nigaṇṭhas began, thinking, “This one finds fault with our doctrine, so we too will accuse him of a fault.” The meaning is this: “Friend Gotama, just as you, wearing fine robes, eating choice rice with meat, and dwelling in a perfumed chamber like a divine mansion, attain happiness through happiness—happiness is not to be attained in that way. Rather, just as we experience various kinds of suffering through practices such as striving in the squatting posture, etc., it is through suffering that happiness is to be attained.” Regarding the phrase “And if, friend, by happiness...”: this was said to show that if happiness were to be attained by happiness, a king would attain it. There, “Māgadha” refers to the ruler of the Magadha country. “Seniya” is his name. “Bimbī” is the name of his person. Because he was the essence of that, handsome and splendid in personal prosperity, he was called Bimbisāra. Regarding “a greater dweller in happiness”: this is what those Nigaṇṭhas say, referring to the king’s enjoyment of prosperity in his three palaces, along with theatrical performances for the three seasons. “Certainly” means without a doubt. “Rashly, without reflection” means having acted recklessly, without proper consideration. It is shown that just as a lustful person speaks under the influence of lust, an angry person under the influence of anger, and a deluded person under the influence of delusion, so too was this speech spoken.

Tattha paṭipucchissāmīti tasmiṃ atthe pucchissāmi. Yathā vo khameyyāti yathā tumhākaṃ rucceyya. Pahotīti sakkoti.

“There, I will inquire”—meaning I will ask about that matter. “As may be agreeable to you”—meaning as it may please you. “He is capable”—meaning he is able.

Aniñjamānoti acalamāno. Ekantasukhaṃ paṭisaṃvedīti nirantarasukhaṃ paṭisaṃvedī. “Ahaṃ kho[V 1.0377], āvuso, nigaṇṭhā pahomi…pe… ekantasukhaṃ paṭisaṃvedī”ti idaṃ attano phalasamāpattisukhaṃ dassento āha. Ettha ca kathāpatiṭṭhāpanatthaṃ rājavāre satta ādiṃ katvā pucchā katā. Satta rattindivāni nappahotīti hi vutte cha pañca cattārīti sukhaṃ pucchituṃ hoti. Suddhavāre pana sattāti vutte puna cha pañca cattārīti vuccamānaṃ anacchariyaṃ hoti, tasmā ekaṃ ādiṃ katvā desanā katā. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānatthamevāti.

“Unmoving”—meaning not stirring. “Experiencing exclusively happiness”—meaning experiencing uninterrupted happiness. “Friends, Nigaṇṭhas, I am able... experiencing exclusively happiness”—this was said showing the happiness of his own attainment of fruition. Here, to establish the topic, the question was asked starting with seven in the section concerning the king. For, if it were said that he is not able for seven days and nights, it would be easy to ask about six, five, or four. But in the pure section, when ‘seven’ is said, mentioning six, five, or four again would be unremarkable. Therefore, the discourse was given starting with one. The rest is clear in meaning everywhere.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

From the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya.

Cūḷadukkhakkhandhasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Cūḷadukkhakkhandha Sutta is finished.

5. Anumānasuttavaṇṇanā

5. Exposition of the Anumāna Sutta.

181. Evaṃ [V 1.0378][M 1.0370] me sutanti anumānasuttaṃ. Tattha bhaggesūti evaṃnāmake janapade, vacanattho panettha vuttānusāreneva veditabbo. Susumāragireti evaṃnāmake nagare. Tassa kira nagarassa vatthupariggahadivase avidūre udakarahade suṃsumāro saddamakāsi, giraṃ nicchāresi. Atha nagare niṭṭhite suṃsumāragiraṃ tvevassa nāmaṃ akaṃsu. Bhesakaḷāvaneti bhesakaḷānāmake vane. “Bhesagaḷāvane”tipi pāṭho. Migadāyeti taṃ vanaṃ migapakkhīnaṃ abhayadinnaṭṭhāne jātaṃ, tasmā migadāyoti vuccati.

181. Thus have I heard—the Anumāna Sutta. Therein, 'in the Bhagga country' refers to a country of that name; the meaning of the words here should be understood according to what has already been stated. 'At Susumāragira' refers to a city of that name. It is said that on the day the site for that city was being determined, a crocodile made a sound and uttered a cry in a nearby lake. Thus, when the city was completed, they named it Susumāragira. 'In Bhesakaḷā Forest' refers to a forest named Bhesakaḷā. There is also a variant reading: 'Bhesagaḷā Forest.' 'In the Deer Park' means that forest arose in a place where safety was given to deer and birds; hence it is called the Deer Park.

Pavāretīti [P 2.0066] icchāpeti. Vadantūti ovādānusāsanivasena vadantu, anusāsantūti attho. Vacanīyomhīti ahaṃ tumhehi vattabbo, anusāsitabbo ovaditabboti attho. So ca hoti dubbacoti so ca dukkhena vattabbo hoti, vutto na sahati. Dovacassakaraṇehīti dubbacabhāvakārakehi upari āgatehi soḷasahi dhammehi. Appadakkhiṇaggāhī anusāsaninti yo hi vuccamāno tumhe maṃ kasmā vadatha, ahaṃ attano kappiyākappiyaṃ sāvajjānavajjaṃ atthānatthaṃ jānāmīti vadati. Ayaṃ anusāsaniṃ padakkhiṇato na gaṇhāti, vāmato gaṇhāti, tasmā appadakkhiṇaggāhīti vuccati.

'He invites' means he expresses his wish. 'Let them speak' means let them speak in the manner of advice and instruction; the meaning is, let them instruct. 'I am one to be spoken to' means I should be addressed by you, advised, and instructed—this is the meaning. 'And he is difficult to speak to' means he is hard to address, and when spoken to, he cannot endure it. 'By way of actions causing one to be difficult to speak to' refers to the sixteen qualities mentioned further on that make one difficult to admonish. 'Not receptive in grasping instruction' means when someone, being addressed, says, 'Why do you speak to me? I know for myself what is allowable and unallowable, blameworthy and blameless, beneficial and unbeneficial.' This person does not take instruction respectfully, but takes it disrespectfully; thus, he is called 'not receptive in grasping instruction.'

Pāpikānaṃ icchānanti lāmakānaṃ asantasambhavanapatthanānaṃ. Paṭippharatīti paṭiviruddho, paccanīko hutvā tiṭṭhati, apasādetīti kiṃ nu kho tuyhaṃ bālassa abyattassa bhaṇitena, tvampi nāma bhaṇitabbaṃ maññissasīti evaṃ ghaṭṭeti. Paccāropetīti, tvampi khosi itthannāmaṃ āpattiṃ āpanno, taṃ tāva paṭikarohīti evaṃ paṭiāropeti.

'Of evil desires' refers to base aspirations for what is not good. 'Opposes' means he stands opposed, becomes an adversary, and disparages, saying, 'What use are your words, you foolish and inept one? Do you really think you are fit to speak?'—thus he rebukes. 'Counter-charges' means he says, 'You too have incurred such-and-such an offense; first, atone for that'—thus he counter-charges.

Aññenaññaṃ paṭicaratīti aññena kāraṇena vacanena vā aññaṃ kāraṇaṃ vacanaṃ vā paṭicchādeti. “Āpattiṃ āpannosī”ti vutte “ko āpanno, kiṃ āpanno, kismiṃ āpanno, kaṃ bhaṇatha, kiṃ bhaṇathā”ti vā vadati. “Evarūpaṃ kiñci tayā diṭṭha”nti vutte “na suṇāmī”ti [V 1.0379] sotaṃ vā upaneti. Bahiddhā kathaṃ apanāmetīti “itthannāmaṃ āpattiṃ āpannosī”ti puṭṭho “pāṭaliputtaṃ gatomhī”ti vatvā puna “na tava pāṭaliputtagamanaṃ pucchāma, āpattiṃ [M 1.0371] pucchāmā”ti vutte “tato rājagehaṃ gatomhī”ti, rājagehaṃ vā yāhi brāhmaṇagehaṃ vā, āpattiṃ āpannosīti. Tattha me sūkaramaṃsaṃ laddhantiādīni vadanto kathaṃ bahiddhā vikkhipati.

'One covers up with another' means one conceals one matter or statement with another matter or statement. When told, 'You have committed an offense,' he says, 'Who has committed an offense? What offense was committed? In what was the offense committed? Whom are you speaking to? What are you speaking of?' Or when told, 'Something like this was seen by you,' he says, 'I do not hear,' and presents his ear. 'Diverts the talk externally' means that when asked, 'Have you committed such-and-such an offense?' he says, 'I went to Pāṭaliputta.' When told, 'We are not asking about your going to Pāṭaliputta, we are asking about the offense,' he says, 'Then I went to the royal palace.' When it is said, 'Go to the royal palace or a brahmin's house, you have committed an offense,' he scatters the talk externally, saying things like, 'There I got some pork.'

Apadāneti attano cariyāya. Na sampāyatīti, āvuso, tvaṃ kuhiṃ vasasi, kaṃ nissāya vasasīti vā, yaṃ tvaṃ vadesi “mayā esa āpattiṃ āpajjanno diṭṭho”ti. Tvaṃ tasmiṃ samaye kiṃ karosi, ayaṃ kiṃ karoti, kattha vā tvaṃ acchasi kattha vā ayantiādinā nayena cariyaṃ puṭṭho sampādetvā kathetuṃ na sakkoti.

'In his conduct' means regarding his own conduct. 'He does not proceed' means that when questioned about his conduct with questions such as, 'Friend, where do you live? On whom do you depend?' or 'You say, "I saw this person committing an offense," but what were you doing at that time? What was he doing? Where were you? Where was he?'—he is unable to give a coherent account.

183. Tatrāvusoti[P 2.0067], āvuso, tesu soḷasasu dhammesu. Attanāva attānaṃ evaṃ anuminitabbanti evaṃ attanāva attā anumetabbo tuletabbo tīretabbo.

183. 'Therein, friend' means, friend, in regard to those sixteen qualities. 'One should infer about oneself thus' means in this way one should infer about, weigh, and investigate oneself by oneself.

184. Paccavekkhitabbanti paccavekkhitabbo. Ahorattānusikkhināti divāpi rattimpi sikkhantena, ratiñca divā ca kusalesu dhammesu sikkhantena pītipāmojjameva uppādetabbanti attho.

184. 'One should reflect' means one should review. 'Training day and night' means training both day and night; by training in wholesome qualities both night and day, one should arouse joy and gladness—this is the meaning.

Acche vā udakapatteti pasanne vā udakabhājane. Mukhanimittanti mukhapaṭibimbaṃ. Rajanti āgantukarajaṃ. Aṅgaṇanti tattha jātakaṃ tilakaṃ vā piḷakaṃ vā. Sabbepime pāpake akusale dhamme pahīneti iminā sabbappahānaṃ kathesi. Kathaṃ? Ettakā akusalā dhammā pabbajitassa nānucchavikāti paṭisaṅkhānaṃ uppādayato hi paṭisaṅkhānappahānaṃkathitaṃ hoti. Sīlaṃ padaṭṭhānaṃ katvā kasiṇaparikammaṃ ārabhitvā aṭṭha samāpattiyo nibbattentassa vikkhambhanappahānaṃ kathitaṃ. Samāpattiṃ padaṭṭhānaṃ katvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhentassa tadaṅgappahānaṃ kathitaṃ. Vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā maggaṃ bhāventassa samucchedappahānaṃ kathitaṃ. Phale āgate paṭippassaddhippahānaṃ, nibbāne āgate nissaraṇappahānanti evaṃ imasmiṃ sutte sabbappahānaṃ kathitaṃva hoti.

'In a clear water pot' means in a clear water vessel. 'The facial image' means the reflection of the face. 'Dust' means adventitious dust. 'A blemish' refers to a birthmark, a mole, or a pimple. By saying, 'All these evil, unwholesome states are abandoned,' he described the abandonment of all. How? For when one generates reflection thinking, 'Such unwholesome states are unsuited for a renunciant,' abandonment by reflection is described. For one who, making virtue the foundation, begins kasina practice and brings forth the eight attainments, abandonment by suppression is described. For one who, making attainment the foundation, develops insight, abandonment by substitution of opposites is described. For one who, having developed insight, cultivates the path, abandonment by cutting off is described. When the fruit is attained, abandonment by tranquilization is described; when Nibbāna is attained, abandonment by escape is described. Thus, in this discourse, the abandonment of all is described.

Idañhi [V 1.0380] suttaṃ bhikkhupātimokkhaṃ nāmāti porāṇā vadanti. Idaṃ divasassa tikkhattuṃ paccavekkhitabbaṃ. Pāto eva vasanaṭṭhānaṃ pavisitvā nisinnena “ime ettakā kilesā atthi nu kho mayhaṃ natthī”ti paccavekkhitabbā. Sace atthīti passati, tesaṃ pahānāya vāyamitabbaṃ. No ce passati, supabbajitosmīti [M 1.0372] attamanena bhavitabbaṃ. Bhattakiccaṃ katvā rattiṭṭhāne vā divāṭṭhāne vā nisīditvāpi paccavekkhitabbaṃ. Sāyaṃ vasanaṭṭhāne nisīditvāpi paccavekkhitabbaṃ. Tikkhattuṃ asakkontena dve vāre paccavekkhitabbaṃ. Dve vāre asakkontena pana avassaṃ ekavāraṃ paccavekkhitabbaṃ, appaccavekkhituṃ na vaṭṭatīti vadanti. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānatthamevāti.

The ancients say that this discourse is called the Bhikkhu Pātimokkha. This should be reviewed three times a day. Having entered one's dwelling place early in the morning and sat down, one should review thus: 'Are these so-many defilements present in me, or not?' If one sees they are present, effort should be made for their abandonment. If one does not see them, one should be glad, thinking, 'I am well-gone-forth.' Having completed the meal duties, one should also review, sitting in the night-place or day-place. In the evening, having sat down in one's dwelling place, one should also review. If unable to do it three times, it should be reviewed twice. But if unable to do it twice, it must be reviewed at least once; it is not proper not to review, they say. The rest is self-explanatory everywhere.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

From the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya.

Anumānasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The exposition of the Anumāna Sutta is concluded.

6. Cetokhilasuttavaṇṇanā

6. The Exposition of the Cetokhila Sutta

185. Evaṃ [V 1.0381][P 2.0068] me sutanti cetokhilasuttaṃ. Tattha cetokhilāti cittassa thaddhabhāvā kacavarabhāvā khāṇukabhāvā. Cetaso vinibandhāti cittaṃ bandhitvā muṭṭhiyaṃ katvā viya gaṇhantīti cetaso vinibandhā. Vuddhintiādīsu sīlena vuddhiṃ, maggena viruḷhiṃ, nibbānena vepullaṃ. Sīlasamādhīhi vā vuddhiṃ, vipassanāmaggehi viruḷhiṃ, phalanibbānehi vepullaṃ. Satthari kaṅkhatīti satthu sarīre vā guṇe vā kaṅkhati. Sarīre kaṅkhamāno dvattiṃsavaralakkhaṇappaṭimaṇḍitaṃ nāma sarīraṃ atthi nu kho natthīti kaṅkhati, guṇe kaṅkhamāno atītānāgatapaccuppannajānanasamatthaṃ sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ atthi nu kho natthīti kaṅkhati. Vicikicchatīti vicinanto kicchati, dukkhaṃ āpajjati, vinicchetuṃ na sakkoti. Nādhimuccatīti evametanti adhimokkhaṃ na paṭilabhati. Na sampasīdatīti guṇesu otaritvā nibbicikicchabhāvena pasīdituṃ, anāvilo bhavituṃ na sakkoti. Ātappāyāti kilesasantāpakavīriyakaraṇatthāya. Anuyogāyāti punappunaṃ yogāya. Sātaccāyāti satatakiriyāya padhānāyāti padahanatthāya. Ayaṃ paṭhamo cetokhiloti ayaṃ satthari vicikicchāsaṅkhāto paṭhamo cittassa thaddhabhāvo, evametassa bhikkhuno appahīno hoti. Dhammeti pariyattidhamme ca paṭivedhadhamme ca. Pariyattidhamme kaṅkhamāno, tepiṭakaṃ buddhavacanaṃ caturāsīti dhammakkhandhasahassānīti vadanti, atthi nu kho etaṃ natthīti kaṅkhati. Paṭivedhadhamme kaṅkhamāno vipassanānissando maggo nāma, magganissando phalaṃ nāma, sabbasaṅkhārapaṭinissaggo nibbānaṃ nāmāti vadanti. Taṃ atthi nu kho natthīti kaṅkhati. Saṅghe kaṅkhatīti suppaṭipannotiādīnaṃ padānaṃ vasena evarūpaṃ paṭipadaṃ paṭipannā [M 1.0373] cattāro maggaṭṭhā cattāro phalaṭṭhāti aṭṭhannaṃ puggalānaṃ samūhabhūto saṅgho nāma, so atthi nu kho natthīti kaṅkhati. Sikkhāya kaṅkhamāno adhisīlasikkhā nāma adhicittasikkhā nāma adhipaññāsikkhā [P 2.0069] nāmāti vadanti. Sā atthi nu kho natthīti kaṅkhati.
