Ayaṃ pañcamoti ayaṃ sabrahmacārīsu kopasaṅkhāto pañcamo cittassa thaddhabhāvo kacavarabhāvo khāṇukabhāvo.

185. The Cetokhilasutta begins with 'Thus have I heard.' Herein, 'mental barrenness' refers to the rigidity, waste-like state, and stump-like state of the mind. 'Mental bondage' means the mind is bound, clenched like a fist, as if seized. In the terms 'growth,' etc., growth is through virtue, development through the path, and abundance through Nibbāna. Or growth is through virtue and concentration, development through insight and the paths, and abundance through fruition and Nibbāna. 'Doubting the Teacher' means doubting the Teacher’s body or qualities. One who doubts the body wonders whether the body adorned with the thirty-two excellent marks of a great man exists or not. One who doubts the qualities wonders whether the omniscient knowledge capable of knowing the past, future, and present exists or not. 'He doubts' means he struggles while investigating, falls into suffering, and is unable to decide. 'Not resolved' means not gaining the conviction that 'it is thus.' 'Not serene' means unable to become clear and free from doubt by immersing oneself in the qualities. 'For ardour' means for the purpose of generating energy that burns up defilements. 'For application' means for repeated application. 'For persistence' means for continuous action. 'For exertion' means for striving. This is the first mental barrenness—this doubt regarding the Teacher is the first rigidity of mind, which is not abandoned in that bhikkhu. 'Dhamma' refers to both the textual Dhamma and the Dhamma of realization. One who doubts the textual Dhamma wonders whether the three baskets of the Buddha’s word, the eighty-four thousand sections of the Dhamma, exist or not. One who doubts the Dhamma of realization wonders whether the path born of insight, the fruition born of the path, and Nibbāna as the relinquishment of all formations exist or not. 'Doubting the Saṅgha' means wondering whether the Saṅgha, the assembly of the four established in the path and the four established in the fruition, those eight types of individuals who are practicing rightly, exists or not. 'Doubting the training' means wondering whether the higher training in virtue, the higher training in concentration, and the higher training in wisdom exist or not. This is the fifth—this anger toward fellow practitioners is the fifth rigidity, waste-like state, and stump-like state of the mind.

186. Vinibandhesu [V 1.0382] kāmeti vatthukāmepi kilesakāmepi. Kāyeti attano kāye. Rūpeti bahiddhā rūpe. Yāvadatthanti yattakaṃ icchati, tattakaṃ. Udarāvadehakanti udarapūraṃ. Tañhi udaraṃ avadehanato udarāvadehakanti vuccati. Seyyasukhanti mañcapīṭhasukhaṃ, utusukhaṃ vā. Passasukhanti yathā samparivattakaṃ sayantassa dakkhiṇapassavāmapassānaṃ sukhaṃ hoti, evaṃ uppannasukhaṃ. Middhasukhanti niddāsukhaṃ. Anuyuttoti yuttapayutto viharati.

186. Among the bondages, 'desires' refers to both desires for objects and desires that are defilements. 'Body' means one's own body. 'Forms' means external forms. 'As much as one wishes' means as much as one desires, that much. 'Filling the belly' means filling the stomach. For it is so called from stuffing the belly. 'Comfort in beds' means comfort in beds and chairs, or comfort in agreeable seasons. 'Comfort in sides' means the comfort that arises for one who lies down turning over, the comfort of the right side and left side. 'Comfort in sleep' means the pleasure of sleep. 'Devoted' means one lives engaged and committed.

Paṇidhāyāti patthayitvā. Sīlenātiādīsu sīlanti catupārisuddhisīlaṃ. Vatanti vatasamādānaṃ. Tapoti tapacaraṇaṃ. Brahmacariyanti methunavirati. Devo vā bhavissāmīti mahesakkhadevo vā bhavissāmi. Devaññataro vāpi appesakkhadevesu vā aññataro.

'Having aspired' means having wished. In the phrases beginning with 'by virtue,' 'virtue' refers to the fourfold purification virtue. 'Vow' means undertaking a vow. 'Austerity' means the practice of asceticism. 'The holy life' means abstaining from sexual intercourse. 'I shall become a god' means I shall become a god of great power. 'Or some other god' means one of the lesser gods.

189. Iddhipādesu chandaṃ nissāya pavatto samādhi chandasamādhi. Padhānabhūtā saṅkhārā padhānasaṅkhārā. Samannāgatanti tehi dhammehi upetaṃ. Iddhiyā pādaṃ, iddhibhūtaṃ vā pādanti iddhipādaṃ. Sesesupi eseva nayo, ayamettha saṅkhepo. Vitthāro pana iddhipādavibhaṅge āgato yeva. Visuddhimaggepissa attho dīpito. Iti imehi catūhi iddhipādehi vikkhambhanappahānaṃ kathitaṃ. Ussoḷhīyeva pañcamīti ettha ussoḷhīti sabbattha kattabbavīriyaṃ dasseti. Ussoḷhīpannarasaṅgasamannāgatoti pañca cetokhilappahānāni pañca vinibandhappahānāni cattāro iddhipādā ussoḷhīti evaṃ ussoḷhiyā saddhiṃ pannarasahi aṅgehi samannāgato. Bhabboti anurūpo, anucchaviko. Abhinibbhidāyāti ñāṇena kilesabhedāya. Sambodhāyāti catumaggasambodhāya. Anuttarassāti seṭṭhassa. Yogakkhemassāti catūhi yogehi khemassa arahattassa. Adhigamāyāti paṭilābhāya. Seyyathāti opammatthe nipāto. Pīti sambhāvanatthe. Ubhayenapi seyyathāpi nāma, bhikkhaveti dasseti[P 2.0070].

189. In the context of the bases of psychic power, 'desire-concentration' is the concentration that arises based on desire. 'Striving-formations' are the formations that constitute striving. 'Endowed' means possessed of those qualities. 'The base of psychic power' is so called because it is the base for psychic power, or the base that is psychic power. The same method applies to the rest; this is the summary here. The detailed explanation, however, is given in the Analysis of the Bases of Psychic Power. Its meaning is also explained in the Visuddhimagga. Thus, with these four bases of psychic power, abandonment by suppression is described. In the phrase 'zeal itself is the fifth,' 'zeal' indicates the energy to be applied in all cases. 'Endowed with the fifteen factors including zeal' means endowed with these fifteen factors: the five abandonments of mental barrenness, the five abandonments of mental bonds, the four bases of psychic power, and zeal. 'Capable' means suitable, appropriate. 'For breakthrough' means for the breaking through of the defilements by knowledge. 'For enlightenment' means for the enlightenment of the four paths. 'Of the unsurpassed' means of the best. 'For security from the yokes' means for the security of arahantship from the four yokes. 'For attainment' means for realization. 'Just as' (seyyathā) is a particle in the sense of a simile. The particle 'pi' is used in the sense of affirmation. Both together indicate the phrase 'Just as, O monks...'

Kukkuṭiyā [M 1.0374] aṇḍāni aṭṭha vā dasa vā dvādasa vāti ettha pana kiñcāpi kukkuṭiyā vuttappakārato ūnādhikānipi aṇḍāni honti, vacanasiliṭṭhatāya pana evaṃ vuttaṃ. Evañhi loke siliṭṭhaṃ vacanaṃ hoti. Tānassūti tāni assu, bhaveyyunti attho. Kukkuṭiyā sammā adhisayitānīti tāya janettiyā kukkuṭiyā pakkhe pasāretvā tesaṃ upari sayantiyā sammā adhisayitāni. Sammā pariseditānīti kālena kālaṃ utuṃ gāhāpentiyā suṭṭhu samantato seditāni [V 1.0383] usmīkatāni. Sammā paribhāvitānīti kālena kālaṃ suṭṭhu samantato bhāvitāni, kukkuṭagandhaṃ gāhāpitānīti attho. Kiñcāpi tassā kukkuṭiyāti tassā kukkuṭiyā imaṃ tividhakiriyākaraṇena appamādaṃ katvā kiñcāpi na evaṃ icchā uppajjeyya. Atha kho bhabbāva teti atha kho te kukkuṭapotakā vuttanayena sotthinā abhinibbhijjituṃ bhabbāva. Te hi yasmā tāya kukkuṭiyā evaṃ tīhākārehi tāni aṇḍāni paripālīyamānāni na pūtīni honti. Yopi nesaṃ allasineho, sopi pariyādānaṃ gacchati, kapālaṃ tanukaṃ hoti, pādanakhasikhā ca mukhatuṇḍakañca kharaṃ hoti, sayaṃ paripākaṃ gacchati, kapālassa tanuttā bahi āloko anto paññāyati, tasmā “ciraṃ vata mayaṃ saṅkuṭitahatthapādā sambādhe sayimhā, ayañca bahi āloko dissati, ettha dāni no sukhavihāro bhavissatī”ti nikkhamitukāmā hutvā kapālaṃ pādena paharanti, gīvaṃ pasārenti, tato taṃ kapālaṃ dvedhā bhijjati. Atha te pakkhe vidhunantā taṅkhaṇānurūpaṃ viravantā nikkhamantiyeva, nikkhamitvā ca gāmakkhettaṃ upasobhayamānā vicaranti.

A hen's eggs are eight, ten, or twelve. Here, although a hen may have fewer or more eggs than the stated number, it is expressed this way for elegance of speech, for such is the elegant way of speaking in the world. 'May they be' means 'they would be'—that is the meaning. 'Properly sat upon by the hen' means that the mother hen spreads her wings over them and sits properly upon them. 'Properly warmed' means that from time to time, she warms them, thoroughly heating them all around. 'Properly nurtured' means that from time to time, she thoroughly nurtures them all around—that is, she imparts the hen's scent. Although for that hen, having carefully performed these three kinds of actions, the wish may not arise, still, those chicks are capable of safely breaking out in the manner described. For since those eggs are protected by the hen in these three ways, they do not rot. The moisture within them is also exhausted, the shell becomes thin, and the tips of the claws and the beak become hard. They mature on their own, and due to the thinness of the shell, the light outside becomes visible inside. Therefore, thinking, 'For a long time, we have lain with contracted limbs in this confinement. Now this outer light is visible—here will be our pleasant abode!'—desiring to emerge, they strike the shell with their feet, stretch their necks, and then the shell splits in two. Then, shaking their wings and chirping as is suitable for that moment, they emerge. Once out, they wander about, adorning the village fields.

Evameva khoti idaṃ opammasampaṭipādanaṃ. Taṃ evaṃ atthena saṃsandetvā veditabbaṃ – tassā kukkuṭiyā aṇḍesu tividhakiriyākaraṇaṃ viya hi imassa bhikkhuno ussoḷhīpannarasehi aṅgehi samannāgatabhāvo. Kukkuṭiyā tividhakiriyāsampādanena aṇḍānaṃ apūtibhāvo viya pannarasaṅgasamannāgatassa bhikkhuno tividhānupassanāsampādanena vipassanāñāṇassa aparihāni. Tassā tividhakiriyākaraṇena aṇḍānaṃ allasinehapariyādānaṃ viya tassa bhikkhuno tividhānupassanāsampādanena bhavattayānugatanikantisinehapariyādānaṃ[P 2.0071]. Aṇḍakalāpānaṃ tanubhāvo viya [M 1.0375] bhikkhuno avijjaṇḍakosassa tanubhāvo. Kukkuṭapotakānaṃ pādanakhamutuṇḍakānaṃ thaddhakharabhāvo viya bhikkhuno vipassanāñāṇassa tikkhakharavippasannasūrabhāvo. Kukkuṭapotakānaṃ pariṇāmakālo viya bhikkhuno vipassanāñāṇassa pariṇāmakālo vaḍḍhitakālo gabbhaggahaṇakālo. Kukkuṭapotakānaṃ pādanakhasikhāya vā mukhatuṇḍakena vā aṇḍakosaṃ padāletvā pakkhe papphoṭetvā sotthinā abhinikkhamanakālo viya tassa bhikkhuno vipassanāñāṇagabbhaṃ gaṇhāpetvā vicarantassa tajjātikaṃ utusappāyaṃ vā bhojanasappāyaṃ vā puggalasappāyaṃ vā dhammassavanasappāyaṃ vā labhitvā ekāsane nisinnasseva vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhentassa anupubbādhigatena arahattamaggena avijjaṇḍakosaṃ padāletvā abhiññāpakkhe papphoṭetvā sotthinā [V 1.0384] arahattappattakālo veditabbo. Yathā pana kukkuṭapotakānaṃ pariṇatabhāvaṃ ñatvā mātāpi aṇḍakosaṃ bhindati, evaṃ tathārūpassa bhikkhuno ñāṇaparipākaṃ ñatvā satthāpi –

Just so, this is the exposition by way of simile. It should be understood by correlating it with the meaning thus: Just as that hen performs three kinds of actions regarding her eggs, so too this monk is endowed with the fifteen factors of energy. Just as the hen’s successful performance of the three actions prevents the eggs from decaying, so too the monk’s successful practice of the three kinds of contemplation prevents the decline of insight knowledge. Just as the hen’s performance of the three actions removes the moisture from the eggs, so too the monk’s practice of the three kinds of contemplation removes the attachment associated with the three realms of existence. Just as the eggshell becomes thin, so too the monk’s eggshell of ignorance becomes thin. Just as the chicks’ claws and beaks become firm and hard, so too the monk’s insight knowledge becomes sharp, firm, clear, and courageous. Just as the time comes for the chicks to mature, so too should be understood the time for the monk’s insight knowledge to mature, grow, and reach its full development. Just as the time for the chicks to break open the eggshell with the tips of their claws or their beaks, flap their wings, and emerge safely, so too should be understood the time for that monk: while cultivating the embryo of insight knowledge and living, having obtained a suitable climate, or suitable food, or suitable companionship, or suitable hearing of the Dhamma, sitting in one seat and developing insight, through the successively attained path of arahantship, he breaks open the eggshell of ignorance, flaps the wings of higher knowledge, and safely attains arahantship. And just as the mother hen, knowing the chicks have matured, breaks the eggshell, so too the Teacher, knowing the maturity of such a monk’s knowledge—

“Ucchinda sinehamattano, kumudaṃ sāradikaṃva pāṇinā;

Santimaggameva brūhaya, nibbānaṃ sugatena desita”nti. (dha. pa. 285) –

“Cut off your affection, like an autumn water lily with the hand; cultivate only the path to peace, Nibbāna, taught by the Sugata.”

Ādinā nayena obhāsaṃ pharitvā gāthāya avijjaṇḍakosaṃ paharati, so gāthāpariyosāne avijjāṇḍakosaṃ bhinditvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti. Tato paṭṭhāya yathā te kukkuṭapotakā gāmakkhettaṃ upasobhayamānā tattha tattha vicaranti, evaṃ ayampi mahākhīṇāsavo nibbānarammaṇaṃ phalasamāpattiṃ appetvā saṅghārāmaṃ upasobhayamāno vicarati.

Thus, having suffused his radiance, he strikes the eggshell of ignorance with the verse. At the conclusion of the verse, having broken the eggshell of ignorance, he attains arahantship. From then on, just as those chicks, adorning the village fields, wander here and there, so too does this great one whose cankers are destroyed, having entered upon the fruition attainment with Nibbāna as its object, wander about, adorning the monastery.

Iti imasmiṃ sutte cattāri pahānāni kathitāni. Kathaṃ? Cetokhilānañhi cetovinibandhānaṃ pahānena paṭisaṅkhānappapahānaṃ kathitaṃ, iddhipādehi vikkhambhanappahānaṃ kathita, magge āgate samucchedappahānaṃ kathitaṃ, phale āgate paṭippassaddhippahānaṃ kathitaṃ. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānatthamevāti.

Thus, in this discourse, four kinds of abandonment are spoken of. How? The abandonment of mental barrenness and mental bonds is spoken of as abandonment by discrimination; abandonment by suppression is spoken of by means of the bases of spiritual power; abandonment by cutting off is spoken of when the path is attained; abandonment by tranquilization is spoken of when the fruit is attained. The rest is clear in meaning throughout.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

From the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Middle Length Discourses.

Cetokhilasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Cetokhila Sutta is concluded.

7. Vanapatthapariyāyasuttavaṇṇanā

7. Commentary on the Discourse on the Ways of the Forest

190. Evaṃ [M 1.0376][V 1.0385][P 2.0072] me sutanti vanapatthapariyāyaṃ. Tattha vanapatthapariyāyanti vanapatthakāraṇaṃ, vanapatthadesanaṃ vā.

190. Thus have I heard. The Discourse on the Ways of the Forest. Therein, 'the discourse on the ways of the forest' means the reason for a forest thicket, or the teaching on a forest thicket.

191. Vanapatthaṃ upanissāya viharatīti manussūpacārātikkantaṃ vanasaṇḍasenāsanaṃ nissāya samaṇadhammaṃ karonto viharati. Anupaṭṭhitātiādīsu pubbe anupaṭṭhitā sati taṃ upanissāya viharatopi na upaṭṭhāti, pubbe asamāhitaṃ cittaṃ na samādhiyati, pubbe aparikkhīṇā āsavā na parikkhayaṃ gacchanti, pubbe ananuppattaṃ anuttaraṃ yogakkhemasaṅkhātaṃ arahattañca na pāpuṇātīti attho. Jīvitaparikkhārāti jīvitasambhārā. Samudānetabbāti samāharitabbā. Kasirena samudāgacchantīti dukkhena uppajjanti. Rattibhāgaṃ vā divasabhāgaṃ vāti rattikoṭṭhāse vā divasakoṭṭhāse vā. Ettha ca rattibhāge paṭisañcikkhamānena ñatvā rattiṃyeva pakkamitabbaṃ, rattiṃ caṇḍavāḷādīnaṃ paribandhe sati aruṇuggamanaṃ āgametabbaṃ. Divasabhāge ñatvā divāva pakkamitabbaṃ, divā paribandhe sati sūriyatthaṅgamanaṃ āgametabbaṃ.

191. ‘Dwells depending on a forest thicket’ means that one dwells practicing the duties of a recluse, depending on a lodging in a forest grove that is beyond the range of human activity. In the phrases ‘unestablished,’ and so on, the meaning is that if mindfulness was previously unestablished, even while dwelling depending on that place, it is not established; if the mind was previously unconcentrated, it does not become concentrated; if the taints were previously undestroyed, they do not go to destruction; and if one has not previously attained the unsurpassed security from bondage called Arahantship, one does not attain it. ‘Requisites of life’ means the supports for life. ‘Should be procured’ means should be collected. ‘They are procured with difficulty’ means they arise with hardship. ‘A portion of the night or a portion of the day’ means in a part of the night or a part of the day. Here, having reflected during the night portion and known, one should depart right at night. If at night there is danger from fierce beasts and so on, one should wait for the rising of the dawn. Having known during the day portion, one should depart right in the day. If there is danger during the day, one should wait for the setting of the sun.

192. Saṅkhāpīti evaṃ samaṇadhammassa anipphajjanabhāvaṃ jānitvā. Anantaravāre pana saṅkhāpīti evaṃ samaṇadhammassa nipphajjanabhāvaṃ jānitvā.

192. ‘Having reflected thus’ means: having thus known the non-accomplishment of the recluse's duty. But in the next instance, ‘having reflected thus’ means: having thus known the accomplishment of the recluse's duty.

194. Yāvajīvanti yāva jīvitaṃ pavattati, tāva vatthabbameva.

194. ‘For as long as life lasts’ means that as long as life continues, so long should one indeed dwell.

195. So puggaloti padassa nānubandhitabboti iminā sambandho. Anāpucchāti idha pana taṃ puggalaṃ anāpucchā pakkamitabbanti attho.

195. The phrase ‘that person’ is connected with ‘should not be followed.’ Here, ‘without asking’ means that one should depart without taking leave of that person.

197. Saṅkhāpīti evaṃ samaṇadhammassa anipphajjanabhāvaṃ ñatvā so puggalo nānubandhitabbo, taṃ āpucchā pakkamitabbaṃ.

197. ‘Having reflected thus’ means: having thus known that the qualities of a recluse are not being accomplished, that person should not be followed; one should depart after taking leave of him.

198. Api [V 1.0386] panujjamānenāpīti api nikkaḍḍhīyamānenāpi. Evarūpo hi puggalo sacepi dārukalāpasataṃ vā udakaghaṭasataṃ vā vālikambaṇasataṃ vā daṇḍaṃ āharāpeti, mā idha vasīti nikkaḍḍhāpeti vā, taṃ taṃ khamāpetvā yāvajīvaṃ vatthabbamevāti.

198. ‘Even if being driven away’ means even if being expelled. For if such a person is made to bring a hundred bundles of firewood, or a hundred water pots, or a hundred loads of sand, or a staff, or is driven out with the words, ‘Do not live here,’ he should ask for forgiveness for each of these things and dwell there for as long as he lives.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

From the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya.

Vanapatthapariyāyasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Discourse on the Ways of the Forest is concluded.

8. Madhupiṇḍikasuttavaṇṇanā

8. The Commentary on the Madhupiṇḍika Sutta

199. Evaṃ [M 1.0377][V 1.0387][P 2.0073] me sutanti madhupiṇḍikasuttaṃ. Tattha mahāvananti himavantena saddhiṃ ekābaddhaṃ aropimaṃ jātivanaṃ, na yathā vesāliyaṃ ropitāropitamissakaṃ. Divāvihārāyāti divā paṭisallānatthāya. Beluvalaṭṭhikāyāti taruṇabeluvarukkhassa. Daṇḍapāṇīti na jarādubbalatāya daṇḍahattho. Ayañhi taruṇo paṭhamavaye ṭhito, daṇḍacittatāya pana suvaṇṇadaṇḍaṃ gahetvā vicarati, tasmā daṇḍapāṇīti vutto. Jaṅghāvihāranti jaṅghākilamathavinodanatthaṃ jaṅghācāraṃ. Anucaṅkamamāno anuvicaramānoti ārāmadassana-vanadassana-pabbatadassanādīnaṃ atthāya ito cito ca vicaramāno. Adhiccanikkhamano kiresa kadāci deva nikkhamitvā evaṃ vicarati. Daṇḍamolubbhāti daṇḍaṃ olumbhitvā gopālakadārako viya daṇḍaṃ purato ṭhapetvā daṇḍamatthake dve hatthe patiṭṭhāpetvā piṭṭhipāṇiṃ hanukena uppīḷetvā ekamantaṃ aṭṭhāsi.

199. Thus have I heard—the Madhupiṇḍika Sutta. There, 'the great forest' means a natural, unplanted forest connected to the Himalayas, not like the mix of planted and unplanted groves at Vesālī. 'For the daytime abiding' means for the purpose of seclusion by day. 'At Beluvalaṭṭhikā' means at a young beluva tree. 'Daṇḍapāṇi' does not mean he held a staff due to the weakness of old age. For he was young, in his first stage of life, but he wandered about holding a golden staff out of a fondness for staffs; therefore he was called 'Daṇḍapāṇi' (Staff-in-hand). 'Walking exercise' means walking about to dispel leg-weariness. 'Pacing and wandering about' means wandering here and there for the sake of seeing the monastery grounds, the forest, the mountain, and so on. It is said he was one who went out spontaneously; he would occasionally just go out and wander like this. 'Leaning on the staff' means that, like a cowherd boy, he leaned on his staff, placing it in front of him, setting both hands on top of it, pressing his chin against the back of his hands, and stood to one side.

200. Kiṃvādīti kiṃdiṭṭhiko. Kimakkhāyīti kiṃ katheti. Ayaṃ rājā bhagavantaṃ avanditvā paṭisanthāramattakameva katvā pañhaṃ pucchati. Tampi na aññātukāmatāya, acittīkārena pucchati. Kasmā? Devadattassa pakkhiko kiresa. Devadatto attano santikaṃ āgacchamāne tathāgate bhindati. So kira evaṃ vadeti “samaṇo gotamo amhākaṃ kulena saddhiṃ verī, na no kulassa vuddhiṃ icchati. Bhaginīpi me cakkavattiparibhogā, taṃ pahāya ‘nassatesā’ti nikkhamitvā pabbaji. Bhāgineyyopi me cakkavattibījanti ñatvā amhākaṃ kulassa vaḍḍhiyā atussanto ‘nassateta’nti tampi daharakāleyeva pabbājesi. Ahaṃ pana tena vinā vattituṃ asakkonto anupabbajito. Evaṃ pabbajitampi maṃ pabbajitadivasato paṭṭhāya na ujukehi akkhīhi oloketi. Parisamajjhe bhāsantopi mahāpharasunā paharanto viya āpāyiko devadattotiādīni bhāsatī”ti. Evaṃ ayampi rājā devadattena bhinno, tasmā evamakāsi.

200. ‘What is his doctrine?’ means ‘What is his view?’ ‘What does he proclaim?’ means ‘What does he state?’ This king, without paying homage to the Blessed One and making only a mere greeting, asks a question. And he does not ask out of a desire to know, but asks disrespectfully. Why? It is said he is a partisan of Devadatta. Devadatta alienates those who come into the Tathāgata's presence. He is said to have spoken thus: ‘The ascetic Gotama is an enemy to our clan; he does not wish for our clan's prosperity. My sister, too, who was fit for a universal monarch, abandoned that status and went forth, as if to say, “Let her perish!” And knowing my nephew was the seed of a universal monarch, being displeased with the growth of our clan, he made him go forth while still a boy, as if to say, “Let him perish!” As for me, unable to live without him, I followed him into homelessness. But even though I have gone forth, from the very day of my going forth, he does not look at me with a straight glance. And when speaking in the midst of the assembly, as if striking with a great axe, he says things like, “Devadatta is destined for the plane of misery.”’ Thus this king, too, was alienated by Devadatta; therefore he acted in this way.

Atha [P 2.0074] bhagavā yathā ayaṃ rājā mayā pañhe pucchite na kathetīti vattuṃ na labhati, yathā [V 1.0388] ca bhāsitassa atthaṃ na jānāti, evamassa [M 1.0378] kathessāmīti tassānucchavikaṃ kathento yathāvādī khotiādimāha.

Then the Blessed One, thinking, ‘I will speak in such a way that this king cannot say, “He did not answer when I asked a question,” and also in such a way that he will not understand the meaning of what is said,’ spoke to him in a suitable manner, beginning with the words, ‘According to what he says...’

Tattha na kenaci loke viggayha tiṭṭhatīti loke kenaci saddhiṃ viggāhikakathaṃ na karoti na vivadati. Tathāgato hi lokena saddhiṃ na vivadati; loko pana tathāgatena saddhiṃ aniccanti vutte niccanti vadamāno, dukkhaṃ, anattā, asubhanti vutte subhanti vadamāno vivadati. Tenevāha “nāhaṃ, bhikkhave, lokena vivadāmi, lokova kho, bhikkhave, mayā vivadati, tathā na, bhikkhave, dhammavādī kenaci lokasmiṃ vivadati, adhammavādīva kho, bhikkhave, vivadatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 3.94). Yathāti yena kāraṇena. Kāmehīti vatthukāmehipi kilesakāmehipi. Taṃ brāhmaṇanti taṃ khīṇāsavaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ. Akathaṃkathinti nibbicikicchaṃ. Chinnakukkuccanti vippaṭisārakukkuccassa ceva hatthapādakukkuccassa ca chinnattā chinnakukkuccaṃ. Bhavābhaveti punappunabbhave, hīnapaṇīte vā bhave, paṇīto hi bhavo vuddhippatto abhavoti vuccati. Saññāti kilesasaññā. Kilesāyeva vā idha saññānāmena vuttā, tasmā yena kāraṇena kāmehi visaṃyuttaṃ viharantaṃ taṃ loke ninnāvādiṃ khīṇāsavabrāhmaṇaṃ kilesasaññā nānusenti, tañca kāraṇaṃ ahaṃ vadāmīti ayamettha attho. Iti bhagavā attano khīṇāsavabhāvaṃ dīpeti. Nillāḷetvāti nīharitvā kīḷāpetvā. Tivisākhanti tisākhaṃ. Nalāṭikanti valibhaṅgaṃ nalāṭe tisso rājiyo dassento valibhaṅgaṃ vuṭṭhāpetvāti attho. Daṇḍamolubbhāti daṇḍaṃ uppīḷetvā. “Daṇḍamālubbhā”tipi pāṭho, gahetvā pakkāmīti attho.

Here, 'He does not dispute with anyone in the world' means he does not engage in contentious talk or dispute with anyone in the world. For the Tathāgata does not dispute with the world; rather, the world disputes with the Tathāgata. When it is said, 'impermanent,' the world says, 'permanent'; when it is said, 'suffering,' 'not-self,' 'unattractive,' the world says, 'attractive,' and thus disputes. Therefore, it is said: 'Monks, I do not dispute with the world; it is the world that disputes with me. Monks, one who speaks the Dhamma does not dispute with anyone in the world; it is one who speaks not-Dhamma who disputes' (Saṃ. Ni. 3.94). 'Because' means for which reason. 'By sensual pleasures' means both by sensual pleasures as objects and sensual pleasures as defilements. 'That brahmin' means that brahmin who is an arahant. 'Without perplexity' means free from doubt. 'With remorse cut off' means with remorse cut off because both remorse due to regret and scrupulousness about hands and feet have been cut off. 'In existence and non-existence' means in repeated existence, or in inferior and superior existences; for a superior existence that has reached its peak is called 'non-existence.' 'Perceptions' means perceptions of defilement. Or here, defilements themselves are referred to by the name 'perceptions.' Therefore, the meaning here is this: I declare the reason for which perceptions of defilement do not obsess that brahmin who is an arahant, who dwells disjoined from sensual pleasures, and is not a devious speaker in the world. Thus the Blessed One reveals his own state as an arahant. 'Sticking out' means having brought it out and waggled it. 'Three-forked' means three-branched. 'A frown on the forehead' means a furrowing of the brow; that is, showing three lines on the forehead, he raised a furrow—this is the meaning. 'Leaning on the staff' means pressing down on the staff. There is also the reading 'Daṇḍamālubbha,' which means having taken the staff, he departed.

201. Aññataroti nāmena apākaṭo eko bhikkhu. So kira anusandhikusalo, bhagavatā yathā daṇḍapāṇī na jānāti, tathā mayā kathitanti vutte kinti nu kho bhagavatā aviññeyyaṃ katvā pañho kathitoti anusandhiṃ gahetvā dasabalaṃ yācitvā imaṃ pañhaṃ bhikkhusaṅghassa pākaṭaṃ karissāmīti uṭṭhāyāsanā ekaṃsaṃ uttarāsaṅgaṃ karitvā dasanakhasamujjalaṃ [P 2.0075] añjaliṃ paggayha kiṃvādī pana, bhante bhagavātiādimāha.

201. 'A certain one' means a monk who was not famous by name. It is said he was skilled in connecting the meaning. When the Blessed One had said, 'I have spoken in such a way that Daṇḍapāṇi would not understand,' this monk grasped the connection, thinking, 'In what way was this matter spoken of by the Blessed One, making it unintelligible?' and 'I will make this matter clear to the Saṅgha of monks.' Having requested the Ten-Powered One, he rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, raised his joined hands, radiant with their ten nails, and said, 'But, venerable sir, what is the Blessed One's doctrine?' and so on.

Yatonidānanti [M 1.0379] bhāvanapuṃsakaṃ etaṃ, yena kāraṇena yasmiṃ kāraṇe satīti attho. Papañcasaññāsaṅkhāti ettha saṅkhāti koṭṭhāso. Papañcasaññāti taṇhāmānadiṭṭhipapañcasampayuttā saññā[V 1.0389], saññānāmena vā papañcāyeva vuttā. Tasmā papañcakoṭṭhāsāti ayamettha attho. Samudācarantīti pavattanti. Ettha ce natthi abhinanditabbanti yasmiṃ dvādasāyatanasaṅkhāte kāraṇe sati papañcasaññāsaṅkhā samudācaranti, ettha ekāyatanampi ce abhinanditabbaṃ abhivaditabbaṃ ajjhositabbaṃ natthīti attho. Tattha abhininditabbanti ahaṃ mamanti abhinanditabbaṃ. Abhivaditabbanti ahaṃ mamāti vattabbaṃ. Ajjhositabbanti ajjhositvā gilitvā pariniṭṭhapetvā gahetabbayuttaṃ. Etenettha taṇhādīnaṃyeva appavattiṃ katheti. Esevantoti ayaṃ abhinandanādīnaṃ natthibhāvova rāgānusayādīnaṃ anto. Eseva nayo sabbattha.

“From which as source” (Yatonidānaṃ): this is an abstract noun in the neuter gender. The meaning is: “by which reason,” or “when that reason exists.” In “the category of perceptions of proliferation” (papañcasaññāsaṅkhā), “category” (saṅkhā) here means a portion. “Perceptions of proliferation” (papañcasaññā) are perceptions associated with the proliferation of craving, conceit, and views; or, by the term ‘perception,’ proliferation itself is stated. Therefore, the meaning here is “the portion of proliferation.” “They arise” (samudācaranti) means they occur. “And if there is nothing to be delighted in here”: the meaning is that when, in the condition designated as the twelve sense-bases, the category of perceptions of proliferation arises, then not even a single sense-base is to be delighted in, spoken of, or clung to. Therein, “to be delighted in” (abhinanditabbaṃ) means to be delighted in as ‘I’ or ‘mine.’ “To be spoken of” (abhivaditabbaṃ) means to be spoken of as ‘I’ or ‘mine.’ “To be clung to” (ajjhositabbaṃ) means that which is fit to be grasped by clinging to, swallowing, and settling upon it. By this, it speaks of the non-occurrence of craving and so forth. “This itself is the end” (eseva anto): this very absence of delighting and so forth is the end of the underlying tendencies of lust, etc. This is the method in all cases.

Daṇḍādānādīsu pana yāya cetanāya daṇḍaṃ ādiyati, sā daṇḍādānaṃ. Yāya satthaṃ ādiyati parāmasati, sā satthādānaṃ. Matthakappattaṃ kalahaṃ. Nānāgāhamattaṃ viggahaṃ. Nānāvādamattaṃ vivādaṃ. Tuvaṃ tuvanti evaṃ pavattaṃ tuvaṃ tuvaṃ. Piyasuññakaraṇaṃ pesuññaṃ. Ayathāsabhāvaṃ musāvādaṃ karoti, sā musāvādoti veditabbā. Ettheteti ettha dvādasasu āyatanesu ete kilesā. Kilesā hi uppajjamānāpi dvādasāyatanāni nissāya uppajjanti, nirujjhamānāpi dvādasasu āyatanesuyeva nirujjhanti. Evaṃ yatthuppannā, tattheva niruddhā honti. Svāyamattho samudayasaccapañhena dīpetabbo –

However, regarding “taking up the rod,” etc.: the intention with which one takes up a rod is “taking up the rod.” The intention with which one takes up or handles a weapon is “taking up the weapon.” A quarrel that has reached its peak is ‘kalaha.’ A mere grasping at various things is ‘viggaha.’ A mere variety of assertions is ‘vivāda.’ That which proceeds as “You! You!” is ‘tuvaṃtuva.’ Making others devoid of what is dear is slander. The intention that produces false speech contrary to its true nature should be known as “false speech.” “Herein, these” (etthete) means: in these twelve sense-bases are these defilements. For defilements, when arising, arise dependent on the twelve sense-bases; and when ceasing, they cease right in the twelve sense-bases. Thus, where they arose, there they are ceased. This meaning should be illustrated by the question on the truth of the origin:

“Sā kho panesā taṇhā kattha uppajjamānā uppajjati, kattha nivisamānā nivisatī”ti vatvā – “yaṃ loke piyarūpaṃ sātarūpaṃ, etthesā taṇhā uppajjamānā uppajjati, ettha nivisamānā nivisati. Kiñca loke piyarūpaṃ sātarūpaṃ? Cakkhu loke piyarūpaṃ sātarūpa”ntiādinā (vibha. 203) nayena dvādasasuyeva āyatanesu tassā uppatti ca nirodho ca vutto. Yatheva ca taṇhā dvādasasu āyatanesu uppajjitvā [P 2.0076] nibbānaṃ āgamma niruddhāpi āyatanesu puna samudācārassa abhāvato āyatanesuyeva niruddhāti vuttā, evamimepi pāpakā akusalā dhammā āyatanesu nirujjhantīti veditabbā. Atha vā yvāyaṃ abhinandanādīnaṃ abhāvova rāgānusayādīnaṃ [M 1.0380] antoti vutto. Etthete rāgānusayādīnaṃ antoti laddhavohāre nibbāne pāpakā akusalā dhammā aparisesā nirujjhanti. Yañhi yattha natthi, taṃ tattha niruddhaṃ nāma hoti, svāyamattho nirodhapañhena dīpetabbo. Vuttañhetaṃ “dutiyaṃ jhānaṃ samāpannassa [V 1.0390] vitakkavicārā vacīsaṅkhārā paṭippassaddhā hontī”tiādi (paṭi. ma. 1.83).

“And where, when arising, does this craving arise? Where, when settling, does it settle?” Having said this, it continues: “Wherever in the world there is what is agreeable and pleasurable, there, when arising, this craving arises; there, when settling, it settles. And what in the world is agreeable and pleasurable? The eye in the world is agreeable and pleasurable,” and so on (Vibh. 203), by which method its arising and cessation in the twelve sense-bases are stated. Just as craving, having arisen in the twelve sense-bases and having reached Nibbāna, is ceased, yet because of the absence of its re-occurrence in the sense-bases, it is said to be “ceased in the sense-bases,” so too should these evil, unwholesome states be understood to cease in the sense-bases. Alternatively, this very absence of delighting and so on is said to be the end of the underlying tendencies of lust and so on. Herein, in Nibbāna, which has obtained the designation “the end of the underlying tendencies of lust and so on,” evil, unwholesome states cease without remainder. For whatever does not exist in a certain place is said to have ceased there. This meaning is to be illustrated by the question on cessation. For it was said: “For one who has attained the second jhāna, thought and examination, which are verbal formations, are stilled” (Paṭi. Ma. 1.83), and so on.

202. Satthu ceva saṃvaṇṇitoti satthārā ca pasaṃsito. Viññūnanti idampi karaṇatthe sāmivacanaṃ, paṇḍitehi sabrahmacārīhi ca sambhāvitoti attho. Pahotīti sakkoti.

202. “And praised by the Teacher” (Satthu ceva saṃvaṇṇito) means praised by the Teacher. “By the wise” (Viññūnaṃ): this is the genitive case used in the sense of the instrumental; the meaning is: esteemed by wise fellow practitioners. “Is capable” (pahoti) means is able.

203. Atikkammeva mūlaṃ atikkamma khandhanti sāro nāma mūle vā khandhe vā bhaveyya, tampi atikkamitvāti attho. Evaṃsampadanti evaṃsampattikaṃ, īdisanti attho. Atisitvāti atikkamitvā. Jānaṃ jānātīti jānitabbameva jānāti. Passaṃ passatīti passitabbameva passati. Yathā vā ekacco viparītaṃ gaṇhanto jānantopi na jānāti, passantopi na passati, na evaṃ bhagavā. Bhagavā pana jānanto jānātiyeva, passanto passatiyeva. Svāyaṃ dassanapariṇāyakaṭṭhena cakkhubhūto. Viditakaraṇaṭṭhena ñāṇabhūto. Aviparītasabhāvaṭṭhena pariyattidhammappavattanato vā hadayena cintetvā vācāya nicchāritadhammamayoti dhammabhūto. Seṭṭhaṭṭhena brahmabhūto. Atha vā cakkhu viya bhūtoti cakkhubhūtoti evametesu padesu attho veditabbo. Svāyaṃ dhammassa vattanato vattā. Pavattāpanato pavattā. Atthaṃ nīharitvā dassanasamatthatāya atthassa ninnetā. Amatādhigamāya paṭipattiṃ dadātīti amatassa dātā. Agaruṃ katvāti punappunaṃ āyācāpentopi hi garuṃ karoti nāma, attano sāvakapāramīñāṇe ṭhatvā sinerūpādato vālukaṃ uddharamāno viya dubbiññeyyaṃ katvā kathentopi garuṃ karotiyeva nāma. Evaṃ akatvā amhe punappunaṃ ayācāpetvā suviññeyyampi no katvā kathehīti vuttaṃ hoti.

203. “Having transcended the root, having transcended the trunk”: if there were essence in the root or the trunk, even that is transcended—this is the meaning. “Thus accomplished” (evaṃsampadaṃ) means endowed with such attainment, meaning ‘of such a kind.’ “Having surpassed” (atisitvā) means having transcended. “Knowing, he knows” means he knows only what is to be known. “Seeing, he sees” means he sees only what is to be seen. For it is not like someone who, grasping pervertedly, does not know even while knowing, and does not see even while seeing; the Blessed One is not so. Rather, the Blessed One, knowing, truly knows; seeing, truly sees. He, by being a guide for vision, is Eye-become. By making things known, he is Knowledge-become. By his unperverted nature, or by setting rolling the Dhamma of the scriptures, or because he is made of the Dhamma uttered by voice after having reflected with the heart, he is Dhamma-become. By his excellence, he is Brahma-become. Alternatively, the meaning in these passages should be understood thus: “become like an eye” is ‘cakkhubhūto.’ He is the speaker (vattā) because he speaks the Dhamma. He is the proclaimer (pavattā) because he causes it to be proclaimed. He is the guide to the meaning (atthassa ninnetā) because of his ability to draw out and show the meaning. He is the giver of the Deathless (amatassa dātā) because he gives the practice for attaining the Deathless. “Without making it heavy”: for one who makes others request again and again indeed makes it heavy. Or one who, standing on his own knowledge of the perfections of his disciples, speaks making it difficult to understand—like one extracting a grain of sand from the foot of Sineru—indeed makes it heavy. The meaning is: “Do not do so; do not make us request again and again, but speak making it easy for us to understand.”

204. Yaṃ [P 2.0077] kho no āvusoti ettha kiñcāpi “yaṃ kho vo”ti vattabbaṃ siyā, te pana bhikkhū attanā saddhiṃ saṅgaṇhanto “yaṃ kho no”ti āha. Yasmā vā uddesova tesaṃ uddiṭṭhova. Bhagavā pana therassāpi tesampi [M 1.0381] bhagavāva. Tasmā bhagavāti padaṃ sandhāyapi evamāha, yaṃ kho amhākaṃ bhagavā tumhākaṃ saṃkhittena uddesaṃ uddisitvāti attho.

204. Regarding “That which for us, friends” (Yaṃ kho no āvuso): here, although it should have been said “That which for you” (yaṃ kho vo), that monk, including himself with them, said “That which for us” (yaṃ kho no). Or it is because the exposition was indeed expounded for them. Furthermore, the Blessed One is the Blessed One of the elder and of them too. Therefore, referring to the word ‘Blessed One,’ he spoke thus. The meaning is: “That which our Blessed One has briefly expounded to you.”

Cakkhuñcāvusotiādīsu ayamattho, āvuso, nissayabhāvena cakkhupasādañca ārammaṇabhāvena [V 1.0391] catusamuṭṭhānikarūpe ca paṭicca cakkhuviññāṇaṃ nāma uppajjati. Tiṇṇaṃ saṅgati phassoti tesaṃ tiṇṇaṃ saṅgatiyā phasso nāma uppajjati. Taṃ phassaṃ paṭicca sahajātādivasena phassapaccayā vedanā uppajjati. Tāya vedanāya yaṃ ārammaṇaṃ vedeti, tadeva saññā sañjānāti, yaṃ saññā sañjānāti, tadeva ārammaṇaṃ vitakko vitakketi. Yaṃ vitakko vitakketi, tadevārammaṇaṃ papañco papañceti. Tatonidānanti etehi cakkhurūpādīhi kāraṇehi. Purisaṃ papañcasaññāsaṅkhā samudācarantīti taṃ apariññātakāraṇaṃ purisaṃ papañcakoṭṭhāsā abhibhavanti, tassa pavattantīti attho. Tattha phassavedanāsaññā cakkhuviññāṇena sahajātā honti. Vitakko cakkhuviññāṇānantarādīsu savitakkacittesu daṭṭhabbo. Papañcasaṅkhā javanena sahajātā honti. Yadi evaṃ kasmā atītānāgataggahaṇaṃ katanti? Tathā uppajjanato. Yatheva hi etarahi cakkhudvāriko papañco cakkhuñca rūpe ca phassavedanāsaññāvitakke ca paṭicca uppanno, evamevaṃ atītānāgatesupi cakkhuviññeyyesu rūpesu tassuppattiṃ dassento evamāha.

In 'And the eye, friend,' etc., this is the meaning: Friend, dependent on the eye-sensitivity as a basis and on forms of the four origins as an object, eye-consciousness arises. 'The meeting of the three is contact' means that from the meeting of those three, contact arises. Dependent on that contact, by way of co-nascence and so on, feeling arises with contact as its condition. Whatever object that feeling feels, that very thing perception perceives. Whatever perception perceives, that very object thought thinks. Whatever thought thinks, that very object proliferation proliferates. 'From that as a source' means from these causes: the eye, forms, and so on. 'Perceptions and notions of proliferation assail a person' means that the classifications of proliferation overwhelm that person who has not fully understood the cause; they occur to him—this is the meaning. Therein, contact, feeling, and perception are co-nascent with eye-consciousness. Thought should be understood as being in thought-accompanied consciousnesses, such as those immediately following eye-consciousness. Notions of proliferation are co-nascent with impulsion. If so, why is reference to the past and future made? Because of arising in that way. For just as proliferation at the eye-door now arises dependent on the eye, forms, contact, feeling, perception, and thought, so too he spoke thus, showing its arising in regard to forms cognizable by the eye in the past and future.

Sotañcāvusotiādīsupi eseva nayo. Chaṭṭhadvāre pana mananti bhavaṅgacittaṃ. Dhammeti tebhūmakadhammārammaṇaṃ. Manoviññāṇanti āvajjanaṃ vā javanaṃ vā. Āvajjane gahite phassavedanāsaññāvitakkā āvajjanasahajātā honti. Papañco javanasahajāto. Javane gahite sahāvajjanakaṃ bhavaṅga mano nāma hoti, tato phassādayo sabbepi javanena sahajātāva. Manodvāre pana yasmā atītādibhedaṃ sabbampi ārammaṇaṃ hoti, tasmā atītānāgatapaccuppannesūti idaṃ yuttameva.

In 'And the ear, friend,' etc., the same method applies. In the sixth door, however, 'mind' means the life-continuum consciousness. 'Dhamma' means the mental object of the three planes. 'Mind-consciousness' means either adverting or impulsion. When adverting is taken, contact, feeling, perception, and thought are co-nascent with adverting. Proliferation is co-nascent with impulsion. When impulsion is taken, the life-continuum together with adverting is called 'mind'; from that, contact and so on are all co-nascent with impulsion. But in the mind-door, since any object whatsoever, with its divisions into past and so on, can be an object, the phrase 'in the past, future, and present' is indeed appropriate.

Idāni [P 2.0078] vaṭṭaṃ dassento so vatāvusoti desanaṃ ārabhi. Phassapaññattiṃ paññapessatīti phasso nāma eko dhammo uppajjatīti evaṃ phassapaññattiṃ paññapessati, dassessatīti attho. Esa nayo sabbattha. Evaṃ imasmiṃ sati idaṃ hotīti dvādasāyatanavasena sakalaṃ vaṭṭaṃ dassetvā idāni dvādasāyatanapaṭikkhepavasena vivaṭṭaṃ dassento so vatāvuso cakkhusmiṃ [M 1.0382] asatīti desanaṃ ārabhi. Tattha vuttanayeneva attho veditabbo.

Now, showing the round of existence, he began the teaching with, 'It is so, friend.' 'He will make known the concept of contact' means he will make known, that is, he will show, the concept of contact thus: 'a certain phenomenon called contact arises.' This method applies everywhere. Thus, having shown the entire round of existence by way of the twelve sense bases according to the principle 'when this exists, that comes to be,' he now shows the rolling back of the round by way of the rejection of the twelve sense bases, beginning the teaching with, 'It is so, friend, when the eye is not present...' Therein, the meaning should be understood according to the method already stated.

Evaṃ pañhaṃ vissajjetvā idāni sāvakena pañho kathitoti mā nikkaṅkhā ahuvattha, ayaṃ [V 1.0392] bhagavā sabbaññutañāṇatulaṃ gahetvā nisinno, icchamānā tameva upasaṅkamitvā nikkaṅkhā hothāti uyyojento ākaṅkhamānā ca panātiādimāha.

Having thus answered the question, he then said, 'But if you wish...' and so on, urging them thus: 'Do not be doubtful because this question was answered by a disciple. The Blessed One is seated, holding the scales of omniscient knowledge. If you wish, approach him and become free from doubt.'

205. Imehi ākārehīti imehi kāraṇehi papañcuppattiyā pāṭiyekkakāraṇehi ceva vaṭṭavivaṭṭakāraṇehi ca. Imehi padehīti imehi akkharasampiṇḍanehi. Byañjanehīti pāṭiyekkaakkharehi. Paṇḍitoti paṇḍiccena samannāgato. Catūhi vā kāraṇehi paṇḍito dhātukusalo āyatanakusalo paccayākārakusalo kāraṇākāraṇakusaloti. Mahāpaññoti mahante atthe mahante dhamme mahantā niruttiyo mahantāni paṭibhānāni pariggahaṇasamatthāya mahāpaññāya samannāgato. Yathā taṃ mahākaccānenāti yathā mahākaccānena byākataṃ, taṃ sandhāya tanti vuttaṃ. Yathā mahākaccānena byākataṃ, ahampi taṃ evamevaṃ byākareyyenti attho.

205. 'By these aspects' means by these reasons: by the individual reasons for the arising of proliferation, and by the reasons for the round and its cessation. 'By these words' means by these collections of syllables. 'By these letters' means by the individual syllables. 'Wise' means endowed with wisdom. Or, one is wise for four reasons: being skilled in the elements, skilled in the sense bases, skilled in the structure of conditionality, and skilled in cause and non-cause. 'Of great wisdom' means endowed with great wisdom capable of grasping great meanings, great dhammas, great expressions, and great analytical insights. 'As by that Mahākaccāna' means as it was explained by Mahākaccāna; with reference to that, it is called the 'text' (tanti). The meaning is: 'Just as it was explained by Mahākaccāna, so too would I explain it.'

Madhupiṇḍikanti mahantaṃ guḷapūvaṃ baddhasattuguḷakaṃ vā. Asecanakanti asecitabbakaṃ. Sappiphāṇitamadhusakkarādīsu idaṃ nāmettha mandaṃ idaṃ bahukanti na vattabbaṃ samayojitarasaṃ. Cetasoti cintakajātiko. Dabbajātikoti paṇḍitasabhāvo. Ko nāmo ayanti idaṃ thero atibhaddako ayaṃ dhammapariyāyo, dasabalassa sabbaññutaññāṇenevassa nāmaṃ gaṇhāpessāmīti cintetvā āha. Tasmāti yasmā madhupiṇḍiko viya madhuro, tasmā madhupiṇḍikapariyāyotveva naṃ dhārehīti vadati. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānatthamevāti.

'Honey-ball' means a large molasses cake or a ball of roasted grain flour. 'Delectable' means that which requires no extra flavouring. Regarding ghee, molasses, honey, sugar, and so on, one should not say, 'This is too little, this is too much,' for the taste is perfectly blended. 'Of mind' means one of a thoughtful nature. 'Of a competent nature' means having the nature of a wise person. 'What is the name of this...?'—thinking, 'This elder is most excellent, this Dhamma exposition is supreme; I will have its name given by the omniscient knowledge of the Ten-Powered One,' he spoke. 'Therefore' means: 'Because it is sweet like a honey-ball, therefore, you should remember it as the "Honey-ball Exposition,"' he says. The rest has a plain meaning everywhere.

Papañcasūdaniyā majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāya

From the Papañcasūdanī, the Commentary on the Majjhima Nikāya.

Madhupiṇḍikasuttavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Honey-ball Sutta is completed.

9. Dvedhāvitakkasuttavaṇṇanā

9. The Commentary on the Discourse on Two Kinds of Thought.

206. [M 1.0383][V 1.0393][P 2.0079] Me sutanti dvedhāvitakkasuttaṃ. Tattha dvidhā katvā dvidhā katvāti dve dve bhāge katvā. Kāmavitakkoti kāmapaṭisaṃyutto vitakko. Byāpādavitakkoti byāpādapaṭisaṃyutto vitakko. Vihiṃsāvitakkoti vihiṃsāpaṭisaṃyutto vitakko. Ekaṃ bhāganti ajjhattaṃ vā bahiddhā vā oḷāriko vā sukhumo vā sabbo pāyaṃ vitakko akusalapakkhikoyevāti tayopi kāmabyāpādavihiṃsāvitakke ekaṃ koṭṭhāsamakāsiṃ. Kāmehi nissaṭo nekkhammapaṭisaṃyutto vitakko nekkhammavitakko nāma, so yāva paṭhamajjhānā vaṭṭati. Abyāpādapaṭisaṃyutto vitakko abyāpādavitakko, so mettāpubbabhāgato paṭṭhāya yāva paṭhamajjhānā vaṭṭati. Avihiṃsāpaṭisaṃyutto vitakko avihiṃsāvitakko, so karuṇāpubbabhāgato paṭṭhāya yāva paṭhamajjhānā vaṭṭati. Dutiyaṃ bhāganti sabbopāyaṃ kusalapakkhikoyevāti dutiyaṃ koṭṭhāsamakāsiṃ. Iminā bodhisattassa vitakkaniggahaṇakālo kathito.

206. 'Thus have I heard' refers to the Discourse on the Two Kinds of Thought. Therein, 'dividing into two, dividing into two' means making them into two parts each. Sensual thought is thought connected with sensual desire. Thought of ill-will is thought connected with ill-will. Thought of harm is thought connected with harm. 'One part' refers to all this thought as being of the unwholesome side, whether internal or external, gross or subtle—thus, I made these three thoughts of sensual desire, ill-will, and harm into one division. Thought connected with renunciation, freed from sensual pleasures, is called the thought of renunciation; that operates up to the first jhāna. Thought connected with non-ill-will is called the thought of non-ill-will; that operates, starting from the preliminary stage of loving-kindness, up to the first jhāna. Thought connected with non-harm is called the thought of non-harm; that operates, starting from the preliminary stage of compassion, up to the first jhāna. 'The second part' refers to all this as being of the wholesome side—thus, I made it the second division. By this, the time when the Bodhisatta restrained his thoughts is explained.

Bodhisattassa hi chabbassāni padhānaṃ padahantassa nekkhammavitakkādayo puñjapuñjā mahānadiyaṃ oghā viya pavattiṃsu. Satisammosena pana sahasā kāmavitakkādayo uppajjitvā kusalavāraṃ pacchinditvā sayaṃ akusalajavanavārā hutvā tiṭṭhanti. Tato bodhisatto cintesi – “mayhaṃ ime kāmavitakkādayo kusalavāraṃ pacchinditvā tiṭṭhanti, handāhaṃ ime vitakke dve bhāge katvā viharāmī”ti kāmavitakkādayo akusalapakkhikāti ekaṃ bhāgaṃ karoti nekkhammavitakkādayo kusalapakkhikāti ekaṃ. Atha puna cintesi – “akusalapakkhato āgataṃ vitakkaṃ mantena kaṇhasappaṃ uppīḷetvā gaṇhanto viya amittaṃ gīvāya akkamanto viya ca niggahessāmi, nāssa vaḍḍhituṃ dassāmi. Kusalapakkhato āgataṃ vitakkaṃ meghasamaye meghaṃ viya sukhette sālakalyāṇipotakaṃ viya ca sīghaṃ vaḍḍhessāmī”ti. So tathā katvā akusalavitakke niggaṇhi, kusalavitakke vaḍḍhesi. Evaṃ iminā bodhisattassa vitakkaniggahaṇanakālo kathitoti veditabbo.

For six years, while the Bodhisatta was striving in his effort, thoughts of renunciation and the like flowed forth in him in heaps and heaps, like floods in a great river. But due to a lapse in mindfulness, thoughts of sensuality and the like suddenly arose, cutting off the wholesome sequence and themselves remaining as sequences of unwholesome impulsion. Then the Bodhisatta thought: 'These thoughts of sensuality and the like remain cutting off the wholesome sequence for me. Come now, I will divide these thoughts into two parts and dwell thus.' Thus, he made thoughts of sensuality and the like one part, as belonging to the unwholesome side, and thoughts of renunciation and the like one part, as belonging to the wholesome side. Then he further thought: 'I will suppress a thought arising from the unwholesome side as one seizing and crushing a black snake with a mantra, or as one treading on an enemy's neck; I will not let it grow. But I will quickly make a thought arising from the wholesome side grow, like a cloud in the rainy season, or like a healthy young sāla sapling in a good field.' Having done so, he restrained unwholesome thoughts and cultivated wholesome ones. In this way, it should be understood that this is spoken of as the time when the Bodhisatta restrained his thoughts.

207. Idāni [V 1.0394][P 2.0080] yathāssa te vitakkā uppajjiṃsu, yathā ca ne niggahesi, taṃ dassento tassa mayhaṃ, bhikkhavetiādimāha. Tattha appamattassāti satiyā [M 1.0384] avippavāse ṭhitassa. Ātāpinoti ātāpavīriyavantassa. Pahitattassāti pesitacittassa. Uppajjati kāmavitakkoti bodhisattassa chabbassāni padhānaṃ padahato rajjasukhaṃ vā ārabbha, pāsāde vā nāṭakāni vā orodhe vā kiñcideva vā sampattiṃ ārabbha kāmavitakko nāma na uppannapubbo. Dukkarakārikāya panassa āhārūpacchedena adhimattakasimānaṃ pattassa etadahosi – “na sakkā āhārūpacchedena visesaṃ nibbattetuṃ, yaṃnūnāhaṃ oḷārikaṃ āhāraṃ āhāreyya”nti. So uruvelaṃ piṇḍāya pāvisi. Manussā – “mahāpuriso pubbe āharitvā dinnampi na gaṇhi, addhāssa idāni manoratho matthakaṃ patto, tasmā sayameva āgato”ti paṇītapaṇītaṃ āhāraṃ upahariṃsu. Bodhisattassa attabhāvo nacirasseva pākatiko ahosi. Jarājiṇṇattabhāvo hi sappāyabhojanaṃ labhitvāpi pākatiko na hoti. Bodhisatto pana daharo. Tenassa sappāyabhojanaṃ bhuñjato attabhāvo na cirasseva pākatiko jāto, vippasannāni indriyāni, parisuddho chavivaṇṇo, samuggatatārāgaṇaṃ viya nabhaṃ paripuṇṇadvattiṃsamahāpurisalakkhaṇappaṭimaṇḍitasarīraṃ ahosi. So taṃ oloketvā “tāva kilanto nāma attabhāvo evaṃ paṭipākatiko jāto”ti cintetvā attano paññāmahantatāya evaṃ parittakampi vitakkaṃ gahetvā kāmavitakkoti akāsi.

207. Now, to show how those thoughts arose in him and how he restrained them, he spoke the passage beginning, 'To me, bhikkhus,' and so on. Here, 'appamattassa' means one who is established in mindfulness without lapse. 'Ātāpin' means one who possesses ardent energy. 'Pahitattassa' means one whose mind is directed. 'A thought of sensual desire arises'—for the Bodhisatta, who had striven in exertion for six years, no thought of sensual desire had ever arisen before regarding royal pleasures, palaces, theatrical performances, harems, or any other prosperity. But when he had reached extreme emaciation through the practice of austerities by cutting off food, he thought: 'It is not possible to produce any distinction by merely cutting off food. What if I were to take substantial food?' So he entered Uruvelā for alms. People thought: 'This great man previously did not accept even what was brought and given. Surely now his aspiration has reached its culmination, which is why he has come himself.' They brought him very excellent food. The Bodhisatta’s body quickly became normal. For an aged and worn-out body does not become normal even with suitable food, but the Bodhisatta was young. Thus, after eating suitable food, his body quickly became normal—his faculties became very clear, his complexion purified, and his body was adorned with the thirty-two major marks of a great man, like the sky with a multitude of stars arisen. Seeing this, he reflected: 'This body, which was so exhausted, has thus become normal again.' Then, due to the greatness of his wisdom, taking even such a small thought, he classified it as a 'thought of sensual desire.'

Paṇṇasālāya purato nisinno camarapasadagavayarohitamigādike magagaṇe manuññasaddaravane moravanakukkuṭādike pakkhigaṇe nīluppalakumudakamalādisañchannāni pallalāni nānākusumasañchannaviṭapā vanarājiyo maṇikkhandhanimmalajalapavāhañca nadiṃ nerañjaraṃ passati. Tassa evaṃ hoti “sobhanā vatime migajātā pakkhigaṇā pallalāni vanarājiyo nadī nerañjarā”ti. So tampi evaṃ parittakaṃ vitakkaṃ gahetvā kāmavitakkamakāsi, tenāha “uppajjati kāmavitakko”ti.

Seated in front of the leaf hut, he sees herds of deer such as chamois, gazelles, wild oxen, and roe deer; flocks of birds such as peacocks and jungle fowls, with pleasant sounds and cries; pools covered with blue lotuses, white lotuses, red lotuses, and so on; rows of trees with branches covered with various flowers; and the Nerañjarā River with its clear water flowing like a stream of jewels. He thinks, 'Indeed, how beautiful are these herds of deer, these flocks of birds, these pools, these rows of trees, and the Nerañjarā River!' Taking even such a slight thought, he classified it as a sensual thought. Therefore, it is said, 'A sensual thought arises.'

Attabyābādhāyapīti [P 2.0081] attadukkhāyapi. Esevanayo sabbattha. Kiṃ pana mahāsattassa ubhayadukkhāya saṃvattanakavitakko nāma atthīti? Natthi. Apariññāyaṃ ṭhitassa pana vitakko yāva ubhayabyābādhāya saṃvattatīti etāni tīṇi nāmāni labhati, tasmā evamāha. Paññānirodhikoti [V 1.0395] anuppannāya [M 1.0385] lokiyalokuttarāya paññāya uppajjituṃ na deti, lokiyapaññaṃ pana aṭṭhasamāpattipañcābhiññāvasena uppannampi samucchinditvā khipatīti paññānirodhiko. Vighātapakkhikoti dukkhakoṭṭhāsiko. Asaṅkhataṃ nibbānaṃ nāma, taṃ paccakkhaṃ kātuṃ na detīti anibbānasaṃvattaniko. Abbhatthaṃ gacchatīti khayaṃ natthibhāvaṃ gacchati. Udakapupphuḷako viya nirujjhati. Pajahamevāti pajahimeva. Vinodamevāti nīharimeva. Byantameva naṃ akāsinti vigatantaṃ nissesaṃ parivaṭumaṃ paricchinnameva naṃ akāsiṃ.

'For self-affliction' means also for self-suffering. This is the method everywhere. But is there a thought that conduces to the suffering of both for the Great Being? No. However, for one who remains without full understanding, a thought can conduce even to the affliction of both; therefore, it obtains these three designations; thus, he spoke. 'Obstructing wisdom' means it does not allow unarisen worldly or supramundane wisdom to arise, and even if worldly wisdom has arisen by way of the eight attainments and five higher knowledges, it uproots and casts it away; therefore, it is one that obstructs wisdom. 'On the side of vexation' means it belongs to the division of suffering. 'Not conducing to Nibbāna' means it does not allow one to directly realize the unconditioned, Nibbāna. 'It goes to ruin' means it goes to exhaustion, to non-existence. It ceases like a water bubble. 'I abandoned it' means I indeed abandoned it. 'I dispelled it' means I indeed removed it. 'I made it utterly vanish' means: I made it gone to its end, without remainder, completely rounded, and entirely cut off.

208. Byāpādavitakkoti na bodhisattassa parūpaghātappaṭisaṃyutto nāma vitakko citte uppajjati, athassa ativassaaccuṇhaatisītādīni pana paṭicca cittavipariṇāmabhāvo hoti, taṃ sandhāya “byāpādavitakko”ti āha. Vihiṃsāvitakkoti na mahāsattassa paresaṃ dukkhuppādanappaṭisaṃyutto vitakko uppajjati, citte pana uddhatākāro anekaggatākāro hoti, taṃ gahetvā vihiṃsāvitakkamakāsi. Paṇṇasālādvāre nisinno hi sīhabyagghādike vāḷamige sūkarādayo khuddamige vihiṃsante passati. Atha bodhisatto imasmimpi nāma akutobhaye araññe imesaṃ tiracchānagatānaṃ paccatthikā uppajjanti, balavanto dubbale khādanti, balavantakhāditā vattantīti kāruññaṃ uppādeti. Aññepi biḷārādayo kukkuṭamūsikādīni khādante passati, gāmaṃ piṇḍāya paviṭṭho manusse rājakammikehi upaddute vadhabandhādīni anubhavante attano kasivaṇijjādīni kammāni katvā jīvituṃ na labhantīti kāruññaṃ uppādeti, taṃ sandhāya “uppajjati vihiṃsāvitakko”ti āha. Tathā tathāti tena tena ākārena. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – kāmavitakkādīsu yaṃ yaṃ vitakketi, yaṃ yaṃ vitakkaṃ pavatteti, tena tene cassākārena kāmavitakkādibhāvo cetaso [P 2.0082] na hi hotīti. Pahāsi nekkhammavitakkanti nekkhammavitakkaṃ pajahati. Bahulamakāsīti bahulaṃ karoti. Tassa taṃ kāmavitakkāya cittanti tassa taṃ cittaṃ kāmavitakkatthāya. Yathā kāmavitakkasampayuttaṃ [M 1.0386] hoti, evamevaṃ namatīti attho. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo.

208. 'The thought of ill-will': This does not mean that a thought connected with harming others arises in the mind of a Bodhisatta. Rather, due to excessive rain, heat, or cold, and so on, a change occurs in his mental state. It is with reference to this that it is said, 'the thought of ill-will.' 'The thought of cruelty': This does not mean that a thought connected with causing suffering to others arises in the mind of the great being. However, his mind becomes agitated and lacks one-pointedness. Taking this, he classified it as a thought of cruelty. For instance, while sitting at the door of a leaf-hut, he sees wild animals like lions and tigers harming small creatures like pigs and so on. Then the Bodhisatta gives rise to compassion, thinking: 'Even in this forest, which is supposed to be free from danger, enemies arise for these creatures of the animal realm. The strong devour the weak, and the weak live on, being devoured by the strong.' He also sees cats and others preying on chickens, mice, and so on. When he enters a village for alms, he sees people oppressed by royal officials, suffering punishments like execution and imprisonment, and unable to make a living despite engaging in farming, trade, and so on. This too gives rise to compassion. It is with reference to this that it is said, 'the thought of cruelty arises.' 'In such and such a way': In this or that manner. This is what is said: Whatever he thinks about, whatever thought he entertains concerning sensual thoughts and so on, his mind does not in that very manner take on the nature of a sensual thought. 'He abandoned the thought of renunciation': He abandons the thought of renunciation. 'He cultivated it frequently': He makes it abundant. 'His mind inclines toward sensual thoughts': His mind inclines for the purpose of sensual thought. The meaning is that just as it becomes associated with sensual thoughts, so it inclines. This is the method in the remaining passages as well.

Idāni atthadīpikaṃ upamaṃ dassento seyyathāpī tiādimāha. Tattha kiṭṭhasambādheti sassasambādhe. Ākoṭeyyāti ujukaṃ piṭṭhiyaṃ pahareyya. Paṭikoṭeyyāti tiriyaṃ phāsukāsu pahareyya. Sannirundheyyāti āvaritvā tiṭṭheyya. Sannivāreyyāti ito cito ca gantuṃ na dadeyya[V 1.0396]. Tatonidānanti tena kāraṇena, evaṃ arakkhitānaṃ gunnaṃ paresaṃ sassakhādanakāraṇenāti attho. Bālo hi gopāloko evaṃ gāvo arakkhamāno “ayaṃ amhākaṃ bhattavetanaṃ khādati, ujuṃ gāvo rakkhitumpi na sakkoti, kulehi saddhiṃ veraṃ gaṇhāpetī”ti gosāmikānampi santikā vadhādīni pāpuṇāti, kiṭṭhasāmikānampi. Paṇḍito pana imāni cattāri bhayāni sampassanto gāvo sādhukaṃ rakkhati, taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Ādīnavanti upaddavaṃ. Okāranti lāmakaṃ, khandhesu vā otāraṃ. Saṃkilesanti kiliṭṭhabhāvaṃ. Nekkhammeti nekkhammamhi. Ānisaṃsanti visuddhipakkhaṃ. Vodānapakkhanti idaṃ tasseva vevacanaṃ, kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ nekkhammamhi visuddhipakkhaṃ addasanti attho.

Now, illustrating the meaning with a simile, he says, 'Just as...' and so on. Here, 'crowded with crops' means crowded with grain. 'He would strike': He would strike straight on the back. 'He would strike back': He would strike sideways on the ribs. 'He would block': He would stand obstructing. 'He would restrain': He would not allow them to go here and there. 'Because of this': Due to this reason; the meaning is, because the unprotected cows eat the grain of others. For a foolish cowherd, not protecting the cows in this way, incurs punishments such as being beaten by the cow owners—who think, 'This one eats our wages, he cannot even protect the cows properly and causes us to have enmity with the families'—and also by the crop owners. But a wise man, seeing these four dangers, protects the cows well. This was said with reference to that. 'Danger': Calamity. 'Fault': A blemish, or an opening in the aggregates. 'Corruption': A state of defilement. 'In renunciation': In renunciation. 'Benefit': The side of purity. 'The side of cleansing': This is a synonym for the same. The meaning is: he saw the side of purity in wholesome states, in renunciation.

209. Nekkhammanti ca kāmehi nissaṭaṃ sabbakusalaṃ, ekadhamme saṅgayhamāne nibbānameva. Tatridaṃ opammasaṃsandanaṃ – kiṭṭhasambādhaṃ viya hi rūpādiārammaṇaṃ, kūṭagāvo viya kūṭacittaṃ, paṇḍitagopālako viya bodhisatto, catubbidhabhayaṃ viya attaparūbhayabyābādhāya saṃvattanavitakko, paṇḍitagopālakassa catubbidhaṃ bhayaṃ disvā kiṭṭhasambādhe appamādena gorakkhaṇaṃ viya bodhisattassa chabbassāni padhānaṃ padahato attabyābādhādibhayaṃ disvā rūpādīsu ārammaṇesu yathā kāmavitakkādayo na uppajjanti, evaṃ cittarakkhaṇaṃ. Paññāvuddhikotiādīsu anuppannāya lokiyalokuttarapaññāya uppādāya, uppannāya ca vuddhiyā saṃvattatīti [P 2.0083] paññāvuddhiko. Na dukkhakoṭṭhāsāya saṃvattatīti avighātapakkhiko. Nibbānadhātusacchikiriyāya saṃvattatīti nibbānasaṃvattaniko. Rattiṃ cepi naṃ, bhikkhave, anuvitakkeyyanti sakalarattiṃ cepi taṃ vitakkaṃ pavatteyyaṃ. Tatonidānanti taṃmūlakaṃ. Ohaññeyyāti ugghātīyeyya, uddhaccāya saṃvatteyyāti [M 1.0387] attho. Ārāti dūre. Samādhimhāti upacārasamādhitopi appanāsamādhitopi. So kho ahaṃ, bhikkhave, ajjhattameva cittanti so ahaṃ, bhikkhave, mā me cittaṃ samādhimhā dūre hotūti ajjhattameva cittaṃ saṇṭhapemi, gocarajjhatte ṭhapemīti attho. Sannisādemīti tattheva ca naṃ sannisīdāpemi. Ekodiṃ karomīti ekaggaṃ karomi. Samādahāmīti sammā ādahāmi, suṭṭhu āropemīti attho. Mā me cittaṃ ūhaññīti mā mayhaṃ cittaṃ ugghātīyittha, mā uddhaccāya saṃvattatūti attho.

209. Renunciation means all wholesome states that have gone forth from sensual pleasures; if included in one dhamma, it is Nibbāna itself. Here is the analogy: The field crowded with crops is like the objects of form and so on. The deceitful cow is like the deceitful mind. The wise cowherd is like the Bodhisatta. The fourfold danger is like the thoughts that lead to harm for oneself, others, and both. Just as the wise cowherd, seeing the fourfold danger, guards the cows diligently in the crowded field, so the Bodhisatta, seeing the dangers of self-harm and so on, while striving for six years, protects his mind so that thoughts of sensuality and the like do not arise in relation to objects like form. It is called 'the growth of wisdom' because it leads to the arising of worldly and supramundane wisdom where it has not yet arisen and to the increase of wisdom where it has already arisen. It does not lead to the suffering of distress—this is the side of non-affliction. It leads to the realization of the Nibbāna element, thus it is conducive to Nibbāna. 'Even if, monks, I were to reflect on it all night': Even if I were to develop that thought for the entire night. 'From that cause': Rooted in that. 'It should be agitated': It would be disturbed, meaning it would lead to restlessness. 'Far': Distant. 'From concentration' refers to both access concentration and absorption concentration. 'I, monks, internally settle the mind': This means, 'Monks, may my mind not be far from concentration.' I establish the mind internally, I place it within its proper domain. 'I calm it': I make it settle right there. 'I unify it': I make it one-pointed. 'I concentrate it': I properly direct it, meaning I skillfully fix it. 'May my mind not be agitated': May my mind not be disturbed, may it not lead to restlessness—this is the meaning.

210. Uppajjati abyāpādavitakko…pe… avihiṃsāvitakkoti ettha yo so imāya heṭṭhā [V 1.0397] vuttataruṇavipassanāya saddhiṃ uppannavitakko kāmapaccanīkaṭṭhena nekkhammavitakkoti vutto. Soyeva byāpādapaccanīkaṭṭhena abyāpādavitakkoti ca vihiṃsāpaccanīkaṭṭhena avihiṃsāvitakkoti ca vutto.

210. The thought of non-ill-will arises… the thought of non-violence arises. Here, the thought that arises together with the preliminary insight described previously is called the thought of renunciation because it opposes sensual desire. The same thought is called the thought of non-ill-will because it opposes ill-will and the thought of non-violence because it opposes violence.

Ettāvatā bodhisattassa samāpattiṃ nissāya vipassanāpaṭṭhapanakālo kathito. Yassa hi samādhipi taruṇo, vipassanāpi. Tassa vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā aticiraṃ nisinnassa kāyo kilamati, anto aggi viya uṭṭhahati, kacchehi sedā muccanti, matthakato usumavaṭṭi viya uṭṭhahati, cittaṃ haññati vihaññati vipphandati. So puna samāpattiṃ samāpajjitvā taṃ paridametvā mudukaṃ katvā samassāsetvā puna vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapeti. Tassa puna aticiraṃ nisinnassa tatheva hoti. So puna samāpattiṃ samāpajjitvā tatheva karoti. Vipassanāya hi bahūpakārā samāpatti.

At this point, the time for establishing insight based on the Bodhisatta’s meditative attainment has been explained. For one whose concentration is still immature, and whose insight is also immature, if he sits for too long after establishing insight, his body becomes fatigued, internal heat arises as if it were fire, sweat pours from his armpits, a column of heat rises from the crown of his head, and his mind is afflicted, distressed, and agitated. He then re-enters meditative attainment, having brought it under control, made it pliable, and soothed it, and again establishes insight. If he sits for too long again, the same thing happens. He re-enters meditative attainment and does the same thing. For insight, meditative attainment is of great benefit.

Yathā yodhassa phalakakoṭṭhako nāma bahūpakāro hoti, so taṃ nissāya saṅgāmaṃ pavisati, tattha hatthīhipi assehipi yodhehipi saddhiṃ kammaṃ katvā āvudhesu vā khīṇesu bhuñjitukāmatādibhāve [P 2.0084] vā sati nivattitvā phalakakoṭṭhakaṃ pavisitvā āvudhānipi gaṇhāti, vissamatipi, bhuñjatipi, pānīyampi pivati, sannāhampi paṭisannayhati, taṃ taṃ katvā puna saṅgāmaṃ pavisati, tattha kammaṃ katvā puna uccārādipīḷito vā kenacideva vā karaṇīyena phalakakoṭṭhakaṃ pavisati. Tattha santhambhitvā puna [M 1.0388] saṅgāmaṃ pavisati, evaṃ yodhassa phalakakoṭṭhako viya vipassanāya bahūpakārā samāpatti.

Just as a warrior's shield-fort is of great benefit—relying on it, he enters battle. There, having fought with elephants, horses, and warriors, when his weapons are spent or he wishes to eat and so on, he retreats, enters the shield-fort, takes up weapons, rests, eats, drinks water, puts on his armor again, and having done all that, he re-enters the battle. After fighting there, if he is afflicted by the need to urinate and defecate, or for some other duty, he enters the shield-fort again. There, he recovers and re-enters the battle. In the same way, meditative attainment is of great benefit to insight.

Samāpattiyā pana saṅgāmanittharaṇakayodhassa phalakakoṭṭhakatopi vipassanā bahūpakāratarā. Kiñcāpi hi samāpattiṃ nissāya vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapeti, vipassanā pana thāmajātā samāpattimpi rakkhati. Thāmajātaṃ karoti.

However, insight is even more beneficial to meditative attainment than the shield-fort is to the warrior who has emerged from battle. Although one establishes insight relying on meditative attainment, insight, once it has become strong, also protects the meditative attainment. It makes it strong.

Yathā hi thale nāvampi nāvāya bhaṇḍampi sakaṭabhāraṃ karonti. Udakaṃ patvā pana sakaṭampi sakaṭabhaṇḍampi yuttagoṇepi nāvābhāraṃ karonti. Nāvā tiriyaṃ sotaṃ chinditvā sotthinā supaṭṭanaṃ gacchati, evamevaṃ kiñcāpi samāpattiṃ nissāya vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapeti, vipassanā [V 1.0398] pana thāmajātā samāpattimpi rakkhati, thāmajātaṃ karoti. Thalaṃ patvā sakaṭaṃ viya hi samāpatti. Udakaṃ patvā nāvā viya vipassanā. Iti bodhisattassa ettāvatā samāpattiṃ nissāya vipassanāpaṭṭhapanakālo kathitoti veditabbo.

For example, on land, they make even a boat and its cargo into a cart-load. But upon reaching water, they make even a cart, its cargo, and the yoked oxen into a boat-load. The boat cuts across the stream and safely reaches a good landing place. Similarly, although one establishes insight relying on meditative attainment, insight, once it has become strong, also protects the meditative attainment and strengthens it. Meditative attainment is indeed like a cart on land, while insight is like a boat on water. Thus, it should be understood that so far, this is spoken of as the time when the Bodhisatta establishes insight relying on meditative attainment.

Yaññadevātiādi kaṇhapakkhe vuttānusāreneva veditabbaṃ, idhāpi atthadīpikaṃ upamaṃ dassetuṃ seyyathāpītiādimāha. Tattha gāmantasambhatesūti gāmantaṃ āhaṭesu. Satikaraṇīyameva hotīti etā gāvoti satiuppādanamattameva kātabbaṃ hoti. Ito cito ca gantvā ākoṭanādikiccaṃ natthi. Ete dhammāti ete samathavipassanā dhammāti satuppādanamattameva kātabbaṃ hoti. Iminā bodhisattassa samathavipassanānaṃ thāmajātakālo kathito. Tadā kirassa samāpattiṃ appanatthāya nisinnassa aṭṭha samāpattiyo ekāvajjanena āpāthaṃ āgacchanti, vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā nisinno satta anupassanā ekappahāreneva āruḷho hoti.

The phrase 'Yaññadeva' and so on should be understood in accordance with what was said in the dark fortnight. Here too, to illustrate the meaning, an example is given with 'just as' and so on. There, 'gathered at the village outskirts' means brought to the edge of the village. 'Only mindfulness is required'—for these cows, merely arousing mindfulness is to be done. There is no need to go here and there to strike them or perform other tasks. 'These phenomena'—these phenomena of serenity and insight—merely arousing mindfulness is to be done. By this, the time when the Bodhisatta’s serenity and insight become strong is explained. At that time, it is said, when he was seated to attain absorption, the eight attainments came into his range with a single advertence. When he was seated after establishing insight, he ascended the seven contemplations with a single stroke.

215. Seyyathāpīti idha kiṃ dasseti? Ayaṃ pāṭiyekko anusandhi, sattānañhi hitūpacāraṃ attano satthubhāvasampadañca [P 2.0085] dassento bhagavā imaṃ desanaṃ ārabhi. Tattha araññeti aṭaviyaṃ. Pavaneti vanasaṇḍe. Atthato hi idaṃ dvayaṃ ekameva, paṭhamassa pana dutiyaṃ vevacanaṃ. Ayogakkhemakāmoti catūhi yogehi khemaṃ nibbhayaṭṭhānaṃ anicchanto bhayameva icchanto[M 1.0389]. Sovatthikoti suvatthibhāvāvaho. Pītigamanīyoti tuṭṭhiṃ gamanīyo. “Pītagamanīyo”ti vā pāṭho. Pidaheyyāti sākhādīhi thakeyya. Vivareyyāti visadamukhaṃ katvā vivaṭaṃ kareyya. Kummagganti udakavanapabbatādīhi sanniruddhaṃ amaggaṃ. Odaheyya okacaranti tesaṃ oke caramānaṃ viya ekaṃ dīpakamigaṃ ekasmiṃ ṭhāne ṭhapeyya. Okacārikanti dīgharajjuyā bandhitaṃyeva migiṃ.

215. 'Just as'—what does this show here? This is a particular connection, for the Blessed One began this teaching to show his service for the welfare of beings and his own perfection of teacherhood. Here, 'in the wilderness' means in a forest. 'In the wood' means in a dense grove. In meaning, these two are indeed the same; the second is a synonym for the first. 'Desiring what is not security from the yokes' means not desiring the safe place free from the four yokes, but rather desiring fear itself. 'Conducive to well-being' means bringing about a state of well-being. 'Leading to delight' means leading to joy. Alternatively, the reading may be 'pītagamanīyo.' 'He would block' means he would cover it with branches and so on. 'He would open' means he would make the entrance clear and open it up. 'A wrong path' means a non-path obstructed by water, forest, mountains, and so on. 'He would place a decoy' means he would place a single decoy deer in one spot, as if it were roaming in its own territory. 'A female decoy' means a female deer bound by a long rope.

Migaluddako hi araññaṃ migānaṃ vasanaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā “idha vasanti, iminā maggena nikkhamanti, ettha caranti, ettha pivanti, iminā maggena pavisantī”ti sallakkhetvā maggaṃ pidhāya kummaggaṃ vivaritvā okacarañca okacārikañca ṭhapetvā sayaṃ paṭicchannaṭṭhāne sattiṃ gahetvā tiṭṭhati. Atha sāyanhasamaye migā akutobhaye araññe caritvā pānīyaṃ pivitvā migapotakehi saddhiṃ kīḷamānā vasanaṭṭhānasantikaṃ āgantvā okacarañca okacārikañca disvā [V 1.0399] “sahāyakā no āgatā bhavissantī”ti nirāsaṅkā pavisanti, te maggaṃ pihitaṃ disvā “nāyaṃ maggo, ayaṃ maggo bhavissatī”ti kummaggaṃ paṭipajjanti. Migaluddako na tāva kiñci karoti, paviṭṭhesu pana sabbapacchimaṃ saṇikaṃ paharati. So uttasati, tato sabbe uttasitvā “bhayaṃ uppanna”nti purato olokentā udakena vā vanena vā pabbatena vā sanniruddhaṃ maggaṃ disvā ubhohi passehi aṅgulisaṅkhalikaṃ viya gahanavanaṃ pavisituṃ asakkontā paviṭṭhamaggeneva nikkhamituṃ ārabhanti. Luddako tesaṃ nivattanabhāvaṃ ñatvā ādito paṭṭhāya tiṃsampi cattālīsampi mige ghāteti. Idaṃ sandhāya evañhi so, bhikkhave, mahāmigasaṅgho aparena samayena anayabyasanaṃ āpajjeyyāti vuttaṃ.

A deer hunter, having gone to the forest, the dwelling place of deer, observes: 'They live here, exit by this path, roam here, drink here, and enter by this path.' Then, he blocks the path, opens a false trail, and sets up both a male decoy deer and a female decoy deer. Concealing himself in a hidden spot, he waits with a spear. In the evening, the deer, roaming the forest free from fear, drinking water, and playing with their young, approach their dwelling place. Seeing the male and female decoy deer, they think, 'Our companions must have come,' and enter without suspicion. Seeing the path blocked, they think, 'This is not the path; that must be the path,' and proceed along the false trail. The hunter does nothing at first, but once they have all entered, he quietly strikes the very last one. That one panics, and then all the deer, panicked and thinking, 'Danger has arisen,' look ahead. Seeing the path blocked by water, forest, or mountains, and unable to enter the thick woods on either side, which are like a chain of fingers, they try to escape by the same path they entered. Knowing they will turn back, the hunter kills thirty or forty deer, starting from the front. Referring to this, it was said: 'In this way, monks, that great herd of deer might later come to ruin and disaster.'

“Nandīrāgassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ, avijjāyetaṃ adhivacana”nti ettha yasmā ime sattā avijjāya aññāṇā hutvā nandīrāgena ābandhitvā rūpārammaṇādīni upanītā vaṭṭadukkhasattiyā [P 2.0086] ghātaṃ labhanti. Tasmā bhagavā okacaraṃ nandīrāgoti, okacārikaṃ avijjāti katvā dassesi.

'This is a designation for delight and lust; this is a designation for ignorance.' Here, because these beings, being ignorant on account of nescience and bound by delight and lust, are led to sense objects such as forms, they receive the strike of the spear that is the suffering of the round of existence. Therefore, the Blessed One showed the male decoy deer to be delight and lust, and the female decoy deer to be ignorance.

Migaluddako hi ekadāpi tesaṃ sākhābhaṅgena sarīraṃ puñchitvā manussagandhaṃ apanetvā okacaraṃ ekasmiṃ ṭhāne ṭhapetvā okacārikaṃ saha rajjuyā vissajjetvā attānaṃ paṭicchādetvā sattiṃ ādāya okacarassa santike tiṭṭhati, okacārikā migagaṇassa caraṇaṭṭhānābhimukhī gacchati[M 1.0390]. Taṃ disvā migā sīsāni ukkhipitvā tiṭṭhanti, sāpi sīsaṃ ukkhipitvā tiṭṭhati, te “amhākaṃ samajātikā aya”nti gocaraṃ gaṇhanti. Sāpi tiṇāni khādantī viya saṇikaṃ upagacchati. Āraññiko yūthapatimigo tassā vātaṃ labhitvā sakabhariyaṃ vissajjetvā tadabhimukho hoti.

On one occasion, the deer hunter, having wiped his body with a broken branch to remove the human scent, placed a male decoy deer in a certain spot. He then released the female decoy deer with a rope, concealed himself, took a spear, and stood near the male decoy deer. The female decoy deer moved toward the grazing area of the herd of deer. Seeing her, the deer raised their heads and stood still. She also raised her head and stood still. Thinking, 'She is one of our kind,' they began to graze. She, pretending to eat grass, slowly approached them. The wild stag, the leader of the herd, catching her scent, sent away his own mate and moved toward her.

Sattānañhi navanavameva piyaṃ hoti. Okacārikā āraññikassa migassa accāsannabhāvaṃ adatvā tadabhimukhīva pacchato paṭikkamitvā okacarassa santikaṃ gacchati, yattha yatthassā rajju laggati, tattha tattha khurena paharitvā moceti, āraññiko migo okacaraṃ disvā okacārikāya sammatto hutvā okacare usūyaṃ katvā piṭṭhiṃ nāmetvā sīsaṃ kampento tiṭṭhati, tasmiṃ khaṇe sattiṃ jivhāya lehantopi “kiṃ eta”nti na jānāti, okacaropi [V 1.0400] sacassa uparibhāgena taṃ migaṃ paharituṃ sukhaṃ hoti, piṭṭhiṃ nāmeti. Sacassa heṭṭhābhāgena paharituṃ sukhaṃ hoti, hadayaṃ unnāmeti. Atha luddako āraññikaṃ migaṃ sattiyā paharitvā tattheva ghātetvā maṃsaṃ ādāya gacchati. Evameva yathā so migo okacārikāya sammatto okacare usūyaṃ katvā sattiṃ jivhāya lehantopi kiñci na jānāti, tathā ime sattā avijjāya sammattā andhabhūtā kiñci ajānantā rūpādīsu nandīrāgaṃ upagamma vaṭṭadukkhasattiyā vadhaṃ labhantīti bhagavā okacaraṃ nandīrāgoti, okacārikaṃ avijjāti katvā dassesi.

For beings, indeed, what is ever new is dear. The female decoy deer, without allowing the wild stag to get too close, and as if facing him, retreated backward toward the male decoy deer. Wherever her rope got stuck, she struck it with her hoof to free it. The wild stag, seeing the male decoy deer, became infatuated with the female decoy deer and jealous of the male decoy deer. Lowering his back and shaking his head, he stood there. At that moment, even while licking the spear with his tongue, he did not realize, 'What is this?' The male decoy deer also, if it was easy for the hunter to strike that stag on the upper part, would lower its back. If it was easy to strike him on the lower part, it would raise its chest. Then the hunter struck the wild stag with the spear, killed him on the spot, took the meat, and left. Just as that stag, infatuated with the female decoy deer and jealous of the male decoy deer, licked the spear with his tongue and knew nothing, so too these beings, infatuated by ignorance and blinded, knowing nothing, approach delight and lust in forms and so on, and obtain their death from the spear of suffering in the cycle of existence. Thus, the Blessed One showed the male decoy deer as delight and lust, and the female decoy deer as ignorance.
